units.la: CUM ex 1. Cor. 10. liquido constet (Amplissimi viri) quae Patribus testamenti veteris in deserto acciderunt, τυπικῶς euenisse, scripta autem esse ad nostri admonitionem, in quos seculorum fines inciderunt: Non est mihi dubium quin hæc diuina Legis illustris repetitio, quam Moses descripsit in hoc libro, qui Joannis Vuolphij patris mei p. m. commentarijs explicatus, in lucem nunc prodit, eodem pertineat, & nobis imitanda proponatur. Ut enim hæc ultimo peregrinationis illorum anno facta est, cum ad fines promissæ terræ iam peruenissent: sic nos in deserto huius mundi fines vitæ alterius iam propius assecuti sumus, quam vulgus obseruat, quemadmodum Domini nostri vaticinia cum rebus præsentibus collata docent. Cumq; Moses in requiem terrenam ingressuris obedientia diuina renouationem tanopere necessariam duxerit, quanto nobis magis, qui in cœlestem requiem ingressuri sumus, Christi Domini nostri Legem nunc repetendam censeas?
units.tr: Since it is clear from 1 Cor. 10 (most distinguished sirs) that what befell the fathers of the Old Testament in the wilderness happened typically [τυπικῶς], and was written down for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the ages have come, I have no doubt that this illustrious repetition of the divine Law, which Moses set down in this book, and which now comes to light explained by the commentaries of my late father, Johannes Wolf, pertains to the same purpose and is set before us for imitation. For just as this repetition was made in the last year of their wandering, when they had already reached the borders of the promised land, so we in the wilderness of this world have already come nearer to the boundaries of the other life than the common people observe, as the predictions of our Lord, compared with present events, show. And since Moses judged that a renewal of divine obedience was so necessary for those who were about to enter the earthly rest, how much more, do you think, must the Law of Christ our Lord be repeated now by us, who are about to enter the heavenly rest?

units.la: Hæc lex autem substantia sua non noua, nec ab illa quam Deus per Mosem tulit, aliena est. Nam idem cibus et idem potus spiritualis, qui teste Apostolo Christus est, animas illorum aluit, qui nostras alit. Et Christus nouum præceptum suum charitatem nominat, quæ veteris legis summa & complementum est. Et Deus apud Jeremiam nouo fœderi, quod pollicetur, veteres articulos illos attribuit, Ero Deus eorum, & ipsi erunt populus meus: Unum hoc adijcitur: Dabo legem meam in interiora eorum, & super cor eorum inscribam eam. Quæ verba non nouam & inauditam legem, sed mage perspicuam & explicatam, non ut vetus in ceremonijs et ritibus abstrusam, sed veritate ac re ipsa conspicuam: nec ut illa inscriptam tabulis lapideis, sed cordibus nostris diuinitus impressam promittunt. Cur ergo noua dicitur? Constat Universa lex duabus partibus, quarum una Dei voluntatem in religione & politia docet, eamq; facientibus pollicetur vitam & salutem, negligentibus vero mortem minatur: Cum vero præstare hanc non possimus, pars altera Legis, ne damnemur, in Christo redemptore nobis ἱλασμὸν vel ἱλαστήριον, expiationem a peccatis & reconciliationem cum Deo monstrat. Prior per charitatem praestatur, posterior fide comprehenditur. Et ambae sunt perpetuae. Unde Paulus Gal. 5. in Christo, in quo vno & solo salvus est, nec circumcisionem, nec praeputium, sed πίστις δ᾽ ἀγάπης ἐνεργουμένῳ fidem per charitatem operantem valere dicit.
units.tr: This Law, however, is not new in its substance, nor is it alien to that which God gave through Moses. For the same food and the same spiritual drink, which according to the Apostle is Christ, nourished the souls of those who lived before us, just as it nourishes ours. And Christ calls his new commandment charity, which is the sum and fulfilling of the old Law. And God, in Jeremiah, ascribes to the new covenant which he promises those old articles: "I will be their God, and they shall be my people." To these is added one thing alone: "I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it upon their heart." These words promise not a new and unheard-of law, but a law clearer and more explained, not hidden, as the old one was, in ceremonies and rites, but made visible in truth and in fact; and not written on stone tablets, but divinely impressed on our hearts. Why, then, is it called new? The whole Law consists of two parts: one teaches God's will in religion and in the polity, and promises life and salvation to those who do it, but threatens death to the negligent. Since we cannot fulfil this, the other part of the Law shows us, in Christ the Redeemer, that we are not condemned: the expiation [ἱλασμὸν] or propitiation [ἱλαστήριον] from sins and the reconciliation with God. The first is performed through charity, the second is grasped by faith; and both are perpetual. Hence Paul, Gal. 5, says that in Christ, in whom alone there is salvation, neither circumcision nor uncircumcision avails, but faith which works through love [πίστις δ᾽ ἀγάπης ἐνεργουμένῳ].

units.la: Sed hac Deus non semper eodem modo, sed aliter alios docuit, secundum diuersa tempora & ingenia hominum. Patres ante legem manu tanquam infantes duxit, nudus promissis & crebris revelationibus: indulsit illis polygamiam, & alia eius generis. Mox vero iam adolescentem ecclesiam, summa legis magna cum maiestate, & cum terrore promulgata, paulo austerius tractavit. Praefecit illi legem tanquam paedagogum, qui externis ritibus & ceremoniis ceu literarum elementis ad Christum illos duceret. Rempub. illorum informavit. Et cessit aliquantisper ferocia[?] iuvenili, ferens illorum pertinaciam, quemadmodum in quaestione de repudiis Christus ipse docuit. Tandem vero per Christum filium suum cum nova ecclesia tanquam cum viris egit, & pueriliibus[?] illis ceremoniis & ritibus externis sublatis, ac veritate & re ipsa exhibita, praestitit ea quae veteribus ab exordio mundi promiserat. Et quamvis infirmitati nostrae aliquid etiam indulserit, duobus externis ritibus sacris institutis, in caeteris tamen genuinum & spiritualem Dei cultum, qui in sincera charitate situs est, ab omnibus corporeis, externis, puerilibus ritibus & crepundiis ita repurgavit, ut nunc in spiritu & veritate rite & legitime colatur Deus. Sunt igitur in lege quaedam temporanea, & veteri ecclesiae & populo Iudaeo propria, ex quibus ecclesiastica quae sunt, quia tantum ad tempus διορθώσεως instituta fuerunt, Hebr. 9. Christus implevit & abrogavit, politica cum ipsa gente desierunt. Quamvis usu suo neutra nunc careant: illa enim Christum adhuc in typo & significatione docent, eiq; testimonium perhibent, hac perfectissimam Reipub. & politiae formam, ut quae Deum ipsum authorem habet, omnibus magistratibus & populis ob oculos ponunt. Quaedam vero sunt perpetua, quae Christus nec soluit nec implevit, nisi quatenus imperfectionem nostram perfecit, eoq; non ante mundi ruinam aboleri poterunt, Matth. 5. Sunt etiam politica quaedam communia, quae a nemine recusari possunt, sed omnibus populis & Rebuspublicis seruanda diuinitus prescribuntur.
units.tr: God, however, did not teach this always in the same way, but taught different people differently, according to the different times and natures of men. Before the Law he led the fathers by the hand, as infants, with bare promises and frequent revelations; he indulged them in polygamy and other things of that kind. Then, however, when the Church had now grown into youth, he dealt with it somewhat more severely, when the sum of the Law was promulgated with great majesty and with terror. He set the Law over it as a pedagogue, to lead them to Christ by external rites and ceremonies, as by the letters of an alphabet. He ordered their commonwealth. And for a while he yielded somewhat to their youthful ferocity, bearing with their obstinacy, as Christ himself taught in the question about divorce. At last, however, through Christ his Son, he dealt with the new Church as with men; the puerile ceremonies and external rites having been removed, and truth and reality having been made present, he granted what he had promised to the ancients from the beginning of the world. And although he has also indulged something to our weakness, by instituting two external sacred rites, nevertheless in all other respects he has so purged the genuine and spiritual worship of God, which rests in sincere charity, from all bodily, external, puerile rites and baubles, that God is now worshipped rightly and lawfully in spirit and in truth. There are therefore in the Law some temporary things, proper to the old Church and to the Jewish people. Of these, the ecclesiastical things, because they were instituted only for a time of correction [διορθώσεως] (Heb. 9), Christ fulfilled and abrogated; the political things ceased together with that nation. Yet neither of them is now without use: the former still teach Christ in type and signification and bear witness to him, the latter set before all magistrates and peoples the most perfect form of commonwealth and polity, since it has God himself as its author. Some things, however, are perpetual, which Christ neither dissolved nor fulfilled, except insofar as he perfected our imperfection; and these therefore cannot be abolished before the ruin of the world (Matt. 5). There are also certain common political things, which no one can refuse, but which are divinely prescribed to be kept by all peoples and commonwealths.

units.la: Hac vero illa esse, quae in lege duarum tabularum summatim prescribuntur, quis dubitet? Qui hac non ut illa ceremonialia & iudicialia per Mosem internuncium, sed ipsius filii Dei, angeli foederis, propria voce promulgata: qui non tam primis illis lapideis tabulis propter peccatum fractis (quae veteris illius foederis imago fuerunt) quam etiam posterioribus per Mosem mediatorem restauratus digito Dei inscripta: qui tabulas illas tabulas foederis dictas, Deut. 9. & in arcam quae Christi typus fuit, impositas: Qui denique ab ipso Christo & Apostolis has decem leges illustratas & confirmatas esse, Matth. 4. v. 10. & 12. Mar. 2. Luc. 6. Rom. 7. Gal. 5. 1. Ioan. 5. Rom. 7. etc. meminerit? Item qui norit peccati notitiam necessariam esse, quae tamen non nisi per legem hanc existit? Roman. 7. Haec enim et alia, quae praetereo, decem illa praecepta prima & praecipua esse inter omnes alias leges, & perpetuo ob-seruanda docent. Quamobrem Origenes in Exod. cap. 20. hom. 8. principium decalogi, Ego sum Dominus Deus, &c. explicans, Non hac, inquit, ad il-los tantum dicuntur, qui de Aegypto profecti sunt: sed multo magis ad te, qui nunc audis ista, si tamen proficiscaris ex Aegypto, & Aegyptijs ultra non seruias. Et quid per Aegyptum & domum seruitutis intelligat, deinceps expli-cat, nempe mundum & negocia secularia: per Hierosolymam vero & domum libertatis, secundum Deum viuere & ecclesiam intelligit. Ac notum est Theologis sub imagine liberationis ex Aegypto redemptionem humani generis adumbratam fuisse: unde huius umbram & illius memoriam unum & idem sacramentum agni Paschalis gesserit. Diuus Irenaeus aduersus haereses Valentini & similium lib. 4. cap. 31. decalogum à caeteris legibus sic di-stinguit, ut illum dicat esse amicitiam cum Deo, & concordiam cum proximo, et vitam: reliqua autem praecepta statuta & iudicia esse seruitutis & signi. Ser-uitus autem & signa vetera sublata sunt quidem, sed caetera illa quae deca-logo tribuit sublata quis dicat? Vere igitur Philo Iudaeus decem praecepta vo-cat legem testamenti sempiterni, & praecepta aeterna, quae non transirent: & alibi legem generalem.
units.tr: That these are the things which are summarily prescribed in the Law of the two tables, who could doubt? These were promulgated not through Moses as an intermediary, like the ceremonial and judicial laws, but in the very voice of the Son of God himself, the angel of the covenant. They were restored, not only on the first stone tables, which were broken on account of sin (and which were an image of that old covenant), but also on the later ones, through Moses the mediator, and inscribed with the finger of God. These tables are called "tables of the covenant" (Deut. 9), and were placed in the ark, which was a type of Christ. Finally, who does not remember that these ten laws were illustrated and confirmed by Christ himself and by the Apostles: Matt. 4 v. 10 and 12; Mark 2; Luke 6; Rom. 7; Gal. 5; 1 John 5; Rom. 7, etc.? Likewise, who does not know that the knowledge of sin, which nonetheless comes into existence only through this Law, is necessary (Rom. 7)? For these and other things which I pass over show that those ten precepts are the first and chief among all other laws, and that they are to be observed perpetually. Wherefore Origen, explaining the beginning of the decalogue in Exod. 20, homily 8, "I am the Lord your God," etc., says: "These words are not spoken only to those who went out of Egypt, but much more to you who now hear them, if you indeed come out of Egypt and no longer serve the Egyptians." And what he understands by Egypt and the house of bondage he then explains: namely the world and secular business; by Jerusalem and the house of liberty he understands living according to God and the Church. And it is known to the theologians that the redemption of the human race was foreshadowed under the image of the liberation from Egypt; hence the one paschal lamb bore the shadow of the one and the memory of the other as one and the same sacrament. Saint Irenaeus, against the heresies of Valentinus and the like, book 4, chapter 31, so distinguishes the decalogue from the other laws that he says it is friendship with God, concord with one's neighbour, and life; but the remaining precepts, statutes and judgments belong to servitude and to sign. Indeed the servitude and the old signs have been abolished; but who would say that those other things which he ascribes to the decalogue have been abolished? Truly, therefore, Philo the Jew calls the ten precepts the law of the everlasting covenant, and eternal precepts, which would not pass away; and elsewhere, the general law.

units.la: Sed obstat, quod D. Augustinus epist. 119. ad Ianuar. & alij quartum praeceptum aiunt ceremoniale aliquid continere, quod sit abrogatum. Qua doctrina ceremoniis in decalogum aperta esse ianua[?] videtur, quae certè, si pateret, mox etiam leges de idolis, honore parentibus debito, matrimonio, caede, furtis & rapinis in typos & umbras resoluendi improbis hominibus an-sam daret. Sed patres & doctores illi non de quarto praecepti verbis, sed eius Mosaica interpretatione, et ut paucis dicam de Iudaico sabbatho loquuntur.
units.tr: But there is an objection: Saint Augustine, Epistle 119 to Januarius, and others say that the fourth precept contains something ceremonial which has been abrogated. By such a doctrine a door seems to be opened to ceremonies within the decalogue, which, if it stood open, would soon give wicked men occasion to resolve the laws about idols, the honour due to parents, marriage, murder, theft and robbery into types and shadows. But those Fathers and teachers do not speak of the words of the fourth precept, but of its Mosaic interpretation, and, to say it briefly, of the Jewish sabbath.

units.la: Lex autem non septimam à mundi exordio diem, sed septem diebus unam, eamq; postremam, nullo termino calculi adhibito, cultui diuino consecrat, & nulla opera certa à quibus hac abstinendum sit definit. Moses autem ad septimam ab initio mundi diem sacrum hoc tempus transtulit, & certa opera eaq; strictim hac die cauenda determinauit. Quae ceremonialia Christus sustulit, dum creationis tempore cum corpore suo mortali sepulto septima die requiem impleuit, & postera die cum nouo & restaurato homine nouum tempus redemptionis inquam, è sepulchro produxit, ut dies ille redemptionis in his terris absolu-ta primus esset, sicut olim septima creationis absolu-ta prima ideoq; sacra fuit. Ita salua lege perpetua de sabbatho septima die reli-gio in septimam à die resurrectionis Domini translata est. gustinus ipse in eodem loco per octauam circumcisionis adumbratum esse & veteres minimè latuisse affirmat.
units.tr: The law, however, consecrates to divine worship not the seventh day from the beginning of the world but one day in seven, and that the last, without any fixed reckoning of the count. It does not define any particular works from which one must abstain. Moses, however, transferred this sacred time to the seventh day from the beginning of the world, and specified certain works to be strictly avoided on that day. Christ abolished these ceremonial things. At the time of creation, with his mortal body buried, he fulfilled rest on the seventh day, and on the following day he brought forth from the tomb the new time of redemption, I mean with the new and restored man, so that the day of redemption, completed on earth, was the first, just as the seventh day, completed at creation, was formerly the first and therefore holy. Thus, with the perpetual law concerning the sabbath kept intact, the observance of the seventh day has been transferred to the seventh day from the day of the Lord's resurrection. Augustine himself, in the same place, affirms that the eighth day was foreshadowed by circumcision, and that the ancients were not at all unaware of this.

units.la: Fortassis etiam libertas Christiana à nonnullis obiicietur. Sed hac non est licentia, & libertas carnis, sed immunitas à legalibus ceremonijs, & iis quæ Reipub. Iudæorum erant propria, item à seruili timore legis: restat tamen decalogi obseruatio, restat ceremoniarum corpus & veritas, restat timor legis ingenuus, qui est filiorum. Non valet in Christo circumcisio, sed nec præputium, quod alienum à lege significat, verum fides per charitatem operans. Vos in libertatem vocati estis (inquit Paulus) tantùm ne libertatem arripite vt datam carni, sed ex charitate seruite alij alijs. Item Spiritu ducimini. Et, si spiritu ducimi, non estis sub lege, sed quid est spiritu duci? Non facere opera carnis quæ lege prohibentur, quæ longo catalogo Apostolus commemorat, sed facere opera spiritus, quæ lege mandantur. Quare subjicit, Aduersus huiusmodi non est lex, qui scilicet legem sponte facit. Qui enim Christi sunt carnem suam crucifixerunt cum affectibus, &c.
units.tr: Perhaps some will also object Christian liberty. But this is not licence and freedom of the flesh, but immunity from the legal ceremonies, and from those things which were peculiar to the commonwealth of the Jews, and likewise from the slavish fear of the law. Yet the observance of the decalogue remains, the body and truth of the ceremonies remain, the free fear of the law remains, which is the fear of sons. In Christ circumcision avails nothing, nor does uncircumcision, which signifies alienation from the law, but faith working through love. "You were called to liberty," says Paul, "only do not seize that liberty as given to the flesh, but serve one another through love." Likewise: "You are led by the Spirit." And, "If you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law." But what is it to be led by the Spirit? It is not to do the works of the flesh, which are forbidden by the law, and which the Apostle recounts in a long catalogue, but to do the works of the Spirit, which the law commands. Therefore he adds, "against such there is no law," namely against one who keeps the law of his own accord. "For those who are Christ's have crucified the flesh with its passions," and so on.

units.la: Quamobrem licet lex non amplius sit pædagogus noster, magistrum tamen & præceptorem adhuc nobis agit: siquidem ea quæ charitatis nomine Christus nobis mandat, speciatim explicat, & teste Apostolo peccatum nos docet, quin etiam Christo testimonium perhibet quemadmodum ipse Dominus testatur.
units.tr: Wherefore, although the law is no longer our pedagogue, it still acts as our master and teacher. For it explains in detail those things which Christ commands us in the name of charity, and, as the Apostle teaches, it shows us our sin; indeed it also bears witness to Christ, just as the Lord himself testifies.

units.la: Sed huic infœlici Magistro idem nunc accidit, quod olim Platoni, quem vt Aelianus libro variarum histor. 4. tradit, Aristoteles discipulus iam satis edoctus Sophisticis quæstionibus circumuentum iam senem è Peripato eiecit, & Philosophiæ præceptoris suam substituit. Vnde illum Plato mulis comparàsse dicitur, qui lacte materno saturi calcibus matrem petunt. Sic enim nos legem quæ Christum & peccata nostra nos docuit (si modo non in vanum docuit) calcibus, hoc est, moribus & doctrina nostris ex ecclesia totam eijcimus, & aut mutilatam, aut humanis traditionibus infectam, adeò vt noua quædam lex sit, in diuina illius locum surrogamus. Et certè si nulla vnquam tempora legis repetitionem, qualem in hoc Deuteronomio suo Moses instituit, postulárunt, hæc magis postulant: quibus ita viuitur, vt Deo nostro nulla lege obstricti, sed nostri iuris & arbitrij esse videamur.
units.tr: But the same thing now happens to this unhappy Master that once happened to Plato. As Aelian relates in book 4 of his Varied History, Aristotle, his pupil, already sufficiently schooled in sophistical questions, circumvented the old man, drove him out of the Peripatos, and put his own doctrine in place of the teacher's philosophy. Hence Plato is said to have compared him to mules, which, having sated themselves on their mother's milk, kick at the mother. Thus we cast out the law, which taught us Christ and our sins (if indeed it did not teach in vain), with kicks, that is, with our morals and doctrine, from the whole Church. And either mutilating it or infecting it with human traditions, so that it becomes some new law, we substitute this in place of that divine law. And certainly, if no times ever demanded a repetition of the law, such as Moses set up in this his Deuteronomy, these times demand it even more, in which people live as if they were bound by no law to our God, but were masters of their own right and choice.

units.la: Lex prima postulat, vt præter mundi creatorem, Deum, hoc est protectorem, auxiliatorem, saluatorem, denique summum bonum, neminem alium habeamus: sed solum illum colamus, inuocemus, testem rebus grauibus adhibeamus, vt Deut. 6. Matth. 4. explicatur. At nunc inuocantur sancti tanquam aduocati & auxiliatores, adoratur bestia illa, de qua Ioan. in Apocalyp. coluntur tanquam summa bona Mammon, Gloria humana, Venter, diȳ huius seculi, suratur per nomina sanctorum, Omnis spes hominum in fœderibus, munitionibus, armis, & brachio carnali sita est.
units.tr: The first law requires that, besides God, the creator of the world, that is, our protector, helper, saviour, in short the highest good, we have no one else; but that we worship him alone, invoke him, and call him as witness in weighty matters, as is set out in Deut. 6 and Matt. 4. But now the saints are invoked as advocates and helpers; that beast of which John speaks in the Apocalypse is adored; Mammon, human glory, the belly and the gods of this age are worshipped as the highest goods; they swear by the names of the saints. All human hope lies in covenants, fortifications, arms, and the arm of flesh.

units.la: Secunda lex prohibet religionem gentilem, quæ fit per imagines & idola, & ne quem locum habeat tergiuersatio, omnis generis idola & imagines cœlestium, terrestrium, aquatilium rerum omnium disserte vetantur. At nunc templa, sacella, fana, compita, & alia loca passim idolis scatent: & hæc lex ne quid obstet, tota expungitur. Ab iis etiam qui reformati videri volunt, idololatria palam defenditur, et qui iuxta mandatum Dei statuas & imagines è templis eiiciunt damnantur. Quæritur typus in re planissima tanquam nodus in scirpo:cum animi idola in primo præcepto prohibuerit Deus.
units.tr: The second law forbids the gentile religion, which is carried on through images and idols. So that no room for evasion remains, idols and images of every kind, of heavenly, earthly and aquatic things, are expressly forbidden. But now temples, shrines, chapels, crossroads and other places everywhere swarm with idols, and this law is wholly struck out lest it stand in the way. Even by those who wish to be seen as reformed, idolatry is openly defended, and those who cast statues and images out of the temples according to God's command are condemned. They look for a knot in a bulrush, in a matter most plain, since God forbade the idols of the mind in the first commandment.

units.la: Tertia lex nominis diuini honorem & reuerentiam mandat, abusum eius temerarium, & iurandi leuitatem prohibet. Quid vero nunc magis in vsu est, quam deierationes & imprecationes, quibus animæ & corpora propria pariter & aliena diru[?] denouentur? Periuria non frequentia sunt tantum, sed ab iis qui legum custodes esse debebant conceduntur, approbantur, & mandantur, dum iuramenta legitima soluunt, hæreticis, hoc est illis qui Romanæ ecclesiæ parere nolunt, fidem nullam seruandam esse docent. Quid dicam nefandum nominis & verbi diuini abusum, quo nunc ex parte altissimi loquuntur (vt Danielis verbis vtar) qui hominum traditiones & statuta pro verbo Dei hominibus obtrudunt?
units.tr: The third law commands honour and reverence for the divine name, and forbids its rash abuse and the levity of swearing. What is now more in use than oaths and imprecations, by which souls and bodies, both one's own and others', are cursed? Perjuries are not only frequent, but are permitted, approved and commanded by those who ought to be guardians of the laws, while they release lawful oaths, teaching that no faith is to be kept with heretics, that is, with those who refuse to obey the Roman Church. What shall I say of the unspeakable abuse of the divine name and word, by which now (to use Daniel's words) they speak on the part of the Most High, those who impose on men the traditions and statutes of men as the word of God?

units.la: Quarta lege de tempore sacro præcipitur, & è septem diebus vnus diuino cultui consecratur, & simul omnia sabbatha, hoc est feria, Deo soli mancipantur, ad quem primæ tabulæ præcepta pertinent. Sed nunc vulgus diem septimam voluptatibus, Baccho, & Veneri dicat, sacrorum antistites sabbathorum honorem à Deo ad creaturas transferunt. Et quam liberè longo iam tempore in feriarum distributione inter sanctos, earumq; mutatione versati sint notum est, atq; nunc tristis eius rei memoria novis correctionibus refricatur. Et temporis quidem ratio huc omnis pertinet: Primum enim Sabbatha tam hæc πρῶτα[?] & perpetua quæ hic mandantur, quàm δευτέρα[?] illa Mosaica sine temporis, neomeniarum, & tekupharum ratione obseruari non potuerunt, vt non immerito coniuncta videantur: Deinde tam sacri, quàm prophani temporis computatio in anno veteri per septenarium numerum procedebat.
units.tr: The fourth law prescribes the sacred time: one of the seven days is consecrated to divine worship, and at the same time all the sabbaths, that is, the weekdays, are handed over to God alone, to whom the precepts of the first table belong. But now the common people dedicate the seventh day to pleasures, to Bacchus and Venus, and the ministers of sacred things transfer the honour of the sabbaths from God to creatures. How freely, for a long time now, men have dealt with the distribution of feast days among the saints and their changing is well known, and now the sad memory of this matter is revived by new corrections. And indeed the whole reckoning of time belongs here. For first, the sabbaths, both these first and perpetual ones commanded here and that second Mosaic one, could not be observed without the reckoning of time, of new moons and of the solstices and equinoxes, so that they seem not without reason to be joined together. Then, the computation of sacred as well as profane time in the old year proceeded by the number seven.

units.la: Secunda tabula à Magistratu incipit, & lege quinta ius suum parentibus in filios Doctorum & præceptorum in discipulos, Magistratui in subditos asserit & defendit, vt legum diuinarum sint patroni & ἐπῳδιώχται[?] & curent vt omnia ordine & decenter fiant. At nunc passim summa ἀταξία[?] est. Armantur liberi in filios, discipuli in præceptores, subditi in magistratus, vt hæc ipsa dies docet. Seditiones, proditiones, perfidiæ antichristi sunt arma, quibus nunc pietas & religio vera oppugnantur. Vt appareat esse illa la tempora, de quibus prædixit Dominus Matth.10. Tradet autem frater fratrem in mortem, & pater filium, & insurgent filij in parentes, & morte eos afficient. Et eritis odio omnibus hominibus propter nomen meum. Item, qui vos occidit putabit se rem gratam fecisse Deo. Qui autem perseueraue-rit vsq; ad finem, hic saluus erit.
units.tr: The second table begins with the magistrate, and by the fifth law it asserts and defends the right of parents over sons, of teachers over disciples, of magistrates over subjects, so that they may be guardians of the divine laws and avengers, and see that all things are done in order and decently. But now everywhere there is the greatest disorder [ἀταξία]. Children are armed against their fathers, disciples against their teachers, subjects against magistrates, as this very day shows. Seditions, treasons and perfidies are the weapons of Antichrist, by which now piety and true religion are assailed. Those are plainly the times foretold by the Lord in Matt. 10: "Brother will deliver up brother to death, and father the son, and children will rise up against parents and cause them to be put to death. And you will be hated by all men for my name's sake. Whoever kills you will think he has done God a service. But whoever endures to the end, he shall be saved."

units.la: Sexta lege homicidium prohibetur cum fontibus suis. Nunc vero militia mercenaria laudi ducitur, per sanguinem & cædem Antichristi regnum defenditur & propagatur. Et vulgò nunc homines, qui in sudore vultus sui panem suum edere nolunt, humano sanguine sibi victum comparant, de quibus vere Antiphanes:
units.tr: The sixth law forbids homicide together with its sources. But now mercenary soldiering is counted praiseworthy, and the kingdom of Antichrist is defended and propagated through blood and slaughter. And commonly now men who are unwilling to eat their bread in the sweat of their face procure their livelihood with human blood, of whom Antiphanes truly says:

units.la: Τὶ δ᾽ οὐχὶ θανάτου μισθοφόρος ὦ φιλτάτη[?] Ὃς ἕνεκα τῆς ζῆν ἤρχετ᾽ ἀποθανεῖν μόνον[?].
units.tr: And is not he a hireling of death, dearest, who goes to die only in order to live? [Τὶ δ᾽ οὐχὶ θανάτου μισθοφόρος ὦ φιλτάτη Ὃς ἕνεκα τῆς ζῆν ἤρχετ᾽ ἀποθανεῖν μόνον]

units.la: Hoc est, Nónne mortis stipendiarius est, ô charissima, qui vitam vt seruet aut sustentet, in mortem abit.
units.tr: That is: Is he not a mercenary of death, my dearest, who goes to his death so as to preserve or sustain his life?

units.la: Septima lex matrimonium tuetur, & eius violationem prohibet. Violatur autem suum cuiq; matrimonium per adulterium coniugis, & commune omnium per scortationem, & omnem alium Veneris vsum illicitum. Hoc enim priuilegium diuinitus huic ordini contigit, vt soli Veneris vsus liber sit, extra hunc omnis illicitus. Et vt olim apud veteres Romanos plebeij homines ius annuli sibi vsurpantes, equestrem & senatorium ordines violabant: Vt Chorai, & R. Ozias laesi sacerdotij poenas dederunt, cum incensa thuribulis suis offerre tentarent, quod solis sacerdotibus licuit: sic vti quacunq; Venere ἀγαμῷ[?] nullus potest, quin laesi matrimonij & violati praecepti huius reus fiat. At nunc adulteria quidem aut fiunt impune, aut leuissimè puniuntur. Scortatio vero palàm defenditur, ganea quae gentibus olim alienis à fide infamia fuerunt, publicè fouentur ab illis, qui Christianissimi videri volunt, & cæteros Christianos omnes haereticos proclamant & persequuntur. Quid quod ijdem illi matrimonium quod Deus ipse instituit, quod Apostolus honestum & purum coram omnibus esse dixit, impurum & spiritui aduersum iudicant, cauendum sacerdotibus, quibus facilius ignoscunt, si fœda scortatione sese polluant, quam si ducant uxores. Nulla eius habita ratione quod Paulus Pseudodoctores satanae doctrinam spargentes facturos hoc praedixit.
units.tr: The seventh law protects marriage and forbids its violation. Each man's marriage is violated by a spouse's adultery, and the marriage common to all is violated by whoring and every other unlawful use of Venus. For this privilege has been granted to this order by God, that only the use of Venus within it is free, and every use outside it is unlawful. And just as among the ancient Romans common men who usurped the right of the ring violated the equestrian and senatorial orders, so Korah and Uzziah suffered the punishment for violating the priesthood, when they tried to offer incense in their censers, which was permitted to the priests alone. In the same way, no one can make use of any Venus outside marriage without becoming guilty of violating this precept and the marriage it protects. But now adulteries either go unpunished or are punished very lightly. Whoring, however, is openly defended, and the brothels which were once a disgrace to the heathen nations, far from the faith, are publicly cherished by those who wish to be seen as most Christian, and who proclaim and persecute all other Christians as heretics. Moreover, these same people judge marriage, which God himself instituted and which the Apostle said is honourable and pure before all, to be impure and hostile to the Spirit, something priests must avoid; they more readily pardon priests who defile themselves with foul whoring than priests who take wives. They take no account of the fact that Paul foretold that false teachers, spreading the teaching of Satan, would do this.

units.la: Octaua lege suâ cuiq; facultates defenduntur, & bonorum proprietas:& omnis generis furta vetantur. Sed quamuis nullum scelus minus nunc tolerabile sit, quia Mammon deus magnus huius seculi vulgò colitur, tamen vsurarij, falsarij, sacrilegi, plagiarij, et qui sunt alij huius generis, qui potentiores sunt quam vt aranearum telas capi possint, impune fere dolos nectunt.
units.tr: By the eighth law the property of each man is defended, with his goods, and every kind of theft is forbidden. But although no crime is now less tolerable, since Mammon, the great god of this age, is commonly worshipped, nevertheless usurers, forgers, sacrilegious persons, kidnappers, and others of this kind, who are too powerful to be caught in the cobwebs of spiders, weave their deceits almost with impunity.

units.la: Mendacia quid dicam & desideria, qua dualus [?] vltimis legibus prohibentur? Simulare & dissimulare, verba in commodum suum apte, & egregie fingere summa nunc prudentia est: Et nemo videtur stultior, quam qui dicit, Est est, & Non non, atque ex suo ingenio iudicans alios facile credit. Desideria vero non amplius sub freno iudicij & pudoris duram in corde seruitutem ferunt, sed iam liberè extra cordis septa in actum erumpunt, & hominum quoque iudicia subeunt, quae olim soli Deo patebant. Multa praetereo ne modum praefationis excedam: sed haec abunde docent, quam necessaria foret seria & diligens Legis diuinae repetitio, & morum ac doctrinae reformatio.
units.tr: Why should I speak of lies and of the desires which are forbidden by the last laws? To dissemble and to pretend, and skilfully and cleverly to shape words to one's own advantage, is now the height of prudence; and no one seems more foolish than the man who says "Yes, yes" and "No, no", and who, judging others by his own nature, readily believes them. As for desires, they no longer bear a hard servitude in the heart under the rein of judgement and modesty, but now burst freely out of the enclosure of the heart into action, and even submit to the judgements of men, which once lay open to God alone. I pass over many things, lest I exceed the bounds of a preface; but these facts sufficiently show how necessary a serious and diligent repetition of the divine Law is, and a reform of morals and of doctrine.

units.la: Scio multa obijci solere, vt sunt verborum architectae qui mendacia sequuntur: Sed omnibus illis vnum illud respondet Deus, dicens: Hoc tantùm facito, quod ego tibi praecipio, nihil adde nihilq; detrahe, ne deflectas, neque ad dextram neque ad sinistram. Item, Frustra me colunt traditionibus humanis. Dominus Matth. 15. dicit: Qui unum ex minimis mandatis hisce soluerit minimus vocabitur in regno coelorum. Quis verò locus illi reliquus erit qui maxima quaeq; soluit, mutat quadrata rotundis, figit atque refigit? Deus illis qui Iosia R. temporibus amissam legem per ignorantiam neglexerant ignoscere noluit, quid fiet nostris qui scientes volentesq; contra legem ante oculos positam tam impudenter peccant? Dolendum est igitur quod nobis Iosiae desunt aut Ezechiae, qui tantis malis medicas manus mature adhiberent, & quod illi quorum officium hoc esset, legem tineas pascere sinunt, & traditiones humanas, quas Deus auersatur, in pretio habent, quasi τὰ τῷ φόβῳ κρέττω. Exorandus est nobis Deus, vt ex hoc veterno nos excitet.
units.tr: I know that many objections are usually raised, as are made by the architects of words who follow lies. But to all of them God answers with this one thing, saying: "Do only what I command you; add nothing and take nothing away, lest you turn aside to the right hand or to the left." Likewise: "In vain do they worship me with human traditions." The Lord says in Matthew 15: "Whoever breaks one of the least of these commandments will be called least in the kingdom of heaven." What place, then, will remain for the man who breaks the greatest commandments, who turns squares into circles, who fixes and refixes? God was unwilling to pardon those who in the times of Josiah had neglected the law lost through ignorance; what will become of ours, who sin so shamelessly against a law set before their eyes, knowing and willing it? It is therefore to be lamented that we lack Josiahs or Hezekiahs, who would promptly apply healing hands to such great evils, and that those whose office this would be allow the law to be eaten by moths, and hold in esteem human traditions, which God abhors, as though they were stronger than the fear [of God]. We must pray to God that he rouse us from this lethargy.

units.la: Haec autem ego eò pluribus exposui, vt legis diuinae, quam Moses in hoc quinto suo libro exponit, lectionem & vsum ab ecclesia Christi non alienum, sed necessarium esse, & patrem meum operam suam, quam huic illustrando dedit, minimè male locasse docerem. Malo quidem alios de hoc eius labore iudicium ferre, qui liberius poterunt: sed tamen vt ad eius lectionem forte non poenitendam praelibantem hac mea inuitem, dissimulare non possum, sub hac breuitate non pauca contineri, quae ad mentem Mosis genuinam, ad intentionem eius typicam, ad omnium et singularum legum ordinem, ad veteris populi historiam, ad vsum locorum communium, denique ad totius legis perpetuae, veteris, atque nouae, aliarumq; rerum intelligentiam tam iurisprudentiae (cuius fontes in lege diuina monstrare studuit) quam Theolo-giæ studiosis, & ad vitæ morumque emendationem omnibus prodesse poterunt.
units.tr: I have set out these things at greater length so that I might show that the reading and use of the divine law, which Moses expounds in this, his fifth book, is not foreign but necessary to the Church of Christ, and that my father did not ill employ the labour he gave to illuminating it. I would rather leave judgement on this work of his to others, who will be able to speak more freely. But since I cannot conceal that, within this brevity, many things are contained which may benefit both students of jurisprudence (whose sources he sought to show in the divine law) and students of theology, as well as all men for the improvement of life and morals, I wish, by this my invitation, to whet the appetite for a reading that will not be regretted. These things concern the genuine mind of Moses, his typological intention, the order of all and each of the laws, the history of the ancient people, the use of the commonplaces, and finally the understanding of the whole law, both old and new, which is perpetual, and of other matters.

units.la: (Cepit autem hunc librum scribere Anno Domini 1554. 5. die Aprilis eumq; in Ianuario anni 1557. absoluit, non vt ederetur, sed in priuatum usum suum, & is nunc demum post eius obitum in lucem prodit: quamob-rem non miraberis, si forte postrema manus in quibusdam desiderabitur. Mihi in paternis scriptis, quae merito amo & magnifacio, mutare aliquid religio fuit. Meum igitur hic nihil est praeter marginales annotationes, & continua orationis distinctionem in paragraphos,quam in gratiam occupati lectoris feci. Catera cum bonis viris malui quam cum tineis habere communia, neque illis hoc meum studium ingratum fore spero.
units.tr: (He began to write this book in the year of the Lord 1554, on 5 April, and completed it in January 1557, not to be published but for his own private use; and it is only now, after his death, that it comes to light. Therefore you will not be surprised if the final hand is perhaps lacking in some places. For my part, I have felt it a scruple to change anything in my father's writings, which I rightly love and greatly esteem. What is mine here is therefore nothing but the marginal notes and the division of the continuous text into paragraphs, which I made for the sake of the busy reader. I preferred to leave the rest to good men rather than to share it with the moths, and I hope this effort of mine will not be unwelcome to them.

units.la: Quod autem vobis (amplissimi Viri) hoc meum paternum opus dedicandum censui, non ideo vobis mirum videri debet, quod mihi notitia et consuetudo hactenus vobiscum nulla fuit. Ea est enim (ut vere Cicero in Laelio suo dixit) virtus vis, ut suapte natura fit amabilis, & nos ad diligendum alliceat eos etiam quos nunquam vidimus, quin etiam (quod maius est) in hoste a nobis diligatur. Qua vero vestrae sint virtutes, quarum delectatio animum meum coeperit, quamvis oculis ego meis nunquam viderim, per famam tamen, quae moenis aut parietibus nullis includitur, facile cognoscere licuit. Et cum ab aliis amicis meis, tum vero in primis a D. M. Ioanne Iacobo Hallero affine meo amantissimo, quocum vobis notitia quaedam familiarior intercedit, saepe de vobis audivi, quae mihi iam pridem officiolo aliquo me in vestram amicitiam insinuandi mirum desiderium excitarunt. Et nunc mihi, postquam diu captatam occasionem tandem arripui, spem non exiguam faciunt, hoc meum qualecunque erga vos studium nec vobis ingratum, nec a meo proposito, et ab ipso opere theologico alienum fore.
units.tr: That I have thought fit to dedicate this work of my father's to you, most distinguished gentlemen, should not seem strange to you, although I have hitherto had no acquaintance or intercourse with you. For virtue, as Cicero truly says in his Laelius, is of such force that by its own nature it is lovable, and attracts us to love even those whom we have never seen, indeed (what is greater) is loved even in an enemy. Though I have never seen with my own eyes what your virtues are, whose delight has begun to move my mind, I have nevertheless been able to learn them easily through report, which is shut in by no walls or partitions. Both from my other friends, and above all from Master Johann Jakob Haller, my most loving kinsman by marriage, who has a rather more familiar acquaintance with you, I have often heard things about you which long ago aroused in me a great desire to insinuate myself into your friendship by some small service. And now, since I have at last seized an opportunity I had long sought, they give me no small hope that this zeal of mine towards you, whatever its worth, will be neither unwelcome to you nor foreign to my purpose and to this theological work itself.

units.la: Ut enim antiqua vestra ZILINORVM familia virtutis, religionis, & pietatis nomine clara semper fuit, quemadmodum monumenta quaedam docent quae in nostris chronicis extant, & quibus vestrarum annalium est copia, facile demonstrare possent. Sic eadem in vestris parentibus atque etiam in vobis ipsis vestigia maiorum apparent. Multos illustres & eximios viros vestra civitas habuit, ut est praestantium hominum fertilissima, sed in his non postremum locum D. IACOBVS ZILINVS pater vester sibi vendicat, singulare ornamentum patriae vestrae. Qui senatorem minoris Consilii Reipub. vestrae, quod (perinde ut apud nos) numero quidem senatorum minus est, sed dignitate & potentia summum: & aliquando etiam Praetorem Vrbanum egit, amplissima virtutum suarum testimonia publico omnium consensu nactus. Nec minus honestissima matrona mater vestra et re et nomine CLARA fuit, è celebri & famosa familia GEISBVRGIORVM Constantiensium oriunda: cuius frater Sebastianus consulatum civitatis illius magna cum laude gessit, infelix quidem propter tristem illum (Constantiensem tumultum, in quem consulatus eius incidit,) vere tamen σεβαστὸς[?], quod dignus est habitus, qui multa pro nomine Christi pateretur. Habuit eodem tempore familia vestra doctos et eruditos viros DD. DOMINICVM et ANTHONIVM Patruos vestros, quos tanquam primogenitos Deo consecrauit: quorum al-ter ecclesiae simul & schola vestra, alter ecclesiae tantum fidelem operam na-varunt. In vos vero (quod citra adulationem dixerim) omnia fere laudis antiquae studia familia vestra quasi in unum contulit. Iucunda sane est et suauissima concors illa vestra & summa animorum pariter & corporum quinq. fratrum coniunctio: Cuius eo memini libentius, quod & pater meus p. m. cuius labores nunc vestro nomini nuncupo, quinq. filios superstites habet, qui & ipsi amori & coniunctioni fraternae pro virili studemus. Faxit Deus ut haec fraterna concordia nostra nobis utrinq. constans & diuturna sit: & vos quinq. fratres nostrum quinq. fratrum amicitiam non aspernemini. Inest etiam vobis singulare quoddam in Ministerium verbi diuini studium, ut iis qui huic inseruiunt, tam vestris quam vicinis quasi tutum apud vos hospitium & asylum paratum sit. Quod ut hoc tempore postremo, quo Dei V. cum ministris suis magis magisq. vilescit & contemnitur, rarum est: sic religionis & pietatis sincerae & integrae non obscuram significationem habet. Solent enim cuiuscunq. legati (quo munere ministri verbi funguntur) con-temptus, & honor è contra eidem exhibitus in ipsum Dominum, à quo missus est, redundare. Neq. vero hoc vestrum erga Dei ministros studium vel a-tra mors abolere potest: quando eorum quoq. liberos, qui fideles in opere Domini fuerunt, patre orbatos educandos suscipitis atq. alitis. Et, ut nunquam desint, qui schola & ecclesia vestra seruire & praeesse possint, docti & eruditi viri, partim communibus sumptibus omnes, partim singuli quidam vestrum privatis stipendiarios alitis, qui in spem patriae & ecclesiae vestrae in bonis literis atq. artibus & in primis in diuina sapientia instituantur. Vt non ipsi tantum Reipublicae vestrae operas vestras quasi devoueritis[?], sed etiam scholae & ecclesiae vestrae seminaria quaedam in ædibus vestris extent. Nemo ergo amplius mirabitur cur insigne familiae vestrae gemina luna sit, quagemina ecclesiae veteris & novae, aut militantis & triumphantis imaginem refert, cum ecclesia Christi tantopere vobis cura sit. Has autem vestras in Deum pietatis, & in S. verbum eius obseruantia quasi primitias, & spontaneas oblationes alias, quas breuitatis causa praetereo, Deus Optimus & remunerator liberalissimus benedictione sua comprobat, qua vos opibus & honoribus, gratia & existimatione & auxit, & magis magisq. auget. Vt celeberrimae et antiquissimae civitatis vestrae familiae patritiae ZOLLICKHOFE-RI, RUTTLINGERI, SCHOVVINGERI, GARVERII, CELLARII, ET ROTTMUNDI amicitia & affinitate coniungi vobiscum desiderarint. Ex illis enim vos coniuges vobis dignissimas delegistis: ha dua[?] vero posteriores ornatissimas matronas MARGARETAM & BARBARAM sorores vestras in gremium suum receperunt. Nam alteram D. HENRICHO CELLARIO Quaestori C.V. amplissimo, alteram BALTHASSARI ROTTMUNDO celeberrimi Doctoris ROTTMUNDI fratri nupsisse accepi. Iam si STUDEROS clarissimam familiam sanguine & affinitate uobis iun-ctam, & alias uestrates uirtutis & nobilitatis uestrae testes commemorare uellem, dicendi finem nullum facerem. Sed & haec & alia multa eiusdem generis pluribus uerbis exponerem, nisi patientia uestra diutius abuti uererer, quasi tamen uos (pro uestra modestia) iam pridem has uestras laudes grauatim audire: Sed dabitis hoc praesenti causae, quae dedicationis huius mea rationes ut redderem, pro more suo postulauit. Et tales quidem causas mihi reddidisse videor, ut ego quidem cum operi huic nouo patrocinium quaererem, & uestra illa quae iam exposui mecum perpendissem, Terentianum illud animo uoluerim: His mandes si quid recte curatum uelis. Quibus enim diuinae legis explicationem rectius ac tutius commisissem, quam tam concordibus & coniunctis, tamq; pietatis & religionis sincerae, puri inquam uerbi Dei, amantibus fratribus? Vos igitur nunc (quod unum superest) amplissimi uiri, oro atque obsecro, ut hoc meum qualecunque in uirtutes & pietatem uestram studium & officiolum boni consulere, & mei erga uos amoris & obseruantiae perpetuum symbolum recipere dignemini. Deum Opt. Max. oro, ut hoc opus nouum in sui nominis gloriam & aedificationem ecclesiae suae fructuosum reddat, uos autem, uestrisq; similes patronos ecclesiae in uera fide & charitate confirmet, & corporis pariter atque animi dotibus aeternum beet, Amen. Data Tiguri 1. Augusti, Anno Domini M. D. LXXXV.
units.tr: For, just as your ancient family of the Zilini has always been renowned for virtue, religion and piety, as certain records in our chronicles show, and as your own annals could easily demonstrate, the same traces of your ancestors appear in your parents and in yourselves. Your city has had many illustrious and outstanding men, since it is a very fertile source of distinguished people, but among them Master JACOB ZILINUS, your father, claims no small place for himself, a singular ornament of your homeland. He served as a senator of the Lesser Council of your Commonwealth, which, as with us, has fewer members but the highest dignity and power, and at one time he also served as Urban Praetor, having gained the most honourable testimonies of his virtues by the public consent of all. Your mother, CLARA, was no less honourable a matron in both reputation and name, sprung from the famous and renowned family of the GEISBURGS of Constance. Her brother Sebastian held the office of consul of that city with great distinction. He was unfortunate because of that sad Constance tumult, during which his consulship fell, yet he was truly "sebastos" [σεβαστὸς], as he was considered worthy, since he suffered much for the name of Christ. At the same time your family had learned and erudite men, Master DOMINIC and Master ANTHONY, your uncles, whom it consecrated to God as its firstborn. One of them served your church and school together, the other rendered faithful service to the church alone. Indeed, to speak without flattery, your family has gathered almost all the ancient pursuits of praise into you. That harmonious and very sweet union of you five brothers, in both mind and body, is truly delightful, and I recall it all the more gladly because my father, of blessed memory, whose labours I now dedicate to your name, has five surviving sons, who also strive, as far as they can, for mutual love and brotherly unity. May God grant that this brotherly harmony of ours be steadfast and lasting on both sides, and may you five brothers not disdain the friendship of our five brothers. There is also in you a singular zeal for the ministry of the divine Word, so that those who serve it find a safe hospitality and a ready refuge with you, with your own people and with your neighbours alike. This is rare in these latter times, when the Lord God, together with his ministers, is increasingly despised and held in contempt, and it gives a clear sign of sincere and whole religion and piety. For the contempt shown to any envoy (which is the office the ministers of the Word fulfil), and honour shown to him in turn, are reflected back upon the Lord himself who sent him. Nor can even dark death abolish this your zeal for God's ministers, since you take up and feed the children of those who were faithful in the Lord's work, orphaned of their fathers, to be brought up. And so that there may never be lack of learned and erudite men who can serve and preside over your school and church, you support some of them at common expense, and some of them individually at your own private cost, as stipendiaries, so that they may be instructed in good letters and arts, and above all in divine wisdom, for the hope of your homeland and church. Thus you have not only devoted your labours to your Commonwealth, as it were, but also certain seminaries of your school and church exist in your own houses. No one, therefore, will any longer wonder why the distinguished emblem of your family is a twin moon, which, as a twin, represents the image of the old and new church, or of the church militant and triumphant, since the church of Christ is such a great concern to you. These acts of yours, your piety towards God and your observance of his holy Word, which I pass over for the sake of brevity, as it were first fruits and other voluntary offerings, God the Best and most generous rewarder approves with his blessing, by which he has increased you in wealth and honours, in grace and esteem, and increases you more and more. Those patrician families of your most famous and most ancient city, the ZOLLICKHOFER, RUTTLINGER, SCHOVINGER, GARVER, CELLAR and ROTTMUND families, your uncles, and so on, have desired to be joined with you in friendship and kinship. For from among them you have chosen wives most worthy of you, and the latter two families have received into their bosom your sisters, most honourable matrons, MARGARET and BARBARA. For I have heard that one was married to Master HENRY CELLAR, most distinguished Quaestor, and the other to BALTHASAR ROTTMUND, brother of the most celebrated Doctor ROTTMUND. Now, if I wished to recall the most illustrious family, joined to you by blood and kinship, and the other witnesses of your virtue and nobility, I would make no end of speaking. But I would set out these and many other things of the same kind at greater length, were I not afraid of abusing your patience for too long, since you (in your modesty) have long borne hearing these praises with reluctance. But you will grant this to the present cause, which, according to its custom, demanded that I give the reasons for this dedication. And I seem to have given such reasons, since, while I sought a patron for this new work, and weighed in my mind those things of yours that I have now set out, I turned over in my mind that line of Terence: "Entrust these to them if you wish something to be properly looked after." For to whom could I more rightly and safely entrust the explanation of the divine law than to brothers so harmonious and united, so devoted to piety and sincere religion, to the pure Word of God, I say? Therefore, most distinguished men, I now beg and entreat you (which is the only thing left) that you deign to accept this my little effort and service, whatever it is, directed to your virtues and piety, and to receive it as a lasting token of my love and respect for you. I pray to God, the Best and Greatest, that he make this new work fruitful for the glory of his name and the edification of his church, and that he confirm you, and patrons like you, of the church, in true faith and charity, and bless you with the gifts of both body and soul for eternity. Amen. Given at Zurich, 1 August, in the year of the Lord 1585.

QUATUOR LIBRORUM HUIUS OPERIS ARGUMENTA ET dispositio.
units.tr: THE ARGUMENTS AND ARRANGEMENT OF THE FOUR BOOKS OF THIS WORK.

units.la: Lib.I. continet Exordium, quo animi hominum sic praeparantur, ut ad percipiendam legem idonei reddantur, quibusdam progymnasmatis, quae sunt,
units.tr: Book I contains the Introduction, by which the minds of men are so prepared that they become fit to receive the law, with certain preliminary exercises, which are:

units.la: 1. Fides & spes. capite primo.
units.tr: 1. Faith and hope. Chapter 1.

units.la: 2. Obedientia. Ubi de Magistratu.
units.tr: 2. Obedience. Here concerning the Magistrate.

units.la: 3. Studium iuris gentium in pace & bello. cap. 2. & 3.
units.tr: 3. The study of the law of nations in peace and war. Chapters 2 and 3.

units.la: 4. In dictis & factis veritas & constantia.
units.tr: 4. Truth and constancy in words and deeds.

units.la: 5. Voluntas propensa erga legis studium. cap. 4.
units.tr: 5. A will inclined toward the study of the law. Chapter 4.

units.la: Lib.II. tractatur Propositio cap. 5. quae est decalogi expositio, continet,
units.tr: Book II treats the Proposition in chapter 5, which is an exposition of the Decalogue, and contains:

units.la: 1. Causam efficientem.
units.tr: 1. The efficient cause.

units.la: 2. Capita legis, praecepta decalogi.
units.tr: 2. The heads of the law, the precepts of the Decalogue.

units.la: 3. Effecta, quae sunt pietas seu timor Domini.
units.tr: 3. The effects, which are piety or the fear of the Lord.

units.la: Lib.III. Confirmationem habet, quae est legis illustratio & enucleatio. Explicatur Tabulae
units.tr: Book III contains the Confirmation, which is the illustration and explanation of the law. The First Table is explained

units.la: Primae lex 1. capp. 6.7.8.9.10.11. Lex 2. capp. 12.13.14. Ubi externus cultus informatur & abusus V.D. in pseudoprophetis prohibetur, qui ad 3. legem pertinet. Lex 4. in capp. 15. & 16.
units.tr: of the First Table: law 1, chapters 6 to 11; law 2, chapters 12 to 14, where external worship is set out and the abuse of the Word of God by false prophets is forbidden, which belongs to the third law; law 4, in chapters 15 and 16.

units.la: Secundae lex 5. de Magistratu cap. 17. Minister cap. 18. Lex 6. capp. 19. 20. 21. Reliquae l. cap. 22. 23. 24. 25. 26. 27. & 28.
units.tr: Of the Second Table: law 5, on the Magistrate, chapter 17; the Minister, chapter 18. Law 6, chapters 19, 20 and 21. The remaining laws, chapters 22 to 28.

units.la: Lib.IIII. Conclusionem complectitur. In qua tolluntur impedimenta legis. Personarum ratio peruersa, & securitas cap. 29. Desperatio, & ignorantia V.D. cap. 30. Deinde Moses, ut populum commoueat, instituit ducem & Leuitas, eosq; confirmat 31. Canticum iussu Dei describit cap. 32. Iosuam substituit. Quibus mortis eius historia attexitur.
units.tr: Book IV contains the Conclusion. In it the hindrances to the law are removed: the perverse reckoning of persons and security, chapter 29; despair and ignorance of the Word of God, chapter 30. Then Moses, in order to move the people, appoints a leader and the Levites and confirms them, 31. He describes the song written at God's command, chapter 32. He substitutes Joshua, and the account of his death is added.

units.la: IOANNIS VVOLPHII TIGURINI IN DEUTERONOMIUM SERMONUM LIBER PRIMUS. CAPUT I.
units.tr: JOHANNES WOLF OF ZURICH, FIRST SERMON ON THE BOOK OF DEUTERONOMY. CHAPTER 1.

units.la: SERMO I.
units.tr: SERMON 1.

units.la: Hæc sunt verba quæ loquutus est Moses ad omnem Israelem cis Iordanem in deserto, in campo ex aduerso maris rubri, inter Paran & Tophel, Laban, Hazeroth, & Dizahab.
units.tr: These are the words that Moses spoke to all Israel beyond the Jordan, in the wilderness, in the plain over against the Red Sea, between Paran and Tophel, Laban, Hazeroth, and Dizahab.

units.la: 2 Itinere vndecim dierum à Horeb per viam montis Seir ad Cades Barnea:
units.tr: 2 It is eleven days' journey from Horeb by the way of Mount Seir to Kadesh-barnea.

units.la: 3 Et factum est in quadragesimo anno, mense vndecimo, primo die mensis, quod loqueretur Moses ad filios Israel, iuxta omnia quæ Dominus per ipsum mandauit ad eos.
units.tr: 3 And it came to pass in the fortieth year, in the eleventh month, on the first day of the month, that Moses spoke to the children of Israel, according to all that the Lord had given him in commandment to them.

units.la: 4 Postquam percussisset Sihon regem Amorræorum, qui habitauerat in Hesbon, & Ogregem Basan, qui habitauerat in Astaroth in Edrei.
units.tr: 4 After he had smitten Sihon king of the Amorites, who dwelt in Heshbon, and Og king of Bashan, who dwelt in Ashtaroth at Edrei.

units.la: VAE nobis de Mose & Deuteronomio deq; reliquis eò spectantibus rebus, more institutoque eorum qui sibi veterum libros exponendos sumunt, prius dicenda videntur esse, quàm ad singularem eius verborum & sententiarum explanationem veniamus: ea commodè & diligenter explicata videntur cum in omni, tum vero maximè in illa nostra interpretatione perquàm multum emolumenti ad propositam rem afferre. Nam & dignitate siue laude scriptoris auditor excitatur atque etiam accenditur, vt eius quem virum tantum esse norit, scriptum nosse quoque quàm cupidissimè enitatur: & summa atque forma libri demonstrata quasi quædam ad inceptum opus via sternitur, multaq; fiunt perspicua quæ futura fuerant obscurissima: deniq; efficitur vtilitatis spe propositá atque factá, vt ad cognoscendum, quod videtur tantopere conducere, mirum in modum animum aduertamus.
units.tr: Before we come to the particular explanation of its words and meanings, it seems right to say something first about Moses, about Deuteronomy, and about the other matters that bear on it, following the custom and practice of those who undertake to expound the books of the ancients. When these things are explained properly and carefully, they are of great help to our purpose in every commentary, and especially in this one of ours. For the hearer is roused and fired by the dignity and reputation of the author, so that he strives most eagerly to read the writings of one he knows to be so great a man. And when the sum and form of the book has been set out, a kind of road is laid down into the work we have begun, and many things that would otherwise be very obscure become clear. Finally, once the hope of benefit has been held out and grasped, our minds are turned, wonderfully, to learning what seems so greatly to serve our purpose.

units.la: Sed quid ego Mosis eius qui nostrum hoc conscripsit opus laudes & dignitatem prædicem, cum maiores sint quam vt oratione efferri possint? Quid de Deuteronomij forma ac summa dicam, quando liber hic ipse summam & caput sacræ philosophiæ continet? Quid denique eius vtilitatem prædicem, quod cum sit ipsissimū Dei verbum, tam salubre est quàm quod saluberrimum? Quamobrem cum illis de rebus sic instituenda sit oratio, vt neq; nimis longa rerum harum commemoratione tempus expositioni propositæ debitum subtrahatur, neq; nimis parum dicendo cupidis animis desimus: Spiritus sancti vestigijs insistendum fuerit, quia principium huius libri ipse sic instituit atque format, vt ex eo rectè ponderato quicquid hanc ad rem requiritur, sanè quàm egregiè cognosci queat.
units.tr: But why should I proclaim the praises and dignity of Moses, who wrote this work of ours, when they are too great to be expressed in speech? Why should I speak of the form and sum of Deuteronomy, when this book itself contains the sum and head of sacred philosophy? Why, finally, should I proclaim its usefulness, since, being the very Word of God, it is as wholesome as anything could be? Therefore, since our discourse on these matters must be arranged so that we neither take up too much of the time owed to the exposition we have set out by a overly long recital of these things, nor leave eager minds unsatisfied by saying too little, we must keep to the footsteps of the Holy Spirit. For he himself arranges and shapes the beginning of this book in such a way that, if what is needed for this purpose is carefully weighed from it, it can be known very well indeed.

units.la: Ac ijs quidem, quæ modo recitauimus, verbis inscriptio libri continetur quæ nobis 1.librum, 2.authorem, 3.locum, 4.tempus ponit ob oculos. Quæ circumstantiæ, si quo modo Spiritus sanctus eas posuit, considerentur, quod de libro ipso deq; eius authore scitu necessarium est abundè significabunt.
units.tr: Now the words we have just recited contain the inscription of the book, which sets before our eyes (1) the book, (2) the author, (3) the place, and (4) the time. If these circumstances are considered, in the way the Holy Spirit has set them down, they will abundantly show what it is necessary to know about the book itself and about its author.

units.la: De libro, Hæc (inquit) sunt verba, & paulo post, ad omnem Israelem: & iterum, iuxta omnia quæ Dominus per ipsum mandauit ad illos. Quibus verbis ostenditur qui qualisq; is sit liber, quorum sit illum nosse & tenere, deniq; quo authore, seu cuius iussu atq; imperio sit editus.
units.tr: Concerning the book: "These are the words," he says, and a little later, "to all Israel," and again, "according to all that the Lord commanded him for them." By these words it is shown what sort of book this is, for whom it is to be known and held, and finally by whose authority, or at whose command and direction, it was published.

units.la: Quis sit, Hæc sunt, inquit, verba. Verbum Hebraeis causam, caput, summam rei significat, & verba sunt illis summæ quædam seu capita rerum: vnde & decem leges quæ duabus tabulis descriptæ sunt, decem verba appellantur.
units.tr: As to what it is: "These are the words," he says. Among the Hebrews the word means a cause, a head, a summary of a matter; and words are for them a kind of summaries or heads of things. This is why the ten laws written on two tablets are called the ten words.

units.la: Quæ leges cum nostro hoc libro & repetantur & exponantur, huic titulū seu inscriptionem apud Hebraeos quidem אֵלֶּה הַדְּבָרִים [?] Elle haddebarim, apud Graecos autè τὸ Δευτερονόμιον [?] fecerunt. Ac quia haddebarim, id est,summæ quædam seu capita libro hoc comprehensa titu-lus seu inscriptio libri significat, intelligi potest, nihil nisi summam breuitatem hic promitti, paucisq; verbis quod facto opus est doceri. Et est profecto omnibus omnium philosophorum enchiridijs præstantior, & ijs qui vel publicis vel domesticis negocijs sunt occupati viris quàm commodissimus, vt mirum sit longos & verbosos sermones à plerisq; magis quàm breues ho-sce legi.
units.tr: Since these laws are both repeated and expounded in this our book, the Hebrews have given it the title or inscription Elle haddebarim [אֵלֶּה הַדְּבָרִים], and the Greeks Deuteronomion [Δευτερονόμιον]. Because haddebarim, that is, the summaries or heads contained in this book, signifies the title or inscription of the book, it can be understood that nothing is promised here but the greatest brevity, and that what needs to be done is taught in a few words. And indeed it is more useful than all the handbooks of all the philosophers, and most convenient for men occupied with public or private affairs. So it is remarkable that many read long and wordy sermons rather than these short ones.

units.la: Iam verò quod δευτερονόμιον [?] quasi δεύτερος νόμος, id est, lex repetita, aut fecundo promulgata, ac Mose precone pariter & interprete rursus proposita Græcis appellatur, id argumento fuerit nobis legem antea latam nunc repeti atq; in memoriam reuocari: quemadmodū iuris ciuilis doctores eum librum quo ius authore Iustiniano, restauratū atq; emendatum est Christianorum impp.atq; principū epistolis, Codicem ex repetita prælectione vocant. Sic Hebræi librum illum quia commentarius est earum quæ in prioribus libris Mosis descripta sunt, משנה [?], id est, repetitam lectionem vocant. Moses enim fœdus cum his qui in deserto nati fuerant restaurat: ac nihil quidem vel perparum affert noui, sed vetera nouo quodam modo exponit. In quo præsens hic liber, quemadmodum præclare est à Rabano annotatum, euangelij typum repræsentat.
units.tr: Now, that it is called in Greek Deuteronomion [Δευτερονόμιον], as if it were deuteros nomos [δεύτερος νόμος], that is, a law repeated or promulgated a second time, and set forth again by Moses as herald and interpreter alike, may serve as a sign for us that the law previously given is now repeated and brought back to memory. In the same way, the teachers of civil law call the book by which the law was restored and emended under the authority of Justinian, from the repeated reading of the Christian emperors' and princes' edicts, the Code. So the Hebrews call that book, because it is a commentary on what is described in the earlier books of Moses, mishnah [משנה], that is, a repeated reading. For Moses renews the covenant with those who were born in the wilderness. He brings almost nothing new, or very little, but sets out the old things in a new way. In this respect the present book, as Rabanus has well remarked, represents the type of the Gospel.

units.la: Sed ex eo nos discimus verbum Dei subinde iterum atque iterum repetendum esse, quia mortales subinde noui nascuntur, qui defunctis natu maioribus succedunt, tum etiam ætate, & fortuna, reliquisq; rebus quæ eueniunt in horas pene mutamur. Etenim alius est iuuenis, alius vir, alius senex: diuersa quoq; est natura viri & fœminæ: alius fit qui cum pauper esset, factus est diues, qui ex priuato homine euasit magistratus. Quæ cum ita sint, exemplo Mosis fœdus su-binde restaurandum est.
units.tr: From this we learn that the Word of God must be repeated again and again, because mortals are constantly being born anew to succeed those who have died, and because we change almost hour by hour through age, fortune, and the other events that befall us. For one man is young, another mature, another old; the nature of a man and of a woman is also different; one who was poor becomes rich, and one who was a private person becomes a magistrate. Since this is so, the covenant must be renewed from time to time, after the example of Moses.

units.la: Sed quam legem repetierit verbo דִּבֵּר [?] in ea qua significatio intenditur forma posita signi-ficat. Idem enim est dibber quod grauiter, vehementer, magno studio dixit. Vnde & hunc-li-brum Hebrei reprehensionum appellant, quod populum duriter alloquatur.
units.tr: But the verb dibber [דִּבֵּר], in the form that expresses intensity, signifies the manner in which he repeated the law. For dibber means to speak gravely, vehemently, with great zeal. Hence the Hebrews also call this book the book of rebukes, because it addresses the people harshly.

units.la: In quo videmus quanto studio verbum Dei prædicari debeat. Vt apud Esa. Sicut tuba vo-cem tuam exalta. Matth. 7. Christus fertur non more Pharisæorum frigide & leuiter sed [illegible, ~9 letters] docuisse.
units.tr: In this we see with how much zeal the Word of God ought to be preached: "Lift up your voice like a trumpet," in Isaiah. In Matthew 7 Christ is reported to have taught not coldly and lightly, as the Pharisees did, but [illegible].

units.la: Eodem modo quæ prioribus libris docuerat hic Moses magno zelo repetita proponit, ac præsenti libro velut epilogo doctrinam suam omnem in vnum colligit, quasiq; iamiam morituruɳ populum ad eius studium quanto potest opere extimulat. Quæ cum ita sint priorum li-brorum hic est epilogus. Nam cum omnis recte facta coclufio motu constet & enumeratione: Moses hic leges prius latas repetit, easq; historijs antea descriptis exponit, quæ ceu exemplo prius pertractata rursus enumerat: tum propositis pœnis atq; premijs ad pietatem eos quasi quodam modo impellit ac de vitæ suæ exitu concionatur, id ad motum pertinet. Ex quo per-spici potest quàm vehemens hæc fit oratio.
units.tr: In the same way, Moses here sets forth with great zeal what he had taught in the earlier books, and in this book, as if in an epilogue, he gathers all his teaching into one place. Like a people about to die, he urges them on to zeal for it with all the effort he can. Since this is so, this book is the epilogue of the earlier books. For since every well-made argument consists of movement and enumeration, Moses here repeats the laws given earlier and explains them by means of the histories described before. Treating these as examples already handled, he enumerates them again. Then, by proposing punishments and rewards, he drives them, as it were, toward piety, and he preaches on the end of his own life. This belongs to movement. From this it can be seen how vehement this discourse is.

units.la: Sed non minus artificiosè fabrefacta est. Nam eius inscriptio primis illis quæ recitauimus verbis, proponitur: inde exorsus est orationem. Ea quadripartita est. Ac partes eius sunt exor-dium, propositio, confirmatio, conclusio. Exordium à primo capite ad quintum vsq; porrigi-tur, quo præparat animos hominum quibusdam progymnasmatis vt ad percipiendam legem Domini fiant idonei. Propositio capite 5. continetur, quo decalogum, quem sibi sumpsit expo-nendum, paucis commemorat. Confirmatio à sexto capite ad trigesimum primum vsq; deduci-tur: quibus leges diuinas adhibitis exemplis, similibus, dissimilibus, exceptionibus, emendatio-nibus enucleat atq; asserit. Inde sequitur conclusio quæ ad finem vsq; extenditur: qua Moses orationem claudit, populo valedicit, canticum canit, Josuam substituit: deniq; etiam historia mortis texitur. Ex quibus omnibus multifariis alijs, quæ lubens hic prætereo, satis perspicuum fit quàm egregius, vehemens, & perspicuus huius libri sit ordo, quàm artificiosa compositio.
units.tr: But it is no less skilfully constructed. For its inscription is set forth in the first words we have recited, and from there he begins the discourse. The discourse is fourfold, and its parts are exordium, proposition, confirmation, and conclusion. The exordium extends from the first chapter to the fifth, preparing the minds of men with certain preliminary exercises so that they may become fit to receive the law of the Lord. The proposition is contained in chapter 5, where he briefly recalls the Decalogue, which he has undertaken to expound. The confirmation is carried from the sixth chapter to the thirty-first, where by means of examples, similar and dissimilar, exceptions, and corrections, he unfolds and establishes the divine laws. Then follows the conclusion, which extends to the end, in which Moses closes his discourse, bids the people farewell, sings the song, appoints Joshua, and finally the story of his death is woven in. From all of these and many other things, which I gladly pass over here, it is sufficiently clear how excellent, vehement, and perspicuous the order of this book is, and how skilful its composition.

units.la: Quorum illum fit nosse,&c. Ad omnem (inquit) Israelem habita scilicet est & pertinet hæc oratio. Quis Israelitæ sunt fideles. Nam fœdus cum Abrahamo renouatum ac factum cum semine eius pertinet ad omnem Abrahæ posteritatem. Ea ab Iacobo nepote eius Israelis cognomentum adepto ipsa quoque Israelitarum nomen accipit. Horum omnium est librum istum nosse.
units.tr: "Which it is for them to know," etc. He says, "The speech was addressed, and it pertains, to all Israel." Those who are faithful are Israelites. For the covenant renewed and made with Abraham pertains to all Abraham's posterity, and that posterity, from Jacob, his grandson, who obtained the name Israel, also receives the name Israelites. It is for all of these to know this book.

units.la: At nos, inquis, neque Israelitæ neque Iudæi sumus, ideoq; legem per Mosem latam non morabimur. Sed respondeo, Mosen dicere ad omnem Israelem, quod perinde est ac si diceret ad omne genus Israelitarum. Sunt ne, rogas, plura populi huius genera? Sunt inquam duo. Nam Paulus Rom. 9. dicit. Non omnes qui sunt ex Israel, hi sunt Israel, neque quia sunt semen Abrahæ statim omnes filij:sed per Ifaac nominabitur tibi femen : hoc est,non qui filij carnis hi filij Dei,sed qui sunt filij promissionis,hi recensentur in femen.Ex quibus verbis potest intel-ligi quod quicunque promissum femen ample&tuntur fide fiue ex Iudæis sint fiue ex gentili-bus,certe veri sunt Israelitæ.Vnde Dominus dicit Ioan.10.fe vnum ouile facere ex duobus o-uium generibus: docent etiam apostoli maceriam qua populus alterab altero diremptus ha-&tenus fuerit,iam Christo authore diruptam deftructamq; esse. Quamobrem non ijs solis qui fecundum carnem sunt Israelitæ, verumetiam illis, qui per Christum in vnum corpus populi Dei coiuerunt,nomen hoc deberi discimus. Igitur cum Moses dicit ad omnem Israelem hæc pertinere,docet vniuersali signo posito neminem excludi, noftraq; etiam, quibus hoc nomen cum primis debetur,interesse vt illum habeamus. Nam cum dicit omnem , vult neminem excipi: veluti fi dicas omnes Heluetios, requiris pagos omnes cum socijs ciuitatibus & prouincijs:sic ille non solum natis sed etiam ascitis Israelitis librum hunc obtrudit.
units.tr: "But we," you say, "are neither Israelites nor Jews, and so we will not dwell on the law given through Moses." I answer that Moses speaks to all Israel, which amounts to saying to every kind of Israelite. "Are there, you ask, several kinds of this people?" There are two, I say. For Paul says in Romans 9: "Not all who are of Israel are Israel, nor because they are Abraham's seed are they all children; but 'in Isaac shall thy seed be called'." That is, "it is not the children of the flesh who are children of God, but the children of the promise are reckoned as the seed." From these words it can be understood that whoever embrace the promised seed by faith, whether they are Jews or Gentiles, are certainly true Israelites. Hence the Lord says in John 10 that he would make one fold out of two kinds of sheep. The apostles also teach that the wall by which one people was separated from the other has now, with Christ as author, been broken down and destroyed. Therefore we learn that this name is owed not only to those who are Israelites according to the flesh, but also to those who have come together through Christ into one body of the people of God. So when Moses says that these things pertain to all Israel, he shows that by a universal sign no one is excluded, and that we also, to whom this name is especially owed, are concerned to have this book. For when he says "all," he means that no one is excepted. It is as if you said "all the Helvetians": you would expect all the cantons together with their allied cities and provinces. In the same way he presses this book upon not only the native-born Israelites but also those who have been admitted.

units.la: Cedo hoc inquis,sed putabam legem abrogatam. Abrogata quidem est sed non deleta aut sublata.Nam fœdus quod cum hominibus Deus pepigit sempiternum est.Idipsum duo capita habet.Prius est,Ego eroDeus tuus Schaddai:posterius,Tu meus populus corá me ambulans. Atque vt & in illud fœdus coire & in illo permanere possemus,Christus Iesus vnigenitus Dei Filius constitutus est arbiter in quo nos Deus suscipit, & Deum nos vicissim accipimus atq; ample&timur.Hic Christus est fœderis huius vinculum,fiue hoc fœdus illud nec pangi potuit nec retineri.Iam quia tanti refert hunc habere,Deus illum alia atque alia ratione commonstra uit. Sed lex omnium princeps forma est proptereaq; ceu pœdagogus ad Christum ducens, Paulo teste,priscis data est mortalibus.Ducit autem ad illum trifariam. Primum enim lex ceri monijs illum adumbrabat: quarum vsus externus Christo iam potitis opus non est,propter eaq; abrogatus : memoria vero, quia significationem illam Christi rebus gestis ceu testem adhiber,retinetur.Idemq; est censendum de promissionibus.
