Quare non amplius sacrificas, verum ex memoria veterum oblationum perennis huius sacrificij vim cognoscis : non amplius tibi promittitur Christus,sed promissum agnoscis atque ample&teris.Dein morum præceptis nos informans lex, nostrarum virium imbecillitate monstrata,Christi vires nos iubet quere-re:Vitia nostra taxans docet nos esse conformes populo Domini.Hæc legis pars minimè gen tium sublata est. Nam adhuc opus est nobis vt imbecillitate nostra agnita in Christi robore spes nostras positas habeamus:vt legis præceptionibus enormia scelera abscindamus,fiamusq; conformes lapidi summo Christo, cui imponamur necesse est.Quare neq; hæc pars legis tollitur.Postremo quando nihil proficitur docendo,iudicijs flagitia coerceri Deus voluit,ne quid effet offendiculi in ecclesia.Iam quia adhuc cauenda ac tollenda sunt offendicula,vultq; Deus etiam in nouo populo magistratus iuris custodes atq; moderatores esse, consequens est iudi-ciorum & forensium rerum vsum atq; exemplum è Mosis rep.petitum atq; ad nostra tempora,quantum religio & conditio cuiufq; populi fert accommodatū non inutilem esse.Acsi Ro-manorum,Atheniensium , aliorumq; populorum iura ac leges atq; consuetudines libenter le-gimus,vt eorum exemplo ciuitates nostras informemus:quanto magis eius reip.quæ Deo do store formata est,cognoscemus.
units.tr: "Granted," you say, "but I thought the law had been abrogated." It has indeed been abrogated, but not destroyed or taken away. For the covenant which God made with men is everlasting. It has two parts. The first is, "I will be your God Shaddai"; the second, "You shall be my people, walking before me." And so that we might both enter into that covenant and remain in it, Christ Jesus, the only-begotten Son of God, has been appointed as mediator, in whom God receives us, and in turn we receive and embrace God. Christ is the bond of this covenant; otherwise that covenant could neither be made nor kept. Now since it matters so much to have him, God has shown him in various ways. But the law, the chief of all, is a form, and therefore, like a schoolmaster leading to Christ, it was given to earlier mortals, as Paul testifies. It leads to him in three ways. First, the law foreshadowed him by ceremonies; the external use of these is no longer needed now that Christ has been obtained, and so they have been abrogated; but the memory of them is retained, since it employs their meaning of Christ as a witness through the events that occurred. The same must be judged of the promises. Therefore you no longer offer sacrifices, but from the memory of the old offerings you recognise the perpetual power of this sacrifice; Christ is no longer promised to you, but you acknowledge the promised one and embrace him. Second, the law, instructing us in precepts of morals, having shown the weakness of our strength, bids us seek Christ's strength. By censuring our vices it teaches us to be conformed to the people of the Lord. This part of the law has by no means been taken away from the nations. For we still need, having recognised our weakness, to place our hopes in the strength of Christ, so that by the precepts of the law we may cut away enormous crimes, and be made conformed to the chief stone, Christ, on whom we must be laid. Therefore this part of the law is not removed either. Lastly, since nothing is gained by teaching alone, God willed that crimes be restrained by judgments, so that there might be no stumbling block in the Church. Now since stumbling blocks still have to be guarded against and removed, and since God wills that in the new people too there be magistrates as guardians and governors of law, it follows that the use and example of judicial and civil matters taken from Moses, adapted to our times as far as the religion and condition of each people allows, is not useless. Just as we gladly read the laws, rights and customs of the Romans, the Athenians and other peoples, so that we may shape our cities by their example, how much more shall we come to know that commonwealth which was formed by God as teacher.

units.la: Quibus de causis libri huius cognitio ad nos quoq; pertinet,qui Israelis nomine censemur, & quibus Christus legem non sustulit sed impleuit.In quam sententiâ D.Paulus 1.Cor.2:5.mul ta docet.Et vt eo maior effet huius libri authoritas,voluit Dominus esi esse publicum,ac iussit vt in arca,quæ & arcana seu mysteria veteris ecclesia retinet omnia, & Christi illiufq; ecclesiæ typum gerit,tum manna,tabulas,virgam Aharonis reliquaq; eiusdem generis sacra habuit,serua retur.Qua de causa Iofias eum repertum populo proposuit. Et Dominus voluit eum regibus esse quàm familiarifsimû.Ergo nos eum ad nos pertinere cumprimis arbitrabimur,nefafq; ducemus esse vt eum qui nostra causa per tot ærumnas conseruatus fit,negligamus.
units.tr: For these reasons the knowledge of this book pertains also to us, who are counted under the name of Israel, and to whom Christ did not abolish the law but fulfilled it. Paul the apostle teaches much to this effect in 1 Corinthians 2. And to make the authority of this book greater, the Lord willed that it be public, and ordered that it be kept in the ark, which also holds the secrets or mysteries of the old Church, and which bears the type of Christ and his Church, together with the manna, the tablets, Aaron's rod and other sacred things of the same kind. For this reason Josiah, when he had found it, set it before the people. And the Lord willed it to be most familiar to kings. Therefore we shall judge that it pertains especially to us, and we shall think it wicked to neglect what was preserved for our sake through so many hardships.

units.la: Quo authore fit editus.Deo ipso iubente & mandante Moses eum populo proposuit:Dicit enim Moses,iuxta omnia,quæ mandauit per ipsum Deus ad eos. In quo vides hunc librum diuini tus allatum proptereaq; magno in precio habendum esse.Sic Efaiæ & reliquorum prophetarū sermones verbum Dei esse illi ipsi testes sunt locupletissimi. Petrus & Paulus nihil humanum sed diuinam doctrinâ afferre fe docent.Christus Ioan.7.Doctrina mea non est mea,&c.Paulus Timotheo scribit omnem scripturam diuinitus inspirata esse.Qua de causa nostrae quoq; cones quoniam nihil aliud habent quàm verba scripturæ eorumq; ex scriptura depromptas explanationes,non humanæ & friuolæ nugæ,sed verbum Dei censeri & haberi debebunt.Atq; hoc sibi de euangelio persuasum habere non tam ad Dei gloriam pertinet , quàm ad nostram salutem momenti multum affert. Igitur qui Deo debitam gloriam perhibere, & saluti suæ consulere cupit, is verbum Dei faciet maximi.
units.tr: By what author it was published: Moses set it before the people at the command and bidding of God himself. For Moses says, "according to all that the Lord commanded him to say to them." In this you see that this book was brought by divine inspiration, and therefore must be held in high esteem. Thus the very witnesses, the words of Isaiah and the other prophets, most fully testify that these are the word of God. Peter and Paul teach that they bring nothing human but divine doctrine. Christ says in John 7, "My doctrine is not mine," etc. Paul writes to Timothy that all Scripture is divinely inspired. For this reason our sermons too, since they have nothing other than the words of Scripture and explanations drawn from Scripture, should be counted and held as the word of God, not as human and trifling trifles. And to hold this persuasion about the gospel is not so much a matter of God's glory as it is of great importance for our salvation. Therefore whoever desires to render God the glory due him and to care for his own salvation will hold the word of God in highest regard.

units.la: De eius authore verbo uno quid sentiendum docet, Mosem dicens. Eius viri multa ac[?] magna laus est. Nos hæc paucis dicimus. 1. Magnum quiddam est quod mirabiliter & in lucem editus & in vita conseruatus est inuito tyranno, qui illi male tractatæ gentis Israeliæ pœnas dedit.
units.tr: Concerning its author, the one word the text teaches us to think, calling him "Moses." Great and manifold is the praise of this man. We say these things briefly. 1. It is a great thing that he was born and brought up in a wonderful way, and preserved in life, though the tyrant was unwilling, who inflicted punishments on the Israelite nation, which he had ill-treated.

units.la: 2 Quod & in aula regis inimici educatus atque omni Ægyptiorum sapientia doctus atque instructus, & à filia regis adoptatus est, illiq; mirum in modum adamatus.
units.tr: 2. That, though brought up in the court of the hostile king, and taught and instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, he was adopted by the king's daughter and was wonderfully beloved by her.

units.la: 3 Quod in ætate iuuenili virilis sanctique animi specimina edidit. Nam ab aula, in qua & illustris & diues & charus esset ad fratres suos tenues, exosos, inglorios transfit. Quod quantæ fidei sit argumentum Paulus Hebr. 11. pulchre docet dicens, Per fidem Moses iam grandis renuit vocari filius filiæ Pharaonis, potius eligens simul malis affici cum populo Dei, quàm temporarijs peccati commodis frui, maiores arbitratus diuitias probrum Christi, quam Ægyptiorum thesauros. Idem etiam tractat Diuus Basilius in prima ad opus hexaemeron homilia ad hunc modum scribens. ὃς (de Mose dicit) τὸν λόγον τῆς πραΰ[?]τητος μισήσας, καὶ πρὸς τὸ πα[?]τρεῖνον τῶν ὁμοφύλων ἀναδραμὼν ἐλέσθαι συγκακουχεῖσθαι τῷ λαῷ τοῦ Θεοῦ πρόσκαιρον ἔχειν ἁμαρτίας [?]καὶ ἀπόλαυσιν[?]. Quibus verbis cum Basilius doceat Mosem ad humilem suorum hominum sortem ex aula tyranni transijsse, quippe quod maluerit simul cum fidelibus aduersam fortunam perpeti, quam breuem & momentaneam perceptam ex peccato voluptatem obtinere: sane perspicuum est hic contineri perpulchram eorum quæ de fide Paulus Hebr. 11. cap. scripsit expositionem. His adde quod neq; Israelitas ab Ægyptiis affligi atque opprimi, neque Israelitas ipsos sese mutuis iniurijs afficere passus est. Quæ profecto magni excelsique animi indicia sunt.
units.tr: 3. That in his youthful age he displayed the marks of a manly and holy spirit. For he passed from the court, where he was famous, rich and dear, to his brothers, who were lowly, hated and without glory. What a proof of faith this is, Paul teaches beautifully in Hebrews 11, saying: "By faith Moses, when he was grown, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter, choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to enjoy the temporary pleasures of sin, esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of the Egyptians." Basil also treats the same in his first homily on the Hexaemeron, writing in this manner: "He (speaking of Moses) hated the reign of gentleness, and ran to the lowly estate of his own kin, choosing to suffer hardship together with the people of God rather than to have the momentary enjoyment of sin [ὃς (de Mose dicit) τὸν λόγον τῆς πραΰτητος μισήσας, καὶ πρὸς τὸ πατρεῖνον τῶν ὁμοφύλων ἀναδραμὼν ἐλέσθαι συγκακουχεῖσθαι τῷ λαῷ τοῦ Θεοῦ πρόσκαιρον ἔχειν ἁμαρτίας καὶ ἀπόλαυσιν]." Since Basil here teaches that Moses passed from the tyrant's court to the humble lot of his own people, preferring to bear adversity together with the faithful rather than to obtain the brief and momentary pleasure gained from sin, it is clearly plain that there is contained here a most beautiful exposition of what Paul wrote about faith in Hebrews 11. To this add that he suffered neither the Israelites to be afflicted and oppressed by the Egyptians, nor the Israelites themselves to inflict wrongs on one another. These are surely signs of a great and lofty spirit.

units.la: 4 Quod ab ipso Deo vocatus est & declaratus dux populi Israelitici: quo officio prudenter & pie, & graviter functus est, resque gessit maximas. Nec moror quod quia de se hæc ipse scripserit, ideo minus vera videantur aliquibus: nam hoc ipse non primus tentauit, nec postremus etiam ausus est, & fecere alij item boni, ut licere Mosi debeat quod licuit aliis. Sed & si nec his contentus velis esse, multæ sunt euidentes & bonæ rationes, quibus idem hoc adstruitur. Primum nihil affectibus datum, sed sua pariter atque aliorum vitia prodidit. Dein illo viuo omnia proposita sunt populo, ut nisi vera fuissent, populus ille furens req; scriptum neque scriptorem tulerit.
units.tr: 4. That God himself called and appointed Moses as leader of the Israelite people is shown by the way he discharged that office: wisely, piously and seriously, and by the great deeds he accomplished. Nor do I dwell on the objection that, because Moses wrote these things about himself, some may think them less true. Moses was not the first to attempt this, nor the last to dare it, and other good men have done the same, so what was lawful for others may be lawful for Moses. But even if you are not content with this, there are many clear and good reasons that confirm the same point. First, nothing in his account is given to passion; he exposed his own faults equally with those of others. Second, while he was still alive, everything was set before the people, so that unless it had been true, that raging people would not have tolerated either the writing or the writer.

units.la: Postremo omnium ætatum decursu firmata est eius authoritas & existimatio cum pietatis tum doctrinæ & solidæ sapientiæ. Et certè si rerum gestarum seriem inspiciamus, ex illo fonte sua plerique sapientes hauserunt. Nam ut omittam Pythagoram Samium, Socratem, Platonem & cæteros prophetis nostris longe recentiores, quippe qui Judæis jam restitutis demum florere ceperint: tum vetustiores his Thaletem & sapientes reliquos: denique eorum omnium vetustissimos Orpheum, Linum, Musæum, his omnibus antiquior Moses fuit. Ac quanquam Ægyptus fortasse gloriari queat hoc nomine, quod Moses ipsius sapientiam ab infantia imbi-berit, suaque ab his omnia hauserit: tamen ipsis etiam Ægyptiis vetustiores doctores diuos pa-triarchas postea nactus est Moses, quando ab Ægyptiis ad Israelem transiit, & in deserto postea Deum ipsum sibi loquentem audivit.
units.tr: Last, through the course of all ages his authority and reputation have been established, both for piety and for learning and solid wisdom. Indeed, if we look at the sequence of events, most of the wise men drew their wisdom from that source. To pass over Pythagoras of Samos, Socrates, Plato and others far later than our prophets, since they only began to flourish once the Jews had been restored; and earlier than these, Thales and the other sages; and finally, the most ancient of all, Orpheus, Linus and Musaeus: Moses was older than all of them. Although Egypt may perhaps boast on this score that Moses drank in its wisdom from infancy and drew everything from it, yet Moses later found teachers older even than the Egyptians, the holy patriarchs, when he passed from the Egyptians to Israel, and afterwards in the desert he heard God himself speaking to him.

units.la: Memorabile est quod Artapanus, quidàquemadmodum in li. 9. præpa. euangel. apud Eusebium scriptum est, tradit Moerim Chenephris Ægyptiarum regis filiam, cum ipsa non pareret, adoptasse puerum Judæum, quem Hebræi Mosem, Græci Mosæum vocant. Ex quo perspici potest tantum Græcis visum esse Mosem ut Musæum, quem fecere maximi, fuisse putaverint. Multa apud Augustinum in lib. 18. de ciuit. Dei itemq; apud Iosephum in eo quem contra Appionem scripsit libro, apud Eusebium & Iustinum Martyrem scripta extant in Mosis laudè ex gentilium hominum scriptis deprompta. Sed etsi illis laudatus cultusq; non fuisset, tamen illum prophetæ & apostoli: & Christus, deniq; etiam doctores Christiani maximis laudibus dignum habuere. Testes sunt illi loci. Psal. 102. & 105. Hier. 15. Mich. 6. Matth. 17. Luc. 24. Paulus & cæteri apostoli in Actis. Quamobrem authoris laus authoritatem libro conciliabit in ecclesia.
units.tr: It is worth remarking what Artapanus relates, as is written in book 9 of the Preparation for the Gospel, as quoted by Eusebius: that Merris, daughter of the Egyptian king Chenephres, when she had no children of her own, adopted a Jewish boy whom the Hebrews call Moses and the Greeks Mosaeus. From this it can be seen that the Greeks thought Moses was so much like Musaeus, whom they held in high regard, that they supposed they were the same. Many writings in praise of Moses, drawn from the works of Gentile authors, are extant: in Augustine's book 18 of The City of God, likewise in Josephus in the book he wrote against Apion, and in Eusebius and Justin Martyr. But even if he had not been praised and honoured by them, the prophets and apostles, Christ himself, and finally the Christian teachers have judged him worthy of the greatest praise. Those passages bear witness: Psalm 102 and 105; Jeremiah 15; Micah 6; Matthew 17; Luke 24; Paul and the other apostles in Acts. Therefore the praise of the author will win authority for the book in the Church.

units.la: De loco, dicit, Cùm Iordanem in deserto, in campis ex aduerso maris rubri, &c. Quibus verbis & loca, in quibus quæ gesta sunt, hic repetuntur, commemorat, & eum ipsum in quo est hæc ora-tio habita monstrat.
units.tr: Concerning the place, it says: "When they were beyond the Jordan in the desert, in the plains opposite the Red Sea," etc. By these words he recalls the places where the events took place, and points out the very place where this discourse was delivered.

units.la: Ac illa quidem loca veluti statuas seu monumenta rerum gestarum commemorat: quippe in quibus maximè peccatum esset. Sunt autem loci quos enumerat septem. In planitie quam Arabam sua lingua vocat Baal, peor solvere. In litore maris rubri contra Deum murmurarunt dicendicentes : an non sepulchra fuerunt in Ægypto? In Paran exploratum perfidis vocibus corru- pti promissæ terræ comparandæ spem extenuarunt ac deposuerunt. Tophel & Laban alibi in Biblijs non ponuntur, fortasse loca aliqua significant quibus etiam alia sunt alibi posita nomi- na. In Hazeroth Core seditio orta est. Per Dizahab aureum vitulum conflatum atq; adoratum putant.Quæ loca Moses enumerans ostendit Deum loci temporisq; quo offenditur meminif- se,peccatiq; facti memoriam renouare,quo pœnitentiam incutiat.Eodem modo nos ipsi mo- neamus vt resipiscamus.
units.tr: He recalls those places as monuments or memorials of the events, since in them especially sin had been committed. There are seven places which he lists. In the plain which he calls Arabah in his own language, they joined themselves to Baal-peor. On the shore of the Red Sea they murmured against God, saying: "Were there not graves in Egypt?" In Paran, by faithless words, they corrupted the spying out of the land and weakened and abandoned their hope of obtaining the promised land. Tophel and Laban are not mentioned elsewhere in the Bible; they perhaps signify some places which are also named otherwise elsewhere. In Hazeroth, the rebellion of Korah arose. At Dizahab they are thought to have cast and worshipped the golden calf. In listing these places, Moses shows that God remembers the place and time at which he was offended, and so renews the memory of the sin committed, in order to stir up repentance. In the same way let us admonish ourselves to repent.

units.la: Hic autem locus in quo præfens hæc est habita concio fuit ampla planicies in campis Moab cis Iordanem.In quo præter rei veritatem, vides etiam parum referre quo loco sacra fiant,mo do fit aptus & idoneus,in quo,veluti Diuus Paulus admonet,omnia decenter & recto fiant or dine. Dein quod in finibus terræ promissæ fui officij admonentur id nobis etiam documento erit,eò deuectis & deductis rebus nostris vt iam pene in tuto simus, aut iam iam futuri esse vi- deamur, tum decere nos vt pietati & probitati quàm maximè studeamus. Igitur vt ætate crescunt corpora,sic animo robur augeant pietas,virtus,probitas.
units.tr: The place where this sermon was delivered was a wide plain in the fields of Moab on this side of the Jordan. Here, besides the truth of the matter, you see that it matters little in what place sacred things are done, provided it is fitting and suitable, where, as the divine Paul advises, all things are done decently and in good order. Then, since we are reminded here, at the borders of the promised land, of our duty, this will also be a lesson for us: when our affairs have been brought and led so far that we are almost in safety, or seem just about to enter into it, then it becomes us to devote ourselves as much as possible to piety and uprightness. Therefore, just as bodies grow with age, so let piety, virtue and uprightness increase strength in the mind.

units.la: De tempore. Anno 40.mense vndecimo, post[?] percussos reges. Duplex est notatio temporis. Vna,cum anni profectionis nominantur: quo diuturnitas laborum & molestiarum dicitur,vt discamus esse patientes.Dat Deus his quæ diu pertuleris malis quoq; finem. Recordare vt Il- raelitæ quadraginta annis vitam duram atq; asperam tulerint.
units.tr: Concerning the time: "In the fortieth year, in the eleventh month, after the kings were struck down." The time is marked in a twofold way. One way is when the years since the departure are named, by which the long duration of labours and troubles is expressed, so that we may learn to be patient. God gives an end even to the evils you have endured for a long time. Remember that the Israelites bore a hard and bitter life for forty years.

units.la: Altera,quando res circa ea tempora factę enumerantur:eo tempore scilicet reges duos de- uictos esse. Vnus erat Seon rex Amorrhæorum qui habitabat in Hesbon. Alter vero Og rex Bafan qui habitabat in Aftaroth, &c. Extat de his Num.21.descripta historia, quaciuitas Hef- bon etiam describitur. Aftaroth autem sunt montes ab ouibus illic pasci solitis denominati.
units.tr: The other is when the events around that time are enumerated: namely, that at that time two kings were defeated. One was Sihon, king of the Amorites, who dwelt in Heshbon. The other was Og, king of Bashan, who dwelt in Ashtaroth, etc. The history of these events is described in Numbers 21, where the city of Heshbon is also described. Ashtaroth, however, are mountains named after the sheep which were accustomed to graze there.

units.la: Nos ex hoc quid deuictis hostibus dataque pace facere deceat addiscimus, nempe vt pa- cis studia ad religionem restaurandam, ad ciuitatis & singulorū ciuium salutem et felicitatem conuertendá. Moses enim data pace populum conuocauit & de religione deq; reipub.salute & dignitate docuit.
units.tr: From this we learn what is fitting to do when enemies have been defeated and peace has been granted: namely, to turn the pursuits of peace to restoring religion, and to the safety and happiness of the state and of each citizen. For Moses, once peace was given, gathered the people and taught them about religion, and about the safety and dignity of the commonwealth.

units.la: Et ex ijs quidé quæ diximus omnibus de libri Mosis, loci,temporis præstantia quod scitu necessarium cognouimus.Sit autè hoc in primis notatu dignū, quod Moses vltimo ætatis suæ tempore lucubratam orationem librohoc proponit,quippe quod argumentum sit doctrinæ defecatissimæ & purissimæ. Eam vt & addiscamus & ad vitam ac mores nostros accommo- demus, Deus pater faxit in Iesu Christo per Spiritum sanctum.Amen.
units.tr: From what we have said about the excellence of the place and time of the books of Moses, we have learned what is needful to know. Let this be especially worth noting, that Moses, at the last time of his life, sets forth in this book a carefully composed discourse, since it contains a doctrine most pure and unmixed. May God the Father grant, through the Holy Spirit in Jesus Christ, that we both learn it and accommodate it to our life and conduct. Amen.

units.la: SERMO II.
units.tr: SERMON II.

units.la: 5 Cùm[?] Iordane in terra Moab constituit Moses explanare legem hanc, & dixit:
units.tr: 5 When Moses undertook to explain this law beyond the Jordan, in the land of Moab, he said:

units.la: 6 Dominus Deus noster loquutus est ad nos in Horeb in hanc sententiam : Sat superà, mansistis apud montem istum.
units.tr: 6 The Lord our God spoke to us in Horeb, saying this: You have dwelt long enough at this mountain.

units.la: 7 Conuersi soluite,et proficiscimini ad montem Amorrhæorum, & ad loca illi vi- cina, fiue sint in planitie, fiue in montanis , fiue in vallibus , fiue in locis sterilibus , fiue in littore maris,ad terram Cananæorum,et adLibanum,& ad fluuium illum magnum, fluuium inquam Euphratem.
units.tr: 7 Turn and set out, and go to the mountain of the Amorrhites and to the places near it, whether they lie on the plain, in the mountains, in the valleys, in barren places, or on the seashore, to the land of the Canaanites, and to Lebanon, and to that great river, I mean the river Euphrates.

units.la: 8 En tradidi in conspectu vestro terram,venite et occupate terram,quam iurauit Dominus patribus vestris Abraha,Ifaac & Iacob,vt daret (eam) ipsis & femini eo- rum post eos.
units.tr: 8 Behold, I have set the land before your eyes. Come and possess the land which the Lord swore to your fathers, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, to give to them and to their seed after them.

units.la: EX recitata atq; explicata præclari illius & eximij libri inscriptione potuit intelligi Mosem antea latam legem hic repetere,& adiectis eò spectantibus exemplis illustrare, & modò præmijs modò pœnis propositis ad diuinæ legis studium homines suos extimulare: Quod quoniam argumento est quàm grandes, vtiles, necessarias res hic liber comprehendat: rectè sanè Moses, qui quidem causam hanc iussu Dei apud populum Ifraeliticum agit, adeò aptam atq; ad auditores accommodatam methodum feruat, vt agnata nobis imbecillitate quàm mi- nimum impediti legibus diuinis obsequamur. Neq; enim subito & fine præparatione quadam animorum has promulgat & inculcat leges,sed quemadmodum artium & doctrinarum omni- um quædam sunt principia quibus tyrones ad eas præparantur : sic diuinæ philosophiæ prin- cipia quædam Moses ponit,quibus ad eius studium & cognitione homines præparari queant, Et qualem, videlicet fidem sive spem in Deo collocatam firmam ac solidam, & obedientiam, & iuris gen-tium studium, & fidem sive eam quae indictis & factis cernitur veritatem & constantiam, deni-que propensam ad studium divini verbi mentem. Quae progymnasmata in prima libri illius parte, nempe in quatuor prioribus Cap. veluti proxime diximus, persequitur.
units.tr: FROM the title of that distinguished and excellent book, once recited and explained, one can understand that Moses here repeats the law he had given earlier, illustrates it with examples that bear on it, and, setting before men now rewards and now punishments, spurs his people on to the study of the divine law. Since this shows how great, useful and necessary the matters are that this book contains, Moses rightly, who indeed conducts this cause before the Israelite people at God's command, observes a method so fitting and so well adapted to his hearers that, given our native weakness, we may obey the divine laws as little hindered as possible. For he does not promulgate and impress these laws suddenly and without some preparation of minds. Rather, just as all the arts and sciences have certain principles by which beginners are prepared for them, so Moses lays down certain principles of divine philosophy by which men may be prepared for its study and knowledge. These are: (1) and what kind of faith, namely, a firm and solid trust or hope placed in God; (2) obedience; (3) a zeal for the law of nations; (4) faith, or that truthfulness and steadfastness which is seen in words and deeds; and finally (5) a mind inclined to the study of the divine word. These preliminary exercises he pursues in the first part of that book, namely in its first four chapters, as we have just said.

units.la: Ac quoniam ex his quinq; fides in Deum vera ac solida prima est ac princeps virtus, à qua reliqua omnia quae diximus principia dependent: ea ipsa primo omnium cognoscenda tenen-daq; est. Quid enim in schola Dei facias, si tibi de eo non sit spes optima? Deus quid facto aut vitato opus sit consulit, si consultoris verbis nil fidas, quid suis apud te consilijs efficiat? Ac ma-gna consulit, & viribus nostris maiora, sed ea nisi spe divinae opis fulti nunquam tentabimus. Magna quoque pollicetur, quae nos nisi spe firmati non credemus, praesertim cum tam multa sint quae retrahant.
units.tr: And since of these five, true and solid faith in God is the first and chief virtue, on which all the other principles we have mentioned depend, it must first of all be known and held. For what will you do in God's school if you have no good hope of him? God advises what must be done or avoided. If you put no trust in his counsellor's words, what will his counsel accomplish in you? He advises great things, greater than our strength, and we will never attempt them unless supported by the hope of divine help. He also promises great things, which we will not believe unless we are strengthened by hope, especially since there are so many things that hold us back.

units.la: Quae cum ita sint quid spes sit aut qualis esse debeat etiam atq; etiam diligenter ponderan-dum est. Est autem spes expectatio futuri alicuius boni: veluti illis terrae promissae spes erat comparanda. Ea inter confidentiam & desperationem media est: utraq; enim in vitio cum sint, haec quia mediocritatem servat, virtus est. Nam quemadmodum nimis magna sperare & appe-tere vitiosum est, & maiora viribus tentare etiam periculosum: sic in magna earum quibus ad magnas res gerendas adiuuamur rerum abundantia semper desperabundum & meticulosum esse cum turpe tum vero maxime perniciosum est.
units.tr: Since this is so, what hope is, and what kind it ought to be, must be weighed again and again with care. Now hope is the expectation of some future good; such was the hope that had to be gained for the promised land. It lies between confidence and despair, for although both are vices, this one, because it keeps the mean, is a virtue. For just as to hope and desire too much is vicious, and to attempt greater things than our strength allows is dangerous, so to be always despairing and fearful amid the great abundance of those things by which we are helped to achieve great deeds is both shameful and, above all, most destructive.

units.la: Igitur ad servandam auream[?] mediocritatem sic de spe & fiducia divinae opis Moses diffe-rit, ut primum eam quae huc pertinet inscriptionis partem repetat, tum impedimenta fidei tol-lit, postremo praesidia atq; adiumenta fidei monstret.
units.tr: Therefore, to preserve the golden mean, Moses speaks of hope and confidence in divine aid in this way: first he repeats that part of the title which bears on this matter; then he removes the hindrances to faith; lastly he shows the defences and aids of faith.

units.la: Inscriptionis pars repetita sic habet, Cis Iordanem in terra Moab constituit Moses explanare legem hanc & dixit: Dominus Deus noster locutus est ad nos in Horeb, &c. Quibus verbis ad ro-borandam spem tria argumenta affert, locum, orationis formam, personam promittentis Dei.
units.tr: The repeated part of the title reads: Beyond the Jordan, in the land of Moab, Moses undertook to explain this law, and said: The Lord our God spoke to us in Horeb, etc. With these words he brings three arguments to strengthen hope: the place, the form of the speech, and the person of the promising God.

units.la: Locus est, cis Iordanem in terra Moab. Nam ad fines terrae Moab, quae quondam ad Iordanem usq; porrecta fuerat, sed eius magnam partem ad Amorrheos Seon rex attraxerat, iam eos peruenisse Moses dicit. Quo ostendit illos decere, ut quoniam eo usq; peruenerint, quasiq; ob oculos positam sibi terram habeant, ne desperabundi terrae huius occupandae conatu desinant, neue de veritate promissionum divinarum sint dubij. Heygeinen[?] Gott so nach zühin[?] gholf-sen so werde er jnen wyter helffen.
units.tr: The place is beyond the Jordan, in the land of Moab. For Moses says that they have now come to the borders of the land of Moab, which once extended as far as the Jordan, though King Sihon had drawn a large part of it to the Amorrhites. By this he shows that they ought, since they have come so far and have, as it were, the land set before their eyes, not to give up in despair of taking possession of it, nor to doubt the truth of God's promises. If God has so far helped you along, he will help you further.

units.la: Eodem modo omnes homines cogitationem de se rebusq; suis instituant atq; informent suam: si Deus hucusq; te fovit, aluit, defendit, promovit, ne desperes, dabit his maiora. Exod. 4. Sic consolatur Moses de suis ad officium necessariis eloquentiae viribus dubium? dicebat e-nim se qui linguam atque os dedisset, usum eorum organorum quoque dare posse. Et Matth. 10. capite apostolos ad eundem modum confirmabat ne de eo quod dicendum esset ad veritatem tuendam sollicitè dubitarent, se qui ipsos vocasset spiritu patris sui instruere velle, ut spiritus ipse fit futurus orator. Sic David ex eo quod ursum & leonem vincere poterat, colligebat sibi spem victoriae contra Goliathum. Eiusmodi ratio ad firmandā spem publicè & privatim semper est servanda. Publice, ut cogitemus Deum nos adversus potentissimos tyrannos, adversus callidissimè structas insidias semper defendisse, idq; etiam ipsum facturum in posterum. Privatim, ut cogites quo pacto in utero matris, in infantia, in adolescentia, in omni deniq; vita tibi semper affuerit: idipsum illum etiam facturum in posterum. Haec anteactae vitae & cogitatae gratiae Domini pia recordatio dici non potest quantopere spem & fiduciam roborent. Recte ergo Moses illos, ne comparandae huius terrae spem deponant, sed promissa Dei magnis a-nimis captent atq; amplectantur, hac ratione extimulat, quod iam quasi praeforibus sint hu-ius terrae promissae.
units.tr: In the same way all men ought to think about themselves and their affairs and shape their own outlook: if God has so far cherished, nourished, defended and advanced you, do not despair, for he will give you greater things. (Exod. 4.) So Moses consoled himself, doubtful of the powers of eloquence necessary for his office; for he said that he who had given the tongue and the mouth could also give the use of those organs. And in Matt. 10 he likewise confirmed the apostles, so that they would not anxiously doubt what they should say in defending the truth; he who had called them would himself teach them by the Spirit of his Father, so that the Spirit himself would become their orator. So David, from the fact that he could overcome the bear and the lion, drew for himself a hope of victory against Goliath. Such reasoning must always be preserved for strengthening hope, both publicly and privately. Publicly, so that we may reflect that God has always defended us against most powerful tyrants and against the most cunningly laid snares, and that he will do the same in future. Privately, so that you may consider how he has been present to you in the womb, in infancy, in adolescence, and in every part of your life; he will do the same in future. A pious recollection of the Lord's past and remembered grace cannot be described in terms of how greatly it strengthens hope and confidence. Rightly, then, Moses urges them by this reasoning, so that they do not give up hope of gaining this land, but seize and embrace God's promises with great eagerness, since they are already, as it were, at the very doors of the promised land.

units.la: Orationis forma, repraesentat hoc ipso quod promittit se nihil noui, nihil obscuri, verum explanationem legis afferre. Dicit enim se legem eo in loco cepisse explanare. Sed quid est ex-planare? est id quod paulò obscurius est adhibitis rebus notioribus & similibus & exèplis illu-strare, & ut fiat magis perspicuum efficere. Veluti si quid sit iustitia docere velim, adhibito vir-tutis ceu notiore nomine eam definiam, dein ut qualis virtus sit intelligatur, dicam illam suum cuique tribuere. Eodem modo praesens haec Moses oratio totius legis explicatio est, quippe qua non solum lex repetitur, sed adhibitis exemplis & similibus illustratur. Quare cum Deus nihil nouum, nihil ambiguum afferat, quod Dij gentium, qui dubijs & obscuris oraculis su-spensos habent, incertos interrogantium animos, solent facere: sanè eius verbis seu promissis sic fidem habere nos decet ut in ijs spem omnem collocemus. Personam promittentis respiciendam hoc ipso ponit ob oculos quod dicit, Dominus Deus noster locutus est ad nos. Est autem hoc ad roborandam spem argumentum optimum. Nam quia Deus per homines suas nobis promissiones effert, satan inde ducit argumenta ad desperatio-nem vocantia, suggeritq; stultum esse hisce credere. Quod Mosi persæpe euenit vt fidem suis apud populum dictis non inuenerit, & Prophetæ quoq; visi sunt vana dicere, & Christus si-mul cū apostolis ceu Galilæus contemptus est: nec secus nostræ se res habent, quando vulgo di ci solet, Quid sacerdotibus istis fidem habes? quid illos moraris? [illegible, ~20 letters] ʒse ren.[?] Id vt cauteat Moses, dicit Dominum Deum terram hanc promisisse, eius iussu mandata hæc ad eos afferri. Sic Dominus dicit in Euangelio, se non suam, sed patris doctrinā afferre. Paulus dicit, se & apostolos reliquos non vt homines, sed vt dispensatores mysteriorum Dei habendos esse. Et nos nihil nisi ex ipso Dei verbo depromptum afferimus, quando & contextum orationis sacræ primum prælegimus, deinceps autem eundem adhibitis aliunde ex scriptura sacra allatis exemplis & sententijs illustramus. Quod ideo dicendum est & inculcandum sæpius, vt intelligant homines se cum sacris concionibus obtemperant, non humanis, sed diuinis iussibus parere. Igitur Dei verbis credis non humanis. Quæ recordatio quantum momenti ad roborandam spem possit afferre, cuius facile est cernere.
units.tr: The form of the speech shows, by the very fact that he promises it, that he brings nothing new and nothing obscure, but an explanation of the law. For he says that he began to explain the law in that place. But what is to explain? It is to illustrate what is somewhat obscure by means of better-known things, similar things and examples, and to make it clearer. For example, if I wish to teach what justice is, I define it by means of the better-known name of virtue, and then, so that it may be understood what kind of virtue it is, I say that it is giving each his due. In the same way, this present speech of Moses is an explanation of the whole law, since in it the law is not only repeated but also illustrated by examples and similar cases. Therefore, since God brings nothing new and nothing ambiguous, unlike the gods of the nations, who keep the anxious minds of their questioners in suspense with doubtful and obscure oracles, we ought certainly to put such faith in his words or promises that we place all our hope in them. He sets before our eyes the person of the promising God to be regarded when he says, The Lord our God spoke to us. This is indeed the best argument for strengthening hope. For because God brings his promises to us through men, Satan draws from this arguments that call to despair, and suggests that it is foolish to believe these things. This often happened to Moses, that he did not find faith for his words among the people; the prophets too were thought to speak in vain, and Christ together with the apostles was despised as a Galilean. Nor is it otherwise with us, when it is commonly said: Why do you trust those priests? Why do you wait on them? [illegible, ~20 letters] To guard against this, Moses says that the Lord God promised this land, and that these commands are brought to them by his order. So the Lord says in the Gospel that he brings not his own teaching but his Father's. Paul says that he and the other apostles are to be regarded not as men but as stewards of the mysteries of God. And we bring nothing except what has been drawn from God's own word, when we first read through the context of the sacred text and afterwards illustrate the same with examples and sayings taken from elsewhere in Holy Scripture. This must be said and impressed often, so that men may understand that when they obey the sacred sermons they are obeying not human but divine commands. Therefore you believe the words of God, not of men. How much weight this remembrance can bring to strengthening hope is easy to see.

units.la: Atq; sic quidem ex inscriptionis parte repetita spei confirmandę fundamenta habes; quod Deus eò vsque te prouexerit vt videas iam coram ob oculos posita quæ promiserat: quod nihil noui, sed idipsum quod iam olim patribus promiserat repetitum atq; explicatum afferat, vt intelligas quid sit sperandum: quod non humanum sed diuinum fidei & spei fundamentum ponitur. Quamobrem tenendus est hic locus animo bene memori, ne qua dubitatio oboriatur de veritate Dei.
units.tr: So, from the part of the inscription that has been repeated, you have the foundations for confirming hope. God has brought you so far that you now see before your eyes what he had promised. What he brings is nothing new, but the very thing he had already promised to the fathers, repeated and explained, so that you understand what is to be hoped for. A foundation of faith and hope is laid here that is not human but divine. Therefore this place must be held in a well-remembering mind, lest any doubt arise about the truth of God.

units.la: Impedimenta fidei, Sat superq; manifestis apud montem i tum, conuersi soluite: Quasi dicat, quod suspensis atq; dubijs animis moram trahitis id spem & fiduciam vestram subinde magis ac magis labefacit, quin posita mora proficiscimini, & promissa bona persequimini? Quo tollitur impedimentum spei maximum: nihil enim est quod spem frangit magis quàm cunctatio. Non quod velit res arduas sine deliberatione & temerè suscipi: sed quod tardis ad præclaras res gerendas ac cunctabundis animis Dæmon mala semper suggerat. Extat Luc. 9. præclarum Domini de cunctatione iudicium duobus exemplis eorum, qui illum sero & non nisi curatis nescio quibus familiaribus negotijs sequi vellent iudicium. Nemo(inquit) qui manu admota aratro respexerit à tergo, aptus est regno Dei. Vxori Lothi malè cessit ista cunctatio. Et in Lege præcepit Dominus, vt ad epulum paschale accedentes festinarent. Israelitæ ipsi subinde Aegyptum recolentes sese mul[?]cum impediuere. Virginibus fatuis sua quoq; parum fœlix fuit cunctatio. Igitur ne fides & spes subinde impedita cunctatione longiore tandem tota frafta euertatur, dicit illos iam totum annum hic commoratos, quoniam respub. constituta, lex lata, tabernaculum extructum, omniaq; curata sint, ad iter tandem accingantur.
units.tr: Impediments to faith: "It is enough for you that you have stayed long at this mountain; turn and set out." As if to say: does your hanging in suspense and doubt, and your delaying, keep wearing down your hope and trust more and more? Stop delaying, set out, and pursue the promised goods. This removes the greatest impediment to hope, for nothing breaks hope more than hesitation. Not that he wants difficult matters undertaken without deliberation and rashly, but the Devil always suggests evils to those who are slow and hesitant in doing noble things. Luke 9 contains the Lord's notable judgment on hesitation, with two examples of those who wanted to follow him late, only after settling some family affairs. "No one," he says, "who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God." That hesitation went badly for Lot's wife. And in the Law the Lord commanded that those coming to the Passover feast should hurry. The Israelites themselves, often recalling Egypt, greatly hindered themselves. For the foolish virgins too, their hesitation was not very fortunate. Therefore, lest faith and hope, repeatedly hindered by lengthy hesitation, be finally overthrown altogether, he says that they, who had now stayed here a whole year, since the commonwealth was set up, the law given, the tabernacle built, and everything attended to, should at last gird themselves for the journey.

units.la: In quo vides quid nobis facto opus sit quando nos Dominus rebus ad negotia nostra necessarijs instruxerit, tunc nostrum esse videlicet iussa capescere. Nā si vel paululum moram trahamus, saran spei fundamenta suffodit eamq; conatur euertere. Moses igitur instructus rebus ad legationem Aegyptiacam necessarijs proficiscitur. Apostoli instructi spiritus sanĉti donis prædicationem Euangelij suscipiunt. Idem hi iubentur facere.
units.tr: In this you see what we must do when the Lord has furnished us with the things necessary for our affairs: then it is our part to take up his commands. For if we delay even a little, Satan digs under the foundations of hope and tries to overthrow them. Moses, therefore, furnished with what was necessary for the embassy to Egypt, sets out. The apostles, furnished with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, take up the preaching of the Gospel. The same people are commanded to do the same.

units.la: Fundamenta fidei tria assert, quorum vnum ducit à facili, alterum ab vtili, tertium à neces-sario: quæ spem & faciunt & sirmant. Ac faciunt quidem persiciendæ rei facilitas, & multa & magna quæ ex re perfecta percipitur vtilitas: sirmat autem hoc ipsum quod quia Deus hoc se velle decreuerit decretumq; iuramento suo confirmauerit, aliter quàm sponsio facta est, euenire nequeat. Quæ baseis vt in rebus nobis promissis nostras spes sirmare queant & fulcire, diligenter ponderandæ sunt.
units.tr: He sets out three foundations of faith: one drawn from ease, another from usefulness, the third from necessity. These both make and strengthen hope. Ease of accomplishment makes it, and so does the many great benefits perceived from the completed thing. But what strengthens it is this: because God has decided to will it and has confirmed his decree with his oath, it cannot turn out otherwise than the promise has been made. These foundations must be weighed carefully, so that they may be able to prop up and sustain our hopes in the things promised to us.

units.la: Facile, dicit qua via ad promissam terram contendatur, ostendens montes, valles & omni no omnia loca quæ vel transeunda vel prætereunda vel superanda sint.
units.tr: Ease: he says by what way the promised land is to be reached, showing the mountains, valleys, and all the places that must either be crossed, passed by, or overcome.

units.la: Eodem modo quicquid promittit, semper vt comparari queat [?]ostendit Dominus. Promittit benedictionem suam patribus factam, sed pietatem & industriam & mediocritatem ceu rationem qua acquirantur opes simul docet. Promittit vitam æternā, sed simul ostendit, Christum, quo ceu duce & via comparetur. Ergo cum ipse Deus rerum abs se promissarum compa-randarum rationem doceat, hocq; ipso quod promisit comparatu facilè effecerit, nō est quod quisquam dubitet, quin ea omnia consequamur.
units.tr: In the same way, whatever he promises, the Lord always shows how it may be obtained. He promises the blessing made to the fathers, but at the same time teaches piety, industry and moderation as the means by which wealth is acquired. He promises eternal life, but at the same time shows Christ, by whom, as guide and way, it is obtained. Therefore, since God himself teaches the way of obtaining the things he has promised, and by the very fact that he promised has made them easy to attain, there is no reason for anyone to doubt that we shall obtain all these things.

units.la: Vtile, quod & terram nominat & terminos eius longos latosq; prædicat, Euphratem, Libanum[?],&c.vt quàm ampla ac magna bona largiatur,doceat.
units.tr: Usefulness: he names the land and proclaims its borders long and broad, the Euphrates, Lebanon, and so on, so that he may teach how ample and great the goods he bestows are.

units.la: Quis igitur magnitudine bonorum non inuitari se patiatur ad ea persequenda? Acre certamen est,sed victoribus amplissima sunt proposita præmia. Quare & si quid difficultatis sit quod spem labefaciat,ei fuerit occurrendum magnitudine præmiorum. Difficile est Christi causa tanta mala perpeti,sed difficultates omnes superat æternæ vitæ perfectio.
units.tr: Who, then, would not allow himself to be invited to pursue such goods by their greatness? The contest is fierce, but the greatest prizes are set before the victors. Therefore, if there is any difficulty that weakens hope, it must be met with the greatness of the rewards. It is hard to suffer such great evils for Christ's sake, but the perfection of eternal life surpasses all difficulties.

units.la: Necessariàm ostendit bifariam. Primum quod bona quæ illi adhuc expectabant apud Deum quasi iam data putentur,dicit enim,En tradidi in conspectu vestro terram. By Gottes schon überbin/was dy vns lang Fünffzig ist. Sic ante iacta mundi fundamenta electi sunt qui fortas-se donum fidei nondum acceperunt. Sed acceptum donum fidei electionis nota est; quæ nos de bonitate Dei non finit dubitare. Est autem hoc ad firmandam spem minimè malum argumentum. Nam quemadmodum quod factum est nequit infectum fieri, sic quod Deus pro eo ac datum sit habet, non potest non dari. Id docet dicens, En tradidi, etc.
units.tr: He shows necessity in two ways. First, the goods they were still awaiting are regarded as already given by God, for he says, "Behold, I have delivered the land before your eyes." Thanks be to God, what is now past, which for us was long fifty (days/years)... So before the foundation of the world the elect were chosen, who perhaps have not yet received the gift of faith. But the gift of faith, once received, is a mark of election, and this does not let us doubt God's goodness. This is in no way a weak argument for strengthening hope. For just as what has been done cannot be undone, so what God has, as though already given, cannot but be given. He teaches this by saying, "Behold, I have delivered," etc.

units.la: Deinceps iuramentum adducit dicens, Deus iurauit patribus, &c. Iuranti Deo fides habenda est. Iurat ideo vt credas. Veluti iurato testi, sic illi iuranti crede. Quod ipsum etiam spem roborat. Quis enim de eo dubitet quod iuramento confirmatum sit?
units.tr: Next he brings in the oath, saying, "God swore to the fathers," etc. God, who swears, must be believed. He swears so that you may believe; believe him swearing as you would a witness under oath. This also strengthens hope. For who could doubt what has been confirmed by an oath?

units.la: Atq; sic quidem spem & fidem in Deum sic firmat, vt sint ad capescendam legem diuinam aptiores. Lex Dei requirit humanis viribus maiora. Iam vt illa possimus præstare, spe & fiducia diuinæ opis firmati simus necesse est. Eam Deus per Mosem his rationibus confirmare docuit, videlicet si præstita Dei beneficia, promissionum perspicuitatem, promittentis personam æstimemus: tum remoueamus cunctationem: deniq; si cogitemus quàm facilè faciat hoc negotium ipse Dominus iter ad id muniens, quàm vtiles res sint propositæ, quòdq; non possit secus quàm speramus euenire. Quibus vt potiamur Deus faxit per Christum, Amen.
units.tr: Thus he so confirms hope and faith in God that they are better fitted to take up the divine law. The law of God demands more than human strength. Now, if we are to be able to perform it, we must be strengthened by the hope and trust of divine help. God taught through Moses that this is to be confirmed by these reasons: if we weigh the benefits already bestowed, the clarity of the promises, and the person of the promiser; then we put aside hesitation; and finally, if we consider how easily the Lord himself makes this business, paving the way to it, how useful the things set before us are, and that it cannot turn out otherwise than we hope. May God grant that we obtain these things through Christ. Amen.

units.la: SERMO III.
units.tr: SERMON III.

units.la: 9 Tum dicebam ad vos hæc verba: Non possum vos solus sustinere
units.tr: 9 Then I spake unto you, saying, I am not able to bear you myself alone.

units.la: 10 Iam Dominus Deus vester auxit vos, nam estis hodie aucti vt stellæ cæli:
units.tr: 10 The LORD your God hath multiplied you, and, behold, ye are this day as the stars of heaven for multitude.

units.la: 11 (Dominus Deus patrum vestrorum auctiores vos reddat, vt fitis millecuplo plures quàm nunc: & bona imprecetur vobis, quemadmodum pollicitus est vobis:)
units.tr: 11 (The LORD God of your fathers make you a thousand times so many more as ye are, and bless you, as he hath promised you!)

units.la: 12 Et nunc quomodo ferrem solus laborem vestrum, onus vestrum, & lites vestras?
units.tr: 12 How can I myself alone bear your cumbrance, and your burden, and your strife?

units.la: CUm Deus Opt.Max. & doctores sui verbi, qui quid facto opus sit docent, & magistratus qui vt id faciamus imperio nos impellant constituerit: certè non solum spe & fiducia bonitatis eius, verumetiam obedientia magistratui debita ad capescendam legem eius præparemur necesse est. Qua de causa Moses obedientiæ in progymnasmatis illis secundum locum tribuit.
units.tr: Since God, most good and great, has appointed teachers of his Word, who teach what must be done, and magistrates, who by their authority drive us to do it, we must certainly be prepared to receive his law not only with hope and trust in his goodness, but also with the obedience owed to the magistrate. For this reason Moses gives obedience the second place in those introductory exercises.

units.la: Ac quoniam difficile est hominem obedientiæ assuefacere, methodo commodissima rem persequitur, quippe qui magistratum cui debetur obedientia & quicquid ad eum pertinet describat egregiè. Nam primum de magistratu, tum eorum & bonorum & malorum exempla affert, denique etiam obedientiæ neglectæ finem docet. Quæ descriptio vsq; ad secundum caput porrigitur.
units.tr: Since it is hard to accustom a man to obedience, Moses pursues the matter by a most suitable method: he describes admirably the magistrate to whom obedience is owed and everything that pertains to him. First he speaks of the magistrate, then he brings forward examples of both good and bad men, and finally he teaches the end of disobedience. This description extends as far as the second chapter.

units.la: Ac de magistratu quidem quid constituat tripartita præceptione persequitur. Docet enim quibus de causis magistratus eligi debeat, deinceps qua ratione fit eligendus, postremò quod nam fit & magistratus & plebis officium. Cæterum causas eligendorum magistratuum hic quidem & proponit & confirmat.
units.tr: As to the magistrate, he treats what he is appointed to do in three parts. He teaches for what reasons magistrates ought to be chosen, then by what method they are to be chosen, and finally what the office of both magistrate and people is. Here, however, he both sets forth and confirms the reasons for choosing magistrates.

units.la: Vt proponat dicit, Non possum vos solus sustinere. Quo docet neque sibi posse bile neque illis vtile esse, vt non sint alij præter ipsum magistratus. Adducit veterem historiam quæ exstat descripta Exod.18.Iethro socer eius videbat eum solum non sufficere publicis negotijs omnibus, unde ei consuluit vt iudices constituerët. Hac significat cum sua tum ipsius populi multum referre, vt sint in ciuitate principes viri, quorum virtute & consilio regantur cæteri. Ipse enim vnus omnibus quì sufficeret? Vnus non videt omnia: vni Deus non dedit omnia: v-nus ferre non potest omnia. Iam tanta turba populi, cui tot res accidunt, qui tot indiget vigili-bus oculis, qui regeretur ab vno tantum homine? Certè non posset vnum malum prius extinguere, quàm alibi grauius aliud exurgeret.
units.tr: That he may set them forth, he says, I am not able to bear you myself alone. By this he teaches that it is neither possible for him nor useful for them that there should be no magistrates besides himself. He adduces the old story, which is recorded in Exodus 18: Jethro, his father-in-law, saw that he alone was not sufficient for all public business, and so advised him to appoint judges. By this he signifies that it matters much, both for the people and for himself, that there should be men of rank in the state, by whose virtue and counsel the rest are governed. For how could one man suffice for all? One man cannot see everything; God has not given everything to one man; one man cannot bear everything. Now, what a vast crowd of people, to whom so many things happen, who need so many watchful eyes, could be ruled by one man alone? Certainly he could not put down one evil before another, more serious, rose up somewhere else.

units.la: Ergo ne diu suspensos habeat, paucis verbis quid velit fieri significat. Quod indicio est non posse vitam in his terris agere sine magistratu quenquam populum.
units.tr: Therefore, lest he keep them long in suspense, he states in a few words what he wishes to be done. This is the sign that no people can live its life on this earth without a magistrate.

units.la: Vt confirmet causas singulas sigillatim enumerat & explanat dicens, Iam Dominus Deus vester auxit vos, &c. Quibus verbis ostendit causas in populi persona, in sua ipsius persona, in officio.
units.tr: That he may confirm the individual reasons, he lists and explains them one by one, saying, Now the LORD your God has multiplied you, etc. By these words he shows the reasons arising from the person of the people, from his own person, and from the office.

units.la: In persona populi sic ostendit causas vt quæ duo poterant obijci, ea prius occupatione prę ueniat. Quorum vnum hoc est: Quid tibi nunc difficile & impossibile factu dicis esse quod hucusq; egregiè perfecisti? fortasse nunc ocio consulis, & in hoc incumbis, vt quiëtam vitam agas repositis in alios negotijs publicis. Id Moses hoc ipso diluit quod dicit se non posse. Quod perinde est ac si dicat, non me studium aut voluntas, sed vires deficiunt: non ocium sed auxilia quæro.
units.tr: He shows the reasons from the person of the people in such a way that he forestalls by his prior statement the two objections that could be raised. The first is this: "What do you now say is difficult and impossible to do, when you have so far carried out so much so well? Perhaps you are now consulting your leisure, and are bent on this, that you may live a quiet life, having handed public business over to others." Moses refutes this by the very thing he says, that he cannot. It is as if he were saying: "It is not zeal or will that fails me, but my strength; I seek not leisure but helpers."

units.la: Atq; hic Moses nobis exemplo est, vt vel leuem ocij suspicionem deuitemus. Nam cum in rerum natura nihil sit ociofum, cur nos ociofi velimus esse? cum ocium sit vt vulgo dici solet, puluinar satanæ, cur tanto tamq; pertinaci atq; impigro hosti penes nos lectum sternimus? cum ocium in ecclesia nihil aliud sit quàm enormis quædam extra ordinem: Christianos excur-sio, cur nos ij qui Diuo Paulo vocantur ἀτάκτοι esse volumus? Igitur exemplo Mosis omnis ocij suspicio cauenda ac remouenda abs se est optimo cuiq; & ciui & principi in repub. viro. Nam ne exprobraretur sibi vel suspicio ocij hac occupatione Moses cauit.
units.tr: And here Moses is an example to us, that we may avoid even the slightest suspicion of idleness. For since nothing in the nature of things is idle, why should we wish to be idle? Since idleness, as is commonly said, is Satan's pillow, why should we spread our bed for so great, so persistent and so tireless an enemy? Since idleness in the Church is nothing other than a monstrous sort of excursion outside the order of Christians, why should we who are called by the name of the divine Paul wish to be disorderly [ἀτάκτοι]? Therefore, following the example of Moses, every suspicion of idleness must be guarded against and removed from himself by every good man, whether citizen or ruler in the commonwealth. For Moses took care that even a suspicion of idleness should not be cast in his face by this occupation.

units.la: Alteram, An inuides nobis quod Dominus Deus noster nobis sic benedixerit, nosq; tantopere auxerit? An velles nostrum pauciores esse, tibi vt ocij plus esset? Minimè vero (inquit Moses) precor vt Deus millecuplo vos augeat. Ex quo discimus inuidiæ & maleuolentiæ suspicionem pariter cauendam & declinandam esse, tantumq; Reipub. tribuendum, vt eam etiam cum nostrarum rerum detrimento auctam velimus. Neq; enim dignitati & vtilitati nostræ fo-lum studendum est, sed ei ipsi publica vtilitas præponenda est. Graue crimen est ex publico suam rem familiarem augere velle. Grauius est eorum crumenas exhaurire velle quibus tuen-dis præfectus sis. Præclarè Bion admonuit eum qui magistratum gerit alicubi in hoc incum-bere debere vt honestior redeat quàm ditior. Nam eo ipso cum sibi tum Reipublicæ quisque optimè consuluerit. Quantoq; plus laudis tulere; meliores fuere Tiberius Cæsar & Alexander Magnus, quorum alter admonitus, vt prouincialibus augeret vectigalia, rescripsit, boni pastoris esse tondere pecus non deglubere: alter cuidam dicenti, longè plus vectigalium a ciuitatibus auferri posse, respondit se eum olitorem odisse qui radicitus herbas exciderat: quàm Vespasianus, qui cum ex lotio vectigal faceret, atq; a filio, ne ê re tam putida lucrum faceret, esset admonitus, pecuniam inde collectam filij naribus admouit, & nunquid ea puteret interrogauit? Igitur dignum quod imitentur exemplum Mosis habent optimi quiq; magistra-tus hic propositum, nempe vt si ille publicum commodum suæ genti inuidere nefas esse ra-tus est: ipsi ea suis populis rapere multò magis esse autument. Graue erat onus tantam homi-num turbam ducere & illius onera omnia sustinere, sed nihilominus millecuplo plures auc-tioresq; eos esse Deum precatus est, ac potius hoc egit vt quia regi non possent vno duce, le-gerentur plures.
units.tr: The second objection is this: "Do you envy us because the Lord our God has so blessed us and increased us so greatly? Or would you wish us to be fewer, so that you might have more leisure?" "Not at all," says Moses; "I pray that God will increase you a thousandfold." From this we learn that the suspicion of envy and ill will is to be guarded against and avoided alike, and that so much is to be given to the commonwealth that we wish it to grow even at the cost of our own affairs. For we must study not only our own dignity and advantage, but public advantage must be placed before it. It is a grave crime to wish to increase one's private estate out of the public purse; it is graver still to wish to drain the purses of those whom you are set over to protect. Bion admirably warned that the man who holds magistracy ought somewhere to take pains to come back more honourable than richer. For by that very means each man will have best provided both for himself and for the commonwealth. And the greater the praise they have won, the better were Tiberius Caesar and Alexander the Great: when Tiberius was urged to increase the provincial taxes, he replied in writing that it was the mark of a good shepherd to shear the flock, not to flay it; Alexander, when a man told him that far more revenue could be taken from the cities, answered that he hated a gardener who tore up the herbs by the roots. How different was Vespasian, who made a tax out of urine, and when his son warned him not to make profit from so foul a thing, held the money collected from it to his son's nose and asked whether it smelt. Therefore the best magistrates have in this example of Moses a purpose worth imitating: just as he thought it wrong to begrudge his nation the public good, so they should think it much more wrong to snatch it from their own peoples. It was a heavy burden to lead so great a crowd of men and to bear all their burdens; yet nonetheless he prayed that God would make them a thousandfold more numerous and greater, and he aimed rather at this, that since they could not be governed by one leader, more should be chosen.

units.la: Ex quo sequitur vnam eligendorum magistratuum causam in persona populi sitam esse. Est enim in ciuitate qualibet turba multa ac varia, agricolarum, artificum, operariorum, militum, mercatorum & aliorum hominum, qui mutuis operis opus habent & propterea sine rerum commutatione & communicatione commodè vitam agere nequeunt. Hæc multitudo quasi multiceps bellua est, & quæ quot capita totidem sensus habet, qui sui ipsius amorem spirant singVli, suum quisque lucrum quærunt, ac sibi quiquè melius esse malunt quàm alteri. Quibus ex studijs contentiones, lites, iniuriæ existunt. Quis illis componendis deligetur arbiter? in sua quisq; causa cæcutit: & verbera citius quàm ius acquiras. Ergo magistratu rectore opus est qui contentiones ex priuato cuiusq; studio natas dirimens turbas ac grauiores motus cauet, ciuilemq; societatem feruet incolumem. Nec ineptè Rempub. animanti comparauit Aristoteles. Nam quemadmodum in humano corpore manus & pedes, aliquâq; membra suum faciunt officium ac cibum comparant, os eum sumit, stomachus [illegible, ~12 letters] coquit, ac ministrat alimenta viresq; toti corpori, quæ regit animus in corpore sum-[illegible, ~10 letters]ceps: sic agricolæ & opifices, & omnino ciues singulì mutuis officijs rempub. fouent, [illegible, ~12 letters] ferueant magistratus prouidet. Igitur vt corpus sine mente gubernante & vt suum quaque [illegible, ~10 letters] bra faciant officium prouidente non constabit, sic sine magistratu gubernante & in suo [illegible, ~6 letters]q; officio ciuem contÎnet. tinente salua nequit esse ciuitas. Atq; hac eadem de causa Moses docet aucto populo opus ef- fe vt magistratum habeant qui sua prouidentia tantam turbam regat.
units.tr: From this it follows that one reason for choosing magistrates lies in the person of the people. For in any city there is a great and varied crowd: farmers, craftsmen, labourers, soldiers, merchants and other men, who have need of one another's work and therefore cannot live well without exchange and sharing of goods. This multitude is like a many-headed beast, and as many heads as it has, so many minds it has, each breathing self-love, each seeking his own gain, and each preferring his own advantage to another's. From these pursuits arise quarrels, lawsuits and injuries. Who will be chosen as arbiter to settle them? Each man is blind in his own cause, and you will sooner get blows than justice. Therefore there is need of a magistrate as ruler, who, settling the disputes born of each person's private interest, guards against tumults and graver disturbances, and keeps civil society safe. Nor did Aristotle compare the commonwealth to a living animal without reason. For just as in the human body the hands and feet and other members perform their office and procure food, the mouth takes it in, the stomach [illegible] digests it, and supplies nourishment and strength to the whole body, which the mind rules in the body as its governor, so farmers and craftsmen, and in general each citizen, cherish the commonwealth by mutual services, and the magistrate provides that they may flourish. Therefore, just as the body cannot stand without a mind governing it and providing that each of its members performs its own office, so without a governing magistrate the citizen cannot be held in his office, and the city cannot exist safe. And for this same reason Moses teaches that when the people has been increased there must be magistrates who by their foresight rule so great a multitude.

units.la: Quod nobis etiam ipsis documento est, vt quando nos Dominus & opibus & copijs auxerit, tanto magis curemus res nostras, nofq; ipsos bonorum & prouidorum magistratuum re &ae disciplinæ permittamus. Nam quò maior fuerit rerum omnium copia, quo maior felicitas, hoc magis est prouidendum ne qua galamitas[?] ingruat.
units.tr: This also serves as a lesson for us: when the Lord has increased us with wealth and resources, we should all the more take care of our affairs, and entrust ourselves to good and prudent magistrates in their public business and discipline. For the greater the abundance of all things and the greater the prosperity, the more care must be taken that no calamity breaks in.

units.la: Etiam priuatis hominibus in honorum atq; opum affluentia, ne fortuna splendida ac lau-ta ebrij in malum aliquod ruant, curandum est. Sed hoc inprimis populofis ciuitatibus præcipitur.
units.tr: Even private persons, amid an abundance of honours and wealth, must take care that splendid and lavish fortune does not drive them, drunk with it, into some ruin. But this is especially enjoined upon populous cities.

units.la: Sed vt in sua ipsius persona causas etiam aliquas monstret, ait, Nunc quomodo ferrem solus? Quod perinde est ac fi dixisset: Sibi quifq; regendo, tuendo & custodiendo vix sufficit, qui igi-tur solus ego sufficerem omnibus? Quo docet non ludum iocumq; esse magistratu fungi. Sūt qui bene secum actum esse putent, fibiq; nunc datum esse locum ocij plenum: at eum qui ma-giftratu rite fungi velit omnium eorum qui suæ fidei crediti sunt cura tangat necesse est. Sed vt intelligas vnum tantæ turbæ gubernandæ nō sufficere, magistratui tibi in conspectum pro ducito mercatorum, opificum, agricolarum, mercenariorum controuersias quæ in dies fingu-los nate ad te referantur: itemq; vrbanarum rerum pariter & prouinciarum curam, et annonā & exterarum gentium legationes, aliaq; innumera negocia, quibus fi in quantacunque repu-blica mediocri singulis singulos magistratus constituas, omnes quotidianis negocijs erunt occupati, ac fi illos omnes vni alicui mandes, etiamsi nunquam dormiat, edat, lauet, tamen non sufficiet. Quid fiet fi mandes nulli? Quæ cum ita sint, in persona sua docuit magistratum in ciuitate esse oportere.
units.tr: But to show in his own person some of the reasons, he says: "How could I bear it alone?" This is just as if he had said: each person hardly suffices for governing, protecting and guarding himself; how then could I alone suffice for everyone? By this he teaches that holding office is no game or jest. There are those who think they have been well treated and that a place full of leisure has now been given to them. But whoever wishes to discharge the magistracy rightly must necessarily concern himself with the care of all those who have been entrusted to his faith. But so that you may understand that one man is not enough to govern so great a crowd, set before your eyes the magistracy's disputes of merchants, craftsmen, farmers and hired workers, which arise day by day and are referred to you; likewise the care of city affairs and of the provinces alike, the grain supply, the embassies of foreign nations, and countless other matters. If in any moderately sized commonwealth you were to appoint a separate magistrate for each of these, all would be occupied with daily business; and if you were to commit all of them to one man, even one who never slept, ate or bathed, he still would not suffice. What will happen if you commit them to no one? Since these things are so, he has taught by his own example that there ought to be a magistracy in the commonwealth.

units.la: In officio vero etiam ipso causas eas monstrat. Laborem vocat seu defatigationem, <bl>mũy vnd arbeit</bl>. Est aliquis quidem corporis, sed animi potissimus ac maximus, quomodo primum in fe tum in ipso populo regendo princeps quifq; habet. Nam qui magistratus officio fungi-tur, atq; alijs velit imperare, primum omnium sibi imperet necesse est, nempe vt sese cohibeat ab omni scelere, vt fe exemplum virtutis præbeat, vt fe ipse quàm optimis moribus assuefaciat. Nam quia difficile est in magna vitæ licentia, qualem fe nactos esse viri principes autumant, af-sectus omnes habere domitos, & res ab humanæ vitæ voluptatibus & illecebris, ab ambitione & auaritia cohibere: certè vt ab harum rerum concupiscentia ad æqui boniq; & rerum præclarum gerendarum studium retrahat animum necesse est.
units.tr: In the very word for the office he shows these reasons. He calls it toil or exhaustion [mühe und arbeit]. It is indeed a labour of the body, but chiefly and above all of the mind, as every ruler has it, first in governing himself and then in governing the people. For whoever discharges the office of magistrate, and wishes to command others, must first of all command himself: namely, he must restrain himself from every wickedness, present himself as an example of virtue, and accustom himself to the best morals. For since it is difficult, amid the great licence of life which rulers claim they have obtained, to keep all the passions tamed, and to restrain affairs from the pleasures and allurements of human life, from ambition and avarice, certainly he must draw his mind away from the desire of these things toward the pursuit of what is just and good and of doing noble deeds.

units.la: Quod efficiet fi primum ad iudicium & voluntatem Dei fe fuasq; actiones omnes diri-gat ac conformet, tum non quod ipse aut velit aut possit, sed quod leges suaserint, agendum sibi putet. Nam vt Paulus iureconsultus in l. non omne, ff. de reg. iur. & Modestinus in l. fem-per in coniunctionibus, ff. eod. docent, non solum quid liceat sed & quid honestum fit confide-randum est. Ex quo sequitur vt in eam curam postea totus incumbat, quo non solum legibus quas ipse posuit alijs, obediat, verumetiam suo populo omni virtutum genere conspicuus pre-ire & prælucere velit. Atq; hic primus labor est viri principis nempe vt sese ipse regat & exem-plum præbeat.
units.tr: He will achieve this if first he directs and conforms himself and all his actions to the judgment and will of God; then he will think that he must act not because he himself wishes or is able, but because the laws have advised. For, as the jurist Paul teaches in l. non omne, ff. de reg. iur., and Modestinus in l. semper in coniunctionibus, ff. eod., one must consider not only what is permitted but also what is honourable. From this it follows that he afterwards applies himself wholly to that care, so that he not only obeys the laws which he has laid down for others, but also wishes to go before his people, conspicuous in every kind of virtue, and to shine before them. And this is the first labour of the ruler: namely, that he govern himself and give an example.

units.la: Alter est vt regat ac gubernet populum, vt singulorum & vniuersorum vtilitates curet, in-commoda propulset. Qui labor qualis & quantus fit exemplis vigilum, pastorum, parentum docent sacræ literæ. Nam cum princeps totus in vtilitate & salute publica cum conferuanda tum promouenda occupatus esse debeat, ipse dormientibus, conuiuantibus, ludentibus reli-quis ciuibus, de legibus vel sanciendis vel retinendis, de pace vel retinenda vel recuperanda, de annona, de educatione liberorum, de coercendis sceleribus, & omnino de cauendis arcen-disue malis & conferuanda communi omnium salute, cogitabit.
units.tr: The second is that he rule and govern the people, that he look after the advantages of individuals and of all together, and ward off harms. What kind and how great this labour is, the examples of watchmen, shepherds and parents teach us in Holy Scripture. For since the prince ought to be wholly occupied with the public advantage and welfare, both in preserving and in advancing it, while the rest of the citizens sleep, feast and play, he will think about whether to enact or retain laws, about keeping or recovering peace, about the grain supply, about the education of children, about restraining crimes, and in general about averting or warding off evils and preserving the common safety of all.

units.la: Eius rei non solum sacræ literæ, verumetiam prophani scriptores pulchra atq; illustria exempla habent. Homerus Iouem Deorum suorum principem cæteris dormientibus vigilan-tem & de euentu belli Troiani deliberantem introducit. Idem Agamemnonem regem ĕ som-no excitat dicens,
units.tr: Not only Holy Scripture but also profane writers have fine and illustrious examples of this matter. Homer introduces Jupiter, the chief of his gods, awake while the others sleep, and deliberating about the outcome of the Trojan war. The same poet rouses King Agamemnon from sleep, saying:

units.la: Εὕδ[illegible, ~8 letters]ἱπποδάμοιο,[?] Οὐ[illegible, ~6 letters]ύχιον δ[?] ἐν βουληφόρον ἀνδρα ῷ λαοῖ[illegible, ~6 letters] τόσα μέμηλε.
units.tr: "Are you sleeping, son of Atreus, tamer of horses? It is not fitting for a counsellor, to whom the people are entrusted and whose care they are, to sleep the whole night." [Εὕδεις, Ἀτρέος υἱὲ δαΐφρονος ἱπποδάμοιο· οὐ χρὴ παννύχιον εὕδειν βουληφόρον ἄνδρα, ᾧ λαοί τε μέμηλε.]

units.la: Quem locum optimus interpres Eufthatius exponens docet, quibus de causis vigilare de-ceat viros principes, videlicet quia sint βουληφόροι[?], id est, confulti, seu qui debeant multis con-sulere, quod noćte, quæ fit aptissima consilijs, omnium optimè efficiant: quia sint illorum cu-ræ mulræ multi populi concrediti: quia magnæ res eis curæ esse debeant.
units.tr: The excellent interpreter Eustathius, expounding this passage, teaches for what reasons rulers ought to keep watch: namely, because they are counsellors [βουληφόροι], that is, men of counsel, or those who ought to give counsel to many; because the night, which is most fitting for deliberation, they can use best of all; because many peoples have been entrusted to their care; and because great affairs ought to be their concern.

units.la: Homerum imitatus Vergilius Æneam suum aut vigilantem introducit, aut dormientem excitat, quando alibi dicit,
units.tr: Imitating Homer, Virgil introduces his Aeneas either awake or rouses him from sleep, when he says elsewhere:

units.la: At pius Æneas per noctem plurima volvens: alibi vero,
units.tr: "But pious Aeneas, turning over many things through the night."

units.la: Ænea potes hoc sub casu ducere somnos?
units.tr: "Aeneas, can you draw out sleep in this condition?"

units.la: Egregium verò & illustre exemplum est Epaminondæ Thebani ducis, qui Thebanis ciuibus conuiuantibus ac potantibus solus vigil ac sobrius arma lustrabat & circuibat mœnia, & cur id faceret rogatus dixisse fertur se νήφειν καὶ ἀγρυπνεῖν ὅπως ἐξῇ τοῖς ἄλλοις μεθύειν καὶ καθεύδειν [?], hoc est, se cibo somnoq; abstinere, vt aliis vino somnoq; indulgere liceat. Quod si Dauidis & Solomonis, & aliorum regum & virorum principum exempla consideres, idem factum apparebit.
units.tr: An outstanding and illustrious example is that of Epaminondas, the Theban general, who, while the Theban citizens feasted and drank, alone and awake and sober, went round inspecting the arms and walls. When asked why he did this, he is said to have replied that he was abstaining from food and sleep [νήφειν καὶ ἀγρυπνεῖν] so that others might be permitted to drink wine and sleep [μεθύειν καὶ καθεύδειν]; that is, that he abstained from food and sleep so that it might be allowed for others to indulge in wine and sleep. If you consider the examples of David and Solomon, and of other kings and princely rulers, the same thing will be found to have been done.

units.la: Eorum omnium exemplis excitati magistratus Christiani cogitabunt quantopere sua rei-que publicæ referat, vt ab ebrietate, & crapula sit abstinendum: tum etiam vt nihil loci sit feg-nitiæ neq; socordiæ, præsertim hisce tam deperditis moribus & temporibus, quibus omnis om-nium scelerum fœditas emergit: quæ si non consilio senum proaldentur, & optimates & ple-bem pessundabunt. Atq; hoc opus hic labor est. 2. Onus dicit, vsus nomine à verbo, quod ferre, parcere, vaticinari, coercere significat, deducto. Quod indicio est dici de populi moribus quos æquo animo ferre, in bonam partem accipere, dissimulare, itemq; quid dicturi sint cum ipsi dicere nequeant quasi vates quispiam diuinare debeas. Id omnium difficillimum est: nam hoc onus interdum sic premit, vt defatigari quempiam necesse sit.
