units.tr: Roused by the examples of all these, Christian magistrates will consider how greatly it concerns themselves and the commonwealth that they abstain from drunkenness and gluttony; and also that there be no room for sloth or heedlessness, especially in these times and among such corrupt morals, when all the foulness of every wickedness rises up. If these are not checked by the counsel of the elders, they will ruin both the nobles and the common people. And this is the work, this is the labour. The Latin word "onus" (burden) is said from its use as a noun, derived from the verb meaning to bear, to spare, to prophesy, to restrain. This is evidence that it is said of the morals of the people, which one must bear with an even mind, take in good part, overlook, and likewise, since they cannot say what they are about to say, one must divine them as some prophet would. This is the most difficult of all, for this burden sometimes presses so hard that someone must needs be worn out.

units.la: 3 Lis siue causa ac iudicium, id est, hoc ipsum, de quo disceptandum est. Hic magistratui incidunt ex personis, rebus, & actionibus negotia. Personarum autem ratio prorsus habenda est, quemadmodum iure præscribitur. Sunt enim omnes homines aut liberi aut serui. Vnde multæ & graues contentiones existunt. Iam res sunt communes, quibus quilibet vti potest, vt aer, aqua, mare, & quæ sunt huius generis alia: tum publicæ, quarum vsus non proprietas communis est, vt flumen, portus, ripa: deinde aliæ res sunt vniuersitatis vt theatrum, palatium: sunt etiam res nullius, vt sacræ: sunt deniq; res singulorum, quæ vel iure gentium, vel ciuili eodemque modos acquirendi alios atq; alios præscribente comparantur. Inde etiam actiones multæ sunt & variæ, quæq; dantur in personam aut in rem, vel sunt ciuiles, vt ex lege, seu senatus consulto decidentes vel prætoriæ. Sed de multitudine & varietate actionum, quarum genera ac formas magistratus norit necesse est, nunc non est dicendi locus.
units.tr: 3. Lawsuit or cause, that is, the very matter to be disputed. Here the business of the magistrate arises from persons, things and actions. The consideration of persons must indeed be taken fully into account, as the law prescribes. For all men are either free or slaves, whence many grave disputes arise. Next, there are common things, which anyone may use, such as air, water, the sea and others of this kind; then public things, whose use, not ownership, is common, such as a river, a harbour, a bank; then other things belong to a community, such as a theatre or a palace; there are also things belonging to no one, such as sacred things; and finally there are the goods of individuals, which are acquired either by the law of nations or by civil law, which prescribes different modes of acquiring. Hence also there are many and varied actions, which are brought either against a person or in rem, and which are either civil, deciding according to law or a senatus consultum, or praetorian. But concerning the multitude and variety of actions, whose kinds and forms the magistrate must know, this is not the place to speak now.

units.la: Ex quibus omnibus multis q; aliis quæ ad enucleandas & exponendas causas eligendorum magistratuum eas, quas hic Moses ponit, laborem scilicet & onus, & forenses lites siue contro-uersias satis perspicuum est magistratum, qui regat vniuersos & singulos, commune bonum esse diuinitus generi nostro conferuando datum, quo carere nequeamus. Nam vt docet Aristo-teles, sine magistratibus esse ciuitas non potest. Sed quid Aristotelem dicimus? Multò maioris momenti sunt ac videri debent quæ D. Paulus in Ep. Rom. 13. scribit, magistratum esse minis-trum Dei nobis vt bene sit datum à Domino. Quemadmodum igitur matrimonium bonum & salubre & necessarium esse nostro generi inde colligimus, quod Deus dixerit non esse bonum homini vt sit solus: sic ex eo quod egregius ille minister Dei dixit nostris commodis curandis magistratu Deo authore constitutum esse, colligemus magistratus omnino oportere esse, quibus recta ac diuino verbo consentanea monentibus atq; imperantibus obsequemur.
units.tr: From all these things, and many others that serve to unfold and explain the reasons for choosing magistrates, which this passage of Moses sets out (the labour and burden, of course, and the lawsuits or disputes of the courts), it is quite clear that a magistrate who governs all and each is a common good given by God to preserve our kind, and one we cannot do without. For, as Aristotle teaches, a state cannot exist without magistrates. But why do we speak of Aristotle? Far weightier, and they ought to be regarded as such, are the words of St. Paul in Romans 13, that the magistrate is the minister of God given to us for our good by the Lord. Therefore, just as we gather that marriage is good, wholesome and necessary for our kind from the fact that God said it is not good for man to be alone, so from the fact that that eminent minister of God said that magistracy was instituted by God's authority for the care of our welfare, we shall gather that magistrates must certainly exist, whom we are to obey when they advise and command things that are right and agreeable to the divine Word.

units.la: SERMO IIII.
units.tr: SERMON IV.

units.la: 13 Adhibete ex vobis sapientes, prudentes & spectatos viros, secundum tribus vestros, & constituam eos, vt præsint vobis.
units.tr: 13 Take wise, prudent and proven men from among you, according to your tribes, and I will set them over you.

units.la: 14 Et respondistis mihi, atq; dixistis: Placet sermo ille quem loquutus es vt faciamus.
units.tr: 14 And you answered me and said: The word you have spoken is good, and we will do it.

units.la: 15 Tuli itaq; capita ex tribubus vestris sapientes & spectatos viros, & constitui eos vt essent principes super vos, tribuni & centuriones, quinquagenarij, decuriones ac præfecti, secundum tribus vestras.
units.tr: 15 So I took the chiefs of your tribes, wise and proven men, and made them rulers over you: tribunes and centurions, leaders of fifties and of tens, and officers, according to your tribes.

units.la: ENumeratis atq; etiam expositis causis ijs ob quas humanum genus sine magistratu vitam in his terris tranquillam & pacatam agere nequeat, quæ huiusce de magistratu tractationis prima ac princeps pars est iam ad secundam, qua de eius electione quæritur, transit, ac docet à quibus, qualis, quas ad res magistratus eligi debeat.
units.tr: Having listed and explained the causes for which the human race cannot live a quiet and peaceful life on this earth without magistracy, we pass from the first and principal part of this treatment of magistracy to the second, which asks about its election. It teaches by whom, of what sort, and for what duties magistrates ought to be chosen.

units.la: A quibus eligi debeat hoc ipso quod sua ad populum verba refert, facilè cernitur. Dicit enim. Adhibete ex vobis sapientes, prudentes, et spectatos viros, et respondistis mihi, placet, et c. Quibus verbis indicat se negotium hoc de eligendo magistratu ad populum retulisse, eiusque consensu & suffragijs magistratum electum esse. Est autem is sensus verborum Mosis: Quoniam vestræ sic se res habent, ut sine magistratu societatem hanc civilem conseruare nequeatis, atque opus fit vobis pluribus ducibus & rectoribus qui sua vos integritate & sapientia regant ac tueantur. Agite ex vestro omnium cœtu præstantissimos atque optimos quosque, seligite, quibusducibus vtamini. Atque hoc quidem consilium vobis tunc probabatur adeo, ut vestro consensu vi ri spectati ex singulis tribubus singuli qui præessent cæteris eligerentur.
units.tr: By whom they ought to be chosen is easily seen from the very fact that he refers his words to the people. For he says: "Take wise, prudent and proven men from among you," and "you answered me, it pleases us," and so on. By these words he shows that he referred the business of choosing magistrates to the people, and that the magistrates were chosen with their consent and votes. The sense of Moses' words is this: "Since your situation is such that you cannot keep this civil society together without a magistracy, and you need several leaders and rulers who may govern and protect you by their integrity and wisdom, pick out from your whole assembly the most outstanding and best men, and choose the leaders you will use." And this plan was so approved by you that, by your consent, proven men were chosen from each tribe to preside over the rest.

units.la: In quo cernimus magistratus electionem sic fieri solitam, ut olim Romæ populus Senato rio magistratu interrogante veluti consule legem constituebat, videlicet ut Mose quasi summo magistratu rogante populi suffragijs optimi deligerentur. Ergo ut ratio constet primum Mosis tum populi persona paulo altius considerari debebunt, electionis formam ac rationem ut intelligamus plenius.
units.tr: In this we see that the election of magistrates was done as it was once done at Rome, where the people enacted a law with the Senate's magistrate asking, as with a consul. So, with Moses as it were the chief magistrate asking, the best men were chosen by the votes of the people. Therefore, so that the argument holds, we must consider first the person of Moses and then that of the people a little more deeply, so that we may understand the form and manner of election more fully.

units.la: Ac Moses quidem & principis & sacerdotis officio fungitur. Principis enim est quod suf‑fragia populi colligit, sacerdotis autem est quod docet electionis formam rectè seruare. Ea est vt sapientes, prudentes, spectatos eligant. Egregia profecto & vtilis & necessaria doctrina hæc est quam qui magistratus eligunt semper seruabunt.
units.tr: Moses indeed discharges the office both of prince and of priest. It belongs to the prince to gather the votes of the people; it belongs to the priest to teach that the form of election is kept correctly. That form is that they choose wise, prudent and proven men. This teaching is indeed excellent, useful and necessary, and those who elect magistrates will always keep it.

units.la: Nam ideo magistratus eligitur vt vniuersis ciuibus se præbeat rectorem. Iam pares pari‑bus rectores dare, nedum minores maioribus præficere stultissimum est, iuxtaque etiam alienum à natura. Neque enim oues ouibus aut equis equos, multo minus ceruos aut asinos leonibus præficimus, sed ijs gubernandis hominem ceu præstantius animal adhibemus. Quod cum ita sit, homini quoque rectorem qui illo ipso sit ac videatur excellentior ac præstantior des necesse est. At quis illo in terris præstantior? nemo: Vnde ergo seu quem ei dabimus pastorem? Dedit Deus verbum suum rectorem præstantissimum, quo ceu lucente pedibus nostris lucerna, vt est in Psal. 119. et 1. Pet. 1. vtimur. Eius iusibus si nos obsequeremur alia re nulla foret opus, sed quia non stamus eius regulis & præceptionibus: magistratus & doctores dedit verbo suo quasi pupillo diuiti tutores & curatores & custodes, quorum alij doctrina alij imperio gubernant homines. Nec satis est tutores esse ni boni sint & prudentes: alioquin nec volent nec pote‑runt vti legibus, eruntque quasi quædam larvæ & personæ comicæ, velutiq; Agamemnonis habitum induti sine opibus & imperio. Ac quemadmodum in comœdia quis imperatoris per sonam refert, exutus autem habitu comico pauper puellus est: sic insipiens, imprudens, igno‑bilis, senator præter habitum ac nomen habet nihil.
units.tr: For a magistrate is chosen so that he may present himself as ruler to all the citizens. Now to set equals over equals as rulers is most foolish, and to set lesser men over greater is more foolish still, and also contrary to nature. For we do not set sheep over sheep or horses over horses, much less stags or asses over lions; for governing these we use man, as the more excellent animal. Since this is so, we must also give man a ruler who is, or seems to be, more excellent and superior to him. But who on earth is more excellent than man? No one. Where then, or whom, shall we give him as shepherd? God has given his Word as the most excellent ruler, by which, as by a lamp at our feet, we are guided, as is said in Psalm 119 and 1 Peter 1. If we obeyed its commands we would need nothing else. But since we do not abide by its rules and precepts, he has given magistrates and teachers to his Word, as guardians, curators and keepers to a rich ward. Some govern men by teaching, others by command. Nor is it enough that they be guardians, unless they are good and prudent; otherwise they will neither wish nor be able to use the laws, and they will be like masks and comic characters, clad in the dress of Agamemnon but without resources or power. And just as in a comedy one man plays the part of an emperor, but when he is stripped of the comic costume he is a poor boy, so a foolish, imprudent, ignoble senator has nothing but the dress and the name.

units.la: Quamobrem ciuibus magistratum electoris doctores indicabunt vt eiusmodi viros eli‑gant, qui sapientia, prudentia, virtute & prælucere & prodesse possint. Atque de eo quidem omnes populi semper admoniti sunt, nec mirabere hodieque te quoque moneri. Nam tua ipsius multum refert qualem eligas. Nam si cæcum tibi ducem eligas, præstabit te solum iter ingredi vel illi præire: si stultum & inprouidum eligas tuis te consilijs vti potius est: si scelestum eligas, quem ad tua peccata conniuere velis, cur non potius fine magistratu peccas? Igitur grande nefas est aut indignos & ineptos malis artibus promouere, aut odio dignos remouere, aut quasi reipub. consulere fit risus & iocus sic negligenter eligere. Atque hæc quidem spectanda cauendaque: Moses docet.
units.tr: Therefore teachers will tell the citizens to choose men of this kind, who can both shine forth and be of use through wisdom, prudence and virtue. All peoples have always been warned of this, and you should not be surprised that you too are admonished today. For it matters greatly to you yourself what sort of man you choose. If you choose a blind leader, it will be better for you to walk the road alone or go ahead of him. If you choose a foolish and improvident man, it is better to use your own counsel. If you choose a wicked man, whom you wish to wink at your sins, why not rather sin without any magistrate? It is therefore a great wrong either to promote the unworthy and unfit by wicked arts, or to remove the worthy out of hatred, or to choose so carelessly, as if the consulting of the commonwealth were a laughing matter. These are the things Moses teaches us to look to and to guard against.

units.la: Iam vero quod respondet populus bonum sibi videri sermonem istum, id perinde est ac si dicat, age quando hoc facto opus est, obsequemur benè monenti. In quo videmus vtilissimum esse, vt bona consilia non respuamus. <bl>Wesn sraaten ist/dem ist sbelffen.</bl> Sæpe veluti pueri solent, sic adulti deteriora eligunt. Eodem modo nos admoniti, non ægrè feramus officij nostri nos admoneri.
units.tr: As for the people's answer that this speech seems good to them, it is just as if they said: "Come, since this action is needed, let us obey the one who advises well." In this we see how useful it is not to reject good counsel. Whose bread one eats, his song one sings (a German proverb). Often, as children do, adults choose the worse. In the same way, when we are admonished, we should not take it badly that we are reminded of our duty.

units.la: Ex his iam perspicuum est quæ nam fuerit vsitata apud illos eligendi ratio, nempe, vt quem admodum diximus, magistratu summo consulente populi suffragijs qui sint optimi declaren‑tur. Eadem nobis Tigurinis est vsitata ratio. Nam & in tribubus tribuno, & in Senatus popu‑li, conuentu, qui ducentorum ciuium dicitur, consule rogantibus eliguntur. Atque hæc ratio Mosi videtur etiam Philone teste placuisse magis, quàm qua magist. atuum creatio forti exercæ & lubricæ committitur. Nemo forte creatis nautis aut medicis potius vteretur quàm arte & vsu probatis & spectatis: cur igitur ciuitatum magnarum & frequentium dominationem forte electis potius quàm spectatis, prudentibus, sapientibus comitteres. Sed quia fortes regit Dominus & ijs ipsis ambitus caueri potest, omniú optima videtur ratio ea, qua vtuntur in eligendis magistratibus Veneti, nempe cum eam mixtâ fortibus & suffragijs adhibét. Cæterú omnes omnium gentiú in hac re mores & rationes hoc videntur significare, quòd & Deus & leges iubent, ne quis magistratus ambiat sed electionem expectet.
units.tr: From these things it is now clear what the customary method of election was among them: namely, as we have said, that with the chief magistrate consulting, those who are best are declared by the votes of the people. Our own Tigurine practice is the same: in the tribes, the tribune is chosen, and in the Senate's assembly, which is called the council of two hundred citizens, the consul is chosen when they ask. Philo bears witness that this method seemed to Moses more pleasing than the method by which the creation of magistrates is left to chance, a slippery and uncertain thing. Perhaps no one would use sailors or doctors chosen by lot rather than those proven and tested by skill and experience. Why then would you entrust the rule of great and populous cities to men chosen by lot rather than to the proven, prudent and wise? But since the Lord governs the lots, and ambition itself can be guarded against by them, the best method of all seems to be that used by the Venetians in choosing magistrates, namely when they combine lot with votes. Moreover, the customs and practices of all nations in this matter seem to signify that both God and the laws command that no one should canvass for a magistracy, but should wait for election.

units.la: Quales eligi debeant primum vno verbo docet, tum enumeratione partium exponit. Vno verbo, quia capita vocat eos quos vult esse principes. Quo ipso similitudinem & sacris literis & prophanis scriptoribus vsitatam eam, qua corpus humanum cum rep. comparatur, adducit, qua vt significet, ciuium multitudini id præstare magistratum oportere, quod humano corpori suapte natura atq; officio præstat caput.
units.tr: He teaches in one word what sort of men should be chosen, and then sets this out by enumerating the parts. He teaches in one word because he calls those whom he wishes to be princes "heads." By this very term he brings forward the comparison common to both sacred and profane writers, in which the human body is compared with the commonwealth. By it he means that the magistrate ought to provide for the multitude of citizens what the head, by its nature and office, provides for the human body.

units.la: Iam si capitis situm, figuram, vsum & vtilitatem consideres, non difficile erit intelligere quales magistratus capitis appellatione Moses significet. Ac si situm consideres, summum locum obtinuit in corpore: id argumento est principis esse loco, vt & ornet & adiuuet. Sic magistratui summus in ciuitate locus debetur, quo non solum honorem ei, sed etiam vtilitatem afferat prohibeatq; dedecus & exitium. Iam si figuram inspicias Galeno videtur optima quæ spherâ bene rotundam, sed vtrinq; paulatim compressam atq; arctatam, seu vt ipse ait, εὐρυθμον hoc est, concinnam ac decoram imitetur. At Hippocrate teste mala figura capitis vitiosam cerebri crafim notat, quemadmodum Homerus Therfitem quia φοξὸς ἐπὶ κεφαλῇ, Peruerso ingenio præditum esse scripsit. Ergo optimè suum officium magistratus seruat, quando naturæ decus seruat, ac ne quam partem nimis spectat, sed in mediocritate consistit. Vtilitas à capite hæc affertur quod cerebrum continet & sensuum organa: in quibus quoniam & cognitio & cogitatio & memoria sunt, optima diuinitatis imago exprimitur. Qua de causa Deus ipse magistratus deos vocat. Hi enim præuident & cognoscunt quæ è re ciuitatis sunt: hi de rebus quæ eueniunt omnibus deliberant: hi rerum præteritarum memoriam retinent, vt quæ futura sint ex ijs conijciant. Ex quibus omnibus multisq; alijs: quæ si velim omnia referre tempus me deficiet, facilè colligimus, quid sibi velit hoc ipso Moses quod magistratus capita appellat, nempe vt aliquid habeant supra fortem popularem, vt sua prouidentia suaq; fide & diligentia corpus suæ ciuitatis tueantur.
units.tr: Now if you consider the position, shape, use and usefulness of the head, it will not be difficult to understand what sort of magistrates Moses signifies by the name of head. If you consider its position, it holds the highest place in the body. This is an argument that the prince should be in the place where he both adorns and helps. So the highest place in the state is due to the magistrate, so that he may bring not only honour but also usefulness, and keep off disgrace and ruin. If you look at its shape, Galen thinks the best is that which imitates a sphere well rounded but gradually compressed and narrowed at the sides, or, as he himself says, eurythmon [εὐρυθμον], that is, well proportioned and graceful. But by the testimony of Hippocrates a bad shape of the head marks a faulty constitution of the brain, just as Homer wrote that Thersites, being pointed on the head [φοξὸς ἐπὶ κεφαλῇ], was endowed with a perverse mind. Therefore the magistrate best keeps his office when he preserves the dignity of nature, and does not look too much to any one part, but keeps to the mean. The usefulness that the head brings is this: it contains the brain and the organs of the senses. In these, since knowledge, thought and memory all reside, the best image of the divine is expressed. For this reason God himself calls magistrates gods. For these foresee and know what is for the good of the state; these deliberate about the events that befall all; these retain the memory of past things, so that from them they may conjecture what is to come. From all these and many other things, which would take too long to report if I wished to list them all, we easily gather what Moses means by calling magistrates heads: namely, that they should have something above the common mob, so that by their foresight, faith and diligence they may protect the body of their commonwealth.

units.la: Enumeratione partium exponit quales velit. 1. Sapientes. At sapientiæ nomine non illa principiorum & causarum, qualis à Platone dialectica dicitur, sed illa potius quæ diuinarum simul & humanarum rerum scientia est & in vniuersam rerum naturam se extendit, intelligi-tur. Quò pertinet, vt primum verbum Dei in quo veræ sapientiæ fundamenta existunt, deinceps linguas, artes, historias in primisq; suæ gentis res gestas, & eam quæ de rerum natura traditur & de moribus doctrinam, itemq; leges præcipueq; suæ patriæ cófuetudines atq; sanctiones norint. Vnde & Philo Iudæus in eo quê de creādo principe scripsit libro, minime malè præcipit, vt sua ipsius manu princeps quisq;, ἐπινομίδα, id est, epitomè, siue, vt ipse exponit, κεφαλαιωδη τύπον [?] ἐπιτεχνασάμενος [?] λαῶν ἡ τύπου ἀπλαστωσαν [?] νόμων, describat, quo ceu insigni siue sceptro glorietur, quem & scribendo & relegendo sic imprimat animo, vt eo ipso descriptas leges omnes quo ties opus est in promptu habeat. Eiusmodi doctos magistratus Athenæ, Massilia, Roma, multæ quæ ciuitates habuere. Sic Moses prius in omni Ægyptiorum sapientia instructus est, quàm ad remp. diuinitus eligeretur. Ergo literarum, artium, philosophiæ, iuris & historiarum cognitio in viro principe requiritur.
units.tr: Enumeration of the parts, showing what kind of men he wants. 1. Wise. By wisdom here we should understand not that skill of first principles and causes which Plato calls dialectic, but rather the knowledge of both divine and human things, which extends over the whole nature of things. To this belongs that the prince should know first the Word of God, in which the foundations of true wisdom lie; then languages, arts and histories, above all the deeds of his own nation, the teaching handed down about the nature of things and about morals, and likewise the laws and especially the customs and sanctions of his own country. Hence Philo the Jew, in his book on appointing a prince, rightly advises that each prince should, with his own hand, draw up an epinomis [ἐπινομίδα], that is an epitome, or, as he himself explains it, a summary outline (typos) of the laws of the people, in which he may take pride as in a badge or sceptre, and which he should so impress on his mind by writing and re-reading that he always has all the laws described at hand whenever need arises. Athens, Massilia, Rome and many other states have had magistrates of this learned kind. So Moses was first instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians before he was divinely chosen for the commonwealth. Therefore a knowledge of letters, arts, philosophy, law and history is required in a prince.

units.la: 2. Prudentes, hoc est qui res cognitas ad vsum publicum possint accómodare. Hæ enim res vniuersales particularibus accómodat. Veluti quod Pharaonis somnium Iosephus intelligit sapientis est, quod ipsum regno potest accómodare, prudentis. Eodem modo sapientis est nos leges & iura, sed earum rigore secundum circumstantiarum varietatem mitigare, & vt seruetur [?] spectare, & vt ne summum ius summa fiat iniuria cauere prudentis. Quid verbis opus est prudentia, personas, facta, locos tempora, causas, & quæ sunt huius generis alia considerat, ac secundum ea quod æquum & bonum est statuit.
units.tr: 2. Prudent, that is, those who can apply known things to public use. For this kind of thing applies universals to particulars. For example, that Joseph understood Pharaoh's dream is the mark of a wise man, but that he could apply it to the kingdom is the mark of a prudent man. In the same way it belongs to the wise man to know laws and rights, but it belongs to the prudent man to soften their rigour according to the variety of circumstances, to look to their preservation, and to take care that the highest right does not become the highest wrong. What need is there of many words? Prudence considers persons, deeds, places, times, causes and other things of this kind, and decides what is fair and good in accordance with them.

units.la: Hæc virtus quoniam prioris quasi quædam perfectio est, in viro principe cumprimis requiritur. Nam quid profuerit te multa nosse, non autem earum quæ noris rerum vsum habere? Certe similis sis eius qui vel aurum vel supellectilem multam ac variâ habet, nec ijs vti queat. Igitur Pythagoras optimè dixit illud, Ἰχὺς καὶ τύχῳ καὶ ὅπλον σοφῆ ἡ φέρνησις. Et Arist. in libello de virtutibus eius vsum in humanis rebus describens ait, ἔργα δ' ἐκ τῆς φρονήσεως δεῖ τὸ εὖ βουλεύεσθαι, τὸ χρῆσθαι καλῶς [?] πάσι τοῖς ὑπάρχουσιν ἀγαθοῖς τὸ ὁμιλῆσαι ὀρθῶς. τὸ σῶμα εἶναι τὰς [?] [illegible, ~45 letters] Ex quibus omnibus potest colligi quantum hæc virtus in publicis & priuatis rebus, vt in negocijs, in conuentibus hominum atq; in foro, in vita, in opum affluentia, in consuetudine & hominum vsu, in moribus, in oratione, in delectu bonorum, in malorum censura atq; iudicio, ad salutem nostram vtilitatis afferat. Vnde non miraberis huic secundum in harum, quæ ad magistratum pertinent, virtutum numero locum tribui, &c.
units.tr: Since this virtue is in a way a kind of completion of the former, it is especially required in a prince. For what good is it to know many things if you do not have the use of the things you know? Certainly you would be like a man who has much gold or many varied furnishings but cannot use them. So Pythagoras said well: "Strength and wealth and arms for the wise is prudence" [Ἰχὺς καὶ τύχῳ καὶ ὅπλον σοφῆ ἡ φέρνησις]. And Aristotle, in his little book on the virtues, describing its use in human affairs, says: "The works of prudence are to deliberate well, to use well all the goods that are present, and to associate rightly" [ἔργα δὲ ἐκ τῆς φρονήσεως δεῖ τὸ εὖ βουλεύεσθαι, τὸ χρῆσθαι καλῶς πάσι τοῖς ὑπάρχουσιν ἀγαθοῖς, τὸ ὁμιλῆσαι ὀρθῶς]. From all these things it can be gathered how much this virtue contributes to our well-being in public and private affairs: in business, in the gatherings of men and in the forum, in life, in the abundance of wealth, in custom and the practice of men, in manners, in speech, in the choice of good men and in the judging and censuring of bad ones. Hence you should not be surprised that this virtue is given the second place among those virtues which pertain to the magistracy, etc.

units.la: 3 Spectatos siue nobiles. Non me fugit ab aliquibus Hebræam vocem actiue accipi vt sciens, & vt septuaginta habent, [illegible, ~8 letters] intelligant. Sed mihi magis eorum arridet atq; placet sententia, qui passiue eam vocem accipiunt. Nam cum prius sapientes dixerit, quid opus erat idem bis dicere, repetita videlicet scientia, quæ nihil à sapientia differt? Præterea verisimile est idem hic sentire dominum quod expressit alibi: nempe rempub. populi sui non alienigenis, sed cognitis hominibus committendam esse. Sed & Philo Iudæus Mosis interpres minime malus, ipsius Dei de hac re præceptum affert ac dicit: præficies tibi ipsi principem non alienigenam, sed vnum ex tuis fratribus. Cæterum cur Deus extero homini reipub. gubernaculæ committi nolit, cum causas ipse duas affert: vnam, ne suam rem familiarem cum detrimento populi Dei velit ac possit augere: alteram, ne spe agri vberioris proposita, sui commodi causa populum vt aliò comigret, inducat. Quæ pericula in homine gentili & noto non solùm nò pertimescenda sunt, verum etiam bona aliqua velut fauor popularis & studiū promouendæ patriæ sperari possunt.
units.tr: 3 Respected, or noble. It does not escape me that some take the Hebrew word actively, as meaning "knowing," and as the Seventy have it, [the Greek is illegible in the scan], that is, "understanding." But I prefer the view of those who take the word passively. For since he has already said "wise," why was it necessary to say the same thing twice, namely "knowing," which differs in no way from wisdom? Moreover it is likely that the Lord here means what he expressed elsewhere: that the commonwealth of his people must not be committed to foreigners, but to men who are known. And Philo the Jew, a not bad interpreter of Moses, cites God's own precept on this matter and says: "You shall set over yourself a prince who is not a foreigner, but one of your brothers." Moreover, as to why God is unwilling to entrust the government of the commonwealth to a foreign man, he himself gives two reasons: first, lest such a man might wish and be able to increase his own private property to the detriment of the people of God; second, lest, with the hope of a more fertile field held out to him, he should lead the people away elsewhere for his own advantage. These dangers are not to be feared only in a gentile and unknown man; rather, some good things may also be hoped for from him, such as popular favour and zeal for promoting the homeland.

units.la: Sed quid sibi vult quod dicit nobiles? an qui maiorum stemmata & reges atauos iactitant, soli sunt ad rempub. admittendi? Est bonum minime contemnendum nobilitas, sed ea maior est & ad hoc quod dicimus potior quæ virtute sua cuiq; parta est.
units.tr: But what does he mean by saying "noble"? Are only those who boast of their ancestral lineage and of kings in their family tree to be admitted to the commonwealth? Nobility is a good not to be despised, but that nobility is greater, and more fitting for our purpose, which each man has won by his own virtue.

units.la: Ergo homines eos eliges quorum tibi cognita sit ac probata pietas, iustitia, prudentia, fortitudo, temperantia, qui vitæ exemplo prælucere plebi suæ queant, qui non minus exemplo suo ad obedientiam voluntariam trahant, ac cogunt inuitos legibus & pœnis. Incognitum le-gere est periculum in repub. facere, quod graue est in re multo minore factu. Nà etsi tranquillum sit mare tamen imperito nautæ nemo se committet, sicut nec imperito medico quisquà cor-pus ægrum curandum committit. Ergo viros, quorum virtus, fides & diligentia tibi sit explorata, cognita ad officia reipub. necessaria eligi necesse est. In eadem cum illis naui fumus; nec potest sine nostro incommodo naufragium fieri. Scite dictum est illud Iamblichi, ὁμοίως [illegible, ~24 letters]. Nam si violento, iniquo, iracundo viro, qui & voluntatem & vim ad nocendum habeat, remp. committas in omnes ciues aut saltem in singulos sæuiet. Igitur quod hic Moses qui sint eligendi significanter indicat, omnibus qui magistratus eligendi ius habent tenendum est.
units.tr: Therefore you will choose men whose piety, justice, prudence, fortitude and temperance you know and have tested, men who can shine before their people by the example of their life, who by their example draw them to willing obedience no less than they compel the unwilling by laws and punishments. It is a dangerous thing to make trial of an unknown man in the commonwealth, a grave matter even in a far lesser business. For even if the sea is calm, no one entrusts himself to an inexperienced sailor, just as no one entrusts a sick body to an inexperienced doctor. Therefore it is necessary to choose men whose virtue, faithfulness and diligence have been tested by you and are known, for the duties of the commonwealth that are necessary. We sail in the same ship with them, and a shipwreck cannot happen without harm to us. The saying of Iamblichus is well put: [the Greek is illegible in the scan]. For if you commit the commonwealth to a violent, unjust, wrathful man, who has both the will and the power to do harm, he will rage against all the citizens, or at least against individuals. Therefore what Moses here significantly indicates about who should be chosen must be observed by all who have the right to elect magistrates.

units.la: Ad quæ officiorum genera? Duo potissimum genera commemorat, vnum eorum qui iubent & imperant, alterum autem eorum qui imperata faciunt.
units.tr: What are the kinds of these offices? He mentions two chief kinds: one of those who command and give orders, the other of those who carry out what is commanded.

units.la: Hi penes quos erat imperium sigillatim singuli recensentur, principes qui mille ciuibus, alij qui centum, rursus alij qui quinquaginta, deniq; etiam qui decem præfecti essent.
units.tr: Those in whom authority lay are listed one by one: princes of a thousand citizens, others of a hundred, again others of fifty, and finally those set over ten.

units.la: His erant ministri quidam attributi qui שֹׁטְרִים vocantur, hoc est exactores siue executores, quos Hebrei ministros publicos vocant & lictores qui loro verberant & sententiæ iudicū exequuntur, qui indicunt silentium, in ius vocant, in concione cogunt, aliaq; generis eiusdem obeunt munera. Hos Leuitas fuisse dicūr, idq; stabilitum adductis ex Paral.19. & Neh.8. testimonijs. Quorum prior sic habet, Sunt exactores Leuitæ ante vos, cofortamini igitur, & viriliter agite, & erit Dominus cum eo qui egerit bonum. Alter aut sic habet, Porro Leuitæ compescebant omnem populum, dicentes tacete.
units.tr: To these were attached certain ministers who are called officers [שֹׁטְרִים], that is, exactors or executors, whom the Hebrews call public ministers, and lictors who strike with a thong and carry out the sentences of judges, who call for silence, summon to court, gather the assembly, and perform other duties of this kind. These are said to have been Levites, and this is held to be established by the testimonies of 1 Chronicles 19 and Nehemiah 8. The first of these reads thus: "The Levites are your officers; therefore take courage and act manfully, and the Lord will be with him who does well." The second reads: "Moreover the Levites kept all the people quiet, saying: Be silent."

units.la: Sed vtut hæc se habeant, tamen scriptura sacra nobis significat populi Israelitici cœtum vniuersum certis quibusdam classibus seu ordinibus distributum esse, quibus singulis sui duces essent. Id exempli vice rebusp. omnibus proponitur, nempe vt quoniam vnus omnibus negotijs non sufficit curandis, plures eligantur in ciuitate magistratus, quorum aliis de-mandentur negotia. Vnde exstant in benè constituta repub. qui rebus sacris, qui rebus vrba-nis, qui rusticis, negotijs & commercijs, qui annonæ, qui publicis ædificijs, qui pupillorum & viduarum bonis conseruandis, qui rebus bellicis, qui iudicijs aliis atq; aliis præfecti sunt magistratus. Quos quibus quæq; ciuitas nominibus appellet, non est huius loci neq; temporis, vt dicamus pluribus. Illud curæ sit cuiq; populo, vt ordinem illum tueatur ac feruet, & iustitiæ distribuentis rationem summa religione custodiat. Quò fiet, vt & dignis tribuantur condigna munera & Resp. personis idoneis potita minus labascat. Æschines dixit si dignis legitimè conferantur munera, fore qui virtute certent: sin cuilibet honores ambienti & ijs qui nihil honore & præmio dignum fecerint, præmia tribuas, effici vt frugi ingenia corrumpantur. Et Solon dixit eam ciuitatem omnium optimè habere, in qua bonis viris honos habeatur, mali vero non solum non honoribus,verumetiam afficiantur supplicijs.
units.tr: But however these things stand, Holy Scripture shows us that the whole assembly of the people of Israel was divided into certain classes or orders, each of which had its own leaders. This is set before all commonwealths as an example, namely that since one man is not enough to manage all affairs, several magistrates should be chosen in the city, to whom different business is committed. Hence in a well-ordered commonwealth there are magistrates appointed: for sacred matters, for city affairs, for rural affairs, for business and trade, for the grain supply, for public buildings, for the preservation of the goods of orphans and widows, for war, and for various kinds of courts. What names each city gives them is not the place or time to say at length. Let it be the concern of every people that it preserves and maintains that order, and guards with the greatest reverence the principle of distributing justice. The result will be that fitting rewards are given to the worthy, and the commonwealth, entrusted to suitable persons, will less totter. Aeschines said that if rewards are conferred lawfully on the worthy, there will be men who compete in virtue; but if you grant honours and rewards to anyone who seeks them, and to those who have done nothing worthy of honour and reward, the result will be that men of good character are corrupted. And Solon said that the city is best ordered in which good men are honoured, and bad men are not only denied honours but are also punished.

units.la: Atque ex his quidem quæ dicta sunt haëtenus perspicuum est , quæ nam verbo diuino consentanea sit eligendorum magistratuum ratio , ea videlicet qua rogante principe populi suffragijs eligantur.In quo discitur penes quos sit eorum creandorum potestas , qui qualesq; debeant eligi,& quibus potisimum opus sit officijs. Quæ res argumento est,Deum velle vt optimo & rectissimo ordine gerantur omnia , quo id & sibi gloriosum sit & nobis ipsis cumprimis commodum & salubre.Amen.
units.tr: Now from what has been said so far it is clear which method of electing magistrates agrees with the Word of God: namely, that they are chosen by the votes of the people, at the request of the prince. From this we learn in whose power it lies to appoint them, what sort of men ought to be chosen, and for which offices they are especially needed. This matter is evidence that God wills all things to be carried on in the best and most right order, which is both glorious to himself and especially advantageous and salutary for us. Amen.

units.la: SERMO V.
units.tr: SERMON V.

units.la: 16 Et præcepi iudicibus vestris tempore illo, & dixi: Audite causas inter fratres vestros, & iudicate iustè inter virum & fratrem eius, & inter peregrinum eius.
units.tr: 16 And I charged your judges at that time, saying, Hear the causes between your brethren, and judge righteously between every man and his brother, and the stranger that is with him.

units.la: 17 Non agnoscetis faciem in iudicio, vt magnum sic et paruum audiatis, nec quem quam mortalem formidetis: iudicium enim hoc Dei est, omnem vero causam difficilē ad me referatis, quam ego audiam.
units.tr: 17 Ye shall not respect persons in judgment; but ye shall hear the small as well as the great; ye shall not be afraid of the face of man; for the judgment is God's: and the cause that is too hard for you, bring it unto me, and I will hear it.

units.la: 18 Eodem quoq; tempore præcepi vobis omnia verba quæ facere debebatis.
units.tr: 18 And I commanded you at that time all the things which ye should do.

units.la: QVanquam his ipsis de causis quas concione proxima recensuimus sine magistratu humanavita in his terris constare nequeat, ac propterea viros sapientes,prudentes,nobiles,e ciuium omnium multitudine lectos,qui ciuitatem totam regant,oporteat: frustra tamen magistratus eligitur,si vel ij ipsi qui electi sunt sic officio suo fungantur malè & inepte,vt ex eorum electione speratos atq; expectatos fructus ciuitas nō percipiat, vel plebs adeo sit ef frenis,vt affectibus suis malit obsequi , quàm pijs & prudentibus magistratibus ,hocq; ipso quod consilia bona respuat,amittat etiam auxilia. Quamobrem Moses propositis atq; etiam explicatis eligendorum magistratuum causis pariter ac modis, iam quid & magistratus ipsos & plebem facere deceat vicissim docet.Quæ doctrina quoniam efficit,vt speratis ex magistratus creatione fructibus potiatur ciuitas, summa diligentia describitur: ac sic quidem,vt primum de magistratus officio,tum autem de eo quod plebis est facere dicat.
units.tr: Although, for the very reasons we reviewed in the previous sermon, human life in this world cannot exist without magistracy, and therefore wise, prudent and noble men, chosen from the whole multitude of citizens, must govern the whole state, the election of magistrates is in vain if either those who have been chosen discharge their office so badly and foolishly that the state does not reap the fruits hoped for and expected from their election, or the common people is so unbridled that it prefers to obey its own passions rather than pious and prudent magistrates, and by rejecting good counsels it also loses the help. Therefore Moses, having set out and explained both the causes and the manner of choosing magistrates, now teaches in turn what both the magistrates and the people ought to do. Since this teaching makes it possible for the state to enjoy the fruits hoped for from the creation of magistrates, it is set out with the greatest care; and he does so in such a way that he first speaks of the magistrate's office, and then of what belongs to the people to do.

units.la: Sed quoniam difficile est,hominem admoneri officij,& omnes homines sunt asperi monitoribus,proptereaq; hoc munus commonendi neq; abs quolibet recte suscipitur, neq; quisquam sapiens sua sponte suscipit:docet hoc loco diuinus Moses primum à quo,tum quo potissimum tempore suscipi,deniq; quid cuiq; parti dici debeat.
units.tr: But since it is difficult to admonish a man of his duty, and all men are harsh toward those who admonish them, this task of admonishing is neither rightly undertaken by just anyone, nor does any wise man undertake it of his own accord. Here divine Moses teaches first by whom it should be undertaken, then at what especially suitable time, and finally what should be said to each part.

units.la: A quo suscipi debeat atq; in bonam partem accipi,suo exemplo docet dicens, Et præcepi iudicibus vestris & dixi vobis. Quod indicio est ministros verbi diuini id officium sibi commisCuius fit comm discipulos prætereo. Nec nunc dico quod pleræq; resp.benè constitutæ fiue eæ liberæ sint,fi ue principis vnius potestati subditæ,iuris doctores & monitores habent, quos tamen operæ precium foret & iuris & sacræ theologiæ peritos esse,vt & de iure & de fide in Deum refpon-dere possent. Quæ exempla docent nequaquam committendum esse,vt hac doctrina ciuitates exuantur:omninoq; opus esse,vt quò magis eam satan explosam cupit,hoc magis retineatur. Nam plebs gaudet magistratibus sua dici vitia,ipsa verò ægre patitur sua corripi : magistratus vicissim plebem vult acriter increpari,fe notari quasi indignissimè factum fit accipit animo i-niquiffimo,nos qui priscam normam sequimur,atq; vtriq; suos mores depingimus,vtriq; in-uisi fumus,firq; vt efficiat satan,quo in odium & explosionem verbi Dei simul ambo confpi-rent. Quid facias? Quia hac doctrina carere ciuitates nequeunt, quocunq; modo potest reti-nenda est.
units.tr: By whom it ought to be undertaken, and received in good part, he teaches by his own example, saying: "And I charged your judges and spoke to you." This shows that the ministers of the divine Word have this duty committed to them; I pass over the disciples. Nor do I now say that most well-ordered commonwealths, whether they are free or subject to the power of a single prince, have jurists and admonishers, who nevertheless would be well worth having skilled both in law and in sacred theology, so that they could answer both concerning law and concerning faith in God. These examples teach that by no means should this doctrine be given up, so that cities are stripped of it; and indeed, the more Satan wishes it cast out, the more it must be retained. For the common people delights to have its magistrates' vices named, but itself bears with difficulty having its own faults rebuked. The magistrates in turn want the people sharply reproached, yet when they are themselves noted, as if something most unworthy had been done, they take it with the utmost ill will. We, who follow the old norm and depict the morals of each side, are hated by both, so that Satan may bring it about that both conspire together against the hatred and expulsion of the Word of God. What is to be done? Because states cannot do without this doctrine, it must be retained by whatever means possible.

units.la: Cæterum vt verbi ministros hoc facere decet,sic plebeios siue priuatos homines dedecet. Suum cuiq; tributum est officium,suum quisq; tueatur.Si idem omnes velint ac conentur fa-cere,magna rerû omniû erit cófufio. Etenim omnibus sibi dicendi partes fumentibus,nemo al-terum intelliget.Ergo dicent hoc ij quibus Deus commisit, & dicent quidem vti par est & vbi vsus postulat.Nam si magistratus delinquat,non solum non prodest quemadmodum debebat sed obest etiàm bene præcipienti remq;p.gerenti plebs nó pareat,frustra bénè regitur ,sin de niq; delinquant ambo,simul ambo sese eunt perditû. Id ab eis auertet malû qui docendo mo-nendoq;vt resipiscant effecerit monitor.Eas partes Moses hic iussu mandatoq; Dei sumpsit.
units.tr: Moreover, as this is fitting for ministers of the Word, so it is unbecoming for plebeian or private men. Each has his own assigned office; let each guard his own. If everyone wished and attempted to do the same thing, there would be great confusion in all affairs. For when all take up the parts of speaking, no one will understand another. Therefore those to whom God has committed it shall speak, and they shall speak as is fitting and where the need requires. For if the magistrate offends, not only does he not benefit as he ought, but if the people do not obey, they hinder even the one who governs well and admonishes rightly; in vain is the state well governed. But if both offend, both together perish. The evil will be averted from them by the admonisher, who by teaching and admonishing has brought them to repentance. Moses took up these parts here by the command and mandate of God.

units.la: Quando.Eodem(inquit Moses)tempore,puta quo magistratus eliguntur. Tunc enim eius rei initiû est,quod si fœlix ac faustû sit,sanè eò plus boni sperari potest.Nâ quod ille dixit,dimi diû facti qui bené coepit habet,sane rerû vsus docet esse verû.Et alter ille nó minus verè etiam hoc,Principijs obsta sero medicina paratur,cum mala per longas conualuere moras.Ex quib. omnibus intelligimus quod exemplo Mosis hic discitur tempus hoc postulare,vt admonean-tur de suo officio cum plebs tum magistratus.Vtrerst den stal su rhün/so 9sû 9:uß sind.
units.tr: When: "At that same time," says Moses, that is, when the magistrates are elected. For then is the beginning of the matter, and if it be happy and fortunate, much good may surely be hoped for. For what that man said, that he who has begun well has half done, experience of affairs shows to be true; and that other saying is no less true: "Remedy is prepared too late when evils have grown strong through long delay." From all of which we understand that Moses' example teaches here that the time itself demands that both the people and the magistrates be admonished of their duty. [Unclear marginal note in German.]

units.la: Ac ne quid hic negligeretur,multi pij & industrij principes in lectione eorum qui de re-pub.scripti sunt librorum sese ipsi exercuerunt,vt Dauid in Psalmis, Salomon in prouerbijs, alij in alijs studijs literarum.Et Demetrius Phalereus Ptolomeum regem adhortatus esse fer-tur,vt libros de regno scriptos emeret ac legeret. Nam de quibus amici regem admonere nõ auderét ea in libris esse scripta.Quare Moses oportune adeo illos monet eo ipso tempore quo creantur magistratus.
units.tr: And lest anything here be neglected, many pious and diligent princes have exercised themselves in reading the books written about the commonwealth: David in the Psalms, Solomon in the Proverbs, and others in other branches of learning. Demetrius of Phalerum is also said to have urged King Ptolemy to buy and read books written about kingship, for the things that his friends did not dare to admonish the king about were written in those books. Therefore Moses admonishes them so opportunely at the very time when the magistrates are created.

units.la: Quod cuiusq; sit officium.Audite causas inter fratres vestros,&c.Quibus verbis indicat quid magistratuum ,quid item plebis sit officium,quo defuncti faciunt , vt tranquillam pacatamq; habeant ciuitatem.
units.tr: What is the duty of each: "Hear the causes between your brethren," etc. By these words he indicates what the duty of the magistrates is, and likewise what the duty of the people is, by performing which they keep the state tranquil and at peace.

units.la: Magistratui suum officium primum exponitur, idq; duobus capitibus omne comprehen-ditur.In quo dicitur primum quid seruandum tum quid cauendum.Seruanda duo sunt, vnû vt audias,alterum vt iudices.
units.tr: The magistrate's duty is set out first, and all of it is comprehended under two heads. Here it is said first what must be observed and then what must be avoided. Two things must be observed: that you hear, and that you judge.

units.la: Vt audias dicit,Audite causas inter fratres vestros. Quo docet quid & quomodo audiendû. Quid igitur audiendum?causam siue litem iubet audire.Nam siue quem indicta causa condem-nes siue absoluas iniquum est.Ergo prius cognoscenda est, ne de re non exploraтè cognita se-renda sit sententia.Iam audiendi studium omnem torporem,& peregrinationem sensuum, & tædium repellit:aures atq; animum præsentes requirit.
units.tr: That he should hear is said in the words Audite causas inter fratres vestros. By these he teaches what is to be heard and how. What then is to be heard? He orders the cause, or the suit, to be heard. For to condemn or acquit someone without a hearing of the case is unjust. Therefore the matter must first be examined, lest sentence be pronounced on a matter not thoroughly known. Moreover, eagerness to listen drives out all drowsiness, the wandering of the senses, and boredom; it requires that the ears and mind be present.

units.la: Quomodo verò sit audiendus hoc ipso docet quod dicit,Inter fratres:non autem inter tuos sufticos,inter tua mancipia, inter subditos,quin dicit fratres,hoc est,eos,qui & sunt & videri fratres debent.Quod argumento est requiri in iudice propensam erga litigatores voluntatē planeq; fraternum animum.Iam si fratres tui litigent,primum tibi id dolet,tum causam vt co-gnoscas das operă,nec prius cõquiescis quàm illos sibi ipsis reconciliaueris, in quo soles eũ qui in alterum sit iniurius increpare,& ab eo qui violetur aut lædatur vim atq; iniuriam arce-re:sed alterius verbis fidem prius non habere quàm audiueris alterû:quando vterq; frater est.
units.tr: How the case is to be heard he teaches by this very phrase, Inter fratres: not between your bondsmen, your slaves, or your subjects, but he says brethren, that is, those who are and ought to be regarded as brethren. This is evidence that a judge should have a well-disposed will towards the litigants and a truly brotherly spirit. Now if your brethren are at odds, first you grieve over it; then you take pains to hear the case, and you do not rest until you have reconciled them to one another. In this you are accustomed to rebuke the one who wrongs the other, and to ward off force and injury from the one who is being violated or harmed. But you do not give credence to the words of one party before you have heard the other, since both are your brother.

units.la: Ex quo perspicuum est audiendam esse tam rei quæ profertur defensionem,quàm actoris quæ reo impingitur culpationem. Notandum enim est,quod non fratrem sed fratres audiri o-portere præcipit.Et egregium est Alexandri illud apophtegma,qui claudebat vnâ ac tantum-modo alteram aurem assantî præbebat , & cur id facerer rogatus dixisse fertur, Alteram se-reo seruare vacuam.Quin & Deus humani corporis conditor idipsum nimirum significauit, quando binas aures homini condidit. Cauenda sunt enim præiudicia, quibus nihil est per-nitiofius.
units.tr: From this it is plain that the defence of the one who is sued, as much as the accusation brought against the defendant by the plaintiff, must be heard. For it should be noted that he commands brethren, not a brother, to be heard. And that saying of Alexander's is outstanding, who kept one ear closed and offered only the other to the petitioner; and when asked why he did so, he is said to have replied that he was keeping the other ear empty for the accused. Indeed God, the maker of the human body, clearly signified this very thing when he made two ears for man. For prejudgments must be guarded against, since nothing is more harmful.

units.la: Vt iudices dicit, Et iudicate iuste inter virum & fratrem eius, & inter peregrinum eius. Pri-mum postulat vt iudicetur. Quid ergo est iudicare? Germanica sane lingua ricpten metaphori cum est. Nam quae curua sunt recta facere est richten, & inde transfertur ad controuersiarum compositionem, qua fit, vt fi quis plus aequo sibi tribuerit, hocq; pacto rectam lineam iustitiae incuruauerit, eam iudex alteri qui iniuriam patitur suum ius reddens, rectam iterum faciat. Ergo iudicare nihil aliud est quam iustam, aequam, legitimam de re controuersa ac dubia fe- re sententiam.
units.tr: As to judging, he says: Et iudicate iuste inter virum & fratrem eius, & inter peregrinum eius. First he requires that judgment be given. What then is to judge? In the German language it is indeed a metaphor: richten. For to make straight what is crooked is richten, and from this it is transferred to the settling of disputes. Thus, if anyone has claimed more than is fair for himself and so bent the straight line of justice, the judge, restoring the right to the one who suffers the wrong, makes it straight again. Therefore to judge is nothing other than to pronounce a just, equitable, and lawful sentence on a disputed and doubtful matter.

units.la: Sed qualia Deus velit esse iudicia, Moses addita differentia significat, dicens, Iuste, hoc est, fe cundum ius. Nam a iure iustitia, & iustum abstrahuntur. Ius est, vt ait Cicero, legitima atq; vsi tata in rebus caufisq; ciuium aequalitatis conseruatio. Iustitia vero, vt inquit Aristoteles, est virtus per quam sua cuique tribuuntur, & eo modo quo praescripta lex vult. Iustum autem ni- mirum id erit quod iustitia duce & magistra secundum ius & aequum & bonum facimus. Ex quibus sequitur, quod quemadmodum in omni vitae genere is recte & iuste se gerit, qui suum cuiq; tribuit, atq; societatem coniunctionis humanae munifice & aeque tuetur: sic recte iudicet quisquis ius in iudiciis & bonum & aequum magis, quam quicquam aliud respicit ac sequitur.
units.tr: But what kind of judgments God wills, Moses indicates by adding a qualification, saying "righteously," that is, according to law. For justice and the just are derived from right. Right, as Cicero says, is the lawful and useful preservation of equality among citizens in their affairs and causes. Justice, as Aristotle says, is the virtue by which each is given what is his, in the way that the prescribed law wills. The just, surely, will be what we do under the leadership and guidance of justice, according to law, equity, and goodness. From these things it follows that just as in every walk of life he acts rightly and justly who gives each his due and generously and fairly maintains the fellowship of human society, so he judges rightly who, in judgments, looks to and follows law, goodness, and equity more than anything else.

units.la: Est autem hoc quod in sua quisq; ciuitate magistratus siue iudex respicit ius, quod ciuile dicimus, partim scriptum, partim non scriptum. Ac scriptum quidem constat legibus, plebiscitis, Senatus consultis, principum placitis siue constitutionibus imperatorum, respondis pru- dentum, magistratuum edictis, vt docet imperator in §. cóstat. Instit. de iur. nat. gent. & ciui. Non scriptum est quod consuetudine & moribus introductum est, ac propterea consuetudinarium appellatur, authore Imp. in §. ex non scripto instit. eod. Consuetudines autem etsi scriptae qui dem non sint, tamen legum scriptarum vim habent.
units.tr: Now in every commonwealth the magistrate or judge looks to that law which we call civil, partly written and partly unwritten. The written law consists of statutes, plebiscites, decrees of the Senate, the decisions of princes or the constitutions of emperors, the responses of the learned, and the edicts of magistrates, as the emperor teaches in the section Constat of the Institutes, on natural, national, and civil law. The unwritten law is that which has been introduced by custom and usage, and is therefore called customary law, as the emperor states in the section Ex non scripto of the same title. Customs, although indeed not written, nevertheless have the force of written laws.

units.la: Sed cum iudex ius respicere debeat in iudiciis, vtrum praestet scriptum ne ius sequatur an secundum naturalem aequitatem siue certa lege cogitatam iudicet, magna quaestio est. Et Aristot. quidem in i. Rethoricorum ad Theodectem statuit in eam curam ac cogitationem incum- bendum esse, vt omnes causae quoad posset fieri comprehensi sint & definitae legibus, & quam minimum arbitrio iudicis relinquatur. Quodipsum vt probet, argumento triplici demonstrat, difficilius esse iudicium ferre, quam leges condere. Vt primum, Vnus & pauci facilius reperi- untur, qui bene sentiant recte; iudicent, quam multi: at leges a paucis conduntur, iudicia ve- ro a multis: ergo facilius est leges quam iudicium ferre. Deinde, quae longo rerum vsu, multa at- que assidua consideratione & penitatione constituuntur, ea meliora sunt & ad id quod iusti & bonum est accedunt propius: at leges vsu rerum longo multaq; deliberatione fiunt, iudi- ia vero de repente emergunt & incidunt: ergo leges ad id quod expedit, quodq; bonum est acce- dunt propius & vt bene iudices efficiunt melius. Melius iudicant qui perturbatione & asse- ctibus omnibus vacant, quam qui ijs succumbunt: at legum latores, quoniam in thesi verfan- tur cui neq; certum tempus neq; persona definita versantur ob oculos, affectibus omnibus va- care facile possunt, iudices autem quia de praesentibus causis & inter singulos iudicant, unde vel beneuolentia, vel odium, vel metus mali, vel emolumenti sui spes oboriantur, facile volup- tatem aut dolorem suum secuti, facultatem dignoscendae veritatis amittunt. Quamobrem & in optimis quibusq; rebus pub. prouisum semper est, vt arbitrio potestatis; iudicis quam mini- mum permissum sit, & in hac sua Moses librum legis aliis commendat seu rectam iudiciorum normam, & oraculum Domini ipse in rebus difficilibus consuluit. Igitur vt suis in ciuitate sal- uus sit honos legibus, & virorum principum libidini frenum fit aliquod optimo cuiq; cogi- tandum est, Athenienses & Romanos vsu comperisse quam non posse finem cripto iure esse pacata tranquillaq; ciuitas: tum etiam quod Deus hanc suam populi Israelitici societatem no- luit carere scriptis legibus.
units.tr: But since a judge ought to regard the law in judgments, the question is a great one: whether he should follow the written law, or judge according to natural equity or a law devised for the particular case. Aristotle, in the first book of the Rhetoric to Theodectes, lays down that care and thought must be devoted to having all cases, as far as possible, comprehended and defined by laws, and as little as possible left to the discretion of the judge. To prove this he demonstrates, by a threefold argument, that it is more difficult to give judgment than to make laws. First, few and one are more easily found who think and judge rightly than many; but laws are made by few, while judgments are given by many; therefore it is easier to make laws than to pass judgment. Next, those things which are established by long experience of affairs and by much constant consideration and deliberation are better and approach more nearly to what is just and good; but laws are made by long experience of affairs and much deliberation, whereas judgments arise and fall suddenly; therefore laws approach more nearly to what is expedient and good, and make judges better. Those judge better who are free from disturbance and all passions than those who yield to them. But lawgivers, since they deal in the abstract, with no certain time and no defined person before their eyes, can easily be free from all passions; whereas judges, since they judge present cases and between individuals, where goodwill or hatred, fear of harm or hope of gain may arise, easily follow their own pleasure or pain and lose the faculty of discerning the truth. Wherefore in the best commonwealths it has always been provided that the discretion of judicial power be permitted as little as possible. In this book Moses too commends to others the law and the right norm of judgments, and in difficult matters he himself consulted the oracle of the Lord. Therefore, so that the honour of the laws may be kept safe in the commonwealth and some bridle may be put on the lust of powerful men, every good man must consider that the Athenians and the Romans learned by experience that a state cannot be peaceful and tranquil without written law; and also that God willed that his people of Israel's society should not lack written laws.

units.la: Caeterum vt iuste iudices, enitendum est, vt quemadmodum Imp. Constantinus & Lici- nius ad Dionysium rescripserunt in l. placuit. C. de iudi. placeat in omnibus rebus praecipuam esse iustitiae equitatis, quam stricti iuris rationem: videlicet ne, quod vulgo dici solet, summum ius, summa fiat iniuria. Ergo rigorem legis aequitate, quae legum interpres moderatrix est, iu- dex mitigabit. Quod diligens circumstantiarum ratio atq; obseruatio facile docuerit & effece rit. Ex quibus omnibus intelligimus, iuste iudicare posse eum, qui iis feruet ac sequatur adhi- bita moderatione aequa & secundum circumstantias, praecipue eas quae legibus expressae sunt. Atq; hoc videtur Moses sensisse, quando dixit, Iudicate iuste.
units.tr: Moreover, to judge justly, one must strive, as the emperors Constantine and Licinius wrote in reply to Dionysius, in the law Placuit of the Code, on judges: that in all matters equity and justice should take precedence over the strict reasoning of law, lest, as is commonly said, the highest law become the highest injury. Therefore the judge will temper the rigour of the law with equity, which is the moderator and interpreter of laws. A diligent consideration and observation of circumstances will easily teach and bring this about. From all these things we understand that he can judge justly who keeps to them, applying fair moderation according to the circumstances, especially those which are expressed in the laws. And this seems to be what Moses meant when he said, "Judge righteously."

units.la: Sed vt magis etiam planum faciat quod sentit, addit etiam personas dicens, Inter virum & fratrem eius, & peregrinum eius, id est, inter eos qui indigenae sunt & fratres, & inter indigenam & peregrinum siue alienigenam.
units.tr: But to make plainer still what he means, he adds the persons as well, saying Inter virum & fratrem eius, & peregrinum eius, that is, between those who are natives and brethren, and between a native and a stranger or foreigner.

units.la: In quo duo quaedam notanda seruandaq; veniunt. Prius est, ut componendis potius quàm vel suscitandis vel fouendis litibus studeas. Hoc enim appellatione fratris significat. Veluti e-nim si tibi cum fratre tuo lis fit, quia fratris iniuriae magis quàm alterius dolori sunt tibi, ideo illi grauius irasceris & calore irae incensus in illum multò vehementius quàm in alienum de-bacharis: mihi nec competit nec consultum est, ut te furentem instigem magis, atque tibi contra fratrem fera 'auxilia, ([illegible, ~9 letters] so mitt ein ander vncine find/sol sich niemand leggen) sed ut cogitem natura duce vos in gratiam redire posse, & omnibus discordia vestram fouentibus inimicos fore: sic optimus quisque iudex partium dissensiones, criminationes, contu-melias & inimicas mentes negliget, ac sibi componendas sedandasq; potius quàm fouendas aut exasperandas intelliget. O quàm malefidi pastores sunt, qui lites suorum ciuium quasi materiam suo quaestui commodam vel captant suffusa[?] frigida, vel fouent crebris dilationibus? Nec potest fieri ut eiusmodi magistratus plebs charos habeat, praesertim astu post cognito & accepto detrimento. Ac quanquam partibus ipsis non fiat iniuria, quandoquidem furore suo atq; odio feré illuc feruntur: tamen à iustitia magistratus alienum est hoc facere. Quamobrem Moses docet iudicem oportere sic actoris calorem refrigerare, ut si illi cum fratribus concili-andis esset negotium.
units.tr: Two things should be noted and observed here. The first is that you should aim to settle quarrels rather than stir them up or feed them. The word "brother" signifies this. For if you have a dispute with your brother, then because his wrongs grieve you more than another's, you are angrier with him and, inflamed by the heat of anger, you rage against him far more violently than against a stranger. It is neither fitting for me nor advisable that I should goad you further while you are raging, or give you savage aid against your brother ([illegible] "so mit ein ander vneins findt, sol sich niemand legen": when people are at odds with one another, no one should meddle). Rather, I should reflect that, with nature as your guide, you can return to harmony, and that anyone who feeds your discord will become your enemy. So every good judge of the parties will disregard their quarrels, accusations, insults and hostile feelings, and will understand that they must be settled and calmed rather than fed or made more bitter. O how faithless are those ministers who seize on their citizens' lawsuits as material convenient for their own gain, either drenching them with cold water or feeding them with constant delays! Nor can the common people hold such magistrates dear, especially once they have recognised the harm done to them by such trickery. Although no injury is done to the parties themselves, since they are carried almost headlong by their own fury and hatred, it is nonetheless foreign to the justice of a magistrate to act in this way. Therefore Moses teaches that the judge must cool the plaintiff's heat in such a way as if he had the business of reconciling brothers.

units.la: Alterum est, ut etiamsi cum peregrino siue hospite quis litiget, tamen à iustitia se nequa-quam patiatur auelli, quin hospiti quod suum est aeque atq; indigenae tribuat. Nam peregrini magna su-stinent odia, magnum etiam contemptum vel infimorum hominum, eaque mala fieri non potest, ut effugiant: siue enim ditescant aliis indigenis luxu atq; inertia pereuntibus, su-stinet inuidiam: siue suas ipsi opes concoquant, ac liberos reipub. educandos relicturi videan-tur esse, odiosi sunt. Quò fit ut omnium iniurijs & libidini sint obnoxij multaeq; eis incidant controuersiae. Quod si nolit eos magistratus tueri & suum illis ius reddere, satius est arcere fi-nibus aut etiam nunquam recipere, ne fit locus iniurijs.
units.tr: The second is that, even if someone is in dispute with a stranger or a guest, he must by no means allow himself to be drawn away from justice, but must render to the guest what is his, just as much as to a native. For strangers endure great hatred and great contempt, even from the lowest of people, and it is impossible for them to escape these evils. If they grow rich while other natives perish through luxury and idleness, they bear the envy; if they manage their own wealth and seem about to leave their children to be brought up for the commonwealth, they are hated. Hence they become liable to the injuries and lusts of everyone, and many controversies befall them. But if the magistrate is unwilling to protect them and to render their right to them, it is better to keep them out of the borders or even never to admit them, lest room be given for injuries.

units.la: Sed peregrinos homines & viduas & pupillos & omnino omnes eos qui vel suis ipsorum viribus vel aliena potentia prefidijsq; destituti sunt, Deus iudicibus siue magistratibus passim committit & commendat. Quare etsi diues & potens & authoritate & dignitate praeditus ho-mo, suum cum pauperrimo, contemptissimo & imbecillimo homine ius experturus in iudi-cium veniat, tamen quod quisq; ius habet id ei tribuendum est siue peregrinus sit siue indige-na. Atq; haec quidem seruanda sunt iudici.
units.tr: But God commits and commends strangers, widows, orphans, and in short all those who are destitute of their own strength or of the power and protection of others, to judges and magistrates everywhere. Therefore, even if a man who is rich, powerful, and endowed with authority and dignity comes into court to contest his right against the poorest, most despised and weakest man, nevertheless whatever right each person has must be granted to him, whether he is a stranger or a native. These things, indeed, are to be observed by the judge.

units.la: Cauenda verò sunt duo itidem, personarum respectus scilicet & metus. De personarum re-spectu dicit, Non agnoscetis facies in iudicio, ut magnum sic & paruum audiatis. Facies hominis, quia animi index est & earum rerum quas animo versamus interpres, pro toto homine accipi-tur, praesertim linguae Hebreae proprietate. Nam moeror apparet in facie, Gen. 40. Cur triftior hodie est? solito facies vestra: laetitia quoq; emicat è facie, ut Prou. 15. Cor gaudens exhilarat fa-ciem: malitiam quoq; prodit vultus ut Eccl. 25. Nequitia mulieris immutat faciem eius: Ose. 5. Respondebit arrogantia Israel in facie eius. Sed quid verbis opus est, ex obtutu faciei quasi quodam modo quis qualisq; sit homo discimus? Laetus exporrigat, iratus corrugat, arrogans & superbus extollit, humilis & abiectus demittit, liuidus auertit, amicus arridet, venerabun-dus suspicit, contemnens despicit.
units.tr: Two things likewise must be guarded against: regard for persons, namely, and fear. Concerning regard for persons he says: You shall not respect persons in judgment; you shall hear the small as well as the great. The face of a man, since it is the index of the mind and the interpreter of those things we turn over in the mind, is taken for the whole man, especially by the peculiarity of the Hebrew tongue. For sorrow appears in the face (Gen. 40): "Why is your face sadder today than usual?" Joy also shines out from the face, as in Prov. 15: "A joyful heart makes the face cheerful." The countenance also betrays malice, as in Eccl. 25: "The wickedness of a woman changes her face." Hos. 5: "The pride of Israel shall answer to his face." But why need we words? From the look of the face we learn, as it were, what sort of man someone is and of what quality. The glad man stretches his face out, the angry man wrinkles it, the arrogant and proud raise it up, the humble and abject lower it, the envious turn it away, the friend smiles, the reverent look up, and the contemptuous look down.

units.la: Iam faciem agnoscere quid aliud est quàm hominis animum, corpus, opes seu fortunas intueri & censere? quid aliud est quàm haec cogitando fenestrà aperire affectibus? Nam aut ira-cundo minacq; vultu metus, aut superbo & excelso inuidia, aut amico beneuolentia suscitatur in animis. Recte ergò Moses, ne quid eiusmodi motuum nostris animis oboriatur, quibus perturbati nebulas & ignorantias accersant sibi, facies iubet non agnoscendas, id est, illud per personarum litigantium siue diuitum siue pauperum iudicium nequaquam esse capiendum.
units.tr: Now, what else is it to regard a face than to look at and judge a man's mind, body, resources or fortunes? What else is it than, by thinking on these things, to open a window to the emotions? For a threatening and angry countenance stirs up fear, a proud and haughty one envy, a friendly one goodwill, in our minds. Rightly, therefore, so that no such motion should arise in our minds, by which we, being disturbed, bring clouds and ignorance upon ourselves, Moses bids us not to regard faces; that is, that judgment must in no way be made on the basis of the persons of the litigants, whether rich or poor.

units.la: Sed se ipse exponit dicens, Vt magnum sic & paruum audiatis. Quo ostendit eas res quae in personis magnae sunt & videntur esse, non tanti fieri debere, ut quia sint & appareant in aliis paruae seu paulò minores, ideo plus iuris ei qui bona maiora habeat tribuamus, & ei qui mino-ra bona possideat suum ius auferamus,
units.tr: But he explains himself, saying: You shall hear the small as well as the great. By this he shows that those things which are great in persons, and seem to be great, ought not to be valued so highly that, because they are or appear small, or somewhat smaller, in others, we should therefore give more right to the one who has greater goods, and take away the right of the one who possesses lesser goods.

units.la: Consideratur autem in personis natale solum, genus, corpus, animus, fortuna, res gestæ & generis huius alia. Iam nobilitatis splendor suo fulgore iudicum oculos plerunq;, sic per-stringit atq; occæcat, ut eos qui ignobili obscuraq; familia nati sunt præ nobilibus illis despi-ciant: ac miser ille quia sua familia parui ducitur, aduersarij verò nobilitas maximi fit, causa ea dat. Et natale solum tantum in his rebus momenti affert, ut vicino vel conciui multò plus tribuamus quàm aduenæ. Sed corporis bona, forma ac recta proportio, dictu mirum est, quanta homini gratiam conciliet:quantum item turpes & deformes homines fastidiamus.Sed hoc est facies agnoscere. Et eos qui minaces, iracundi sunt,sæpe ne damnum dent metuentes, nolitis offendere, & potius imbecilliorem, quem tueri nostrum fuerat deferimus. Quid autem benefacta in nos antea locata,& munera possunt? Munera crede mihi placant hominesq; Deosq;,Placatur donis Iupiter ipse datis. Hæc magna sunt & eum qui dederit, aut adiuuerit, magnum faciunt:nihil dedisse parui ducitur.Opes autem usus docet,quanti fiant,ac paupertas quàm contempta iaceat.Iam Moses admonet,ut quem natio longinqua aut barbara, quem generis ignobilitas,quem forma turpis,animus pusillus,artes contemptæ, paupertas paruum faciunt,æque audias,&si causam iustam foveat,tueare, atque eum qui propter accepta multa ac magna animi corporis & externa bona magno estimapud omnes in precio. Atque hoc est quod & hoc in loco Moses & spiritus sanctus alibi dicit,veluti Leuit.19.Prouerb.18.&alibi. Etiam hoc docet Plutarchus in libro de Iside Thebanorum iudicum eiusmodi imaginem describens esse,quod sine manibus visantur,&summi iudicis conniueant,videlicet quia iustitia nec homi-num aspectu flectatur nec munera curet. Ex quibus potest intelligi cauendum esse iudici, ne quod hic Moses docet & Christus quasi quodam modo exponit Ioan.7.ne [illegible, ~12 letters] iudicet.
units.tr: Now in persons one considers native soil, family, body, mind, fortune, deeds done, and other things of this kind. The splendour of noble birth, with its brightness, very often so dazzles and blinds the eyes of judges that they despise those born of an obscure and ignoble family in comparison with the nobles; and the fact that that wretched man is thought little of because of his family, while the nobility of his opponent is thought great, gives occasion for this. Native soil also brings so much weight in these matters that we give a neighbour or fellow citizen far more than a newcomer. But the goods of the body, beauty and right proportion, it is wonderful to say how much they win favour for a man, and how much we despise the ugly and deformed. But this is to regard faces. And we often leave to be defended the weaker man, whom it was our duty to protect, not wanting to offend those who threaten and are angry, fearing lest they do us harm. But what can past good deeds done for us, and gifts, achieve? "Believe me, gifts placate men and gods, and Jupiter himself is appeased by gifts given." These things are great, and make great the one who has given or helped; to have given nothing is thought small. Experience teaches how much riches are worth, and how despised poverty lies. Now Moses warns that whoever is made small by a distant or barbarous nation, by ignoble birth, by ugly form, by a small mind, by despised arts, or by poverty, you should hear equally, and if his cause is just, protect him, just as you would one who is held in great esteem by all for the many great goods of mind, body and external fortune he has received. And this is what Moses here, and the Holy Spirit elsewhere, says, as in Lev. 19 and Prov. 18, and elsewhere. Plutarch also teaches in his book on Isis and Osiris that such an image of the Theban judges was described as being without hands, and with eyes closed, namely because justice is not swayed by the look of men, nor does it care for bribes. From these things it can be understood that the judge must beware lest, as Moses teaches here and Christ in some sense expounds in John 7, he [illegible] judge.

units.la: De metu,quem ceu malum alterum cauebit iudex,hoc dicit, Non metuatis à facie viri, id est,non metuatis quenquam.Quo metum,qui pessimus consultor est,procul ab animo iudicis remouet.Atque id quidem ut intelligas rectius,quid sit metus,& quæ res timeantur,& quomodo do qui timent affecti sint considerandum est.
units.tr: Concerning fear, which the judge must guard against as another evil, he says: You shall not be afraid of the face of any man; that is, you shall fear no one. By this he removes from the judge's mind fear, which is the worst counsellor. And so that you may understand more rightly what fear is, which things are feared, and in what state those who fear are, this must be considered.

units.la: Ac metus quidem aliud nihil est,quàm trepidatio animi, quæ ex cogitatione futuri mali, quod vel exitium vel molestiam magnam videatur afferre,nata.
units.tr: Fear is nothing other than a trembling of the mind, born from the thought of a future evil which seems to bring either ruin or great trouble.

units.la: Timentur ergo quæ iam iam imminere videntur aut non ita multò post affutura cum magna nostra molestia aut etiam pernicie. Quò fit ut etiam earum rerum indicia nos terreant, metumque nobis incutiunt.
