Eorum genere continentur iræ inimicitiæque præpotentium hominum, & eorū qui iniusti sunt,omninoq; eorum omnium qui videntur & velle & posse nocere.Sed videntur velle qui iniuriam à nobis passi sunt aliquam,ut alias à nobis etiam non volentibus offensi,qui sunt aut videntur æmuli,&c.Posse vero videntur ij cumprimis qui valent robore,potentia,opibus,honoribus,authoritate,amicitijs,fauore populari, quiqueQue nostri facti alicuius ingentis & vehementer ardui conscij sunt, quorum in potestate & arbitrio fortunæ atq; opes nostræ videntur esse collocatæ.
units.tr: Therefore those things are feared which already seem to hang over us, or which will come upon us not long afterwards, with great trouble or even destruction to us. Hence even signs of such things terrify us and strike fear into us. In this class are included the anger and enmity of powerful men, and of those who are unjust, and in general of all who seem both to wish and to be able to harm us. They seem to wish to harm us who have suffered some injury at our hands, as well as those who have been offended by us in other matters even against our will, who are or seem to be rivals, and so on. They seem able above all who excel in strength, power, resources, honours, authority, friendships, popular favour, and those who are conscious of some great and very difficult deed of ours, in whose power and discretion our fortunes and resources seem to be placed.

units.la: Qui igitur timent ij sibi persuasum habent eiusmodi suam fortunam esse ut appeti libidine possint,& esse potentiores,vel etiá pares qui iam læsi sint.Quæ pericula prouidere & declinare sit huius loci atq; temporis. Eò rhetorum arte iudicum animi quandòq; rapiuntur,cum hæc illis suggerunt.Sed Athenis in Ariopago minime male cautum est legibus ne quis rhetor asse ctus mouerent iudicibus.Nam si magistratus eos metuat, quibus gubernandis præfectus est, nihil in ciuitate præclare faciet.Pilatus metueas Cæsarem multum reluctante conscientia Christi iniquissimo iudicio condemnauit. Et antea ab eiusmodi iudicibus Nabothus condemnatus est.Quamobrem Democritus dixit,iudicem debere neminem timere quam seipsum.
units.tr: Those who fear, therefore, are persuaded that their fortune is such that they can be attacked by another's lust, and that those who have already been wronged are more powerful than they are, or at least their equals. To foresee and avoid these dangers is the business of this place and time. By the art of the rhetoricians the minds of judges are sometimes carried away when these things are suggested to them. But at Athens in the Areopagus it was very wisely provided by law that no orator should move the judges in this way. For if a magistrate fears those whom he is appointed to govern, he will accomplish nothing excellent in the commonwealth. Pilate, fearing Caesar, condemned Christ by a most unjust judgment, though his conscience greatly resisted. And before him Naboth was condemned by such judges. Wherefore Democritus said that a judge ought to fear no one but himself.

units.la: Atq; hæc quidem duo quæ diximus seruanda,& illa due in quibus exponendis modo versamur cauenda sunt ei qui velit officio boni iudicis fungi.
units.tr: These two points we have mentioned are to be observed, and those two which we are now setting forth are to be guarded against by anyone who wishes to discharge the office of a good judge.

units.la: Sed ut possit animus eo perpelli causa non leuis additur quia(inquit)iudicium Dei est.Quo significat non nostram hic sed Dei rem agi. Quemadmodum igitur Deus audit attente & benevolenter quæ geruntur & dicuntur quæq;ad illum referuntur omnia, deq; ijs iustam fert atq; exequitur sententiam: contra vero nec obtutu personarum ab æquo & bono vel tantillum flectitur,nec vllius periculi quanticunq; metu frangitur:sic qui fungitur iudicis officio,atq; ex officio nomen Dei accepit, & audiendis iudicandisq; causis intentus esse & personarum respectu metuq; omni vacare debet. In quam sententiam tot extant scripti sacræ scripturæ loci ut enumerare me volentem tempus citius quam materia deficiat.
units.tr: But so that the mind may be moved to do this, a not slight reason is added: "because (he says) the judgment is God's. By which he signifies that the matter here is not ours but God's. Just as God hears attentively and kindly all that is done and said, and all that is referred to him, and pronounces and executes a just sentence on them, whereas he is not turned aside from what is fair and good even a little by regard for persons, nor is he broken by fear of any danger, however great; so he who discharges the office of judge, and from his office has received the name of God, ought to be intent on hearing and judging causes, and free from respect of persons and from all fear. Passages of holy Scripture to this effect are so numerous that, if I wished to enumerate them, time would run out sooner than material.

units.la: Sed hæc non ita magistratui imponuntur onera ut nulla sit iuxtà concessa leuandæ molestiæ difficultatisq; propinata ratio. Nam quia mens hominis in corpus mortale quasi tumulum condita aliis atque aliis opinionibus fallitur,ne quis iudex seipso fiat deterior, veritatem respuens & sententias cæcas proferens, Moses quid de iure dubitantem facere deceat adhunc modum exponit, Et negotium,inquit,quod difficilius vobis fuerit quam ut iudicando sitis, ad me re-fertis. Quod perinde est ac si dicat, Quando non satis perspicitis causas quippe quod perple-xæ sint & obscuræ,tunc iudicis officium poteritis recusare, & litigatores ad accuratius tribu-nal ablegare.Atque hic sensus ex verbis Mosis videtur colligi.Nam quia verbum שְׁפַט[?] significat asperum, grauce, & difficile esse, consequens est de rebus sententiam seu iudicium impedi-entibus dici: & verbum à suo primitiuo פָּרַךְ[?] deductum relationem siue remissionem significat, facile est colligere quod diximus.
units.tr: But these burdens are not so laid upon the magistrate that no reason is offered for easing the trouble and difficulty bestowed upon him. For since the human mind, buried in a mortal body as in a tomb, is deceived by one opinion after another, lest any judge become worse than himself, rejecting the truth and pronouncing blind sentences, Moses sets out in this way what it befits one who is doubtful about the law to do: "And the matter which shall be too difficult for you to judge, you shall refer to me." This is just as if he said: when you do not see the causes clearly, since they are intricate and obscure, then you may refuse the office of judge and send the litigants away to a more careful tribunal. And this sense seems to be gathered from the words of Moses. For since the word שְׁפַט [shaphat] signifies harsh, grievous and difficult, it follows that it is said of matters that hinder sentence or judgment; and the word derived from its root פָּרַךְ [parakh] signifies referral or remission, so it is easy to gather what we have said.

units.la: Sunt autem magnæ illæ atq; arduæ causæ, non vt Iosepho placuit controuersiæ quæ inter claros, diuites, potentesq; incidunt: sed quemadmodum Philoni visum est, quando priuati, egeni, obscuri homines premuntur à potentioribus adeo, vt nisi in summo iudice spes præsidij nulla sit reliqua. Earum cognitionem & iudicium ad summum iudicem pertinere Moses hic docet.
units.tr: But those great and arduous causes are not, as Josephus thought, the disputes that arise among the famous, rich and powerful; they are rather, as it seemed to Philo, the cases in which private persons, needy and obscure, are oppressed by the more powerful, so that unless there is hope of protection in the supreme judge, none remains. Moses teaches here that the cognizance and judgment of these belong to the supreme judge.

units.la: Atque eo ipso & iudicibus & subditis consultum est. Ac iudicibus quidem hoc modo con-sulitur, vt si de iure dicendo dubitent, causam ad superiorem iudicem remittant. In quo tamen iura ciuilia modum & legitimas causas seruari volunt. Neque enim eò confugere eis semper licet, præsertim si de facto sit dubium, veluti colligitur ex l. eum quem temere ff. de iudiciis. Oportet etiam euidentem ambigendi causam esse: nam si iudex ideo deprehendatur causam ad superiorem retulisse, vt onus cognitionis declinaret, pœnâ ei leges irrogant, vt est videre in l.ij.C.de legibus. Quod ipsum etiam Mosis sententiæ consentaneum est. Nam si labores omnes vnus ferre posset, electione iudicum inferiorum non opus esse censuisset. Facient igitur illi quod poterunt, ac quod ferre nequeunt ad Mosem referant.
units.tr: By this very thing both judges and subjects are provided for. Judges are provided for in this way: if they doubt how to give the law, they refer the case to a higher judge. In this, however, the civil laws want the proper manner and lawful causes to be observed. For it is not always permitted them to flee there, especially if the doubt concerns the facts, as is gathered from the law "eum quem temere" in the Digest on judgments. It is also necessary that the cause of doubt be evident; for if a judge is found to have referred a case to a superior in order to escape the burden of hearing it, the laws impose a penalty on him, as can be seen in the second law of the Code on laws. This is also consistent with the sentence of Moses. For if one man could bear all the labours, he would not have thought it necessary to appoint lower judges by choice. They will therefore do what they can, and bring to Moses what they cannot bear.

units.la: Neq; vero Moses hoc ipso quod grauiorum contr ouerfiarum iudicium sibi reseruauit, Iudi[?] cum persone consuluit tantum, verum etiam suorum subditorum libertati, quæ bono principi non minus curæ esse debet, quàm obedientia suis magistratibus delegatis debita, vt docet A-lexander Seuerus imp. in l. imperator. ff. de appellat.
units.tr: Nor indeed did Moses, in reserving to himself the judgment of the weightier controversies, consult only the persons of the judges, but also the liberty of his subjects, which ought to be a concern to a good prince no less than the obedience owed to his delegated magistrates, as the emperor Alexander Severus teaches in the law "imperator" in the Digest on appeals.

units.la: Sunt autem subditis ad declinandum iniusta iudicum imperia duo potissimum præbita remedia, videlicet appellatio & suspecti iudicis recusatio. Et appellatio quidé, est vti vulgo de minore iudice ad maiorem prouocatio finiri solet. Ea fit, vel coram iudice à quo appellatur, vel si appellans non possit aut non audeat ipse conuenire iudicem, per denunciationem ei ad quem appelatur factam. Sed ad eum qui gradu superiore proximus est, debet fieri. Ad eam dantur dies decem: quod sic est accipiendum, vt intelligas, si à lata sententia intra decem dies vtiles, hoc est, quibus adeundi iudicis in publico potestas facta est, non fit appellatum, porrò non admittatur ad appellandum. Appellatione facta datur aliud spacium eam prosequendi, vi delicet iure nouis. vt intra annum eam prosequare.
units.tr: For subjects, two chief remedies have been provided to escape the unjust commands of judges, namely appeal and the challenge of a suspect judge. Appeal is, as it is commonly defined, a challenge from a lesser judge to a greater. It is made either before the judge from whom one appeals or, if the appellant cannot or dares not approach the judge himself, by a notice given to the one to whom one appeals. But it must be made to the judge who is next in higher rank. Ten days are given for it; which is to be understood thus: if within ten useful days from the pronouncement of sentence, that is, days on which the power of approaching a judge in public is granted, no appeal is lodged, then afterwards he is not admitted to appeal. Once the appeal has been made, another space is given for pursuing it, namely by the newer law, so that you may pursue it within a year.

units.la: Sed recusatio suspecti iudicis minus offensæ habet. Nam iure ciuili iudex etiam delegatus, si fit suspectus, ante litis contestationem recusari potest, quod de nostra causa male iudica-turus esse videatur. Quin idem licet, etiam post litis contestationem, si tibi suspicionis causa tum demum oborta sit. Qua de re leges extant cum alibi multæ, tum vero maxime in l. non di-stinguemus. §. cum quidam. ff. de arbi. Hæc eo commemoro, vt intelligant homines quibus ex fontibus has de iudiciis leges iureconsulti sibi sumpserint. Genera sunt illa quæ Moses annotat, species autem iure ciuili introductæ sunt ita rectè & legitimè, vt scripturæ Mosis siue ma-uis[?] iuri diuino sint omnino consentaneæ. Nam magnas causas sic vides secundum illas ratio-nes ad summum magistratum referre, vt modo iudicibus delegatis ne plus æquo ferre necesse habeant: modo plebeis hominibus, ne premantur præpotentium hominum iniurijs: modo si-mul ambobus, vt retineantur in officio & saluo statu.
units.tr: But the challenge of a suspect judge carries less offence. For by civil law even a delegated judge, if he is suspected, can be challenged before the joining of issue, on the ground that he seems likely to judge our case badly. Indeed the same is permitted even after the joining of issue, if the cause of suspicion has arisen for you only then. There are laws on this in many places, but especially in the law "non distinguemus", §"cum quidam", in the Digest on arbiters. I mention these things so that people may understand from what sources the jurists have taken these laws on judgments. The kinds are those which Moses notes, but the species have been introduced by civil law so rightly and lawfully that they are wholly consistent with the writings of Moses, or rather with divine law. For you see that great causes are referred, on those grounds, to the supreme magistrate: now so that delegated judges need not bear more than is fair; now so that common people are not oppressed by the injuries of the most powerful men; now both together, so that they may be kept in their office and in a secure state.

units.la: Atq; hæc quidem omnia magistratibus prædicanda Moses docuit, vt sui suorumq; ho-minum semper meminerint. Alibi verò Deus alias rationes enumerat, quarum suo loco me-minerimus.
units.tr: Moses taught that all these things are to be proclaimed to magistrates, so that they always remember themselves and their people. But elsewhere God enumerates other reasons, which we shall recall in their proper place.

units.la: Plebis autem officium vt simplex est & minimè varium, sic paucis & simpliciter ostendit dicens, Eodem tempore præcepi vobis (cum tota populi Israelitici concione colloquitur) quæcunq; facere debeatis. Quod idem est ac si dicat, vobis autem, quoniam magistratus mandato iussuq; Dei nec non vestro ipsorum consensu atque etiam arbitratu delectus est, non immerito præ-cepta legitimæ & debitæ obedientiæ dedi. Nam si magistratus edictis non obediatur, frustra magistratus eligitur. Seditionibus quassantur omnia. Quæ quantam afferant rebuspub. perniciem, Menenius Agryppa in oratione ad plebem Romanam, quæ in Auentinum montem secesserat, habitam perpulchre docuit, introducto de ventre & membris apologo. Alicubi Dij vocantur, vt intelligas diuinam illis authoritatem apud te esse debere, quod secundum Deum illis debeatur obedientia maxima. Paulus Rom. 13. dicit tibi in bonum datos esse diuini-tus, propterea quæ consciențiæ suæ cuiusque tunc maximè consuli, cum obeditur magi-stratui. Dominus in Euangelio de ea re consultus dicit, Date Deo quod Dei est, & Cæsari quod Cæsaris est. Ipse etiam tributum poscentibus nō negauit, sed Petro iußit vt utriusque nomine redderet. Egregium exemplum plebis obedientis Israelitæ de se præbent quando Iosuæ suam fidem & obedientiam quantam maximam præstitissent Mosi, verbis magnifice pollicentur & reuera præstant. Eam si pijs magistratibus præstent homines magnam ex ea felicitatem sibi comparabunt. Atque sic quidem Moses & eos quibus est obediendum rerum gerendarum præceptis: illos quorū est obedire doctrina de obedientia imbuit, quæ si feruemus magna cum ad hanc caducam, tum ad illam sempiternam vitam accedet nobis vtilitas. Amen.
units.tr: The duty of the common people, since it is simple and not at all varied, he sets out briefly and plainly, saying: "At the same time I commanded you (he speaks to the whole assembly of the Israelite people) all that you ought to do." This is as if he said: but to you, since the magistrate has been chosen by the command and order of God, and also by your own consent and judgment, precepts of lawful and due obedience have not been given without reason. For if the magistrate's edicts are not obeyed, the magistrate is chosen in vain. Everything is shaken by seditions. What great ruin these bring upon commonwealths, Menenius Agrippa taught very beautifully in his speech to the Roman plebs, who had withdrawn to the Aventine mountain, by introducing the fable of the belly and the members. In some places magistrates are called gods, so that you may understand that they ought to have divine authority with you, since the greatest obedience is owed them next after God. Paul in Romans 13 says that they are given to you by God for your good, and that each man's conscience is then most consulted when the magistrate is obeyed. The Lord in the Gospel, being asked about this matter, says: "Give to God what is God's, and to Caesar what is Caesar's." He himself also did not deny tribute to those demanding it, but ordered Peter to pay it on behalf of both of them. The Israelite people present a splendid example of an obedient commonalty, when they magnificently promise Joshua, in words, and indeed perform, as great faith and obedience as they had shown to Moses. If men render such obedience to godly magistrates, they will procure great happiness for themselves. And so Moses has imbued the magistrates with the precepts of governing, and those who must obey with the doctrine of obedience. If we hold to this with great zeal, usefulness will come to us both in this frail life and in that everlasting one. Amen.

units.la: SERMO VI.
units.tr: SERMON VI.

units.la: 19 Profecti itaque de Horeb, per universum desertum vastum, & horridum transiuimus, (quod vidistis) per viam montis Amorrhæi, sicut præcepit nobis Dominus Deus noster, & venimus in Cades Barnea.
units.tr: 19 So we departed from Horeb and passed through all that vast and dreadful wilderness (which you saw), by the way of the mountain of the Amorites, as the Lord our God commanded us, and we came to Kadesh-barnea.

units.la: 20 Et dixi vobis, venistis ad montem Amorrhæi, quem Dominus Deus noster nobis daturus est.
units.tr: And I said to you, "You have come to the mountain of the Amorites, which the Lord our God is about to give us."

units.la: 21 Ecce Dominus Deus tuus dedit coram te terram istam, ascende, & occupa, sicuti pollicitus est tibi Dominus Deus patrum tuorum, ne timeas, neque terrearis.
units.tr: Behold, the Lord your God has set this land before you. Go up and take possession, as the Lord God of your fathers has promised you. Do not fear, nor be dismayed.

units.la: 22 Accessistis autem ad me omnes vos, & dixistis, Mittamus viros ante nos & explorent terram, & nobis renuntient per quod iter ascendamus, & civitates ad quas veniemus.
units.tr: And you all came to me and said, "Let us send men before us, to search out the land and bring us word of the way by which we shall go up, and of the cities to which we shall come."

units.la: 23 Placuit hoc mihi, & tuli ex vobis duodecim viros, ex quaq; tribu vnum.
units.tr: This pleased me, and I took from among you twelve men, one from each tribe.

units.la: 24 Qui versi ascenderunt in montem, venerunt q; ad torrentem Eschol, & explo-rauerunt eam.
units.tr: They turned and went up into the mountain, came to the valley of Eshcol, and searched it out.

units.la: 25 Et accipientes in manus suas de fructibus terræ illius, attulerunt ad nos, re-nuntiarunt q; nobis responsum tale: Bona est terra, quā Dominus Deus noster dat nobis.
units.tr: And taking in their hands some of the fruit of that land, they brought it to us, and they brought back this report: "The land is good, which the Lord our God gives us."

units.la: 26 At vos noluistis ascendere, sed exacerbastis os Domini Dei vestri.
units.tr: But you would not go up; you rebelled against the mouth of the Lord your God.

units.la: 27 Et murmurantes in tentoriis vestris dixistis: Quādoquidē Dominus nos odit, ideo eduxit nos de terra Ægypti, vt traderet nos in manum Amorrhæi, & perderet nos.
units.tr: And murmuring in your tents you said, "Because the Lord hates us, he brought us out of the land of Egypt, to deliver us into the hand of the Amorites and to destroy us."

units.la: 28 Quo ascendemus nos? fratres nostri liquefecerunt cor nostrum in hoc quod dixerunt: Populus ille maior & excelsior nobis est, habens vrbes magnas, et in cœlum vsq; munitas, & vidimus quoq; illic filios Enakim.
units.tr: Where shall we go up? Our brothers have made our hearts melt, saying, "That people is greater and taller than we are; their cities are great and walled up to heaven; and we saw there the sons of the Anakim."

units.la: 29 Tum dixi vobis, ne sitis animo consternato neq; timeatis ab eis.
units.tr: Then I said to you, "Do not be struck with dread, nor fear them."

units.la: 30 Dominus Deus vester, qui incedit ante vos, ipse pugnabit pro vobis, secun-dum omnia ea quæ fecit nobiscum in Ægypto vobis spectantibus.
units.tr: The Lord your God, who goes before you, will himself fight for you, according to all that he did for us in Egypt before your eyes.

units.la: 31 Quin & in deserto quoque vidisti quomodo gestarit te Dominus Deus tuus, quemadmodum gestat homo filium suum, in omni via quaivistis [?] donec veniretis ad locum istum.
units.tr: Moreover, in the desert also you saw how the Lord your God carried you, as a man carries his son, in all the way you went until you came to this place.

units.la: 32 Et hac in re non credebatis Domino Deo vestro.
units.tr: Yet in this matter you did not believe the Lord your God.

units.la: 33 Qui præcessit vos in via, vt exploraret vobis locum vbi quiescéretis: nocte quidem (præcessit) in igne, vt videretis viam, in qua incederetis, interdiu autem in nube.
units.tr: Who went before you on the way, to search out a place where you might rest: by night indeed in fire, so that you might see the way in which you should go, and by day in a cloud.

units.la: Quoniam non satis est nos Deum nosse & verbum eius tenere, sed requiritur etiam vt in ipsum credamus & eius verbo obsequamur, eaq; de causa, Deus magistratum constituit, qui nos ad ea studia pro suo imperio adigat: nobis certe est opus vt magistratus suas leges omnes eò dirigat, vt Deo atq; eius verbo adhereamus, contraq; prouideat ne qua deficiamus, plebs aut hoc agenti magistratui pareat. Quod ni fiat necessarium est genus nostrum pessum ire. Atq; vtinam hæc credere quam experiri mallemus. Cæterum ne sine exemplis nudam præceptionem haberemus, exempla suis de magistratus atq; plebis officio præceptionibus addit. Et adducit ex annalibus suæ gentis historiam, quæ Num.13.14.extat, quâ sic tractat, vt primum boni magistratus exemplum, iuxtaq; positum obedientiæ, quæ ei præstita est, fructu-tum mali magistratus exemplum iuxtaq; descriptionem eorum quæ per illum ingruerunt in rempub. malorum proponat.
units.tr: Since it is not enough for us to know God and hold his word, but it is also required that we believe in him and obey his word, for this reason God has set up the magistrate, who by his authority drives us to those pursuits. Certainly we need the magistrate to direct all his laws to this end: that we cling to God and his word, that he take care we lack nothing, and that the common people obey the magistrate who does this. Unless this is done, our race must necessarily perish. Would that we preferred to believe these things rather than to learn them by experience! But lest we have a bare precept without examples, he adds examples to his precepts on the duties of magistrate and people. And from the annals of his own nation he brings forward the history found in Num. 13–14, which he handles in such a way that he first sets forth an example of a good magistrate, together with the obedience rendered to him and its fruit, and then an example of a bad magistrate, together with a description of the evils that came upon the commonwealth through him.

units.la: Exemplum boni Magistratus in suo ipsius illis omnibus notissimo facto proponit, quippe qui captata ex rebus gestis sui populi, occasione eum ipsum ad suscipiendum quod praeceperat Dominus negocium adhortatus sit: cui monitioni cum paruissent, omnis res ea ex animi sententia cesserit. Verum ut ea res plenius ac melius intelligatur, videbimus illam occasionem quo pacto usurpauerit, tum quomodo plebs ei sit obsecuta, denique ut res succesSerit.
units.tr: He sets forth the example of the good magistrate in a deed well known to all of them. Seizing the occasion offered by the affairs of his people, he urged them to undertake the task the Lord had commanded. When they obeyed this admonition, the whole matter turned out according to their wishes. But so that this may be understood more fully and better, we shall see how he seized that occasion, how the people obeyed him, and finally how the affair turned out.

units.la: Occasio ut fit usurpata ex eo potest intelligi quod hic dicitur eam primum à Mose animad-versam, tum autem populo ut arriperet mirifice propositam. Est autem animaduersa quando Moses secum reputauit quos quantosque labores populus hucusque tulisset, quas itineris mo-lestias superasset, dum per vastum hoc & horridum desertum transijsset usque ad Cadesbar-nea. Ex quo colligit populo hos labores recolenti minus difficile fore quod supererat, nempe terram hanc ut occuparent.
units.tr: The seizing of the occasion can be understood from what is said here: that Moses first noticed it, and then set it before the people so that they might eagerly grasp it. He noticed it when he reflected on what great labours the people had borne up to that point, and what hardships of the journey they had overcome while passing through this vast and dreadful desert as far as Kadesh-barnea. From this he concluded that for a people recalling these labours, what remained, namely to occupy this land, would be less difficult.

units.la: Sic magistratus, quandoquidem titulum prouidorum sibi vendicant, prouideat omnia quae possunt euenire ciuitati, ac non modo quae ante pedes sunt, sed & praeterita & futura con-tueatur. Dij vocantur in Psalmis, ergo Dei prouidentiam imitabuntur. Veluti nostri maiores senatus populusque Tigurinus cogitantes bella mercenaria seditionum & tumultuum civili-um seminaria fore,eaque de causa voluere eis ipsis in posterum abstinere. Et in illis tantis re-rum difficultatibus data fuerat ad tollendum luxum occasio, sed socordia nostra neglecta est. Iam cum uberes sint rerum proventus abolendae mendicitati prebetur occasio, sed & ea ipsa negligitur. At Moses & acceptat & usurpat occasiones.
units.tr: So the magistrate, since he claims for himself the title of provident, should foresee all things that can befall the commonwealth, and should attend not only to what lies at his feet but also to past and future. In the Psalms magistrates are called gods; therefore they should imitate God's providence. Thus our ancestors, the senate and people of Zurich, reckoning that mercenary wars would be seedbeds of sedition and civil tumults, were willing for that reason to abstain from them in future. And in those great difficulties of affairs an opportunity had been given to curb luxury, but our sloth neglected it. Now, when the harvests are abundant, an opportunity is offered to abolish beggary, and this too is neglected. But Moses both accepts and seizes opportunities.

units.la: Sed & populo ad hunc modum est propositum. Eò v/q[?] venistis (inquit) en coram vobis,&c. Quo ostendit facile facta[?] fore quod dicit. Iam quis res praeclaras cum faciles facta[?] sunt suscipiendas esse neget? Deinceps dicit, Deum promiss[?], quod argumentum est optimum, nempe Deus promisit, igitur dabit. Quis promittenti Deo fidem non habeat? Tertio, ne terreãris, inquit. Turpe est in re tam certa ac facili impediri formidine. Atque sic quidem publice & privatim occasiones non negligemus eas quibus vel ad religionem, vel ad utilitatem publicam, vel ad singulorum hominum utilitatem aliquid emolumenti possit afferri.
units.tr: But the matter was also put to the people in this way: "Now you have come (he says), behold, before you," and so on. By this he shows that what he says will be easily done. Who, then, can deny that noble undertakings should be taken up when they have been made easy? Next he says, "God has promised," which is an excellent argument: God has promised, therefore he will give. Who would not have faith in a God who promises? Third, he says, "do not be terrified." It is shameful to be hindered by fear in a matter so certain and easy. And so, both publicly and privately, we shall not neglect the occasions by which some advantage may be brought either to religion, to the public good, or to the good of individual men.

units.la: Ceterum sequitur ut quemadmodum occasione istam usurpanti & proponenti Mosi populus Israel obsecutus sit indicemus. Ac primum quidem censent exploratores mittendos esse: quae historia Num.13. describitur: qui cognoscant ac nuncient quae qualisque haec sit terra & quomodo inuadi atq; occupari queat.
units.tr: It remains to show how the people of Israel obeyed Moses when he offered and set before them this occasion. And first, they judge that spies should be sent, an action described in Num. 13: men who would learn and report what sort of land this is, and how it might be invaded and occupied.

units.la: In quo proponitur consilij capiendi ratio. Est autem consilium nihil aliud quam ratio qua adhibita dispicimus quid sit faciendum aut non faciendum. Ei proposita est ad quam dirigatur norma, verbu[m] Domini videlicet: quae certissima est. Nam quod istic prohibitum est, de eo non opus est ut capias consilium: de eo vero quod istic praecipitur, an expediat fieri, non consul-tandum quidem est, sed tamen quo pacto mandatum Dei exequamur, erit deliberandum. Sic illi rectè quidem exploratores mittendo faciunt, quippe quod iussisset Dominus, consultando vero prudenter faciunt, quippe quod quae Deus velit ac iubeat sapienter sint suscipienda & prudenter perficienda. Ac quanquam haec ipsa populi Israelitici consultatio male eis cesserit: tamen bene & prudenter suscepta est. Nec ex eventu facta notanda sunt. Res consultò suscepte plerunq; succedunt prospere. Explorant etiam Iosue & Danitae. Explorare sibi suisq; civibus malum non est, at patriam hostibus prodere est pessimum.
units.tr: In this is set out the manner of taking counsel. Now counsel is nothing other than a method by which, once applied, we consider what is to be done or not done. A rule is set before it to direct it, namely the word of the Lord, which is most certain. For about what is forbidden there, there is no need to take counsel; but about what is commanded there, whether it is expedient to do it, there is indeed no need to consult, yet how we may carry out God's command must be deliberated. So those men act rightly in sending spies, since the Lord had commanded it; and they act prudently in consulting, since what God wills and commands should be undertaken wisely and carried out with prudence. And although this very consultation of the Israelite people turned out badly for them, it was nonetheless undertaken well and prudently. Nor should actions be judged by their outcome: matters undertaken with deliberation usually succeed. Joshua and the Danites also sent spies. To spy out for oneself and one's fellow citizens is no evil; but to betray one's country to enemies is the worst.

units.la: Eliguntur ex singulis tribubus singuli. Quod facit ad concordiam.
units.tr: Single men are chosen from each tribe. This serves concord.

units.la: Rei sic suscepte causae ex mandatis cognosci possunt, nempe quod urbes, homines, natu-ram terrae & itinera cognoscere cuperent. Quarum rerum cognitio quàm necessaria atq; uti-lis ipsis futura fuerat, adeo cuius perspicuum est, ut dicto opus non fit. Quantum enim ad vi-ctoriam adiumentum est hostem suum qualis sit quaque parte facillime & minimo cum detri-mento atque periculo superetur nosse? Ergo magistratuum prouidorum interest ut in res a-libi, in primisq; apud hostes, fieri solitas intenti sint, quo possint ex eo ipso res suas instituere: Contrà sic res instituat atque gerat suas ut exploratorum oculos atq; aures sine periculo pos-sit sustinere. Egregium Scipionis exemplū est, qui missos ab Hannibale in sua castra viros non solum non ultus est supplicio, sed etiam circumduci voluit ut spectarent omnia: quoniam tanta disciplina suos regebat ut eius nuntio hostes terreri magis, quàm animari posse consideret. Eodem modo maiores nostri in edito colle, cui quondà arx fuit imposita, suas copias hosti spectandas praebuere. Et Sempachij duci Austriacorum Leopoldo nunciarunt exploratores Hel-vetios paucos quidem esse, sed eosdem tamen gnauos atq; alacres. Nunc sic passim comparati sunt mores hominum, vt qui hinc inde veniunt, cernant effœminatos, luxu perditos omni disciplina solutos, in Bacchum pariter ac Venerem effusos: Nec tamen sunt prouidi, vt vel sibi caueant ab exploratoribus, vel ipsi illorum, qui eos oderunt, cane peius & angue, con-silia conatusq; explorent. Securitas certè semper cessit pesimè.
units.tr: The cause of such an undertaking can be known from the commands: namely, that they wished to know the cities, the men, the nature of the land, and the routes. How necessary and useful the knowledge of these things would be for them is so plain that it needs no saying. For how much does knowing what sort of enemy one faces, and in what part he may most easily be overcome with least loss and danger, contribute to victory? Therefore it concerns provident magistrates to be attentive to affairs elsewhere, and especially among enemies, that they may shape their own plans from this very knowledge. Conversely, they should so order and conduct their affairs that they can endure the eyes and ears of spies without danger. The noble example of Scipio is well known: he did not even punish with death the men sent by Hannibal into his camp, but wished them to be led round so that they might see everything, since he ruled his men with such discipline that he judged the enemy would be frightened rather than encouraged by their report. In the same way our ancestors, on a high hill where a citadel once stood, offered their forces to be seen by the enemy. And spies reported to Leopold, Duke of Austria, at Sempach that the Swiss were indeed few, but nonetheless vigorous and eager. Now human manners are so disposed everywhere that those who come from here and there see men effeminate, ruined by luxury, loosed from all discipline, given over to Bacchus and Venus alike; yet they are not provident enough to guard against spies themselves, nor to spy out the plans and attempts of those who hate them, worse than dog or snake. Certainly security has always turned out very badly.

units.la: Postremò cognoscendum est vt illis hi conatus successerint. Venerunt, inquit, ψ[?] ad torrentem Eschol. 2. explorant eam. 3. attulerunt etiam fructus terræ. Vide quàm felices successus? Quousq; volunt peruenum, nec solum transeunt, sed explorant, & vt quæq; res se habeant cognoscunt deniq; etiam fructus nemine prohibente efferunt. Quid velles amplius?
units.tr: Finally, we must learn how those attempts turned out for them. "They came," it says, "to the brook Eshcol." (2) "They explored it." (3) "They also brought back fruit of the land." See how fortunate the outcome was? They reached the place they wanted, they did not merely pass through but explored it, they learned at last how matters stood, and they brought back the fruit with no one forbidding them. What more could you want?

units.la: Magna quidem & difficilis res est terras hostiles explorare, sed id ipsum tamen felicissimè efficitur cum prouidenter atq; ex mandato Dei suscepto sit. Sic quæ pie & prudenter fusci-piuntur, vt aut difficilia sint, tamen facillimè perficiuntur. Quàm difficile fuit patrum nostrorum memoria mercenariam militiam plebeijs alienis ocio, & pensiones optimatibus luxu deperdi tis eripere? Quantæ molis fuit sacerdotibus missam reliquosq; cultus papisticos, vnde eis esset quæstus vberrimus, eripere? Et tamen Deus dedit vt posset effici. Qui id quæso? Magistratus erat fortis & industrius, plebs zelo pietatis feruebat tota. Iam cum paruæ sint harum rerum reliquiæ, veluti sacella, festi dies, commercia cum impijs, regnant etiam pristina scelera, vt vsu-ræ, ebrietas & quæ sunt huius generis alia. Hæc si quis iubeat è medio tollere, videntur sustolli non posse: in ore est omni populo: Man mags niemandt bringen: Es mag nit erhebt werden. Qui fit quod tolli non potest? an ne grauius quiddam est? aliquanto quidem: nam ceu lignum diu in aquis iacuit, & vt solet zizania, radices egit altius: sed illud ἀλλ' ἄ ἄντ ὑτοῦ videtur magis per sonis quàm rebus ipsis existere. Ac nos ipsi infirmiores facti sumus: quippe quorum corpora luxu crapulaq; emollita, animi vero pecuniæ studio, & ambitione, & inertia fracti sunt. Magistratus enim modò renuit, modò non audet leges bonas ferre, easq;, si ferat ac promulget maximè, tamen euestigio negligit: plebs fide caret & charitate, nec spem habet nisi rerum quas putat amitti non posse. Inde existit illa ad rectum & bonum ἀλλ' ἴωσεγ ὑτοῦ.
units.tr: It is indeed a great and difficult thing to explore hostile lands, yet this very task is accomplished most happily when it is undertaken prudently and at God's command. Thus things undertaken piously and wisely, though difficult, are carried out most easily. In our fathers' memory, how hard was it to free the mercenary soldiery from the idleness of the commons and the pensions of the nobles, who were squandering them in luxury? How great a task was it to tear the Mass and the other papistical rites away from the priests, from which they drew their rich profits? And yet God granted that it could be done. Why, I ask? The magistrate was strong and diligent, and the whole common people burned with zeal for piety. Now that remnants of these things are few, such as chapels, feast days and dealings with the wicked, the old sins also reign, such as usury, drunkenness and other things of this kind. If someone orders these to be removed from the midst, they seem unable to be removed. It is on everyone's lips: "Man mags niemandt bringen: Es mag nit erhebt werden." Why is it that it cannot be removed? Is it something more serious? Somewhat, certainly: like wood that has lain long in water, and like tares, it has put down roots deeper. But that "but ..." [ἀλλ' ἄ ἄντ ὑτοῦ] seems to exist more in sounds than in the things themselves. We ourselves have also become weaker: our bodies are softened by luxury and drunkenness, and our minds are broken by the pursuit of money, ambition and sloth. For the magistrate now refuses, now does not dare, to enact good laws, and even if he enacts and promulgates them, he at once neglects them. The common people lack faith and charity, and have no hope except in the things they think cannot be lost. Hence arises that "but ..." [ἀλλ' ἴωσεγ ὑτοῦ] against what is right and good.

units.la: At Israelitis illis in suscipiendo eò, quod Dominus mandauerat, concordibus atq; fortibus felicissimè succedunt omnia. Quod quidem magistratui præbitas ad bonum occasiones vsurpanti & vt arripiantur populo persuadenti non immeritò acceptum ferimus. Vt orandus sit Dominus qui magistratus nobis velit esse bonos, cum ex ijs maxima ad rempub. bona redeat. Sed & de malo sequitur.
units.tr: But for those Israelites, who undertook what the Lord had commanded in harmony and with courage, everything succeeded most happily. For this we rightly credit the magistrate who makes use of the opportunities offered for good and persuades the people to seize them. We ought to pray that the Lord would be pleased to give us good magistrates, since great benefits for the commonwealth come from them. But let us also come to what follows concerning evil.

units.la: Exemplum mali proponit in persona decem exploratorum, qui reuersi populum ad desperationem adegere eò, effecerè vt sese miserijs & molestijs maximis obiecerint. Et id quàm vt intelligamus, primum ipsorum tum populi factum æstimandum est.
units.tr: He sets before us an example of evil in the person of the ten explorers, who on their return drove the people to despair, and brought it about that they exposed themselves to the greatest miseries and troubles. To understand this, we must first weigh their own deed and then that of the people.

units.la: Ipsorum factum in verbis plebis proponitur. Fratres nostri, inquiunt, liquefecerunt cor no-strum. Vide, exploratum missi fuerant: quid afferunt? 1. populus ille maior & excelsior nobis est. Ratio puerilis est & cogitatu & vt ea terreare. Quid enim hoc argumenti est? magno & vasto corpore præditus est, igitur inuidus fuerit. Wenn es an Ser große lege/so erlüffein Zu einhäsen. Sed & hoc ipsum quod ceu locustæ ab ipsis contemnerentur spem victoriæ potest facere. Facilè enim est eum qui te contemnat vincere. 2. Vrbes esse magnas & munitas. Et ipsum hoc nihil erat. Nam viri fortes hoc semper contemnere. Pulchrum conclave mulierum Theb. quidam appellabat vrbem munitâ. Et Alexander Magnus arcem munitâ videns, si illuc aurum ferri posset, aiebat capi posse. Nostrate prouerbio dici solet humana manu frangi posse quæcunq; ea facta fuerint. Omitto quod quo plus illis in rebus & præsidijs spei ponitur, hoc maior nascitur securitas, & ex eo fit hosti maior ad vincendum facilitas, quæ iam erat illis explorate cognita.
units.tr: Their deed is set out in the words of the people: "Our brothers," they say, "have melted our heart." Consider: they had been sent to explore; what do they bring back? (1) That people is greater and taller than we are. This reasoning is childish, both as a thought and as a means of frightening us. For what kind of argument is it? He has a large and vast body, therefore he must be fierce. "Wenn es an Ser große lege/so erlüffein Zu einhäsen." But even this, that they were despised by them as locusts, can give hope of victory, for it is easy to conquer one who despises you. (2) The cities are large and fortified. And this itself was nothing, for brave men always despise such things. A certain man (at Thebes) called a fine chamber of women a fortified city, and Alexander the Great, seeing a fortified citadel, said that it could be taken if gold could be carried up to it. A proverb of our own says that whatever has been made by human hands can be broken by human hands. I pass over the fact that the more hope is placed in such things and defences, the greater the security that is born, and from that comes greater ease for the enemy in conquering, which was already clearly known to them.

units.la: 3 Filij Enacim. At horum maiores iam vicerant: inde etiam spes esse bona poterat. Sed nihil quicquam.
units.tr: (3) The sons of Anak. But their ancestors had already conquered these, so hope could be good. Yet there was nothing at all in this.

units.la: His sermonibus, inquiunt, fratres nostri liquefecerunt cor nostrum. Quo verbo metum perditissimum significant. verba sunt Hebraea quæ quod diximus omnino sonant. Est enim הִמִּיס hiffil. à verbo נָמַס deducta forma quod significat instar ignis aliquid liquefacere. Veluti Psalmo 22. in eandem sententiam vsurpatum est. Cor meum (inquit Psalmista) sicut cera דּוֹנַג liquefactum est. Ex quo potest intelligi cor hominis, quod pulchrum est, prorsus deformatum imò destructum esse metu. Ac quemadmodum cera aut quicquid excera factum est, pulchrum est ipsum quidem, sed igne totum absumitur: sic cor humanum multis magnis præclarisque muneribus exornatum, pium, sapiens, forte est, & virtutes maximas affert, verum admonitis illis ignibus totum absumitur, vt illarum virtutum nulla sit ac manet. reliqua: non amplius sapit, nihil audet, nihil potest, ist der man nit einer schlehen[?] wert/ob er gleich von lyb groß/starck/vnd hüpsch ist. Eiusmodi factos se esse dicunt Israelitæ sermonibus improbis malorum magistratuum.
units.tr: "By these speeches," they say, "our brothers have melted our heart." By this word they signify the most destructive fear. The words are Hebrew, and they sound just as we have said. For the form הִמִּיס [hiphil] is derived from the verb נָמַס, which means to melt something as fire does. In the same sense it is used in Psalm 22: "My heart," says the Psalmist, "is melted like wax [דּוֹנַג]." From this it can be understood that the human heart, which is beautiful, is utterly deformed and indeed destroyed by fear. Just as wax, or whatever is made of wax, is beautiful in itself but is wholly consumed by fire, so the human heart, adorned with many great and excellent gifts, is pious, wise and brave, and brings forth the greatest virtues, but when those fires are applied it is wholly consumed, so that none of those virtues remains. It no longer has wisdom, dares nothing, can do nothing. "Ist der man nit einer schlehen wert, ob er gleich von lyb groß, starck, vnd hüpsch ist." Such is the state, the Israelites say, into which they were brought by the wicked words of the evil magistrates.

units.la: Eò res deueniunt si cuiq; quidlibet dicendi potestas est, præsertim in ciuitate libera. Ibi su[?] furri plurimum nocent: sed magistratuum desperabundi sermones longè sunt pestilentiores. Etenim si tu qui magistratum geris de emendatione morum desperare, te fateare, quid tuos hosce sermones audiēs homo plebeius cogitet? quid dicat aliud, quàm si tu desperes quid ipse speret? Malum est inde per te deduci quò duci debebant homines. Sua sponte illuc ibant: te duce redeundum erat in viâ.
units.tr: Things come to this when each person has the power to say whatever he likes, especially in a free city. There rumours do the most harm, but the despairing speeches of magistrates are far more pestilential. For if you, who bear the magistracy, confess that you despair of the amendment of morals, what does a common man think when he hears these words of yours? What else does he say than: if you despair, what does he himself hope for? It is harmful for you to lead men to where they ought to be led. They were going there of their own accord; with you as leader, they had to turn back on the way.

units.la: Sed vt intelligas sermonibus improbis vitiari mores probos, iam factū plebis commemorat. 1. Noluerunt ascendere: sind jrs fürnemmens[?] abgstanden. Hoc sequitur ex illa stolida creduli-tate. Non temere credendum est etiam ijs qui sibi videntur rem exploraste cognouisse: potuit fieri, vt peregrinarentur sensibus, non omnia aduerterent, cognita non bona fide recenseant. Quin natura cum omnibus partibus orationis conferenda est, & qui sit qui dicat, & quare, & quomodo dicat considerandum. Atque his quidem opponenda promissa & anteaćta eodem q; modo in cæteris.
units.tr: But so that you may understand that good morals are spoiled by wicked speeches, he now recalls the deed of the people. (1) "They were unwilling to go up." "Sind jrs fürnemmens abgstanden": they gave up their undertaking. This follows from that foolish credulity. One must not rashly believe even those who seem to themselves to have known the matter well. It may be that they wandered in their senses, did not notice everything, and report what they knew without good faith. Indeed, the nature of the matter must be compared with every part of the speech, and it must be considered who is speaking, why, and how. Against these things must be set the promises and past deeds, in the same way as for the rest.

units.la: 2 Aeterbastis[?] es Domini: Hoc est, dulces illius promissiones vos quasi felle infectas insidias accepistis,& odio vestri susceptum hoc consilium. Amore & benevolentia Dominus eos eduxerat, vt est Exod. 1. & 3. id illi in malam partem vertunt atque accipiunt, metu mali dementati. Sic fit, fidelis in bonum accipit omnia, in malum impius. An quia mala patimur, ideo videatur nos odisse Dominus? Amauit Abelem, & tamen ab eo mortem diram non repulit. Nohe, Abraham, Loth, Iacob, Ioseph, Iob, Dauid, Prophetæ, vnigenitus filius, apostoli, quos Deus pater omnes habuit charissimos, mala maxima perpesi sunt. Caue quæ Deus iuuandi tui studio facti-tat, ea tu tui perdendi causa fieri dictites. Atque hoc eos conqueri tantò peius est, quod mali nihil dum passi fuerant. Satis mature accusassent iniuriarum, vbi illata fuisset. Quin ipso hoc nomine etiam ipsi in Deum sunt iniurij quòd de malo nondum accepto querelas euomunt.
units.tr: (2) "The Lord hates you." That is: you took his sweet promises as snares infected with gall, and this plan was undertaken out of hatred of you. The Lord had led them out in love and goodwill, as in Exod. 1. and 3.; they turn this to the bad and take it so, madmen with fear of evil. Thus the faithful take all things for good, the impious for evil. Or because we suffer evils, does the Lord seem to hate us? He loved Abel, and yet did not spare him a dire death. Noah, Abraham, Lot, Jacob, Joseph, Job, David, the prophets, the only-begotten Son, the apostles, whom God the Father held all most dear, suffered the greatest evils. Beware lest you call what God does out of zeal to help you something done for your destruction. And it is so much worse that they complain when they had not yet suffered any evil. They would have complained of wrongs soon enough, once they had been inflicted. Indeed, by this very complaint they themselves wrong God, in that they pour out grievances about evil not yet received.

units.la: 3 In tam desperatam, desperationem lapsi sunt, vt nullis etiam optimis argumentis erigi possent. Idq; ex Mosis oratione colligitur. Qui quidem ne timeant eis conatur persuadere. 1. Deus præcedit. Non ipse vos præire iubet sibi cauens post principia: quin ceu optimus impera tor vos præcedit, viam facit, vos tantùm præeuntem sequimini.
units.tr: 3 They have fallen into such a desperate despair that not even the best arguments can raise them up. This is gathered from Moses' speech, and he tries to persuade them not to be afraid. (1) God goes before you. He does not order you to go in front of him, guarding himself behind the vanguard. Rather, like an excellent commander, he goes before you, makes the way, and you only follow him as he goes ahead.

units.la: 2 Pugnat pro vobis. Ille vires ministrat, quod hactenus cognouerant.
units.tr: 2 He fights for you. He supplies the strength, as you have experienced up to now.

units.la: 3 Vt infantem gestauit.
units.tr: 3 As he carried the infant.

units.la: 4 Singula castra vobis sixit, quasi loca tuta monstrans.
units.tr: 4 He pitched each camp for you, showing you places that were safe.

units.la: Vide quanta auxilia. Quæ ad victoriam requiruntur ijs rebus omnibus diuintus præditi fuerant, scilicet numine propitio, viribus diuinis, cura ac prouidétia diuina, militari disciplina, prorsus diuina. Quis timeat quando Deus viæ dux est, vires suppeditat, rebus necessarijs & tu tela prospicit, gubernatione recta continet? Optimæ quidem sunt illæ rationes, sed tamen his ipsis apud desperabundos nihil efficitur. Atque eò res deueniunt culpa malorum magistratuum, qui se suosque eunt perditum. Igitur qui sibi bene consultum[?] cupiunt mali, exemplum cauant, imitentur bonum. Id faxit Deus in Christo Iesu. Amen.
units.tr: See how great the aids are. Everything required for victory was divinely provided: a propitious divine power, divine strength, divine care and providence, military discipline, all wholly divine. Who would fear when God is the leader of the way, supplies strength, watches over the weapons, and holds all things in check by right government? Those reasons are indeed excellent, yet among the despairing they achieve nothing at all. And things come to this pass through the fault of wicked magistrates, who ruin themselves and their people. Therefore let those who desire their own good beware the bad example and imitate the good. May God grant this in Christ Jesus. Amen.

units.la: SERMO VII.
units.tr: Sermon 7.

units.la: 34 Audiuit itaq; Dominus vocem verborum vestrorum, & indignatione commo tus, iurauit in hanc formam.
units.tr: 34 And the Lord heard the voice of your words, and being moved with indignation, he swore, saying:

units.la: 35 Nemo ex istis viris, & ex hac praua generatione videbit terram istà bonam, quam iuraui me daturum patribus vestris.
units.tr: 35 Not one of these men, of this evil generation, shall see that good land which I swore to give to your fathers.

units.la: 36 Præter Caleb filium Iephunæ is videbit eam, atq; ei dabo terram, quam calca uit, atq; filijs eius, eò quod perfectè implerit post Dominum.
units.tr: 36 Except Caleb the son of Jephunneh: he shall see it, and to him will I give the land on which he trod, and to his sons, because he has fully followed the Lord.

units.la: 37 Etiam contra me iratus est Dominus vestri causa, vt diceret, Neq; tu illuc venies.
units.tr: 37 The Lord was angry with me also because of you, saying: Neither shalt thou go in thither.

units.la: 38 Iehosua vero filius Nun, qui coram te stat, is introibit in eam, hunc corrobo-ra, nam is distribuet hanc terram Israelitis.
units.tr: 38 But Joshua the son of Nun, who stands before you, he shall go in. Encourage him, for he shall divide this land among Israel.

units.la: 40 Et pubes vestra quam dixistis prædam fore, & liberi vestri qui hodie inter bonum & malum nihil discernunt, ij ingredientur illuc, & illis dabo eam, ipsiq; eam occupabunt.
units.tr: 40 And your children, whom you said would be a prey, and your sons, who today cannot distinguish between good and evil, they shall go in there, and I will give it to them, and they shall possess it.

units.la: 40 Vos autem conuersi proficiscemini versus desertum viam maris careftofi.
units.tr: 40 But you, turning back, shall set out for the desert by the way of the Red Sea.

units.la: QVos honores quasq; utilitates ex bonorum magistratuum fide, & diligentia, atq; etiam ex obedientia populi tota ciuitas percipiat: quantam contra perniciem atq; ignominiam cum sibi tum suis subditis magistratus accersant improbitate & negnitie, Moses his ipsis verbis quae concione proxima commemorauimus atq; exposuimus suo ipsius & explorato- rum decem exemplo docuit. Iam vero Dei super hac relatam sententiam introducit, qua signi- ficat quid Deus de bonis & de malis magistratibus sentiat: quodq; sit eiusdem de plebis obe- dientis & inobedientis moribus iudicium. Atq; hoc quidem loco primum inobedientiam gene- ratim omnem damnat, tum quid sentiat partium enumeratione explicat, deniq; concludit to- tum negotium.
units.tr: How great the honours and benefits that a whole state receives from the faithfulness and diligence of good magistrates, and from the obedience of the people, and how great the ruin and disgrace that magistrates bring upon themselves and their subjects through wickedness and negligence, Moses taught by his own example and that of the spies, in the very words we recalled and expounded at the last sermon. Now he introduces God's judgment on this matter, by which he shows what God thinks of good and bad magistrates, and what his judgment is on the conduct of an obedient and a disobedient people. In this passage he first condemns disobedience in general, then explains what he thinks by listing the parts, and finally concludes the whole matter.

units.la: Summatim. Audiuit itaq; Dominus vocem verborum vestrorum & indignatione commotus in rauit[?]. Quibus verbis indicat Deum sensisse & improborum magistratuum & ipsius plebis per fidiam, eamq; tulisse egerrime, & iuramento sententiam condemnante firmasse. Qui locus egregius est, videlicet & plebi & magistratui indicans Deum res humanas cernere, mala ferre aegerrimo animo, iudicio seuero & constanti illa vindicare. Quibus partibus huius rei summa ac capput comprehenditur.
units.tr: In summary: And the Lord heard the voice of your words, and being moved with indignation, swore. By these words he indicates that God perceived the perfidy both of the wicked magistrates and of the people themselves, that he took it very grievously, and that he confirmed his condemning sentence with an oath. This is an outstanding passage, showing both people and magistrates that God sees human affairs, bears evil with a most grieved mind, and avenges it with a severe and constant judgment. In these parts the sum and chief point of the matter is contained.

units.la: Humanas res cernere eo ipso dicitur, quod Moses ait ab eo voce illorum verborum auditam esse. Atq; hoc ipsum scriptura passim inculcat omnibus hominibus magistratui scilicet & plebi. Magistratum videre se testis est Psal.8z. Deus (inquit psalthes) stat in medio Deorum iudicans ipsos. Quare meminerint se Deum habere testem suarum actionum, & assessorem, & spectatorem, & quasi quendam coryceum in iudicia sua, recta ne sint an iniqua prorsus intentu. Quod qui cogitant multo minus & errabunt & peccabunt in ferendis sententijs. Neq; enim erunt negligentes, sed quanta maxima poterunt diligentia rimabūtur ac ponderabunt omnia: neq; etiam ab eo quod bonum & aequum norunt ulla siue spe lucri, seu fauoris, siue metu mali diuelli poterunt. Hoc si ministri Isabellae reginae Israeliticae, qui Nabothum hominem innocentem condemnarunt, aut Pilatus Christum condemnans secu reputassent, minimè sic deliquissent. Rectius Iosephus Arimatheensis, qui senatui Christum condemnanti interesse noluit.
units.tr: That God sees human affairs is said by this very fact, that Moses says his voice was heard in those words. Scripture repeatedly impresses this on all men, magistrates and people alike. That magistrates are seen by him is witnessed by Psalm 82: "God," says the psalmist, "stands in the assembly of gods, judging them." Therefore let them remember that they have God as the witness of their actions, as assessor, as observer, and as a kind of spectator of their judgments, whether they are right or altogether unjust. Those who consider this will be much less likely to err and sin in pronouncing sentences. For they will not be negligent, but will search out and weigh all things with the greatest diligence they can, and they will not be torn away from what they know to be good and fair by any hope of gain, or of favour, or by fear of harm. If the ministers of Jezebel, the Israelite queen, who condemned the innocent man Naboth, or Pilate, when he condemned Christ, had considered this, they would never have sinned as they did. Joseph of Arimathea acted more rightly, who refused to take part in the condemnation of Christ by the senate.

units.la: Caeterum hoc ipsum non minus plebeijs hominibus cogitandum est quàm magistratibus: his enim homines etiam occulatissimos fallere fortasse non est adeo difficile: sed Deum fallere nequeunt, nec si id tentarint, manus eius euadere. Sed & in excelso throno, sed nihilominus & coelestia & terrena videt omnia: nam & humiles euehit & steriles facit matres: superbos autem agit praecipites. Egregie describit hoc Psal.112. Egregie etiam dictū est illud àDiuo Basilio. Οὐδ᾽ἐν(inquit)ἀπεγνόντον ὡς ἠμεληένον παρὰ θεῷ, πάντα σκοπεύει ὁ ἀκοίμητος ὀφθαλμός, πᾶσι πάρεστι σκοπιζον ἐκάστῳ τῶν σωτηρίαν[?]. Idem exempla significant. Gen.2. Abelis sanguis illius ad aures clamans penetrauit. Gen.6. Malitia carnis in conspectum eius ascendit. Gen.19. Sodomae iniquitas audita ab illo est. Esa.5. emptiones locupletum in auribus Domini sonuerunt. Haec cogitata faciunt cautos & officij sui studiosos populos, haec neglecta faciunt impios atq; improbos. Nullae tam clandestinae sunt artes, insidiae, machinae, quin has ille cognouerit: nihil tam magno astu potentium est supressum, quod ille vel sub maxima mole non vide at esse positum. Haec non cogitata faciunt vt trutina, mensura, dolis, scelere turbes conscientia. Atq; hoc quidem hic inculcat Moses dicens, Deum audisse verba populi murmurantis.
units.tr: But this same thing must be considered no less by common people than by magistrates. For it may perhaps not be so difficult to deceive men, even the most watchful; but they cannot deceive God, nor, if they try, escape his hand. He sees all things, both heavenly and earthly, from his high throne: for he exalts the humble and makes barren mothers fruitful, but he casts the proud down headlong. Psalm 112 describes this admirably. Admirably also said is that saying of the divine Basil: "Not even those who despair, thinking themselves neglected by God: the unsleeping eye observes all things, and it is present to each as a watchman for the salvation of all." [Οὐδ᾽ ἐν ἀπογνόντων ὡς ἀμελουμένων παρὰ θεῷ, πάντα σκοπεύει ὁ ἀκοίμητος ὀφθαλμός, πᾶσι πάρεστι σκοπιὸς ἑκάστῳ τῶν σωτηρίαν]. The examples also show the same. Gen. 2: Abel's blood reached his ears, crying out. Gen. 6: the wickedness of the flesh came up before his face. Gen. 19: the iniquity of Sodom was heard by him. Isa. 5: the purchases of the rich sounded in the ears of the Lord. Such thoughts make peoples careful and eager for their duty; neglect of them makes men impious and wicked. There are no arts, plots, or machinations so secret that he has not known them; nothing done by the great cunning of the powerful is so hidden that he does not see it set down, even under the greatest mass of things. Thoughts of this kind not being entertained, the scales, the measures, and the frauds and crimes of deceit trouble the conscience. And this is exactly what Moses insists on here, saying that God heard the words of the murmuring people.

units.la: Sed his addit etiā vt placeat: dicit enim irasci, imo dicit eum indignatione grauiter commotum esse. Nam [illegible, ~6 letters] iram grauem & oppido quam vehementem significat, quippe quod spumam etiam qui indignantiū fere est propria simul innuat. Vnde & lxx. Interpretes eū παροξυνόντα, hoc est, concitatum, irritatum, acerbatum dicunt. Quid verbis opus est: iram maximam spiritus sanctus significat. Sed quid? an Deus affectibus obnoxius est? minimè vero, cur hic irasci dicitur? Locutio est à sensu nostro ducta, qua spiritus sanctus haec scribens innuit rem gestā Deo mirum in modum displicuisse. Vt enim nos eas ob res irascimur quae nobis vehementer displicent, sicq; huic nostrę naturae omnes assueuimus, vt nisi quis ob rem factam irascatur, ea nō offensus esse videatur, sed sit ne an non sus- deq; ferre. Ex quo potest intelligi, Deum ijs rebus vehementer offendi, quibus iratus esse in scripturis dicitur. Iam vero quoniam murmuranti- bus illis iratus esse dicitur, indubium est illi magnopere displicuisse.
units.tr: But he adds something more, so that it may be pleasing: for he says that God was angry, indeed that he was greatly moved with indignation. For [illegible, about six letters] signifies a grave and very vehement anger, since it also suggests the foaming that is almost the mark of the indignant. Hence the Seventy translators render it as provoked, that is, stirred up, irritated, embittered. Why use many words? The Holy Spirit signifies the greatest anger. But what then? Is God subject to passions? By no means. Why then is he said to be angry here? It is an expression drawn from our own feeling, by which the Holy Spirit, writing these things, indicates that the deed done displeased God in a remarkable way. For just as we are angry at those things that displease us greatly, and we are so accustomed to this nature of ours that unless someone is angry at a deed done, he seems not to be offended by it but to be able to bear it with indifference, from this it can be understood that God is greatly offended by those things at which he is said in the Scriptures to be angry. Now, since he is said to be angry with those who murmured, it is beyond doubt that the thing greatly displeased him.

units.la: In quo videmus quantum nefas sit magistratum qui seruandæ ciuitati datus sit, eam sua per dere perfidia: itemque vt magnum scelus sit plebem malis potius magistratibus contra Deum quam bonis obsequi. Vult enim Deus & ciuitatem & magistratus suis ipsorum operis mutuis conseruare: illi contra se mutuum ambo eunt perditum. Ideo Moses Deum irasci dicit: nec desunt Mosem in hoc adiuuantia prophetarum suffragia. Esa. 1. Cum dixisset principes infideles, socios furum, amantes munerum, negligentes pupillos atque viduas, addit hoc, propterea ait Dominus Deus exercituum, heu ego consolabor super hostibus meis & vindictam sumam de inimicis meis. Esa. 24. cum dixisset, quia transgresi sunt leges, mutauerunt ius, disipauerunt foedus sempiternum, subiicit, Cataractæ de excelsis aperientur, & concutientur fundamenta terræ, confractione confringetur terra, agitatione agitabitur sicut ebrius. Prouer. 16. in iustitia firmabitur solium. Ciuitates paceæ sunt in quibus ciues pascendi fuerant: sed magistratus atque viri principes in his se ipsi solent pascere, vides enim vt iudicibus, & lictoribus & notarijs opima sint in egentium hominum marsupijs posita vectigalia. Sed sunt irati Dei minime vana minimeq; leuia indicia, tempestates, terræmotus, pruinæ, grandines, annonæ caritas in magna rerum copia atq; frugum omnium prouentibus vberrimis, itemq;, bella & clades publicæ, deniq; maledictio omnium conatuum humanorum publica <bl>sic Chastenbeit ferbet vß</bl>. Vt tabes​cent homines sic refpub.sensim consumuntur. Nam pulmo reip.Christianæ exulceratus est, hypocrisi scilicet & adulatione, & simulando dissimulandoq; deperdita veritate. Exempla noua & vetera tot sunt, vt referri, præsertim in præsentia nequeant.
units.tr: In this we see how great a wickedness it is for a magistrate, who has been given to preserve the state, to ruin it by his own faithlessness; and likewise how great a crime it is for the people to obey wicked magistrates rather than good ones, against God. For God wills both the state and the magistrates to be preserved by their mutual work; but they, on the contrary, both go to ruin together. Therefore Moses says that God is angry, and the testimonies of the prophets are not lacking to help Moses in this. Isa. 1: when he had spoken of unfaithful princes, companions of thieves, lovers of bribes, neglecting orphans and widows, he adds this: "Therefore says the Lord God of hosts: Ah, I will be comforted over my enemies, and I will take vengeance on my adversaries." Isa. 24: when he had said, "Because they have transgressed the laws, changed the right, broken the everlasting covenant," he adds, "The floodgates from on high shall be opened, and the foundations of the earth shall be shaken; the earth shall be broken with a breaking, shall be moved with a moving like a drunken man." Prov. 16: "By righteousness the throne shall be established." Cities are at peace in which the citizens were fed; but magistrates and leading men are accustomed to feed themselves in these cities, for you see that the taxes placed in the purses of poor men are rich pickings for judges, lictors and clerks. But the signs of God's anger are not vain or trivial: tempests, earthquakes, frosts, hailstorms, dearth amid great abundance of goods and most plentiful yields of all crops, likewise wars and public disasters, and finally the curse on all human undertakings, public: <bl>sic Chastenbeit ferbet vß</bl>. As men waste away, so the commonwealth is gradually consumed. For the lung of the Christian commonwealth has been ulcerated, namely by hypocrisy and flattery, the truth being lost through pretending and dissimulating. The examples, new and old, are so many that they cannot be recounted, especially at present.

units.la: Sed ad tam deperditas mores quid quæso dicit Dominus? Iurauit, inquit, non ingressuros in terram illam. Et hoc ipsum sceleris magnitudinem significat. Nam quæ Deus iuramento suo asserit ea tam certa sunt, vt non posint nō esse certissima. Nā si quod hominis iuramento promissum est, pro vero & certo accipis. Cur de eo quod iurauit se facturū Dominus sit dubium? Ergo hoc ipso Moses innuit sententiā contra hoc scelus diuinitus latam esse eam à quo nemini fassit ad vllū alium iudicem appellatione prouocare. Ergo magistratui recta bonaq; iubenti non obtemperare, sed impijs à Deo seuocantibus obsequi scelus eiusmodi est quod terræ benedictæ possessione, hoc est, sine humanæ vitæ, felicitate scilicet homines exuit. Vnde fit vt mise​ri sint, & perditi, quicunq; bonis legibus reluctantur.
units.tr: But what, I ask, does the Lord say to such abandoned morals? He swore that they would not enter that land. This very thing signifies the greatness of the crime. For what God affirms by his oath is so certain that it cannot fail to be most certain. If you accept as true and certain what a man has promised by oath, why should there be doubt about what the Lord has sworn he will do? By this very statement Moses indicates that a sentence has been pronounced by God against this crime, and that God, to whom no one may appeal to any other judge, has pronounced it. So to refuse obedience to a magistrate who commands what is right and good, and to obey impious men who call us away from God, is a crime of this kind: it strips men of possession of the blessed land, that is, of the happiness of human life. Hence it follows that all who resist good laws are wretched and lost.

units.la: Atque his quidem verbis Moses docuit summam ac caput eius quod Deus de malis magistratibus atq; ciuibus tulerit iudicij, quando indicauit illum hæc omnia cernere, ei vehementer displicepe, illis grauissimam pœnam minitari.
units.tr: In these words Moses has taught the sum and chief point of the judgment that God has pronounced against wicked magistrates and citizens, since he shows that he sees all these things, that he is greatly displeased with them, and that he threatens them with the gravest punishment.

units.la: Expositio particularis sequitur, qua de singulis ciuibus quid statuerit edocet. 1. De viris istis, & c. nemo ingredietur. Quibus verbis & magistratus, & plebeia quæ secuta fuerat, simul intelligit, simul enim omnes generationem prauam vocat, veluti Baptista progeniem viperarū, & Christus prauam sobolem seu diabolo genitos, & prophetæ filios Belial apellant. Veluti Germani dicunt, ein Gösse Bube Funde Gott von güter ärd nit an.
units.tr: A particular exposition follows, in which he teaches what he has decided concerning each class of citizens. 1. Of these men, etc.: none shall enter. By these words he understands both the magistrates and the common people who followed them, for he calls them all a wicked generation, as the Baptist calls them a brood of vipers, Christ calls them a wicked seed begotten of the devil, and the prophets call them sons of Belial. As the Germans say: "a bastard, a rascal, a fiend; God and good earth will not endure him."

units.la: Sed ne temere eis notam hanc inustam putes Num. 14. peccatum ipsum plenius describitur. Quo in loco dicuntur. 1. abusi esse Dei longanimitate. 2. obsignatis promissionibus fidem non habuisse. 3. Deum tentasse. 4. vocem eius audire noluisse. 5. Deum irritasse. 6. scortati esse. 7. aduersus Deum conspirasse. 8. de eius fide conquesti esse. 9. tam bonam terram respuisse. Ex quibus quasi partibus quale peccatum sit inobedientia perspicuum est.
units.tr: But lest you think that this mark is branded on them carelessly, the sin itself is described more fully in Numbers 14. In that passage they are said: (1) to have abused God's patience; (2) to have not believed his sealed promises; (3) to have tempted God; (4) to have refused to hear his voice; (5) to have provoked God; (6) to have played the harlot; (7) to have conspired against God; (8) to have complained about his faithfulness; (9) to have spurned so good a land. From these parts, as it were, it is plain what kind of sin disobedience is.

units.la: Sed pœnam dicit; Non videbunt terram istam bonam: ac proditores morte subita, reli​qui partim bello, partim peste sublati sunt omnes vt indigni benedictæ terræ possessione exclusi.
units.tr: But he speaks of the punishment: They shall not see that good land. And the traitors were all carried off by sudden death, and the rest partly by war, partly by plague, all excluded as unworthy of possession of the blessed land.

units.la: Sic euenit impijs quod metuunt. Et indigni sunt pace, qui illam contra Deum quærunt: eodem modo censendum est de bonis reliquis.
units.tr: Thus what the wicked fear befalls them. And those who seek peace against God are unworthy of it. The same judgment must be made about the rest of the good.

units.la: 2 De Chalebo dicit Dominus. Is simul & omnes eius posteri terram illam & videbunt & possidebunt, quia Domino satisfecerit. In quo proponitur exemplum boni viri: qui mandata Dei exequitur. Nam & vestes scindit, & desperatos plebis animos erigit. In earum virtutum studium omnibus hominibus in primisq; magistratibus est incumbendum. Sed cedo premium. Plebs quidem eum vult obruere lapidibus, verum Deus eum coronat ac terræ Cananeæ fruitione dignum iudicat. Sic Ioannes Baptista, Stephanus, apostoli, Christus ipse, quia pro Dei patris gloria & pro salute publica cum impijs hominibus decertarunt, ab illis quidem ipsis morte, & infamia sunt obruti, sed à Deo sempiternis premijs, atq; laudibus digni habiti. Idem enitere quisquis pius es & studiosus salutis publicæ.
units.tr: 2. Concerning Caleb the Lord says: He and all his posterity shall both see and possess that land, because he has fully followed the Lord. In this a pattern of a good man is set forth, one who carries out God's commands. For he tears his garments and raises up the despairing spirits of the people. Every man, and above all magistrates, must labour for the pursuit of these virtues. But consider the reward. The people indeed wish to stone him, but God crowns him and judges him worthy of enjoying the land of Canaan. So John the Baptist, Stephen, the apostles, and Christ himself, because they contended with wicked men for the glory of God the Father and for the public welfare, were overwhelmed by those very men with death and infamy, but were counted worthy by God of everlasting rewards and praises. Strive to do the same, whoever you are that are godly and zealous for the public welfare.

units.la: 3 De Mose quam sententiam tulerit ipse indicat. Etiam (inquit) contra me iratus Dominus dixit, &c. dixit, etc. Peccati sui quod Num.20. describitur causam dicit, populi pertinaciam, qua victus non ita vti par erat Domino suam debitā gloriam dederit. Quod Procopius exponens quomo do Deus Mosi propter populum iratus fit, sic docet. Ἐγὼ δὲ φησὶ ὅτι ἀπειθήσατε τῆς ἐμῆς φωνῆς, ἃ ὑμᾶς διὰ τὸ ἀποθνῄσκειν ... Sed peccatum ipsum etiā alibi notatur. Esa.3. magnum di citur. Psalm.106. populus ipse & Deum & Mosem irritasse dicitur. Deus ipse dicit in Num. Quia non credidistis. Apparet in verbis quaedā diffidentia. Vt sanctificaretis me, scilicet oratio ne pia ac sancta coram populo habita. Vides quanta sit in Deo constantia, iustitia contra quan- tum scelus affectibus populi cedere. Certe eiusmodi vt terrae promissae possessione excludat Mosem.
units.tr: 3. Concerning Moses, the sentence he himself pronounced is indicated: The Lord was angry with me also, saying, etc. He gives the cause of his own sin, described in Numbers 20: the stubbornness of the people, by which, being overcome, he did not give the Lord his due glory as he should have. Procopius, expounding how God was angry with Moses on account of the people, teaches thus: "But I say that you have disobeyed my voice, which ... because of dying ..." [Ἐγὼ δὲ φησὶ ὅτι ἀπειθήσατε τῆς ἐμῆς φωνῆς, ἃ ὑμᾶς διὰ τὸ ἀποθνῄσκειν ...] But the sin itself is noted elsewhere too: it is called great in Isaiah 3, and in Psalm 106 the people themselves are said to have provoked both God and Moses. God himself says in Numbers: Because you did not believe. In the words there appears a certain distrust, that you might sanctify me, namely in the pious and holy address delivered before the people. See how great is God's constancy and justice, and how much wickedness, by contrast, yields to the passions of the people. Certainly it is of such a kind that it excludes Moses from possession of the promised land.

units.la: 4 De Iosua dicit: Qui coram te stat, id est, minister tuus est: is videbit, dividet, possidebit eam. Hic honos habitus est ministro fideli. Sic Dauid loco Saulis rex factus. Virtute sua semper pa- rata praemia.
units.tr: 4. Concerning Joshua he says: He who stands before you, that is, your minister, he shall see it, divide it, and possess it. This honour was given to a faithful minister. So David was made king in place of Saul. Rewards always stand ready for virtue.

units.la: 5 Pubes vestra quae videbatur praeda futura, & liberi, quibus quid inter bonum & malum in tereffet nondum adhuc fuit cognitum, intrabunt. Quia inermes erant & imprudentes, ideo vi dentur praeda fore, ipsi vero tuti, quia adulti essent: sed contra ac rationem ipsi inierant, accidit. In Dei potentia ac viribus salus omnis est posita. Liberi tui non erunt praeda tutoribus. Simi- lis pueri fias necesse est, siquidem ingredi in regnum Dei velis. Atqui sic habemus quis sit bono rum & malorum finis.
units.tr: 5. Your youth, which seemed destined to be booty, and your children, who did not yet know the difference between good and evil, shall enter. Because they were unarmed and inexperienced, they seemed destined to be booty, while those who were grown up would be safe; but things turned out contrary to what they had reasoned. All safety lies in the power and strength of God. Your children will not be booty for their guardians. You must become like a child, if you wish to enter the kingdom of God. And so we have here what the end of good and evil men is.

units.la: Concludit: Vos autem (inquit) reuertimini mare versus, etc. Quasi dicat: Summa, quia redi- re mauultis quàm progredi, agite redite: & oportet quidem vos redire. Vides quid sit male con- fulere, & malis consultoribus obsequi: nempe retrocedere, hoc est deficere viribus atque opi- bus, pessum ire. Vides quàm iustus, seuerus, & constans sit Deus in condemnandis ijs qui magi stratus donum sibi diuinitus datum sic contaminant.
units.tr: He concludes: But you, turn back, toward the sea, etc. As if he said: Since you prefer to turn back rather than go forward, go on and turn back; and indeed you must turn back. You see what it is to take bad counsel and to obey bad counsellors: namely, to go backward, that is, to fail in strength and resources, and to go to ruin. You see how just, severe, and constant God is in condemning those who so defile the office of magistrate given to them by God.

units.la: Felices fuere ciuitates ex quibus essent boni magistratus: perditae contra quibus mali. Quin etiam ex vno atqui altero principis peccato saepe magnam cladem accepit tota ciuitas: contra virtute principum respublicae mirum in modum auctae sunt. Propter Pharaonis feuiti am & crudelitatem & pertinaciam populus Aegyptius cum alias atqui alias accepit clades, tum vero simul vniuersus tandem marinis aquis cum immani atqui iniusto principe suffocatus inte rijt. Propter Dauidis peccatum percussa sunt in populo septuaginta virorum millia. Sed Iose- phi, Moisi, Iosuae, Dauidis, Iosiae aliorumque similium virtute Deus ciuitates mirum in modum auxit. Id ipsum nostra tempestate cernimus. Dum magistratus euangelij bonarumq; legum studio feruerent, & in hoc toti incumberent, vt pietas & probitas florerent, tunc optime habe bant omnia: iam vero in contemptum euangelij & in improbitatem conuersis eorum studijs, clades aliae alijs cumulatae passim ingruunt.
units.tr: Cities were happy whose magistrates were good, and lost whose magistrates were wicked.
