Indeed, often a whole city has suffered great disaster because of the single sin of one or another ruler; on the other hand, the commonwealths have been wonderfully increased by the virtue of their rulers. Because of the savagery, cruelty and obstinacy of Pharaoh, the Egyptian people suffered now one plague and now another, and at last the whole people, together with their monstrous and unjust prince, perished, drowned in the sea waters. Because of David's sin, seventy thousand men were struck down among the people. But by the virtue of Joseph, Moses, Joshua, David, Josiah and others like them, God wonderfully increased cities. We see this same thing in our own time. While magistrates were zealous for the gospel and for good laws, and devoted themselves wholly to making piety and uprightness flourish, all things were then in the best state; but now that their zeal has been turned to contempt of the gospel and to wickedness, various disasters, heaped one upon another, rush in everywhere.

units.la: Quamobrem omnibus in repub. priuatis pariter & magistratu fungentibus hominibus cogitandum est Deum omnia quae geruntur cernere, mala ferre aegerrime, eademq; feuerisi- me vindicare: tum bonos praemijs, malos supplicijs afficere. Quae cogitatio faciet, vt magistra- tus quidem ipsi bene imperent, plebs autem recta praecipientibus obediat: hocq; modo simul ambo conferuentur, per Iesum Christum dominum nostrum. Amen.
units.tr: Therefore all people in the commonwealth, both private citizens and those who hold magistracy, ought to consider that God sees all that is done, bears evil most grievously, avenges it most severely, and rewards good men with prizes and punishes the wicked with penalties. This thought will make magistrates govern well, and the common people obey those who give right commands; and in this way both will be preserved together, through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

units.la: SERMO VIII.
units.tr: SERMON VIII.

units.la: 41 Et respondentes dixistis mihi, Peccauimus Domino, ascendemus, & propu- gnabimus iuxta omnia quae praecepit nobis Dominus Deus noster: Et accinctus est quisque armis suis bellicis, mutuoq; adhortati estis ad ascendendum in montem.
units.tr: 41 And you answered and said to me, We have sinned against the Lord; we will go up and fight, according to all that the Lord our God commanded us. And every man girded on his weapons of war, and you were eager to go up into the mountain.

units.la: 42 Et dixit Dominus ad me, Dic eis, Ne ascendatis, neque pugnetis, ego enim non sum in medio vestri, ne affligemini ante hostes vestros.
units.tr: 42 And the Lord said to me, Tell them, Do not go up and do not fight, for I am not in the midst of you, lest you be struck down before your enemies.

units.la: 43 Loquebar igitur vobis, at vos non audiebatis, sed exacerbantes os Domini, insolenter ascendebatis in montem.
units.tr: 43 So I spoke to you, but you would not listen; you rebelled against the mouth of the Lord and went up into the mountain presumptuously.

units.la: 44 Egressus Amorraeus qui habitabat in monte illo, obuiam vobis, persequutae est vos quemadmodum apes facere solent, & percussit vos in Seir vsque Horma.
units.tr: 44 Then the Amorite who dwelt in that mountain came out against you, and pursued you as bees do, and struck you down in Seir as far as Hormah.

units.la: 45 Et reuersi fletis coram Domino, & Dominus non audiuit vocem vestram, & non attendit vos.
units.tr: 45 And you returned and wept before the Lord, but the Lord did not hear your voice nor give ear to you.

units.la: Sententia Dei de Iosua.
units.tr: The sentence of God concerning Joshua.

units.la: Magistratus virtutes comme modi, viti ve ro damna ma ximae plebi asse runt.
units.tr: The virtues of magistrates bring the greatest good to the common people, and their vices the greatest harm.

units.la: Sedistis itaq; in Cades diebus multis, secundū dies videlicet, quibus manifestis.
units.tr: So you dwelt in Kadesh many days, that is, for the number of days during which...

units.la: NEmo est eorum qui verbi diuini simul ac rerum humanarum vsum aliquem habent, quin & ex ipso Dei verbo & ex humanarum rerū decursu explorarè cognitum habeat, quod satan generis nostri pertinacissimus hostis in angelum lucis se transformat, ac rebus pe[r]fimis & turpissimis boni pariter & honesti colorem [splendoremq;] illinit, nempe vt dementa ti & seducti pro eo quod bonum atq; pulchrum est, id quod turpe est & malum amplexi in ea dem, quibus ipse est illapsus, mala incidamus. Qua de causa nobis æquè atq; trapezitis numerorum cognitio boni simul ac mali necessaria est: vt amplecti bonū, fugere verò & odisse malum queamus. Eò Moses respiciens proposita atq; explicata obedientiæ, vt eræ doctrinæ, iuxta que, vt bene contemplemur, inobedientiæ fine ob oculos posito suam aduersus satanæ dolos munit, ac spectandam præbet imaginem falsæ & fictæ & ementitæ & [illegible, ~10 letters] obedientiæ. Quod in præsentia sic Moses facit, vt obedienti falsam primum describat vt cognoscatur tum ostendit quantum miseriarum ex falsa illa obedientia promanet, vt eo diligentius ab ea no bis caueamus.
units.tr: No one who has any acquaintance with the divine Word and with the course of human affairs fails to know, from the Word of God itself and from the history of human events, that Satan, the most persistent enemy of our race, transforms himself into an angel of light, and paints with the colour of goodness and honesty the most wicked and shameful things. Thus, deceived and mad, we embrace what is foul and evil instead of what is good and fair, and fall into the same evils into which he himself has slipped. For this reason we need knowledge of good and evil, just as money-changers need to know coins, so that we may be able to embrace the good and flee from and hate the evil. Looking to this end, Moses sets before our eyes the proposed and explained doctrine of obedience, and along with it the end of disobedience, so that we may contemplate both well; and by this he fortifies us against the snares of Satan and sets before us the image of false, feigned and counterfeit [illegible] obedience to be looked upon. Moses does this now in this way: he first describes the false obedience, so that it may be recognised, and then shows how much misery flows from that false obedience, so that we may be the more diligently on our guard against it.

units.la: Qualis sit illa egregie docet, nempe quod primum omnia quàm optima simulet, cum falsa ac mala habeat omnia, seq; tandem det quàm turpissimè. Ac quemadmodum moriones præclara habent suorum sermonum initia, & in conclusiones absurdas ac ridiculas definiunt: sic illa malum initio pulchrè celat, imposita videlicet boni maximi & pulcherrimi specie: sed tandem larua detracta aut deposita apparet turpissima. Igitur ne quis specie ea fallatur Moses & larua illam sive pulchram boni formam, & eius subsistantiæ, quæ qualifq; subtus tecta lateat, in conspectum omnium hominum protrahit.
units.tr: He teaches admirably what such obedience is: namely, that it first imitates everything in the best manner, although it has everything false and evil, and at last it gives itself up in the most shameful way. And just as fools have fine beginnings to their arguments and end in absurd and ridiculous conclusions, so this obedience cleverly hides its evil at the start, by putting on the appearance of the greatest and most beautiful good; but when the mask is finally removed or laid aside, it appears most foul. Therefore, lest anyone be deceived by that appearance, Moses drags the mask, with its fair form of the good, and what substance and quality lies hidden beneath it, into the sight of all men.

units.la: Ac larua quidem est quod & peccati pœnitentiam & recti studium cum verbis simulatum etiam factis aliquo modo repræsentat.
units.tr: Now the mask is that which imitates, in words and to some extent in deeds, both repentance for sin and zeal for what is right.

units.la: Verbis, vt Moses hoc exemplo commemorat. 1. Peccauimus Domino. Hæc verba sunt pœnitentium [illegible, ~12 letters]. Nam qui se fatetur deliquisse, is quasi promittit se melio rem fore. Atq; hoc ipso quid pulchrius? quid melius[?]? quid deniq; venia ac commiseratione dignius? Nam peccati turpitudo nulla alia re tegi potest quàm pœnitentia decora. Postquā peccaueris nihil est quod conducat magis, quàm ab eo desinere, cum reus fis nihil est ad remouendam pœnam potius, quàm criminis confessio atq; deprecatio.
units.tr: In words, as Moses records in this example: (1) "We have sinned against the Lord." These are the words of penitents. For he who confesses that he has done wrong seems to promise that he will do better. And what is more beautiful than this? What is better? What, finally, is more worthy of pardon and pity? For the shamefulness of sin can be covered by no other thing than by a becoming repentance. Once you have sinned, nothing is more useful than to cease from it; when you are guilty, nothing serves better to remove punishment than the confession and entreaty of the crime.

units.la: 2 Attendemus[?], verba sunt promittentium se facturos quod anteà facere noluerant. Quid etiam hoc ipso melius? Nam si peccatum fit hoc ipso quod noluerit, iam si velis ac facias, videberis vitium virtute obliterare.
units.tr: (2) "We will attend to it" are the words of those who promise that they will do what they had previously been unwilling to do. What could be better than this? For if sin consists in being unwilling, then once you are willing and act, you will seem to have wiped out the vice by virtue.

units.la: 3 Pugnabimus iuxta omnia quæ præcepit Dominus. Et hoc est omnium optimum videlicet non solum quod Deus iubet facere, sed & modum in eo perficiendo nequaquam alium, quàm quem Deus ipse præscripserit, seruare.
units.tr: (3) "We will fight according to all that the Lord has commanded." And this is the best of all: not only to do what God commands, but also to keep, in carrying it out, no other manner than the one God himself has prescribed.

units.la: Atq; hæc sunt eorum qui veram præferunt obedientiam verba, quibus omnia de se quæ diuinissima pollicentur. His nos quidem, qui in intimos animorum humanorum recessus non possumus inspicere, quidq; istic lateat cernere, facile percellimur: at Deus ne tantillum moue tur. Dicit enim in veteri quidem testamento: Populus hic labijs me honorat, cor autem eorum procul abest à me: in nouo, Non quisquis dicit Domine intrabit in regnum Dei, sed qui fecerit voluntatem patris, &c. Quod argumento est Deum isto verborum fuco nō decipi. Quemadmodum igitur vir prudens nullis neq; splendidis promissis, neq; blanditijs suauibus se demulceri patitur [illegible, ~20 letters] nec Deus illis simulatis cultibus deluditur.
units.tr: These are the words of those who put forward true obedience, and by them they promise all things about themselves that are most divine. We, who cannot look into the innermost recesses of human hearts and see what lies hidden there, are easily moved by these words; but God is not moved in the least. For he says in the Old Testament: "This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me"; and in the New: "Not everyone who says, Lord, Lord, shall enter the kingdom of God, but he who does the will of my Father," etc. This is proof that God is not deceived by this varnish of words. Just as a wise man allows himself to be soothed by no splendid promises or sweet flatteries, so God is not deluded by these feigned worships.

units.la: Igitur hæc, ne decipiaris, sic depicta ponuntur ob oculos. Sic Papistæ & eorum similes bo na nescio quæ promittunt, ac prætexunt, vt quam suo more præstant, veram esse probent obedientiam. Hic sunt prætextus optimi & tamen veri non censentur nec sunt. Sed ludū iocūmq; dicas esse, præ verbis, quando opera quoq; videris.
units.tr: Therefore, lest you be deceived, these things are set before our eyes thus painted. So the Papists and their like promise and put forward I know not what good things, so that they may prove the obedience they render in their own way to be true. These are the best of pretexts, yet they are not and are not considered true. But you may say it is all play and jest, judging by words, when you see also the works.

units.la: Factis igitur declarant illi ad hunc modum. 1. Armis accinctus est quisq; suis: In quo vides eos quæ ad rem perficiendam requiruntur sibi comparare. Quod prudentiæ pariter & industriæ est indicium.
units.tr: By their deeds, then, they declare themselves in this way. (1) "Every man girded on his own weapons": here you see them providing for themselves what is required to accomplish the task. This is a sign of prudence and diligence alike.

units.la: 2 Mutuum adhortantur, <bl>ein anderen zügrüffi/ift[?] allen ernst gsin</bl>. Mutuæ cohortationes quoniam in omnibus rebus sunt optimæ, præclara videntur esse verææ pœnitentiæ signa atq; indicia. Sed tamen est falsum.
units.tr: (2) They urge one another: "They called to one another, and it was all in earnest." Mutual exhortations, since they are excellent in all matters, seem to be splendid signs and indications of true repentance. But nevertheless it is false.

units.la: Eius exempla cum in papatu tum in nobis vides. In Papatu non solum verba habes sed & facta, vt conuentus sacros, peregrinationes, preces, elemosynas, absolutiones, satisfactiones, præclaram scilicet friuolæ pietatis speciem. Deus dicit, obedientiam quam sacrificium malo. Et, frustra me colunt traditionibus hominum. Sic in nostris ecclesijs hypocritæ verbum augiunt, orant, sacramenta celebrant, eleemosynas elargiuntur, magnam etiam probitatem simulant, intus autem magni sunt nequam. Eius generis homines quondam fuere Cain, Saul, Ana-nias & innumeri alij. Ergo ne vel ipse decipias alios hypocritä, vel decipiare ab alijs, detracta larua qualis in se existat docet Moses.
units.tr: You see examples of this both in the papacy and among ourselves. In the papacy you have not only words but also deeds: sacred assemblies, pilgrimages, prayers, almsgivings, absolutions, satisfactions, a splendid show of trifling piety. God says, "Obedience is better than sacrifice," and, "In vain do they worship me with the precepts of men." So in our churches hypocrites add to the Word, pray, celebrate the sacraments, distribute alms, and even feign great uprightness, while inwardly they are very wicked. Men of this kind once were Cain, Saul, Ananias and countless others. Therefore, lest you either yourself deceive others as a hypocrite, or be deceived by others, Moses teaches what such a person is in himself, once the mask is removed.

units.la: Substantia vero quæ qualifquefit illius fictæ & falsæ obedientiæ, & quam turpiter ila la sese dare soleat, trifariam Moses edocet, videlicet quod Deum dissuadentem non audiat, quod rationibus optimis à proposito suo deflecti nequeat, quod denique verbi ministerium, optimum mortalium calamitatibus auertendis diuinitus propinatum remedium negligunt atq; etiam respuunt.
units.tr: Moses teaches, threefold, what the substance and quality of that feigned and false obedience is, and how shamefully it is wont to show itself: namely, that it does not listen to God when He dissuades; that it cannot be turned from its purpose by the best reasons; and finally, that it neglects and even spurns the ministry of the Word, the best remedy divinely provided for averting the calamities of mortals.

units.la: Ac primum quidem quod etiam renuente & dissuadente conatus illos Domino nihilo-minus ipsi pergunt atque in susceptis suis consilijs pertinacissime perseuerant id satis euiden-ti claroque argumento fuerit, eos à vera obedientia quàm longissime abfuisse. Est enim obse-quentis & pij ingenij Deo nolente & prohibente quod ceperis omittere.
units.tr: First, that they went on with their attempts, even though the Lord was unwilling and dissuaded them, and that they persevered most obstinately in their undertaken plans, is sufficiently clear and evident proof that they were as far as possible from true obedience. For it is the mark of an obedient and pious disposition to leave off what you have begun when God is unwilling and forbids it.

units.la: Eodem modo clamitante per verbum suum Deo quam sœdi sint in religione errores, quàm tetra sint, in vita flagitia, qui verè sunt obedientes mox desinunt: qui perseuerant, eo ip-so se accusant inobedientiæ.
units.tr: In the same way, when God through his Word cries out how foul the errors in religion are, how hideous the crimes in life, those who are truly obedient soon cease; those who persevere thereby accuse themselves of disobedience.

units.la: Sed Moses iussu Domini monet illos vtà pugna cessent, illi nihilo minus pergunt. Quæ hæc est obedientia? Disuadet nobis & vituperat auaritiam, ambitum, adulterium, ebrietatem: nos pergimus; quæ hæc est pietas? Ergo vtut simules pietatem, tamen hæc nulla videbitur quam diu tuos vitiosos motus potius sequeris, quam salutaria Dei monita.
units.tr: But Moses, by the Lord's command, warns them to stop fighting, and they nevertheless press on. What kind of obedience is this? It rejects and condemns for us covetousness, ambition, adultery and drunkenness, and we carry on. What kind of piety is this? Therefore, however much you pretend to piety, it will appear to be no piety at all, as long as you follow your own sinful impulses rather than God's saving admonitions.

units.la: Porrò hoc turpius hæc se dat obedientia, quod non solum fidissimis atque amantissi-mis Dei patris monitis non obediunt, verùm etiam firmissimis atque optimis eius argumen-tis vt desistant persuaderi atque adduci nequeunt. Et argumenta quidem Moses commemo-rat. 1. Proponit ne ascendatis, neue pugnetis. Ist suttuss jr sondo mit thun. Clarum & expres-sum est de multis rebus cauendis verbum Domini, sed tamen eorum studia nihilo magis de-ferimus. 2. Argumenta ipsa sigillatim singula enumerat. Vnum, Ego enim non sum in medio ve-stri. Quo significat eos nihil feliciter factûros. Nam cum in Deo sumus & moueamur, veluti docet apostolus sequitur illo absente nos omnem vim mouendi prorsus amittere. Qui igitur nos ruebimur? quo pacto hostes propulsabimus, cum ne moueri quidem possimus? ꝏ wir vns nit gregen fonnen? Ergo vt Paulus dicit, si Deus pro nobis quis contra nos? sic dicimus cum Mose, si Deus nolit nobis adesse pugna desistendum esse. Argumentum optimum: quid enim illo nos deserente faceremus?
units.tr: Moreover, this obedience shows itself all the more shameful because they not only refuse to obey the most faithful and loving admonitions of God the Father, but also cannot be persuaded or induced to desist by his most solid and excellent arguments. Moses does set out the arguments. (1) He says: "Do not go up, and do not fight." (German gloss: you shall not do it.) The word of the Lord is clear and explicit about many things to be avoided, yet we pay no more heed to their zeal. (2) He enumerates the arguments themselves one by one. The first: "For I am not in the midst of you." By this he signifies that they will accomplish nothing successfully. For since we are in God and move and have our being, as the apostle teaches, it follows that when he is absent we lose all power of moving at all. How, then, shall we rush forward? How shall we drive back enemies when we cannot even move? (German gloss: how can we not hold our own against them?) Therefore, as Paul says, "If God is for us, who is against us?" So we say with Moses: if God is unwilling to be present with us, we must give up the fight. It is an excellent argument: for what could we do if he forsook us?

units.la: Alteram ab vtili ducit, ne affligamini. Sed cæca natura nec quod sibi conducit facile cer-nit. Ergo surdis narrentur bona consilia. Non flestuntur rationibus.
units.tr: The second he draws from what is useful: "that you be not smitten." But blind nature does not readily perceive even what is to its own advantage. Therefore good counsel is told to the deaf. They are not moved by reasons.

units.la: Postremò verbi diuini ministerium hoc ipso respuunt quod Mosem iussu Dei hæc asse-rentem non audiunt. Quod eos fecisse Moses indicat: Hæc, inquit, ego loquebar, am prædi-gen ist, cum mangel grün. Promulgarunt hæc Dei mandata patriarchæ, Moses, prophetæ, Christus, apostoli, & nostrates ecclesiastæ. Quid fit? At vos (inquit Moses) non audi batis. Id est, nolebatis obsequi. Sic non audiunt cõciones qui eas fugiût, aliud sog tantes audiunt, quid dicatur sus-serunt, Et, exacerbantes os Domini. Hoc est, quod Deus vobis ceu honestū & bonum con-sulebat, id vobis cum turpe tum perniciosum fore videbatur. Sie warheit müßt vnrecht han. Dein, insolentes ascendebatis. Id est, qui Deum aut me liberet irritare sic contemptis meis mo-nitionibus, rem aggressi estis. Eadem nunc quoque regnat inobedientia superba atque insolens, s she den pfaffen nit an/wile thün/solts jm ein lyden sint. Atq; hæc est illa obedientia sci licet. Hanc tu Christianæ caueto.
units.tr: Finally, they reject the ministry of the divine Word itself, since they do not listen to Moses declaring these things by God's command. Moses indicates that this is what they did: "These things," he says, "I was speaking [to you]." (German gloss: when I preach, there is lacking the green.) The patriarchs, Moses, the prophets, Christ, the apostles and our own churchmen have proclaimed these commands of God. What happens? "But you," says Moses, "did not hear," that is, you were unwilling to obey. So those who flee sermons do not listen to them, but they hear other things and take up whatever is said, "and provoked the mouth of the Lord." This means that what God advised you as honourable and good seemed to you both shameful and harmful. (German gloss: so truth must be wrong.) Then: "insolently you went up." That is, you set about the business, despising my admonitions, as if to provoke God or me. The same proud and insolent disobedience reigns now too: (German gloss: whatever they will not do for the priests, let them suffer it.) And this is that obedience, namely. Beware of it as Christians.

units.la: Exitus qui fuerit singularum descriptione docet. 1. Funduntur: nam illorum montiũ incolæ egressi ceu apes in illos impetu facto quicquid habuerunt obuiũ prostrauere. Atq; hisunt rerum cõtra Deũ susceptarũ euentus. 2. Fleuerunt luctus sequitur. 3. Dominus non audit. 4. Sedistis. Neque progredi neque regredi datum est. Quare hæc obedientia ca-uenda fuerit, enitendumque erit potius vt benemonentibus parea-mus. Quò fiet vt ad legem Domini futu-ri simus aptiores in Chri-sto. Amen.
units.tr: The outcome of each of these things the description teaches. (1) They were routed: for the inhabitants of those mountains came out like bees, made an attack on them, and struck down whatever they met. Such are the outcomes of undertakings against God. (2) They wept, and mourning follows. (3) The Lord does not hear. (4) You sat still. It was granted to them neither to advance nor to retreat. Wherefore this obedience ought to be avoided, and we should rather strive to obey those who admonish us well. This will make us the more fit to keep the law of the Lord in Christ. Amen.

units.la: IN DEVTERONOMIVM CAPVT II. SERMO IX.
units.tr: IN DEUTERONOMIUM CHAPTER II. SERMON IX.

units.la: Versi igitur profecti sumus in desertum viam maris carectosi[?], quemadmodum Dominus loquutus erat ad me, & circuimus montem Seir diebus multis.
units.tr: So we turned and set out into the wilderness by the way of the Red Sea, as the LORD had spoken to me, and we compassed Mount Seir for many days.

units.la: 2 Et loquebatur Dominus ad me dicens.
units.tr: And the LORD spoke to me, saying:

units.la: 3 Satis circuistis montem istum vertite ad aquilonem.
units.tr: You have compassed this mountain long enough; turn northward.

units.la: 4 Et populo praecipe dicens, Vos transibitis limitem fratrum vestrorum filiorum Esau, qui habitant in Seir, qui timebunt a vobis, cauete tamen diligenter.
units.tr: And command the people, saying: You are to pass through the territory of your brethren the children of Esau, who dwell in Seir. They will be afraid of you, so take diligent heed.

units.la: 5 Ne offendatis vos feroces contra eos, quoniam nihil dabo vobis de terra eorum, ne vestigium quidem pedis, quoniam dedi montem Seir ipsi Esau possidendum.
units.tr: Do not provoke them, for I will not give you any of their land, not even so much as a foot's breadth, because I have given Mount Seir to Esau as a possession.

units.la: 6 Cibum emetis ab eis pecunia, ut comedatis, quin aquam emetis ab eis argento ut bibatis.
units.tr: You shall buy food from them for money, that you may eat, and you shall also buy water from them for money, that you may drink.

units.la: 7 Nam Dominus Deus fausta tibi precatus est in omni opere manuum tuarum, novit proficiſci tuum in deserto isto vasto hos quadraginta annos, fuitq; tecum Dominus Deus tuus, ut tibi nihil defuerit.
units.tr: For the LORD your God has blessed you in all the work of your hands. He has known your journeying through this great wilderness; these forty years the LORD your God has been with you, and you have lacked nothing.

units.la: 8 Transeuntes vero a fratribus nostris filiis Esau habitantibus in Seir a via plana, ab Elath & Esion Gaber, defleximūs & transiuimus viam deserti Moab.
units.tr: And when we passed by our brethren the children of Esau, who dwell in Seir, by the way of the plain, from Elath and from Ezion-geber, we turned and passed along the way of the wilderness of Moab.

units.la: 9 Dixitq; Dominus ad me, Moabitas non premas hostiliter, neq; ferocias in eos bello, quoniam non dabo tibi de terra eius possessionem, quandoquidem filiis Lot dedi Ar possidendam.
units.tr: And the LORD said to me: Do not distress the Moabites or contend with them in war, for I will not give you any of their land as a possession, because I have given Ar to the children of Lot as a possession.

units.la: 10 Emim antea in ea habitarunt, populus magnus & multus, tum etiam proce-rus ut Anakim, quos Moabitae vocant Emim.
units.tr: The Emim dwelt there formerly, a great and numerous people, and tall as the Anakim; the Moabites call them Emim.

units.la: 11 In Seir vero olim habitarunt Horaei, quorum possessionem occuparunt filij Esau, & vastarunt eos ante se, habitaruntq; in loco eorum, quemadmodum fecit Israel in terra possessionis suae, quam eis Dominus dedit.
units.tr: The Horites also dwelt in Seir formerly, but the children of Esau took their possession, destroyed them before them, and dwelt in their place, as Israel did in the land of its possession, which the LORD gave them.

units.la: Quinque progymnasmatis iis quibus Moses populum suum, ac deinceps eius exemplo omnes homines ad divinae legis studium praeparare voluit, tertium, quod est studium iuris gentium, nunc sequitur. Quod quoniam non minus quam quae modo sunt expositae hanc ad rem momenti affert, Moses exorsus a secundo usq; in tertium caput productâ tractatione, sanè quam egregie describit, & commendat, adhibitis exemplis vi-uis[?], quae potiora praeceptionibus fore putavit. Ac primum ipsis ius gentium commendat, tum quomodo & pace & bello servandum sit declarat. Atq; eius doctrinae pars ea, qua studium hoc commendatur, itemq; ea quae ut pace servetur, iis verbis quae praelecta sunt exponitur.
units.tr: Of the five preliminary exercises by which Moses wished to prepare his people, and after their example all men, for the study of the divine law, the third now follows: the study of the law of nations. Since this bears no less on the matter than those just set out, Moses, beginning at the second chapter and carrying the treatment on into the third, describes and commends it most admirably, with lively examples which he judged more effective than precepts. First he commends the law of nations itself, and then declares how it is to be observed both in peace and in war. The part of this teaching by which the study is commended, and also that by which it is kept in peace, is set out in the words just read.

units.la: Ut commendet ius gentium argumenta duo affert: quorum alterum ab eorum ipsorum anteacta vita, alterum a mandato seu voluntate Dei ducit. Ab anteacta vita, dum repetit itineris molestias, quas annis illis perpessi fuerant, dicens, versi igitur profecti sumus, &c. Quae mala Moses non ideo revocat in memoriam, ut exprobret, sed ut suo ipsorum exemplo moniti quae qualisque sit afflictorum hominum conditio recordentur, ac propterea minus alios affligant, sed iuri gentium sic addicti sint, suas ut res sic curent, ne quem ledant alium. Nam ut praeclare est a Cicerone scriptum in officiis, detrahere aliquid alteri, & hominem hominis incommodo augere suum commodum magis est contra naturam quam mors, quam paupertas, quam dolor, quam caetera, quae possunt aut corpori accidere, aut rebus externis. Primum enim hoc ipso quod propter suum emolumentum aliquis alterum spoliat aut violat, omnis hominum societas coniunctioq; dissoluitur. Quippe quod perinde fiat, ac si uno quoq; membro omnem proximi membri valetudinem ad se traducente, corpus totum debilitetur atq; intereat. Deinceps non solum natura atque etiam iure gentium, sed etiam singulorum populorum singulis constitutum est, ut non liceat sui commodi causa alteri nocere. In quo vides quemadmodum omnia in hunc quasi Oceanum iura confluant, hocq; uno consensu quod hic Moses docet approbent.
units.tr: To commend the law of nations he brings forward two arguments, one drawn from their own past life and the other from the command or will of God. From their past life, when he recalls the hardships of the journey they had endured in those years, saying, "So we turned and set out," and so on. Moses does not recall these evils in order to reproach them, but so that, warned by their own example, they may remember what the condition of afflicted people is, and therefore afflict others less, and so be bound by the law of nations, managing their own affairs in such a way as not to harm anyone else. For, as Cicero splendidly writes in his On Duties, to take something from another and to increase one's own advantage at another's disadvantage is more contrary to nature than death, than poverty, than pain, or than anything else that can befall the body or external circumstances. For first, by the very fact that someone despoils or injures another for his own gain, the whole fellowship and union of men is dissolved. It is as if, with each member drawing the health of a neighbouring member to itself, the whole body were weakened and perished. Further, it has been established not only by nature and the law of nations, but also by the particular laws of individual peoples, that it is not lawful to harm another for one's own advantage. In this you see how all laws flow together into this, as it were, ocean, and by one common consent approve what Moses teaches here.

units.la: Ius naturae Cicero vocat rationem summam insitam in natura, quae iubet ea quae facienda sunt, prohibetq; contraria. Paulus autem Apostolus Rom. 2. conscientiam vocat quæ factum vel accusæt vel defensione recta tueatur. Iure consulti vero hoc vocant quod natura docuit omnia animantia, vt est in l. 1. §. ius naturale. ff. de iust. & iur. Vnde existunt maris & fœminæ conjunctio, liberorum procreatio pariter atq; educatio. Nam cum omnia animantia mortalia sint, commixtione liberos procreare, & insita erga natos benevolentia fouere eos atque educare, hocq; modo conseruare genera animalium natura docuit. Quod Theophilus Inst. de iur. na. gen. & ciui. in prin. sic exponit, [?] φύσεως ὁρῶντα τὸ καθ' ἕκαστον τῆς [?] θανάτῳ [?] [illegible, ~12 letters] [?] Inde etiam libertas existit. Inst. de libert. Et iniuriarum propulsio l. 1. §. cum arietes. ff. si quadrupedes. Et communis omnium rerum possessio ca. ius naturale. d. 1. Quod omnium minime permittit vt suum quisque commodum quærat ex alterius incommodo, quando vides eo ipso statui, vt omnibus sint salus, libertas, diuitiæ, & tuta rerum fruitio.
units.tr: Cicero calls natural law the supreme reason, implanted in nature, which commands what ought to be done and forbids the contrary. The Apostle Paul in Romans 2 calls it conscience, which either accuses or defends a deed by right judgment. Jurists, however, call it what nature taught all living creatures, as in l. 1 §. ius naturale, ff. de iust. et iur. Hence come the union of male and female and the procreation and rearing of offspring. For since all living things are mortal, nature taught them to produce offspring by mating, to cherish the young with innate goodwill, and to bring them up, and in this way to preserve the kinds of animals. Theophilus expounds this in the Institutes, de iur. nat. gen. et civ., at the beginning, in a passage of which the Greek is in part illegible in the scan. From this also comes freedom: Inst. de libert. And the repelling of injury: l. 1 §. cum arietes, ff. si quadrupes. And the common possession of all things: ca. ius naturale, d. 1. This by no means permits each man to seek his own advantage at another's disadvantage, since you see that it is established precisely so that all may have safety, liberty, riches, and the secure enjoyment of things.

units.la: Ius gentium est quod naturalis ratio inter omnes gentes constituit, atq; apud omnes populos peraeq; constituit, vt ait Iustinianus Inst. eod. tit. vel illud est quo gentes humanæ vtuntur, vt ait Vlpianus in l. 1. §. vltimo ff. de iusti. & iur. Et hoc differt à naturali, quod illud animalibus, hoc solis hominibus inter se commune est. Inde existunt religio, & debita patriæ & parentibus obedientia, seruitus, bellum, & emptio, venditio, locatio, conductio, societas, depositum, mutuum, & vt iniuria cum moderatione inculpatæ tutelæ propulsetur, vt est Inst. de iur. na. gen. & ciui. §. quod vero in gl. 1. Existit inde contractuum omnium origo. Atque hoc iure quicquid introductum est omnium hominum, qui quidem, vt Theophilus Paraphrastes indicat, rationem vitæ ducem habent ac feruant, vno consensu receptum est, nempe vt homicidia, adulteria, reliquaq; enormia scelera capitalibus supplicijs coerceantur, & quicquid in alteram partem nimis inclinat, id arceatur.
units.tr: The law of nations is what natural reason has established among all nations, and has established equally among all peoples, as Justinian says in the same title of the Institutes. Or it is that which human nations use, as Ulpian says in l. 1 §. ultimo, ff. de iust. et iur. It differs from natural law in that the latter is common to animals, whereas the former is common to men alone among themselves. From it arise religion, the due obedience owed to country and parents, slavery, war, and buying, selling, letting, hiring, partnership, deposit, and loan; and it also arises that injury is repelled with moderation by blameless defence, as in Inst. de iur. nat. gen. et civ., §. quod vero, gl. 1. From this comes the origin of all contracts. And by this law whatever has been introduced for all men has been received by common consent. These men, as Theophilus the paraphrast indicates, have reason as their guide and keep it. Namely, murders, adulteries, and other heinous crimes are restrained by capital punishments, and whatever inclines too far to one side is warded off.

units.la: Ab hoc iam differt ciuile ius, quippe quod non omnium simul populorum, sed vnius alicuius populi consensu receptum sit. Nam vt ait Imp. quod quisq; populus ipse sibi ius constituit, id ipsius proprium ciuitatis est, vocaturq; ius ciuile, quasi ius proprium ipsius ciuitatis. In hoc tamen conueniunt, quod ipsum quoq; ius ciuile requirit quæ non prorsus aliena sunt à lege natur. Vnde & Vlpianus in l. vj. ff. de iust. & iur. dicit, vel ius ciuile est quod neq; in totum à iure naturali vel gentium recedit, neq; per omnia ei seruit. Imò ius gentiam fit ciuile quando omnium consensu recipitur, sed tamen accomodatum publicæ necessitati. Veluti in leg. xij. tab. Ius naturæ præcipiés liberis, vt alant parentes, hac moderatione mitigatum est, vt filius si parentis iniuria nullam artem didicerit, eo non teneatur. Illa vero iuris à natura discessio fit esse Matth. 19. Dominus Christus indicat. His adde quod locorum & temporum, & personarum ratio diuersa facit, vt vnum idemq; ius omnibus gentibus esse nequaquam posit, propter eaq; & à iure gentium interdum discedit & naturæ ius ciuibus accomodatur, fiuntq; leges aliis populis aliæ. Quemadmodum Theophilus indicat Athenienses lege constituisse, vt eorum respub. multos habeat [?] ad sedandam penuriam, cum Alexandrijs frumento abundan tibus hac lege non opus fit. Eodemq; modo in alijs. Sed ius ciuile suum qui contemnit aut vio lat, is quemadmodum inquit Cic. vincula non modo iudiciorum, sed etiam vtilitatis vitæ q; com munis reuellit. Nā iure ciuili sublato, vt idè dicit, nemo scire potest, quid suū aut quid alienū. Ex quibus omnibus multisq; alijs quæ huc afferri possunt, potest intelligi, sic omnes debe re sibi cofulere, vt faluū fit fuū ius alijs. Nā fi vnus ad fe rapiat omnia, quid reliquū erit alijs? Et ipse sibi licet omnia posideat, solus nō sufficiet, eueniētq; ei quod ijs qui vouent, vt omnes ho mines decedant, eorumq; bona ad fe redeant hereditate. Id enim fi tibi cōtingat maxime, ta men hoc eris miserior, quia ipse arare, sementé facere, vineta colere, pecus pascere, vestes farci re, calceos fuere, & omnino omniū artificiū operas facere necesse habeas. Quæ res docet quàm stulta sit & misera [?] quà inutile sit suā rem familiaré cū alterius detrimento augere vel le: quàm cōtra cōueniens sit iuri naturæ, gentiū & ciuili vt suū cuiq; tribuatur. Et id vt prestes cuiq; Moses recordatione eorū quæ pasi fuerat malorū, admonet. Quasi dicat, Magna affectis ab Amorrheis clade & iniuria: ne fitis in quenquā iniurij vel hic ipse lu&us vester vos admone at. Atq; sic quidé ab anteacta vita, velut ab exemplis nostris argumenta ad feruandum ius pof. fumus ducere.
units.tr: Civil law now differs from this, since it is received not by the consent of all peoples together, but by the consent of some one people. For, as the Emperor says, what each people establishes for itself as law is its own and belongs to that state, and is called civil law, as it were the proper law of that state. Yet they agree in this, that civil law too requires things not wholly alien to the law of nature. Hence Ulpian also says, in l. 6, ff. de iust. et iur., that civil law is that which neither wholly departs from natural law or the law of nations, nor wholly follows them. Indeed the law of nations becomes civil when it is received by the consent of all, but adapted to public necessity. As in the Twelve Tables: natural law requires parents to feed their children, but this was tempered by a moderation, so that a son who, through his father's wrong, learned no trade is not bound by it. That departure of law from nature Christ the Lord indicates in Matthew 19. To these add that the differing circumstances of places, times and persons mean that one and the same law cannot be for all nations; for this reason law sometimes departs from the law of nations and is adapted to the citizens, and different peoples have different laws. As Theophilus indicates, the Athenians by law established that their commonwealth should have many ... to relieve scarcity, whereas at Alexandria, which abounds in grain, no such law is needed, and so likewise in other cases. But whoever despises or violates his civil law, as Cicero says, tears away the bonds not only of judgments but also of the usefulness and common life of living. For with civil law removed, as he says, no one can know what is his own or what is another's. From all these things and many others that could be brought forward here, it can be understood that all ought so to provide for themselves that the right of others remains safe. For if one man seizes everything for himself, what will be left for others? And even if he himself possesses everything, he alone will not suffice; and it happens to him what happens to those who wish that all men would die, so that their goods might return to them by inheritance. For even if that should happen to you, you would be the more wretched, since you would have to plough yourself, sow, tend the vines, pasture the flocks, mend your clothes, make your shoes, and in short perform the work of all the crafts. This shows how foolish and wretched it is, and how unprofitable, to wish to increase one's own household wealth to another's loss; and how contrary it is to natural, national and civil law that each should be given his due. Moses admonishes each to render this, by recalling the evils he suffered. As if he said: great was the slaughter and injury inflicted by the Amorites; take care not to be unjust to anyone, lest this very grief of yours admonish you. And so indeed from our past life, as from our examples, we may draw arguments for keeping the right.

units.la: Sed à mandato Dei sic ducit rationes, Et loquebatur (inquit) Dominus, &c. Afferre fe diuini- tus hoc mandatū docet. Nam Deus constituerat fuū populū in promissam terrā introducere, verum ne quid ex eo detrimenti paterentur alij populi. Idq; etiamnum Deus finit. Vult ali-quem augere diutiis & honoribus, sed fine hominum innocentium periculo. Ergo omnium consensu puniuntur latrones, homicidæ, adulteri, fures, & omnino omnes scelerati homines: item q; sint contractus, & distincta rerum dominia, & legitimi res aquirendi modi, quos homines non transfiliant. Nam hoc Deum velle, Moses eo ipso docet, quod dicit, se hæc Israelitis iuf su Domini præcipere. Ergo nō tam natura tuæ quam voluntas Dei, quæ est ipsa iustitia, postulant, ut sua cuiq; relinquas bona, ac nihil nisi legitimis modis acquiras tibi. Si naturam tuā vitiat[?] corruptio, retrahat ad officia diuinæ voluntatis imperium. Abs te quasi a minore ad Deum ceu id quod maius est, Moses transfit: docetq; tuarum esse partium hoc velle, sin autem nolis Deum, ut velis, pro imperio suo iubere, (Gott wills ben [?] / wirs noch nit / so warr was dir dar nach gang. Atq; hæc omnino cogitanda sunt hominibus: alioquin ad capescendā legē Dei su-mus ineptissimi. Qui secus affectus est, ius, humanitatem, naturam deniq; exuit, eftq; non homo, sed ratione destituta bellua. At belluam quid literas, nedū spiritus sancti mysteria doceas? laterem laueris.
units.tr: But he draws his reasons from the command of God: "And the Lord spoke," etc. He shows that this command was given by divine authority. For God had determined to lead his people into the promised land, yet so that the other peoples would suffer no loss from it. God still permits this today. He wills to enrich some with wealth and honours, but without endangering innocent people. Thus by common consent robbers, murderers, adulterers, thieves, and in general all wicked men are punished; likewise there are contracts, distinct ownership of things, and lawful modes of acquiring property, which men do not overstep. Moses shows that God wills this by the very fact that he says he commands these things to the Israelites by the Lord's order. Therefore it is not so much your nature as the will of God, which is justice itself, that requires you to leave each person his own goods and to acquire nothing for yourself except by lawful means. If corruption vitiates your nature, let the command of the divine will draw you back to your duties. From you, as from the lesser, Moses passes to God, as to the greater, and teaches that it is your part to will this. But if you are unwilling for God to command as he wills, by his authority (German gloss: "If God wills it, and we are not yet willing, then it will go with you accordingly"). These things must be thought through by men altogether; otherwise we are most unfit to grasp the law of God. Whoever is otherwise disposed has cast off right, humanity, indeed nature itself, and is not a man but a beast deprived of reason. But what do you teach a beast letters, let alone the mysteries of the Holy Spirit? You wash a brick.

units.la: Igitur vt legibus diuinis pedetentim assuescamus & ius inter nos feruando diuino iuri parere discamus, Moses ius gentium leges diuinas audituris prius commendat, eoq; vt diximus, quasi quodam progymnasmate ad eas capiendas præparat.
units.tr: So that we may gradually grow accustomed to the divine laws, and learn to obey divine right in keeping justice among ourselves, Moses first commends the law of nations to those who are about to hear the divine laws. In this way, as we said, he prepares them to receive those laws, as by a kind of preliminary exercise.

units.la: Vt pace feruetur, tres gentes commemorat quarum possessiones Deus ab his nolit occupari, vt petant ius transeundi, victumq; emant ab incolis omnem, etiam aquæ potum. Eas sunt Idumæi, Moabitæ, Ammonitæ.
units.tr: So that peace may be kept, he mentions three peoples whose possessions God does not want to be seized by Israel: they are to ask the right of passage and buy from the inhabitants all food, even water to drink. These peoples are the Edomites, Moabites and Ammonites.

units.la: Ergo Idumæos, vt ius feruent, docet egregie. Exordium ab eorum persona ducit, fratres appellans, & vt illam cognationem norint exactius, filios Esau nominans. Erat enim admodum propinqua cognatio. Idumæi montium horum incolæ ab Esauo, qui & Edom, hoc est, rufus nominatus est, & ortu & cognomine hoc adepti sunt: Israelitæ vero ab Iacobo fratre eius qui Israel etiam appellatus est, descenderunt. Vnde eit perspicuum illos populos quasi patrueles fratres sibi inuicem extitisse. Ergo sanguinis coniunctio, quæ naturæ est consentanea, debebat eos prohibere, quo minus eos afficerent iniuria.
units.tr: Thus he teaches the Edomites excellently to keep right. He begins from their person, calling them brothers, and, so that they may know that kinship more exactly, he names them the sons of Esau. For the kinship was very close. The Edomites, inhabitants of these mountains, were named after Esau, who is also called Edom, that is, red; they obtained both their origin and their surname from him. The Israelites descended from Jacob, his brother, who was also called Israel. Hence it is clear that those peoples were, as it were, cousins to one another. Therefore the bond of blood, which accords with nature, ought to have restrained them from doing them injury.

units.la: In quo discimus ortum nostri semper spectandum esse. Sæpe gens gentem, familia familiā, homo hominem despicit, qui si respicerent originem, maioribus ijsdem nati esse viderentur, minimeq; causam habarent iustam sese efferendi præ cæteris. Neq; enim duæ fuerunt Euæ, quarum altera nobiles, rusticos altera peperit. Vnde ergo nobiles? virtus fecit: vnde nati sunt ignobiles[?], ignauia ac scelus fecit inglorios: Mitte ergo contemptum proximi: fratres esse memineris.
units.tr: In this we learn that our origin should always be considered. Often nation looks down on nation, family on family, man on man; if they considered their origin, they would see that they were born of the same ancestors, and they would have least just cause for exalting themselves above others. For there were not two Eves, one of whom bore noble children and another rustic ones. Whence then the nobles? Virtue made them. Whence the ignoble? Cowardice and crime made men inglorious. Put away then your contempt for your neighbour; remember that they are brothers.

units.la: Ad personam etiam animus pertinet, quem ipsum etiam, qui iniuriam patiatur, indignum esse dicit, quippe quod timidi sint, ac nolint ipsi quidem nocere, sed timeant, ne sibi quis noceat. Quo modo qui affecti sunt nequaquam debebunt iniuria affici. Timidis & imbellibus homi-nibus optimus quisq; minimum iniuriarum intentat.
units.tr: The disposition also pertains to the person, and he says that it is itself unworthy even in one who suffers injury, since such people are timid. They themselves indeed do not want to harm, but they fear lest someone harm them. In this way those who have been so treated ought by no means to be injured. The best of men inflict the least injury on the timid and unwarlike.

units.la: 2. Quod iustus sit proponit, iubens, vt ne feroces sint. Quo vel vultum minacem vetat, nedum animum aut voluntatem ad nocendum patiatur. Adeo vult iuris obseruantes nos esse, vt nec velimus nocere, si fit facultas maxime. Vnde & iustitia voluntatis appellatione quasi genere definitur.
units.tr: 2. He sets out that it is just, bidding them not to be fierce. He forbids even a threatening look, let alone allowing mind or will to harm. So much does he want us to observe right that we should not even wish to harm, when the opportunity is especially given. Hence justice is defined by the name of will, as if by its genus.

units.la: 3 Confirmat 1. à voluntate Dei, quæ constituerat nihil Israelitis de terra hac dare, sed Idumæis illam conferuare.
units.tr: 3. He confirms it first from the will of God, who had determined to give nothing of this land to the Israelites, but to preserve it for the Edomites.

units.la: In quo vides, Deum terrena pariter & cœlestia bona distribuere, & omnino velle, quod ipse dederit alij, id te non solum non rapere, sed etiam non concupiscere. Hic iuris gentium cardo vertitur, ne quod Germanis datum est, Galli sibi petant aut rapiant: neue Germani, seu Helvetij Gallorum aut Italorum agros depopulentur, fruges demetant. Vtinam hoc secum reputent huius ætatis principes pariter ac priuati homines: bone Deus quanto minus esset bellorum, litium & iurgiorum? Nam si quod Deus tibi fauet, ego tibi quoq; non solum permittam, sed etiam faueam, constans & syncera erit inter nos concordia.
units.tr: In this you see that God distributes earthly and heavenly goods alike, and wills altogether that what he has given to another you not only do not seize, but do not even covet. Here turns the hinge of the law of nations: that what has been given to the Germans, the Gauls should not seek or seize for themselves; nor should the Germans or the Helvetians lay waste the fields of the Gauls or Italians and reap their crops. Would that the princes of this age, and private men alike, would consider this with themselves! Good God, how much less there would be of wars, lawsuits and quarrels! For if I not only permit you what God favours for you, but also favour it myself, a constant and sincere concord will exist between us.

units.la: 2 Ab occupatione. Quæris: vnde viuam si nemini quod suum est rapiam? Respondet Moses: Dominus benedixit tibi, nouit iter tuum, &c. Cibum & potum ab illis emes. Sunt acquirendæ possessionis iusti & legitimi diuinitus concessi modi, his vtere: est Dei benedictio, qua quod iusta & legitimè agimus, felix nobis fit ac faustum: est deniq; Dei prouidentia, qua fit vt iter, hoc est, vitæ nostræ cursum totum norit atq; dirigat. His medijs viuimus magis, quam cura nostra. Eò dem pertinent quæ de victu Matth. 6. concionatur Dominus. Iam quia spretis his medijs, ali-ter ipsi ter ipsi acquirimus,ingruunt omnis generis aerumnæ, annonæ caritas,pestis,bella, dissidia.At Israelitæ pro vt iusi fuerant faciunt,ideoq; tuto transfeunt.Eadem nos fortuna vtemur si me-dijs diuinitus constitutis & concesis vtamur:inhonestas & iniustas artes missas faciamus: so <bl>ist glück[?] Sarby.</bl>
units.tr: 2. From occupation. You ask: whence shall I live, if I seize nothing that belongs to another? Moses answers: "The Lord has blessed you, he knows your journey," etc. "You shall buy food and drink from them." There are just and lawful modes of acquiring possessions, granted by God; use these. There is God's blessing, by which what we do justly and lawfully becomes happy and prosperous for us. And finally there is God's providence, by which he knows and directs the whole of our journey, that is, the whole course of our life. We live by these means more than by our own care. To the same end pertains what the Lord preaches about food in Matth. 6. Now, since men who have scorned these means acquire otherwise, all kinds of miseries crowd in: dearth of grain, plague, wars, dissensions. But the Israelites did as they had been commanded, and therefore pass over safely. We shall have the same fortune if we use the means divinely established and granted, and dismiss dishonourable and unjust arts (German gloss: "so is luck").

units.la: Moabitas ipsos etiam lædi noluit.Id primum proponens ait,ne lædas, neue premas hostiliter, nec bello ferocias.Summa,nec oneri fis nec damno.Tum cofirmat à voluntate Domini, Quod is antea propter fastum & iniquitatem priores incolas punierit,hisq; eiectis terram Moabitis dederit:ergo Moabitis permittendam.Vide vt ius suum cuiq; reddat.Loth inde expulsus,Abrahamo victori debita,iam Lothi filio,qui Moab erat,datur & retinetur.Vt detur, expellit E-mim horrendos & tremendos incolas,populum magnum,procerum,multum , similem Ena-kim,id est,gigantū. Vt retineatur Israelitas aditu prohibet. Vide sic efficit Dominus, vt quod nostrum est alisquamur,quodq́ue sumus assequuti idipsum retineamus. Et addit robur argumento hoc ipso , quod Idumeæ terræ priores cólonos ceu exemplí vice commemorat, dicens,in Seir fuisse Horeos.Quo docet etiam idipsum quod modo diximus.
units.tr: He did not want the Moabites themselves to be harmed. Setting this forth first, he says: do not harm them, nor oppress them as enemies, nor be fierce against them in war. The sum is: be neither a burden nor a loss to them. Then he confirms it from the will of the Lord: that he had punished the earlier inhabitants because of their pride and iniquity, and, having cast them out, had given the land to the Moabites; therefore it must be left to the Moabites. See how he renders to each his own. Lot had been expelled from there; what was owed to Abraham the victor is now given to and retained by Lot's son, who was Moab. That it might be given, he drives out the Emim, dreadful and terrible inhabitants, a great and tall people, numerous, like the Anakim, that is, giants. That it might be retained, he forbids the Israelites access. See how the Lord brings it about that we obtain what is ours, and keep the very thing we have obtained. He adds strength to the argument by this very fact: he mentions as an example the earlier inhabitants of the land of Edom, saying that the Horites were in Seir. By this he also teaches the very thing we have just said.

units.la: Ammonitas etiam vetat affici iniuria.Et exorditur orationem à recordatione cladis prius exceptæ,docens cauendum esse ne se Deum offendendo retardent iterum , & damno assi-ciant,quemadmodum maiores eorum fecerint. Vtile est res olim gestas ex annalibus repeti-tas in memoriam reuocare. 2. Non premas Moab,non ferocias:animum siue voluntatem simul ac vim omnem prohibet. 3. Confirmat iterum vt supra.Non tib. (inquiens)/sed filio Loth de-di eam.Tum addit exemplum Seir.Atque ex his omnibus perspicuum est quomodo Deus ve-lit ius gentium saluum esse. Quo si ducamur,viam quæ est ad legem Dei proxima sumus ipsam ingressi.Sin autem id negligamus,nulla spes est ad legem diuinam perueniendi. Deus eo nos deducat.Amen.
units.tr: He also forbids the Ammonites to be injured. He begins his speech from the recollection of the defeat previously suffered, teaching that we must take care lest by offending God we again hold back and suffer loss, as their forebears did. It is useful to call to mind in memory things done long ago, repeated from the annals. 2. Do not oppress Moab, nor be fierce against it: he forbids mind or will as well as every kind of force. 3. He confirms it again, as above: "I did not give it to you," he says, "but to the son of Lot." Then he adds the example of Seir. From all these things it is plain how God wills the law of nations to be kept safe. If we are led by this, we have entered upon the way nearest to the law of God; but if we neglect it, there is no hope of attaining the divine law. May God lead us there. Amen.

units.la: SERMO X.
units.tr: SERMON X.

units.la: 13 Surgite igitur, & transite torrentem Zared : & transiuimus torrentem Zared.
units.tr: 13 Now rise up, and go over the brook Zared. And we went over the brook Zared.

units.la: 14 Et dierum quidem quibus profecti sumus à Cades Barnea,donec transiremus torrentem Zared,fuerunt triginta octo anni , donec vniuersa ætas virorum qui bello apti erant,consumeretur de medio castrorum,quemadmodum iurauerat eis Dominus.
units.tr: 14 And the days in which we travelled from Kadesh-barnea until we crossed the brook Zared were thirty-eight years, until the whole generation of the men of war was consumed from the midst of the camp, as the LORD had sworn to them.

units.la: 15 Quin & manus Domini fuit contra eos, vt perderet eos è medio castrorum, donec plane consumpti essent.
units.tr: 15 Indeed the hand of the LORD was against them, to destroy them from the midst of the camp, until they were utterly consumed.

units.la: 16 Quumq́ue iam omnes viri bello apti confecti essent, interiissentq; è populo:
units.tr: 16 So when all the men of war had perished and died out from among the people,

units.la: 17 Loquutus est Dominus ad me,in hanc sententiam.
units.tr: 17 the LORD spoke to me, to this effect:

units.la: 18 Tu transis hodie limitem Moab,nempe Ar.
units.tr: 18 Today you are to cross the border of Moab, namely Ar.

units.la: 19 Et quum appropinquaueris filiis Ammon,ne premas eos hostiliter,neq; feroci in eos bello:de terra enim filiorum Ammon nihil dabo vt possideas,filiis enim Loth dedi eam possidendam.
units.tr: 19 And when you come near to the children of Ammon, do not press them hostilely, nor wage fierce war against them, for I will give you nothing of the land of the children of Ammon to possess, since I have given it to the children of Lot to possess.

units.la: 20 Terra Rephaim & ipsa reputatur,sederuntq; in ea iam olim Rephaim,quos Ammonitæ vocant Zamzummim.
units.tr: 20 That land too is reckoned a land of giants. Giants lived there in former times, whom the Ammonites call Zamzummim.

units.la: 21 Populus fuit magnus & multus,tum etiam procerus , quemadmodum Enakim,quos Dominus excidit ante eos,& occuparunt eos,habitaruntq; illic pro ipsis.
units.tr: 21 They were a great and numerous people, and tall like the Anakim; but the LORD destroyed them before the Ammonites, and they dispossessed them and dwelt in their place.

units.la: 22 Quemadmodum fecit filiis Esau habitantibus in Seir , cum extirparet Horæos à facie eorum,vt ipsi possiderent eos,habitarentq; illic illorum loco in hunc vsq; diem.
units.tr: 22 So he did for the children of Esau, who dwell in Seir, when he destroyed the Horites from before them, and they dispossessed them and dwelt in their place, even to this day.

units.la: 23 Hauers[?] quoq; habitantes in Hazerim vsq; Gaza,Caphtorim egressi ex Caphtor exciderunt eos,& habitarunt ipsi loco illorum.
units.tr: 23 The Avvim too, who dwelt in villages as far as Gaza, were destroyed by the Caphtorim, who came out of Caphtor, and these dwelt in their place.

units.la: 24 Surgite itaq; soluite,& traicite torrentem Arnon,ecce dedi in manum tuam Sihon regem Hefbon Amorræorum atq; terram eius,incipe possidere , & capesce ad-uersus eum prælium,
units.tr: 24 Rise up then, set out, and cross the river Arnon. Behold, I have given into your hand Sihon the Amorite, king of Heshbon, and his land. Begin to possess it, and engage him in battle.

units.la: 25 Incipiam hoc ipso die immittere pauorem tuum, & timorem tuum super populos qui ubiq; sub cælo sunt, vt qui vel famam de te audierint, contremiscant, et coram te infirmentur.
units.tr: 25 This very day I will begin to put your dread and your fear upon the peoples who are under the whole heaven, so that when they hear report of you they will tremble and be undone before you.

units.la: 26 Misi ergo nuncios à deserto Kedemoth ad Sihon regem Hesbon tum mandatis pacificis, nempe huiusmodi:
units.tr: 26 So I sent messengers from the wilderness of Kedemoth to Sihon king of Heshbon, with words of peace, to this effect:

units.la: 27 Liceat quæso, vt transeam per regionem tuam, via recta ibo: non declinabo neque ad dextram neq; ad sinistram.
units.tr: 27 Let me, I pray, pass through your land. I will go by the highway; I will not turn aside either to the right hand or to the left.

units.la: 28 Commeatum pecunia vendes mihi vt comedam, & aquam pecunia dabis mihi vt bibam, liceat saltem vt pedes transeam,
units.tr: 28 You shall sell me food for money, that I may eat, and give me water for money, that I may drink. Only let me pass through on foot,

units.la: 29 Quemadmodum fecerunt mihi filij Esau qui habitant in Seir, & Moabitæ habitantes in Ar, quousq; traiecero Iordanem, in terram quam Dominus Deus noster tradidit nobis.
units.tr: 29 as the children of Esau who dwell in Seir did for me, and the Moabites who dwell in Ar, until I cross the Jordan into the land which the LORD our God gives us.

units.la: 30 Sihon autem rex Hesbon non permisit vt transiremus per sua: nam induravit Dominus Deus tuus animum eius, & corroborauerat cor eius, vt traderet eum in manum tuam, quemadmodum hodiernus dies (declarat.)
units.tr: 30 But Sihon king of Heshbon would not let us pass through his territory, for the LORD your God hardened his spirit and made his heart obstinate, so that he might deliver him into your hand, as is shown this day.

units.la: 31 Et dixit Dominus ad me: Ecce cœpi tradere coram te Sihon & terram eius, incipe occupare vt possideas terram eius.
units.tr: 31 And the LORD said to me, "See, I have begun to deliver Sihon and his land before you. Begin to take possession, that you may possess his land."

units.la: 32 Egressus itaq; obuiam nobis Sihon, ipse & universus populus eius, vt congrederetur (nobiscum) in Iaza.
units.tr: 32 Then Sihon came out against us, he and all his people, to fight at Jahaz.

units.la: 33 Et tradidit eum Dominus Deus noster coram nobis, & percussimus eum, & filios eius, atq; cunctum populum eius.
units.tr: 33 And the LORD our God delivered him up before us, and we struck him down, with his sons and all his people.

units.la: 34 Cepimus quoq; eodem tempore omnes ciuitates eius, & excidimus ad internecionem vsq; omnes ciuitates, viros, mulieres, & pubem, neminem reliquimus superstite.
units.tr: 34 We took all his cities at that time and utterly destroyed every city, men, women and children; we left no survivor.

units.la: 35 Cæterum iumenta diripuimus nobis, & prædam ciuitatum quas ceperamus.
units.tr: 35 Only the cattle we took as spoil for ourselves, and the plunder of the cities we had taken.

units.la: 36 Ab Aroer quæ est ad littus torrentis Arnon, & à ciuitate, quæ est in torrente vsq; ad Gilead, non fuit ciuitas quæ superior esset nobis, Dominus Deus noster tradidit eas omnes ante nos.
units.tr: 36 From Aroer, which is on the edge of the river Arnon, and from the city that lies in the valley, as far as Gilead, there was not a city too strong for us: the LORD our God delivered them all up to us.

units.la: 37 Duntaxat ad terram filiorum Ammon non accessisti, ad omnem limitem torrentis Iabok, & ad ciuitates montanas, & ad omnia quæ præcepit Dominus Deus noster.
units.tr: 37 Only you did not approach the land of the children of Ammon, nor any part of the banks of the river Jabbok, nor the cities of the hill country, nor anything else which the LORD our God forbade.

units.la: Iure gentium, quod quidem Moses quasi quoddam progymnasma diuinæ legi dantibus operam commendat, religio, vel debita parentibus & magistratibus obedientia, quicquid denique cum hominibus homines habent commercij continetur. Quamobrem interest omnium qui legi studere volunt, vt primum mandatum ac voluntatem Dei, tum finem diuinæ voluntatis consentaneum spectent vnicè, postremo sui pariter & eorum quibus cum eis res est, rationem habeant. Quò fiet vt & pace & bello nihil quod Deo displiceat, sibi noceat, erga alios ini [?] quum fit, illis indignum videatur, faciat, hocq; pacto ius gentium seruent quàm pulcherrimè. Id admodum egregiè Moses præsenti cap. docet, indicans eas terras, quas cuiq; genti Deus assignarit, tibi non affectandas esse: in ijs autem quas iniustè possident alij, tibi voluntatem Dei, finem tuorum conatuum, gentem aduersariam, teq; ipsum, qui quantusq; sis considerari oportere. Ergo res eas quo ordine propositæ sunt in præsentia considerabimus.
units.tr: The law of nations, which Moses commends as a kind of preliminary exercise for those who labour at the divine law, comprises religion, the obedience owed to parents and magistrates, and, in short, whatever dealings men have with men. Therefore it concerns everyone who wishes to study the law to look solely to the first command and will of God, then to the end that accords with the divine will, and lastly to take account both of himself and of those with whom he has to deal. The result will be that in both peace and war he does nothing that displeases God or harms himself, nothing unjust toward others and nothing that seems unworthy to them, and so he keeps the law of nations most beautifully. Moses teaches this most admirably in the present chapter, showing that you must not covet the lands which God has assigned to each nation, but in those which others hold unjustly you must consider the will of God, the end of your undertakings, the hostile nation, and yourself, who and how great you are. Let us therefore consider these matters in the order in which they are set forth.

units.la: Voluntatem Dei, quæ norma est ad quam ius naturæ, gentium & ciuile examinandum est, promisionis verbis explicatam ponit ob oculos, dicens, Surgite itaq;, soluite & traijcite torrentem Arnon, &c. Quibus verbis huius terræ promissionem renouat iterum, eaq; voluntatem Dei sic ob oculos Moses ponit, vt quid nostrum, quid illius sit facere, ex ea non difficile fit cognitu. Voluntas Dei fert, vt Edomei, Moabitæ, Ammonitæ terras quas habebant retinerent: ideoq; & gentes à quibus iniustè tenebantur expellit & Israelitas hac iter habentes, his arcet ac prohibet. Verum Ogem & Seonem iniustè tenentes eas terras quæ debebantur Israelitis, expellit, vt eis reddat.
units.tr: The will of God, which is the rule by which the law of nature, of nations and civil law are to be judged, he places before our eyes, explained in the words of the promise, saying, "Rise up therefore, set out and cross the river Arnon," and so on. By these words he renews again the promise of this land, and Moses sets the will of God before our eyes in such a way that from it it is not difficult to learn what is ours to do and what is God's. God's will is that the Edomites, Moabites and Ammonites should keep the lands they had; therefore he drives out the nations by whom they were unjustly held, and he keeps the Israelites, passing that way, away from them and forbids them. But Og and Sihon, who unjustly held the lands that were owed to the Israelites, he drives out, so that he may restore them.

units.la: Ex quo patet ius, si quemadmodum dici solet, ipsum ab ouo repetitum consideres, à voluntate diuina scilicet, statuere, vt sua cuiq; salua sit possessio. Hoc in religione, vt Deo suus ho-
units.tr: From this it is clear that law, if you consider it traced back to its very beginning, as the saying goes, namely to the divine will, ordains that each person's possession be kept safe. This holds in religion, so that God has his due honour;

units.la: nos habeatur;in republica,vt magistratibus debitam præstes obedientiam;in re familiari ; vt parentes honore & obsequijs prosequamur : omninoque in rebus omnibus ,vt si cum vici- no contrahas,ne plus mercium accipias quàm exponas pecuniarum, nèue plus accipias pe- cuniæ quàm ipse tu mercium dederis.Sed adeò nunc curæ est iuris obseruatio , vt huius ἀνισότητι[?] nomine plerique etiam glorientur , ac si quas res minus éxili precio sibi com- parauerint, quasi re benè gesta passim factum suum prædicent. At eiús qui feruare ius gen- tium velit,interest,in pace quidem,vt officium viri boni faciat, in bello verò iusti militis par- tes tueatur.Dei promissio constanter obseruata multò citius atq; etiam plenius expectata da- bit,quàm si tentes iniqua.
units.tr: in the commonwealth, so that you render the obedience owed to magistrates; in domestic affairs, so that we honour and serve our parents; and in all things generally, so that if you deal with your neighbour, you take no more goods than you pay out in money, nor take more money than you yourself have given in goods. But observance of law is now so much a matter of neglect that many even boast of this inequity, and if they have bought something for less than its worth, they proclaim their deed everywhere as if it were some well-managed achievement. But it is the concern of one who wishes to keep the law of nations that in peace he performs the duty of a good man, and in war he plays the part of a just soldier. A promise of God constantly kept will bring what is hoped for much sooner and more fully than if you attempt unjust things.

units.la: Hæc Dei voluntas antea reuelata est de ijs,quibus cum pax feruanda fuit : sed hoc loco repetita ac secundo repetita est, vt ex ea quomodo in bello ius gentium seruandum esset in- telligerent.Quod ipsum sic proponitur,vt & quid nostrarū sit partium, & quid Deus ipse ve- lit facere ,doceat.
units.tr: This will of God was revealed earlier concerning those with whom peace had to be kept; but here it is repeated, and repeated a second time, so that they may understand from it how the law of nations is to be kept in war. This is set out so as to teach both what our part is and what God himself will do.

units.la: Illorum esse dicit;vt surgant,soluant,traijciant torrentem Arnon. Surgendi verbo voluntas ad propositam rem propensa , siue magnum & intentum studium significatur. Ergo Deus vult nos iuuare, sed ea lege, vt ipsi quoque gnaui simus atque impigri. Pigris enim & ster tentibus quid daret ? Quàm corrupta nunc sunt quæso omnium ferè mortalium ingenia veternus obruit nos,vt otiosè ditescere, vincere, ad honores euehi concupiscamus. Dnser Wing wär mit müssig gang rydcn[?] Inde existunt vsurarij, circulatores, mercenarij milites, caupones,fures,latrones,falsi doctores , & nescio quæ sex hominum. At Deus laboribus sua vendidit.
units.tr: He says that it is theirs to rise up, loose, and cross the river Arnon. By the word "rise up" is signified a will inclined toward the matter proposed, that is, a great and eager zeal. Therefore God wishes to help us, but on this condition, that we ourselves also be vigorous and active. For what would he give to the sluggish and the drowsy? How corrupt, I ask you, are the minds of almost all mortals now! Lethargy overwhelms us, so that we long to grow rich idly, to conquer, and to be raised to honours. (The German proverb says: whoever rides with idleness is paid with poverty.) From this arise usurers, hucksters, mercenary soldiers, innkeepers, thieves, robbers, false teachers, and I know not what sort of men. But God sells his gifts for labour.

units.la: Soluendi verbo moram seu impedimenta notat,quæ deponi debent,vt expediti simus. Vt enim in via sic in vita sunt impedimenta : veluti luxus , crapula,& otium nos impediunt,quò minus ditescamus;itemq; in rep.simultates natæ ex ambitu causæ existunt ciuilium dissensio- num,quibus respub.ne crescat aut proficiat retrahitur.Sic ne in cognitione & fide Christi pro sicias cura terrenarum rerum te remoratur.Vnde dicit Dominus,Qui manu admota aratro à tergo respicit non est me dignus. Quamobrem Moses iubet soluere ,ne dum littore hærent nusquam progrediantur.
units.tr: The word "loosen" (solvere) denotes a delay or hindrances, which must be laid aside so that we may be free. For as on a journey, so in life there are hindrances: luxury, gluttony and idleness keep us from growing rich; likewise in the commonwealth, rivalries born of ambition give rise to civil dissensions, by which the commonwealth is held back from growing or prospering. So too, lest you make progress in the knowledge and faith of Christ, the care of earthly things holds you back. Hence the Lord says, "He who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is not worthy of me." Therefore Moses orders them to loose (cast off), so that they do not stay stuck on the shore and never advance.

units.la: Traijciendi verbo laborem significat & industriam,quibus nihil est ad gerendas res mag- nas cum aptius tum etiam magis necessarium.Multa remigantibus aduersa sunt,sed tamen est traijciendum.Nihil est pernitiosius,quàm cedere. Labor improbus omnia vincit. Atq;sic ita omni vitæ genere cui nos destinauit Dominus cogitabimus nostrarum esse partium esse vigi- lantes & gnauos & impigros.
units.tr: By the word "cross over" (traicere) he signifies labour and diligence, which are both more suitable and more necessary for carrying out great undertakings. Many things are adverse to those who row, yet they must still cross over. Nothing is more harmful than giving way. Unrelenting labour overcomes all things. And so, in whatever walk of life the Lord has appointed us, we should consider it our part to be watchful, diligent and energetic.

units.la: Sed quid facit Deus? Dedi(inquit)eum in manus? Quomodo dabat eum ? Tuprælium sapesce, ego faciam vt ille timeat ac fugiat, fortis ipse sis & vincas.Vides auxilium diuinitus paratum ijs qui res magnas gerendas strenuè suscipiunt.Ergo quod poeta dicit,audentes for- tuna iuuat,tu dic,fortes Deus adiuuat.Deus enim laborantes auget opibus, virtuti studentes dignatur honoribus,gnauiter & prudenter belligerantes donat victoria.Exemplorum plenæ sunt omnes historiæ.Iofuam pugnantem adiuuabat,itemq; Dauidem & Machabeos:apostolo- rum conciones sua quoq; cooperatione prouehebat.Nos si nostro sungamur officio,habebi- mus illũ cooperariū.Ergo cum omnibus in rebus tum in iure gentiū Deum pariter ac te ser- ua,vt quod tua: um sit partium facias,& ab eo quod eius est fidenter expectes. Nam te gnaui- ter enitentem & laborantem ille egregiè promouebit.
units.tr: But what does God do? "I have delivered him into your hands," he says. How did he deliver him? "Begin the battle, and I will make him fear and flee; you yourself be brave and conquer." You see that help is divinely provided for those who bravely undertake great tasks. So, what the poet says, "fortune favours the bold," you should say, "God helps the brave." For God enriches those who labour with resources, deigns to honour those who strive for virtue, and gives victory to those who fight energetically and wisely. All histories are full of examples. He helped Joshua when he fought, and likewise David and the Maccabees; he also advanced the sermons of the apostles by his own co-operation. If we apply ourselves to our duty, we shall have him as our co-worker. Therefore, in all things, and especially in observing the law of nations, serve God and yourself alike: do what is your part, and confidently look for from him what is his. For he will powerfully advance you when you strive and labour with energy.

units.la: Israelitarum studia sic describit,vt intelligas fuisse iuri gentium consentanea.Israelitæ in- structi quidé promissione sciunt quid sit futurum,& tamen eo ipso nõ superbiunt,verum ius gentium nihilominus seruant hoc ipso,quod priusquam ad Seonis terras veniant,nuncios de pace & transitu mittunt propositis conditionibus æquisimis.Et vt eundem omnibus te præ- beas orationem expende.
units.tr: He describes the Israelites' conduct in such a way that you may understand it was in accordance with the law of nations. The Israelites, indeed, having been instructed by the promise, know what is going to happen, and yet for that very reason they do not become arrogant; rather, they nonetheless keep the law of nations, in this very thing, that before they come to the lands of Sihon they send messengers with proposals of peace and passage, on the most equitable conditions. And that you may show yourself the same to all, weigh their language well.

units.la: Exordium à beneuolentiæ captatione ducunt, quia tantum pacem petunt & promittunt. Propositio,qua summam ac caput complectitur,nihil nisi transitum petit, vt appareat quàm non sit iniqua postulatio.Confirmatio repellit quicquid videbatur impedimento fore.Via re- &ta,non declinabo,cõmeatum,etiá aquam ipsam pecunijs meis abs te emam , pedes transibo, quod ipsum etiam leuius est: exempla habeto eorum qui idé mihi præstiterût officium,Edom & Moab.Concludit,hoc transitu nihil aliud quæro quàm vt ad Iordanem peruenia m.
units.tr: They begin by winning goodwill, because they ask and promise only peace. The proposition, which sums up the whole matter, asks only for passage, so that it may appear how unjust the request is not. The confirmation rebuts whatever seemed likely to be an obstacle: "I will not turn aside, by the king's highway; I will buy provisions from you, even water with my money; I will cross on foot, which is itself the lighter course. Take as examples those who have done the same service for me, Edom and Moab." The conclusion is: "By this passage I seek nothing else than to reach the Jordan."

units.la: In quo vides quanta sit adhibenda diligentia,vt saluum sit ius gentium,& vt de tuo iure ce- das potius quàm alium suo pellas.
units.tr: In this you see how much care must be applied, so that the law of nations is kept intact, and so that you yield something of your own right rather than strip another of his.

units.la: Seonis studia dicit, Seon autem rex Hesbon non permisit, &c. Quo ostendit æquissimas illas conditiones ab impio & superbo rege spretas esse, idq; vt intelligatur melius adiecta causa discutitur, nempe quia Deus induraverit cor eius.
units.tr: He describes Sihon's conduct: "But Sihon king of Heshbon would not allow us to pass, etc." By this he shows that those most equitable conditions were scorned by an impious and proud king; and, so that this may be better understood, the added cause is examined, namely that God hardened his heart.

units.la: Quod vt rectius intelligatur, paulò altius est repetendum. Seon tenet terram partim Moa bitis partim Abrahæ iure belli debitam: populus eius Amorrhæi sunt: contra quos iam olim lata fuit sententia, ac qui tunc peccatis suis Deum offenderant, pœnasq; iure daturi fuissent: sed tot annorum dilatione cum emendati non sint, ac mensura veluti solet dici, nunc plena sit, tempus exitio destinatum est. Ideo rex simul cum omni populo sic ad suam messem maturuit, vt neq; remittere, neq; tenere, quemadmodum vulgo dicitur, sciat, seq; suosq; eat perditum. Ac quanquam ipse Seon adeo iniustus & superbus esset, vt neque suum cuique redderet, neq; precibus vagantis populi flecti posset, Satanaq; his usus scalis [?] illius animum occupasset, ac ne cederet æquis postulationibus, ipsum obduraret: tamen quia hæc non fiunt sine Dei providentia, nempe vt Israelitæ sibi debita terra potirentur & peccata tanti nebulonis adeo longo tempore impune patrata coercerétur, Spiritus sanctus finem huius optimum respiciens opus indurationis Deo tribuit.
units.tr: So that this may be understood more correctly, we must go back a little further. Sihon held the land, owed partly to the Moabites and partly to Abraham's seed by right of war. His people are the Amorites, against whom sentence was long ago pronounced, and who at that time had offended God by their sins and would have had to pay the penalty by right. But since they had not been amended over so many years, and their measure, as is commonly said, was now full, the time was fixed for their destruction. So the king, together with the whole people, ripened for his harvest in such a way that he did not know whether to give way or to hold on, as the common saying goes, and so went to his own destruction.
