And although Sihon himself was so unjust and proud that he would not render to each his own, nor could be moved by the prayers of a wandering people, and Satan, using these stairs, had seized his mind and hardened him so that he would not yield to equitable requests: yet, because these things do not happen without the providence of God, namely that the Israelites might possess the land owed to them and that the sins of so great a scoundrel, committed with impunity over so long a time, might be punished, the Holy Spirit, looking to the best end of this work, attributes the hardening to God.

units.la: Quemadmodum hoc etiam fit alibi & in exemplo Pharaonis cernitur. Vbi Deus dicitur excæcare & indurare reprobos, eorumq; corda vertere & impellere, idq; duplici nomine. Primum cum sublato eius lumine cæcitas superest: cum abducto à nobis eius spiritu corda ceu lapides obduruerunt: cum eius nobis negato ductu in obliquum tendimus, tunc excæcare, indurare, inclinare dicitur: quia facultatem videndi, obsequendi, recte res gerendi adimit. Velut Iob 12. aufert labium à veracibus, rationem tollit à senioribus, cor aufert ab iis qui præsunt populo terræ, errare eos facit per inuium. Qui locus indicat quales Deus faciat homines eos, quos deserit. Deinceps est alia quoq; ratio quæ propius accedit ad verborum proprietatem: quod Deus iræ suæ ministro satana agitat impios, vt 1. Reg. 16. Spiritus Domini malus dicitur Saulem modo rapuisse, modo dimisisse. Quod indubie de Satana diuinæ iræ ministro debet intelligi.
units.tr: In the same way this also happens elsewhere, and it is seen in the example of Pharaoh. Where God is said to blind and harden the reprobate, and to turn and drive their hearts, and this in a twofold way. First, when, with their light taken away, blindness remains; when, with his Spirit withdrawn from us, hearts have hardened like stones; when, with his guidance denied us, we tend towards what is crooked: then he is said to blind, harden and incline, because he takes away the ability to see, to obey and to act rightly. Thus in Job 12: he takes away speech from the truthful, takes reason from the elders, takes the heart from those who rule the people of the land, and makes them wander in a pathless waste. That passage shows what kind of people God makes of those whom he forsakes. Next there is another reason, which comes closer to the proper sense of the words: that God, through Satan, his minister of wrath, stirs up the impious, as in 1 Samuel 16, where an evil spirit of the Lord is said to have seized Saul at one time and to have left him at another. This must undoubtedly be understood of Satan, the minister of divine wrath.

units.la: Multum tamen etiam in eodem opere inter id quod Deus agit interest, & inter id quod agunt satan & impij. Deus enim mala instrumenta, quorum ius potestatem habet, suæ iusti-tiæ vti seruiant efficit. Satan autem & impij pro sua prauitate mala faciunt. Exemplo sit ea, quâ Iobi sanctissimo homini intulerunt Chaldæi, calamitas. Iobis pastoribus trucidatis gregem totum abducunt Chaldæi. Satana instigante totum hoc factum esse testis est historia. Iob autem agnoscit hoc opus esse Dei, quem dicit ea, quæ dederit antea, nunc auferre.
units.tr: Yet in the same work there is still much difference between what God does and what Satan and the impious do. For God brings it about that evil instruments, over which he has right and power, serve for the exercise of his justice. But Satan and the impious, out of their own perversity, do evil. Let the calamity which the Chaldeans inflicted on the most holy man Job serve as an example. The Chaldeans slaughtered Job's shepherds and carried off the whole flock. That all this was done at Satan's instigation is attested by the history. Yet Job acknowledges that this work is God's, saying that he who gave the things before now takes them away.

units.la: Quomodo idem opus ad Deum, ad satanam, ad Chaldæos referimus? Certè vel satanam excusabimus Dei consortio, vel eius mali Deum authorem dicemus? Minimè fiet hoc, si suum in agendo finem cuiq; propositum consideremus. Dei consilium est serui sui patientiam calamitate exercere, satan eum cupit ad desperationem adigere. Chaldæi constituerant ex aliena relucrum [?] præter iis [?] & fas accipere. Sic in quodam Psalmo Dauid Iosephi in Ægyptum venditi casum considerat.
units.tr: How do we refer the same work to God, to Satan, and to the Chaldeans? Surely either we shall excuse Satan by associating him with God, or we shall call God the author of that evil? By no means will this happen, if we consider the purpose each one set before himself in acting. It is God's purpose to exercise his servant's patience by calamity; Satan desires to drive him to despair. The Chaldeans had determined to make gain from another's misfortune and to take booty beyond what is lawful. So in a certain Psalm David considers the fate of Joseph, sold into Egypt.

units.la: Eodem modo suum Israelitis ius reddere & diu patrata ac sceleribus cumulata scelera punire Deus voluit. Satan eum regem fascinatum cupidè secum in exitium rapit: rex autem quò plus rogatur, hoc minus exoratur, im <bl>grosset der Kopff/meint es sych nieman dann er</bl> [?]: ideoq; iniustè retentat alienum & superbè despicit populum supplicem. Idem etiam in Heli sacerdotis filijs cernitur. 1. Reg. 2. qui ideo salutaribus monitis non obtemperabant, quod Dominus il-los puniturus esset. Inquis, Cur oculos non aperuit? Inquam quia voluit istum Seonem trade-re, cur tradere? quia sic erat dignus. Cur nō ignoscit, vt aliis peccatoribus? quia voluit punire: cur voluit: nimis progrederis: voluntas Dei summa rerum causa est, ac nihil hac potest maius existere, & cum natura diuinitatis pugnat, aliquid habere cui sit aligata. Ergo quicquid Deus vult, hoc ipso quod vult, iustum est. Hæc probè tenenda sunt, vt & Deum agnoscas, & tempo-re pœnitentiæ dato non abutare, quasi ipse velis ac possis quoties libeat resipiscere.
units.tr: In the same way God willed to render his due to the Israelites and to punish the crimes long committed and piled up by wickedness. Satan eagerly drags the bewitched king with him to ruin; but the more the king is entreated, the less he is moved, and (as the German saying goes, "when the head swells, no one thinks it means anyone but himself") therefore he unjustly holds on to what is another's and proudly despises the suppliant people. The same is seen also in the sons of Eli the priest, 1 Samuel 2, who for that reason did not obey salutary warnings, because the Lord was going to punish them. You ask, "Why did he not open their eyes?" I answer: because he willed to hand over that Sihon; why hand him over? Because he was thus worthy. Why does he not pardon him, as he does other sinners? Because he willed to punish: why did he will it? You go too far: the will of God is the highest cause of all things, and nothing can exist greater than this, and it is contrary to the nature of divinity to have anything to which it is bound. Therefore whatever God wills, by the very fact that he wills it, is just. These things must be held firmly, both so that you may acknowledge God, and so that you do not abuse the time of repentance given to you, as if you could and might repent whenever it pleases you.

units.la: Finem siue euentum sic describit docens, 1. Egressum illum & deuictum esse: Pereunt cū eo simul omnes omnis generis atq; sexus homines, quippe qui cum rege peccassent. Sic cum Pharaone Ægyptij, cum Saule Israelitæ, cum scribis & pontificibus Iudæi, cū principibus Germanicis Germani. Hoc est iudicium Dei. Nos discamus voluntate Dei cum persona nostra com-parare: eos quibus cum nobis res est iniuria nulla afficere: & finem Deo gloriosum, nobis salutarem habere propositum, quem etiam diuinitus adiuti per Christum assequemur. Amen.
units.tr: He describes the end or outcome thus, teaching (1) that the one who went out was also overcome: all people of every kind and sex perish together with him, since they had sinned along with their king. So the Egyptians perished with Pharaoh, the Israelites with Saul, the Jews with the scribes and high priests, and the Germans with the German princes. This is the judgment of God. Let us learn to apply the will of God to our own persons, to do no injury to those with whom we have a quarrel, and to hold as our purpose an end that is glorious to God and salutary to us, which we shall also reach, aided by God through Christ. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: SERMO XI.
units.tr: SERMON XI.

units.la: VErsi autem ascendimus per iter Basan. Et egressus rex Basan occurrit nobis ipse & vniuersus populus eius, vt congrederetur nobiscum in Edrei.
units.tr: And we went up by the way of Bashan. Then Og, king of Bashan, came out against us, he and all his people, to fight with us at Edrei.

units.la: 2 Tum dixit Dominus ad me: Ne timeas eum, nam tradidi eum in manum tuam, & cunctum populum eius, atque terram eius, tu facies ei, quemadmodum fecisti Sihon regi Amorræorum, qui habitauit in Hesbon.
units.tr: 2 And the Lord said to me: "Do not fear him, for I have delivered him into your hand, with all his people and his land. You shall do to him as you did to Sihon, king of the Amorites, who dwelt at Heshbon."

units.la: 3 Tradiditque itaque Dominus Deus noster in manum nostram etiam Ogipsum, regem Basan, & vniuersum populum eius, percussimusque eum, vt non superesset ei reliquus.
units.tr: 3 So the Lord our God delivered into our hand also Og, king of Bashan, with all his people, and we struck him down so that no survivor was left to him.

units.la: 4 Et cepimus eodem tempore omnes ciuitates eius, nec fuit ciuitas vlla quam non caperemus ab eis, sexaginta ciuitates per vniuersum tractum Argob regni Og in Basan.
units.tr: 4 At that time we took all his cities, and there was no city we did not take from them: sixty cities, the whole region of Argob, the kingdom of Og in Bashan.

units.la: 5 Erant sq; omnes illæ vrbes altis muris, foribus & repagulis munitæ, præter ciuitates quæ muros non habebant, quarum erant admodum multæ,
units.tr: 5 All those cities were fortified with high walls, gates and bars, besides the unwalled towns, which were very many.

units.la: 6 Has ad internecionem vsq; excidimus, sicut feceramus Sihon regi Hesbon, vastando funditus omnes vrbes, viros, mulieres, & pubem.
units.tr: 6 These we destroyed utterly, as we had done to Sihon, king of Heshbon, laying waste every city, men, women and children.

units.la: 7 Cuncta tamen iumenta, & spolia ciuitatum diripuimus nobis.
units.tr: 7 But all the cattle and the spoil of the cities we took for ourselves.

units.la: 8 Ademimus itaque eodem tempore terram istam de manu duorum regum Amorrhæorum, quæ erat cis Iordanem, à torrente Arnon vsq; ad montem Hermon.
units.tr: 8 So at that time we took the land out of the hand of the two kings of the Amorites, the land on this side of the Jordan, from the torrent Arnon to Mount Hermon.

units.la: 9 Porrò Sidonij vocant (montem) Hermon Sirion, & Amorrhæi uocant eum Senir.
units.tr: 9 (The Sidonians call Hermon Sirion, and the Amorites call it Senir.)

units.la: 10 Omnes ciuitates in planicie sitas, & vniuersum Gilead, atq; omnem Basan, vsq; ad Salcha & Edrei, quæ erant ciuitates regni Og in Basan.
units.tr: 10 All the cities of the plain, all Gilead, and all Bashan, as far as Salcah and Edrei, which were cities of the kingdom of Og in Bashan.

units.la: 11 Solus enim Og rex Basan remanserat ex reliquiis Rephaim, & en lectus eius erat lectus ferreus, qui adhuc uisitur in Rabbath filiorum Ammon, nouem cubitos habet longitudo eius, & quatuor cubitos latitudo eius iuxta cubitum virilem.
units.tr: 11 For Og, king of Bashan, alone remained of the remnant of the Rephaim. Behold, his bed was an iron bed, which is still shown in Rabbah of the children of Ammon: its length is nine cubits and its breadth four cubits, by the common cubit.

units.la: VOD vulgo dici simul atq; credi solet, ex suis quenq; virtutibus bona, & ex sceleribus mala percipere, & omnino sua quenq; fide & synceritate promoueri, impediri vero perfidia: deniq; vt suas quisq; res auspicetur, sic earum euentum sortiri solere: id cum in omni vitæ genere, tum vero perpulchrè in hoc seruati & non seruati iuris gentium exemplo pulcherrimo, quod Moses nobis describit in præsentia verum esse perspicitur. Nam vt ius gentium doceat ac persuadeat, exempli vice graue bellum intro ducit, quod olim cum Og Basan rege maiores eorum gesserant, & in eo describendo 1.susceptum 2.vt gestum sit indicat. Vbi facile est cernere quàm sint felices rerum recte suscepta rum euentus, quàm infelices exitus habeant res perperam susceptæ.
units.tr: It is commonly said and believed that each person receives good things from his own virtues and evil things from his own crimes, and that in general each is advanced by his own faith and sincerity but hindered by treachery; and that, as each begins his affairs, so he is accustomed to obtain their outcome. This is shown to be true in every kind of life, and most beautifully in this most excellent example of the law of nations, kept and broken, which Moses here describes for us. For in order to teach and persuade us about the law of nations, he brings in, as an example, a grave war which their forefathers once waged with Og, king of Bashan; and in describing it he indicates, first, how it was undertaken and, second, how it was carried out. Here it is easy to see how happy is the outcome of things rightly undertaken, and how unhappy the end of things wrongly undertaken.

units.la: Quomodo susceptū sic docet, vt quod dicimus clarissimè videas: dicit enim Israelitas verbum Domini secutos, Og em autem illum his occurrisse, & temerè bellum intulisse. Israelitas vt iniuriam abs se repellerent, quod est iuris gentium, Deum precatos, & ab eo cum auditos tum confirmatos hostem illum repulisse. Summa hæc est: ipsas autem personas describit ordine. Israelitæ verbum Dei vocans in terram promissam sequuntur. Idq; Moses indicat dicens eos ascendisse per iter Basan. Ex quo discimus verbum Dei propositum sequi, illiusq; ve stigia nusquam deserere. Non dubium erat quin Oges ille offenderetur, & tamen progredi endum fuit, ne quod antea ex inobedientia damnum acceperant, nunc sibi iterum accerse rent. Sic cuilibet magistratui finis est propositus, salus videlicet atq; incolumitas ciuiũ, eò ci ues erunt deducendi etiamsi rumperentur hostibus ilia. Illi transitum petunt, licita monstra taq; diuinitus via eunt. Ergo magistratus ad Deum recta via deducat suos, nec hostes vllos moretur. Offenduntur, sed quid tum? priuatim quisq; salutis suæ curam habeat, eat per illud iter quod Christus verus Moses ducit, vt ut fremant gentes.
units.tr: He teaches how it was undertaken so that you may see clearly what we are saying: he says that the Israelites followed the word of the Lord, but that Og came out to meet them and rashly made war upon them. The Israelites, to repel the injury done to them, which is in accordance with the law of nations, prayed to God, and, being heard and strengthened by him, drove back that enemy. This is the sum; but he describes the persons themselves in order. The Israelites, following the word of God, which calls them to the promised land, go forward. Moses indicates this when he says they went up by the way of Bashan. From this we learn to follow the word of God that is set before us, and never to desert its footsteps. There was no doubt that Og would be offended, yet they had to proceed, lest they bring upon themselves again the loss they had earlier suffered through disobedience. So every magistrate has a goal set before him, namely the safety and wellbeing of his citizens, and to that end the citizens must be led even if the enemies rage. They seek passage and go by a way that is lawful and divinely given. Therefore let the magistrate lead his people by the straight way to God, and let him not be delayed by any enemies. They are offended, but what of it? Let each private person take care of his own salvation, and go by that way which Christ, the true Moses, leads, though the nations rage.

units.la: Oges ipse & vniuersus populus eius egressi illis occurrunt, vt manum consererent. Pau-D cis ostendit tyrannum hunc bellum his intulisse, qui nulla eum lacesiuerint iniuria. Nam oc currendi verbo celeritas, belli nomine finis indicatur. Ac in bello quidem gerendo bonum maximum est celeritas, in suscipiendo verò cunctatio. Benedixit ille, deliberandum esse diu, verum vbi deliberaueris maturè facto opus esse. Hic non diu deliberat, sed statim occurrit, nullis tentatis pacis conditionibus. Improbanda temeritas: labile est almæ pacis studium. Et dulce bellū est inexpertis. Nam homines nō occumbunt si sint pauperes, sed si non sint, egen tes siunt. Nō vt velis ac libeat pax reddi-tur. Nemo nisi victor pace belli mutauit. Recte ergo dixit ille, Sapientem decere vt omnia prius tentet, quàm armis res gerat. Sed ô Deus bone quàm temerè & violéter bella cum suscipi tum geri solent hoc tempore? Cares ijs bella infe-rebant à quibus non essent vlla lacesiti iniuria: verum ipsi quoq; tandé præda fiebant exte-ris. Quid inter nos & illos interest? An non bella nunc suscipimus atq; gerimus neglecto iu-re gentiū? Quibus enim iniurijs nos lacesiuerunt Itali? Pedemontani? Belgæ? aut si qua acce-pta sit ab his iniuria, cur non prius more maiorum, & secundam rectam formam iuris gen-tium eis bellum indicimus? an illis non præmonitis belligerantes sic satis existimationi fa-mæq; nostræ consultum est? Acsi qua nobis sit illata ab his iniuria, communi gentis nostræ consensu cōmunibusq; copijs & auxilijs erat vindicanda: sin nulla ab his, quod magis credi-derim, affecti simus, omnium erat ab atroci facinore nostros homines reuocare, & ne effusio-ne sanguinis innocentis male dictione toti genti accerserent, cauere. O quàm iucundū Tur-cis, nobis triste spectaculū sunt quæ nunc geruntur bella? Sed hoc ipso ferè defendimus fce-lus, quod impune iam diu patrauerimus: at ex eo nō sequitur impunè semper patrari posse.
units.tr: Og himself and all his people came out and met them to join battle. Moses shows in few words that this tyrant made war upon them although they had given him no provocation. For the word "came out" indicates speed, and the word "war" indicates the end. In waging war, speed is the greatest good; in undertaking it, however, delay is best. That man said that one must deliberate long, but once you have deliberated, you must act promptly. Here he did not deliberate long but at once came out, without trying any terms of peace. Rashness is to be condemned; the zeal for gentle peace is slippery. And war is sweet to those who have not tried it. For men do not perish if they are poor, but if they are not poor they become needy. Peace is not restored for the sake of what one wishes or pleases. No one has ever changed war for peace except as victor. Rightly, then, did that man say that it befits a wise man to try everything before he wages war by arms. But, good God, how rashly and violently are wars in this age usually both undertaken and waged! They make war upon those by whom they have been provoked by no injury; but in the end they themselves become the prey of foreigners. What difference is there between us and them? Do we not now undertake and wage wars, neglecting the law of nations? For what injuries have the Italians, the Piedmontese, or the Belgians provoked us with? Or if some injury has been received from them, why do we not first, after the custom of our ancestors and the proper form of the law of nations, declare war on them? Or do we think we have sufficiently consulted our reputation and good name by waging war without warning them? And if some injury has been done to us by them, it ought to be avenged by the common consent of our nation, with common forces and aids; but if we have been affected by no injury from them, which I would rather believe, then it was the duty of all to call our men back from that savage crime, and to take care that by the shedding of innocent blood they do not bring a curse upon the whole nation. Oh, how pleasing to the Turks are the wars now waged among us, and how sad a spectacle for us! Yet we almost defend this crime by the very fact that we have committed it with impunity for so long; but it does not follow that it can always be committed with impunity.

units.la: Et hic noster Oges diu bellis vicinas gentes presseratiam idem facturus ipse opprimitur: si si si si si si si si si si si si ne nobis euenìat pœnitentia ac precibus ad Deum fusis cauebitur.
units.tr: And here our Og, who for a long time had oppressed the neighboring nations by wars, is himself overwhelmed while about to do the same thing. It will be guarded against, so that it does not befall us, by repentance and prayers poured out to God.

units.la: Iac[?]ael quid facit? Dixit Dominus, ne timeas eum. Quibus verbis ipsius Dei consilium ponit ob oculos ceu typum rectæ de pace & bello deliberationis. Sed considera singula. 1. Neti-meas eum. Quasi dicat: Etsi sæuiat magnopere, tamen eum propterea non est quod metuas.
units.tr: What does Iac[?]ael do? The Lord said, do not fear him. By these words he sets before our eyes the counsel of God himself, as a type of the right deliberation about peace and war. But consider each point. 1. Do not fear him. As if he said: Although he rages greatly, there is nonetheless no reason for you to fear him.

units.la: Quibus verbis metum pessimum consultorem remouet. Nam metus consilijs pariter atque facti-s honestis præclarisq; semper obfuit. Metus suadet turpem pacem, qua, vt ait Demosthe-nes, bellum potius est. Nam honestè mori præstat quàm turpiter viuere. [illegible, ~8 letters] inquit Demosthenes, [illegible, ~10 letters]. Metus etiam deditiones & defectiones suadet. Ergo vacare metu viri principes debent, quippe in quibus alijs spes est & solatium. At hostem potentem quis non metuat? Ne timeas eum, inquit Dominus, scilicet occurrente & volentem pugnare. Quo magis demit metum, cum iubeat etiam minas negligere. Duces populi non decet esse ceruos, sed leones, qui magnis animis & hostiles minas & suorum ho-minum impatientiam superent.
units.tr: By these words he removes fear, the worst counselor. For fear has always been an obstacle to counsels as well as to honorable and distinguished deeds. Fear recommends a shameful peace, which, as Demosthenes says, is rather a war. For it is better to die honorably than to live shamefully. [illegible] says Demosthenes, [illegible]. Fear also recommends surrenders and desertions. Therefore princes ought to be free from fear, since others place their hope and comfort in them. But who would not fear a powerful enemy? "Do not fear him," says the Lord, that is, though he comes out to meet you and wishes to fight. By so much more does he remove fear, since he commands us to disregard even threats. Leaders of the people ought not to be stags but lions, who by great courage overcome both the threats of the enemy and the impatience of their own men.

units.la: 2. Tradidit ipsum, populum, terram. id est, ipsum qui videtur animo valere & viribus, eius au-xilia, eius opes, vt belli neruos. Quo magis hostis superbierit hoc certius poterit intelligi ip-sum esse diuinitus traditū. [illegible, ~9 letters]. Superbia signum victoriæ est humilibus quos despicias.
units.tr: 2. He delivered him, his people, his land. That is, him who seems strong in spirit and resources, together with his allies, his wealth, the sinews of war. The more proudly the enemy carries himself, the more clearly it can be understood that he has been delivered by God. [illegible]. Pride is a sign of victory over the humble whom you despise.

units.la: 3 Ab exemplo Seonis argumentum ducit. Quo docet ex anteactis consolationem capere. Imperatoris est animo renouare memoriam victoriæ veteris. Atq; sic videmus rectam de bello suscipiendo deliberationē, quæ etiá alibi descripta cernitur, esse proposita. Nempe vt deceo deliberans primum te cōsideres, id est ciuitatis tuæ vires quantæ sint, quantæq; cōpa-rari queant, quot qualesq; habeas vicinos atq; socios, tecū ne an cū hostibus sint futuri: tum quos habeas hostes, quibus ij sint præditi viribus, quos socios vicinosq; habeat. Inde institue-tur vtrarumq; partiū cōparatio, ex qua perspicuū fiat, pax ne sit futura potior, an bellū. Hanc cogitationem Deus moderabitur, quando primū eius verbū, ac deinceps ius gentium respe-xeris. Verbum eius iubebit omni metu vacare: ius gentiū docebit iure primū experiri num pax obtineri possit, tum si illo ipso nil proficias, inculpatam tutelam rebus suis feruandis ad-hibere. Sed vt metum excutias, bella quæ prius gesseris reuocanda sunt ob oculos, vt pecca-ta priora nunc vites, virtutes imiteris, euentu cōsoleris. Atq; hæc cogitatio cum vtilis est tū necessaria. Vtilis quia benè & maturè deliberata bene cadunt. Necessaria quia non semper pax est, sed occasiones sunt multæ & variæ. Aliquando defendendi sunt qui patiuntur iniu-riam, veluti socij, vicini subditi, quib.scelus est negare auxilia. Aliquando nos ipsi lacessimur iniurijs. Si iure nil proficitur, tunc arma sumi necesse est. Vt Abraham & 5. reges, Dauid contra Ammonitas coacti sumpseruntarma. Lydi contempti sunt ob timiditatem. Summa, sic affectos esse viros bonos æquum est, ut in quadam Corinthiorum concione dictum esse Thucydides perhibet. Ἀθηναῖοι γὰρ σωφρονῶν[?] μᾶλλον ἐξὸν εἰ μὴ ἀδικοῦντο [illegible, ~20 letters] ἐν εἰρήνῃ πολεμεῖν. Qui sic animo comparati, iis quæ conantur omnia succedunt ex animi sententia.
units.tr: 3. He draws an argument from the example of Sihon, teaching us to take comfort from past events. It is the commander's part to renew in his mind the memory of an earlier victory. So we see that the sound deliberation about undertaking war, which is also described elsewhere, is set out here. Namely, as a prudent man deliberating, you should first consider yourself: how great your city's strength is and how much it can be increased, how many and what kind of neighbours and allies you have, and whether they will be with you or against you. Then consider what enemies you have, what forces they possess, and what allies and neighbours they have. From a comparison of the two sides it will become clear whether peace or war is the better course. God will guide this reflection, if you first heed his word and then the law of nations. His word will bid you be free of all fear. The law of nations will teach you first to test by right whether peace can be obtained, and then, if nothing is gained by that, to use blameless defence to keep your possessions safe. But to shake off fear, the wars you have fought before must be brought back before your eyes, so that you avoid earlier sins, imitate virtues, and console yourself with the outcome. This reflection is both useful and necessary. It is useful, because things well and maturely deliberated turn out well. It is necessary, because there is not always peace; occasions are many and various. Sometimes those who suffer injury must be defended, such as allies, neighbours and subjects, to whom it is wicked to deny help. Sometimes we ourselves are provoked by injuries. If nothing is achieved by right, then arms must be taken up. So Abraham and the five kings, and David against the Ammonites, were compelled to take up arms. The Lydians were despised for their timidity. In sum, it is fitting that good men be disposed in this way, as Thucydides reports was said in a certain assembly of the Corinthians: [Ἀθηναῖοι γὰρ σωφρονῶν μᾶλλον ἐξὸν εἰ μὴ ἀδικοῦντο [illegible] ἐν εἰρήνῃ πολεμεῖν]. Those so disposed in spirit find that everything they attempt succeeds according to their wish.

units.la: Ut gestum & perfectum. Dominus cum tradidit &c. Quo ostendit populo Israelitico victoriam contigisse cum utilem tum honestam. Utilem quia metuendus hostis, qui voluit simulac visus est potuisse damnum dare, bello hoc domitus est. Unde & onere maximo levati sunt. Sed & hoc nomine fuit utilis victoria, quod in illorum cassces incidit, fera non solum imanis ac metuenda, verumetiam pinguis, quippe ex qua magna splendidaque spoliatu[illegible, ~12 letters] rint. Quod argumento fuerit eos non solum damno levatos, verumetiam maximis auctos esse commodis. Unde perspicuum est utile esse quandoque operam & oleum fumere: [illegible, ~15 letters]. Sæpe fit ut quæ videatur pax non fit, in qua videlicet subinde metus sit & damnum. Eam profecto præstaret non esse quàm tantopere nocere. Ergo hoc onere levati, hisce polisi ditati Israelitæ vi victoriam supra modum utilem reportarunt.
units.tr: As done and completed. When the Lord delivered them, etc. Here he shows that the victory came to the Israelite people both useful and honourable. It was useful, because the enemy, who was to be feared, and who wished to do harm as soon as he seemed able, was subdued by this war. Hence they were relieved of a very great burden. But the victory was useful also in this respect: it fell upon their folds, a beast not only huge and frightening but also fat, from which great and splendid spoils were taken. This is evidence that they were not only relieved of harm but greatly enriched with advantages. Whence it is clear that it is sometimes useful to take up toil and effort [illegible]. It often happens that what appears to be peace is not peace, since fear and loss are at times present within it. Certainly it would be better not to be harmed so greatly. Therefore, relieved of this burden and enriched with these spoils, the Israelites gained a victory exceedingly useful.

units.la: Honestam etiam fuisse Moses hoc ipso docet quod ostendat hostem minime contemnendum, sed potentissimum superatum esse, sed etiam urbes exceptis vicis & castellis sexaginta magnæ & munitæ fuerunt. Ipse gygantibus ortus maioribus, adeo vasto corpore præditus, ut lectio describit. Hic quoniam dominus dedit vincere, est egregia victoria. Exempla sunt Gen.14. Abraham, Israelitæ contra Pharaonem pro libertate, & contra Madianitas pro ultio ne iniuriarum. Iosue contra Hierichuntem. Dauid pro liberanda Ziclag. Eiusmodi bella maiores nostri gesserunt contra Austriacos principes, contra Burgundionum ducem, contra Anglos, contra Sueuos aliosq; innumeros penè magnos & exiguos hostes. Quæ eis bella cesserunt optimè. Gesta sunt patrum nostrorum notaraq; ipsorum memoria quædam, quæ minus prosperos exitus habuere. Qui id factum est? Sanè quia non ita iuste suscepta sunt, ut illa à nostris maioribus. Eodem modo bellum hoc etiam Israelitis succesisset felicius quàm quæ dam priora. Qui id? Quod hoc iussu Dei suscepit sit, & iustissimè gestum.
units.tr: Moses also shows that it was honourable by this very fact: that it demonstrates the enemy was by no means to be despised, but a most powerful one was overcome; and that the cities, besides villages and fortresses, were sixty in number, large and fortified. Og himself was descended from the giants and endowed with so vast a body, as the text describes. Since the Lord gave them the victory, it is an outstanding victory. Examples are in Genesis 14: Abraham; the Israelites against Pharaoh for liberty, and against the Midianites in vengeance for injuries; Joshua against Jericho; David for the liberation of Ziklag. Our ancestors waged such wars against the Austrian princes, against the duke of Burgundy, against the English, against the Swabians, and against countless other enemies, almost great and small. Those wars turned out very well for them. There are deeds of our fathers, and some memorable events of theirs, which had less prosperous outcomes. Why did this happen? Surely because they were not undertaken as justly as those of our ancestors. In the same way, this war would have turned out more happily for the Israelites than some earlier ones. Why? Because it was undertaken at God's command and carried out most justly.

units.la: Ex quo potest intelligi, ut res suscipiuntur sic solere perfici: propterea q; iusta & Deo auspice suscipiendas esse, ut euentus habeant felices. Quod fiet si ipse lædas neminem, læsus autem ab aliis, inculpata tutela, quæ iure gentium concessa est vtare. Id te facientem Deus semper adiuuabit per Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum. Amen.
units.tr: From this it can be understood that, as things are undertaken, so they usually turn out; therefore they should be undertaken justly and under God's auspices, so that they have happy outcomes. This will happen if you harm no one, but when you are harmed by others, you use the blameless defence which the law of nations allows. God will always help you in doing this, through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

units.la: SERMO XII.
units.tr: Sermon 12

units.la: 12 Et hanc quidem terram nunc occupavimus, ab Aroer quæ est ad torrentem Arnon, & dimidium montis Gilead, & civitates eius dedi Rubenitis & Gaditis:
units.tr: 12 And this land we have now occupied, from Aroer, which is by the river Arnon, and half the mountain of Gilead, and its cities I gave to the Reubenites and the Gadites.

units.la: 13 Reliquam vero partem Gilead, & universam Basan, regnum videlicet Og dedi dimidiæ tribui Manasse, omnem scilicet trallum Argob cum tota Basan, quæ & ipsa vocatur terra Rephaim.
units.tr: 13 But the rest of Gilead, and all Bashan, the kingdom of Og, I gave to the half-tribe of Manasseh: that is, all the region of Argob with all Bashan, which is also itself called the land of the Rephaim.

units.la: 14 Iair filius Manasse occupavit omnem trallum Argob usq; ad limitem Gefuri[?] & Maachati, & nominavit ea (loca) iuxta nomen suum, Basan Havoth Iair usq; in hodiernum diem.
units.tr: 14 Jair, the son of Manasseh, occupied all the region of Argob as far as the border of Geshuri and Maacathi, and he named those places after his own name, Bashan-havoth-jair, even to this day.

units.la: 15 Ipsi Machir vero dedi Gilead.
units.tr: 15 But to Machir I gave Gilead.

units.la: 16 Porro Rubenitis & Gaditis dedi de Gilead, usq; ad torrentem Arnon, medium torrentis, & limitem, usq; ad Iabok torrentem, qui limes est filiorum Ammon.
units.tr: 16 Moreover, to the Reubenites and the Gadites I gave from Gilead as far as the river Arnon, the middle of the river being the border, and as far as the river Jabbok, which is the border of the children of Ammon.

units.la: 17 Vasta quoq; loca, & ipsum Iordanem atq; limitem a Cinereth usq; ad mare solitudinis, mare videlicet salis, sub scatebris collis ad orientem.
units.tr: 17 Also the plain, and the Jordan itself with its border, from Chinnereth even to the sea of the wilderness, that is, the Salt Sea, under the springs of the slope toward the east.

units.la: 18 Eodem tempore præcepi vobis, dicens, Dominus Deus vester dedit vobis terram istam, ut possideatis eam: in primo pilo transibitis ante fratres vestros filios Israel, omnes scilicet qui viri estis.
units.tr: 18 At that time I commanded you, saying: The Lord your God has given you this land to possess it. You shall pass over armed before your brothers, the children of Israel, all of you who are men of war.

units.la: 19 Tantum uxores vestræ, pubes vestra, pecora vestra (scio enim quod multum pecoris est) vobis manebunt in civitatibus vestris, quas dedi vobis.
units.tr: 19 Only your wives, your little ones and your cattle (for I know that you have much livestock) shall remain in your cities which I have given you.

units.la: 20 Donec Dominus requiem dederit fratribus vestris, sicut vobis, & occupa-uerint ipsi quoq; terram, quam Dominus Deus vester dedit eis ultra Iordanem, tunc revertimini unusquisq; ad possessionem suam quam dedi vobis.
units.tr: 20 Until the Lord gives rest to your brothers as he gave it to you, and they too possess the land which the Lord your God has given them beyond the Jordan; then each of you shall return to his possession which I have given you.

units.la: 21 Et ipsi Iehosua præcepi eodem tempore hisce verbis: Viderunt oculi tui cun-cta[?] quæ fecit Dominus Deus vester duobus istis regibus, sic faciet omnibus regnis ad quæ tu iam transis.
units.tr: 21 And at the same time I commanded Joshua, saying: Your eyes have seen all that the Lord your God did to these two kings; so will he do to all the kingdoms into which you are passing.

units.la: 22 Ne timeatis eos, quia Iehoua Deus vester ipse est qui pugnat pro vobis.
units.tr: 22 Do not fear them, for the Lord your God himself is the one who fights for you.

units.la: Postquam diuinus Moses suum populū iuris gentiū studio ad intelligendā ac feruandā legem Dei præparare voluit, idq; ipsum v: efficeret exempla quædā ex ipsius gentis historijs demonstrandi causa adduxit: iam aliud progymnasma sumit, nempe fidē: siue eā, quæ in dictis & in factis cernitur, veritatem & constantiam: quo virtutis genere non minus nos, quàm priore præparat ad intelligendam pariter ac feruandam legē Domini. Quemadmodū enim qui ius gentiū in omni vitæ genere, & in comutatione & comunicatione rerum atq; officiorum seduló semper feruat, eo vsu tam præclaro studio sic assueuit, vt ad studium iuris diuini adduci facillimè possit: sic qui fidelis esse mortalibus assueuerit, idem etiam Deo fidem seruabit constantius. Nam ea quæ Deo debetur & ea quæ potest atq; debet præstari mortalibus fides, coniunctæ sunt & cognatæ. Vulgo dici solet non fore fidelē in magnis qui in parvis non fuerit: ita profecto fidelis in Deum non erit, qui in hominēs non fuerit. Quemadmodum D. Ioan. dicit: Quomodo Deū, quē non videt, potest diligere: qui proximū, quem videt, non diligit? Ergo primum homines hominibus fideles esse debent, tunc ipse[?] erit eos etiā in Deum eosdem fore. Ad id Moses hac vltima parte præsentis cap. nos extimulat, adductis tribus exemplis bonæ fidei, quorū duo præsenti cōtextu verborū cōpleētitur: sic ea proponēs, vt primum materiam in qua fides exerceri mutuumque præstari queat, tum exemplarimul ambo afferat.
units.tr: Since divine Moses wished to prepare his people, by their zeal for the law of nations, to understand and keep the law of God, and in order to do this he brought forward certain examples from the histories of that same nation by way of demonstration, he now takes up another preparatory exercise, namely faith: that is, the faithfulness and constancy shown in words and deeds. This kind of virtue prepares us no less than the former to understand and likewise to keep the law of the Lord. For just as one who diligently observes the law of nations in every kind of life, and in the exchange and sharing of goods and duties, becomes so accustomed to that very praiseworthy practice that he can very easily be led to the study of divine law, so one who has become accustomed to being faithful to mortals will also keep faith with God more steadfastly. For the faith owed to God and the faith which can and must be given to mortals are joined and akin. It is commonly said that one who is not faithful in small things will not be faithful in great things; so certainly one who has not been faithful to men will not be faithful to God. As St John says: How can he who does not love his neighbour, whom he sees, love God whom he does not see? Therefore men must first be faithful to men, and then they will be the same toward God as well. To this Moses urges us in the last part of the present chapter, adducing three examples of good faith, of which two are comprised in the present context of words. He sets them out in such a way that he first offers the matter in which faith can be exercised and mutually rendered, and then brings forward the examples together.

units.la: Materia ad hunc modum describitur: Et hanc quidem terram occupauimus tunc ab Aroer etc. Quibus verbis terræ diuinitus datæ descriptione ponit, quasi illius & iā occupatæ portio, & adhuc accipiēdæ possessio materia sit futura, in cuius distributione & fruitione fides & veritas siue dictorū factorumq; constantia sit exercedenda. Magnū est vincere, sed multò magis est victoria rectè vti. Præclarè est illud quidē de Hannibale dictum: Vincere scis Hannibal victoria vti nescis. At licet bona magna possideas, non aut fides in eorū distributione & vsu feruetur, seruari parta non poterunt. Nam regna, ciuitates, familiæ, fœdera quæ fide caruerūt, nunquam diu stare potuerunt. Quæ magnis laboribus Alexand. Magnus cōparauerat dum ab heredibus parum fidelibus inique diuiderentur, sensim amissa sunt. Numidiæ regnum quod Micipsa rex Iugurthæ & Hiempsali & Adherbali filijs florentissimum reliquerat, perfidia discordiaq; postestate Rom. venit. Rom. rempub. Cæsar & Pomp. mutua perfidia deiecerunt. Sæpe etiam magni exercitus victores dum prædam quæ potiti fuerant, perfide diuidunt, obruti sunt & superati. Et certè Ermetingæ victoria vespere amissa quentis diei diluculo per hostilem discordiam & parum fidam concordemq; prædæ diuisionem maioribus nostris recuperata est. Nam dum regiæ copiæ de duobus tormentis inter se decertarent, eaq; quiq; habere vellent, nostri in illos subito impetu facto cum tormentis reliquisq; spoliis victoriam, fusis fugatisq; hostibus recuperant. Idem Æsopicus ille de mure & rana apologus significat. Quamobrem iubet Moses non solum erga exteros ius gentium seruare, verum etiam erga se mutuam fidem colere, videlicet vt rebus quæsitis vti queant.
units.tr: The matter is described in this way: And this land we have occupied then, from Aroer etc. By these words he sets out a description of the land given by God, as if a portion of it already occupied, and the possession still to be received, were to be the matter in whose distribution and enjoyment faith and truth, that is, constancy in words and deeds, must be exercised. Conquering is a great thing, but using victory well is much greater. That saying about Hannibal is rightly famous: "You know how to conquer, Hannibal; you do not know how to use victory." But although you may possess great goods, unless faith is kept in their distribution and use, what has been gained cannot be preserved. For kingdoms, cities, families and covenants that lacked faith could never stand long. The things that Alexander the Great had acquired with great labours were gradually lost while they were unjustly divided among heirs who were little faithful. The kingdom of Numidia, which Micipsa, the king, left most flourishing to his sons Jugurtha, Hiempsal and Adherbal, through treachery and discord came into the power of the Romans. Caesar and Pompey overthrew the Roman commonwealth by mutual treachery. Often too great armies, victorious, when they treacherously divided the spoil they had seized, were overwhelmed and defeated. And surely at Ermetinga, the victory lost in the evening was recovered by our forefathers at dawn the next day, through the hostile discord and the unfaithful, unharmonious division of the booty. For while the royal forces were contending among themselves over two cannons, each wanting to have them, our men made a sudden attack on them, and recovered the victory with the cannons and the other spoils, routing and putting the enemy to flight. That Aesopic fable of the mouse and the frog means the same. Therefore Moses commands not only that the law of nations be kept toward foreigners, but also that mutual faith be cultivated among themselves, so that they may be able to enjoy the goods they have acquired.

units.la: Quid igitur est fides? Sanè ex eo quod quæ dicta sunt fiant, dici videtur. Et est dictorum conuentorumque constantia & veritas. Est etiam & iustitiæ & amicitiæ fundamentum, & Rerumpublicarum conseruatrix. Nec enim, vt ait in officijs Cicero, vlla res vehementius rempub. continet quàm fides. Et vt idem dicit alibi, nihil stabile est quod infidum est. Quid igitur vulgo dicimus? <bl>Verheissen ist adenlich / halten püwer sch/meinst du werdist zum puwren/ wäre wäger zum puwren / denn zum schelmen..</bl> Sed non solum verbis effertur, verum etiam adeò manet alta mente repostum, vt placere nobis declaret res ipsa. Nam simulare & dissimulare, & foro se parare, & seruire tempori summa nunc videatur esse prudentia: at eundem esse & sibi semper constare stultitia putetur. Quàm bene satis docent hæc tempora. Turcæ fidem seruando non solum Asiam, verum etiam magnam Europæ partem acquisiuerunt, quippe quod vsu compertum habeant multi populi plus illorum promissis nudis, quàm nostris tabulis tribuendum esse. Romani cum fidem seruarent rem suam publicam auxerunt: eandemque cum cepissent violare fidem, pessundederunt. Id eo ipso Moses cauere voluit, quod suos hanc seruare docuit. Et Christus docet, Sit sermo vester est est, non non. Nostrum quoq; erat in illa pace, quam di uinitus his annis confequuti fumus maximam, sic fideles & amantes veritatis esse, vt non effent in rebus contrahendis tam frequentia mendacia. Sed forum tam frequens fatis magno est indicio sermones nostros alios esse, quàm Christus docuerit. Ergo quia nusquam tuta fides est, ideo minus apti verbo Dei fumus. Nulla nobis est reliqua religio. Qui fit rogas? quia cum nobis ipsis fideles non fimus, quàm quæso præstaremus Deo? Coniunctæ res sunt fides quæ feruatur hominibus & quæ datur ac feruatur Deo. Effigies fidei manus coniunctas habet, eoq; ipso significat, fi tu non minus teneas meam atq; ego tuam, sic nos inter nos coniunctos fore, vt seiungi nequeamus. Sic fi nos Deum adeo firmis nexibus amplectamur atq; ille nos tenet, indubie firma semper erit coniunctio. Sed à nostra ad illam diuinam proxima via ascenditur. Quod etiam homines Ethnici docuerunt qui Romæ fimulachrum fidei proximum esse Iouis imagini voluerunt. Quamobrem fi terram hanc promissam, quam partim acceperant, partim erant adhuc accepturi Israelitæ, & illa promissa bona quæ Deus partim dedit, partim adhuc daturus est materiam exercendæ veritatis atque fidei videlicet, inter nos recte & fideliter diuiserimus nosque mutuo amore persequemur, certe eo facto nos assuefecerimus etiam, vt Deo fidem dare & feruare possimus facilius. Hoc Moses proposita descriptione illa docere voluit.
units.tr: What then is faith? Surely it seems to be said from the fact that what has been said is done. It is the constancy and truth of words and agreements. It is also the foundation of both justice and friendship, and the preserver of commonwealths. For, as Cicero says in his De officiis, nothing holds a commonwealth together more strongly than faith. And as he says elsewhere, nothing is stable that is faithless. What then do we commonly say? "A promise is a debt; keep your word. Do you think you will be a peasant? It is better to be a peasant than a scoundrel." But it is not only expressed in words; it is also so deeply fixed in the mind that the thing itself shows it pleases us. For to dissemble and pretend, to fit oneself to the market and to serve the times, is now thought to be the height of prudence; but to be the same and always consistent with oneself is held to be folly. How well these times sufficiently teach this! The Turks, by keeping faith, have acquired not only Asia but also a great part of Europe, since many peoples have learned by experience that more is to be given to their bare promises than to our documents. The Romans, while they kept faith, increased their commonwealth; and when they began to violate faith, they destroyed it. Moses wanted to guard against this very thing, in that he taught his people to keep it. And Christ teaches: Let your speech be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay. It was also our duty, in that peace which by God's gift we have obtained these years past, which is very great, to be so faithful and lovers of truth that there would not be so many lies in making contracts. But that the market is so full of lies is a great sign that our speech is other than Christ taught. Therefore, because faith is nowhere safe, we are the less fit for the word of God. We have no religion left. How so, you ask? Because since we are not faithful to ourselves, how, I ask, should we render faith to God? The faith kept toward men and the faith given and kept toward God are joined together. The image of faith has joined hands, and by this very thing it signifies that if you hold mine no less than I hold yours, so we shall be bound together so that we cannot be separated. Thus, if we embrace God with such firm bonds, and he holds us, the union will undoubtedly always be firm. But the nearest way from ours to that divine way is climbed. The heathen too have taught this, who at Rome wished the image of Faith to be next to the image of Jupiter. Therefore, if we Israelites, who have partly received this promised land and were partly still to receive it, and the good promises which God has partly given and partly will still give, the matter for exercising truth and faith, I mean, divide rightly and faithfully among ourselves and pursue one another with mutual love, we will certainly by that act accustom ourselves also to be able to give and keep faith to God more easily. This is what Moses wished to teach by setting out that description.

units.la: Exempla duo commemorat seruatæ videlicet fidei: quorum alterum singulis ciuibus, magistratibus alterum proponitur, quippe quod duabus his partibus constet tota ciuitas: ac fi ciues singuli mutuam erga fe fidem feruent, & suam erga ciues vniuersos magistratus firmam habeat, tunc ciuitas ipsa salua est & ad legem Dei tota apta atq; idonea.
units.tr: He recalls two examples of preserved faith. One is set before individual citizens, the other before the magistrates, since the whole city consists of these two parts. If individual citizens keep faith with one another, and the magistrates keep firm faith toward all the citizens, then the city itself is safe and wholly fit and suited to God's law.

units.la: Exemplum singulorum in tribubus illis duabus cum dimidia, quæ suis fratribus reliquis Israelitis datam fide seruauerunt, ponitur ob oculos. Rubenitis, Gaditis, & Manafleis cis Iordanem sita terra commoda erat, quod effet pascua hanc petunt sibi dari, quippe qui abundent pecoribus: Israelitæ reliqui illam eis cedunt, sed ea lege, vt quoniâ primi quieti fuę con fuluerint, primi quoq; periculorum & laborum onus in fe suscipiant atq; ferant. Quod propter missum & receptum est, vtrinq; summa fide feruatur. Id Moses, quoniam summam æqualitatem reprefentat, & infigne est exemplum fidei, nunc commemorat. Hæ tribus iam suis vxori bus atq; liberis consuluerant, eratq; vbi coquiefcerent. Vnde & parentes expeditiores ad res gerendas, & familiabus datum vnde plus acquirerent. Reliquæ suas secum familias atq; etiâ impedimenta reliqua ducere, nec loco quietis aut tranquillitatis vllo potiri, sed prelia habere passim obuia, vnde, fi quis eorum occumberet, liberis & paupertas & orbitas. Ergo sic inita atq; facta commutatione rerum & periculorum, vt qui res haberent simul onera ferret atq; subirent pericula, qui minus rerum haberent obirent minus periculorum. Iam facile est res occupare, promittere contra suum officiû: sed vbi rebus potitus, pericula subire malefidis, difficile factu est. Illis quia fidi sunt, non tam promiffu quàm factu facile fuit.
units.tr: The example of individuals is placed before our eyes in the two and a half tribes, who kept the faith they had given to their remaining brothers, the Israelites. The Reubenites, Gadites, and Manassites, whose land lay on this side of the Jordan, were well suited to pasture, so they asked that it be given to them, since they abounded in livestock. The other Israelites ceded it to them, but on this condition: since they were the first to be settled in rest, they should also be the first to take up and bear the burden of dangers and labours. This agreement was made and accepted, and both sides kept it with the greatest faith. Moses now recalls this because it represents the highest equality and is a notable example of faith. These tribes had already provided for their wives and children, and had a place where they could rest. So the parents were freer for waging war, and the families had land from which they might acquire more. The others had to lead their households with them, along with their remaining baggage, and they found no place of rest or tranquillity; instead they met battles everywhere, so that if any of them fell, their children faced poverty and orphanhood. Thus the exchange of goods and dangers was arranged and carried out so that those who had possessions also bore the burdens and faced the dangers, while those who had fewer possessions met fewer dangers. It is easy to seize property and to promise against one's duty, but once a man has got possession, to undergo dangers is hard for one who is faithless. Since these men were faithful, it was no harder in deed than it had been easy in promise.

units.la: Hæc æqualitas atq; fides omni in ciuitate feruanda fuerit. Dum pace fruimur, pauperes diuitibus ne inuideant: nec diuites sua pauperibus denegent auxilia. Si bellum ingruat alius fo-letur[?] & magnas res extimulet. Qui dignitatibus auĉti[?] sunt, ij præcedant ordines pro salute publica, pro aris & focis, pro charissimis liberis & coiugibus dimicent. Reliquos suis paruis & inopibus liberis saluos seruies[?] & incolumes. Qui in acie pugnantes cecidere, quoniam sua morte diram à ciuitate totam mortem auerterunt, hoc digni sunt, vt eorum liberis magnifice prospiciatur. Est in eo genere publica salus semper respicienda, vt rempub. adiuues, & vt homo priuatus ei quoq; studeat augendæ. Rubenitæ promoti sunt, iam suos fratres ipsi quoq; promouent. In distribuedis honoribus & beneficijs hæc feruetur ratio. Sed in cômutatione rerum atq; in contractibus eandem seruabis æquitatem, omninoq; cauebis ne tuis rebus augendis solum natum te putes esse. Nam vt iniquum est eum qui confert operas, socordem negligentemq; esse: sic iniustum est ei, & quem conduxeris vel nimium oneris imponere, vel mercedem parum bona fide reddere. Et hæc quidem sicut fidos faciunt homines homini-bus recte cogitata: sic etiam nos præparant & quasi quodammodo instruunt ad eam quæ debetur Domino fidem. Hodieq; maior effet religio, fi in dictis & factis omnibus maior effet veritas & constantia. Quamobrem hoc exemplum sic considerandum, ad noftramq; vitam accomodandum est.
units.tr: This equality and faith ought to be kept in every city. While we enjoy peace, the poor should not envy the rich, nor should the rich deny their help to the poor. If war threatens, let those who have been raised to dignities go first for the public safety, and fight for the altars and hearths, for their dearest children and wives. Let them leave the rest safe and unharmed for their small and needy children. Those who fell fighting in battle, since by their death they turned the dreadful death away from the whole city, deserve that provision be made generously for their children. In this kind of matter the public welfare must always be kept in view, so that you help the commonwealth, and the private person should also strive to increase it. The Reubenites were promoted; now they in turn promote their brothers. This principle should be observed in distributing honours and benefits. But in the exchange of goods and in contracts you will keep the same equity, and above all take care not to think you were born only to increase your own wealth. For just as it is unjust for one who contributes labour to be idle and negligent, so it is unjust either to impose too great a burden on the man you have hired, or to pay his wage with little good faith. These things, rightly thought through, make men faithful to men, and they also prepare us, and as it were instruct us, for the faith owed to the Lord. Even today religion would be greater if all our words and deeds showed greater truth and constancy. Therefore this example must be considered in this way and applied to our own life.

units.la: Exemplum singulorum sequitur id, quod magistratibus ponitur ob oculos, in persona Iofuę eius qui populi dux creatus fuerat, quem admonet suæ toti populo debitæ fidei, illum extimulans vt metu periculorum non absterreretur, sed populum in promissam terram in-troduceret. Quo exemplo magistratus discunt sua referre vt populum in promissam terram introduccant, hoc est, pia prudentiq; gubernatione ad beatae vitae possessionem prouehant.
units.tr: The example for individuals is followed by what is set before the magistrates, in the person of Joshua, who had been appointed leader of the people. Moses reminds him of the faith owed to the whole people, urging him not to be frightened off by fear of dangers but to lead the people into the promised land. From this example magistrates learn to bring the people into the promised land, that is, by pious and prudent government to advance them to the possession of the blessed life.

units.la: Et ponit primum obstaculum, tum quibus hoc remoueatur. Obstaculum est metus. De quo supra. Hic impedit interdum, vt vel nostros ipsorum vel exteros homines metuamus. Nostros, quando eos malae & remissae disciplinae assuefecimus, quando eos nō pauimus, sed depauimus, quando non iure, sed vel odio vel amore moti ius diximus. Sic Iudaeos Pilatus metuit. Exteros autem metuimus, quando & nos eiusmodi sumus, quibus facile noceant homines, vt inprouidis, imbellibus, effeminatis, atq; timidis: & ita nos gesimus cum nostris, vt nulla nobis in eis praesidij spes posset esse. Hinc ille magistratuum metus.
units.tr: He sets out first the obstacle, and then how it is to be removed. The obstacle is fear, of which we spoke above. It sometimes hinders us so that we fear either our own people or foreigners. We fear our own people when we have accustomed them to bad and lax discipline, when we do not pasture them but devour them, when we have pronounced judgement not justly but moved by hatred or love. Thus Pilate feared the Jews. We fear foreigners when we ourselves are such that men can easily harm us, being unprepared, unwarlike, effeminate, and timid, and when we have so behaved toward our own people that no hope of protection from them could be ours. Hence comes that fear of magistrates.

units.la: Quomodo autem obstandum erit his malis: Fide & veritate: Vt introducas in terrā, hoc est, vt promoueas rempub. vt adiuues singulos & vniuersos. Si fidei tibi conscius fis, nunquam metues. In eo te confirmes duabus rebus. 1. Exemplorum veterum recordatione. Vt maioribus cesserit videlicet. Hic Og & Seon deuictos narrat.
units.tr: How these evils must be resisted: by faith and truth, so that you may lead the people into the land, that is, so that you may advance the commonwealth and help both individuals and all together. If you are conscious of your faith, you will never fear. Strengthen yourself in two things. (1) By remembering old examples, how the enemies of the fathers gave way to them. Here he tells of Og and Sihon, who were defeated.

units.la: 2. Praesentia numinis, Deus aderit pugnans pro vobis. Qui iustam causam tuentur recte, ij Deum sibi praesentem habent. <bl>Rächt mit vnbgaan</bl>[?] Iudex non adiuuat eum, qui causam bonam agat male: quanto minus speres hoc Deum facere? Nos auari, ambitiosi: hos animos Deus non adiuuat, faceret peiores. Quin fis humilis simul ac constans, & Deus iuuabit aeque ac maiores iuuit. Fidelibus fidelis est Dominus. Ei sit honos in secula, Amen.
units.tr: (2) By the presence of the divine power: "the Lord will fight for you." Those who rightly defend a just cause have God present with them. A judge does not help a man who pleads a good cause badly; how much less, then, should you hope that God will do so? We are greedy and ambitious, and God does not help such minds; he would make them worse. Rather, be humble and steadfast at once, and God will help you just as he helped the fathers. The Lord is faithful to the faithful. To him be honour for ever. Amen.

units.la: SERMO XIII.
units.tr: Sermon XIII.

units.la: 23 Oraui autem illo tempore ad Dominum, dicens,
units.tr: 23 And I prayed to the Lord at that time, saying,

units.la: 24 Domine Deus tu coepisti ostendere feruo tuo magnitudinem tuam, & manum tuam robustam, (quis enim est Deus in coelis aut in terra, qui faciat secundum opera tua, & potentiam tuam?
units.tr: 24 O Lord God, you have begun to show your servant your greatness and your mighty hand (for what God is there in heaven or on earth who can do according to your works and your power?)

units.la: 25 Liceat quaeso vt & ego transeam, & videam terram istam bonam, quae est vltra Iordanem, montem & illum bonum & Libanum.
units.tr: 25 Let me pray you, that I may also cross over and see that good land beyond the Jordan, that good mountain and Lebanon.

units.la: 26 At Dominus commotus aduersum me vestri causa, non exaudiuit me, sed dixit ad me Dominus: Sat fit tibi, ne quid amplius hac de re ad me loqueris.
units.tr: 26 But the Lord was angry with me because of you, and did not hear me, but the Lord said to me: Enough for you; do not speak to me any more about this matter.

units.la: 27 Ascende in verticem collis, & sublatis oculis tuis ad mare, ad Septentrionem, ad Meridiem & ad Orientem, circumspice oculis tuis, quia non traijcies Iordanem istum:
units.tr: 27 Go up to the top of the hill, and lifting up your eyes to the sea, to the north, to the south and to the east, look around with your eyes, because you shall not cross this Jordan.

units.la: 28 Et praecipe ipsi Iehofua, robora & anima eum, quoniam ipse praecedet populum istum, & ipse forte diuidet eis terram istam quam vides.
units.tr: 28 But charge Joshua, strengthen and encourage him, for he shall go before this people, and he shall divide among them that land which you see.

units.la: 29 Mansimus vero in valle e regione domus Peor.
units.tr: 29 So we stayed in the valley opposite the house of Peor.

units.la: PRoximè commemoratis atq; explicatis verbis adduxit Moses exempla duo, quibus docuit quantopere Deus postulet, vt fides & veritas inter nos feruentur, hocq; si fiat, magnis praemijs dignum ducat atq; afficiat. Sed quoniam non modo boni spe ad bonum allicimur, sed etiam incusso mali metu à malo absterreamur necesse est: recte sane duobus illis fidei seruatae exemplis, vnum non seruatae & punitae subiungit. Quemadmodum igitur praemia praebita fidelibus ad fidem & veritatem non immerito excitant: sic violatae fidei supplicia ab infidelitate nos absterrent. Rubenitae & coniunctae cum his sesqui tribus, itemq; Iofua magnam sua fide laudem cofecuti sunt: at Moses quia non fatis constans in sua erga Deum atq; etiam populum sibi creditum fide fuit, ideo punitus est iustissimo pariter & conftantif-fimo Dei iudicio. Quod hoc loco sic ipse commemorat, vt primum suas preces, quibus cu-pam deprecabatur, tum Dei super ea postulatione respondum describat.
units.tr: Having just recounted and explained these words, Moses brings forward two examples by which he taught how earnestly God requires that faith and truth be kept among us, and that if this is done, he judges it worthy of and rewards it with great prizes. But since we are drawn to good not only by the hope of good, but must also be turned away from evil by the fear of evil, he rightly adds, to those two examples of faith kept, one of faith not kept and punished. Just as the rewards given to the faithful rightly stir them to faith and truth, so the punishments of broken faith turn us away from unfaithfulness. The Reubenites and the half-tribe joined with them, and Joshua too, gained great praise for their faith; but Moses, because he was not steadfast enough in his faith toward God and toward the people entrusted to him, was therefore punished by the most just and at the same time most steadfast judgment of God. Here he relates this as follows: first he describes his prayers, by which he begged for his desire, and then God's answer to that request.

units.la: Precum descriptio.Oraui (inquit)illo tempore dicens, Domine Deus tu coepisti ostendere &c. Quibus verbis & factum & facti qualitatem docet. Factum ipsum est, quod oraffe fe dicit. Atque hoc facit Moses pressus magnis angustijs animi. Nam cum terrae benedictae fruitione fe priuatum recordatur animo angitur, ideoque suas angustias Deo licet offenso per preces aperit.
units.tr: The description of the prayer. "I prayed," he says, "at that time, saying, O Lord God, you have begun to show &c." By these words he teaches both the deed and the manner of the deed. The deed itself is that he says he prayed. Moses does this, pressed by great distress of mind. For when he recalls that he has been deprived of the enjoyment of the blessed land, his mind is troubled, and therefore he opens his distress to God by prayer, though God is offended.

units.la: Est id exemplo in omni rerum aduersarum genere preces esse sacram anchoram. Iacob Efauum fratrem metuens eiufq; aduentu territus Deum implorat. Anna sterilitatis malo mœsta Deũ, vt id auertat precatur. Dauid quocunq; mali genere pressus ad preces confugit. Christus & cũ discipulos emittere et cũ sese pro nobis offerre vellet,quę res erant arduę,pré cibus ad eas gerendas sese præparat. Cum Petrus ab Herode captus esset,ecclesia cupiens damnum hoc vitare,Deum exorat qui illum liberat vinculis pariter & carceribus. Iam nè- scio quo prius confugimus,quàm ad preces: inde fit vt res minus succedant prospere. Qui diuitias affectant,ad vsuras,& fraudes,& bella nefaria:qui magnos honóres,ad ambitum:qui valetudinem bonam,ad magos: qui res amissas ad ariolos : qui pacem ad abnegationes fidei, & ad turpes paces,confugiunt. At,inquis,magnus sum nebulo, meisq; fœleribus Deum sic offendi,vt nullus ad eum mihi pateat trames ? Et Mosi Deus iratus fuerat, & tamen Moses non alió quàm ad illum confugit. Quò enim confugias?illo, qui omnipotens est,renuente, nemo poterit te iuuare.
units.tr: In every kind of adversity prayer is a sacred anchor. Jacob, fearing his brother Esau and terrified at his coming, implores God. Hannah, sorrowful at the evil of barrenness, prays God to turn it away. David, pressed by whatever kind of evil, flees to prayer. Christ, when he was about to send out his disciples and to offer himself for us, prepared himself for these difficult tasks by prayer. When Peter had been seized by Herod, the Church, wishing to avert this loss, entreated God, who freed him from chains and prisons alike. Now I know not to which thing we first resort rather than to prayer; hence it happens that things turn out less prosperously. Those who aim at riches resort to usury, frauds and wicked wars; those who seek great honours, to ambition; those who seek good health, to magicians; those who seek lost things, to soothsayers; those who seek peace, to denials of the faith and to shameful peace-treaties. But, you say, I am a great scoundrel, and by my crimes I have so offended God that no path to him lies open to me? Yet God was angry with Moses too, and still Moses fled to no one but him. For where will you flee? If he who is almighty refuses, no one will be able to help you.

units.la: Nulla ergo sanctorum inuocatio.Nam alioqui Moses patriarchas sibi parasset aduoca- tos.Túne ais,Mosi te sceleste comparas?non equidem ei me æquiparo,sed tamè meam cum illius angustia comparare non vereor.Erat & is peccator,& quidem tantus,vt ob suum cri- men promissæ terræ finibus excluderetur.Si is Deum recta accessit,cur ego non idem face« rem?Imò Dominus iussit omnes qui laborarent ad se venire Matth. 11. & eos qui sitirent ad se ceu fontem aquæ viuæ potatum venire,Ioan. 7.Cur ego qui laboro magnopere & oppido quam vehementer sitio,non illum accederem ? Quin ideo missus est,vt miseris atq; affli&is succurreret.Ergo quod Moses fecit ipsi quoq; nobis faciundum arbitrabimur.
units.tr: There is therefore no invocation of the saints. For otherwise Moses would have provided himself with the patriarchs as advocates. Do you say, "Do you compare yourself with Moses, you wretch?" I do not indeed make myself equal to him, but I do not hesitate to compare my distress with his. He too was a sinner, and indeed so great a one that because of his crime he was shut out from the borders of the promised land. If he approached God rightly, why should I not do the same? Indeed the Lord bade all who labour to come to him (Matt. 11), and those who thirst to come to him to drink as from a fountain of living water (John 7). Why should I, who labour greatly and thirst most vehemently, not approach him? Indeed he was sent precisely to help the wretched and afflicted. Therefore we shall judge that what Moses did must also be done by us.

units.la: Sed quomodo quaq; via aggrediemur tantum opus?hoc describens factì sui qualitatem Moses pulchre docet. Facti qualitas orationis eius,quæ ad Deum rectè fit,figuram siue for- mam indicat. Domine Deus tu cepisti,et c.inquit.Forma egregia. Nam primũ deprecatur cul pam,tum exponit animi sui sententiam.Culpam deprecatur confessione potentiæ,cui prius dissidebat,iá luculenter edita.Quasi dicat,Tu Domine Deus potens es,fateor, nũc'agnosco: Ostendit sese Dei potentiá agnoscere, ac non simpliciter confitetur quasi id in Dei gratiam faciat,aliàs apud se non satis certò persuasus;verum hoc se scire & constanter affirmare posse argumento duplici probat. Vno,quod operibus ostenderit magnitudinem & potentiam, & robustã manú.Nam vt cuiusq; facta quis qualisq; sit produnt,àc probant: sic quæ Deus facit indicio possunt esse,qualé eum esse existimare debeamus.Ergo vt Deũ subinde magis ac ma gis noscas,eius opera contemplabere.Altero,comparatione Deorum aliorum:quod videli- cet nullum habeat sibi parem , quod in tanta Deorum multitudine & varietate nullus exi- stat vspiam qui vel tantillam portionem huius omnipotentiæ repræsentet.
units.tr: But by what way shall we go about so great a work? In describing this, Moses teaches beautifully the manner of his deed. The manner of his prayer, which is rightly made to God, indicates its figure or form. "O Lord God, you have begun," etc., he says. An excellent form. For first he deprecates his fault, then sets out the judgment of his mind. He deprecates his fault by confessing the power in which he had previously disbelieved, now clearly set forth. As if he said: You, Lord God, are powerful; I confess it, I now acknowledge it. He shows that he acknowledges God's power, and does not simply confess it as if he did so for God's favour, since otherwise he was not sufficiently persuaded of it in himself; rather he proves by a twofold argument that he knows this and can firmly affirm it. First, because by his works God has shown greatness and power and a mighty hand. For just as the deeds of anyone show and prove what kind of person he is, so what God does can be a sign of what kind of being we ought to think him. Therefore, that you may know God more and more, you will contemplate his works. Second, by comparison with other gods: namely, that he has no equal, and that in so great a multitude and variety of gods there is nowhere anyone who represents even the smallest portion of this omnipotence.

units.la: Atq; hæc est recta potentiæ diuinæ comparatio & cognitio & confessio:nempe vt agno- scas Deum sic omnia posse,vt cesset ac desideat sunquam, sed manu contineat omnia,proui dentia sua gubernet omnia,nutu cósilio; suo gerat omnia. Ex eo sane fides nostra consola- tionem duplicem capit, primum quod in eo sit immensa quædam nos tuendi vis,tum quod quasi in portu securè conquiscas.Nam si Deus pro nobis,quis contra nos?
units.tr: This is the right comparison, knowledge and confession of divine power: namely, that you acknowledge God to be able to do all things in such a way that he never ceases or rests, but holds all things in his hand, governs all things by his providence, and carries out all things by his nod and counsel. From this our faith certainly takes a twofold consolation: first, that in him there is a certain immense power to protect us, and second, that we may rest safely as in a harbour. For if God is for us, who is against us?

units.la: Hæc confessio secum trahit agnitionem imbecillitatis nostræ. Vt Moses hoc ipso se peç casse confitetur,quod omnipotentiæ Domini,quá hic prædicat, non ita multú vti æquú fuè rat,tribuere voluerit.Et hoc exéplo discimus preces nostras à deprecatione culpę exordiri.
units.tr: This confession carries with it the recognition of our own weakness. Moses confesses that he sinned in this very thing, that he was unwilling to ascribe to the omnipotence of the Lord, which he here proclaims, the power that it was not so very right for him to use. And from this example we learn to begin our prayers with a confession of our fault.

units.la: Iam petitio sic habet,Sine quæso terram hanc bonam ego quoq; ingrediar, et possideam,et c. Quæ hæc est petitio? Deum precatur vt det ipsum frui terræ huius confpeętu & possessio- ne caduca ac terrena.Quod non est aliud,quàm terrenum quiddam ac caduceum petere.Er- go humanum quiddam Moses patitur.Homo erat: quid mirum si humani ab eo nihil fuerit alienum? Sed tamen hoc laudabile est, & quod im teris dignum,quod suum istum affectum non exponit vlli mortalium,sed in sinum Dei quidquid animo comprehensum habuit,effun dere voluit.Quo certe nihil est nobis honestius,tutius,salubrius.Ipse enim Deus non ettutit se certò sibi credita,& vtiliter quid expediat ac deceat fieri,consulit.
units.tr: Now the petition runs thus: "Let me pray you, let me too enter this good land and possess it," etc. What is this petition? He asks God to grant that he may enjoy the sight and the frail and earthly possession of this land. This is nothing other than to ask for something earthly and perishable. Therefore Moses suffers something human. He was a man; why wonder if nothing human was foreign to him? Yet this is commendable, and worthy of praise, that he does not reveal this affection of his to any mortal, but wished to pour out into the bosom of God whatever he held in his mind. Certainly nothing is more honourable, safer or more wholesome for us than this. For God himself does not hesitate to consult him about what is useful and fitting to be done, since he is certainly trusted with what is entrusted to him.

units.la: Cæterum quod Moses his precibus non solum agnoscit peccatum,sed id quod antea no luerat iam vult ac conatur suscipere,videlicet Deũ etiam in ipsam terram spe & fidutia pœ- nitentiæ eius fretus sequi:id etiam exemplo est sic confitenda nobis esse peccata nostra,vt ab ijs resipiscamus,faciamus; meliora. Nostra ætate in ore est omni populo nostram vitam ac mores Deo displicere, ère nostra fore, si mutemur in melius : sed quis mutatur in melius? Certe si sic pergamus bene confitendo, turpiter delinquendo : quid aliud fiet,quam vt con- demnemur nostris ipsorum calculis?Ergo Mosem imitabimur,& hanc precum formam sem per habeamus ob oculos nostros positam. Responsio Domini descriptio. Dicit, At Dominus commotus aduersum me vestri causa, non ex audiuit me, & te. Quibus verbis & responditte Dominū & quomodo responderit indicat. Responsi loco fuit, quod iratus fuit Dominus. Quo dicit. Peccatum ad quod vestra impatientia veftraq; impotentia perpulsus sum, Dominus tulit indignissime.
units.tr: Moreover, that Moses in these prayers not only acknowledges sin, but now wills and attempts that which he had not previously taken up, namely, relying on the hope and confidence of his repentance, to follow God even into the land itself; this too is an example that we must so confess our sins that we return from them and do better. In our age it is on everyone's lips that our life and morals displease God, and that it will be better for us if we change for the better; but who is changed for the better? Surely if we continue thus, confessing well and sinning shamefully, what else will happen than that we are condemned by our own tallies? Therefore we shall imitate Moses, and always keep this form of prayer set before our eyes. Description of the Lord's response. He says: "But the Lord was angry with me because of you, and did not hear me, and you." By these words he indicates both how the Lord responded and in what manner he responded. His anger was the response. By this he means: the Lord bore most indignantly the sin to which I was driven by your impatience and your impotence.

units.la: Vide quantum malum fit prębita ad peccatum occasio. Ideo dicit apostolus abstinendum etiam ab omni specie mali. Dominus & cauit & cauenda docuit offendicula, quando turbas ad regnum aspirantes, & ipsum deposcentes cum ipse fugit, tum etiam discipulos, vt ab his abesse procul, in vlteriorem ripam compulit vt traijcerent Ioan. 6. Improbus popu lus magistratum ignauum, vterque ministrum verbi socordem facit. Id Deus fert aegerrimè. Ergo ne quis offendat alium cauebimus. Sed & nos omnes qui gloriamur euangelij nomine, quando non minus vino, Veneri, Mammonæ indulgemus quam quiuis impij populi: quoniam vicini in vitam nostram magis intenti sunt, quàm in euangelium, fieri non potest, quin eos offendamus plurimum. Id etiam D. Chryfoft. in homil. 4. Pauli ad Hebr. epistolæ dicit, ad hunc modum. Οὐ γὰρ τοῖς λεγομένοις παρ' ἡμῶν προσέχειν ἐθέλωσιν, ἀλλὰ τοῖς γινομένοις παρ' ὑμῶν. Hoc est, non in meam doctrinam, sed in vestram vitam intenti sunt Graeci. Quamobrem enitendum est vt qui nobiscum versantur, ex commercio nostro boni potius quàm mali causam atq; ansam habeant.
units.tr: See how great an evil is the opportunity given to sin. For this reason the apostle says we must abstain even from every appearance of evil. The Lord both guarded against stumbling-blocks and taught us to guard against them. When the crowds, aspiring to the kingdom and demanding him as king, were hurrying towards him, he himself fled, and he also compelled the disciples to go away far from them, to the further bank (John 6). A wicked people makes the magistrate idle, and each makes the minister of the Word careless. God bears this very badly. Therefore let no one give offence to another; we will take care. But also we all who boast of the name of the gospel, when we indulge in wine, Venus and Mammon no less than any impious people, since our neighbours are more intent on our way of life than on the gospel, it cannot be that we do not offend them greatly. St. Chrysostom also says this in his fourth homily on Paul's Epistle to the Hebrews, in this manner: "For they are not willing to attend to what is said by us, but to what is done by you" [Οὐ γὰρ τοῖς λεγομένοις παρ' ἡμῶν προσέχειν ἐθέλωσιν, ἀλλὰ τοῖς γινομένοις παρ' ὑμῶν]. That is, the Greeks are intent not on my teaching but on your life. Therefore we must strive that those who live with us may gain from our dealings a cause and occasion for good rather than for evil.

units.la: 2 Non exaudiuit me. Qui id arbitrabar precum fidelium vim esse maximam. Audiuit De us, sed quod petijt non dat. Neque enim expediebat, vt daretur. Ergo quid petas vide. Sæpe nobiscum ipsi pugnamus precantes: tunc Deus qui ipsa sapientia est, melius nobis consulit, quàdo petita negat. Etenim qui diuinitus sibi dari postulat, quæ èrefua peculiariter fore du xerit, is versatur in ea Dominicæ precationis parte, quæ panem nostrum quotidianum petit. Id ille, si sapit, obtinere nequaquam volet, nisi saluis petitionibus prioribus, nempe ijs, sanctificetur nomen tuum, aduenniat regnum tuum, fiat voluntas tua, &c. Quis enim mentis compos vna eademque oratione diuersa, secumque pugnantia petierit? Christus petit, vt transeat calix, suum ipsius hoc erat: sed redit ad priores petitiones, dicens, fiat voluntas non mea, sed tua. Apostolus 2. Corinth. 12. petit ab angelo satanæ liberari, sed id non impetrat ea ipsa de causa, quam addit. Sic quod Moses petit, quoniam cum gloria, regno, voluntate Dei pugnabat, quæ Moses ipse noluissec violari: sané quod petita non assequitur, pro sua pietate boni consulit. Ex quo vides cur interdum non audiamur, videlicet quando non est èrè nostra.
units.tr: 2 He did not hear me. I had thought that the power of faithful prayers was very great. God heard, but does not give what he was asked. For it was not expedient that it be given.
