So see what you ask. Often we struggle against ourselves when we pray; then God, who is wisdom itself, provides for us better when he denies what is asked. For whoever asks God for what he has himself judged will be peculiarly his own good is engaged in that part of the Lord's Prayer which asks for our daily bread. He, if he is wise, will by no means wish to obtain it, unless the earlier petitions stand: namely, "hallowed be your name, your kingdom come, your will be done," and so on. For who in his right mind would ask, in one and the same prayer, for things that are different and at odds with one another? Christ asks that the cup pass from him; that was his own wish. But he returns to the earlier petitions, saying, "not my will, but yours be done." The apostle, in 2 Corinthians 12, asks to be freed from the angel of Satan, but does not obtain it, for the very reason he adds. So too with what Moses asks: since he was contending against the glory, kingdom and will of God, which Moses himself would not have wished to be violated, he certainly takes it in good part, out of his piety, that he does not obtain what he asked for. From this you see why we are sometimes not heard, namely when it is not to our advantage.

units.la: Responsi forma hæc est. 1. Sat tibi sit. Quasi dicat. Stat animo fixa sententia, nolo mihi de re ea verbum vllum feceris amplius. Vides Dei de perfidia graue & constans iudicium. Ἐτ will ghalten ban. Optimus quisq; maxime succenset mendacibus.
units.tr: The form of the answer is this. 1. Let it be enough for you. As if he were saying: my resolve is fixed; I do not want you to say any more to me about this matter. You see God's grave and steadfast judgment on faithlessness. Honour must be kept [Ehr will ghalten ban]. The best of men are most angry with liars.

units.la: 2 Ascende, mitigat sententiam de poena latam. Illic iustitiam, hic misericordiam habes. Nam quod Mosem punit est iustitiæ, quod terræ negatæ conspectu dignatur misericordiæ, qua fit, vt si totum dare non sinat iustitia, aliquid huius opefaltem impetret. Sic Deus non supra, quàm ferre possis tentari te finit. Tempora nostrarum ærumnarum contrahit, ne redemptionis mora longior fessum onere calamitatis ad desperationem adigat. Etiam vires, ferendo vt simus, ipse suppeditat. Ergo in hac Dei bonitate magna nobis spes debet esse posita.
units.tr: 2 Go up, softens the sentence of punishment that has been pronounced. In the one you have justice, in the other mercy. For that he punishes Moses is justice; that he deigns to let him see the land that was denied him is mercy. By this it comes about that, if justice does not allow him to give the whole, he at least obtains some part of this. So God does not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear. He shortens the times of our troubles, lest a longer delay in our deliverance, wearying us with the burden of calamity, drive us to despair. He himself also supplies the strength to bear it. Therefore we ought to place great hope in this great goodness of God.

units.la: 3 Iosuæ mandata impone, eumq; præfice populo, & firma adhortatione. Iosua fidus fuit igi- tur nunc euehitur & afficitur præmijs. In quo vides quam verum fit quod dicitur alibi magnis honoribus dignari Deum illos, qui dignos habeant ipsi. Exemplo sunt Ioseph, Phinees, Iosue, Chaleb, Saul, Dauid, Hester, Mardochæus, in primis Christus, qui cum se totum humiliasset supra cœlos omnes euectus est, itemque apostoli, qui Dei causa infames facti sunt, iam existunt celeberrimi. Quamobrem & in homines & in Deum fidi simus: tunc fiet autho ritatem nobis comparemus maximam.
units.tr: 3 Lay your commands on Joshua, set him over the people, and encourage him with firm exhortation. Joshua was faithful, and therefore he is now raised up and honoured with rewards. In this you see how true it is, as is said elsewhere, that God honours with great honours those who are worthy of them. Examples are Joseph, Phinehas, Joshua, Caleb, Saul, David, Esther, Mordecai, and above all Christ, who, when he had wholly humbled himself, was exalted above all the heavens; likewise the apostles, who became infamous for God's cause and now are most renowned. Therefore let us be faithful both to men and to God: then we shall win for ourselves the greatest authority.

units.la: Atq; hæc de fide & veritate dicta sufficiunt. Satis apta ad studium diuinæ legis hæc est præparatio. Etenim qui infuerit hominibus datam fidem feruare, is etiam Deo datam præstabit. Id Deus faxit vt præstemus in eo, qui ipsa veritas est, Iesu Christo. Amen.
units.tr: These things said about faith and truth are enough. This preparation is well suited to the study of the divine law. For whoever is faithful in keeping a pledge given to men will also perform what is given to God. May God grant that we do so in him who is truth itself, Jesus Christ. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT IIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER IIII.

units.la: SERMO XIIII.
units.tr: SERMON XIIII.

units.la: 3 Audi igitur Israel statuta & iudicia, quæ ego doceo vos, vt faciatis, vt vi- uatis. natis, introeatis & possideatis terram, quam Dominus Deus patrum vestrorum dat vobis.
units.tr: 3 Hear therefore, Israel, the statutes and judgments which I teach you, that you may do them, that you may live, go in and possess the land which the Lord God of your fathers gives you.

units.la: 2 Ad verbum meum, quod ego praecipio vobis, nihil adijcietis, nihil item ei detrahetis, vt obseruetis praecepta Domini Dei vestri, quae ego praecipio vobis.
units.tr: 2 You shall not add anything to the word that I command you, nor take anything from it, so that you may keep the commandments of the Lord your God which I command you.

units.la: 3 Oculi vestri viderunt quae fecit Dominus in Baal Peor, nam omnem virum, qui inceßit post Baal Peor, huc perdidit Dominus Deus tuus e medio tui.
units.tr: 3 Your eyes have seen what the Lord did at Baal Peor, for the Lord your God has destroyed from among you every man who went after Baal Peor.

units.la: 4 Vos contra qui adhaesistis Domino Deo vestro, omnes etiamnum hodie viuitis.
units.tr: 4 But you who clung to the Lord your God are all alive today.

units.la: 5 Ecce docui vos statuta & iudicia, sicut praecepit mihi Dominus Deus meus, vt sic faciatis in medio terrae, ad quam vos venitis, vt eam occupetis.
units.tr: 5 Behold, I have taught you statutes and judgments, just as the Lord my God commanded me, that you may do so in the midst of the land into which you are going to occupy it.

units.la: [?]LVD quidem non solum ex praeceptis sapientum, verum etiam vsu rerum omnes explorate cognitum habemus, quod quarumcunque doctrinarum sine re- rum studio hominem deditum esse volumus, ad eas percipiendas alia re nulla, quam voluntate & quasi quadam naturali animi propensione plus momenti af- fertur. Etsi enim quis ingenio, memoria, reliquisq; naturae praesidijs & auxilijs praeditus fue- rit, non autem voluntate eam ad rem vlla propendeat, nihil in ea proficitur. Quemadmo- dum igitur prudentes doctores voluntatem in animis discipulorum excitant, sic etiam au- ditor verbi diuini prius ad amorem & studium verbi diuini debet excitari, quàm ad ipsum audiendum deducatur. Qua de causa Moses positis quibusdam progymnasmatis, quae nos hactenus exposuimus: idem vltimo loco, quando ad legis tractationem accessit proxime, hanc orga legis studium voluntatem propensam excitat in animis audientium.
units.tr: This indeed we all know, not only from the precepts of the wise but also from experience, that whatever teaching a man is to take up, he cannot be brought to it by any other means than by the will and a kind of natural inclination of the mind, to which the greatest weight is given. For even if someone is endowed with talent, memory and the other aids and helps of nature, yet if his will does not incline toward the matter at all, nothing is achieved in it. Just as wise teachers stir up the will in the minds of their pupils, so the hearer of the divine Word must first be roused to love and eagerness for the divine Word before he is led to hear it itself. For this reason Moses, having set down certain preliminary exercises, which we have so far expounded, now at the last point, when he comes close to the handling of the law, stirs up in the minds of the hearers a willing inclination toward the study of the law.

units.la: Atque vt idipsum efficiat : quarum rerum spe & admiratione eo perpelli possumus, eas hoc praef.4.cap.singulas singulatim explicat:ac docet, legem Dei fui cultoribus vtilem, ho- nestam,diuinam,priscam,æquam.
units.tr: And so that he may accomplish this, we can be moved by the hope and admiration of these things, which he sets out one by one, and he teaches that the law of God is useful, honourable, divine, ancient and just to its worshippers.

units.la: In quarum rerum tractatione minime malum ordinem sequitur. Etenim quia prima vtilitatis, posterior honestatis cura nobis esse solet, ab his locis primum argumenta ducit: tum quia curatá re & vtilitate nostra nihil prius nobis est, quàm quod diuinum est & pri- scum, etiam ab his.ipsis locis argumenta ducit: postremo ne vel difficultas aliqua vel rigor vllus ab hoc doctrinæ genere nos absterreret, æquam eam & plenam omnis moderationis atque æquitatis docet esse. Ergo hoc capite primum vtilem, tum honestam, tertiò diuinam, quarto priscam, quintò æquam dicit esse legem Domini: vt si quæ nostræ nos salutis tangat cura, si quis amor honesti nostris animis insideat, si qua sit animis nostris indita religio, si quā nos ducat antiquitatis admiratio, si quod nos trahat æqui boniq; studium: non possimus non incitatis omnibus animi sensibus atq; viribus ad illud tam salubre & honestum & diui- num & priscis mortalibus vsitatum & æquitatis plenum studium ferri.
units.tr: In handling these matters he follows a not at all bad order. For since we are usually concerned first with usefulness and second with honour, he draws his arguments first from these topics; then, since once our well-being and usefulness are secured nothing is more important to us than what is divine and ancient, he also draws arguments from these same topics; finally, lest any difficulty or harshness in this kind of teaching should frighten us away, he shows that it is just and full of all moderation and equity. Therefore in this chapter he says first that the law of the Lord is useful, then honourable, third divine, fourth ancient, fifth just. So that if the care of our salvation touches us, if the love of what is honourable dwells in our minds, if religion is implanted in our minds, if the admiration of antiquity draws us, if the zeal for what is fair and good carries us along, we cannot help being borne, with all the feelings and powers of our minds stirred up, toward that study which is so wholesome, honourable, divine, customary among the ancient mortals, and full of equity.

units.la: Ac quod ad primum locum attinet, quem, vti modo diximus, ab vtilitate huius doctri- næ ducit: sic eum hic persequitur vt à fine, à forma, à causa efficiente eius argumenta fumat ad demonstrandum & probandum quod proposuit.
units.tr: As for the first topic, which, as we have just said, he derives from the usefulness of this teaching, he pursues it here in such a way that he takes his arguments from its end, its form and its efficient cause, to demonstrate and prove what he has proposed.

units.la: A fine, Audi Israel statuta & iudicia quæ ego doceo vos vt faciatis, vt vivatis, introcatis, & possideatis, &c. Quibus verbis ad demonstrandam vtilitatem verbi diuini, argumenta à fi- ne ducta profert. Iq triplex ostenditur, nempe vt addiscatur & fiat, vt vita contingat, vt pos- sessio obtineatur.
units.tr: From the end: "Hear, Israel, the statutes and judgments which I teach you, that you may do them, that you may live, go in and possess," and so on. By these words, to demonstrate the usefulness of the divine Word, he brings forward arguments drawn from the end. This end is shown to be threefold: namely, that it may be learned and done, that life may be attained, and that possession may be obtained.

units.la: Vt addiscatur, docet quis edoctor, quæ doctrina, cur doceatur. Ac doctorem quidem ipse Deus nos vo- dicit esse. In quo vides Deum nobis verbum suum non obtrudere violenter, sed vsum ho- minum opera docere, & eo nos ducere vt velimus. Sic Abraham edoctus est vt auelli non potuerit à Domino. Moses ipse sic edoctus est, vt maluerit populi Dei, quàm Pharaonis nu- mero adscribi. Sic prophetæ & apostoli, & omnino omnes Christi martyres doctrinam ver- bi diuini sic imbiberunt animis, vt obfirmatis aduersus omnia mala, omnesque etiam diros cruciatus animis illam constanter retinuerint. Non Deus illos, non Moses, non vllus Dei mi- nister hos coegit, sed tantum ipsa doctrinæ veritas eos sibi sic deuinxit, vt auelli nequiuerint. Idem vides hodieq; fieri, vt qui veritatis doctrinam rectè norint, atque etiam putam suis a- nimis imbiberint, ij sua sponte eam & audiunt, & sequuntur, & cupide retinent. Iudæi vero & Turcæ, & papistæ, & omnino omnes tyranni suam doctrinam docere nequeunt, quod malis fit fundata basibus:ideoque eam violenter obtrudunt hominibus. Quæ sua natura bona sunt,ad ea boni & sapientes homines sponte sua feruntur:quæ vero vid entur quidem, reue-ra autem bona non sunt,ad ea qui sapiunt,& qui boni sunt,ne cogi quidem possunt. Quam-obrem Deus nos,qui natura ab eo quod vere est bonum abhorremus, ipse docet & ratione ducit,ut velimus amplecti quod ipse proposuit.Quamobré ne eum offendamus contemptu huius doctrinæ,etiam atque etiam cauendum est.
units.tr: That it may be learned: he teaches who the teacher is, what the teaching is, and why it is taught. God himself says that he is our teacher. In this you see that God does not force his Word upon us violently, but teaches us through the work of human beings and leads us to will it. Thus Abraham was taught so that he could not be torn away from the Lord. Moses himself was so taught that he preferred to be counted among the people of God rather than among the number of Pharaoh's. So the prophets and apostles, and indeed all the martyrs of Christ, so drank in the doctrine of the divine Word in their minds that, steeled against all evils and even all dreadful torments, they held it constantly. It was not God, not Moses, not any minister of God who compelled them, but the very truth of the doctrine so bound them to itself that they could not be torn away. You see the same happening even today: those who rightly know the doctrine of truth, and have truly drunk it into their minds, of their own accord hear it, follow it and cling to it eagerly. But the Jews, the Turks, the Papists, and in short all tyrants cannot teach their doctrine, because it is founded on bad foundations; therefore they force it violently upon people. Good and wise men are carried of their own accord toward those things which are good by their nature; but those things which seem indeed to be good, yet in truth are not, the wise and good cannot even be compelled to accept. For this reason God, who teaches us and leads us by reason, though by nature we shrink from what is truly good, wills that we embrace what he has set forth. Therefore, lest we offend him by contempt of this doctrine, we must take heed again and again.

units.la: Quæ vero fit hæc doctrina quidque comprehendat duobus nominibus expo-nit, nem-pe pe חֻקִּים[?] & מִשְׁפָּטִים, seu ut lxx. transferunt, δικαιωμάτων καὶ κριμάτων[?], & ut expo-nunt nostri,rituum atque legum. Nam priore nomine ritus sacros seu ceremonias,seu quæ ad cultum Dei pertinent omnia complectimur,ut de doctrina, de auscultatione, de preci-bus, de sacrificijs, de ministério seu officijs ecclesiæ. Quæ quoniam ad diuinam iustitiam, quæ nos indutos coram Deo oportet apparere,sunt exercitia ducentia, Græci non inepte δικαιώματα reddiderunt,quippe quod & Christum, qui nostra est iustitia monstrant,& in ipsa nos exerceant iustitia. Atq; huius quicquid est, verbo Dei contineri id Moles hoc lo-co docet.
units.tr: What this doctrine is and what it comprehends he sets out under two names, namely חֻקִּים [chukkim] and מִשְׁפָּטִים [mishpatim], or, as the Seventy translate them, δικαιωμάτων καὶ κριμάτων [dikaiōmatōn kai krimatōn], and, as our people expound them, rites and laws. For under the former name we embrace the sacred rites or ceremonies, or whatever pertains to the worship of God: concerning doctrine, hearing, prayers, sacrifices, the ministry or offices of the Church. Since these are exercises leading to the divine righteousness, which we ought to appear before God clothed in, the Greeks not inaptly rendered them δικαιώματα [dikaiōmata], since they both point to Christ, who is our righteousness, and exercise us in that very righteousness. And Moses here teaches that whatever there is of this kind is contained in the Word of God.

units.la: Quod cum ita fit,magno onere quærendi,disputandi,iudicandi leuati fumus: quo quid quæso potest esse utilius.Multum sese torserunt pleræque gentes in hoc negocio, & tamen grauibus & perniciosis erroribus nihilominus immersi sunt. Hic quicquid hanc ad rem requiritur omne comprehensum est.
units.tr: Since this is so, we are relieved of the great burden of seeking, disputing and judging. What, I ask, can be more useful than this? Most nations have tormented themselves greatly over this matter, and yet they have nonetheless been plunged into grave and pernicious errors. Here whatever is required for this purpose is all comprehended.

units.la: Posteriore nomine iudicia,fiue totum ius ciuile completitur,& quicquid ad forum,ad officia publica,ad disciplinam rei militaris,ad annonæ curam,& omnino ad remp.totam per tinet idipsum hic describitur. Romani à Græcis sua iura sumpserunt , nostrum nos ab ipso Deo per Mosem & Christum accepimus. Ergo hoc quoque nomine hæc doctrina est utilisima, quod totum ius ciuile,fine quo vita nostra in his terris constare nequit,continet.
units.tr: Under the latter name, judgments, the whole civil law is embraced, and whatever pertains to the courts, to public offices, to the discipline of military affairs, to the care of the grain supply, and in general to the whole commonwealth, is here set out as well. The Romans took their laws from the Greeks; we have received ours from God himself through Moses and Christ. Therefore this doctrine is most useful under this name too, because it contains the whole civil law, without which our life cannot subsist in this world.

units.la: Cæterum ut qua de causa doceatur intelligas,addit,Ut faciamus. Neq; enim in sola cotem platione cófiftit hoc ftudiu,sed versatur etiam in actione, Beati qui audiunt & faciunt verbu Dei.Et Dominus viro sapienti simile esse dicit eum Mat.7.qui cognoueritatq; fecerit voluntatem Dei patris.Et Diuus Iacobus dicit fidem fine factis esse mortuam. Rom. 2.non audito res legis,sed factores iustificabuntur. Et in eo speculo fi vitam nostram contemplemur, intelligemus euangelicam doctrinam his temporibus ideo patefactam esse ut pie,sobrie,caste, non impie,intemperanter,turpiter viuamus. Inanis est & turpis nostra gloriatio quoad mo-ribus ad doctrinam,quam audimus, non accedimus. Ac quemadmodum nobis nostræ miseriæ parum confultum est, fi Deus nobis de summo bono deque reliquis inferioribus bonis diu multumque concionetur, nihil autem eorum nobis impertiat:sic neque Dei vo-luntatis & honori,neque nostræ saluti confultum est,fi de pietate multum loquamur, vita au-tem nostra nihilo fit melior. Ergo primus est finis ut discamus & faciamus quicquid Deus fe velle suo verbo declarauerit.
units.tr: Moreover, so that you may understand why it is taught, he adds: that we may do. For this study consists not only in contemplation but also is carried out in action: "Blessed are those who hear and do the word of God." And the Lord says that the man who knows and does the will of God the Father is like a wise man (Matt. 7). And the divine James says that faith without works is dead. (Rom. 2): "Not the hearers of the law, but the doers, will be justified." And if we look at our life in this mirror, we will understand that the gospel doctrine has been revealed in these times so that we may live piously, soberly and chastely, not impiously, intemperately and basely. Our boasting is empty and shameful if we do not conform our morals to the doctrine we hear. And just as it is little help to our misery if God preaches at length to us about the highest good and the other lesser goods, yet imparts none of them to us, so it is no help either to the honour of God's will or to our salvation if we speak much of piety, while our life is none the better for it. Therefore the first end is that we learn and do whatever God has declared in his Word that he wills.

units.la: Ut vita contingat nobis alter finis est. Vita autem & mors opposita sunt. Ac diaboli ver-bis aurem præbentes atque etiam obsequentes parentes nostri mortem in mundum introduxerunt: Christus author vitæ malis his obuiam iuit allato in orbem vitæ verbo, ut qui i-pfum audiant ac sequantur vitam recuperent. Unde & Ioan. 5.dicit, videmini vobis in illis, puta scripturis,vitam habere,& Paulus dicit,per Euangelium ego vos genui,hoc est,ideo <bl>euch erft rechtzlüten gmacht</bl>/effeci vos viuos,qui fueratis mortui.
units.tr: That we may attain life is the second end. Life and death are opposites. Our parents, giving ear to the devil's words and even obeying him, brought death into the world. Christ, the author of life, met these evils by bringing the word of life into the world, so that those who hear and follow it may recover life. Hence John 5 says, "you think that in them, that is, in the Scriptures, you have life," and Paul says, "through the gospel I have begotten you," that is, "I have made you alive, who were dead."

units.la: Est autem vita in hoc mundo caduca,& in cœlis æterna: utramque hic intelligit. Nam qui verbum Dei cum discunt tum sequuntur agnitum, ij vere viuunt: qui illud neque cognitum habent neq; sequuntur vitam ac moribus,ij licet videantur viuere, tamen reuera non viuunt funtq; cadauera sensu boni carentia. Omitto quod præceptis diuinis additur vitæ promissio,veluti in primo præcepto fecundæ tabulæ.Atq; viuere quidem,qui finis est homi-nis,diu multumq; quæsitus à philosophis:nunquâ ab his,facile vero à nobis qui diuinæ legis duétum sequimur,inuentus est.Hic enim ostenditur quomodo amissa, restituta fit.Hinc fan-ctiin ipso mortis obiutu,vitæ spem hauserunt.O lætum doctrinæ genus,nec perperam di&um euangelium.Quid enim affert aliud,quàm vitam mortalibus.Quisquis igitur cupit vi-uere,verbi Dei studio hoc efficiet.An non hæc est magna utilitas?
units.tr: Life in this world is perishable, but in heaven it is eternal, and he means both here. Those who learn the word of God and follow it once known truly live. Those who neither know it nor follow it in life and conduct, though they may seem to live, do not really live; they are corpses lacking any sense of good. I pass over the fact that a promise of life is added to the divine precepts, as in the first commandment of the second table. To live, which is the end of man, was sought long and hard by the philosophers and never found by them; but it is easily found by us, who follow the guidance of divine law. For here it is shown how what was lost is restored. Hence the saints, even at the sight of death, drew in hope of life. O joyful kind of teaching, and not wrongly called gospel! For what does it bring to mortals but life? Whoever therefore desires to live will achieve this by zeal for the word of God. Is this not a great benefit?

units.la: Ut terræ promissæ possessio contingat tertius finis est doctrinæ huius. Atque hoc qui-dem peculiariter ad Israelitas pertinet, sed allegoria ab his ad omne hominum genus trahi potest. Vides pios bonis affluere,Iobem[?], Abrahamum, Dauidem, Solomonem,Tobiam, Constantinum[?], multos pios hoc tempore: impios contra adeo miseros atque infelices esse, ut etiam cum opibus atq; honoribus abundent, tamen vel animis vel corporibus afflicti sint. Nec mirum est hac aetate multos esse miseros, cum verbi contemptus eis infit maximus. Nō imus inficias optimos quosq; maximis interdum miseriarum fluctibus iactatos esse, verum tamen si quantorum bonorum largitione recreati sint consideres, illorum aerumnas impio rum felicitati facile praetuleris. Quis enim adeo stolidus est, ut Herodes quam Baptista, Pilatus quam Christus, Nero quàm Paulus esse malit: Recte ergo Moses dicit verbi divini studio hoc consequi homines ut terrae promissae possessione perfruantur.
units.tr: That the possession of the promised land should come to us is the third end of this doctrine. This pertains particularly to the Israelites, but by allegory it can be extended from them to the whole human race. You see the godly abounding in good things: Job, Abraham, David, Solomon, Tobias, Constantine(?), many godly people in this age. The wicked, on the other hand, are so wretched and unhappy that, even when they abound in wealth and honours, they are afflicted either in mind or in body. Nor is it surprising that many are wretched in this age, since contempt for the word is greatest among them. We do not deny that the best men are sometimes tossed by the greatest waves of misery; yet if you consider how they are refreshed by the abundance of so many goods, you would readily prefer their troubles to the happiness of the wicked. For who is so stupid as to prefer to be Herod rather than the Baptist, Pilate rather than Christ, or Nero rather than Paul? Rightly, then, Moses says that by zeal for the divine word men attain this: that they enjoy possession of the promised land.

units.la: Ex quibus omnibus intelligimus huius studij finem esse bonum. Quid enim utilius est quàm discere; discendo subinde nobis consulimus melius. Solomon sapientiam opibus praeferebat. Quid utilius quàm vera vita potiri, mortem autem effugere? Mors omnibus bonis exuit, vita vero dat his ipsis perfrui. Quid utilius quàm iis, quae Deus dederit, bonis suaviter afficiì? Nà etsi Croesi divitias habeas, animo vero non valeas, Iro[?] pauperior es. Hoc verbum Dei docet efficere, ut bonis quaesitis laetemur, & suaviter afficiamur. Ex quibus omnibus perspicuum est verbi Dei finem esse, quemadmodum diximus optimum, & eiusmodi quidem ut quemadmodum Timotheum suum apostolus, 1. Tim. 4. Admonet, sic nos merito omnes simus admoniti, ut attendamus nobis ipsis & doctrinae, & perstiamus in his: quod id si fecerimus servaturi simus & nos, & qui nostrae fidei commissi sunt. Hic finis est huius doctrinae.
units.tr: From all these things we understand that the end of this study is good. For what is more useful than to learn? By learning we continually consult our own good better. Solomon preferred wisdom to wealth. What is more useful than to possess true life and escape death? Death strips us of all goods; life, on the other hand, grants us the power to enjoy them. What is more useful than to be pleasantly affected by the goods God has given? For even if you have the riches of Croesus but lack spiritual health, you are poorer than Irus. This word of God teaches us to rejoice in the goods we have acquired and to be pleasantly affected by them. From all these things it is clear that the end of the word of God is, as we said, the best, and of such a kind that, just as the apostle admonishes his Timothy (1 Tim. 4), so we too are rightly admonished to attend to ourselves and to the doctrine, and to persist in these things; for if we do this we shall save both ourselves and those committed to our faith. This is the end of this doctrine.

units.la: Forma, Ad verbum meum, quod ego praecipio vobis nihil addetis, nihil item detrahetis, &c. Quibus verbis ostendit doctrinam hanc omnibus suis partibus atq; numeris sic perfectam, ficq; absolutam esse, ut nihil quod ad bene beateq; viuendi rationem pertinet, vel desit vel redundet: ideoq; nefas esse ei vel addere quicquam velle, vel detrahere. Quae cum ita sint, enitendum nobis est, ut haec formae illius descriptio quàm rectissime consideretur.
units.tr: Form: "You shall add nothing to my word which I command you, nor take anything away," etc. By these words he shows that this doctrine is so perfect and complete in all its parts and numbers that nothing pertaining to the right and blessed manner of living is either lacking or superfluous. Therefore it is wrong for anyone to wish either to add anything to it or to take anything away. Since this is so, we must strive to consider this description of that form as accurately as possible.

units.la: Nihil, inquit, addetis. Proclivis est mens hominis ad excogitandos novos cultus, quibus Deum demereatur: eaq; effingende religionis affectatio omnibus seculis sese prodidit. Velut Moses vitulum se absente erectum cogitur destruere, dum Hieroboam cultum novum instituit in Israel, dum Esaias clamare cogitur frustra coli Deum humanis traditionibus, dum Christus ad demoliendum cultus novos idem prophetae dictum in evangelio adducit. Sed nostra tempora morbo hoc adeo laborat ut humanis divina penè cesserint. Quid enim aliud est, quod aiunt scripturâ sacram nō omnia quae scitu sint ad salutem necessaria comprehendere? Quod oporteat ecclesiam subinde comminisci novas? Et eò dementiae deuenerunt isti homines, ut ecclesiam Dei per purum & solum Dei verbum rite gubernari posse prorsus negent. Hinc est, ut quidam iureconsultus dicit, quod duobus ad episcopi munus electis, quorum unus sit theologus, alter autem canonista, sintq; alias pares, & haeresis vel in ea cui praeficiendus sit, vel in vicina ecclesia prorsus nulla pullulet: praeferendus sit Canonista secundā Host. Ioh. Andr. Panor. & doc. in c. j. de confang. & affini. quippe quod is textus Host. & Io. And. authoribus expresse statuat ecclesiam non posse regi per puram & solam theologiam. Omitto plura quibus ostenditur hoc hominum genus, ut auderent suas sanctiones mortalibus obtrudere, dixisse scriptura non omnia, quae scitu necessaria sint, ad salutem comprehen-sa esse. Nos autem Mosis verbis stamus, & dicimus his legibus nil addendum esse. Hanc enim novas condendi libidinem Deus hoc edicto coercere voluit. His praestita vera est & recta obedientia, quae mater, & custos, & origo virtutum est omnium.
units.tr: "You shall add nothing," he says. The human mind is prone to devise new forms of worship by which to earn God's favour, and this eagerness to fashion religion has shown itself in every age. Thus Moses was forced to destroy the calf set up in his absence; Jeroboam instituted a new worship in Israel; Isaiah was forced to cry out that God is worshipped in vain with human traditions; and Christ, to overthrow new forms of worship, cites the same prophet's saying in the gospel. But our times are so afflicted with this disease that human things have almost displaced divine ones. For what else is it that they say, that Holy Scripture does not comprehend all things that must be known for salvation, and that the Church must therefore continually invent new ones? These men have fallen into such madness that they flatly deny that the Church of God can be rightly governed by the pure and sole word of God. Hence a certain jurist says that when two men are chosen for the office of bishop, one a theologian and the other a canonist, and they are otherwise equal, and no heresy sprouts either in the church over which he is to be placed or in a neighbouring church, the canonist is to be preferred (Host., Io. Andr., Panor., and the teacher on c. 1, de consang. et affin.). Indeed, Host. and Io. And. expressly lay down that the Church cannot be ruled by pure and sole theology. I pass over many other things by which this kind of men is revealed, men who dared to thrust their own sanctions upon mortals, saying that Scripture does not comprehend all things necessary to know for salvation. But we stand by the words of Moses, and say that nothing is to be added to these laws. For God wished to restrain this lust for devising new things by this edict. True and right obedience is rendered to Him, and it is the mother, guardian and origin of all virtues.

units.la: Nil detrahetis, inquit. Id est, ab eius expressa sententia discedere, simulare vel dissimula-re, hostibus eius aliquid cedere, vita ac moribus alium se quam Dei verbum docet referre, nefas esse ducite. Summa, Hoc Deus statuit non ut in humanis rebus solemus, sic in divinis pacifici, dare quicquam adversariis velimus: non addamus quae finximus ipsi nova, quasi nos plus sapiamus, quàm Deus. Sacrae literae sunt perfectae, quia nihil eis addi nihilque detrahi voluit Dominus. Ut infra cap. 12. Quicquid ego vobis praecipio id observabitis, ut faciatis, ad hoc nihil addes, ab eo nihil detrahes. Proverbior. 30. Omnis sermo Dei purgatus est scutum his qui eo nituntur: nec addas sermonibus eius, ne redarguat te & mendax inveniaris.
units.tr: "You shall take nothing away," he says. That is, you must regard it as wrong to depart from its express sense, to pretend or dissemble, to yield anything to its enemies, or to show in life and conduct a different face from the one the word of God teaches. In sum: God has decreed this, that we, unlike the way we are accustomed to act in human affairs, should in divine matters be peaceable and not wish to concede anything to adversaries. Let us not add new things of our own devising, as if we were wiser than God. The sacred letters are perfect, because the Lord wished nothing to be added to them nor taken from them. As below, in chapter 12: "Whatever I command you, you shall observe to do; you shall add nothing to it, nor take anything away from it." Proverbs 30: "Every word of God is purified; he is a shield to those who trust in him. Do not add to his words, lest he reprove you and you be found a liar."

units.la: Ex quo perspicuum est scripturam sacram plenam perfectamque esse. Et usu comper-tum est etiam quòd dicimus verum esse. Quacunque enim de re Christus rogatus esset, eam petitis ex scriptura sacra legibus & iudicijs explicavit. Ut de summa legis, de matrimonio, de resurrectione, de vectigalibus, & de rebus reliquis. Et Paulus de coena Domini rogatus respondit ex Evangelio. Constantinus iussit secundum scripturas componere controuerfias de religione. Ergo merito magna est eius apud nos authoritas.
units.tr: From this it is clear that Holy Scripture is full and perfect, and experience has also proved that what we say is true. For whatever matter Christ was asked about, he explained it from Holy Scripture, from its laws and judgments: concerning the sum of the law, marriage, the resurrection, tribute, and other matters. And Paul, asked about the Lord's Supper, answered from the gospel. Constantine ordered controversies about religion to be settled according to the Scriptures. Therefore its authority is rightly great among us.

units.la: Sed vt eadem illis fit hac in parte religio, refert exemplum ex annalibus dicens. Oculi vestri viderunt quae fecit Dominus in Baal Peor. Extat historia Num.25. Exemplo hoc deterret illos ab apostasia. Nam qui tunc constanter in propo-sito verbo Dei perseverabant ij seruabantur, qui vero deficiebant ad idololatriam, hos Deus simul omnes perdebat. In quo ex-emplo praemia bonis parata non minus descripta sunt, quam quae malis sunt decreta supplicia. Vt igitur ad virtutem praemia alliciunt, sic absterreant a malo supplicia. Ex quibus per-spicuum est scripturam sacram, quoniam plena perfectaq; est, si formam consideres, esse vtilissimam. Quid enim est vtilius quam eiusmodi doctrinae genus nactum esse, è quo quicquid omnino quaestionis incidat, recta peti queat explicatio? Sane erit hic magister optimus.
units.tr: But so that the same religion may hold among them in this respect, he cites an example from the annals, saying: "Your eyes have seen what the Lord did at Baal-peor." The history is found in Numbers 25. By this example he deters them from apostasy. For those who then persevered steadfastly in their purpose in the word of God were preserved, while those who fell away to idolatry were all destroyed together by God. In this example the rewards prepared for the good are described no less than the punishments decreed for the wicked. Therefore, just as rewards attract men to virtue, so punishments turn them from evil. From these things it is clear that Holy Scripture, since it is full and perfect, is most useful if you consider its form. For what is more useful than to have obtained a kind of teaching from which a right explanation can be sought for whatever question may arise? Surely this will be the best teacher.

units.la: Causa efficiens. Ecce(inquit)docui vos statuta & iudicia sicut praecepit mihi Dominus Deus meus, &c. Quod perinde est ac si dicat: Religio mihi foret vos fallere. Deus meus maiore est apud me in precio, quam vt vel latum vnguem a mandatis eius discedam. Quin aliud nihil vos doceo, quam quod ille in mandatis dedit. Atq; sic quidem causam efficientem huius doctrinae Deum ipsum statuit, eoque ipso docet eius studium esse longe vtilissimum. Quod ra-tionibus minime leuibus confirmatur. Primum quod cum diuina sit, puram & affectibus malis vacuam esse oporteat, hocque ipsum quod expedit tantum consulere. Deinceps quod non potest esse suspecta doctrina Domini, quasi ipse suis commodis aut honoribus haec nobis suadens aut difuadens consulat, quia Deo siue facias iusta, siue ea negligas, iustic nec feritur nec metitur. Postremo quia rectum Dei verbo prebitum obsequium aeque eum nobis amicum facit atque homines hominibus amicos faciunt obsequia. At Deo coniunctum esse amicitia summum bonum est: quo nihil potest esse nostro generi salubrius. Quamobrem cum a Deo nihil nisi bonum proficisci queat, etiam hoc nomine verbi Dei studium est vtile, quod non aliunde ipsum, quam a Deo accepimus. Atque sic quidem finis simul & materia & efficiens verbi Dei causa nobis vtilitatem ex hoc studio pollicentur maximam. Quare sit Deo patri & filio & spiritui sancto honos sumus in secula seculorum. Amen.
units.tr: Efficient cause. "Behold," he says, "I have taught you statutes and judgements, just as the Lord my God commanded me," etc. This is as much as to say: it would be a sin for me to deceive you. My God is of greater worth to me than that I should depart from his commands by so much as the breadth of a fingernail. Indeed, I teach you nothing other than what he has given in his commands. In this way he names God himself as the efficient cause of this teaching, and by that very fact shows that its pursuit is by far the most useful. This is confirmed by no slight reasons. First, since it is divine, it ought to be pure and free from evil affections, seeking only what is truly expedient. Next, the teaching of the Lord cannot be suspected, as though he advised us to do or avoid things for his own advantage or honour, since to God it makes no difference whether you do what is right or neglect it; he is neither harmed nor benefited. Lastly, because obedience rendered according to the word of God makes him our friend, just as services make men friends to men. To be joined to God in friendship is the supreme good, and nothing can be more wholesome for our kind. Therefore, since nothing but good can come from God, the study of the word of God is useful on this count too, since we have received it from no other source than God. And so the end, the matter and the efficient cause of the word of God together promise us the greatest usefulness from this study. Therefore let there be honour to God the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, for ever and ever. Amen.

units.la: SERMO XV.
units.tr: Sermon 15.

units.la: 6 Custodieris itaq; & facietis: haec enim est sapientia & intelligentia vestra coram populis, qui audient omnia statuta ista, vt dicant, duntaxat populus sapiens & intelligens est gens haec magna.
units.tr: 6 You shall therefore keep and do them, for this is your wisdom and your understanding before the peoples, who shall hear all these statutes and say, "Surely this great nation is a wise and understanding people."

units.la: 7 Quae enim gens ita magna est, quae sic habeat Deum suum sibi amicum & familiarem, quemadmodum Dominus Deus noster est in omnibus quibus inuocamus eum?
units.tr: 7 For what great nation is there that has its God so near to it as the Lord our God is to us, whenever we call upon him?

units.la: 8 Et quae gens ita magna est, cui sint statuta & iudicia iusta, secundum uni-versam legem istam, quam ego propono vobis hodie?
units.tr: 8 And what great nation is there that has statutes and judgments so righteous as this whole law which I set before you today?

units.la: 9 Modo caue tibi, & custodi animum tuum diligenter, ne vnquam obliuiscaris eorum quae viderunt oculi tui, & ne forte recedant a corde tuo cunctis diebus vitae tuae, sed nota facias ea filijs tuis, & nepotibus tuis.
units.tr: 9 Only take heed to yourself, and keep your soul diligently, lest you forget the things your eyes have seen, and lest they depart from your heart all the days of your life; but make them known to your sons and your grandsons.

units.la: QVemadmodum omnes homines sic natura sua comparati sunt, vt ad id quod conducere sibi videatur, facile expetendum ferantur: sic etiam hoc a natura sibi insitum habent, vt ad honores mirum in modum propendeant, & subinde cupiant esse in precio, eaq; de causa res eas in quibus est aliqua spes honorum posita, licet magnae sint & arduae, confidentibus animis aggrediuntur ac gerunt. Ac si quae sint artes, aut studia, aut vitae gene-ra, quibus ad honores iter panditur, eo videmus omnium animos atque studia applicari. Neque enim fine causa vulgo dici ceptum est, artes honoribus ali. Quamobrem vt Moses vtilitatis spe suum populum ad diuinae legis studium voluit allicere, sic in praesentia spem honorum offert, eaq; vult animos ad diuinarum legum studium excitare, docens ex eo non minus honorum quam vtilitatum comparari. Atque vt intelligant honestissimum hoc esse studium, primum hoc summatim proponit, tum probat argumentis, denique claudit exhorta-tione totum negocium. Proponit dicens, Custodietis itaque & facietis: hæc enim est sapientia & intelligentia vestra coram populis. Quod idem est ac si dicat. Datæ operam huic doctrinæ, quia hæc sola vobis cum sapientiam conferet, quæ vestram vobis augere potest apud omnes gentes existimationem & dignitatem.
units.tr: Just as all human beings are so constituted by nature that they are readily carried toward whatever seems to serve their advantage, so they also have it implanted in them by nature to lean remarkably toward honours, and to desire to be held in esteem. For this reason they take up and carry out with confident hearts those undertakings in which some hope of honour is placed, however great and difficult they may be. And if there are any arts, pursuits or ways of life by which a path to honours is opened, we see the minds and efforts of all men directed to them. Indeed, it is not without cause that it has become a common saying that the arts are nourished by honours. Therefore, just as Moses wished to draw his people to the study of the divine law by the hope of advantage, so now he holds out the hope of honours and wishes to stir their minds to the study of the divine laws, teaching that from this study honours are gained no less than advantages. And so that they may understand that this study is most honourable, he first sets it out in brief, then proves it by arguments, and finally concludes the whole matter with an exhortation. He sets it out, saying: You shall therefore keep and do them, for this is your wisdom and your understanding before the peoples. This is as much as to say: Give your attention to this teaching, since this alone will bring you wisdom, which can increase your reputation and dignity among all nations.

units.la: Quo ostendit nihil esse ad comparandam præclaram apud homines existimationem efficacius verbi diuini studio. Nam si id sit honestum quod sua vi naturaq; nos alliciens laudabile est: certe sapientia quæ suo ipsius splendore, tum etiam bonitate & suauitate sua ad se nos allicit atq; atrahit, non poterit non hoc genere contineri.
units.tr: By this he shows that nothing is more effective than the study of the divine Word for gaining a splendid reputation among men. For if that is honourable which, by its own power and nature, draws us to itself and is praiseworthy, then certainly wisdom, which by its own splendour, and also by its goodness and sweetness, draws and attracts us to itself, cannot but be contained within this kind.

units.la: Cæterum, vt quomodo sapientiam sacra scriptura conferat, intelligas, verbis Mosis hoc demonstrabitur. Nam custodiendi verbo causam sapientiæ veræ efficientem siue principium, faciendi vero eius formam significat.
units.tr: But so that you may understand how Holy Scripture bestows wisdom, this will be shown from the words of Moses. For by the word "keep" he signifies the efficient cause or principle of true wisdom, and by the word "do" its form.

units.la: Ac principium quidem eius est timor Domini, quem propheta custodiendi verbo notat. Id enim custodimus atq; etiam asseruamus assidue, quod omnium minime volumus per ditum, vt thesauros, & vestes, & omnino quæ chara magnique precij sunt omnia, nempe vt non amittamus, vt ne corrumpantur, aut aspergantur maculis. Eodem modo leges ne violentur, aut abrogentur custodiri solent. Ea custodia coniunctam habet solicitudinem: nam vbi nil timetur periculi, ibi nulla requiritur custodia. Inde fit, vt qui ne qua diuinæ legis violatione Deum offendat, timet, hacq; de causa quicquid Deus iusserit gnauiter efficit, Deum timere dicatur. Is timor quoniam nos in officio, hoc est in eo quod rectum, honestum, vtile, necessarium est retinet, nosq; ab eo quod nobis detrimento pariter, & dedecori fuerit cohibet, non inepte sane dicitur initium sapientiæ, &c. Quis enim eum sapientem neget esse qui in omnibus vitæ suæ partibus ab eo, quod diximus, alienum nihil faciat? Ergo Psalmo cxj. principium sapientiæ timor Domini dicitur. Et alio Psalmo, Sculti propter transgressionem suâ & propter afflictiones suas affliguntur. Quo dicit stultos solere mandata sua negligere, eoq; ipso sibi mala adcersere: at sese affligere, vel cedere colaphis, vel quoquo malo afficere quis neget esse stulti & dementis hominis? Quis suam rem recte gerere & suis commodis rite studere neget esse sapientis? Vt Pharao quia Deum non timuit sese pariter ac suos pessundedit: Ioseph quia Deum timuit, cum sibi tum toti Ægypto bene consuluit. Saul quoad Deum timeret bene habebat, dum illius timore vacuus mandata Dei negligeret sese perdidit. Ergo opus est ad veram sapientiam pietate. Veluti Lucas Actor. 10. de Cornelio perhibet, quod prius timens Dei fuerit antequam ad solidam eius cognitionem atq; fidem, veram sapientiam videlicet peruenirèt[?]. Actor. 13. Paulus verbum salutis ijs mitti dicebat qui timerent Deum. Et Esa. 66. dicitur Dominus eos respicere qui ad sermonem eius cotremiscunt. Quare Moses custodiendi verbo timorem Dei ceu initium veræ sapientiæ significat.
units.tr: Now its principle is the fear of the Lord, which the prophet signifies by the word "keep." For we keep and also diligently guard that which we least of all wish to lose, such as treasures, garments, and in general all things that are dear and of great value: namely, that we do not lose them, that they are not spoiled or stained. In the same way laws are customarily kept so that they are not violated or repealed. This keeping is joined with anxiety, for where there is no fear of danger, there is no need for guarding. Hence it comes about that the one who fears to offend God by any violation of the divine law, and for this reason diligently performs whatever God has commanded, is said to fear God. Since this fear keeps us in our duty, that is, in what is right, honourable, useful and necessary, and restrains us from what would be harmful and shameful to us, it is not foolishly said to be the beginning of wisdom, and so on. For who would deny that he is wise who in every part of his life does nothing foreign to what we have described? Therefore in Psalm 111 the fear of the Lord is called the beginning of wisdom. And in another Psalm: "Fools are afflicted because of their transgression and because of their iniquities." By this he says that fools are accustomed to neglect his commands and so bring evils upon themselves; but who would deny that a man who afflicts himself, or submits to blows, or suffers any evil whatever, is a foolish and senseless man? Who would deny that a man who manages his affairs rightly and rightly attends to his own advantage is wise? Thus Pharaoh, because he did not fear God, destroyed both himself and his people alike; Joseph, because he feared God, provided well both for himself and for all Egypt. Saul, so long as he feared God, was doing well, but when he was empty of the fear of God and neglected God's commands, he ruined himself. Therefore a godliness is needed for true wisdom. As Luke says in Acts 10 about Cornelius, that he was first a fearer of God before he came to solid knowledge and faith in him, that is, to true wisdom. In Acts 13 Paul said that the word of salvation was sent to those who feared God. And in Isaiah 66 the Lord is said to look upon those who tremble at his word. Therefore Moses, by the word "keep," signifies the fear of God as the beginning of true wisdom.

units.la: Formam autem verbo faciendi cum intelligentiæ nomine coniuncto notat. Dicit enim facite, siue facietis, & deinceps addit, intelligentia. Est autem intelligentia animæ rationalis facultas, qua res eæ quæ possunt intelligi percipiuntur & cognoscuntur. Vnde eius proprium est inuenire, librare & censere, & quale quidq; sit cognoscere. Quod quid aliud est quà sapientiæ? Esa. 11. Spiritus sapientiæ spiritus intelligentiæ dicitur. Ex quo Basilius definit sapientiam dicens, Σοφία ἐστὶν ἐπιστήμη θείων καὶ ἀνθρωπίνων πραγμάτων καὶ τῶν τούτων αἰτίων. Hoc est, quæ diuinas simul ac humanas res earumq; etiam causas explorate cognitas habet. Diuinarum autem rerum numero quicquid religionis est, & humanarum quicquid homines cum hominibus siue singuli cum singulis, siue vniuersi cum vniuersis habent negocij continentur. Quæ doctrina duobus à Christo capitibus, Dei videlicet & proximi dilectione tota comprehensa est, ac deinceps multis sacris prophanisq; scriptoribus explicata fusius. Atq; hæc quidem nosse est intelligentiæ. Vnde Solon dixit τοσοῦτο[?] ... διαφέρειν τὴν φρόνησιν τῶν ἀρετῶν, ὅσῳ θεῶν [?] ... τῶν ἄλλων ἀνθρώπων.
units.tr: But by the word "do," joined with the name of understanding, he indicates the form. For he says "do," or "you shall do," and then adds "understanding." Now understanding is the faculty of the rational soul by which those things which can be understood are perceived and known. Hence its proper function is to discover, weigh and judge, and to know what kind of thing anything is. And what is this other than wisdom? Isaiah 11 says: "the spirit of wisdom and the spirit of understanding." From this Basil defines wisdom, saying: Wisdom is the knowledge of divine and human things and of their causes [Σοφία ἐστὶν ἐπιστήμη θείων καὶ ἀνθρωπίνων πραγμάτων καὶ τῶν τούτων αἰτίων]. That is, it is that which has accurately known both divine and human things and their causes as well. Under divine things is included whatever belongs to religion, and under human things whatever business men have with men, whether individuals with individuals or all with all. This teaching, comprised entirely under the two heads taught by Christ, namely the love of God and the love of neighbour, has afterwards been explained more fully by many sacred and profane writers. And to know these things is indeed the office of understanding. Hence Solon said that prudence differs from the virtues as much as ... [τοσοῦτο ... διαφέρειν τὴν φρόνησιν τῶν ἀρετῶν, ὅσῳ θεῶν ... τῶν ἄλλων ἀνθρώπων] ... the other men.

units.la: Iam ne scientia sola contenti simus, faciendi verbum intelligentiæ coniungit eoque docet quod Diuo Augustino multisque præclaris theologis & philosophis placuit, sapientiæ studium non minus in actione quam contemplatione versari. Qua de causa Diuus Basilius alibi quoque sapientiâ definiens ait, ἀλλ' ἀληθὴς φρόνησις ἐπιγνώσις ἐστι τῶν τε ποιητέων καὶ πρακτέων[?]. Hoc est, quæ doceat non solum quid facere, verum etiam quid non facere debeas. Et Dauid in eo quem modo diximus, Psalmo, cum dixisset initium sapientiæ timor Domini, mox addit, intellectus bonus omnibus FACIENTIBVS EA. Quo docet tum demum vtilem esse nobis intelligentiam quando quæ cognita habemus recta ac bona faciamus: non boñam autem, hoc est inutilem imò perniciosam, quando bona ac recta noris, non autem eafa-cias. Nam rectum scire nec facere non solum non prodest, sed obest etiam. Non prodesse, vulgi illud dictum notat, Odi sapientem qui sibi ipse non sapit. Et certe quid profuerit multa de re familiari, de repub. nec nō de religione differere, nec eorū quidquā facere? Sed obesse Dominus hoc ipso docet in euangelio, quod dicit, seruus sciens non autem faciens voluntatem Domini plagis multis vapulabit. Quare et in Euangelio Dominus eum sapientē Dicit esse qui non solum norit spem salutis in mundanis caducisq; rebus collocandam non esse, verum etiam in ijs spem nullam, omnem autem in Deo positam habeat. Mat. 7. Et Matt. 10. prudentes nos esse vult quemadmodū serpentes, ut se qui caput nostrū est, unice studeamus coseruare: simplices autē ut sunt columbæ, ut res nostras sine proximi detrimento agamus. Hæc omnia quoniā sacræ literæ docent non possunt non conferre eam, quę vere est honori, sapientiam.
units.tr: Now, lest we be content with knowledge alone, the word "do" joins with understanding, and thereby teaches what pleased the divine Augustine and many excellent theologians and philosophers: that the study of wisdom is concerned no less with action than with contemplation. For this reason Basil, defining wisdom elsewhere, also says: But true prudence is knowledge of things to be made and things to be done [ἀλλ' ἀληθὴς φρόνησις ἐπιγνώσις ἐστι τῶν τε ποιητέων καὶ πρακτέων]. That is, it is that which teaches not only what you ought to do, but also what you ought not to do. And David, in the Psalm we have just mentioned, after saying "the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom," immediately adds: "good understanding to all who DO them." By this he teaches that understanding is then useful to us when we do the right and good things we know; but it is not good, that is, it is useless and indeed harmful, when you know what is good and right but do not do it. For to know what is right and not to do it not only does not profit, but even harms. That it does not profit is shown by the common saying: "I hate the wise man who is not wise for himself." And indeed what does it profit to discuss at length matters of household, of the commonwealth, and of religion too, and to do none of these things? That it harms the Lord shows in the Gospel, where he says: "the servant who knows the Lord's will but does not do it shall be beaten with many stripes." Therefore also in the Gospel the Lord calls wise the one who knows not only that the hope of salvation is not to be placed in worldly and perishable things, but also that he has no hope in them, and places all his hope in God. Matthew 7. And in Matthew 10 he wills that we be wise as serpents, so that we may earnestly strive to preserve him who is our head, and simple as doves, so that we may conduct our affairs without harm to our neighbour. Since the sacred letters teach all these things, they cannot but bestow that wisdom which is truly honourable.

units.la: Propositā argumentis probat duobus, quorum unum ab effectis, à materia alterum du-cit. Ab effectis, Populus(inquit) audientes discent, duntaxat populus sapiens & intelligens, &c. Quæ enim gens magna est, &c. Quo docet verbi Dei studio effici, ut Deum nobis amicū, familiarē, auxiliarium habeamus: quod est longè honestissimum. Amicus, quippe qui beneuelit: at qui bus fit amicior quam sui verbi studiosis, dicit, honorantes me vicissim honore prosequor, diligentes me redamo. Christus fratres & sorores appellat facientes voluntatē patris sui. Familiaris, quippe qui nos ipse doceat consoletur, ac roboret: ut patriarchis locutus est, præiuit dux viæ, misit nuncios suæ voluntatis interpretes. Egregie D. Hieron. in 1. aduersus Iouinianum libro dicit, sapientē nunquam solum esse, habere eum secum omnes qui sunt quiq; unquam fuerunt boni, & animum liberum quocunq; velit transferre, quippe qui quod corpore nō possit cogitatione cōplectatur, & si hominū inopia fuerit cū Deo colloquatur. Auxiliarius, omnibus inuocantib⁹ opē ferens accurrat. Utlosepho[?], Dauidi, Danieli, &c. Quis igitur eū qui Deū amicū, familiarē, auxiliarē habeat sapientē propterea, honestissimū neget esse.
units.tr: Having set out the point, he proves it by two arguments, one drawn from effects and the other from matter. From effects: "The people (he says) who hear shall learn, the wise and understanding people only, etc. For what great nation is there, etc." By this he teaches that devotion to the Word of God brings it about that we have God as our friend, intimate and helper, which is by far the most honourable thing. God is a friend, since he does good; and who is made more friendly to us than those who are diligent in his word? He says: "Those who honour me I will honour in return; those who love me I will love again." Christ calls those who do his Father's will his brothers and sisters. God is intimate, since he teaches us himself, comforts us and strengthens us; as he spoke to the patriarchs, he went before them as the leader of the way, and he sent messengers to interpret his will. Saint Jerome, in the first book against Jovinian, rightly says that the wise man is never alone: he has with him all who are or ever have been good, and a free mind that can go wherever it wishes, since it grasps in thought what it cannot reach in body, and if he lacks human company he converses with God. God is a helper, who runs to aid all who call on him, as he did for Joseph, David, Daniel, and others. Who then would deny that the man who has God as friend, intimate and helper is wise, and therefore most honourable?

units.la: A materia, Et quæ gens est cui sint statuta & iudicia iusta. Materia circa quā sapiens animus versatur sunt primū statuta siue sacri ritus & quicquid ad religionem pertinet. Quæ non alibi unde melius, quam è verbo Dei petuntur, Omnes gentes quæ quidem verbum Dei non habuerunt magistrum religionis, pudore suffusi sunt propter vanitatem excogitatarum absque superstitionum: at gens Israelitica verbo Dei instructa veritatem agnouit, hocq; nomine sapientiæ laudem consecuta est.
units.tr: "From matter: And what great nation is there that has statutes and righteous judgements." The matter with which the wise mind is concerned is first of all the statutes, that is, the sacred rites, and whatever pertains to religion. These are sought nowhere better than from the Word of God. All the nations that did not have the Word of God as their teacher of religion were put to shame, because of the vanity of the superstitions they had devised; but the Israelite nation, instructed by the Word of God, knew the truth, and by this gained the praise of wisdom.

units.la: Dein sunt leges siue iura quæ iudiciorum nomine comprehenduntur. Ea Romani quondam à Græcis petierunt, & à Lacedemonijs: sed in singula secula mutata sunt: gens Israelitica ab ipso Deo religionem docta cum legibus aliunde iura petere necesse non habuit. Quod quoniam est honestissimū magnam laudem attulit huic populo. Utq; Iudæa magnū ex hac re nomen adepta, & Capernaum usq; ad cœlum exaltata, sic nos quoq; eo nomine celebres facti sumus. Omnes hoc relicto facti sunt contemptissimi.
units.tr: Next there are the laws or rights, which are comprehended under the name of judgements. The Romans once sought these from the Greeks, and from the Lacedaemonians; but they were changed in every age. The Israelite nation, taught its religion by God himself, had no need to seek its rights from elsewhere along with its laws. Since this is most honourable, it brought great praise to this people. And just as Judaea gained a great name from this fact, and Capernaum was raised up to heaven, so we too have become famous on this account. All who have abandoned this have become most contemptible.

units.la: Quamobrem cum verbū Dei cerimonias simul atq; leges ciuiles rectas suppeditent, illud retinebimus ceu materiā & effecta veræ, quæ honores affert, sapientiæ. Conclusio, Caue, &c. Summam ac caput huius loci duabus partibus comprehendit. Una, ut ne earum memoria animis excidat, verum perpetuo hæreat Obliuio verbi Dei malorum omnium causa est. Ergo ut caueamus mala noli committere ut eius obliuiscare. Hinc prædicatio verbi diuinitus instituta est. Etsi scias, tamen excidunt animo: ideo revocat in memoriam prædicatio, ut vere scias. Siquidem id demū verè scimus, quod tenemus memoria. Atq; sic se pij semper exercue-runt audiendo, meditandoq; verbo Domini, itemq; precibus, & lectionibus, & colloquijs, ut Moses, Maria, Zach. Simeon, in primisq; diuinus psaltes. Quamobrem ut diuini verbi semen animis nostris acceptum perpetua memoria custodiamus, audiendo, meditando, precando, pijsq; colloquijs efficitur.
units.tr: Therefore, since the Word of God supplies both the ceremonies and the civil laws that are right, we shall hold to it as the matter and the effects of true wisdom, which brings honour. "Conclusion: Take heed, etc." He comprehends the sum and head of this passage in two parts. The first is that the memory of them should not slip from our minds, but cling to us perpetually. Forgetting the Word of God is the cause of all evils. So, if we want to avoid evils, do not commit them, and do not forget it. Hence the preaching of the word was instituted by God. Even if you know it, still it slips from the mind; so preaching calls it back to memory, so that you truly know it. For we truly know only what we hold in memory. And thus the godly have always exercised themselves in hearing and meditating on the word of the Lord, likewise in prayers, readings and godly conversations, as Moses, Mary, Zechariah, Simeon, and above all the divine psalmist did. Therefore, that the seed of the divine word received in our minds may be kept by perpetual memory, this is brought about by hearing, meditating, praying and holy conversation.

units.la: Altera, Liberos nostros idem etiam doceamus: dicit enim, nota facies ea filijs tuis & nepotibus, &c. Quibus verbis Catechismum in ecclesia instituit, quemadmodum Dominus postulat adduci sibi liberos. Extant in hanc sententiam multa passim scripta. Discè liberorum curā habere: opes liberis colligis, cum præstaret sapientes effici: tunc enim opes ipsi sibi possunt quærere. Stulti quæsitas non possunt retinere. Egregie sanè Pythagoras illud dixit, Οὔτε ἵππον χωρὶς χαλινῶν, ὅτε πλοῦτον ἄνευ φρονήσεως ὁ νατὸν κρατεῖσθαι[?]. Quod indicio est divitias non prodesse sine ratione recta siue sapientia. Unde vetus dictum est illud nostris hominibus usitatum: Ser sin Fund ʒüchte/lege im gold in Büsen. Itaq; liberi sunt in pietate & bonis moribus instituendi pariter atq; educandi. Quod hoc loco Moses admonet.
units.tr: The second part is that we should teach the same to our children also: for he says, "You shall make these things known to your sons and grandsons, etc." By these words he establishes the catechism in the Church, just as the Lord requires that children be brought to him. Many writings on this subject are found everywhere. Learn to have care for your children: you gather riches for them, when it would be better to make them wise; for then they can seek riches for themselves, whereas fools cannot keep what has been sought. Pythagoras said this admirably: neither a horse without bridles nor wealth without wisdom can be held [Οὔτε ἵππον χωρὶς χαλινῶν, ὅτε πλοῦτον ἄνευ φρονήσεως ὁ νατὸν κρατεῖσθαι]. This is evidence that riches do not profit without right reason or wisdom. Hence that old saying, familiar among our people, runs: sow the seed, gather the crop, and lay the gold in your bosom. Therefore children are to be instructed and brought up in piety and good morals, both alike. This is what Moses urges in this place.

units.la: Ex quibus omnibus intelligitur verbi diuini studium ijs qui se ei rectè dediderunt esse honestisihonestissimum. Nam si id quod confert sapientiam honestum est, certe verbi diuini studium quoniam eam confert, omnium honestissimum esse necesse est. Ac sapientiam quidem honori nobis esse hoc ipso Moses indicat, quod dixit, eum populum qui ista sapientia pollet omnibus gentibus admirationi fore, deque eo dictum iri, en populus ille sapiens & intelli-gens: quæ est tanta gens, &c. Quis enim neget verum esse, quod poeta vetus dixit, Pulchrum est monstrarier digito, & dici hic est? Sed hoc studio conferri sapientiam cum materia tum effecta significant. Efficit enim, vt Moses indicat, hoc studium vt Deum, qui nobis amicus, familiaris, auxiliarius semper assit, quicquid facto opus est perpetuo consulat. Materia vero quam sapientissimus quisque versat maxime; doctrina de religione & de iure nullibi melius ac plenius, quàm in his literis sacris traditur. Ergo concludit ei non solum nos, qui prouesti sumus ætate, verum etiam liberos nostros deditos esse oportere. Id vt fiat ac saluti sit faxit Deus in Christo. Amen.
units.tr: From all these things it is understood that devotion to the divine Word is most honourable for those who have rightly given themselves to it. For if what brings wisdom is honourable, then surely devotion to the divine Word, since it brings wisdom, must be the most honourable of all. And that wisdom is a credit to us, Moses himself indicates by saying that the people who possess this wisdom will be an object of admiration to all nations, and that of them it will be said: "Behold, that wise and understanding people; what a great nation it is, etc." For who would deny the truth of what the old poet said: "It is a fine thing to be pointed at with the finger and to be said, 'There he is'"? But that wisdom is brought by this devotion, both as to matter and as to effects, they signify. For, as Moses shows, this devotion brings it about that God, who is always present to us as friend, intimate and helper, takes perpetual counsel for whatever deed is needed. The matter, which the wisest men handle above all, the doctrine of religion and of law, is nowhere handed down better or more fully than in these holy writings. Therefore he concludes that not only we, who are advanced in years, but also our children ought to be devoted to them. May God grant that this come about and be for our salvation in Christ. Amen.

units.la: SERMO XVI.
units.tr: SERMON XVI.

units.la: 10 Diem præsertim quo stetisti coram Domino Deo tuo in Horeb, cum diceret Dominus ad me: Congrega mihi populum, & faciam vt audiant verba mea, quæ discant, vt timeant me cunctis diebus quibus ipsi viuturi sunt super terram, et filios suos doceant.
units.tr: 10 Especially the day on which you stood before the Lord your God in Horeb, when the Lord said to me: Gather the people to me, and I will make them hear my words, which they shall learn, so that they may fear me all the days they live upon the earth, and may teach their sons.

units.la: 11 Accessistis autem & stetistis sub monte, mons autem ardebat igne ad medium cæli vsq; in quo erant tenebræ, nubes & caligo.
units.tr: 11 You came near and stood under the mountain, and the mountain burned with fire up to the midst of heaven, where there was darkness, cloud and mist.

units.la: 12 Loquebaturq; Dominus ad vos de medio ignis, et quidem vocem verborum vos audiebatis, at simulachrum nullum videbatis vltra vocem.
units.tr: 12 And the Lord spoke to you out of the midst of the fire; you heard the voice of the words, but you saw no form, only a voice.

units.la: 13 Tum promulgabat vobis fœdus suum, quod præceperat vobis vt faceretis, decem verba nempe, quæ scripsit super tabulas duas lapideas.
units.tr: 13 Then he set forth to you his covenant, which he commanded you to keep, namely the ten words, which he wrote upon two tablets of stone.

units.la: 14 Mihi vero eodem tempore præcepit Dominus, vt docerem vos statuta & iudicia, vt faceretis ea in terra, in quam transitis, vt eam possideatis.
units.tr: 14 At the same time the Lord commanded me to teach you statutes and judgments, that you should do them in the land into which you are crossing to possess it.

units.la: QUanquam homo reuera nihil animo suo pluris faciat, quam suam ipsius vtilitatem, atque gloriam: tamen præseferet ac constanter simulat maiore apud se esse in precio Deum, eius verbum, eiusque etiam gloriam: quippe quod eo sua quenque cogat conscien-tia, vt agnoscat pluris esse numen, & quicquid est diuinum, quàm hominem. Ex eo hoc consecutum est, vt quicunque vel seipsos, vel sua ipsorum consilia, atque placita magni momenti esse voluerint, eo ipso hoc efficere conati sint, quod se Deos appellari, suaque consilia diuina esse dixerunt. Veluti quidam adulatores suis principibus numen tribuerunt, & quidam principes se ipsi Deorum nomine vocarunt, nonnulli suas, quas populis vellent obtrudere, leges diuinitus se accepisse gloriati sunt, quidam etiam doctores & philosophi sua placita siue dogmata diuinarum reuelationum titulo ornata proposuere. Vt Alexander Magnus à suis Deus appellatus est: Cæss. nonnulli se Deos appellari voluere. Et vt Minos leges suas ab Ioue, Numa suas ab Ægeria nympha accepisse gloriati sunt. Sic Francifcus ille, qui Francifcanis monachis nomen dedit, & Brigitta illa nota Christianis populis quæ docuere, sibi diuinitus reuelata esse docuere, hocque ipso fidem dictis apud homines repererunt. Iam si illi sua consilia atque inuenta nomine diuinitatis vt acciperentur effecerunt, quanto magis est enitendum, vt hæc doctrina diuina agnoscatur? Igitur vt Diuinus Moses ostendit leges ab se latas cum vtiles tum honestas esse ijs, qui recipiunt atque seruant eas: hoc iam nomine docet esse recipiendas, quod authore Deo latæ sint, & promulgatæ. Qua de causa quisquis diuina magnifacit, quod videri volumus omnes facere, etiam harum studium amplectetur. Docet enim hoc loco Moses hanc doctrinam & diuinam esse, & diuinam permanere in æternum. Ac diuinam quidem esse ex eo docet, quo proposita atque pro-mulgata fit modo perspicuum fieri. Quem vt exponat circumstantias omnes enumerat, personam, modum, remipsam.
units.tr: Although a man in truth values nothing more than his own advantage and glory, yet he professes and constantly pretends that God, his word, and also his glory, are held in greater esteem by him; for his own conscience compels each person to acknowledge that the divine power, and whatever is divine, is greater than man. From this it has followed that whoever has wished himself or his own counsels and decisions to be of great importance has tried to achieve this very thing by calling themselves gods and by saying that their counsels were divine. Thus certain flatterers have ascribed divinity to their princes, and certain princes have called themselves by the name of gods; some have boasted that they received from God the laws they wished to thrust upon the peoples; and some teachers and philosophers have put forward their opinions or doctrines adorned with the title of divine revelations. Thus Alexander the Great was called a god by his followers. Caesar: some wished to be called gods. And as Minos boasted that he received his laws from Jupiter, and Numa his from the nymph Egeria. So that famous Francis, who gave his name to the Franciscan monks, and that well-known Bridget, who taught Christian peoples, taught that they had been divinely revealed to them, and by this very means they found credit for their words among men. Now if those men made their own counsels and inventions to be received under the name of divinity, how much more must we strive that this divine doctrine be recognised! Therefore, just as the divine Moses shows that the laws he proposed are both useful and honourable to those who receive and keep them, so he now teaches that they are to be received for this reason, that they were given and promulgated with God as their author. For this reason whoever holds divine things in high esteem, as we all wish to appear to do, will also embrace the study of these laws. For Moses teaches in this place that this doctrine is divine, and that it remains divine for ever. He teaches that it is divine from the fact that the manner in which it is set forth and promulgated makes this clear. To explain this, he enumerates all the circumstances: the person, the manner, and the matter itself.

units.la: Persona legem dans est Deus ipse, id indicat Moses diligentissime circumstantijs adhibitis scilicet. 1. Diem quo stetisti coram Domino, scilicet recordare. Tempus dicit, quo & ipsos testes, & Deum nomothetam agnitum indicat. Dies quinquagesimus ab egressu populi ex Ægypto:qui & missione spiritus sancti celebris est, & anno iubileo numerum illum referen-te. Sed Dei nomine renouat quicquid eo ipso acciderat: quemadmodum Paulus noctem, qua Dominus fuerat proditus in memoriam revocat. Ita nimirum lætus dies erat, quo Ægypto erepti benignissimum illum Deum pro tyranno truculentissimo nacti, legem acci-piebant.
units.tr: As to the person giving the law, it is God himself; Moses indicates this most carefully by the circumstances he adds, namely: (1) The day on which you stood before the Lord, that is, remember. He names the time, by which he shows both that the witnesses themselves and God the lawgiver were recognised. It was the fiftieth day after the people's departure from Egypt, which is celebrated both for the mission of the Holy Spirit and, in the reckoning of the year of Jubilee, refers to that number. But by the name of God he renews whatever had happened on that very day, just as Paul calls to mind the night in which the Lord was betrayed. So indeed it was a joyful day, on which they received the law, having been freed from Egypt and having found that most kind God in place of a most savage tyrant.

units.la: Iam & persona verbi secunda ipsos testes appellat, quasi dicat has leges non sibi soli, vel duodecim viris, vel septuaginta viris declaratis magistratibus, sed toti coetui stanti coram Domino datas. Est aute hoc certissimum veritatis indicium quod omnes rei gestæ testes esse possunt, aut saltem plærique. Unde Deus omnia palàm fecit aperte, & in conspectu hominum, ne qua posset esse fraudis suspicio. Sic natiuitas, ascensio, refurrectioDomini testes multos habuere.
units.tr: Moreover, the second person in the verb calls the witnesses themselves, as if to say that these laws were given not to them alone, nor to the twelve men or seventy men appointed as magistrates, but to the whole assembly standing before the Lord. This is a most certain sign of truth, because all who were present at an event can be witnesses, or at least most of them. Hence God made all things openly, plainly and in the sight of men, so that there could be no suspicion of deceit. Thus the nativity, ascension and resurrection of the Lord had many witnesses.

units.la: Sed & locum dicit montem Horeb, qui idem Sina.
units.tr: But he also names the place, Mount Horeb, which is the same as Sinai.

units.la: Persona Dei quoque producitur qui id iusserit: non enim ipse hæc dixit, sed Deus iussit vt dicerentur.
units.tr: The person of God is also brought forward as the one who commanded it: for he did not himself say these things, but God commanded that they be spoken.

units.la: Sed quid his suis legibus Deus sibi velit etiam addit, 1. Vt cogregemur: dicit enim, Congrega mihi populu[?]. Ex quo potest intelligi Deu[?] verbo suo homines colligere: humanas aut traditiones dissidiorum causas esse. Secundum verbum Dei Deus unus colitur unanimiter, nemini damnum datur, nemo publica pacem turbat. Sed superstitio parit dissidia & flagitia: Vt Cain in Abelum fratre incitauit superstitio, Achabi tempore tumultus peperit, itemq; Christi & apostolorum memoria, nostraq; etiam ipsorum. Ambitio & auaritia Herodem & Pila-tum, omnesq; principes discordes fecere. At quod Deus iubet ac docet, eo homines congregantur, ut apostoli, ut populus Israel.
units.tr: Moreover, he also adds what God wishes by these his laws: (1) that we be gathered together; for he says, Gather the people to me. From this it can be understood that God gathers men by his word, and that human traditions are the causes of dissensions. According to the word of God, God is worshipped as one with one mind; no one is harmed, no one disturbs the public peace. But superstition brings forth dissensions and wickedness: superstition stirred up Cain against his brother Abel, it caused tumults in the time of Ahab, and likewise in the memory of Christ and the apostles, and in our own time too. Ambition and avarice made Herod and Pilate, and all princes, discordant. But men are gathered together by what God commands and teaches, as the apostles were, as the people of Israel were.

units.la: 2 Audiant & discant me timere cunctis diebus, &c. Audiendi verbo notat obedientiam, qua fit ut admittamus sana consilia: quod est initium salutis: nam quod bona consilia respuit, ei succurri nullo modo potest, quemadmodum vulgo dici solet. Discendi verbo significatur studium & diligentia ad propositā re adhibita: quod quasi medium est quo rebus nostris cosulitur[?].
units.tr: (2) That they may hear and learn to fear me all their days, and so on. By the word hear he denotes obedience, by which we come to admit sound counsels, which is the beginning of salvation; for one who rejects good counsel can in no way be helped, as is commonly said. By the word learn is signified the zeal and diligence applied to the matter proposed; this is, as it were, the means by which our affairs are provided for.

units.la: Sed ne quid defit quid disci hinc queat dicit, nempe se timere. At Deum timere, quoniam efficit ut recte, & honorifice, & pie de eo sentias, divinis monitis atq; iussibus obedias, dictis eius & pollicitis fidem habeas, quid aliud est, quam mera pietatis perfectio? In quo videmus etiam ut timor Domini non in humanis traditionibus, sed in solo verbo Dei, in quo Deus ipse quomodo timeri velit & debeat, verè nos edocet, addisci possit. Sunt qui Deum timeant hoc ipso, quod delectum ciborum aut dierum quemadmodum ab hominibus introductus est neglexerint: sed inanis hic timor est, quippe quoniam in verbo Dei non didiceris.
units.tr: But lest anything be lacking, he says what may be learned from this, namely that they should fear him. To fear God, since it brings it about that you think rightly, honourably and piously of him, that you obey his divine warnings and commands, and that you have faith in his words and promises, what else is it than the pure perfection of piety? In this we also see that the fear of the Lord is truly taught to us, and can be learned, not from human traditions, but from the word of God alone, in which God himself teaches us how he wishes and ought to be feared. There are those who fear God in this very respect, that they neglect the choice of foods or days as introduced by men; but this fear is empty, since you have not learned it from the word of God.

units.la: Quamobrem cum Deus ipse leges in illum finem promulgaverit, ut audias atq; discas verum Dei timorem, certe divinam esse hanc doctrinam necesse est. Id ut indicet Moses verbis apertis dicit se divinitus has accepisse. Et prophetæ verbum à Domino factum ad se esse dixerunt. Et Christus, Doctrina mea nō est mea, sed eius qui misit me patris. Apostolis dictū est, Non vos estis illi loquentes, sed spiritus patris vestri, qui est in cœlis. Paulus dixit se & reliquos apostolos quæstores esse mysteriorum Dei.
