units.tr: Wherefore, since God himself has promulgated these laws to this end, that you may hear and learn the true fear of God, it is certainly necessary that this doctrine be divine. To show this, Moses says in plain words that he received these things from God. And the prophets said that the word of the Lord came to them. And Christ said, My doctrine is not mine, but his who sent me, the Father's. It was said to the apostles, It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who is in heaven. Paul said that he and the other apostles were stewards of the mysteries of God.

units.la: Iam sit impudens necesse est qui doctrinæ, quam divinam esse certo sciat, repugnet. Atq; utinam Gamalielis consilium sequantur aliqui, videlicet, ut si ipsi id audire nolint, saltem eius auscultatione non prohibeant alios: si ipsi nolint obsequi mandatis Domini, saltem eos qui docent quiq; volunt parere missos, faciant. Atq; hæc quidem ex eo, quod Deum doctrinæ huius authorem, tempus, locus, auditores, finis indicant, cognosci possunt.
units.tr: Now whoever opposes a doctrine which he knows for certain to be divine must of necessity be shameless. And would that some would follow the counsel of Gamaliel, namely, that if they themselves are unwilling to hear it, they at least do not forbid others by hindering their hearing; if they themselves are unwilling to obey the commands of the Lord, at least let them not hinder those who teach and who wish to obey those sent. And indeed these things can be known from the fact that the circumstances, namely the time, place, hearers and purpose, indicate God as the author of this doctrine.

units.la: Cæterū etiam hoc nomine divinam esse probat, quod, ut sit perpetuus eius usus in ecclesia, liberis quoq; tradi voluit. Neq; enim Euripi simile est Euangeliū, ut modo hoc modo illud credas, & ut vulgo dici pariter atq; fieri solet, foro te pares & volubilitati fortunæ rerum tu-am fidem sive religionem accommodes: sed in omnem posteritatem vult eam propagare: quæ proxima ad æternitatem via est, successione scilicet ut conservetur in nobis mortalibus hæc sapientia.
units.tr: Moreover, he proves that it is divine also on this ground: he wished it to be handed down to our children as well, so that its use in the Church might be perpetual. For the Gospel is not like the tide of the Euripus, so that you believe this now and that later, and, as people commonly say, adjust your faith or religion to the market and to the fickle turns of fortune. Rather, God wills that it be propagated into every future generation. This is the nearest path to eternity, namely that this wisdom be preserved among us mortals by succession.

units.la: Quomodo? Accessistis (inquit) & stetistis coram, &c. Quibus verbis legem divinam publice, miraculose, expresse prodita ait. Publice accessistis et stetistis sub monte. Nō ego solus affui, qui promulgantem Deum audiuerim: coram vobis omnibus publice proposita est. Quod cū ita sit, suspecta esse nō potest. Et certe Christus nec ipse clàm quicquā docuit, nec voluit apostolos clàm sua dogmata spargere. Qui enim susurros spargunt, ij sese produnt non syncerā causam fovere quippe, cui timeant: quæ divina est, adeò non potest occultari ut in publicum semper eruperit. Miraculose, quia miraculis partim naturam, partim effecta verbi diuini indicare voluit. Ignis illustrat, purificat, inflammat, absumit: ficDeus suo verbo cæcas mentes illuminat, impu-ras sanctificat, frigidas atq; tepidas inflammat, rebelles consumit. Vim & potentiam verbi to-nitruis atq; terræmotibus significat. Euangelium est potentia Dei (inquit Apostolus) ad sa-lutem omni credenti. Quis hæc audiens diuinum esse negetʼ At populus totus vidit.
units.tr: How? "You came near and stood," he says, "before, etc." By these words he says that the divine law was published publicly, miraculously and expressly. "You came near and stood publicly under the mountain." I was not the only one present who heard God proclaiming; it was set forth publicly before all of you. Since this is so, it cannot be suspected. And indeed Christ himself taught nothing in secret, nor did he want his apostles to spread his doctrines in secret. Those who spread whispers betray that they are not defending a sincere cause, since they fear something. What is divine cannot be hidden to such an extent that it has not always broken out into the open. "Miraculously," because by miracles he wished to indicate partly the nature of the divine word and partly its effects. Fire lights up, purifies, inflames and consumes. So God by his word illuminates blind minds, sanctifies the impure, inflames the cold and lukewarm, and consumes the rebellious. By thunderbolts and earthquakes he signifies the force and power of the word. "The Gospel is the power of God (says the Apostle) unto salvation to everyone who believes." Who, hearing these things, would deny that they are divine? But the whole people saw it.

units.la: Expresse, sic promulgauit legem suam Deus, vt quo pacto le coli velit expressis verbis significauerit. Non visus est, sed auditus tantum. Quod videri noluit argumento est, eum vo-luisse fingendarum imaginum occasionem omnem eis præripuisse. Ergo Deus imaginum vsu & sacrificijs nequaquam rite colitur. Nam cum sit inuisibilis qui posses eum vsibili mo-do colere, cum sit Deus, qui possis illum humano more venerari. Ita quisq; colitur vti natu-ræ eius est accommodatum atq; consentaneum. Nam eum caseo vel alio quocunque cibi ge-nere velle pascere, qui caseo non vescitur, quid aliud est quàm ἀχαιρῶ ἐννοια. Igitur & De-us cum sit spiritus spirituali cultu colatur necesse est. Agnouit hoc qui dixit,
units.tr: "Expressly": God so proclaimed his law that he signified in express words how he wishes to be worshipped. He was not seen, but only heard. That he did not wish to be seen is evidence that he wished to take away from them every occasion of fashioning images. Therefore God is by no means rightly worshipped by the use of images and sacrifices. For since he is invisible, how could he be worshipped in a visible way? Since he is God, how could he be honoured in a human manner? Thus each thing is worshipped as is suited and consonant with its nature. For to want to feed God with cheese, or with any other kind of food, when he does not eat cheese, is what else but an inept notion [ἀχαιρῶ ἐννοια]? Therefore, since God is spirit, he must be worshipped with spiritual worship. He who said this recognised it:

units.la: Si Deus est animus nobis vt carmina dicunt
units.tr: "If God is mind, as the poets sing,"

units.la: Hic tibi præcipue sit pura mente colendus.
units.tr: "let him above all be worshipped by you with a pure mind."

units.la: Agnouit hoc etiam atque docuit Dei filius vnigenitus Iesus Christus qui dixit Ioan.4.veros adoratores Deum adorare in spiritu & veritate. Atque vt hic cultus in ecclesia Dei semper retineri posset Deus verbum suum magistri partes habere voluit: ac ne quis statuis & simu-lachris hoc auderet vnquam arrogare, nullam sui imaginem spectandam populo, quo cum loquebatur præbuit. Ex quo cum perspicuum sit externum cultum verboDei respui, nihilq; nisi quod spirituale sit requiri, sanè sequitur doctrinam hanc diuinam esse.
units.tr: The only-begotten Son of God, Jesus Christ, also recognised and taught this, when he said in John 4 that the true worshippers worship the Father in spirit and in truth. And so that this worship might always be retained in the Church of God, God willed his word to have the role of teacher, and, lest anyone should ever dare to claim this for statues and likenesses, he offered to the people, to whom he spoke, no image of himself to be looked upon. Since it is therefore plain that external worship is rejected by the word of God, and that nothing but what is spiritual is required, it certainly follows that this doctrine is divine.

units.la: Quid? Res ipsa scilicet dicitur: Tum promulgabat vobis (inquit) fœdus, &c. In hoc ipso quod hic dicitur cardo rei vertitur. Finis hominis est coniungi cum Deo. Eadé ratio quæ patrono clientem, seruum hero, filium patri, nos Deo coniungit. Boni spe ducuntur homines, vt mu-tua cum hominibus iungant auxilia, nempe vt coniunctis copijs atque opibus plus promo-ueant res suas. Eadem spes homines etiam vt cum Deo coniungi concupiscant adigit. Sed quo modo quaq; re media mortales homines cum immortali Deo coire in societatem pos-sunt? fœdere, nam hoc ipso partes partibus obligari consueuere.
units.tr: What? The matter itself is plainly stated: "Then he declared to you the covenant, etc." The hinge of the matter turns on what is said here. The end of man is to be joined to God. The same reason which joins a client to a patron, a servant to a master, a son to a father, joins us to God. Men are led by hope to join their mutual aid with other men, namely so that, with their forces and resources united, they may promote their affairs more. The same hope drives men to desire to be joined also with God. But by what means, and by what medium, can mortal men unite in fellowship with the immortal God? By covenant; for it is by this very means that parties are customarily bound to parties.

units.la: Vnde nobis eius capita? à Deo certe accipiantur necesse est: nam is liberauit è durissima seruitute. Ergo in hac concione Moses ea partim digito Dei scripta, partim verbis suis ex-plicata commemorat. Quę Deus duabus lapideis tabulis exarauit, hic decem verba hoc est, de cem rerū summas ac sententias nominat. Quæ vero Moses explicauit, & post eum pluribus verbis etiam persecuti sunt prophetæ, & Christus, & apostoli, ea omnia verbi diuini nomine comprehenduntur. Ex quo rursus sequitur hanc Mosis doctrinam prorsus diuinam esse. Iam cum legis latoris persona, modus legum latarum, deniq; earum ipsarum nomen quod videlicet fœdus diuinum appellentur, spectatur, sequitur omnes qui in eo permanent so-lidum fundamentum habere, vt est Matth.7. Id vt retineamus Deus orandus est in Iesu Christo Domino nostro. Amen. fatis indicat sese purum,sanctum, ac prorsus diuinum doctrinæ genus esse: sic Deus ipsum in hac pura,simplici,sancta,diuinaq; substantia perpetuo conseruat hoc ipse,quod non solum præcipit,vt eius ipsius verbis omnino stemus, verum etiam ad hoc studium beneficijs allicit, atq; ab eius contemptu pœnis abstderret. Quod ipsum Moses hac demonstratione qua diuinitatem suarum legum astruit,egregie significat. Nam quod antea docuisset leges suas diuinas esse,quia Deus ipse eas publice,miraculose,expresse promulgauerit,fuiq; fœderis nomine dignas duxeritим quod dixisset etiam non vllam Dei formam visam,ac tantum eius vocem auditam esse,quæ quid facto opus sit significaret:idipsum in præsentia paulo altius repetit,atq; etiam explicat, docens eo facto Deum significare voluisse quam nolit doctrinæ suæ puritatem nostrarum opinionum & fictionum sordibus inquinari.Idq; vt efficiat duas quasdam humanarum fictionum capita profert:quorum prius est visus cultusq; imaginum: alterum cultus creaturarum.Quæ quoniam religionis puritatem contaminant ambo remouet.
units.tr: From where are we to get its terms? They must certainly be received from God, for he set us free from the hardest slavery. Therefore in this sermon Moses recalls them, partly those written by the finger of God, partly those explained in his own words. What God engraved on the two stone tablets, here he names, that is, the ten words, the summaries and sentences of the ten matters. But what Moses explained, and what the prophets, Christ and the apostles afterwards pursued in more words, all these are comprehended under the name of the divine word. From this again it follows that this doctrine of Moses is wholly divine. Now when the person of the lawgiver, the manner of the laws given, and finally the very name of these laws, namely that they are called a divine covenant, are considered, it follows that all who persist in it have a solid foundation, as in Matthew 7. "That we may retain this, God must be prayed to in Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen." It sufficiently shows itself to be a pure, holy and wholly divine kind of teaching. Thus God preserves it perpetually in this pure, simple, holy and divine substance, and he not only commands that we should stand fast in his very words, but also allures us to this zeal by benefits and deters us from contempt of it by punishments. Moses clearly signifies this very thing in the argument by which he establishes the divinity of his laws. For what he had taught before, that his laws are divine because God himself published them publicly, miraculously and expressly, and that they were deemed worthy of the name of covenant, and what he had said too, that no form of God was seen, but only his voice heard, which signified what needed to be done: this same point he now takes up again somewhat more deeply and also explains, teaching that by this act God meant to signify that he does not wish the purity of his doctrine to be defiled by the filth of our opinions and fictions. And to bring this about, he sets forth two heads of human fictions: the first is the sight and worship of images, the other the worship of creatures. Since these two contaminate the purity of religion, he removes both.

units.la: Ac de cultu seu visu imaginum dicit,Cauete ergo diligenter,&c. Quibus verbis imaginum visum omnem,qui quidem in sacris & in religione esse solet remouet.Id vt nobis maiori curæ sit,videndum est quomodo proponat,atq;explicet.Proponit autem magno studio. Nam quicquid ad mouendos animos plurimum momenti habet, id in medium profert. 1. Cauete siue custodite diligenter. Vox est magnum idq; etiam præsens periculum prænunciantis atque etiam vt ab eo sibi quisq; caueat admonentis.Ac veluti in maxima turba hominum qui molem magnam gestat aut curru trahit,ne quis offendatur,alta voce cauere iubet.Ergo periculum sit necesse est.Quid igitur in re tam plena periculi tantum operæ ponimus.
units.tr: And concerning the sight or worship of images he says: "Take heed therefore diligently, etc." By these words he removes every sight of images, which is usually found in sacred matters and in religion. That we may give greater attention to this, we must consider how he sets it forth and explains it. He sets it forth with great earnestness. For whatever has the greatest weight in moving minds, this he brings forward. 1. "Take heed," or guard diligently. It is the voice of one announcing a great and present danger, and also warning each to beware of it. And just as, in a huge crowd, one who carries a great burden or drags a cart bids them beware in a loud voice, lest anyone be hurt, so here. Therefore there must be danger. Why then do we spend so much effort on a matter so full of danger?

units.la: 2 Animas vestras custodite:quid custodiri debeat, id quod omnium carissimum est anima videlicet.Quod genus exhortationis rebus maximis solet adhiberi.Et certe de vitæ periculo hic agitur.Quis enim nescit ei vitam satis tuto committi non posse,qui suæ ipsius tuendæ non sufficiat? At qui idola colunt,ijs se suaq; bona commendant,rebus inanibus se committunt.Æneas Diuos penates suos,quorum erat ipsum cum patre,& omnino omni familia ex incendio eripere & in Italiam deportare,ipse ceu truncos(quod erant)efferre necesse habuit. Quid quod Tyrios ferunt suos Deos vinculis constringere,& alligare solitos esse,ne quo hostili carmine possent euocari?Miseri profecto Dij,qui nisi ligati mortaliumq; opera custodi ti fuerint ab infestationibus dæmonum tuti non sint. Ist fritich ein schlechter Gott/Ben Verrüffel mag hinfüren. Quamobrem si hisce imbecillibus Dijs tete credas potius,quaDeo vero omnipotenti, sane vitam tuam exponis magnis periculis. Nam ab eo,in quo tuta erat loco, in eum in quo tuta non est transfers. Quam bene curasti res tuas? Certe haud secus ac si quis Euchlio thesaurum domo sua elatum in publico aliquo condat loco. Ergo iubat nostras res Deo potius,quam idolis committamus.
units.tr: 2. "Guard your souls": what ought to be guarded is what is dearest of all, namely the soul. This kind of exhortation is usually used in the greatest matters, and indeed here it is a matter of peril to life. For who does not know that a life cannot be committed safely enough to one who is not sufficient to protect his own? But those who worship idols commend themselves and their goods to them, and entrust themselves to empty things. Aeneas, who had to carry his household gods, of whom both himself and his father and his whole family were, out of the fire and convey them to Italy, was obliged to bear them himself, as though they were mere trunks (which indeed they were). And what of the report that the Tyrians used to bind their gods with chains and fetter them, lest they be called away by some hostile incantation? Truly wretched gods, who, unless they are bound and guarded by the work of mortals, are not safe from the assaults of demons. "Ist fritich ein schlechter Gott; Ben Verrüffel mag hinfüren." Wherefore, if you trust these feeble gods rather than the true almighty God, you surely expose your life to great dangers. For you transfer it from the place where it was safe to one where it is not safe. How well have you looked after your affairs? Surely no differently from someone who buries in some public place the treasure that Euclio carried out of his house. Therefore let us commit our affairs to God rather than to idols.

units.la: 3 Quia nullum vidistis simulachrum,&c.Dicit Deum ideo videri noluisse,ne præberet occasionem fingendis imaginibus,& potius in simplici legum suarum studio retineret.Id argumento est verbum debere esse eum,qui nos religionem doceat,magistrum.
units.tr: 3 Because you saw no image, etc. He says that God chose not to be seen, so that he would not give occasion for making images, and would rather keep people in the simple study of his laws. This is evidence that the Word ought to be the teacher who instructs us in religion.

units.la: Quid igitur hodie clamitant,statuas & imagines esse libros laicorum,hoc est,vulgarium hominum? An Deus,Israelitas doctorus religionem aureum vitulum,aut aliam aliquam statuam propositum,è qua discerent? Non hoc eum fecisse id significat,quod erectum ab Aaron demoliri iusserat. Cur ergo monachi vel sacrificuli pro viua diuini verbi doctrina crucifixa,quæ vocant,adhibent? Sunt,inquiunt,libri laicorum.Quomodo quæso docebunt? Esto enim ob oculos tuos posita vel Saturni, vel Iouis, vel Apollinis statua:quis tibi fabularum quæ de eis describuntur extant,interpres,qui sint dixerit? esto ob oculos tuos posita Laurentij vel Verenæ statua, quis Turcæ alicui legendarum nostrarum ignaro,qui nam illi sint, dixerit? Etsi enim sit imago fœminæ impexis crinibus, & pectine quem manu gestet:positaq; ... men quis mihi illam Verenam fuisse indicauerit? An illæ ipsæ statuæ? at Paulus in 1.ad Corinthios epistola mutas esse edocet:aliquis,qui illis astet,edituus aut sacrificus? tunc illæ nō docent sed sacrificus.Quod si ita est,magistros esse non posse certo sequitur. Nam cum aures quidem habeant, non autem audiant, te rogantem aut consulentem aliquid non audient: cum ora habeant non autem loquantur, te errantem non poterunt castigare: cum oculos habeant,non autem videant, te siue pecces siue recte tuum munus obeas, non videbunt. Quales igitur magistri? Sanè cæci duces cæcorum,surdi,muti:quibus impedimentis efficitur,nihil vt habeant,quod ad docendum aptum sit atque idoneum. Ergo plus vtilitatis afferent & verius nos quid facto opus sit docebunt, Petri, Pauli,Ioannis,aliorumque epistolæ quàm cæcæ,surdæ,mutæ statuæ. Sed ne me putes hæc solum constituere, en tibi prophetarum testimonia. Hierém. 10: lignum, hoc est, ligneas statuas doctrinam vanitatis: Abacac 2. conflatile demonstrationem mendacij vocant. Ex quo colligis esse doctores vanos, qui multum quidem promittant, ac nequicquam præstent: esse mendaces, qui falsum doceant, atq; id quod non sunt, præ se ferant. Vnde & Lactantius minime malè dixit li. 2. Inst. ca. 19. Quicquid simulatur id falsum esse oportere. At simulachra nomen ex eo quod simulare soleant, habeant. Omitto quæ Sap. 14. multa alia de simulachris scripta sunt. Atque vt ab his nos decipulis ad doctorem optimum reducèret Dominus: ac significaret verbum suum, non simulachra, magistrorum loco haberi velle, non videri, sed audiri voluit.
units.tr: What, then, do they now cry out, that statues and images are the books of the laity, that is, of ordinary people? Did God teach the Israelites religion through the golden calf, or through some other statue set before them from which they might learn? He did not mean that, since he ordered the thing Aaron had set up to be pulled down. Why, then, do monks or sacristans use so-called crucifixes in place of the living doctrine of the divine Word? "They are," they say, "books of the laity." But how, I ask, will they teach? Suppose a statue of Saturn, or Jupiter, or Apollo is set before your eyes: who would explain to you the fables written about them, and tell you who they were? Suppose a statue of Laurentius or Verena is set before your eyes: who would tell some Turk, ignorant of our legends, who they were? Even if there is the image of a woman with unkempt hair and a comb in her hand, and the ... who would show me that she was Verena? Would the statues themselves? But Paul, in his first epistle to the Corinthians, teaches that they are dumb. Would someone standing beside them, a sexton or sacristan? Then it is not the statues that teach, but the sacristan. If so, it certainly follows that they cannot be teachers. For though they have ears, they do not hear; if you ask them or consult them about anything, they will not listen. Though they have mouths, they do not speak; if you err, they cannot correct you. Though they have eyes, they do not see; whether you sin or rightly discharge your duty, they will not see. What sort of teachers, then? Truly blind guides of the blind, deaf and dumb, with such defects that they have nothing fit and suitable for teaching. Therefore the epistles of Peter, Paul, John and the others will bring more benefit and will more truly teach us what needs to be done than blind, deaf and dumb statues. But lest you think I am setting up these points alone, here are the testimonies of the prophets. Jer. 10: a "wood," that is, wooden statues, teach the doctrine of vanity. Hab. 2: they call the molten image a demonstration of lies. From this you gather that they are vain teachers, who indeed promise much but deliver nothing in vain, and liars, who teach falsehood and present themselves as what they are not. Hence Lactantius also said quite rightly (Inst. 2.19) that whatever is feigned must be false. But images have their name from the fact that they usually simulate. I pass over the many other things written about images in Wisdom 14. And so that the Lord might lead us back from these snares to the best teacher, and show that his Word, not images, is to be held in the place of teachers, he wished to be heard, not seen.

units.la: 4 Ne corrumpatis, nēue perdatis. Nam verbum Hebræum תשחית[?] hoc significat. Ergo dicit vsu statuarum veram religionem vitiari. Quod vtinam agnosceremus. Sed agnouit hoc, vt Diuus Augustinus lib. 4. de Ciuit. Dei cap. 31. docet, Varro homo Ethnicus. Is dixit simulachrorum inuentores duo damna pietati dedisse. Vnum, vt hominum animis Dei timor omnis exemptus sit, quia cum viderint ligneas & lapideas statuas Dijs poni, circaq; eas multas ac varias imposturas sieri, coepisse eos omnem Deorum cultum ridere & despectui habere. Alterum, quod errorem circa theologiam auxerint, data videlicet occasione pictoribus atque poetis subinde nouas fabulas excogitandi. Atque hoc ipsum nō tam verè dixit Varro, quàm patrum nostrorum, nostraq; ipsorum memoria verum esse comperimus. Nam introductis in ecclesiam statuis, ceptum est subinde nouos Deos comminisci, noua miracula fingere, et fallacijs alijs atq; alijs vulgus hominum circumuenire. Quo factum est, vt qui paulò sagacio- re essent præditi ingenio, tucos odorarent, eaq; simplicioribus etiam proderent, & efficeret, vt non modo plebei homines, sed ipsi quoq; antistites sensim occiperent eam contemnere, & pro figmento sibi sustentandis excogitato ducere.
units.tr: 4 Lest you corrupt yourselves, or destroy. For the Hebrew word [תשחית] means this. So he says that true religion is corrupted by the use of statues. Would that we acknowledged this. But Varro, a heathen man, recognised it, as the divine Augustine teaches (De Civitate Dei 4.31). He said that the inventors of images brought two harms upon piety. One: all fear of God was taken from men's minds, because when they saw wooden and stone statues set up as gods, and many and varied impostures practised around them, they began to laugh at all worship of the gods and hold it in contempt. The other: they increased error about theology, by giving painters and poets occasion to devise new fables from time to time. And this Varro said not so much truly as we have found to be true in the memory of our fathers and in our own. For once statues were introduced into the Church, it began from time to time to invent new gods, to feign new miracles, and to deceive the common people with one fallacy after another. The result was that those of somewhat keener wit smelled out the frauds and revealed them even to simpler people, and brought it about that not only ordinary folk but the leaders themselves gradually began to despise them and to regard them as a fiction devised to sustain themselves.

units.la: Passim clamitatur, nullam reliquam esse pietatem[?] quæ causa est in promptu causa est: quando hominis est Deos quoscunq; velit quotidie ponere, certè etiam hominis videtur esse eosdem, si displiceant, respuere. Quicunq; saluam esse religionem volunt, ij sibi, quemadmodum Dominus hoc loco per Mosem docet, ab omni statuarum vsu caueant.
units.tr: Everywhere it is cried out that no piety remains. The cause is at hand: since it is up to man to set up whatever gods he likes every day, it certainly seems also to be up to man to reject the same gods if they displease him. Whoever wish religion to be kept safe should, as the Lord teaches here through Moses, beware of every use of statues.

units.la: Et ne quid erroris oboriatur, expressis verbis quid sibi velit edocet. Nullum, inquit, simulachrum, idolum, nullam formam maris, feminæ, animalis, auis, & omnino omnium siue cœlestium siue terrestrium, aquatilium subterranearum[?] rerum. Adeo diligenter remouet quicquid excipi poterat. Deus, quoniam immensus est & inuisibilis, & incorporeus, effingi non potest. Christus homo quidem factus est, sed nō vt effingeretur aliqua eius forma, verum vt miserias nostras exploraret ac morte sua mortem à nobis auerteret. Sed & si humanitas eius effingatur & colatur: tantum semi Christum colis, qui tamen totus coli postulat. Angeli quia cœlestium rerum numero continentur, Diui homines, quia terrestres sunt, effingi non debent. Atque Deus omnino postulat, vt quoniam in vsu statuarum præsens est & quidem vitæ periculum, quia Deus nullum sui simulachrum cerni, sed audiri vocem voluit, quia religio hoc ipso vitiatur, ab eo nobis quàm diligentisimè caueamus.
units.tr: And lest any error arise, he states in express words what he means: "No image," he says, "no idol, no likeness of male, female, beast, bird, and in short of all things, whether heavenly or earthly, aquatic or subterranean." So carefully does he remove whatever could be excepted. God, since he is immense, invisible and incorporeal, cannot be fashioned. Christ indeed was made man, but not so that some form of him should be fashioned; rather so that he might explore our miseries and by his death turn death away from us. But even if his humanity is fashioned and worshipped, you worship only half a Christ, who nevertheless demands to be worshipped whole. Angels, since they are counted among the heavenly things, and holy men, since they are earthly, ought not to be fashioned. And God altogether requires that, since in the use of statues there is both a present danger to life, because God wished no image of himself to be seen but his voice to be heard, and religion is thereby corrupted, we guard against it as diligently as possible.

units.la: De cultu creaturarum dicit, Et ne forte attollas oculos tuos in cœlos, & videas. Quibus verbis admonet ne creaturarum cœlestium maiestate, pulchritudine, vi, effectus ducti illas i- psas Deorum loco haberemus. Nec Deum fefellit hæc cogitatio. Nam quia sol, luna, reliquæque sydera, deniq; etiam cœlum ipsum magnum eumq; definitum cursum conficiunt, terrarum orbem & omnino omnia inferiora corpora non solum splendore suo atq; lumine exhilarant, verumetiam vi sua mirifice & varie solent afficere, Deorum loco haberi cœperunt. Vnde & in Cratylo suo Plato scribit, homines cum viderent Solem, lunam, astra, cœlum ipsum currendo semper circumuolui, Deos esse putasse, & vt idem dicit, ἀπὸ ταύτης τῆς φύσεως τῆς τὰ θεῖα θεὸς αὐτῆς ἐπιπροσάγῃ[?]. Quod etiam Proclus eius interpres docet. Et Lactantius hac de causa stellas à Stoicis cultas esse asserit. Idem sensisse Anaximandrum Milefium Pra- xiadæ filium D. August. testis est. Hinc illa Deorum varietas & copia.
units.tr: On the worship of creatures he says, "Lest perhaps you lift your eyes to heaven and see." By these words he warns that we should not, led by the majesty, beauty, power and effects of the heavenly creatures, hold those very things in the place of gods. Nor did God miss this thought. For because the sun, moon, the other stars, and finally the heaven itself with its great and fixed course, not only cheer the orb of the earth and all lower bodies with their splendour and light, but are also wont to affect them wonderfully and variously by their power, they began to be held in the place of gods. Hence Plato also writes in his Cratylus that men, seeing the sun, moon, stars and heaven itself ever revolving in their course, thought them to be gods, and as he says, [ἀπὸ ταύτης τῆς φύσεως τῆς τὰ θεῖα θεὸς αὐτῆς ἐπιπροσάγῃ]. Proclus, his interpreter, teaches this too. And Lactantius asserts that for this reason the Stoics worshipped the stars. Augustine is witness that Anaximander of Miletus, son of Praxiades, held the same view. Hence that variety and abundance of gods.

units.la: Iam præter hunc errorem est etiam alius, quod his omnium fortunarum nostrum dextrum pariter & sinistrum cursum acceptum ferimus: veluti si quis hoc aut illo natus sydere credatur hac aut illa fortuna vsurus esse. Sed quo quæso nati sunt sydere Iacob & Efau certè eadem hora ambos dedit licet dissimillimos. Et cum in ijs bellis, quæ Magnus Alexander cū Dario gessit tribus prælijs totidemq; annis quinquies decies centena millia hominum cæsa sint: an vsus & idem omnium fuit horoscopus? Et an fuit vnum idemq; Basternarum eorum qui fracta glacie Danubij fluminis aquis suffocati sunt, sydus? Fortasse prælium increuit ariete & tauro,& cápricorno cornibus suis impetum non sustinentibus:aut alluuionem fecit à‐quarius.Ridiculum hoc est,fateor,sed & hoc ridiculum est, quod vbi vescis noua fit sumen‐da,cœleste lignum potissimum consulitur.An non stultum atq; impium est immortales ani‐mas creaturis perituris obnoxias statuere.
units.tr: Moreover, besides this error there is another: we attribute to the stars all the fortunes of our life, both the favourable and the unfavourable, as when someone is believed to be born under this or that star and to be going to enjoy this or that fortune. But under what star, I ask, were Jacob and Esau born? Surely God gave both in the same hour, though most unlike. And in those wars which Alexander the Great waged against Darius, with three battles in as many years, five hundred thousand men were slain: was the horoscope the same for all of them? And was there one and the same star for those Bastarnae who were suffocated in the waters of the Danube when the ice broke? Perhaps the battle grew hot under Aries and Taurus, with Capricorn unable to withstand the onset with its horns, or Aquarius made a flood. This is ridiculous, I admit; but it is also ridiculous that when a new meal from the harvest is to be eaten, the heavenly wood is especially consulted. Is it not foolish and impious to subject immortal souls to perishable creatures?

units.la: Quin Mosem respice.Is dicit, Ne prosternare, ne adores, ne colas. Quibus verbis diuinus eis honos omnis adimitur. Nam prosternendi verbo significationes obseruantiæ velut ge‐nuum flexio,& quod nunc solemus caput aperire,& si quid est generis eiusdem aliud remo uet.Adorandi verbo spem & fiduciam opis eorū tollit.Colendi verbo timorem& ob seruan‐tiam significat,ne quid ab his mali timeas,neue boni cuiusquā spe honore eis vllum habeas.
units.tr: Look also at Moses. He says, Do not bow down to them, do not worship them, do not serve them. By these words all divine honour is taken away from them. For the word "bow down" signifies acts of reverence, such as bending the knee and, as we now commonly do, uncovering the head, and it removes anything of that kind. The word "worship" takes away their hope and trust in help. The word "serve" signifies fear and observance, so that you do not dread any evil from them and do not show them any honour in hope of some good.

units.la: Causam addit Moses, Quia Deus hæc omnibus populis distribuit, nempe vt vsui non ti‐mo‐ri essent.Vsum Gen.i.docet,in signa,dicens,& in temporā,hoc est,ad agriculturam,ad medi‐cinam,ad rempublicam. Magna nobis confert Deus per hæc beneficia,sed non illis verum Deo datori debentur gratiæ.
units.tr: Moses adds the reason: Because God has distributed these things to all peoples, namely so that they might be used, not feared. Genesis 1 shows their use, when it says "for signs, and for seasons" (Gen. 1), that is, for agriculture, for medicine, and for government. God bestows great benefits on us through these things, but the true thanks for them are owed not to them but to God, the giver.

units.la: Vsus est aliquando hominum operis ad subleuandam mortalium miseriam,sed ideo ho‐minibus illis diuinus honos non debuit perhiberi.Et hoc nomine grauiter reprehenduntur gentes quod Herculi,Æsculapio, alijsq; magnis heroibus, qui diuinitus hoc acceperant,vt præclara in rempublicam beneficia conferrent,ceu Dijs litarunt.Eodem iure Christiani re‐prehendi possent,qui præclaris viris atq; fœminis,quorum opera Deus nostram salutem iu‐uit,diuinos honores habuerunt: quasi vero hoc ipsi suo Marte ac non potius diuina graria præditi potuerint præstare.Detestatus est hoc diuus Apostolus cum sibi & Barnaba Lystrij ceu Dijs acclamarent.Et certe si illa sit Deorum fingedorum rÉta causa,res eò nostræ deue nient,vt quicquid vsibus nostris seruiat,id ipsum in numerum Deorum sit referendum.Vti‐lis est præceptor bonus,erit ille mihi Deus. Vtilis est qui multis magnisq; ex malis me eri‐puit:erit is igitur mihi Deus.Nec peccauit Tityrus ille Vergilianus qui Cæsarem, quod otij sibi causa fuisset,Dei loco habere voluit.Igitur Mammona qui me captiuum redimit,qui me ære alieno liberat,qui mihi victum & amictum comparat,qui me palsim ornat,auget,tuetur ceu Deum vtilissimum venerabor. Namq; erit ille mihi semper Deus,illius aram Sæpe tener nostris ab oviligus imbuet agnus.
units.tr: Sometimes the work of men has been used to relieve the misery of mortals, but for that reason no divine honour ought to have been paid to those men. The nations are severely rebuked on this account: they sacrificed to Hercules, Aesculapius and other great heroes, as though to gods, although these men had received from God the gift of conferring outstanding benefits on the commonwealth. By the same right Christians could be rebuked who paid divine honours to outstanding men and women through whose labours God helped our salvation, as though they could have accomplished this by their own might and not rather by divine grace. The divine Apostle detested this when the people of Lystra acclaimed him and Barnabas as gods. And certainly, if that were the true reason for making gods, our situation would come to this: whatever serves our uses would have to be counted among the gods. A good teacher is useful, so he would be a god to me. Someone who has rescued me from many great dangers is useful, so he would be a god to me. Nor did that Vergilian Tityrus err when he wished to regard Caesar as a god because Caesar had given him leisure. So I shall worship Mammon as my most useful god, since he redeems me from captivity, frees me from debt, provides me with food and clothing, and adorns, increases and protects me in every way. For he will always be a god to me, and "often the tender lamb will stain his altar with the blood of our flocks."

units.la: Nec peccauit Menander qui Aurum & Argentum , quibus in vita nihil vtilius esse creditur in numero Deorum haberi voluit, quemadmodum festiuo & qui hic scribatur digno car‐mine docuit: Ὁ μὲν ἡλιος ἐστι θεὸς εἶναι λέγει, ἀνέμους, ἥλιον, γῆν, ὕδωρ, πῦρ, ἀστέρας. ἐγὼ δ᾽ ὑπολαβὼν χρησμὸς εἶναι θεὸς. τὸ ἀργύριον ἡμῶν καὶ τὸ χρυσίον ἰσρυσάμεν τούτοις δὲ εἰς τὸ δίκαιον ἀξιαὶ τι βελτίω ταῦτα σοι γινώσεται. ἀγεῖς, οἰκίαι, θεοὶ πόντες, ἀργυρώματα, φίλοι, δικαστικοὶ, μάρτυρες, μόνον δὲ. αὐτὰς γὰρ ἔχεις τὰς θεὰς ὑπηρέτας.
units.tr: Menander did not err when he wished gold and silver, which are believed to be the most useful things in life, to be counted among the gods, just as he taught in a witty and worthy verse: "The sun, they say, is a god; winds, sun, earth, water, fire, stars. But I, taking the opposite view, say that money is a god: our silver and our gold. For these things, rightly considered, will show you something better. Lands, houses, gods of the sea, silver-work, friends, judges, witnesses, but only these; for you have these goddesses as your servants." [Ὁ μὲν ἡλιος ἐστι θεὸς εἶναι λέγει, ἀνέμους, ἥλιον, γῆν, ὕδωρ, πῦρ, ἀστέρας. ἐγὼ δ᾽ ὑπολαβὼν χρησμὸς εἶναι θεὸς. τὸ ἀργύριον ἡμῶν καὶ τὸ χρυσίον ἰσρυσάμεν τούτοις δὲ εἰς τὸ δίκαιον ἀξιαὶ τι βελτίω ταῦτα σοι γινώσεται. ἀγεῖς, οἰκίαι, θεοὶ πόντες, ἀργυρώματα, φίλοι, δικαστικοὶ, μάρτυρες, μόνον δὲ. αὐτὰς γὰρ ἔχεις τὰς θεὰς ὑπηρέτας.]

units.la: Sed nugas has Deus hic cauere iubet,& persuadet etiam addita causa probabili, quod com‐moda magna ferant hæc mortalibus, sed eam vim vtilitatis diuinitus acceperint, ac ni Deus vt prosint det,ea prodesse non posse.Quamobrem à creaturis neque boni neque mali quic‐quam Deo renuente proficiscitur : estq; Deus , vt nostris vsibus illa seruiant exorandus. Ergo si quid suscipias Deum potius quàm stellas respice,& an pia causa sit, quomodo pie su‐scipi atque geri possit,& vt Deum habeas auxiliarem elabora.Hic est rectus vsus astrolabij: sic recte vertitur, quæ in illo est, regula. Atq; ex his omnibus colligi potest Deum velle,vt quemadmodum verbū suum simplex est & purum, sic neq; simulachrorum vsu,neque crea‐turarum obseruatione & cultu polluatur : sed quoniam ipse visus non est, & auditus tan‐tum, nos omissis visibilibus rebus illius verbi ductum sequentes, eum in spiritu & veritate veneremur per Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum,Amen.
units.tr: But God here commands us to beware of these trifles, and he also persuades us, with a plausible reason added, that these things bring great advantages to mortals, yet they have received this power of usefulness from God, and unless God grants that they should benefit us, they cannot benefit us. Therefore nothing good or bad comes from creatures against God's will, and God is to be entreated that these things may serve our uses. So if you undertake anything, look to God rather than to the stars, consider whether the cause is pious, how it can be undertaken and carried out piously, and strive to have God as your helper. This is the right use of the astrolabe: thus the rule within it turns correctly. And from all this it can be gathered that God wishes his word to remain simple and pure, just as it is, and not to be polluted either by the use of images or by the observance and worship of creatures. Since he himself has not been seen, but only heard, let us set aside visible things and follow the guidance of his word, and worship him in spirit and truth through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

units.la: SERMO XVIII.
units.tr: SERMON XVIII.

units.la: 20 Vos autem assumpsit Dominus, atq; eduxit vos de fornace ferrea, de Ægypto scilicet, ut essetis ei in populum & hæreditatem, ut hæc dies (declarat.)
units.tr: 20 But the Lord took you and led you out of the iron furnace, namely out of Egypt, that you should be to him a people and an inheritance, as this day (declares).

units.la: 21 Commouitq; se Dominus adversum me vestri causa, ut juraret ne transirem Jordanem, neq; introirem in terram illam bonam, quam Dominus Deus tuus dat tibi in hæreditatem.
units.tr: 21 And the Lord was angry with me on your account, and swore that I should not cross the Jordan or enter that good land which the Lord your God gives you for an inheritance.

units.la: 22 Sed morerer in hac terra, & non transirem Jordanem, vos autem transibitis & possidebitis terram illam bonam.
units.tr: 22 But I shall die in this land and not cross the Jordan; you, however, will cross and possess that good land.

units.la: 23 Cavete ergo ne quando obliviscamini fœderis Domini Dei vestri quod pepigit vobiscum, ut faciatis vobis sculptile, aut simulachrum cuiusq; rei, quod prohibuit tibi Dominus Deus tuus.
units.tr: 23 Take heed therefore lest at any time you forget the covenant of the Lord your God which he made with you, and make for yourselves a graven image, or the likeness of anything, which the Lord your God has forbidden you.

units.la: 24 Nam Dominus Deus tuus ignis consumens est, & Deus indignè ferens.
units.tr: 24 For the Lord your God is a consuming fire, and a God who is jealous.

units.la: 25 Si genueris filios & nepotes, & commorantes in terra perverse egeritis, faciendo scilicet quamcunq; sculptam imaginem, feceritisq; malum in oculis Dei tui, ut ad iram provoces eum.
units.tr: 25 If you beget sons and grandsons, and dwelling in the land you act perversely, namely by making any carved image, and do evil in the eyes of your God so as to provoke him to anger,

units.la: 26 Obtestor contra vos hodie cælum & terram, quod subito peribitis de terra, ad quam vos traiecto Jordane transitis ut eam possideatis, nec prolongabitis dies, su[?] per eam, sed omnino exterminabimini.
units.tr: 26 I call heaven and earth to witness against you today, that you will quickly perish from the land to which you go over the Jordan to possess it, and you will not prolong your days upon it, but will be utterly destroyed.

units.la: 27 Dissiciet vos Dominus in populos, et reliqui eritis pauci numero in gentibus, ad quas vos Dominus ducturus est.
units.tr: 27 The Lord will scatter you among the peoples, and you will be left few in number among the nations to which the Lord is about to lead you.

units.la: 28 Serviētisq; ibi diis qui sunt opus manuum hominum, nempe ligno & lapidi, qui non vident, neq; audiunt, neq; comedunt, neq; odorantur.
units.tr: 28 And there you will serve gods that are the work of men's hands, namely wood and stone, which neither see nor hear, nor eat, nor smell.

units.la: 29 Inde tum quæres Dominum Deum tuum, atq; invenies, siquidem eum investigaveris toto corde tuo, atq; toto animo tuo.
units.tr: 29 Then from there you will seek the Lord your God, and you will find him, if indeed you search for him with all your heart and all your soul.

units.la: 30 Quum fueris in afflictione, & deprehenderint te omnia quæ hic dicuntur, tandem reverteris ad Dominum Deum tuum, & obedies voci eius.
units.tr: 30 When you are in affliction, and all these things that are spoken here have overtaken you, at last you will return to the Lord your God and obey his voice.

units.la: 31 Nam Deus misericors est Dominus Deus tuus, non faciet te languere, neq; disperdet te, neq; obliviscetur fœderis patrum tuorum, quod illis juravit.
units.tr: 31 For the Lord your God is a merciful God; he will not let you languish, nor destroy you, nor forget the covenant of your fathers, which he swore to them.

units.la: Quoniam nihil est in omni rerum natura, quo verbum Dei veraq; religio magis inquinetur, depravetur, deniq; etiam suffocatur, quàm visus imaginum, & cultus creaturarum: rectè Moses docet, Deum, qui quidem verbum ut est, sic velit purum conservare, hæc duo vitia non solum sevērissimè vitare, verumetiam eos qui sibi ab his caveant, præmiis, qui contra faciant supplicis afficere. Ac cum illa modo vetasset, argumenta ad persuadendum duo affert: quorum unum à beneficiis Dei, ab eius natura alterum ducit.
units.tr: Since there is nothing in all of nature by which the Word of God and true religion are more defiled, corrupted, and finally even suffocated, than by the sight of images and the worship of creatures, Moses rightly teaches that God, who wishes his Word to be preserved pure as it is, not only most severely forbids these two vices, but also rewards with favours those who keep themselves from them and punishes those who act contrary to this. And when he had just forbidden these things, he brings forward two arguments to persuade: one of which he derives from the benefits of God, the other from his nature.

units.la: A beneficiis Dei sic ducit, Vos autem, inquit, assumpsit Dominus atq; eduxit è fornace ferrea, &c. Quibus verbis eiusmodi argumentum texit, Deus vos suscepit atq; auxit beneficiis, ergo æquum est vos illius iussibus obsequi. Id nemo it inficias. Quis enim ei qui benefecerit neget gratiam? perditur quicquid in ingratum confertur. Et nihil est tam alienum à natura, quàm beneficia parum grato animo accipere, cum terra culta fruges reddat. Quò fit, ut homine homini ingratum esse fit ac videatur turpissimum. At quanto quæso turpius est ingratum esse Deo? Docet igitur eos, si discedant à divini verbi puritate, crimen ingratitudinis effugere non posse, quandoquidem Deus immensa in ipsos beneficia contulerit.
units.tr: He derives it from the benefits of God thus: But the Lord took you, he says, and led you out of the iron furnace, etc. By these words he weaves an argument of this kind: God has received you and enriched you with benefits; therefore it is right that you obey his commands. No one denies this. For who would deny gratitude to one who has done good? Whatever is bestowed on an ungrateful person is wasted. And nothing is so contrary to nature as to receive benefits with an ungrateful mind, since cultivated land yields its crops. Hence it is held to be most shameful for one man to be ungrateful to another. But how much more shameful, I ask, is it to be ungrateful to God? He therefore teaches that if they depart from the purity of the divine Word, they cannot escape the charge of ingratitude, since God has bestowed immense benefits upon them.

units.la: Ac ne videatur plura, quàm sint dicere, ea ipsa sigillatim singula commemorat, ut antecedens asserat.1. Assumpsit vos, nimirum miseros, afflictos, desertos ab omnibus Diis atq; hominibus. Hoc facere solet Deus, estq; eius proprium, tunc demum opem ferre, quando opis humanæ spes nulla est reliqua. Sic assumpsit Adamum perditum, Abrahamum in medio hominum idololatrarum: sic Diva virgo sui rationem esse habitam confitetur; sic Paulus è peccatis suis ereptus est, ut vß Gellend[?] vnd Gättel[?] vffgnon[?]
units.tr: And lest he seem to say more than there is, he recounts these very benefits one by one, so as to confirm what goes before. 1. He took you, namely wretched, afflicted, and forsaken by all gods and men. This is what God is accustomed to do, and it is his property to bring help precisely when there is no hope of human aid left. Thus he took up Adam when lost, and Abraham in the midst of idolatrous men; thus the blessed Virgin confesses that her lowliness was regarded; thus Paul was snatched from his sins, so that [obscura].

units.la: 2 Eduxit è fornace ferrea. His si quid fornax ferrea, quid item educendi verbum significent diligenter compares, magnum vides his præstitum beneficium. Ac fornace ferrea tyranni-dem intolerabilem significat. Nam ut fornace conclusus æstu seu calore suffocatur quidem, at fornace ferrea clausus etiam aduritur, & ferrum candens cutem, carnem, ossa, medullam adurit atq; absumit: sic grauibus oneribus premebantur Israelitæ, verum hoc omnium gra‑uissimum fuit, quod in recens editos partus Pharao tentauerat. Hinc ereptos in libertatem, qua nihil est iucundius, vtilius, preciosius, eduxit illos. Hac potiri quibus datum est, ij sunt li‑beri, & suis rebus vti frui possunt vt libet, tuto. Explicari dicendo non possunt libertatis commoda.
units.tr: 2 He led us out of the iron furnace. If you carefully compare what an iron furnace signifies, and likewise what the word "to lead out" means, you will see a great benefit conferred on them. An iron furnace signifies intolerable tyranny. For as a man shut up in a furnace is indeed suffocated by the heat or glow, but one shut in an iron furnace is also burned, and the glowing iron burns and consumes skin, flesh, bones, and marrow: so the Israelites were oppressed by heavy burdens, but the most grievous of all was what Pharaoh had attempted against the newly born children. Having taken them from there into liberty, than which nothing is more pleasant, more useful, or more precious, he led them out. Those to whom this has been granted are free, and can use and enjoy their possessions as they please, safely. The advantages of liberty cannot be explained in words.

units.la: Ergo cum seruitute libertatem comparat Moses, vt amplificet beneficij magnitudinem, eosq; excitet ad gratitudinem. Id publicè & priuatim fieri conducit. Publicè vt cogitemus fornacem ferream, in qua nos Austriaci duces tenuere: in quam nos Burgundionum dux Ca‑rolus includere conatus est, mit sinen fiuor ysen; itemq; bella, quæ maioribus nostris ab An‑glis, Boemis, Sueuis, alijsq; populis illata sunt: in primisq; tyrannidem papisticam, qua non solum corpora, verum etiam animi carceribus angustissimis Antichristus concluserat: seor‑sim singulí morbos, egestatem, exilia, naufragia, reliquaq; incommoda, è quibus nos in dies singulos eripit. Cogitemus quæ mala nunc multi populi perferant, quibus quamque graui‑bus bellis adterantur. Sic grati erimus Domino, eumq; statuis omnibus præferemus.
units.tr: Therefore Moses sets liberty against servitude, in order to magnify the greatness of the benefit and to stir them up to gratitude. It is profitable that this be done both publicly and privately. Publicly, so that we may think of the iron furnace in which the Austrian dukes held us, into which the Duke of Burgundy, Charles, tried to shut us up, "mit sinen fiuor ysen" (with its fiery iron); likewise the wars which were waged against our forefathers by the English, the Bohemians, the Swabians, and other peoples; and above all the papal tyranny, by which Antichrist had shut up not only bodies but also minds in most narrow prisons. Privately, each of us should think of illnesses, poverty, exiles, shipwrecks, and other misfortunes from which he rescues us day by day. Let us think what evils many peoples now endure, and by how grievous wars they are worn down. So we shall be grateful to the Lord, and we shall place him before all things.

units.la: 3 Vt effetis ei populus, et hæreditas. Iam beneficij magnitudo hoc ipso magis perspicua est, quod Deus pro suis istis laboribus, & pro tutela perpetua non annua tributa, nulla ve‑stiga‑lia, nullas operas requisiuit, sed tantummodo gratum & officij bene memorem animum, eumq; etiam in mutua beneuolentia constantem, ac quoniam vidissent neminem amicum fuisse eis, ipsi quoq; neminem quam illum ipsum charum habeant. Annon hoc æquum? Sanè: æquum enim est, vt quoniam ego te amo, tu me redames. Quare eius iugum quod lene est suscipiamus potius quàm satanicum illud, quod multis nos molestijs & laboribus & omni‑bus malis obruit ac deprimit.
units.tr: 3 That you should be to him a people and an inheritance. Now the greatness of the benefit is all the more evident from this: that for these labours of theirs, and for his perpetual protection, God has demanded no yearly tributes, no taxes, no services, but only a grateful and mindful spirit of duty, and that this spirit should also remain constant in mutual goodwill. And since they had seen that no one had been a friend to them, they likewise hold no one as dear as him. Is this not fair? Certainly: for it is fair that, since I love you, you should love me in return. Therefore let us take up his yoke, which is gentle, rather than that satanic one, which overwhelms and crushes us with many troubles and labours and every kind of evil.

units.la: 4 Dies declarat. Nemo factum negabit. Vsu compertum est Deum esse beneficum. Nam si indeab incunabilis repetamus quæ in nos beneficia contulerit, erunt immensa atque in‑numera.
units.tr: 4 The day declares it. No one will deny the fact. It is known by experience that God is beneficent. For if from our cradles we go back over the benefits he has bestowed upon us, they will be immense and innumerable.

units.la: 5 Mihi quoq; vel tra causa suerent suit, &c. Auget beneficentiam Domini pulchra compara‑tione, qua docet quanto maiora habeant ipsi bona à Domino, quàm ille. Ipsis datur terræ promissę possessio, sibi vero nihil, nisi illam contemplari. Quod genus comparationum est ad excitandam pietatem atq; gratitudinem efficacissimum. Sæpe enim videmur nobis esse o‑mnium miserrimi, malaq; maxima perpeti cum habeamus longè melius, quàm ij quos puta‑bamus non tam miseros. Inde existunt illæ querelæ: Me miserū: omnes aduersum me Deos conspirasse puto. At si nostras cum aliorum miserijs ærumnas comparemus, leues sunt præ‑ijs, quas alij perferunt. Ærumnas maximas Euangelij causa ferimus, fateor, sed nullæ sunt præ‑ijs, quas prisci patres pertulerunt. Quanta passos legimus Abrahamum, Isephum, Mosem ipsum, Dauidem, Iofiam, Machabæos, apostolos, martyres, Christum ipsum? Ergo pro tanta tamq; alta pace Deo grati simus curandum est: ac ne quæ mala frangant animos, comparabi‑mus nostras cum aliorum miserijs. Moses hic dicit Israelitas multò feliciores esse, quàm i‑pse qui terræ promissę fruitione prohibeatur. Atq; ex his omnibus iubet eos colligere, quàm beneficus sit in illos Deus.
units.tr: 5 For my sake the Lord was angry with you, etc. He enhances the Lord's beneficence by a fine comparison, by which he teaches how much greater the good things they have from the Lord are than his own. To them is given the possession of the promised land; to himself nothing except to look upon it. This kind of comparison is most effective for stirring up piety and gratitude. For often we seem to ourselves the most wretched of all, and suffer the greatest evils, when we are in fact far better off than those whom we thought not so wretched. Hence arise those complaints: "Woe is me; I think all the gods have conspired against me." But if we compare our hardships with the miseries of others, they are light beside those that others endure. I confess we bear the greatest hardships for the sake of the Gospel, but they are nothing beside those which the ancient fathers suffered. How many sufferings do we read of in Abraham, Joseph, Moses himself, David, Josiah, the Maccabees, the apostles, the martyrs, and Christ himself? Therefore we must take care to be grateful to God for so great and so high a peace; and so that evils may not break our spirits, we shall compare our troubles with the miseries of others. Moses here says that the Israelites are far happier than he himself, who is prohibited from enjoying the promised land. And from all these things he bids them gather how beneficent God is toward them.

units.la: Que Deo vi-cissim præstan- da sunt.
units.tr: What is to be rendered to God in return.

units.la: Igitur explicata atq; confirmata ad hunc modum argumenti parte priore, consequens nunc illustrat dicens, Cauete ergo ne foederis oblivi scamini, &c. Quo ostendit, quoniam Deus tam bene meritus sit de ijs, enitendum esse, vt hæc duo præstemus ei: primum ne obliuisca‑mur foederis: id est, vt quæ diuino fœdere continentur rata habeamus. Ea sunt vt auxilia non aliunde iperemus, quàm à Domino, vt Deo nos totos dedamus, vt proximum perinde ac nos ipsos adamemus. Deinde ne faciamus idola, quippe quod nostros animos abstrahant à Domino.
units.tr: Having explained and confirmed the first part of his argument in this way, Moses now draws the consequence, saying: Take heed therefore lest you forget the covenant, etc. By this he shows that, since God has deserved so well of us, we must strive to render him two things. The first is that we not forget the covenant, that is, that we hold firm what is contained in the divine covenant. These are: that we seek help from no one but the Lord, that we give ourselves wholly to God, and that we love our neighbour as ourselves. The second is that we not make idols, since these draw our minds away from the Lord.

units.la: Atq; hæc quidem ex Dei in nos beneficijs colligit Moses. Et ea de causa Deus ipse in De‑calogo obijcit audienti populo, quod ipse eos ex Ægypto eduxerit. Et pascha sanciuit Do‑minus, vt memoria redemptionis eius extaret sempiterna. Eadem de causa constitutum est in ecclesia, vt cœna Dominica celebraretur ceu monumentum eorum quæ morte Christi pa‑rata sunt beneficiorum. Quare ne discedamus à verbi diuini puritate, memoria seu recor‑datione Dei in nos beneficiorum efficiemus. Vnde & argumento eiusmodi Moses vtitur.
units.tr: Moses draws these points from God's benefits toward us. For this reason God himself, in the Decalogue, sets before the people as they listen that he brought them out of Egypt. The Lord also instituted the Passover, so that the memory of his redemption might remain for ever. For the same reason it was established in the Church that the Lord's Supper should be celebrated, as a memorial of the benefits won by the death of Christ. Therefore, so that we do not depart from the purity of the divine Word, we shall keep alive the memory and remembrance of God's benefits toward us. Moses also uses this kind of argument.

units.la: A natura Dei: Quia Dominus Deus tuus (inquit) ignis consumens est. Quibus verbis docet sic comparatam esse naturam Domini, vt in peccatores impœnitentes animaduertat seueris‑simè: ac rursus eorum qui pœnitentia ducuntur, misereatur. Quamobrem vt verbi Dei ve‑stigijs insistamus, imaginabimur nobis eiusmodi Deum, qui vindex sit sui verbi, ipsumque contemni neutiquam patiatur;quiq; etiam Dominus fit misericors, eofq; venia non dedig-netur qui redeant ad præscriptam è verbo suo viam.
units.tr: From the nature of God: For the Lord your God, he says, is a consuming fire. By these words he teaches that the nature of the Lord is such that he punishes most severely impenitent sinners, but on the other hand shows mercy to those who are led to repentance. Therefore, so that we may keep to the footsteps of God's Word, let us picture to ourselves a God who is the avenger of his own Word, and who in no way suffers it to be despised; who also becomes merciful, and does not refuse pardon to those who return to the way prescribed in his Word.

units.la: Ac vindicem quidem esse docet bifariam. Primum(inquit) Dominus Deus tuus ignis con-sumens est. Ac quid eo ipso sibi velit verba docent, nempe ut quemadmodum ignis stipulas & obvia quæq; consumit, sic Deus absumit quicquid cùm eius natura ac voluntate pugnaue-rit. Quemadmodu igitur densa ac solida materia nos aduersus ignem munire consueuimus: sic nediuinus ignis nos absumat, densa ac solida fide nos tuebimur. Quod fiet si in unum Deum potius, quàm vel in creaturas vel in statuas intenti simus. Sed ignis huius exempla multa habentur. Absumpsit enim hic ignis Caini hypocrisim, impuritatem Sodomæ, Aaronis vitu-lum, cultum Baaliticum, Pharisaicas cerimonias, & id genus alia.
units.tr: He teaches that God is an avenger in two ways. First, the Lord your God is a consuming fire. The words themselves show what he means by this: just as fire consumes stubble and whatever lies in its way, so God destroys whatever is opposed to his nature and will. Just as we are accustomed to protect ourselves against fire by means of dense and solid material, so let us, against the divine fire, guard ourselves with a dense and solid faith. This will happen if we fix our attention on the one God rather than on creatures or on statues. Many examples of this fire are to be found. For this fire consumed the hypocrisy of Cain, the impurity of Sodom, the calf of Aaron, the worship of Baal, the Pharisaic ceremonies, and other things of that kind.

units.la: Dein ait & Deus zelotes est. Quemadmodum enim maritus non fert, vt vxor amet alium, & est inter collegas æmulatio quædam mutua, ita vt quod Dominus dicit, nemo possit duo-bus dominis seruire: sic Deus indignissimè fert esse nobis quenquam aliud[?], quem illi vel parem vel superiorem habeamus. Ita enim vult nos sibi totos esse deditos, vt nihil alij tribua-mus. Et certè eam suam naturam adeo multis in locis profitetur, vt tempus non sufficiat si commemorare illos omnes oporteat.
units.tr: Then he says also: God is a jealous God [ζηλωτής]. For just as a husband does not bear that his wife should love another man, and there is a certain mutual rivalry among colleagues, so that, as the Lord says, no one can serve two masters, so God most unworthily bears that we should have anyone else whom we hold equal or superior to him. For he wishes us to be wholly given over to himself, so that we attribute nothing to others. And indeed he declares this nature of his in so many places that there would not be time enough to recount them all.

units.la: Hunc autem locum illustrat hypotiposi; quà quasi in conspectum producit facie huius vindicationis. Quod si, inquit, vos vestriue posteri terra hac potiti sic ab eius Verbi præscri-pto in illa deuia declinaueritis, profectò cœlum ac terram testor fore, vt Deus id grauissimo ge-nere supplicij vlciscetur: subito peribitis; idolis turpiter subijciemini, in totum terrarum or-bem miseri dispergemini; amissa scilicet ac funditus perdita republica. En vt graphicè descri-batur exitium, quod euenisse postea testes sunt historiæ. Eorum exemplo vtinam nos terreat & à malis quæ designamus nos cohibeat. Atqui hæc cum sit natura Dei impatiens scilicet falsi, æmus[?] operam, vt verbum Dei purum putum retineamus,
units.tr: He illustrates this point by a vivid description, by which he sets before our eyes the face of this vengeance. If, he says, you or your posterity, having possessed this land, shall turn aside from the precept of his Word into those byways, I call heaven and earth to witness that God will avenge this with the most grievous kind of punishment: you will perish suddenly; you will be shamefully subjected to idols; you will be wretchedly scattered over the whole orb of the earth; the commonwealth, of course, will be lost and utterly destroyed. See how graphically the ruin is described, which history bears witness did afterwards come upon them. Would that by their example it might terrify us and restrain us from the evils we are contemplating. And since this is the nature of God, who cannot bear falsehood, let us take pains to keep the Word of God pure and unmixed.

units.la: Misericordem autem esse Dominum in eos; qui in viam rectam à qua declinauerant re-deunt, sic dicens docet: Inde tum quæres Dominum, &c. Quemadmodum in eos qui deficiunt seuerus est: sic erga eos qui resipiscunt est misericors. Magni boni loco est imò immensi, quod Deus est misericors. Quis enim, si ille suum ius velit persequi consisteret[?] nemo certè, ait Psalthes. Et apud homines (inquit Christus) impossibile est quendam[?] fieri, apud Deum omnia sunt possibilia. Quare vt in nobis est causa desperationis, sic in illo spei basis est. Ergo hoc loco Moses quomodo adsequamur Dei misericordiam, quæ qualisq; fit, & quid præstet indicat.
units.tr: That the Lord is merciful toward those who return to the right way from which they had strayed, he teaches by saying: Then from there you shall seek the Lord, etc. As he is severe toward those who fall away, so he is merciful toward those who repent. It is a great good, indeed an immense one, that God is merciful. For who, if he wished to press his right, could stand? No one certainly, says the Psalmist. And as Christ says, with men it is impossible, but with God all things are possible. Therefore, as the ground of despair lies in us, so the basis of hope lies in him. Here, then, Moses indicates how we may obtain the mercy of God, what sort of mercy it is, and what it accomplishes.

units.la: Ac si quomodo eam assequamur roges, dicit, Quæres Dominum Deum tuum, si quidem eum inuestigaueris toto corde tuo &c. Quibus verbis omnia quæ ad reconciliandum Deum requi-runtur docet, Eafant[?] Deum quærere, afflictionibus agitari, obedire voci Domini. Iam quæ-rere significat idè quod vestigare, scrutari, cófulere, scire cupere, captare, & omnino si res sit quæ sciri possit, cognoscere: sin res sit quæ venire in potestatem nostram possit, obtinere velle. Ergo Deum quærit qui illum sibi cognitum, consultum, auxiliarem, coniunctum cupit.
units.tr: And if you ask how we may obtain it, he says: You shall seek the Lord your God, if indeed you search for him with your whole heart, etc. In these words he teaches all that is required for reconciling God: to seek God, to be stirred by afflictions, to obey the voice of the Lord. Now to seek means the same as to track down, to search, to consult, to desire to know, to strive after, and, in general, if the thing is one that can be known, to come to know it; but if it is a thing that can come into our power, to wish to obtain it. Therefore he seeks God who desires him to be known, consulted, helpful and joined to himself.

units.la: Id quanto studio velle debeamus hoc ipso Moses docet, quod addit, toto corde, toto animo. Iam vero cor quia spiritus vitalis fons est, quippe quod sanguinem crassiorem ex epate attra-ctum purgare & calefacere, & spiritus vitales gignere soleat, ideo virtutum omnium instru-mentum est ac dicitur: tum quia sunt in eo mirifici motus omnes, res lætæ & tristes ipsum statim feriunt, omnium etiam sedes est affectuum. Ergo omnes nostri conatus, omnes virtu-tes, quicquid denique est in nobis virium id omne sibi deberi dicit Dominus, quando cor totum sibi postulat. Anima vero, siue quid de ea sentiant philosophi, siue eam vt definiant Theologi, respicias: quid aliud est, quàm vita ac Spiritus intelligens & sapiens hominis? Igi-tur cum ea sit in nobis vegetans, sentiens, rationis particeps, omnem ætatem hominis sibi Deus vendicat: cum in ea sit intelligentia, memoria, voluntas seu iudicium: id omne sibi Deus reddi vult cum totam animam postulat. Ex quo perspicuum est tunc rectè quæri Dominum cum quicquid in nobis est ingenij, virium, vitæ denique, id omne Deo tribuimus, ni-hil alijs.
units.tr: How eagerly we ought to desire this Moses shows by what he adds: with the whole heart, with the whole soul. Now the heart is the source of the vital spirit, since it is wont to purify and warm the thicker blood drawn from the liver and to generate the vital spirits; therefore it is, and is called, the instrument of all virtues. Moreover, all the wonderful motions are in it, joyful and sad things strike it at once, and it is the seat of all the affections. Therefore the Lord, when he demands the whole heart, says that all our efforts, all our virtues, and in short whatever strength there is in us, all of this is owed to him. If you consider the soul, whatever the philosophers may think of it or the theologians may define it as, what else is it but the life and the intelligent and wise spirit of man? Since it is in us the principle that gives life, feels and shares in reason, God claims the whole age of man for himself; and since intelligence, memory and will or judgement are in it, God wishes all of this to be rendered to him when he demands the whole soul. From this it is clear that the Lord is rightly sought when we attribute to him whatever there is in us of wit, strength and, in short, life, and attribute nothing to others.

units.la: Ac tunc (inquit Moses) inuenies eum: quod perinde est ac si dicas, tunc erit ille tibi Deus, tunc ille tuis vsibus subseruiet. Afflictionibus agitari ideo prodest, vt quia secundis rebus abstrahimur: aduersis ad illum retrahamur. Dicit enim, Cum fueris in afflictione, & deprehenderint te quæ hic dicuntur omnia, tunc tandem reuerteris ad Dominum Deum tuum. Nostrum erat beneficijs duci potius, quàm verberibus trahi ad Dominum, sed quia adeò seruilibus ingenijs prædíti sunt homines pleriq; vt neq; verbis Domini fidisimis atq; amantisimis monitis,neq; eius beneficijs meliores reddamur,(sané ceu Phryges plagis Deus nos emendat. Exempla sunt in libris Iudicum Israelitarum illustria. Sed ipse sibi quisq; exemplo est. Vnde & afflictiones ad id conducunt, vt nos ad officium ad Deum retrahant. Boni patris officio fungitur Dominus quando sic castigat nos. Nam quod vulgò dici solet, vexatio dat intellectum. Quamobrem eam æquis animis consulemus, cum instrumentum sit, quo nos ad Deum retrahimur.
units.tr: And then, says Moses, you will find him, which is just as if you were to say: then he will be God to you, then he will serve your uses. Being stirred by afflictions is profitable because, when we are drawn away by prosperity, we are drawn back to him by adversity. For he says: When you are in affliction, and all these things that are spoken here have overtaken you, then at last you will turn back to the Lord your God. It would have been better for us to be led to the Lord by benefits rather than dragged by blows; but since most men are so slavish in disposition that we are not made better either by the Lord's most faithful and loving words of warning or by his benefits, God indeed, like the Phrygians, corrects us with blows. There are illustrious examples of this in the Book of Judges concerning the Israelites. But each man is an example to himself. Hence afflictions also serve to draw us back to our duty toward God. In chastising us in this way the Lord performs the office of a good father. For what is commonly said, that suffering gives understanding, is true. Therefore we shall take it with an even mind, since it is an instrument by which we are drawn back to God.

units.la: Tertium est, Obedire voci Domini. Quod nihil aliud est, quàm ab ijs rebus, quas illum offendere nouimus, abstinere, & ea quæ iusserit sedulo facere. Veluti solent frugi filij familiàs, & ferui quæ pater herúsue mandauerit capessere. Quæ verò verò iubeat quæque prohibeat ex eius verbo cognosci potest, propterea q; dicitur eorum studium, obedientia verbo Dei præbita. Atq; hoc est tertium, quo Deus nobis conciliatur. Quis enim non gaudet sua coasilia, sua monita, sua mandata curæ esse hominibus? Quare si quis Deum sibi benignum ac propitium velit, is illi se totum dedat, illius virgæ se submittat, illius iusibus obediat. Eius rei fuere exempla Iosephi, Dauid, Christus ipse.
units.tr: The third is "to obey the voice of the Lord." This is nothing other than abstaining from those things which we know offend him, and diligently doing what he commands, as thrifty sons of a household and servants usually carry out what the father or master has ordered. What he commands and what he forbids can be known from his word, and for that reason their zeal is called obedience to the word of God. This is the third thing by which God is won over to us. For who does not rejoice that his counsels, his warnings and his commands are a concern to men? So if anyone wishes God to be kind and gracious to him, let him give himself wholly to him, submit himself to his rod, and obey his commands. Examples of this were Joseph, David, and Christ himself.

units.la: Cæterum si quæ qualisq; sit Dei gratia siue misericordia roges, dicit Moses, Nam Deus misericors est Dominus Deus tuus. Vbi [illegible, ~6 letters] lxx. interpretes οἰκτίρμονα καὶ ἐλεήμονα vocat, hoc est eum quem ceu patrem nostrarum miseriarum misereat. At patrem etiam cum castigat filium, eius miseret, & si resipiscat afficitur mirifice, & quemadmodum Terentianus ille senex audiens seruulum prædicantem virtutes sui Ctesiphonis gaudio lachrumabat. Ita profecto Deus nihil perinde cupit ac peccatores resipiscere, quod & dictis testatur, & reipsa præstat. Quoties enim dicit se nolle mortem peccatoris, sed vt resipiscat ac viuat? Quàm miseri corditer exclamans atq; etiam lachrumans dicit Dominus: O Hierusalem Hierusalem, quæ lapidas prophetas &c. quoties volui te congregare &c? Quàm egregiè expressit affectum illum paternum in parabola de filio prodigo? Quàm bene ducit argumenta à patris & matris erga liberos animis cum in prophetis tum in Euangelijs descripta? Sic igitur erga nos affectus est Dominus, vt optimus parens erga suos charissimos liberos.
units.tr: But if you ask what kind and quality of grace or mercy God has, Moses says: "For the Lord your God is a merciful God." Where the Seventy translators call him οἰκτίρμων καὶ ἐλεήμων [merciful and compassionate], that is, one who has pity on us as a father does on our miseries. But a father, even when he chastises his son, pities him, and when the son comes to his senses he is wonderfully moved, just as that old man in Terence, hearing his slave praise the virtues of his son Ctesipho, wept for joy. Truly God desires nothing so much as that sinners come to their senses, as he testifies both by his words and by his deeds. How often does he say that he does not wish the death of the sinner, but that he repent and live? With what tender feeling does the Lord cry out, even with tears: "O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who stonest the prophets, etc.... how often would I have gathered you, etc."? How admirably did he express that fatherly affection in the parable of the prodigal son? How well does he draw his arguments from the feelings of fathers and mothers toward their children, as described both in the prophets and in the Gospels? So the Lord is disposed toward us as an excellent parent is toward his dearest children.

units.la: Quid autem hæc nobis præstet misericordia iam quoq; dicit.{1} Non faciet te remissum. Id quale sit ex Hebræa veritate & eius expositione Græca perspici poterit. [illegible, ~4 letters] verbum significat remissum, negligentem, ociosum, & laxatum, debilitatum. Veluti sunt manus & brachia membraq; reliqua, vel morbo vel labore, vel imbecillitate fracta. Vnde Græcus illam vim formam reddidit ad hunc modum: ἐκ ἐγκαταλείψει σε [?], hoc est, non deseret te, in crimine, in imbecillitate tua non derelinquet te. Quod quid aliud est quàm Deum nolle nos nobis relinquere, ne cum simus imbecillibus cruribus atq; brachijs præditi, propterea atque nostro Marte [?] neq; stare neq; nos tenere posimus, prorsus corruamus. Exemplo sit pater ducens te nerum filiolum, quem si sibi ipsum relinquat, præcipitat. Sic ille dicit Deum non velle nos nobis relinquere, sed tenere & sua manu ducere.
units.tr: Now he also says what this mercy will do for us: "He will not make you remiss." How this is so can be seen from the Hebrew truth and from its Greek exposition. The Hebrew word means slack, negligent, idle, loosened, weakened, as the hands and arms and other limbs are broken by sickness, labour or feebleness. Hence the Greek rendered that force in this way: οὐκ ἐγκαταλείψει σε [he will not forsake you], that is, he will not desert you in your sin, he will not leave you in your weakness. What else is this than God not willing to leave us to ourselves, lest, since we are endowed with feeble legs and arms, we should, by our own strength, be able neither to stand nor to hold ourselves up, and so utterly fall? Take as an example a father leading his tender little son, whom if he left to himself, the child would fall headlong. So he says that God does not wish to leave us to ourselves, but to hold us and lead us by his own hand.

units.la: 2 Non disperdet te, non vt dignus eras, te multabit. Ita mortem meritam auertit Dei misericordia.
units.tr: "2. He will not destroy you, nor, as you deserve, will he punish you." So the mercy of God turns away the death that we have merited.

units.la: 3 Non obliuiscetur fœderis patrum tuorum, quod illis iurauit. Fœdus hoc pollicetur Deum fore nobis nostrum. Id eius gratia fit, vt Deus ratum habeat. Nos enim ipsum subinde violamus. Sed is nobis misericorditer ignoscit, & fœdus seruat. Quæ Deus facit omnia, vt ad veri sui studium redeamus. Ex quibus omnibus colligitur doctrinam hanc diuinam esse, quia sit ab ipso Deo tradita, habeatq; nomen diuini fœderis: quia non solum diuina sit, verumetiam sic sit ac maneat perpetuo, quandoquidem ipsam Deus ab omni labe & interitu custodiat, eosq; etiam, qui illam violat puniat, ac pœnitentes in gratiam sanè quàm misericorditer recipiat. Quæ cum ita sit amplectemur eam perpetua quadam diligentia atque obseruantia in Christo Iesu Domino nostro, Amen.
units.tr: "3. He will not forget the covenant of your fathers, which he swore to them." This covenant promises that God will be ours and we his. This comes about by his grace, so that God holds it firm, for we ourselves repeatedly violate it, but he mercifully forgives us and keeps the covenant. He does all this so that we may return to a zeal for his truth. From all these things it is gathered that this doctrine is divine, because it was delivered by God himself and bears the name of a divine covenant; not only is it divine, but it also is and remains so perpetually, since God preserves it from every stain and destruction, punishes those who violate it, and mercifully receives back into favour those who repent. Since this is so, let us embrace it with a constant diligence and observance in Christ Jesus our Lord, Amen.

units.la: SERMO XIX.
units.tr: SERMON XIX.

units.la: 32 Etenim scisciteare, idq; à prisciis temporibus quæ ante fuerunt, ex eo die, quo creauit Dominus hominem super terram, & (percurrite) ab extremitate cæli, si vn-quam facta sit huiusmodi res magna, aut audita sit similis huic.
units.tr: 32 For ask now of the former ages which were before you, from the day that God created man upon the earth, and from one end of heaven to the other, whether there hath been any such great thing as this is, or hath been heard like it.

units.la: 33 Num audiuit vnquam populus vocem Dei loquentis de medio ignis (sicut tu audiuisti) & vivus mansit?
units.tr: 33 Did any people ever hear the voice of God speaking out of the midst of the fire, as you have heard it, and live?

units.la: 34 Aut tentauit ne Deus, vt ingrederetur & tolleret sibi gentem e medio gentis, per tentationes, signa, prodigia, bella, manum validam, brachium exertum, perq; terrores magnos, iuxta omnia quæ fecit vobis Dominus Deus vester in Ægypto, [illegible, ~5 letters] antibus id oculis tuis.
units.tr: 34 Or hath God tried to go and take himself a nation from the midst of another nation, by temptations, signs, wonders, wars, a mighty hand, a stretched-out arm, and great terrors, according to all that the Lord your God did for you in Egypt before your eyes?

units.la: 35 Tu per apparitiones edoctus es Dominum ipsum esse Deum, nec esse alium præter eum.
units.tr: 35 To you it was shown, so that you might know that the Lord is God, and that there is none other besides him.

units.la: 36 De cœlis fecit te audire vocem suam, vt erudiret te, & in terra ostendit tibi ignem suum magnum, & verba eius audiuisti e medio ignis.
units.tr: 36 Out of heaven he made you hear his voice, that he might instruct you, and upon earth he showed you his great fire, and you heard his words out of the midst of the fire.

units.la: 37 Et quoniam dilexit Patres tuos, elegit semen eorum post eos, & eduxit te in facie sua virtute sua magna ex Ægypto.
units.tr: 37 And because he loved your fathers, he chose their seed after them, and brought you out of Egypt in his own presence by his great power.
