units.la: 38 Vt gentes magnas, & te robustiores ante te eijceret, atq; te introduceret, & daret tibi terram illarum in hæreditatem, id quod hæc (probat) dies.
units.tr: 38 To drive out before you nations greater and mightier than you, and to bring you in and give you their land for an inheritance, as this day bears witness.

units.la: 39 Agnoscas igitur hodie & in cor tuum reuoca, quod Dominus ipse est Deus in cœlis superne, & in terra inferne, nec est alius.
units.tr: 39 Know therefore this day, and consider in your heart, that the Lord himself is God in heaven above and on earth beneath, and there is no other.

units.la: 40 Et custodi statuta eius & præcepta eius, quæ ego mando tibi hodie, vt bene sit tibi, & filijs tuis post te, vt proroges dies super terram, quam Dominus Deus tuus dat tibi cunctis diebus.
units.tr: 40 Keep therefore his statutes and his commandments, which I command you this day, that it may go well with you and with your children after you, and that you may prolong your days upon the earth, which the Lord your God gives you for all time.

units.la: Antiquitas adeo magno in precio apud omnes homines semper fuit, vt nō solum quæ cunq; prisca sunt, veluti homines, tabulas, cōsuetudine, [?]snumos, ædes, hoc ipso quod antiquitatem referat adm[?] ratione & laude dignemur, atq; etiam chara habeamus, verumetiā existimemus ea, quoniam Deus omnium rerum est principium, quo vetustiora sint hoc esse Deo viciniora. Qua de causa in libris de legibus præclare dixit Cicero, in exemplis authoritatem habere antiquitate, & eam ipsam etiā ad Deos proxime accedere. Igitur ostendit Moses hanc ipsam, quam proponit Moses, doctrinam veram, antiquissimam ac certissimam religionem esse, quæ iam inde ab origine rerum vsq; ad nostra tempora salua atq; integra permanserit. Quo ceu optimo argumento vult eam rursus populo suo commendare. Et est hoc quidem nostris temporibus vtilissimum cognitu pariter ac cogitatu, quippe quibus Euangelij contemptum inde proficisci putemus, quod nouum quoddam ac nostra demũ memoria natum doctrinæ genus existimetur. Quod quo pacto sit refutandum hoc loco Moses docet. Nam antiquam esse doctrinam suam 1. proponit, 2. confirmat, 3. concludit.
units.tr: Antiquity has always been held in such high esteem among all men that we not only value and hold dear whatever is old, such as men, tablets, customs, coins and buildings, for the very reason that they recall antiquity, but we also think them the closer to God the older they are, since God is the beginning of all things. For this reason Cicero rightly said in his books On the Laws that in precedents antiquity carries authority, and that antiquity itself comes nearest to the gods. So Moses shows that the very doctrine he sets forth is the true, most ancient and most certain religion, one that has remained safe and whole from the beginning of things down to our own times. He wishes to recommend it again to his people as the best of arguments. This is especially useful for us today to know and to consider, since we think the contempt for the Gospel arises from this: that it is regarded as a new kind of teaching, born in our own memory. Moses teaches how this must be refuted. For he sets out to show that his doctrine is ancient in three steps: (1) he sets it forth, (2) he confirms it, (3) he concludes.

units.la: Proponit, Scisciscitare (inquit) à prisc is temporibus &c. Quibus verbis ostendit si quis ætatum omnium decursum perquirat, ac si quid sit antiquius scire velit, nil prorsus inueniri posse. Remittit enim ad rerum originem, ad superiora tempora, deniq; ad eum ipsum diem, quo primus homo conditus est. Ac si repetas vetera, verum esse quod Moses dicit intelliges. Adami namq; fides & religio quæ fuit? Sanè ex ea quam audiuit & recepit doctrina percipi potuit. Illud ei Deus ipse prædicauit, Ponere se inimicitias inter semen mulieris & serpentem, & serpentis caput calcatum iri per semen mulieris &c. Hoc est quemadmodum satan astutè per mulierem introduxit mortem in mundum, ac sibi regnum quàm amplissimum comparauit: sic prudenter Deus per mulierem natum virum vitam miseris ac deperditis mortalibus restaurabit, ac serpentis caput, hoc est, regnum & potentiam omnem franget. Quam doctrinam vt ab initio diuinitus promulgata est, sic Apostolus exposuit Rom. 8. Peccatum per peccatum sustulit. 1. Peccatum per hostiam pro peccatis fieri solitam sustulit. Et 1. Cor. 1. Christus nobis diuinitus factus sapientia, iustitia, sanctificatio, redemptio, vt qui glorietur in Domino glorietur. Atque hæc est illa doctrina prima. Hanc Adamus assensu suo comprobauit ac recepit docendoq; etiam demisit ad posteros. Nam quod vxorem suam Heuæ nomine appellauit, id argumento poterit esse eum credidisse natos Heua non mortuos, sed per Christum viuos fore. Nec sacrificia, quæ typum veri illius sacrificij in ara crucis pro peccatis nostris oblati referunt, aliam spem significant. Vnde enim Abelo & Caino fratribus sacrificiorum ritus innotuissent, quàm ab Adamo patre? Ergo Adamus & didicit & credidit hoc ipsum quod Moses postea docuit.
units.tr: He sets it forth: Ask (he says) of the former times, etc. By these words he shows that if anyone searches through the whole course of the ages, and wishes to know whether anything is older, he will find nothing at all. For he refers us back to the origin of things, to the earliest times, and finally to that very day on which the first man was made. And if you go back to the old things, you will understand that what Moses says is true. What was the faith and religion of Adam? Surely it could be grasped from the doctrine he heard and received. God himself declared to him that he would put enmity between the seed of the woman and the serpent, and that the serpent's head would be crushed by the seed of the woman, etc. Just as Satan cunningly brought death into the world through the woman and procured for himself the widest possible kingdom, so God wisely, through a man born of a woman, would restore life to wretched and lost mortals, and would break the serpent's head, that is, all its kingdom and power. This doctrine, as it was published from the beginning by divine command, the Apostle expounded in Rom. 8: "He removed sin through sin." 1: "He removed sin through the victim customarily offered for sins." And in 1 Cor. 1: "Christ was made for us by God wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption, so that he who glories, may glory in the Lord." And this is that first doctrine. Adam confirmed it by his assent, received it, and by teaching it passed it down to his posterity. For that he called his wife by the name Eve may be an argument that he believed her children would be born not dead but alive through Christ. Nor do the sacrifices, which represent the type of that true sacrifice offered on the altar of the cross for our sins, signify any other hope. For whence would the rite of sacrifices have become known to the brothers Abel and Cain, if not from their father Adam? Therefore Adam both learned and believed the very thing Moses later taught.

units.la: Iam si inde ad Abelum transeas, testis est Hebr. 11. Diuus Apostolus eum per fidem sacrificasse Deo gratum sacrificium. In quo hoc ipsum, quo de nunc est maximè controuersia, si des ne an opera iustificent perspicuum fit. Nam si Caini idem quod Abeli opus fuit, & tamen alterius approbatum, alterius autem reiectum est: consequens est, Deum non opus ipsum vel externum eius speciem, verum animum atq; voluntatem facientis respexisse, & fide effectum ut Abeli sacrificium reciperetur.
units.tr: Now if you pass from there to Abel, Heb. 11 is the witness: the divine Apostle says he offered a sacrifice acceptable to God through faith. In this passage it becomes clear whether works justify or not, which is the very point now most in controversy. For if Cain's work was the same as Abel's, and yet the one was approved and the other rejected, it follows that God looked not at the outward deed or its external appearance, but at the heart and will of the doer, and that it was by faith that Abel's sacrifice was accepted.

units.la: Inde ex Setho natus Enos: quo tempore coepit inuocari nomen Domini, hoc est, tunc coepit religio Abeli morte passa naufragium restaurari & in integrum restitui.
units.tr: From Seth was born Enos, in whose time men began to call upon the name of the Lord; that is, then the religion of Abel, which had suffered shipwreck by his death, began to be restored and made whole again.

units.la: Post ea tempora Enochus adeo veritati studuit, ut immortalitatis animorum & resurrectionis corporum typus fuerit: nam & eius fidem commendat Apostolus.
units.tr: After that time Enoch so devoted himself to the truth that he became a type of the immortality of souls and the resurrection of bodies; for the Apostle also commends his faith.

units.la: Noha dein is fuit quo cum fœdus suum Deus renouauit.
units.tr: Then came Noah, with whom God renewed his covenant.

units.la: Eum autem omnium gentium origo dispersioque sequuta est. Nam à Chamo descendunt Ægyptij, Æthiopes, Numidæ, Mauri, Babylonij: à Semo Indi, Medi, Persæ, Ismaelitæ, Israelitæ: ab Japeto Schytæ, Turcæ, Sarmatæ, Græci, Itali, Romani, Germani & qui cunq; Europam simul atq; adiacentes insulas occupant.
units.tr: After him followed the origin and dispersion of all nations. For from Ham descend the Egyptians, Ethiopians, Numidians, Moors and Babylonians; from Shem the Indians, Medes, Persians, Ishmaelites and Israelites; from Japheth the Scythians, Turks, Sarmatians, Greeks, Italians, Romans, Germans, and all who occupy Europe and the islands adjacent to it.

units.la: Ex hac dispersione & varietate populorum nascentium omnis idololatria nata est, ut delicet[?] plus minus M D C C C. annis vera fide recentior, quando ut apparet Adamus Deum unum simpliciter agnouit atque coluit, hæcque superstitionum multitudo & varietas simul cum multitudine & varietate gentium enata est. Ac quanquam non in solius Chami posteris, sed etiam in reliquis serpens suos cultores habuit, tamen vera pietas omnium est antiquissima, quippe quam Adamus & agnouerit & seruauerit, & ab eo Deus hanc ad omnem posteritatem subinde propagauerit.
units.tr: From this dispersion and the variety of the nations as they arose, all idolatry was born, some roughly 1800 years later than the true faith, since, as is evident, Adam knew and worshipped the one God purely, and this multitude and variety of superstitions came forth together with the multitude and variety of nations. And although the serpent had his worshippers not only among the descendants of Ham but also among the rest, true piety is nonetheless the most ancient of all, since Adam both knew and kept it, and from him God then continued to propagate it to every posterity.

units.la: Etenim à Semo natus est Abrahamus. Eius fidei fundamentū est semen benedictū Gen. 22.Gal.3[?].Joan.8 Christo pariter & Apostolo testibus. Inde lex per Mosem lata est, quæ ceu pædagogus ad Christum duceret.
units.tr: For Abraham was born from Shem. The foundation of his faith is the blessed seed of Gen. 22, Gal. 3, John 8, as Christ and the Apostle both bear witness. From there the law was given through Moses, which was to lead us as a schoolmaster to Christ.

units.la: Sequuti sunt Josua, Dauid, Solomon, Josias, alijque magni heroes typi & testes Domini. Quid enim clarius dici de Christo potuit, quàm quod Psalmus C IX. totus de Christo canit.
units.tr: Joshua, David, Solomon, Josiah followed, and other great heroes, types and witnesses of the Lord. For what could be said more clearly of Christ than that Psalm 109 sings of Christ throughout?

units.la: Ab his ad Prophetas accedito, quorum alius ortum & occasum filij hominis resque gestas & miracula commemorat, alius locum, alius tempus, alius resurrectionem & triumphū Christi fataq; ecclesiæ referunt.
units.tr: Come next to the Prophets, one of whom recounts the rising and setting of the Son of Man, his deeds and miracles, another his place, another his time, another the resurrection and triumph of Christ and the fortunes of the Church.

units.la: Sed Mesiam ipsum digito monstrauit Joan. Baptista dicens, Hic est agnus ille Dei, qui tollit peccatum mundi.
units.tr: But John the Baptist pointed to the Messiah himself with his finger, saying, "Here is that Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world."

units.la: Sub ea tempora Christus & Apostoli docuerunt sequutiq; sunt ecclesiarum aliarum episcopi. Ex quibus omnibus perspicuum est, Christianum quidem nomen, veluti Lucas per hibet[?] Antiochiæ demum natum esse, sed fidei capita ab orbe condito semper eadem diuinitus prædicata esse.
units.tr: In those times Christ and the Apostles taught, and the bishops of the other churches succeeded them. From all of this it is clear that the name "Christian" was, as Luke relates, only finally born at Antioch, but the articles of faith were always the same and had been divinely proclaimed since the creation of the world.

units.la: Sed quod multi in ecclesiam Christianam errores inuecti sunt, quos nunc Antichristus mordicus retinet, ac vult loco religionis auitæ retineri: contra sancti Euangelij puram pu-tam doctrinam abse varijs superstitionibus inquinatam antea, nunc verò ad exemplum viuum repurgatam ceu nouam quandam, bonis moribus nocuam, hæresim reijcit, id iam inde à Christi ascensione statim cœpit fieri. Nam tunc occepit satan & falsam doctrinam serere & ecclesiam crudeliter persequi, cumq; neq; mendacijs & erroribus eam inficere, neq; persecutione delere posset, tandē conuersis studijs, pacē diuinitus ecclesiæ datā abusu quietis infecuri[?]tatem, negligentiā, & delitias detorsit, ut præcipitaret huiusce tam præclaræ structuræ columina ac tandē etiam fundamenta, si posset, eriperet. Sensim enim à simplicitate fidei ad alias atq; alias traditiones & cerimonias secessionem fecerunt.
units.tr: But that many errors have been introduced into the Christian Church, which Antichrist now clings to with his teeth and wants retained in place of the ancestral religion, and which reject the pure and unadulterated doctrine of the holy Gospel, once polluted by various superstitions and now restored to its living pattern, as some new heresy harmful to good morals, this began straight after Christ's ascension. For then Satan began to sow false doctrine and to persecute the Church cruelly. And since he could neither infect it with lies and errors nor destroy it by persecution, he at last turned his efforts elsewhere: he twisted the peace divinely given to the Church into an abuse of quiet, into carelessness and luxury, so that he might overthrow the pillars of this so splendid structure and, if he could, tear away its very foundations. For gradually they drifted from the simplicity of faith toward other and other traditions and ceremonies.

units.la: Ac quanquam æmulatio, ambitio, auaritia, securitas[?] aliaq;, eiusdē generis vitia ante Constantini tempora atq; etiam in plerisq; Orientis ecclesijs cœpissent grassari: tamen Romæ ex ortum est malorum caput. Nam quia Rom. ecclesia cæteris omnibus præstaret, & episcopos Germaniæ, Galliæ, Angliæ, Italiæ prouincijs mittere consueuisset, & Petrum crederetur, Paulum autem constaret precones seu ministros habuisse, haberetq; semper pios, gnauos cōstantes episcopos & populum religionis supra modum deditum, deniq; pontificibus Romanis multi præclari & præpotentes reges atq; principes magnos ac propè diuinos honores habere, ac vellent ab ipsis tanquam Christi ministris inaugurari: certè quæ est ingenij humani imbecillitas, hinc ambitioni data videtur occasio.
units.tr: Although ambition, rivalry, greed, complacency and other vices of the same kind had begun to rage even before the time of Constantine, and in most of the churches of the East, yet Rome became the head of these evils. For since the Roman Church excelled all the others, and used to send bishops to the provinces of Germany, Gaul, England and Italy, and since it was believed that Peter, and it was certain that Paul, had had heralds or ministers, and since it always had godly, diligent and steadfast bishops and a people exceedingly devoted to religion, and finally since many distinguished and very powerful kings and princes gave great and almost divine honours to the Roman pontiffs and wished to be installed by them as by Christ's ministers, surely this is the weakness of the human mind: here ambition seems to have been given its opportunity.

units.la: Laudatur quidē Gregorius qui Ioan. Costantinopolitano oecumenici epis. & patriarchæ titulum ambitiose adepto,itemque Mauritio Cæsari illum ipsum ambitum defendere cona-to restitit,ac|scripsit Antichristi præcursorem esse qui velit appellari vniuersalis episcopus: sed eum posteri nequaquam imitati sunt,ac potius authoritate ecclesiæ suæ abusi primatum affectarunt.
units.tr: Gregory is indeed praised, who resisted John of Constantinople when he ambitiously obtained the title of ecumenical bishop and patriarch, and likewise resisted Emperor Maurice when he tried to defend that same ambition. Gregory wrote that whoever wished to be called universal bishop was a forerunner of Antichrist. But later generations by no means imitated him; rather, abusing the authority of their Church, they aspired to primacy.

units.la: Nam cum hoc Gregorius anno à nato Christo DC.constanter renuisset. Bonifacius papa affectauit ipsum atq; etiam Phocæ Cæsaris auxilijs vt Roma esset ecclesiarum omnium caput impetrauit atq; obtinuit anno Do.DCVIII. Hoc tempore caput ecclesiæ datum est,quo tot seculis antea caruerat.Atq; hic est primus gradus ad culmen Antichristianæ monarchiæ.
units.tr: For although Gregory had steadfastly refused this in the year 600 after the birth of Christ, Pope Boniface laid claim to it, and with the help of the Emperor Phocas he obtained and secured that Rome should be the head of all the churches, in the year of the Lord 608. At this time a head was given to the Church, which it had lacked for so many centuries before. And this is the first step to the summit of the Antichristian monarchy.

units.la: Alter est quod Constantinus Constantis filius,is qui imperio præfuit anno Domini DCLXX.multa bona animi in Benedicto cernens(vt ait Sabellicus)statuit vt quem ante cle-rus populusq; Romanus cum exercitu creassent episcopum, is verè vicem Christi in terris gerere crederetur,nulla imperatoris aut exarchi approbatione expectata.Quo factum est,vt quemadmodum antea consecutus erat pontifex imperium in episcopos & ecclesias,sic nūc imperium atq; iugum Rom.imperatorum excusserit.
units.tr: The second is that Constantine, son of Constans, who ruled the empire in the year of the Lord 670, seeing many good qualities of mind in Benedict (as Sabellicus says), decreed that the one whom the clergy and Roman people, together with the army, had first created bishop should be believed to bear truly the place of Christ on earth, without waiting for any approval from the emperor or the exarch. As a result, just as the pontiff had earlier gained power over bishops and churches, so now he shook off the power and yoke of the Roman emperors.

units.la: His duobus gradibus tertius tunc est impositus,cum papa primum Philippico propter Monothelitarum hæresim,dein Leone III.propter deletas imagines & deiectas,quæ in templis essent pictæ & positæ statuas excommunicatis,post superato Luitprando Longobardorum rege,oppressa regnoque eiecta Merouignorum familia,atq; ad regnum euecto Pipino Pusillo Exarchatum Rauennæ,quicquid Padum & Apenninum interiacet,& quæ inter Ifaurum flumen Apenninum & Hadriaticum media sunt,quæq; Aistulphus de Hetrufcis & Sabinis coeperat,omnia Pipini beneficio consecutus,ficq; imperio Italiæ potitus esset.Quod anno Domini DCCLVI.ecclesiæ Romanæ datum deinceps vltimo Longobardorum rege De fiderio oppressio per Carolum Magnum confirmatum atque auctum est priuilegijs.
units.tr: To these two steps a third was then added, when the pope first excommunicated Philippicus on account of the Monothelite heresy, and then Leo III because the images painted and set up in the churches had been destroyed and thrown down, and afterwards, when King Liutprand of the Lombards had been overcome, and the family of the Merovingians had been crushed and expelled from the kingdom, and Pepin the Short had been raised to the kingship: by Pepin's favour the papacy obtained the Exarchate of Ravenna, everything lying between the Po and the Apennines, and what lay between the river Isaurus, the Apennines and the Adriatic, and what Aistulf had begun to seize from the Etruscans and the Sabines; and so it gained rule over Italy. This was in the year of the Lord 756. Afterwards, the grant was confirmed and enlarged with privileges to the Roman Church by Charlemagne, after the last Lombard king, Desiderius, had been overthrown.

units.la: Quartus est his tribus impositus.quando Leo III. papa imperium à Græcis ad Francos transfert & circa annum Do. DCCCIII. Carolum magnum Imperatorē decernit & coronat, dein ab eius filio Ludouico Pio beneficia plura accipit, ac tandem etiam vrbis Romanæ ditione,omnibusq; circa terris,ciuitatibus,portubus & maritimis locis Hetruriæ potitus est. Exemplum donationis Ludouici Pij Volaterranus lib.3.Geographiæ descripsit.Inde factum est vt Berengario Ottonis Germanorum regis viribus oppressio Ioannes XIII.papa ad Germanos transferret imperium,idq; eis Gregorius V.Saxo, qui Othonis III.Imp,consanguineus erat,confirmaret ita vt solis Germanis liceret,Principem qui Cæsar siue Romanus rex esset eligere,& imperator & Augustus appellaretur si ipsum Romanus pontifex confirmasset. Cæterum electionis ius penes tres episcopos & totidem principes esse voluit quibus rex Bohemiæ septimus adderetur.Quod factum est anno Do.M II. His gradibus itum est ad æthera papisticum,
units.tr: A fourth step was added to these three, when Pope Leo III transferred the empire from the Greeks to the Franks, and around the year of the Lord 803 decreed and crowned Charlemagne as Emperor. Then from his son Louis the Pious he received many benefices, and at last he also gained possession of the territory of the city of Rome, and of all the lands, cities, ports and maritime places of Etruria round about. Volaterranus, in the third book of his Geography, has described the example of Louis the Pious's donation. From this it came about that, when Berengar had been crushed by the forces of Otto, King of the Germans, Pope John XIII transferred the empire to the Germans; and Gregory V, a Saxon who was a kinsman of Otto III, confirmed this for them, so that the Germans alone might be allowed to elect the prince who would be Caesar or Roman king, and he would be called emperor and Augustus if the Roman pontiff confirmed him. Moreover, he wished the right of election to rest with three bishops and as many princes, to whom the seventh, the king of Bohemia, would be added. This was done in the year of the Lord 1002. By these steps they proceeded to the papal heaven.

units.la: Quis iam mirabitur pontifices Romanos obtinere potuisse,vt quod ipsis placuisset pro orthodoxo haberetur,contraq; nouum & hæreticum censeretur quicquid Euangelium potius quàm ipsorum decreta saperet? Igitur agnoscimus multis seculis Antichristū regnasse, sed tamen veram synceramq; religionem,quam nos profitemur,antea & quidē ab orbe condito proditam fuisse,propterea; nostram non nouam,sed vetustissimam recuperatam esse. Quemadmodum enim Helias non nouam sed veterem doctrinam, & Christus non nouam, sed antiquissimam illam attulit,sic exemplo Mosis originem religionis nostræ nos ad eum diem,quo homo conditus est,referimus. Ergo si quid valet antiquitatis existimatio,magni precij nostra nobis,quæ est antiquissima,fuerit religio.
units.tr: Who will now be surprised that the Roman pontiffs were able to bring it about that whatever pleased them was held to be orthodox, and whatever savoured more of the Gospel than of their decrees was deemed new and heretical? Therefore we acknowledge that Antichrist reigned for many centuries, but that the true and pure religion which we profess had been handed down before, indeed from the creation of the world, and that therefore what we have recovered is not new but most ancient. For just as Elijah brought not a new but an old teaching, and Christ brought not a new but a most ancient one, so by the example of Moses we trace the origin of our religion back to that day on which man was created. Therefore, if the judgement of antiquity has any weight, our religion, being the most ancient, will be of great value to us.

units.la: Confirmat dicens,Non audiuit vnquam populus vocem Dei loquentis ex. Quibus verbis argumenta tria affert:quorum vnum ab authore,alterum ab ecclesia, tertium à modo reuelatæ seu promulgatæ legis affert.
units.tr: He confirms this by saying, "Did ever a people hear the voice of the living God speaking out of the midst of the fire?" By these words he brings three arguments: one from the author, another from the Church, and the third from the manner in which the law was revealed or published.

units.la: Ab authore Num audiuit(inquit)populus vocem Dei,&c.Quo ostendit Deum,qui summa sapientia est , quemque verisimile non est à quoquam aliquid didicisse ,hanc doctrinā illis audiētibus promulgasse.Quomodo Philo quoq; colligit ideo nihil esse antiquius verbo Domini,quod ad Deum ipsum eius origo referatur. Ergo hoc ipso quod vere diuina est,antiquissima sit necesse est nostra religio.Ac nos quidem malumus eius originē ad Deum ipsum quam ad patres & concilia referre,& hoc nomine nouam esse dicimus papisticam, quod ab illis patribus orta est. Nam his multò est antiquior Deus.Igitur vt ostenderet Moses hanc antiquam esse,dixit Deum ipsum huic genti locutum esse.
units.tr: From the author: "Did a people ever hear the voice of God," etc. By this he shows God, who is supreme wisdom, and whom it is not likely anyone taught anything, that this doctrine was published to those hearing it. Philo also infers in the same way that nothing is older than the word of the Lord, since its origin is traced back to God himself. Therefore, because it is truly divine, our religion must necessarily be most ancient. We prefer to trace its origin to God himself rather than to the Fathers and councils; and on this account we say that the Papist religion is new, because it arose from those Fathers. For God is far older than they are. So that Moses might show that this doctrine is ancient, he said that God himself had spoken to this people.

units.la: Ab ecclesia sic argumenta ducit, Aut tentauit ne Deus(inquit)vt ingrederetur & tolleret sibi gentem è medio gentis &c. Quibus verbis ostendit ecclesiam ab ipso Deo electam, & amatam mirificè, & præpotenter eductam in hanc terram: quod argumento maximo possit esse doctrinam huius populi vetustissimam esse. Nam è media Ægypto selegit Israelitas Deus, & amorem erga eos suum hoc ipso quod illis familiariter affuit, egregiè declarauit. Est autem electio, & dilectio & defensio, quæ bona diuinitus præstitit ecclesiæ Dominus, argumentum verae fidei. Ac si libeat argumenta ab euentu ducere, sanè quod ecclesiam suam per tot pericula saluam atq; incolumem conseruauit Deus, id esse potest argumento optimo nostram causam minimè malam esse.
units.tr: From the Church he draws his arguments thus: "Or has God attempted to go and take for himself a nation from the midst of another nation," etc. By these words he shows that the Church was chosen by God himself, wonderfully loved, and mightily brought out into this land; and this can be a very strong argument that the doctrine of this people is most ancient. For God chose the Israelites from the midst of Egypt, and by the very fact that he was present with them in a familiar way, he plainly declared his love towards them. Moreover, the election, the love and the protection which the Lord has divinely granted to his Church are a proof of the true faith. And if it pleases us to draw arguments from the outcome, surely the fact that God has preserved his Church safe and sound through so many dangers can be a most excellent argument that our cause is by no means bad.

units.la: A modo, quo proposita est lex, argumentatur, ostendens miraculis, verbo, beneficijs, firmatá esse. Miracula, tentationes, signa, bella, manum validâ & terrores commemorat, vt quemadmodum miraculis diuinis falsa superabantur, sic diuina hac doctrina superaret falsam. Sic euangelium confirmatum est miraculis. Verbum ipsum expressum dicit, quippe quod vox Dei fit audita, & alia sint edita præsentiæ Domini indicia. Nulla hic impostura qualibus vsi sunt Dij gentium. Beneficia quoq; significabant quid quæreret, non quæ sua sunt videlicet, sed quæ pertinerent ad salutem populi. Sic benefica est doctrina Domini. At falsæ doctrinæ semper suis professoribus plus quàm auditoribus acquirunt. Ex quo perspicuum est, doctrinâ hanc quia sit à Deo primùm prodita, & ecclesiæ populi colligendæ destinata, & ita suæ naturæ coparata, vt argumentis optimis firmata, & clara ac perspicua, & benefica ac salutaris sit, omnium antiquissimè esse.
units.tr: He argues from the manner in which the law was set forth, showing that it was confirmed by miracles, by the word, and by benefits. He recounts miracles, trials, signs, wars, a strong hand and terrors, so that just as false things were overcome by divine miracles, so this divine doctrine might overcome the false. Thus the Gospel was confirmed by miracles. He says the word itself was openly declared, since the voice of God was heard, and other evident signs of the Lord's presence were given. There is no imposture here, such as the gods of the nations used. The benefits also signified what he sought, not what is his own, namely, but what pertains to the salvation of the people. Thus the teaching of the Lord is beneficial. But false doctrines always gain more for their professors than for their hearers. From this it is clear that this doctrine, since it was first set forth by God and destined for gathering the people of the Church, and since it is by its nature so constituted that it is confirmed by the best arguments, and is clear and perspicuous, and beneficial and salutary, is the most ancient of all.

units.la: Concludit iam dicens, Agnoscas igitur hodie &c. Quo docet quale debeat esse diuini verbi studium. 1. Contemplatio, vt agnoscas, hoc est credas perfuasumq; habeas, videlicet hunc esse solum Deum salutarem. Ex quo colligis qualis sit cognitio Domini, videlicet quæ iuxta Deum nemini locum esse sinat, sed eum ipsum solum habeat quem adoret. Sic Christi cognitio ea vera est, quæ eum solum viuificâ oblatione, intercessione, remissione, via, sanctificatione agnoscat. Agnoscitur quidem à multis Dominus, sed non solus & unus arbiter, id falsum est. Unum agnoscas necesse est.
units.tr: He now concludes by saying, "Acknowledge therefore today, etc." In this he teaches what the study of the divine word ought to be like. (1) Contemplation, so that you may acknowledge, that is, believe and be persuaded, that this one is the only saving God. From this you gather what the knowledge of the Lord is: namely, that knowledge which allows no place beside God for anyone, but holds him alone as the one to be worshipped. So the true knowledge of Christ is that which acknowledges him alone as the one who gives life by his offering, intercession, forgiveness, the way, and sanctification. Indeed the Lord is acknowledged by many, but not as the sole and only judge; that is false. You must acknowledge the one.

units.la: 2 Actio requiritur, nempe vt custodias. Neq; enim satis est scire quin id quod rectum esse noris facias.
units.tr: (2) Action is required, namely that you keep it. For it is not enough to know that you should not do what you know to be right.

units.la: 3 Finis, vt bene fit. Id Deus faxit, Amen.
units.tr: (3) The end, that it may go well. May God grant this, Amen.

units.la: SERMO XX.
units.tr: SERMON XX.

units.la: 41 Tunc segregauit Moses tria oppida cis Iordanem ad solem orientem.
units.tr: 41 Then Moses set apart three cities on this side of the Jordan, toward the rising of the sun.

units.la: 42 Vt illuc confugeret homicida, qui per imprudentiam proximum suum occideret, neq; odio eum fuerit prosecutus antea, fugeritq; ad unum ex illis oppidis, vt viuat.
units.tr: 42 That a manslayer might flee thither, who killed his neighbour unintentionally, and had not hated him before, and that fleeing to one of those cities he might live.

units.la: 43 Nempe Bezer in deserto in terra plana Rubenitis, & Ramoth in Gilead Gaditis, & Golan in Basan Manassitis.
units.tr: 43 Namely Bezer in the wilderness, in the plain country, for the Reubenites; and Ramoth in Gilead for the Gadites; and Golan in Bashan for the Manassites.

units.la: 44 Hæc itaq; est lex, quam proposuit Moses in conspectu Israelis,
units.tr: 44 This therefore is the law which Moses set forth before the children of Israel.

units.la: 45 Hæc sunt testimonia, statuta & iudicia, quæ locutus est Moses ad filios Israel, quum exijssent ex Ægypto,
units.tr: 45 These are the testimonies, statutes and judgments which Moses spoke to the children of Israel when they came out of Egypt.

units.la: 46 Cis Iordanem iuxta Beth Peor in terra Sihonis regis Amorræorum, qui habitauerat in Hesbon, quæ percusserat Moses & filij Israel, quum exijssent ex Ægypto.
units.tr: 46 On this side of the Jordan, near Beth-peor, in the land of Sihon, king of the Amorites, who dwelt in Heshbon, whom Moses and the children of Israel struck when they came out of Egypt.

units.la: 47 Et occupauerunt terram eius, & terram Og regis Basan, duos reges Amorræorum, qui erant cis Iordanem ad exorientem solem.
units.tr: 47 And they possessed his land, and the land of Og king of Bashan, the two kings of the Amorites, who were on this side of the Jordan toward the rising of the sun.

units.la: 48 Ab Aroer, quæ est ad ripam torrentis Arnon, vsq; ad montem Sion, qui & Hermon.
units.tr: 48 From Aroer, which is on the bank of the torrent Arnon, as far as mount Sion, which is Hermon.

units.la: 49 Et omnem planitiem cis Iordanem ad orientem vsq; ad mare, quod est in planitie sub scatebris collis.
units.tr: 49 And all the plain on this side of the Jordan toward the east, as far as the sea that lies in the plain below the slopes of the hill.

units.la: Quanquá ea omnia quæ putantur utilia, honesta, diuina, priscà deniq; esse magno sunt in precio, & concupisci solent à plerisq;: tamen vt æquum sit & bonum, & facile quicquid apud multitudinem obtinere velis, multum refert. Quid enim conduceret rem mihi magnopere placere, nō aut obuenire posse? Certè eó stultior sim, qui id expetā, quod neq; consequi, neq; si impetrem, sustinere possim. Ergo cum Moses docuisset suá, quá afferebat doctrinâ utilé, hone-stam, diuinâ, priscâ, propterea q; & admirandâ & expetendâ esse: iam docet æquâ etiâ ac tole-rabilem esse, vt à nemine queat respui, eiq; demonstrationi conclusionem totius primæ partis subiungit quasi quandam ad quintum caput, quo præcepta decem commemorat, transi-tionem. Æquam esse exemplo positorum asylorum docet. Quasi dicat, ut intelligatis hanc doctrinam non solum ita uti prædicaui utilem, honestam, diuinam, priscam esse, verum etiam æquam & omnino facilem fore, exemplum è multis unum profero: nempe quod cum lege vetitum sit homicidium, & tamen usu venire sæpe enumero soleat, ut quis alium occidat fortuito, non proposito seu destinato consilio, Deus æquitatem & moderationem ceu interpretem legis admisit, constitutis asylis in quæ tales homicidæ confugiant. Atque hoc Nu. 35. & Iof. 20. describitur. Ac quanquam hæc de re multa cum ex historiis tum ex utroque iure huc afferri possent: tamen quia caput aliud eadem de re sequitur peculiare, omissa tractatione ea, verbi divini æquitatem considerabimus.
units.tr: Although all those things which are thought useful, honourable, divine, and indeed ancient, are held in great esteem, and are commonly desired by most people, yet for a thing to be fair and good, and easily acceptable, it matters much whether it can be obtained among the multitude. For what would it profit me that a thing pleases me greatly, if it cannot come to me? Surely I would be the more foolish if I aimed at what I could neither attain nor, if I did attain it, bear. Therefore, when Moses had taught that his doctrine, which he set forth, is useful, honourable, divine, ancient, and for that reason both admirable and to be desired, he now teaches that it is also fair and bearable, so that no one can reject it. To this demonstration he appends, as it were, the conclusion of the whole first part, a kind of transition to the fifth chapter, in which he recounts the ten commandments. He teaches that it is fair by the example of the cities of refuge that were appointed. As if he were to say: so that you may understand that this doctrine is not only useful, honourable, divine and ancient as I have said, but also fair and altogether easy, I offer one example out of many: namely, that although homicide is forbidden by the law, and yet it often happens that someone kills another by chance, not by settled purpose or deliberate design, God, as the interpreter of the law, admitted equity and moderation, by appointing cities of refuge into which such manslayers may flee. And this is described in Numbers 35 and Joshua 20. And although many things on this matter could be brought forward here, both from histories and from both laws, yet because another chapter follows that deals with the same matter in particular, I will set aside that treatment and consider the equity of the divine Word.

units.la: Quod igitur Deus homicidia imprudenter facta, non secundum ius strictum, sed secundum æquitatem iudicat, & concedit aliquid imprudentiæ & socordiæ nostræ, id argumento est Deum nos magis curare & respicere, quàm quicquam aliud. Veluti si quis feram petens hominem feriat, aut si quis in tecto fabrefaciens aliquid, non magis prouideat, quàm ut ei bi-pennis è tecto lapsa prætereuntem aliquem perimat: ne vel magistratus, vel propinqui sive vindices eius, qui interijt, illium subito obruant atq; opprimant, asyla, in quæ confugiant rei, instituit Dominus. Atq; hoc quidem satis evidens est illius æquitatis exemplum: sed sunt etiam alia non minus illustria. Veluti quod sabbathum violari maluit, quàm non ope subleva-ri hominem, & obstetrices Ægyptias mentiri maluit, quàm perire fidelium liberos, & panes propositionis è templo auferri, quàm Dauidem cum suis fame emori, itemq; discipulos spicas sabbatho vellere, quàm esurire, multaque præterea generis eiusdem alia.
units.tr: Therefore that God judges homicides committed unintentionally not according to strict law but according to equity, and grants some allowance for our carelessness and thoughtlessness, is a proof that God cares for and regards us more than anything else. Just as if someone, hunting a wild beast, strikes a man, or if someone working on a roof does not take enough care, so that a axe falling from the roof kills a passer-by; the Lord instituted cities of refuge, so that the magistrates, or the relatives or avengers of the dead man, may not suddenly overwhelm and crush the accused as they flee. And this is indeed a quite clear example of that equity; but there are also other examples no less illustrious. For instance, that he preferred the Sabbath to be broken rather than a man not be helped; and that he preferred the Egyptian midwives to lie rather than the children of the faithful perish; and that the showbread be taken from the temple rather than David and his men die of hunger; and likewise that the disciples pluck ears of corn on the Sabbath rather than go hungry; and many other things of the same kind besides.

units.la: Ex quibus intelligimus Deum non minus ad misericordiam quàm ad iustitiam propen-dere, ideoq; non posse de verbo Dei, quasi de doctrina dura atq; difficili, quenquàm conqueri: sed esse nostrarum partium potius agnoscere, quod lenis sit & naturæ, non corruptæ, iucun-da. Unde etiam Dominus dixit Matth. 11. iugum suum lene est & suave.
units.tr: From these things we understand that God leans no less toward mercy than toward justice, and therefore no one can complain of the word of God as if it were a hard and difficult doctrine; rather it is our part to acknowledge that it is gentle and agreeable to a nature that is not corrupted. Whence also the Lord said, Matthew 11: My yoke is easy and my burden is light.

units.la: Carni quidem magis adlubescit licentia, quemadmodum iuventuti indomitæ, cum longè suavior sit disciplina recta, animis, qui in pietate maturuerint. Quanto enim securior est αὐτάρκεια, quam πλεονεξία: pudica ac casta vita, quàm libido, humilitas, quàm ambitio: charitas quàm invidia: sobrietas quàm ebrietas. Exemplorum plenæ sunt omnes historiæ.
units.tr: Indeed, licence is more pleasing to the flesh, just as to untamed youth; yet right discipline is far sweeter to minds that have matured in piety. For how much safer is self-sufficiency [αὐτάρκεια] than covetousness [πλεονεξία]; a chaste and modest life than lust; humility than ambition; charity than envy; sobriety than drunkenness. All histories are full of examples.

units.la: Ergo Deus nihil requirit nisi quod factu facile est, quod naturæ bonæ consentaneum est. Nec solum leges sunt faciles, sed & si illas fis transgressus, adeo propendet ad misericordiam Dominus, ut exorari se, quo concedat veniam, patiatur facillimè. Cuius rei spem faciebat Dominus instituto & usu sacrificiorum, itemq; expiationum & lustrationum veterum, denique perenni sacrificio Domini nostri Iesu Christi pro nobis in ara crucis oblato. Unde & Evangelium, quia remissionem peccatorum & vitam æternam nunciaret, læti nuncij nomen accepit. Quamobrem nullum est tam suave & gratum doctrinæ genus, atq; hoc ipsum quod Deus primum per Mosem & prophetas promulgatum per Christum & Apostolos postea renovavit, nec quisquam satanæ, qui id nobis durum fingit, fidem habendam censeat, præsertim cum res ipsa atq; eius usus diversum nobis indicent.
units.tr: Therefore God requires nothing but what is easy to do, and what agrees with a good nature. Nor are the laws only easy; but even if you have transgressed them, the Lord is so inclined to mercy that he allows himself, in order to grant pardon, to be most easily entreated. The Lord gave hope of this by the institution and practice of the sacrifices, and likewise of the old expiations and purifications, and finally by the perpetual sacrifice of our Lord Jesus Christ offered for us on the altar of the cross. Whence also the Gospel, because it announces the forgiveness of sins and eternal life, received the name of good news. Wherefore there is no kind of doctrine so sweet and welcome; and this very doctrine, which God first promulgated through Moses and the prophets and afterwards renewed through Christ and the apostles, let no one, who pictures it to us as hard, be believed, especially since the thing itself and its use show the opposite to us.

units.la: Sed ex hoc etiam, siquidem Dei imitatores esse volumus, ipsi bonitati atq; æquitati stu-dere discimus. Ea est perfecta ratio, quæ leges & omne scriptum dictumq; interpretatur & emendat, ex qua ius manat, quod bonum & æquum dicitur, nullo scripto comprehensum, sed in circumstantijs rerum, personarum, locorum sita. Hæc rigorem legis mitigat, & ne summum ius degeneret in summam iniuriam, ipsa cavet. Ei magistratus cumprimis studere debet, quando casus omnes scripto comprehendi non possunt, & subinde nascuntur noui. In quibus omnia comparanda sunt. Hanc ergo se mutuo servabunt singuli. Sed de hac re quo-niam post sequitur in 19.cap.locus peculiaris, cum eo ventum erit dicetur pluribus. Utrumque coniunctum est, & alterum consequitur alterum. Ideo dixit Deus oremus, remitte no-bis, sicut & nos remittimus debitoribus nostris. Et Petrus ait, eos qui remiserint culpam fra-tribus, tanto orare felicius & fidentius. Jam hoc teneamus Deum benignum esse, & faciles leges ponere, easque etiam ipsas sic mitigare æquitate, ut illis obsequi non sit difficile.
units.tr: But from this also, if indeed we wish to be imitators of God, we learn to strive after goodness and equity itself. That is the perfect reason, which interprets and corrects laws and every written and spoken word; from which comes the right that is called good and fair, comprehended in no writing, but lying in the circumstances of things, persons and places. This softens the rigour of the law, and itself guards against the highest right degenerating into the highest wrong. Magistrates above all ought to strive for this, since not all cases can be comprehended in writing, and new ones keep arising. In these matters all things must be weighed. Let each therefore preserve this towards one another. But since, on this matter, a particular passage follows later in chapter 19, it will be discussed more fully when we come to it. The two are joined, and the one follows the other. Therefore God said: pray, forgive us our debts as we also forgive our debtors. And Peter says that those who have forgiven their brothers' faults pray all the more happily and confidently. Let us hold this now: that God is kind, and lays down easy laws, and even softens them by equity, so that it is not difficult to obey them.

units.la: Concludit deinceps & hoc ipsum, quod prosecutus est quarto capite progymnasma, & primam libri partem totam. Illud progymnasma sic concludit, Hæc (inquiens) est lex quam proposuit Moses. Atqui talis est hæc doctrina, qualem modò vobis dixi, utilis, honesta, diuina, prisca, æqua. Quid ab illa abhorretis? Quin illam summo studio accipitis? Sanè qui respuit hanc, is suum ipsius commodum reijcit, quod stultissimum est: suum ipsius honorem, quod & turpe est, & ab optimo quoq; alienum: res sacrosanctas atq; diuinas despicit, quod impium est & periculosum: qui etiam antiquitatem despicit,quod ab hominis natura atq; etiam usu prorsus est alienum: æquum & bonum renuit,quod est iniquissimum,& pugnat cum totius orbis concordia.
units.tr: He then concludes this very thing which he pursued in the fourth chapter as an exercise, and the whole first part of the book. He concludes that preliminary exercise thus: This (he says) is the law which Moses set forth. But this doctrine is such as I have just told you: useful, honourable, divine, ancient, fair. Why do you shrink from it? Why do you not rather receive it with the greatest zeal? Surely whoever rejects it casts away his own advantage, which is the height of folly; his own honour, which is both shameful and foreign to all the best people; he despises holy and divine things, which is impious and dangerous; he who also despises antiquity, which is wholly contrary to human nature and even to custom; he refuses what is fair and good, which is most unjust, and he fights against the harmony of the whole world.

units.la: Vide quid fit religionis tædio laborare,itemq; quales nos simus quibus Euangelium, le-gesq; secundum ipsum factæ tantopere sordeant,quibus ministri verbi Dei pariter atq; eius asseclæ tam sunt molesti,contempti,inuisi.Præsagia sunt imminentis excidij. Quod significant exempla Nohæ temporum,& Sodomæ,& Ægypti,& Saulis,itemq; Israelis,Iudeæ, Germaniæ,moresq; nostri.Experti sumus utilitates,& gloriam, quæ bona accepimus cumulatissimè[?],cognouimus doctrinam diuinam esse,certum est nouam non esse,æquam & facilem esse subinde sentimus. Quare nullæ sunt iustæ contemptus causæ.
units.tr: See what it is to labour under weariness of religion, and what sort of people we are, for whom the Gospel and the laws made according to it are so despised, and for whom the ministers of God's Word and their followers are so troublesome, contemptible and hateful. These are omens of impending destruction. This is what the examples of the times of Noah, of Sodom, of Egypt, of Saul, and likewise of Israel, Judah, Germany and our own morals signify. We have experienced the benefits and the glory we have received in the fullest measure. We have come to know that the divine doctrine is not new, and from time to time we feel that it is just and easy. Therefore there are no just causes for contempt.

units.la: Sed totam hanc operis partem enumeratione præcedentium claudit, quæ docet eiusmodi quoq; esse priora progymnasmata. Testimonij appellatione fidem in Deum postulat. Nam ut testium sic etiam Dei verba habentur rata ac vera,& quæ nefas sit negare. Atque eo primum progymnasma dirigitur,nempe ut credatur Deo.
units.tr: But he closes this whole part of the work with a recounting of the preceding matters, which teaches that the earlier exercises are likewise of this kind. By the term "testimony" he demands faith in God. For, as with witnesses, so also God's words are held to be firm and true, and it is wrong to deny them. And so the first preliminary exercise is directed to this, namely that God be believed.

units.la: Statutorum & iudiciorum appellatione repetit obedientiam magistratui debitam:hæc enim ut seruemus leges cogit.
units.tr: By the term "statutes and judgments" he repeats the obedience owed to the magistrate, for these compel us to keep the laws.

units.la: Deuictorum regum nominibus repetitis ius gentium in memoriam reuocat ac seruandum admonet.Terræ cis Iordanem sitæ descriptione repetita veritatis atq; bonæ fidei, quæ sanctè seruanda est,admonet. Quæ omnia ceu principia quædam ad diuini verbi studium requiruntur.Inde fit ad decalogum,qui nunc proximum ab hinc locum habet, transitio.
units.tr: By repeating the names of the defeated kings, he recalls the law of nations to memory and admonishes that it be kept. By repeating the description of the land on this side of the Jordan, he admonishes us of truth and good faith, which must be kept sacredly. All these things are required as certain principles for the study of the divine Word. From here comes the transition to the Decalogue, which now has the next place.

units.la: Deus faxit ut bene iaciantur initia. Nam dimidium facti qui be-nè coepit habet. Id fiet in Christo, cui sit ho-nos in secula, Amen.
units.tr: May God grant that the beginnings be well laid. For he who has well begun has half the work done. This will be accomplished in Christ, to whom be honour for ever. Amen.

units.la: IOANNIS VVOLPHII TIGVRINI IN DEVTERONOMIVM SERMONVM LIBER SECVNDVS. CAPVT V. SERMO I.
units.tr: The Second Book of the Sermons of Johann Wolf of Zurich on Deuteronomy. Chapter 5. Sermon 1.

units.la: Vocauitq; Moses vniuersum Israelem, & dixit ad eos, Audi Israel ritus & iudicia, quæ ego hodie loquor in auribus vestris, vt discatis ea, & in hoc feruetis, vt faciatis.
units.tr: And Moses called all Israel, and said unto them, Hear, O Israel, the statutes and judgments which I speak in your ears this day, that ye may learn them, and be careful to do them.

units.la: 2 Dominus Deus noster pepigit nobiscum fœdus in Horeb.
units.tr: The LORD our God made a covenant with us in Horeb.

units.la: 3 Non cum patribus nostris (tantū) excidit Dominus fœdus hoc, sed nobiscū, qui omnes etiamnum hodie hic viuimus,
units.tr: The LORD made not this covenant with our fathers only, but with us, even us, who are all of us here alive this day.

units.la: 4 Facie ad faciem loquutus est Dominus nobiscum in monte de medio ignis.
units.tr: The LORD talked with you face to face in the mount out of the midst of the fire.

units.la: 5 Et ego stans inter Dominum, & inter vos eodem tempore, annuntiaui vobis verbum domini, vos enim timuistis ab igne, nec montem ascendistis: Sic autem dixit.
units.tr: (I stood between the LORD and you at that time, to shew you the word of the LORD: for ye were afraid by reason of the fire, and went not up into the mount;) saying,

units.la: EXPLICATA fuscepte scriptionis parte priore, quaMoses animos nostros ad diuinæ legis cognitionem atque studium præparauit, sequitur altera, qua legem ipsam seu eius summam ac caput comprehendit, idq; sane quâ methodicè. Nam primum efficientem eius causam, tum ipsam simul formam ac materiam, id est, eius capita sigillatim & suo quoq; ordine posita commemorat, deniq; eius effecta refert pietatem videlicet seu timorem Domini.
units.tr: Having explained the first part of the passage we have undertaken, in which Moses prepared our minds for the knowledge and study of the divine law, there follows the second part, in which he sets out the law itself, or its sum and head, and he does so in an orderly method. For first he mentions its efficient cause, then its form and matter at once, that is, its chapters, set out one by one and in their own order, and finally he reports its effects, namely piety, or the fear of the Lord.

units.la: Ac quantum ad efficientem causam pertinet, quam verbis illis persequitur: hæc est rei summa: Deum ipsum huius legis authorem esse, quippe qui Mose vsus internuncio populum vniuersum in concionem vnam conuocarit, eiq; coram astanti ipse facie ad faciem, hoc est, vt Græce & secundum Theophilactum dicam planius, αὐτοπροσώπως apparens decalogum promulgauit: eoq; ceu sancti illius inter se & populum initi fœderis esse capita voluerit.
units.tr: As for the efficient cause, which he pursues in these words, the substance of the matter is this: God himself is the author of this law. Using Moses as his intermediary, he gathered the whole people into one assembly, and in the presence of those standing by him, he appeared face to face [αὐτοπροσώπως], as I may put it in Greek and, following Theophylact, more plainly, and proclaimed the Decalogue, and so willed these to be the heads of the holy covenant made between himself and the people.

units.la: Quod quemadmodū sese habeat tunc plane cognoscemus cum considerabimus 1. Concionem populi. 2. fœdus. 3. Deum ducem siue Dominum: quæ Moses eo ponit ordine, vti fœdus cuius apellatione leges illæ continentur, inter ambas partes medium, quasi illas diuisas, in vnum colligens ac vinciens vinculum emineat. Quæ cum ita sint, sequitur concionem populi, ipsam doctrinam, Deum qui proponit vno ore dicere leges illas diuinitus ortas esse.
units.tr: We shall understand how this stands when we consider: (1) the assembly of the people; (2) the covenant; (3) God as leader, or Lord. Moses arranges these in such an order that the covenant, by whose name those laws are contained, stands out as the middle bond between the two parties, joining and binding them together as if they were divided. Since this is so, there follows the assembly of the people, the doctrine itself, and God who sets it forth, speaking with one voice, and saying that those laws were given by divine inspiration.

units.la: Concio populi diligentissime describitur. Vocauitq; Moses vniuersum Israelem & dixit ad eos, &c. Quibus verbis docet populum eum, qui cum Deo coniungi cupiat, omnino conuocandum esse, vt fœderis capita percipiat, ac custodiat.
units.tr: The assembly of the people is described with great care: And Moses called all Israel, and said unto them, etc. In these words he teaches that the people who wish to be joined with God must indeed be called together, so that they may receive and keep the heads of the covenant.

units.la: Dicit autem primum quo precone populus in concionem conuocatus sit, nempe Mose. Id indicio nobis est oportere esse designatos ministros Ecclesiæ, qui præsint populo, ne qua sit ἀταξία <bl>vil birten hütend nie wol</bl>. Vnde Israelijs Moses & Aharô duces dati, inde Leuitæ, tum apostoli, episcopi, parochi præfecti sunt ecclesijs. Est hæc perpulchra harmonia ciuitatis, qua multos vnus colligit in vnum corpus, vt coalescant, qui illorū curet, foueat, seruet incolu-mitate: veluti in republica aliqua magnis cœtibus consules, triumuiri, tribuni præficiūtur: ve-lutiq; magistratus minores summus semper colligit ac gubernat. Eiusmodi boni ordinis & legitimæ dominationis speciem pulchram Moses præfert.
units.tr: He first says by what herald the people were called to the assembly, namely by Moses. This is an indication to us that the ministers of the Church must be appointed to preside over the people, lest there be any disorder [ἀταξία]; the German gloss in the margin says: "too many herders, never well." Hence Moses and Aaron were given to the Israelites as leaders, and then the Levites, and afterwards the apostles, bishops and parish pastors were set over the churches. This is a most beautiful harmony of a commonwealth, by which one man gathers many into one body, so that they may grow together, and so that he who cares for them may cherish and keep them safe, just as in some republic consuls, triumvirs and tribunes are set over great assemblies, and as a chief magistrate always gathers and governs the lesser magistrates. Moses presents this fair image of good order and lawful rule.

units.la: 2 Qui cogi debeant,Vniuersus Israel. Omnibus enim hominibus vult Deus innotesce-re:ergo omnium est velle eum cognoscere. Peccant igitur non tantum in homines, sed in Deum etiam ipsum quicunque lectione Bibliorum homines prohibent. Rara est domus, quæ nullam habeat regulam, habeat libram nullam, quæ careat mensura ac pondere: cur ergo vitæ regula domos hominum destituunt? Nec minus peccant qui ipsi sese prohibent sa-cris concionibus & lectionibus, quiqué dicunt eam nihil ad se pertinere, sacerdotum hæc exercitia esse propria: an ergo solis sacerdotibus, ac non etiam tibi vis salutem impetiri? an non pro eo quod ipsis penduntur decimæ, tibi Deus alijs prouentibus consuluit? O stultos qui tenebras, quam lucem malunt, qui in Alpium niuibus aut Oceano glaciali malunt, quam in locis apricis habitare. Quamobrem cogitabimus Deum, quoniam totum fui populi cœtum in vnum conuocat nolle vel dispersionem vel conuenticula, sed vnam omnium concionem.
units.tr: (2) Who ought to be called? All Israel. For God wishes to make himself known to all men; therefore it is the duty of all to wish to know him. Those therefore sin not only against men but against God himself who keep men from reading the Bible. Rare is the house that has no rule, no scales, no measure or weight: why then do men leave their homes without the rule of life? Those also sin no less who shut themselves off from sacred sermons and readings, and say that these things do not concern them, and that these exercises belong to priests alone. Do you then wish salvation to be obtained only for priests, and not for yourself too? Has God not provided for you, since tithes are paid to them, by other means of support? O fools, who prefer darkness to light, who would rather live in the snows of the Alps or on the icy ocean than in sunny places! Therefore let us consider that God, when he calls together the whole assembly of his people, does not want scattering or little conventicles, but one assembly of all.

units.la: Quid proponendum sit suo exemplo Moses indicat, Audi (inquiens) Israel, ritus et iudicia quæ ego hodie loquor in auribus vestris. Non humanæ traditiones, aut fabulæ proponentur, sed sacrosanctum Dei verbum. Nam illis nec sat doceri, nec castigari, nec castigatione coerceri, nec consolatione confirmari possumus: Quippe quod sint tenebris Cimmerijs obscuriores, quod homo nolit ab homine gubernari, quod verbis humanis parum fidimus. Igitur non pascitur ecclesia Pharifaico fermento, Papisticis, Iudaicis, Turcicis siue ceremonijs siue fabulis. Quid enim vel doctrinæ vel consolationis ex ecclesiasticis illis non intelligtis cantibus & ceremonijs haurias? quod scelus vnquam hisce ritibus digne notari & reprehendi potuit? Equidem arbitror diabolum hos ritus atque cantus excogitasse propterea, vt ne cognitione veritatis imbuerentur homines doctrina, tolleretur e medio: tum populo hos ipsos ideo sic arridere, vt ne qua audiatur amplius iniustitiæ reprehensio. Quæ cum ita sint, male cadet illis pastoribus (qui ceu πυρασπισταὶ rei pro bono pabulo dant paleas) sua cum improbitas tum impietas.
units.tr: Moses shows by his own example what should be proposed to the people: "Hear, O Israel," he says, "the statutes and judgments which I speak in your ears this day." Human traditions or fables are not to be put forward, but the holy Word of God. For we cannot be taught enough by those, nor rebuked, nor restrained by rebuke, nor strengthened by consolation; indeed they are darker than Cimmerian shadows, a man will not be governed by a man, and we have little trust in human words. Therefore the Church is not fed with the leaven of the Pharisees, of the Papists, the Jews or the Turks, whether in ceremonies or in fables. For what doctrine or consolation can you draw from those ecclesiastical songs and ceremonies that you do not understand? What crime could ever be rightly marked and rebuked in these rites? Indeed I think the devil devised these rites and songs for this reason: so that men might not be imbued with the knowledge of the truth, which doctrine would remove from the midst; and so that the people might be so pleased with these very things that no rebuke of injustice would be heard any more. Since this is so, the wickedness and impiety of those ministers will fall badly upon them, who, like pyraspists [πυρασπισταί] of a sort, give chaff instead of good fodder to the flock.

units.la: Quin omnes exemplum Moisi habeant ob oculos positum, qui verbum Dei syncere prædicat. Sed id duabus partibus distribuit, legibus videlicet ac ritibus. Rituum appellatione quicquid est ecclesiasticum & ad religionem pertinet, intelligit. Ergo religionem vere & recte tradi Moses iubet. Legum autem leu iudiciorum nomine quicquid ad ciuitatis statum spectat intelligimus. Ergo verbi minister de magistratuum creatione & officio, de iudiciorum forma, de reiudicata, de testamentis, de controuersijs forensibus, de bello & re militari, de locis, de pace & inducijs, deq; reliquis rebus ciuilibus verba faciens minime extra suæ vocationis septa excurrit. Nam hic locus indicat verbi Domini summam philosophiam esse, qua ceu toto partes illæ contineantur. Ac fi magistratus hæc ad nos, non pertinere clamitet, causa est, quod doceri nolit. Moses autem exemplum ostendit leges non minus prædicandas quam ritus, hoc est, sacras cerimonias.
units.tr: Let all have before their eyes the example of Moses, who preaches the Word of God sincerely. He divides it into two parts, namely laws and rites. By the name of rites he understands whatever is ecclesiastical and pertains to religion. Therefore Moses orders that religion be taught truly and rightly. By the name of laws or judgments we understand whatever concerns the state of the commonwealth. Therefore a minister of the Word, when he speaks about the appointment and duty of magistrates, the form of courts, appeals, wills, lawsuits, war and military affairs, boundaries, peace and truces, and other civil matters, does not in the least run outside the bounds of his calling. For this passage shows that the sum of the Word of the Lord is a philosophy in which those parts are contained as the whole. And if the magistrate cries out that these things do not pertain to us, the reason is that he does not want to be taught. Moses, however, shows by example that laws are to be preached no less than rites, that is, the sacred ceremonies.

units.la: 4 Quorsum hoc nempe vt audiant, discant, ferunt, faciant. En tibi quid requirat Dominus, non vult surdis cani fabulam, audiri postulat. Nam ex auditu fides. Non creauit aures impuris fabulis, sed audiendo verbo suo Dominus. Grande nephas est aures ei prebere nolle, qui tibi illas creauit. Quàm grauiter peccat, qui patri, cuius beneficio ædes atque opes habeas, negare hospitium? quanto grauius est hoc quod dicimus?
units.tr: (4) Why? Namely that they may hear, learn, bear in mind and do them. See what the Lord requires of you: he does not wish a tale to be sung to the deaf; he demands to be heard. For faith comes by hearing. The Lord did not create ears for impure fables, but for hearing his word. It is a great wickedness to refuse to offer ears to him who made them for you. How gravely does he sin who denies hospitality to a father, by whose kindness you have a house and wealth? How much more gravely is what we are saying?

units.la: Discere iubet: quod attentionem deficerat: nō vult quasi παροικος audiri: sed vt reliquis curis familiaribus aut ludis atque iocis, vel etiam nugis & fabulis verbum audiatur. Memento ecclesiam non stoam aliquam, non tonstrinam, non forum in quo garrias, sed scholam in qua discas, esse.
units.tr: He bids them learn, because attention is wanting. He does not want the word to be heard as a stranger [παροικος], passing through, but so that it may be heard among the other family cares, or games and jokes, or even trifles and tales. Remember that the Church is not some porch, nor a barber's shop, nor a marketplace where you chatter, but a school in which you learn.

units.la: lubet etiam seruare, hoc est tenere memoriu. Obliuio verbi diuini mater est & errorum & peccatorum omnium. Discipuli verbi Christi memoria lapsi, resurrectionis spem quoque amiserunt. Igitur cum tempus, locus, res omnes adiumenta pijs studijs suppeditent: occasio ne quisquis sapit vtetur, ac quemadmodum thesaurus in magna annonæ copia collectus ingruente rerum caritate solatio est maximo-sic verbi diuini, dum prædicatur & auditur tutò, thesauros collegisse & animo condidisse, quando vel morbis, vel quacunque aduersa fortuna corripimur, est immensa vtilitas. Vnde & à Domino in Euangelio margarita dicitur. Matth. 7. Sapienter sibi consuluisse dicitur, qui verbum Dei cum animo suo bene perceperit, tum vita ac moribus expresserit. Hac enim de causa Dei verbum nobis traditur.
units.tr: He also commands you to keep, that is, to hold in memory. Forgetfulness of the divine Word is the mother of all errors and all sins. The disciples of Christ, having slipped from memory of his word, lost also the hope of the resurrection. Therefore, since time, place and all things supply aids to pious studies, whoever is wise will use the occasion; and just as a treasure gathered in a great abundance of grain is the greatest comfort when scarcity comes on, so it is of immense use to have gathered the treasures of the divine Word, while it is preached and heard safely, and to have stored them in the mind, when we are seized by sickness or by whatever adverse fortune. For this reason the Lord also calls it a pearl in the Gospel. Matt. 7. He is said to have provided wisely for himself who has well perceived the Word of God in his own mind, and then expressed it in his life and conduct. For it is for this reason that the Word of God is delivered to us.

units.la: Atque sic habes imaginem ecclesiæ quàm paucissimis descriptam verbis. Est cœtus populi Dei, qui ab ipso per ministrum designatum ad studium verbi cultusque Dei colligitur, vt cum ipso Deo coniungatur ac viuat. Habes enim sub Deo pastorem, populum, verbum, studia. Cum his Deus est fœderatus: odit populos ministrorum persecutores, discurrentes ab ecclesia, sua magis quærentes quàm verbum, malis potius deditos quam bonis operibus. Ergo nostræ leges bonæ erunt, si sint eiusmodi vt hæc nobis mandent studia: vita recta fuerit si ad eas accommodata: alioquin Deus hic non sibi figet tentoria.
units.tr: And so you have an image of the Church, described in as few words as possible. It is the assembly of God's people, gathered by him, through the minister he has appointed, to attend to the Word and the worship of God, so that they may be joined to God himself and live. For you have under God a minister, a people, the Word, and their zeal for it. God has entered a covenant with these: he hates the persecutors of ministers, those who wander away from the Church, who seek their own interests rather than the Word, and who are given over to evil rather than to good works. Therefore our laws will be good only if they are such as to commend these pursuits to us, and our life will be upright only if it is adjusted to them; otherwise God will not pitch his tents here.

units.la: Fœdus, Dominus Deus noster pepigit nobiscum in Horeb, &c. Verbum diuinum, quia Deus quid ab illo sit nobis expectandum, ac rursus quid à nobis requiratur edocet, fœdus appellatur nempe vt intelligamus quanti referat his stare quæ dicit Dominus. In fœdere enim fit obli-gatio duarum in vnum corpus coeuntium partium. Quod ego tibi promitto hoc tu ratum habebis, nec vnquam dubitabis: nec potes negare quod & tabulas & iuramentum & sigilla hæ-beas: quod tu mihi debes, id ni præstes, violati fœderis crimen incurris. Sic promissis diuinis obsignatis, scriptis, iuratis non potes saluo honore tuo diffidere: præceptis eius non potes non obsequi, nisi velis fœdus irritum. Magnam hoc nomine Deus suo verbo authoritatem quærit ac vendicat.
units.tr: Covenant: the Lord our God made a covenant with us in Horeb, etc. The divine Word is called a covenant, because it teaches us what we may expect from him, and again what is required of us; so that we may understand how much it matters that we abide by what the Lord says. For in a covenant an obligation arises between two parties coming together into one body. "What I promise you, you shall hold fast, and you shall never doubt it": you cannot deny that you have the tablets, the oath and the seals; if you do not render what you owe me, you incur the guilt of breaking the covenant. Thus, with the divine promises sealed, written down and sworn, you cannot, without losing your honour, distrust them; you cannot fail to obey his precepts, unless you wish the covenant to be void. By this title God claims and asserts great authority for his Word.

units.la: Et hoc quidem fœdus dicit, non cum patribus, puta, foliis factum, sed etiam nobis cum. Ne putes patribus dictum: quod enim vni dicit, omnibus dictum puta. Semen Abrahæ post Abrahamum elegit, quod exponit apostolus. Ergo hoc fœdus vinculum est Dei pariter ac hominum. Qui id despicit, is rumpit diuinum vinculum. Qui igitur Sacra Biblia cremant, qui do-ctrinam euangelicam diris blasphemijs conspuunt, malis artibus persequuntur, profligant, vbi possunt, opprimunt ij vincula quibus Deus & humanum genus coniuncti sunt, rumpunt. Si igitur grande nephas est etiam horum ipsorum iudicio matrimonia dirimere: quanto maius est scelus matrimonium inter Deum atq; homines contractum dirimere? Sed Deus ipse suam vlciscitur iniuriam.
units.tr: And he says that this covenant was made not with the fathers, that is, with the leaves, but also with us. Do not think it was spoken to the fathers only: what he says to one, consider it said to all. He chose the seed of Abraham after Abraham, as the apostle explains. Therefore this covenant is a bond of God and of men alike. Whoever despises it breaks the divine bond. Those, then, who burn the holy Bibles, who spit on the evangelical doctrine with dreadful blasphemies, who persecute it with wicked arts, who destroy it wherever they can and crush it, break the ties by which God and the human race are joined. If, then, even by their own judgment it is a great wickedness to dissolve a marriage, how much greater a crime is it to dissolve the marriage contracted between God and men? But God himself avenges his own injury.

units.la: Deus facie ad faciem (inquit) locutus est eis. Quo ostendit hoc fœdus, plane diuinum esse, & leges has authore Deo promulgari. Demonstrat hoc argumentis à modo reuelatæ legis sumptis. 1. facie ad faciem, seu vt Græce dici posset αὐτοπροσώπως. Sic enim præsens hæc agens Deus fuit, vt ipsius præsentiæ sensus perciperetur. 3. Locutus: Vocem quocunq; modo voluit articulatam ac claram edidit. Igitur vt humana sunt quæ locutus est homo: sic quæ Deus dixit diuina sint necesse est. 3. Nobiscum, scilicet cum Mose & tota gente. Testes sunt auriti, qui metuerunt sibi & petierunt, vt per Mosem loqueretur. Quid magis perspicuum? Diuinam esse, qui recte hæc perpenderit, nemo negauerit.
units.tr: God (he says) spoke with them face to face. By this he shows that this covenant is plainly divine, and that these laws were promulgated with God as their author. He proves this by arguments taken from the manner of the revealed law. First, face to face, or, as it could be said in Greek, αὐτοπροσώπως [in person]: for God acted in this way as one present, so that the sense of his very presence was perceived. Second, spoke: he uttered a voice, articulate and clear, in whatever manner he wished. Therefore, just as what a man speaks is human, so what God spoke must necessarily be divine. Third, with us, namely with Moses and the whole nation. They are witnesses with ears, who were afraid for themselves and asked that he might speak through Moses. What could be more evident? Whoever weighs these things rightly will deny no one that it is divine.

units.la: Quamobrem hoc Dei verbum eo maiore erit nobis in precio quod ipsum Deus ipse promulgarit: quod eo nos ceu vinculo optimo cum sibi, tum nobis ipsis copulauit, atq; coniunxit: quod deniq; ipsum prius noluit proponere, quàm cœtum omnem Moses in locum vnum coegisset: nempe vt perciperetur ab omnibus. Quæ profecto res sunt eiusmodi, vt verbo Dei magnam authoritatem conciliare debeant: nosque ad eius studium mirum in modum excitare. Amen.
units.tr: Wherefore this Word of God will be all the more precious to us because God himself has promulgated it; because by it he has bound and joined us both to himself and to ourselves, as with the best of bonds; and because, finally, he was unwilling to set it forth until Moses had gathered the whole assembly into one place, namely so that it might be perceived by all. These things are surely of such a kind that they ought to win great authority for the Word of God, and to stir us wonderfully to its study. Amen.

units.la: SERMO II.
units.tr: SERMON II.

units.la: 6 Ego Dominus Deus tuus, qui eduxi te de terra Ægypti, de domo seruitutis.
units.tr: 6 I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.

units.la: CVm Moses hoc cap. summam ac caput doctrinæ suæ, seu diuinæ voluntatis proponat: ac quod potissimum ad hanc rem pertinet, causam efficientem verbis ijs, quæ nuper exposuimus, ostenderit: sequitur etiam vt describat eius formam & materiam.
units.tr: Since Moses in this chapter sets forth the sum and head of his teaching, or of the divine will, and since, as far as this matter requires, he has shown the efficient cause in the words we have recently explained, it follows that he also describes its form and matter.

units.la: Ac materia quidem, quemadmodum hoc loco proponitur: duabus partibus omnis con-tinetur, amore Dei videlicet & proximi. Nam primum ea commemorat, quæ ad Dei cultum pertinent: dicens, ego sum Deus tuus, non habebis Deos alienos: non pones statuas: non assumes nomen Domini frustra: sabbatum non prophanaueris. Quæ vero pertinent ad amorem proximi, ea in alteram tabulam reijcit: dicens, honora parentes: non occides: non mechaberis: non furaberis: non dices falsum testimonium: non concupisces. Atq; hæc est illa, quam Mat. 22. Dominus de summa legis rogatus duabus ijs, quas diximus, partibus comprehendit materiam.
units.tr: The matter, as it is set out in this place, is contained in two parts, namely the love of God and the love of neighbour. For first he recalls the things that pertain to the worship of God, saying: "I am your God; you shall have no other gods; you shall not make graven images; you shall not take the name of the Lord in vain; you shall not profane the sabbath." Those things that pertain to love of neighbour he places on the second tablet, saying: "Honour your father and mother; you shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness; you shall not covet." This is that summary which the Lord, when asked about the chief of the law, comprehended in the two parts we have mentioned (Matt. 22).

units.la: Ex quo potest intelligi quid Christianus lector hoc libro fit cogniturus: primùm, vt Deum verum, vnum, summo studio sicuti hic præscribitur, reuereamur: ac neque dæmonia, neque creaturas vllas simul cum Deo coniungamus: & ipsum Deum neque negligenter, neque aliter atque ab ipso præscriptum est honoremus: tum autem quod tibi nolis fieri alteri ne feceris: quod præstari tibi cupias id ipse præstes alijs fidem & dilectionem: In quod studium si incumberent homines, neque de religione, neque de bonorum possessione controuerteretur. Igitur quod ad materiam pertinet: non est quod hæreticam, falsam, seditiosam, turbulentam hic doctrinam proponi putes: sed diuinam, veram, salutarem.
units.tr: From this one can understand what the Christian reader is going to learn from this book: first, that we should revere the one true God with the highest zeal, as is prescribed here, and join neither demons nor any creatures with God, and that we should honour God himself neither carelessly nor otherwise than as he has prescribed; then, that you should not do to another what you would not want done to you, and that you should show to others the faith and love that you desire to receive. If men were devoted to this zeal, there would be no dispute either about religion or about the possession of goods. Therefore, as far as the matter is concerned, you should not think that a heretical, false, seditious or turbulent doctrine is put forward here, but a divine, true and wholesome one.

units.la: Iam quoniam Deus nobis, quibus hæc materia percipienda proponitur, consuluit: ne rudis esset & indigesta moles, quasi quoddam informe chaos: in ordinem optimum disposita proponitur hæc materia. Ac quemadmodum philosophi veteres rerum, quæ sunt, omnium classes decem, quas κατηγορίας Graeci vocant, fecere: sic Deus omnis diuinę humanæq; sapientiæ decem capita posuit.
units.tr: Now since God, who has proposed this matter to us to be grasped, has taken thought for us, so that it should not be a rough and undigested mass, a kind of formless chaos, this matter is set out in the best order. And just as the ancient philosophers made ten classes of all the things that exist, which the Greeks call categories, so God has set down ten heads of all divine and human wisdom.

units.la: Nec prætereundum est, quod quidam ex primis duobus vnum faciunt, & vltimum quod vnum est in duo secant, vt illud de fimulachris expungant. Augustinum secutos se dicunt, qui eo numero triadis sanctæ mysterium adfirmauerit in libr.2.quæst.super Exod.cap.71.
units.tr: Nor must it be passed over that some make the first two into one, and divide the last, which is one, into two, so as to strike out the prohibition of images. They say they follow Augustine, who, in book 2 of his Questions on Exodus, chapter 71, asserted the mystery of the holy Trinity by this number.

units.la: Sed Augustino primum vetustiores patres, tum illum ipsum sibi, deniq; Mosem etiam opponimus.
units.tr: But against Augustine we set the earlier Fathers, then Augustine himself, and finally Moses himself.

units.la: Athanas.in Synopsi sua, argumentū fiue summam Exodi describens: vbi ad decalogū ventū est, sic ait: ἡ πρὸ αὐτῶν τὰ ἐν πλαξὶ ἃ ἐκ[?] ἐντολὰς ταύτας. Πρῶτος, ἐγώ εἰμι κύριος ὁ θεός σου. Δευτέραν, Οὐ ποιήσεις σεαυτῷ εἴδωλον, ἀλλ' ἐ[?] πάντος ὁμοίωμα. Τρίτον, Οὐ λήμψῃ τὸ ὄνομα κυρίου τοῦ θεοῦ σου ἐπὶ ματαίῳ. Τέταρτον, μνήσθητι τὴν ἡμέραν τῶν σαββάτων. Πέμπτην, τίμα τὸν πατέρα σου καὶ τὴν μητέρα σου. Ἕκτον, οὐ φονεύσεις. Ἑβδόμην, μοιχεύσεις. Ὄγδοον, οὐ κλέψεις. Ἔνατον, οὐ ψευδομαρτυρήσεις κατὰ τοῦ πλησίον σου μαρτυρίαν. Δέκατον, οὐκ ἐπιθυμήσεις τὴν γυναῖκα τοῦ πλησίον σου, οὔτε οἰκίαν τοῦ πλησίον σου, [?] Ex quibus perspicuum fit Athanasium has decem leges, & duabus tabulis distribuere, & eodem quo nos ordine collocare: non autem ex duabus primis vnam: vel ex vltima vna duas facere.
units.tr: Athanasius, in his Synopsis, in which he describes the argument or sum of Exodus, when he comes to the Decalogue, says: "The things written on the tablets, these commandments.
