First: 'I am the Lord your God.' Second: 'You shall not make for yourself an idol, nor any likeness.' Third: 'You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain.' Fourth: 'Remember the day of the sabbaths.' Fifth: 'Honour your father and your mother.' Sixth: 'You shall not kill.' Seventh: 'You shall not commit adultery.' Eighth: 'You shall not steal.' Ninth: 'You shall not bear false witness against your neighbour.' Tenth: 'You shall not covet your neighbour's wife, nor his house.'" [Ἡ πρὸ αὐτῶν τὰ ἐν πλαξὶ ἃ ἐκ[?] ἐντολὰς ταύτας. Πρῶτος, ἐγώ εἰμι κύριος ὁ θεός σου. Δευτέραν, Οὐ ποιήσεις σεαυτῷ εἴδωλον, ἀλλ' ἐ[?] πάντος ὁμοίωμα. Τρίτον, Οὐ λήμψῃ τὸ ὄνομα κυρίου τοῦ θεοῦ σου ἐπὶ ματαίῳ. Τέταρτον, μνήσθητι τὴν ἡμέραν τῶν σαββάτων. Πέμπτην, τίμα τὸν πατέρα σου καὶ τὴν μητέρα σου. Ἕκτον, οὐ φονεύσεις. Ἑβδόμην, μοιχεύσεις. Ὄγδοον, οὐ κλέψεις. Ἔνατον, οὐ ψευδομαρτυρήσεις κατὰ τοῦ πλησίον σου μαρτυρίαν. Δέκατον, οὐκ ἐπιθυμήσεις τὴν γυναῖκα τοῦ πλησίον σου, οὔτε οἰκίαν τοῦ πλησίον σου, [?]] From which it is plain that Athanasius distributes these ten laws into two tables, and arranges them in the same order as we do; he does not make one out of the first two, nor two out of the last.

units.la: Origenes autem homilia super Exodum 8. docet scire se nonnullos esse, qui primum & secundum mandatum in vnum cogant: sed eorum sententiam cum veritate decalogi pugnare: concludendum ergo esse, quod primum mandatum sit, Non erunt tibi Dij alij præter me: secundum vero, non facies tibi idolum, neque vllam similitudinem: & cætera. Ac deinceps exposito mandato primo ad secundi expositionem veniens: ait, Posthæc videamus quid etiam secundum videtur continere mandatum. Non facies tibi ipsi idolum, &c.
units.tr: Origen, however, in Homily 8 on Exodus, teaches that he knows some who force the first and second commandments into one, but that their opinion conflicts with the truth of the Decalogue. It must therefore be concluded that the first commandment is, "You shall have no other gods before me," and the second, "You shall not make for yourself an idol, nor any likeness," and so on. And then, after expounding the first commandment and coming to the exposition of the second, he says: "Let us next see what the second commandment also seems to contain: You shall not make for yourself an idol, etc."

units.la: Et Chrysostomus homilia super Matthæum expositionis secundæ 49. dicit legis iustitiam decem mandatis haud secus atq; decem mensibus annus efficitur, constare: primum (inquit) cognoscere vnum Deum: secundum, abstinere ab idolis: tertium, non peierare: quartum, colere sabbatum spirituale: quintum, honorare patrem & matrem: sextum, non occidere: septimum, non adulterari: octauum, non furtum facere: nonum, non falsum testimonium dicere: decimum, nullam rem proximi concupiscere. Ex quibus omnibus perspici potest eandem etiam huic decalogi distributionem placuisse, quæ recepta est.
units.tr: Chrysostom, in his second exposition, Homily 49 on Matthew, says that the righteousness of the law consists of ten commandments, just as a year is made up of ten months. "The first," he says, "is to know the one God; second, to abstain from idols; third, not to swear falsely; fourth, to keep the spiritual sabbath; fifth, to honour father and mother; sixth, not to kill; seventh, not to commit adultery; eighth, not to steal; ninth, not to bear false witness; tenth, not to covet anything that belongs to one's neighbour." From all of these it can be seen that this same division of the Decalogue, which has been received, was also pleasing to him.

units.la: Iam & Gregorius Nazianzenus in eo volumine, quo poemata viri illius in vnum collecta Aldus edidit: decem versibus heroicis leges decem sic conscripsit vt prope singulis præceptis singuli versus respondeant.
units.tr: Again, Gregory of Nazianzus, in that volume in which Aldus published the poems of that man collected together, wrote the ten laws in ten heroic verses, so arranged that nearly each precept corresponds to a single verse.

units.la: Eandem diuisionem Hieronymus in cap.6.epistolæ ad Ephesios, & Ambrosius in eundem locum scribentes retinent.
units.tr: Jerome, in chapter 6 of the Epistle to the Ephesians, and Ambrose, writing on the same passage, keep the same division.

units.la: His adde Phil.& Iosephum si nō Christianos, tamen antiquissimos, atq; rerū Hebræarū peritissimos: qui eandem legum diuisionem retinent, ac tantum in eo quod cuiq; tabulæ quinq; leges assignat, à nostris variant. Philo enim in eo quæ de decalogo scripsit libro leges illas omnes, ait, in duas πεντάδας diuinitus distributas, ac duabus tabulis descriptas esse: quas deinceps sic enumerat. ἡ μὲν οὖν (inquit) ἀμείνων πεντάς τοιαύτη τῶν περὶ μοναρχίας [?], ᾗ μοναρχεῖται ὁ κόσμος, περὶ ξοάνων, καὶ ἀγαλμάτων, καὶ σωμάτων ἀφιδ' ὑμνάτων χειροποιήτων, περὶ τὸ μὴ λαμβάνειν ἐπὶ ματαίῳ θεὸν ἐπὶ πρίστας [?], περὶ γονέων τιμῆς. In quo habes quinque leges priores, de monarchia Dei, qua solus ipse mundum regit: tum de idolis: tertio de nomine Domini: quarto, de sanctificatione sabbathi: quinto, de parentum obseruantia. Ac quanquam hæc ipsa verborum collocatio, & distinctio ad id, quod volumus, demonstrandum sufficiant: tamen ipse postea rem hoc ipso magis aperit: quod cum multa de statuis atque imaginibus disseruisset, ait se ita ad hunc modum enarrata lege secunda, ad sequentem transfire. Quod indicio est hanc de idolis illi secundam visam esse. Mox de altera classe legum sic scribit: ἡ δ' ἑτέρα πεντάς τὰς πάσας ἀγορεύσεις περιέχει μοιχείας, φόνου, κλοπῆς, ψευδομαρτυρίας, ἐπιθυμίας. Ac quanquam hic etiam ordo satis perspicue legem vltimam de concupiscentia doceat esse: tamen idem in epilogo huius in Decalogum descriptionis singulas sigillatim repetens: secundam de idolis, decimam de concupiscentia nominat. Ergo & hic vir, quem illi ceu Iudæum non respuent, cum illi & vetus ecclesia multum tribuerit: & sua opera quæ pie & docte scri-pta sunt. pta sunt opera maximam laudem concilient: harum legum seriem eam seruat: quam nos sequimur.
units.tr: To these add Philo and Josephus, if not Christians, yet very ancient and most expert in Hebrew matters, who keep the same division of the laws and differ from us only in that they assign five laws to each table. For Philo, in his work on the Decalogue, says that all those laws were divinely distributed into two pentads and written on two tables, and then he enumerates them thus: "The better pentad, then, is of this kind: concerning the sole rule of God, by which the world is governed; concerning images, statues and bodies made by hand; concerning not taking God's name in vain [...]; concerning honour of parents." [ἡ μὲν οὖν ἀμείνων πεντάς τοιαύτη τῶν περὶ μοναρχίας [?], ᾗ μοναρχεῖται ὁ κόσμος, περὶ ξοάνων, καὶ ἀγαλμάτων, καὶ σωμάτων ἀφιδ' ὑμνάτων χειροποιήτων, περὶ τὸ μὴ λαμβάνειν ἐπὶ ματαίῳ θεὸν ἐπὶ πρίστας [?], περὶ γονέων τιμῆς.] In this you have the first five laws: on the monarchy of God, by whom alone the world is ruled; then on idols; third, on the name of the Lord; fourth, on the sanctification of the sabbath; fifth, on observance towards parents. Although this very arrangement and distinction of the words is enough to show what we want, he himself later makes the matter clearer, for after discussing at length statues and images, he says that, having thus explained the second law in this way, he passes to the next one. That is evidence that he saw this as the second law, the one about idols. Soon afterwards he writes of the second class of laws in this way: "The other pentad contains all the prohibitions: of adultery, murder, theft, false witness, and covetousness." And although this order also makes it quite clear that the last law concerns concupiscence, nevertheless in the epilogue to his description of the Decalogue, when he repeats each law separately, he calls the second the one about idols and the tenth the one about concupiscence. Therefore this man too, whom they will not spurn as a Jew, since the ancient Church attributed much to him, and whose works, written piously and learnedly, win the greatest praise, keeps the sequence of these laws that we follow.

units.la: Iosephus autem lib.3. Iouδαικῆς ἀρχαιολογίας cap.4. Decalogum sic enumerat.
units.tr: Josephus, however, in book 3 of his Jewish Antiquities, chapter 4, enumerates the Decalogue thus:

units.la: Διδάσκει μὲν οὖν ὁ πρῶτος λόγος ὅτι θεὸς εἷς, καὶ τοῦτον σέβεσθαι μόνον.
units.tr: The first word teaches that God is one, and that he alone is to be worshipped. [Διδάσκει μὲν οὖν ὁ πρῶτος λόγος ὅτι θεὸς εἷς, καὶ τοῦτον σέβεσθαι μόνον.]

units.la: ὁ δὲ δεύτερος κελεύει μηδένος εἰκόνα ποιήσαντας προσκυνεῖν.
units.tr: The second commands that no one make an image and worship it. [ὁ δὲ δεύτερος κελεύει μηδένος εἰκόνα ποιήσαντας προσκυνεῖν.]

units.la: ὁ τρίτος δὲ τὸ μηδὲν φαύλως τὸν θεὸν ὀμνύειν.
units.tr: The third forbids swearing by God lightly. [ὁ δὲ τρίτος δὲ τὸ μηδὲν φαύλως τὸν θεὸν ὀμνύειν.]

units.la: ὁ τέταρτος παραγγέλλει τὰς ἑβδομάδας ἀναπαυομένους ἀπὸ παντὸς ἔργου.
units.tr: The fourth bids us rest from every work on the seventh day of each week. [ὁ τέταρτος παραγγέλλει τὰς ἑβδομάδας ἀναπαυομένους ἀπὸ παντὸς ἔργου.]

units.la: πέμπτος γονεῖς τιμᾶν.
units.tr: The fifth: to honour parents. [πέμπτος γονεῖς τιμᾶν.]

units.la: ἕκτος ἀποκτείνειν φόνον.
units.tr: The sixth: not to commit murder. [ἕκτος ἀποκτείνειν φόνον.]

units.la: ὁ ἕβδομος μὴ μοιχεύειν.
units.tr: The seventh: not to commit adultery. [ὁ ἕβδομος μὴ μοιχεύειν.]

units.la: ὄγδοος μὴ κλέπτειν.
units.tr: The eighth: not to steal. [ὄγδοος μὴ κλέπτειν.]

units.la: ἔνατος μὴ ψευδομαρτυρεῖν.
units.tr: The ninth: not to bear false witness. [ἔνατος μὴ ψευδομαρτυρεῖν.]

units.la: δέκατος μηδὲ ἐπιθυμίαν λαμβάνειν.
units.tr: The tenth: not to conceive desire (not to covet). [δέκατος μηδὲ ἐπιθυμίαν λαμβάνειν.]

units.la: Ex quibus verbis colligi potest hanc illarum legum seriem vel ipsa vetustatis authoritate comprobari: cuius Iosephus, & Eusebius, qui illum non in vno in loco celebrat: & Sozomeno, qui illum cum multas ob res tum ob praeclarum Christo perhibitum testimonium mirifice extollit: minime malus testis visus est.
units.tr: From these words it can be gathered that this sequence of those laws is confirmed even by the authority of antiquity. Josephus and Eusebius, who praises him in more than one place, and Sozomen, who greatly extols him for many reasons but above all for the excellent testimony he bore to Christ, seem to be by no means poor witnesses of it.

units.la: Sed quemadmodum hic nouus, quem statuarum patroni obtrudunt, ordo pugnat cum vniuersa antiquitate: & illi sibi nisi Diuum Augustinum, quem praetexant, habent neminem: & illis ipsis, & Augustino, ipsum Augustinum opponemus. Is in lib. Quaest. Vet. & Nou. Test. decalogum sic refert. Non sint tibi Dij alij praeter me: primum verbum hoc est.
units.tr: But just as this new order that the defenders of the statues push forward clashes with all of antiquity, they have no one on their side except Augustine, whom they put forward as cover. So we will set Augustine himself against them, and against them too. In his book Quaestiones veteris et novi Testamenti, he gives the Decalogue as follows: "Let there not be other gods for you besides me: this is the first word."

units.la: Et subiecit secundum, Non facies tibi vllam similitudinem eorum quae sunt in coelo sursum & in terra deorsum: neque in aqua quae est sub terra.
units.tr: And he added the second: "You shall not make for yourself any likeness of the things that are in heaven above or on the earth beneath, nor in the water that is under the earth."

units.la: Deinde adiecit tertium, Non sumes nomen Dei tui in vanum: Non enim mundabit eum Dominus, qui sumpsit nomen eius in vanum: hoc est, non in mendacio nomen Dei tui assumes vt periures per illud.
units.tr: Then he added the third: "You shall not take the name of your God in vain, for the Lord will not hold guiltless him who has taken his name in vain." That is, "you shall not take the name of your God in a lie, so as to swear falsely by it."

units.la: Dehinc quarto loco dicit, Sabbathum Domini Dei tui seruabis, & non facies in illo vllum opus seruile.
units.tr: Next, in the fourth place, he says: "You shall keep the Sabbath of the Lord your God, and you shall do no servile work in it."

units.la: Haec quatuor verba sunt de decem: ista ad Deum proprie pertinent. Haec sunt in prima tabula scripta.
units.tr: These four words belong to the ten, and they properly pertain to God. They are written on the first tablet.

units.la: Deinde in secunda tabula haec continentur, Primum verbum est, honora patrem tuum & matrem tuam.
units.tr: Then the second tablet contains the following. The first word is: "Honour your father and your mother."

units.la: Secundum, Non occides.
units.tr: The second: "You shall not kill."

units.la: Tertium, Non fornicaberis.
units.tr: The third: "You shall not commit adultery."

units.la: Quartum, Non furaberis.
units.tr: The fourth: "You shall not steal."

units.la: Quintum, Non falsum testimonium dices.
units.tr: The fifth: "You shall not bear false witness."

units.la: Sextum non concupisces quicquam proximi tui. His Augustinus paulo post adiecit etiam haec verba: Itaq; habes inquit, & mandata distincta, & numerum eorum consummatum & quae & quot singulis tabulis scripta sunt. Si igitur placuit Augustino librum hunc tribuere: age placeat etiam, quod is in eo cum veteris ecclesiae; tum totius antiquitatis consensum secutus: primae tabulae quatuor, secundae sex leges assignat: ac neque ex duabus primis vnam, neque ex vltima vna duas facit.
units.tr: "Thou shalt not covet anything that belongs to thy neighbour." After this, Augustine added shortly afterwards these words: "So you have, he says, both the commandments set apart, and their number complete, and what and how many are written on each tablet." If it therefore pleased Augustine to attribute this book, then let it also please us that in this he followed the agreement of both the ancient Church and all antiquity: he assigns four precepts to the first tablet and six to the second, and he neither makes two out of the first nor one out of the last into two.

units.la: Mosem deniq;, si veritatem Hebraicam penitius inspicias, ipsum habes diuisionis huius authorem. Is enim concupiscentiam vnico verbo vetat omnem. Et Paulus vno peccati genere eam omnem comprehendit. Quae eo libentius commemoraui, vt extaret certa ac recta harum legum diuisio. Sed ad primum.
units.tr: Finally, Moses himself, if you examine the Hebrew text more closely, is the author of this division. For he forbids covetousness in every form with a single word. And Paul includes all of it under one kind of sin. I have mentioned these things the more gladly so that a certain and correct division of these laws may stand. But to the first.

units.la: Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus, qui eduxi te de terra Aegypti, e domo seruitutis. Non habebis Deos alienos coram, &c. Hoc praeceptum primum est non solum ordine, sed & sua natura ac vi: quippe quod hoc neglecto, reliqua sunt irrita: hoc seruato, rata sint reliqua: tum quod Deus sit rerum omnium principium: in eius reuerentia si impingas, in portu impegeris: & pietas cum sapientiae tum virtutum omnium initium est. Quibus de causis hoc recte principium statuitur. Sed & hoc spectauit Dominus, ne quod vsu venire solet, in contemptum aliquem lex abiret sua: quoniam primo hoc praecepto quasi trifariam remouet. Primum enim ostendit abs se, quasi rerum omnium fonte, quicquid vspiam fit pendere, vt ei fit parendum necessario: dein promittit suam gratiam, quod Deus nobis sit futurus, quod vnum bonum merito nos ad eum amandum allicit; denique beneficium commemorat quod gratos animos moueat ad pietatem. Et certe hæc lex summam omnis,quæ de vera ac falsa religione traditur,doctrinæ continet: quippe quæ doceat, quis Deus sit colendus,qui item Dij non colendi. Pars prior sic habet: Ego sum Deus,&c. Singula considera.
units.tr: I am the LORD thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. Thou shalt have no other gods before me, etc. This precept is first not only in order but also in its nature and force: for if it is neglected the rest are void, and if it is kept the rest are valid. Moreover, God is the beginning of all things, and if you strike against reverence for him, you will have run aground in the harbour itself; and piety is the beginning both of wisdom and of all virtues. For these reasons this is rightly set down as the first principle. But the Lord also had this in view, that his law should not fall into some contempt, as often happens; for by this first precept he removes such contempt, as it were, in three ways. First, he shows that whatever happens anywhere depends on him as the fount of all things, so that obedience to him is necessary. Second, he promises his grace, that God will be ours, a single good which draws us rightly to love him. Third, he recalls the benefit which moves grateful hearts to piety. And certainly this law contains the sum of all the teaching handed down concerning true and false religion, for it teaches which God is to be worshipped and likewise which gods are not to be worshipped. The first part reads thus: I am God, etc. Consider each part separately.

units.la: Ego sum Iehova, Id est, ego sum illud ens in quo, per quod, quicquid est existit uspiam, & conservatur. Atque sic significat divinitatem veram, quæ est principium, conservatio, vita rerum. Nam Iehova existentiam significat & αὐτουσίαν: non pendet ab alio, non eget alterius opera. Exod.3. Ego sum qui sum. Apoc.1. Sum Α & Ω[?]. Est suus stellis & splendor & cursus: sed divinitus attributus: est sua lepori celeritas, vulpi versutia, robur leoni: Solomoni sapientia: sunt alijs alia munera, sed data divinitus.
units.tr: I am Jehovah. That is, I am that being in whom, through whom, and by whom whatever exists anywhere exists and is preserved. Thus it signifies the true divinity, which is the principle, preservation and life of all things. For Jehovah signifies existence and self-subsistence [αὐτουσία]: he depends on no other, and needs no other's help. Exod. 3: "I am who I am." Rev. 1: "I am the Alpha and the Omega [Α and Ω]." The stars have their own brightness and course, but these are given by God. The hare has its swiftness, the fox its cunning, the lion its strength, Solomon his wisdom: other creatures have other gifts, but all are given by God.

units.la: Iam cum sint & consistant in ipso omnia, Rom.11. Vide quàm portentosum sit, ab eo vel-le secessionem facere, extra quem vitæ nullus sit locus: ei velle cultum negare, qui dignita-tes & honores, quibus quisq; potitus est, dedit. Quamobrem animis considerandaac tenen-da hæc est ratio, ut Deum summo honore & amore prosequare, & ei quicquid habes bonorum acceptum feras.
units.tr: Since all things both are and consist in him (Rom. 11), see how monstrous it is to wish to withdraw from him, outside of whom there is no place for life, or to wish to deny worship to him who gave the dignities and honours that each one has obtained. Therefore this reasoning must be considered and held in mind: that you should pursue God with the highest honour and love, and ascribe to him whatever good things you have as received from him.

units.la: Elohim, Vox ipsa potentiam significat eam, quæ rebus conservandis ac tuendis præsens est omnibus: ut intelligas ab illo te vel defendi, vel eripi, vel conservari. Semper enim Deus adest creaturis suis, cum opus est. Hierem.23. Putas ne Deus è vicino sum, dicit Dominus, & non Deus de longe? Ibi. Num non cœlum & terram ego impleo. Psal.138. Quo ibo à spiritu tuo, & quo à facie tua fugiam? Si ascendero, &c. Acto.17. Paulus ait, Non procul abest ab uno quoque nostrum Deus: per ipsum vivimus movemur & sumus. Unde & Θεὸς ἀπὸ τοῦ θεῖν[?], hoc est, ab accurrendo.
units.tr: Elohim. The word itself signifies that power which is present to all things to preserve and protect them, so that you may understand that by him you are either defended, or rescued, or preserved. For God is always present to his creatures when there is need. Jer. 23: "Am I a God at hand, says the Lord, and not a God afar off?" And there: "Do I not fill heaven and earth?" Ps. 138: "Where shall I go from your Spirit, or where shall I flee from your face? If I ascend..." Acts 17: Paul says, "God is not far from each one of us; for in him we live, move and have our being." Hence also θεὸς from θεῖν [God from running], that is, from hastening to help.

units.la: Atque sic Deus non solum vi, quemadmodum supra, sed & dulcedine quadam vultu al-licere: cum promittit se nobis ubique præsentem esse velle, ut sua nos conservet virtute. In qua nobis tam bene stabilitata spes esse potest, ut immortalitatem animarum & resurrec-tionem corporum, id est, perennem felicitatem inde probari posse Christus ipse docuerit. Nam quibus se Deus promisit Deum fore, eos vivere oportere dixit. Quocirca audiens Deum ti-bi esse: spem retine & præsentis & futuræ felicitatis.
units.tr: And so God allures us not only by force, as above, but also by a certain sweetness of countenance, when he promises that he wishes to be present with us everywhere, so as to preserve us by his power. In this God we can have a hope so well established that Christ himself taught that from it the immortality of souls and the resurrection of bodies, that is, everlasting happiness, can be proved. For he said that those to whom God has promised to be God must live. Therefore, hearing that God is yours, hold fast to the hope of both present and future happiness.

units.la: Cæterum quod hæc vox pluraliter ponitur & cum singulari nomine & pronomine con-iungitur: id docet Deum nobis esse eiusmodi, qui quidem unus sit substantia, trinus autem personis.
units.tr: Moreover, that this word is put in the plural, and joined with a singular noun and pronoun, teaches that God is to us such that he is indeed one in substance, but three in persons.

units.la: Estque positum omnibus hæresibus repagulum. Nam si quis Deos plures obijciat, tu contra, Ego, pronomè obijce: sin quis trinitatem abneget, Elohim plurale nomen obijce. Quo fiet unum substantia: personis trinum habeas Deū. Extant autem in sacris literis, & in rerum natura, & in nobis ipsis sacrosanctæ triadis mysteria. Scriptura Gen.1. Matth.3. Apoc.4. & alibi trinitatem docet. Sol sua substantia, suo calore, & splendore Deum trinum & unū repræsentat. Anima cuiusque nostrum propria, cum offert in se considerandam inte-ligenti-am, memoriam, voluntatem: an non sanctæ trinitatis nos admonet? Sic patri principium a-gendi rerumque origo tribuitur: filio sapientia & consilium. Spiritui sancto virtus actionis. Sed hæc de Deo satis hoc quidem loco.
units.tr: And this is a bulwark placed against all heresies. For if anyone objects to you that there are several gods, you reply with the pronoun "I"; but if anyone denies the Trinity, you object the plural name Elohim. By this it becomes one in substance, and you have God three in persons. The mysteries of the sacred Triad are found both in the holy writings and in the nature of things and in ourselves. Scripture teaches the Trinity in Gen. 1, Matt. 3, Rev. 4 and elsewhere. The sun, by its substance, its heat and its brightness, represents the triune and one God. Does not the soul of each of us, when it offers in itself understanding, memory and will to be considered, remind us of the holy Trinity? Thus the Father is attributed the origin of acting and the source of things; to the Son, wisdom and counsel; to the Holy Spirit, the power of action. But this is enough about God for the present place.

units.la: Quod autem addit, Tuus, qua tantam multitudinem hominum singulari numero allo-quitur: id significat Deum & communem omnium & singulorum Deum esse. Ergo singulis & universis colendus, timendus, patroni, vindicis, patris loco habendus est.
units.tr: Moreover, what he adds, "your," in which he addresses so great a multitude of men in the singular number, signifies that God is the God both of all in common and of each one. Therefore he is to be worshipped and feared by individuals and by all together, and is to be held in the place of patron, avenger and father.

units.la: Qui eduxi te de domo seruitutis. Hoc, ne quid desit, & ut eum se esse facto probet, addit. Indeed enim quod dicitur iam multo certius est esse rerum. Satis esset obsignatas habere literas, sed factum hoc magis probat. Veluti ignotus aliquis adveniens, atque commendationem scripto obsignato comprehensam porrigens, si, se eum præstet, quem literæ prædicant: vita, mores, ars illum multo faciunt, quàm literæ celebriorem. Quare ne tantum haberes literas, factis se Deus ostendit eum esse, quem sacræ literæ prædicant. Verum observa singula. Eduxi, inquit: non mitigaui, non leniui tyranni iugum: sed opem præsis tuli talem, ut iugo fa-cti sitis liberi. Vides perfecta esse quæ Deus fert auxilia. Ex Ægypto, de domo seruitutis. Vides regna aliud nihil esse nisi ergastula, pistrina, molas. Magnum hoc est beneficium: pro inde constituta est ei perpetua memoria: tum etiam typus est eius ser-vitutis, à qua nos Christus eripuit. Ex quibus intelligimus eum esse Deum in quo nobis sit vita, salus, æterna felicitas in Iesu Christo. Amen.
units.tr: Who brought you out of the house of bondage. He adds this, lest anything be lacking, and to prove by the deed that he is who he is. For what is said by deed is far more certain than what is said by word. It would be enough to have sealed letters, but the deed proves it more. Suppose some unknown man arrives, presenting a letter of commendation sealed up; if he shows himself to be the man the letter describes, his life, character and skill make him far more celebrated than the letter. So, lest you have only the letters, God shows by his deeds that he is the one whom the sacred writings proclaim. But observe each detail. He brought out, he says: he did not soften or lighten the tyrant's yoke, but brought such help that you were made free from the yoke. You see that the aids which God brings are complete. Out of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. You see that kingdoms are nothing other than prisons, mills and millstones. This is a great benefit, and for this reason a perpetual memorial has been established for it. Moreover, it is also a type of that bondage from which Christ has rescued us. From these things we understand that he is the God in whom we have life, salvation and eternal happiness in Jesus Christ. Amen.

units.la: SERMO III.
units.tr: SERMON III.

units.la: 7 Non erunt tibi Dij alij coram me.
units.tr: 7 You shall have no other gods before me.

units.la: CVm hæc ipsa,quam proponit Moses,doctrina:sit ac nominetur fœdus Domini,seu de scriptio capitum eius,quod est inter Deum,atque homines fœderis: certe & proposi-tæ rei & eius tractationi competebat:vt primo omnia loco,quid partibus partes vltro citro que promisissent describeretur. Nam cum hæ partes in vnum fœdus coire velint: primum quid is nobis velit præstare:quid item à nobis is requirat indicandum est.
units.tr: Since this very teaching which Moses sets forth is called the covenant of the Lord, a writing down of its terms, which exists between God and men, the covenant partners, it was certainly fitting both for the matter proposed and for its treatment that first of all it should be described what each party promised to the other. For since these parties wish to come together into one covenant, it must first be shown what he wishes to grant us and what he in turn requires of us.

units.la: Ac qualem quidem nobis se præstare velit, hoc ipso docet,quod ait, Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus,qui eduxi te de terra Ægypti,&c. Id indicio semper fuit omnibus mortalibus: De-um esse vitam,& salutem suorum,req; ipsa voluntatem hanc probasse. Nam id omnium gen-tium consensu receptum est. Quod eo potest intelligi,quod & in scripta philosophorum,& in leges atq; iura populorum,quidquid de religione dici potest,relatum est. Veluti in II.xij. tab.primi tituli duo priora capita significant.Eadem abre non est alienum quod Pomponi-us Iureconsultus religionem erga Deum inter iuris naturalis exempla refert, l.vt vim. ff.de iust.&iur.Et Cicero,de ipsis quidem(inquit)hominibus nulla gens est neq; tam mansueta, neq; tam fera,quæ non etiamsi ignoret qualem habere Deum deceat, tamen habendum sci-at.Omitto complura alia, quæ & ex Iustinianeo Codice & ex Nouellis constitutionibus af-ferri possent,testimonia. Quæ profecto significant omnia, Deum velle,vt nobis persuasum sit:se curam ac memoriam nostri perpetua cum beneuolentia custodire.
units.tr: As for the kind of God he wishes to show himself to us, he teaches this by saying, I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, etc. This has always been a sign to all mortals that God is the life and salvation of his people, and that by this very fact he has proved his goodwill. For this is accepted by the consent of all nations. This can be understood from the fact that whatever can be said about religion has been handed down both in the writings of the philosophers and in the laws and rights of peoples. Thus the first two chapters of the first title of the Twelve Tables signify this. Nor is it irrelevant here that the jurist Pomponius counts religion towards God among the examples of natural law, l. ut vim, ff. de iust. et iur. And Cicero says: "There is no nation, among men themselves, so gentle or so savage that, even if it does not know what sort of God it ought to have, it does not know that it ought to have one." I omit many other testimonies which could be brought from the Justinianic Code and the Novels. All of these certainly show that God wills us to be persuaded that he keeps watch over us and remembers us with perpetual goodwill.

units.la: Cæterum quales erga ipsum nos esse deceat,hoc ipso dicit quod ait, Non habebis Deos alienos coram me. Quod quasi præcedentis particulæ consequens est, & perinde di&tum,ac si dicas,cum Deus tibi se totum despondeat:tu illi vicissim vni totus sis deditus.Sed quid si-bi velit singula verba suppeditant.Non habere:Dij alieni:Coram facie.
units.tr: Moreover, what sort of attitude we ought to have towards him, he shows by saying, You shall not have other gods before me. This follows as a consequence of the preceding clause, and is said in the same way as if you were to say: since God has pledged himself wholly to you, you in turn should be wholly devoted to him alone. But what he wishes by each single phrase, the words themselves supply: "to have," "other gods," "before the face."

units.la: Non habebis, Siue nō sint tibi. Quo prohibet ne quis sibi faciat aut constituatDeos alienos: quasiq; cultum Dei notat,& ab eo quicquid alienum est remouet. Ergo quid ei sit contrari-um,quid item consentaneum inuestigetur necesse est.
units.tr: You shall not have, that is, whether they are not yours. By this he forbids anyone to make or set up for himself other gods. He marks out the worship of God, and removes from it whatever is foreign to it. Therefore it is necessary to investigate what is contrary to it and what is in agreement with it.

units.la: Contrarium est religioni veræ: 1. Si pro vero Deo colas eos, qui reuera Dij non sunt. Quod genus cultuum plena fuerunt in gentibus omnia.Nam in cœlo,terra,inferis,Dij quæsi-ti & culti sunt.Sap. 13. Si ipsorum pulchritudinem,potentiam,& virtutes alias mirati sunt: cur non eorum conditorem mirantur & venerantur magis?Stultus sis qui plus operi,quàm opifici tribuas.Opus ab artifice restaurari potest,à se ipso nunquam.
units.tr: The following is contrary to true religion: (1) if you worship as the true God those who are in truth not gods. Kinds of worship of this sort were everywhere in the nations. For gods were sought out and worshipped in heaven, on earth, and in the underworld (Wisdom 13). If they admired their beauty, power and other virtues, why do they not admire and venerate their Maker all the more? You would be foolish to attribute more to the work than to the workman. A work can be restored by its craftsman; it can never restore itself.

units.la: 2 Quando verus quidem & vnicus Deus : sed non rite & ex eius præscripto colitur. Hoc enim alienum à vero cultu dicunt esse & scriptura sacra & recta ratio.Ac scriptura qui-dem Matth.15.frustra me colunt traditionibus hominum. Quo omnis,quæ in obseruatione legum humanarum poni posset, fiducia frangitur ac sternitur. Sed ratio hoc ipsum etiam pulchre docet.Deo seruire est eius voluntatem speƈtare & sequi:at eam sacris literis expref-sam si negligas,ac tuam speƈtes potius:vtri quæso, tibi ne an Deo seruis?Dein beneficij lo-co non accipitur quod nolenti & respuenti datur. Vere enim dictum est, ἀχαρ&ς ἐντοιαι ἐχθρας ὡσ' ἐν διαφέρει. Quamobrem ei qui Deo seruire velit non vlla humana, sed sola di-uina voluntas speƈtanda est: procul esto quod nobis videtur bonum : ex verbo Dei metie-mur bonum.
units.tr: (2) When the God who is indeed true and one is worshipped, but not rightly and not according to his prescription. For both Holy Scripture and sound reason say that this is alien to true worship. Scripture says, in Matthew 15: "In vain do they worship me with the traditions of men." By this, all confidence is broken and overthrown which might be placed in the observance of human laws. But reason also teaches this beautifully. To serve God is to look to his will and follow it. If you neglect his will as expressed in the sacred writings, and look rather to your own, I ask you: which of the two do you serve, yourself or God? Again, that is not received as a benefit which is given to one who is unwilling and refuses it. For it is truly said: [ἀχάριστος ἔντοιο ἐχθρᾶς ὥσ' ἐν διαφέρει], that is, the ungrateful man is no different from an enemy. Therefore, for one who wishes to serve God, not any human will but only the divine will is to be looked to. Let what seems good to us be far away; we shall measure what is good by the Word of God.

units.la: 3 Cum verus quidem Deus colitur,sed tantum ore & verbis:non autem vita recta ac bo na,quæ verbo Dei fit consentanea. Veluti nobis in ore est euangelium : in vita ac moribus Epicuri religio.Atq; hæc omnia nisi caueantur primo præcepto non statur.
units.tr: (3) When the true God is worshipped, but only with the mouth and in words, and not with a good and upright life which agrees with the Word of God. For example, the gospel is on our lips, but the religion of Epicurus is in our life and morals. Unless all these things are guarded against, the first commandment does not stand.

units.la: Sed Deum tum recte habes: quando eum adoras & veneraris, & honeste persequeris: quando eum quacunque re opus fit inuocas : quando fidutia auxiliorum eius te confirmas: quando quicquid habes bonorum illi soli acceptum fers & gratias dignas agis.Id fecere Io-seph,Moses,Diuid,& tota fidelium ecclesia.Quamobrem hæc possessio illud habere,seu no-bis esse refertur ad animum & ad vitam:Vtanimus noster alio non respiciat:vita nihil aliud referat,quam Deum hunc vnum & verum.
units.tr: But you have God rightly when you adore and venerate him and honourably pursue him; when you call upon him in whatever need arises; when you strengthen yourself by trust in his help; when you ascribe to him alone whatever good you have and give him worthy thanks. Joseph, Moses, David, and the whole company of the faithful have done this. Therefore this having, or belonging to us, is referred to the mind and to life: so that our mind looks to nothing else, and our life refers to nothing else than this one and true God.

units.la: Dij alieni, Qui-nam illi:Hic tibi Deus est quem amas,colis,reuereris. Iam Deus præter se nihil amari,coli,timeri patitur.Sed vide quomodo hoc requirat,Nō dicit:Nō habebisDeos: ne si veros habeas,tibi id licere putes: sed dicit, alienos: id est, quoscunq; alios, siue ij sint veri, siue falsi: hocq; ipso disputationem omnem amputauit, quæ de quorumuis Deorum diuinitate possit instituì. Et recte. Nam si quis sit falsus: hoc ipso quod falsus est, coli nō debet: sin quis esse verus existimetur: ipse quoq; iuxta Deum coli non potest, cum Deus solus sit, colendus. Ac quemadmodum uxor ab eo, qui vir non sit, ideo quod vir non est: & ab eo qui vir quidem sit, non autem eius ipsius maritus, hoc ipso quod maritus non est pariter abstinebit: sic ecclesia quæ sponsa est Christi, & à Deo & à falso Deo abstinebit: ac solum Deum patrem, qui Deus unus & verus est, respiciet.
units.tr: Other gods. Who are they? Here is your God: the one you love, worship and revere. For God does not allow anything else to be loved, worshipped or feared beside himself. But see how he requires this. He does not say, "You shall not have gods," lest, if you had true ones, you should think it lawful for you; but he says, other, that is, whatever others there are, whether they are true or false. By this he has removed all dispute that could be raised about the divinity of any gods whatever. And rightly so. For if someone is false, by the very fact that he is false he ought not to be worshipped; but if someone is thought to be true, even he cannot be worshipped alongside God, since God alone is to be worshipped. And just as a wife will abstain from a man who is not her husband, because he is not her husband, and likewise from one who is indeed a man but is not her own husband, because he is not her husband, so the Church, which is the bride of Christ, will abstain both from God and from a false god, and will look to God alone, the Father, who is the one and true God.

units.la: Sed qui sunt Dij illi quorum cultum sic vetat? Quicquid supra Deum amatur, colitur, timetur: veluti si quis angelos, Diuos, astra, Deos gentiles, pecuniam, ventrem, mundum, denique omne genus defectionis sequatur. Qua in re quemadmodum peccatum fit ab gentibus, à Christianis, testantur ægrorum, naufragorum, captiuorum vota ac precationes. Nec minor est error Christianorum, quam fuerit olim gentium. Quis enim nescit multitudinem & varietatem patronorum, qui ciuitatibus, casibus, & rebus singulis singuli quæsiti sunt[?]? Nautis Christophorus & Nicolaus pro Neptuno: Georgius militibus pro Marte: alijs alij pro alijs culti sunt. Sed contra Deus clamat: Inuoca me in die tribulationis & eripiam te.
units.tr: But who are those gods whose worship he forbids in this way? Whatever is loved, worshipped or feared above God: for example, if someone follows angels, saints, stars, the gods of the Gentiles, money, the belly, the world, in short, every kind of apostasy. In this matter, as sins are committed by the Gentiles, so too by Christians, the vows and prayers of the sick, the shipwrecked and the captives bear witness. The error of Christians is no less than that of the Gentiles of old. For who does not know the multitude and variety of patrons who have been sought out, one for each city, each misfortune, and each single thing? For sailors Christopher and Nicholas stand in for Neptune; George for soldiers in place of Mars; others are worshipped in place of others. But God cries out against this: "Call upon me in the day of trouble, and I will deliver you."

units.la: Verum vide quod nam habeant suis pudendis perizoma. 1. Non colimus eos vt Deos, inquiunt. Quid tum, inquam: si illos nihilominus colas? Perinde enim te excusas, ac coniunx impudica dicat amatorem suum se non habere loco coniugis: cum tamen ei corpus marito soli debitum, ceu maritus esset, impertiat: sic illi cultum soli Deo debitum ijs tribuunt, quos Deorum loco habere videri nolunt. Quo fit vt & in Deum, cui debitos honores auferunt: & in illos, quibus maiores honores habent, quam eos ipsos faciant, peccent. Ergo hoc prætextu se ipsi accusant.
units.tr: But see what they have as a loincloth to cover their shame. (1) "We do not worship them as gods," they say. What then, I answer, if you worship them nonetheless? You excuse yourself in the same way as an unchaste wife who says that her lover is not in the place of a husband, while she nevertheless gives her body, which is owed to her husband alone, as if he were her husband. So they give to those whom they do not wish to seem to hold in the place of gods the worship which is owed to God alone. Hence they sin both against God, from whom they take away the honours due to him, and against those others, to whom they give greater honours than they themselves would make them. Therefore they accuse themselves by this very pretext.

units.la: 2 Aiunt se Deum in sanctis colere: & allegant Psalm. 150. verba: Laudate eum in sanctis eius. At si sic velis colligere: Deus etiam in coelo, terra, mari, denique etiam creaturis omnibus laudandum se esse docet alibi. Sed si id obtineas: etiam suos errores obtinebunt gentes: nempe vt Iunonem, Venerem, &c. Vos & Deas colant. Est etiam aliud laudare, quam colere. Vnde & effugij loco distinctionem hanc promunt quod λατρείαν Deo, δουλείαν [?] sanctis tribuant. Sed quid hoc est? Quod leuissimum est, cultum Deo præstant: quod maius est, seruitium creaturis exhibent. Vtrum enim facilius est honorem habere an seruire alicui.
units.tr: (2) They say that they worship God in the saints, and they cite the words of Psalm 150: "Praise him in his saints." But if you want to infer from this, God elsewhere teaches that he is to be praised also in heaven, on earth, in the sea, and indeed in all creatures. But if you maintain this, the nations will also maintain their errors: namely that they should worship Juno, Venus, etc., and goddesses too. There is also another thing: to praise is other than to worship. Hence they bring forward this distinction as a means of escape, saying that they give latreia to God and douleia [?] to the saints. But what is this? What is the least, they give to God as worship; what is greater, they offer as servitude to creatures. For which is easier: to show honour to someone, or to serve him?

units.la: 3 Miracula nobis obijciunt: at si certandum sit miraculis: habebunt ethnici non pauca, quibus suorum Deorum cultum probent.
units.tr: 3 They throw miracles at us; but if we must contend by miracles, the heathen too will have not a few by which they prove the worship of their gods.

units.la: 4 Dij gentium, inquiunt, erant dæmonia, cum hi sancti sint: at illos scimus non fuisse dæmones: scimus autè fuisse homines, eosdemq; ex parte sanctissimos: & homines æque colendos non esse ac dæmones.
units.tr: 4 The gods of the nations, they say, were demons, whereas these are saints. But we know that those were not demons: we know they were men, and in part most holy men; and men are not to be worshipped in the same way as demons.

units.la: 5 Aiunt, inuocamus eos, vt intercessores: cum tamen eis ceu Dijs templa, aras, statuas, se staponant. Tum Christus vnus intercessor est 1.Tim.2. Ergo nihil his argumentis efficiunt.
units.tr: 5 They say, "We invoke them as intercessors," although they set them up with temples, altars and statues, as if they were gods. Yet Christ alone is the intercessor (1 Tim. 2). Therefore these arguments achieve nothing.

units.la: Sunt præter hos etiam pecunia, venter, & aliæ res: quas Deorum loco habere solent aliqui. Vnde Paulus auaritiam idololatriam vocat. Colos.3. & alibi dicit ventrem aliquibus Deum esse. Quamobrem relictis rebus illis omnibus Deum vnum, qui solus rebus gerendis semper sufficit, adoremus.
units.tr: Besides these there are also money, the belly and other things which some are accustomed to hold in the place of gods. Hence Paul calls covetousness idolatry (Col. 3), and elsewhere says that the belly is the god of some (Phil. 3). Wherefore, putting aside all those things, let us adore the one God, who alone is always sufficient for managing affairs.

units.la: Coram facie mea. Solum se coli vult: nec fert partem: nec iniuria. Nam primum cauendum est, ne mendacium veritati coniungatur: quippe quod sine veritatis contemptu non fiet. Deinceps cum Deus vnus sit vnice colendus erit: ne pluribus additis vnitas tollatur. Tertiò, cum Deus omnibus rebus efficiendis sic sufficiat, vt procossi[?] seu vicarijs opus non habeat, solus ille semper est inuocandus. Quartò, cum illius in nos amor sit indefessus, nos illum redamando simus impigri necesse est. Quintò, zelus eius nos eò propellat. Nam cum alij suos honores habere nolit: sane stulte fecerimus illius in nos iram vocando. Qui enim illum negligat, aut alij illos honores habeat: is sane Deum quasi iniuria lacescat. Dixit se esse zelotem: cur hoc sciens, colis aliū? Certe hic quasi in portu impingunt idololatræ.
units.tr: Before my face. He wills to be worshipped alone and does not bear a partner, and rightly so. For first, we must take care lest a lie be joined to the truth, since this cannot happen without contempt for the truth. Next, since God is one, he is to be worshipped uniquely, lest by adding many the unity be destroyed. Thirdly, since God is so sufficient for effecting all things that he has no need of substitutes or deputies, he alone is always to be invoked. Fourthly, since his love towards us is unwearied, we must of necessity be untiring in loving him in return. Fifthly, his zeal drives us to this. For since he is unwilling to have others' honours, we would surely be foolish to provoke his anger against us. For whoever neglects him, or gives those honours to another, surely provokes God as if by injury. He has said that he is a zealot: why, knowing this, do you worship another? Certainly here, as if in harbour, the idolaters run aground.

units.la: Ergo hoc præceptum ceu caput fœderis primo loco ponitur: vt naturam ad superstitiones propensam reprimat: vt idololatriam tollat atque ab ea reuocet ad Deum verum.
units.tr: Therefore this precept is placed first, as the head of the covenant, so that it may restrain our nature, which is prone to superstitions, so that it may remove idolatry and recall us from it to the true God.

units.la: Summa enim legis est huius: vt quoniam Deus totum se promittit & impertit no-bis: iure sibi vicissim nos deposcat ac vendicet. Ergo ei soli sit honos in sœcula.
units.tr: For the sum of this law is this: since God promises and bestows the whole of himself upon us, by right he in turn demands and claims us for himself. Therefore let honour belong to him alone for ever.

units.la: Amen.
units.tr: Amen.

units.la: SERMO IIII.
units.tr: SERMON IV.

units.la: Ne feceris tibi statuam,cuiuscunq; effigiei(eius)quod est in cælo desuper,& quod est in terra subtus,& quod in aquis est sub terra.
units.tr: "Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the waters under the earth." (Exod. 20.4)

units.la: QUanquam primum præceptum recte perceptum & seruatum fatis superque docet,quis qualisque sit Deus,& quomodo colendus esse videatur:tamen animus hominis ad externum Dei cultum,qui tamen internæ & incorporeæ Dei naturæ,atque essentiæ non competit,adeo propendet: ut necesse habuerit Dominus etiam de eo ipso quid sibi videretur,apertis verbis significare.Igitur quemadmodum in primo præcepto cultum inter num suæ maiestati soli debitū postulauit: ita secundo hoc præcepto remouet omnem exter-num.Atq; quem in eo hoc agit,ut nos à crasis Dei imaginationibus retrahat,atq; omne cultum in spiritum dirigat.Quod quidem ita clarum est & apertum,ut ab omnibus queat intelligi.Nam & verbis perspicuis exprimitur:& serie partium recta ac commoda proponitur.
units.tr: Although the first commandment, rightly understood and kept, teaches quite sufficiently who and what kind of God is, and how he seems to be worshipped, the human mind is still so inclined to an outward worship of God, which does not suit his inward and incorporeal nature and essence, that the Lord found it necessary to state plainly what he himself thought of this matter. So, just as in the first commandment he demanded for his majesty alone the worship due to him, so in this second commandment he removes all outward worship. His aim here is to draw us back from fleshly images of God and to direct all worship towards the spirit. This is so clear and plain that everyone can understand it. For it is expressed in plain words, and its parts are set out in a sound and fitting order.

units.la: Ac præceptum ipsum tribus partibus distribuit:ut etiam fiat eo clarius: quarum prima vetat idola facere:secunda vetat diuinum illis honorem haberi: tertia pœnam transgressori-bus,præmium obedientibus ponit.
units.tr: The commandment itself is divided into three parts, which makes it clearer still. The first part forbids making images; the second forbids giving them divine honour; the third sets a penalty for transgressors and a reward for those who obey.

units.la: Jam vero cum ab externo cultu reuocet nos ad internum ac spiritualem: omnibusq; per nos inuentis cultibus posthabitis velit nos ei,quam ipse præscripserit,religioni deditos esse: ex omni genere externorum cultuum eum potissimum nominat,qui sit omnium fœdissimus: diuinaq; maiestate minime dignus. Quis enim est qui nesciat simulachro quasi quodā plaustro cerimoniarum genus omne vehi:facta enim atque posita statua,non sub dio,neque in ripa fluminis,neq; in foro,neq; in communibus pascuis([illegible, ~7 letters])coli potest:sed eius gratia templum seu sacellum extrui,postaram erigi,mox sacrificia atq; anathemata afferri,sacerdotes eligi:qui sint inuentores,magistri,ministri cerimoniarum:iisq; homines ad se conuertendum pelliceant. Verum subuersa deiectaq; statua,quis neget hæc omnia corruere.
units.tr: Now since he calls us from outward worship to inward and spiritual worship, and wishes us, setting aside all the worships we have devised ourselves, to be devoted to the religion he himself has prescribed, he names above all the kind of outward worship that is the most foul of all and least worthy of the divine majesty. For who does not know that every kind of ceremony is carried along, as it were, on the cart of an image? Once a statue is made and set up, it cannot be worshipped in the open air, on a riverbank, in the marketplace, or on common pasture (illegible, about seven letters). Instead a temple or shrine must be built for its sake, an altar erected, then sacrifices and offerings brought, and priests chosen, who become the inventors, teachers and ministers of the ceremonies, and who entice people to turn to them. But once the statue is overthrown and cast down, who would deny that all of this collapses?

units.la: Atq; ut mentem & sententiam Dei probè percipiamus: eo quo dictum est ordine hæc lex erit existimanda.Ergo ut primam legis partem intelligamus: intelligendum est 1. quibus rebus Deus interdicat:2.qua ratione quoque modo hoc agat.
units.tr: So that we may properly grasp God's mind and meaning, this law must be considered in the order in which it has been stated. Therefore, to understand the first part of the law, we must understand (1) what things God forbids, and (2) by what reason and in what manner he does so.

units.la: Quibus interdicat,simpliciter omni simulachrorum effictione & prostitutione. Hocq; non solum ad sculptores,verum etiam ad eos,qui illos conducunt,& per eos hæc fingi,sculpi,prostitui curant:pertinet.Quis enim est qui nesciat eum qui jubet,& eum qui obsequitur eadem lege teneri? quis nescit regem decertasse,& vicisse prælio,quando hoc fecerunt eius copiæ? Eodem modo,siue ipse sculpas,siue sculpi cures:in illam legem peccaueris.Simpliciter enim hoc ceu initium omnis idololatriæ remouet.
units.tr: He forbids, simply, every shaping and setting forth of images. This applies not only to the sculptors but also to those who hire them and see to it, through them, that such things are formed, carved and set up. For who does not know that the one who commands and the one who obeys are bound by the same law? Who does not know that a king was defeated and beaten in battle when his troops did this? In the same way, whether you carve the image yourself or have it carved, you have sinned against that law. For God simply removes this, as the beginning of all idolatry.

units.la: Obicis:Non licet mihi in fenestra aliqua habere pictam historiam:aut in pariete pictam parentis imaginem,aut alias generis eiusdem siue picturas siue imagines? Quin obiciunt etiam papistæ nostrorum amicorum,aut præceptorum imagines.Respondeo,Dissimilis ratio est.Si Solomon sic præceptum hoc accepisset,certe in suo regio solio non finxisset leonum imagines.Deus hoc præcepto remouet eas imagines,quæ ad cultum prostituuntur in templis.
units.tr: You object: "May I not have a painted scene in a window, or a painted likeness of a parent on the wall, or other pictures or images of the same kind?" Indeed the Papists object to images of our friends or teachers as well. I answer that the case is different. If Solomon had received this commandment in this way, he would certainly not have carved images of lions on his royal throne. God, by this commandment, removes those images that are set up for worship in temples.

units.la: Obiciunt iterum:tantum à simulachris Deorum gentilium interdici:nec esse illicitas Christi & Diuorum imagines.Responsum ad hanc obiectionem sequentia suppeditabunt.
units.tr: They object again that only the images of the heathen gods are forbidden, and that images of Christ and of the saints are not unlawful. The following will supply a reply to this objection.

units.la: Obiciunt alii idola esse adiaphora:hoc est eorum,quę habeas nec ne parui referat,genere.Sed pro responso iubeo expendant dicta Paulina,Omnia mihi licet,at non omnia expediunt:tum quæ mala secum trahant,considerent. Ea. ca.15.liber Sapientiæ commemorat.1. Abstrahunt à vero cultu Dei. Augustinus enim dicit alicubi,hominem,si in templum,quod idola habeat,ingrediatur,imaginis specie pellici,& orare coram ipso:si succedat,pergere: sin minus,putare se non satis reuerenter habuisse imagines,atq; sic fieri illum subinde superstitiosorem.2.Abstrahunt à contemplatione diuinorum operum:etenim si simulachrum sit elegans,admiratur opificis ingenium:sin turpe,& idoli turpitudinem & ineptias sculptoris demiratur: quò fit ut opera Dei,ex quibus multo plura ac meliora cognosci possent,negligamus.Veluti vitem inspiciens,cogitas quod Christus dixit se esse veram vitem: viam incea-deas[?] cogitas Christum esse viam veram,eodemq; modo in ostij,portæ,& aliarum rerum conspectu.Omitto cœlum,terram,maria,& quæ his continentur: ex quibus & Dauid atque Solomon,& suo exemplo philosophi docuerunt creatoris bonitatem,sapientiam,prouidentiam,potentiam æstimare. Ab his rebus trunci illi nos abstrahunt.3. A charitate,quod est omnium pefsimum,nos abstrahunt:ac faciunt,vt eam,quæ est fidelium hominum teftera, vir tutem negligamus.Plus enim amoris & sumptuum impendimus ligneis imaginibus,& lapideis statuis:quàm viuis Dei imaginibus,nempe hominibus, quos nostræ curæ Deus commi fit.Clemens scribit Iacobo fratri Domini ad hunc modum:Si vultis honorem habere imagini Dei nos vobis quod verum est,aperimus:vt homini,qui ad imaginem Dei creatus est, benefaciatis,honorem habeatis,esurienti cibum,sitienti potum,nudo vestimentum,ægro ministerium,peregrino hospitium,captiuo necessaria suppeditetis.Idem etiam dicit diabolum serpentis eius,quo Adamus deceptus est,exuuio tectum effecisse,vt homines plus ligneis & lapideis statuis,quam viuis Dei imaginibus,hominibus videlicet tribuerent. Ac profecto verum est multos pauperes opifices ægre sibi parent: cum interea multæ in clarissima luce in templis frustra & inutiliter ardeant. Et recte concludit Athanasius idolorum inuentum,quia sit ex malo principio natum,totum malum esse. Qua de causa priscorum patrum memoria lex hæc tanto studio custodita est,vt idolum nufpiam vllum extiterit.Vnde Epiphanius Anablattam veniens,velum habens imaginem sicut Christi siue sancti alicuius hominis in ecclesia Christi contra authoritatem scripturarum pendere visum scidit,& custodibus consuluit, vt pauperem mortuum eo ipso potius obuoluerent & efferrent. Quod & Ioanni Hierosolymitano episcopo,vt presbyteris omnibus mandet Epiphanius author est.
units.tr: Others object that images are things indifferent, that is, of the kind whose presence or absence matters little. But in reply I bid them weigh the words of Paul, "All things are lawful for me, but all things are not expedient" (1 Cor. 6.12), and consider the evils they bring with them. The fifteenth chapter of the Book of Wisdom records these. (1) They draw us away from the true worship of God. For Augustine says somewhere that if a man enters a temple that has idols, he is enticed by the appearance of the image and prays before it; if he succeeds in doing so, he goes on; but if not, he thinks he has not shown the images sufficient reverence, and so he becomes more and more superstitious. (2) They draw us away from contemplating the works of God. For if the image is elegant, we admire the craftsman's skill; if it is ugly, we marvel at the ugliness of the idol and the clumsiness of the sculptor. The result is that we neglect the works of God, from which far more and better things could be known. When we look at a vine, we think of what Christ said, that he is the true vine; when we see a door or a gate, we think that Christ is the true way; and so with the sight of other things. I pass over heaven, earth, the seas and what is contained in them, from which David and Solomon, and the philosophers by their example, taught us to judge the goodness, wisdom, providence and power of the Creator. Those blocks of wood draw us away from these things. (3) They draw us away from love, which is the worst of all evils: they make us neglect that love which is the mark of faithful people. For we spend more affection and expense on wooden images and stone statues than on the living images of God, namely the men whom God has committed to our care. Clement writes to James the brother of the Lord in this manner: "If you wish to honour the image of God, I tell you what is true: be kind to man, who was created in the image of God; honour him; give food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, clothing to the naked, care to the sick, hospitality to the stranger, and necessities to the prisoner." He also says that the devil, covered in the skin of that serpent by which Adam was deceived, has brought it about that men give more to wooden and stone statues than to the living images of God, that is, to men. And indeed it is true that many poor craftsmen can barely support themselves, while meanwhile many lamps burn uselessly and in vain in the temples, in the brightest light. Athanasius rightly concludes that the invention of idols, since it arose from an evil origin, is wholly evil. For this reason, in the memory of the ancient Fathers this law was kept with such zeal that no idol was ever found anywhere. Hence Epiphanius, coming to Anablatha, saw a veil bearing the image of Christ, or of some holy man, hanging in the church of Christ, contrary to the authority of the Scriptures; he tore it, and advised the guardians to wrap the dead pauper in it and bury him with it instead. Epiphanius also vouches that he instructed John, bishop of Jerusalem, to give this order to all the elders.

units.la: Sed contrafimulachrorum cultum atque vsum tres grauissimos testes sistimus Mo-fem[?],Efaiam,Paulum:quorum primus fœderis contaminationem vocat, Deut. 4. alter cap. 4.suæ prophetiæ,dicit Deum non posse effingi cum sit sua natura immensus, æternus,ingenitus ἀόρα[?]:⊙:vt finitæ,caducæ,creatæ seu fabrefactæ,visibili rei similis esse non possit:tertius autem Actor.17.dicit auro,argento,lapidi arte sculpto, & inuento hominis numen non esse simile. Ex quibus omnibus alij q;[?] penè innumeris huic legi assentientibus testimonijs intelligitur quibus Deus prohibeat rebus.
units.tr: But against the worship and use of images we set three very weighty witnesses: Moses, Isaiah and Paul. The first calls it a contamination of the covenant (Deut. 4); the second, in his prophecy, says that God cannot be fashioned, since by his nature he is immeasurable, eternal, unbegotten, and invisible [ἀόρατος], and so cannot be like a visible thing that is finite, perishable, created or made by hands; the third (Acts 17.29) says that the divinity is not like gold, silver or stone carved by art and invented by man. From all these testimonies, and from nearly countless others that agree with this law, we understand the things which God forbids.

units.la: Quomodo prohibeat sequentia legis verba docent. Nam vt futilis & effugijs omnibus repagulum ponat:primum ea communi nomine appellat, quasi posito summo genere, appeliat enim fulptum aut excisum simulachrum : tum ne quid putes permissum esse: quid sibi velit per species explanat:siue partium enumeratione remouet omnia.
units.tr: The following words of the law show how he forbids them. For, to block every evasion, first he names them with a general term, as if setting down the highest genus: he calls them a carved or hewn image. Then, lest you think anything is permitted, he explains by species what he means, and by enumerating the parts he removes everything.

units.la: Ac tribus generibus res,quæ effingi possunt omnes comprehendit.1. Quæ in cœlis sunt, effingi non vult. Ibi Deus,qui totum aliâs orbem essentia ac vi sua continet, quasi in summa regia sedet. Effingi illum non posse,quæ significant multæ sunt rationes. Nam quia natura suapte est immensus:qui posset effingi?Homo vero,qui creatura est, vt Deum creatorem effingat,est indignissimum. Si materiam,puta ligna,lapides,argentum,aurum,quæ caduca sunt omnia,consideres: qui quæso referent æternam essentiam? Si finem spectes tantus illis neque potest nec debet honos exhiberi quantus Deo debetur.
units.tr: And he comprehends all things that can be depicted under three kinds. (1) Things that are in heaven he does not want depicted. There God, who otherwise contains the whole world by his essence and power, sits as on a supreme throne. That he cannot be depicted, there are many reasons which show. For since by his own nature he is immeasurable, who could depict him? Indeed, for man, who is a creature, to depict the Creator is most unworthy. If you consider the material, say wood, stones, silver, gold, all of which are perishable, who, I ask, will represent his eternal essence? If you look at the end, neither can nor should such honour be given to those things as is due to God.

units.la: Eò refer cœlestium corporum & spirituum omnia genera:vt solem,lunam,sidera: angelos,& felices animas:quibus omnibus detrahis plurimum de sua felicitate & gloria:si quæ solida sunt & lucentia,tu caduca atque obscura pingas : si quæ sunt incorporea, æterna,pura,tu corporea,momentanea,squaleri obnoxia finxeris.
units.tr: To this belong all kinds of heavenly bodies and spirits: the sun, the moon, the stars; the angels and the blessed souls. By depicting all of these you take away much of their happiness and glory: if you paint solid and shining things as perishable and dark, and if you fashion incorporeal, eternal and pure things as corporeal, momentary and subject to filth.

units.la: 2 Quæ in terris sunt pingi & coli negat. Eorum numero continentur homines, omnia animantia, stirpes & plantæ & quicquid terrenum est. Cur igitur humanæ effigies positæ? cur leones,tauri,ciconiæ,aliaque animalia culta sunt? Vnde Rom. 1. Paulus dicit, mutauerunt gloriam incorruptibilis Dei,in similitudinem imaginis corruptibilis hominis, & volucrum & quadrupedum & serpentum.
units.tr: (2) Things that are on earth he forbids to be painted and worshipped. Among these are included men, all living creatures, plants and shrubs, and whatever is earthly. Why, then, are images of men set up, and why are lions, bulls, storks and other animals worshipped? Hence Paul says in Romans 1, that they "changed the glory of the incorruptible God into an image made like to corruptible man, and to birds and four-footed beasts and creeping things."

units.la: 3 Quæ in aquis sunt, vt pisces & monstra marina: quibus omnibus effingi se Deus vetat. Vult enim internum cultum: & vt colatur in spiritu & veritate. Amen.
units.tr: (3) Things that are in the waters, such as fish and sea monsters: God forbids himself to be depicted in all of these. For he wants internal worship, and that he be worshipped "in spirit and in truth." Amen.

units.la: SERMO V.
units.tr: Sermon V.

units.la: 9 Non adorabis ea,neque coles ea.
units.tr: 9 You shall not adore them, nor serve them.

units.la: VSu[?] rerum iam inde ab orbe condito gestarum cognitum est: nullum esse tam grande, tam vehementer vetitum, tam turpe, deniq; tam perniciosum scelus: quod satan nesci-at adeo pulchro & specioso colore pingere & tanto pere commendare mortalibus: vt ad id patrandum pertrahat. Ac quemadmodum in vita malos mores, tetraq; scelera colore virtutis ornat: sic in religione foedos errores, praeclara specie veritatis decore vestit. Nam quod in fecundo praecepto statuarum atq; imaginum vsum fiue cultum vetuit: veluti rem, quae sensus externos primum, tum ipsam etiam mentem à Deo soleat auocare: id satan euertit, & imagines ponens, ait, Deum in illis coli. Quo figmento pene totus orbis delusus est: ac foli ij fuerunt immunes, qui mandatu Dei praesenti lege expressum respexerunt ac seruandum exiftimarunt.
units.tr: From the deeds done since the world was made, it is known that there is no sin so great, so strictly forbidden, so shameful, and finally so destructive, that Satan does not know how to paint it in so fair a colour and commend it so highly to mortals that he draws them into committing it. Just as in life he dresses bad morals and foul crimes in the colour of virtue, so in religion he clothes foul errors in the becoming appearance of truth. For what the second commandment forbids, the use or worship of statues and images, as something that is wont to draw the external senses first and then the mind itself away from God, Satan overturns: setting up images, he says that God is worshipped in them. By this fiction almost the whole world has been deceived. Only those were immune who looked to what was expressly written in God's command and judged that it must be kept.

units.la: Etenim quod ait, Non adorabis ea neque coles ea: hoc ipso excusationes, & praetextus idololatriae quaesitos omnes tollit. Verum vt intelligas primum excusationes, tum oppositam legem considera.
units.tr: For when he says, "You shall not adore them nor serve them," he removes by this very word all the excuses and pretexts for idolatry that have been sought. But so that you may understand the excuses first, and then the law set against them, consider the following.

units.la: Excusatio fiue gentilium, fiue Iudaeorum, fiue papistarum eadem est omnium: fe Dei gratia scilicet, eo dementiae nondum peruenisse: vt ipsas statuas aut imagines honore prosequantur: ac potius dum ante eas prouoluti precantur, vel Deos, vel Diuos, qui repraesententur, sicque in illis Deum ipsum adorare. Praeclara scilicet excusatio: quippe qua fateantur duo se facere: vnum quod ante imagines procumbant: alterum quod Diuos colant: quae De usambo[?] lege hac remouit: & alterum quidem hoc ipso quod dicit non incuruaberis ante ea: alterum autem eo quod dicit, non seruies eis. Quae sunt paulo altius repetenda.
units.tr: The excuse, whether of the Gentiles, the Jews or the Papists, is the same for all: that, by the grace of God, they have not yet fallen into such madness as to pay honour to the statues or images themselves. Rather, while they prostrate themselves before them and pray, they call upon either the gods or the saints who are represented, and so in them they adore God himself. A fine excuse indeed, since by it they confess that they do two things: one, that they fall prostrate before images; the other, that they worship the saints. This law removes both: the first by the words "you shall not bow down before them", the second by "you shall not serve them." These must be traced a little more deeply.

units.la: Non adorabis ea. Verbum Hebraeum significat incuruandi, genuaflectendi, & omnino omnem externam gestum, quo honoris gratia erga aliquem utimur. Quemadmodum principum Deo, tum magistratibus & principibus viris habetur: ac Deo quidem vt conditori, altori, conseruatori: magistratibus autem & principibus, vt ijs per quos Deus commoda nostra promoueat. Eum geltum Graeci προσκυνεῖν verbo, quod significat esse supplicem & genua flectere, exponunt. Vnde & Deo & regibus hic honos habitus passim in scripturis legitur. Iam fi illi dicant, fe ante statuas supplices prouolutos precari: feque eo praetextu probe defensos putent: quid lex diuina mandet vide. Non incuruabis te eis: nit neigen bür abziehen[?].
units.tr: "You shall not adore them." The Hebrew verb signifies bowing, kneeling, and in general any outward gesture by which we show honour to someone. Such honour is paid to God, and also to magistrates and princely men: to God as creator, sustainer and preserver; to magistrates and princes as those through whom God advances our welfare. The Greeks express this gesture by the verb proskynein [προσκυνεῖν], which means to be a suppliant and to bend the knee. Hence this honour is read everywhere in Scripture as given both to God and to kings. Now if they say that they pray prostrate as suppliants before statues, and think that they are thereby well defended, let them see what the divine law commands: "You shall not bow yourself down to them."

units.la: Iam honores eis habitos considera.1. In templis positae: quae domus est Dei, in qua Deus quaeritur, colitur, adoratur: an non satis honoris? fi consulari sella seruum collocem, an non indigno consularis honos habitus. Recte ergo his è templis eiectis, Deo diuinus ho-nos defertur. Recte ergo templa idolis sacra non Dei, sed idolorum domos voces: <bl>nit Gottes/ sonder götzenhûser</bl>[?]. Deinceps idololatrae statuas sequuntur, quasi Deos salutares: neque enim longe remotos eremos proficiscere, si in proximo pago positum idolum esset: vt ta-cem, quod aliud alio praeciosius est, & videtur dignius. Tertio ante ea procumbitur, & illis quasi Dijs acclamatur, & preces Deo debitae, eis dicuntur. Iam nisi illis vim saluandi tribuere, Deum, qui vbiq; est, etiam domi tuae posses precari. Quarto sacrificia & anathemata ad eorum aras afferuntur. Quas ceremonias hic vides vno verbo omnes remoueri: ac si vel caput eis aperias, hanc legem violatam esse.
units.tr: Next, consider the honours paid to them. (1) First, they are placed in temples, which is the house of God, where God is sought, worshipped and adored. Is that not honour enough? If I were to seat a slave in a consular chair, would not consular honour be unworthily bestowed? Rightly, then, when these images are cast out of the temples, divine honour is rendered to God; and rightly do we call the temples consecrated to idols not houses of God but houses of idols. (2) Second, idolaters follow the statues as if they were saving gods. You would not travel far to find one, if an idol stood in the nearest village; I say nothing of the fact that one is more precious than another and seems more worthy. (3) Third, people prostrate themselves before them, hail them as if they were gods, and address to them the prayers due to God. Now unless you attribute to them the power to save, you could pray to God, who is everywhere, even in your own house. (4) Fourth, sacrifices and votive offerings are brought to their altars. You see that by one word all these ceremonies are removed; and if you uncover your head before them, this law is violated.

units.la: Neque sine causa Deus externum cultum istum remouit. Fit enim vt in externas gestus tota conuertatur & pietas & probitas. Veluti si suum cuique idolo quotidie pensum reddas: iam immunem te esse ab omni suppliciorum genere: nec damnum vllum dari praeterea, vt vt potes, blasphemes, (corteris[?], & pecces: quando sic peractis sacrificijs, atque precibus Deus caetera susque deque ferat. At obedientiam & misericordiam non sacrificium vult Dominus. Testes sunt Cain, Saul, Pharisei. Inde etiam accidit, vt quemadmodum externe Deum colimus: sic etiam hominem honore externo deludamus: veluti blanditijs, gestibus, leuibus officijs: quibus maiorem, quàm animo comprehensam habeas beneuolentiam simulas[?]. Nam qui Deum fallere consueuerit: quanto magis audebit caeteros. Igitur quod externe faciunt qui simulachra colunt: id Deus incurandi verbo remouet.
units.tr: Nor without cause did God remove this external worship. For it comes about that all piety and uprightness is turned into outward gestures. If, for example, you pay each idol its daily dues, you then think yourself free of every kind of supplication, and no further loss is counted against you. You may then blaspheme, lie and sin as you please, since, with sacrifices and prayers so performed, God lets everything else go hang. But the Lord wants obedience and mercy, not sacrifice. Cain, Saul and the Pharisees are witnesses. Hence it also happens that, just as we worship God outwardly, so we deceive men with outward honour: with flatteries, gestures and light services, by which you feign a greater goodwill than you hold in your mind. For he who is accustomed to deceive God will dare all the more to deceive others. Therefore what those who worship images do outwardly, God removes by the word "bow down."

units.la: Neque coles ea, Verbum Hebraeum significat idem quod λατρεύειν seu δουλεύειν, hoc est, seruire. עבד[?] eum est alicuius iuri, potestati, imperio subditum esse.
units.tr: "Nor serve them." The Hebrew word means the same as the Greek latreuein [λατρεύειν] or douleuein [δουλεύειν], that is, to serve. To serve is to be subject to someone's right, power and command.

units.la: Iam rifti[?] se excusant, ac dicunt se simulachris cultum duliae, non latriae praestare: ideóque Deo debitum honorem non detrahi: illis seruitium praestari. Vnde haec eis excusatio. Qui LXX[?] interpretes verbo λατρεύειν vsi sunt: illi se non λατρεύειν, sed δουλεύειν aiunt praeclarum effugium scilicet. Etsi enim Graecis idem vtrumque significat: tamen vt demus eis inter sentiendum. ipsorum & istum vetitum cultum aliquid interesse: consequens erit eos idola sua absque cultu colere,eis seruire quidem,honorem autem non habere. Quod quid aliud est quàm ei ser‑uire,quem despicias: quemadmodum maligni serui faciunt? Sed etiam hoc ipsum Deus re‑mouet. Vtrumque enim, & honorem,& seruitium sibi vendicat. Nam seruire quid est aliud quam se præbere seruum alicui, quem agnoscas pro Domino,timeas, sequare, eius iussa ca‑pessas,ei acquiescas,ei te vsurpandum,alendum, conferuandum dedas,ac commendes? Hoc omne deberi Deo soli,nemo est qui neget. Honorem autem siue cultum Deo deberi, quem ipsi concesserunt: non est quod pluribus euincamus.
units.tr: Now the idolaters excuse themselves, saying that they render to images the cult of dulia, not of latria, so that the honour due to God is not taken away, and service is rendered only to the images. Hence this excuse. The Seventy translators used the verb latreuein [λατρεύειν]; the idolaters say that they do not latreuein but douleuein [δουλεύειν]. A fine escape, certainly. For although to the Greeks both words mean the same, let us grant them, for the sake of argument, that there is some difference between their own worship and this forbidden cult. It would follow that they worship their idols without cult, serving them indeed, but not giving them honour. But what is this other than serving someone whom you despise, as wicked servants do? God removes even this, however, for he claims both honour and service for himself. For what is serving other than offering oneself as a servant to someone whom you acknowledge as Lord, whom you fear and follow, whose commands you obey, to whom you yield, and to whom you give and commit yourself to be used, nourished and preserved? That all this is owed to God alone, no one denies. That honour or worship is owed to God, which they themselves have conceded, there is no need to prove at length.

units.la: Iam si negent se statuas colere : fateantur autem sanctos abse coli:in eo ipso quoque peccant: sancti enim, creaturæ cum sint, etiam ipsi coli non debent. At hac larua detracta, alia rursus subest: adeo multis tecta est idololatria. Aiunt enim se Deum in illis colere. Ve‑rum hoc antea refutatum est. Sic enim gentes Deum principem in creaturis, velut sole & luna,& Mercurio,& cæteris colere visi sunt. Quin hæc omnia Deus remouet. Præstat Chri‑stianum mentem suam quam oculos pascere. Turpe est, vt docet Gregorius, fidem habere potius in coloribus: vbi facile eluitur, quam in corde vbi queat radices agere. Quanto præ‑stat spectare & cognoscere sanctorum patrum libros,quàm statuas: cum statuæ eorum cor‑pora solum,si modo vere possint, referant: libri vero, quemadmodum ait Chrysostomus, eorum animas quæ qualesquæ fuerint exhibeant? Neque enim imago Pauli diuinam illius apostoli fidem, pietatem, fortitudinem, industriam referat: cum hoc præstet vel vnum ali‑quod eius epistolarum caput. Sed nec corporum bona,vt valetudinem, formam,celerita‑tem referent imagines. Nec leuis causa est quæ Diuo Athanasio lachrimas excusserit,quan‑do cogitaret eos qui viderent,ijs qui sensum oculorum nullum habent inseruire. Quamob‑rem reiectis statuis, Deum quoniam spiritus est, in spiritu & veritate veneremur. Amen.
units.tr: Now if they deny that they worship statues, but admit that the saints are worshipped by them, they sin in this too, for saints, since they are creatures, ought not to be worshipped either. But with this mask removed, another lies beneath it, so widely is idolatry concealed. They say they worship God in the images. But this has been refuted already. For in this way the Gentiles seemed to worship God as the chief among creatures, as in the sun and moon and Mercury and the rest; indeed God removes all of these. It is better for a Christian to feed his mind than his eyes. It is shameful, as Gregory teaches, to have faith in colours, which are easily washed away, rather than in the heart, where it can take root. How much better it is to look at and read the books of the holy Fathers than their statues, since statues can represent only their bodies, if indeed they could do so truly, whereas books, as Chrysostom says, exhibit their souls, whatever those were like. For an image of Paul does not show that divine apostle's faith, piety, courage and industry; yet a single chapter of his epistles does this. Nor do images show bodily goods such as health, appearance and swiftness. Nor is the cause a slight one which drew tears from the godly Athanasius, when he thought of those who see, yet serve things that have no sense of sight. Therefore, with statues rejected, since God is spirit, let us worship him in spirit and in truth. Amen.

units.la: SERMO VI.
units.tr: SERMON VI.

units.la: 19 Quia ego sum Dominus Deus tuus, fortis, indignabundus, prosequens iniquitatem patrum in filijs, in tertijs & quartis, odientibus (scilicet) me.
units.tr: 19 For I am the Lord your God, strong, jealous, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, upon the third and fourth generations, of those hating (namely) me.

units.la: 20 Et prosequens bonitatem in mille, his qui me diligunt, & præcepta mea obseruant.
units.tr: 20 And showing mercy unto thousands, to those who love me and keep my commandments.

units.la: NItio huius in secundum præceptum institutæ expositionis ostendimus ipsum præceptum tribus partibus,omne distributum esse: quarum prima Deus ab omni simulachrorum vsu nobis interdicat: altera cultum eorum remoueat: iam vero tertia sequitur, quanonnulla ad stabiliendam legem hanc argumenta,afferuntur: quæ etsi sint duplicia,tamen à natura Dei simul omnia desumpta sunt. Nam vt in rebus humanis plurimum refert:vt eum quo cum ti‑bi res est,recte noris: sic in religione & diuinis rebus momenti plurimum ad pietatem ve‑ram affert vera ac recta Dei cognitio.
