Quocirca Deus vt præceptum hoc stabiliat, argumen‑ta à natura sua sumit,eaq; vt diximus duplicis generis:nempe quædam quibus benigne sua‑deat vitandam idololatriam:ac rursus quædam quæ seuere & duriter ab ea absterreant. Ergo primum rationes,tum minas considerabimus.
units.tr: At the beginning of our exposition of the second commandment we showed that the commandment itself is divided into three parts. The first forbids us by God's command all use of images. The second removes their worship. The third now follows, in which several arguments are brought to confirm this law. Although these arguments are of two kinds, they are all drawn together from the nature of God. For, as in human affairs it matters greatly that you know rightly the person with whom you have to deal, so in religion and divine matters the true and right knowledge of God contributes most to true piety. Therefore, in order to establish this commandment, God takes arguments from his own nature, and these are, as we have said, of two kinds: some by which he kindly persuades us to avoid idolatry, and others by which he sternly and harshly frightens us away from it. So we shall consider first the reasons, then the threats.

units.la: Rationes, Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus, fortis. Quibus verbis ad firmandam legis huius bafim argumenta tria affert,quibus vt vitemus idolorum cultum fidem faciat.
units.tr: The reasons: For I am the Lord your God, strong. In these words he brings three arguments to confirm this law, so that we may avoid the worship of idols.

units.la: 1 Ego sum (inquit) Dominus. Quo docet iure sibi soli cum honores deferri, tum operas præstari: quod ipse sit Dominus. Est autem argumentum sumptum ab iusto. Idem habe‑mus etiam in Psalm. vt 98. Dominus,qui in Zion colitur magnus est & sublimis super omnes populos:& post, quasi concludens,ait: Euchant nomen tuum magnum formidabile,& san‑ctum. Et psalm. 112. ad laudes diuinas extimulaturus, seruos appellat: hempe vt intelligant quantum sua referat hoc facere. Dicit enim, Laudate ferui Domini, laudate nomen Domini. est omnium illustrissimum illud Psalm. 122. feruorum atque ancillarum simile. Ac ne quis hallucinetur, Ego (inquit) sum ille Dominus. Non à iudicio nostro pendet religio: sed intel‑ligendum est: Deum, quisquis tandem cuique videatur, tamen Dominum esse. Quod si Do‑minus est, iustum est vt illi obediatur.
units.tr: 1. For I am (he says) the Lord. By this he teaches that honour and service are rightly due to him alone, because he is the Lord. This argument is drawn from what is just. We find the same in the Psalms, for example Psalm 98: "The Lord, who is worshipped in Zion, is great and high above all peoples," and afterwards, as if concluding, he says: "Let them praise your great, awesome and holy name." And in Psalm 112, when about to stir us up to praise God, he calls us servants, so that we may understand how much it concerns us to do this: "Praise, servants of the Lord, praise the name of the Lord." The most famous Psalm 122 is similar, speaking of menservants and maidservants. And lest anyone be deceived, I (he says) am that Lord. Religion does not depend on our judgment; rather, we must understand that God is God, whatever anyone may think of him. And if he is Lord, it is just that he be obeyed.

units.la: 2 Deus tuus. Deum esse est vitam, salutem, & id quo opus est, esse. Veluti cum Abrahamo promitteret salutem, patrocinium, rerum omnium satietatem: ait, ego ero Deus tuus: ego e‑ro tecum ro tetum vbiuis gentium:ego sum fchaddai,i d est,sufficiens. Igitur fi quare fit opus,ab illo potius qui habet petemus : quàm ab idolis,quæ nihil habent. Igitur non opus habet vica‑rijs qui vbiq; est:nec eget sociis aut auxilijs, qui ipse sufficit omnibus. Ex quibus intelligi‑tur,vtilifimum esse nobis fi quàm proxima cognatione & societate illi coniunēti fimus:con tra quàm pernitiofum esse ab illo ad idola abstrahi.
units.tr: 2. Your God. To be God is to be life, salvation, and whatever is needed. So when he promised Abraham salvation, protection and the fullness of all things, he said: "I will be your God; I will be with you and go before you everywhere among the nations; I am El Shaddai, that is, sufficient." Therefore, if anything is needed, we shall seek it from him who has it, rather than from idols, which have nothing. Thus he has no need of deputies, since he is everywhere; nor does he need companions or helpers, since he himself suffices for all. From these things it is understood that it is most useful for us to be joined to him by the closest kinship and fellowship, and on the contrary most harmful to be drawn away from him to idols.

units.la: 3 Fortis:Nam ּשַׁדַּי fortis à fortitudine verè & proprie Deus dicitur: quippe qui vires ha‑beatad omnia perficienda.Quod eò de Deo scire necesse est,quia spem firmat:ac facit, vt & fi quempiam religionis verae studio offenderimus : neque eius minas,neque vim vllam me‑tuamus confirmati potentia Domini,qua possimus defendi.Is potius quærendus est scius qui sua manu tenet omnia:is timendus est qui in animam simul ac corpus habet imperium. Atque hoc argumentum alta mente reponi debet.Cum suæ potentiæ & victoriarum nomi‑ne gloriari consueuerint idololatræ. Veluti Romanus ille gloriatur, ea religione sub leges suas orbem vniuersum subactum:his sacris vrbe profligatum Hannibalem,pulsos à Capito‑lio Senones.Idem solent etiamnum papistæ.Quibus oppones quod dixit Dominus, Noli ti mere pusille grex.Atq; hoc argumento ostenditur,non ita vt videtur, esse difficile,verum re ligionis genus sequi,cum suos Deus cultores tueatur.
units.tr: 3. Strong: For God is truly and properly called strong, Shaddai [שַׁדַּי], since he has the power to accomplish all things. It is necessary for us to know this about God, because it strengthens hope, and makes it so that, even if we have offended someone by our zeal for true religion, we do not fear his threats or any violence, being confirmed by the power of the Lord, by which we can be defended. We should rather seek him who holds all things in his own hand; we should fear him who has power over soul as well as body. And this argument ought to be deeply fixed in the mind, since idolaters are accustomed to boast of their power and of their victories. Thus the Roman boasted that by this religion the whole world had been subdued under his laws, that Hannibal had been routed in the city by these rites, and that the Senones had been driven from the Capitol. The Papists are still doing the same. To them you may answer what the Lord said: "Do not fear, little flock." By this argument it is shown that it is not, as it appears, difficult to follow the true kind of religion, since God protects his worshippers.

units.la: Ex quibus perspicuum est,Deum,quoniam Dominus est,& Deus,& fortis fiue potens, vnice colendum & diligendum esse:idola autem,ne nos ab hoc auocent, prorsus abijcienda esse,ceu sacrosanctæ religionis impedimenta. Quæ qui rectè secum reputauerit:is quoniam omnia sibi in Deo bona scit esse posita,ac propterea non opus habere statuarum reuerentia, ab idolis facillimè abstinebit.
units.tr: From these things it is plain that God, since he is Lord, God and strong, that is powerful, is to be worshipped and loved alone; and that idols, lest they draw us away from this, must be utterly cast aside as obstacles to the most holy religion. Whoever has rightly considered this, since he knows that all good things are placed for him in God, and therefore has no need of reverence for statues, will most easily abstain from idols.

units.la: Minæ,zelotes, visitans iniquitatem patrum in filijs in tertiam & quartam generationem eorū, qui oderunt me,& faciens misericordiam in &c.Quibus verbis refert rationes cogentes & iu‑bentes hoc præceptum feruare,vel experiri deteriora. Eæ sunt omnino duæ.Vna quod fe zelotem vocat.Sed zeli nomine æmulationem significat,qua fit,vt quis consortis fit impatiens. Est enim amor Dei idem in nos,qui boni & pij mariti in coniugem. Qua de re multum in fa cris literis scriptum est.
units.tr: The threats: jealous, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, and showing mercy to &c. In these words he sets out the reasons compelling and urging us to keep this commandment, or else to experience worse things. There are two of these altogether. The first is that he calls himself jealous. But by the name of zeal he signifies rivalry, by which someone cannot bear a partner. For the love of God towards us is the same as that of a good and pious husband towards his wife, and much is written about this in the Sacred Scriptures.

units.la: Vnde is zelus?equidem eum in Deo ¿liunde quàm ex amore nostri proficisci non puto. Neq; enim zelus existit vbi non fit amor:quando eum huc illucq; ferri finis,quem non dili‑gis:eum verò tibi foli vis addiētum esse quem amas. Vnde vero Dei in nos amor potest pro‑ficifci?an ne est aliquid in nobis,quod illi dignum amore suo videatur?non arbitror quod a‑more quicquam:sed quod odio dignum fit permultum. Vnde ergo diuini in nos amoris cau‑fa?Ex eius ipsius bonitate & gratia. Quæ cum ita sint, iure zelum suum idololatriæ quasi quoddam repagulum ponit.Ac quemadmodum grauius peccat adultera,quàm maritus ve‑hementer amauit:sic nos etiam ingratitudinem simul cum fcortatione committimus:quan‑do despecto Deo confugimus ad statuas.Ergo quod ius est in adulteram marito:idipsum in nos Deo competit.Quamobrem idololatrarum fortunæ,vtut floreant ac vigeant:tamen eæ dem sunt,quæ adulterarum. Quemadmodum enim illæ voluptatibus illicitis indulgent, ac simul metu pœnæ & conscientiæ stimulis conficiuntur anxiæ:sic illi quoq; rerum prosperi‑tate & copia gaudeat,ac simul metu mortis & pœnarum mœrent. Igitur idololatria & adul‑teria pariter honesta,tuta,felicia studia sunt:tum vt marito grata est vxor adultera, sic idolo latris delectatur Deus:quos odit constantissimè.Quare zelo Dei retrahi debemus à cultu i‑dolorum:quæ prima ratio est.
units.tr: Whence does this zeal come? Indeed I do not think it can arise in God from anything but love of us. For zeal does not exist where there is no love; since you are unwilling for the one you do not love to be carried hither and thither, but you wish the one you love to be devoted to you alone. But whence can God's love for us arise? Is there anything in us which seems worthy of his love? I do not think there is anything worthy of love, but there is very much that is worthy of hatred. Whence then is the cause of his divine love for us? From his own goodness and grace. Since these things are so, he rightly sets his zeal against idolatry as a kind of barrier. And just as an adulteress sins more gravely than the husband has loved her vehemently, so we also commit ingratitude together with fornication, when, despising God, we flee to statues. Therefore what right a husband has over an adulterous wife, the same belongs to God over us. Wherefore, however much idolaters flourish and thrive, they are the same as adulteresses. For just as the latter indulge in illicit pleasures and at the same time are consumed with anxious fear of punishment and the stings of conscience, so the former also, though they rejoice in the prosperity and abundance of things, at the same time mourn in fear of death and punishments. Therefore idolatry and adultery are equally shameful, unsafe and unhappy pursuits. Just as an adulterous wife is pleasing to her husband, so God takes delight in idolaters; yet he hates them most constantly. Therefore we ought to be drawn back from the worship of idols by God's zeal; this is the first reason.

units.la: Altera,quod Deus non solum ægrè fert,sed etiam vlciscitur iniuriam. Ac ne putes eum has iniurias negligere,facto simul ac dicto probat,vt ne fit dubium.Facto:Visitans ,inquit,i‑niquitatem,&c.Visitandi verbo sacris literis vsitato dicit idem,quod est Latinis animaduer‑tere:quodq; Germanica lingua dicimus ein infehen thûn/zû einer fach lögen : aliquem ob‑feruare & deprehensum punire.
units.tr: The second is that God not only bears this with displeasure but also avenges the wrong. And lest you think he neglects these wrongs, he proves it both by deed and by word, so that there may be no doubt. By deed: "visiting," he says, "the iniquity," and so on. By the word "visiting," which is used in Sacred Scripture, he means the same as what the Latins call to take notice of (animadvertere), and what we Germans call ein Infehen thun, that is, to take notice of a matter and call someone to account: to observe someone and, when caught, to punish him.

units.la: Iniquitatem,hoc est,rem,quæ in immeritum committitur.Quid enim ést iniquius,quàm eum contemnere qui sic te adamet,vt nequeat magis?Magis peccatur quando vel ipsam etiá æquitatem negligimus,quàm fi ius præterceatur.Nam ius strictum est & rigorè videmur fer‑re non posse:at æquitas eius moderatrix,& ad nos demittit sese:vt fi illam quoq; violaris ,fis ac videare pefsimus. Veluti iniustus sum qui proximū non diligam:sed multò sum iniuftior, qui amantem non redamem:sic enim ipsam etiá æquitate violo.Quare Deus dicit iniquitate esse maximam statuas,quæ sunt res inanimatæ,quæq; nec solent, nec possunt fi velint nobis benefacere:maiore honore prosequi, quàm Deum ipsum, qui nos àdeò tenere diligit. Sed hæc iniquitas quæ quantaq; pestis sit ipsius legis verbis notatur: nam verba legis sic habent: iniquitatem patrum in filiis eorum qui oderunt me. Quo docet morbum esse pestilenti-ssimum[?]: quippe qui in omnem fere posteritatem serpat: ac vbi semel grassari cœperit, nunquā cesset: vnde & Deus magis irascatur, suaeq; longanimitatis nolens volens finem faciat: cumq; exemplo patrum filij nihilo meliores facti malint peccare, quàm resipiscere: ipse simul omnem veterem & nouam iniuriam vlciscatur. Veluti paterfamiliàs, qui primo pepercerit peccanti filio: secundo peccanti poenas graviores irroget.
units.tr: "Iniquity," that is, the thing which is committed against one who does not deserve it. For what is more unjust than to despise one who loves you as much as he possibly can? A greater sin is committed when we neglect even equity itself than when right is passed over. For right is strict, and we seem able to bear it only with difficulty; but equity tempers it and lets itself down to us, so that if you violate that too you are the worst of men and seem so. For example, I am unjust if I do not love my neighbour; but I am much more unjust if I do not love back one who loves me, for in that way I violate even equity. Therefore God says that the greatest iniquity is to honour with greater reverence statues, which are lifeless things, which neither are accustomed nor are able, even if they wished, to do us good, than God himself, who loves us so dearly. But what a plague this iniquity is, is noted in the very words of the law, for the words of the law read thus: "the iniquity of the fathers upon their children, who hate me." By this he teaches that the disease is most pestilential, since it creeps into almost all posterity, and once it has begun to rage it never ceases. Hence God is the more angered, and willy-nilly brings to an end his longsuffering; and when the children, made no better by the example of their fathers, prefer to sin rather than to repent, he at the same time avenges every old and new wrong. Just as a father of a household, who at first spared a sinning son, afterwards inflicts heavier punishments on the son who sins again.

units.la: Alioqui Deus filios innocentes non punit ob delicta parentum: quod ipse pluribus verbis docet Ezechielis 18. sed eos inquit, qui oderunt me, hoc est, quando filij suos parentes vel imitantur vel superant in malo. Vt apparet in ratione temporum: quorum alia sunt tenebrarum, alia lucis. In tenebris ad multa conniuet Dominus: quæ dein cum lux est, punit. Erant magnæ patrum memoria tenebræ: sed nunc clarissima lux est euangelij: qua despecta si malimus tenebras, graues nos poenæ manent. Sunt qui velint auitam religionem retinere: quam lux hæc prodidit esse meram superstitionem: sed in tantis tenebris antea à maioribus nostris cerni non potuit.
units.tr: Otherwise God does not punish innocent sons for the sins of their parents; he teaches this himself at greater length in Ezekiel 18. But, he says, "those who hate me": that is, when sons either imitate their parents in evil or surpass them. This is evident from the arrangement of the times, some of which are times of darkness, others of light. In the darkness the Lord overlooks many things, but when the light comes he punishes them. The darkness was great in the memory of our fathers, but now the light of the gospel is most clear; if, having despised it, we prefer the darkness, grievous punishments await us. There are some who wish to retain the religion of our ancestors, which this light has shown to be pure superstition; but in such great darkness it could not be discerned by our forefathers before.

units.la: Odij nomine cultum simulachrorum appellat Dominus, vt intelligas simulachra colere nihil esse nisi Deum odisse. Jam odium sui Deus jure punit, cum diligendus fuerit qui te diligit. Quod docet Apostolus Rom. 1. dicens gentes propter peccatum idololatriæ suis concupiscentijs traditas. Et regnum Israel vbi idololatria infectum est, cecidit. Idem Judæis accidit. Sic Christianorum idololatria Turcas potentes fecit, & eos ipsos calamitatibus attriuit.
units.tr: The Lord calls the worship of images by the name of hatred, so that you may understand that to worship images is nothing other than to hate God. Now God justly punishes the hatred of himself, since he ought to be loved who loves you. The Apostle teaches this in Romans 1, saying that the Gentiles, on account of the sin of idolatry, were given over to their lusts. And the kingdom of Israel, where idolatry had infected it, fell. The same happened to the Jews. So the idolatry of Christians has made the Turks powerful, and has worn them down with calamities.

units.la: Auget has minas comparatione, qua misericordiam suam cum nostra comparat dicens, Faciens misericordiam in millia hīs qui me diligunt, & seruant præcepta mea. In quo vides primum vt maior sit Dei erga nos misericordia quàm ira, vt quæ eam in nos malit exercere quàm iram. Visitatio enim siue vindicta in quatuor generationes: misericordia vero in mille porrigitur. Quod argumento est eum tanto magis propendere ad misericordiam, quod quia repetit, significat se malle diligere, quàm punire, bonis quàm malis afficere. Eam autem bonitatem pollicetur iis qui ipsum diligunt, puta quemadmodum Matt. 22. requiritur ex tota anima: & qui custodiunt eius præcepta: quorum numero hoc ipsum etiam continetur. Igitur ab idolis abstinendum est, vt vites mala, ac compares bona, quæ Deus mauult dare quàm mala. Ei sit honos in sæcula, Amen.
units.tr: He increases these threats by a comparison, in which he sets his mercy against our wrath, saying, "showing mercy to thousands of those who love me and keep my precepts." In this you see first that God's mercy towards us is greater than his wrath, since he prefers to exercise mercy upon us rather than wrath. For his visitation or vengeance extends to four generations, but his mercy extends to a thousand. This is evidence that he inclines the more to mercy, because by repeating it he signifies that he would rather love than punish, and rather bestow good things than evil. He promises that goodness to those who love him, namely, as in Matthew 22, with the whole soul; and to those who keep his commandments, which number includes this very thing as well. Therefore we must abstain from idols, so that you avoid evils and obtain goods, which God would rather give than inflict evils. To him be honour for ever and ever, Amen.

units.la: SERMO VII.
units.tr: SERMON VII.

units.la: Nō sumes nomen Domini Dei tui vane, quia neutiquam impunitum dimittet Dominus eum qui nomen eius vane sumpserit.
units.tr: You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain, for the Lord will by no means leave unpunished him who takes his name in vain.

units.la: POstquam Dominus Deus in primo & secundo præcepto offendit & à Diis alienis, & ab eius ipsius, qui verè & propriè Deus est, cultu falso abstinendum esse: iam porrò docet ne sanctum eius nomen contemptim & vanè & malitiosè sumatur. Nam cum suam quanquam rem sequatur nomen haud secus ac vmbra corpus: consentaneum erat: vt exposita sua ipsius essentia atq; etiam sui cultus recta ratione: deinceps exponeret de suo nomine. Atq; eum ordinem & Deus ipse probat alibi, & secutus est etiam Dominus Christus unigenitus eius filius. Ipse Deus pater ait Mich. 1. Filius honorat patrem & seruus Dominum suum: si pater ego sum, vbi est honor meus? & si Dominus ego sum, vbi est timor meus? dicit Dominus exercituum. Quod perinde est ac si dicat: Cùm sciatis me patrem & Dominum: qui fit, vt non intelligatis etiam me honore & cultu prosequendum? Eodem argumento Matth. 6. nos uti in precum formula docuit Dei filius dicens: Pater noster, qui es in cœlis, sanctificetur nomen tuum. Quo iubemur Deum patrem agnoscere, ne confugiamus ad alium: agnoscere eum cœlestem, propterea; non honorandum terrenis cultibus: denique eum qui pater cœlestis sit sanctificandum. Eo spectat etiam hoc præceptum, quippe quo doceat se velle nominis sui maiestatem nobis esse sacrosanctam. Vnde sequitur eam nec contemptu, nec abusu vllo prophanandam. Quę est huius præcepti summa. Continetur autem duabus partibus, interdicto & pœna.
units.tr: Having shown that the true and proper God is to be worshipped and that false gods must be avoided in the first and second commandments, the Lord now teaches that his holy name must not be taken contemptuously, vainly, or maliciously. For although a name follows its thing as a shadow follows a body, it was fitting that, after his own essence and the right manner of his worship had been set forth, he should then set forth what concerns his name. God himself approves this order elsewhere, and his only-begotten Son, the Lord Christ, followed it too. God the Father says in Mic. 1: "A son honours his father, and a servant his lord: if I am a father, where is my honour? and if I am a lord, where is my fear? says the Lord of hosts." This is as much as to say: since you know that I am your Father and Lord, why do you not understand that I must also be honoured and worshipped? By the same reasoning, in Matt. 6, the Son of God taught us to use this form of prayer: "Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name." By it we are bidden to acknowledge God as Father, so that we do not flee to another; to acknowledge him as heavenly, and therefore not to be honoured with earthly worship; and finally to hallow him who is our heavenly Father. This commandment also aims at the same thing, since in it he teaches that he wishes the majesty of his name to be sacred to us. Hence it follows that it must not be profaned by any contempt or misuse. This is the sum of the commandment. It consists of two parts: a prohibition and a penalty.

units.la: Interdictum: Non assumes nomen Domini Dei tui vane. In quo rationem eandem, qua in præceptis reliquis usus est, servat: ut non quid velit, nempe sanctificari nomen suum: sed quid non velit, videlicet ipsum prophanari, doceat. Veluti contra. Ego sum Deus tuus, non habebis Deos alienos coram me, ait: non autem, Ego sum Deus, me solum coles. Sic hoc loco potius dicit, non prophanabis, quàm sanctificabis, nomen meum. Ratio est, quod more gentium omnium Israelitæ per nomen Dei sui iuraturi erant: corruptam naturam nostram sciebat, ut quemadmodum gentes iurarent temere, sic etiam Israelitæ leuiter sese essent gesturi: quod hic expressis verbis vetuit.
units.tr: The prohibition: "You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain." Here he keeps the same method he used in the other commandments: he teaches not what he wills, namely that his name be hallowed, but what he does not will, namely that it be profaned. Compare the earlier one: "I am the Lord your God; you shall have no other gods before me," he says, not "I am God; you shall worship me alone." So here he says rather that you shall not profane, than that you shall hallow, my name. The reason is that, after the manner of all nations, the Israelites were about to swear by the name of their God. He knew our corrupt nature: just as the nations swore rashly, so the Israelites too would behave lightly, and this he forbids here in express words.

units.la: Ex quo sequitur, ut maiestatem nominis diuini tam religiosa veneratione prosequamur, ut de eo nihil nisi honorificum mens concipiat, lingua proferat, ut neque nomine, neque verbo neque sacrosanctis eius mysteriis, vel ad ambitionem, vel ad auaritiam, vel ad ludicra nostra abutamur: semper ipsum habeamus in precio. Idq; verba legis exprimunt.
units.tr: It follows that we must honour the majesty of the divine name with such religious reverence that the mind conceives nothing about it but what is honourable, and the tongue utters nothing but what is honourable; that we never abuse his name, his word, or his most sacred mysteries, whether for ambition, for greed, or for our own frivolous purposes; and that we always hold it in high esteem. The words of the law express this.

units.la: Nomen enim quid aliud est, quàm ea nota, qua rerum inter se distinctio & natura, & effectus cognoscuntur? Res enim sunt multæ & variæ: quæ dignosci non possunt nisi nominibus.
units.tr: For what is a name but that mark by which the distinction and nature of things, and their effects, are known among themselves? For there are many and various things, which cannot be told apart except by names.

units.la: Sed Deus quia parem non habet, nomine nequaquam indiget propter differentiam, quæ inter eum & creaturas omnes tanta est, ut omnibus sit hominibus notissima. Unde & Dij gentium hoc ipso, quod habent nomina, declarant se Deos non esse. Deinceps autem Deus nomen certum & finitum non habet, quia suapte natura sit immensus, & incircumscriptus. Ergo definiendæ & definiendæ naturæ diuinæ causa Deus nomen non habet, cum eius tam immensa natura sit, ut nullo nomine comprehendi possit. Sed quatenus effectum significamus nomine, & propterea nomen pro fama rerum præclarè gestarum accipitur: nomen Dei est qualiscunque eius naturæ & virtutum, ut iustitiæ, veritatis, omnipotentiæ, prouidentiæ, misericordiæ notatio. Unde & Exodi decimoquinto cap. omnipotens nomen eius. Et Psalmo 83.[?] Dominus nomen eius. Sperabunt in te qui nouerunt nomen tuum, quoniam non derelinques quærentes te. Ergo Dei nomen est quicquid de eo scribitur & prædicatur, ut iustitia, misericordia, &c. quarum æstimatio fit animis nostris maxima.
units.tr: But God, since he has no equal, has no need of a name for the sake of distinction, for the difference between him and all creatures is so great that it is known to all men. Hence even the gods of the nations, by the very fact that they have names, declare that they are not gods. Moreover, God does not have a fixed and finite name, because by his nature he is immense and unbounded. Therefore God has no name for the sake of defining or describing the divine nature, since that nature is so immense that it can be comprehended by no name. But insofar as we signify an effect by a name, and so the word "name" is taken for the fame of illustrious deeds, the name of God is whatever mark there is of his nature and virtues, such as justice, truth, omnipotence, providence, and mercy. Hence in Exod. 15 we read "omnipotent is his name," and in Ps. 83 [?] "The Lord is his name. They who know your name will trust in you, for you do not forsake those who seek you." Therefore the name of God is whatever is written and proclaimed of him, such as justice, mercy, and so on; and the esteem of these things is very great in our minds.

units.la: Sumendi verbo notat omnem eius usum, hoc est, ut animo cogites, recolas: ore prolo-quare nihil de Deo, quod non fit augustissimum.
units.tr: The word "take up" signifies every use of it: that is, to think of it in the mind and call it to remembrance, and to utter with the mouth nothing about God that is not most majestic.

units.la: Vanè dicit, hoc est, falsò, contemptim, frustra. In quo verbo totius legis basis est posita: Hoc enim, quia cum verbo coniunctum est, indicio fuerit, sumptionem, hoc est, usum nominis diuini rectum non remotum esse, & solum à nominis Dei prophanatione seu abusu nobis interdictum esse.
units.tr: "In vain" means falsely, contemptuously, to no purpose. On this word the whole basis of the law is laid. For since it is joined with the word "take", it shows that the taking, that is, the right use of the divine name, is not forbidden, and that only its profanation or abuse is forbidden to us.

units.la: Iam ut & usum rectum & abusum sciamus: intelligendum est quibus in rebus uti nomine Dei consueuerimus: tunc enim virtus pariter & vitium apparebunt. Igitur Dei nomine primum utimur iuramento, quod verum est asseuerantes. Hoc enim quid est aliud, quàm Dei in rebus dubijs testimonium. Eius usum hac lege Deus nequaquam remouet: alioqui di-xisset, non assumes nomen Dei tui. Sed cum dicit, ne vanè sumatur, intelligi potest recte su-mi posse. Quod & infra cap.6. præcipit, ut per nomen suum iuretur videlicet. Anabaptistæ ergo in Christum impingunt, quasiq; eum patri contrarium faciunt, quando per euangelium iusiurandum è medio tolli putant. Esset quidem optandum nos omnes sic assueuisse veritati, ut iuramentis opus non esset, ac simplex hominis oratio talis esset, ut iurisiurandi vim obti-neret:id autem cum fieri nequeat, proximum est, ut recte iuretur.
units.tr: Now, so that we may know both the right use and the abuse, we must understand in what matters we are accustomed to use the name of God; for then virtue and vice will equally appear. First, then, we use the name of God in an oath, when we affirm what is true. For what is this but calling God to witness in doubtful matters? God does not in any way remove this use by this law; otherwise he would have said, "You shall not take the name of your God." But since he says, "not in vain," it may be understood that it may rightly be taken. He also commands this in chapter 6 below, namely that one swear by his name. The Anabaptists therefore strike against Christ, and as it were make him contrary to the Father, when they think that by the gospel oaths are removed from the midst. Indeed it would be desirable that we were all so accustomed to truth that oaths were unnecessary, and that a man's plain speech had the force of an oath. But since this cannot happen, the next best thing is that one swear rightly.

units.la: Iam cum pro nostra vitiositate nec hoc ipsum præstemus, sitq; periurium peccatum maximum: Deus ipsum quasi sui nominis prophanationem hoc præcepto remouet. Quid enim gravius quàm doli, falsi, mali testem Deum citare & sisteret? Non ausis ab amico postulare, ut tua causa peccet, cur hoc ipsum petis à Deo qui sit iustissimus? Si illum inscium aut negligentem rerum putas, cur testem sistis impudens? Sin eum rerum gnarum noris, impius es qui scientem sistis. Sed hæc omnia superat quod periurio naturæ eius detrahitur: quid e-nim in natura Dei sit reliquum ablata veritate? Iosua Achan orat, ut confessione veri det gloriam Domino. Exemplum Iudæorum extat Ioan.9.
units.tr: Now, since on account of our vice we do not even achieve this, and perjury is the greatest sin, God removes it by this commandment as a profanation of his name, so to speak. For what is more grievous than to summon God as a witness of fraud, falsehood, and wrong, and to set him before the court? You would not dare to ask a friend to sin for your sake; why do you ask this of God, who is most just? If you think he is ignorant or careless of affairs, why do you shamelessly summon him as a witness? But if you know he is aware of all things, you are impious to summon one who knows. Yet all these things are surpassed by what is taken away from his nature by perjury: for what remains in the nature of God once truth is removed? Joshua urges Achan to give glory to the Lord by confession of the truth. An example of the Jews is found in John 9.

units.la: Gentium omnium consensu iusiurandi religio sanctissima semper habita est. Existimarunt enim ipsum esse religiosam actionem, quæ pertineret ad iustitiam fidemque publicam: quam iureiurando violato læsam arbitrati sunt. Cornelius Nepos in quinto libro Exemplorum de captiuis Carthagine Romam misis scribens ostendit, quam infames semper sint habiti qui iurisiurandi fidem violarent. Cornelius Pontifex Max.iusiurandum à ieiunis praestari voluit. Inde existunt etiam cerimoniae quae iuramento solent adhiberi: veluti quod Iouem lapidem iurasse Romanis sanctissimum est habitum: item quod lapidem filicem tenerent iurantes per Iouem dicentes: Si sciens fallo me Diespiter salua urbe arceq; bonis eijciat, ut ego hunc lapidem. Et prisci Romani religionem eius tam sanctam esse voluere, ut si actor delato sibi per reum sacramento debitum adstruxisset, non amplius quaerendu videretur an reus debeat. Veluti videre est in l. actori. C. de re b. creditis. l. non erit. §. dato. l. nam posteaquam §. actor. & l. duobus ff. de iureiurando.
units.tr: By the consensus of all nations the religion of the oath has always been held most sacred. For they judged it to be a religious act, one pertaining to justice and public faith, which they thought was harmed when an oath was violated. Cornelius Nepos, in the fifth book of his Examples, writing about captives sent from Carthage to Rome, shows how infamous those have always been held who violated the faith of an oath. Cornelius the Pontifex Maximus wished oaths to be sworn by those who were fasting. Hence also arose the ceremonies that are usually employed with oaths: for example, that the Romans held it most sacred to swear by Jupiter the stone; likewise, that those swearing by Jupiter held a flint stone, saying: "If I knowingly deceive, may Diespiter cast me out of the city, the citadel, and my goods, as I cast this stone." And the early Romans wished the religion of the oath to be so sacred that if a plaintiff, having been offered the oath by the defendant, proved the debt owed to him, it did not seem necessary to inquire further whether the defendant ought to pay. This may be seen in l. actori, C. de rebus creditis; l. non erit, §. dato; l. nam posteaquam, §. actor; and l. duobus, ff. de iureiurando.

units.la: At periurijs melius obuiam iri non potuit, quàm si ipsum iusiurandum tantam apud omnes authoritatem obtineret: & periuria grauissimis supplicijs afficerentur. Quam in eurâ ac cogitationem magistratibus nostris est etiam incumbendum. Id fiet si cauebunt ne eo nimis temere & ad res quaslibet utantur. Veluti ridiculum est iurisiurandi & quinq; solidorum poenae nomine vocari in curiam: quò si non venias, quinq; solidorum multa tibi irrogetur nulla habita iurisiurandi ratione. Barbaræ gentes hoc non facerent.
units.tr: But perjuries could not be better met than if the oath itself carried such authority among everyone that perjuries were punished with the gravest penalties. Our magistrates must also give attention and thought to this. It will happen if they take care not to use oaths too rashly and for just any matter. For example, it is ridiculous to summon someone to court by oath under a penalty of five shillings, so that if you do not come, a fine of five shillings is imposed on you with no regard for the oath. Barbarous nations would not do this.

units.la: Dein cauendum, ne leuibus quibusuis deferatur: ut ebriosis in arcenda ebrietate, blasphemis in blasphemijs. Et certè Plato in 12. de legib. Epicureos homines, quod vel Deum ne gent esse: vel si sit, res humanas negligere credunt: hoc ait habere sibi peculiare, ut temerè peierent. Quamobrem pietas ad id non parum profuerit, ut iurisiurandi maior fiat ac sanctior religio. Nec parum profuerit etiam meminisse quod in xij tab. ll. periurij poena, diuina, exitium: humana dedecus videretur. Nec male scribitur in Iure Canonum de iuramenti religione & usu recto. Hoc enim statuitur, ut iuramentum tres habeat comites: veritatem, iudicium iustitiam, uti videre est in xxij.q.1. iurabunt. q.ij. c. animaduertendum. Quod deinceps sic exponitur alibi. Veritatem habet, quando corde sentitur quod ore iuratur xxij.q.2. animad uertendum. Iustitiam, quando iustum & licitum est, quod iuratur. xxij.q.4. innocens. §. illici tum. Iudicium quando cum deliberatione & cautela fit xxij.q.4. §. illicitum. 2.q.5. sacrum. Ex quibus omnibus potest intelligi nomen Dei, quando eius usus est in iureiurando necessarius: tunc rectè sumi cum iuratur verè, & iuste, & scienter siue prouidenter.
units.tr: Next, care must be taken that oaths are not imposed for trivial matters of any kind: as on drunkards, to restrain drunkenness; on blasphemers, to restrain blasphemies. Indeed Plato, in the twelfth book of the Laws, says that Epicureans, who believe either that there is no God or that, if there is one, he neglects human affairs, have this peculiarity: they swear rashly. Therefore piety will contribute not a little to making the religion of the oath greater and holier. It will also help not a little to remember that in the Twelve Tables the penalty for perjury was divine destruction and human disgrace. It is also well put in the Canon Law concerning the religion and right use of oaths. For it is laid down that an oath has three companions: truth, judgment and justice, as may be seen in 22 q.1 "iurabunt" and q.2 c. "animadvertendum". This is explained elsewhere thus: truth is present when what is sworn with the mouth is felt in the heart (22 q.2, "animadvertendum"); justice, when what is sworn is just and lawful (22 q.4, "innocens", §. "illicitum"); judgment, when it is done with deliberation and caution (22 q.4, §. "illicitum"; 2 q.5, "sacrum"). From all of this it can be understood that the name of God, when its use is necessary in an oath, is rightly invoked when one swears truly, justly and knowingly or prudently.

units.la: Secundo nomine diuino utimur in priuatis asseuerationibus. In quo profecto grauissimè delinquitur. Nam & temerè & leuiter & nulla cogente necessitate res obscaenas, impuras, turpes dicentibus Dei nomen in ore est: ut omittam, quod eius diros cruciatus, & vulnera leuiter usurpamus. Hoc utut magistratus ferat, Deus inultum non sinet. Nam si nomen suum non vult vanè sumi: sic sumi nequaquam volet.
units.tr: Second, we use the divine name in private asseverations, and in this we certainly sin most gravely. For we rashly, lightly and without any compelling necessity put the name of God in our mouths when speaking of obscene, impure and shameful things; to say nothing of how lightly we invoke its dreadful torments and wounds. However the magistrate may tolerate this, God will not leave it unpunished. For if he does not wish his name to be taken in vain, he will by no means wish it to be taken thus.

units.la: Tertio cum omnibus rebus suscipiendis Deus felix ac faustus dux sit, eo solemus auspice & turpissima carmina & obscaenas fabulas incipere.
units.tr: Third, since God is a happy and propitious leader in all undertakings, we are accustomed, under his auspices, to begin even the most shameful songs and obscene tales.

units.la: Quarto solent incantationibus suis hoc nomen adhibere maleficae.
units.tr: Fourth, sorceresses are accustomed to use this name in their incantations.

units.la: Quinto annullis inscribimus & torquibus.
units.tr: Fifth, we inscribe it on rings and necklaces.

units.la: Sexto falsi episcopi suum quaestum hoc obtegunt. Conspurcatur itidem à magistratu, qui sibi nomen hoc ipsius Dei beneficio habet: sed ipsum foede contaminat obscoena vita. Atque his aliisq; rebus innumeris Dei nomen polluitur: quod tamen sanctissimè erat usurpandum.
units.tr: Sixth, false bishops cover their profit with this name. It is likewise defiled by the magistrate, who holds his office by God's benefit but foully contaminates it by an obscene life. By these and countless other things the name of God is polluted, though it ought to have been used most holily.

units.la: Pœna: Quoniam non insontem habebit Deus eum qui sumpserit nomen ipsius vane. En verba. Non habebit insontem. Tu tibi videris impunè peierare, blasphemias vomere, ludere: at Deus rei loco te habet. Quid expectandum reo? nihil certè quàm supplicium. Quae de periurijs & blasphemijs dixi, quo loco sint ac habeantur, video: sufq; deq; ferri scilicet: at quid Deo videatur haec lex testis est. Iocorum & vanitatis est reddenda ratio teste Domino Matth.12. Et si, ut ait Psalthes, perituri sunt omnes mendaces: quid eueniet periuris & blasphemis? Sa-nè Leuit.24. lapidibus obruitur. Extant etiam descriptae poenae periuriorum in Nouellis constitutionibus. Sed ex his satis perspicuum est, quàm periculosum sit nomine Dei abuti: quàm contra bonum eo recte uti. Quare quod in precationis à Domino praescripta formula didicimus, dabimus operam, ut nomen Dei per nos sanctificetur, Amen.
units.tr: Punishment: "For the Lord will not hold him guiltless who takes his name in vain." Behold the words: he will not hold him guiltless. You suppose you can perjure yourself, vomit blasphemies and make sport with impunity; but God holds you in the place of a guilty party. What can the guilty expect? Certainly nothing but punishment. Whatever I have said about perjuries and blasphemies, I see the place they hold and the regard in which they are held: they are evidently carried lightly, as the saying goes. But what God thinks of this law is the witness. An account must be rendered for jests and vanity, as the Lord witnesses in Matth. 12. And if, as the Psalmist says, all liars shall perish, what will become of perjurers and blasphemers? Indeed in Levit. 24 they are stoned to death. The punishments for perjuries are also set out in the Novel constitutions. But from these things it is clear enough how dangerous it is to abuse the name of God, and how contrary to what is good it is to use it rightly. Wherefore, what we have learned from the form of prayer prescribed by the Lord, we shall take pains that the name of God be sanctified through us. Amen.

units.la: SERMO VIII.
units.tr: SERMON VIII.

units.la: 12 Obserua diem sabbathi, ut eum sanctifices, quemadmodum praecepit tibi Dominus Deus tuus.
units.tr: 12 Observe the day of the sabbath, to keep it holy, as the Lord your God has commanded you.

units.la: POstquá Dominus in primo & secundo præcepto omnem quę abs se fit defectionem & idololatriam: tum in tertio sui nominis prophanationem vetuisset: ex quo nos quod vera in Deum unum fides, eius solius adoratio, nomin s diuini sanctificatio verus Dei cultus sint colligere potuimus: iam quartam fert legem ac statum tempus deputat, sabbathum videlicet: quod sanctum esse & ab omni rerum terrenarum cura liberum, & suo cultui soli sacrum velit. Ac præceptum quidem ipsum tribus partibus omne distribuit, quarum prima summa rei ponit ob oculos: altera legem adhibita circumstantiarum eo spectantium enumeratione explicat, postrema legem argumentis firmat.
units.tr: After the Lord, in the first and second commandments, had forbidden every defection and idolatry that turns from him, and in the third had forbidden the profanation of his name, from which we could gather that true faith in the one God, the worship of him alone, and the sanctification of his name are the true worship of God, he now brings forth a fourth law and assigns a set time, namely the sabbath. He wills that this time be holy, free from all care for earthly things, and consecrated to his worship alone. The precept itself divides into three parts: the first sets the substance of the matter before our eyes; the second explains the law by listing the circumstances that bear on it; the last confirms the law with arguments.

units.la: Ac quantum ad præcepti primam partem attinet: quam seorsim ab aliis in præsentia (quod Deus bene vertat) explicare volumus, ea sic habet. Observa diem sabbathi ut eum sanctifices, quemadmodum tibi præcepit Dominus Deus tuus. Quibus verbis, ut diximus, summam ac caput legis comprehendit. Ea est, ut quoniam vera pietas & religio, quam præceptis superioribus requisivit, opus habet quodam exercitio, quo cum discatur tum foveatur ut subinde magis ac magis crescat: statum ei tempus definit, idque ei soli sacrum esse iubet. Iam si verba singula consideres: habes quod diem ipsum nominat, & eius usum & rationem assignat: præmisso uno verbo quo commendat legem.
units.tr: As for the first part of the precept, which for now (God willing) we want to explain separately from the rest, it reads: Observe the day of the sabbath, to keep it holy, as the Lord your God has commanded you. In these words, as we have said, he sums up the whole law and its heart. The point is this: true piety and religion, which the earlier precepts required, need a certain exercise by which they are both learned and nourished, so that they grow more and more. He therefore fixes a time for this and orders that it be holy to him alone. If you consider the individual words, you find that he names the day, assigns its use and purpose, and prefaces it with one word that commends the law.

units.la: Commendationem legis uno custodiendi verbo affert, quo exponit illud verbum, quo Deus ipse legem ferens usus fuerat, Memento videlicet. Quae duo verba coniuncta quo pacto & hæc ipsa & reliquæ Dei leges omnes servandæ sint, indicant. Nam זכור memento, animum servandis Dei legibus sic deditum postulat, qui relictis rebus omnibus has unas servet.
units.tr: He commends the law with the one word remember, which explains the word God himself used when giving the law, namely "Remember." These two words taken together show how this law, and all the other laws of God, are to be kept. For zakhor [זכור], "remember," requires a mind so devoted to keeping God's laws that, setting aside all other things, it keeps these alone.

units.la: Nam divini verbi oblivio & peccatorum omnium fons est & contemptus Dei iudicium. Ac quod vitiorum omnium fons sit nostris ipsorum sermonibus & usu vitæ & hoc ipso verbo probabitur. Nos enim si quis vel dicto vel facto peccet: solemus dicere eum sui oblitum esse: veluti senex, quem gravitas decet, scurrilia dicens aut faciens: dicitur personæ quam gerit, oblitus esse: eodemque modo amicus amicum calumniis proscindens, episcopus vel magistra-tus ebrius, qui si personarum suarum meminissent, id magis quod decorum est facerent, quam quod dedecet. Sic qui legis huius memoriam perpetua cum obedientia custodiat: is nihil quo prophanet sabbathum committerit.
units.tr: For forgetfulness of the divine word is the source of all sins, and contempt of God is the judgment on it. That forgetfulness is the source of all vices can be shown from our own everyday speech, from the conduct of life, and from this very word. When someone sins by word or deed, we usually say that he has forgotten himself: for example, an old man who should be dignified but speaks or acts in a buffoonish way is said to have forgotten the character he bears. In the same way a friend who tears another to pieces with slander, or a bishop or magistrate who is drunk, has forgotten himself. If they remembered their station, they would do what is fitting rather than what is unbecoming. So whoever keeps the memory of this law with constant obedience will commit nothing by which he profanes the sabbath.

units.la: Usu vitæ comperimus hoc fieri. Israelitæ enim quoties peccatis Deum offenderent: Scri-ptura causam commemoratura, dicit oblitos fœderis. Apostoli in resurrectione Domini ideo minus firmi fuere credenda, quod oblivisci essent eius quod dixerat se præiturum in Galilæam. Nostra ætate Christus ideo sursum vorsum ostenditur atque quæritur, quia non meminimus dixit se Dominum fore qui illum hic aut illic monstrent, qui non sint audiendi. Et usu ciborum atque matrimonii interdictum est, quia sumus obliti, quod ea interdicta Paulus doctrinas dæmo-niorum vocat. Sic Divos implorant, quibus excidit illud Perri dicto. Nullum est nomen &c. Act. 4. sic sua in religione iudicia probant ac sequuntur obliti veteris dicti: No facies mihi quod tibi videtur bonum, frustra me colitis traditionibus hominum.
units.tr: We learn from the conduct of life that this is so. Whenever the Israelites offended God by their sins, Scripture, when it sets out the cause, says that they had forgotten the covenant. The apostles were slow to believe at the resurrection of the Lord because they had forgotten what he had said, that he would go before them into Galilee. In our own age Christ is shown and sought here and there, because we do not remember that he said many would come saying that they were Christ, and that those who point him out in this place or that are not to be heard. And the use of certain foods and marriage is forbidden, because we have forgotten that Paul calls these prohibitions "doctrines of demons." So men call on saints who have forgotten that saying of Peter, "There is no other name..." (Acts 4). So too they approve and follow their own judgments in religion, forgetting the old saying: "You shall not do what seems good to you; in vain do they worship me with the traditions of men."

units.la: Quamobrē hoc verbo iubemur meminisse ut sabbathum custodiamus, hoc est ne prophanetur caveamus. At oblivione fit ut ab ea discedamus. Igitur cum oblivio fit quasi quædam huius impietatis procreatrix: ab illa cumprimis est abstinendum. Sed eius oblivisci contemptus Dei iudicium est. Eius enim verborum maxime oblivisci-mur, cuius non magna apud nos sit authoritas. Sin quid meminisse tua referat, id ne excidat, scripto, iussis te admonere amicis aut ser-vulis, signis quacunque iter est positis, caues. Cur hic non tantopere laboramus? Quia serve-tur ne an non, parum nostra referre credimus. At in hoc salutis nostræ cardo vertitur, ut di-vinis legibus obedias. Ignorantia non excusabit. Culpæ est enim nescire quod tua ut scias interest. Quamobrē seriū[?] quiddā innuit recordādi verbo, eoque studium excitat & requirit animum. Verum שמור custodiendi verbum praxin notat, ut quod præstes. Eiusmodi sis necesse est. Nam custodiendi verbo laboriosam actionem notat. Verum ex his prolegominis quàm sit augustum hoc præceptum facile potest intelligi.
units.tr: Therefore we are bidden by this word to remember, so that we keep the sabbath, that is, take care that it is not profaned. Forgetfulness, however, is what makes us drift away from it. Since forgetfulness is, as it were, the begetter of this impiety, we must above all abstain from it. But to forget it is a sign of contempt for God. For we forget most readily the words that carry little authority with us. Yet if something matters to you to remember, you take care, lest it slip away, to remind yourself in writing, or by ordering your friends or servants, or by setting signs wherever you go. Why do we not labour so hard here? Because we think it matters little whether this is kept or not. Yet the hinge of our salvation turns on this, that you obey the divine laws. Ignorance will not excuse. For it is a fault not to know what it is in your interest to know. Therefore the word "remember" hints at something further, and rouses zeal and demands the mind. But the word shamor [שמור], "keep," marks practice, so that you actually do it. You must be such a person. For the word "keep" denotes a laborious action. From these preliminaries it can easily be understood how weighty this precept is.

units.la: Diem dicit seu nominat diem sabbathi, hoc est, eum quem a quiete & recreatione nomi-nat. Nam שבת quiescere significat.
units.tr: He speaks of, or names, the day of the sabbath, that is, the day he names from rest and recreation. For shabbat [שבת] means to rest.

units.la: Atque hunc quidem Deus non sine causa cultui suo destinavit: nimirum ut valere iussis o-mnibus malis & mundanis curis & negotiis divina cogitaremus & faceremus.
units.tr: God appointed this day for his worship not without reason: clearly so that, bidding farewell to all evil and worldly cares and business, we might think and do divine things.

units.la: Inde ab usu tam sacrosancto ipse quoque est factus sanctior: aliàs neque numerus neque tempus sanctimoniæ quicquam conferunt: quid enim in illis situm fit? Igitur & mandato Domini, & sacrarum rerum usu factus est cæteris sanctior. Veluti templa, si formam spectes & materiam nihil aut perparum inter hæc & reliquas domos interest: sin finem consideres, plurimum, plurimum: sunt enim sacris vsibus dedicata. At quemadmodum nulla apud Deum est personarum ratio, nosque si genus spectes & originem, ijdem omnes sumus, homines scilicet, & tamen dignitate & officio superat alius alium: sic dies septimus idem est qui sextus & quintus & reliqui: sed tamen propter diuina sanctaq; exercitia reliquis factus est sanctior.
units.tr: From this most sacred use the day itself has also become holier. Otherwise neither number nor time contributes anything to holiness: for what is there in them? So by the Lord's command and by the sacred use of it, the day has become holier than the rest. Take temples: if you look at their form and material, there is little or no difference between them and other houses; but if you consider their purpose, the difference is very great, because they are dedicated to sacred uses. And just as there is no distinction of persons with God, and if you look at race and descent we are all the same, namely human beings, yet one surpasses another in dignity and office, so the seventh day is the same as the sixth and fifth and the rest; yet on account of divine and holy exercises it has become holier than the others.

units.la: Ac poterat Deus omnes dies istis vsibus destinare: sed quoniam ex sudore vultus alimur, & per eos labores ab rerum diuinarum studijs auocamur: vnum illum selegit, quo deposita rerum terrenarum cura diuinis illis toti vacaremus. Vt enim tu molestè ferres amicum, interea dum vel tu cum illo, vel ille tecum loqueretur, aliud animo voluere: sic Deus videtur velle, vt siue eum ipsum audias, siue is tuis precibus suas aureas præbeat: ne quid agas aliud.
units.tr: God could have assigned all days to these uses; but since we are fed by the sweat of our face, and are drawn away from the study of divine things by those labours, he chose one day on which, with earthly cares laid aside, we might be wholly free for those divine things. For just as you would be annoyed with a friend who, while you are speaking with him or he with you, turns his mind to something else, so God seems to will that, whether you hear him himself or he offers his golden words in answer to your prayers, you do nothing else.

units.la: Iam vt in omnibus, sic in hac etiam lege est aliquid æternum, & rursus aliquid quod abrogatur, vt in fœdere, eius ipsius nota quæ est circumcisio, baptismo cessit: vsus circumcisionis internus perpetuus est: victus ministris ecclesiarū semper debetur, sed decimæ nē an definita stipendia reddanturperinde est. Eodem modo perpetuum hoc est, vt certus aliquis dies religioni sit sacer: sed septimus nē an octauus is sit parui refert. Priscis septimus erat ob memoriam orbis conditi: nobis est octauus ob memoriam orbis restaurati. Nam eo Christus orbis restaurator resurrexit à mortuis morte superata ac domata. Quæ mutatio licet sacris literis expressa non sit, tamen diei dominicæ in Apocalypsi fit mentio. Igitur eam ratam ac sanctam habere exemplum Apostolorum docet, & nostra vtilitas, quæ ex eutaxia percipitur, postulat.
units.tr: Now, as in all things, so also in this law there is something eternal and something that is abrogated. As in the covenant, the sign of which is circumcision, that sign yielded to baptism, while the inner use of circumcision remains forever; and the living of the ministers of the churches is always owed, though it makes no difference whether tithes or fixed stipends are paid. In the same way it is perpetual that some definite day be set apart for religion; but whether that day is the seventh or the eighth matters little. For the ancients the seventh day was for the memory of the created world; for us it is the eighth, for the memory of the restored world. For on that day Christ the restorer of the world rose from the dead, death having been overcome and subdued. Although this change is not expressed in Holy Scripture, yet mention is made of the Lord's day in the Apocalypse. Therefore the example of the apostles teaches us to hold it as valid and holy, and our own profit, which comes from good order, requires it.

units.la: Vsum indicaturus ait, Vt sanctificet[?]:quo verbo cum vsum eius rectum, tum abusum notat. Vsus rectus est, eum sanctificare. Quid id est: rebus sanctis accomodare & tribuere videlicet. Quæ nam hæ sunt: quæ nimirum ad Dei, qui solus est sanctus, cultum pertinent: vt docere & audire verbum Dei, orare, sacrificare, & quæ sunt huius generis alia. De quibus Nehem. 8. Iam Christiani diem dominicam doctrinæ, precibus, mysterijs, collectis siue eleemosynis re-ctè tribuent. Sic Christus & Apostoli semper sunt vsi sabbatho, seu die dominica. Et quemadmodum Iudæi conditi mundi, sic nos eius conditi pariter & in integrum restituti memoriā celebrandam arbitrabimur. Quo pertinebit etiam grata beneficiorū Dei recordatio, & peccatorum etiam ad resipiscendum vocans cogitatio. Qui ipsum rebus alijs tribuit, prophana re videbitur, vt qui corpus curant, sumptus supputant, animam autem negligunt, verbum Dei non audiunt, sed dum prædicatur, aut potant, aut obambulant. Hi meminerint, vt gladius non scindendis arboribus sed tuendo corpori, vt vestis non abstergendis sordibus, sed tegendo & ornando corpori: vt poculum non lotio, sed vino capiendo: sic sabbathum non Mammonæ, Baccho, Veneri, sed Dei Opt.Max.cultui factum esse. Summa, sabbathum sancti-ficandum[?] est.
units.tr: In stating the use, he says, that you sanctify it. By this word he marks both its right use and its abuse. The right use is to sanctify it, that is, to devote and assign it to holy things. What are these? Clearly those that pertain to the worship of God, who alone is holy: to teach and hear the word of God, to pray, to offer sacrifice, and other things of this kind, concerning which see Nehemiah 8. Now Christians will rightly devote the Lord's day to teaching, prayers, the mysteries, and collections or alms. So Christ and the apostles always used the sabbath, that is, the Lord's day. And just as the Jews remembered the creation of the world, so we shall think it right to celebrate the memory of its creation and of its restoration to completeness. To this will also belong the grateful remembrance of God's benefits, and the thought that calls us to repentance for our sins. Whoever assigns this day to other things will seem to treat it as a profane thing, like those who take care of the body, reckon expenses, and neglect the soul, who do not hear the word of God, but while it is preached either drink or stroll about. Let such people remember that a sword is not for cutting trees but for defending the body, that clothing is not for wiping away filth but for covering and adorning the body, that a cup is not for washing but for drinking wine; so the sabbath was made not for Mammon, Bacchus, or Venus, but for the worship of God, most good and most great. In sum, the sabbath is to be sanctified.

units.la: Quemadmodum Dominus Deus tuus præcepit tibi. Quod perinde est ac si dicat ideo feruandum esse sabbathū quia Deus ipsum sacrosanctum esse voluerit. Nimirum enim voluit Dominus quietem, & intermissione carnalium operum hac quasi figura demonstrare, vt cessantes ab operibus carnis, Deum in nobis agere pateremur. Tum voluit esse ἀνάπαυσιν[?] quandam in ecclesia: ne si promiscuè quicquam fieret, nihil rectè fieret. Postremo, vt ijs qui sub aliorum sunt imperio dies aliquis esset, quo donis etiam inuitis possent quiescere. Quid enim durabile est quod caret alterna requie? Atq; hæc Dei voluntas expressa verbis, vt haberet vim legis, pro ratione siue causa voluntatem seu mandatum Dei habet.
units.tr: As the Lord your God commanded you. This is as much as to say that the Sabbath is to be kept because God willed it to be holy. Indeed the Lord willed, by this kind of figure, that rest and the cessation from carnal works should show that, while we cease from the works of the flesh, we allow God to work in us. He also willed there to be a certain ἀνάπαυσις [anapausis, rest] in the Church, so that if everything were done indiscriminately, nothing would be done rightly. Last, he willed that there should be a day for those who are under the authority of others, on which even unwilling servants could rest. For what can endure that lacks a regular rest? And this will of God, expressed in words so that it would have the force of law, has for its reason or cause the will or command of God.

units.la: Sed eam vt est expressa, considera. Quod dicit quemadmodum, eo docet non ab arbitrio nostro sed suo pendere formam & rationem sabbathi. Præcipiendi verbo quasi ius & imperium iustum obtendit cui repugnare nephas arbitrere. Quod ait, tibi, id ad omnes huius legis cognitores hæc pertinere significat.
units.tr: But consider it as it is expressed. By saying as, he teaches that the form and reason of the Sabbath depend not on our judgment but on his. By the word of commanding he puts forward a kind of right and a just authority, which you should think it wrong to resist. By saying your, he signifies that this law pertains to all who know it.

units.la: Ergo nostra non minus quàm Iudæorum interest, vt hanc legem feruemus. Idq; exemplo omnium gentium sic esse accipiendum probari potest. Etenim in xij.tab. II.feriæ sic sanctæ sunt habitæ, vt liberis hominibus requiem litium, feruis autem operum & laborum præstiterint. Et lex de ferijs sic habet: Ferijs iurgia amouento, easq; in famulis, operibus patratis habento. Et Vlpianus pridie calendas Februarias magistratus nec ius dicere, nec sui potestatem facere cõsueuisse asserit in l. pridie ff. de ferijs. Idem dicit lege cautum esse, ne feriatis diebus iubus iudicium fit, nisi ex voluntate partium. Extant praeterea in Codice & Nouellis constitutionibus tituli de ferijs. Ex quibus omnibus intelligimus, ferias omnibus hominibus sanctas esse oportere.
units.tr: Therefore it concerns us no less than the Jews that we keep this law. And this can be shown by the example of all nations to be the correct understanding. For in the Twelve Tables the festival days were so held sacred that they gave free men a rest from lawsuits, and slaves a rest from work and toil. And the law concerning holidays reads: "Keep quarrels away from holidays, and let slaves have them once their tasks are done." And Ulpian, in the law Pridie in the Digest, De feriis, asserts that on the day before the Kalends of February magistrates were accustomed neither to pronounce judgment nor to exercise their power. The same writer says that the law provided that judgment should not be given on holidays, unless by the will of the parties. Moreover, there are titles on holidays in the Code and in the Novels. From all these we understand that holidays ought to be holy to all men.

units.la: Quod postremo addit, Dominus Deus tuus:hoc ipso legem eam cum iure tum necessario feruare docet. Nam si dominus iubet,iure parueris: si Deus mandet, necesse est facias: siquidem eum tibi velis esse Deum. Sed quis ex septem diebus unum ei neget a quo reliquos omnes habet? Quamobrem Deum cum aliis tum praecipue sabbatho celebrabimus per Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum, Amen.
units.tr: What he finally adds, your God the Lord, by this very phrase teaches that this law must be kept both by right and of necessity. For if a master commands, you will obey by right; if God commands, you must do it, since you wish him to be your God. But who would deny one of the seven days to him from whom he has all the rest? Wherefore we shall honour God, both in other things and especially on the Sabbath, through Jesus Christ our Lord, Amen.

units.la: SERMO IX.
units.tr: SERMON IX.

units.la: 13 Sex diebus operaberis & conficies omnia negotia tua.
units.tr: 13 Six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work.

units.la: 14 Septimo autem die Sabbathum est Domini Dei tui:non facies vllum opus, neq; tu neq; filius tuus, filia tua, famulus tuus atq; ancilla tua, bos tuus, asinus tuus, atque omnia iumenta tua, sed & peregrinus tuus, qui est intra portas tuas, vt quiescat seruus tuus, & ancilla tua sicut & tu.
units.tr: 14 But the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God: in it thou shalt not do any work, thou, nor thy son, nor thy daughter, thy man-servant, nor thy maid-servant, nor thy ox, nor thy ass, nor any of thy cattle, nor thy stranger that is within thy gates; that thy man-servant and thy maid-servant may rest as well as thou.

units.la: QVando ex prima quarti praecepti parte, perspicuum est, sabbathum, ceu statum quoddam ac religioni debitum tempus à Deo Opt.Max. instituturum esse, eoq; ipso factum quasi quoddam temporum inter se discrimen: iam sequitur eius legis expositio longior: qua tempus aliud laboribus & negotijs humanis ostenditur: aliud rursus religioni & diuinis negotijs deputatur. Ac primum quod humanis, deinceps autem quod diuinis est debitum negotijs haec legis pars persequitur.
units.tr: Since it is plain from the first part of the fourth commandment that God the best and greatest has appointed the sabbath as a certain time set apart and due to religion, and that by this very act a kind of distinction has been made between times: the longer exposition of the law now follows, in which one time is shown to be given to human labours and business, and another time is in turn assigned to religion and divine business. This part of the law pursues first what is due to human affairs, and then what is due to divine ones.

units.la: Tempus humanis operis datum sic exponit: Sex diebus operaberis & facies omnia opera tua. Quibus verbis primum tempus ipsum tum labores dicit. Tempus dies sex continet, quibus operas fieri praecipit, vt ne eum otio putes oblectari: aeque laboris atque ocij tempus nuncupat.
units.tr: The law sets out the time given to human work thus: Six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work. In these words it first names the time itself, both labours and rest. The time of six days is what he commands to be spent in work, lest you think it is given over to leisure; he calls it an equal time for labour and for rest.

units.la: Ex quo perspicuum est, & otium illud segne, & multas illas ferias Deo displicere: quippe quod multis ferijs auocemur ab operis ad otium, & otium fit, quod dicitur, puluinar fatha-næ[?]. Ergo vt septimo quietem, sic sex illis diebus labores mandat. Quod primę legi consenta-neum est, quae dicit: In sudore vultus tui vescieris pane tuo. Et, Maledicta terra in opere tuo. Et, In laboribus comedes ex ea cunctis diebus vitae tuae. Quare cum omnes peccatum habeamus, omnes peccati poenas, labores scilicet & molestias perferemus, ne si illos labores fugiamus, incidamus in animi labores & molestias. Accedit ad legem diuinam etiam Dei ipsius exemplum. Quemadmodum enim Deus die septimo quieuit, sic diebus sex labores orbis conditi pertulit, vt non tam recreationis quàm laboris & industriae exemplum praeferret. Quod etiam Dominus Iesus docet in euangelio, dicens cum se tum patrem subinde operari. Igitur exemplum Dei non est negligendum.
units.tr: From this it is clear that both idle leisure and those many holidays displease God, since we are drawn by many holidays from work to idleness, and idleness becomes, as the saying goes, "a pillow for fools." So, just as he commands rest on the seventh day, so he commands labour on those six days. This agrees with the first law, which says: "In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread." And: "Cursed is the ground for thy sake." And: "In toil shalt thou eat of it all the days of thy life." Therefore, since we all have sin, we all bear the penalties of sin, namely labours and troubles; lest, if we flee those labours, we fall into labours and troubles of the mind. God's own example is also added to the divine law. For just as God rested on the seventh day, so on the six days he laboured in creating the world, so as to offer an example not so much of recreation as of labour and diligence. The Lord Jesus also teaches this in the Gospel, saying that both he and the Father work continually. Therefore the example of God is not to be neglected.

units.la: Sed quoniam Deus in illa maxima lege diem vnum destinauit ocio sacro, videmus illum tenuisse quàm sufficiat hoc tempus religioni, quamquè non opus sit pluribus ferijs.
units.tr: But since God, in that greatest law, set aside one day for holy rest, we see that he has held that this time is enough for religion, although there is no need for more holidays.

units.la: Et ceterę feriae ante meridianum tempus tantum pietatis non habent, quantum vulgo pomeridiano tempore patratur scelerum. Vnde nulli de ferijs illis extant in scriptura Canonica tituli, quales post in iure Canonum sunt excogitati. Et prisci Christiani sanctis Mar-tyribus memorias non ferias instituerunt. Socrates libro 5. Eccles. hist. cap. 22. multis Diui Pauli testimonijs ostendit feriarum vsum esse liberum: tum apponit Constantini & Quartadecimanorum de ijs iudicia: denique suum etiam ex Apostolis. Quartadecimani enim obseruationem quartae decimae ab Ioanne Apostolo sibi traditam afferebant. Romani verò & Occidentales suarum ecclesiarum consuetudinem ab Apostolis Petro & Paulo datam asseuerabant, sed, vt ipse dicit, & res comprobat, neutra pars demonstrationem aliquam hac de re scripto traditam potest proponere.
units.tr: The other holidays before midday have no more piety in them than the crimes committed commonly in the afternoon. Hence there are no titles for those holidays in the canonical Scripture, such as were later invented in the canon law. And the early Christians established memorials for the holy martyrs, not holidays. Socrates, in book 5 of his Ecclesiastical History, chapter 22, shows by many testimonies of the Apostle Paul that the use of holidays is free; then he adds the judgments on them of Constantine and of the Quartodecimans; and finally his own from the Apostles. For the Quartodecimans claimed the observance of the fourteenth day handed down to them by the Apostle John. The Romans and Westerners, however, asserted that the custom of their churches was given by the Apostles Peter and Paul; but, as he himself says, and the facts prove, neither side can put forward any demonstration of this matter committed to writing.

units.la: Iam leges de ferijs Papa tulit, quarum ante annos ducentos extabat nulla. Nam in Con-cilio Lugdunensi demum latae sunt, vt est de Conse.d.iij.ca.pronunciandum.
units.tr: Now the Pope has issued laws on holidays, of which there were none two hundred years ago. For they were first enacted at the Council of Lyons, as is to be declared in De Consecratione, distinction 3, chapter "Pronunciandum."

units.la: Nos ex verbis huius legis facile colligimus tam negotium probari quàm ocium.
units.tr: From the words of this law we easily gather that business is approved just as much as leisure.

units.la: Opera verò vno pronomine exponit dicens, tua. Quo ostendit quae nobis honesta, vtilia, necessaria sunt. Iam honestum est suis quenque deditum esse studijs & officijs : non irhiarę[?] alienis: ut aliud episcopi,magistratus,patrum,dominorum,aliud ecclesię,plebis,liberorum, servorum est facere. Si servus herilia faciat,non suum opus facit,sed alienum,quod est in vitio. Utile est quod te decet atq; æquum est facere,& bonum:si pecces in Deum, in bonas leges,in proximum,non tuum sed diaboli facis opus,aut etiam suis, asini, lupi,vulpis. Quod singulari numero utitur id argumento est,singulorum officia significari. Hæc de laboribus.
units.tr: He sets out the works with one pronoun, saying thy. By this he shows what is proper, useful and necessary for us. Now it is proper for each person to be devoted to his own studies and duties, not to those of others: it is one thing for a bishop, magistrate, father or master to do, and another for the church, the common people or children, or servants, to do. If a servant does his master's work, he is not doing his own work but another's, which is a fault. What is useful is what it becomes you to do and what is right and good; if you sin against God, against good laws, or against your neighbour, you are doing the work not of yourself but of the devil, or even of your ass, wolf or fox. That he uses the singular number is an argument that the duties of individuals are meant. So much for labours.

units.la: Tempus diuinis operis datum sic docet : Septimo autem die sabbathum Domini Dei tui est,non facies omne opus in eo. Quibus verbis primum nominatur & commendatur sabbathum:dein ostenditur quibus rebus atq; studijs dicatum sit:postremo quorum causa Deus ipsum instituerit.
units.tr: He teaches the time given to divine work thus: But the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God; in it thou shalt not do any work. In these words the sabbath is first named and commended; then it is shown to what things and studies it is dedicated; lastly, for whose sake God instituted it.

units.la: 1 Commendatur & nominatur dies septimus. Umbra secundum Paulum,nec ei nos astricti sumus.Christiani dominicam octauo die celebrant. De quo satis alibi. Commendatur autem hoc ipso quod dicitur sabbathum Domini Dei tui esse. Quod cum ita sit,sequitur ipsum creaturis ullis,nec nostris voluptatibus usurpandum.
units.tr: 1 The seventh day is commended and named. "A shadow," according to Paul, "and we are not bound to it" (Col. 2). Christians celebrate the Lord's day on the eighth day. Concerning this there is enough said elsewhere. It is commended, moreover, by the very fact that it is called the sabbath of the LORD thy God. Since this is so, it follows that it must not be used for any creatures or for our pleasures.

units.la: Feriæ diuis institutæ partim cum ecclesiæ veteris consuetudine , partim cum hac ipsa lege pugnant.Etenim vetus ecclesia non habuit ex tanta patrum copia quenquam , cui dies festos agerent:cum Nohe,Abraham,Jacob,Juseph , alijq; alijs de causis fuerint celeberrimi. Igitur illæ feriæ nec veterem nec Apostolicam ecclesiam , sed merum gentilismum sapiunt. Hæc autem lex sabbatha Domino Deo nostro vendicat.
units.tr: Holidays instituted by men are partly at odds with the custom of the ancient Church, and partly with this very law. For the ancient Church did not have, among so great a number of fathers, anyone to whom they kept festival days, though Noah, Abraham, Jacob, Joseph and others were very famous for various reasons. Therefore those holidays savour not of the ancient or Apostolic Church, but of pure paganism. This law, however, claims the sabbaths for the Lord our God.

units.la: Sed voluptatibus dari cum lege prorsus pugnat. Esa.58. Ne faciamus voluntatem nostram in die sancto suo jubet Dominus:sed glorificabimus Dominum , si faciamus vias ejus. Igitur abutimur sabbatho Domini cum nostrae gulae & voluptati inserviimus.Recte ergo ob scaenas voluptates Imp.Leo & Antemius diebus dominicis fieri noluerunt.l. dies festos.C. de feriis.Ergo soli Deo sacrum esto.
units.tr: But that they should be given to pleasures is utterly contrary to the law. Isaiah 58: "The Lord commands: Do not do your own will on my holy day; but we shall glorify the Lord if we do his ways." Therefore we abuse the sabbath of the Lord when we serve our gluttony and pleasure. Rightly, then, because of stage pleasures, the Emperors Leo and Anthemius did not wish things to be done on the Lord's days (law "dies festos," Code, concerning holidays). Let it therefore be holy to God alone.

units.la: 2 Quibus studijs destinatum sit: Non facies,inquit,omne opus in eo. Docet contrario quid facto opus sit.Antea cum de laboris tempore diceret,ait:Facies opera tua:quibus verbis labores licito significabat:jam cum dicit opus nullum faciendum esse,ostendit etiam honestas atque licitas operas hoc die non debere fieri,quippe quibus aliqua cura impenditur, quæ nos à cultu Dei retrahit.At Deus,qui vult animum sibi deditum , hæc omnia removet, per quæ possumus avocari. Proinde remoras mitte. Noli corpus templo inferre: animum quo opus est maxime ,foris habere. Sapientis est viri impedimenta removere : justi vero quod debeat plenè facere. In quo nostros abusus vides. Pars etiam in templis sedens res mundanas animis voluit,ac sabbathis operas suscipit,ficq; à sacris studijs retrahitur.Pars dita est rebus & sabbatho & quouis tempore illicitis,ut crapulæ & nugis. Hi sic servant sabbatha,ut equi & vaccæ ferientur melius : quippe quæ si bona non agant, tamen non faciunt mala.Quin leges proferuntur & servantur jam dudum hisce de rebus læta. Sed quid verbis opus est?Quibus rebus impediuntur verbi divini studium,preces,mysteria,conventus sac-ri,& his similia pia studia.Bene etiam Scævola,rogatus,quid ferijs agi liceret:quod noceret, inquit prætermissum. Nec aberrauit à Christiana doctrina gentilis homo , mea quidem sententia.Quid enim Christus docuit?Sabbathum hominis causa factum dicebat ille: nimirum ut homo quietem corpori negotium animæ præberet hoc die.
units.tr: 2 For what studies it is set apart: "Thou shalt not do," he says, "any work in it." By the contrary he teaches what work must be done. Earlier, when speaking of the time of labour, he said: "Thou shalt do thy works"; by which words he plainly signified labours; now, when he says that no work is to be done, he shows that even honest and lawful works ought not to be done on this day, since they involve some care which draws us away from the worship of God. But God, who wants the mind devoted to him, removes all these things by which we can be distracted. Therefore put away hindrances. Do not bring the body into the temple and keep outside the mind, which is most needed there. It is the mark of a wise man to remove impediments; of a just man, to do fully what he owes. In this you see our abuses. Some, sitting in the churches, give their minds to worldly things, and take up business on the sabbaths, and so are drawn away from holy studies. Others are given to things both unlawful on the sabbath and at any time, such as drunkenness and trifles. These keep the sabbaths in such a way that horses and cows are better kept, for if they do no good, at least they do no evil. Indeed, laws have long been put forward and observed on these matters. But why need words? By what things are the study of the divine word, prayers, the mysteries, holy assemblies, and similar pious studies hindered? Scaevola also answered well when asked what it was lawful to do on holidays: "What would harm," he said, "if left undone." Nor, in my opinion, did this Gentile stray from Christian doctrine. For what did Christ teach? That the sabbath was made for man's sake, as he said: namely, so that on this day man might give rest to the body and nourishment to the soul.

units.la: Quorum causa factum sit sabbathum jam dicit:Tu,inquit,& filius tuus &c. Quibus verbis & homines & jumenta dicit. Homines, tu & filius &c.ait. Cum omnes crearit Deus: sabbathum omnium causa factum, omnibus vult esse solatio tam servis quàm liberis,tam ex teris quàm indigenis.In religione enim jus personarum non ita uti in externis & civilibus rebus servatur,cum omnibus servandis Christus venerit.Rectum & bonum omnium inter-est facere:quiescere & refici necessarium est omnibus.
units.tr: He now states for whose sake the sabbath was made: Thou, he says, and thy son, etc. In these words he names both men and beasts. Men: "thou and thy son" etc. Since God created all, he wants the sabbath, made for the sake of all, to be a comfort to all, to servants as much as to free men, to strangers as much as to natives.
