For in religion the distinction of persons is not kept as it is in external and civil matters, since Christ came to save all. It is right and good for all to do the work; it is necessary for all to rest and be refreshed.

units.la: Jumenta vero,cum quia recreatione etiam ipsa opus habent:tum quia dux illis & magi-ster laborantibus tribuendus esset:Deus etiam sabbatho suo digna duxit. Quamobrem hæc singularis creaturarum notatio,quam ista lex habet,minime est negligenda, atq; enitendum ut suum cuiq;,veluti est à Deo datum,salvum sit privilegium.
units.tr: As for the beasts of burden, since they too need refreshment, and since an ox or an ass that labours ought to be given its guide and master, God has also deemed them worthy of his Sabbath. Therefore this particular mention of the creatures, which this law contains, is by no means to be neglected, and we ought to strive that each creature keeps its own privilege, as it has been given by God.

units.la: Atque ex his quidem potest intelligi , Deum velle suo quæq; tempore fieri, ac diebus sex labores peragi : septimo autem agi ferias : tum ut labores quisque suos habere , sic uni Deo ferias agere debeamus. Ei sit honos in secula , Amen.
units.tr: Indeed from these things it can be understood that God wills each thing to be done in its own time, and the labours to be carried out over six days, while on the seventh day rest is to be taken; so that just as each of us has his own labours, so we ought to keep our rest for the one God alone. To him be honour for ever and ever, Amen.

units.la: SERMO X.
units.tr: SERMON X.

units.la: 15 Et memineris quod & tu seruus fueris in terra Aegypti, & eduxerit te Dominus Deus tuus illinc per manum validam, & brachium exertum. Idcirco praecepit tibi Dominus Deus tuus, ut obserues diem sabbathi.
units.tr: And remember that you too were a servant in the land of Egypt, and the Lord your God brought you out from there by a strong hand and an outstretched arm. Therefore the Lord your God commanded you to keep the day of the Sabbath.

units.la: INitio interpretationis in quartam legem nostrae demonstratum est: Deum velle religioni certum ac statum tempus esse sabbathum: quo sepositis mundanis negotijs, diuinorum & coelestium cura suscipiatur. Atque ut haec eius lex non solum animis comprehendi, ve-rumetiam recte & vere percipi, atque rata haberi queat: tribus partibus eam omnem di-stribuit. Ac prima quidem parte summam ac caput legis: secunda eius expositionem: ter-tia rationes & argumenta, quibus ut seruetur, adduci quisque debeat, ob oculos posuit. Igi-tur explicatis duabus partibus, quibus summa atque explicatio legis propositae sunt: reli-quum est, ut exponatur tertia, qua legem argumentis firmat.
units.tr: At the beginning of our exposition of the fourth law it was shown that God wills the Sabbath to be a fixed and appointed time for religion, so that, with worldly business set aside, care for divine and heavenly things may be taken up. So that this law may be not only grasped by the mind but also rightly and truly understood and held as binding, he divides the whole of it into three parts. In the first part he sets before our eyes the sum and heart of the law; in the second, its explanation; in the third, the reasons and arguments by which each person ought to be led to keep it. Having explained the two parts, in which the sum and explanation of the proposed law are given, it remains that we expound the third, in which he confirms the law by arguments.

units.la: Ea sic habet: Memineris quod seruus fueris in terra,&c. Quorum verborum summa argumentum habet ab ijs quae cum aliquo conferuntur: quae [illegible, ~6 letters] Graeci vocant, du-ctum. Quod genus magnam profecto vim habent. Nam adeo propinqua cognatione si-bi coniuncta sunt ipsa, ut altero sublato sustuleris alterum. Veluti pater & filius, vxor & ma-ritus, dominus & seruus. Etenim hic docet, si seruus hero suo hoc aut illud imperanti iure debet obsequi: profecto meus populus sabbathi religionem requirenti mihi iustam ac debi-tam obedientiam praestabit. Igitur si sabbathi religionem docenti simul atque requirenti mi-hi multum obijcias: ecquid tandem hoc sit: ego, inquam: cedo quis es? an non es seruus Do-mini Dei tui, qui te viuum conseruauit? non opinor negabis. Cur igitur inquam, obe-dientiam neges ei, cui quod modis omnibus maius est, ipsam etiam vitam debes? Quamob-rem satis causae est cur serues sabbathum, quod Dei seruus es: quodq; e durissima seruitute ereptum te sibijpsi libertum fecit.
units.tr: It reads thus: Remember that you were a servant in the land, etc. The sum of these words has an argument drawn from things that are related to one another, which the Greeks call [πρός τι]. This kind of argument has indeed great force. For such things are joined to one another by so close a kinship that, if you remove one, you remove the other: for example, father and son, wife and husband, master and servant. For here he teaches this: if a servant rightly owes obedience to his master in commanding this or that, then surely my people will render me the just and due obedience when I require the observance of the Sabbath. Therefore, if, while I teach and require the observance of the Sabbath, you raise many objections against me, I say to you: Come now, who are you? Are you not a servant of the Lord your God, who has kept you alive? I think you will not deny it. Why then, I ask, do you refuse obedience to him to whom you owe in every way something greater, even your very life? Therefore there is reason enough why you should keep the Sabbath: because you are the servant of God, and he, having snatched you from the hardest slavery, has made you free for yourself.

units.la: Verum ut maiore sit in precio quae proponitur ratio, docet primum, quo in loco res eo rum fuerint: tum in quo statu nunc sint Dei beneficio: deniq; quod ea de causa Deus hanc le-gem tulerit ac seruari postulet.
units.tr: But so that the reason set forth may be held in greater esteem, he teaches first in what place these things were; then in what state they now are by God's benefit; and finally, that for this reason God has enacted this law and requires it to be kept.

units.la: Quo in loco fuerint, Memineris quod seruus fueris in terra Aegypti. Id idem est ac si dicat: Non est quod vel meae legis iugum decutias, quasi tui iuris sis, ac totus liber: vel seruos tuos tractes asperius, quasi nihili mancipia: quin cogita potius quis fueris, ipse seruus scilicet: atq; etiā ut Comicus ille dicit, [illegible, ~12 letters] Igitur cum antea liber nó fue-ris, nec Deum potes contemnere nec homines. Atque sic quidem Deus humilitatem pri-stinae fortis recordatione ingerit, ut per eam extorqueat & debitam Dei verbo obedientiam & charitatem erga proximum. Nam arrogantia & superbia solae faciunt, ut & verbum Dei ne-gligamus & despiciamus proximum.
units.tr: As to the place where they were: Remember that you were a servant in the land of Egypt. This is the same as if he said: There is no reason for you to shake off the yoke of my law, as if you were your own master and wholly free; nor should you treat your servants more harshly, as if they were worthless chattels. Rather, consider who you were: a servant, of course. And, as that comic poet says, [illegible]. Therefore, since you were not free before, you can despise neither God nor men. In this way God, by recalling your former lowly condition, presses upon you both the obedience to his Word that is owed and charity toward your neighbour. For arrogance and pride alone make us neglect and despise both the Word of God and our neighbour.

units.la: Igitur pristinae fortis recordatione tumor ille reprimendus est. Vnde enim haec Ar-damo[?] superbia[?]: qua dustus[?] & verbum Dei de ligno vitae datum negligeret, & Deum quod illi tunc esset proximus, gloria superare contenderet? Certe non aliunde quam e fortis obli-vione proficisci potuit. Etenim si se creaturam & quidem e puluere & coeno genus duxisse, & spiritum vitalem ab eo quem volebat superare, cogitasset: minime vero hoc peccatum tantum commisisset. Ergo tumorem eum repressurus Deus, fortem pristinam obijcit, ac dicit, e puluere genus duxisti, in puluerem redibis. Quae cogitatio docebat utrum erigeret cristas an demitteret. Sauli idem accidit. Nam oblitus suae fortunae pristinae elatus est animo praeque se verbum Dei pariter ac homines contemptui habuit. Tempus me deficiat si similia passos omnes commemorem. Quin etiam haec aetas eius rei plurima exempla tulit. Videas enim aliquem e rherore[?] factum consulem mirum in modum superbire: nec quicquam quod ipse non fecerit rectum ducere: omnes prae se etiam verbum Dei contemnere. Qui ita? quia quis fuerit oblitus est. Nec priuatis hominibus solis malum hoc accidit: quin ipsum principes maximi, & potentissimae Reipublicae patiuntur. An non fortis nostrae nos etiam obliti sumus? Heluetij maiores nostri pauperes, & iugo tyrannorum crudelissimorum pressi rustici, atque ciues fuere: nos ope Dei libertate potiti superbimus mirifice, ac suam sibi quisq; nobilitatem comminiscitur, cuius opinione elatus & homines & Euangelium despiciat. Iam si de nobis, quibus datum est nosse Euangelii, seorsim fit oratio, certè euangelium, cuius beneficio cum opes ingentes, tum etiam illustre nomen comparauimus, negligimus, despicimus, quacunq; de causa deferimus. Qui fit: quia veteris inopiae memoria deposita, ac pacata rerum possessione perfruentes cristas attollimus, quasi fossas omnes superauerimus. Ei malo non melius ibitur obuiam, quàm si tumorem illum recordatione veteris miseriae retundamus. Sic Deus suos Israelitas adducturus ad obedientiam legibus suis debitam, tolera tae in Aegypto durae seruitutis admonet.
units.tr: Therefore that swelling of pride must be checked by the remembrance of our former condition. For whence came this arrogance, by which a man who had received the Word of God, the tree of life, would neglect it, and strive to surpass God in glory, since God was then nearest to him? Surely it could have arisen from nothing but forgetfulness of his condition. For if he had considered that he was a creature, and indeed one whose origin was dust and mire, and that the vital breath came from him whom he wished to surpass, he would never have committed so great a sin. Therefore God, about to check that swelling, sets before him his former condition and says: You have taken your origin from dust, and to dust you shall return. This thought taught him whether to raise his crest or lower it. The same happened to Saul. For, forgetting his former fortune, he was lifted up in mind and held the Word of God as well as men in contempt. Time would fail me if I were to recount all who have suffered similar things. Indeed this very age has produced very many examples of this. For you may see someone, made consul out of a rhetorician's class, puffed up in a marvellous way, thinking nothing right that he himself has not done, and despising before his eyes even the Word of God. Why so? Because he has forgotten who he was. Nor does this evil befall private men alone; the greatest princes and most powerful commonwealths suffer it too. Have we not also forgotten our own condition? Our forefathers, the Helvetians, were poor, and were peasants and citizens pressed under the yoke of the most cruel tyrants. We, having gained liberty by God's help, are wondrously proud, and each one invents for himself a nobility, and, puffed up by this opinion, despises both men and the Gospel. Now if I speak separately of us, to whom it has been given to know the Gospel, certainly we neglect, despise and abandon for whatever reason the Gospel, by whose benefit we have acquired both great wealth and an illustrious name. Why is this? Because, having put aside the memory of our former poverty, and enjoying the peaceful possession of our affairs, we raise our crests as if we had overcome all the ditches. The surest way to meet this evil is to beat back that swelling by recalling our former misery. So God, about to lead his Israelites to the obedience due to his laws, reminds them of the bearable but harsh slavery of Egypt.

units.la: Quo in loco nunc sint, Et eduxerit te Dominus Deus tuus illinc per manum validam & brachium exertum. Id est, Is Deus, qui sabbathum suum vult abs te ratum ac sacrosanctum haberi, sua te potentia ex illa miserrima forte eripuit. Et haec ita dicit, ut quis illos adiuuerit, quis eos inde extraxerit, & quomodo hoc effecerit intelligant.
units.tr: As to the condition in which they now are: And the Lord your God brought you out from there by a strong hand and an outstretched arm. That is: this God, who wills his Sabbath to be held by you as valid and sacred, has by his power snatched you from that most wretched condition. And he speaks thus so that they may understand who helped them, who drew them out from there, and how he did it.

units.la: Quis igitur eos eripuit? Dominus Deus tuus inquit: ne erres, non tuo robore, tua sapientia, non hominum aut Deorum auxilijs, sed eius Dei manu, cuius sabbathum sanctio, liberatus es. Id eò facit, vt Deum redamemus & grati simus.
units.tr: Who then rescued them? "The Lord your God," he says. Do not be mistaken: you were freed not by your own strength, nor by your own wisdom, nor by the help of men or gods, but by the hand of that God whose Sabbath is sanctioned. He does this so that we may love God in return and be thankful.

units.la: Est in hoc permultum situm, vt agnoscas benefactorem tuum. Quid enim Dominus ad pud Efaiam conqueritur? Cognouit bos possidentem se, & asinus praesepe magistrorum suorum: Israel non cognouit, populus meus non intellexit. Ex eiusmodi ingratitudine contemptus & obliuio diuinarum legum proficiscitur.
units.tr: Much in this depends on your acknowledging your benefactor. For what does the Lord complain of through Isaiah? "The ox knows its owner, and the ass its master's crib; but Israel does not know, my people does not understand." Contempt and forgetfulness of the divine laws arise from ingratitude of this kind.

units.la: Sed quid nobis oblitis beneficiorum diuinorum accideritconfidera. Quia fumus obliti Christi redemptoris, ideo sanctis hominibus potius, quàm illi sabbatha facimus: quasi verò per illos ac non potius per Christum redempti & conseruati simus. Sanè ea sabbatha sancti ipsi non recipient: quippe quae norunt esse Christo debita, satis eorum voluntatem probant Ioannis & Pauli & Barnabae exempla, qui mortales abs se ad Christum remiserunt Actorum 3.16. Redeamus igitur ad eum qui benefecit, ac propterea suo iure sibi gratos poscit. Cur Dei fidissimis atque amantissimi patris monitis non obsequimur? Quoties, inquit Dominus, volui te congregare? Ex quibus omnibus colligi potest, Deum quia nos è malis maximis in lautam ac pacatam fortunam traduxerit, iure sibi sabbatha poscere.
units.tr: But consider what has happened to us who have forgotten the divine benefits. Because we have forgotten Christ the Redeemer, we make Sabbaths for holy men rather than for him, as if we had been redeemed and preserved not through Christ but through them. Surely the holy men themselves would not accept such Sabbaths, since they know that these are owed to Christ; the examples of John, Paul and Barnabas prove their will well enough, who sent mortals away from themselves to Christ (Acts 3.16). Let us then return to him who has done good and therefore rightly demands the gratitude that is his due. Why do we not obey the admonitions of God, the most faithful and most loving Father? "How often," says the Lord, "have I wished to gather you?" From all these things it can be gathered that God, because he has brought us out of the greatest evils into a rich and peaceful fortune, rightly demands the Sabbaths for himself.

units.la: Quomodo verò hoc effecerit, iam dicit, Per manum validam & brachium exertum. Hoc est diuina virtute & potentia, citra quam auxilium vobis ferri non poterat. Manus enim pro magna aliqua vi, pro potestate & potentia sumitur: vnde & in sacris literis Spiritus sanctus rebus, quas vult dicere maximas, nomen hoc tribuit. Veluti Psalmo centesimo se-ptimo, quos redemit, inquit, de manu angustiae: quod perinde est ac si dixisset de maxima angustiae vi: de immensa calamitatis & miseriae magnitudine. Hinc & Dei & cuiusuis etiam hominis potentia manus appellatione significatur. Qua de causa fideles Deus auxilij sui promisso consolaturus, suam illis manum paratam dicit: ac rursus opem diuinam implorantes manum sibi porrigi postulant. Vt Psalmo octovagesimonono, Manus mea parata erit cum eo, id est, meum illi in promptu erit auxilium. Et Psalmo centesimo decimo nono: Sit manus tua ad auxiliandum mihi: id est manu tua me extrahas precor.
units.tr: But how he has done this he now says: By a strong hand and an outstretched arm. That is, by divine power and might, apart from which help could not be brought to you. For "hand" is taken for some great force, for power and might; hence also in the sacred letters the Holy Spirit gives this name to things he wishes to call very great. For example, in Psalm 107: "whom he redeemed," he says, "from the hand of distress," which is just as if he had said: from the great force of distress, from the immense magnitude of calamity and misery. Hence the power both of God and of any man is signified by the name "hand." For this reason God, about to comfort the faithful with the promise of his help, says that his hand is ready for them; and again, those who implore divine aid ask that a hand be stretched out to them. As in Psalm 89: "My hand shall be ready with him," that is, my help shall be at hand for him. And in Psalm 119: "Let your hand be to help me," that is, I pray that you draw me out by your hand.

units.la: Idem de brachio dici potest. Nam Spiritus sanctus Psalmo 89. dicens, Brachium meum corroborabit eum: itemque Psalmo eodem dicens, tibi brachium est cum potentia, firmas manum tuam, exaltas dexteram tuam: hoc satis asserit. Ex quibus perspicuum fit etiam hoc loco manum validam, pro maxima potentia: brachium exertum pro porrecto atq; praestito auxilio accipi.
units.tr: The same can be said of the arm. For the Holy Spirit, saying in Psalm 89, "My arm shall strengthen him," and likewise in the same Psalm, "You have an arm with power; you strengthen your hand and lift up your right hand," asserts this sufficiently. From these passages it is also clear that here a strong hand is taken for the greatest power, and an outstretched arm for help that has been extended and given.

units.la: Iam quoniam populus Israel nisi diuina virtute ex istis malis miserijsque eripi non potuit: honestum, iustum, salubre erit ei, illum Deum vt colat, atq; eius iussibus obsequatur. Sed & historia testis est vera dici. Israelitae enim à tergo Pharaonis immensas atq; instructas copias: à fronte mare rubrum habebant, vt quasi inter sacrum & saxum positis nusquam pateret effugium. Hic Deus, quod alterius nullius vi potuisset effici, per fluctus marinos illis vt sua viam fecit.
units.tr: Now, since the people of Israel could not have been rescued from those evils and miseries except by divine power, it will be right, just and salutary for them to worship that God and obey his commands. History also bears witness that this is true. For the Israelites had Pharaoh's vast and fully armed forces behind them and the Red Sea in front, so that, placed as it were between the sacred and the rock, they had no way of escape. Here God did what could have been accomplished by the power of no other being: he made a way for them through the waves of the sea.

units.la: Iam quemadmodum Moses admirabilis illius auxilij recordatione populum Israel ad obedientiam diuinis legibus debitam excitat: sic nos quoque primum omnes quotquot per Christum mirificè conseruati sumus: tum qui vim diuinae gratiae senserunt etiam aliter: eò nos ipsos propellemus, vt leges Dei ratas habeamus. Heluetijs maioribus nostris modo vniuersis , modo singulis opem tulit : quam aliunde sperare nunquam ausi fuissent.Et nos quibus Euangelium suum attulit, in medio hostium subinde infidiantiû conseruauit. Cur ergo vel hanc ipsam de fabbatho , vel reliquas eius leges non haberemus sanctas?Sed de his fatis.
units.tr: Just as Moses, by recalling that wonderful help, stirs the people of Israel to the obedience due to the divine laws, so we too, first of all, all of us who have been wonderfully preserved through Christ, and then those who have felt the power of divine grace in other ways as well, should urge ourselves on to hold God's laws as binding. God brought help to our Helvetian forefathers, sometimes to all of them together and sometimes to individuals, help which they had never dared to hope for from any other source. And to us, to whom he has brought his Gospel, he has kept us safe in the midst of enemies who lay constant snares for us. Why then should we not regard as holy this very law about the Sabbath, or his other laws? But enough on these points.

units.la: Conclusio docet,quod ideo iure fabbathum seruari postulet.Iccirco præcepit,inquit,tibi Dominus Deus tuus,vt obserues diem fabbathi.Id idem est ac fi dicat:Cum Deus hoc tibi dede rit beneficium,iure sibi illud reddi postulat.Vnde sic concludit:Seruus Dei cum fis,Domi-no Deo tuo obedies.Iam fi seruitus, vt est in l.seruitutum.ff.de reg.iur.morti comparatur: sequitur hominem,qui manu missus fit,ac fi prius in rerum natura non fuisset: hominem no-uum factum esse.Igitur Deus primum hanc promulgans legem,creationis meminit, qua fa-ctum est,vt effet homo:iam eam renouans Moses,meminit redemptionis: qua restitutus est in integrum homo,vt iam fit quasi noua creatura Domini.
units.tr: The conclusion teaches that it therefore rightly demands that the Sabbath be kept. Therefore he commanded, he says, the Lord your God, that you should keep the day of the Sabbath. This amounts to saying: since God has bestowed this benefit upon you, he rightly demands that it be returned to him. Hence he concludes thus: "Since you are a servant of God, you shall obey the Lord your God." Now if servitude is compared to death, as in the law "Servitutum" in the Digest, de regulis iuris, it follows that a man who is manumitted becomes, as it were, a new man, as if he had not previously existed in the nature of things. Therefore God, in first promulgating this law, recalled the creation, by which man was made to exist; and Moses, in renewing it, recalls the redemption, by which man has been restored to his original state, so that he is now, as it were, a new creature of the Lord.

units.la: Quamobrem vt veteribus vetus fabbathum fuit,sic nobis nouis nouum esto facrofan-ctum. Sunt enim quæ fabbatho par est fieri, cum suauia tum salubria omnia. Quid enim est salubrius quàm à rerum terrenarum cura ac cogitatione sese ad diuinarum ac cœlestium rerum contemplationem conferre ? quid est vtilius quàm resipiscere à peccatis & bonum facere?tum autem suauis est creationis recordatio:suauior reftaurationis ac redemptionis memoria : omnium autem iucundissima semper est æterni sabbati, id est, cœlestis illius & sempiternæ recreationis & quietis & tranquillitatis spes & fiducia.Deus faxit, vt in his ter-ris sic festos dies agamus,vt in cœlis apud illum æternum feriemur per Iesum Christum Do-minum nostrum,cui sit honos in secula seculorum,Amen.
units.tr: Wherefore, just as the old Sabbath was an old one for the old people, so let the new Sabbath be a holy new one for us who are new. For there are things that ought to be done on the Sabbath, all of them both pleasant and wholesome. For what is more wholesome than to turn one's mind away from the care and thought of earthly things and to devote oneself to the contemplation of divine and heavenly things? What is more useful than to repent of sins and do good? Moreover, the remembrance of creation is pleasant, more pleasant still the memory of restoration and redemption; but most delightful of all is always the hope and confidence of that eternal Sabbath, that is, of that heavenly and everlasting refreshment, rest and tranquillity. May God grant that we so keep festal days on this earth that we may keep holy rest with him in heaven, eternally, through Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom be honour for ever and ever. Amen.

units.la: SERMO XI.
units.tr: SERMON XI.

units.la: 16 Honora patrem tuum & matrem tuam,sicut præcepit tibi Dominus Deus tuus,vt prolongentur dies tui, vtq; bene tibi sit in terra, quam Dominus Deus tuus dat tibi.
units.tr: 16 Honour your father and your mother, as the Lord your God has commanded you, that your days may be prolonged and that it may go well with you in the land which the Lord your God gives you.

units.la: QVod Dominus noster Iesus Christus interrogatus quibus in rebus summa legis & Prophetarum posita sit,in duabus respondit,videlicet & amore & reuerentia Dei & dilectione proximi : id & ex omni genere sacrarum literarum & ex duum tabularum legi-bus cumprimis perspicuum est. Eæ enim sic duabus tabulis descriptæ sunt, vt quæ reli-gionis sunt in prima, quæ vero charitatis in secunda descriptæ sint. Ac quoniam prius ca-put primæ tabulæ descriptum legibus audiuimus,consequens est, vt ex secundæ tabulæ sex reliquis caput alterum addiscamus.
units.tr: When our Lord Jesus Christ was asked in which things the sum of the Law and the Prophets lies, he answered: in two, namely in the love and reverence of God and the love of neighbour. This is shown most clearly by every kind of Holy Scripture, and especially by the laws of the two tables. For these are so written on the two tables that the matters of religion are set down on the first, and those of charity on the second. And since we have heard the first chapter of the first table set out in laws, it follows that we should learn the second chapter from the remaining six laws of the second table.

units.la: Earum prima sic habet:Honora patrem tuum & matrem tuam,&c. Qua lege docet eos qui nobis præfecti sunt honore, obedientia, gratitudine prosequi, nempe vt salua sit Ταξία.Atque hæc quidem lex duabus partibus comprehenditur:quarum prima quid fa-cto opus sit,secunda quibus de causis fieri debeat ostenditur.
units.tr: The first of these reads: Honour your father and your mother, etc. By this law he teaches that those set over us are to be honoured, obeyed and thanked, so that good order [Ταξία] be preserved. This law is comprised of two parts: the first shows what must be done, the second shows for what reasons it ought to be done.

units.la: Prima pars,Honora patrem tuum & matrem tuam.Quibus verbis iubet eos omni honore & officio prosequi,itemque eis obedire,qui nobis ortus nostri secunda causa sunt parentes videlicet.Quod vt quale sit intelligamus plenius & officium debitum & personas quibus de beatur indicat.
units.tr: The first part: Honour your father and your mother. In these words he commands that they be honoured and served in every way, and likewise obeyed, those who are, after ourselves, the cause of our birth, that is, our parents. So that we may understand more fully what kind of duty this is, he also indicates both the duty owed and the persons to whom it is owed.

units.la: Personæ quibus debetur officium sunt parentes, cùm dicat, patrem tuum & matrem tuam. In quo duo obserua. Vnum quod & patrem & matrem ponit. Est quidem ma-ior patris quàm matris dignitas , estque propter insitam muliebri sexui imbecillitatem mi-nor matris authoritas : sed idipsum filio, si matrem minus honorificè habeat,non patroci-nabitur. Primum quia alia patris cum matre tua , quàm filij cum mâtre est comparatio: suum in illam ius pater tuus habet , illa suum item in te filium. Consul aliter alloquitur proconsulem, quàm ego eum qui priuatus sum alloqui debeam. Deinceps quia licet pa-ter te genuerit, tamen mater te & concepit & gestauit vtero & peperit, lactauit, educauit. Qua de causa Deus non minus vult honorari matrem,quam patrem. His duabus causis ac-cedit etiam tertia quod Deus parentes matrimonij lege sic coniunxit tamque arcto mutui amoris nexu sibi inuicem copulauit, vt alter sine altero verè & proprie coli nequeat.
units.tr: The persons to whom the duty is owed are parents, since he says: your father and your mother. Note two things here. The first is that he names both father and mother. The father's dignity is indeed greater than the mother's, and the mother's authority is less, because of the weakness inherent in the female sex; but this will not excuse a son who honours his mother less. First, because the relation of your father to your mother is not the same as that of a son to his mother: your father has rights over her, and she likewise over you, her son. A consul addresses a proconsul differently from how I ought to address a man who is a private person. Next, because although a father begot you, your mother both conceived you, carried you in her womb, bore you, nursed you and raised you. For this reason God wills that the mother be honoured no less than the father. To these two causes a third is added: God joined parents by the law of marriage and bound them to one another with so close a bond of mutual love that the one cannot truly and properly be honoured without the other.

units.la: Alterum quod obseruēs est, quod nulla adhibita conditione quosuis parentes nominat; sed qualescunque reuerendos præcipit: id enim est indicio eos etiam si ignobiles, inopes; imprudentes, improbos habeamus, tamen hoc ipso quod parentes sunt colendos esse. Etenim si pater non fungatur patris officio, peccat ipse: tu non ideo patrem venerari definens peccabis. Quin doleat tibi illorum imbecillitas, pro eis ores Deum, modestè & submissè monebis, cæles eorum peccata, feres æquo animo quod mutari non potest. Summa, nihil excipit Dominus.
units.tr: The second thing to note is that he names parents without any added condition, but commands that parents of whatever kind be revered. For this shows that we are to honour them even if they are ignoble, poor, unwise or wicked, since the very fact that they are parents means they are to be honoured. Indeed, if a father does not perform a father's duty, he himself sins; you will not sin by continuing to honour your father. Rather, let their weakness grieve you, pray to God for them, admonish them modestly and humbly, conceal their sins, and bear with an even mind what cannot be changed. In short, the Lord excepts nothing.

units.la: Officium autem dicit vno verbo honorandi. Quod profecto si spectes originem Hebraei thematis כָּבֵד [?] & כָּבֵד [?] à gravitate & pondere deductum nomen, maiestatem & gravitatem & excelsam quandam gloriam significat, qualem sacræ literæ quandoque Deo, quandoque regibus tribuunt. Quamobrem cum hac voce utatur Dominus, magnam quandam atque excellentiam parentum authoritatem & existimationem vult in animis nostris suscitari. Neque dixit, time ceu herum seruus, noluit enim timeri quidem, non autem coli & diligi: neque dixit dilige ceu æqualis æqualem amat magis quam honoret, noluit enim contemptim aut citra obseruantiam diligi: sed honorandi verbo reuerentiam, amorem, denique omnis generis officia complectitur. Itaque eiusmodi in animis nostris parentum nostrorum existimationem vult residere, vt nobis post Deum nihil sit illis prius, augustius, antiquius. Nam ipsi sunt parentes nostri, id est, illa instrumenta quibus Deus ad creandum nos vsus est.
units.tr: He states the duty in one word: honour. If you consider the origin of the Hebrew word kabed [כָּבֵד], which is derived from weight and heaviness, it signifies majesty, gravity and a certain lofty glory, such as Holy Scripture sometimes ascribes to God and sometimes to kings. Therefore, since the Lord uses this word, he wants great and excellent authority and esteem for parents to be raised up in our minds. He did not say "fear," as a slave fears his master, for he did not want to be merely feared and not honoured and loved; nor did he say "love," as an equal loves an equal, for that love would be greater than honour, and he did not want to be loved in a contemptuous way or without respect. Rather, in the word "honour" he embraces reverence, love and, finally, every kind of duty. Thus he wills that such esteem for our parents should dwell in our minds, that after God nothing should be prior, more venerable or more ancient to us than they. For they are our parents, that is, those instruments by which God used to create us.

units.la: Sed idipsum non solum sic sentire, verumetiam factis ostendere præcipit. Præstabis autem si verbis honorificis, & benignis & vt res vsusque postulat appelles, si illos opera adiuues, si denique ægros consoleris, mœstos reficias, languentes cures, inopes foueas. Sed quis omnia genera enumerare? Totum te eis præbeas Dominus præcipit. Quod est honore parentes prosequi.
units.tr: But he commands us not only to think this but also to show it by our deeds. We shall do so if we address them with honourable and kind words, as the matter and custom require; if we help them in their work; and finally, if we comfort them when they are sick, cheer them when they are sad, care for them when they are weak, and cherish them when they are in need. But who could list every kind of service? The Lord commands you to give yourself wholly to them. This is what it is to honour one's parents.

units.la: Neque verò honos ille primarius est: prior enim est illo qui debetur Deo, quo de nobis primæ tabulæ præceptum est legibus. Ex quo potest intelligi quousque sese porrigat ista parentibus debita reuerentia, nempe, vt ille dixit, vsque ad aras. Iubet Deus parentibus obedias, non autem vult illis, si quid impium, improbum, absurdum, indignum bono viroiubeant, obsequi. Ionathas Sauli patri in persecutione Dauidis nequaquam obsequitur. Petrus iubet magistratibus obsequi, sed ipse magistratui contra Christum imperanti silentium non obsequitur, dicens, oportere Deo magis obsequi quàm hominibus. Christus dicit eum qui parentes pluris quam ipsum faciat indignum esse qui sit ipsius discipulus. Ex quibus omnibus multisque aliis quæ præterco [?] perspicuum est, obedientiam illam parentibus atque magistratibus debitam ad ea nos minime cogere, quæ pugnant cum pietate & iustitia, sed velle Deum in ijs rebus nos parentibus atque magistratibus esse morigeros, in quibus possumus piè & iustè. Atque hæc est legis sententia.
units.tr: Nor is this honour the first in order: for it comes after the honour owed to God, which is laid down for us in the laws of the first table. From this it can be understood how far that reverence owed to parents extends, namely, as that man put it, even as far as the altars. God commands you to obey your parents, but he does not want you to obey them if they order anything impious, wicked, absurd or unworthy of a good man. Jonathan does not obey his father Saul in the persecution of David. Peter commands obedience to magistrates, yet he himself does not obey a magistrate who orders him to be silent against Christ, saying that we must obey God rather than men. Christ says that one who values his parents more than himself is not worthy to be his disciple. From all these and many other examples, which I pass over, it is clear that the obedience owed to parents and magistrates does not compel us to those things which fight against piety and justice; rather, God wills that we be obedient to parents and magistrates in those matters in which we can be so with piety and justice. This is the meaning of the law.

units.la: Finis autem est vt quibus aliqua in nos potestas concessa est, ijs quantam maximam possumus pietatem atq; obseruantiam exhibeamus.
units.tr: The purpose is that we should show the greatest possible piety and respect to those over whom some power has been granted to us.

units.la: Nam ex hoc præcepto ius personarum, quo fit vt alij sui sint iuris alij alieni, defluxit. Idq; patris à quo patria appellatur, nomen non obscure significat. Inde sequitur, vt quicquid appellatione patriæ comprehensum est, quod quidem ad eam conseruandam pertinet, vt magistratus, tutores, magistri, senes, agnati atq; affines, denique etiam episcopi, eos omnes patrum loco nobis habendos esse.
units.tr: For from this commandment arises the law of persons, by which some are their own masters and others are under another's authority. The name "patria" (fatherland), from which "pater" (father) is derived, clearly signifies this. It follows that whatever is included under the name of fatherhood, insofar as it pertains to preserving that authority, such as magistrates, guardians, teachers, elders, agnates and kinsmen by marriage, and finally even bishops, are all to be regarded by us in the place of fathers.

units.la: Ac magistratus quidem omnium gentium consensu patres, & quidem Romæ patres conscripti nominati sunt: quod quemadmodum liberorum parentes sic illi plebis saluti curandæ essent dediti. Quis vero neget obediendum ijs esse qui nostri cura non minus quàm si patres nobis essent tanguntur.
units.tr: Magistrates, indeed, are called fathers by the consent of all nations, and at Rome they were named "conscript fathers," because just as parents are devoted to their children, so they should be devoted to caring for the safety of the people. Who would deny that those must be obeyed who concern themselves with us no less than if they were our fathers?

units.la: Tutores autem quia liberis testamento dabantur ab ipsis patribus iure legum xij.tab.i. temq; ciuili,ijq; eo pacto in patrum locum succedebant: quis illis neget conuenire, vt eos quos pater moriens præfecerat, parentum instar honorarent?
units.tr: Guardians, since they were appointed for children by testament from the fathers themselves, under the law of the Twelve Tables and civil law, and in this way succeeded to the place of fathers: who could deny that it is fitting for us to honour as parents those whom a dying father had appointed?

units.la: Magistri quia animos formabant, erantq; nobis quasi vitæ melioris authores: quis non videt quanto sint habendi in precio? Aristotelem patris loco habendum sibi duxit Alexander Macedo, propterea quod eo præceptore esset vsus.
units.tr: Teachers, since they formed our minds and were, as it were, the authors of a better life for us: who does not see how highly they are to be valued? Alexander the Macedonian thought Aristotle should be held in the place of a father, because he had been taught by him.

units.la: Senes autem omnes, quoniam viri nos filios, fœminæ virgines filias quasi iure nominant atq; alloquuntur omnium consensu honorandi visi sunt. Nec Sparta hanc rem minus floruit ac viguit. Agnati vero quia non datis testamento tutoribus ipsi iure tutores fiunt quasi tuitores: quo nomine sunt etiam ceu parentes venerandi.
units.tr: Elders, since men address us as sons and women address girls as daughters, as it were by right, have by the consent of all been seen as deserving honour. Nor did Sparta flourish and thrive less in this matter. Agnates, indeed, because when no guardians have been given by testament they become guardians by law, as it were protectors: under this name too they are to be venerated as parents.

units.la: Episcopis vero,cum quod sunt legati Dei opt. max. tum quod doctrina vitam nostram in Christo nouam faciunt,patres appellantur;& habentur. Vnde & apostolus dicit se Corinthios in fide genuisse in Domino.
units.tr: Bishops, however, are called and regarded as fathers, both because they are the ambassadors of God most good and great, and because by their teaching they make our life new in Christ. Hence the apostle also says that he begot the Corinthians in the faith in the Lord.

units.la: Atq; his omnibus quoniam ad tuendam suam apud nos dignitatem Deus nomen suum ipsius vsurpandum concessit,nempe vt & patres & Dii & Domini appellentur,sacris literis testibus certe vel praeclaris istis titulis moti, summam reuerentiam habere debebimus. Ac quia nomina diuina sine causa nequaquam gerunt, arbitrabimur habere eos no parum honoris cum Deo optimo maximo commune. Pater enim vere & proprie solus Deus dicitur,sed id nomen etiam iis qui patres mundani sunt impertit, vt maiorem eis honorem habeamus: Dei nomen soli illi ipsi competit, sed vt magnos propeq; diuinos magistratibus habeamus suum ipsius proprium illis quoque tribuit nomen. Dominus ipse vere & proprie solus dicitur, & tamen vt obediendum magistratibus arbitraremur,ipsos quoque eo nomine dignatus est.
units.tr: Since God has allowed his own name to be used to maintain their dignity among us, so that they are called fathers, gods and lords, we ought to show them the greatest reverence, moved by these splendid titles, as Scripture itself attests. And since divine names are never borne without reason, we shall consider that they have no small share of honour in common with God most good and great. For God alone is truly and properly called Father, yet this name is also given to earthly fathers, so that we may give them greater honour. The name of God belongs to him alone, but he also grants his own name to magistrates, so that we may regard them as great and almost divine. The Lord alone is truly and properly called Lord, and yet, so that we may judge that magistrates are to be obeyed, he has also honoured them with that title.

units.la: Iam cum & sententiam & finem legis habeamus,etiam in vitam ac mores nostros intueamur necesse est,nempe vt quando seruetur aut negligatur lex Domini intelligamus.
units.tr: Since we have both the sense and the purpose of the law, we must also look at our life and conduct, namely, so that we may understand when the Lord's law is kept and when it is neglected.

units.la: Ac transgressores quidem duabus classibus omnes comprehendimus: quarum altera au-thores,altera autem eos ipsos includimus.
units.tr: We may sum up all transgressors under two classes: one class consists of the instigators, the other of those who commit the offences themselves.

units.la: Authores sunt aliis vti legem hanc violent multi & varij. Primum magistri falsae religio-nis,de quibus etiam Dominus Matth.15. conqueritur, dicens, Quare & vos transgredimini praeceptum Dei propter traditionem vestram? Nam Deus praecipit dicens: Honora patrem et matrem: & qui maledixerit patri & matri morte moriatur. Vos aut dicitis quicunq; dixerit patri & matri: quicquid doni a me profecturum erat, id in tuum vertitur commodum, & non honorabit patrem suum, aut matrem suam, & irritum fecistis praeceptum Dei propter traditionem vestram. Id vt intelligas quale sit, eiusmodi est. Quod parentibus dari poterat id illi in v-sus templi seu thesauros ecclesiasticos conferendum potius iudicabant, quippe quod inde fructus vberrimos & parentes & liberi perciperent. Speciosum quidem erat documentum, sed & sacrificorum magis, quàm parentum vsibus commodum, & officijs parentum victum debitis summe perniciosum. Quare eam traditionem Dominus quasi quoddam debitae parentibus pietatis impedimentum vituperat. Eorum similes sunt monachi nostri qui parentibus & liberos & facultates auferunt, acq; etiam inopibus pernegant, quíque mortuis potius quàm viuis parentibus officia postulant. Quos qui non dicas liberis authores esse, vt legem de pietate parentibus debitam hanc transgrediantur.
units.tr: Many and various people instigate others to break this law. First, the teachers of false religion, about whom the Lord also complains in Matthew 15, saying: "Why do you also transgress the commandment of God by your tradition? For God commanded, saying, Honour your father and mother; and, whoever curses father or mother, let him die the death. But you say, whoever shall say to his father or mother, Whatever gift is mine that might have profited you, it is devoted to God, he shall not honour his father or his mother; and you have made the commandment of God void by your tradition." To see what sort of thing this is, consider the following. What could have been given to parents, they judged should rather be contributed to the uses of the temple or to the ecclesiastical treasury, since parents and children would both draw most abundant profit from it. It was a specious teaching, but it served the uses of the priests more than those of the parents, and it was utterly harmful to the support that parents are owed by their children's duty. Therefore the Lord censures that tradition as a kind of hindrance to the piety owed to parents. Similar to them are our monks, who take away from parents both their children and their property, deny them even to the needy, and who demand services for the dead rather than for the living. Would one not say that they are instigators of children to break this law concerning the piety owed to parents?

units.la: Qui vero filios familiàs & virgines iniscijs parentibus iungunt connubijs, quod patriae potestati derogat,iidem etiam liberis authores sunt,vt legem istam violent. Etenim filius familiàs,quoniam est in potestate patris, non potest matrimonium contrahere nisi patre consentiente. Vnde iustae nuptiae censentur non solum qui iunguntur, sed etiam parentes, sub quorum sunt potestate. Dicit enim in l. nuptiae, ff. de ritu nuptiar. Paulus Iurecol. ad hunc modum. Nuptiae consistere non possunt nisi consentiant omnes, id est, qui coeunt, quorum-que in potestate sunt. Ac quanquam leges ciuiles tantummodo patrum & auorum, ac non etiam matrum, quarum in potestate liberi iure ciuili esse non possunt, consensum requirant, eoque matrem, cuius obseruantiam haec lex aeque ac patris reuerentiam praecipit, excludat: tamen ad hoc praeceptum Domini propius accedunt, quàm pontificum canones, quos oportebat esse verbo Dei proximos. Pontifices enim in iis quae nubunt, quiq; matrimonium contrahunt consensum esse contenti sunt, ac docent parentum assensum honestatis magis, quàm iuris nomine requiri. Vti scriptum est ab illis in c. sufficiat. xxvij, q. ij. & c. hoc sanctum. xxxij. q. ij. & c. cum locum. extra. de sponsa, & matri. Quamobrem proxime accedunt ad sententiam legis diuinae qui parentum consensum in matrimonijs non negligunt: contra hanc violant, qui liberis, vt illis inscijs & inuitis sese iungant connubijs authores praebent.
units.tr: Those who join sons under their father's authority and unwedded daughters in marriage without their parents' knowledge, which detracts from paternal power, are likewise instigators of children to break this law. For a son under paternal authority cannot contract marriage unless his father consents. Hence a marriage is held to be lawful not only if the couple are joined, but also if the parents under whose power they stand give consent. For the jurist Paulus says in the law "Nuptiae", Digest, on the rite of marriage, in this manner: "Marriage cannot exist unless all consent, that is, those who come together and those under whose power they are." And although the civil laws require the consent only of fathers and grandfathers, and not of mothers, whose children cannot by civil law be under their power, and so exclude the mother, whose reverence this law commands just as much as the father's, nevertheless the canons of the pontiffs, which ought to have been closest to the Word of God, come less near to this command of the Lord than the civil laws do. For the pontiffs are content with the consent of those who marry and contract matrimony, and they teach that the assent of parents is required out of decency rather than by right, as is written by them in the chapter "Sufficiat" (27, q. 2), the chapter "Hoc sanctum" (32, q. 2), and the chapter "Cum locum" (Extra, on betrothal and marriage). Therefore those who do not neglect the consent of parents in marriages come nearest to the sense of the divine law; those who violate it are those who lend themselves as instigators to children, so that they may join themselves in marriage without, and against the will of, their parents.

units.la: His adnumerandi sunt tertij qui fe-tenerae aetati praebent magistros nequitiae, & omnis generis flagitiorum, vt inuitis ac renitentibus parentibus potare, scortari, ludere, & omnino recti nihil facere consuescant. Quo in numero sunt etiam qui filiosfamiliàs procul hinc abducunt militatum: quod, quoniam plerunque occidunt, plagij simile est. Hi sunt authores inobedientiae, autho-res inobedientiae. Cæterum vsuenit,vt ipsi quoq; parentes violatæ legis huius liberis authores sint,quando nimis illis indulgent, quando magis coaceruandis opibus, quàm illis erudiendis dediti sunt, quando solutæ & impuræ vitæ exemplo suo offendunt ipsi liberos, denique cum eos asperius quàm par fit habeant. Quò fit,vt alieniores fiant eorum à parentibus animi, vt quæ patrum consilijs atque monitis fugere debuerant, ea sectentur ipsorum exemplo perciti,vt ingenia non acuant disciplina ac studio,sed consumant inertia,vt parentum imperium,quando ei non assueuerunt à pueris, intolerabile esse iudicent, etiam cum iustum bonum & æ-quum est.
units.tr: To these must be added the third sort, who give tender youth teachers of wickedness and of every kind of disgrace, so that, against the wishes and resistance of their parents, they learn to drink, to whore, to gamble, and to do nothing right at all. In this number are also those who lead sons of the household far away to serve as soldiers; since they mostly perish there, this is like kidnapping. These are the instigators of disobedience. Moreover, it happens that the parents themselves become instigators of their children to break this law, when they indulge them too much, when they are devoted more to heaping up wealth than to educating their children, when by the example of a loose and impure life they offend their children themselves, and finally when they treat them more harshly than is right. The result is that their children's minds become more estranged from their parents, so that they pursue, stirred up by the parents' own example, the very things they ought to have avoided at their fathers' counsel and warnings; they do not sharpen their wits by discipline and study, but waste them in idleness; and since they have not been accustomed to parental authority from childhood, they judge it intolerable, even when it is just, good and fair.

units.la: Itaque enitendum est parentibus,vt educatione,disciplina,exemplo iustæ & debitæ obedientiæ liberos assuefaciant,eosque non vt tyranni mancipia,quod Ephesijs scribens apostolus admodum detestatur,sed vt patres suos ipsorum natas,chara scilicet pignora,benignè,& amanter foueant.
units.tr: Therefore parents must strive to accustom their children, by upbringing, discipline and example, to just and due obedience; and they must cherish them kindly and lovingly, not as a tyrant's slaves, which the apostle, writing to the Ephesians, utterly condemns, but as their fathers' daughters and sons, dear pledges indeed.

units.la: Ipsi vero liberi suos parentes quandoque non quo par erat honore, prosequuntur & officio, sed vel simulant verbis praesertim in conspectu hominum, quam animis nullam habent pietatem: vel si magnificiant eos, tamen officio non satisfaciunt: vel netrum praestant. Ac nostra quidem aetate admodum procax est & inobediens adolescentia, quippe quæ non solum quosvis senes,verum etiam suos ipsorum parentes parum pie et decore tractet. Quod genus homines hac lege coercendi sunt.
units.tr: The children themselves, for their part, sometimes do not show their parents the honour and service that is fitting. They either pretend with words, especially in the sight of men, when in their hearts they have no piety at all; or if they do magnify their parents, they still do not fulfil their duty; or they render neither. In our own age the youth is very insolent and disobedient, since it treats not only any old people, but even its own parents, with little piety and decency. Such people must be restrained by this law.

units.la: Pars altera. Sicut præcepit tibi Dominus Deus tuus, vt prorogentur dies tui, vtq; bene sit tibi in terra quà Dominus Deus tuus dat tibi. Rationes sunt tres. 1. præceptū Domini, videlicet Exod. 20. in monte Sina quando leges illas decem toti populo proposuit. Igitur si quæris, cur honorandi sint, quia Deus preceperit respondeo. An non hoc ipsum satis causæ est? Nos enim quando hoc affirmamus in disputando, quare sic se habeat sciscitantibus iustius respondemus ὅτι αὐτὸς ἔφα, quàm Pythagorici, quàm alicuius heri famuli, quàm ministri regij. In eam sententiam scribit etiam Colossensibus apostolus cap. 3. dicens, Filij obedite parentibus per omnia, sic enim placitum est Domino.
units.tr: The second part: As the Lord your God has commanded you, that your days may be prolonged, and that it may be well with you in the land which the Lord your God gives you. There are three reasons: (1) the command of the Lord, namely Exodus 20, where on Mount Sinai he set out those ten laws before the whole people. So if you ask why they are to be honoured, I answer: because God has commanded it. Is this itself not reason enough? When we affirm this in disputation, and are asked why it is so, we answer more justly "he himself has said it" (ὅτι αὐτὸς ἔφα) than the Pythagoreans would, or any servant of some master, or a royal minister. The apostle also writes to the Colossians to this effect, in chapter 3: "Children, obey your parents in all things, for this is well pleasing to the Lord."

units.la: Sed & omnium hominum & brutorum animantium mentibus, atque sensibus hæc de pietate erga parentes lex Domini indubie diuinitus impressa est. Nam priscis Romanis adeo cordi fuit vt parentes honorarētur à liberis, vt & patriæ potestatis ius sanxerint & idipsum postea in immensum auxerint. Ac Romulus quidè earum, quas curiatim rogauit legū numero comprehendit hanc etiam, Filius quamdiu vixerit, in patris potestate manet, quare eam neq; nuptiæ, soluunt, sed nisi legitime pareat, est perpetua: verum leges xij. tab. eam sic auxerunt vt vendendi filij patri potestatem fecerint. Quam etsi iniustam legiq; Dei contrariam posteri mitigarint, atq; ad naturalem diuinoq; iuri consentaneam æquitatem traduxerint, vt videre est in l. qui filios. C. quæ res pign. obliga. poss. vel non, & l. Diuus Adrianus. ff, ad leg. Pompe. de patric. tamen adhuc reliquam fecerunt parentibus honestam emendationem & ex maxima causa exheredationem. Qua de re scribitur C. de emenda. propinquo. & Nouell. vt cum de appella. cognosci. §. aliud quoque. His adde quod tantus honos habitus est parentibus, vt actione iniuriarum non teneantur l. pretor edixit. §. præterea. ff. de iniuri. ac si liberis iniurij sint, cœcessum [?] est liberis hoc solum, vt officium iudicis implorent, qui compellat iniquos parentes ad emancipationem. l. vltima. ff. si à parent. quis manumiss. fuerit. Ex quibus omnibus multisque alijs legibus ciuilibus perspicuum est quantopere cauerint prisci seculi homines ne qua liberis daretur occasio parentes contemnendi.
units.tr: But the Lord's law concerning this piety towards parents is undoubtedly impressed by God on the minds and senses of all men and of the brute animals as well. For the ancient Romans so cherished the principle that parents should be honoured by their children that they enshrined the right of paternal power in law, and afterwards greatly extended it. Romulus indeed included among the laws which he proposed by the curiae this one also: "A son remains under his father's power as long as the father lives," so that marriage does not dissolve it, but unless the father legitimately releases him, it is perpetual. The Twelve Tables, however, so extended it that they gave fathers the power of selling their sons. Although later generations softened this, which was unjust and contrary to the law of God, and brought it back to the natural equity consonant with divine law, as may be seen in the law "Qui filios" (Code, on what things may be pledged or not) and the law "Divus Hadrianus" (Digest, on the Pompeian law concerning parricide), nevertheless they left parents an honourable correction, and disinheritance for the greatest cause. On this matter it is written in the Code, "On emancipation by a relative", and in the Novels, in the rule "When it is to be known on appeal", paragraph "Aliud quoque". To these add that such great honour was given to parents that they cannot be held liable for injury by an action for wrongs (the law "Praetor edixit", paragraph "Praeterea", Digest, on injuries); and if children are wronged by them, it is permitted to the children only to implore the office of a judge, who may compel unjust parents to emancipate them (the last law, Digest, "If a man has been manumitted by his parent"). From all these and many other civil laws it is plain how greatly the men of earlier ages took care that no occasion should be given to children to despise their parents.

units.la: Quin illius vim legis in scriptis poetarum & philosophorum multò magis cernimus. Menander ait, Νόμῳ γονέυσιν ἰσοθέως τιμὰς νέμειν. Id est, lex iubet parentibus honores diuinos perhibere. Et Euripides ait eum qui parentes colat & viuum & mortuum Dijs charum esse. Quo quid dicit aliud quàm hic fortunata ac prospera, illic autem beata vita perfrui illum qui in parentes pius fuerit? Platonis, Isocratis, aliorumque in hanc sententiam scite dicta praetereo, nec exempla quibus Græcæ & Romanæ plenæ sunt historiæ lubens omitto: quæ tamen omnia significant illud ipsum Dei verbum in omnium hominum animis altas radices egisse. Sed etiam brutis animantibus impressam esse hanc legem exemplum ciconiæ describens, & ad nostras illas tabulas accommodans indicat Aristophanes in Auib. Dicit autem apud eum Pischetærus.
units.tr: Indeed, we see the force of this law even more clearly in the writings of poets and philosophers. Menander says, "To honour parents as gods by law" [Νόμῳ γονεῦσιν ἰσοθέως τιμὰς νέμειν]. That is, the law requires that divine honours be paid to parents. Euripides says that the man who honours his parents, both living and dead, is dear to the gods. What else does this mean than that the man who has been dutiful to his parents enjoys a fortunate and prosperous life here and a blessed one hereafter? I pass over the wise sayings of Plato, Isocrates and others to the same effect, and gladly leave aside the examples with which Greek and Roman histories abound. Yet all of these show that this very word of God had struck deep roots in the minds of all men. Aristophanes, in the Birds, shows that this law was even stamped upon brute animals, when he describes the stork as an example and applies it to our tables. There, Peisthetairos speaks as follows.

units.la: Ἀλλ' ἔξεστιν ἡμῖν τοῖσι ὄρνισιν νόμῳ
units.tr: But it is permitted for us birds by law [Ἀλλ' ἔξεστιν ἡμῖν τοῖσι ὄρνισιν νόμῳ]

units.la: Παλαιὸς ἐν τοῖς τὰν πελαργῶν χύβιστιν [?]
units.tr: Ancient in the custom of storks [Παλαιὸς ἐν τοῖς τὰν πελαργῶν χύβιστιν]

units.la: Ἐπλῶ ὁ πατὴρ ὁ πελαργὸς ἐκπετησίμες [?] Πάντας ποιήσῃ τῆς πελαργιδεῖς τρέφων [?] Δεῖ τῆς νεοττῆς τὸν πατέρα πάλιν τρέφειν. [?]
units.tr: The father stork, having flown forth, nourishing all his brood, must in turn feed his young, as they fed him [Ἐπλῶ ὁ πατὴρ ὁ πελαργὸς ἐκπετησίμες Πάντας ποιήσῃ τῆς πελαργιδεῖς τρέφων Δεῖ τῆς νεοττῆς τὸν πατέρα πάλιν τρέφειν.]

units.la: Quibus verbis docet legem tabulis ciconiarum inscriptam esse eiusmodi ; ut quemadmodum ciconiæ pullos suos educarunt, sic pulli vicissim suos parentes nutriant senio confectas. Qui locus etiam tabularum in quibus leges describi solent meminit : quod indicio est hanc legem æque aliarum gentium tabulis, atque Hebræis illis diuinitus allatis inscribi solitas. Et Scholiastes Aristophaneus cõparatione ciconiæ & hippopotami siue equi fluuiatilis ex Aristotele adducta probat exemplum ciconiarum minimè fabulosum esse. Vnde potest intelligi ; illius legis sententiam etiam brutis animantibus probari. Quamobrem cum hoc verbum Domini cum hominum omnium, eorum quidem qui rationem ducem sequuntur, tum etiam brutorum animantium consensu recepta sit: consequens est eius causam satis pro batam ac firmatam esse verbo Domini.
units.tr: By these words he teaches that a law of this kind is inscribed on the tables of the storks: just as storks have reared their young, so in turn the young should nourish their parents when they are worn out with age. The passage also mentions the tables on which laws are usually written, which is evidence that this law was customarily inscribed on the tables of other nations as well as on those tables of the Hebrews that were delivered by divine means. The Scholiast on Aristophanes, adducing from Aristotle the comparison of the stork with the hippopotamus or river horse, shows that the example of the storks is by no means fabulous. From this it can be understood that the sense of that law is confirmed even by brute animals. Therefore, since this word of the Lord has been received by the agreement of all men, at least of those who follow reason as their guide, and also of the brute animals, it follows that its reason has been sufficiently proved and confirmed by the word of the Lord.

units.la: Altera causa est; ut prorogentur dies tui. Quibus verbis longævitatem ceu maximum quod-dam huius virtutis præmium pollicetur. Nam cum vita hæc beneficium sit Domini, quis ne get illud cumulari si vita contingat longior. Ergo hoc premiu etiam gentiles scriptores pol licentur. Extat in eâm sententiam Senarius Græcus:
units.tr: The second reason is that your days may be prolonged. In these words he promises long life as a kind of greatest reward for this virtue. For since this life is a gift of the Lord, who would deny that it is increased if it proves to be longer? Therefore the Gentile writers also promise this reward. To this effect there is a Greek iambic line:

units.la: Ἱκανὸς βιῶσαι γηροβοσκεῖν τὰς γονεῖς. [?]
units.tr: It is enough to have lived, to have nourished one's aged parents [Ἱκανὸς βιῶσαι γηροβοσκεῖν τὰς γονεῖς.]

units.la: Est autem hac virtute dignum premium longævitas. Quis enim vita dignior est, quàm qui instrumentum ipsum, per quod vitam accepit, summo habet in precio: Quamobrem si velis senex venerandus haberi, senes ipse prius veneraberis.
units.tr: Long life is a reward worthy of this virtue. For who is more worthy of life than the one who holds in highest esteem the very means by which he received life? Therefore, if you wish to be considered an honourable old man, you must first honour the aged yourself.

units.la: Tertia causa est, Vt bene sit tibi in terra quam Dominus Deus tuus dat tibi. Hoc est, ut vita bonisque reliquis, quibus Deus te donauit quiete & suauiter perfruare. Quod exempla docent fieri. Cham quia patrem turpiter habuit, seruitati subiectus est: Iosephus autem quia patrem summo habuit in precio, totius Ægypti dominationem consecutus est. Absolon contra patrem suscitatæ seditionis miserabili morte pœnas dedit: Tobias autem quia senio confectos parentes honorauit ideo Deum semper sibi propitium patronum habuit. Nostra tempestate magnas ex eo clades accipimus quod parentes parum reueremur atque etiam eos pars maxima contemnimus. Deus faxit ut & hanc & alias eius leges ratas habeamus. Amen.
units.tr: The third reason is that it may be well with you in the land which the Lord your God gives you. That is, that you may enjoy life and the other good things with which God has blessed you, in quiet and sweetness. Examples show that this comes to pass. Ham, because he treated his father shamefully, was made subject to slavery; but Joseph, because he held his father in highest esteem, obtained dominion over all Egypt. Absalom, on the other hand, who stirred up sedition against his father, paid the penalty with a wretched death; but Tobias, because he honoured his parents when they were worn out with age, always had God as a kind and favourable patron. In our own time we suffer great calamities from this cause, that we pay little reverence to our parents, and indeed the greater part of us despise them. May God grant that we hold this law and his others as valid. Amen.

units.la: SERMO XII.
units.tr: SERMON XII.

units.la: 17 Ne occidas.
units.tr: 17 You shall not kill.

units.la: QVemadmodum Deus quinque prioribus præceptis sic quæ veram religionem spectant comprehendit, vt à summo genere ad imum quasi per gradus descendat: eodem modo quinq; reliquis à maximo flagitio descendit ad minimam quæ fit iniuriam. Nam quod ad religionem attinet, maximum peccatum est Deum negare, & ab eo prorsus deficere: proximum, trrare in eius cultu seu religione: tertium, abuti illius san&o nomine: quartum, prophanis & interdum nefarijs rebus illius ferias polluere: vltimum, quos ille nobis præfecit tanquam legum suarum custodes & magistros despicere. Igitur primo præcepto Deos alienos, secundo simulachrorum vsum atque cultum, tertio nominis sui sumptionem friuolam, quarto sabbathi prophanationem, quinto parentum contemptum vetat. Quo ordine vides Deum, qua parte plus est periculi, ea ipsa primum curare & arcere malum. Itaque in ijs quæ proximum nostrum speƈtant rebus eundem seruat ordinem, vt primum cedem, qua nulla accidit homini maior iniuria, deinde adulterium, quo nobis, vxores & liberi quibus nihil est charius de fama, deq; sua salute periclitantur, tertiò furtum, quo opes ause-runtur, quarto linguam siue maledicentiam, quinto voluntatem nocendi vetat.
units.tr: Just as God has comprehended the first five commandments, which concern true religion, so that he descends as by steps from the highest kind to the lowest, in the same way he descends through the last five from the greatest wrong to the least injury to our neighbour. As for religion, the greatest sin is to deny God and wholly fall away from him. The next is to err in his worship or religion. The third is to abuse his holy name. The fourth is to profane his festival days with secular and sometimes wicked deeds. The last is to despise those whom he has set over us as guardians and teachers of his laws. Accordingly, the first commandment forbids strange gods, the second the use and worship of images, the third the frivolous taking of his name, the fourth the profaning of the Sabbath, and the fifth contempt for parents. You see that in this order God first guards against and repels the evil where the danger is greatest. He keeps the same order in matters concerning our neighbour: first he forbids murder, which does no greater wrong to a man; then adultery, by which wives and children, who are dearer to us than anything, are put at risk of their reputation and their salvation; third, theft, by which our goods are taken away; fourth, the tongue, that is, slander; and fifth, the will to harm.

units.la: Ac sextum quidem illud sic habet, Non occides. Ac quanquam breuis est lex, tamen ob id non erit leuiter consideranda. Quin nobis quo breuior est, hoc fuerit altius repetenda, cum breuitas legislatorum sit propria. Considerabitur autem rectissime, si primum quid, tum quo iure Deus vetet inspiciamus.
units.tr: The sixth commandment reads thus: You shall not kill. Although the law is brief, it should not for that reason be considered lightly. Indeed, the briefer it is, the more deeply we should go back into it, since brevity is the mark of lawgivers. It will be considered most rightly if we first examine what it forbids and then on what authority God forbids it.

units.la: Quid vetet verbo רצח dicens, non occides, significat, quippe quo atrocem iniuriam, qua corpus aut pulsatur aut leditur aut perimitur. Ac scelus quidem eo ipso repellit, sed tamen etiam virtutem commendat. Quis enim neget virtutem commendari cum reprehendi tur vitium, praesertim cum sit quaedam virtutis & vitij comparatio & contentio? Nam si modo neam te ne fis auarus: quis non intelligit, me velle te liberalem esse? si dicam ne fis contentio sus, te amicum esse? Eodem modo certum est Deum velle nos studere conseruandis tuendisque hominibus quando praecipit, ut ne eos trucidemus. Flagitium enim est hominis falu[?]ti insidias tendere: virtus autem illius salutem defendere.
units.tr: What it forbids is shown by the Hebrew verb [רצח] in the words "you shall not kill," since it signifies a grave wrong by which the body is struck, injured or destroyed. The commandment certainly repels the crime by that very fact, but it also commends virtue. For who would deny that virtue is commended when vice is rebuked, especially since there is a kind of comparison and contrast between virtue and vice? For if I say, "Do not be greedy," who does not understand that I want you to be generous? If I say, "Do not be quarrelsome," who does not understand that I want you to be friendly? In the same way it is certain that God, when he commands that we not slaughter people, wills us to labour to preserve and protect human beings. For it is a crime to lay snares for a man's safety, but a virtue to defend his safety.

units.la: Iam quia virtus est ἕξις, vitium autem κακεξία[?]: sequitur facti nomine etiam conatum remoueri. Nam quemadmodum in rebus laude dignis voluisse sat est, sic in rebus, quae sunt in vitio, conatum quoque Deus improbat. Quod cum ita sit, consequens est, non solum eum qui manu quempiam percutiat condemnari, verum etiam eum qui verbis aut voluntate damnum dederit. Neque ego solus hanc interpretationem cogito atque affero, sed mecum sentit prae caeteris ipse Dominus Iesus Christus, qui cum hanc ipsam tum reliquas leges omnes sic explanat Matth. 5. De omnibus dicit: Nisi veltra iustitia abundauerit plus quam scribarum & Pharisaeorum, non poteritis ingredi in regnum coelorum. In foro ciuili qui manum abstinuit innocens est: in foro diuino, quod vocant conscientiae, etiam animus affectu cedis vacet necesse est. Iam quia Pharisaei humano seu ciuili more legem metiri solerent, ac cordis affectus malos nisi in cedem erumperent non improbarent, dicit Christus eos a coelesti regno procul abesse. Hanc autem ipsam eodem in loco sic exponit, dicens, audistis quod dictum sit veteribus, Non occides, at ego dico vobis, quisquis irascitur fratri suo temere, &c. Quibus verbis Dominus tria genera commemorat. Vnum facti, nō occides: alterum animi, non irascare: tertium, oris, ne dixeris racha aut fatue.
units.tr: Now since virtue is a state [ἕξις] and vice a bad state [κακεξία], it follows that even the attempt is removed along with the deed. For just as in things worthy of praise it is enough to have willed them, so in things that belong to vice God disapproves even the attempt. Since this is so, it follows that not only the man who strikes someone with his hand is condemned, but also the man who harms him by words or by his will. Nor am I alone in thinking and advancing this interpretation; the Lord Jesus Christ himself agrees with me above all others, for he explains this very law, and all the other laws, in this way at Matthew 5. He says of them all: "Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you cannot enter the kingdom of heaven." In the civil court, the man who has kept his hand from harm is innocent; in the divine court, which they call conscience, the mind must also be free of the feeling of murder. Now since the Pharisees were accustomed to measure the law by human or civil custom, and would not disapprove of evil feelings of the heart unless they burst out into murder, Christ says that they are far from the heavenly kingdom. He sets out this same point in the same place, saying: "You have heard that it was said to the ancients, 'You shall not kill'; but I say to you, whoever is angry rashly with his brother, etc." By these words the Lord mentions three kinds. One concerns the deed: "You shall not kill." The second concerns the mind: "You shall not be angry." The third concerns the mouth: "Do not say raca or fool."

units.la: Facto peccatur trifariam, ut destinato, necessario, casu. Destinato, Cum quis dedita opera vel seipse vel alium quempiam occiderit. Seipse, quando malorum impatientia, desperatione, vitae beatae praepostero desiderio sibi quispiam mortem consciuerit, ut Cato Vticensis, ut Lucretia, ut Nero, ut Iudas, ut Saul, ut vsurarij moerore propter annonae copiam, ut Cleombrotus, & alij: Quod genus homicidij malum est. Primum vitae necisque potestas Dei, non nostra, est: unde suum Deo ius aufert quisquis illius iudicium anteuertit. Deinceps quia causae etiam ipsae velut impatientia, desperatio, detrectatio comeriti supplicij, & aliae similes malae sunt, nec potest ex malis causis quicquam boni prouenire. Postremo in se ipse peccat homo, quippe qui sibi tuendo natus se se ipse damno efficit. Samsonis exemplum dissimile est: is enim ut ulcisceretur iniurias & contumelias populi Dei, ut hostes trucidaret, aedium ruinam in suos humeros traxit, ac multitudinem hostium maximam secum rapuit. Iam quia alia via non erat, qua pateret exitus, hac eundem sibi censuit. <bl>Er müßt ins wasser / Da zog er sine sind mitt sin</bl>[?] Hoc autem eius consilium Deus ipse approbauit, quando illi viros per hostium fraudes amissas restituit.
units.tr: Sin is committed in the deed in three ways: by intention, by necessity, and by chance. By intention, when someone has killed either himself or another person on purpose. Himself, when someone, through impatience with evils, through despair, or through a perverse desire for a happy life, has brought death on himself, as Cato of Utica did, as Lucretia did, as Nero did, as Judas did, as Saul did, as usurers do out of grief over the abundance of grain, as Cleombrotus did, and others. This kind of homicide is evil. First, the power over life and death belongs to God, not to us; so whoever anticipates his judgment takes away his right. Next, since the causes themselves, such as impatience, despair, and the refusal to bear a deserved punishment, and other similar things, are evil, no good can come from evil causes. Lastly, a man sins against himself, since by being born to protect himself he destroys himself. The example of Samson is different, for to avenge the wrongs and insults done to the people of God, and to slaughter the enemies, he drew the collapse of the building upon his own shoulders and carried off a very great multitude of enemies with him. Since there was no other way by which an exit could be found, he judged this one to be his. <bl>Er müßt ins wasser / Da zog er sine sind mitt sin</bl>[?] — He must go into the water; then he drew his sins along with him. Moreover, God himself approved this purpose of his, when he restored to him the men who had been lost through the deceits of the enemy.

units.la: Sed desperabundis illis hominibus consulendum est, ut aduersus hosce mali spiritus insidias pijs precibus, verbo Domini, consilijs amicorum sese muniant. Videntur quidem mala quaedam effugere, sed in lernam malorum incidunt.
units.tr: But those desperate men must be counselled to fortify themselves against these snares of the evil spirit by devout prayers, by the Word of the Lord, and by the advice of friends. They seem indeed to escape certain evils, but they fall into the pit of evils.

units.la: Alios autem qui destinato occidunt homines qui spe precij, inuidia, aemulatione, odio cedes patrant, uti fit in conuiuijs, in choreis, in aleae lusu, in mercenaria militia. Magnum pro facto scelus.
units.tr: Others, however, kill people on purpose: those who commit murder from hope of gain, from envy, from rivalry, or from hatred, as happens at feasts, at dances, at games of dice, and in mercenary soldiery. This is a great crime for the deed.

units.la: Necessario quis patrat cedem, quando se suosque tueri, vimque vi propellere cogitur. Quod genus quoniam ex necessitate non voluntate causa proficiscitur, venia dignum censetur. Nam, ut Iureconsultus ille in l. ut vim. ff. de iust. & iur. ait, iure euenit, ut quod quisque ob tutelam corporis sui fecerit iure fecisse existimetur. Sed etsi id ita se habeat, tamen Christiano homini doleat hoc abs se oportuisse fieri, & Deo supplex fiat cum Paulo dicens: etsi mihi conscius non sim, tamen in eo non sum iustificatus. Adeo standum est praecepto Domini, ut id nunquam transilias. Unde & Iura gentium voluerunt esse inculpatam & moderatam tutelam nostri.
units.tr: A man commits murder by necessity when he is forced to defend himself and his own, and to repel violence with violence. Since this kind of cause arises from necessity and not from will, it is judged worthy of pardon. For, as that jurist says in the law ut vim, Digest, de iustitia et iure, it is rightly the case that whatever someone has done in defence of his body is considered to have been rightly done. Yet even if this is so, a Christian ought to grieve that this had to be done by him, and should become a suppliant before God, saying with Paul: "Though I am not conscious of anything against myself, yet I am not thereby justified." So firmly must the precept of the Lord be kept that you never pass it over. Hence the laws of nations also wished our defence to be blameless and moderate.

units.la: Casu fit cedes, cum quis aliud agens occidit aliquem: veluti quod de Lamech Hebraei dicunt, quod feram percussurus Cainum iaculo traiecerit. Etiam hoc genere Deus nos vacare vellet, propterea quae non prorsus omni culpa vacat, qui sic occidit aliquem, sed tamen absoluitur. Alibi enim illiusmodi in exilium abibant, & Deus eis asyla posuit. Atque sic quidem facto cedes patratur.
units.tr: Murder happens by chance when someone, while doing something else, kills another person. Thus the Hebrews say of Lamech that, while about to strike a wild beast, he pierced Cain with an arrow. God would also wish us to be free of this kind of act, because someone who kills another in this way is not entirely free of all blame, yet he is nonetheless acquitted. Elsewhere such persons used to go into exile, and God set up cities of refuge for them. And so the deed of murder is committed in this way.

units.la: Animo vero patratur quando ira, indignatione, inuidia, odio, quae caedis causae existi-mantur infecti sumus. Nam ira armis instruit, frigidam subfundit: inueterata autem odium generat, & inuidiam, quæ si non adiuuant, tamen clam collaudant eos qui inuiso tendunt in-fidias. Estque radix huius vitij in animo. Iam vide quàm pauci vacemus illo crimine. Sæpe non nocemus, non quia nolumus, verum quia non possumus. Ergo facultas nos, non volun-tas, deficit. Hoc quale fit Ioannes in 1. epist. 3. docet dicens, Quisquis odit fratrem suum homi-cida est. Quanti igitur sunt homicidæ, qui non solum indignantur, sed etiam culpam condo-nare nolunt.
units.tr: We are infected in the mind when anger, indignation, envy, and hatred, which are considered the causes of murder, take hold of us. For anger arms itself, and cold hatred sets in beneath it; but long-standing hatred breeds envy, which, if it does not help, nevertheless secretly applauds those who lay snares for the hated person. This root of the vice is in the mind. Now see how few of us are free of this crime. Often we do no harm not because we do not want to, but because we cannot. Therefore it is ability, not will, that fails us. John in his first epistle, chapter 3, teaches what this amounts to, saying: "Whoever hates his brother is a murderer." How many, then, are murderers who not only feel indignation but are also unwilling to forgive the fault!

units.la: Verbis patratur cedes qualem vetat dicens ne cui vel racha, vel fatue dicatmus. Quo ge-nere comprehendimus consilia, mandata, proditionem, falsa testimonia, diras imprecatio-nes. Consilio Baptistam Herodias, Christum Caiáphas occidit, mandato Saul sacerdotes Do-mini, Herodes infantes Bethlehemicos, proditione Christum Iudás: falso testimonio princi-pes illi Sufannam, Iezabel Nabothum, &c. diris imprecationibus denique mala precamur ijs, quibus irascimur, quæ si illis ingruerent de eis actum esset. Quod eò maius est si infantibus & charissimis nostris liberis sic pestem & nescio quæ precamur malè sani mala. Atque hi qui dem omnes in legem istam peccant, etiam Christo, quo nemo melius nouit patris voluntá-tem, teste & interprete.
