units.tr: Murder is committed by words, which is what the commandment forbids when it says that no one should call another "Raca" [ῥακά] or "fool." Under this kind we include counsel, command, betrayal, false witness, and dire curses. By counsel Herodias killed the Baptist and Caiaphas killed Christ; by command Saul killed the priests of the Lord and Herod the infants of Bethlehem; by betrayal Judas killed Christ; by false witness those princes destroyed Susanna and Jezebel destroyed Naboth, and so on. Finally, by dire curses we pray evils upon those with whom we are angry, and if those evils fell on them it would be their end. This is all the greater when, like madmen, we pray plague and I know not what other evils upon infants and our dearest children. And indeed all these sin against that law, even against Christ, who knows the Father's will better than anyone, as both witness and interpreter.

units.la: Quo iure vetet non potest aliunde cognosci melius, quam ex Dei ipsius voluntate & consilio, & ex causis hominis conditi. Dei voluntas & consilium bifariam perspicitur, nem-pe & ex verbo & ex eius executione. Verbum cum hic tum alibi clarum est & expressum. Quare negare nemo potest, quin iuri diuino consentaneum sit, vt ne quis occidat al-terum.
units.tr: By what right it forbids can be learned better from nowhere else than from God's own will and counsel, and from the causes of the human being who was made. God's will and counsel are seen in two ways, namely from his word and from its execution. The word is clear and express, both here and elsewhere. Therefore no one can deny that it is consistent with divine right that no one should kill another.

units.la: Executio vero in hoc perspicitur quod verbo suo magistratus quasi tutores dedit, qui legis huius transgressores vel lege talionis, vel alio supplicij genere afficiant. Vnde est Gen. 9. Quicunque fuderit sanguinem humanum, fundatur sanguis eius. Et Rom. 13. magistratui ius gladij tribuitur.
units.tr: The execution is seen in this: by his word God has given the magistrates, as it were, as guardians, to punish the transgressors of this law either by the law of retaliation or by some other kind of punishment. Hence Gen. 9: "Whoever sheds human blood, his blood shall be shed." And Rom. 13: the right of the sword is granted to the magistrate.

units.la: Iam vero magistratus etiam ipse legem hanc violat, quando suæ rationis magis, quàm diuini verbi dučtum sequitur, ac non occidendos occidit, & conseruat occidendos, cum ceu iudex delegatus Dei opt. max. principis rescriptum sequi deberet. Occidi iubet Dominus Exod. 22. immolantes Dijs, Leuit. 20. consulentes magos & phytonicos, Leuit. 24. prophetas falsos & blasphemos, Leuit. 21. rebelles liberos. At Saul occidit sacerdotes Domini quos tue ri debuerat, Achabus Nabothum innocentem hominem: contra Saul Amelechum occiden-dum viuum seruat, Achabus sacerdotes Baal trucidandos fouet. Igitur quo iure magistra-tus nostræ ætatis Iudæos, blasphemos, mercenarios milites tanto habeant in precio, confes-sores nominis Christiani perimant, ipsi viderint. Certe & quia legem sibi creditam non tu-entur, & quia eam ipsi violant pœnas dabunt. Est enim consilium Domini, vt quod verbo suo mandarit, id magistratus iure & legibus exequatur. Quamobrem duobus illis ordi-nibus doctorum scilicet & magistratuum Deus testatus est, se nolle tales iniurias impu-ne fieri.
units.tr: But the magistrate himself also violates this law when he follows his own reason rather than the guidance of the divine word, and kills those who should not be killed, and spares those who should be killed, although as a judge delegated by God most good and great he ought to follow the rescript of the prince. The Lord commands killing: Exod. 22 for those who sacrifice to gods; Lev. 20 for those who consult magicians and soothsayers; Lev. 24 for false and blaspheming prophets; Lev. 21 for rebellious children. But Saul killed the priests of the Lord, whom he ought to have protected; Ahab killed the innocent man Naboth. On the contrary, Saul spared Amalek, who was to be utterly destroyed, and Ahab cherished the priests of Baal, who were to be slaughtered. Therefore, by what right the magistrates of our age hold Jews, blasphemers and mercenary soldiers in such high regard, and destroy the confessors of the Christian name, let them see to it themselves. Surely they will pay the penalty, both because they do not defend the law entrusted to them and because they violate it themselves. For it is the Lord's counsel that the magistrate should carry out by right and by laws what God has commanded by his word. Wherefore, through those two orders, namely teachers and magistrates, God has declared that he is unwilling for such injuries to go unpunished.

units.la: Causæ vero hominis conditi idipsum etiam signifieant. Efficiens, ipse Deus creator est, qui tam præclarum opus produxit. Iam si hominem trucides opus diuinum destruxisti: an non eodem aduersus te iure Deus aget, quo tu posses vti contra eum, qui tibi vel horreum, vel quodcunq; ædificiolum demolitus esset?
units.tr: The causes of the human being who was made signify the same thing. The efficient cause is God himself, the Creator, who produced so excellent a work. Now if you kill a man, you have destroyed a divine work. Will not God act against you by the same right by which you could act against someone who had demolished your barn or any small building of yours?

units.la: Materia vna eademque est omnibus: nec quisquam potest dicere se ex auro proximum suum ex cupro factum esse, se ex argento proximum è plumbo fabricatum: terrena est omni um materia. Cur igitur alius sericum se esse, lineum autem alium audet dicere? Igitur cum natura pugnat hæc rabies, qua alij in alios ferimur. Florentinus in l. vt vim. ff. de iust. & iur. Et cum inter nos (inquit) cognationem quandam natura constituerit: consequens est homi-nem homini insidiari nefas esse. Leo leonem non sic impetit, vt homo hominem, Christianus Christianum. Effodere sepulchra, & mortuos pulsare grande nephas semper est habitum antiquitus, at quia viui dolores sentiunt, hoc longe maius visum est.
units.tr: The matter is one and the same for all. Nor can anyone say that he was made of gold and his neighbour of copper, or that he was fashioned from silver while his neighbour was made of lead; the material of all is earthly. Why then does one person dare to say that he is silk and another linen? Therefore this frenzy by which we are carried against one another is contrary to nature. Florentinus, in l. ut vim, ff. de iust. et iur.: "And since nature has established a certain kinship among us, it follows that it is wrong for one man to lay snares for another." A lion does not attack a lion as a man attacks a man, a Christian a Christian. To dig up graves and strike the dead has always been counted a great crime from antiquity, but because the living feel pain, this has been thought far greater.

units.la: Iam si formam consideres, sacræ literæ & res ipsa comprobant ad imaginem Dei conditos nos esse. Quocirca si positam tibi statuam deijci nolis: cur tu Dei imaginem deijcis? Egregi-um profecto Macedonij heremitæ responsum Theodosio Imperatori datum, quando ob sub ueriam Placillæ Augustæ statuam Antiochenis ciuibus mortem intentare vellet, missum est illud imperatoris legatis nuncijs videlicet: O amici (inquit) dicite Imperatori. Non es Impe-rator solummodo sed etiam homo, noli crudeliter Dei delere imaginem, irritas creatorem cum illius ġeles imaginem. Considera illud etiam quod tu æneæ duntaxat statuæ gratia contristaris. Quantum vero differat res inanimata ab animata viuente & rationali, omnibus est aperrissimum. Sed & facile erit pro vna statua aerea plures reparare statuas aereas, impossibile autem fuerit vnum peremptis capillum restituere. Quid putas Macedonius ille diceret si redeat ac videat nostra aetate maiore esse in precio statuas, quàm viuos homines? si videat capitis poena affici illos, qui imagines, aut deiecerint aut adorare noluerint: magno vero in precio esse eos, qui viuas Dei imagines cateruatim trucident? Nec absurdum est quod Graeci veteres homicidium sacrilegio comparant: siquidem sacrosanctam Dei imaginem hominem violare grauius est, quàm idolis sacratas res tollere.
units.tr: If you consider the form, Holy Scripture and the thing itself prove that we were created in the image of God. Therefore, if you do not want a statue set up for you to be thrown down, why do you throw down the image of God? Remarkable indeed is the reply given by the Macedonian hermit to Emperor Theodosius, when, on account of an offence against the statue of the Augusta Placilla, the emperor wished to threaten the citizens of Antioch with death. That message was sent to the emperor's legates, namely: "O friends, tell the emperor: you are not only an emperor but also a man. Do not cruelly destroy the image of God; by destroying the image of his creature you provoke the Creator." Consider too that you are distressed only for the sake of a bronze statue. How much an inanimate thing differs from a living, rational one is most evident to everyone. Moreover, it will be easy to replace one bronze statue with several bronze statues, but impossible to restore a single hair to one who has been destroyed. What do you think that Macedonian would say if he returned and saw that in our age statues are held in higher esteem than living men? If he saw that those who throw down images or refuse to adore them are punished with capital penalty, but that those who slaughter the living images of God in crowds are held in high regard? Nor is it absurd that the ancient Greeks compared homicide with sacrilege, since to violate a man, the sacrosanct image of God, is more grievous than to take away things consecrated to idols.

units.la: Sin finem reputes, homo conditus est vt viuat: an non voluntati Dei renititur quisquis eum vult esse mortuum?
units.tr: If you consider the end, man was made to live. Does not whoever wishes him dead resist the will of God?

units.la: Quæ cum ita sint & manum & os & cor abstinebimus à cede hominum, ac potius eorum saluti defendendę dabimus operā, vt & nobis conseruandis deditum ac paratum habeamus Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, cui sit honos in sæcula. Amen.
units.tr: Since these things are so, let us abstain with hand, mouth and heart from the slaughter of men, and rather let us devote our effort to defending their safety, so that we may have our Lord Jesus Christ, devoted and ready to preserve us, to whom be honour for ever and ever. Amen.

units.la: SERMO XIII.
units.tr: SERMON XIII.

units.la: 18 Non moechaberis.
units.tr: 18 You shall not commit adultery.

units.la: CVm generis humani propagandi & conseruandi gratia Deus instituerit, sanctam, iustam, legitimam maris & fœminæ coniunctionem, ne ea vel impura, nefaria, promiscua libidine contaminaretur, sed matrimonium ceu ratio propagandi nostri generis hone-stissima pariter ac sanctissima perpetuo maneret, septima hac lege Deus cauit adulteria, eorumque nomine quicquid ad contemptionem, violationem, destructionem matrimonij faceret, comprehensum voluit. Idque Deum patrem voluisse tam verum est & certum, vt eius rei locupletissimum testem habeamus eius filium vnigenitum Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, qui Matth. 5. sic explanat legem de adulteris, vt etiam obscœnas libidines animo cogitatas, ac nondum re patratas vetitas esse dixerit & impuram illam luem radicitus euulse rit. Quamobrem vt legem intelligamus melius, primum quod qualeque vitium, tum quare, & quomodo vetat Dominus, postremo quomodo ipsum nos cauere posimus.
units.tr: Since God instituted marriage for the propagation and preservation of the human race, he willed that the holy, just and lawful union of man and woman should not be defiled by impure, unlawful or promiscuous lust, but that marriage, as the most honourable and most holy means of propagating our kind, should remain perpetually inviolate. By this seventh law God forbade adultery, and under the name of adultery he meant to include whatever tends to the contempt, violation or destruction of marriage. That God the Father willed this is so true and certain that we have a most complete witness to it in his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, who in Matthew 5 explains the law concerning adulterers so as to say that even obscene lusts thought in the mind, though not yet carried out, are forbidden, and so he pulled up that impure pestilence by the roots. Therefore, that we may understand the law better, we must consider first what kind of sin is forbidden, then why and how the Lord forbids it, and finally how we ourselves can guard against it.

units.la: Quod qualeque fit verbo נאף[?] Moses indicat, videlicet matrimonij violationem scelestam ac nefariam. Sic enim verbum hoc etiam alibi, vt Num.20. Prouer. 7. & 9. ac compluri-bus locis alijs acceptum est. Quomodo nos Germanice quoque accipimus ein <bl>Ehebruch</bl>, dictione composita, ab <bl>Ehe</bl> matrimonio, & <bl>Bruch</bl> fractione. Quæ vox multas habet similes <bl>Beinbruch</bl>/<bl>Schiffbruch</bl>/cum eos fractum, nauem fractam dicimus. Frangitur autem quicquid integrum cum effet corrumpitur, soluitur, destruitur. Iam matrimonium integrum saluumque est, quoad fides data vtrinque seruatur: soluitur autem & corrumpitur, si pars alteru-tra fallat.
units.tr: What kind of sin is meant, Moses indicates by the Hebrew word [נאף], namely the wicked and unlawful violation of marriage. For this word is used in this sense elsewhere too, as in Numbers 5, Proverbs 7 and 9, and in many other places. We in German likewise use the compound word <bl>Ehebruch</bl>, from <bl>Ehe</bl>, marriage, and <bl>Bruch</bl>, breaking. There are many similar words, <bl>Beinbruch</bl> and <bl>Schiffbruch</bl>, since we call a broken leg or a wrecked ship a "break." Now whatever was whole and is corrupted, dissolved or destroyed is broken. A marriage is whole and sound as long as the pledge given on both sides is kept; but it is dissolved and corrupted if either party deceives the other.

units.la: Neque vere me latet & scholasticos aliquos interpretes & Iurisprudentes diuersum di-cere. Lyranus enim sic definit adulterium. Moechia est copula carnalis cum vxore alterius viri quæ reputatur vna caro cum ipso. Quæ definitio satis certo significat ei videri committi in nupta solum adulterium. Sed Modestinus in l. inter stuprum .ff. de verb. sig. dicit inter stuprum & adulterium hoc interesse, quod adulterium in nupta n[?], stuprum autem in viduam committatur. Quod ipsum etiam in l. stuprum, §. adulterium. ff. ad leg. Iul. de adulter. coercend. idem asseuerat. Et ratio redditur in l. inter liberas. §. lex stuprum. ff. eod. tit. videlicet propter partum ex altero conceptum composito nomine, in nuptam proprie committi adulterium. Ex quibus intelligitur adulterium illorum iudicio à marito non committi, si cum virgine vel vidua, aut cum qualibet soluta muliere coierit: ab vxore vero committi quocunque admisso.
units.tr: I am well aware that some scholastic interpreters and jurists say otherwise. Lyranus defines adultery thus: adultery is carnal intercourse with the wife of another man, who is regarded as one flesh with him. This definition clearly indicates that he thinks adultery is committed only with a married woman. But Modestinus, in the law "inter stuprum" in the Digest, On the meaning of words, says that the difference between stuprum and adultery is that adultery is committed with a married woman, stuprum with a widow. The same thing he affirms in the law "stuprum," §"adulterium," in the Digest, On the Lex Julia on the punishment of adultery. And the reason is given in the law "inter liberas," §"lex stuprum," in the same title: namely, that because of the offspring conceived from another man, adultery is properly committed with a married woman, the word being compounded. From these passages it is understood that, in the judgment of these writers, a husband does not commit adultery if he has intercourse with a virgin, a widow, or any unmarried woman, but a wife commits adultery by any such act.

units.la: Sed hæc opinio neque ciuili, neque gentium, neque diuino iuri consentanea est. Non ci-uili, quia si mulieres propter fidem lubricam non fide iubent, non satis dant, non possunt es-se procuratrices, non semper dignæ censentur quibus iuramentum deferatur: quæ signifi-cant illis non tribui, quod sint fidæ & constantes: cur ab eis in hoc genere solis, vt fidem datam seruent postulas? Profecto iure sic abutimur, & hoc ipso quod marito hoc conceditur, ipsis ad peccatum suum quasi quodam modo via sternitur.
units.tr: But this opinion agrees neither with civil law, nor with the law of nations, nor with divine law. Not with civil law: for if women are not trusted to give bail or security because of their unstable faith, if they cannot act as guardians, and if they are not generally thought worthy to be put under oath, which signifies that these things are not granted to them because they are faithful and constant, then why do you demand of them alone in this matter that they keep the faith they have pledged? Indeed, by such a law we abuse our authority, and by the very fact that this is granted to the husband, a way to sin is, as it were, paved for the wife.

units.la: Noniuri gentium. Nam si in contractibus omnibus, qui quidem iure gentium introdu-cti sunt[?] si[?] sunt, vtrinque existit obligatio, & eo genere matrimonium continetur: cur non æque maritum vxori, atque vxorem marito obligari statuis? Quæ enim fuit vnquam emptio, in qua non emptor precium, & mercem venditor æque reddere tenerentur? Quod vnquam ictum est fœdus, in quo non ambæ partes tenerentur? Sane in suo, quod cum nostro genere pepigit Deus ipse nobis obligare sese non dedignatus est: tu marito plus, quam ipsi Deo tribues?
units.tr: Nor with the law of nations. For if in all contracts, which indeed were introduced by the law of nations, an obligation arises on both sides, and marriage belongs to that class, why do you decide that the husband is not bound to his wife just as the wife is bound to her husband? For what sale has ever been made in which the buyer and the seller were not equally bound to pay the price and deliver the goods? What covenant has ever been struck in which both parties were not bound? Surely God himself did not disdain to bind himself to us in the covenant he made with our race. Will you grant a husband more than God himself?

units.la: Non diuino, Nam quod Deus duo in vnam carnem coalescere voluit id in 1. Corinth.7. Paulus sic exponit, vt ostendat mariti corpus iure matrimonij in potestatem vxoris concessisse, contraque corpus vxoris mariti pastum esse: quod argumento sit maritum æque sui iuris non esse atque vxorem. Quod si ita est, sequitur etiam maritum cum quacunq; rem habeat, adulterium committere, quod vxori debitum corpus impertit pellici.
units.tr: Nor with divine law. For Paul, in 1 Corinthians 7, explains that God willed the two to become one flesh, in such a way as to show that by the right of marriage the husband's body has been given into the power of the wife, and the wife's body into the power of the husband. This proves that the husband is no more his own master than the wife is. If this is so, it follows that the husband also commits adultery with whatever woman he has to do with, since he gives to a concubine the body that is owed to his wife.

units.la: Nec moror quod obijcitur maius ab adultera damnum dari: nihil hoc ad propositū. Ma ius scelus est fateor, vxorem committere adulterium, sed ideo culpa adulterij sui maritus non absoluitur. Quamobrem est adulterium sancte & legitime contracti inter marem & fœminam matrimonij violatio scelesta ac nefaria.
units.tr: Nor do I dwell on the objection that the greater harm falls on the adulteress: that is beside the point. I admit it is a greater wickedness for a wife to commit adultery, but the husband is not on that account absolved of the guilt of his own adultery. Therefore adultery is the wicked and unlawful violation of a holy and lawfully contracted marriage between a man and a woman.

units.la: Ex quo sequitur scelus hoc esse nefarium, quippe quod propinqua cognatione coniun ctum sit cum periurio, plagio, furto. Nam periurio quo pacto liber erit, qui publice Deum, ec clesiam dextra iuncta testatus est ac recepit, vxori se fidum fore? Plagij reus quomodo non erit, qui suæ sese coniugi ipse subduxerit? Furto maius esse dicit Solomon Prouerb.6. quia adulterini partus & falsis patribus & filijs familiàs coheredibus sua bona auferunt. Ergo De us volens sacrosanctam esse maris & fœminæ coniunctionem adulteria lege cauenda arbi tratus est.
units.tr: From this it follows that this sin is wicked, since it is closely connected with perjury, kidnapping and theft. For how will he be free from perjury who has solemnly called God and the Church to witness, and has received the right hand, pledging himself faithful to his wife? How will he not be guilty of kidnapping who has himself withdrawn from his own spouse? Solomon says in Proverbs 6 that it is theft: for children born of adultery steal their goods from false fathers and from the legitimate heirs of the household. Therefore God, wishing the holy union of man and woman to be safeguarded, decided to guard it by a law against adultery.

units.la: Sed quoniam violatio commune est nomen, & non solum hoc genus, verum etiam con cupiscentiam, & alia genera significat, videmus etiam per eos violari matrimonium qui vel ardent impuris motibus, & tamen à coniugio prorsus abstinent: vel patrant impuras & illi-citas libidines. Impuris affectibus plenus est cœlibatus papisticus. Variæ libidines sunt scor tatio, Sodomiticum crimen, incestus, & alia quæ pudet horreteq; animus dicere. Hæc omnia Deus vetuit, & vt esset honestum aduersus libidinum omne genus remedium, suam cuique tribuit vxorem. Videmus igitur Paulum sic consulere, & Dominum etiam ipsum, vt quan do casti non sumus, contrahamus matrimonia, sitque thorus pudicus nobis potior, quam scortatio.
units.tr: But since "violation" is a common term, and signifies not only this kind of sin but also concupiscence and other kinds, we see that marriage is also violated by those who burn with impure desires yet refrain entirely from marriage, or who commit impure and unlawful lusts. The Papist celibacy is full of impure passions. The varieties of lust are fornication, the crime of Sodom, incest, and others which shame and horror forbid the mind to name. God forbade all of these, and, so that there might be an honourable remedy against every kind of lust, he gave each person his own wife. Thus we see Paul advising this, and the Lord himself too: that, since we are not chaste, we should contract marriages, and that a chaste marriage bed should be preferable to us than fornication.

units.la: Quare & quomodo vetet Dominus operæprecium est cognoscere, vt quanti sit momen ti quod dicimus intelligas. Cur vetet ex eo potest intelligi, quod impuritas ista maximarum calamitatum causa semper fuerit, vt exempla suppeditant historiæ. Vt Nohæ seculum, & So- domæ excidium, vt Pharaoni immissæ propter Saram raptam plagæ, vt vrbs Salem & exem plum Abimelechi, & tribus Beniamin. Quo refer etiam bellum Troianum, & raptam princi pem Britanniæ. Omitto mala ciuilia, vt cedem, infamiam, æmulationes, odia, miseriam. His malis arcendis Deus hanc legem opposuit.
units.tr: It is worth our while to know why and how the Lord forbids this, so that you may understand how important what we are saying is. The reason why he forbids it can be understood from the fact that this impurity has always been the cause of the greatest calamities, as the examples of history show: as in the age of Noah, the destruction of Sodom, the plagues sent upon Pharaoh because of Sarah's abduction, the city of Salem and the example of Abimelech, and the tribe of Benjamin. To these belongs also the Trojan War, and the abduction of the princess of Britain. I pass over civil evils such as slaughter, infamy, rivalries, hatreds and misery. God set this law against these evils, in order to ward them off.

units.la: Quomodo vero vetuerit & verbo & legibus ciuilibus & exemplis omnium gentium ad discitur. Verbo suo, Leuit.20. & Deut. 22. Si mœchatus quisquam fuerit cum vxore alterius & adulterium perpetrauerit cum coniuge proximi sui morte moriantur ambo. Quo perti net exemplum Sufannæ. Et quæ Christus hac de re dicit Ioann.8. & quod regno cœlesti Pau lus excludit adulterum. Quæ docent verbo Dei prorsus remoueri adulteria.
units.tr: How he forbade it, however, is learned from his word, from civil laws and from the examples of all nations. By his word, in Leviticus 20 and Deuteronomy 22: "If anyone commits adultery with the wife of his neighbour, both shall surely die, the adulterer and the adulteress." To this belongs the example of Susanna, and what Christ says about this matter in John 8, and that Paul excludes adulterers from the heavenly kingdom. These teach that adulteries are wholly removed by the word of God.

units.la: Porro leges ciuiles ea quoque seuere vindicant. Vt in II.xij.tab. sic scriptum extat. Vim ingenuæ virgini inferre, aut eam suasione in tuam sententiam trahere cæueto. Et, Sororem aut filiam in stupro deprehensam vendito. Et, Mœchum in adulterio deprehensum neca to. Extant etiam in Iure tituli de ritu nuptiarū, de fecundis nuptijs, de iure dotium, ad legem Iuliam de adulterijs. Omitto priuilegia quæ passis illam iniuriam leges indulserunt. Ergo le ges argumento sunt quàm seuere Deus crimen hoc punitum velit.
units.tr: Moreover, civil laws also punish these things severely. As is written in the Twelve Tables: "Beware of using force against a freeborn virgin, or of drawing her to your opinion by persuasion." And: "Sell a sister or daughter caught in illicit intercourse." And: "Kill an adulterer caught in adultery." There are also titles in the Law on the rite of marriage, on second marriages, on the right of dowries, and on the Julian law concerning adulteries. I pass over the privileges which the laws granted to those who suffered that injury. Therefore the laws are evidence of how severely God wishes this crime to be punished.

units.la: Exempla gentium omnium hoc ipsum etiam docent. Romæ, in Tenedo, & in Arabia ca- pite plexi sunt adulteri. Opilius Macrinus ignibus cremabat eos. Nos soli tam leui pœna tantum scelus vindicamus. Adeò omnibus gentibus insita fuit huius criminis detestatio. Ex quibus omnibus colligi potest Deum hoc scelus & expresso verbo & naturali seu intus in animis hominum agente vi procul arcere voluisse, vt id nobis merito fit cauendum.
units.tr: Examples of all peoples also teach this very thing. At Rome, in Tenedos and in Arabia, adulterers were put to death by beheading. Opilius Macrinus used to have them burned with fire. We alone avenge so great a crime with so light a punishment. So deeply was abhorrence of this crime implanted in all peoples. From all these things it can be gathered that God, both by an express word and by the power that acts naturally, that is, inwardly in the minds of men, wished this crime to be kept far away, so that we rightly ought to take care to guard against it.

units.la: Quomodo vero caueri possit: non aliter certe ac mala alia, sublatis causis videlicet. Quæ vero sunt illæ? Ac dubium non est quin author suasorque sit satan, quippe qui impellit ad ueri possit hoc scelus. omnia scelera: sed tamen habet causas medias quibus nos ceu escis hamo fixis illicit ac ca-pit. Prima ac princeps est verbi Dei negligentia, qua fit vt pro iusto & vero quod prauā na-tura dictitat sequamur, vsuras & dolos auarus, libidines impurus: nec superat etiam multum latrans conscientia, cum sint colores qui illinuntur vitijs. Quo fit vt quod quisque amat maximè, id quam minime esse malum autumet. Audiendum est igitur verbum Dei, vt natu-ram emendes.
units.tr: How it can indeed be guarded against is certainly no differently than other evils, namely with their causes removed. And what are those causes? There is no doubt that the author and persuader of this crime, as of all crimes, is Satan, who drives men on; yet he has middle causes by which, like fish caught on a hook, we are enticed and seized. The first and chief is neglect of the Word of God, through which it comes about that we follow, as just and true, what our corrupt nature keeps asserting: the greedy man follows usury and fraud, the lustful man impure desires. Nor does conscience, though it barks loudly, prevail much, since there are colours spread over vices. Hence it happens that whatever each person loves most, he thinks is least of all evil. The Word of God must therefore be heard, so that you may amend your nature.

units.la: Altera causa est segnis & socors liberorum educatio, illis enim ad choreas, ad impura car-mina, ad mala commercia assuefactis via ad hoc vitium sternitur.
units.tr: The second cause is the slack and careless upbringing of children; for once they have been accustomed to dances, to impure songs and to bad dealings, the way to this vice is paved.

units.la: Tertia est ocium, quo efficitur vt liberi sint oculi contemplandis seu spectandis illece-bris, vt aures vacent audiendis impuris carminibus & dicterijs, vt omittam quod de reli-quis sensibus dici potest. Exemplo sunt Dauid quem ociosum in has cafles illexit satan cum spectaret lauantem Bersabam. Notū est quod de Ægisto dicit Ouidius. Vsu compertum est in vrbibus quæ fouent ocia, plura committi scelera.
units.tr: The third is idleness, by which it comes about that children have eyes free for gazing upon and watching enticements, and ears free for hearing impure songs and sayings, to say nothing of what can be said of the other senses. David is an example: Satan enticed him, being idle, into this snare when he watched Bathsheba bathing. It is well known what Ovid says of Aegisthus. Experience has shown in cities that foster idleness that more crimes are committed.

units.la: Quarta causa est, impunita scortatio, per hanc enim ad adulteria fit aditus.
units.tr: The fourth cause is unpunished fornication, for through this an approach is opened to adulteries.

units.la: Quinta est omnium hominum tam plebis quàm magistratuum officij remissio. Singuli vocati vt dicant quæ sciunt hinc inde committi flagitia, tacent, etiamsi antea multum quesi-ti sint. Magistratus aut fontes absoluit aut leuibus pœnis afficit. Sed redeundum est ad præcep-tum Domini, quod omnium gentium consensu receptum est. Oremus.
units.tr: The fifth is the neglect of the duty of all men, of the common people as much as of the magistrates. Individuals who are summoned to tell what they know of the disgraces committed here and there keep silent, even if they have previously been questioned at length. Magistrates either absolve the offenders or punish them with light penalties. But we must return to the precept of the Lord, which has been received with the consent of all peoples. Let us pray.

units.la: SERMO XIIII.
units.tr: SERMON XIV.

units.la: 19 Nefureris.
units.tr: 19 Thou shalt not steal.

units.la: POstquam Deus in secunda tabula ius personarum descripsit, ac deinceps & vitæ & famæ singulorum aduersus vim omnem positis legibus consuluit: iam alia lege docet vt ve-lit suas cuique facultates saluas esse. Ac quoniam non omnium opis est violenter sua alijs ra-pere, propterea; ad malas artes atq; dolos pleriq; confugiant: Deus quod à plerisq; fit sce-lus hac lege nominatim repulit, eoq; ipso quod pauciores patrant comprehensum voluit. Quod & vltima lex de concupiscentia, & huius ipsius omnes causæ docent. Siquidem consi-deremus 1. Quid. 2. Quomodo. 3. Qua de causa vetet Dominus.
units.tr: After God, in the second table, had set out the rights of persons, and then by laying down laws had provided against all violence to each person's life and good name, he now teaches by another law that everyone's possessions should be safe. Since not everyone has the means to rob others openly, many resort to wicked arts and tricks. God forbade by name this crime, which many commit, and by the very fact that fewer commit it, he wanted it to be restrained. The last law, on covetousness, and all the reasons for this one teach the same thing. Let us consider: 1. what is forbidden; 2. how; 3. for what reason the Lord forbids it.

units.la: Quid vetet hoc ipso quidè docet quod ait, ne furtum facias: sed id multò plenius ac me-lius cognoscitur si quid fit, & quotuplex esse videatur, & quod modis fiat furtum inuestige-mus. Quid sit cum nominis interpretatione tum rei definitione discitur. Verbum Hebræ-um clam aliquid moliri, damnum dare, surripere quidpiam significat. Et ad res non corpo-reas transfertur hæc significatio. Vt. 2. Reg. 15. furatus est Absolon cor Israelis, hoc est dolo traxit in suas partes, visus aliud agere videlicet. Sic Germani quicquid clam, & sub alio præ-textu fit, dicimus <bl>verstålen</bl>: <bl>Du hast mir Das verstolen.</bl> Et Græce κλέπτης ἀπὸ τῆς κλά-πτω dicitur: κλέπτειν δ' ἀφαιρεῖσθαι [?] & significat aliquem decipere, alicui id quod verū est fur-ripere. Latinè furtum à furuo, id est, nigro, dictum esse dicit Labeo.
units.tr: The very words "thou shalt not steal" show what is forbidden, but this is understood much more fully and better if we investigate what theft is, how many forms it seems to take, and in how many ways it is committed. What it is, is learned both from the meaning of the word and from the definition of the thing. The Hebrew word means to plot something secretly, to cause loss, to snatch something away. This meaning is also carried over to things that are not bodily. For example, 2 Sam. 15: "Absalom stole the heart of Israel," that is, he drew them to his side by deceit, while seeming to be doing something else. So the Germans call whatever is done secretly and under another pretext verstålen: "Du hast mir das verstolen" ("you have stolen that from me"). And in Greek the thief is called klepths from klaptō, and klepteín means to deceive someone, to snatch away from someone what is theirs [κλέπτης ἀπὸ τῆς κλάπτω; κλέπτειν δ' ἀφαιρεῖσθαι]. Labeo says that the Latin furtum is derived from furuus, that is, black.

units.la: Furtum igitur est, vt Iulius Paulus definit, alienæ rei contrectatio fraudulenta, quæ fit inuito Domino, lucrifaciendi gratia, vel ipsius rei, vel vsus eius, vel possessionis, quod lege naturali prohibitum est admittere.
units.tr: Theft, then, as Julius Paulus defines it, is the fraudulent handling of another's property, done against the owner's will, for the sake of gain, whether of the thing itself, or its use, or its possession, which natural law forbids.

units.la: Quotduplex autem fit furtum ex hoc ipso potest colligi. Nam alienam rem contrectare & inuito Domino sibi vendicare & acquirere, & ea suam rem familiarem augere, proximi facultates minuere, genere eodem comprehendi perspicuum est. Vnde rapina, plagium, dolus, & cum pondere & mensura proximus fallitur. Ergo coram Deo rei sunt huius criminis mercatores, qui merces malas pro bonis vendunt, & operarij male fidi, qui mercedem pro diurna integra opera accipiunt, ac vix dimidium temporis impendunt operæ: malefidi serui, & quicunque secus quàm conuentum est funguntur officijs. Quid verbis opus est, tam late patet hoc genus vt totum comprehendi nequeat. Testes nos ipsi fumus, qui, fi quis nos aliquo modo fefellerit, dicimus, <bl>er het mirs äben als mär vß dem seckel gstolen.</bl> Quod verbum indicio est impostu-ras tales nos furti genere comprehendere.
units.tr: How many kinds of theft there are can be gathered from this same definition. For it is plain that handling another's property, claiming and acquiring it for oneself against the owner's will, and so increasing one's own household goods and diminishing a neighbour's means, all fall under the same genus. Hence come robbery, kidnapping, fraud, and when a neighbour is cheated in weight and measure. So before God are guilty of this crime the merchants who sell bad goods for good, and the workmen of bad faith who take a full day's wages but give barely half a day's work, and the faithless servants, and whoever performs his duties otherwise than was agreed. Why say more? This kind of theft extends so widely that it cannot all be covered. We ourselves are witnesses: if someone has cheated us in any way, we say, "He has got more out of me than if he had stolen it from my purse." That saying shows that we count such trickeries as a kind of theft.

units.la: Quot modis furtum committatur alia scelera significant. 1. Ope & opera: Veluti su-rem ducas, custodias, instrumentis adiuues. <bl>Dem Dieben den sack nach tragist.</bl>
units.tr: The ways in which theft is committed are shown by other sins. (1) By help and work: for example, when you lead on a thief, keep watch, or assist him with tools. "You carry the sack behind the thief" (German proverb).

units.la: 2 Mandato:is quia author est peior fuerit,mali pædagogi,magistri improbi.
units.tr: (2) By command: because the one who gives the order is the worse author, like bad tutors and wicked masters.

units.la: 3 Consilio,suadet malum facere.
units.tr: (3) By counsel: when one advises doing evil.

units.la: 4 Consensu, fiue id ante factum aut in facto aut post factum fiat; Nam consentienti & facienti idem iuris est.
units.tr: (4) By consent, whether it happens before the act, during it, or after it; for the one who consents and the one who does are under the same law.

units.la: 5 Abblandiendo & audiendo;
units.tr: (5) By flattering and by listening.

units.la: 6 Occultando,ⴱer ḥéler Ꞵóser ⴱer stȋler.
units.tr: (6) By concealing: as the German saying goes, "the receiver is as bad as the thief."

units.la: 7 Communicatione rei furto ablatæ.
units.tr: (7) By sharing in the goods taken by theft.

units.la: 8 Promittendo quod prohibere poteras.
units.tr: (8) By promising what you could have forbidden.

units.la: Quæ eò ponderanda sunt exactius vt & cæueamus peccata; & cum facta sunt non putemus nos vacare culpa. Ac multi sic peccant publice & priuatim; qui tamen sibi quasi innocentibus blandiuntur. Sed instar Pilati innocentes sunt, qui condemnato Christo manus abluerat. Quare si velis esse innocens nec consilio; nec opera, nec tacendo; nec consummen do malum adiuua. Ac si iterum atque iterum solicitere, tamen ne deficias. Christus tertio tentatus perstitit, denique etiam in passione. Nam si velis premium, oportet vincere: at sine sanguine & sudore non vincitur. Summa; diabolus ad peccatum multum solicitat & varie. Enitendum est contra, vt quoad potest fieri nulla specie peccati, contaminemur. Quod effi- ci poterit, si quemadmodum vetitum, quoddq; sit peccatum intelligamus.
units.tr: These things must be weighed more carefully, so that we both guard against sins and, when they have been committed, do not think ourselves free of guilt. Many people sin in this way, in public and in private, and yet flatter themselves as if they were innocent. But those who, like Pilate, wash their hands when Christ has been condemned are not innocent. Therefore, if you wish to be innocent, do not help evil by counsel, by work, by silence, or by consenting. And if you are tempted again and again, do not give up. Christ, tempted three times, stood firm, and finally even in his passion. For if you want the prize, you must conquer, and no one conquers without blood and sweat. In short, the devil urges us to sin much and in many ways. We must strive against him so that, as far as possible, we are not defiled by any kind of sin. This can be done if we understand both what is forbidden and what sin is.

units.la: Quo modo vetitum sit rogas; dico expresso pariter & intrinsecus agente verbo. Expres so verbo, cum multis in locis aliis tum hac ipsa lege cumprimiis. Alibi Exod. 20. Qui furatus bouem vel ouem, & occiderit vel venditerit, quinque boues pro vno boue restituet; & qua tuor oues pro vna oue. Ephes. 4. Qui furabatur iam non amplius furetur: magis autem la- boret operando manibus quod bonum est; vt habeant vnde tribuat necessitatem pati- enti. Hic autem iubens indicat illi ius imperandi esse; nostra referre vt obediamus eius iussibus;
units.tr: You ask how it is forbidden. I say, by an express word and by a word that works inwardly as well. By an express word, both in many other places and especially in this very law. Elsewhere, Exod. 20: "If anyone steals an ox or a sheep, and kills or sells it, he shall restore five oxen for an ox, and four sheep for a sheep." Eph. 4: "Let him who stole steal no more, but rather let him labour, working with his hands what is good, so that he may have something to give to the one in need." Here, moreover, the command indicates that he has the right to command, and it is our part to obey his orders.

units.la: Intrinsecus agit hoc etiam vt hæc lex omnium animis hæreat. Vnde & omnium genti- um consensu furtum punitum est: Idque testantur historiæ de pœnis huic sceleri decretis: Dracoṅis leges capitalem pœnam furibus irrogarant. Solon dupli pœna vindicabat. Leges xij.tab.quibus vtebantur Romani; furem ἐν ἀυτοφόρῳ deprehensum tunc occidi iubebant, cum noctu furatus esset, aut se telo vel interdiu niteretur defendere. Inde Romani prætores pœnam quadrupli irrogarunt: Nonnullis postea visum est membris fures mutilari. Sed ab eo genere supplicij iterum recessit Iustinianus. Denique Fœdericus Imperator eius nomi- nis primus constituit eum, qui rem quinque solidis æstimatam furatus esset laqueo suspen- dendum: sin minoris precij fuisset, quod furatus esset, scopis castigandum;
units.tr: This also works inwardly, so that the law may cling to the minds of all. Hence theft has been punished by the consent of all nations, and histories bear witness to the penalties decreed for this crime. The laws of Draco imposed capital punishment on thieves. Solon punished with double damages. The Twelve Tables, which the Romans used, ordered that a thief caught in the act [ἐν ἀυτοφόρῳ] be killed then and there, if he had stolen at night, or if he tried to defend himself with a weapon even by day. Afterwards the Roman praetors imposed a fourfold penalty. Some later thought it right to mutilate thieves' limbs. But Justinian went back from that kind of punishment. Finally, the Emperor Frederick, the first of that name, decreed that whoever stole a thing valued at five shillings should be hanged, but if what he stole was of less value, he should be whipped with twigs.

units.la: Aberrarunt à vero Ægyptij & Lacedemonij, quorum permissu furtum erat liberum: aberrant quicunque non æstimant quantopere Deus ab hoc genere sceleris abhorreat, nõ- que abstinere iusserit. Sed negligentia diuinæ legis factum est vt & furta committerentur multa & varia & nullo supplicio vindicarentur. Vnde Marcus Varro queritur priuatos su- res in neruo atque compedibus ætatem agere, fures publicos in auro atque in purpura. Mul- ta possent ex iure, ex historijs & varijs omnium gentium moribus huc afferri, sed ex his ipsis satis perspici potuit quam seueram legem huic vitio Deus opposuerit.
units.tr: The Egyptians and the Spartans were wrong, for by their permission theft was free. They are wrong too, all who do not consider how greatly God abhors this kind of sin, and how he commanded us to abstain from it. But through neglect of the divine law it has come about that many and various thefts are committed and go unpunished. Hence Marcus Varro complains that private thieves spend their lives in chains and fetters, while public thieves live in gold and purple. Many examples could be brought from law, from histories and from the customs of all nations, but from these alone it can be seen well enough how severe a law God has set against this vice.

units.la: Quia de causa Deus hanc legem tulerit hoc ipso docet, quod ex eius feruandæ studio se- quitur. Quid id est? Nempe quod suis quisque bonis tranquillè pacateque frui potest: Nam si nemo bonis alterius inhiet, si nemo alteri quod suum est abstulerit: quis neget suum cuiq; in tuto fore? Igitur id egit Deus vt vigeret iustitia quæ suum cuiq; tribueret, nec foret vlla confusio.
units.tr: Why God gave this law he shows by what follows from keeping it. And what is that? Namely, that each person can enjoy his own goods in peace and tranquillity. For if no one covets another's goods, and no one takes from another what is his, who would deny that each person's own will be safe? So God intended that justice, which gives each person his own, should flourish, and that there should be no confusion.

units.la: Quod si ita sit, vti vere est, vel sola hac lege euerti illorum opinionem oportet, qui rerum proprietatem tollunt è medio. Vetus quidem nec nostra demum ætate nata opinio, sed ma- la tamen ac falsa. Plato li. V. de II.censet eas ciuitates esse beatissimas, in quibus omnium o- mnia sint communia. Eum secutus Seneca putauit omnia habitura quā optimè, si verborum illorum Meum & Tuum nullus amplius vsus foret. Exemplo sunt apud Strabonem Noma- des. Eodem numero nostros anabaptistas comprehende, qui scripturis sacris hanc rerum perturbationem approbare conati sunt. Sed necquicquam. Nam primum Abraham & pa- triarchæ reliqui, homines summa pietate præditi fuerunt ditisimi. Dein Josue publice & priuatim sua populo Israelio bona distribuit. Extant præterea & in Solomone & in prophe- tis præcepta de rerum proprietate cum plurima tum pulcherrima. Et legi illi qui locus esset, si nihil cuiquam sit proprium? Nam si nihil habeam proprium nihil mihi quod fureris erit. Nec credibile est Deum legem hanc laturum fuisse, si voluisset omnia esse communia.
units.tr: If this is so, as it truly is, then the opinion of those who abolish the ownership of property must be overturned, and by this law alone. The opinion is old, not born only in our own age, but it is nonetheless bad and false. Plato, in the fifth book of the Laws, held that those states are most blessed in which all things are held in common. Following him, Seneca thought that all things would go as well as possible if the words "mine" and "yours" were no longer used. Strabo gives the nomads as an example. In the same category I include our Anabaptists, who have tried to approve this upheaval of property from the sacred Scriptures. But in vain. For first, Abraham and the other patriarchs, men endowed with the highest piety, were very rich. Then Joshua publicly and privately distributed goods to the people of Israel. Moreover, both in Solomon and in the prophets there are many and very beautiful precepts about the ownership of property. And what place would there be for that law, "thou shalt not steal," if nothing belonged to anyone? For if I have nothing of my own, there will be nothing that can be stolen from me. Nor is it credible that God would have given this law if he had wanted all things to be common.

units.la: Porro si veteris testamenti testimonia, quod solent, repudiauerint, en[?] alia adducta ex nouo. Christus iubet eleemosynas largiri, & pascere famelicos: at id non poterit quisquam si nihil habeat proprium. Apostolus hortatur ad curam rei familiaris: at ea nisi rem familiarem propriam habeas, suscipi non poterit. Et Petrus Ananię dicit, poteras retinere totum agrum, &c. Quod argumento est Christiano opus non esset, ut bonorum possessione cedat. Quamobrem iubet hac lege Dominus iustitiam colere, & suis quenque rebus contentum esse, & non solum non damnum dare proximo, verum etiam eius utilitati & saluti studere. Oremus.
units.tr: Moreover, if they reject the testimonies of the Old Testament, as they usually do, then look, other passages drawn from the New. Christ commands us to bestow alms and to feed the hungry; yet no one can do that if he has nothing of his own. The Apostle exhorts us to care for our household affairs; yet this cannot be undertaken unless you have a household property of your own. And Peter says to Ananias, "You could have kept the whole field," etc. This is evidence that a Christian has no need to surrender his goods into common possession. Therefore the Lord, by this law, bids us cultivate justice, to be content with our own things, and not only not to do harm to our neighbour, but also to labour for his advantage and welfare. Let us pray.

units.la: SERMO XV.
units.tr: Sermon XV.

units.la: 20 Ne respondeas falsum testimonium aduersus proximum tuum.
units.tr: 20 You shall not bear false witness against your neighbour.

units.la: QUemadmodum Dominus in ijs tribus, quae proximae sunt, legibus seuitiae, libidini, furto, quibus ceu atrocibus iniurijs damnum datur, repagulum posuit: sic praesenti istac lege mendacium remouet, ceu tetrum vitium, quod verbis noceat.
units.tr: Just as the Lord, in the three laws that come next, against cruelty, lust and theft, which do harm as grave wrongs, has set up a barrier, so in this present law he removes lying, a foul vice that injures by words.

units.la: Ea vero sic habet. Ne respondeas falsum testimonium aduersus proximum tuum. Refponden[?] di verbo, quo Hebrei שׁוא[?] vtuntur, significat nostrum esse, ut de persona, rebus, negocijs proximi rogati quod verum est dicamus.
units.tr: The law reads: "You shall not bear false witness against your neighbour." The verb for "bear witness" that the Hebrews use [שׁוא] signifies that it is our duty to say what is true when we are asked about a neighbour's person, property or affairs.

units.la: Rogamur autem priuatim iuxta ac publice. Priuatim quando in conuentibus, & conuiuijs, & colloquijs incidit in absentis alicuius mentionem aliquis: tunc enim offertur occasio vel obtrectandi vel commendandi. Publice cum in foro seu iudicio rogati testimonium dicimus.
units.tr: We are asked in private as well as in public. In private, when in gatherings, feasts or conversations someone happens to mention an absent person, an occasion then arises either to disparage or to commend. In public, we give testimony when we are asked in the marketplace or in court.

units.la: Quicquid igitur in absentem dicitur quoniam ei vel prodest vel obest, testimonij nomen obtinet.
units.tr: Therefore whatever is said about an absent person, insofar as it either benefits or harms him, takes on the character of testimony.

units.la: Proximus autem is est, de quo verba fieri fecerit occasio.
units.tr: Now a neighbour is whoever gives occasion for words to be spoken about him.

units.la: Ex quo perspicuum est summam legis huius esse, ne vel calumnijs alicuius nomen vio-lemus vel maledictis offendamus, vel mendacijs eius saluté ledamus. Aut enim obtrectatio-ne fama proximi leditur, aut mendacijs illius comodis detrahitur. Igitur non solum iudicia-ria testimonia, sed etiam vulgares calumnias & mendacia remouet. Hoc enim quasi caput summum ex omni genere falsi proponit, ad quod cetera genera referas: quando in hoc gene-re vitij turpitudo maxime eminet, quippe quod cum periurio coniunctum sit.
units.tr: From this it is plain that the sum of this law is that we must not violate anyone's name by slander, nor offend him by insults, nor harm his welfare by lies. For a neighbour's reputation is injured either by disparagement or his advantage is diminished by lies. So the law removes not only false testimony in courts but also common slander and lies. For it sets out this as the chief head of every kind of falsehood, to which you may refer the other kinds, since the foulness of this kind of vice stands out most, being joined with perjury.

units.la: Ergo praeceptum hoc seruatur quando lingua cum famae, tum utilitati proximi seruie-rit: violatur autem cum ea ipsa vel famae vel commodis eius nocuerit. Atque ea quidem legis sententia ex causis, contrario, testimonijs, exemplis colligi poterit.
units.tr: So this precept is kept when the tongue serves both a neighbour's reputation and his advantage, but it is violated when the tongue harms either his reputation or his interests. The meaning of this law may be gathered from causes, contraries, testimonies and examples.

units.la: Causa est, quod quemadmodum mendacijs in peccatum detrusi fumus, sic ad mendacia subinde adhuc propendent animi omnium mortalium. Hęcq; naturae nostrae deprauatio vel scripturę sacrę testimonio confirmatur. Nam cum nusquam scriptum extet, omnis homo fur, vel adulter, aut latro: sæpe tamen & multum scribitur, omnis homo mendax. Quod indicio fuerit, quantopere natura propendeamus ad mendacia. Omitto teste huius mali vulgarem, & pene continuâ, mentiendi consuetudinem. Ut immensa cavi spirant mendacia folles. Quo refer obtrectationes, calumnias, mendacia, testimonia, assentationem, & huius generis alia, quibus nisi mature eatur obuiam, damna dantur maxima. Quare Deus & remouere malum & normam legum idem facientium proponere voluit.
units.tr: The cause is that, just as we have been thrust into sin by lies, so the minds of all mortals still lean toward lying. This corruption of our nature is confirmed by the testimony of Holy Scripture. For although nowhere is it written that every man is a thief, an adulterer or a robber, yet it is often and repeatedly written that every man is a liar. This is a sign of how strongly our nature inclines to lies. I pass over the common and almost constant custom of lying, a witness to this evil: "like bellows that breathe out immense lies." To this belong backbiting, slander, lies, false witness, flattery, and other things of this kind, which cause the greatest harm unless they are speedily opposed. Therefore God wished both to remove the evil and to set before us the rule of laws doing the same.

units.la: Contra vero si tam propensae ad falsum naturae non iretur obuiam, innumera mala fe-qui necesse esset.1.Sancta violatur veritas, qua nihil est in rerum natura sacratius, quippe quę ceu sol quispiam ne quid lateat è tenebris protrahit & illustrat omnia.
units.tr: On the other hand, if we did not oppose this nature so prone to falsehood, countless evils would necessarily follow. First, the holy truth is violated, than which nothing in the nature of things is more sacred, since truth, like some sun, drags out all things from darkness so that nothing may remain hidden, and illumines everything.

units.la: 2 Rerum notitia mendacijs quasi tenebris atque nebulis legitur. Quo malum aliud vix est maius ullum. Etenim si quid dicam pulcherrime & falsum sit argumentum, quid nisi nihil dixi?
units.tr: Second, knowledge of things is lost, as if in darkness and fog, brought about by lies. Hardly any other evil is greater than this. For if I say something very beautifully, but it is a false argument, what have I said but nothing?

units.la: 3 Iniusti adiuuantur, indigni laudantur: iusti vero sunt inglorij, & impediuntur atque op-primuntur quibus est illata iniuria. Nam in iudicijs quidem testium verbis quasi legibus est addictus iudex, ac si falsa sint illa pronunciare pro iure & veritate non potest, sitq; ut causa cadant qui poterant vincere. Idem accidit in priuatis negotijs.
units.tr: Third, the unjust are helped, the unworthy are praised, while the just are unrecognised, and those who have been wronged are hindered and oppressed. For in courts the judge is bound by the words of witnesses as if by laws; if these are false, he cannot pronounce in accordance with right and truth, and it comes about that those who could have won lose their cases. The same happens in private affairs.

units.la: 4 Fides quæ est basis societatis humanæ, tollitur, fitque vt quicquid tentes nil efficias. Nam cum verbis quid de te mihi persuasum esse debet tuis cognosci possit; verba autè sint friuola ac falsa: ego quando illis niti volo non lóngius nec felicius meas res gessero, quàm qui aëre ceu ponte vti velit, wirt nit wit vfflufft gaan.
units.tr: Fourth, faith, which is the basis of human society, is destroyed, and it comes about that whatever you attempt, you achieve nothing. For when I ought to be persuaded of anything concerning you, it can be learned from your own words; but if the words are frivolous and false, then when I wish to rely on them I shall have acted no further and no more successfully than one who wishes to use air as a bridge, to walk as it were on the wind and go off like a puff of breath.

units.la: 5 Neque cum Deo neq; cum hominibus nobis res esse possit, si legi illi nòn stetur. Nam quia Deus est ipsissima veritas, odit atque execratur mendacium: ac quò nobis cum illo pós fit intercedere commercium, opus est nos veraces esse. Vt enim mundus bonus, iustus ipse est, vultúque etiam nos propterea mundos bonos atque iustos esse: ita quia verax est etiam nos veraces esse iubet. Iam si in vsu familiaritatis humanæ eam rationem inire soles; vt quo-niam simile simili gaudeat, tu quorum amicus esse cupias eorum moribus tete accommo-des: cur non etiam vt Dei sis amicus illius te naturæ & moribus accommodas? At si legè hac neglecta mendacijs studeas actum est de eâ amicitia. Neque sperari par est eum amicum tibi fore à cuius moribus tui tantopere varient. Ergo vt amicitia tibi cum Deo non possit esse fa-ciunt mendacia.
units.tr: Fifth, we cannot have any dealings either with God or with men if we do not abide by that law. For since God is very truth itself, he hates and abhors lying; and so that a relationship with him may come about for us, we must be truthful. For as God is good and just, and therefore wills that we too be good and just, so because he is truthful he commands that we too be truthful. Now if in the practice of human friendship you are accustomed to follow this rule, that since like delights in like, you adapt yourself to the manners of those whose friend you wish to be, why not also adapt yourself to the nature and manners of God, so that you may be his friend? But if, neglecting this law, you devote yourself to lies, that friendship is at an end. Nor is it right to expect that one will be a friend to you whose manners differ so greatly from yours. Therefore lies make it impossible for you to have friendship with God.

units.la: Sed nec cum hominibus vlla potest intercedere mendacibus amicitia. Cui enim libèat habere cum eo quicquam negocij qui quicquid dixerit mentiatur? Nihil illi tuto credideris: ac si nihil dixeris tamen periculum est ne quid esse dictum mentiatur alibi. Atq; hæc quidem ex mendacijs.
units.tr: But no friendship with men can arise with liars either. For who would wish to have any business with one who lies whatever he says? You would trust him in nothing; and even if you said nothing, there is still a danger that he will lie elsewhere about what has been said. So much for lies.

units.la: Testimonia verò si requiras multa pássim extant. Exod. 23. Non suscipies vocem mendacij, nec iungas manum tuam vt pro impio dicas falsum testimonium. Leuit. 19. ne quis deci-piat fratrem suum. Psalm. 15. Non relinquitur locus mendacibus in monte Domini. Eódem sua quoque præcepta dirigunt apostoli. Paulus Coloss. 3. nolite mentiri inuicem. Et 1. Tim. 1. mendacibus & periuris dicit legem esse positam, scilicet repagulum. Eadem de re extat non nihil étiam Iacob. 3.
units.tr: If you seek testimonies, many are scattered everywhere. Exod. 23. "You shall not take up a false report, nor put your hand with the wicked to be a false witness." Lev. 19. "Let no one deceive his brother." Ps. 15. "There is no place for liars on the mountain of the Lord." The apostles too direct their precepts to the same end. Paul, Col. 3: "Do not lie to one another." And 1 Tim. 1 says the law has been laid down for liars and perjurers, clearly as a barrier. Something on the same matter is also found in Jas. 3.

units.la: His accedunt etiam Christianorum theologorum sententiæ. Basilius inquit, Οὔτε ἐν ἀλ-ηθείᾳ ... ἀληθῆ πρὸς λόγους τῆς βίᾳ. Chrysostomus ait. ὅσπερ τὸ καλῶς λέγειν καὶ ἐγκωμιάζειν ἀρ-χὴ φιλίας ἐστιν οὕτω τὸ καλῶς λέγειν καὶ ἀμαβάλλειν ἐχθρᾶς καὶ ἀπιχθείας καὶ μυείων κακῶν ἀρχὴ καὶ ὑπὸ θεσίς γέγονε.
units.tr: To these are added the opinions of Christian theologians. Basil says: "Neither in truth ... true in words of violence." [Οὔτε ἐν ἀλήθεια ... ἀληθῆ πρὸς λόγους τῆς βίᾳ.] Chrysostom says: "Just as speaking well and praising is the beginning of friendship, so speaking well and slandering is the beginning of enmity, hatred and countless evils, and has come into being as a pretext." [ὅσπερ τὸ καλῶς λέγειν καὶ ἐγκωμιάζειν ἀρχὴ φιλίας ἐστιν οὕτω τὸ καλῶς λέγειν καὶ ἀμαβάλλειν ἐχθρᾶς καὶ ἀπιχθείας καὶ μυρίων κακῶν ἀρχὴ καὶ ὑπόθεσις γέγονε.]

units.la: Eódem & poetæ & Philosophi respiciunt. Menander enim dicit,
units.tr: Poets and philosophers look to the same thing. For Menander says:

units.la: Ἀεὶ κεχρῆσθαι τῇ ἀληθῆ λέγειν.
units.tr: "Always to use the truth in speaking." [Ἀεὶ κεχρῆσθαι τῇ ἀληθῆ λέγειν.]

units.la: Ἐν παντὶ καιρῷ τοῦτ᾽ ἐγὼ παρεγγυῶ
units.tr: "In every circumstance I charge this:" [Ἐν παντὶ καιρῷ τοῦτ᾽ ἐγὼ παρεγγυῶ]

units.la: Εἰς ἀσφάλειαν τῷ βίῳ πλεῖστον μέρος.
units.tr: "For safety in life, it is the greatest part." [Εἰς ἀσφάλειαν τῷ βίῳ πλεῖστον μέρος.]

units.la: Iam & Pythagoras interrogatus quid possent homines facere quod Deo simile esset, respon-dit ἐαν ἀληθεύωσιν. Et Magi suum maximum Deum, quem Oromagden nominabant, cor-pore quidem luci, anima autem veritati similem esse tradiderunt. Sed præceptum hoc Theo-gnis omnium optime expressit dicens, μαρτυρεῖν ψευδῆ φεύγειν, τὰ δίκαια ἀγορεύειν. Sic enim cauendum falsum testimonium, & ad eum modum gubernandâ esse linguam nostram vt quod iure cuiusq; sit idipsum ei tribuatur, docuit.
units.tr: Again, when Pythagoras was asked what men could do that was like God, he answered: "if they speak the truth." [ἐαν ἀληθεύωσιν.] And the Magi taught that their greatest god, whom they called Oromazes, was like light in body and like truth in soul. But Theognis expressed this precept best of all, saying: "to bear witness to avoid falsehood, to speak just things." [μαρτυρεῖν ψευδῆ φεύγειν, τὰ δίκαια ἀγορεύειν.] For he taught that false witness is to be avoided in this way, and that our tongue is to be governed so that what is due to each person by right is given to him.

units.la: Exemplis autem perspicuum fit quàm turpe & pernitiosum & malum fit mentiri. Doeg Idumæus sua delatione & sacerdotes Domini 85. & omnes vrbis Nobe incolas perdidit. Da-uid exilij sui causam tribuit mendacibus delatoribus dicens ad Saulem: Domine mi rex, qua-re audis verba hominum dicentium ad te, Dauid quærit malum aduersum te? Amanus etiam suis apud Assuerum calumnijs, ni Deus auertisset, Iudæam gentem penè totam oppresserat. Sed falsorum testium exempla sunt in iudicijs Nabothi, Susannæ, Christi, Stephani, & alio-rum. Exemplo fit populus Romanus, qui legibus & supplicijs hoc malum semper vindica-uit. In leg. xij. tab. tit. viij. sic scriptum extat. Qui falsum testimonium dixisse conuictus erit, ä faxo Tarpeio deijcitor. Et in ijsdem tit. vij. sic. Iudicem arbitrûmue iure datum, qui ob rem di-cendam accepisse pecuniam conuictus est, capite punito. Eódem refer quæcunq; in Iure ex-tant de iudicijs, actionibus, probationibus, testibus, calumniatoribus, libellis famosis & alijs rebus similibus, itemq; illa pulchra l. diffamari. c. de ingenu. manumiss. Quæ cum ita sint, vt perspicuum sit hanc legem & causis & exemplis & sententijs optimorum hominum appro-bari: sequitur nobis etiam illam recipiendam esse vt obtineamus veritatem, rerum notitiam, ius, fidem, deniq; & Dei & hominum amici-tiam. Id faxit Deus. Amen.
units.tr: By examples it is also clear how shameful, pernicious and wicked it is to lie. Doeg the Edomite, by his accusation, destroyed both the priests of the Lord, eighty-five of them, and all the inhabitants of the city of Nob. David attributed the cause of his exile to lying informers, saying to Saul: "My lord the king, why do you listen to the words of men who say to you, 'David seeks harm against you'?" Haman too, by his calumnies before Ahasuerus, had nearly oppressed the entire Jewish nation, had God not turned it aside. Examples of false witnesses are also found in the trials of Naboth, Susanna, Christ, Stephen and others. The Roman people set an example, which always punished this evil by laws and penalties. In the Twelve Tables, title 8, it is written thus: "Whoever is convicted of having given false testimony shall be thrown from the Tarpeian Rock." And in the same title 7: "A judge or arbiter appointed by law who is convicted of having taken money for the case shall be punished with death." To this belong all the things in the law concerning trials, actions, proofs, witnesses, slanderers, defamatory pamphlets and other similar matters, and likewise that fine law, "diffamari", C. de ingenuis manumissis. Since these things are so, and it is plain that this law is approved by reasons, by examples and by the opinions of the best men, it follows that we too must receive it, so that we may obtain truth, knowledge of things, right, faith, and finally the friendship of both God and men. May God grant it. Amen.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAPTER 5.

units.la: 21 Ne concupiscas vxorem proximi tui, neue domum proximi tui desideres, nec agrum eius, nec ancillam eius, nec bouem eius, nec asinum eius, nec quidquà quod est proximi tui.
units.tr: 21 You shall not covet your neighbour's wife, nor desire your neighbour's house, nor his field, nor his manservant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor anything that is your neighbour's.

units.la: CVm velit Dominus & in omnibus tabulæ fecundæ legibus eò solũ spectet, vt animus noster totus amore seu dilectione proximi posideatur: iam vltimo hoc præcepto contra cupiscentiam aduersam dilectioni remouet, atq; iubet, vt aut penitus excutiatur, aut quando hoc obineri non potest, saltem reprimatur.
units.tr: Since the Lord wills, in all the laws of the second table, to aim solely at this, that our whole mind be possessed by love or affection for our neighbour, he removes by this last precept the desire that is opposed to love, and commands that it be either utterly cast out or, when this cannot be obtained, at least restrained.

units.la: Ipsum autem præceptum sic habet, Ne concupiscas vxorem proximi tui, neue domum proximi tui desideres, nec agrum eius, &c. Eius summa hæc est: Ne qua cogitatio subeat animos nostros, qua agitata concupiscentia in proximi nostri detrimentum noui quicquam moliatur, atque eius bonis inhiet. E diuerso præcipitur, vt omnis cogitatio, omne studium & institutum nostrum ad vtilitatem, & salutem proximi referatur.
units.tr: The precept itself reads: You shall not covet your neighbour's wife, nor desire your neighbour's house, nor his field, etc. Its sum is this: no thought should enter our minds by which, once desire is stirred, we would undertake some new scheme to our neighbour's loss and gape after his goods. On the contrary, it is commanded that every thought, every effort and every purpose of ours be directed to our neighbour's advantage and welfare.

units.la: Ac quoniam concupiscentia dilectioni, quæ Christianorum hominum, vt docent Christus & apostoli, tessera pariter ac perfectio est, tantopere solet reluctari: hæc lex, quam Deus quasi quoddam huic bestiæ repagulum posuit, paulò altius reperenda est, inuestigandumq; erit vnde hæc existat pestis, & quæ qualisque sit, & quænam secum mala trahat. Nam his cognitis perspicuum erit quomodo huic malo sit eundum obuiam, vt seruetur lex Domini: quid Deus expetendum concesserit quidue nolit expeti: quibus deniq; de causis hanc legem Deus tulerit, & ea malum hoc remouere voluerit.
units.tr: Since desire is so strongly resisted by love, which, as Christ and the apostles teach, is both the mark and the perfection of Christian people, this law, which God has set as a kind of barrier against this beast, must be sought out somewhat more deeply. We must inquire whence this plague arises, what kind of thing it is, and what evils it brings in its train. For once these are known it will be clear how this evil is to be met, so that the Lord's law may be kept; what God has allowed us to desire and what he is unwilling for us to desire; and finally, for what reasons God gave this law and wished to remove this evil by it.

units.la: Sed vnde existat concupiscentia Philo minime malus interpres Mosis, hanc eum reli- quis animi perturbationibus conferens ad hunc modum docet: <bl>μόνη</bl> inquit, <bl>αὕτη ἔστὶν μιᾶ τῶν ἀρχῶν ἐξ ἡμῶν λαμβάνει</bl>, <bl>ἀρχή ἔστιν ἰουδαίων</bl>. Ac ne verbis illis fidè habere graue sit & molestum tibi Christiano, habemus ex multis etiam hæc Christi testimonia. Is Matth. 15. Pharifæis causam seu fontem malitiæ in eorum ipsorum cordibus monstrat dicens, eos cum mali sint, & intus & in cute improbi, nō posse quicquam boni proloqui, quippe quod è bono thesauro cordis bona boni loquantur ac rursus è malo mala mali. Et alibi dicit frustra coli mundiciem corporum, quando animi intus fœtore concupiscentiæ, auaritiæ, ambitionis, inuidiæ & similium affectuum sint inquinati. Quibus locis quod docet Philo confirmatur inhærere animis nostris illam pestem.
units.tr: But whence desire arises, Philo, no unfriendly interpreter of Moses, teaches in this manner, comparing it with the other disturbances of the mind: "This," he says, "is one of the first principles, which we receive from ourselves, the beginning of injustice" [μόνη αὕτη ἔστιν μιᾶ τῶν ἀρχῶν ἐξ ἡμῶν λαμβάνει, ἀρχή ἔστιν ἰουδαίων]. And lest it be burdensome or troubling for you as a Christian to trust these words, we have many testimonies of Christ on this point too. In Matthew 15 he shows the Pharisees the cause or fountain of wickedness in their very hearts, saying that since they are evil, wicked both within and in their outward skin, they cannot speak anything good, for out of the good treasure of the heart good men bring forth good things, and again out of the evil, evil men bring forth evil. And elsewhere he says that the cleanness of bodies is vainly cultivated when the mind within is defiled by the stench of lust, greed, ambition, envy and similar passions. From these passages it is confirmed that what Philo teaches, that this pestilence clings to our minds, is true.

units.la: Iam fi in nobis oriatur, quis illam pestem nostris animis indidit? Indidit Deus affectus, & appetitum bonorum rationi & naturæ & vero diuino consentaneum, quibus quasi stimulis seu calcaribus ad bonum propelleremur. Et vsu rerum comperimus vtiles esse hos stimulos: quid enim inuita Minerua, quod aiunt, efficimus? Cæterum nobis Adæ lapsu vitiatis simul hæc animi bona vitiata sunt omnia, & haud secus ac in fœtido dolio vinum occipit fœtere, sic in nobis omnia bona corrupta sunt illo originali vitio. Quo fit, vt illi quoq; stimuli qui bus ad bonum excitari debebamus, nos inuitent atq; agitent ad malum.
units.tr: Now if it arises in us, who put that pestilence into our minds? God put in the affections and the appetite for good things, agreeable to reason, to nature and to the true divine will, by which as by goads or spurs we would be driven to the good. And by experience we have found these goads useful: for what, as they say, do we accomplish against Minerva's will? But when we were corrupted by Adam's fall, all these good gifts of the mind were corrupted together, and just as wine begins to stink in a foul cask, so in us all good things have been corrupted by that original vice. Hence it comes about that those very goads by which we ought to have been roused to good now invite and drive us to evil.

units.la: Cæterum vt satan huius corruptionis author atque effector extitit, sic illa nostra κακία subinde in perniciem nostram abutitur, eamq; solet obiectis illecebris ciere. Vt vsu perse- runtur ad nos amœnæ, pulchræ, bonæ, iucundæ res, quibus illectus animus concupiscentiam sequitur. Veluti Nohæ seculo vident filij Dei filias hominum, eoq; aspectu sunt in illorum amores incitati: videt Dauid lauantem Berfabam, eiusq; visa forma animus captus est instigante videlicet concupiscentia. Has sensuum facultates, atque vires non nescieuit Balaamus, qui Moabitides in conspectum filiorum Israel adduci iusit, vt eorum aspectu deliniti viri concupiscentiam incitatam sequerentur. Sic Achab visa Nabothi vinea concupiscentia supe ratus est. Auditu idé accidit. Nam ex colloquijs, rumoribus, cantilenis, & sonis Musicis affici mur, vt concupiscamus. Vt Paris audita forma Helenæ prius non quieuit, quàm illa videret, eius potiretur conuiétu, deniq; etiam ea tota. Nam primum auditus, tum visus, inde etiam tactus, mox vsus seu eius consuetudo cupidinem adiuuarent, vt tota in sua vota mentem ho minis pertraherent. Contactu siue commercio quis nescit infici mentem ac mores hominis? Ab Gößer gichli chafft ward Ser man sied.
units.tr: Moreover, just as Satan was the author and maker of this corruption, so our own wickedness [κακία] from time to time abuses it to our destruction, and is accustomed to stir it up by means of enticing objects. Pleasant, beautiful, good and agreeable things are brought to us through experience, and the mind, lured by them, follows desire. Thus in Noah's time the sons of God saw the daughters of men, and by that sight they were inflamed with love for them. David saw Bathsheba bathing, and his mind was captured by her beauty, desire of course urging him on. Balaam did not fail to know these powers of the senses, for he had the Moabite women brought into the sight of the sons of Israel, so that men softened by their appearance would follow the desire thus kindled. So Ahab, having seen Naboth's vineyard, was overcome by desire. The same happens through hearing: we are moved to desire by conversations, rumours, songs and the sounds of music. So Paris, having first heard of Helen's beauty, was not at rest until he saw her, possessed her company, and finally possessed her entirely. For first hearing, then sight, then touch, and soon use or habit, aid desire, so that they draw the whole mind of a man toward their wishes. Through touch or contact who does not know that a man's mind and morals are infected? Ab Gößer gichli chafft ward Ser man sied (a German proverb).

units.la: Atq; earum quas hic diximus rerum ductu venire ad radices huius mali potes, quæ eò ponderandæ sunt exactius, quod illis cognitis malo obstare possumus facilius. Nam sublata causa tollitur effectus. Igitur consulit Dominus Matth. 5. eruehdum oculum illum, qui inui-tat ad malum: & Solomon dicit, auerte oculos ne videant vanitatem. Ex quibus intelligimus euitatis obiectis, & repulsis sensibus rerum iucundarum nuncijs effici, vt concupiscentia minus accensa, peccemus minus.
units.tr: By the guidance of the things we have mentioned here, you can come to the roots of this evil, which must be weighed the more exactly because, once they are known, we can more easily resist the evil. For when the cause is removed the effect is removed. Therefore the Lord advises in Matthew 5 that the eye which invites us to evil be plucked out, and Solomon says, "Turn away your eyes lest they see vanity." From these things we understand that by avoiding objects and by repelling the senses from the news of pleasant things, it is brought about that desire is less kindled, and we sin less.

units.la: Sed praeterea amplius quiddam requiritur. Etsi enim nec audias, videas, contingas quicquid mala tamen malae subeunt animum cogitationes, quibus aeque atq; extrinsecus oblatis rebus haec impigra bestia suscitatur. Quid hic agas? praecludes illis aditum continuis occupationibus, precibus, curis publicis & domesticis, honestis studijs & laboribus: ac si sit recreandus animus, fumendae sunt refocillationes honestae & licitae. Id docet Matth. 13. Dominus quando has cogitationes auibus comparat, quae verbi diuini semen in animos nostros iactum deuorent, vt qui id semen saluum retinere velit, auibus ne qua possint aduolare, praecludat aditu.
units.tr: But beyond this something more is required. For even if you neither hear, see nor touch anything, nevertheless evil thoughts come into the mind, and by these, no less than by objects offered from outside, this tireless beast is stirred up. What are you to do here? You will shut them out by constant occupations, prayers, public and domestic cares, honourable studies and labours. And if the mind needs refreshing, honest and lawful recreations are to be taken. Matthew 13 teaches this, when the Lord compares these thoughts to birds that devour the seed of the divine word sown in our minds; so he who wishes to keep that seed safe must close off access, lest any birds may fly down upon it.

units.la: His etiam aliud accedit malum, quo bestiae huic fores aperiuntur, earum quas dedit Deus minus rerum satietas: haec enim si nos coeperit alterius res, statim concupiscimus. Vt vxoris suae pertesus, obuiam quanq; concupiscit, officij sui tedio ductus alienam appetit, eodem modo in bonis omnibus. Quid hic facias? profecto opus est cito remedio. Nam vt ille dixit, vulgare est hoc vitium, & optat ephippia bos piger, optat arare caballus. Tu contra quod Mar-tialis cofulit sequitor. Quod fis, inquit, esse velis nihil, malis. Est virtus αὐτάρκεια cuius au-xilijs multum efficitur. Atq; hoc consulit D. Chrysostomus dicens, ὁ ἀεὶς τὰς ὑπερέχοντας βλέπων, τῆς ἐνώσεως αὐτῷ ἐυπρείας ἀδ' ἵποτε ἃ δύναται λαβεῖν αἴσθησιν· ἀλλ' ἀεὶ αὐ-τάρκως ἔσεις ἰδία ἔχειν, ἡ δ' ἀχαριστεῖν τῷ θεῷ. Praeclarum profecto & ad tranquillam iucundamq; praesentium rerum fruitionem momenti plurimum afferens. Qui enim tuarum rerum sensu vllo potes afici, subinde inte-ntus alienis fortunis? Quare si concupiscentia reprimenda fit, oculi in tuarum ipsius fortunarum aspectum conuertendi sunt, nempe vt eo quod Dominus dedit, contentus sis & illi datori gratias agas atq; habeas. Nec temere dictum est illud Spartam quam nactus es, hanc orna. Sed omnium optime Christus consuluit, hac vi delicet praescripta quotidianarum precum formula, fiat voluntas tua in terra, sicut & in coelo. Quod quid est aliud, quam eodem velle nos esse loco, quo nos Deus constituat. Idem coelites, quod Deo videtur ac placet, voluntidem in terris nos, quod illi videtur ac placet velle debebimus. Atq; sic quidem & radices mali illius habes, & qua sit eundum obuiam.
units.tr: To this another evil is added, by which the doors are opened to this beast: satiety with the things God has given us in smaller measure. For if the things of another begin to take hold of us, at once we desire them. As a man weary of his wife, though he desires some other woman, led by the tedium of his duty, seeks what belongs to another, so in regard to all goods. What are you to do here? Surely a quick remedy is needed. For as he said, this vice is common: "the lazy ox wishes for a saddle, the horse wishes to plough" [Horace]. You, on the contrary, follow what Martial advised: "What you are, you should wish to be; nothing else should you prefer." There is the virtue of self-sufficiency [αὐτάρκεια], by whose aid much is accomplished. And this is what St John Chrysostom advises, saying: "He who always looks at those above him never perceives what he could obtain for his own good; but he who is always content with what he has, and does not fail to give thanks to God" [ὁ ἀεὶ τοὺς ὑπερέχοντας βλέπων, τῆς ἑαυτοῦ εὐπραγίας... ἀλλ' ἀεὶ αὐτάρκως ἕξει ἃ ἔχει ἰδίᾳ, καὶ μὴ ἀχαριστεῖν τῷ θεῷ]. Truly a remarkable saying, and one contributing very much to the calm and pleasant enjoyment of present things. For how can you be affected by any sense of your own possessions, if you are constantly intent on the fortunes of others? Therefore, if desire is to be restrained, your eyes must be turned to the sight of your own fortunes, namely so that you may be content with what the Lord has given, and may give thanks to and hold in regard that giver. Nor was that saying rashly uttered: "Adorn the Sparta you have obtained." But Christ advised best of all, by prescribing this formula in the daily prayers: "Your will be done on earth as it is in heaven." What is this other than wishing ourselves to be in the place where God has set us?
