As the heavenly ones wish what seems right and pleasing to God, so we on earth ought to wish what seems right and pleasing to him. In this way you have both the roots of that evil and the way to meet it.

units.la: Quid ea fit ideo scire est operae precium, vt quid Deus concesserit quidq; vetuerit hac lege constet. Est igitur concupiscentia rerum iucundarum & voluptatem afferentium appetitio.
units.tr: It is worth knowing what this is, so that it is clear from this law what God has permitted and what he has forbidden. Concupiscence, then, is the appetite for pleasant things that bring pleasure.

units.la: Iam quemadmodum res diuiduntur in eas quae & licitae sunt, & diuinitus praebitae, quarumq; voluptate pie fruimur, itemq;, in eas quae & negatae sunt nobis diuinitus, & perniciosae sunt & nefariae: sic ipsa sese concupiscentia diuidit, & est alia concessa ac licita, alia contra vetita & nefaria. Licita ac bona concupiscentia ea est, quae verè bona, recte & moderate expetit, vt honores, opes, vxorem, liberos pacem, amicitias & huius generis alia quis non expeteret? His oblatis quis non gauderet, & frueretur? Paulus episcopatum expetere non improbauit, sed honestum duxit. Abraham, Sara, Anna mater Samuelis, Zacharias, Elizabeth desiderarunt liberos, idq; tantum abest vt Deus improbarit, vt etiam ipsum concesserit. His addemo-tus, quos animis Deus ceu virtutum cotes indidit, vt amore erga liberos, patriam, & omnino nostros omnes, vt irā, vt spem & his similes alios nobis vtilisimos. Liberos enim tantis curis & molestijs quis posset eorum amore vacuus, educare? Fortitudine quid acuit magis quàm ira? Patientia & constantiam quid aliud quàm spes vna firmat ac sustinet? Quid verbis opus est? Res ipsa probat hosce motus esse bonos & vtiles, & errorem esse Stoicorum ἀπάθειαν. Nam qui victum appetit, impellitur ad implorandam opem Dei: qui illo potitus est, quoniam eum non fine labore & molestia acquisiuit, vsum eius rectum ac moderatum feruat, proque eo sibi concesso Deo gratias habet atq; agit. Quis improbet haec studia? at ea nobis peperit haec ipsa quam probamus concupiscentia. Quamobrem eam hac lege Deus nequaquam improbat.
units.tr: Just as things are divided into those that are both lawful and divinely granted, the enjoyment of which we use piously, and, on the other hand, into those that are both denied us by God and are harmful and wicked, so concupiscence itself divides: one kind is permitted and lawful, another is forbidden and wicked. Lawful and good concupiscence is that which seeks, rightly and in moderation, things that are truly good, such as honours, wealth, a wife, children, peace, friendships, and other things of this kind, which no one would fail to desire. When these are offered, who would not rejoice and enjoy them? Paul did not disapprove of desiring the episcopate, but considered it an honourable thing. Abraham, Sarah, Hannah the mother of Samuel, Zechariah and Elizabeth desired children, and God was so far from disapproving of this that he actually granted it. To these are added the impulses which God has placed in our minds as whetstones of the virtues: love towards children, country, and in general towards all our own, anger, hope, and other similar ones that are most useful to us. For who could bring up children, with so many cares and troubles, if he were devoid of love for them? What sharpens courage more than anger? What else but a single hope strengthens and sustains patience and constancy? Why need we say more? The thing itself proves that these emotions are good and useful, and that the Stoics' apatheia is an error. For he who desires food is driven to implore the help of God; he who has obtained it, since he acquired it not without labour and trouble, keeps its use right and moderate, and for what has been granted to him he has and gives thanks to God. Who would condemn these pursuits? Yet this very concupiscence, which we approve, brought them forth for us. Wherefore God by this law by no means condemns it.

units.la: Sed alia est magistra mala quae concupiscit illicita, turpia, nefaria, & omnino ea quae pugnant cum voluntate Domini & cum vtilitate proximi. Nam cum summa doctrinae Christianae haec fit: Deum prae rebus omnibus, ac proximum aeque ac teipsum amare: sane quicquid aduersum est ac displicet Domino, quicquid vergit in perniciem proximi, id fine scelere & violatione legis affectari non potest.
units.tr: But there is another, evil mistress, which desires things unlawful, shameful, wicked, and in general those things which conflict with the will of the Lord and with the good of our neighbour. For the sum of Christian doctrine is this: to love God above all things and our neighbour as ourselves. Surely whatever is contrary to the Lord and displeasing to him, whatever tends to the ruin of our neighbour, cannot be pursued without wickedness and violation of the law.

units.la: Atque hoc ipsum verba legis docent. Non enim dicit, Non concupiscesvxorem, domum, seruum, ancillam &c. quia non negat hæc votis nostris: sed dicit, Non concupisces vxo-rem proximi, quod eá sibi vendicare, quæ sint alterius, sit ac videatur nefarium.
units.tr: And the words of the law itself teach this. For it does not say, "You shall not covet wife, house, manservant, maidservant, etc.", because it does not forbid these to our wishes; but it says, "You shall not covet your neighbour's wife", since to claim for oneself what belongs to another is, and appears, wicked.

units.la: Ac quo foret illustrior hæc præceptio, summa quædam rerum genera numerat, quarum appetitu proximo nostro damnum datur: nempe vt quod Deus cuiq; dedit id ipse ei cum permittas integrum, tum etiam si possis non auferas. Sunt diuinis & humanis legibus definiti rerum commutandarum atq; acquirendarum modi, quos vult seruari, & adeo quidem seruari[?] vt ne in mentem quidem veniat alterius. Summa, iniquum est quenquam velle cum al-terius detrimento rem suam familiarem augere, cum diligendus sit potius quam damno af-ficiendus proximus.
units.tr: And to make this precept the clearer, it enumerates certain general kinds of things, by the desire for which damage is done to our neighbour: namely, that one should, while allowing him to keep what God has given him, not even if one could take it away. There are, by divine and human laws, defined ways of exchanging and acquiring things, which God wills to be observed, and indeed to be observed so strictly that it does not even enter the mind to seize what belongs to another. In sum, it is unjust for anyone to wish to increase his own household property to the detriment of another, since the neighbour is to be loved rather than harmed.

units.la: Mali quid afferat concupiscentia bifariam cognosci posse existimo, vel si cum reliquis animi perturbationibus comparetur, vel si illius effecta consideres. Vtroque experiemur in præsentia.
units.tr: I think that the harm which concupiscence brings can be known in two ways: either if it is compared with the other disturbances of the mind, or if you consider its effects. Let us experience both at present.

units.la: Cum alijs comparata reliquas omnes superat. Etsi enim ex mentem[?] sua pristina sanitate soleant dimouere, tamen ipsam hæc ferit omnium grauissimè. Alijs enim extrinsecus obre-pentibus hæc in nobis ipsis oritur & grassatur: at quis nescit intestina bella nocentiora esse exteris? Ergo vt intestinis tumultibus ciuitas magis lædítur, quàm externis: sic animus re-bus extrinsecus obuenientibus minus premitur, quàm intus ortis & grassantibus.
units.tr: Compared with the others, it surpasses them all. For although other passions are wont to move the mind from its former soundness, yet this one strikes it most gravely of all. For the others creep upon us from outside, but this one arises and rages within ourselves; and who does not know that civil wars within are more harmful than foreign ones? Therefore, as a state is harmed more by internal tumults than by external ones, so the mind is less oppressed by things coming upon it from outside than by those which arise and rage within.

units.la: Dein affectus reliquos & si tranquilli sint & pacati ipsa suscitat, ac perturbatos reddit: quando nunc in spem propositi boni cuiuspiam erigit, nunc metu mali venturi cruciat, mo-do accepti mali dolore conficit. Spe vero dictu mirum est quantopere excruciet, dum ani-mum quàm longissimè porrigit, quasiq; ad captandum corripiendumq; bonum propellit, nempe persuadens adeò propinquum esse, vt iam attingi possit. Hic animus haud secus ac ciurus quispiam in orbiculari machina semper sequendo, nunquam assequendo, sursum vor-sum ac circumcirca agitur. An vero sit vllum tormentum maius? Si verbis res satis depingi nequeat, en Tantalum illum, quem Horatius dicit sitientem fugientia à labris pocula capta-re. In quo vides quàm nullus sit quietis & tranquillitatis locus ei quem concupiscentia coe-pit, ac deuinctum & constrictum tenet.
units.tr: Further, it both stirs up the other affections, even when they are calm and at peace, and makes them disturbed: for now it raises them up in hope of some good proposed, now it torments them with fear of an evil about to come, now it overwhelms them with the pain of an evil already received. Hope, indeed, it is wonderful to say how greatly it racks, while it stretches the mind as far as possible and drives it, as it were, to seize and grasp the good, persuading it that the good is so near that it can now be touched. This mind, no otherwise than some runner on a wheel-shaped machine, is always following and never attaining, and is driven up and down and round about. Is there any torment greater than this? If the matter cannot be sufficiently depicted in words, behold that Tantalus whom Horace says tries to catch the cups that flee from his lips while thirsting. In him you see how there is no place for rest or tranquillity for one whom concupiscence has seized and holds bound and fettered.

units.la: Effectus autem eius & multi sunt & varij. Primum fulgore bonorum obiectorum sic præstringit oculos vt eos prorsus excæcet, vnde & gentilibus Cupido cæcus pingitur.
units.tr: Its effects, moreover, are both many and various. First, by the glitter of the good things set before it, it so dazzles the eyes that it utterly blinds them; hence also Cupid is painted blind among the pagans.

units.la: Dein cum verbum sit lux data nostris pedibus, vt ait in Psal.118. Dauid, ne qua affulgeat inde lux nobis, verbum ipsum hæc bestia suffocat in animis nostris, vt qui fumus maneamus cæci & stupidi. Docet hoc Dominus Marc.4. Dicit enim: Et alij sunt qui in spinas semen ex-cipiunt. Hi sunt qui sermonem audiunt & solicitudines seculi huius, ac deceptio diuitiarum cæterarumq; rerum cupiditates introeuntes, suffocant sermone, ac redditur infrugifer. Ergo hæc neq; ipsa quæ è re nostra sunt consulit, neq; eos qui cosulerent admittit, sed tota hoc agit vt nos eat perditum.
units.tr: Then, since the word is a light given to our feet, as the Psalm 118 says, "lest any light shine on us from it", this beast suffocates the word itself in our minds, so that we remain blind and stupid like smoke. The Lord teaches this in Mark 4. For he says: "And others are those who receive the seed among thorns. These are they who hear the word, and the cares of this world, and the deceit of riches and the desires for other things, entering in, choke the word, and it becomes unfruitful." Therefore this passion neither considers what is for our good, nor admits those who would counsel us, but does all it can to make us perish.

units.la: Tertio sic etiam est affecta, vt quo magis obstes hoc sæuiat ac grassetur illa magis, nec ve-lit vllis coerceri legibus, sed si quibus illi interdicas rebus, hæc eas tanto magis expetat. At-que hoc non solum sacris sed etiam prophanis literis celebratum probatumq; est & vsu rerum quotidianarum exploratum. Nam hoc dixit ille nobilis Poeta,
units.tr: Thirdly, it is so disposed that the more you oppose it, the more it rages and spreads, and it will not be restrained by any laws, but if you forbid it certain things, it desires them all the more. And this has been celebrated and approved not only in the sacred but also in profane writings, and has been proved by the everyday experience of things. For that noble poet said this:

units.la: Nitimur in vetitum semper cupimusq; negata.
units.tr: We strive always for what is forbidden, and we desire what is denied.

units.la: Et Paulus Ro.7. dicit, Peccatum occasione accepta per mandatum, operatum est in me omnem concupiscentiam. Quæ hæc est miseria? Si illam sinas suo more furere, periis-ti: si illi relu-cteris[?] furit magis.
units.tr: And Paul, Romans 7, says: "Sin, taking occasion through the commandment, wrought in me all concupiscence." What misery is this! If you allow it to rage in its own way, you perish; if you resist it, it rages the more.

units.la: Quartò parens est & ministra vitiorum omnium: quicquid enim est, cuius modo in mentem veniat id expetit. Et inde existunt φιλοπορνία, φιλοδοξία, γαστριμαργία & alia innumera. Nam quicquid cogitat hoc expetit.
units.tr: Fourthly, it is the parent and minister of all vices: for whatever comes to mind at all, it desires. And from this arise love of whores, love of glory, gluttony and countless others. For whatever it thinks of, it desires.

units.la: Quintò perennis seu continuata quædam perturbatio est, quippe quæ cum sit in iuue-nibus vehemens atq; impotens, tamen in senibus non occidat. Nam aliarum pertesa alias se-quitur, & quæ factis præstare nequit, ea cura ac solicitudine, & iussibus & dictis exequitur.
units.tr: Fifthly, it is a kind of perpetual or continuous disturbance, since, although it is vehement and uncontrollable in young men, yet it does not die out in old men. For, weary of one thing, it follows another, and what it cannot accomplish in deeds, it pursues with care and anxiety, both in commands and in words.

units.la: Iam quoniam videmus malum hoc nobis insitum esse: quis non agnosceret accurrendū esse ad Christum medicum? quoniam videmus magnum esse, quis non videat Deum hoc vetando nobis optimè consultum voluisse? Quamobrem cognita nostra iniustitia, Christi iustitiam fide capiamus, eaque sic potiti si malum istuc totum reprimere nequeamus, saltem hoc efficiamus, vt non obtineat in nobis imperium Roman. 6. Christus autem regnet in nobis, Amen.
units.tr: Now, since we see that this evil is implanted in us, who would not acknowledge that we must run to Christ the physician? Since we see that it is great, who does not see that God, by forbidding it, wished to provide most well for us? Wherefore, having recognised our injustice, let us grasp by faith the righteousness of Christ; and having obtained it, if we cannot restrain all that evil, let us at least bring it about that it does not obtain dominion over us (Romans 6). May Christ reign in us, Amen.

units.la: SERMO XVII.
units.tr: SERMON XVII.

units.la: Verba hæc loquutus est Dominus ad cunctam congregationem vestram in monte, de medio ignis, nubis ac caliginis, voce magna, nec quidquam adiecit, scribens ea in duas tabulas lapideas, tradensq; eas mihi.
units.tr: The Lord spoke these words to your whole congregation on the mountain, out of the midst of the fire, the cloud and the darkness, with a loud voice, and added nothing, and he wrote them on two tables of stone and gave them to me.

units.la: IN principio nostræ in quintum caput interpretationis ostensum est hoc capite summam quandam doctrinæ Mofaicæ comprehendi, sicque proponi populo, vt primum eius auctor, tum fortuna simul ac materia, denique effecta demonstrentur. Authorem esse Deum ipsum probauit argumentis à concione populi, à fœdere, à Deo legumlatore sumptis: materiam autem, seu res, de quibus præciperetur, ordine concinno rececensuit. Reliquum est igitur, vt de forma dicatur & de effectis.
units.tr: At the beginning of our interpretation of the fifth chapter it was shown that this chapter contains a certain summary of Mosaic doctrine, and is so set before the people that its author, its fortune and matter, and finally its effects, are made clear. He proved that God himself is the author, from arguments drawn from the assembly of the people, from the covenant, and from God as lawgiver. He then reviewed in orderly fashion the matter, or the things commanded. It remains, therefore, to speak of the form and of the effects.

units.la: Ac de forma quidem dicit ad hunc modum: Hæc verba loquutus est Dominus ad cunctam congregationem vestram in monte &c. Summa ac caput horum verborum est, hanc doctrinam esse plenam, perfectam, omnibus suis numeris atq; partibus absolutam, & quasi quoddam diuinæ & humanæ sapientiæ penuarium. Id ita se habere singula argumenta singulis verbis suppeditat.
units.tr: As to the form, he speaks thus: These words the Lord spoke to your whole congregation on the mountain, and so on. The sum and chief point of these words is that this doctrine is full and perfect, complete in all its parts and members, and is, as it were, a storehouse of divine and human wisdom. The individual words supply separate arguments for this.

units.la: Verba illa. Verba vocans ostendit illis legibus ceu summis rerum notis & generibus & communibus vocabulis quicquid & ad Deum & ad homines spectat contineri. Nam cum Hebræi verbum pro tota causa, pro summa rei capiant, ac Christus, quia redemptor noster est & Dei patris de salute nostra consilium re expressit, verbum patris dicitur: quis non intelligat hoc modo leges illas verba dici? Iam si genera sint quis neget illorum appellatione species omnes contineri? Quare & decem verba, & δέκα λόγοι nominantur, hoc est decem generna. Ac si philosophi decem categorijs res omnes complecti potuere, cur dubites hoc non potuisse Dominum?
units.tr: These words. By calling them words he shows that in those laws, as in the highest headings and kinds of things and common terms, everything that concerns both God and man is contained. For since the Hebrews take word for the whole cause, for the sum of a matter, and since Christ, because he is our redeemer and has expressed in fact the Father's plan for our salvation, is called the Word of the Father, who would not see that those laws are called words in this way? And if they are kinds, who would deny that all species are contained under their name? Therefore they are called both the ten words and the Ten Words [δέκα λόγοι], that is, the ten kinds. And if the philosophers could embrace all things under ten categories, why do you doubt that the Lord could do the same?

units.la: Sed omnium virtutum & vitiorum, omnium actionum humanarum hoc decalogo contineri nomina Christus interpres legis Matth. 5. & 7. significat. Et Moses cum Prophetis & Apostolis ei suffragantur quoties harum legum mentionem faciunt. His ipsum addes decalogum. An non prima lex multitudinem Deorum, & varietatem earum rerum, in quibus plus spei quam in Deo ponunt homines, omnem vetat. Siue enim Deos alienos colas, siue in diuitijs aut honoribus, aut amicitijs felicitatem quæras, siue in voluptate summum bonum colloces, hæc lex repugnat. Iam secunda cum simulchra tum cerimonias ab hominibus infti tutas & omnino omnem religionem falsam remouet. Tertia vero blasphemiarum omne genus vetat & iusiurandum informat. Quarta quicquid de ferijs & de temporibus religioni sacris dici potest, continet. Quod si inde ad alteram tabulam transeas, prima de magistratibus tutoribus, magistris, parentibus, & omnino omnibus senibus: secunda de cæde & latrocinijs: tertia de omni genere libidinis: quarta de recta pariter & iniqua rerum commutatione: quinta de vero falsoq; linguæ vel sermonis vsu atque omnibus virtutibus & vitijs, quæ eodem pertinent: Sexta de concupiscentia seu temperantia. Quæ cum ita sint, omnia decem illis generibus contineri necesse est. Si illis continentur omnia, perfecta fir negari non potest.
units.tr: But Christ, the interpreter of the law, shows in Matthew 5 and 7 that the names of all virtues and vices and of all human actions are contained in this Decalogue. Moses, with the Prophets and Apostles, supports him whenever they mention these laws. Add to these the Decalogue itself. Does not the first law forbid every multiplicity of gods and the variety of those things in which men place more hope than in God? For whether you worship strange gods, or seek happiness in riches, honours or friendships, or place the highest good in pleasure, this law opposes you. The second law removes both images and the ceremonies devised by men, and every false religion altogether. The third forbids every kind of blasphemy and prescribes the oath. The fourth contains whatever can be said about holidays and times sacred to religion. If you pass from there to the second table: the first concerns magistrates, guardians, teachers, parents and, in general, all elders; the second concerns murder and robbery; the third concerns every kind of lust; the fourth concerns the just and unjust exchange of goods; the fifth concerns the true and false use of the tongue and speech, and all the virtues and vices that pertain to the same; the sixth concerns concupiscence or temperance. Since this is so, all things must necessarily be contained under those ten kinds. If all things are contained in them, it cannot be denied that they are perfect.

units.la: Loquutus est Dominus. Iam ab authore seu artifice huius methodi sumit argumentum. Deum dicit hæc summa rerum genera posuisse. Quis enim summam disciplinæ cuiusquam traderet melius & felicius quàm eius ipsius optimus artifex? Der der Kunst voll ist. Iam cum sua sapientia Deus omnia contineat, quis illum neget plenam sapientiæ methodum potuisse constituere.
units.tr: The Lord spoke. Next he takes an argument from the author or craftsman of this method. He says that God laid down these highest kinds of things. For who would hand down the sum of any discipline better and more happily than its most excellent craftsman? Der der Kunst voll ist, the master full of his art. Since God contains all things by his own wisdom, who would deny that he could establish a full method of wisdom?

units.la: Errant igitur & falluntur vana suæ sapientiæ opinione, qui quasi Deum quid fugerit, quasiq; Deus obliuione vel insicitia præpeditus quid omiserit, sacris oraculis nouas traditio nes addunt.
units.tr: They err, therefore, and are deceived by the empty opinion of their own wisdom, who add new traditions to the sacred oracles, as if God had overlooked something, or as if God, hindered by forgetfulness or ignorance, had left something out.

units.la: Quin illi cogitet Dominū posuisse hæc genera, ac velle ea firma ac rata haberi. Nā hoc verba Mosis innuit. Verbo Dabar in Piel, id est ea forma posuit, quæ vim verbi intendit, vt intelligas ferio dixisse, & id etiā atq; etiā vehementer nos monere. Domini vero nomen idipsum quoq; significat. Siue enim Ædo Heb. Græce χυρίον fiue δεσπότης reddas imperiū significat, & authoritatē iusib. cóciliat. Nā vt alibi Philo docet χύριος παρὰ τὸ κύρος hoc est ab auctoritate dicitur, qua ratum fit aliquid, sicut irritū dicit ἄχυρον. Quod si igitur cogites hæc mandasse Dominum, authoritate mandantis ad obedientiam inuitaris. Δεσπότης[?] autem, id est herus, παρὰ τὸν δεσμόν[?], id est, à vinculo dicitur. Iam si illum herum, quì sua potentia suo- què herili imperio sibi deuincta atque obligata habet omnia, leges has tulisse cogites, prose- ćto simul animum subeat quàm te expedire illis nexibus nequeas, necesse est. Ex quibus omnibus perspicuum est Deum ipsum, cuius authoritas apud te debet esse sanctissima, augu- stissima, maxima, cóstituisse hæc genera, & velle ea rata haberi. Valeant igitur cum nouis suis traditionibus homines;
units.tr: Indeed, let him consider that the Lord has laid down these kinds and wishes them to be held firm and valid. For this is what the words of Moses imply. The verb dabar in the Piel, that is, in the form which intensifies the force of the verb, shows that he said it solemnly, and that he warns us again and again, and very earnestly. The name Lord also signifies this same thing. For whether you render it Adon in Hebrew, [χύριον] in Greek, or [δεσπότης] (master), it signifies command and gains authority for its orders. For as Philo teaches elsewhere, kyrios is so called from [κύρος], that is, from authority, by which something is made valid, just as the invalid is called [ἄκυρον]. If, then, you consider that the Lord has commanded these things, you are invited to obedience by the authority of the one who commands. [Δεσπότης], that is, master, is so called from [τὸν δεσμόν], that is, from the bond. If you think that this master, who has all things bound and obligated to himself by his power and by his mastery, has enacted these laws, it must necessarily come into your mind how you could not escape those bonds. From all these things it is plain that God himself, whose authority ought to be most holy, most august and greatest with you, has established these kinds and wishes them to be held valid. Let men, then, with their new traditions, go their way.

units.la: Ad cunctam congregationem vestram. Argumentum ab ipsa concione sumit. Nam si Deus hæc capita vniuersis & singulis in toto hoc cœtu versantibus conuenire censuit: sequitur illis ipsis quid quend; deceat edoceri. Sic enim omnes appellat vt assari singulos videatur. Nö habebis, non facies, non sumes, non occides, singulariter præcipiens.
units.tr: To your whole congregation. He takes the argument from the assembly itself. For if God judged that these heads were to suit all and each of those who stood in this whole company, it follows that each of them is taught what is fitting for whom. For he addresses them all in such a way that he seems to speak to each one singly, commanding in the singular: You shall not have, you shall not make, you shall not take, you shall not kill.

units.la: Ergo hoc decalogo masculi pariter ac fœminæ, senes & iuuenes, magistratus & priuas[?]-ti, pauperes æque ac diuites suæ vitæ documenta habent. Id ipsum Paulus innuit etiam, di- cens, scripturas sacras vtiles esse ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem, ad insti- tutionem quę est in iustitia, vt integer sit Dei homo ad omne opus bonum apparatus. Quam obrem rectè dicimus hanc doctrinam, quoniam omnia omnium officia doceat plenam ac perfectam esse.
units.tr: Therefore, by this Decalogue, men and women alike, old and young, magistrates and private persons, poor and rich equally, have the lessons of their life. Paul also implies this when he says that the holy Scriptures are profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness, so that the man of God may be complete and equipped for every good work. Wherefore we rightly say that this doctrine is full and perfect, since it teaches the duties of all men.

units.la: In monte de medio ignis &c. Argumentum à modo reuelatæ legis sumit, ac docet eam sic reuelatam esse, vt veram esse negari nequiuerit. Nam dum reuelaretur edita esse signa con- stat, quibus ostendi poterat hanc & præpotentem & apertam esse. Præpotens esse videbatur ideo quod signis diuinæ præsentiæ fumo scilicet atque ignibus terrerentur auditores: clara, quòd non quasi tectu quiddá musitans, sed alta voce promulgaret eam Dominus. Vtrumq; est certum veritatis indicium.
units.tr: On the mountain, out of the midst of the fire, and so on. He takes an argument from the manner in which the law was revealed, and teaches that it was so revealed that its truth could not be denied. For it is clear that signs were given while it was being revealed, by which it could be shown that this doctrine was both mighty and clear. It seemed mighty because the hearers were terrified by the signs of the divine presence, namely smoke and fires. It was clear because the Lord proclaimed it not as if murmuring something hidden, but with a loud voice. Both are sure signs of truth.

units.la: Veritate enim nihil est potentius, quippe quæ tunc demum surgit feq; exerit maximè cum videtur oppressa penitus. Eius rei testes sunt historiæ. Qui doctrinam hanc respuit, is ábit in tenebras: qui illam videtur superare sua sapientia, is oberrat in nubibus & videtur cū Aristophaneo illo Socrate ἀσεβατεῖν[?]: qui illam oppugnat ignibus eius absumitur. Rursus veritate nihil est aperrius & simplicius.
units.tr: For nothing is more powerful than the truth, since it rises up and shows itself most of all when it seems utterly crushed. History bears witness to this. He who rejects this doctrine goes into darkness; he who thinks he overcomes it by his own wisdom wanders among the clouds, and, like that Socrates of Aristophanes, seems to be [ἀσεβατεῖν], playing the impious fool; he who attacks it is consumed by its fires. Again, nothing is more open and simple than the truth.

units.la: Iam quoniam quicquid simplex est ac clarum, idem etiam compositum & obscurum esse non potest: sequitur huic clarę & simplici doctrinæ nihil addi posse. Atq; hoc ipsum ea pro- bant etiam quæ videntur contra facere.
units.tr: Now since whatever is simple and clear cannot also be compound and obscure, it follows that nothing can be added to this clear and simple doctrine. And even those things which seem to tell against it prove this very point.

units.la: Nam voces hoc ipso in loco non modò aliæ sed etiam plures, quàm in Exodo ponun- tur: tum & puncta sunt alia, & mutatæ sententiæ. Obseruarunt Iudei in Exodo 161.hic autem 173.voces poni. Et quartum præceptum alia quàm istic ratione firmatur. Quod adeo non de- rogat existimationi legis, vt eam multò magis roboret. Nam Moses hoc loco non præconem vti phius sed interpretem legis agit. Est autem proprium interpretis rem propositam alijs at- que alijs verbis explicare, nempe vt subinde fiat illustrior.
units.tr: For in this very place the words are not only different but also more numerous than in Exodus; there are also other pointings and altered sentences. The Jews observed that in Exodus there are 161 words, but here 173. And the fourth precept is grounded in a different way than there. This does not in the least detract from the authority of the law, but rather strengthens it much more. For Moses in this place acts not as a herald but as an interpreter of the law. It is the proper task of an interpreter to explain the matter proposed in different words and phrases, so that it may become clearer as he goes on.

units.la: Quamobrem ex hoc loco potius colligamus quales cognitores requirat veritas, non vi- delicet literarum aut syllabarum atq; vocum aucupes, sed rerum æstimatores industrios. Et ridendi sunt potius quàm audiendi, qui si vocula saltem vnam mutatam videant, cœlũ ter- ræ miscent. Quemadmodum nostra ætate pro dimitte, remitte: pro verbo, sermonem dici qui- dam ægreferunt: quasi verò nos verbis simus obnoxij, non autem verba nobis potius serui re æquum sit. Summa, sic apertis verbis & alta voce reuelata est hæc doctrina vt nihil illi pos- sit addi.
units.tr: Let us therefore draw from this passage what kind of examiners the truth requires: not hunters after letters, syllables and words, but diligent weighers of things. And those people are to be laughed at rather than listened to, who, if they see but a single little word changed, stir heaven and earth together. Just as in our own age some take offence when "dimitte" is said instead of "remitte", or when "sermonem" is used instead of "verbum": as if we were bound to words, rather than words being rightly bound to us. In short, this doctrine has been revealed in such plain words and with such a loud voice that nothing can be added to it.

units.la: Nec quicquam adiecit. Quod Deus passim vetat, ne quid verbo suo vel addatur vel detra- hatur, id hic suo ipsius exemplo feruandum esse docet. Nam si ille ipse paucissimis illis legi- bus nihil addendum esse censuit, atq; is ipse etiam, qui id omnium optimè potuisset præsta- re, nihil addere voluit: cur nos illis quicquam volumus quasi imperfectis addere? Ergo sacræ literæ sic plenæ & perfectæ sunt, vt quicquid ad salutem nostram pertinet, ijs ipsis compre- hensum sit, nec opus sit vllis constitutionibus alijs. Valeant igitur cum Alcorano suo Tur- cæ, cum suo Thalmud Iudæi, cum suis Decretis & decretalibus, & Clementinis & quocun- que vagantibus canonibus: nobis, qui Christum confitemur, sacræ literæ sufficiunt.
units.tr: Nec quicquam adiecit. What God forbids everywhere, namely that anything be added to or taken away from his word, he here teaches must be observed by his own example. For if he himself judged that nothing should be added to those very few laws, and he who could have done this best of all did not wish to add anything, why should we want to add anything to them as though they were imperfect? Therefore the holy Scriptures are so full and perfect that whatever pertains to our salvation is contained in them, and there is no need for any other constitutions. Let the Turks farewell with their Alcoran, the Jews with their Talmud, and with their Decrees and Decretals, their Clementines, and whatever wandering canons there are: for us, who confess Christ, the holy Scriptures suffice.

units.la: At, inquiunt Ioannis 20. dicitur ad hunc modum: Multa quidem & alia signa fecit Iesus in conspectu discipulorum suorum quæ non sunt scripta in libro hoc. Ex his autumant col- ligi, non omnia quæ quidem ad salutem nostram requiruntur, comprehendi sacris literis. Qui id ita? Quia non respiciunt ad ea quæ consequuntur. Hæc autem (inquit Ioannes) scri-pta sunt, vt credatis quod Iesus est Christus filius Dei, & vt credentes vitam habeatis per nomen eius. Quid verò hoc est aliud, quàm dicere: multa alia fecit & dixit, sed hæc nosse ad beatam vitam sufficiunt. Neque verò aliter hoc expono, quàm Cyrillus libro duodecimo in Ioannem scribens id exponit. Dicit enim: Magna, ait Ioannes, multitudo signorum Domini & immensus numerus est, sed hæc quæ retulimus sufficiunt ad plenissimam fidem attente le [?] gentibus faciendam. Eodem modo Chrysostomus in Acto. cap. 1. scribens ait ipsum non dixisse omnia de omnibus, perinde ac si dixisset, In genere de omnibus ad salutem necessarijs scripsi.
units.tr: But, they say, John 20 speaks in this way: "Many other signs also did Jesus in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book." From this they claim it is gathered that not everything which is indeed required for our salvation is comprehended in the holy Scriptures. How so? Because they do not look at what follows. "But these things (says John) are written, that you may believe that Jesus is Christ the Son of God, and that believing you may have life through his name." What else is this than to say: he did and said many other things, but to know these is enough for a blessed life? Nor do I explain it otherwise than Cyril does in his twelfth book on John. For he says: "Great, says John, is the multitude of the Lord's signs and the number is immense, but those which we have related are sufficient to produce full faith in those attending." In the same way Chrysostom, writing on Acts chapter 1, says that he did not say everything about everything, just as if he had said: "In general I have written about all things necessary to salvation."

units.la: Quod porro obijciunt, Apostolos non omnia scripsisse, quid aliud est, quàm quod hæretici veteres apud Tertullianum dicebant Apostolos non omnia sciuisse. Ego verò censeo Diuos Apostolos, quoniam docendis hominibus diuinitus missi fuerant, & quæ nobis scitu necessaria sunt, Spiritu sancto doctore cognouisse, & pro sua fide & diligentia proque summa erga nos benevolentia sua tradidisse omnia. Ac si quid tradiderint quod literarum monumentis ad posteritatem transmittere non voluerint aut potuerint: quis censeat eos tam leues atque inconstantes fuisse homines, vt diuersum traderent ab eo quod scripsissent? Quamobrem & si summas rerum gestarum & concionum descripserint, tamen eorum quæ nos scire nostra refert maximè nihil prætermissum ab his esse credendum est. Fortasse enim plures quàm Iairi filiam & viduæ filium & Lazarum suscitauit à mortuis Christus: multos leprosos mundauit, multis cæcis visum donauit: sed horum exemplis sat probatum est omnibus hominibus idem per illum præstari posse.
units.tr: As for what they further object, that the Apostles did not write everything, what else is this than what the ancient heretics said in Tertullian, that the Apostles did not know everything? I, however, judge that the divine Apostles, since they had been sent by divine command to teach men, and since the Holy Spirit was their teacher in what is necessary for us to know, both knew all things and handed them down, by their faith and diligence and by their great goodwill towards us. And if they handed down anything which they did not wish or were not able to transmit to posterity by written monuments, who would think them so light and inconstant that they taught something different from what they had written? Therefore, even if they described the main outlines of the deeds and sermons, we must nevertheless believe that nothing of those things which especially concern our knowledge was omitted by them. For perhaps Christ raised from the dead more people than the daughter of Jairus, the widow's son and Lazarus: he cleansed many lepers and gave sight to many blind: but by the examples of these it has been sufficiently proved that the same things can be performed by him for all men.

units.la: Quamobrem sacras literas esse perfectas arbitrator, Deíque exemplo coerce confidentiam, ne eis quicquam vel ausis addere, vel detrahere. Nam si Deus addere nihil voluit, quid tu poteris?
units.tr: Therefore I judge that the holy Scriptures are perfect, and by God's example restrain confidence, so that you dare neither to add anything to them nor to take anything away. For if God was unwilling to add anything, what could you be able to add?

units.la: Scribens ea in duas tabulas, &c. Quibus verbis docet Dominum has leges quasi decoro ordine distributas, iamque perfectas atque elaboratas inscripsisse, & Mosi dedisse.
units.tr: Scribens ea in duas tabulas, &c. By these words he teaches that the Lord inscribed these laws, as it were arranged in a fitting order and already complete and finished, and gave them to Moses.

units.la: Vnde perspicuum est in ijs nihil desiderari. Idque docent hæc tria. 1. Ordo quo distributæ sunt. Duabus enim tabulis eas sic complexus est, vt altera quicquid Deo, altera verò quicquid proximo debent homines descripserit. Quem ordinem Christus etiam de summa legis rogatus seruauit. Ergo nouus ordo cogitandus esset si quid velis addere, quod est impium.
units.tr: Hence it is clear that nothing is lacking in them. And these three things teach this. 1. The order in which they are arranged. For he gathered them into two tables in such a way that on one he described whatever men owe to God, and on the other whatever they owe to their neighbour. Christ also kept this same order when asked about the sum of the law. Therefore, if you wished to add something, a new order would have to be devised, which is impious.

units.la: 2 Ipsa inscriptio. Manca & imperfecta membranis siue schedis annotamus, post in exemplum ipsum inscripturi: Deus has leges statim in ipsas tabulas, in quibus extare voluit, retulit: quod argumento potest esse nihil in his desiderari.
units.tr: 2. The inscription itself. We note that things written in a rough and imperfect state on membranes or tablets are afterwards inscribed as a model; God set down these laws at once on the very tables on which he wished them to stand, which can be an argument that nothing in them is lacking.

units.la: 3 Traditio. Quod Mosi illas tradidit. Nam si magistratus nullas nisi perfectas promulgat leges, quid tu putes Deum semifactas promulgasse? Quæ cum ita sint, vti diximus, omnia, sequitur doctrinam hanc perfectam, nobisque vnicè seruandam, atque custodiendam esse in Christo. Amen.
units.tr: 3. The delivery. That he handed them to Moses. For if the magistrate promulgates no laws except perfect ones, what do you suppose God promulgated half-made? Since these things are so, as we have said, it follows that this doctrine is perfect, and is to be kept and guarded by us alone in Christ. Amen.

units.la: SERMO XVIII.
units.tr: Sermon XVIII.

units.la: 23 Cumq; audisseris vocem de medio tenebrarum, monte ipso igne ardente, accessistis ad me unà cum principibus & seniorum vestrorum.
units.tr: When you had heard the voice out of the midst of the darkness, while the mountain burned with fire, you came near to me, together with the princes and elders of your tribes.

units.la: 24 Et dixistis: Ecce ostendit nobis Dominus gloriam suam & magnificentiā [?] suam, & vocem eius audiuimus de medio ignis: hoc ipso die vidimus quod Deus cum homine loquitur, illo viuo manente.
units.tr: And you said: Behold, the LORD our God has shown us his glory and his greatness, and we have heard his voice out of the midst of the fire. We have seen this day that God speaks with man, and man still lives.

units.la: 25 Cur igitur moriemur, vt devoret nos ignis ille magnus? Si iterum audieri-mus vocem Domini Dei nostri, moriemur.
units.tr: Why then should we die? For this great fire will consume us. If we hear the voice of the LORD our God any more, we shall die.

units.la: 26 Quæ enim unquam caro fuit, quæ audierit vocem Dei viuentis, loquentis de medio ignis vt nos, & viua [?] manserit?
units.tr: For who of all flesh has ever heard the voice of the living God speaking out of the midst of the fire, as we have, and remained alive?

units.la: 27 Accede tu, & audi omnia quæ dicturus est Dominus Deus noster, & tu loqueris ad nos omnia quæ loquuturus est Dominus Deus noster ad te, & nos audiemus & faciemus.
units.tr: Go near yourself, and hear all that the LORD our God shall say. Then speak to us all that the LORD our God shall speak to you, and we will hear it and do it.

units.la: 28 Audiuit autem Dominus vocem verborum vestrorum quum loqueremini ad me. Et dixit Dominus ad me: Audiui vocem verborum populi huius, quae sunt ad te loquuti.: esse[?] senserunt in omnibus quae sunt loquuti.
units.tr: And the LORD heard the voice of your words when you spoke to me. And the LORD said to me: I have heard the voice of the words of this people, which they have spoken to you. They have spoken well in all that they have said.

units.la: 29 Vtinam sit tale cor in eis, vt timeant me, & seruent omnia praecepta mea a cunctis diebus, vt bene sit illis, & filijs eorum perpetuo.
units.tr: O that there were such a heart in them, that they would fear me and keep all my commandments always, so that it might go well with them and with their children for ever!

units.la: 30 Vade, dic eis: Reuertimini in tentoria vestra.
units.tr: Go and say to them: Return to your tents.

units.la: 31 Tu vero hic sta mecum, & loquar ad te omnia praecepta, ritus, iudicia, quae docebis illos, vt sciant in terra, quam ego do eis possidendam.
units.tr: But as for you, stand here with me, and I will speak to you all the commandments, the statutes and the judgments, which you shall teach them, so that they may know them in the land which I give them to possess.

units.la: 32 Obseruabitis igitur, vt opere exequamini sicut praecepit vobis Dominus Deus vester, ne recedatis neque ad dexteram neque ad sinistram.
units.tr: You shall therefore take care to do as the LORD your God has commanded you. You shall not turn aside to the right hand or to the left.

units.la: 33 Per vniuersum iter quod praecepit Dominus Deus vester incedetis, vt viuatis, & bene sit vobis, prorogetisque dies in terra, quam possidebitis.
units.tr: You shall walk in all the way which the LORD your God has commanded you, that you may live, and that it may go well with you, and that you may prolong your days in the land which you shall possess.

units.la: Quanquam Diuus Moses in prima libri huius parte suum populum progymnasmatis quibusdam ad verbi Dei studium praeparauit: tamen eius summam, quam hac secunda parte comprehendit, eo ponit ordine, quo plebem in officio contineat. Nam vbi causam efficientem & materiam & formam huius doctrinae demonstrauit, ac de effectis quicquid dicendum esset, vltimo loco dicere voluit: quo maiore pietate & diligentia audiretur, sic illius vires & effecta praedicat, vt simul etiam eius vsum indicet. Quo profecto nihil pene est cognitu magis necessarium. Quis enim vti remedio queat cuius vim facultatem q; nesciat[?] Vtilis igitur est, & cumprimis necessaria quae verbis hisce comprehenditur praeceptio. Et duabus constat partibus: quarum priore quae diuini verbi vis sit & efficacia, posteriore vero quo modo eo sit vtendum dicitur.
units.tr: Although divine Moses, in the first part of this book, prepared his people for the study of God's word with certain preliminary exercises, nevertheless he sets out the substance of it, which he comprehends in this second part, in the order by which he keeps the people in their duty. For when he had shown the efficient cause, the matter and the form of this doctrine, and had wished to speak last of its effects, he so proclaims its powers and effects, so that it may be heard with greater reverence and diligence, that at the same time he also points out its use. Indeed there is almost nothing more necessary to know than this. For who can use a remedy whose power and efficacy he does not know? The precept contained in these words is therefore useful and especially necessary. It consists of two parts: in the first is said what the power and efficacy of the divine word is, and in the second how it is to be used.

units.la: Verbi diuini vis quae sit, Moses partim suiipsius partim populi sui verbis exponit. Suis, Cumq; audiissetis[?],inquit,vocem de medio tenebrarum,monte ipso igne ardente,accessistis ad me unà cum principibus tribuum vestrarum & seniorum vestrorum. Quibus verbis Moses vt diuini verbi vim demonstret, primum signa, quae circa legis promulgationem facta sunt, tum autem metum, quo populus lege promulgata perculsus est repetit, atque in memoriam reuocat. Nam illis indicijs quid verbum Dei in animis hominum efficiat quodam modo repraesentari potest.
units.tr: Moses explains what the power of the divine word is, partly in his own words and partly in the words of his people. In his own words: "When you had heard the voice out of the midst of the darkness, the mountain burning with fire, you came near to me, together with the princes of your tribes and your elders." By these words Moses, in order to show the power of the divine word, first recalls the signs that were made at the promulgation of the law, and then repeats and brings to mind the fear by which the people were struck when the law was promulgated. For by those indications one can in some measure depict what the word of God effects in men's minds.

units.la: 1 E medio tenebrarum & densa caligine vox diuina audita est. Quod est indicio densas tenebras inter nos & Deu esse, quibus nobis ad illam sempiternam lucem aditus omnis praecludatur, verbumq; Dei tenebris illis dispellendis ceu solem coelitus oriri. Quae cum ita sint, semper cogitandum est, tenebras penes nos esse, penes Deum lucem.
units.tr: A divine voice was heard out of the midst of darkness and thick mist. This is an indication that there is a dense darkness between us and God, by which every access to that everlasting light is shut off from us, and that the word of God, like the sun rising from heaven, arises to disperse those shadows. Since this is so, we must always bear in mind that the darkness is on our side and the light on God's.

units.la: Quis illas inter nos & Deum posuit? Satan qui parentes nostros labefecit, eoq; lapsu nostros animos luce data priuatos in Cimmerias tenebras praecipitauit.
units.tr: Who placed those shadows between us and God? Satan, who overthrew our parents, and by that fall, deprived of the light given to them, plunged our minds into Cimmerian darkness.

units.la: Sunt quidem scintillae quaedam in animis nostris reliquae, quae nisi istac luce adhibita ac cendi non possunt. Inde Matthaeus cap.4. vbi commemorasset quo pacto Christus per Gali-læam obambulans tenebricosis animis verbi sui lucem admouerit, praeclarum illud quod Esa.9. descriptum extat vaticinium tunc completum dicit esse, nempe quod sedentibus in te nebris & vmbra mortis lux oritura sit. Et certe id accidit. Nam docente Christo omnes omnium Iudaeorum & philosophorum errores animaduersi inq; lucem protracti sunt. Et nostra aetate Papistarum fraudes in tam clara luce Euangelij vidimus. Quamobrem noli committere, vt lucem hanc cuiquam permittas extinguendam, ni velis magis quam antea caecutire, veluti qui e loco lucidissimo aut lato niuibus obtecto campo, in aedes quanutmuis luci das ingressus, nihil videt tamen. Quin cogitemus quas ad res conducat haec lux, videlicet vt luceat nostris pedibus. Psal.118. vt docet Dauid.
units.tr: There indeed remain in our minds certain sparks, which cannot be kindled unless this light is brought to them. Hence Matthew, in chapter 4, after relating how Christ, walking about through Galilee, brought the light of his word to minds in darkness, says that the famous prophecy described in Isaiah 9 was then fulfilled, namely that light would rise for those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death. And certainly this happened. For when Christ taught, the errors of all the Jews and philosophers were detected and brought into the light. And in our own age we have seen the frauds of the Papists in the very clear light of the Gospel. Therefore do not allow this light to be put out by anyone, unless you wish to become blinder than before, like one who, coming from a very bright place or from an open field covered with snow into a house however well lit, sees nothing at all. Rather let us consider to what ends this light is useful, namely that it may shine on our feet, as David teaches, Psal. 118.

units.la: Dein ait, monte ipso igne ardente. Quo ostendit alterum miraculum quod sit indicio, verbum Dei ignis naturam atq; vim obtinere, nempe vt in suam, puta, candentem, vrentem & consumentem naturam conuertat quae corripit omnia. Quemadmodum igitur ignis quae natura suapte sunt frigida & humida, sicca ac calida facit, vt ligna, metalla, saxa, ipsas etiam aquas: sic qui suapte natura terreni, frigidi, impuri, inimici Dei & hominum, mendaces, iniusti, stolidi sunt, eos verbum Dei coelestes, feruidos, puros, amantes Dei pariter & hominum, veraces, iustos, sapientes atq; prouidos efficit. Ac quemadmodum ignis rebus humidis atq; putridis nonnihil impeditur,interdumq; etiam opprimitur,verum vbi inualuerit, extingui non po-teft:sic putidis artibus & mendacijs damnum veritati verbi datur,& cursus eius nonnunquá impeditur,& interdum etiam opprimitur,sed rursus exurgit,& ita increscit,vt extingui non possit.Ac certè compertum est iam inde ab orbe condito vsq; ad nostra tempora,quæ aquæ sunt extinguendo huic igni apportatæ,sed adhuc ardet,& verbum illud nondū oppressum est,ac cœlum prius ruet,quàm ipsum opprimatur.
units.tr: Next he says: "the mountain burning with fire." By this he shows another miracle, which is a sign that the word of God has the nature and power of fire, namely to convert whatever it seizes into its own nature, that is, to make it glowing, burning and consuming. Just as fire makes things that are by nature cold and moist, such as wood, metals, stones and even water itself, dry and hot, so the word of God makes those who are by nature earthly, cold, impure, enemies of God and men, liars, unjust and foolish, heavenly, fervent, pure, lovers of God and of men alike, truthful, just, wise and provident. And just as fire is somewhat hindered by moist and rotten things, and sometimes even overpowered, but once it has taken hold cannot be extinguished, so by rotten arts and lies harm is done to the truth of the word, and its course is sometimes impeded and sometimes even overpowered; but it rises again and grows so that it cannot be extinguished. And indeed it has been established that from the foundation of the world until our own times many waters have been brought to quench this fire, but it still burns, and that word has not yet been overcome, and heaven will fall before it is overcome.

units.la: His addit iam Moses his visis diuinæ potentiæ circa verbum illud versantis indicijs populum totum concussum esse,& principes viros legatos ad se misisse,qui de alio docendi modo secum consultarent. Quod erat euidens diuinæ potentiæ indicium, & quod verbi diuini motus sit citissimus,quodq; non vti noster pedetentim,sed cito agat.Vnde & in Actis vento comparatur,qui subitò simul omnia rapit. Nos grana sigillatim singula colligimus, at ea si-mul omnia aut pleraq; ventus sursum rapit. Veluti istoc loco Deus concione simul omnem concussit.Ex quo perspicuum est indomitam vim diuini verbi esse,eamq; nec consilijs eludi nec viribus vllis frangi posse.Dixit hoc Esaias cap.40.ad hunc modum.Omnis caro fœnum & omnis gloria eius quasi flos campi.Exaruit fœnum & emarcuit flos. Verbum autem Dei nostri consurget & firmum stabit in æternum.Quid quod Matthæus dicit Christum non ita vti Pharisæi solebant frigidè docuisse verum ὡς ἐξουσίαν ἔχοντα.Et Paulus eandè verbi vim passim prædicat.Rom.1.Non(inquit)me pudet euangelij siquidem est potentia Dei ad salu tem omni credenti.Et 1.Cor.2.dicit verbum Dei non habere volubilitatem verborum huma næ sapientiæ,sed ostensionem spiritus & potentiæ, nempe vt fides nostra non sit in sapientia hominum,sed in potentia Dei.Et 1.Cor.4. Non enim in sermone est regnum Dei, sed in virtute.Ex quibus omnibus colligimus quod suis verbis Moses docet verbi diuini vim im-mensam esse.
units.tr: Moses adds that, after these signs of divine power working around that word had been seen, the whole people was shaken, and that they sent princes as envoys to him to consult with him about another way of teaching. This was clear evidence of divine power, and of the fact that the motion of the divine word is most swift, and that it does not act slowly, as our own word does step by step, but quickly. Hence also in Acts it is compared to a wind, which suddenly seizes and carries away everything at once. We gather grains one by one, but the wind carries them all up together. So at this place God shook the whole assembly at once. From this it is plain that the divine word has an untameable force, and that it can be neither eluded by plans nor broken by any strength. Isaiah said this in chapter 40 in this way: "All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field. The grass withers and the flower fades, but the word of our God shall rise and stand firm for ever." What of the fact that Matthew says Christ did not teach coldly, as the Pharisees used to, but as one having authority [ὡς ἐξουσίαν ἔχοντα]? And Paul everywhere proclaims the same power of the word. Rom. 1: "I am not ashamed," he says, "of the gospel; for it is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes." And 1 Cor. 2 says that the word of God does not have the flowing persuasiveness of human wisdom, but the demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that our faith may rest not in the wisdom of men but in the power of God. And 1 Cor. 4: "For the kingdom of God is not in word but in power." From all these things we gather that, as Moses teaches in these words, the power of the divine word is immense.

units.la: Sed vt hoc plenius ac melius doceat atq; etiam firmet magis, ipsius populi super hac re verba atq; editam confessionem recitat,vt suis ipsorum verbis doceantur.Et dixistis(inquit) ecce ostendit nobis Dominus gloriam suam & magnificentiam suam,& vocem eius, &c. Quibus verbis Moses,vt iam diximus,populo suam ipsorum confessionem reuocat in memoriam, quippe quæ & ipsa vim diuini verbi doceat.Atq; ea quidem duas facultates naturæ verbi tri buunt.Vnam quod monstret gloriam & magnitudinem Domini.Est autem certissimum verbo Dei sacrarium cœleste,quo recondita sunt Dei mysteria,nobis pandi,ac nos quantum fas est carnem indutos cernere,tantum nobis ob oculos poni: tum vt ex verbis quisq; suis quis qualisq; sit cognoscitur,sic ex suo verbo Deum etiam cognosci. Opera prædicant illius magnitudinem & potentiam,gubernatio prouidentiam,aliæ res virtutes eius alias, sed in ijs æ-stimandis viæ dux est verbum.Testes sunt Psalmi,qui nos docent hæc considerare,vt in Psal mo 104.& non paucis alijs vel creatæ res vel iudicia ac facta Domini considerantur.Summa verbum Dei nos docet eius opera suo modo metiri,& recte perpendere:sine verbo Dei cæ-cutiunt philosophi.Ergo verbum duplici de causa laudibus maximis dignum est:vna, quod ipsum nobis Deum qualis sit prædicat:altera,quod operum , ex quibus etiam cognosci po-teft,censusam optimam suppeditat.Quò fit,vt alia re nulla Deus cognoscatur melius,quàm verbo suo magistro.
units.tr: But so that he may teach this more fully and well, and confirm it more firmly, he recites the people's own words and their declared confession on this matter, so that they may be taught in their own words: "And you said, Behold, the LORD our God has shown us his glory and his greatness, and his voice, etc." By these words Moses, as we have already said, recalls to the people's memory their own confession, which itself also teaches the power of the divine word. And this confession ascribes two faculties to the nature of the word. The first is that it shows the glory and greatness of the Lord. Now the Word of God is most certainly a heavenly sanctuary, in which the mysteries of God are hidden, which are opened to us, and which are set before our eyes, so far as it is lawful for us to see them while clothed in flesh. Just as a person is known by his own words, so God is also known by his Word. Works proclaim his greatness and power, governance proclaims his providence, and other things proclaim other of his virtues, but the Word is the guide in estimating these. The Psalms bear witness, which teach us to consider these things, as in Psalm 104 and in not a few others, where created things or the judgments and deeds of the Lord are considered. In sum, the Word of God teaches us to measure his works in their own way and to weigh them rightly; without the Word of God the philosophers grope in blindness. Therefore the Word is worthy of the greatest praise for two reasons: first, because it proclaims to us what God is like; second, because it supplies the best measure of his works, by which he can also be known. Hence it comes about that God is known better by no other thing than by his Word as teacher.

units.la: Alteram vim verbi diuini maiorem esse,quàm vt ei ferendo sint homines. Dicunt illi Is-raelitæ inauditum hoc esse,quod quisq; hominum postquam Deum audisset potuerit viue-re,se verè eo audito viuos permansisse,sed periculum tamen esse,ne si ipsum iterum audiant, moriendum sit.Iu est,indicio homines,quia terreni sunt & caro,ijq; vel pij vel impij , verbo Dei ferendo non esse.
units.tr: The second power of the divine word is too great for men to bear. Those Israelites say that it is unheard of that any man, after he has heard God, could live; they say that they had truly remained alive after hearing him, but that there is nevertheless a danger that, if they hear him again, they must die. Thus they judge that men, because they are earthly and flesh, whether pious or impious, are not able to bear the Word of God.

units.la: Impij id ridẽt,fastidiunt,despiciunt:at eius vi tandé prostrati iacebunt.Et certù est Christũ nec Herodi,nec Pharisæis,nec Luciano,alijsq; tyrannis & nebulonibus amplius esse ludi brio,sed illum triumphare:hos algere & angi. Sunt ætate nostra complures impij veritatis hostes qui vel ridentvel persequuntur euangelium,sed ijdem aliquando trement,& dolebút pro eo quod pios ipsi nunc terrent & mœrore afficiunt.Est enim indomita vis euangelij:im pij in secundis rebus hoc non ferunt victi impotentia animorum: in aduersis desperabundi concidunt.
units.tr: The impious laugh at it, scorn it and despise it, but at last, cast down by its power, they will lie prostrate. And it is certain that Christ is no longer a plaything for Herod, the Pharisees, Lucian, or other tyrants and scoundrels, but that he triumphs while they grow cold and are distressed. In our own age there are many impious enemies of the truth who either mock or persecute the gospel, but these same men will at some time tremble and grieve over that which they now terrify and afflict the pious. For the power of the gospel is untamable: the impious do not bear it in prosperity, being conquered by the impotence of their minds; in adversity they fall down in despair.

units.la: Pij verò quoniam & ipsi sunt homines,tremunt ac ferre vim illam nequeunt,agnita vi-delicet nuditate sua,sed ideo non despondent animos, sed supplices tendunt ad sydera pal-mas:ah Christe tu nos legis onere pressos subleua,tu quod nos præstare non possumus effi-ce.His Christus à lege quasi à pœdagogo ostenditur.Ex quo perspicuum est humanas traditiones fugiendas,quippe nostras nobis vires,quæ nullæ sunt monstrant: verbum divinum auté,quod nos à nostris viribus ad Christum mittit,ac vim illustrandi,accendendi,fuperan-di seu suscitandi habet,eligendum esse.
units.tr: But the pious, since they too are men, tremble and cannot bear that power, recognising of course their own nakedness; yet they do not for that reason lose heart, but stretch out their hands in supplication to the stars: "Ah Christ, you raise us up, who are pressed down by the burden of the law; you make effective what we cannot accomplish." Here Christ is shown to us as one who leads us to himself from the law as from a schoolmaster. From this it is clear that human traditions are to be shunned, since they show us our own powers, which are nothing; but the divine word, which sends us from our own powers to Christ, and which has the power to enlighten, to kindle, to overcome, or to raise up, is to be chosen.

units.la: Quomodo hoc vtamur Moses partim populi, partim Dei ipsius verbis iudicat. Populi verbis, Accede tu & audi(inquiunt) quæ dicturus est Dominus, & tu loquere ad nos quæ &c. Op-timum docendi modum,quo homo hominem doceat,indicant,eumq; recipi cupiunt,atque postulant. Id qui possit fieri dicunt.1. Vnus aliquis divinitus electus accedat & audiat Domi-num. Id documento fuerit doctrinam non ex hominum opinionibus, sed Dei sententia su-mendam esse. Christus eius rei typum nobis prætulit Ioan. 6. discipulis suis cibos quos tur-bis ipsi distribuerent dederat. Matth.10. Non vos estis illi loquentes &c. Audire ergo Deum, id est exercere fe legendo & precando & meditando decet episcopum.
units.tr: Moses judges how this should be used, partly from the words of the people and partly from the words of God himself. In the words of the people: Go near, you (they say), and hear what the Lord will say, and you speak to us, etc. They point out the best method of teaching, by which a man teaches a man, and they desire and ask that it be accepted. They also say how this can come about. 1. Let some one man, divinely chosen, approach and hear the Lord. This is an example that doctrine is to be taken not from human opinions but from the judgment of God. Christ set before us a type of this in John 6, when he gave his disciples food which they themselves were to distribute to the crowds. Matt. 10: "It is not you who speak," etc. So it is fitting for the bishop to hear God, that is, to exercise himself in reading, praying and meditating.

units.la: 2 Ipse cognita proponat populo, quippe quod fit familiariter cognitus, qui fit eiusdem naturæ & substantiæ. Spiritus timentur,præstat habere doctores homines.
units.tr: 2 He himself should set forth to the people what is known, since he is familiarly known and of the same nature and substance. Spirits are to be feared; it is better to have men as teachers.

units.la: 3 Audiemus & faciemus. Ergo meminerimus non frustra prædicari verbum Domini,sed audiendum & enitendum, vt id faciamus.
units.tr: 3 We shall hear and do. So let us remember that the Word of the Lord is not preached in vain, but must be heard and striven for, so that we may do it.

units.la: Exemplo populi illius discimus,verbi Dei interpretes homines audire malle,quàm habere reuelationes,præsertim cum diabolus fe transformet in angelum lucis,eaq; specie quis decipi queat. Christus hominibus Mosem & Prophetas, quàm mortuorum spiritus audien-dos potius censuit. Ergo homines petierunt verbi ministerium sibi institui. Cur igitur re-spuis quod te postulante est institutum? Iudæi,inquis,petierunt,non ego. Iudæi,inquis gens pertinax, & præfracta. Vnde eorum inquam , pertinacia tibi cognita est? Ex sacris literis dicis. Noui inquam,sed fi nostra nobis vitia tam sedulò notarentur,quales nos cerneres? certè peiores. Ergo confiteberis te non minus malum atq; imbecillem esse,quàm fuerunt illi,ti-biq; æquè atq; illis hoc docendi genus competere.
units.tr: From the example of that people we learn that they preferred to hear men as interpreters of the Word of God rather than to have revelations, especially since the devil transforms himself into an angel of light, and by that appearance anyone can be deceived. Christ judged that men should rather be heard, Moses and the Prophets, than the spirits of the dead. So the people asked that a ministry of the Word be instituted for them. Why, then, do you reject what was established at your own request? "The Jews," you say, "asked for it, not I." "The Jews," you say, "are a stubborn and obstinate people." Whence, I ask, do you know their stubbornness? You say it is from the sacred writings. I know it, I answer; but if our own faults were noted with such care, what sort of people would you see? Certainly worse. So you will confess that you are no less evil and feeble than they were, and that this manner of teaching suits you just as well as it suited them.

units.la: Verbis Dei, Audiuit(inquit) Dominus vocem verborum vestrorum &c.1. Deus audit. Me-mineris Deum nihil latere,eiq; ceu exploratori prudentissimo omnium machinarum falu-tem nostram commendandam. Audiuit Abelis sanguinem,Israelis in Ægypto fusas lachry-mas atq; etiam gemitus,& orbarum matrum in Bethlehem planctus.
units.tr: By the words of God: The Lord heard the voice of your words, etc. 1. God hears. Remember that nothing is hidden from God, and that our salvation is to be committed to him as to the most prudent of spies, who knows all the schemes. He heard the blood of Abel, the tears and even the groans shed by the Israelites in Egypt, and the lamentation of the bereaved mothers in Bethlehem.

units.la: 11 Consilium hoc approbat.En patrem amicissimum,qui sese nobis accomodat, ac quos-cunq; velis doctores mittit.Sed requirit vicissim duo.1. Vt ipsum timeat cor nostrum.2. Vt studeamus eius mandatis.Et addit causam,Vt bene fit nobis.Sane si nos ipsi charos habeamus, hæc præstemus necesse est.
units.tr: 11 He approves this counsel. Behold a most loving Father, who accommodates himself to us and sends whatever teachers you wish. But he requires two things in return. 1. That our heart fear him. 2. That we strive after his commandments. And he adds the reason: so that it may go well with us. Indeed, if we hold ourselves dear, we must necessarily practise these things.

units.la: 3 Instituit verbi ministerium.Ergo hoc retinendum,non petenda signa.
units.tr: 3 He has instituted the ministry of the Word. Therefore this is to be retained; signs are not to be sought.

units.la: Id asserit Moses addita clausula,qua cum præsentem locum claudit,tum ad insequentem sibi viam munit.1.Quid fit feruandum,præceptum Dei videlicet.2.Quomodo, Neq; ad dex-teram,neq; ad sinistram.Ad dextram itur quando opinionum noftrarū speciem bonam secuti à recto tramite deflectimus,vt qui bona,veluti solent dicere,intentione faciunt quæ Deus nec iussit nec docuit.Ad sinistram itur quando cultus prophanos,& scelera patramus ac sequimur. Hic docet media via nobis eundum esse , hoc est rectè , & ad præscriptum verbi Dei cum in religione,tum in vita ac moribus omnia debere fieri.Id Deus faxit in Christo Iesu Domino nostro, cui fit honos in secula,Amen.
units.tr: Moses asserts this by the added clause, with which he both closes the present passage and prepares a way for what follows. 1. What is to be kept, namely the command of God. 2. How: Neither to the right hand nor to the left. One goes to the right when, following the good appearance of our own opinions, we turn aside from the straight path, as those who act with what they are accustomed to call good intention, doing things which God neither commanded nor taught. One goes to the left when we commit and follow profane worship and crimes. Here he teaches that we must walk the middle way, that is, rightly, and that everything, both in religion and in life and conduct, must be done according to the prescription of the Word of God. May God grant this in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be honour for ever, Amen.

units.la: JOANNIS VVOLPHII TIGURINI IN DEUTERONOMIUM SERMONUM LIBER TERTIUS. CAPUT VI. SERMO I.
units.tr: The Third Book of Johannes Wolphius of Zurich's Sermons on Deuteronomy. Chapter 6, Sermon 1.

units.la: HÆc sunt autem præcepta, ritus, iudicia, quæ præcepit Dominus Deus vester, ut docerem vos, ut faciatis ea in terra, ad quam vos transitis ut possideatis.
units.tr: These are the precepts, rites and judgments which the Lord your God commanded, that I should teach you, that you should do them in the land into which you are crossing to possess it.

units.la: 2 Ut scilicet timeas Dominum Deum tuum, & custodias omnes ritus eius atq; præcepta eius quæ ego tibi præcipio, tu & filius tuus atq; nepos tuus cunctis diebus vitæ tuæ, ut prorogentur dies tui.
units.tr: 2 That you may fear the Lord your God, and keep all his rites and precepts which I command you, you, your son and your grandson, all the days of your life, that your days may be prolonged.

units.la: 3 Audies igitur Israel, & seruabis ut facias, ut bene tibi sit, & ut crescatis valde, sicut pollicitus est Dominus Deus patrum tuorum tibi &[?] terram fluentem lacte & melle.
units.tr: 3 Hear therefore, Israel, and take care to do them, that it may be well with you, and that you may increase greatly, as the Lord God of your fathers promised you, a land flowing with milk and honey.

units.la: POSTQVAM Divus Moses populo suo ad studium legis aditum fecisset, propositis quibusdam progymnasmatis, ac deinceps eius ipsius summam pro posuisset: iam tertiam huius libri partem aggreditur, qua diuinarum legum ex positionem pleniorem affert, atq; etiā docet, quo pacto hæ Dei leges, quæ dua-bus illis tabulis sunt descriptæ & propositæ, debeant intelligi, inq; nostros ut ius & salutem conuerti.
units.tr: After Moses had opened the way to the study of the Law for his people, setting out certain preliminary exercises and then presenting their sum, he now begins the third part of this book. In it he gives a fuller exposition of the divine laws, and also teaches how these laws of God, which were written and set out on the two tablets, ought to be understood and turned to our right use and salvation.

units.la: Est autem hæc ad ipsas tabulas accommodata explicatio, nempe ut à 6.cap.usq; ad 31. ambæ quidem, sed à 6. ad 17. prima, & à 17. ad 31. secunda tabula exponatur.
units.tr: This explanation is fitted to the tablets themselves: from chapter 6 to chapter 31 both tablets are expounded, but from 6 to 17 the first tablet, and from 17 to 31 the second.

units.la: In qua habes leges speciales, & casus, & similitudines & exempla legum istarum breuium: & discis cum scripturam sacram universam tum omnes omnium philosophorum præceptiones ad istas decem leges tanquam summas rerum notas referre atq; accommodare.
units.tr: In it you have special laws, cases, comparisons and examples of those brief laws. And you learn that both the whole of Holy Scripture and all the precepts of all the philosophers are to be traced back to and fitted to these ten laws, as to their known summaries.

units.la: Ac quoniam omnis quæ de re aliqua suscipitur disputatio à definitione proficis-ci debet, nempe ut quid sit cogniturus auditor intelligat: recte sanè Moses etiam hanc suam divinarum legum expositionem à definitione est auspicatus, quam non nudam quasi dia-lecticus quispiam ponit ob oculos, verum ceu orator & interpres pluribus verbis pressam.
units.tr: Since every disputation about any subject ought to begin from a definition, so that the hearer may understand what he is about to learn, Moses rightly began this exposition of the divine laws with a definition. He does not set it before us bare, as some dialectician might, but, like an orator and interpreter, compresses it into more words.

units.la: Ac si illud ipsum caput huius expositionis initium recte expendamus, talis ex ea doctrinæ sacræ definitio colligetur. Lex est diuinum eloquium Dei ipsius per Mosem præconem generi mortalium propositum, quo pietas & diuinæ voluntatis omnis obseruatio præcipitur in summam salutem atq; utilitatem omnium, qui has seruant hominum. Atq; hæc quidem definitio longior quidem est, sed tamen & ad verba Mosis accommodata, & affinis ei quam Philo in suo περὶ ἀναμιξίας libro ponit. Ac Philonis quidem definitio sic habet: νόμος δὲ[?] ἀρχὴ ἢ λόγος[?] θεῖος[?] ἀπαγορεύων[?] ἀμὴ χρή[?]. Mosis autem verbis conuenire eam & Philo & Mosis ipsius hæc verba docent. Etenim Philo definitioni illi quam adduximus basin quandam addes dicit, ὡς μαρτυρεῖ φάσκων ὅτι ἐξ[?] ἔστι[?] τῶν λόγων αὐ-τῷ νόμου. Quod perinde est ac si dicat legem aliud nihil esse quàm quod diximus Moses ipse qui legem à Deo accepit locupletissimus testis est.
units.tr: If we weigh well the opening of this exposition, a definition of this sacred doctrine can be gathered from it as follows: The Law is the divine utterance of God himself, proclaimed to the human race through Moses the herald, by which piety and every observance of the divine will are prescribed for the highest salvation and advantage of all who keep them. This definition is longer, but it fits the words of Moses and is akin to the one Philo gives in his book On Adultery (περὶ ἀναμιξίας). Philo's definition runs: νόμος δὲ ἀρχὴ ἢ λόγος θεῖος ἀπαγορεύων ἀμὴ χρή. That Philo and Moses's own words agree with it is shown by these words of Moses. For Philo, adding a kind of foundation to that definition, says: ὡς μαρτυρεῖ φάσκων ὅτι ἐξ ἔστι τῶν λόγων αὐτῷ νόμου. This amounts to saying that the Law is nothing other than what we have stated, and that Moses himself, who received the Law from God, is the fullest witness to it.

units.la: Jam Mosis verba genus siue nomen legis, & finem & utilitatem, quæ tria hac à nobis posita definitione continentur, pluribus exponunt atq; enumerant.
units.tr: Now Moses's words set out and enumerate, at greater length, the three things contained in the definition we have given: the kind or name of the Law, its end, and its use.

units.la: Ac genus quidem siue nomen legis sic dicit, ut simul & species eius & differentiam indicet. Nam quod triplex ei nomen tribuit, quid id est aliud, quàm specierum enumeratio?
units.tr: As to the kind or name of the Law, he speaks in such a way that he also indicates its species and its differences. For what is his threefold naming of it, if not an enumeration of its kinds?

units.la: Sed primum præcepta, quæ Græcis & Hebræis itemq; Germanis à mandando ducun-tur, ut à מִצְוָה[?] ab ἐντέλλομαι ἐντολαί, ab Germanico verbo <bl>gebüten gebott</bl> dici solita adducit. Unde ex interpretatione nominis perspici poterit, intelligi præcepta moralia, quæ pro imperio quid facto opus sit, quidq; vitandum sit indicant ac præcipiunt. Nam Deum adorare, parentes honorare, à cæde & libidine, & furto & falso abstinere tam iustum & æquum est ut hæc iubenti legi non possis resistere. Et hæc mandanti partem necesse est, siquidem vir bonus esse velim: Sin me iubeas cedere possessione, sin domum postulas, obsequar ne, annō mei fuerit arbitrij. Quò fit ut hæc præcepta vocentur, quia non possit eorum imperio obsi-sti, illa petitionis aut donationis nomina habeant. Possum enim iure vel donare vel negare quod postulaueris: at parentes reuereri, Deum colere, abstinere ab iniurijs, siquidem viri bo-ni officio fungi velim, necesse habeo.
units.tr: First, he brings in the word "precepts," which the Greeks, the Hebrews and the Germans derive from commanding: the Hebrew מִצְוָה, from the Greek ἐντέλλομαι, ἐντολαί, and from the German verb gebieten, Gebot. From this the meaning of the name can be seen: moral precepts are understood, which by command indicate and prescribe what must be done and what must be avoided. For to worship God, to honour parents, to abstain from murder, lust, theft and falsehood is so just and fair that one cannot resist a law that enjoins them. And this is necessarily the part of one commanding, if I wish to be a good man. But if you command me to give up my property, or demand my house, I am not bound to obey; it is up to my own will. Hence these precepts are called precepts, because one cannot resist their command, whereas those other things bear the names of request or gift. For I may by right either give or refuse what you ask; but to revere parents, to worship God, to abstain from wrongs, I am bound to do, if I wish to discharge the duty of a good man.

units.la: Ex quo sequitur has leges ideo præcepta dici quod sint latæ de bonis moribus, quorum usus est sempiternus. Igitur non quod quidam autumant Iudæis solis, sed omnibus gentibus latæ sunt. Testantur hoc patriarcharum, qui his legibus prius studuerunt, quàm eas Deus tulisset, pietas & probitas: Testantur hoc ipsum Pythagoræ, & Phocilidis & Epicteti, & aliorum præcepta de moribus.
units.tr: From this it follows that these laws are called precepts because they were enacted concerning good morals, whose use is everlasting. Therefore they were given not, as some assert, to the Jews alone, but to all nations. The piety and uprightness of the patriarchs testify to this, who studied these laws before God had given them. The moral precepts of Pythagoras, Phocylides, Epictetus and others testify to it as well.

units.la: Dein ponit חֻקִּים[?], id est ritus, Septuaginta ab effectu δικαιώματα[?] appellant. Sunt enim cerimoniæ, quibus iustificatio per Christum nobis parta repræsentatur. Quod genus sunt sa-crificia, purgationes, & circumcisio, & pascha, ex quibus constat huius doctrinæ pars altera.
units.tr: Next he sets down חֻקִּים (chukkim), that is, rites, which the Septuagint call δικαιώματα from their effect. For they are ceremonies by which the justification won for us through Christ is represented. Of this kind are the sacrifices, the purifications, circumcision and the Passover, from which the second part of this doctrine consists.

units.la: Earum usus abijt, sed superest significatio. Usus ceu umbra quædam Christum repræsentabat, oblato pro nobis Christo, rebusque[?], ut ipse crucifixus ait, consummatis, illas omit-timus. Significationis autem, quoniam ipsa vim, seu virtutem, seu utilitatem mortis Christi pulchre docet, recordatio retinenda est. Sed cerimoniæ ex manent, quas Christus & Apostoli instituerunt, veluti Baptismus, & Eucharistia, & manuum impositio. Unde Paulus Hebræis scribens ex promissione Domini, quæ extat apud Ieremiam de novo testamento condendo colligit, hoc ipso quod nouum dixerit, antiquatum esse vetus. Et Ierem. 3. extat oraculum, nul-lam fore posthmodum arcæ fœderis & quæ penes eam sunt rituum memoriam. Sed tamen Iudæis & toti Israelitæ genti ritus hi dati sunt, ut illis usi Christum venturū discerent potius, quàm si gentilibus usi à Christo abducerentur.
units.tr: Their use has passed away, but their meaning remains. As a kind of shadow, their use represented Christ, when Christ was offered for us and, as he himself said on the cross, things were accomplished; so we let those go.
