But the memory of their meaning is to be retained, since it clearly teaches the force, the power and the benefit of the death of Christ. There remain also the ceremonies which Christ and the apostles instituted, such as Baptism, the Eucharist and the laying on of hands. Hence Paul, writing to the Hebrews, from the promise of the Lord which stands in Jeremiah concerning the making of a new covenant, infers that by calling it new he has made the old obsolete (Heb. 8). And Jeremiah 3 contains an oracle that there would afterwards be no remembrance of the ark of the covenant and of the rites that belong to it. Yet these rites were given to the Jews and to the whole nation of Israel so that, by using them, they might learn that Christ was to come, rather than, if the Gentiles used them, be led away from Christ.

units.la: Postremo loco ponit משפטים iudicia quæ Septuaginta vocant κρίματα[?] à iudicijs seu re iudicata. Unde colligi potest forenses leges intelligi.
units.tr: Last, he sets down משפטים (mishpatim), judgments, which the Septuagint call κρίματα, from judgments or matters already adjudged. From this it can be gathered that forensic laws are meant.

units.la: Eæ quoniam partim iuri naturæ & ciuili sunt consentaneæ, partim Israelitis solis ceu iura municipalia sunt accommodatæ: partim perpetuæ sunt, partim abrogatæ. Nam quæ bonis moribus omnium hominum atq; gentium sunt necessariæ, & iuri naturæ consentaneæ, eas nemo hominum recte deleuerit. Quæ vero solis nobis minimè conueniunt, eas nobis iure ne-mo obtruserit. Exemplo sint illæ duæ inter se contrariæ. Extat lex generalis de non ducenda fratria: itemq; extat altera de eadem ducenda. Ut ducerent fratrias defunctis seu fine liberis decedentibus fratribus Deus voluit, nempe ut & familiæ & possessiones conseruari possent. Iam cum illa familiarum & possessionum conseruatio non requiratur amplius: nos hac abrogata generalem illam de cauendis incestis nuptijs legem iuri naturali gentium, & ciuili consenta-neam feruathus. Esto hoc ex ipso iure sumptum exemplum. Etiamsi pleræq; ciuitates Germanicæ ius ciuile sequantur ac seruent, tamen etiam hoc saluo singulis singula sunt iura municipalia. Eodem modo suum Iudæis priuatum ius esto, itemq; nobis nostrum, & tamen diuinum illud commune, quoad cuiq; est aptum reipublicæ simul omnes seruamus ac sequimur. Quod genus sunt leges illæ de pietate in Deum, parentes, patriam, de potestate patriæ de pace publica tuenda, de contractibus, de dolo malo, & de rebus reliquis, quas interest omnium ratas esse. Multa huc referri possent, quæ breuiter ut sim, prætereo.
units.tr: Since these are partly consistent with the law of nature and with civil law, and partly were fitted to the Israelites alone as municipal law, some are perpetual and some have been abrogated. For those laws which are necessary to the good morals of all men and nations, and consistent with the law of nature, no one can rightly abolish. But those which in no way suit us alone, no one can rightly impose upon us. Let those two laws, which are contrary to each other, serve as examples. There is a general law forbidding the marrying of a brother's widow; and there is another commanding it. God willed that brothers should marry the widows of those who died, or who departed leaving no children, so that both families and possessions might be preserved. Now since that preservation of families and possessions is no longer required, we, with that law abrogated, keep that general law concerning the avoidance of incestuous marriages, which agrees with the law of nature of the nations and with civil law. Let this example be taken from the law itself. Although most German cities follow and keep the civil law, nevertheless, with this law still in force, individual places also have their own municipal laws. In the same way, let the Jews have their own private law, and let us have ours; yet we all together keep and follow that divine common law so far as it suits each commonwealth. Of this kind are those laws concerning piety towards God, parents and country, concerning paternal power, concerning the maintenance of public peace, concerning contracts, concerning malicious deceit, and concerning other matters in which it is in everyone's interest that they be upheld. Many more could be referred here, but, to be brief, I pass them over.

units.la: Sed ex tribus istis huius doctrinæ nominibus colligimus tria legum genera hac tractatione contineri, ut præcepta de moribus, cerimonias seu ritus sacros, & leges forenses.
units.tr: But from these three names of this teaching we gather that three kinds of laws are contained in this treatment: precepts concerning morals, ceremonies or sacred rites, and civil laws.

units.la: Eas ut secernat ab humanis Moses, dicit eas abs se quidem propositas, sed id illis ipsis po-stulantibus & mandante Domino. Quasi dicat non suas esse has, sed Dei leges, non illo ipso rogante, sed postulante populo per ipsum ex ore Dei acceptas & promulgatas. Ex quo po-test intelligi quod diximus species quidem esse præcepta, ritus, iudicia, sed commune omnium nomen, diuinum eloquium. Unde sequitur eas non Minois, non Draconis, non Solonis, non Lycurgi, sed Dei Opt. Max. leges esse: non à Mose inuitis illis obtrusas, sed postulantibus & cupientibus diuinitus impetratas. Quod si ita est, nec contemni nec tespui poterant: quando contemptum religio,repulsionem consensus vetarent. Atq; hoc inter illas & humanas leges interest,quod prima parte definitionis ostenditur.
units.tr: Moses, to separate these from human laws, says that he has indeed set them out, but at the request of the people themselves and at the command of the Lord. It is as if he said that these are not his own laws but God's, received and promulgated through him from the mouth of God, at the people's request and not at his own. From this it can be understood, as we said, that precepts, rites and judgments are kinds of law, but the common name for them all is the divine utterance. It follows that they are not the laws of Minos, Draco, Solon or Lycurgus, but the laws of God, the best and greatest. They were not forced upon an unwilling people by Moses, but were obtained from God at the people's own request and desire. If this is so, they could be neither despised nor spurned, since religion forbade contempt and consent forbade rejection. And this is the difference between those laws and human laws, which is shown by the first part of the definition.

units.la: Finis ad hunc modum exponitur: Vt timeas Dominum Deum tuum custodiens &c. Qui- bus verbis huius studij finem dicit esse pietatem,quæ cùm nostram vtilitatem simul cum vi-uina gloria coniunctam habeat,& semper & ab omnibus requiritur.Igitur si quæras cur do-ceantur sacræ literæ, & vt nostra ætate multi dictitant,ꝛwas πiedijen nũ:ςe responderi ex hoc loco potest,vt plantetur pietas.
units.tr: The end is set out in this way: That you may fear the Lord your God, keeping etc. By these words the end of this study is said to be piety, which, since it has our advantage joined with the divine glory, is both always and by all required. So if you ask why the holy letters are taught, and as many in our age keep saying, [garbled Greek], the answer can be drawn from this passage: that piety may be planted.

units.la: Hæc est fundamentum omnium virtutum:hæc parens est & procreatrix omnium honestarum actionum.Nam qui timore numinis aliquo afficitur,is ita sese gerit,vt nec Deum offendat,nec eos quos putet illi charisimos.Sin hæc absit,perinde vita ducitur ac solent absen-tibus parentibus liberi viuere.Etenim hæc magistra quædã est,quę nos quasi freno cohibeat, quò minus indulgeamus,atq; obsequamur malesuadis affectibus.Docet hoc Dauid in Psal-mo 14.quando vitæ perditissimæ causam efficientem ostensurus ait, Non est timor Domini ante oculos illorum.Gen.20.Abraham cogitabat se tutò versari istic nō posse, vbi timor Dei nullus esset.Matth.27.Iatro crucifixus ideo dicitur Christo illudere, quod Deum non time-ret.Neq; verò seruilis quidam timor requiritur,sed ingenuus qualis est in liberis. Grata est & placet Domino voluntas pietatis index.Hac,vt Philo monet,nullum potest esse verius sa crificium , quippe quod relatum in Dei tabulas cum sole & luna & mundo perpetuum sit. Hæc,inquit Apostolus,ad omnia est vtilis.
units.tr: This is the foundation of all virtues; this is the parent and begetter of all honourable actions. For he who is moved by some fear of the divine power conducts himself so that he offends neither God nor those whom he thinks dear to God. But if this is absent, life is lived as children usually live when their parents are away. For this is a kind of teacher, which restrains us as with a bridle, so that we do not indulge or yield to evil desires. David teaches this in Psalm 14, when he wants to show the efficient cause of the most abandoned life and says, "There is no fear of the Lord before their eyes." Gen. 20: Abraham thought that he could not live safely where there was no fear of God. Matt. 27: the thief crucified is said to have mocked Christ because he did not fear God. Yet it is not a servile fear that is required, but a free fear such as children have. The will that is an index of piety is pleasing and acceptable to the Lord. As Philo warns, there can be no truer sacrifice than this, since it is offered in God's tablets and lasts forever with the sun, moon and world. This, says the Apostle, is profitable for all things.

units.la: Sed quibus in rebus posita sitrogas?Dicit Moses, Vt custodias omnia mandata Domini, quæ ego tibi præcipio hodie.Vide quæso quantum errent homines cum eam in cerimonijs,seu externis ritibus,& in ἐυθλοβρησκείᾳ quadam positam autumant.Quanto rectius Philo dicit à recta via pieratis aberrare eos qui in cerimonijs sanctitatem collocant,ac dona offerunt ei qui his non capitur,adulantur ei cui palpum obtrudi non possit: quin Deum hoc cultu de-lectari maximè,quo solet animasolum & vnicum sacrificium nempe veritatem offerre. Ea veritas hoc loco ostenditur, vt custodias omnia mandata quæ iussu Dei Moses præceperit. Ergo pietatis veræ est,quæ Deus iussit,non quæ tibi videantur bona,facere.
units.tr: But you ask in what things this piety consists? Moses says, That you may keep all the commandments of the Lord which I command you this day. Please see how greatly men err when they think it consists in ceremonies or external rites, or in some sort of showy worship [ἐυθλοβρησκείᾳ]. How much more rightly does Philo say that those stray from the straight path of piety who place holiness in ceremonies and offer gifts to one who is not moved by them, who flatter one to whom no flattery can be offered; indeed, that God is especially delighted by the worship in which the soul offers its one and only sacrifice, namely truth. That truth is shown here, namely that you keep all the commandments which Moses taught at God's command. Therefore true piety consists in doing what God has commanded, not what seems good to you.

units.la: Abstinebant olim Iudæi cibis aliquibus,habebantsua ieiunia,sua sabbatha,sed id & De-us pater improbat apud Esaiam ,& reprehenditin Euangelio Dominus. Frustra me colunt traditionibus homipum. Labijs me honorat hic populus, cor autem eorum procul abest à me.Quid quæso fit nostra memoria?Cibis,matrimonio , rebus honestis atq; licitis abstinent homines:dona ferunt & suppendunt statuis,in stas vouent & peregrinationes & vigilias ,ex truunt altaria, & opibus augent sacerdotia : sed quid hoc pietatis, cum Deus horum nihil præceperit?
units.tr: The Jews formerly abstained from certain foods, and had their own fasts and their own sabbaths; but God the Father disapproves of this in Isaiah, and the Lord rebukes it in the Gospel: "In vain do they worship me with the traditions of men. This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me." What, I ask, is the case in our own memory? Men abstain from foods, from marriage, from honest and lawful things; they bring gifts and hang them on statues, they vow pilgrimages and vigils, they build altars and enrich priesthoods with their wealth. But what is this piety, since God has commanded none of these things?

units.la: At bona,aiunt,intentione facimus:faciant quocunq; velint etiã optimo animo,tamen mi hi nunquá fidem facient gratam esse posse <bl>ἀχαμεχν εννοιαν</bl>. Quis enim herus est, qui videat seruum omissis & posthabitis herilibus iussis , quæ sibi probarentur facere ,& id non ferat ægerrimè ? Quocirca nullo tam pulchro colore depingi potest , vt Deo placeat <bl>ἐυθλο-βρησκεια.</bl>
units.tr: "But we do them," they say, "with a good intention. Let them do whatever they like, even with the best mind; still they will never persuade me that it can be pleasing to God [ἀχαμεχν εννοιαν]." For what master is there who, when his servant sets aside and disregards his master's orders in order to do what he himself approves, does not bear it very badly? Therefore no colour, however fine, can be painted over this so that it pleases God [ἐυθλο-βρησκεια].

units.la: Ac longe præstaret blasphemijs,corruptela munerum ,ꝛæde & rapina,& adulterijs & stu-pris &vsuris abstinere,quàm rebus ijs,quarum Deus vsum nobis permisit liberum.Eò Cato nis versus nos vocant etiam , qui docent Deum,qui sit animus,præcipue pura mente colen-dum esse.Huc vocat nos diuinæ voluntatis interpres optimus Christus Ioan.4.dicens in spi-ritu & veritate patrem rectè adorari.
units.tr: And it would be far better to abstain from blasphemies, the corruption of gifts, murder and robbery, adultery, debauchery and usury, than from those things of which God has allowed us free use. Even the verses of Cato call us to this, which teach that God, whatever his nature, must be worshipped above all with a pure mind. Christ, the best interpreter of the divine will, calls us to this too, John 4, saying that the Father is rightly worshipped in spirit and truth.

units.la: Iam quorum sit pietati studere si quis roget,Moses dicit,Tu,& filius tuus,nepos tuus: id est,omnium tam patrum quàm liberorum. Falluntur ergo sua ipsorum stultitia qui diuina-rum legũ onus ab humeris deponere & ministris Euangelij iniungere cōsueuerunt.Etenim si illi quia habent sacerdotia,religioni docendæ iure vacant:tu , quia habes victum & amictũ & vitam,& ocium ei cognoscendæ eodem iure vacabis. Habent ministri stipendia, sed vt te doceant,Si illorum est te docere,tuum est discere & facere.Omnium enim est Dominus, er go omnes si seruient:omnium est Deus,ergo omnes ab eo pendeant.
units.tr: Now if someone asks for whom it is proper to be devoted to piety, Moses says, You, and your son, and your grandson: that is, of all, both fathers and children. Those therefore are deceived by their own folly who are accustomed to lay the burden of the divine laws from their shoulders and impose it on the ministers of the Gospel. For if those men, because they hold the priesthood, are by right free to teach religion, you too, because you have food and clothing and life, and leisure to learn it, will be free by the same right. Ministers have stipends, but so that they may teach you. If it is their task to teach you, it is yours to learn and to do. For the Lord belongs to all; therefore all shall serve him. God belongs to all; therefore all shall depend on him.

units.la: Si roges quando aut quamdiu,dicit, Cunctis diebus vitæ tuæ:Id est,quam diu viuis.In quo videmus qualem requirat Deus pietatem,constantem videlicet. Nam cum pietas virtutum genere contineatur, ac potiùs virtutum omnium , vti paulò ante est à nobis exPhilone di-ctum,fundamentum sit:virtutes autem ipsæ sint habitus,hoc est,vt exponit Cicero, constan tiores & perfectiores animi absolutiones:tum Aristoteles habitus omnes πολυχρονιως και [illegible, ~9 letters] dicat esse, ea demum erit vera pietas, quae tempore & consuetudine fit confirma-ta. Quapropter Moses qui pietatem veram postulat, eam nullo tempori alligatam, sed perpe-tuam iubet esse & continuam. Idem pasim docent sacrae literae, ut 1.Cor.9.sic currite ut com-prehendatis. Hebr.12. Manus remissas & soluta genua erigite. Similis locus est Hebr.3. Matth. 10. & alibi. Ergo vera pietas erit quae constans fuerit & perpetua.
units.tr: If you ask when or how long, he says, All the days of your life: that is, as long as you live. In this we see what kind of piety God requires, namely constant piety. For since piety is contained in the class of virtues, and is rather the foundation of all virtues, as Philo said a little earlier, and since the virtues themselves are habits, that is, as Cicero explains, more constant and perfect settled states of mind, and since Aristotle says that all habits [πολυχρονιως και] [illegible], then true piety will be that which is confirmed by time and custom. Therefore Moses, who demands true piety, orders that it be bound to no time but be perpetual and continuous. The holy letters teach the same everywhere, as in 1 Cor. 9: "So run that you may obtain." Heb. 12: "Lift up the drooping hands and the weak knees." A similar passage is in Heb. 3, Matt. 10, and elsewhere. Therefore true piety will be that which is constant and perpetual.

units.la: Quamobrem autem haec abs te requiritur? ut inde aliquid emolumenti accedat Deo? Minime vero: Deus enim is est, qui neq; ex pietate tua fit ditior, neq; ex impietate fit pauperior. Hoc Deus agit, Ut prorogentur dies tui, [illegible, ~9 letters] [illegible, ~10 letters] Dicit longaevos esse pios homines, exemplo sunt prisci saeculi homines. Non autem esse diu superstites impios, exemplo sunt nostri saeculi homines. Ergo hoc agitur verbi Dei ministerio, ut plantetur pietas, quam Deus requirit ab omni hominum genere, quae debet esse perpetua, quae est saluberrima.
units.tr: But why is this required of you? So that some profit may accrue to God from it? By no means. For God is one who does not become richer from your piety, nor poorer from your impiety. God does this: that your days may be prolonged [illegible] [illegible]. He says that pious men are long-lived; the men of the early age are examples. Impious men, on the other hand, do not survive long; the men of our age are examples. Therefore this is done by the ministry of the Word of God, so that piety may be planted, which God requires from every kind of man, which ought to be perpetual, and which is most wholesome.

units.la: Ac quoniam vita moresq; nostri indicant pietatis parum nobis inesse, doctrinae multum requiritur. Nam quoad pietas te nondum eo copulerit ut vsuras, luxum, adulteria, reliquaq; scelera caveas, certe eges multa ac valida verbi Dei praedicatione. Et haec quidem de fine doctrinae huius.
units.tr: And since our life and conduct show that little piety dwells in us, much teaching is required. For as far as piety has not yet bound you so that you avoid usury, luxury, adultery and other crimes, you certainly need much and strong preaching of the Word of God. And these things are said about the end of this teaching.

units.la: Utilitatem sic exponit, Audies igitur Israel, &c. Quibus verbis huius studij, commoda enumerat. 1. Ut bene fit tibi: ut animo sis pacato, quieto, securo, tranquillo, quali profecto sunt, qui dicto factoque laedunt neminem, quiq; Deum semper venerantur, & ne quo pacto offendant cavent, qui deniq; si periculi quid immineat, in illo omnes spes opesq; sitas habent. Haec quies & tranquillitas verbis atq; oratione humana sat digne efferri non potest. Habes exempla eorum, qui cum Deum offendissent peccatis, furijs agitati nusquam possent consistere, ut Caini, Saulis, Judae, Neronis, Orestis & aliorum: contra Josephi, Davidis, Apostolorum, martyrum, quorum in periculis maximis animi quieti fuere & infracti. Jam corpora pij non gravant crapula, non inquinant scortatione, & si quis ingruat morbus, eum quia sibi ipsi non accersiuerunt vel scortando vel potando, patienter ferunt. Fortunis uti visum est Deo magnis aut mediocribus aut infimis contenti sunt. Quod sunt esse volunt nihilq; malunt. Quid quaso his felicius.
units.tr: He sets out the benefit thus: Hear therefore, Israel, etc. By these words he lists the advantages of this study. 1. That it may go well with you: that you may be at peace in mind, quiet, secure, and tranquil, as indeed those are who harm no one in word or deed, who always revere God and take care not to offend him in any way, and who, if any danger threatens, place all their hopes and resources in him. This quiet and tranquillity cannot be expressed worthily enough in words or human speech. You have examples of those who, having offended God by their sins, were driven by the furies and could find rest nowhere, such as Cain, Saul, Judas, Nero, Orestes and others. On the contrary, there were Joseph, David, the Apostles and the martyrs, whose minds were quiet and unbroken in the greatest dangers. Again, the pious do not burden their bodies with gluttony, nor defile them with fornication; and if any sickness comes upon them, they bear it patiently, since they have not brought it on themselves by fornicating or drinking. They are content whether God has given them great, moderate or meagre fortunes. They want to be what they are, and prefer nothing else. What, I ask, is happier than this?

units.la: 2 Ut crescatis. Et hoc bonum est haud exiguum. Nam movere & non promovere, quanti doloris est & taedij? At inuenies homines, qui cum noctes atq; dies sese fatigent laboribus & vigilijs, tamen nihilo fiunt ditiores. Qui fit? deest illis res bene fortunans Dei benedictio: Celebre est illud Israelitis quondam usurpatum proverbium, Benedicat tibi Dominus, sicut Ephraim. Haec enim tribus opibus, potentia, dignitate sic erat aucta divinitus, ut reliquis omnibus praeluceret. Unde Psal.57. precatur psalthes. Terra dat prouentus suos, benedicat nobis Deus, Deus noster. Benedicat nobis Deus. Si igitur vis bonis abundare, non a mundo, sed a Deo datore petas ea. Nam & si quid mundus dederit, tamen id perpetuum non est, nec felix ac faustum. Ea nunc est hominum impietas ut prolis multiplicatio, quae huc etiam pertinet, in bonis amplius non habeatur.
units.tr: 2 That you may increase. And this is no small blessing. For to move about and not to advance: how much grief and weariness that is! Yet you will find men who wear themselves out night and day with labours and watchings, and yet become no richer at all. How so? The thing that makes wealth prosper is lacking: the blessing of God. That famous proverb once used among the Israelites is well known: "May the Lord bless you, as Ephraim." For this tribe was so greatly enriched by God, in power and dignity, that it outshone all the rest. Hence the psalmist prays in Psalm 67: "The earth gives its increase; may God, our God, bless us. May God bless us." If therefore you wish to abound in goods, seek them not from the world but from God the giver. For even if the world gives anything, it is not lasting, nor happy and prosperous. Such now is the impiety of men that the multiplication of offspring, which also belongs here, is no longer counted among blessings.

units.la: 3 Ut promissa terra potiare. Locus promittitur in quo pedem sistas, ne semper exul erres. At Christiani patriam sibi in coelis esse arbitrantor, in qua cum Christo aeternum conquie-scant, Amen.
units.tr: 3 That you may possess the promised land. A place is promised in which you may set your foot, so that you do not wander forever as an exile. But Christians think their fatherland is in heaven, where with Christ they rest in eternity. Amen.

units.la: SERMO II.
units.tr: SERMON II.

units.la: 4 Audi Israel Dominus Deus noster Deus unus est.
units.tr: 4 Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God is one LORD.

units.la: 5 Diliges itaq; Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo, & tota anima tua, et pro omni virili tua.
units.tr: 5 Thou shalt therefore love the LORD thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy strength.

units.la: 6 Sint verba ista quae ego tibi hodie praecipio in corde tuo.
units.tr: 6 And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart.

units.la: 7 Et inculces ea filijs tuis, & loqueris de eis, quum domi tuae resides, & quum in via in cedis, quum cubitum vadis, & quum surgis.
units.tr: 7 And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.

units.la: 8 Ligabis deniq; ea in signum ad manu tuam, eruntq; monumenta intera tuos.
units.tr: 8 And thou shalt bind them for a sign upon thine hand, and they shall be as frontlets between thine eyes.

units.la: 9 Scribes quoq; ea super postes domus tuae, & in portis tuis.
units.tr: 9 And thou shalt write them upon the posts of thy house, and on thy gates.

units.la: 10 Quum introduxerit te Dominus Deus tuus in terram, quam juravit Patri bus tuis Abraham, Isaac & Jacob, & dederit tibi civitates magnas & bonas quas tu non aedificasti.
units.tr: 10 And it shall be, when the LORD thy God shall have brought thee into the land which he sware unto thy fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, to give thee great and goodly cities, which thou buildedst not,

units.la: 11 Domos quoque plenas omnibus bonis, quas tu non implevisti, & puteos ex-cisos, quos tu non effodisti, vineas & oleas, quas tu non plantasti, comederisq; & sa-tiatus fueris.
units.tr: 11 And houses full of all good things, which thou filledst not, and wells digged, which thou diggedst not, vineyards and olive trees, which thou plantedst not; when thou shalt have eaten and be full;

units.la: 12 Cave ne obliviscaris Domini, qui te eduxit de terra Ægypti, de domo ser-vorum.
units.tr: 12 Then beware lest thou forget the LORD, which brought thee forth out of the land of Egypt, from the house of bondage.

units.la: POsita[?] definitione legis, Moses praecepti primi interpretationem auspicatur. Ac quoni-am illud ipsum primum praeceptum duabus constat partibus, ipsam quoq; expositionem in partes duas destribuit: ita ut cum vna praecepti pars sic habeat, Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus qui eduxi te de terra Ægypti, de domo servitutis: ipse eam exponens doceat, v-num nobis Deum esse quanto maximo fieri potest amore comprehendendum: cumq; pars altera sic habeat, non eruni tibi Dij alij coram me, ipse eam exponens doceat, illam de mul-titudine & varietate Deorum esse minuendam.
units.tr: Having set out the definition of the law, Moses begins his exposition of the first commandment. And since that first commandment itself consists of two parts, he also divides the exposition into two parts. One part of the commandment reads: "I am the LORD thy God, which brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage"; in expounding it, he teaches that the one God is to be embraced with the greatest love possible. The other part reads: "Thou shalt have no other gods before me"; in expounding it, he teaches that the multitude and variety of gods is to be diminished.

units.la: De prima praecepti parte dicit in praesentia, & eam sic exponit, vt primum ostendat quid sit illud; Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus: tum quid illud, qui te eduxi de terra Ægypti, &c.
units.tr: For the present he speaks of the first part of the commandment, and expounds it so as first to show what this means, "I am the LORD thy God," and then what that means, "which brought thee out of the land of Egypt," and so on.

units.la: Illud membrum, Audi Israel. Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus, &c. hoc ipso exponit, quod dicit, Dominus Deus noster Deus vnus est. Audi, inquit. Tempus audiendi nunc esse dicit, vt quae sit mens legis intelligamus: neq; enim excusat crassa ignorantia.
units.tr: The clause "Hear, O Israel. I am the LORD thy God," etc., he expounds by means of the words "the LORD our God is one LORD." He says, "Hear." He tells us that now is the time for hearing, so that we may understand the mind of the law; for gross ignorance is no excuse.

units.la: Dein exponit Ego Dominus Deus tuus per illa, Dominus Deus noster Deus vnus est. In quo habes, pro Ego, Deus vnus. Quo docet vnum se esse, qui vnice coli & timeri debeat. Exi-stimare Deum vnum esse est religionis salus & perfectio. Et haec expositio ad veram fidem pertinet maxime. Nemo enim Deum vnum habent[?], nisi qui ab eo solo pendet, & ei soli fidit. Iam etiam considera[?] quoniam vnius nomen ipsam Dei naturam comprehendat, quod vnus existat, creet, regat, seruet omnia, deniq; vnus quicquid de Deo dici potest faciat.
units.tr: Then he expounds "I am the LORD thy God" through the words "the LORD our God is one LORD." Here, in place of "I," you have "one God." By this he teaches that he is the one who ought to be worshipped and feared alone. To hold that God is one is the safety and perfection of religion, and this exposition pertains above all to true faith. For no one has God as one unless he depends on him alone and trusts in him alone. Consider also how the word "one" embraces the very nature of God: that he alone exists, creates, rules and preserves all things, and in short that he alone does whatever can be said of God.

units.la: Quamobrem examina te an Deū vnū habeas. Credo in vnum Deum, inquis: sed diuersum tefentire facta declarant tua. Veluti si curras ad divos petitum ab his auxilium; subijceris & cedis impijs & prophanis hominibus, pios aut tradis aut deseris, honores, opes, amicos, ventrem pluris quam Deum facis: at qui Deum vnum habet is ei posthabet omnia, quippe qui sciat ideo Deum vnum esse, quod non aliunde, sed ex eo ceu vna rerum origine pronanent[?] omnia. Quam causam in 1.Corinth.8.reddit etiam apostolus.
units.tr: Therefore examine yourself, whether you have one God. "I believe in one God," you say; but your deeds show that you feel otherwise. For example, if you run to idols and seek help from them; if you submit to and yield to impious and profane men, betray or desert the godly, and make honours, wealth, friends and your belly more important than God, then you do not have one God. But he who has one God puts all things after him, since he knows that God is one because all things flow not from elsewhere but from him as from one origin of things. The apostle also gives this reason in 1 Corinthians 8.

units.la: Pro eo vero quod in ipsa lege dictum fuit, Dominus Deus, quoniam nihil poni potest aliud, hoc ipsum iterum repetit. Etenim Domini vox authoritatem, qua Deum apud nos pollere par est, significat: at Iehoua nomen summam illam essentiam significat, qua res quae existunt omnes continentur. Quo nomine cum nullum aliud sit sublimius seu communius: sane pro eo nullum erit aliud, quo Deum definias.
units.tr: As for what was said in the law itself, "the LORD our God," since nothing else can be put in its place, he repeats the same thing. For the word "Lord" signifies the authority by which God ought to hold sway among us, but the name Jehovah signifies that supreme essence by which all existing things are contained. Since no other name is more sublime or more general than this, surely no other will be found by which you could define God.

units.la: Caeterum haec audiens Dei nomina, supremam illam numinis maiestatem, seu excelsum hoc eius in omnes creaturas imperium: tum illam rerum quae existunt omnium essentiam animo comprehende & considera tuo. Quo fiet ut illum Deum tibi cum venerandum, tum patroni loco retinendum semper arbitrere.
units.tr: Moreover, as you hear these names of God, grasp and consider in your mind that supreme majesty of the divine power, or that lofty dominion of his over all creatures, and also the essence of all things that exist. By this you will come to judge that he is to be revered as your God, and to be kept always as your patron.

units.la: Iam quod in lege positum fuerat Deus tuus, id hoc ipso exponit quod nunc dicit, Deus noster. Quas formulas si in vnum ipse conferas, disces eum & singulorum & vniuersorum Deum esse. Quare siue singuli siue vniuersi periculis obruamur, Deus nobis adiutor erit. Ni-hil enim profuerit Deum vnum & summum & optimum maximum esse, ni illum etiam tu-um esse noris. Daemones credunt esse Deum, sed non suum. Eorum similes sunt Cain, Iudas, & qui de eius ope spem omnem deposuerunt. Ex quo perspicuum est quid sibi velit Deus hoc ipso quod vnum se esse dicit Deum nostrum.
units.tr: Now, what was put in the law as "thy God," he expounds by what he now says, "our God." If you compare these forms with one another, you will learn that he is the God both of individuals and of all together. So whether we are overwhelmed by dangers as individuals or as a people, God will be our helper. For it will profit nothing that God is one, supreme, best and greatest, unless you also know that he is your God. The demons believe that there is a God, but not that he is their God. Like them are Cain, Judas, and those who put all their hope away from his help. From this it is plain what God means when he says that he is "our God" who is one.

units.la: Caeterum quid ex hoc axiomate concludi possit atque colligi Moses adhunc modum edocet. Diliges itaque Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo, & tota anima tua, &c. In quibus habes illius argumenti quasi quoddam consequens, Deum omnino diligendum esse. Si Deus est vnus, erit vnice diligendus. Quod nemo iverit inficias. Est enim verum hoc in omni vitae genere. Si istæc tua sit coniunx, eam vnicam adamandam arbitrare: si is sit herus ei ser-vies: eodemq; modo in caeteris. Sic si Deus vnus sit, vnice colendus & diligendus est. Iam diligere quid aliud est, quam habere magno in precio, & velle vt idem sit ac videatur apud omnes, illi gratificari, &c.
units.tr: Moreover, Moses teaches in this way what may be concluded and drawn from this axiom: "Thou shalt therefore love the LORD thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul," etc. Here you have, as it were, a consequence of that argument: God must altogether be loved. If God is one, he is to be loved uniquely. No one will deny this, for it holds true in every kind of life. If this is your wife, you judge that she alone is to be loved; if he is your master, you serve him; and likewise in other things. So, if God is one, he is to be worshipped and loved alone. Now, what else is loving than holding in high esteem, wishing that he be honoured and seen to be so by all, and pleasing him?

units.la: Sed ipse exponit sese & enumeratione partium & exemplo, vt quam in partem illud VNICE accipi debeat, intelligas. Enumerat enim cor, animam, vires. Cor est sedes affectuum vt iræ, odij, voluptatis, amoris, gaudij, & cæterorum. Hos sibi Deus vendicat vt impijs irafca re, impiorum mores odio prosequare, Diuini verbi proscriptione & perditis moribus triste re:bona grata acceptaq; elfe tibi velis, Deum ames, in illo solo solida gaudia habeas. Iam fi De um vnicè delegeres nihil magis offenderet te quàm illius legû negligentia ac proculcatio. Exemplo Paulus est, qui Corinthijs & Galatis scribens, flet Dei gloriam conculcari. Iam cum Antichristus in gregem Domini grassatur, adeò non dolet nobis hæc ignominia, vt plus fit conuiuiorum & festorum, quàm fuerit antea. Vbi cor nostrum est ibi thesaurus fit necesse est. Iam fi voluptatibus alius, honoribus atq; opibus alius inhiet: quis non videat nostra nos habere chariora, quàm Deum?
units.tr: But he explains himself, both by the enumeration of the parts and by an example, so that you may understand in what sense that word "ALONE" should be taken. For he enumerates the heart, the soul and the strength. The heart is the seat of the affections, such as anger, hatred, pleasure, love, joy and the rest. God claims these for himself, so that you should be angry at the impious, hate the morals of the impious, grieve at the proscription of the divine word and at depraved morals, and wish good things to be pleasing and acceptable to you. Love God, and have solid joys in him alone. Moreover, if you chose God alone, nothing would offend you more than the neglect and trampling of his laws. Paul is an example, who, writing to the Corinthians and Galatians, laments that the glory of God is trampled underfoot. Now, when Antichrist rages against the flock of the Lord, this disgrace does not grieve us so much that there are more feasts and festivals than there were before. Where your heart is, there your treasure must be. Now, if one person pants after pleasures, another after honours and wealth, who does not see that we hold our own things dearer than God?

units.la: Anima vero est ipsa vita mortalium, quæ Hebræis dicitur, quæ habet facultates su- as & organa, vt visum, auditum, &c. Ergo omnes sensus debentur Domino. Cur igitur aures præbemus impuris aut blasphemis sermonibus? Cur oculos in malarum rerum obtutum conuertimus? Cur intellectum fiue νοῦς rebus nihili potius exercemus quàm sanctis & grauibus.
units.tr: The soul, moreover, is the very life of mortals, which the Hebrews call nephesh, and which has its faculties and organs, such as sight, hearing, and so on. Therefore all the senses are owed to the Lord. Why then do we lend our ears to impure or blasphemous speech? Why do we turn our eyes to the gazing upon wicked things? Why do we exercise our intellect, or nous [νοῦς], on worthless things rather than on holy and serious ones?

units.la: Vires vehementiam, facultatem, studium significant, ἐνέργεια ernft/vnd yffer. Ex quibus intelligis requiri totum hominis posse. Veluti fi quis eloquentia, robore, sapientia, virtute bellica polleat, is quidquid ipsum est in vsum reip. conferat. Exemplo sunt Aharon, Samfon, Salomon, Iofue, Dauid, & alij. Quæ docent totum hominem deberi Domino.
units.tr: "Strength" signifies vehemence, ability and zeal, energia [ἐνέργεια], that is, earnestness and zeal. From these you understand that the whole power of a man is required. For example, if someone excels in eloquence, physical strength, wisdom or military valour, he should put whatever he is to the service of the commonwealth. Examples are Aaron, Samson, Solomon, Joshua, David, and others. These teach that the whole man is owed to the Lord.

units.la: Sed idem illustrat exemplo dicens, Sint verba ista, &c. Quo docet in omnem vitæ vsum hæc conferenda, vt sensus inde distrahi in aliarum rerum curam ac cogitationem neque-ant. Ac sigillatim refert singula.
units.tr: But he illustrates the same point with an example, saying, "Let these words be," and so on. By this he teaches that these things are to be applied to every use of life, so that the mind cannot be drawn away from them into the care and thought of other matters. And he goes through each item separately.

units.la: 1 Sint in corde tuo. Hoc est, fac non solum audias, aut dicas, aut semel cogites, sed iterum atque iterum repete & considera vt ne mente elabatur tua.
units.tr: "1. Let them be in your heart." That is, do not only hear, speak, or think of them once, but repeat and consider them again and again, so that they do not slip from your mind.

units.la: 2 Acues ea filijs tuis. Ne videlicet hebescant animi, ceu culter eos acue. Id de liberis quidem dicit, quia ab his auspicamur doctrinam, sed omnibus factum expedit. Omnes enim vsu vitæ humanæ subinde atterimur, vt minus acutè res diuinas geramus, minus bene verbum Domini secemur. Alium negociatio, alium conuiuia, alium alia, quò minus ferueat in negocijs Domini, obtusum reddunt. Ergo opus est verbo Domini ceu cote, quo acuamur.
units.tr: "2. You shall teach them diligently to your sons." This is so that your minds do not grow dull, as a blade does, and so that they are sharpened as a knife is sharpened. He says this of children in particular, because it is with them that we begin teaching, but it is useful for everyone. For all of us are worn down from time to time by the business of human life, so that we handle divine things less keenly and hold the word of the Lord less firmly. Business dulls one person, feasts another, and other things still others, so that they grow less fervent in the affairs of the Lord. Therefore we need the word of the Lord, like a whetstone, by which we may be sharpened.

units.la: 3 Loqueris domi tuæ sedens de ijs. Docet patrum familiàs esse, vt quasi catechistæ sint, sic pro nenijs & obfcœnis sermonibus Christianæ vitæ præceptis & exemplis augeant liberos.
units.tr: "3. When you sit at home and talk of them." He teaches that parents should be like catechists, so that instead of trifles and obscene talk they enrich their children with the precepts and examples of the Christian life.

units.la: 4 In via incedens, &c. Exemplo sint euntes Emaum. Incitet nos ad pias confabulationes, quod Dominus promittit, fe ijs qui de fe colloquantur affore medium: quod contra certum fit diabolum res malas agentibus assistere.
units.tr: "4. When you walk along the way." Let the disciples going to Emmaus be the example. It should move us to pious conversation, since the Lord promises that he will be present among those who speak of him; on the contrary, it is certain that the devil stands by those who are engaged in evil things.

units.la: 5 Si cubitum eas, & surgas. Quod ipsum etiam facto opus est. Nam fi dormitum eas, quando horam aduentus Christi nescis, qui non te Domino commendes maxime: sin euigiles, cur non aduersus innumera pericula tete munias precibus?
units.tr: "5. When you lie down and when you rise up." This too needs to be done in practice. For if you go to sleep, when you do not know the hour of Christ's coming, will you not commend yourself especially to the Lord? And if you wake, why do you not fortify yourself with prayers against countless dangers?

units.la: 6 Monumenta in sinu tuo, in portis, in postibus, in oculis. Hæc attendite, qui torques, atq; an nulos potius habetis, non Dei, sed superbiæ monumenta. Sic enim amoris nostri, quàm Dei facilius admonemur. Ex his intelligis te in amorem Dei tuas curas ac cogitationes omnes debere conuerte re. Vult enim Deus hominem sibi totum, quantus quantus est, esse dicam. Ni id fiat primo præcepto non statur. Sed hactenus de eo quod dictum est, Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus.
units.tr: "6. Signs on your breast, on the gates, on the doorposts, and on your eyes." Pay attention, you who wear necklaces, or rather who have rings: these are monuments not of God but of pride. For thus we are more easily reminded of our own love than of God. From these things you understand that you must turn all your cares and thoughts to the love of God. For God wills to have the whole man for himself, however great or small he is. Unless this is done, the first precept does not stand. But so much for what was said: "I am the Lord your God."

units.la: Illud alterum, Qui eduxi te de terra Ægypti, de domo seruitutis, &c. sic exponit. Cum introduxerit Dominus, &c. Quibus verbis eos gratitudinis admonet, idque sic facit, vt simul etiam quæ res à religione soleant auocare, ijs omnibus interdicat, videlicet nimio rerum ter renarum amore. Dicit enim ciuitatibus, domibus, vineis, puteis, oleu potitus & satiatus ne obli-uiscaris Domini. Vnde in Pfalm. dicitur, Diuitiæ fi affluant, nolite cor apponere. Dominus hæc bona mortalibus non vt instrumenta malorum dedit, sed vt cum gratiarum actione su-mantur, veluti in 1. Tim. 4. de cibis dicit apostolus. Et idem in 1. Corinth. 10. fiue inquit, edi-tis, fiue bibitis, fiue quid facitis, omnia in gloriam Dei facite. Multa in hanc sententiam Pfal. 32, 36. scripta sunt. Quamobrem meminerimus beneficia diuina, quoniam sunt Dei in nos amoris testimonia, sic esse accipienda, atque vsurpanda vt eò magis ipsum Deum adoremus & diligamus in Iesu Christo Domino nostro.
units.tr: The other, "who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage," and so on, he explains thus: "When the Lord has brought you in," and so on. In these words he reminds them of gratitude, and he does so in such a way that he also forbids all those things which are wont to draw us away from religion, namely an excessive love of earthly things. For he says to them: cities, houses, vineyards, wells, olive oil; when you have possessed them and are satisfied, beware lest you forget the Lord. Hence it is said in the Psalm, "If riches abound, do not set your heart upon them." The Lord has given these goods to mortals not as instruments of evil, but to be taken with thanksgiving, as the apostle says of foods in 1 Tim. 4. And in 1 Cor. 10 he says: "Whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God." Many things to this effect are written in Psalms 32 and 36. Therefore let us remember that the blessings of God, since they are testimonies of his love towards us, are to be received and used in such a way that we adore and love God himself all the more, in Jesus Christ our Lord.

units.la: Amen.
units.tr: Amen.

units.la: SERMO
units.tr: SERMON

units.la: SERMO III.
units.tr: SERMON III.

units.la: 13 Dominum Deum tuum timebis, & illum coles, iurabisq; per nomen eius.
units.tr: Thou shalt fear the Lord thy God, and serve him, and swear by his name.

units.la: 14 Ne sequamini Deos alienos, Deos videlicet populorum, qui circum vos habitant.
units.tr: Ye shall not go after other gods, the gods of the peoples who dwell round about you.

units.la: 15 Quoniam Dominus Deus tuus, qui in medio tui est, Deus est zelotes, ne forte indignetur vultus Domini Dei tui contra te, & exterminet te de terra.
units.tr: For the Lord thy God, who is in the midst of thee, is a jealous God, lest perhaps the countenance of the Lord thy God be kindled against thee, and destroy thee from the earth.

units.la: 16 Ne tentetis Dominum Deum vestrum, sicut tentastis in Massa.
units.tr: Ye shall not tempt the Lord your God, as ye tempted him at Massah.

units.la: 17 Diligentissime custodietis praecepta Domini Dei vestri, atq; testimonia eius, & ritus eius quae praecepit tibi.
units.tr: Ye shall diligently keep the commandments of the Lord your God, and his testimonies, and his statutes, which he hath commanded thee.

units.la: 18 Facies, quod rectum & bonum est ante oculos Domini, ut bene sit tibi, ut introeas, & possideas terram illam bonam, quam iurauit Dominus patribus tuis.
units.tr: Thou shalt do what is right and good in the sight of the Lord, that it may be well with thee, and that thou mayest go in and possess that good land which the Lord sware unto thy fathers.

units.la: 19 Ut pellere possis ante te omnes hostes tuos, quemadmodum locutus est Dominus.
units.tr: That thou mayest drive out all thine enemies from before thee, as the Lord hath spoken.

units.la: 20 Cumque interrogauerit posterus temporibus filius tuus, dicens: Quid sibi volunt haec testimonia, ritus, & iudicia, quae praecepit Dominus Deus vester vobis?
units.tr: And when thy son shall ask thee in time to come, saying: What mean these testimonies, statutes and judgments, which the Lord your God hath commanded you?

units.la: 21 Respondebis filio tuo, serui fuimus Pharaonis in Aegypto, & eduxit nos Dominus ex Aegypto manu valida.
units.tr: Then thou shalt say unto thy son: We were Pharaoh's servants in Egypt, and the Lord brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand.

units.la: 22 Ediditq; Dominus signa & portenta magna, & noxia in Aegypto, in Pharaone, & in cuncta familia eius, idq; nobis spectantibus.
units.tr: And the Lord shewed signs and great and grievous wonders upon Egypt, upon Pharaoh, and upon all his household, before our eyes.

units.la: 23 Nos vero eduxit illinc, ut introduceret nos, & daret nobis terram quam iurauit patribus nostris.
units.tr: And he brought us out from thence, that he might bring us in, and give us the land which he sware unto our fathers.

units.la: 24 Praecepitque nobis Dominus ut faceremus omnia statuta ista, & timeremus Dominum Deum nostrum, idque bono nostro, cunctis diebus, ut viviamus quemadmodum est hodie.
units.tr: And the Lord commanded us to do all these statutes, and to fear the Lord our God, for our good always, that he might preserve us alive, as it is at this day.

units.la: 25 Erit iustitia nobis, si custodierimus, & fecerimus omnia praecepta ista in conspectu Domini Dei nostri, sicut praecepit nobis.
units.tr: And it shall be our righteousness, if we observe to do all these commandments before the Lord our God, as he hath commanded us.

units.la: Quod Moses in fine suae in secundam partem expositionis dicit, Dominum Deum tuum timebis & illum coles iurabisq; per nomen eius: id quasi quaedam ambarum partium connexio est, significans Deum hoc agere, ut ipsum quanto maximo cultu, amore, timore, summa pietate prosequamur, iuxtaq; eum Dei loco habeamus neminem.
units.tr: Moses, at the end of his exposition, comes to the second part and says: Thou shalt fear the Lord thy God, and serve him, and swear by his name. This is, as it were, a link joining both parts, signifying that God wills us to pursue him with the greatest possible worship, love, fear and utmost piety, and to hold no one beside him in the place of God.

units.la: Dicit autem tria: primum Dominum Deum tuum timebis: Quo timore coerceet[?] omnem petulantiam & libidinem, ac iubet etiam ne rebus ex animi sententia succedentibus prorsus omni pietate vacemus.
units.tr: He says three things. First, Thou shalt fear the Lord thy God. By this fear he restrains all wantonness and lust, and he also bids us not to become utterly careless of piety when things go according to our wishes.

units.la: Deinceps ait, illum coles, seu illi seruies. Seruire est alicui deditum esse, veluti in heri nutus & mandata sic in verbum Domini intentos esse. Quae est illa δουλία quae fingitur.
units.tr: Next he says serve him, or be his servant. To serve is to be devoted to someone, to be attentive to his nod and commands; so too to be intent upon the word of the Lord. What is that so-called servile worship [δουλία] which is invented?

units.la: Postremo dicit, Iurabisq; per nomen eius. Equidem iurandi consuetudinem illam leuem atque impiam non probat nec praecipit: verum si res postulet, vult per Deum iurari. Igitur iuramentum est alicuius rei confirmatio quae fit religione interposita. Id pertinet ad externam religionem. Additur autem hic ad primum praeceptum, quia partim ad primi, partim,ad tertij praecepti praescriptum iurandum est. Primum enim praeceptum iubet per solum Deum,tertium vt ne temere seu vane iures. Ergo primum praeceptum transgredimur iurantes creaturis adhibitis. Sed ea de re suo loco dicentur plura.
units.tr: Finally he says, and swear by his name. Indeed he neither approves nor prescribes that light and impious custom of swearing; but if the matter requires it, he wills that we swear by God. An oath, therefore, is the confirmation of some matter, made with religion interposed. This pertains to external religion. It is added here to the first commandment, because an oath must be sworn partly in accordance with the first commandment and partly with the third. For the first commandment bids us swear by God alone, and the third that we not swear rashly or in vain. Therefore we transgress the first commandment when we swear by creatures. But more will be said on this matter in its proper place.

units.la: Iam quemadmodum iurantes praeter vnum Deum respicere debent neminem: sic in omnibus alijs vitae partibus nullum nobis fingamus alium in quo potius, quam in Deo ipso omnes nobis spes opesque sitas esse arbitremur. Quod docet secundae partis expositio quae verbis illis comprehenditur. In ea sic versatur Moses vt primum doceat cauendum esse πολυθεΐαν[?] siue ἀλλοθεΐαν: tum praebet optima contra hanc remedia.
units.tr: Now, just as those who swear ought to regard no one but the one God, so in all other parts of life let us imagine no other in whom we think all our hopes and resources should rest rather than God himself. The exposition of the second part, comprised in those words, teaches this. In it Moses proceeds in such a way that he first teaches that polytheism [πολυθεΐα] or allotheism [ἀλλοθεΐα] is to be avoided, and then offers the best remedies against it.

units.la: Vt eam cauendam esse doceat, sic ait, Ne sequamini Deos alienos Deos videlicet populorum qui ei cum vos habitant. In ipso praecepto dixerat, Non erunt tibi alieni coram me. Iam quid fit esse Deos aliosqui item Dij alieni, pulchrè docet. Dij alieni sunt inquit, populorum qui circum vos habitant, hoc est, quos populi vicini Deorum loco habent ac colunt. Est autem hoc perinde ac si dicat, in Ægypto vidisti, in Canaan videbis Deos multos & varios, hos tu caueto. Erant Ægyptijs, Chaldæis, alijs etiam populis Dij alij. Chaldæis ignis Deus erat aureorum & argenteorum & ligneorum Deorum victor: nam quibuscunque statuis ignem suum admouerent Chaldæi, omnes uti credibile est, consumebantur. Igitur in Ægyptum profecti suum cum Canopo Deo Ægyptio commiserunt ignem. Atastutus erat illi Canopo sacrificus, qui hydriam, quales habent in illis partibus maximas, perforatam circumquaque & rursus cera obstructis foraminibus pulchre pictam ferreis pedibus impositit, & illi ipsi caput indidit eius Dei, vt iam simulachri formam obtineret. Huic Ignis suppositus cera liquefacta aquis effluentibus extinctus est. Quæ res magnum Canopo nomen fecit. Omitto iam Græcos & Romanos Deos quorum alij terris, alij aëri, alij alijs rebus præfecti sunt, quàs Deus regendo & conferuando opificio suo non amplius sufficeret. Ab his ille dicit abstinendum.
units.tr: To teach that it is to be avoided, he says: Ye shall not go after other gods, the gods of the peoples who dwell round about you. In the precept itself he had said: Thou shalt have no other gods before me. Now he beautifully teaches what the gods of others are, and what strange gods are. "Strange gods," he says, "are the gods of the peoples who dwell round about you": that is, those whom the neighbouring peoples hold as gods and worship. This is as if he said: in Egypt you have seen, and in Canaan you will see, many and various gods; beware of these. The Egyptians, the Chaldeans and other peoples had other gods. For the Chaldeans fire was a god, the conqueror of gold, silver and wooden gods; for whatever images the Chaldeans applied their fire to, all of them, as is credible, were consumed. Therefore, when they went into Egypt, they committed their fire to Canopus, the Egyptian god. And a crafty priest of Canopus, having pierced a jar, such as they have in those parts, very large, all round, and having stopped the holes again with wax and painted it beautifully, set it on iron feet and placed on it the head of that god, so that it now had the form of an image. Fire placed beneath it melted the wax, and the water ran out and extinguished it. This trick won Canopus great renown. I now pass over the Greek and Roman gods, of whom some are set over lands, some over the air, and some over other things, as if God, in ruling and preserving his work, were no longer sufficient. From these, he says, we must abstain.

units.la: Idem ad nos dictum puta, nempe vt abijs quos vicini colunt Dijs abstineamus. Qui nam illi Iudæi Deum agnoscunt quidem, sed non qualem se expressit, atque exhibet in filio. Eum nos errorem cauebimus & Deum in filio Iesu Christo, in quo bonitas, iustitia, sapientia maxime cernitur, adorabimus. Turcæ eodem pene errant modo, quòs ipsos etiam cauebimus. Papistæ agnoscunt Deum in Christo, sed non solo: vnde fit, vtinstar Iudæorum fingant opera, & instar gentium plures sibi Deos ponant aliarum atque aliarum rerum præsides. Qui illorum error eò vsque creuit, vt inter illos & gentes nihil videamus interesse.
units.tr: Take this as said to us too, namely that we abstain from those gods which our neighbours worship. What of those Jews, who indeed acknowledge God, but not as he has revealed and shown himself in the Son? We shall beware of that error, and shall adore God in the Son Jesus Christ, in whom goodness, justice and wisdom are chiefly seen. The Turks err in almost the same way, and we shall beware of them too. The Papists acknowledge God in Christ, but not in Christ alone; hence it comes about that, like the Jews, they fashion works, and, like the heathen, they set up for themselves many gods, patrons of this and that thing. Their error has grown so far that between them and the heathen we can see no difference.

units.la: At inquiunt, nos Deum vnum agnoscimus. Quid tum, inquam si agnoscas vnum multos colas,[?] autem colas? agnorunt & illi vnum summum, & tamen multos coluerunt. Pythagoras μόνας, quæ rerum omnium visa est exister principium, quid aliud, quàm Deum vnum repræsentauit? Multa sunt, inquit 1.Corinth.12. & varia dona, sed vnus omnium largitor Deus. Igitur hosce qui seducunt ab vno & vero Deo errores caue.
units.tr: But they say: we acknowledge one God. What then, I say, if you acknowledge one but worship many? They too acknowledged one supreme god, and yet worshipped many. Pythagoras, what else did he represent by the monad [μονάς], which seemed to be the principle of all things, than one God? "There are many and various gifts," says 1 Corinthians 12, "but one God who gives them all." Therefore beware of those errors which lead you away from the one and true God.

units.la: Idem etiam singulis dictum putabimus. Sunt enim vicini, quorum alius opes, alius optimatum amicitiam, alius alias res pluris quam Deum facit, in ijsque sibi spem suam positam habet. Ex quibus perspicuum est Iudæam, Turcicam, papisticam, aliasque superstitiones i-temq; ventrem & Mammonam, & Bachum & Venerem ceu Deos alienos caueri deberi. Quin etiam homo sibi ipsi quandoq; Deus est, adeò magni sese facit, & tenere sese diligit. Quicquid abducit à Deo, hoc totum ceu Deus alienus sit caue.
units.tr: We shall think this said to each individual too. For there are neighbours, one of whom makes wealth his god, another the friendship of the great, another makes other things more of than God, and places his hope in them. From this it is clear that Judaism, Turkishness, papistry and other superstitions, and likewise the belly and Mammon, and Bacchus and Venus, are to be beware of as strange gods. Indeed, a man is sometimes a god to himself, so greatly does he make much of himself and love to hold himself dear. Whatever draws you away from God, beware of it all as a strange god.

units.la: Esse Deum quid sit exponit hoc ipso quod dicit, ne sequamini. Quod Hebræi dicunt post aliquem ire, id est, habere aliquem sibi delectum viæ ducem, vitæ magistrum præeuntem, salutis atq; fortunarum patronum atq; vindicem. In quo dicto mirum est quantopere excrescat superstitio. Etenim si Deum quempiam preceris aliquid, idque contigerit ex animi sententia: quid fit? certe quod dicit Tityrus.
units.tr: What it is to have God he explains by this very thing he says: ye shall not go after. The Hebrews say that to go after someone is to have someone chosen as the guide of one's way, the teacher of one's life going before, the patron and defender of one's safety and fortunes. In this saying it is remarkable how greatly superstition grows. For if you pray to some god for something, and it happens according to your wishes, what follows? Surely what Tityrus says:

units.la: O Melibœa Deus nobis hæc otia fecit / Namq; erit ille mihi semper Deus, illius aram / Sæpe tener nostris ab ovilibus imbuet agnus.
units.tr: O Meliboeus, a god has made us this leisure, for he will always be a god to me, and often the tender lamb from our folds shall stain his altar.

units.la: Sin quod petieras non consequare, subit animum cogitatio, ne non satisfeceris, eaque cura ad maiorem superstitionem impelleris. Quid verbis opus est? semper te suspensum tenet atque anxium, quod res sit plena timoris superstitio. Vtinam ne peccares tam solicite caveres. Quamobrem esse Deum, aut habere aliquem Dei loco est ei ceu Deo salutifero, patrono, vindici addictum esse, omnes in eo spes opesqué collocare, vnum quem spectes, colas, vereare semper habere ob oculos positum. Vnde sequitur præcepti sensum esse, vt neminem nisi Deum optimum maximum colas, timeas, inuoces, & sequaris. At, inquis, qui possum? Se-quitur iam in remedijs.
units.tr: But if you do not obtain what you asked for, the thought comes to mind that you have not satisfied God, and that anxiety drives you into greater superstition. Why say more? It keeps you always hanging and anxious, because superstition is full of fear. Would that you did not sin, so that you might take care not to. Therefore, to have God, or to have something in God's place, is to be bound to him as to a saving God, patron and avenger, to place all hope and help in him, to regard, worship and always keep before your eyes the one God. From this it follows that the sense of the precept is that you should worship, fear, invoke and follow no one except the best and greatest God. "But," you say, "how can I?" Now it follows in the remedies.

units.la: Remedia contra πολυθεΐαν tria præbet, de natura Dei rectè sentire, ne Deum tentes cauere, eius verbo studere. Has res, quoniam nos vni Deo coniunctos tenent, sigillatim exponit singulas.
units.tr: The text offers three remedies against polytheism: to think rightly of the nature of God, to beware of tempting God, and to devote yourself to his Word. Since these things bind us to the one God, he sets out each of them separately.

units.la: I Syncerum de natura Dei iudicium. Quoniam, inquit, Dominus Deus tuus, qui in medio tui est, Deus zelotes est, ne indignetur contra te, & excindat te. Obserua notas quibus Dei natura describitur. Primam, In medio tui est, videlicet vbique præsens, audiens videnséque omnia. Quo circa falli non potest, vti possunt homines à falsis amicis: Vnde si illum simul ac peregrinos Deos sequi velis actum est. Difficile est imò non potest fieri, vt videntem & scientem decipias. pias. Quamobrem stolidus fis iuxta ac impius, qui Deum coneris fallere.
units.tr: I. A sound judgment of the nature of God. "Since," he says, "the Lord your God, who is in the midst of you, is a jealous God, lest his anger be kindled against you and he destroy you." Observe the marks by which the nature of God is described. The first is "he is in the midst of you," that is, present everywhere, hearing and seeing all things. Therefore he cannot be deceived, as men can be deceived by false friends. Hence, if you wish to follow him and also foreign gods, it is over for you. It is difficult, indeed it is impossible, that you should deceive one who sees and knows; therefore you become as foolish as you are impious if you try to deceive God.

units.la: Altera, Sua natura ζelotes est. Esa.42. dicit gloriam meam alteri non dabo. Nec thiruth, cum ipse crearit omnia, conferuet omnia: cur alium quasi conditorem colas: cur alium quasi patronum inuoces? Et aemulatio illa matrimonij similitudine exprimitur, quippe in quo coniugum amor sic mutuus esse debeat, vt tertium non admittat. Igitur Deum scito non ferre, vt ipsum simul colas, & sequare mammona.
units.tr: The second is that by his nature he is jealous. Isaiah 42 says, "my glory I will not give to another." Nor, since he himself created all things and preserves all things, why should you worship another as though he were the creator, or invoke another as though he were the patron? That jealousy is expressed by the likeness of marriage, in which the love of the spouses ought to be so mutual that it admits no third party. Therefore know that God will not tolerate your worshipping him and at the same time following Mammon.

units.la: Tertia, Ne iratus excindat te. Discis iram illius terrori esse debere, ac non quasi formica irritaris negligendam esse. Exempla testata sunt quid sit illius indignatio. Nohæ seculum, Ægyptus, Saul, Israel, Iuda, Roma, Germania. Quamobrem ne cum mundo peccemus etiam reluctante Deo & prohibente. Neq; enim impune abierit is, cui Deus indignatur.
units.tr: The third is "lest, angry, he destroy you." You learn that his anger ought to be a terror to you, and that you must not provoke it as if it were an ant to be neglected. Examples bear witness to what his indignation is: the age of Noah, Egypt, Saul, Israel, Judah, Rome, Germany. Therefore let us not sin with the world, even when God resists and forbids. For he to whom God is angry will not go away unpunished.

units.la: II Ne eum tentes cauere. Ne tentetis Dominum Deum vestrum, inquit, sicut in Massa. Pau cis verbis eam, quæ Num.21. describitur, historiam repetit. De qua nonnihil & quantum ad præsentem locum attinet dicendum est.
units.tr: II. To beware of tempting him. "You shall not tempt the Lord your God, he says, as you tempted him at Massah." In a few words he repeats the story described in Numbers 21. About this, something must be said, and as far as the present passage is concerned.

units.la: Tentare est actio hominis propria, videlicet quale quiddam sit experiri periculum aliquâ de refratre, & qualem sit euentum habitura velit cognoscere, veluti de equo, de cultro sit periculum. Qui naturam causas atque euentus rerum nouit, is verè & proprie non tentat, quippe qui prius norit quale quiddam sit futurum, quàm ipsum fiat eiusmodi. Veluti medicus in iis morbis, quos cognitos habet curandis remedia non tentat, sed in raris & in nouis, in quibus certas rationes nullas habet. Deus autem quia scit successus & euentus rerum, vt eos cognoscat minimè tentat: homo qui illos nescit, tentat. Sic Solomonem regem, an quanta audit us erat pollere sapientia, præstaret, regina Saba quæstionibus tentasse dicitur: sic Christū Sadducæi tentant: sic Æsopicus ille tenebrio manu comprehensam auem tentat Apollinem. Eodem modo se res in tentatione Dei habet, vt qui illius bonitatem & veritatem recte norit, de ea nolit facere periculum, quippe qui sciat illum secus, quàm pro sua natura, nihil posse facere: qui vero hanc fidei [?]ἁπλησφορίαν non habet, quique de tam bona quàm prædicatur Dei natura dubitat, is Deum tentare solet, & an iustus, verus, bonus, clemens sit experiri velle.
units.tr: To tempt is a human action: to try a danger in some matter, wishing to know what sort of thing it is and what outcome it will have, as one tests a horse or a knife for danger. One who knows the nature, causes and outcomes of things does not, truly and properly speaking, tempt, since he knows beforehand what sort of thing will happen before it happens. Thus a physician does not try remedies in the diseases he knows how to cure, but in rare and new ones, in which he has no certain principles. But God, because he knows the successes and outcomes of things, does not tempt at all in order to learn them; man, who does not know them, tempts. So it is said that the Queen of Sheba tested King Solomon with questions, to see whether the wisdom he was said to possess was real; so the Sadducees tempted Christ; so that Aesopian trickster tempted Apollo with a bird he held in his hand. In the same way it stands with temptation of God: one who rightly knows his goodness and truth is unwilling to make trial of it, since he knows that God can do nothing otherwise than according to his nature. But one who lacks this full assurance of faith, and doubts whether God's nature is as good as it is proclaimed, is accustomed to tempt God, and wishes to try whether he is just, true, good and merciful.

units.la: Quod accidit trifariam. 1. Cum media vel parando bono, vel declinando malo defti-nata relpuit, & quod cupit alio modo conatur efficere, vt qui fine velte frigere, fine labore ditescere, non ponte transflumen strato vti, sed tranare non postulante necesitate velit. Quod Christus Matth.4. suo exemplo, quando scalis vti maluit, quàm è pinnis templi defi-lire, ne tentaret Deum indicauit. Iudæi vero & nostra ætate multi contemptis ijs quæ habe-mus signis, noua petunt hoc: ipso Deum tentant.
units.tr: This happens in three ways. (1) When, rejecting the means appointed either for obtaining a good or for avoiding an evil, a man tries to achieve by another way what he desires: as one who wishes to be warm without fire, to grow rich without work, or to cross a river by swimming when no necessity demands it, instead of using a bridge. Christ showed in his own example that this is tempting God, in Matthew 4, when he preferred to use the stairs rather than throw himself down from the pinnacle of the temple. The Jews, and in our own age many, having despised the signs we have, seek new ones, and by this very thing tempt God.

units.la: 2. Cum habemus promissa quidem amplissima, sed deficiunt nos media, quando qui sunt impatientes & increduli statim deficiunt, deo; & tempus præscribunt, & modum au-xilij. Non agnoscunt omnipotentem esse Deum, nec secum repetunt morae causas. Exemplo sunt quod diximus Num.21. descriptum esse; & illud 1.Cor.10. depictum ab Apostolo. Sed extat præclara hac de reludithæ oratio.
units.tr: (2) When we have very ample promises, but the means fail us; then those who are impatient and unbelieving at once lose heart in God, and prescribe to him the time and the manner of help. They do not acknowledge that God is almighty, nor do they reckon up again the causes of the delay. Examples are what we said is described in Numbers 21, and what the Apostle portrays in 1 Corinthians 10. But there is a notable discourse on this matter in Hebrews.

units.la: 3. Cum impœnitentia nostra Dei longanimitatem prouocamus. Vulgaris proh dolor nostri seculi tentatio hæc est. Nam vt vt graues pœnas Deus minitetur, tamen rarus est qui resipiscat: plæriq; ogganniunt iam diu minas has auditas, mala hactenus nunquam visa esse, quod de iudicio Domini dicimus incertum esse & dubium. Atque hæc tentatio omnis, vti nunc exposita est à Deo, prorsus auocat homines primum ad nos ipsos, tum ad creaturas & illicita media, denique etiam ad ventrem & præsens seculum. Quamobrem ab his est abstinendum, vt Deum vnum rebus omnibus rectis sequare, & venerere.
units.tr: (3) When by our impenitence we provoke God's long-suffering. Alas, this is the common temptation of our age. For although God threatens grievous punishments, yet few repent; most have long been mocking these threats, since they have heard them, and say that evils have never yet been seen, and that the judgment of the Lord is uncertain and doubtful. And all this temptation, as it has now been set out, utterly draws men away, first to themselves, then to creatures and forbidden means, and finally to the belly and the present age. Therefore we must abstain from these things, so that we may follow and revere the one God in all right things.

units.la: III. Eius verbo studere: id quoniam est primarium contra hanc pestem remedium, diligentissimè exponitur. Docet enim hoc loco Moses, vti verbi diuini studio cum nos ipsos, tum etiam nostros omnes exerceamus, ne vel nos ipsi, vel liberi nostri, quo minus vni Deo adhæreamus, impediant.
units.tr: III. To devote oneself to his Word. Since this is the chief remedy against this plague, it is set out most diligently. For Moses teaches in this place that we should exercise ourselves, and our children too, in the study of the divine Word, so that neither we ourselves nor our children may hinder us from cleaving to the one God.

units.la: Ac de nobis dicit diligentissimè.1. Custodienda præcepta, testimonia, ritus Domini, quæ præcepit: quasi dicat omnia, quocunque nomine, Dei placita summo studio feruanda sunt.
units.tr: He speaks most carefully about us: (1) "the precepts, testimonies and rites of the Lord, which he has commanded, you shall keep," as if to say that all the things God has pleased to lay down, under whatever name, must be kept with the greatest care.

units.la: 2. Quod rectum & bonum est in oculis Domini id facies: non quod tibi videtur bonum. Dei solius est de religione statuere, nō hominis. Respuitur, hic ἐθελοθρησκία, gilt gmeint/ gutdunckt/ dünckt ab vō Gott. Valeant ergo bonę intentiones, quibus superstitio defenditur.
units.tr: (2) "You shall do what is right and good in the eyes of the Lord," not what seems good to you. It belongs to God alone to decide about religion, not to man. Here self-chosen worship is rejected: what seems good to oneself, what one thinks, what one supposes is from God. Let good intentions, by which superstition is defended, therefore fare badly.

units.la: 3 Vt bene sit, tibi, vt introeas, possideas, superes, quemadmodum promisit Dominus. Sic memi-nerimus nos promisionibus diuinis in officio retinendos esse. Nam cum tanta, ac tam præclara bona suarum legum studijs promiserit & preftare etiam consueuerit Dominus: certe in fe ipse & in Deum impius erit quisquis illarum desiderio non du[?]tus leges has seruauerit.
units.tr: (3) "That it may go well with you, and that you may go in and possess, and overcome, as the Lord has promised." So let us remember that we must be kept to our duty by the divine promises. For since the Lord has promised such great and splendid goods to those who study his laws, and is accustomed to perform them, certainly whoever keeps these laws without being moved by desire for those goods will be impious towards himself and towards God.

units.la: Liberos autem sic vult instrui: Cumq; interrogauerit te, &c. Quo iubet vt dicamus liberis quales fimus, quales fuerimus, quis nos redemerit, & quo pacto hoc effecerit, quid item requirat a nobis, vt grati fimus, vt seruiamus ei. Inde existit vera iustitia. Hanc quoniam assequi nostris viribus non possumus, Christus fide comprehendendus erit, vt sufficiat. Amen.
units.tr: He wishes children to be taught in this way: "And when he asks you, etc." By this he bids us tell our children what we are, what we were, who redeemed us and how he did it, and further what he requires of us, that we may be thankful and serve him. From this true righteousness arises. Since we cannot attain this by our own strength, we must lay hold of Christ by faith, so that he may suffice. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT VII. SERMO IIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII. SERMON IV.

units.la: Cum introduxerit te Dominus Deus tuus in terram ad quam tu proficisceris, vt eam possideas, & eiecerit gentes multas ante te, nempe Hithæum, Gergesæum, Amorræum, Chananæum, Pherizæum, Hiuæum, & Iebusæum, septem gentes maiores & robustiores te.
units.tr: When the Lord your God has brought you into the land which you are going to possess, and has driven out many nations before you, namely the Hittite, the Girgashite, the Amorite, the Canaanite, the Perizzite, the Hivite and the Jebusite, seven nations greater and stronger than you.

units.la: 2 Tradideritq; eas Dominus Deus tuus ante te, feries eas, & omnino exter-minabis, nec feries cum eis pactum, neq; miseriaris earum.
units.tr: 2 And when the Lord your God has delivered them up before you, you shall strike them and utterly destroy them; you shall make no covenant with them, nor show mercy to them.

units.la: 3 Neiungas cum eis affinitatem, filiam tuam ne des filio earum, neq; filiam earum despondeas filio tuo.
units.tr: 3 You shall not make marriages with them: do not give your daughter to their son, nor take their daughter for your son.

units.la: 4 Quoniam auocabit filium tuum à me, seruiet Dijs alienis, & commouebitur furor Domini contra vos, vt cito te deleat.
units.tr: 4 For they will turn your son away from me, so that he serves other gods; and the anger of the Lord will be kindled against you, and he will quickly destroy you.

units.la: 5 Sic autem facies eis, aras eorum diruetis, statuas eorum confringetis, lucos eorum succidatis, & sculpta eorum simulachra igne comburetis.
units.tr: 5 But this is how you shall deal with them: you shall break down their altars, smash their pillars, cut down their groves, and burn their carved images with fire.

units.la: BI Diuus Moses hoc vj. capite primæ legis expositionem est auspicatus, iuxtaque docuit quoniam nos ad eius obseruantiam accommodare oporteat: iam septi-mum cap. sequitur, quo nos admodet, vt ab omni incredulorum hominum consortio abstineamus. Qua in re quoniam & magnum est, & præsens periculum, diligentissime eam ipse rem persequitur. Ac primum proponit ob oculos quasi depictam causam totam, simul etiam docens, quomodo fit efficiendum quod Deus postulat: dein quasi densum quoddam argumentorum agmen adducit, quibus eò propellat: denique concludit in vnum aggregata rei totius perficiendæ ratione.
units.tr: Divine Moses began the exposition of the first law in the sixth chapter, and he taught at that point how we ought to adapt ourselves to its observance. Now the seventh chapter follows, in which he urges us to keep away from all association with unbelieving men. Since this matter is both of great importance and a present danger, he pursues it with the greatest care. First he sets before our eyes, as if painted, the whole case, and at the same time teaches how what God demands is to be carried out; then he brings forward a dense column of arguments by which he drives us toward it; finally he sums up the whole method of accomplishing the matter, gathered into one.

units.la: Sed in præsentia propositio seu narratio rei proponitur absoluta suis numeris omnibus, & ad viuum depicta suis circumstantijs, vt tempore, loco, persona, reipsa, causa, modo. Omnium summa ac caput est. Cum Deus vos in has terras introduxerit & collocarit, tum ab omni societatis peregrinæ genere prorsus abstine:hæc[?] enim est exitio, & vt tutus fis tibi potius extirpandæ sunt omnes gentes illæ.
units.tr: But here the proposition, or narrative of the matter, is set out complete in all its parts and painted to the life with its circumstances: time, place, person, thing itself, cause, and manner. It is the sum and head of the whole. When God has brought you into these lands and settled you there, then abstain altogether from every kind of foreign association; for this is destruction. And so that you may be safe, all those nations must rather be utterly rooted out.

units.la: Cum introduxerit te Dominus. Id est, quando occasiones iustas & legitimas tibi Deus suppeditarit, iusque belli in illas gentes habueris, tunc eas excindas iubeo. Qua de re & supra quoque dictum est in exemplis iurisgentium. Erat eos in has terras introducturus, sed eam ad rem adhibendæ erant legitimæ rationes, & prius comparandum ius belli, quam terram adorirentur. Non enim iubet Dominus suum alijs iniuste eripere. Quamobrem tempus occupandis his terris id definit, quo eius incolæ conditionibus æquissimis repudiatis iustam belli causam præberent. Hac occasione tam bona ac pulchra ne abutantur, vt in turpem pacem cum impijs coeant, admonet. Ex quo discimus non præuenire ius, verum ob latum persequi. Sic optimus quisque tempus oportunum spectat.
units.tr: When the Lord has brought you in. That is: when God has furnished you with just and lawful occasions, and you have the right of war against those nations, then I command you to destroy them. On this matter something has also been said above, in the examples of the law of nations. He was going to bring them into these lands, but for this purpose lawful grounds had to be applied, and the right of war had to be obtained before they attacked the land. For the Lord does not command his people to seize what belongs to others unjustly. Therefore he fixes the time for occupying these lands as the point when their inhabitants, having rejected the most equitable terms, had given a just cause for war. He warns them not to abuse this so good and fine an opportunity by joining in a shameful peace with the impious. From this we learn not to anticipate the right, but to pursue it when it is ripe. In this way every good man watches for a fitting time.

units.la: Locus, In terram, inquit, ad quam possidendam proficisceris. Vbi igitur te Deus esse voluit & longa profectione fessum fatigatumq; quiete recreauit: ibi ne pace & quiete abutare.
units.tr: As to place: "into the land," he says, "which you are going to possess." Where therefore God has willed you to be, and has refreshed you with rest after your long journey, weary and worn out: there do not abuse peace and quiet.

units.la: Sed multa sunt istic res quibus, parum firmi si simus, adducimur vt etiam cum hominibus impijs commercia haberi iure posse autumemus. Primum quia sedes ea nobis sit tribu-ta diuinitus in qua habitent illi.
