Proptereaque manendum istic esse vbi Deus collocarit: dein ululandum cum lupis, cum quibus esse cupis: denique bene cum sit hominibus præsens seculum magis,quàm Deum quem oculis non cernimus,reueremur.
units.tr: But there are many things in that place by which we, if we are not firm enough, are drawn to think that we may rightly have dealings with impious men as well. First, because that dwelling has been assigned to us by God, in which those others live; and therefore we must remain where God has placed us. Next, we must howl with the wolves among whom we wish to be. Finally, since the present world is nearer to men, we tend to revere men more than God, whom we do not see with our eyes.

units.la: Quamobrem cum locus videtur ad malum inuitare, danda est opera, vt animum aduersus has illecebras muniamus cogitatione contraria.Etenim cum bene habeas,cur non illum potius sequeris,qui illam tibi fortunam tam lautam atque opimam dedit? Quod fi sic cogites, locus pietatis potius, quàm praeposterae pacis aut alicuius peregrinae iocietatis nos admoneat.
units.tr: Therefore, when the place seems to invite us to evil, care must be taken to fortify our minds against these allurements by contrary thoughts. For since you are doing well, why not rather follow him who gave you such a rich and plentiful fortune? If you reflect in this way, the place should remind us rather of godliness than of a perverse peace or of some foreign fellowship.

units.la: Personas nominat Hittæum, Gergefæum, Amorrhæum, Chananæum, Pherefæum, Hiuæ-um, Iebufæum septem gentes maiores & robustiores, &c. Istos populos Deus auxerat honoribus, opibus, viribus: illi his abusi grauiter peccabant cede,rapina,luxu,fastu. Conniuet Deus diu:tandem fatis irritatus Israelitas adducit, ijsque mandat vt sint executores diuinae iustitiae potius,quàm humanae iniustitiae participes.Habes testimonia de his cum multis in locis alijs tum Genef.decimo quinto,& Amos fecundo.cap. Ac de peccatis eorum Gen. decimo quinto. cap. Vbi posteris Abrahae terras eas pollicetur, sed indicat nondum tempus hoc adesse,quia nondum sint completa peccata eorum.De poena vero Amos 2.dicitur: Amorhæum deleueram ante vos instar cedrorum procerum & instar quercuum robustorum,at supernè fructus &inferne radices perdidi.
units.tr: He names the peoples: the Hittite, the Girgashite, the Amorite, the Canaanite, the Perizzite, the Hivite and the Jebusite, seven nations greater and stronger, and so on. God had increased these peoples with honours, wealth and strength; but they abused these things and sinned grievously by slaughter, robbery, luxury and pride. God for a long time overlooked it, but at last, provoked enough by their crimes, he brings the Israelites in and commands them to be executors of divine justice rather than partners in human injustice. You have testimonies about these people in many places, among them Genesis 15 and Amos 2. And concerning their sins, Genesis 15 speaks; there he promises those lands to the posterity of Abraham, but shows that the time has not yet come, because their sins were not yet complete. Concerning the punishment, Amos 2 says: "I destroyed the Amorite before you, like tall cedars and strong oaks; yet I destroyed his fruit above and his roots below."

units.la: Qui duo loci fatis perspicue docent quam diu conniueat ad peccata hominum Deus: quàm contra puniat & vindicet grauiter scelera. Quamobrem fi longanimitate Dei fiat,vt diu tyrannidem exerceant impij,noli illorum exemplo offendi. <bl>Der Frug gaat fo Dict zum Brunnen bis er bricht.</bl> Magnifici,illustres tertremendi sunt, verum illos propterea noli tu pluris quam Deum facere. Noli æmulari in malignantibus. Pulchra species est personæ,sed Deum imitatus personam ne respicias, Deum amicum tibi retine: Deus est bonus, fidus, potens,æternus: illi videntur quidem, sed non sunt boni, promittunt, sed non seruant fidem,videntur,sed non sunt potentes,quin Deus illos brachium carnis appellat,æterni adeo non sunt,vt mortalitatem quotidie sentiant.Verum hoc esse exempla docent.Vbi enim sunt Esau,Nimroth,Saul,illi Cananæi,Antiochus,Iulius,Alexander & cæteri? Verisimum sane est quod de his scripsit Horatius idem exemplis colligens ad hunc modum.
units.tr: These two passages teach quite clearly how long God overlooks the sins of men, and how severely, on the other hand, he punishes and avenges crimes. Therefore, if it happens through the patience of God that the impious exercise tyranny for a long time, do not be offended by their example. The pitcher goes to the well until it breaks. The magnates and illustrious men are to be feared, yet do not for that reason esteem them above God. Do not emulate those who do evil. The appearance of a person is fine, but in imitating God, do not look at the person; keep God as your friend. God is good, faithful, powerful and eternal. They seem indeed to be so, but they are not good; they promise, but they do not keep faith; they seem powerful, but they are not, since God calls them "arm of flesh"; and they are so far from eternal that they feel their mortality every day. Yet examples teach that this is so. For where are Esau, Nimrod, Saul, those Canaanites, Antiochus, Julius, Alexander and the rest? What Horace wrote about these men is truly very apt, gathering examples in this way:

units.la: Quo pius Æneas,quo Tullus dines & Ancus? Pulvis & umbra sumus.
units.tr: Where are pious Aeneas, where rich Tullus and Ancus? We are dust and shadow.

units.la: An non erat potentissimus Æneas superato Turno & acquisito Latio? & certe cum illo affinitatem contrahere videbatur operaeprecium esse: & tamen hic illum appellat puluerem. Quare etsi Cananæi isti potentes sint,& robusti, tamen cum illis non est contrahenda ami-citia,siquidem rebus nostris bene confultum velimus.
units.tr: Was not Aeneas most powerful, once Turnus was overcome and Latium acquired? And certainly it seemed worth while to form a marriage alliance with him; yet here Horace calls him dust. Therefore, even if these Canaanites are powerful and strong, friendship must not be made with them, if we wish our affairs to be well ordered.

units.la: Res ipsa sic exprimitur, Omnino exterminabis,nec feries cum eis pactum,nec miserearis earum,nec iungas cum eis affinitatem, filiam tuam ne des filio earum, &c. Quibus verbis indicat Deum velle eas deletas,propterea que eorum qui Deo obedire volunt, vt idem velint intelligere:non autem contra quicquam faciant. Omnino ait,exterminabis: Vti malum est maximum bonos opprimere,sic fouere & tueri malos peccatum est maximum.
units.tr: The matter itself is expressed thus: You shall utterly destroy them; you shall make no covenant with them, nor show mercy to them, nor make marriages with them, do not give your daughter to their son, and so on. By these words he shows that God wishes them to be destroyed, and therefore that those who want to obey God should also will the same, and should not do anything to the contrary. He says "utterly destroy": just as it is the greatest evil to oppress the good, so it is the greatest sin to foster and protect the wicked.

units.la: Sed eccum nostros mores. Fideles eijciuntur finibus,blasphemi sunt in pretio: qui carnibus vescitur diebus iure papistico illicitis,punitur: qui humano sanguine victum sibi quærunt sunt in pretio. Omitto quæ putantur vulgaria scelera, quibus virtutes maximas anteponimus. An non hoc est contra ire Domini iudicio? Si magistratus iniquissimis animis ferrent,si quis de sua sententia discederet, aut eam impugnaret? Quamobrem vt nostra facta sint iudicio Domini conformia,prohibet omni illarum gentium societate.
units.tr: But look at our own manners. The faithful are driven out of the lands, blasphemers are held in high esteem; the man who eats meat on days forbidden by papistical law is punished, while those who seek their living by human blood are held in high esteem. I pass over the crimes that are thought commonplace, while we prefer the greatest virtues to them. Is this not contrary to the judgment of the Lord? What if the magistrates were to endure with the most unjust spirit anyone who departed from their opinion, or who opposed it? Therefore, so that our deeds may conform to the judgment of the Lord, he forbids all association with those nations.

units.la: Ac duo potisfima amicitiarum genera nominat, vnum publicum, priuatum alterum. Publicum est foedus, seu quaecunque societas. Ea est mutua duorum aut plurium in vnam vitæ, & fortunarum societatem coeuntium, ad se tuendum & conseruandum facta obligatio.
units.tr: And he names two chief kinds of friendship, one public and the other private. The public kind is a covenant, or any society whatever. It is a binding obligation, mutually undertaken by two or more who come together into one society of life and fortunes, for defending and preserving one another.

units.la: Ex quo perspicuum est eum, qui fit obligatus & coniunctus alicui, iam purum putum amplius non esse, verum mixtum atque ex se & illo socio compositum. Veluti argentum si quid metalli coniunctum habeat vt cupri,purum putum esse desijt. Ergo Deus, qui nos fi-bi totos vendicat,hæc fœdera vetuit. Si Senatus nulli prouinciæ permittit, vt cum alienis populis in quodcunque foedus coeant: cur Deus nobis clientibus suis hoc permiserit?
units.tr: From this it is clear that the one who is bound and joined to someone is no longer pure and simple, but a mixture composed of himself and that partner. Just as silver, if it has some metal joined to it, such as copper, ceases to be pure. Therefore God, who claims us wholly as his own, forbids these covenants. If the Senate permits no province to enter into any covenant with foreign peoples, why would God have permitted this to us, who are his clients?

units.la: Priuatum est matrimonium, quippe quod eo ipso priuati inter se homines in vnam sociëtatem coëant.In quo omnino eadem est ratio.Quare iubet etiam hoc abstinéamus.
units.tr: Marriage is a private matter, since by that very fact private individuals join together in one society. The reasoning here is entirely the same, so he commands us to abstain from this too.

units.la: Nec miserearis,inquit. Videtur præclarum esse si quis parcat nocentibus:at eos qui Deum volunt imitari decet, vt coniunctam cum misericordia habeant iustitiam. Sic enim & Deus nostri misertus est,vt iustitiæ nihil detraheretur. Saul Amelechitis, Achab Benhadæ Syro pepercerunt non fine suo damno maximo. Et nostra ætas nobis exempla dedit cum in Heluetia primum,tum deinceps in Germania. Quamobrem occasione & victoria qui sa-pit vtitur.
units.tr: "Nor shall you show pity," he says. It may seem a fine thing to spare the guilty, but those who want to imitate God ought to join justice with mercy. For God himself showed mercy to us without any loss to his justice. Saul spared the Amalekites, and Ahab spared Ben-hadad the Syrian, and not without their own very great loss. Our own age has also given us examples, first in Helvetia and afterwards in Germany. Therefore the wise man makes use of the opportunity and the victory.

units.la: Causa Quoniam anocabit filium tuum a me, seruiet, Diis alienis & commonebitur, &c. Causas duas commemorat: vnam, quod ab amore & cultu Dei recto & integro reuocent:alte-ram,quod Dei in nos iram vocant,accersantque exitium.
units.tr: Because he will turn your son away from me, and he will serve other gods, and he will be provoked, &c. He mentions two reasons: first, that such marriages turn people away from the true and sincere love and worship of God; second, that they provoke God's anger against us and bring on destruction.

units.la: Auocant,modis multis & varijs videlicet. Ac potissimum quod amicitia similitudinem morum & mutuas operas atq; auxilia, denique etiam plenas consensiones generet. Iam quia pietas in homine est imbecillis,& naturæ prauæ motu facile vincitur, periculum est ne bo-nus degeneret potius, quàm malus fiat melior. Est sociorum habere communes hostes,& communes amicos:quid putas fiet de Deo Deiqúe cultoribus, quos impius socius hostium loco habet?Vnde Psalm. 83.conqueritur Dominus quod populus Dei fœderatus sit impio-rum,quodq; impijs gentibus sese brachium præbuerint aduersus Dominum.
units.tr: They turn us away, in many ways and by various means, of course. Above all, friendship produces a likeness of morals, mutual services and help, and finally full agreement. Since piety is weak in a human being and is easily overcome by the pull of a corrupt nature, there is a danger that the good man will degenerate rather than the bad man becoming better. Allies share common enemies and common friends. What do you suppose will happen to God and to those who worship God, when an ungodly ally regards them as enemies? For this reason the Lord complains in Psalm 83 that the people of God have made a league with the ungodly, and that the nations have given their arm to the Lord's enemies.

units.la: Dei in nos iram nostrumque exitium nobis accersunt, quod exempla populi Dei do-cent.Rex Afa quamdiu sideret Domino saluus est,vbi cum impijs inijt fœdera,malum sibi con-sciuit.Exemplum præclarum est Iofaphat cum Achabo bellum contra Syros gerens. In ma-trimonio Solomon exemplo est & Samson,&c.Achab etiam.
units.tr: They bring upon us God's anger and our own ruin, as the examples of the people of God teach. King Asa was safe as long as he trusted in the Lord, but when he entered into covenants with the ungodly, he brought evil upon himself. Jehoshaphat's case is a notable example, when he waged war against the Syrians together with Ahab. In marriage, Solomon and Samson are examples, &c. Ahab too.

units.la: Quid igitur faciasʼan rescindenda fœdera & matrimoniaʼminime vero: Hoc enim ne-que euangelium docet,neque ratio suaserit. Euangelium enim iura non tollit, nec fidem da-tam violat. Quid hic facto opus fit Diuus Paulus in 1.Corinth. 7. docet:Dicit enim:Si quis vxorem habeat infidelem , & hæc assentitur vt habitet cum illo, ne dimittat eam. Et muli-er quæ,&c. Ex quo perspicuum est matrimonia atque fœdera antea cum impijs contracta non dissolui religione Christiana, verum noua cauenda esse : Etenim ipsa quoque fœdera non parum momenti ad augendam remp. afferunt. Aucta est exterarum gentium societa-te Roma. Vti in Orat.pro Cornelio Balbo confitetur Cicero. Nec mirum sic augeri ciuita-tes,quia sese mutuo conferuant, vt extat in l. non dubito.ff.de capti.& postlim.reuerf. Vbi dicit Bartholus in sociorum æque atque in nostros ipsorum hostes animaduerti posse. Sed quoniam in fœderibus est seruanda æqualitas,vti præcipit Imp.in Authen. de non eligend. secund.nup.§.illud quoque dubium: sane quis non videat hæc fœdera quæ cum impijs se-riuntur,quoniam sunt dissimillimorum populorum,nec recta nec vtilia esse? Quamobrem quæ habemus à maioribus iŏta[?], quoad pars volet altera,seruabimus , neperfidiæ notam E-uangelio inuramus:noua autem quæ feriri possent, cauenda nobis arbitrabimur. Sic enim videtur præcipere coniugibus apostolus. Est enim iniquum, vt idem ait, nos iugum trahe-re cum infidelibus:est illicitum vt Hieronymus contra Iouinianum scribens ait,templa Chri-sti idolis prostitui. Vnde Ambrosius in epistola 70.ad Vigilium scribens ait, Christiani ho-minis esse à fidelibus non infidelibus matrimonia petere. Est enim hic præsens periculum, quando religionis studium impeditur,& amor Deo non omnis,vti par erat,tribuitur,& qui Dei gloriam promouere debebat,is impijs in causa mala iure societatis affert auxilium.
units.tr: What then should you do? Should covenants and marriages be annulled? By no means. Neither the gospel teaches this nor does reason advise it. For the gospel does not abolish rights or violate a pledge once given. What must be done in this matter, the divine Paul teaches in 1 Corinthians 7, for he says: "If any brother has a wife who is an unbeliever, and she is content to dwell with him, let him not put her away." And "the woman who..." &c. From this it is plain that marriages and covenants entered into with the ungodly before are not dissolved by the Christian religion; rather, new ones must be guarded against. Indeed, covenants themselves contribute no little to the growth of the commonwealth. Rome grew by its alliance with foreign nations, as Cicero admits in his speech for Cornelius Balbus. Nor is it surprising that states grow in this way, since they mutually preserve one another, as is set out in the law "Non dubito", Digest on captives and postliminy. There Bartolus says that this can be observed both in allies and in our own enemies. But since equality must be maintained in covenants, as the emperor prescribes in the Authentic "de non eligendis secundo nuptiis", paragraph "illud quoque dubium", who does not see that covenants struck with the ungodly, since they are between most dissimilar peoples, are neither right nor useful? Therefore we shall keep those inherited from our forefathers, so far as the other party is willing, and we shall not brand the gospel with the mark of faithlessness; but those new ones which might be struck we shall consider must be guarded against. For this is how the apostle seems to instruct spouses. For it is unfair, as he says, to draw the yoke with unbelievers; and it is unlawful, as Jerome writes against Jovinian, for the temples of Christ to be prostituted to idols. Hence Ambrose, writing in his letter 70 to Vigilius, says that it belongs to a Christian man to seek marriages from among believers, not unbelievers. For the danger is present here whenever zeal for religion is hindered and love for God is not given wholly, as it ought to be, and one who ought to promote the glory of God gives aid to the ungodly in an evil cause by the right of alliance.

units.la: Dicit aras,statuas,lucos,simulachra succidite,ne quid sit reliquiarum facito. Sem-per male cessit Israelitis quod excelsa non euerterent. Christo pure seruiant omnia. Ni-hil habeat sibi seruiens Belial. Sic prima de amore Dei pleno & perfecto lex seruabitur. Id faxit Dominus.Amen.
units.tr: Break down their altars, their statues, their groves, and their images, and leave nothing of them. It has always gone badly for Israel that they did not overthrow the high places. Let everything serve Christ purely; let Belial have nothing to do with the one who serves. In this way the first law, concerning full and perfect love of God, will be kept. May the Lord grant this. Amen.

units.la: SERMO V.
units.tr: SERMON V.

units.la: 6 Nam populus sanctus es tu Domino Deo tuo, te elegit Dominus Deus tuus vt sis ei populus peculiaris præ omnibus populis qui sunt super faciem terræ.
units.tr: For you are a holy people to the Lord your God. The Lord your God has chosen you to be his peculiar people above all the peoples who are upon the face of the earth.

units.la: 7 Neq; ob id vos tam ardenter dilexit atque elegit Dominus quod plures sitis alijs populis, (quum sitis pauciores omnibus populis.)
units.tr: The Lord did not set his love and choice upon you because you were more numerous than other peoples, since you are fewer than all peoples.

units.la: 8 Sed quia dilexit vos, & seruáre voluit iuramentum quod iurauit patribus vestris, eduxit vos Dominus, ualida manu, & redemit te de domo seruitutis, de manu Pharaonis Regis Ægypti.
units.tr: But because he loved you and wished to keep the oath he swore to your fathers, the Lord brought you out with a mighty hand and redeemed you from the house of bondage, from the hand of Pharaoh, king of Egypt.

units.la: 9 Scias itaq; quod Dominus Deus ipse est Deus, Deus fidelis seruans fœdus illud, & misericordiam diligentibus se, & seruantibus præcepta eius in mille secula.
units.tr: Know therefore that the Lord your God is God, the faithful God who keeps that covenant and mercy towards those who love him and keep his commandments, to a thousand generations.

units.la: 10 Reddit denique ijs, qui oderunt eum in faciem suas, ut perdat eos, nec tardat, quin ijs qui eum oderunt, in faciem suas reddat.
units.tr: And he repays to their face those who hate him, so as to destroy them. He does not delay, but repays to their face those who hate him.

units.la: 11 Custodies itaq; præcepta ritus & iudicia, quæ ego præcipio tibi hodie vt facias ea.
units.tr: You shall therefore keep the precepts, the rites and the judgments which I command you today, that you may do them.

units.la: QVod vulgo dici solet malorum consortio nos ceu peste quadam infici, & vnius ouis scabiem in gregem vniuersum serpere: id adeo omnes quotidie experimur verum esse, vt nemo sit cuius persuadendi gratia dictum hoc longiore probatione egeat. Quo circa Diuus Moses, quo nos in amore Dei vero ac pleno retineat, ab incredulorum commercio dehortatur, ac docet nos, si Deum perinde, vt prima lege præcipitur, amore veneratione fide velimus prosequi, inimicorum Dei commercium omne fugiamus necesse esse.
units.tr: It is commonly said that we are infected by the company of wicked men as by a kind of plague, and that the scab of one sheep creeps through the whole flock. We all experience daily that this is true, so that no one needs a lengthy proof to be persuaded of it. Therefore divine Moses, in order to keep us in the true and full love of God, dissuades us from dealings with unbelievers, and teaches us that if we wish to pursue God with love, reverence and faith, as the first law prescribes, we must necessarily flee every association with the enemies of God.

units.la: Sed quia mundanarum illarum amicitiarum illecebræ, ceu magnes quispiam, omnia ad se trahunt, nosque eas ægre deserimus: quo nos istuc adigat, in secunda præsentis Cap. parte bonas causas affert, atque indicat; primum id nos decere, tum nobis conducere, denique facile factu fore.
units.tr: But since the allurements of those worldly friendships, like some magnet, draw everything to themselves, and we abandon them only with difficulty, he gives good reasons to bring us to this, and points them out in the second part of the present chapter: first, that it befits us; then, that it is to our advantage; finally, that it will be easy to do.

units.la: Ac quantum ad decorum pertinet, de eo primum omnium disserit, & eum ipsum locum sanè quàm diligenter explicat, quippe quod præclara sit decori ratio. Minuenda enim atque explodenda est quorundam hominum opinio, qui mortales siue pares esse, siue æquales omnes autumant, cum ætas, sexus, fortuna, artes, quæque sunt generis eiusdem alia inter nos mille discrimina faciant. Unde fit ut aliud divitem, aliud pauperem deceat: aliud item senem, aliud juvenem, & eodem modo in reliquis. Exempla pictores & poetæ suppeditant: Quis enim est qui Delphinum syluis appingat, fluctibus aprum? Suum cuique [?]τὰ ἴδια[?] affingitur. Id qui seruauerit officium fecisse dicitur. Ac Moses hinc argumento sumpto suos admonet, ut quoniam populus Dei sint ac videri velint, relictis Dijs & hominibus ei aduersarijs Deum unum colant ac sequantur.
units.tr: As far as propriety is concerned, he first of all discourses on it, and explains that very passage most carefully, since the reasoning from propriety is excellent. The opinion of certain men must be diminished and driven out, those who claim that mortals are all alike or all equal, when age, sex, fortune, skills and a thousand other differences of this kind make distinctions among us. Hence one thing becomes the rich man and another the poor; likewise one thing the old and another the young, and similarly in the rest. Painters and poets supply examples. For who paints a dolphin in the woods or a boar on the waves? Each thing is given its own [τὰ ἴδια]. Whoever keeps to this is said to have done his duty. And Moses, taking his argument from this, admonishes his people that, since they are God's people and wish to be seen as such, they should abandon the gods and men hostile to him, and worship and follow the one God.

units.la: Et quanquam hoc ipsum quo de verba facimus decorum latissime pateat: tamen ipse eum locum duabus partibus omnem distribuit, ita ut iubeat qui simus, quisque sit is quo cum nobis fœdus est, existimare.
units.tr: And although this very propriety of which we speak extends very widely, he himself divides the whole passage into two parts, so that he bids us consider who we are and who he is with whom we have a covenant.

units.la: Qui sint dicit, Nam populus sanctus es tu Domino Deo tuo, te elegit, &c. Vt sis ei, &c. Quibus verbis ostendit eos, si in suam ipsorum fortunam & officiu spectent, facile visuros, quâ minimè sese deceat cum impijs quicquam habere commercij.
units.tr: He says who they are: "For you are a holy people to the Lord your God; he has chosen you," and so on, "that you may be to him," and so on. By these words he shows that if they look to their own fortune and duty, they will easily see how little it becomes them to have any dealings with the impious.

units.la: Primum enim tu es, inquit, populus sanctus Domino Deo tuo. Sanctum est autem quicquid Deo divinisque vsibus consecratum est, vt mystæ, loca, tempora, sacrificia. Unde & angeli & Leuitæ, & Nazaræi, & frugum primitiæ, & victimæ, & templa & festa. Iam quemadmodum illa prophanis vsibus, ni velis polluere, adhibere nequeas: sic homo fidelis in amicitiam cum homine impio coire non potest nisi polluatur.
units.tr: "For first," he says, "you are a holy people to the Lord your God." Now whatever is consecrated to God and to divine uses is holy: ministers, places, times, sacrifices. Hence also angels, Levites, Nazirites, the first fruits of the harvest, victims, temples and feasts. Just as you cannot use those things for profane purposes unless you wish to defile them, so a faithful man cannot enter into friendship with an impious man without being defiled.

units.la: Quamobrem admonemur in sacris literis, ut ad eorum, qui sunt ac nominantur sancti, exempla nos componamus, ac conformemur. Angelis similes fore nos Christus dicit, cum omni mortalitate deposita resurrexerimus. Nazaræorum exemplum proponitur Num. 6. Templa dicimur Apostolo 1. Corinth. 6. victima dicimur eidem Roman. 12. Primitiæ frugum dicuntur Israelitæ Hierem. 2. Inde extant exhortationes illæ per totum corpus scripturarum sparsæ. Exod. 22. viri sancti eritis mihi. 1. Pet. 3. considerantes in timore sanctam conuersationem vestram.
units.tr: Therefore we are admonished in the sacred letters that we should model ourselves and conform to the examples of those who are and are called holy. Christ says we shall be like the angels when, having laid aside all mortality, we have risen. The example of the Nazirites is set forth in Num. 6. We are called temples by the Apostle, 1 Cor. 6; we are called victims by the same, Rom. 12; the Israelites are called first fruits, Jer. 2. Hence those exhortations scattered through the whole body of Scripture: Exod. 22, "You shall be holy men to me"; 1 Pet. 3, "considering your holy conversation in fear."

units.la: Sed sanctum & totum purum esse non potest quicquid vel parum sordium sibi commixtum habet, veluti purum putatum argentum non est, quod æris cupriue quicquam admixtum habeat. Eodem modo sanctum te esse tui sodales impij non sinent: aliqua enim illorum pars eris: aliquid illorum causa facies quod hominem sanctum dedeceat. Igitur ne pro phaneris totum te sibi vendicat Dominus.
units.tr: But whatever has even a little dross mixed into it cannot be wholly holy and pure, just as silver thought to be pure is not pure if it has any bronze or copper mixed in. In the same way, your impious companions will not allow you to remain holy: for you will become a part of them, and you will do something on their account which does not befit a holy man. Therefore the Lord claims you wholly for himself, not for profane things.

units.la: Dein te elegit Dominus Deus tuus, hoc est, ex omni genere nationum te sibi soli segregauit. Quod si impijs illis admixtum te voluisset, non te [?]selegisset[?]. Sed quoniam electio causa princeps est, qua fit, ut eo in loco res nostræ sitæ sint, sanè quod de ea ipsa dici par est, id describit egregiè, rem ipsam videlicet ab ipsius electionis causis tanquam fontibus repetens. Ac duas quidem, finalem videlicet & efficientem causas commemorat.
units.tr: "Then the Lord your God has chosen you," that is, he has set you apart from every kind of nation for himself alone. If he had wished you to be mixed with those impious people, he would not have chosen you. But since election is the chief cause by which our affairs stand where they do, he describes this very thing admirably, tracing the matter itself back to the causes of election as to their sources. He mentions two causes, namely the final and the efficient.

units.la: Causam finalem dicit, vt fis ei populus peculiaris præ omnibus populis qui sunt super terram. Deus, inquit, non voluit confusum quoddam atque indiscretum hominum chaos sed ex omni sece mortalium te selectum ac perpurgatum peculium sibi voluit. Qua de re passim extant testimonia. Malac. 3. Erunt mihi ait Dominus usq; in peculium, & parcam eis. Et in 1. epist. 2. Petrus nos electum & regale genus vocat.
units.tr: He states the final cause: "that you may be to him a peculiar people above all the peoples that are upon the earth." God, he says, did not wish a confused and indiscriminate chaos of men, but wished you, chosen and purified out of all the race of mortals, to be his own possession. There are testimonies to this scattered everywhere. Mal. 3: "They shall be mine, says the Lord, for a possession, and I will spare them." And in 1 Pet. 2, Peter calls us an elect and royal race.

units.la: Ex quo perspicuum est eos qui in Christo sunt electi, si in aliqua siue fœdera siue matrimonia cum hominibus impijs coeant, electionis finem præterijsse. O quàm parum hoc cogitamus? Non cuiuis datur versari in sancto monte, & tabernaculo Domini, vt in 15. Psal. scribi- tur sed per baptismū loti rursus ijs polluimur flagitijs, quibus in 1. Cor. 6. Paulus docet nos expelli regno Dei. Quod quid aliud est quàm ad cœnum redire, & pollui ceu amica luto sus? Quare finis electionis semper est animo versandus homini, vt quo quenq; loco Deus collocarit, vt præluceat alijs, in eo permaneamus.
units.tr: From this it is clear that those who are elect in Christ, if they unite in any covenants or marriages with impious men, have passed beyond the purpose of election. Oh, how little we think of this! It is not given to everyone to dwell on the holy mountain and in the tabernacle of the Lord, as is written in Ps. 15. Rather, we who have been washed through baptism are again defiled by those vices by which Paul teaches in 1 Cor. 6 that we are expelled from the kingdom of God. What is this other than to return to the mire and be defiled like a sow, a friend of mud? Therefore a man must always keep the purpose of election in mind, so that wherever God has placed him, there he may remain, to shine before others.

units.la: Sed electionis cauSam efficientem perpulchrè perquè accuratè explicat, quippe qui & contrariàm ei opinionem refutet, & quod verum est assueret. Contrarium vero est electionis causas efficientes in nobis quærere, quasiq; nos tam boni vel futuri vel iam visi fuerimus, vt inde adductus Dominus nos elegerit, sic à nostrarum virtutum atq; virium splendore pen- dens iudicium Dei fingere.
units.tr: But the efficient cause of election he explains most beautifully and carefully, since he both refutes the contrary opinion and establishes what is true. The contrary opinion is to seek the causes of election in ourselves, as if we were, or were going to be, so good that the Lord was led by this to choose us, thus fashioning a judgment of God that depends on the splendour of our own virtues and powers.

units.la: Ergo hoc ipsum prius refutat quàm ipsam causam aggrediatur. Et ad hunc modum dicit: Neq; vero propterea vos tantopere dilexit & elegit Dominus, quod plures esset alijs populis, cum sitis pauciores omnibus. Quibus verbis omnem superbiendi causam his præripit, & dicit eos non adeo potentem & populosam, & egregiam Deo visam gentem, vt præ cæteris, quos eligeret digniores autumaret.
units.tr: Therefore he refutes this first, before he takes up the cause itself, and he speaks in this way: "Nor indeed for this reason did the Lord love and choose you so greatly, because you were more numerous than other peoples, since you are fewer than all." By these words he takes from them every reason for pride, and says that they are not a nation so powerful, so populous and so distinguished in God's sight that they should think themselves more worthy than the rest to be chosen.

units.la: Idem docetur passim in sacris literis, videlicet electionem Dei non ab hominum persona, hoc est ijs quæ mortalibus vel gratiam & dignitatem, vel odium & contemptum pariunt rebus pendere. Quò fit vt Actor. 10. & Rom. 2. Petrus & Paulus doceant Deum non respicere quibus quis terris oriundus fit: & Iacobus in sua ep. c. 2. dicat, Deû nullius opum splendore duci: & Paulus alibi indicet Deum in eligendo nec seruitutis nec libertatis rationem habere. Quamobrem electio minimè ab hominis respectu provenit, veluti illo ipso etiam exemplo per Mosem ostenditur.
units.tr: The same is taught throughout the sacred writings: God's election does not depend on the person of men, that is, on those circumstances which bring grace and dignity or hatred and contempt among mortals. Hence Peter and Paul teach in Acts 10 and Romans 2 that God does not regard the land from which anyone comes; James in his epistle, chapter 2, says that God is not led by the splendour of wealth; and Paul elsewhere shows that in choosing God takes no account of servitude or freedom. Therefore election does not arise from any regard for man, as Moses also shows by this very example.

units.la: Quibus igitur ex rebus provenit? Iam causas efficientes dicit Moses: Sed quia dilexit vos, et seruare voluit iuramentum quod iurauit patribus vestris. En causas electionis duas quidè, sed alteram principem gratiam & veritatem. Elegit nos quia promisit, promisit autem quia dilexit nos. Iá quia in Christo omnes eligimur, eaq; ex gratia ac veritate Dei provenit electio, rectè scriptum est Ioan. 1. Lex per Mosem data est, gratia & veritas per Iesum Christum exorta est. Qua sententia euincitur causas electionis, quoniam cum Christo æterno Dei filio coeperunt existere, & nostris ipsorum meritis atq; viribus, & lege Mosaica, & nobis ipsis antiquiores & priores esse. Quamobrem cum electionis nostræ causas in nobis quidem nullas, in Deo vero veritatem habeamus & gratiam: enitendum est illam Dei in nos misericordiam, ac plane paternam propensionem cum humiliter suspiciamus, tum vero gratissimis animis amplectamur.
units.tr: From what, then, does it arise? Moses now names the efficient causes: But because he loved you, and was willing to keep the oath which he swore to your fathers. Here are the causes of election: two, but the first and chief is grace and truth. He chose us because he promised, and he promised because he loved us. Since we are all chosen in Christ, and election comes from the grace and truth of God, it is rightly written in John 1: The law was given through Moses, grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. This statement proves that the causes of election, since they began to exist together with Christ, the eternal Son of God, are older and prior to us, to our own merits and strength, and to the Mosaic law. Therefore, since we have no causes of our election in ourselves but find grace and truth in God, we must strive, when we humbly look up to that mercy of God towards us and his truly fatherly goodwill, to embrace it with the most grateful hearts.

units.la: Ac quemadmodum Deus olim potuisset alios, quàm Israelitas, quibus benefaceret elige- re, reiq; eius Mosesi eos admonet, vt illum solum colerent & sequerentur: sic nos Heluetij co- gitabimus etiam alios populos siue Sueuos, siue Italos, siue Gallos potuisse diuinitus eligi totq; Dei beneficijs augeri, quot nos aucti sumus & ditati: verum nos adeo dilexit Dominus, vt eligeret & promoueret. Quamobrem danda est opera vt grati simus & eum vicissim omni- bus gentibus præferamus.
units.tr: Just as God could once have chosen other peoples than the Israelites to bless, and Moses warns them to worship and follow him alone, so we Helvetians may think that other peoples, whether Swabians, Italians or Gauls, could have been divinely chosen and enriched with as many benefits of God as we have been increased and enriched. But the Lord loved us so much that he chose and advanced us. Therefore we must take care to be thankful, and in turn to prefer him to all nations.

units.la: Ex quibus omnibus perspicuū est, quàm dedeceat aliquem eximio gradu collocatum turpiter viuere, diuinis beneficijs ornatum atque auctum verbo Dei sese opponere. Ergo qui se vocant euangelicos eorum est agere vitam euangelicam: qui se vocant sanctos eorum est agere vitam sanctam: eodemq; modo in cæteris. Certè multum offendimus alios, & nos ipsos etiam turpiter damus, quando nostræ personæ decorum adeo negligimus: quin cogitamus quod Moses dicit nos sanctos esse Domino, nos ab illo immeritos electos eiq; sacros esse.Iam si finem electionis sanctimoniam existimes, quemadmodum Paulus Ephesijs scribens cap.1.admonet:nostrum erit vt sanctam & inculpatam vitam peragamus.
units.tr: From all these things it is plain how unbecoming it is for someone placed in a distinguished rank to live shamefully, and to set himself against the word of God when he has been adorned and enlarged with divine benefits. So those who call themselves evangelical must lead an evangelical life; those who call themselves holy must lead a holy life; and likewise in other things. Certainly we offend others greatly and bring shame upon ourselves when we so neglect the dignity of our persons; we do not consider that Moses says we are holy to the Lord, chosen by him though we did not deserve it, and consecrated to him. Now if you think that the end of election is holiness, as Paul writing to the Ephesians in chapter 1 admonishes, it will be our task to lead a holy and blameless life.

units.la: Quo cum nobis fit negocium,Cum Domino Deo nostro. Dicit enim: Scias itaque quod Dominus Deus tuus ipse est Deus, Deus fidelis,&c. Et id quidem sic agit Moses, vt quemadmodum discessio a Deo ad mundum inde existit,quia mundus videtur Deo potior esse,hoc est, quod nec mundum quam perfidus atque impotens sit, nec Deum,quam fidus atque omnipotens existat,recte noris:Deum qui qualisq; sit aliquibus naturae diuinae notis & indicijs depingit. Earum autem notarum duo genera affert, videlicet vnum earum quae consolantur nos atque etiam inuitant ad eius consortium: alterum terrentium, mixtum tertium.
units.tr: Our business is with the Lord our God, for he says: Know therefore that the Lord your God is God, the faithful God, etc. Moses deals with this in such a way that, just as a turning away from God to the world arises from thinking the world better than God, that is, from not rightly knowing how faithless and powerless the world is and how faithful and almighty God is, so he portrays God, and what sort of being he is, by certain marks and indications of the divine nature. He brings forward two kinds of these marks: one kind that comforts us and also invites us to fellowship with him, and another that terrifies, with a third mixed kind.

units.la: Consolantur & ad Dei consortium inuitant haec tria. Primum. 1. Quod ipse est Deus, hoc est,vita,salus, robur, & summum bonum omnium fidelium. Nam hoc Christus Matth. 22.cum Sadducèis disputans pulchre colligit.Et nomen tetragrammaton essentiam summam significans,argumento est, extra Deum & sine Deo non posse quenquam existere. An non hoc inuitet nos,vt cum eo malimus versari,in quo solo possunt res opes; nostrae saluae esse, quam cum mundo qui subinde ruit & perit ipse? Cur malos magis ames,quam bonum? Cur eum amicum malis in quo peris,quam eum in quo saluus es? Ergo si Deum recte noris,illum potius quam mundum tibi fociun voles.
units.tr: These three comfort us and invite us into fellowship with God. First: That he is God, that is, life, salvation, strength, and the highest good of all the faithful. For Christ, disputing with the Sadducees in Matthew 22, draws this conclusion finely. And the name tetragrammaton, signifying the supreme essence, is proof that no one can exist outside God and without God. Does this not invite us to prefer to dwell with him, in whom alone our affairs and resources can be safe, rather than with the world, which itself keeps falling and perishing? Why do you love evil men more than the good? Why do you make friends with those by whom you are ruined rather than with him in whom you are safe? Therefore, if you rightly know God, you will want him rather than the world as your companion.

units.la: Alterū, Deus fidelis ac feruans foedus. Qui quid Deus promittit id bona fide praestat:homo contra vanus ac fallax est.Idq; experimur quotidie.Ergo qui verum, fidum,constantem quo cum habeat commercium mauult quam mendacem, perfidum, lubricum:is Deum etiam amicum habebit potius quam mundum.
units.tr: Second: God is faithful and keeps the covenant. Whatever God promises, he performs in good faith; man, on the contrary, is empty and deceitful. We experience this every day. Therefore whoever prefers to have dealings with one who is true, trustworthy and constant rather than with one who is lying, faithless and unstable, will have God as a friend rather than the world.

units.la: Tertium, Misericors erga amantes & feruantes mandata. Quae nota multam ac magnam constituit inter homines differentiam. Homines in eos, qui benefaciunt,plerunque ingrati sunt:veluti in seruos bonos heri, in ciues bonos patria, & amicos amici: vt in Iacobum Laban,in Iofephum Potiphar,in Mosem gens Israelia,in Dauidem Saul alij in alios ingrati fuerunt.At Deus nullam virtutem dedignatur premio,nullis officijs non refert gratias. Er laat ihm nüt vergeben thün. Quippe qui amantem redamet,sibi seruientem atq; oblequentem tue atur ac conferuet. Igitur fi diuitibus largiris munera, vt auferas maiora: fi munificis officia facis,vt accipias amplam gratiam: cur non Deo,qui ita suapte est natura comparatus, vt omnibus sibi seruientibus maximas referat gratias,totum tete praebeas? Atq; hae quidem res fi ad studium conferuandae cum Deo amicitiae te excitare nequeunt: quid te excitet aliud neicio.
units.tr: Third: Merciful towards those who love and keep his commandments. This mark makes a great and considerable difference among men. Men are for the most part ungrateful to those who do them good: as good servants to their masters, good citizens to their country, friends to friends; so Laban was ungrateful to Jacob, Potiphar to Joseph, the people of Israel to Moses, Saul to David, and others to others. But God disdains no virtue without reward and does not fail to give thanks for any service. Er laat ihm nüt vergeben thün: he lets nothing go unrewarded for him. For he who loves in return, and who is served and obeyed by him, cherishes and preserves him. Therefore, if you give gifts to the rich in order to receive greater ones, if you do favours to the generous in order to get ample thanks, why will you not give yourself wholly to God, who by his very nature is so made that he repays with the greatest thanks all who serve him? And if these things cannot stir you to strive to keep friendship with God, I do not know what else will.

units.la: Earum autem quae nos terreant hanc vnam notam affert, quod etiam in inimicos suos,at que eos qui resistunt ei grauiter animaduertat,eosque etiam, vt digni sunt,perimat. Igitur fi praepotentem aliquem hominem metuis,eumq; fi non aimes,saltem reuereare, vtne noceat:cur Deum,quo non est potentior alter,adeo secure despicis? Non equiqem id impune aufes.Malos male perdet.Exempla non desunt,fi recoles.
units.tr: Of the marks that terrify, he brings forward this one: that he also punishes severely his enemies and those who resist him, and destroys them too, as they deserve. Therefore, if you fear some very powerful man, and if you do not love him, at least reverence him, lest he harm you; why do you so carelessly despise God, than whom there is no one more powerful? Indeed you will not get away with it unpunished. He will destroy the wicked with wickedness. Examples are not lacking if you call them to mind.

units.la: Medium inter has notas,& ex vtrifq; mixtum est quod eum ꝑ, id est,fortem, robustum, praepotente appellat:hoc enim&solari bonos fuu amicos,& terrore malos fiue hostes potest.
units.tr: Between these marks, and mixed from both, is that he calls him El [אל], that is, strong, robust, mighty; for this can both comfort the good as his friends and terrify the wicked or enemies.

units.la: Ex his omnibus collige num decorum fit eo qui salus tua, fidelis patronus tuus, misericors & propitius in amicos suos,asper vero in hostes, potens ad feruandos suos & perdendos hostes fit,relicto,te qui illi sanctus fis cum prophanis & impuris coniungere. Haec qui secum recte reputat reliquis rebus omnibus solum Deum sequitur in Christo Iesu.Amen.
units.tr: From all these things gather whether it is fitting for you to join yourself to the profane and impure, leaving him who is your salvation, your faithful patron, merciful and kind to his friends but harsh to his enemies, powerful to save his own and destroy his enemies. Whoever rightly considers these things, setting aside all other things, follows God alone in Christ Jesus. Amen.

units.la: SERMO VI.
units.tr: SERMON VI.

units.la: 12 Quod fi audieritis iudicia ista, & custodieritis atque feceritis ea, seruabit & tibi Dominus Deus tuus foedus & beneficentiam, sicut iurauit patribus tuis.
units.tr: 12 If you hear these judgments, and keep and do them, the Lord your God will also keep for you the covenant and the kindness which he swore to your fathers.

units.la: 13 Diliget te,fortunabit te,atque multiplicabit te, fortunabit quoque fructum ventris tui, & fructum terrae tuae,frumentum tuum, vinum tuum, & oleum tuum, foetum boum tuorum, & greges porcorum tuorum, in terra quam iurauit patribus tuis vt daret tibi.
units.tr: 13 He will love you, bless you, and multiply you; he will also bless the fruit of your womb and the fruit of your land, your grain, your wine and your oil, the increase of your herds and the flocks of your sheep, in the land which he swore to your fathers to give you.

units.la: 14 Fortunatus eris pra omnibus populis,nō erit in te sterilis,neq; in iumentis tuis.
units.tr: 14 You will be blessed above all peoples; there will be no barren person among you, nor among your livestock.

units.la: 15 Auferet quoq; Dominus à te omnem languorem, & cunctas ægritudines Ægypti malas (de quibus tu scis) nō inferet tibi, sed ponet eas super vniuersos hostes tuos.
units.tr: 15 The Lord will also take away from you all sickness, and will not bring upon you any of the evil diseases of Egypt (which you know), but will lay them upon all your enemies.

units.la: IN ea Mosis exhortatione, qua vir ille diuinus admonet, vt abstineant fideles ab impiarum gentium consortio: quo primam de plena ac perfecta Dei dilectione legem nullis impedi-ti rebus feruent, facilius: præclarum est argumentum quod à decoro ducitur. Quis enim ossi-cium sui nō patiatur sese admoneri? Quamobrē vsus hoc ipso Moses admonet suos homines vti prophanarum gentium consortijs & fœderibus omnibus abstineant, quippe quod deco-rum non sit fideles ijs rursus immisceri, à quibus sunt diuinitus segregati, tum etiam ipso ceu peculium quoddam congregati.
units.tr: IN this exhortation of Moses, in which that divine man urges the faithful to keep away from fellowship with the impious nations, so that they may more easily keep the first law, of full and perfect love of God, undisturbed by any hindrances, there is a notable argument drawn from what is fitting. For who does not suffer himself to be reminded of his duty? Therefore Moses, using this very argument, admonishes his people to keep away from every partnership and alliance with the profane nations, since it is not fitting for the faithful to mix again with those from whom they have been divinely set apart, and gathered as a kind of special possession.

units.la: Sed quoniam hæc de electione doctrina videtur ijs, qui sua magis humana, quàm diuina ratione duci solent, absurda & perniciosa: quippe qua abstrahantur homines à vitæ sanctimonia, ac pars securitate, pars desperatione rapiantur ad scelera: Moses ostensis electionis causis hos antea quidem refutauit, iam vero ostendens etiam pœnas & premia non confun-di, refellit magis. Illi enim quod à decoro sumptum expo-suimus argumento nunc aliud ab vtili sumptum subdit. Quod quoniam vtilitatis falsa specie plærunque decipimur, considera tu dignum pariter ac necessarium est. Nam propterea impijs coniungimur quod quæsisse nostram vtilitatem videri volumus: cum ex hoc loco perspicuum est quod illis omissis Deum secuti melius nobis consulamus. Moses autem hoc argumentum sic tractat vt primum sum-matim tum sigillatim vtilitatem hanc exponat. Quo nos ordine eum locum ponderabimus.
units.tr: But since this teaching about election seems absurd and harmful to those who are accustomed to be led more by human reasoning than by divine, for it draws men away from holiness of life, and some are carried off to crimes by security, others by despair, Moses, having shown the causes of election, earlier refuted these men; but now, by showing that rewards and punishments are not confused, he refutes them even more. For to that argument taken from what is fitting, which we have set out, he now adds another taken from what is useful. Since we are very often deceived by the false appearance of usefulness, it is equally worthy and necessary to consider this. For we are joined to the impious because we wish to seem to have sought our own advantage, whereas from this passage it is plain that, by leaving them aside and following God, we consult our own good better. Moses, however, handles this argument in such a way that he sets out this usefulness first in summary and then in detail. Let us weigh the passage in that order.

units.la: Summatim, Quod si audieritis iudicia ista & custodieritis atq; feceritis ea, seruabit tibi Dominus Deus tuus fœdus istud & gratiam, &c. Id est, si ita quod vos decet quodq; iustum atque æquum est ab impiorum hominum consortio abstinueritis, certè Deus & fœdus initum cum patribus seruabit, quæ patribus promisit ea vobis large præstabit beneficia. Ex quo perspicuum est Mosem docere & quæ sit ista quam promittat vtilitas, & quæ sit eius acquiren-dæ ratio optima.
units.tr: In summary: If you hear these judgments and keep and do them, the Lord your God will keep for you that covenant and grace, etc. That is: if you abstain from fellowship with impious men in the way that befits you and is just and fair, then certainly God will keep the covenant made with your fathers, and will generously grant you those benefits which he promised to the fathers. From this it is plain that Moses teaches both what this usefulness is that he promises, and what is the best way of obtaining it.

units.la: Rationem comparandæ eius, quoniam prior est, priore loco traditur. Si (inquit) audie-ritis iudicia ista &c. Iudicij nomine decorum seu officium, de quo paulò ante dixerat, intel-ligit. Sæpe enim pro eo quod cuiusq; iaterest [?] facere sumitur. Veluti Psalm. 119. Aspice ad me & miserere mei, sicut est iudicium eorum qui diligunt nomen tuum: hoc est, veluti consue-uisti illorum qui te diligunt misereri.
units.tr: The manner of obtaining it is given first, since it comes first. "If," he says, "you hear these judgments, etc." By "judgments" he means what is fitting, or duty, of which he spoke a little earlier. For the word is often taken to mean what is the concern of each person to do. So in Psalm 119: "Look upon me and have mercy on me, as is the judgment of those who love your name"; that is, have mercy on me as you are accustomed to show mercy to those who love you.

units.la: Dein audiendi verbo obedientiæ principium notat, quod qui aures præbeat, iam quasi quodam modo annuerit: sed eius perfectionem sequentibus custodiendi & faciendi. Quorum priore postulat ratum haberi, & sic teneri mordicus, vt nullam aduersam cogitationem admittas. Posteriore vero, vt ad eam persuasionem totam vitam ac mores accommodes: non verbis Christum, factis Antichristum referas. Sic expetitur vtilitas.
units.tr: Then the word "hear" marks the beginning of obedience, since he who lends his ears has already, in a certain way, given assent; but its perfection is indicated by the words that follow, "keep and do." By the former he requires that these things be held as settled and held fast with the teeth, so that you admit no contrary thought. By the latter, that you adapt your whole life and conduct to that persuasion, referring Christ in words and Antichrist in deeds. In this way the usefulness is sought.

units.la: Quæ vero ea sit ad hunc modum dicit: Seruabit tibi Dominus Deus tuus fœdus & benefi-centiam, sicut iurauit patribus tuis. Fœdus hoc Gen. 17. describitur, ero Deus tuus: in semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes. Id hic vno gratiæ, seu beneficentiæ nomine reddit. Vbiuis [?]συμμαχον se promittit fore, & fœdus ratum habiturum. Iam si Deus pro nobis quis contra nos? Rom. 8. Et Matth. 17. portæ inferorum non præualebunt. Esa. 52. Non propere ibitis, non fugietis, quia præit Dominus. Et idem Psalm. 27. habemus. Idem Christus ait, Ego ero vobiscum vsq; ad consummationem seculi. Quid verbis opus est? Si Deum amicum habueris, erit ille fœderatus vtilissimus, quippe qui vim propulsare illatam ab hostibus & inferre pos-sit vbi res postulet. Atq; sic quidem vtilitatem istam summatim exposuit.
units.tr: What that usefulness is, he says in this manner: "The Lord your God will keep for you the covenant and kindness, as he swore to your fathers." This covenant is described in Genesis 17: "I will be your God; in your seed all nations will be blessed." Here he expresses it by the single name of grace, or kindness. He promises that he will everywhere be an ally [σύμμαχος] and will hold the covenant firm. If God is for us, who is against us? Romans 8. And Matthew 16: the gates of hell will not prevail. Isaiah 52: "You will not go in haste, nor will you flee, for the Lord goes before you." And we have the same in Psalm 27. Christ himself says the same: "I will be with you even to the end of the age." Why do we need words? If you have God as a friend, that covenanted friendship will be most useful, since he is able to repel force brought by enemies and to inflict it when the matter requires. And so indeed he has set out this usefulness in summary.

units.la: Sigillatim exponit adhibita enumeratione partium. Diliget te, ait, & benedicet te, &c. Quibus verbis totam [?]εὐδαιμονίαν complectitur, quæ consistit in hoc, vt animis, corporibus, & externis bonis quam optime valeamus. Quæ bona Moses in præsentia commemorat. Ac primum quæ sunt animi, quibus primæ partes debentur, hoc ipso notat quod dicit, Diliget te Dominus Deus, &c. Est enim hic & principium fœlicitatis & tranquilli pacatiq; animi basis. Nam quonam Dei in nos amor bonorum omnium efficiens causa est, sensus eius sic animum percellit nostrum, vt eum ipsum mirum in modum exhileret.
units.tr: In detail he sets it out by listing the parts. "He will love you," he says, "and bless you, etc." In these words he embraces the whole happiness [εὐδαιμονία], which consists in this, that we fare as well as possible in soul, body and external goods. Moses recalls these goods for the present. And first, the goods of the soul, to which the first place is owed, he marks by what he says: "The Lord your God will love you, etc." For here is both the beginning of happiness and the foundation of a calm and peaceful mind. For since God's love toward us is the efficient cause of all good things, the sense of it so stirs our mind that it gladdens it in a wonderful way.

units.la: Ac pij quidem non solum ex beneficijs: hæc enim cum impijs habent à Deo patre com-munia: sed & ex promissis & ex spiritus sancti testimonio Dei in se amoris cognitionem cer-tam habent. Qua confirmati semper læti, securi, intrepidi sunt. Scire enim se Deo charum esse, est omnium quæ nobis obueniunt animo iucundissimum. Hoc Iobem, Iosephum, Dauidem, apostolos, Christum ipsum confirmauit. Quare enitendum est, ne peccatis onerata conscientia reclamet animo sic fe consolari volenti, vt dilectionis huius cognitio non perturbetur, ac male habere mens occipiat. Nam fi id fiat actum est de animi tranquillitate. Vt oceifo fratre Cain animi tranquillitatem amisit. Idem accidit Sauli, Iudae, & caeteris.
units.tr: The godly indeed have certain knowledge of God's love toward them not only from benefits (for in these they share with the impious what they have from God the Father), but also from the promises and from the testimony of the Holy Spirit. Strengthened by this they are always glad, secure and fearless. For to know oneself beloved of God is the most delightful thing to the mind of all that befall us. This confirmed Job, Joseph, David, the apostles, and Christ himself. Therefore we must strive that a conscience burdened with sins does not cry out against the mind that wishes to console itself in this way, so that the knowledge of this love is not disturbed, and the mind does not begin to be ill at ease. For if this happens, the tranquillity of the mind is undone. Thus Cain lost the tranquillity of his mind after the killing of his brother. The same happened to Saul, Judas, and others.

units.la: Igitur fi quis peccet statim ductus poenitentia, ad Christum, in quo vt dilectissimo diligi mur, confugiat. Sic enim animo pax sua recuperatur. Iam animi tranquillitate nihil est maius, nobilius, melius omnium consensu mortalium. Nil conscire sibi, nulla pallescere culpa, hic murus aheneus esto. Hoc bono Moses eum potiri dicit, qui defertis & posthabitis mundanis amicitijs, Deum habeat ac sequatur unum.
units.tr: Therefore, if anyone sins, let him at once, led by repentance, flee to Christ, in whom we are loved as most beloved. For in this way peace is recovered for the mind. Now there is nothing greater, nobler or better than tranquillity of mind by the agreement of all mortals. To be conscious of nothing, to turn pale at no fault: let this be a wall of bronze. Moses says that he who forsakes and sets aside worldly friendships, and has God alone and follows him, obtains this good.

units.la: Iam quoniam opes & honores, & quae sunt huius generis externa alia bona plurimi fiunt, ac pene sint maiore in precio apud omnes quàm illa quae diximus animi bona: secundas his tribuit, ac dicit, Benedicet te, augebit te, &c. In quo benedicere quid sit paulo altius repetendum est. Benedicere adeo frequens scripturis verbum est, vt expositione longiore minimè egeat. Omnibus enim constat idem esse quod bene velle, precari, benefacere, &c.
units.tr: Now since wealth and honours, and other external goods of this kind, are valued most highly, and are almost held in greater esteem by all than those goods of the mind that we have mentioned, he assigns these second place and says: "He will bless you, increase you, etc." Here we must go a little further back to explain what it is to bless. "To bless" is so frequent a word in the Scriptures that it needs no lengthy explanation. For everyone agrees that it means the same as to wish well, to pray for, to do good, etc.

units.la: Sed quis benedicit? Alicubi, vt Num. 6. sacerdos benedicit ex praescripta formula: alibi Deus benedicit ipse, vt in praesentia. Id indicio est Deum interdum vti sacerdotis aut alterius persona ceu arbitraria, semper autè ipsum benedicere. Formula significat in nomine Domini bona omnia euenire, à Deo nostraq; custodiri, vultum illius nobis affulgere, eum benefacere, eum sua nos providentia curare & conservare, pacem ab illo nobis omnem conferri. Quae bona abs Deo patre, in ea, quam Dominus Christus praescripsit formula, precamur indies.
units.tr: But who blesses? Sometimes, as in Numbers 6, the priest blesses according to a prescribed formula; elsewhere God blesses himself, as here. This shows that God sometimes uses the person of a priest or another as an instrument, but always blesses himself. The formula signifies that all good things come to pass in the name of the Lord, are kept by God for us, that his face shines upon us, that he does us good, that he cares for us and preserves us by his providence, and that all peace is conferred upon us by him. These goods we ask for daily from God the Father, in the form of prayer which the Lord Christ prescribed.

units.la: Sed illud benedicendi verbum Moses augendi verbo exponit. Quod indicio est benedicere illud aliud nihil esse, quàm quae dedit bona sic fœcundare, vt subinde crescant aliaq; generentur ex alijs: veluti in frugibus, in iumentis & pecoribus, in lucro, & omnino omnibus rebus. Quod ipsum Germani vocant <bl>erschöpfen</bl>.
units.tr: But Moses explains the word "bless" with the word "increase." This indicates that to bless means nothing other than to make the goods that have been given fruitful, so that they grow again and new things are produced from them: for example in crops, in livestock and cattle, in profit, and in all things generally. The Germans call this erschöpfen, to make abundant.

units.la: Sed & enumeratione partium exponit latius. Primum liberos commemorat, quos, vt animum percellat magis, fructum ventris appellat. Nam sunt, veluti vulgo dici solet, caro & sanguis nostep, quibus laboramus & sudamus cum alendis tum etiam prouehendis: si illis sit bene, nos habemus eo melius: sin male, contra. Dein habere etiam ex nobis indolem videntur: vt quemadmodum ex fructibus arborem, sic nos cognosces ex illis. Vnde vulgus nostrum dicit <bl>Guß schlaat grummen nach</bl>. Quid verbis opus est: magna terrenæ felicitatis pars in hoc nobis est repossita liberos vt bonos habeas. Ac multò rectius ratione instituas si illos Deo commendes, quàm eorum causa malis hominibus contra Deum obsequare.
units.tr: Moses also explains it more fully by listing the parts. First he mentions children, whom he calls the fruit of the womb, so as to move us more deeply. For they are, as people commonly say, our own flesh and blood, for whom we toil and sweat both to feed them and to advance them: if things go well for them, we fare the better for it; if badly, the reverse. Next, they also seem to have inherited something of our nature, so that just as one knows a tree by its fruit, so you will know yourselves by them. Hence our common people say, "Good calves follow a good cow" [Guß schlaat grummen nach]. Why use many words? A large part of earthly happiness lies in this, that you have children who are good. And you will act much more rightly, reasonably, if you commend them to God, than if for their sake you humour wicked men against God.

units.la: Secundo loco opes commemorat, vt proventus agrorum & pecora. At opes magno sunt ornamento pariter & adiumento, velutiq; malis sunt irritamenta malorum, sic bonis sunt instrumenta bonorum maximorum. Etenim diuites & si in magistratu non sint, tamen apud eum possunt omnia, eoq; etiam timentur & habentur in pretio: tum ornant omnia dicta ac facta: nec vllum est vel animi vel corporis bonum, quod in diuite non splendeat magis, quàm in paupere: [illegible, ~55 letters] Omitto quod benemereri possunt de omnibus. Quamobrem opes & sunt & videntur magnum Dei donum fidelibus. Testes sunt Abraham, Isaac, Iacob, Ioseph, Dauid, Solomon, ipse etiam Iob.
units.tr: In second place he mentions wealth, the produce of the fields and the flocks. Yet riches are at once a great ornament and a help; and just as they are incitements to evil for the wicked, so for the good they are the most powerful instruments of good. For the rich, even if they hold no office, nevertheless have influence over everything through their standing; they are therefore feared and held in esteem; moreover they adorn all their words and deeds, and there is no good of mind or body that does not shine more in the rich man than in the poor. [illegible, about 55 letters] I pass over the fact that they can do good service to everyone. Wherefore riches both exist and appear to be a great gift of God to the faithful. Witnesses are Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, David, Solomon, and Job himself.

units.la: Tertio loco bonam atq; integram valetudinem commemorat: qua nihil est optatius praesertim aegris, qui illius praestantiâ agnoscunt optimè. Qui valent corporibus, ij magis opibus & honoribus inhiant: at aegri agnoscunt illam opibus & honoribus praestare. Quare Dominus pollicetur se morbos Aegyptios ab illis auersurum esse, qui ipsum dignis modis venerantur.
units.tr: In third place he mentions good and sound health, than which nothing is more desirable, especially to the sick, who best recognise its excellence. Those who are in good health in body hanker more after wealth and honours; but the sick recognise that health surpasses wealth and honours. That is why the Lord promises that he will turn the diseases of Egypt away from those who worship him in a worthy manner.

units.la: Sunt quaedam peccata, quae morbos ipsos secum trahunt, vt ebrietas, crapula, scortatio: ex quibus podagram, morbum intercutem, phtisim, morbum Gallicum & huius generis alia flagella nostris corporibus solemus accersere.
units.tr: There are certain sins which bring diseases with them, such as drunkenness, gluttony, and whoredom; from these we are wont to bring upon our bodies gout, dropsy, consumption, the French pox, and other scourges of this kind.

units.la: In quibus omnibus vides quàm erret imò peccet vulgus, quod euangelio recepto morbos imputat, cum hic locus doceat eo profligato hosce nobis oboriri. Ac de nobis quidem solis vt dicam, pecunia non euangelium discordes fecit: luxus & crapula pauperes: pestem & annonę charitatem & bella partim ambitio, partim impietas accersiuerunt. Idem Achabi tem poribus factum est.
units.tr: In all these things you see how greatly the common people err, or rather sin, when they impute diseases to the gospel once received, since this passage teaches that when the gospel has been cast out these evils arise among us. And to speak only of ourselves: money, not the gospel, has created discord; luxury and gluttony have made men poor; plague, dearth of food, and wars have been brought on partly by ambition, partly by impiety. The same happened in the times of Ahab.

units.la: Quin hic vides idem docere Mosem, quod fecit Solomon, quod Christus consuluit. Solomon veram sapientiam petijt à Domino, cumq; ea diuitias etiam consecutus est. Christus nobis suasit,ante omnia quærendum regnum Dei,& reliqua omnia adijci. Moses hic docet, omnium etiam maximarum gentium societati fœdus amicitiamq; Dei præferre, sicque animum cuiusq; persuasum esse oportere,Deo amicos suos diligere,benedicere,& omni bonorum genere augere. Eiusmodi in Psal.1.iii.127. &c. habes pulcherrima documenta. Deo sit honos in secula,Amen.
units.tr: Indeed here you see that Moses teaches the same thing that Solomon did, and that Christ advised. Solomon asked the Lord for true wisdom, and along with it he also obtained riches. Christ urged us that above all things the kingdom of God is to be sought, and all the rest will be added. Moses here teaches that the covenant and friendship of God is to be preferred even to fellowship with the greatest nations, and that the mind of each person ought to be persuaded that God loves his friends, blesses them, and increases them with every kind of good. You have most beautiful examples of this in Psalms 1, 3, 127, etc. To God be honour for ever, Amen.

units.la: SERMO VII.
units.tr: SERMON VII.

units.la: 16 Tu devorabis omnes populos,quos Dominus Deus tradet tibi : oculus tuus non parcat eis,neq; colas deos eorum:nam id tibi in laqueum foret.
units.tr: 16 You shall devour all the peoples whom the Lord your God shall deliver to you: your eye shall not spare them, neither shall you serve their gods: for that would be a snare to you.

units.la: 17 Si dixeris in corde tuo: Plures sunt gentes istæ quàm ego, quomodo possem eijcere eas?
units.tr: 17 If you say in your heart: These nations are more numerous than I; how could I drive them out?

units.la: 18 Ne timueris eas,sed diligenter recole,quæ fecerit Dominus Deus tuus Pharaoni,& toti Ægypto.
units.tr: 18 Do not fear them, but diligently call to mind what the Lord your God did to Pharaoh and to all Egypt.

units.la: 19 Tentationes magnas quas viderunt oculi tui, & signa atq; prodigia, & manum validam atq; brachium extentum, per quæ eduxit te Dominus Deus tuus cunctis populis,à quibus tu metuis.
units.tr: 19 The great trials which your eyes saw, and the signs and wonders, and the mighty hand and outstretched arm, by which the Lord your God brought you out, so will the Lord your God do to all the peoples of whom you are afraid.

units.la: 20 Sed & crabrones mittet Dominus Deus tuus in eos, donec pereant hi qui reliqui sunt,quiq; absconditi fuerunt metu tui.
units.tr: 20 Moreover the Lord your God will send hornets among them, until those who remain and who hid themselves from you are destroyed.

units.la: 21 Ne consternaris metu illorum,quoniam Dominus Deus tuus est in medio tui, Deus fortis & terribilis.
units.tr: 21 Do not be dismayed at their presence, for the Lord your God is in the midst of you, a God mighty and terrible.

units.la: 22 Eijciet autem Dominus Deus tuus gentes illas paulatim ante te,nec poteris eas subito excindere,ne forte multiplicentur contra te bestiæ agrestes.
units.tr: 22 The Lord your God will drive out those nations before you little by little; you will not be able to destroy them at once, lest the wild beasts multiply against you.

units.la: 23 Sed Dominus Deus tuus tradet eas coram te, & tumultu magno perdet eas,donec deleverit eas.
units.tr: 23 But the Lord your God will deliver them before you, and will destroy them with a great confusion, until they are wiped out.

units.la: 24 Sed & reges earum tradet in manum tuam, & abolebis nomen earum sub cælo,nec quisquam consistere poterit coram conspectu tuo, donec vastaveris eas.
units.tr: 24 And he will deliver their kings into your hand, and you shall blot out their name under heaven; no one shall be able to stand before you, until you have destroyed them.

units.la: 25 Sculptilia deorum ipsarum igne combures, argentum & aurum quod in illis est,ne concupiscas, ut tibi collas,ne forte impingas in eo, quoniam abominanda res est domino deo tuo.
units.tr: 25 You shall burn with fire the graven images of their gods, and you shall not covet the silver and gold that is on them, nor take it for yourself, lest you be ensnared by it, since it is an abomination to the Lord your God.

units.la: 26 Ne ergo inferas abominationem in domum tuam,ne fias Hærem, quemadmodum illud est: omnino execreris illud,planeq; ab eo abhorreas. Hærem enim est.
units.tr: 26 Therefore you shall not bring an abomination into your house, lest you become accursed like it: you shall utterly detest it and utterly abhor it, for it is accursed.

units.la: Quanquam Deus ipse iubeat pariter ac doceat,quàm prudenter quæ ad tuendam publicam pacem,atq; incolumitatem pertinent,suscipere atq; exequi debeamus,ipsaqué etiam prudentia sit eximium Dei munus: tamen hæc prudentia cum in rerum æstimatione versatur,ne quam incredulitatem pariat cauendum est:nempe vt comparata cum mundi viribus imbecillitate nostra:forsan à Deo solo pendere nolimus,ac spei nonnihil & præsidij in impiarum gentium societate collocemus. Ac pulchram me Hercle speciem habet,quod obtendunt impij:esse potentissimos quosq; populos nostræ religionis profesioni inimicos,& coactis consilijs atq; opibus illam oppugnare:nos paucos numero,eosq; etiam imbelles, & rerum gerendarum rudes,nisi fœderibus atq; amicitijs munitos solos non posse subsistere. Quibus cogitationibus & rationibus obuiam itur fide,quæ docet ex præscripto primæ legis à solo & vnico Deo pendere,& omnino persuasum habere:quibus rebus efficiendis nos non satis prudentes & firmi simus,ijs ipsum & prudentem & potentem esse:quæq; sint ac videantur facitu difficillima,ea auxilio Dei fieri facillima.
units.tr: Although God himself commands and teaches us how prudently we ought to undertake and carry out the things that pertain to securing public peace and safety, and although prudence itself is an outstanding gift of God, yet this prudence, when it is exercised in weighing circumstances, must be guarded against producing any unbelief: namely, that, comparing our weakness with the strength of the world, we may be unwilling to depend on God alone, and may place some hope and protection in alliance with ungodly nations. And indeed, by Hercules, the wicked put forward a fine appearance: that the most powerful peoples are enemies of our religion and attack it with combined counsels and resources; that we are few in number, and moreover unwarlike and unskilled in conducting affairs, and cannot hold out unless we are protected by treaties and friendships alone. These thoughts and reasons are met by faith, which teaches that, according to the prescription of the first commandment, everything depends on the one and only God, and which holds firmly that where we are not wise and strong enough to accomplish things, he is both wise and mighty, and that things which seem most difficult to do are made most easy by the help of God.

units.la: Id Moses iam argumenti tertij loco contra amicitias impias suis Israelijs affert, ac docet eos ne sint adeo pusillanimes,qui putent se,si Deum solum ac præterea neminè amicum habeant,non posse salvos esse: quin istam animi titubationem fide sistant, Deumq; sciant sibi sufficere,modo ipsi blasphemis resistant,presos defendant &c. Qua in re & deliberatione tria tempora statuit:ac quid in quoq; vel impediat vel promoveat exponit: Ea sunt,ante factum,in facto,post factum.
units.tr: Moses now brings forward this, as a third argument, against impious friendships to his Israelites, and teaches them not to be so faint-hearted as to think that they cannot be saved if they have God alone and no one else as a friend. Rather, they should check this wavering of mind by faith, and know that God is enough for them, provided they resist the blasphemers and defend the oppressed, and so on. In this matter and deliberation he sets out three times, and explains what in each either hinders or advances us. These are: before the deed, in the deed, and after the deed.

units.la: Ante factum existit prudens deliberatio, qua vires nostræ cum finitimarum gentium po-tentiæ comparantur: ubi videmus vel non satis firmi, vel non satis instructi: unde & metus exoritur, qui circumspicit qua parte sit vel in hominibus falsus aliqua. Quod animos nostros quandoque totos à Deo revocat, atque efficit, ut metu periculi impediti vitam[?], otium, ami-citias humanas præ confessione & promotione veritatis, præque Dei fœdere sibi deligant. Ut illi Cananæos robustos & potentes & bellicosos esse iudicant, sese vero nec viribus nec ullis adversus hos rebus idoneis instructos esse. Sed eum metum hic egregie retundit Moses, quippe qui studio quietis, atque ocij mandatum Dei: potentiæ hostili potentiam Dei: imbecillitati nostræ omnipotentiam Dei opponat. Sic fiet ut si caro te vocet ad tuendam hanc terrenam quietem, reclamitet spiritus & obijciat mandatum Domini: si terreare Cananæa potentia, contra confirmare divina omnipotentia: si tua te revocet à gerendis rebus imbecillitas, incitet atq; inflammet rursus omnipotentia Domini.
units.tr: Before the deed, prudent deliberation arises, in which our strength is compared with the power of the neighbouring nations; here we see ourselves either not firm enough or not sufficiently equipped. From this fear also arises, which looks around to see on what side there is some falsehood, whether in men or elsewhere. This sometimes calls our whole minds back from God and brings it about that, through fear of danger, men choose for themselves a life of ease and human friendships in preference to the confession and furtherance of the truth, and in preference to the covenant of God. So the Israelites judge the Canaanites to be strong, powerful and warlike, while they themselves are neither equipped with strength nor with any means suitable against them. But Moses powerfully checks this fear, since he sets against the zeal for quiet and leisure the command of God; against the enemy's power the power of God; against our weakness the almighty power of God. So it will come about that if the flesh calls you to defend this earthly quiet, the spirit will cry out against it and set before you the command of the Lord; if the power of the Canaanites terrifies you, the divine omnipotence will on the contrary strengthen you; if your own weakness recalls you from undertaking things, the omnipotence of the Lord will again stir up and inflame you.

units.la: Sed quoniam hæc animos nostros firmandi ratio melius ex verbis Mosis perspici pote-rit, eorum ipsorum nobis est suscipienda consideratio: Ac primum mandatum Domini sic proponit ut volenti nec sit nec videatur difficile: Deuorabis (inquit) omnes populos quos tradet Dominus, oculus tuus non parcat eis, illorum Deos non coles: nam id tibi in laqueum foret. Deuorandi verbo ostendit utra pars altera sit potior, quæ consumit, an quæ consumi-tur. Si Deus vobis Israelijs hoc dedit ut ceu leones illos homines consumatis: quid illos metuitis.
units.tr: But since this method of strengthening our minds can be better seen from the words of Moses, we must take up their consideration. First he sets out the command of the Lord in such a way that it is not and does not seem difficult to one who is willing: "You shall devour," he says, "all the peoples whom the Lord delivers to you; your eye shall not spare them; you shall not serve their gods, for that would be a snare to you." By the word "devour" he shows which side is the stronger, the one that consumes or the one that is consumed. If God has given you Israelites this, that you should devour those men like lions, why do you fear them?

units.la: Deinceps tradendi verbo ostendit victoriam fore facillimam. Nam si Dominus, qui potentissimus est omnium, tradat eos, qui tu non superes? Veluti pater filio comprehensum aliquem verberibus cedendum tradat ac teneat, sic Deus pater suis filiis impios tradit superandos.
units.tr: Next, by the word "deliver" he shows that the victory will be very easy. For if the Lord, who is the most powerful of all, delivers them, how could you not overcome them? Just as a father hands over someone caught by his son to be beaten and held, so God the Father delivers the wicked to his sons to be overcome.

units.la: Quæ cum ita sint, imperat ne parcas illis, ne qua clementia dignos ducas ut impunitos dimittas: nec eorum Dijs honores ullos habe: est enim hoc perinde ut laqueus aliquis quo miser irretiare.
units.tr: Since these things are so, he commands you not to spare them, lest by some clemency you think them worthy to be dismissed unpunished; nor should you show any honour to their gods, for this is just like a snare in which you would wretchedly be entangled.

units.la: In quo præclarum exemplum nobis est propositum, ut in rebus gerendis ipsum Dei mandatum semper ob oculos positum habeamus, quod sequi conveniat. Ac quæ Deus iubeat magno animo suscipe & feliciter efficies. Arduum erat negotium, quod Moses popu-lum Israeliticum, in quem Pharao diuturnum imperium habebat, quod sibi iure præscriptionis poterat vendicare, sibi permitti postularet: sed quoniam non ambitiose, non temere, verum iussu Dei susceperat, effectu facillimum fuisse legimus. Idem in exemplo Iosephi, Heliæ, Dauidis, Apostolorum perspicimus, qui mandatum Dei magis, quàm humanas rationes sequuti sine vi, sine armis res maiores gesserunt, quàm quæ potuerint armis perfici.
