Quod ipsum Episcopi, magistratus, singuli considerent. <bl>On grund Gotts wort sol man nit an-faahn / weß mann aber in Gottesworte grund hat / Seht[?] sol man redlich nachgaan.</bl> Veluti nostra ætate verum est esse solos atque impares adversarijs, qui veritatem Euangelicæ fidei retinent: ut pietas patriæ debitæ suadeat qualemcunque pacem præferendam defensioni civili: sed quoniam sine verbi divini abnegatione pax apud adversarios obtineri nequit, ac mandatum Dei par est respici: præstat homines offendi quàm Deum, corporum quàm animarum iacturam facere. Id hic Moses doceat quando iubet mandatum Domini potius, quàm adversariam vim respici.
units.tr: In this a remarkable example is set before us, that in carrying out affairs we should always keep the very command of God before our eyes, and follow it. And whatever God commands, undertake with a great spirit, and you will carry it out successfully. The task was arduous, when Moses asked that the Israelite people, over whom Pharaoh had long held rule, which he could claim by the right of prescription, be allowed to leave; yet since he undertook it not ambitiously, not rashly, but by the command of God, we read that it was very easy in its outcome. We see the same in the examples of Joseph, Elijah, David and the Apostles, who, following the command of God rather than human reasons, without force and without arms, accomplished greater things than could have been done by arms. Let bishops, magistrates and each individual consider this. <bl>On God's Word one should not begin anything; but whoever has a foundation in God's Word should then go forward with it honestly.</bl> So in our own age it is true that those who hold to the truth of the evangelical faith are alone and unequal to their adversaries; so that the duty of piety to one's homeland may persuade us to prefer some kind of peace to civil defence; but since peace cannot be obtained with the adversaries without denying the divine Word, and the command of God must be respected, it is better to offend men than God, and to suffer loss of bodies rather than of souls. This Moses teaches here, when he commands that the command of the Lord be respected rather than the hostile force.

units.la: Sed ut hostili potentiæ divinam opponas, eam ipsam quo pacto ex operibus Dei colli-gas iam edocet. Si dixeris (inquit) in corde tuo, hoc est, si cogitaueris plures sunt gentes istæ quàm ego: quomodo possem eas eijcere? Ne timueris eas: sed diligenter recole quæ fecerit Dominus, &c. Quibus verbis iubet illarum gentium potentiæ Dei omnipotentiam opponere. Ex procera Cananæorum statura atq; ex eorum oppidis, arcibus & terra tam munita colligebant eam gentem esse potentissimam: iubet ergo Moses ex Ægyptiorum internecione, ex Ægyptiorum plagis, & signis istic editis Dei vindicis omnipotentiam colligere, præq; ea Cananæam istam despicere.
units.tr: But how you may oppose divine power to the enemy's power, he now teaches by showing how to gather that very power from the works of God. "If you say," he says, "in your heart, that is, if you think: these nations are more numerous than I; how could I drive them out? Do not fear them, but diligently call to mind what the Lord did," and so on. By these words he commands that the omnipotence of God be set against the power of those nations. From the tall stature of the Canaanites, and from their towns, citadels and land so well fortified, they concluded that the nation was most powerful; so Moses commands them to gather from the destruction of the Egyptians, from the plagues of the Egyptians, and from the signs performed there, the omnipotence of God the avenger, and in the light of that to despise that Canaanite power.

units.la: Est autem hæc adversus metum præclarissima ratio. Etenim si victoriæ malorum nos terrent, cur non consolentur Dei opera? Eodem modo se Dauid adversus Goliathum, & Machabæi contra Antiochum, & Apostoli contra Herodem sese consolati sunt. Sic nos animis repetamus eas victorias, quas Deus dedit nostris maioribus, cum vires nostræ nos defice-rent, & ipse eas suis confirmaret. Is Deus adhuc superstes est, nec minus valet viribus quàm olim valuit: nec uti propheta ait, manus eius abbreviata est.
units.tr: This is a most excellent argument against fear. For if the victories of the wicked terrify us, why should not the works of God console us? In the same way David console himself against Goliath, the Maccabees against Antiochus, and the apostles against Herod. So let us call to mind those victories which God gave to our forefathers, when their own strength failed them, and he himself strengthened them with his power. This God is still alive, and is no less mighty than he once was; nor, as the prophet says, has his hand been shortened.

units.la: Obseruandum est autem quod crabronum exemplo ostendit Dominum posse omnium creaturarum rerum ministerio suos hostes ferire & opprimere. Nam aquis, ignibus, animalibus, aliisque rebus quos vult potest afflìgere: veluti centurio de morbis dicit Matth. 8. quod sint quasi quidam serui: & Propheta de Assyrio quod sit quasi quaedam virga Domini. Ergo si Deus velit, quicquid est obuium, potest in perniciem suorum hostium conuertere.
units.tr: We should also observe, from the example of the hornets, that the Lord can strike down and crush his enemies by the service of all created things. For he can afflict them with waters, fires, animals and other things as he wills. So the centurion says of the diseases in Matthew 8 that they are like servants; and the prophet says of the Assyrian that he is like a rod of the Lord. Therefore, if God wills, whatever lies in the way he can turn to the destruction of his people's enemies.

units.la: Vt deniq; nostrarum virium atq; auxiliorum cum paucitati tum etiam imbecillitati vires & auxilia Dei contra ponas, ait: Ne consternaris metu illorum, quoniam Dominus Deus tuus est, &c. Quo metu omne procul abigit, quia Deus sit in medio eorum. Habes in eam sententiam nonnihil Psal. 45 & 1. Ioan. 4. Maior est (inquit) qui in nobis est, quàm qui in mundo: In medio nostri Deum esse cum promissiones tum natura significant. Nam & natura se in immensum porrigit, & promittit suis semper affore. Sed quid hoc profecerit? Si Deus pro nobis quis contra nos? Nam ipse est robustus & terribilis, inquit hoc loco Moses. Quamobrem si Deum, qui ipse etiam terribilis est & fortis, à tuis partibus habeas, non est quod metuas. Ex quibus omnibus intelligitur initia rerum gerendarum vtut sint terribilia: tamen ab eo, quod diuinitus est mandatum non debere nos reuocare. Atq; haec de primo quod est ante factum tempore.
units.tr: Finally, so that you may set the strength and help of God against the fewness and also the weakness of your own forces and helps, he says: "Do not be terrified by their fear, since the Lord your God is among you, etc." By this fear he drives out every kind of dread, because God is in the midst of them. You have something to this effect in Psalm 45 and 1 John 4: "Greater is he who is in us than he who is in the world." That God is in the midst of us is signified both by his promises and by his nature: for his nature extends itself immeasurably, and he promises always to be present with his own. But what does this profit us? "If God is for us, who can be against us?" For, as Moses says in this place, he is mighty and terrible. Therefore, if you have God, who is himself terrible and strong, on your side, there is no reason for you to fear. From all of these things it is understood that the beginnings of undertakings, however dreadful they may be, must nevertheless not turn us back from that which has been commanded by God. And this is said concerning the first point, which concerns the time before the deed.

units.la: In facto: Eijciet autem Dominus Deus tuus gentes istas paulatim, nec poteris eas subito exciudere, &c. Secundum tempus in ipsa actione est, qua robur magnum requiritur, vt perseueres. Saepe enim res magnis animis aggredimur, verum si non ex animi sententia statim successe-rit, deficimus, remq; imperfectam relinquimus. Vnde & in hoc opus est diuinis rationibus, igitur docet non vno conatu, posse gentes has deleri: sensim hoc effici: nec si posset è re & fa-iute[?] sua fore, quippe quod periculum esset à bestijs.
units.tr: Concerning the deed itself: "The Lord your God will drive out those nations little by little; you will not be able to exterminate them at once, etc." The second time is in the action itself, in which great strength is required, so that you may persevere. For we often undertake things with great spirit, but if they do not succeed immediately as we wished, we give up and leave the matter unfinished. Hence in this work there is need of divine reasons; therefore he teaches that these nations cannot be destroyed in a single attempt, but that this is accomplished gradually; nor would it be for their advantage and safety if it could be done, since there would be danger from the wild beasts.

units.la: In quo videmus quàm non deceat nos, rebus contra ac sperauimus eueneintibus animos despondere: Deum qui magis sapit eas sic dirigere.
units.tr: In this we see how unfitting it is for us to lose heart when events turn out contrary to what we hoped, since God, who is wiser, directs them in this way.

units.la: Sic si zizania omnia funditus euellerentur, nec vlla esset vnquam persecutio, non apparet vbi nam esset ecclesia: quin plena forent hypocritis omnia.
units.tr: Likewise, if all the tares were uprooted completely, and there were never any persecution, it would not be clear where the Church would be; indeed, everything would be full of hypocrites.

units.la: Idem de peccati in nobis haerentibus reliquijs esto iudicium. Conemur saltem hoc efficere, vt in nobis imperium nō obtineat. Carthagine deleta Romana Respublica cecidit: Hel uetij deletis exteris hostibus sese ipsi persequi coepere. Quare si non omnia simul & semel efficis, non ideo desperabis. Sat cito si fiat bene. Perge vt potes.
units.tr: The same judgment is to be made concerning the remnants of sin that cling to us. Let us at least strive to bring it about that sin does not gain dominion over us. When Carthage was destroyed, the Roman commonwealth fell; when the Helvetii had destroyed their external enemies, they began to persecute one another. Therefore, if you do not accomplish everything at once and in a single stroke, you should not on that account despair. It is quick enough if it is done well. Press on as far as you can.

units.la: Post factum, Sculptilia Deorum &c. Tempus tertium notat, quod in finem facti cadit. In quo plerumq; damnum dat incuria, veluti si reliquiae non tollantur. Sed ostendit hic peccari bifariam: in idolorum reliquijs videlicet, & bonis eorum. Idolorum vsus pestis est scropha fœcundior alba.
units.tr: After the deed: "The graven images of the gods, etc." This marks the third time, which falls at the end of the deed. In this, neglect usually causes loss, as, for example, if the remnants are not removed. But here he shows that sin is committed in two ways: namely in the remnants of the idols, and in their goods. The use of idols is a plague, more fruitful than a white sow.

units.la: Magnae sunt nostra aetate contentiones cum pars statuas antea in papatu positas recon-dit, pars eas nec locis suis remouet, sed retinet, pars eorum haec complectitur numero, quae vocantur Διάχορα[?]. At Moses ea iubet demoliri & abominationem vocat. Quamobrem qui verbo Dei stare velint, ij statuas omnes templis excisas ignibus absument. Nidos, inquit, vulgus nostrum, tolle ne redeant ciconiae.
units.tr: In our own age there are great contentions: some men hide away the statues once set up in the papacy, some do not remove them from their places but keep them, and some embrace them in the number of those things which are called [adiaphora]. But Moses commands that they be demolished and calls them an abomination. Therefore those who wish to stand by the Word of God should burn all the statues cut out of the temples with fire. "Tear down the nests," as our common saying has it, "lest the storks return."

units.la: Bonorum autem seu praedae fruitio semper fuit exitio. Vnde hic maledictionem vocat, quam ne in aedes tuas importes mandat. חרם[?] vocat seu anathema.
units.tr: But enjoyment of goods or of plunder has always been a ruin. Hence here he calls it a curse, which he commands you not to bring into your house. He calls it [herem], that is, anathema.

units.la: Id documento fit nobis ne bonis ijs, quae sacrifici Antichristiani iniuste collegerunt abutamur: est enim, vt dicitur, aurum Tolosanum: quin elargire pauperibus, ne fi in tuos vsus conferas, anathemate feriare.
units.tr: This is given to us as a lesson, that we should not make use of those goods which the Antichristian priests have unjustly gathered: for it is, as the saying goes, Toulouse gold; rather, distribute them to the poor, lest, if you bring them into your own use, you be struck with anathema.

units.la: Atq; ex his omnibus perspicuum fit, vti Deus à societate, à religione, ab idolis, à bonis impiorum velit nos abstinere, quippe quod ab ipso nos haec omnia auocent. Igitur qui salutis suae rationem vllam habent, ij dabunt operam, vt his reliquis rebus foli Deo semper adhaerant, Amen.
units.tr: From all of these things it is plain that God wills us to abstain from fellowship, from religion, from idols, and from the goods of the impious, since all these things turn us away from him. Therefore those who have any regard for the reason of their salvation will take care that, with these remaining things set aside, they cling always to God alone. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT VIII. SERMO VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII. SERMON VIII.

units.la: OMne praeceptum, quod ego tibi praecipio hodie, custodietis vt faciatis, vt viuatis & crescatis, vtq; introeatis & possideatis terram, quam iurauit Dominus patribus vestris.
units.tr: All the commandment which I command thee this day shall ye observe to do, that ye may live, and multiply, and go in and possess the land which the LORD sware unto your fathers.

units.la: 2 Recorderis cuncti itineris, per quod duxit te Dominus Deus tuus his quadraginta annis per desertum, vt affligeret te, & tentaret te, vt experimento quodam innotesceret quid esset in corde tuo: num scilicet seruares præcepta eius an minus.
units.tr: 2 And thou shalt remember all the way which the LORD thy God led thee these forty years in the wilderness, to afflict thee and to try thee, that it might be known by some experience what was in thy heart: namely, whether thou wouldest keep his commandments or not.

units.la: 3 Afflixit itaque te, & passus esset te fame laborare, aluitque te manna, quod nec tu nec patres tui nouerunt, vt scilicet ostenderet tibi, quod non in solo pane viuit ho-mo, sed in omni eo quod prodit ex ore Domini homo viuet.
units.tr: 3 So he afflicted thee and suffered thee to labour with hunger, and fed thee with manna, which neither thou nor thy fathers knew, that he might show thee that man does not live by bread alone, but man lives by everything that proceeds from the mouth of the Lord.

units.la: 4 Vestimentum tuum super te vetustate non est detritum, nec pes tuus intu-muit hisce quadraginta annis.
units.tr: 4 Your garment has not worn out upon you with age, nor has your foot swollen these forty years.

units.la: 5 Sed & hoc expendas tecum in corde tuo, vt sicut quis castigat filium suum, sic castigat te Dominus Deus tuus.
units.tr: 5 But consider this also in your heart: that as a man chastens his son, so the Lord your God chastens you.

units.la: VEMADMODVM ex septimo capite potuit intelligi: perfectam Dei dilectio-nem, quæ præcepto primo requiritur, consortio prophanarum gentium mirum in modum impediri, interdumque totam frangi: sic ex hoc 8. cap. colligi poterit, homines victus atq; rerum terrenarum cura ferè à Deo solere auocari. Quo fit, vt Moses qui primum præceptum ratum haberi postulat, etiam hoc impedimentum remo-ueat. Bifariam autem victus nos à Deo auocat: vel cum aduersis in rebus atq; in rerum penuria fides nos deficit: ac non omne eius spem & curam in Dei bonitate & munificentia ponimus: vel cum rebus ex animi sententia nobis affluentibus secuti Deum negligimus: quasi rebus nostris sic stabilitis illius ope non amplius fimus[?] indigi. Vtram igitur in partem pec-ces pietati magnum damnum datur. Etenim aduersæ res tales animos ad desperationem adigunt, eoq; propellunt etiam: vt quoniam Deus non det, abs quouis etiam cacodæmone accipias: secundæ verò sic efferunt, vti neq; Deum respicias, neq; homines: ac si quid diuinum afferatur, nisi placeat respuas: hominibus autem ni spes lucri vel honoris affulgeat, quàm mi-nimum inseruiamus.
units.tr: As it could be understood from the seventh chapter that the perfect love of God, which the first commandment requires, is wonderfully hindered by association with profane nations, and at times wholly broken, so from this eighth chapter it may be gathered that people are usually drawn away from God by concern for food and worldly things. Hence Moses, who wants the first commandment kept as valid, also removes this hindrance. Now there are two ways in which food draws us away from God: either when, in adversity and want of things, faith fails us, and we do not place all our hope and care in God's goodness and generosity; or when, with things flowing to us as we wish, we forget God, as if, our affairs being so secure, we no longer need his help. Whichever way one goes wrong, great harm is done to piety. For adverse circumstances drive minds to despair and push them on, so that, since God does not give, you accept help from any devil whatever; while prosperous circumstances so puff people up that they neither regard God nor men, and reject anything divine unless it pleases them, and serve men only as little as they must, unless the hope of gain or honour shines upon them.

units.la: Igitur docet Moses hoc cap. Deum vnum semper debere respici: à Deo nec in auaritiam nec in securitatem esse deflectendum. Quæ doctrina cum ex se ipsa bipertita sit, etiam hoc caput quo proponitur, distributum est duabus partibus: quarum priore, vti res aduersas: posteriore quo pacto secundas feramus, vt à Deo nos nō auocent, præscribit Moses. Ac priore quidem, quæ verbis istis continetur, primum docet verbum Dei ceu scopum quendam ad quem collimes, ob oculos semper habendum: deinceps argumenta ad affirmandum hoc affert.
units.tr: Therefore Moses teaches in this chapter that God alone must always be regarded, and that one must not be turned aside from God either into greed or into complacency. Since this doctrine is itself twofold, this chapter also, in which it is set forth, is divided into two parts. In the first, Moses prescribes how we should bear adverse things; in the second, how we should bear prosperous things, so that they do not draw us away from God. In the first part, which is contained in these words, he first teaches that the word of God is to be kept constantly before our eyes as a kind of goal at which we aim, and then he brings forward arguments to confirm this.

units.la: De scopo, Omne (inquit) præceptum quod ego tibi præcipio hodie &c. Quibus verbis ostendit eos, si modo Deum respiciant, ab eo pendeant: in ipso omnes sibi ipsi opesq; sitas esse credant: & vita fausta ac felici fruituros & copijs atq; opibus auctiores fore. En præclarum consilium ei, qui si Deum in uno mundo sequatur, timet ne egestate pereat. Idem Math. 6. Christus consulit: Ante omnia (inquiens) quærite regnum Dei & iustitiam eius, & reliqua omnia adijcientur vobis. Idem Dauid multis in Psalmis consulit. Vt Pf. 33. Eos qui inquirunt Domini num, inquit, non deficient vlla bona. Psal. 37. de iustorum forte differens ait, Non pudefient in tempore malo, & in diebus famis saturabuntur. Et ibidem paulo post ait iterum: Iunior fui & senui, & non vidi iustum derelictum, nec semen eius quærens panem. Psal. 112. promittuntur opes & honores pijs. Prouerb. 30. Solomon petebat ad victum necessaria: diuitias depre-cabatur. Præclare etiam D. Petrus admonet omnem curam victus in Deum reijciendam, quod illi sit de nobis cura.
units.tr: Concerning the goal: Every commandment (he says) which I command you this day, etc. In these words he shows that if people do regard God, they depend on him; they believe that all their resources and wealth are in him, and that they will enjoy a happy and prosperous life and be richer in means and wealth. Here is an excellent counsel for one who fears he will perish in want if he follows God in this world alone. Christ gives the same counsel in Matthew 6: Seek first (he says) the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you. David gives the same counsel in many Psalms. Thus in Psalm 33: Those who seek the Lord, he says, shall lack no good thing. In Psalm 37, speaking of the fortunes of the righteous, he says: They shall not be ashamed in the evil time, and in the days of famine they shall be satisfied. And a little later in the same psalm he says again: I have been young and am now old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging for bread. Psalm 112 promises wealth and honours to the godly. In Proverbs 30 Solomon asked for the necessities of life; he prayed against riches. St Peter also admirably urges that all care for sustenance be cast upon God, since he cares for us.

units.la: Hæc ratio si rectè reputetur, dici non potest quantum vitiorum agmen profligaret. Neque enim vt familiarem rem nostram augeremus, vt liberis immensas opes colligeremus: vel hominibus impijs adularemur: vel conscientia reclamante superstitionibus applauderemur: vel usuris, peculatu, sacrilegio, oppressione viduarum atq; pupillorum, alijsq; sceleribus potiueremur[?]: sed earum quæ licitæ sunt, artium exercitio contenti, Dei benedictionem respice-remus. Quanto enim præstaret & nobis & liberis nostris pietas, quàm hæc impia atq; iniu-sta industria!
units.tr: If this reasoning is rightly considered, one cannot say how great a host of vices it would put to flight. For we would not seek to enlarge our household goods, or to amass immense wealth for our children, or to flatter wicked men, or, with conscience protesting, to lend our approval to superstitions, or to gain our ends by usury, embezzlement, sacrilege, the oppression of widows and orphans, and other crimes; rather, content with the practice of lawful occupations, we would look to God's blessing. For how much better would piety be for us and for our children than this impious and unjust diligence!

units.la: Sed quid fit, quod Deum non respicimus? cur illi non fidimus? Egestas, quoniam præ-fert nescio quam illius de rebus nostris negligentiam, facit, vt quando ipse videtur nobis nolle consulere: nos nobis consulturi fimus. At error hic est. Tantum enim abest vt egestas argumento fit, Deo res nostras curæ non esse, vt etiam ipso doceat magis illum nos curare: tum etiam hoc agere, vt intelligamus illum nos fouere posse naturalibus alimentis deficien- tibus. Stat igitur hæc sententia: eos qui legum diuinarum studio sint dediti, valere, & viuere, & florere. Qui id ita reclamante summa rerum omnium penuria ƒlam dicetur.
units.tr: But why is it that we do not regard God? Why do we not trust him? Want, since it suggests some neglect of our affairs on his part, makes us, when he seems unwilling to provide for us, ready to provide for ourselves. But this is an error. For want is so far from being a proof that God does not care for our affairs, that it rather teaches us that he cares for us all the more, and also shows that he can sustain us with natural food when it fails. This statement therefore stands: those who are devoted to the study of divine laws will be strong, will live, and will flourish. Anyone who says otherwise, when the greatest scarcity of all things protests, will be contradicting it.

units.la: Argumenta quibus probet à contrario, hoc est, ab ipsa paupertate sumit. Nam cum ea videatur obstare, quo minus quod dicimus verum sit: ipse docet Deum etiam in summa pau- perie suos sustentare posse: & quæ videtur vitæ exitium minari, ea ad iuuandam felicitatem nostram quàm plurimum momenti affert. Ac ne quis sibi verba dari putet, vtilitates pauper- tatis & inopiæ refert. Eæ sunt fidei nostræ probatio, immensæ Dei potentiæ demonstratio, paterna castigatio.
units.tr: He proves the point by the opposite argument, that is, he takes it from poverty itself. For since poverty seems to stand in the way of our statement being true, he shows that God can sustain his people even in the greatest poverty; and what seems to threaten the ruin of life contributes very much to helping our happiness. And lest anyone think he is being fooled with words, he sets out the advantages of poverty and want. These are the proof of our faith, the demonstration of God's immense power, and fatherly correction.

units.la: Nostræ fidei probatio: Recorderis (inquit) cunctì itineris per quod duxit te Dominus Deus tuus his quadraginta annis per desertum, vt affligeret te &c. Reuoca, ait, in memoriam afflictio- nes priscas, quibus Deus non hoc egit vt perderetis, sed vt probareris, qui qualisq; futurus sis si res postulet.
units.tr: The proof of our faith: Remember (he says) all the way by which the Lord your God led you these forty years in the wilderness, to afflict you, etc. Call to mind, he says, the former afflictions, by which God did not act to destroy you, but to prove you, and to show what sort of people you would be if the situation required it.

units.la: Eam probationem tentationem vocat. At tentatio mali quidem speciem habet, & mole- sta mortalibus, ijs videlicet, qui quid agat, quidq; afferat, non considerant. Ergo Moses hoc docet. Notum, inquit facit quid in corde tuo lateat, vtrum sis seruaturus an non præcepta Domini. Cor hominis & abstrusum est & sinuosum: idemq; potest frigidum & calidum effla- re: nec fenestras vllas habet, per quas quid intus lateat perspicias. Quo fit, vt posit simulare virtutes maximas: quas tamen nullas habet: sed afflictione quasi quodam igne probatur: ve- luti Matth. 13. de præcoci semine Dominus disserit. Ac veluti in tenebris omnes æque benè cernimus: vbi in lucem prodijmus quantum quisq; superet alterum perspicuum fit: sic in re- bus secundis pietatis existimationem pleriq; obtinent, quam tamen rebus afflictis soli fide- les tueri possunt. Sic satan dicit Iobi facile esse Deum colere qui illum tot tantisq; augeat be- neficijs. Sed rebus aduersis Iob cum sibi tum alijs hominibus factus est notior. Idem accidit Mosi, Dauidi, Ezechiæ, Petro, Apostolis omnibus. Et nobis facile est habere euangelium qui- bus tantum profuit eius professio. Quid enim interea habuimus mali, quod non vel luxu & crapula, vel imprudentia nostra nobis accersiuerimus? Igitur dicit Moses Deum penuria rei familiaris & alijs miserijs periculum de nobis facere, & experiri velle quales nos ei simus præ- stituri. Quæ cum ita sint, egestas, cuius nomine tantopere angimur, non est exitio, sed saluti: quippe quæ nostram nobis probet, & declaret fidem & constantiam.
units.tr: He calls this proving a temptation. Yet temptation certainly has the appearance of evil and is troublesome to mortals, namely to those who do not consider what it does and what it brings. Therefore Moses teaches this: it makes known, he says, what lies hidden in your heart, whether you will keep the commandments of the Lord or not. The heart of man is both hidden and tortuous, and can show cold and hot alike; it has no windows through which one may see what lies within. Hence a person can pretend to the greatest virtues which yet he does not have; but he is tested by affliction, as by a kind of fire, as the Lord discourses concerning the seed that sprang up quickly, in Matthew 13. And just as in darkness we all see equally well, but when we come into the light it becomes clear how much each surpasses the other, so in prosperous circumstances most people maintain a reputation for piety, which only the faithful can preserve in afflicted circumstances. Thus Satan said to Job that it was easy to worship God when he heaped so many great benefits upon him. But in adversity Job became known both to himself and to other men. The same happened to Moses, David, Hezekiah, Peter, and all the apostles. And for us it is easy to possess the gospel, since its profession has brought us so much benefit. For what evil have we suffered in the meantime that we have not brought upon ourselves through luxury and drunkenness, or through our own imprudence? So Moses says that God, by want of household means and by other miseries, makes trial of us and wishes to test what sort of people we will prove to be before him. Since these things are so, poverty, on account of which we are so greatly troubled, is not a ruin but a salvation, since it proves and declares our faith and constancy.

units.la: Immensæ Dei potentiæ demonstratio: Afflixit (inquit) te, & passus est te fame laborare, aluitq; te manna, &c. Penuria videtur nobis significare exitium: at nulla res est alia, qua meli- us sentiamus immensam Dei potentiam. Cum enim res nostræ in angustum coactæ sunt, tunc Deus ostendit maximè quantum possit præstare. Idque Moses hic ostendit bi- sariàm.
units.tr: A demonstration of God's immense power: "He afflicted you," it says, "and suffered you to hunger, and fed you with manna, etc." Want seems to us to signify ruin, yet there is no other thing by which we may better perceive the immense power of God. For when our affairs are brought into straits, then God shows most fully how much he is able to do. And Moses shows this here in two ways.

units.la: 1 Ideo afflixit te vt aleret te manna, cibo nec tibi nec patribus tuis cognito. Cibum consuetum videtur natura suppeditare: verum Deus ostendit Schaddai illum rerum abs se conditarum creatorem esse: qui possit vndiquaq; alimenta præstare. Quis enim putaret ei in aere esse ag- ros, hordea, molas, pistrina? Samariam affliétam fame, postea cibis hostium recreauit. Turbas in deserta loca se secutas Dominus mirabiliter pauit Ioan. 6. Quare & si naturalia nos desici- ant, tamen supra naturam Deus nos iuuare potest. Sic nos in summa rerum penuria Deus mirabiliter sustentauit.
units.tr: 1 "So he afflicted you that he might feed you with manna, a food known neither to you nor to your fathers." Nature seems to supply the customary food; but God shows that he, Shaddai, is the creator of all things he has made, who is able to provide sustenance from every quarter. For who would think that there were fields, barley, mills and bakeries in the air? He refreshed Samaria, afflicted with famine, afterwards with the food of its enemies. The Lord miraculously fed the crowds who followed him into the desert (John 6). Therefore, even if natural means fail us, God is still able to help us beyond nature. So in our greatest scarcity God has sustained us wonderfully.

units.la: 2 Vt ostenderet quod non in solo pane viuit homo sed &c. Præclara sententia. Vnum negat, alterum asserit. Negat in solo pane, hoc est, victu terreno vitam sibi positam. Caro nostra sem- per in externis hæret: eaq; si desint, murmurat. Ergo Moses negat omni ex parte nobis con- sultum esse, si cibos caducos habeamus.
units.tr: 2 "That he might show that man does not live by bread alone, but..." An excellent saying. It denies one thing and asserts another. It denies that life is set for us in bread alone, that is, in earthly sustenance. Our flesh always clings to external things, and if these are lacking, it murmurs. Therefore Moses denies that it is in every respect good for us to have only perishable food.

units.la: Asserit autem ex verbo hoc est voluntate seu decreto Dei vitam nobis constare: ac quem admodum initio fiebant quæ dicebat Deus omnia: sic quæ dicat, hoc est, decernat etiamnum euenire.
units.tr: But he asserts that life subsists for us by the word, that is, by the will or decree of God; and just as at the beginning all the things that God spoke came to be, so whatever he speaks, that is, decrees, still comes to pass.

units.la: In quo cernitur communis hominum error: qui se putant omnia consecutos esse quan- do bonis terris aucti sunt: quasi Deus alia nobis alendis instrumenta non habeat quàm terre- nos cibos. Quomodo enim Mosem, Heliam, Sareptanam, Sunamitidem, Christum vnigenitum filium sine cibo terreno diu sustentauit?
units.tr: Here is seen the common error of men, who think they have obtained everything when they are enriched with good lands, as if God had no means of nourishing us other than earthly food. For how else did he sustain Moses, Elijah, the woman of Sarepta, the Shunammite woman, and his only-begotten Son Christ for a long time without earthly food?

units.la: 3 Neq; vestes attritæ sunt neq; pedes intumuerunt. En etiam corpus simul ac vestimenta di- nitus conseruata. Sic omnia benedicente Domino firma ac vegeta. Vides vt hominum pauperum liberi firmioribus ac pulchrioribus sunt corporibus præditi quàm diuitum. Huc affer etiam quod Matth.6.supra hac re Christus disserit. Summa potentia Dei hic in primis cernitur vbi vires nostræ nos deficiunt.
units.tr: 3 "Neither were their garments worn out, nor did their feet swell." Behold the body and the clothing preserved by divine power. Thus all things are firm and vigorous, the Lord blessing them. You see how the children of poor men are endowed with stronger and more beautiful bodies than those of the rich. Add to this what Christ discourses about this matter in Matthew 6. The power of God is chiefly seen here, where our own strength fails us.

units.la: Castigatio, Ut quis castigat filium suum, sic castigat te Dominus. Præstat nos coerceri pœnis leuioribus, & desituris quàm & diris & æternis. At Deus in his terris libidines nostras coercens vel inopia vel alijs ærumnis & molestijs: id vnū agit vt adigamur ad pœnitentiam & conseruemur. Multa possent exempla afferri, sed sibi quisq; esse exemplo potest. Quocircanobis est cogitandum, Deum, etsi nos patiatur premi rerum inopia: tamen ideo de sua erga nos paterna beneuolentia nihil deposuisse: ac potius nostram virtutem probare: suam potentiam demonstrare: nos castigatos ad se in portum attrahere & æterna felicitate dignos efficere in Christo Iesu Domino nostro, Amen.
units.tr: Correction: "As a man corrects his son, so the Lord corrects you." It is better to be restrained by lighter punishments, which will cease, than by dreadful and eternal ones. But God, restraining our lusts in this earthly life by want or by other troubles and annoyances, does this one thing: that we are driven to repentance and preserved. Many examples could be brought forward, but each one may be an example to himself. Therefore we must consider that God, although he allows us to be pressed by scarcity of things, has nonetheless not diminished his fatherly goodwill toward us on that account; rather, he tests our virtue, displays his power, and draws us, corrected, to himself as to a harbour, and makes us worthy of eternal happiness in Christ Jesus our Lord, Amen.

units.la: SERMO IX.
units.tr: SERMON IX.

units.la: 6 Custodi igitur præcepta Domini Dei tui, ut incedas in viis eius, & ut timeas eum.
units.tr: 6 Therefore keep the precepts of the Lord your God, that you walk in his ways, and that you fear him.

units.la: 7 Quoniam Dominus Deus tuus introducet te in terram bonam, terram in qua sunt torrentes aquarum, fontes & abyssi erumpentes ex vallibus & montibus.
units.tr: 7 For the Lord your God will bring you into a good land, a land in which there are streams of waters, springs and deeps welling out from valleys and mountains.

units.la: 8 Terram in qua est triticum & hordeum, vineæ, ficus, & mala punica, terra in qua est oleum olearum & mel.
units.tr: 8 A land in which there is wheat and barley, vines, fig trees and pomegranates, a land in which there is olive oil and honey.

units.la: 9 Terram in qua absque penuria panem comedes, nec quoquam egebis in ea: terram cuius lapides ferrum, & de cuius montibus chalybem effodies.
units.tr: 9 A land in which you will eat bread without scarcity, and in which you will lack nothing; a land whose stones are iron, and from whose mountains you will dig out copper.

units.la: 10 Quum igitur comederis & satur, satus fueris [?], age gratias Domino Deo tuo in terra illa bona quam dedit tibi.
units.tr: 10 When therefore you have eaten and are full, and satisfied, give thanks to the Lord your God in that good land which he has given you.

units.la: Quanquam naturæ humanæ malitia multis & varijs modis sese prodat: tamen ea in vsu diuinorum beneficiorum in primis cernitur. Nam si parum det Dominus, impatientes, blasphemi, apostatæ sumus: sin multum aut quod satis est suppeditet, in Dei contemptum & nostram ipsorum perniciem datis abutimur. Quod malum Matth. II. Iudæorum ex emplo Christus notat: ac morosis pueris, quibus nec tristia, nec læta placent carmina, Iudæos comparat: quod nec Ioannes sua grauitate, nec sua Christus cõitate eis placuissent. Quod genus ingenij naturam aranearum resipit, quæ ex omnibus bonis ac malis floribus venenum æque sugunt. Iam quemadmodum hæc morositas homines ad ciuilem societatem ineptos facit: sic eosdem etiam ab amicitia ac fœdere Dei, quo nos primo præcepto allicimur, abstrahit.
units.tr: Although the malice of human nature shows itself in many and various ways, it is seen above all in the use of God's blessings. For if the Lord gives little, we are impatient, blasphemers and apostates; but if he supplies much, or what is enough, we abuse his gifts to the contempt of God and to our own ruin. Christ notes this evil from the example of the Jews in Matthew 11, and compares the Jews to fretful children, whom neither sad songs nor happy ones please; they were not pleased by John's gravity, nor by Christ's affability. This kind of disposition resembles the nature of spiders, which suck poison from all flowers, good and bad alike. Just as this peevishness makes people unfit for civil society, so it also draws them away from the friendship and covenant of God, to which we are drawn by the first commandment.

units.la: Qua de causa Moses & impatientiam vituperat ac rationibus declinat, vt audiuimus: luxum autem & abusum beneficiorum Domini sequentibus remouet: tum inter hæc duo media virtutes duas ponit: quarum studio malum vtrumq; reprimatur. Eæ sunt pietas & gratitudo.
units.tr: For this reason Moses both condemns impatience and turns it aside with arguments, as we have heard; but he removes luxury and the abuse of the Lord's blessings by what follows. Then he sets two virtues between these two extremes, by zeal for which each evil is restrained. These are piety and gratitude.

units.la: Pietatem sic commendat: Custodi igitur (inquit) præcepta Domini Dei tui, vt incedas in vijs eius, & vt timeas eum. Quod perinde est ac si dicat. Quin obserua quæ præcepit tibi Dominus, vt ea præstes, & Deum reuereare. In eam enim curam ac cogitationem si incumbas, non multum auget te rerum terrenarum angustia. Hoc enim verum est quod dicit Dominus. Vbi thesaurus tuus, ibi cor tuum, & quod poeta dixit trahi sua quenq; voluptate. Iam si Deum & verbum eius spectes, illius fruitione potitus, satis habere videbere: victu modico eris contentus. Idq; sic habere sese vides in omni vitæ genere. Quod quisq; facit maximè, eo ipso vt potiatur elaborat: ac prius non conquiescit, quàm id sit assecutus, vt ebriosus omnes suos reditus, omnia lucra, omnes prouentus, etiam mutuò comparatas pecunias, si proprię non sint, in conuiuia insumit: eodemq; modo in vestes, qui saltuosus [?]: in Venerem qui libidi nosus est. Ad hunc modum nos Moses instruit erga Deum affecti simus: nam si illum solum maximi facias, ad eum religiosis [?] spretisq; reliquis rebus omnibus pertraheris: tantum abest vt illarum penuria magnopere doleas.
units.tr: He commends piety thus: Therefore keep (he says) the precepts of the Lord your God, that you walk in his ways, and that you fear him. This is just as if he said: Indeed, observe what the Lord has commanded you, so that you may perform it and revere God. For if you apply yourself to that care and thought, the narrowness of earthly things will not greatly trouble you. For what the Lord says is true: "Where your treasure is, there is your heart," and what the poet said, that each is drawn by his own pleasure. Now if you look upon God and his word, and enjoy him, you will seem to have enough; you will be content with modest food. And you see this to be so in every kind of life. Whatever each man does most, he labours to possess by that very means, and does not rest until he has attained it. So the drunkard spends all his income, all his gains and profits, even money borrowed, if it is not his own, on feasts; and in the same way the extravagant man on clothes, and the lustful man on sensual love. In this way Moses instructs us how we ought to be disposed towards God. For if you esteem him alone as greatest, and are drawn to him religiously, with all else despised, you are so far from grieving greatly at their want.

units.la: Verum hoc ipsum verbis Mosis discamus.1. Custodi præcepta Domini Dei tui. Laborem imponit, quo ceu onere aliquo vitiosos motus sedes seu reprimas. Vt enim animalium custodia reliquas curas abigit, inq; se intentum esse iubet: sic verbi seu præceptorum Dei ob-
units.tr: But let us learn this very thing from the words of Moses. 1. Keep the precepts of the Lord your God. He imposes labour, as if a burden, by which you may restrain or curb vicious motions. For as the keeping of animals drives away other cares and bids one be intent on it alone, so the observance of God's word or precepts is such a laborious matter that it drives trifles far from oneself.

units.la: {y} seruatio adeo operosa res est, ut nugas procul abs se abigat. Nam ut lupi, vrsi, leones gregi-bus insidiantur, sic caro nostra, mundus, satan etiam diuinis legibus infeste sunt bestię. Quod ex praeceptis ipsis cognosci potest. Nam cum Deorum alienorum cultum, a quo lege prima prohibemur, vitare velimus: Deus bonae quam multa sunt quae nos inde reuocent? Mam-mon, venter, mundus ipsi quoque Deorum loco solent haberi. Si secundum praeceptum, quo vetantur imagines, seruare velis: praetextus sunt, quibus ipsum eripiatur multi et varij. Alius enim dicit esse rerum gestarum monumenta: libros hominum indoctorum esse clamitat alius: quibus dum aures praebes praeceptum diuinum ablatum est. Sic conuictus cum impijs, temeritas, impia consuetudo, aliaque praeceptum tertium de cauendis blasphemijs et per-jurio praeripiunt. Idem fit in reliquis omnibus. Quamobrem opus est impigra pariter atque as-sidua[?] custodia. Ea curas illas prophanas abiget.
units.tr: For as wolves, bears and lions lie in wait for the flock, so our flesh, the world and Satan too are beasts hostile to the divine laws. This can be known from the precepts themselves. For when we wish to avoid the worship of other gods, from which the first law forbids us, how many things there are that call us back from it! Mammon, the belly and the world itself are wont to be held in the place of gods. If you wish to keep the second commandment, by which images are forbidden, there are many and various pretexts by which it is snatched from you. One says these are monuments of deeds done; another cries out that they are books of unlearned men; while you lend your ears to these, the divine precept is taken away. So too, association with the impious, rashness, impious custom and other things snatch away the third commandment, concerning the avoiding of blasphemy and perjury. The same happens with all the rest. Therefore there is need of a vigilant and at the same time constant guard. This will drive away those profane cares.

units.la: Age ergo quae praecepta Dei potissimum seruanda sint tecum animo reputa: ac si in eam cogitationem incumbas, sentiés te factum meliorem. Iob quia Dei voluntatem & prouidentiam haberet ob oculos positam: ablatis facultatibus dicebat: Dominus dedit, Dominus abstulit. Abraham cogitans Deum sibi velle esse Schaddai, hoc est, saturantem: sequutus est eum quoquo voluit. Apostoli cognito Christo vitae pane etiam secessione ab eo facientibus aliis, ipsi remanserunt. Igitur ad pietatem suscitandam conducet assidua verbi diuini re-cordatio;
units.tr: Come then, consider in your mind which precepts of God are chiefly to be kept; and if you apply yourself to that thought, you will feel yourself made better. Job, because he had the will and providence of God set before his eyes, said when his possessions were taken away: "The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away." Abraham, thinking that God wished to be to him Shaddai, that is, the one who satisfies, followed him wherever he willed. When the apostles recognised Christ, the bread of life, they remained with him, while others withdrew from him. Therefore constant recollection of the divine word will help to stir up piety;

units.la: 2 Vt intedas[?] in viis eius. Non otiosam contemplationem, sed actionum honestarum studium postulat: & haec ipsa ad αὐτάρκειαν momenti plurimum afferet exercitatio. Nam viae Domini minime magnos sumptus postulant, cum ea, quam ad verbi diuini studium agis, vita, sumptus mundanos minuat. Mundus ad luxum, ad fastum, ad crapulam multis: quibus pietas ad mediocritatem admodum exiguis opus habet sumptibus. In hospitalitatem & eleemosynas insumit plurimum. Memineris igitur diuinarum legum studijs nostros nobis sumptus minui. Id agit Moses.
units.tr: 2. That you walk in his ways. It demands not idle contemplation but the pursuit of honourable actions; and this very exercise will contribute greatly to self-sufficiency [αὐτάρκειαν]. For the ways of the Lord require by no means great expenses, since the life you lead for the study of the divine word diminishes worldly expenses. The world spends much on luxury, on display and on gluttony for many, whereas piety, which needs only a moderate outlay, has very modest expenses. It spends much on hospitality and alms. Remember therefore that by study of the divine laws our own expenses are reduced. This is what Moses aims at.

units.la: 3 Vt timeas eum. Timor Dei cum praesentis fortis impatientiam, tum abusum lautae fortu-nae reprimit. Semper enim veretur iudicium Domini. Quod Deus imposuit aequo animo fert malum: Bono quod dedit & contentus est & recte fruitur. Ex quibus colligi potest verisi-mum esse quod praeclare scriptum est a D. Paulo ad Timoth. pietatem videlicet utilem esse ad omnia. Recte ergo Moses hanc commendat nobis.
units.tr: 3. That you fear him. The fear of God restrains both impatience in adversity and the abuse of prosperous fortune. For he always reveres the judgment of the Lord. What God has imposed he bears with an even mind; what he has given, he enjoys with contentment and rightly. From these things it can be gathered that what St Paul wrote excellently to Timothy is true, namely that piety is profitable for all things. Rightly therefore Moses commends it to us.

units.la: Gratitudinem vero sic docet: Quoniam Dominus Deus tuus introducit te in terram bonam, in qua sunt &c. Ex quibus verbis perspicuum est ad gratitudinem requiri duo: primum, ut beneficium quanti sit recte aestimetur animo: alterum, ut quod noris esse magnum beneficium, id laudes ac magnifice praedices.
units.tr: He teaches gratitude thus: For the Lord your God brings you into a good land, in which there are etc. From these words it is clear that two things are required for gratitude: first, that the worth of a benefit be rightly estimated in the mind; second, that what you know to be a great benefit you praise and extol magnificently.

units.la: Vt æstimes, hoc ipso docet, quod terram hanc adeo diligenter describit: ac primum bonam dicit: tum id probat enumeratione partium. Commemorat autem quæ ad incolumitatem vitæ pertinent bona potissima: aquas videlicet, & prouentus, & metalla.
units.tr: He teaches us to estimate it by this very fact, that he describes this land so carefully, and first calls it good; then he proves this by enumerating its parts. He mentions the chief goods that pertain to the safety of life: namely waters, produce and metals.

units.la: Aquarum genera tria ponit, nempe flumina, fontes, abyssus siue lacus aut maria: flumina cum aerem, ne stando putrescat, refrigerent: cum apta sint nauigationibus & alijs rebus com pluribus: & ad sanitatem & alimoniam hominum conducunt plurimum. Fontes autem cum pecori tum ipsis hominibus potandis seruiunt. Stagna vero siue maria, quoniam & piscium omne genus fouent: & vehendis mercibus & hominibus seruiunt, dictu mirum est quanto-pere nostram ad vtilitatem pertineant.
units.tr: He sets down three kinds of waters: rivers, springs, and deeps, that is lakes or seas. Rivers cool the air, lest it rot by standing; they are suitable for navigation and for many other uses, and they contribute greatly to people's health and nourishment. Springs serve for watering livestock and humans themselves. Pools or seas, since they also nourish every kind of fish, and serve for carrying merchandise and people, it is wonderful to say how greatly they pertain to our use.

units.la: Prouentus dein eos refert, qui non solum necessitati, sed etiam sanitati & voluptati ser-uiunt: quod genus sunt triticum, hordeum, oleum, vinum, mel, ficus, mala punica.
units.tr: Next he mentions the produce, which serves not only necessity but also health and pleasure; of this kind are wheat, barley, oil, wine, honey, figs and pomegranates.

units.la: Metalla vero [illegible, ~4 letters] appellatione complectitur, ut æs, chalybem ferrum. Quo referas aurum etiam, & argentum, & salem, & quae terris effodiuntur opes.
units.tr: Under the term "metals" he includes bronze, steel and iron. To these you may add gold and silver, salt, and whatever wealth is dug out of the earth.

units.la: Atque haec est illa tam beata terra, quam habitantes, ait, nec vllius rei penuria sint labo-raturi Israelitæ: qua sola potitis[?] perspicuum esse potuit, diuinarum legum studiosis bene es-se. Etenim res ad necessitatem, ad sanitatem, ad suauitatem & delectationem produxit mul-tas ac varias.
units.tr: This is that very rich land which, he says, the Israelites would inhabit and would never lack anything to work at. From this alone it could be plain that those who study the divine laws fare well. For the land has produced many and varied things, for necessity, for health, and for pleasure and delight.

units.la: Sed quid hac commemoratione effecit Moses? nempe ut illa non contenti regem sibi dari poscerent, qui illos in aula foueret. Eos profecto nos imitamur: qui nostræ terræ bonis non contenti inhiamus alienis: ac quæ non sufficit otiosis & truncis fruges consumere natis terra ea dicitur nobis non sufficere. Vulgo dicimus: <bl>Eß muß es einer Bälen der Schü[?]d mit wyden</bl> <bl>wyden Ginndtes wile aber nieman mit wyden Ginden : es muß alle syden vnd sammes sn[?].</bl> Quo fit, vt ad suppeditandos nostro luxui sumptus:eos, quibus nostri maiores non sine sudore & sanguine liberarunt se & nos,reges nobis repetamus. His regibus sunt miseri qui per soluant rustici. Quin bona data diuinitus agnoscamus.
units.tr: But what did Moses achieve by this recital? Surely that the people, not content with it, demanded a king to be given them, who would cherish them at court. We certainly imitate them: not content with the goods of our own land, we covet what belongs to others, and the land is said not to suffice for us, since it cannot support idle and worthless men who consume its fruits. We commonly say: "One must have a [farm] with wide [acres]; but nobody wants to be content with wide [acres]; it must all be silk and velvet." Hence, to supply the expenses of our luxury, we seek back as kings those whom our ancestors freed themselves and us from, not without sweat and blood. For these kings the poor countryfolk are wretched and are ground down. Rather, let us acknowledge the goods given us by God.

units.la: Vt agnita prædices sic docet:Cum igitur (inquit) comederis & satur factus fueris, age gratias &c. Agnitionem beneficij gratiarum actio sequitur. Vt quæ magna accepisti, de ijs Deo datori gratias dignas agas. Exemplo sunt Psalmi & cantica Dauidis, Mosis, Deborę, Mariæ virginis, Simeonis, Zachariæ, & aliorum. Et ad gratiarum actionem assuefaciendi sunt etiam liberi. Et gratiarum actionis atque laudis sacrificium solum ex omni sacrificiorum genere sempiternum est. De quo scriptum est: Inuoca me in die tribulationis & eripiam te, & glorificabis me. Et immola Deo sacrificium laudis. Et sacrificiū laudis honorificabit me.
units.tr: So that we may recognise them, he teaches as follows: When therefore you have eaten and been filled, give thanks, etc. Thanksgiving follows the acknowledgement of a benefit, so that you may render fitting thanks to God the giver for the great things you have received. The Psalms and songs of David, Moses, Deborah, the virgin Mary, Simeon, Zechariah and others are examples of this. Children too are to be accustomed to giving thanks. And the sacrifice of thanksgiving and praise alone, of every kind of sacrifice, is everlasting. Of it is written: Call upon me in the day of trouble, and I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me. And offer to God the sacrifice of praise. And the sacrifice of praise will honour me.

units.la: Iam cum omnium hominum rationem Deus habeat, ac sine munere vacuum dimiserit neminem: omnes homines canendis seu prædicandis eius laudibus dediti sint æquum est. Et si præter Christum Iesum patronum ac vindicem nihil dedisset hominibus, satis gratia- rum illi nunquam haberemus.
units.tr: Since God takes account of all men, and has never let anyone go empty-handed without a gift, it is right that all men should devote themselves to singing or proclaiming his praises. And if he had given men nothing beside Christ Jesus, our patron and deliverer, we could never render him thanks enough.

units.la: Ergo vt ne qua desperatione à Deo te auelli patiare, docet Moses pietate & gratitudine effici. vt cum Deum solum facias maximi, rerum mundanarum curam non ita magnam habeas: tum autem vt agnoscas & magnificè prædices, quę habes Dei beneficia. Quæ ratio Deo gratissima fuerit. Ei sit honos, Amen.
units.tr: Therefore, so that you do not allow yourself to be torn away from God by any despair, Moses teaches that it is brought about by piety and gratitude: so that, while you hold God alone in highest regard, you may have less concern for worldly things, and that you may acknowledge and magnificently proclaim the benefits of God that you possess. This is the course most pleasing to God. To him be honour. Amen.

units.la: SERMO X.
units.tr: SERMON X.

units.la: 11 Caue ne forte obliuiscaris Domini Dei tui, & non custodias præcepta eius atq; iudicia eius, & ritus eius, quæ ego præcipio tibi hodie.
units.tr: 11 Take heed lest perhaps you forget the Lord your God, and do not keep His commandments and His judgments and His statutes, which I command you today.

units.la: 12 Ne forte comedas, & satur factus domos pulchras extruas & inhabites.
units.tr: 12 Lest perhaps you eat and, being full, build fine houses and dwell in them.

units.la: 13 Armenta tua, & greges tui augescant tibi, aurum & argentum multum sit tibi, & quicquid deniq; habes augescat.
units.tr: 13 Let your herds and your flocks increase for you, let there be much gold and silver for you, and whatever you have at last, let it increase.

units.la: 14 Et hinc eleuetur cor tuum, & obliuiscaris Domini Dei tui, qui te eduxit de terra Ægypti, de domo seruitutis.
units.tr: 14 And then your heart be lifted up, and you forget the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.

units.la: 15 Qui dux tuus fuit in deserto magno & horribili (in quo fuerunt) serpentes vrentes, scorpiones & siccitas absque vlla aqua. Ipse vero produxit tibi aquam è petra durissima.
units.tr: 15 Who was your leader in the great and dreadful desert (in which there were) fiery serpents, scorpions, and drought without any water. But he brought forth water for you out of the hardest rock.

units.la: 16 Ipse te aluit manna in deserto, quod nesciérunt patres tui, vt scilicet afflige ret & tentaret te, atq; sic tibi tandem benefaceret.
units.tr: 16 He fed you with manna in the desert, which your fathers did not know, so that he might afflict you and test you, and thus at last do you good.

units.la: 17 Ne diceres in corde tuo: Virtus mea & robur manus meæ parauit mihi banc opulentiam.
units.tr: 17 Lest you say in your heart: My power and the strength of my hand has gained me this wealth.

units.la: 18 Memineris itaque Domini Dei tui, quia ipse est qui dat tibi virtutem, vt opes tibi pares, vt scilicet confirmet fœdus suum quod iurauit patribus tuis, vt esta tur dies hæc.
units.tr: 18 Remember, therefore, the Lord your God, for it is he who gives you the power to gain wealth, so that he may confirm his covenant which he swore to your fathers, as it is this day.

units.la: 19 Si vero omnino oblitus fueris Domini Dei tui, atque sequutus fueris Deos alios, & coluerís eos, adorauerisque eos, certissime (quod & testor vobis hodie) peribitis.
units.tr: 19 But if you indeed forget the Lord your God, and follow other gods, and serve them and worship them, you will most surely perish (as I also testify to you today).

units.la: 20 Quemadmodum gentes quas Dominus perdidit ante vos, sic peribitis & vos, eò quod non obedieritis voci Domini Dei vestri.
units.tr: 20 Just as the nations which the Lord destroyed before you, so you too will perish, because you did not obey the voice of the Lord your God.

units.la: CVm primum præceptum, cuius expositionem capp.istis Moses affert, hoc requirat, vt Deo toti dediti simus: pietatem & gratitudinem quasi in medio collocat, vt nos doceant Dei voluntatem solam spectare, eíque nos & in secunda & in aduersa fortuna sic subijcere, vt si is parum det, contenti simus, sin multum suppeditet, etiam eo ipso recte fruamur. Qua mediocritate efficitur, vt duo maxima crimina, ingratitudo scilicet & impatientia reprimantur. Quemadmodum igitur Moses eorum alterum remouit antea: sic in præsentia remouet alterum. Ac quo melius caueri possit, ipsum describit diligentissime. Primum enim cau sam efficientem: tum effecta pingit cum suis remedijs.
units.tr: SINCE the first commandment, whose exposition Moses gives in these chapters, requires that we be wholly devoted to God, he places piety and gratitude, as it were, in the middle, to teach us to look to God's will alone, and to submit ourselves to him in both prosperity and adversity, so that if he gives little we are content, and if he supplies much we also enjoy it rightly. By this moderation it comes about that the two greatest crimes, namely ingratitude and impatience, are restrained. Therefore, just as Moses earlier removed the one, so now he removes the other. And so that this may be guarded against more effectively, he describes it very carefully. First he sets out the efficient cause, then he portrays the effects together with their remedies.

units.la: Efficiens causa ad hunc modum describitur: Cauene forte obliuiscaris Domini Dei tui, &c. Quibus verbis causam efficientem ingratitudinis sic describit, ut quibus assurgat gradi-bus intelligamus. Causa ipsa est Dei datoris obliuio. Dicit enim: Cauene obliuiscaris Domini Dei tui. Id est, si vis ingratitudinem euitare, fac Dei, quo datore bona habes omnia, memoriam perpetua cum pietate custodias.
units.tr: The efficient cause is described in this way: Take heed lest perhaps you forget the Lord your God, etc. In these words he describes the efficient cause of ingratitude in such a way that we may understand the steps by which it rises. The cause itself is forgetfulness of God the giver. For he says: Take heed lest you forget the Lord your God. That is, if you wish to avoid ingratitude, keep the memory of God, by whom you have all good things, with constant piety.

units.la: Quod indicio fuerit ingratitudinem ex obliuione proficisci. Nec mirum. In eum enim cuius meminisse desieris, facile est ingratum fieri. Exempla docebunt. Adam oblitus eius quod ipsum produxerat ac ditauerat Dei, peccat: idem usu evenit Sauli, Dauidi, Solomoni, Israeli-tis, Iudæis, nobis ipsis. Dedit nobis Dominus, ut animas, simul ac corpora liberaremus à iu-go seu tyrannide: eius libertatis iam pertesum est, & toleratæ seruitutis deposita atq; obscurata memoria: quò fit ut & donis abutamur, & in eum qui dedit ingrati sumus. Sic priuatim alius ditatus se fuisse pauperem: alius auctus honoribus se fuisse obscurum atq; ignobilem: alius valetudine bona recuperata se fuisse ægrum obliuiscimur. Quando malis angimur, tum Deum precamur: at vbi illis defuncti fumus, Deo posthabito conuertimur ad luxum & crapulam. Qui id ita? Quia veteris mali deposita est memoria.
units.tr: That this is a sign that ingratitude arises from forgetfulness is no surprise. For it is easy to become ungrateful toward one whom you have ceased to remember. Examples will teach us. Adam, forgetting that God had made and enriched him, sinned. The same thing happened to Saul, David, Solomon, the Israelites, the Jews, and to ourselves. The Lord gave us, as we were freed from the yoke or tyranny, both bodies and souls. We are now weary of that liberty, and the memory of the slavery we endured has been laid aside and obscured. Hence it happens that we both abuse his gifts and are ungrateful to him who gave them. Thus privately, one forgets that he was once poor though now rich; another forgets that he was once obscure and ignoble though now raised by honours; another forgets that he was sick though his health has been restored. When we are troubled by evils, then we pray to God; but when we have been freed from them, we turn, setting God aside, to luxury and drunkenness. Why is this so? Because the memory of the former evil has been put away.

units.la: Sed quibus gradibus ascendat in nos obliuio, Moses hoc loco paulò altius repetit, ac primum ait, Quia non custodis præcepta, iudicia, ritus Domini. Hoc est quæ Deus de moribus, de iure & æquitate, de religione deniq; tradidit, ea tute negligis. Ostendit verbi diuini, ex quo Deus omnium optime cognoscitur, usum nullum esse: unde hæc existit obliuio. Quemadmodum artes sine exercitio non hærent animis, nec radices agunt altius: sic animis nostris non imprimetur sine verbi Dei studio, solida Dei cognitio. 3ßt sich ab[?] Discis exemplis. Saul quò magis Samuelis sermones despiceret ac suis opinionib⁹ posthaberet, hoc magis in Deū ingratus evadebat. Iudæi quò plus operæ in traditionibus suis ponerent, hoc magis diuinarum legū obliuiscebantur. Idem papistis qui cerimonias magis respiciunt quà euangelii usuenit. Idé nostris hominibus qui deambulationibus magis delectantur quàm sacris con-cionibus, accidit. Summa, qui sua magis respiciunt quàm Dei consilia: ii sui magis quàm Dei sunt memores.
units.tr: But by what steps forgetfulness creeps upon us, Moses here traces a little more deeply, and first says: Because you do not keep the precepts, the judgments, and the rites of the Lord. That is, you neglect those things which God has handed down concerning morals, law and equity, and finally religion. He shows that where there is no use of the divine Word, by which God is best known, this forgetfulness arises. Just as skills do not remain in the mind without practice, nor take deeper root, so a firm knowledge of God will not be impressed on our minds without diligent study of the Word of God. Learn from examples. The more Saul despised Samuel's words and preferred his own opinions, the more ungrateful he became toward God. The more the Jews devoted their effort to their own traditions, the more they forgot the divine laws. The same happens to the Papists, who regard ceremonies more than the gospel. It happens to our own people too, who take more delight in walks than in holy sermons. In sum, those who regard their own affairs more than the counsels of God are more mindful of themselves than of God.

units.la: Deinceps dicit, Ne comedas, satieris, domos habites: pecus, aurum, argentū, deniq; opes respicias: in his oblectes te te. Diuitiæ si affluant, nolite cor apponere. Tum enim non cogitatur de bene dictione, sed ut census censum, pecus pecus, fructus fructum augeat. Tua tibi sapientia ac prudentia acquiri: tua cura diuitiæ conseruari ac cumulari videbuntur: nec erit benedictionis diuinæ ratio. Quibus ex curis atq; studiis obliuio Dei proficiscitur.
units.tr: Next he says: Do not eat and be full, dwell in houses, look to flocks, gold, silver, and finally to wealth; take your delight in these. If riches flow in, do not set your heart upon them. For then one does not think about the blessing, but only how money may increase money, flock flock, and produce produce. Your own wisdom and prudence seem to acquire wealth, and your own care seems to preserve and heap it up, and there is no account of the divine blessing. From these cares and pursuits forgetfulness of God proceeds.

units.la: Postremo ait, Et hinc eleuetur cor tuum & obliuiscaris &c. Uti hæc bestia cum enascatur tum excrescat vides: videlicet posthabito verbo Domini tua consilia, tuas opes, tuam spe-ctas magnitudinem, tunc tibi places. Atque hæ sunt illæ, quibus verbi diuini semen suffocatur, spinæ: hæ sunt illæ quibus hoc semen devoratur, aues. Unde existit obliuio. Quid mirum est nullam in animis nostris esse Dei memoriam? Certè cum nihil in Ecclesiis habeamus reliquum præter missas ac statuas, nihil est quod eius in nobis conseruet memoriam. Iam si meminisse desieris, non amplius diliges: si non diligas, ab eius lege discesseris. At tetrum vitium est ingratitudo. Nam & accepta ut pereant efficit: perit enim in ingratum quicquid contuleris: & iis quæ daturus erat indignos facit: quis enim suos thesauros in cribrum effunderet.
units.tr: Finally he says: And then your heart be lifted up, and you forget, etc. You see how this weed, once it sprouts, also grows: namely, when the Lord's word is set aside and you look to your own counsels, your own wealth, your own greatness, then you are pleased with yourself. And these are the thorns by which the seed of the divine Word is choked; these are the birds by which this seed is devoured. From these forgetfulness arises. Why wonder that there is no memory of God in our minds? Surely, since we have nothing left in our churches but masses and statues, there is nothing that preserves his memory in us. Now if you cease to remember, you will no longer love; if you do not love, you will have departed from his law. But ingratitude is a foul vice. For it causes even what was received to perish: whatever you have bestowed is lost on an ungrateful person; and it makes people unworthy of what he was about to give. For who would pour out his treasures into a sieve?

units.la: Quamobrem cauendum est hoc vitium, & enitendum ut obstes principiis: nam sero medicina paratur, cum morbi per longas conualuere moras. At sublata causa, quod efficitur, sustuleris. Id qui fiat Moses jam edocet: nempe si in partem contrariam conuertare: id est, si beneficia data subinde recolas, ac quæ quantaq; sint tecum animo reputes. Quod indicat longa beneficiorum commemoratione.
units.tr: Therefore this vice must be guarded against, and we must strive to withstand it at the beginning, for medicine is prepared too late when the disease has grown strong through long delay. But once the cause is removed, you will have removed what it produces. Moses now teaches how this is done: namely, by turning to the opposite course, that is, by frequently recalling the benefits given and by considering in your mind how great and how many they are. This he indicates by a long recounting of the benefits.

units.la: 1 Eterra Ægypti, domo seruitutis, &c. Magnum est beneficium libertatis, & tanti semper fuit manumissio, ut ingratos libertos in seruitutem reuocare patroni iure possent. Sic nos cogitabimus quibus ex malis miseriisque erepti sumus: & in quæ mala rua-mus ingrati.
units.tr: 1 Out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage, etc. The benefit of liberty is great, and manumission has always been so valued that patrons could by law reduce ungrateful freedmen to slavery again. So let us consider from what evils and miseries we have been rescued, and into what evils we rush when ungrateful.

units.la: 2 Dux fuit in deserto magno. Describit auersa mortis, famis, aliaq; pericula. Ostendit mo-dum opis latæ fuisse difficilem. Oÿe nitring ʒugangen / nit cin[?] yeder herte mögen.
units.tr: 2 He was your leader in the great desert. He describes the dangers of death, famine, and other perils. He shows that the means of help was difficult to come by. Without struggle, which not every heart can endure.

units.la: Sic Christi sanguine, quo solo mundari potuimus, liberati: sic ingentibus victoriis, magnisq; præliis libertas oppressis reddita est: sic papatus oneribus mirabiliter leuati sumus. Quæ cogitatio retinenda est animis, ut ingratorum crimen deuitemus. Adinuabunt conciones sacræ & lectio biblica, & pia colloquia, & sancta carmina, quibus ne turpes illas & obscoenas anteponas, caue. Sic itur obuiam obliuioni.
units.tr: So we have been freed by the blood of Christ, the only thing by which we could be cleansed; so liberty has been restored to those oppressed by great victories and great battles; so we have been wonderfully relieved of the burdens of the papacy. This thought must be kept in our minds, so that we may avoid the sin of ingratitude. Holy sermons, the reading of the Bible, pious conversations, and sacred songs will help, and beware of putting base and obscene things before these. In this way forgetfulness is met.

units.la: Effecta. Et dices in corde tuo, virtus mea &c. Quo ostendit ex ea, quam nobis peperit obliuio, ingratitudine magnam superbia atq; arrogantiam proficisci: quam prosopopœia describit. En nostram potentiam atq; opulentiam: en nos tam bellicosos & inuictos populos. Sic introducit Iudæos: quid de nobis? Papistæ sua prædicant opera, quorum splendore ductus Deus eos amet. Inde nostra nobis placet euangelica sententia. Quid Dominus? Caro & sanguis non reuelat hæc. Omne donum bonum cœlitus datur. Summa stultitia est arrogare sibi quæ non habeas bona.
units.tr: The effect: Moses shows that the forgetfulness we are prone to breeds great pride and arrogance out of ingratitude, and he describes this by a prosopopoeia. "Behold our power and wealth; behold such warlike and unconquered peoples we are." Thus he introduces the Jews. What of us? The Papists proclaim their own works, and God, dazzled by their splendour, loves them. Hence our own evangelical opinion pleases us. But what does the Lord say? "Flesh and blood has not revealed this" (Matt. 16). "Every good gift comes down from heaven" (James 1). It is the height of folly to claim for oneself good things one does not have.

units.la: Sed hanc docet Moses reprimere duplici remedio. Vno, ut cogites naturam Dei. Memineris (inquit) Domini Dei tui. Ipse est robur, opes, & omnia: quia promisit benigne & præstitit fideliter. En Deum fontem omnium bonorum: si hinc promanant, cur eorum te fontem facis.
units.tr: Moses, however, teaches that this pride must be checked by a twofold remedy. The first is that you should consider the nature of God: "Remember the Lord your God; he is strength, wealth and all things," because he has promised kindly and performed faithfully. Behold God, the fountain of all good things: if good things flow from him, why do you make yourself their fountain?

units.la: Altero ut cogites euentum, quod sapientissimus quisq; suaserit. Eum sic describit: Siillius[?] opt.max. Dei deposita atq; ex animo tuo deleta memoria ad alios defeceris: hoc testor fore, ut pessum eatis haud secus ac gentes ea, quas vidistis iam ante vos deletas esse, quod non obedieritis vocI Domini. Idem cogitandum est nobis qui pulsis ob ingratitudinem Israelitis, in ecclesiam Christianam asciti, successisimus: idem nobis etiam qui in Heluetia pulsis & eiectis iniustis tyrannis, ipsi nunc dominamur. Etenim si verbum Dei sicut ipsi neglexerimus, eadem qua ipsi pœna plectemur. Ergo per Christum conuertamur ad Deum patrem. Cui sit honos in secu-la, Amen.
units.tr: The second is that you should consider the outcome, as every wise man would advise. Moses describes it thus: "If you forget the Lord your God, the best and greatest God, and blot his memory from your mind, and turn aside to others, I testify that you will surely perish, just as the nations which you saw destroyed before you, because you did not obey the voice of the Lord." The same must be considered by us, who, with the Israelites cast out for their ingratitude, have been received into the Christian Church and have succeeded them; the same also by us who, in Helvetia, with the unjust tyrants driven out and ejected, now rule ourselves. For if we neglect the word of God as they did, we shall be punished with the same punishment. Therefore let us turn through Christ to God the Father, to whom be honour for ever and ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT IX. SERMO XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX. SERMON XI.

units.la: Audi Israel, tu transis hodie Iordanem, ut ingrediaris, & possideas gentes magnas & robustiores te, civitates magnas ac munitas in cœlum usq.
units.tr: Hear, O Israel, you are crossing the Jordan today to go in and possess nations greater and stronger than you, cities great and fortified up to heaven.

units.la: 2 Populum magnum & procerum, filios Enakim, de quibus tu nosti & audisti. Quis staret coram filiis Anak?
units.tr: 2 A great and tall people, the sons of the Anakim, of whom you know and have heard. Who can stand before the sons of Anak?

units.la: 3[?] Scias itaq; hodie, quod Dominus Deus tuus ipse est qui præcedit te, ignis devorans, ipse delebit eos, & ipse prosternet eos ante te, ipse exterminabit eos, atq; cito perdet eos, quemadmodum pollicitus est tibi Dominus.
units.tr: 3[?] Know therefore today that the Lord your God himself goes before you as a consuming fire; he himself will destroy them, he himself will cast them down before you, he himself will drive them out and will quickly destroy them, just as the Lord has promised you.

units.la: 4 Ne in corde tuo, cum expulerit eos Dominus Deus tuus ante te, sic cogites propter iustitiam meam introduxit me Dominus ut possiderem terram hanc, nam propter impietatem gentium istarum Dominus expellet eas ante te.
units.tr: 4 Do not say in your heart, when the Lord your God has driven them out before you, "Because of my righteousness the Lord has brought me in to possess this land"; for it is because of the wickedness of these nations that the Lord will drive them out before you.

units.la: 5 Non propter iustitiam tuam & propter rectitudinem cordis tui, tu venis ut possideas terram eorum, sed propter impietatem gentium istarum Dominus Deus expellit eas ante te, ut scilicet verbum quod iurauerat patribus tuis, Abrahamo, Isaac, & Iacob, inconcussum seruaret.
units.tr: 5 It is not because of your righteousness or the uprightness of your heart that you are coming to possess their land, but because of the wickedness of these nations the Lord your God is driving them out before you, and so that he might keep unbroken the word that he swore to your fathers, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

units.la: 6 Scias igitur quod non propter iustitiam tuam dat tibi Dominus Deus tuus terram istam bonam possidendam, quum sis populus præfracta ceruicis.
units.tr: 6 Know therefore that the Lord your God is not giving you this good land to possess because of your righteousness, since you are a stiff-necked people.

units.la: O[?]mni genere earum rerum quæ perfectum Dei cultum & amorem vitiant, prima ac princeps est quæ ex opinione propriæ pietatis & iustitiæ nascitur arrogantia: quippe qua satan non vulgus hominum fidelium, sed eos qui pietatis laudem obtinent maximam, adoritur. Est etiā hic morbus hoc nomine pestilentior, quod ne Deo datori grati simus, facit: ne quas hic dedit, virtutes exercitatione, & studio perficiamus, cum putemus esse maximas. Quamobrem ad eam explodendam iam accedit Moses, ac docet, quod Deus pulsis gentibus ipsos in hanc terram collocarit. Unde non captanda sit ullius arrogantiæ occasio, cum eiectarum gentium impietate & veritate & gratia sua ductus Dominus hoc illis beneficium dederit.
units.tr: Of all the kinds of things that spoil the perfect worship and love of God, the first and chief is the arrogance that arises from the opinion of one's own piety and righteousness; for Satan attacks with it not the common mass of believers but those who have the greatest reputation for piety. This disease is also more pestilent for this reason, that it keeps us from being grateful to God, the giver, and keeps us from perfecting, through exercise and zeal, the virtues he has given us, since we think we already have them in the greatest measure. Therefore Moses now approaches to drive out this arrogance and teaches that the Lord planted them in this land after casting out the nations. Hence no occasion for any arrogance is to be seized, since the Lord, moved by the wickedness, truth, and his own grace of the expelled nations, has bestowed this benefit upon them.

units.la: Agitur autem hoc ordine. Primum summam ac caput rei proponit, tam argumenta ad probandum tria affert:quorum primum ducit à persona deletarum gentium:alterum à persona Dei:tertium ab ipsorum Israelitarum persona.Quorum duo priora, quæ breuia sunt,simul cum propositione exponemus in præsentia.
units.tr: The argument proceeds in this order. First he sets out the sum and head of the matter, and he brings three arguments to prove it: the first he draws from the person of the destroyed nations, the second from the person of God, the third from the person of the Israelites themselves. We will now expound the first two, which are brief, together with the proposition.

units.la: Propositio sic habet: Audi Israel tu transis hodie Jordanem, &c. Quibus verbis arrogantiam suis hominibus sic eximit,ut quibus ex rebus ipsi causam eius acciperent : earum ipsarum exemplo doceat ipse eam deuitandam.Cananæas gentes propter impuram atq; impiam vi-tam eijciebat. Israelitas propter fœdus quo dignos eos duxerat,in promissam terram intro-duxit.Jam contrariorum,ut philosophis placuit, eadem est ratio:inde illi colligebant:si illos ob peccata eijcit,hos ob virtutes introducit.Ergo earum nomine sibi placeant. Sed opinionem eam frangit ac refellit Moses,dicens,res gestas eorum esse maximas:errorem tamen esse in causis:ipsos has res sibi tribuere, cum Deus eas dederit.Quod quale sit intelligi poterit facilius,si quemadmodum hic à Mose proponitur,primum illas res gestas, tum earum causas æstimemus.
units.tr: The proposition reads: Hear, O Israel, you are crossing the Jordan today, etc. In these words he removes arrogance from his people in such a way that, from the very things from which they might draw a cause for it, he teaches by the example of those same things that it must be avoided. He drove out the Canaanite nations because of their impure and impious life; he brought the Israelites into the promised land because of the covenant by which he had judged them worthy. Now, as the philosophers have held, the reasoning of contraries is the same: from these things they were inferring, "If he casts out those for their sins, he brings these in for their virtues. Therefore let them take pleasure in those things." But Moses breaks and refutes this opinion, saying that their achievements are indeed great, yet the error lies in the causes: they attribute these things to themselves, though God has given them. What this amounts to will be more easily understood if, as Moses here proposes, we first weigh the achievements and then their causes.
