units.la: Res gestas æstimat ex deuictis ac deletis tam magnis & robustis gentibus earumq; terræ possessione,ut magnis,altis,&munitis urbibus,populo procere & vasto. Quarum rerum laude suas ipsi cumulabant:<bl>hettinð nit Find überwunden</bl>.. Quemadmodum Rom.Imperatores ex deuictis gentibus Aphricani,Germanici,Numidici,Scauici,vocabantur,quemadmodum nos rerum gestarum gloria turgemus,ac bella Austriaca,Burgundica, Sueuica iaćitamus.Unde existit in nobis peregrinarum gentium contemptus maximus:quasi præ cæteris nescio quid simus,Sed & priuati sic superbiunt homines,quorum alius opes,aliis,nobilitatem,alius res alias iaćitant. Quin & in religionis causa , in qua quàm minimum arrogantiæ decet esse,plurimum est superbiæ.Quis enim non videat quantum nobis tribuamus,aliis de trahamus ? Docet igitur Moses ab inanis gloriæ studio & ab isthac arrogantia prorsus ab-stinere.
units.tr: He estimates the achievements from the defeat and destruction of such great and strong nations, and from the possession of their land, and from great, high, and fortified cities, and a tall and vast people. By the praise of these things they heaped up their own glory: Hettin nit, find überwunden (Hettin not found, overcome). Just as the Roman emperors were called Africanus, Germanicus, Numidicus, Scauricus from the nations they had conquered, so we too swell with the glory of our deeds and boast of the Austrian, Burgundian, and Swabian wars. Hence arises in us the greatest contempt for foreign nations, as if we were, I know not what, above the rest. But private persons too are proud in this way: one boasts of wealth, another of nobility, another of other things. Indeed, even in the cause of religion, where as little arrogance as possible should be present, there is very much pride. For who does not see how much we ascribe to ourselves and how much we detract from others? Moses therefore teaches us to abstain entirely from the pursuit of empty glory and from that arrogance.

units.la: Causas aut horum bonorũ,& eas quæ veræ sunt, & eas quæ veræ quidé non sunt,eiusmo-di vero videntur esse:iuxta ambas ponit. Ac summa quidé horum bonorũ causa Deus est:di cit enim:Scias itaq; hodie quod Dominus Deus tuus &c. Quo ostendit Deum nobis hæc dare: & ut credas dicit eum hæc pro sua providentia,potentia,veritate & gratia suppeditare.
units.tr: As for the causes of these goods, both those that are true and those that are not truly so, he sets them out in accordance with both. The chief cause of these goods is God; for he says: Know therefore today that the Lord your God, etc. By this he shows that God gives us these things, and that you may believe it, he says that he supplies them through his providence, power, truth, and grace.

units.la: Providentia, quod is inquit præcedit te : quomodo? In Exodo & Numer. dicitur in columna nubis & ignis ceu suæ præsentiæ certis indicijs. Cauet autem sua cura ceu lux prælucens , ne qua pedem impingas tuum. Cura terrenarum rerum penes Deum est. Igitur si nos recta via processerimus : illius non nostræ providentiæ successus hos tri-buamus,
units.tr: Providence: because he says, "He goes before you." How? In Exodus and Numbers it is said that he goes before in a pillar of cloud and fire, as sure signs of his presence. And his care, like a shining light, guards lest you strike your foot. The care of earthly things lies with God. Therefore, if we have proceeded by the right way, we must ascribe the success to his providence and not to ours.

units.la: Potentia,quod is ceu quidam ignis devoret has stipulas,ceu lapis sternit ac conterit:ceu mallius consumit,sceptro ferreo confringit hæc vasa figulina.
units.tr: Power: because he, like a fire, devours these stubble, like a stone he strikes down and crushes, like a hammer he consumes, and with an iron sceptre he breaks these earthen vessels.

units.la: Veritate & gratia,quemadmodum(inquit) pollicitus est tibi Dominus. Promisit hæc Dominus pro sua erga nos propensa voluntate & gratia:non enim quicquam debuit:præsti-tit autem pro sua veritate & fide. Quamobrem illi soli non nobis hoc acceptum feremus. Nam si Deus aut non promisset, aut præstare noluisset nil haberemus. Atq; hæc est bono-rum causa vera.
units.tr: Truth and grace: "as he has promised you," he says. The Lord promised these things out of his own inclined will and grace toward us; for he owed us nothing, yet he has performed them for the sake of his truth and faithfulness. Therefore we shall credit this to him alone and not to ourselves. For if God had either not promised or been unwilling to perform, we would have nothing. And this is the true cause of the goods.

units.la: Putatitia causa est,cum dicis (inquit) in corde tuo te fuissi: tam justum , ut dignus esset his præmijs,Hic morbus est,quem cauebis & curabis.Quin rectius de rebus,quas Deus facit judicare.Israelitæ premuntur in Ægypto:sed ideo Pharao,qui illos premit,non est eis melior. Nec Saul Dauide melior,nec Achabus Helia, nec Judæi Christo,nec papa Christianis quos persequitur. Sic quidam Germaniæ populi sunt afflicti,nos autem adhuc tuti sumus & se-curi:non sane quia simus meliores:hos afflixit justo judicio,nobis parcit ex gratia.Sic Chri-stus de turri Siloensi deque iis quos Pilatus sacrificantes interemerat.Omnes sumus pecca-tores:si quos punit, est id justi judicij:sin quibus parcat,est gratiæ.Adulter aliquis & αὐτο-φόρῳ[?] deprehensus à marito occiditur:quæ est merces condigna flagitio: sin tibi idem ite-rum atque iterum patranti scelus hactenus parcit Dominus , huius exemplo diuinitus ad-monitum arbitrator:sic ebrius tibi casus ebriorum proponito:Sic usurarius, &c. Lucæ de-cimo tertio capite inquit Dominus:nisi resipueritis simul omnes peribitis. Roman.ii.capite Paulus monet gentes ne efferantur vocationis suæ præstantia,quod æque possent repudiari ac Judæi.Roman.i.existimas[?] o homo qui judicas talia facientes & eadem facis quod effugias judicium Dei. Hoc nobis etiam cogitandum est.Si Deus nobiles expulit,poterit etiam nos expellere:si Deus papistas puniuit propter abusum religionis, eadem de causa nos quoque poterit excindere. Quamobrem non nos sed Deum respiciamus, & ad hunc modum de iudicijs eius statuamus.
units.tr: There is a fancied cause, when you say (he says) in your heart that you were so just as to be worthy of these rewards. This is the disease you must guard against and cure. Rather, one should judge about things according to what God does. The Israelites were oppressed in Egypt, yet Pharaoh, who oppressed them, was not better than they were. Nor was Saul better than David, nor Ahab than Elijah, nor the Jews than Christ, nor the Pope than the Christians whom he persecutes. So some peoples of Germany have been afflicted, while we are still safe and secure; not surely because we are better, but he has afflicted those with a just judgment and spares us out of grace. So Christ spoke about the tower of Siloam and about those whom Pilate had slain while they were sacrificing. We are all sinners: if he punishes some, that is the sign of just judgment; if he spares some, that is of grace. Someone who is an adulterer and is caught in the act [αὐτόφωρῳ] by his husband is killed, which is the wage fitting for the shameful deed; but if the Lord has hitherto spared you, though you commit the same crime again and again, take it as a divine admonition by the example of that man; likewise let the fate of drunkards be set before you as a drunk; likewise the usurer, etc. In Luke chapter 13 the Lord says: unless you repent, you will all likewise perish. In Romans chapter 2 Paul warns the Gentiles not to be puffed up by the excellence of their calling, since they too could be rejected just as the Jews were. Romans 1: "Do you suppose, O man, who judge those who do such things and do the same, that you will escape the judgment of God?" This too we must consider: if God has cast out the nobles, he can also cast us out; if God punished the Papists for their abuse of religion, for the same cause he can also destroy us. Therefore let us look not to ourselves but to God, and judge about his judgments in this way.

units.la: Argumentum primum à persona deletarum gentium sic tractat: Non propter iustitiam tuam, & propter rectitudinem cordis tui venis, ut possideas, &c. Quod perinde est ac si dicat. Nō ideo Deus has eiecit gentes, ut earum terris te quasi tuæ iustitiæ præmijs donaret, verum ut illos propter sua scelera indignos eijceret.
units.tr: He treats the first argument, from the person of the destroyed nations, thus: It is not because of your righteousness, or the uprightness of your heart, that you come, that you may possess, etc. This is just as if he were saying: God has not cast out these nations so that he might give you their lands as rewards for your righteousness, but so that, being unworthy because of their crimes, he might cast them out.

units.la: In quo vides Deum in eos quos punit impios non esse iniurium. Igitur impij sua culpa pereunt. Sic Saul, Pharao, Sodomitæ, Iudæi, Cananæi, &c. Ac si iustissimus aliquis affligatur, non habet de quo conqueratur cum Domino: in peccatis enim, ut ait Dauid, omnes nati sumus & concepti. Ergo colligit Moses: si hæc gens propter sua peccata, igitur non propter vestram iustitiam eiecta est. Ac si verborum eius seriem conuertas, habes argumentum: Impietate sua pellentur isti, igitur non pietate tua, &c.
units.tr: In this you see that God is not unjust toward those impious whom he punishes. Therefore the impious perish through their own fault. So Saul, Pharaoh, the Sodomites, the Jews, the Canaanites, etc. And if some most righteous man is afflicted, he has no ground for complaint against the Lord; for in sins, as David says, we were all born and conceived. Therefore Moses concludes: if this nation was cast out because of its sins, then it was not cast out because of your righteousness. And if you reverse the sequence of his words, you have the argument: "These men will be driven out by their wickedness, therefore not by your righteousness, etc."

units.la: Argumentum secundum à persona sua ducit ad hunc modum: Ut erigeret verbum quod iuramento promiserat patribus Abraham, Isaac, Iacobo. Ex fœdere promissionem eam conti-nente: igitur non ob vestra merita venit vobis hæreditas. Ibi enim fides in promissionum spe conquiescens est, non meritum. Est argumentum optimum, videlicet quod Deus pro-missum suum non humana merita spectet: Vbi enim erant, aut quid fecerant Israelitæ, quan-do hoc bonum Deus promisit patribus. Sic Paulus omne genus hominum admonet gratiæ scribens Romanis & Galatis. Quare cauendum est ne nos Deorum loco habeamus, ne o-peribus nostris meritum aliquod & nobis nimium tribuamus: hoc enim pugnat cum præ-cepto primo, quoꝯ[?]iubemur Deum solum spectare, & in eo ipso totis animis conquiescere. Id ut fiat ipse faxit per Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum. Amen.
units.tr: The second argument he draws from the person of God, in this way: "That he might confirm the word which he had sworn to our fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob." The promise, containing the covenant, is by covenant: therefore the inheritance has come to you not on account of your merits. For there faith rests in the hope of the promises, not in merit. It is an excellent argument, namely that God regards his promise and not human merits: for where were the Israelites, or what had they done, when God promised this good to the fathers? So Paul admonishes every kind of man, writing to the Romans and the Galatians, that they should attend to grace. Wherefore we must take care not to put ourselves in the place of gods, nor to attribute to ourselves too much merit from our works; for this conflicts with the first commandment, by which we are bidden to regard God alone and to rest wholly in him with all our souls. May he himself grant that this come to pass, through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

units.la: SERMO XII.
units.tr: SERMON XII.

units.la: 7 Reuoca in mentem, & ne obliuiscaris quomodo irritaueris Dominum Deũ tuum in deserto, ab eo die quo egressus es de terra Ægypti, & venisti ad locum istum, quàm fueritis rebelles aduersus Dominum.
units.tr: Remember, and do not forget, how you provoked the Lord your God in the wilderness, from the day you went out of the land of Egypt until you came to this place; how rebellious you were against the Lord.

units.la: 8 Sed & in Horeb ad iram concitastis Dominum, & iratus Dominus contra vos, voluit vos excindere.
units.tr: Also in Horeb you provoked the Lord to anger, and the Lord was angry with you and wished to destroy you.

units.la: 9 Quum scilicet ascenderem in montem, ut acciperem tabulas lapideas, tabu-las fœderis quod Dominus ferijt vobiscum, & manerem in monte quadraginta dies, & quadraginta noctes, quando nec panem comedi neq; aquam bibi.
units.tr: When, to be sure, I went up into the mountain to receive the tablets of stone, the tablets of the covenant which the Lord made with you, and I remained on the mountain forty days and forty nights, when I neither ate bread nor drank water.

units.la: 10 Et dedit quidem mihi Dominus duas tabulas lapideas, scriptas digito Dei erantq[?], in eis omnia verba quæ locutus erat Dominus vobiscum in monte de medio ignis, in die comitiorum.
units.tr: And the Lord indeed gave me two tablets of stone, written with the finger of God, and on them were all the words which the Lord had spoken with you on the mountain out of the midst of the fire, on the day of the assembly.

units.la: 11 Exactis quadraginta diebus & quadraginta noctibus, dedit mihi Dominus duas tabulas lapideas, tabulas fœderis.
units.tr: When the forty days and forty nights were past, the Lord gave me the two tablets of stone, the tablets of the covenant.

units.la: 12 Et dixit mihi Dominus, Surge & festinanter hinc descende, quoniam petpe-[?]ram egit populus tuus quem eduxisti de Ægypto: recesserunt citò de via quam præscri-pseram eis: fecerunt enim sibi simulachrum fusum.
units.tr: And the Lord said to me, Arise and go down quickly from here, for your people whom you brought out of Egypt have acted corruptly; they have quickly turned aside from the way which I had prescribed to them, for they have made for themselves a molten image.

units.la: 13 Et rursum dixit Dominus ad me in hæc verba: Vidi populam[?] istum, & en populus est præfractæ ceruicis.
units.tr: And again the Lord spoke to me in these words: I have seen this people, and behold, it is a stiff-necked people.

units.la: 14 Sine ut excindam eos, & deleam nomen eorum sub cælo, & faciam te in gentem robustiorem & fortiorem quàm sint illi.
units.tr: Let me alone, that I may destroy them and blot out their name under heaven, and make you a nation stronger and mightier than they.

units.la: Initio præsentis Cap. ostensum est Mosem ab arrogantia atque à propriæ pietatis opinio-ne suos Israelitas dehortari: nempe ut cogitent sese non suo ipsorum merito, sed diuina gratia terram hanc adeptos esse. Atque eam ad rem probandam argumenta tria affert: quo-rum primum à persona gentium expulsarum: quæ sua malitia sic iram Dei in se prouocarint: alterum à persona Dei, qui fœdus cum Abrahamo factum sibi tam sancte seruandum duxerit: tertium ab ipsorum Israelitarum persona ducit, idq; etiá diligentissime persequitur. Ac summam quidem eius sic dicens exponit, Scias itaq; quod non propter tuam iustitiam, &c. Quo o-stendit non potuisse fieri vt suæ ipsorum iustitiæ gratia terra hæc eis obuenerit, cum sint ac semper fuerint gens pertinacissima.
units.tr: At the beginning of the present chapter it was shown that Moses dissuades the Israelites from arrogance and from the opinion of their own piety: namely, that they should recognise they obtained this land not by their own merit but by divine grace. To prove this he brings three arguments. The first is from the persons of the expelled nations, who by their wickedness so provoked God's anger against themselves. The second is from the person of God, who held the covenant made with Abraham to be kept so sacredly. The third he takes from the persons of the Israelites themselves, and pursues this most diligently. He sets out the sum of it thus: Know therefore that not for your righteousness, etc. By this he shows that this land could not have come to them through their own righteousness, since they are, and always have been, a most stubborn people.

units.la: Hoc doctrinæ genus nostra tempestate cumprimis est necessarium. Nam hic peccatur varie Papistæ suis meritis & satisfactionibus salutem tribuunt: nos syncerioris religionis no mine efferimur: neutrorum autem tanta pietas est, vt Deus si iuste malit, quàm clementer nos tractare: non possit nostro nos merito non excindere. Etenim si inspicias vtrinque sum mos atque imos ordines: digna reperias grauibus pœnis flagitia: ad quæ Deus pro sua longa himitate & clementia pœnitentiam expectans, clementer conniuet.
units.tr: This kind of teaching is especially necessary in our own time. For here people err in various ways. The Papists attribute salvation to their merits and satisfactions; we boast of the name of the purer religion. Yet neither side is so pious that God, if he wished to deal justly, could not destroy us on account of our merit. Such is the mercy with which he treats us. For if you look on both sides, from the highest orders to the lowest, you will find crimes worthy of heavy punishments, at which God, waiting for repentance in his long patience and clemency, mercifully winks.

units.la: Sed argumentum hoc confirmat Moses enumeratione seu exemplis, sed præmissa expo sitione summaria. Recordare, inquit, quomodo irritaueris Dominum, &c. Quod idem est ac si di cat, exempla petite ex vestris annalibus rerumque in deserto gestarum commentarijs. Ipse vero primum peccatum commemorat eiq; exagerando reliqua adhibet. Et nostrum esset ex nostris annalibus peccata nostra recolere. Sed accurate persequitur omnia. 1. tempus. 2. dete stum scelus. 3. expiatum peccatum.
units.tr: But Moses confirms this argument by enumeration, or by examples, with a summary explanation placed first. Remember, he says, how you provoked the Lord, etc. This is the same as if he said: seek examples from your own annals and the records of what was done in the wilderness. He himself first recalls the sin and then adds the rest, amplifying it. It would be ours to recall our sins from our own annals. But he follows up everything carefully: (1) the time; (2) the crime committed; (3) the sin expiated.

units.la: Tempus, Sed in Horeb, inquit, ad iram concitastis Dominum, & iratus Dominus contra vos voluit vos extinguere cum scilicet ascenderem in montem vt acciperem, &c. Id est, quo tempore Dominus quid vobis ad bene beateq; viuendum opus esset, mihi traderet, ac duabus ipse tabulis hoc describeret: tunc vos illo deserto vitulum aureum vobis adorandum erexistis. En primam huius iustitiæ partem. Quo tempore Deus hoc agebat vt illorum saluti consul-tum esset: eo ipso deficiebant à Domino, etiam nondum descriptis fœderis initi condi-tionibus.
units.tr: The time: But in Horeb, he says, you provoked the Lord to anger, and the Lord was angry with you and wished to destroy you, when, to be sure, I went up the mountain to receive, etc. That is, at the very time when the Lord was handing over to me what you needed for living well and happily, and was himself writing this on the two tablets, you set up for yourselves a golden calf to worship in that desert. Here is the first part of this justice. At the very time when God was taking thought for their salvation, they were at that very moment falling away from the Lord, even before the conditions of the covenant had been written down.

units.la: Quod exaggerat adhibitis circumstantijs 1. Ascenderem in montem. Hoc est vestro, qui ipsum Deum loquentem audire non valebatis, iussu montem conscendi Deum auditurus. Erant in Mosem legatum impij, quippe quem quasi prodidissent.
units.tr: He enlarges on this by adding circumstances. (1) I went up into the mountain. That is, at your command, since you could not hear God speaking himself, I climbed the mountain to hear God. The impious were against Moses as their envoy, since they had, as it were, betrayed him.

units.la: 2 Tabulas lapideas, videlicet fœderis vt acciperem. Impij igitur in Deum erant quod prius deficerent quam describi fœdus posset.
units.tr: (2) The tablets of stone, namely of the covenant, that I might receive them. The impious, therefore, were against God, in that they would have given up before the covenant could be written down.

units.la: 3 Dedit mihi suo digito descripta quæ vobiscum locutus est verba omnia. Digitus Dei quid fit duobus ex locis disci potest. Primum Exo. 8. ex verbis Ægyptiorum magorum: tum Luc. 11. Christi in Euangelio: qui dicit digito Dei fieri miracula, & eijci dæmonia. Est igitur agens Dei virtus qua tabulæ hæ sunt descriptæ.
units.tr: (3) He gave me the words he spoke with you, all written with his own finger. What the finger of God is can be learned from two passages: first Exodus 8, from the words of the Egyptian magicians; then Luke 11, where Christ in the Gospel says that miracles are done and demons cast out by the finger of God. So the tablets were written by the active power of God.

units.la: Commendat autem has ab argumento simul & scriptore. Deus ipse non vllus angelus scripsit hasce. Est etiam, vt ait apostolus scriptura diuinitus inspirata. Quare etsi illam præ-dicent homines, tamen diuina doctrina est, cum diuinitus accepta sit. Argumentum erat ea-rum quas coram pronunciasset legum. En summam ingratitudinem pro ea quam iactabant iustitia. Sic nos interea dum salutem nostram molitur Deus in illum ipsum peccamus. Dum concionatur, oratur, multi ventri, Mammonæ alijsque idolis seruiunt. Quæ est ingratitudo maxima.
units.tr: He commends them both by their subject and by their author. God himself, not any angel, wrote these. It is also, as the apostle says, Scripture inspired by God. Therefore, although men preach it, it is divine teaching, since it was divinely received. Its subject was the laws which he had proclaimed before them. Here is the greatest ingratitude for the justice they boasted of. So we too, while God is working out our salvation, sin against that very thing. While the sermon is preached and prayers are offered, many serve the belly, Mammon and other idols. What greater ingratitude could there be?

units.la: Vt detectum scelus, Dixit Dominus, surge & festinanter descende, &c. Quibus verbis o-stenditur Deum & vidisse scelus & idipsum detexisse. 1. Iam quod Dominus etiam cum Mo-se res alias agens videt hanc fui populi idolomaniam: id nobis documento fuerit, quàm per-spicax sit in omnia quæ geruntur natura Domini: ac non vnius rei impediatur cura, quo minus videat & intelligat alteram. Videt & audit cefum Abelum, turris Babel extructionem, prisci seculi scelera, Sodomorum malitiam, Ægypti violentiam, Pauli conatus aduersus ec-clefiam nefarios. Idem etiam quæ hodieq; fiunt non videat?
units.tr: As to the crime uncovered: The Lord said, Arise and go down quickly, etc. By these words it is shown that God both saw the crime and himself revealed it. (1) That the Lord, even while dealing with Moses about other matters, sees this idolatry of his people, should be a lesson to us: how perceptive the nature of the Lord is in all that happens, and how the care of one matter does not prevent him from seeing and understanding another. He sees and hears the blood of Abel, the building of the tower of Babel, the crimes of the earliest age, the wickedness of the Sodomites, the violence of Egypt, Paul's impious attempts against the Church. Will he not see what is done even today?

units.la: 2 Cæterum quod ipsum detegit, id documento est nil tam occultum esse, quod non ali-quando protrahatur in lucem, cum hæc Deus ipse proferat ac detegat. Mosem hoc est, mi-nistrum aliquem mittens qui detegat. Eius generis ministri sunt homines, indices, signa, sua cuiusq; conscientia, quibus peccatum proditur, treist etwan Ꝑen Ɓalꝕ selbꝺ sůbin.
units.tr: (2) But that he himself uncovers it is a lesson that nothing is so hidden that it is not sometime brought out into the light, since God himself brings these things forth and reveals them. He sends Moses, that is, some minister, to expose them. Ministers of this kind are men, judges, signs, and each person's own conscience, which sometimes drives the guilty to confess, by which sin is betrayed.

units.la: 3 Quod exponit factum, ac quod qualeque fit ostendit, idipsum etiam est annotandum, nempe vt qualia quoq; videantur Domino reputemus. Quid igitur fecerant? Simulachrum fusum, vitulum videlicet. Quid tum postea? Dicit, perperam agit populus: en simulachris debitum nomen: peccatum & iniquitatem: recefsionem à via tradita. Habes quid fit idolola-tria peccatum & defectio. Cur igitur Volumus? cur sic defendimus?
units.tr: (3) What he sets out as done, and what kind of thing it is, this too is to be noted: namely, that we should consider how such things appear to the Lord. What then had they done? They made a molten image, namely a calf. And what came of it afterwards? He says: your people have acted corruptly. Here is the name due to images: sin and iniquity, departure from the way that was handed down. You have what idolatry is: sin and defection. Why then do we resist? Why do we defend it in this way?

units.la: 4 Quod denique populum qui id facit ipsum, qualis fit depingit: & ipsum est notan-dum. Vidi, inquit, populum istum, & en populus est præfracta ceruicis: sine eos excindam, nomen eorum
units.tr: (4) Finally, what sort of people he depicts as doing this, that too is to be noted. I have seen, he says, this people, and behold, it is a stiff-necked people: let them alone, that I may destroy them and blot out their name.

units.la: Ꝑ 3 eorum deleam, te magnam in gentem faciam. Quæ verba sunt paulò altius repetenda. 1. Vidi populum. Deus cordium cognitor est. Christus in Euangelio sæpe & multum hoc docet & te-stantur etiam alibi sacræ literæ: denique etiam natura quæ eum agnoscit artificem.
units.tr: 3. I will blot out their name, and make you a great nation. These words must be taken again from a little higher up. (1) I have seen the people. God is the knower of hearts. Christ often and emphatically teaches this in the Gospel, and the holy letters bear witness to it elsewhere; finally, nature too, which acknowledges him as its maker.

units.la: 2 Populum durae cervicis vocat, hoc est & impudentem & pertinacem. Sed [illegible, ~7 letters]. Audierant, viderant, norant leges, & tamen eos non pudet has negligere & transgredi. Quid de nobis Christianis, qui novæ pariter ac veteris Scripturæ testimonijs edocti simulachra mordicus retinemus? an non est magna impudentia.
units.tr: (2) He calls the people stiff-necked, that is, both shameless and obstinate. But [illegible]. They had heard, they had seen, they knew the laws, and yet they are not ashamed to neglect and transgress them. What of us Christians, who, taught by the testimonies of both the new and the old Scripture, cling stubbornly to images? Is this not great shamelessness?

units.la: 3 Sine eos excindam. Premium idololatriæ dicit, exitium. Nec aliud est expectandum or-bi Christiano tam impudenter idola retinenti: & idipsum iam sentiscimus.
units.tr: 3 Let me destroy them. He calls destruction the reward of idolatry. Nor is anything else to be expected for the Christian world, which so shamelessly retains idols; and we are already feeling this very thing.

units.la: 4 Deleatur nomen eorum. Indigni sunt idololatræ quorum extet memoria: quippe qui diuinam legem obliterauerint. Quid ijs euenient qui legem hanc etiamnum prætermittunt, vt idola retineant? Sane & eos ipsos obliterabit Dominus vt suæ voluntati consentaneam religionem obtineat.
units.tr: 4 Let their name be blotted out. Idolaters are unworthy that their memory should remain, since they have blotted out the divine law. What will happen to those who still neglect this law, so as to keep idols? Indeed the Lord will blot out even those very people, so that he may obtain a religion that agrees with his own will.

units.la: 5 Te faciam in gentem magnam. Deus ex lapidibus illis potest Abrahæ filios suscitare: ex-Mose potest gentem facere: sic etiam nobis deletis potest ecclesiam colligere. Etiam alibi ma-teriam habet unde hoc opus extruat. De expiato peccato post dicetur.
units.tr: 5 I will make you into a great nation. God can raise up the sons of Abraham from those stones; he can make a nation from Moses; so too, once we are destroyed, he can gather a church. He has material elsewhere from which to build this work. What is to be said later concerning sin that has been expiated.

units.la: Iam meminerimus iustitiam nostram esse nullam: Dei gratiam esse maximam: hac vt digni simus per Christum exorandus est Deus pater, cui sit honos in secula.
units.tr: Let us now remember that our righteousness is nothing, that God's grace is very great, and that through Christ we must pray to God the Father that we may be made worthy of it, to whom be honour for ever.

units.la: SERMO XIII.
units.tr: Sermon XIII.

units.la: 15 Vertens itaq; descendi de monte, mons autem igne ardebat, erantq; tabulæ fœderis in ambabus manibus meis:
units.tr: 15 So I turned and came down from the mountain, and the mountain was burning with fire. The two tables of the covenant were in my two hands.

units.la: 16 Et vidi, & ecce peccaueratis in Dominum Deum vestrum, feceratis vobis vitulum fusum, recesseratis cito de via quam vobis præscripserat Dominus.
units.tr: 16 And I looked, and behold, you had sinned against the LORD your God. You had made yourselves a molten calf, and you had turned aside quickly from the way which the LORD had commanded you.

units.la: 17 Et apprehensis duabus tabulis, abieci eas de ambabus manibus meis, atq; confregi eas vobis spectantibus.
units.tr: 17 So I took hold of the two tables and threw them out of my two hands, and broke them in front of your eyes.

units.la: 18 Prostratus ergo coram Domino (vt antea) quadraginta dies & quadraginta noctes, nec panem comedi, neque aquam bibi, propter omnia peccata vestra quæ perpetraueratis, faciendo malum in oculis Domini, vt eum ad iram provocaretis.
units.tr: 18 Then I fell down before the LORD, as before, forty days and forty nights. I neither ate bread nor drank water, because of all your sins which you had committed, doing evil in the sight of the LORD to provoke him to anger.

units.la: 19 Expaui enim a naso & calore Domini, quo indignabatur Dominus contra vos, vt etiam statuerit vos perdere, sed exaudivit me Dominus etiam tunc.
units.tr: 19 For I was afraid of the anger and the heat of the LORD, with which the LORD was angry against you, so that he was minded to destroy you. But the LORD heard me even then.

units.la: 20 Et adue[?]sum Aharonem quoq; exarsit Dominus valde, volens delere eum, tum supplicabam & pro Aharone illo ipso tempore.
units.tr: 20 The LORD was also very angry with Aaron, and wished to destroy him. But I prayed for Aaron at that same time.

units.la: 21 Peccatum quoq; vestrum quod fecistis, nempe vitulum, tuli, & igne illum combussi, & contudi eum molendo, idq; bene, donec pulvis fieret tenuis, abieciq; pul-verem eius in torrentem qui e monte defluit.
units.tr: 21 Your sin which you had made, the calf, I took and burned it in the fire, and I crushed it, grinding it well until it became fine dust, and I cast its dust into the brook that ran down from the mountain.

units.la: 22 Et in Tabera quoque, in Massa, & in Kibroth Hataaba iritastis Domi-num.
units.tr: 22 And at Taberah, at Massah, and at Kibroth-hattaavah you also provoked the LORD.

units.la: 23 Et quum Dominus misisset vos de Kades Barnea, huiusmodi mandatis, Ascendite & occupate terram quam dedi vobis, exacerbastis os Domini vestri, & non credidistis ei, neque auscultastis vocem eius.
units.tr: 23 And when the LORD sent you from Kadesh-barnea with this command, "Go up and possess the land which I have given you," you rebelled against the mouth of the LORD your God, and did not believe him, nor did you obey his voice.

units.la: 24 Amarifuistis in Dominum à die quo vos cognovi.
units.tr: 24 You have been rebellious against the LORD from the day that I knew you.

units.la: 25 Procidi itaq; coram Domino per quadraginta dies & quadraginta noctes, quibus me ipsum prostraui, quoniam decreuerat Dominus quod vellet vos delere.
units.tr: 25 So I fell down before the LORD for forty days and forty nights, in which I prostrated myself, because the LORD had decided that he would destroy you.

units.la: 26 Oravi igitur ad Dominum, & dixi, Domine Deus, ne perdas populum tu-um, & hæreditatem tuam, quam redemisti magnitudine tua, atq; de Ægypto manu valida eduxisti.
units.tr: 26 I prayed therefore to the LORD and said, "O Lord GOD, do not destroy your people and your inheritance, which you have redeemed through your greatness, and which you have brought out of Egypt with a strong hand."

units.la: 27 Recordare servorum tuorum Abrahæ, Isaac, & Iacob, & ne respicias ad duritiam huius populi, ad impietatem eius, & ad peccatum eius.
units.tr: 27 "Remember your servants Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and do not look to the stubbornness of this people, nor to its wickedness and its sin."

units.la: 28 Ne forte dicant in terra de qua eduxisti nos, Non potest eos Dominus introducere in terram quam pollicitus est& eis[?],odio habuit eos,& ob hoc eduxit eos,ut interficeret eos in deserto.
units.tr: 28 "Lest perhaps those in the land from which you brought us say, 'The LORD was not able to bring them into the land which he promised them, and he hated them, and for this reason he brought them out, that he might kill them in the wilderness.'"

units.la: 29 En ipsi,populus tuus & hæreditas tua,quos virtute magna & brachio exerto eduxisti.
units.tr: 29 "Behold, they are your people and your inheritance, whom you brought out by your great power and your outstretched arm."

units.la: Quemadmodum arrogantia,ac virtutum opinio vana propterea perniciosa est, quod nos ab amore Dei revocet ad nostrum ipsorum amorem: sic etiam ea ipsa propterea nocens est, quod nos ab obedientia diuinis legibus debita ad obsequium carnis & nostrorum affectuum pertrahit,hocque ipso efficit:ut vbi scelerum & malitiæ est plurimum,ibi ia-ctitet innocentiam & virtutes maximas. Qua de causa difficile est eam, vbi radices altius egerit,animis eximere.
units.tr: Just as arrogance and a vain opinion of one's own virtues are harmful for this reason, that they call us back from the love of God to love of ourselves, so also that very thing is harmful, in that it draws us away from the obedience owed to the divine laws and toward the compliance of the flesh and of our own affections. And it brings about this result: where there is the greatest amount of crime and malice, there men boast of their innocence and their greatest virtues. For this reason it is difficult to remove it from minds once it has struck its roots deeper.

units.la: Igitur Moses,ut hanc ab oculis removeat nebulam, peccata populo commemorat sua, eaque sic depingit,ut ex tempore,ex facti qualitate, ex eius ipsius expiatione perspiciant in illis esse nihil innocentiæ. Tempus enim ostendit summam malitiam: tunc enim peccatum est cum oportuit minime,benefaciente videlicet eis Domino. Facti qualitas ostendit peccatum grande:neque enim ab homine liuido,sed ab ipso Deo cum proditum tum depictum est,ita ut quale sit ipsum & quales sint qui fecerunt intelligatur. Quod nuper est expositum.
units.tr: Therefore Moses, in order to remove this mist from their eyes, recalls to the people their own sins, and so portrays them that from the time, from the quality of the deed, and from its very expiation, they may see that there is nothing of innocence in them. For the time shows their great malice: sin was committed when it was least fitting, since the Lord had been doing them good. The quality of the deed shows the sin to be grave: for it was not reported by a spiteful man, but was both disclosed and depicted by God himself, so that it may be understood what kind of thing it was and what kind of people they were who did it. This was explained just now.

units.la: Facti ipsius expositio nullis ipsorum neque precibus neque studijs, sed aliena prorsus opera comparata est: quippe quæ per Mosem suscepta ac per Deum ipsum perfecta fit. Vbi Moses Christi typum gerit. Sed hæc expositio, ut nobis seruiat paulo altius repetenda est. Discitur enim hic quoniam expientur peccata. 1. eorum odio seu detestatione. 2. coërcitione, 3. deprecatione culpæ.
units.tr: The exposition of the deed itself was obtained not by any prayers or efforts of theirs, but wholly by the work of another, since it was undertaken through Moses and completed by God himself. Here Moses bears the type of Christ. But this exposition, so that it may serve us, must be taken up a little more deeply. For here we learn how sins are expiated: (1) by hatred or detestation of them; (2) by restraint; (3) by entreaty for the fault.

units.la: Detestatione, Vertens itaq; descendi, &c. Ostendit se peccato fama audita vidisse & cognouisse ipsum,eoque sic ad iram commotum esse,ut tabulas quibus esset lex descripta,abijciens fregerit,sicque sit affectus,ut neque comedendum,neque bibendum sibi duxerit priusquam scelus rite vindicatum atque expiatum esset. Quod ipsum etiam argumento est peccatum fuisse maximum,& extitisse eius expiandi initium hoc ipsum,quod hic Moses dicit.
units.tr: Detestation: "So I turned and came down," etc. He shows that, having heard the report, he saw the sin and recognised it, and was so moved to anger by it that, casting away the tables on which the law had been written, he broke them. And he was so affected that he thought he should neither eat nor drink until the crime had been duly avenged and expiated. This itself is evidence that the sin was very great, and that this very thing which Moses here describes was the beginning of its expiation.

units.la: In quo perspici potest ad odium peccatorum hæc tria requiri, nempe ut & inquiratur, & odio habeatur & mœrore afficiat. Inquisitionem hoc ipso significat, quod se dicit prote-nus conuersum de monte descendisse,nempe ut acta cognosceret.
units.tr: In this it can be seen that three things are required for hatred of sins: namely, that one both inquires, and hates, and is affected with grief. He signifies inquiry by this, that he says he came down from the mountain immediately after turning, namely, so that he might learn what had been done.

units.la: Est autem magistratuum, episcoporum, parentum, singulorum inquirere atque animad uertere in ciuitatis,ecclesiæ,familiæ,suos ipsorum mores: ut quæ peccata grassentur & ver-gant in perniciem publicam. Audis nunc Euangelio parum consentaneam agi vitam:si inquiras,intelliges etiam cum legibus tuis pugnare. Audis querelas de liberorum procacitate & petulantia:tu tuos hoc obserua magis. Audis omnes homines peccatores esse:tuos mores tuum animum in speculo verbi diuini contemplare & scrutare quibus tu fis inquinatus peccatis. Optima sunt hæc examina. Magnus est ad sapientiam pariter atque probitatem gradus hic de monte descensu. Videmur enim quandoque sidera contingere,cœlos scandere, Deo proximi esse:verum præstaret de monte illo excelso in nos ipsos descendere, & qui qualesque simus cognoscere. Et certe non abs re conquesti sint veteres simul ac recentiores philosophi,quod in alios magis,quàm in nos ipsos descendere consueuerimus. Plærique enim sufq; deq; ferunt, ut ut viuatur priuatim æque atque publice. Quo fit impune liceat quicquid libet facere. Moses autem audita fama sceleris patrati id visum descendit.
units.tr: It is the duty of magistrates, bishops, parents, and each individual to inquire into and examine the morals of their own state, church, and household: what sins are spreading and tending toward public ruin. You hear that a life hardly in agreement with the Gospel is being lived: if you inquire, you will understand that it also conflicts with your own laws. You hear complaints about the insolence and wantonness of children: you should rather observe your own children. You hear that all men are sinners: contemplate and scrutinise your own morals and your own soul in the mirror of the divine word, and see with what sins you yourself are stained. These examinations are the best. This step of coming down from the mountain is a great step toward wisdom and integrity alike. For we sometimes seem to touch the stars, to climb the heavens, to be near God; but it would be better to come down from that lofty mountain into ourselves and to know who and what sort of people we are. And certainly the ancient and the more recent philosophers complained, not without reason, that we are accustomed to descend more upon others than upon ourselves. For most people care not a jot, however they live, in private as well as in public. From this it comes that whatever one likes is permitted with impunity. But Moses, on hearing the report of the crime committed, came down for this purpose.

units.la: Odium vero seu zelum, quo erga malum æstuet, eo ipso significat, quod tabulas, quas tamen habebat in maximo precio, commotus abiecerit ac perfregerit. Sic igitur odio perse-quare malum et rerum charissimarum, & tui ipsius præ illius vindicatione obliuiscare, nempe ut omnes hinc conijciant probitate & iustitia tibi nihil esse antiquius. Exemplo sunt Phine-es in scortatorem, Dauid in Goliam, Stephanus in Antichristianos, Christus in templi pro-phanatores. At hac ætate nulla fere est iustitiæ ratio: ac plærique si quid pro ea tuenda faci-ant:tamen id vel odio, vel inuidia, vel ambitione ducti moliantur:qui pœnitentiam & resipi-scentiam spestant raros esse,id ipsum est indicio,quod secus quàm deceat quamque æquum est res illas gerant. Idq; fit & priuatim & publice: amicus absoluitur,inimicus reprimitur. Ali-lio zelo Moses fertur.
units.tr: His hatred or zeal, with which he burned against evil, he shows by this, that, moved, he cast away and broke the tables, which nevertheless he held in the highest value. So then pursue evil with hatred, even of the dearest things, and forget yourself in avenging it, so that all may thus infer that nothing is more important to you than integrity and justice. Examples are Phinehas against the fornicator, David against Goliath, Stephen against the Antichristians, Christ against the profaners of the temple. But in this age there is almost no regard for justice; and most men, if they do anything to defend it, nevertheless carry it out led by hatred, envy, or ambition. That those who look for repentance and repentance-producing change are rare is itself a sign that they carry on those affairs otherwise than is becoming and otherwise than is just. And this happens both in private and in public: a friend is acquitted, an enemy is repressed. Moses is reported to have been moved by a different zeal.

units.la: Dolorem vero quem ex eo facto cepit eo ipso prodit quod à cibo & potu quadraginta diei continuos abstinuerit. Sic igitur nos peccata mœrore afficiant, vt si cibo potuq; prorsus omni nolimus abstinere, saltem adhibeamus modum ludis & conuiuijs. At licet in perditissima tempora inciderimus, quippe quibus non modo vetera peccata crescant, verumetiam pullulent atq; emergant noua: tamen id adeo nos non angit, vt eo magis dediti simus luxui pariter & crapulæ. Moses autem, quod solent qui anguntur animis, nec edit nec bibit prius; quàm re bene gesta. Atq; hæ res ad peccatorum expiationem viam sternunt.
units.tr: The grief which he felt from that deed he reveals by this, that he abstained continuously from food and drink for forty days. So then let sins affect us with grief, so that if we do not wish to abstain altogether from food and drink, at least we may apply some restraint to games and feasts. But although we have fallen into most desperate times, in which not only old sins increase but new ones also sprout and emerge, nevertheless this does not so trouble us that we are the more given over to luxury and drunkenness alike. Moses, however, as those who are troubled in spirit usually do, neither ate nor drank until the matter had been well handled. And these things pave the way to the expiation of sins.

units.la: Coercitione seu castigatione & disciplina qua se quisq; coercet, aut castigat eos quorum curam suscepit. Peccatum quoq; vestrum (inquit hanc docens Moses) quod fecistis nempe vitu-lum, tuli & igne cum combusti, &c. In quo videmus factum populi primum verbis castigari, tum deleri; denique exaggerari exemplis. Ac verbis quidem castigat, quod vitulum quem fecerant non dicit simulachrum, seu imaginem, verum peccatum appellat, usus eo scilicet, quod rei debebatur; nomine. At peccatum quid aliud est, quam quod contra voluntatem Dei lege expressam committitur? Vides ergo quæ debeantur, ac tribuenda sint idolis nomina. Vulgus Christianorum Christo & Diuis apostolis ac martyribus statuas ponit, quas dignatur ipsius Christi & Diuorum nominibus: at Moses peccata vocat.
units.tr: Restraint, or chastisement and discipline, by which each person restrains himself or corrects those whose care he has undertaken. "Your sin also" (Moses says, teaching this) "which you made, namely the calf, I took and when I had burned it in the fire," etc. Here we see the people's deed first rebuked by words, then destroyed, and finally magnified by examples. He rebukes them by words, in that he does not call the calf they had made an image or idol, but calls it sin, evidently using the name that was owed to the thing. But what is sin other than what is committed against the will of God expressed in the law? You see then what names are due to idols and ought to be given to them. The common run of Christians sets up statues to Christ and to the holy apostles and martyrs, which they honour with the names of Christ himself and of the holy ones; but Moses calls them sins.

units.la: Ergo Mosis exemplo discimus & ijs quæ in religione, & ijs quæ in vita ac moribus contra Deum fiunt rebus peccati nomen tribuere. Hoc agit Satan, vt falso nomine pingat ac celet vitium: sed veritatis est eam peccato larvam detrahere. Missas, superstitiosos ritus, preces hypocriticas, ieiunia, peregrinationes vocat bona opera Satan: at veritas hypocrisim, peccatum, abominationem, superstitionem vocat. Dicit enim Dominus se non coli traditioni-bus hominum. In vita, qui sunt auari frugi patres: qui profusi & prodigi, boni sodales: obscœni faceti: quicunq; deniq; vitijs sunt aliquibus dediti, ij sese nomine virtutis ornant ac tegunt. Iam ne longa subducamur fallacia cum optimorum quorumq; ciuium, tum fidelium doctorum in primis est officium, digna rebus nomina tribuere. Atq; hoc etiam docet in prophetarum libris Dominus. Esa. 5. cap. Væ dicentibus malum bonum, & bonum malum: qui ponunt tenebras in lucem, & lucem in tenebras: qui ponunt amarum in dulce, & dulce amarum. Igitur ea demum est vera ac recta vitiorum castigatio: qua malum ipsum quod qualeque sit, & quid afferat incommodi seu exitij verbis apertis & dignis explicatur. Quod profecto Moses hic exemplo suo docet.
units.tr: Therefore, following Moses' example, we learn to attach the name of sin both to things done against God in religion and to things done in life and conduct. Satan does the opposite: he paints and conceals vice under a false name. It is the mark of truth to strip that mask from sin. Satan calls masses, superstitious rites, hypocritical prayers, fasts and pilgrimages good works, but truth calls them hypocrisy, sin, abomination and superstition. For the Lord says that he is not worshipped with the traditions of men. In daily life, those who are greedy are called thrifty fathers, those who are wasteful and lavish are called good fellows, the obscene are called witty, and in short, whoever is given over to some vice dresses it up and covers it with the name of virtue. So that we are not led on by such long-standing deception, it is above all the duty of the best citizens and especially of faithful teachers to give things their proper names. The Lord also teaches this in the books of the prophets: Isaiah 5: "Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who put darkness for light and light for darkness, who put bitter for sweet and sweet for bitter." True and right correction of vices is therefore that in which the evil itself, whatever it is, and what harm or ruin it brings, is set out in plain and fitting words. This is exactly what Moses teaches here by his example.

units.la: Delet autem peccatum hoc ipso quod é medio sublatum ignibus quantum est absumit, & cineres contusos in profluentem abijcit: ne quid eius sit reliquum videlicet. Atque hoc modo sacra ab Antichristo in ecclesiam inuecta nobis quoque erant funditus extirpanda. Quid enim idola, sacella, templa, aras, cœnobia, denique etiam ipsa festa solennia, quæ reliqui mus, aliud poterunt parturire, quam hoc ipsum malum quod deletum volumus? Bene profecto vulgo dici solet nidum tollendum esse ei, qui nolit redire in sua tecta ciconias. Sane vetus Testamentum significat Deum semper hoc nomine succensuisse regibus, quod excelsa non sustulissent. Ac quemadmodum Heluetijs maioribus nostris nil perinde libertatem constabiliuit suam, ac quod in acie quidem principes viros trucidare quàm captos vendere maluerunt: in agris autem omnibus arces solo æquarunt: sic nobis ad conseruandam, quam habemus, euangelij puritatem nil perinde erit adiumento, ac cœnobiorum & papatus deletio.
units.tr: Moreover, this sin is destroyed by the very fact that, once removed from the midst, it is consumed by fire as far as possible, and its crushed ashes are thrown into a flowing stream, so that nothing of it remains. In this way the rites that Antichrist introduced into the Church must also be utterly rooted out among us. For what could idols, chapels, temples, altars, monasteries, and even the solemn feasts that we have kept, produce but this very evil that we want destroyed? Indeed, it is commonly said well that the nest must be taken away from one who does not want the storks to return to his roof. Certainly the Old Testament shows that God was always angered against kings for this reason, that they did not remove the high places. And just as our forefathers the Swiss secured their liberty by nothing so much as by preferring, in battle, to slaughter their leading men rather than sell them as prisoners, and by levelling the citadels to the ground throughout the countryside, so for us, for preserving the purity of the gospel that we have, nothing will be as helpful as the destruction of monasteries and of papacy.

units.la: Atq; hoc Moses docet.
units.tr: And this is what Moses teaches.

units.la: Exemplis demum factum hoc exaggerat. 1. In Tabera, id est, incendio. Locus inde nomen accepit, quid ignis Domini exarsit in eos, qui contra Deum murmurarent. Num. 11. &c.
units.tr: Finally, he magnifies this matter by examples. (1) At Taberah, that is, by fire. The place took its name from this, because the fire of the Lord blazed up against those who murmured against God. Numbers 11, etc.

units.la: 2 In Massa, quando in Raphidim propter aquas Deum tentarunt, & cum Mose contenderunt. Vnde, vt est Exod. 17. locus Massa & Meriba à contentione & tentatione dicitur.
units.tr: (2) At Massah, when in Rephidim they tempted God because of the waters and contended with Moses. Whence, as is said in Exodus 17, the places Massah and Meribah are named from contention and temptation.

units.la: 3 In Cibroth Hataeba, id est, sepulchris concupiscentiæ: qui locus ob crapulam mortiferam sic dictus est Num. 11. &c.
units.tr: (3) At Kibroth-hattaavah, that is, the graves of lust, a place so called because of deadly gluttony, Numbers 11, etc.

units.la: 4 In Cades Barnea. Num. 13. cum exploratorum verbis plus tribuerunt quam promissis Dei.
units.tr: (4) At Kadesh-barnea. Numbers 13, where they gave more weight to the words of the spies than to the promises of God.

units.la: In quo catalogo discimus etiam nostra peccata colligere. Papistæ preces & merita, nos syncerioris cultus professionem iactitamus: cur non etiam peccata referimus? impatientiam laborum & paupertatis, dira in Deum & ministros conuicia, luxum & crapulam, metum mundi maiorem fide & pietate, &c. Hæc nisi castigentur, non placabimus iratum Deum.
units.tr: In this catalogue we also learn to gather up our own sins. The Papists boast of their prayers and merits, and we of our profession of a purer worship; why do we not also list our sins? Impatience in labours and poverty, dreadful reproaches against God and his ministers, luxury and gluttony, fear of the world greater than faith and piety, and so on. Unless these are corrected, we shall not appease an angry God.

units.la: Deprecatione culpæ eam vt describat plenam, ostendit pro quibus, quo ritu, quibus ver-bis orarit. Pro quibus pro populo & pro Pharaone. Populus peccauerat, eum Moses non a-bijcit, sed usus ijs quæ data sunt medijs Deum pro eo orat. Sic magistratus & ministri Dauid, Daniel, Christus, apostoli pro suis hominibus orarunt. Idem etiam parentum est facere.
units.tr: In describing his prayer of intercession for the fault in full, he shows for whom, in what manner, and in what words he prayed. For whom: for the people and for Pharaoh. The people had sinned, yet Moses does not cast them off, but, using the means that have been given, prays to God for them. So too magistrates and ministers, David, Daniel, Christ and the apostles prayed for their people. It is also the duty of parents to do the same.

units.la: Aharon is erat qui populo malū petenti morem gesserat: cum eius fuisset coercere. Sue[?] censet igitur Dominus. Exemplum est mollium magistratuum.
units.tr: Aaron was the one who had yielded to the people when they asked for evil, though it was his duty to restrain them. The Lord therefore judges accordingly. This is an example for weak magistrates.

units.la: Orat etiam pro eo ipso Moses. Ergo pro iis qui præsunt orandum est etiam ex præscri-pto Petri & Pauli. Nec non iubet hoc ipsum charitas.
units.tr: Moses also prays for the very man who had sinned. Therefore we must pray also for those who rule over us, as is prescribed by Peter and Paul. Charity itself also commands this.

units.la: Quo pacto 1.prostratus, quo gestu significat animum deiectum ac humilem. Nam cum peccatum sit arrogans ac superba Dei contemptio, requiritur ad placandum iratum Deum humiliatio, qua testemur nos eius imperio cedere. Sed cauendum est ne quam gestibus referi-mus, animo nullam habeamus humilitatem & modestiam.
units.tr: In what manner: (1) prostrate, he signifies by his posture a cast-down and humble spirit. For since sin is a proud and haughty contempt of God, humiliation is required to appease an angry God, by which we bear witness that we yield to his command. But care must be taken that we do not express humility in gestures while having no humility and modesty in our hearts.

units.la: 2 Jeiunus. Nullum hic stabilitur ieiunium papisticum: sed exemplum animi sobrij, qui solus ad præces sit aptissimus. Unde & apostolo placuit ut matutinæ horæ peragendis sacris tribuerentur.
units.tr: (2) Fasting. No Papistical fast is established here, but an example of a sober mind, which alone is most fit for prayers. Whence it also pleased the apostle that the morning hours be assigned to the performance of sacred duties.

units.la: Quibus verbis, Egregie deprecatur culpam, fatetur peccatum, sed ostendit utrum præ-stet deleri an seruari populum. 1.à persona populi, tuus est, hæreditas tua, eductus & ereptus mirifice: ideo non sic perdendus. In quo discimus argumenta nobis etiam suppeditari ab e-lectione & liberatione per Christum præstita. Sic Deus dilexit mundum, &c. Ioan.3. quid porro negabit? 2.à promissione, quàm cum peccato comparat. 3.ab offendiculo, ne præbeatur hostibus calumniæ materia.
units.tr: By what words: he earnestly deprecates the fault, confesses the sin, but shows which is better, that the people be destroyed or preserved. (1) From the person of the people: they are yours, your inheritance, wonderfully led out and rescued; therefore they must not be destroyed in this way. In this we learn that arguments are also supplied to us from the election and liberation brought about through Christ. So: God so loved the world, etc., John 3. What then will he deny? (2) From the promise, which he sets against the sin. (3) From the stumbling-block, lest an occasion of slander be given to enemies.

units.la: Atque hæc ratio satis indicat nihil esse eis iustitiæ: peccatum autem multum & varium: non illorum sed Mosis opera expiatum, nec illorum meritis, sed Dei gratia. Illi igitur honos omnis debetur per Christum, in quo nos elegit, & sibi reconciliari patitur. Amen.
units.tr: This reasoning sufficiently shows that they had no righteousness of their own, and that their sin was great and manifold; it was atoned for not by their works but by the works of Moses, and not by their merits but by the grace of God. All honour is therefore due to him through Christ, in whom he chose us and allows us to be reconciled to himself. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT X. SERMO XIIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER X. SERMON XIIII.

units.la: IN illo tempore dixit Dominus ad me, Scalpe tibi duas tabulas lapideas instar priorum, & ascende ad me in montem, faciesq; tibi arcam ligneam.
units.tr: At that time the Lord said to me, Hew for yourself two tables of stone like the former ones, and come up to me into the mountain, and make for yourself a wooden ark.

units.la: 2 Et scribam in tabulas illas verba illa quæ fuerant in prioribus tabulis quas confregisti. ponesq; eas in arcam.
units.tr: And I will write on those tables the words that were on the former tables which you broke, and you shall put them in the ark.

units.la: 3 Feci igitur arcā de lignis Sitim, & scalpsi duas tabulas lapideas instar prio-rum, ascendiq; in montem, habens duas tabulas in manu mea.
units.tr: So I made an ark of shittim wood, and hewed two tables of stone like the former ones, and went up into the mountain, having the two tables in my hand.

units.la: 4 Et scripsit in tabulis secundum priorem scripturam, decem verba quæ locutus fuerat Dominus ad vos in monte de medio ignis in die comitiorum, deditque eas Dominus mihi.
units.tr: And he wrote on the tables, according to the former writing, the ten words which the Lord had spoken to you in the mountain out of the midst of the fire in the day of the assembly; and the Lord gave them to me.

units.la: 5 Et conversus descendi de monte, & posui tabulas in arcam quam extruxe-ram, & sunt ibi quemadmodum præceperat mihi Dominus.
units.tr: And I turned and came down from the mountain, and put the tables in the ark which I had made, and there they are, as the Lord commanded me.

units.la: 6 Filii autem Israel proficiscebantur de Beeroth filiorum Jaekan in Mosera, ubi mortuus est Aharon atq; sepultus, & functus est sacerdotio pro eo Eleazar fi-lius eius.
units.tr: And the children of Israel journeyed from Beeroth Bene-jaakan to Mosera, where Aaron died and was buried, and Eleazar his son ministered as priest in his place.

units.la: 7 Hinc proficiscebantur in Gudgoda, & de Gudgoda in Jotbata terram quæ torrentes habet aquarum.
units.tr: From there they journeyed to Gudgodah, and from Gudgodah to Jotbathah, a land of brooks of water.

units.la: 8 Tunc temporis separavit Dominus tribum Levi, ut portaret arcam fœderis Domini, & ut astaret coràm Domino ad ministrandum ei, benedicq; imprecaretur in nomine eius usq; in præsentem diem.
units.tr: At that time the Lord separated the tribe of Levi, to bear the ark of the covenant of the Lord, and to stand before the Lord to minister to him, and to bless in his name, unto this day.

units.la: 9 Et ob hanc causam non cessit Levitis pars & hæreditas cum fratribus suis, sed Dominus est hæreditas illorum, sicut Dominus Deus tuus illis loquutus est.
units.tr: Therefore Levi has no portion nor inheritance with his brethren; the Lord is his inheritance, as the Lord your God spoke to him.

units.la: 10 Ego autem steti in monte iuxta priores dies, quadragin-ta dies & quadraginta noctes, exaudivitq; me Dominus etiam tum, & noluit te Dominus perdere.
units.tr: And I stood in the mountain as at the first days, forty days and forty nights; and the Lord heard me at that time also, and the Lord would not destroy you.

units.la: 11 Et dixit Dominus ad me, Surge & præcede in profectione populum istum, ut ingrediantur, & possideant terram, quam iuravi patribus eorum, ut trade-rem eis.
units.tr: And the Lord said to me, Arise, and go before the people on their journey, that they may enter in and possess the land which I swore to their fathers to give them.

units.la: VANQVAM accurata morum atq; animorum inspectio,tum etiam anteactæ vitæ recordatio,qua de fatis est priore cap.expositum, plane doceat non extare vl la nostra de Deo merita, quorum is ratione ductus vel hæc mundana ac caduca, vel illa cœlestia ac sempiterna beneficia conferat:tamen recta factorum & naturæ Dei consideratio cum moribus nostris comparata magis hoc præstabit. Nã veluti colores coloribus oppositi,qui qualefq; sunt apparent magis:sic res cum rebus comparatæ magis elu cefcunt. Ac veluti auarum hominem omnes odio dignum ducimus:magis autē eum odimus fi fit comparatus cum aliquo homine liberali & munifico: sic diuina iustitia cum iniustitia nostra compata facit,vt nostra magis sordeat iniustitia.
units.tr: Although a careful inspection of our morals and minds, together with a recollection of our past life, which was set out in the earlier chapter, plainly teaches that we have no merits before God by which he might bestow either these worldly and frail benefits or those heavenly and everlasting ones, nevertheless a right consideration of his deeds and nature, set against our conduct, will show this even more clearly. For just as colours set against colours appear more plainly what they are, so things compared with things become more evident. And just as we consider a greedy man deserving of hatred by all, but hate him all the more when he is set beside some generous and liberal man, so the divine justice, when compared with our injustice, makes our injustice appear all the more foul.

units.la: Qua de causa Moses,vt ne quid nobis arrogemus: primum quidem depingit humanam malitiam:tum autem cum diuina bonitate comparans , ostendit per nos exitium per Deum salutem effici. Ac superiore quidem cap.docuit,quot modis Israelitæ Dei in fe prouocarint indignationem : hoc autem docet quàm multis ille modis suam erga eos beneuolentiam demonftrarit. Per illos doctrina salutis acquirendæ monftratrix fracta : per illos sacerdotium quasi quoddam salutis perficiendæ instrumentum corruptum : per illos magistratus suscepti in promissam terram itineris dux fractus atque impeditus: contra per Deum hæc omnia restituta in integrum. Sed & Moses præterea mentem & voluntatem Dei pulchrè & exactè exponit:ostendens Deum hoc solum agere,vt cum ipso quàm arctiffimo necessitudinis vin culo coniuncti,ipsius bonorum omnium confortes fimus.
units.tr: For this reason Moses, so that we may claim nothing for ourselves, first indeed depicts human wickedness, and then, setting it beside the divine goodness, shows that ruin comes from us and salvation is effected by God. In the previous chapter he taught in how many ways the Israelites provoked God's anger against them; but here he teaches in how many ways he showed his goodwill towards them. Through them the teaching that shows how salvation is to be obtained was broken; through them the priesthood, as a kind of instrument for bringing salvation to completion, was corrupted; through them the magistracy, taken up as the leader of the journey into the promised land, was broken and hindered; on the other hand, through God all these things were restored to their whole state. Moreover, Moses also sets forth beautifully and exactly the mind and will of God, showing that God's only aim is that we, bound to him by the closest tie of kinship, should share in all his good things.

units.la: Ex quo perspicuum est diuinæ gratiæ seu bonitatis magnitudinem hoc quidem loco primum operibus domini,tum eius verbo demonstrari. Eius demonstrationis pars prior verbis illis exponitur. Quæ docent,Deum adeo benignum esse & propitium,vt quæ suis peccatis Israelitæ corruperint,tabulas videlicet & sacerdotium,& magistratum,ea Deus reftaurarit omnia. De quibus singulis.
units.tr: From this it is clear that the greatness of the divine grace or goodness is shown in this passage first by the works of the Lord, and then by his word. The first part of this demonstration is set out in those words. They teach that God is so kind and propitious that he restored everything the Israelites had corrupted by their sins: namely the tables, the priesthood and the magistracy. Let us consider each of these.

units.la: De tabulis,In illo(inquit)tempore dixit,&c.Quo ostendit, tabulas populi culpa fractas, Dei bonitate restauratas esse:idq; circumstantijs eo spectantibus illustrat. Ac de tempore quidem,quoniam dicit,in illo tempore : videmus hæc aptissimè connecti cum superioribus: Vt enim sua culpa has amiserant,sic easdem Dei beneficio recipiebant. In quo videmus,vt à nobis eodem tempore exitium obtingat,quo salus existit à Domino.Quid igitur nobis tribuimus?cur desperamus rebus perditis?
units.tr: Concerning the tables: In that time (he says) the Lord spoke, etc. By this he shows that the tables, broken through the people's fault, were restored by the goodness of God; and he illustrates this with the circumstances that bear on it. As for the time, when he says at that time, we see that these words are very aptly connected with what precedes: for just as they had lost these through their own fault, so they received them back by the benefit of God. In this we see that ruin befalls us at the same time that salvation comes from the Lord. Why then do we attribute anything to ourselves? Why do we despair when things are lost?

units.la: Causa eff ciens etiam hoc ipse exponitur,quod illis in mœrore luctuq; iacentibus, nec audentibus hoc à domino petere dat vltrò dominus. Sic in iuuandis & redimendis nobis prior ipse est semper Deus. Adamum lapsum quærit,& fugientem sequitur, & in cœno iacentem erigit.Abrahamum in prophanis cultibus sedentem elegit,atq; in societatem suscipit.Israelitas vltrò eligit:vniuersos fideles ante iacta mundi fundamenta in Christo eligit.Igitur illius gratia maior est nostris meritis.
units.tr: The efficient cause is also set forth here: while the people lay in grief and sorrow, not daring to ask this of the Lord, the Lord gives it of his own accord. Thus in helping and redeeming us God is always the first to act. He seeks Adam when he has fallen, follows him when he flees, and raises him up when he lies in the mire. He chose Abraham when he sat in profane worship, and took him into fellowship. He chose the Israelites of his own accord; he chose all the faithful in Christ before the foundation of the world. Therefore his grace is greater than our merits.

units.la: Personæ quarum opera res hæ geruntur,Mosis quidem est vna,altera Dei:nullæ in his partes aut operæ populi.Tabulas Moses parat,sed in eas leges inscribit Deus.Id argumento est ministrorum opera Deum vti in præparandis ad percipiendum verbum suum humanis animis:sed eum ipsum verbum in animos inscribere. Vnde Paulus Verbi ministērium agriculturæ comparat:quod istic ferant ac plantent homines . Deus autem det incrementum. Non est inquit volentis neq; currentis sed miserentis Dei.Igitur gratia semper est maior operibus.
units.tr: Of the persons by whose work these things are done, one is Moses and the other is God; there is no share or labour of the people in them. Moses prepares the tables, but God writes the laws on them. This is evidence that the ministers' work is for God to use in preparing human minds to receive his word, but it is God himself who writes the word on their minds. Hence Paul compares the ministry of the Word to farming, in which men plant and water, but God gives the increase. "So it is not of him that wills, nor of him that runs, but of God who shows mercy." Therefore grace is always greater than works.

units.la: Forma fit eadem quæ priorum fuit.Nam eadem constabant materia, quippe effent etiã lapideæ:idem erat quod priorum argumentum videlicet decem verba: eodem scribebantur authore nempe Deo.In quo vides verbum Dei semper vnum & idem esse, nec vlla re varia-re.Vnde hæc doctrina corrupta ad primum exemplum fui reformabitur,veluti cœna Domi nica apud Corinthios per apostolum ad institutum Domini.
units.tr: The form is the same as that of the former tables. For they were made of the same material, being of stone as well; the subject was the same as before, namely the ten words; and they were written by the same author, namely God. In this you see that the word of God is always one and the same, and does not change in any respect. Hence this doctrine, when corrupted, is to be reformed according to its first pattern, just as the Lord's Supper among the Corinthians was restored by the apostle according to the Lord's institution.

units.la: Locus in quo reftaurataæ sunt hæ sigillatim quoq; dicitur.Acceptæ sunt quidem in Sina monte sacerrimo:conditæ verò in arca.
units.tr: The place where these were restored is also named individually. They were indeed received on the most sacred mountain of Sinai, but were written again in the ark.

units.la: Erat autem arca sanctissimum instrumentum quo tabulæ istæ simul cum manna ac virga Aharonis seruarentur. Ligna ex quibus hæc erat effecta Hebraei[?] שִׁטִּים[?] Lxx.interpretes ligna ἀσηπτά[?],Iosephus autem ἰσχυρὰ τῶν ξύλων καὶ σήψιν ἢ παθεῖν ἀ λωάνευα[?], alij cedrum, alij buxum,alij quodcunq; genus in Sina monte nascentium arborum autumant. Et Philo doctissimus in 3. de vita Mosis libro cedro hoc tribuit quod fit ἀσηπτότατον[?] atq; ex ea materia tabernaculum fabrefactum ait. Ex quibus est perspicuum quod firmissima ac maximè durabilis materia ad arcam illam deligenda fuerit. Nam cum leges in ea ipsa ceu thefau-rum quendam recondi voluerit: opus erat thecam tanto thesauro fatis bonam deligi. Εἰς γὰρ τὸν [?] (inquit Philo) κατατίθεται τὰ χρηματιζόμενα λόγια. Vnde idem dicit eodem loco ar-cam ἀγγεῖον τὰν νόμων esse.
units.tr: The ark was the most holy vessel in which these tables were kept together with the manna and the rod of Aaron. As to the wood of which it was made, the Hebrews [say] שִׁטִּים [shittim]; the Seventy [render it] incorruptible wood; Josephus [says it was] strong wood and resistant to rot [ἰσχυρὰ τῶν ξύλων καὶ σήψιν]; others think it was cedar, others box, others any kind of tree growing on Mount Sinai. And Philo, most learned, in the third book of his Life of Moses, assigns to cedar the quality of being most incorruptible, and says the tabernacle was built of that material. From these things it is clear that the firmest and most durable material was chosen for that ark. For since he wished the laws to be stored in it as in a kind of treasure chest, it was necessary to choose a box fit for so great a treasure. For (as Philo says) the oracles that were given are deposited in it. Hence the same Philo says in the same place that the ark is a vessel of the laws.

units.la: Hæc indicio sunt ecclesiam esse receptaculum verbi diuini in Christo firmissimum atque ab omni putredine alienum. Ac quemadmodum in arca decem legum tabulæ conde-bantur: sic in ecclesia Christiana verbum Dei perpetua cum obseruantia conseruandum est. Eius enim obliuio cum errorum tum malorum & vitiorum omnium fons est. Quare magni beneficij est in loco Deum id nostra culpa amissum, nobis tam benigne restituere.
units.tr: These things are signs that the Church in Christ is the most firm receptacle of the divine word, and free from all corruption. And just as the tables of the ten laws were stored in the ark, so in the Christian Church the word of God must be preserved with constant observance. For forgetting it is the source of errors, of evils and of all vices. Therefore it is a great benefit that God, having been lost through our fault in that place, has restored it to us so graciously.

units.la: Sacerdotium restitutum, Filij Israel, inquit, proficiscebantur, &c. Ostendit quo pacto & corruptum & restitutum sit sacerdotium.
units.tr: The priesthood restored: The children of Israel, he says, journeyed, etc. He shows how the priesthood was both corrupted and restored.

units.la: Corruptum hoc ipso fuit, quod Aharon obsecutus impijs populi postulationibus vitulum aureum fecerat: qua de causa moritur in Mosera qui sacerdos fuerat.
units.tr: This was itself the corruption of the priesthood: Aaron, yielding to the impious demands of the people, made the golden calf, and for that reason he who had been priest died at Mosera.

units.la: Exemplum est: ministris tacentibus, & conniuentibus, & obsequentibus amitti minifte-rium. Quod populus omnium vult & optat maxime, nempe vt ad omnia scelera conniue-ant episcopi: id in eius perniciem vergit maxime. Sic Achab falsus est assentationibus pseu-doprophetarum.
units.tr: This is an example that when ministers keep silent, connive and comply, the ministry is lost. The people of every kind most want and desire that bishops should connive at all wickedness, and this tends most of all to their ruin. Thus Ahab was deceived by the flattery of the false prophets.

units.la: Restitutum est hoc ipso ministerium quod & Eleazar Aharoni substitutus est, & Leuitarum officia redintegrata sunt omnia. Atq; id adeo diligenter describit, vt de electione, de officio, de eorum victu quid statuendum sit ex his eius verbis perspicias.
units.tr: The ministry was restored by this very fact, that Eleazar was substituted for Aaron, and all the duties of the Levites were renewed. And he describes this so carefully that from his words you may see what must be decided about their election, their office and their maintenance.

units.la: De electione eorum dicit: Separauit eos Dominus. Verbum Hebræum, quo Moses vsus est in de-scriptione creationis, cum firmamentum quasi quoddam aquarum interstitium describeret, significat Leuitas ab omni genere mortalium seiunctos, quasique peculium quod-dam factos esse.
units.tr: Concerning their election he says: The Lord separated them. The Hebrew verb which Moses used in describing the creation, when he described the firmament as a kind of separation of the waters, signifies that the Levites were set apart from all the rest of mankind and made, as it were, a peculiar possession.

units.la: Id autem non factum est propterea vt ipsi vel efferantur animis, reliquosq; præ se con-temnant homines: vel à reliquis odio habeantur, aut contemnantur hominibus: sed vt ef-sent Nazaræi siue sancti Domini, siue, vt Petrus ait, exemplaria gregis Domini.
units.tr: This was not done so that they might be puffed up in spirit and despise other men, nor so that they might be hated or despised by others. It was done so that they might be Nazirites, that is, holy to the Lord, or, as Peter says, examples of the Lord's flock.

units.la: Obseruandum est autem quod hæc separatio non ab illis ipsis sed Deo authore facta est: quemadmodum apostoli non à seipsis sed à Christo sunt è mundo selecti atq; segregati: vt nulla sit monachorum illa αὐτομάτῃ[?] segregatio.
units.tr: It must be observed, however, that this separation was made not by themselves but by God as its author, just as the apostles were chosen and set apart from the world not by themselves but by Christ. So there is no such self-chosen [αὐτομάτῃ] separation of the monks.

units.la: De officio disserit.1. Arcam portent. Id non erat omnium Leuitarum, sed Aharonis filiorum in primis, reliqui instrumenta tabernaculi ferebant. Igitur quoquo fit eundum ecclesiæ, semper est ad eam ipsam accommodanda verbi diuini prædicatio. Onus & curam eius gubernandæ suis humeris sustinebunt Leuitæ.
units.tr: He treats of their office. (1.) Let them carry the ark. This was not the duty of all the Levites, but chiefly of the sons of Aaron; the others carried the instruments of the tabernacle. Therefore, wherever the Church goes, the preaching of the divine Word must always be adapted to it. The Levites will bear on their shoulders the burden and the care of governing it.

units.la: 2 Stent coram Domino, id est, ministrent, docendo, sacramenta administrando, precando.
units.tr: (2.) Let them stand before the Lord, that is, let them minister by teaching, by administering the sacraments, and by praying.

units.la: 3 Benedicent populo in nomine Domini: salutem ecclesiæ pro virili sua propagabunt. Atq; hoc quidem eorum officium confirmat Christus dicens in euangelio. Scribæ sedent in cathedra Mosis, quæ docent facite, &c.
units.tr: (3.) They shall bless the people in the name of the Lord: they shall extend the salvation of the Church as far as in them lies. And Christ confirms this very duty of theirs in the gospel, saying: The scribes sit in the seat of Moses; what they teach, do, etc.

units.la: Postremo de victu illorum disserit ad hunc modum: Dominus est hæreditas eorum: partem cum fratribus non habebunt. Quo significat decimas, victimas, primitias, quæ Domino oblatæ Leuitis cedebant in alimoniam. Et ita restituit Dominus sacerdotium.
units.tr: Finally, he speaks of their maintenance in this manner: The Lord is their inheritance; they shall have no part with their brothers. By this he signifies the tithes, the sacrifices and the firstfruits, which were offered to the Lord and went to the Levites as their food. And so the Lord restored the priesthood.

units.la: Magistratus redditus. Moses qui magistratu summo fungebatur, non potuit operam dare gubernandæ reipublicæ, quod occupatus esset negocio placandi iratum Deum. Inde erat vt populus, quasi nullum haberet magistratum, sic desertus esset. Quod quam perniciosum sit, ex interregnis, seditionibus, magistratuum socordia perspicuum est. Restituit autem hoc ipso Dominus Israelijs Mosem quod se placari passus est: quod populum vti dignus e-rat perdere noluit: quod Mosem eis ducem quasi de integro dedit. Ex quibus omnibus col-ligi potest diuinæ gratiæ magnitudo, quæ est salutis nostræ causa efficiens vnica. Christo sit honos in secula. Amen.
units.tr: The magistracy was restored. Moses, who held the highest magistracy, could not devote his effort to governing the commonwealth, because he was occupied with the business of appeasing an angry God. Hence the people, as though they had no magistrate, were left deserted. How harmful this is is clear from interregnums, seditions and the negligence of magistrates. The Lord, however, restored Moses to the Israelites by this very fact, that he allowed himself to be appeased; that he was unwilling to destroy the people, which deserved to be destroyed; that he gave them Moses again as their leader, as if anew. From all these things the greatness of divine grace can be gathered, which is the one efficient cause of our salvation. To Christ be honour for ever. Amen.

units.la: SERMO XV.
units.tr: SERMON XV.

units.la: 12 Et nunc Israel, quid Dominus Deus tuus petit à te, nisi vt timeas Dominum Deum tuum, & vt incedas in cunctis viis eius, diligas eum, & seruias Domino Deo tuo toto corde tuo, & tota anima tua?
units.tr: 12 And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you, but that you fear the Lord your God, walk in all his ways, love him, and serve the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul?

units.la: 13 Ut scilicet custodias præcepta & statuta tua, quæ ego præcipio tibi hodie bono tuo.
units.tr: 13 That is, that you keep his precepts and statutes, which I command you today for your good.

units.la: 14 En Domini Dei tui cælum est, & cæli cælorum, terra quoque & quicquid in ea est.
