units.tr: 14 Behold, the heaven is the Lord your God's, and the heaven of heavens, the earth also, and all that is in it.

units.la: 15 Duntaxat tamen in patres tuos amorem effudit Dominus, ut eos diligeret, & eligeret semen eorum post eos, nempe vos, præ[?] omnibus populis, ut hodie (videre licet.)
units.tr: 15 Yet the Lord set his love only upon your fathers, to love them and choose their seed after them, namely you, above all peoples, as it is today (you may see).

units.la: 16 Circuncidite igitur præputium cordis vestri, & ceruicem vestram amplius ne induretis.
units.tr: 16 Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and do not harden your neck any more.

units.la: 17 Quia Dominus Deus vester ipse est Deus Deorum, & Dominus Domi-norum, Deus magnus, fortis, metuendus, qui personam non recipit nec accipit munus.
units.tr: 17 For the Lord your God is himself God of gods and Lord of lords, a great, mighty and terrible God, who does not respect persons nor take a bribe.

units.la: 18 Ipse ius dicit pupillo & viduæ, atq; amat peregrinum, ut det illi victum[?] & vestitum.
units.tr: 18 He executes judgment for the fatherless and the widow, and loves the stranger, to give him food and clothing.

units.la: 19 Diligite igitur & vos peregrinum, quia peregrini fuistis in terra Ægypti.
units.tr: 19 Love therefore also you the stranger, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt.

units.la: 20 Dominum Deum tuu[?] time, & ei serui, adhærere ei, & iura per nomen eius.
units.tr: 20 Fear the Lord your God, serve him, cleave to him, and swear by his name.

units.la: 21 Ipse est laus tua, & Deus tuus, qui fecit tecum magnalia hæc, & terribilia illa quæ viderunt oculi tui.
units.tr: 21 He is your praise and your God, who did with you these great and terrible things which your eyes have seen.

units.la: 22 Cum septuaginta animabus descenderunt patres tui in Ægyptum, & nunc posuit te Dominus Deus tuus, & multiplicauit te velut stellas cæli.
units.tr: 22 Your fathers went down into Egypt with seventy souls, and now the Lord your God has set you, and multiplied you like the stars of heaven.

units.la: IN hoc prorsus incumbit Moses, ut agnoscamus diuina beneficia non nostro merito, sed Dei bonitate & gratia nobis obuenire, eaq; de causa nos ipsos nihili, illum vero maximi faciamus. Quod ut nobis persuadeat utriuq; partis personarum descriptione efficit. Ac Israelitarum quidem descriptionem ex eorum ipsorum sumptam annalibus sic ponit ob oculos, ut intelligant se non bene de Deo, sed male esse meritos: quippe quem peccatis subinde suis offenderint, ac mala sibi magis accersiuerint quam præmia: Dei vero personâ ut depingat, eius ex factis atq; ex verbo descriptionem sumit, quippe quibus suam erga illos beneuolentiam summe declarauerit. Iam quoniam tabulas, sacerdotium, magistratū, quæ sua culpa populus amiserat, ipse reddidit, uti nuper est expositum, eo facto suum in illos amorem satis te-statum facit: sed id verbo nihilo minus probat sese esse bonum & placabilem. Id etsi suis par-tibus omnibus verbum nobis comprobet: tamen fine multo magis docet, quippe quo significet Deum unum agere ut nos arctissimo necessitudinis vinculo sibi deuinctos beatæ vitæ consortes efficiat. Quod hic Moses docet non posse secus efficí, quàm pietate, nostrum ipsorum castigatione, Dei ipsius imitatione.
units.tr: Moses labours precisely in this, that we should acknowledge that divine benefits come to us not by our own merit but by God's goodness and grace, and for this reason we should count ourselves as nothing and him as the greatest. To persuade us of this he sets out a description of both parties. He places before our eyes a description of the Israelites, taken from their own annals, so that they understand they have not deserved well but badly of God, since they repeatedly offended him by their sins and brought more evils upon themselves than rewards. To portray the person of God, he takes his description from God's deeds and from his word, by which he has most fully declared his goodwill towards them. Now, since he himself restored the tables, the priesthood and the magistracy, which the people had lost through their own fault, as was lately explained, by that deed he sufficiently testifies his love towards them; yet he nonetheless proves by his word that he is good and placable. Although the word proves this to us in all its parts, it teaches it much more fully, since it signifies that God alone works to make us, bound to himself by the closest bond of kinship, partakers of a blessed life. Moses teaches that this cannot be brought about otherwise than by piety, by our own self-chastisement, and by imitation of God himself.

units.la: Pietate: Et nunc (inquit) o Israel quid Dominus Deus tuus requirit abs te, nisi ut timeas Dominum Deum tuum.&c: Quibus verbis non solum ostendit pietate nos coniungi cum Deo maxime, uerumetiam pietatem ipsam, veluti suis partibus omnibus absoluitur, descriptam ponit ob oculos.
units.tr: Piety: "And now," he says, "O Israel, what does the Lord your God require of you, but that you fear the Lord your God," etc. By these words he shows not only that we are joined most closely to God through piety, but also sets piety itself before our eyes, described in all its parts.

units.la: Et ad pietatem quidem primum est quod requiritur: ut timeas, inquit, 'Dominum Deum tuum. Recte sane primus locus timori Dei datur, cum timor Domini sit initium sapientiæ, Prou.1. Et thesaurus maximus, Esa.33. & frenum quo coerceamus impuras concupiscentias, ut exemplis & usu rerum constat. Neq; vero ceu seuum tyrannum, sed ut patrem amabilem reuerebimur: quod genus timoris Paulus tribuit liberis ingenuis: nempe ut amore Dei timor ille mitigetur.
units.tr: And for piety, what is required first is that you fear, he says, the Lord your God. Rightly indeed is the first place given to the fear of God, since the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, Prov. 1, and the greatest treasure, Isa. 33, and the bridle by which we restrain impure lusts, as experience and practice show. Nor should we revere him as a cruel tyrant, but as a loving father; this kind of fear Paul attributes to free-born children, namely that the fear is softened by the love of God.

units.la: Sed quorsum hic timor? Ut ambules, inquit, in omnibus viis eius. Atalicuius viam ire, se-cundum Hebræos, idem est quod illum seu eius vitæ genus quod sequatur habere propositum: veluti in viis Dauid, in viis regum Iuda, in viis gentium ambulare: quod perinde est ac illorum more viuere. Id Græci Latiniq; scriptores peculiaribus verbis exprimunt, ut Græcizare, patrissare, Cretizare, id est patrem, Cretes, Græcos moribus referre. Docet ergo Moses, Deum patrem sic honorandum esse & venerandum, ut iisdem quibus ille est deditus & delectatur rebus, studiis atq; artibus, iisdem etiam nos afficiamur ac studeamus. Quod sacræ literæ docent esse verum Dei filiorum signum. Nam qui spiritu Christi non ducuntur, hi, in quiùt non sunt eius. Et, oves meæ vocem meam audiunt. Et Iudæos ideo negat esse vel Dei vel Abrahæ filios ,quod veritate quam & Abraham & Deus haberent charisimam,ipsi canes[?] peius & angue odissent. Sic si nos verbum Dei fugiamus, despiciamus, persequamur,non Dei filij sumus,cum diuinam indolem hæc non sapiant: sed quemadmodum Christus de Iudæis colligit,patrem alium referimus,sind nit <bl>(Gottesfürchtig) sonder tüfelsfürchtig.</bl>
units.tr: But why this fear? "So that you walk," he says, "in all his ways." For to walk in someone's way, according to the Hebrews, is the same as to have as one's aim the person or manner of life one follows: as to walk in the ways of David, in the ways of the kings of Judah, in the ways of the nations, which is just the same as living after their manner. Greek and Latin writers express this by special words, such as Hellenizing, Patrizing, Cretizing, that is, to reproduce in one's conduct the father, the Cretans, the Greeks. Moses therefore teaches that God the Father is to be honoured and revered in such a way that we are affected by the same things to which he is devoted and in which he delights, and that we apply ourselves to the same studies and arts. Holy letters teach that this is the true sign of God's children. For those who are not led by the Spirit of Christ, these, it says, are not his; and "my sheep hear my voice." And he denies that the Jews are sons of God or of Abraham, because, though Abraham and God held the truth most dear, they themselves hated it worse than a dog or a snake. So if we flee from, despise, or persecute God's word, we are not God's sons, since these things do not savour of the divine disposition; but, as Christ infers about the Jews, we refer to another father: <bl>not God-fearing but devil-fearing.</bl>

units.la: Alterum est quod ad pietatem pertinet: Vt diligas inquit,eum. Quo docet Deum rebus omnibus praeferendum ac magis amandum esse. Vulgus germanorum dicit, wenn lieb ers kompt/ so ist leidero vß: quo docet fieri solere, vt aliquem diligamus, sed fiquis alius accedat,ex quo plus honoris atq; commodi,itemq; voluptatis & delectationis percipi possefe confidamus:iam priore illo derelicto sequamur alterum. At Deus sic se vult diligi, vt nihil diligamus magis. Dicit enim Dominus,qui parentes,liberos,familias diligi præcipit:eum qui parentes,liberos,agros magis quam ipsum diligat indignum ipso esse. Et cor totum hicamor postulat.
units.tr: The second thing that pertains to piety is "that you love," he says, "him." By this he teaches that God is to be preferred to all things and loved more than all. The common people of the Germans say: <bl>when love comes, alas, it is soon over.</bl> By this he teaches that it usually happens that we love someone, but if someone else appears from whom we trust more honour, advantage, pleasure and delight can be received, then, having left the former, we follow the other. But God wills to be loved in such a way that we love nothing more. For the Lord, who commands us to love parents, children and families, says that one who loves parents, children and fields more than himself is unworthy of him. And this love demands the whole heart.

units.la: Tertium est,vt seruias,inquit, Domino Deo tuo,hoc est,vt illius honori,commodo,voluntati fis totus deditus:vt quemadmodum serui intenti sunt ad omnes nutus herorum,sic si nos quoq; Deus vocet eamus,quicquid iubeat parati simus facere.
units.tr: The third is "that you serve," he says, "the Lord your God," that is, that you be wholly devoted to his honour, advantage and will: just as servants are attentive to every nod of their masters, so if God calls us, we should go, ready to do whatever he commands.

units.la: Sed quomodo seruies Domino? Ex toto corde tuo & ex tota anima tua, inquit. Quemadmodum enim Deus vnus est:sic vni sibi nos totos vult esse deditos. Vnde dicit Helias, non esse claudicandum in vtramq; partem:vnde Christus, neminem posse seruire duobus Dominis: vnde Paulus,nihil esse Christo cum Belial,vel luci cum tenebris. Quare cauebimus ne partem nostri mundo,partem satanæ,minimum autem Deo tribuamus.
units.tr: But how will you serve the Lord? "With all your heart and with all your soul," he says. For just as God is one, so he wants us wholly devoted to himself alone. Hence Elijah says that one must not limp to both sides; hence Christ, that no one can serve two masters; hence Paul, that there is nothing in common between Christ and Belial, or light with darkness. Therefore we will take care not to give part of ourselves to the world, part to Satan, and the least part to God.

units.la: Sed quod cor & ipsam etiam animam requirit,id est indicio:Deum,ni mens illi sit dedita, ritus externos,& corporis gestus,& verborum volubilitatem non magni facere. Vnde & apud Esa.quaeritur, populum suum ore quidem ipsum colere,sed corde esse ab eo prorsus alienum.
units.tr: But that he requires the heart and even the soul itself is a sign that God does not value outward rites, bodily gestures and fluency of words, unless the mind is devoted to him. Hence also in Isaiah it is complained that the people honour him indeed with their mouth, but with their heart are utterly alienated from him.

units.la: Sed quibus illi feruitur officijs? Vt custodias,inquit,praecepta Domini,& statuta eius,quae ego praecipio tibi in bonum. Quemadmodum sese quisq; gereret & quid quenq; deceret,est expressum praeceptis Dei:quibus,qui Deo seruire volet,habit. Ergo pietas hoc ipso perficitur diuinarum legù studio,quo fit,vt si quid secus,quàm Deus præceperit,feceris, totus expauescas,totus horreas, nec prius conquiescas,quam iratum patrem placaueris. Sir selb ein gwüssine Brumb machest/ so du vnrecht thust. At nostra secula tales ferunt homines,quibus ridiculi sint ac videantur, qui vitam suam vtcunq; diuinis præceptionibus accommodant. vulgus enim ridet eum qui paulum sibi temperauerit à luxu atq; à crapula. Ser wil auch die zehen Gott hallten. Plæriq; si commodum fit recipiunt,sin minus,repudiant.
units.tr: But in what duties is he served? "That you keep," he says, "the precepts of the Lord and his statutes, which I command you for your good." How each person should conduct himself and what befits each is set out in God's precepts, which whoever wishes to serve God must have. Therefore piety is accomplished by this very zeal for divine laws, so that if you have done anything otherwise than God has commanded, you are wholly terrified, wholly horrified, and do not rest until you have appeased your angry father. <bl>You yourself make a sure reckoning when you do wrong.</bl> But our age produces such men that those who in any way fit their lives to divine precepts seem ridiculous to them; for the common people laughs at one who has restrained himself a little from luxury and drunkenness. <bl>He wants to keep the Ten Commandments too.</bl> Most accept them if it is convenient, but if not, they reject them.

units.la: Iam qui ritus sacri Deo placeant expressum est eius verbo:verbi studio,sacramentis,precibus,eleemosynis colitur. His studijs,qui pius est,sese dedit. Sic seruitur Domino.
units.tr: Now, what kind of ritual pleases God has been stated in his word: he is worshipped through zeal for the Word, through the sacraments, through prayers and through alms. The man who is godly devotes himself to these pursuits. In this way the Lord is served.

units.la: Ex quo perspicuum est τῇ ἐθελοθρησκείᾳ locum nullum esse. Verum est enim quod vulgo dici solet ἄκαιρον ἐννοίαν ἐχθρᾶς [?] διαφέρειν. Frustra, inquit Dominus,coluntme traditionibus hominum: videlicet cum hic Moses dicat eum coli suarum ipsius præceptionum atq; cerimoniarum studio.Nec ratio hoc iuerit inficias. Nam si quod mihi placet ac gratum est facio:num quasi tibi seruire videor? non certe existimo,ni idem ipsum tibi quoque placeat. Qui igitur Deo seruies si non quod illi placet,verum quod tibi ipsi videtur rectum facias? sane tibi ipsi seruire diceris. Quis igitur bonæ illi,quam iactitant,intentioni locus est reliquus? Non Missis,idololatria peregrinationibus,indulgentijs, vigilijs,ieiunijs Deo seruies cum ille horum nihil iusserit.Igitur nulla est hæc pietas. Sed illis,quas diximus ,partibus vera pietas perficitur.
units.tr: From this it is plain that there is no place for will-worship [ἐθελοθρησκείᾳ]. The common saying is true, that one who entertains an unseasonable thought differs from an enemy [?]. "In vain," says the Lord, "do they worship me with the traditions of men" (Matt. 15.9). Clearly Moses here says that God is worshipped through zeal for his own precepts and ceremonies. Reason cannot deny this. For if I do what pleases and suits me, do I seem to be serving you? Certainly I do not think so, unless the same thing also pleases you. So if you serve God by doing not what pleases him but what seems right to yourself, you are said to be serving yourself. What room, then, is left for the good intention they boast of? You will not serve God by Masses, idolatrous pilgrimages, indulgences, vigils or fasts, since he has commanded none of these. Therefore this is not piety. True piety is achieved in the parts we have mentioned.

units.la: At mihi,inquis,hoc est difficile præstitu. Vellem quidem,sed carnis meæ stimulis ab hoc studio rursus abigor.Age ergo ratione Moses retrahit in viam, propones Dei in nos amore, cuius recordatione permoti in viam redeamus. En (inquit) Domini Dei tui cœlum est, & cœli cœlorum, & terra, & quicquid in ea est: sed patres tuos amauit, &e. Quod perinde est ac si dicat. In tam immensa rerum creatarum varietate & copia an non Deus habuit quæ diligeret,& augeret suis beneficijs? abunde satis erat inquam,quod diligeret: sed maiores vestros, vofq; eorū posteros rebus omnibus chariores habuit. Hæc vos recordatio ad eum redamandum impellat. Nam si in vos ille sic affectus est, vt nihil meritos tantopere dilexerit: quanto magis vos illum de vobis benemeritum amabitis?
units.tr: "But," you say, "this is hard for me to do. I would indeed like to, but the goads of my flesh drive me away from this pursuit again." Then let Moses lead you back onto the way by reason. Set before yourself the love of God toward us, so that, moved by remembering it, we may return to the way. "Behold," he says, "the heaven of the Lord your God, and the heaven of heavens, and the earth, and all that is in it. Yet he loved your fathers, etc." This is much the same as if he said: In such an immense variety and abundance of created things, did God not have things to love and to enrich with his benefits? It was enough, I say, that he could love; yet he held your forefathers, and you and their descendants, dearer than all things. Let this remembrance drive you to love him in return. For if he has so disposed himself toward you that he loved you so greatly though you had done nothing to deserve it, how much more will you love him, who has deserved well of you?

units.la: In quo videmus Deum omnes homines amare & iuuare, sed in primis suos electos tueri solere. Omnibus legem naturæ,sed suam suis reuelauit:omnibus promisit & reuelauit redemptorem. demptorem Christum,sed electis suis peculiariter:omnibus hominibus etiam improbis demittit solem & pluuiam,sed pios ditat inprimis : omnes in vita conseruat homines, sed electos suos Iosephum,Dauidem,Prophetas, Apostolos & omnino omnes diligentissime conseruauit.
units.tr: In this we see that God loves and helps all men, but that he is accustomed above all to protect his elect. He revealed the law of nature to all, but his own law to his own people. He promised and revealed the Redeemer, Christ, to all, but in a special way to his elect. He sends sun and rain to all men, even the wicked, but he enriches the godly above all. He preserves all men in life, but he most diligently preserved his elect, Joseph, David, the Prophets, the Apostles, and in short all of them.

units.la: Ex quo colligent ipsi Deum illum propterea sibi tanto magis redamandum. Omnibus Europae populis beneficia quaedam contulit,atq; euangelium suum non tam viva voce quàm typographorum opera atq; industria editis libris promulgauit:sed Germanis utroq; modo clarissimè reuelauit. Ergo ipsum Germani prae caeteris colent. An non potuit Dominus Suevos,Flandros,Anglos,Saxones aliosque populos tanta libertate & existimatione virtutis donare,quanta nos Heluetios pro sua erga nos paterna voluntate dignatus est? Sane potuit. Sed maiores nostros nosq; ipsos tantopere dilexit ut his dignos duxerit beneficijs. Ergo nos eū vicissim amabimus,& pietate reliquos populos anteibimus. Quod si quoniam haec ad pietatem non excitant,nihil est quod eum possit ad officium propellere, quippe qui sit ingratus, & naturae monstrum,quando beneficium non reddit. Atq; haec de pietate satis sit dixisse.
units.tr: From this they may themselves conclude that God is therefore all the more to be loved in return. He has bestowed certain benefits on all the peoples of Europe, and he has published his gospel not so much by living voice as by the work and industry of printers and books. But he has revealed it most clearly to the Germans in both ways. Therefore the Germans will worship him above the rest. Could not the Lord have granted the Swabians, Flemings, English, Saxons and other peoples the same liberty and reputation for virtue that he has deigned to give us Swiss, out of his fatherly goodwill toward us? Certainly he could. But he loved our forefathers and ourselves so greatly that he thought us worthy of these benefits. Therefore we in turn will love him, and we will surpass the other peoples in piety. But if these things do not stir us to piety, nothing can drive us to duty, since we are ungrateful and a monster of nature when we do not return a benefit. Let this be enough said about piety.

units.la: Castigatione seu repraesione subinde emergentis ac sese erigentis malitiae Deo coniungimur etiam. Nam si peccatum nos à Deo separat: eius repraesio atq; castigatio cum eodem nos coniungET. Id qui fiat circumcisione,docet,dicens,Circumcidite praeputium cordis vestri,et ceruicem vestra ne induretis amplius.Circumcisio signū erat facti cum Deo foederis:sed ea quid intus in animo deceret,atq; etiam oporteret fieri signo quodam seu externo opere significabat. Quod ipsum quale sit verbis suis docet Moses.Circumcidite,inquit,praeputiū cordis vestri,id est crassam illam ignorantiā & contemptionem Dei pariter & verbi diuini,quam comprehensum vestris animis retinetis. Haec enim secum trahit impurum & scifcosum humorem, vitiosos affectus,& quicquid est aduersum Deo. Ut igitur preputium abscinditur quo glans aperta ac pura sit:sic animi humani refecata crassitie erunt aperti & puri.
units.tr: We are also joined to God by the correction or rebuke of malice, which from time to time rises up and lifts its head. For if sin separates us from God, his rebuke and correction join us to him again. Circumcision teaches how this happens, saying: "Circumcise the foreskin of your heart, and do not harden your neck any more" (Deut. 10.16). Circumcision was a sign of the covenant made with God, but it signified by an external sign or outward act what ought to be, and needed to be, within the mind. Moses himself teaches what this is in his own words. "Circumcise," he says, "the foreskin of your heart," that is, that thick ignorance and contempt of God and likewise of the divine Word, which you hold fast in your minds. For this brings with it an impure and filthy moisture, vicious affections, and whatever is hostile to God. Therefore, as the foreskin is cut away so that the glans is open and clean, so the human mind, once its thickness has been cut off, will be open and pure.

units.la: Quod Moses vocat circumcidere,Christus eruere & excindere,Paulus mortificare. Christus enim dicit in Euangelio,si te offenderit oculus tuus,erue illum:praestat enim ire in coelum seu beatam vitam monoculum, quàm ambobus praeditum oculis in gehennam ingredi: eodemq; modo dicit ibidem de manibus atq; pedibus:non hoc agens ut membris mutilaremus corpora,sed ut oculorum,auriū, & reliquos sensus, quibus ducibus res ad cor intro aduectae animos sua cupidine inflammant,reprimantur:praestare enim sic luctari & decertare cum impuris motibus, quo beatae vitae possessione potiamur : quàm illis obsecutum perire & sempiternis cruciatibus implicari. Paulus autem Col.3.ait,Mortificate igitur membra vestra terrestria,stuprum,immunditiam,molitiem,&c.Etenim si mundo viuamus mortui sumus Christo:sin mundo moriamur Christo viuimus. Qua de causa Moses argumento à vero circumcisionis vsu ducto monet eos,qui velint amicitiam sibi cum Deo contrahere,malum, propter quod à Deo separati sunt,resecare debere. Estq; ea demū verā circumcisio, qua mala cordibus nostris innata amputatur. Quā ipsam celebrat apostolus Rom.2.Phil.3.Col.2.
units.tr: What Moses calls circumcising, Christ calls plucking out and cutting off, and Paul calls mortifying. For Christ says in the Gospel, "If your eye offend you, pluck it out; for it is better to enter heaven, or the blessed life, with one eye than to go into hell with both eyes" (Matt. 18.9). He says the same in the same place about hands and feet. He does not mean that we should mutilate our bodies, but that the eyes, ears and other senses, by whose guidance things brought inward to the heart inflame the mind with their desire, should be restrained. For it is better to struggle and contend in this way against impure motions, so that we may gain possession of the blessed life, than to yield to them, perish and be entangled in everlasting torments. Paul, moreover, says in Colossians 3: "Mortify therefore your earthly members: fornication, uncleanness, lust, etc." For "if we live in the world we are dead to Christ; if we die in the world we live to Christ." For this reason Moses, arguing from the true use of circumcision, warns those who wish to make friendship with God that they must cut away the evil on account of which they were separated from God. That is the true circumcision, by which the evils innate in our hearts are cut off. The apostle celebrates this very thing in Romans 2, Philippians 3 and Colossians 2.

units.la: Sed ut ad Mosem redeamus,ait ipse:& ceruicem vestram ne induretis amplius. Qua metaphora à bobus iugo sua colla submittentibus ducta iubet obedientiam. Nescio enim quo naturae malo fiat,ut eam disciplinam, quae non solum ad animorum verumetiam ad corporum incolumitatem plurimum utilitatis affert,omnium aegerrime sustineamus. Quis enim est qui vitae rationem praescriptam à medico non grauate suscipiat ac victum quem vocant medicum,non autumet esse miserum? Adeo libet,quod non licet atque expedit. Sic iugum ferre vix possumus,ac semper nitimur in vetitum. At Christus ait Matth. 11. iugum suum suave esse & facile. Et quoniam nil imponit,nisi quod est naturae consentaneum,qui potest esse grave? Nobis vero quia magistrum naturae bonae corruptorem audimus, hoc iugum respuimus. Testantur animos impatientes disciplinae prisca pariter ac recentia seculā. Lothum Sodomitae,Iosephum fratres,Mosem Israelitae,prophetas,apostolos,episcopos, etiam philosophos & omnino omnes quibus quod malum & iniquum est adeo displicuit ut id auderent reprehendere,mundus aegre pertulit. At eiusmodi homines, quoniam & vitiosi sunt & meliores reddi non possunt: ad societatem diuinam inepti sunt. Recte ergo Moses ad eam ipsam nos alliciens admonet nos circumcisionis, qua docet nos ceu arbores ut proferendis fructibus fiamus magis idonei,putari debere.
units.tr: But to return to Moses, he also says: "and do not harden your neck any more." By this metaphor, taken from oxen that submit their necks to the yoke, he commands obedience. For I do not know by what evil of nature it happens that we bear with the greatest difficulty that discipline which brings great advantage not only to the soundness of our minds but also of our bodies. For who does not take up with reluctance the regimen of life prescribed by a physician, and does not think the diet, which they call medicine, a miserable thing? So much do we desire what is not permitted and not expedient. Thus we can scarcely bear the yoke, and we always strive toward what is forbidden. But Christ says in Matthew 11 that his yoke is sweet and easy. And since he imposes nothing except what agrees with nature, how can it be heavy? But because we hear a corrupter of good nature as our teacher, we reject this yoke. The minds impatient of discipline attest this, both the ancient and the recent ages. The Sodomites were displeased with Lot, the brothers with Joseph, the Israelites with Moses, and the world has scarcely endured the prophets, apostles, bishops, even the philosophers, and in short all those whose displeasure at evil and iniquity was so great that they dared to rebuke it. But such men, since they are both wicked and cannot be made better, are unfit for the divine fellowship. Rightly, therefore, Moses, enticing us to that very fellowship, admonishes us that we ought to be pruned, as by circumcision, in which he teaches us, like trees, to become the more fit to bring forth fruit.

units.la: Sed & hoc ipsum,inquis,factu difficile est. Fateor ego inquam, sed unde haec orta nobis est difficultas ? Ex eo sane quod quis qualisque sit Deus aut ignoramus, aut non ita vti par est reputamus. Recte ergo Moses,ut nos ad officium excitet,Deum suis coloribus quantum potest ab homine cum exprimi tum percipi, depingit, ac dicit. Nam Dominus Deus ve-ster ipse est Deus Deorum, & Dominus Dominorum, Deus magnus, robustus, tremendus, qui non recipit personas nec munera. Quo docet eum esse Deum nostrum, cui maxime sit obedien-dum. Etenim si illi parere nolis, cui pareas iustius habebis neminem. Siue enim maiorem quæras aliquem, nihil egeris, cum hic omnium sit optimus maximus, siue minorem tibi de-ligas, idipsum & illo & te ipso indignum fuerit. Esse vero hunc maximum argumento est, quod est Deus Deorum, Dominus Dominorum, Deus magnus, præpotens & tremendus. Hæc qui rectè secum reputat facile adducitur ut Deo obediat.
units.tr: "But," you say, "this too is difficult to do." I grant it, I say, but whence has this difficulty arisen for us? Certainly from the fact that we either do not know what and how great God is, or do not reckon him as we ought. Therefore Moses rightly, to stir us to our duty, depicts God in his own colours, as far as he can be expressed and perceived by man, and says: "For the Lord your God is the God of gods, and the Lord of lords, a great, mighty and terrible God, who does not accept persons nor gifts." By this he teaches that he is our God, to whom we must most of all render obedience. For if you are unwilling to obey him, you will have no one to whom you could more justly obey. For if you seek some greater being, you will accomplish nothing, since he is the best and greatest of all; and if you choose some lesser one for yourself, that would be unworthy both of him and of yourself. That he is the greatest is shown by the fact that he is the God of gods, the Lord of lords, a great, all-powerful and terrible God. Whoever rightly considers these things in himself is easily led to obey God.

units.la: Ex quibus est perspicuum homines, ut ad societatem cum Deo ineundam fiant idonei verbo Dei moneri: primum ut malum, cuius causa ab illo repulsi fuerant, resecent seq; totos perpurgent: idein[?] ut iugo verbi Dei opt.max. sua colla non grauate subijciant. Quo fiet ut in numerum suorum Deus nos recipiat.
units.tr: From these things it is clear that, if men are to become fit to enter into fellowship with God, they must be admonished by the Word of God: first, that they cut away the evil on account of which they had been repulsed by him, and thoroughly cleanse themselves; and then that they willingly submit their necks to the yoke of the Word of God, most good and great. In this way God will receive us into the number of his own people.

units.la: Imitatione vero hoc totu[?] quod dicimus perficitur. Nam cum simile simili gaudeat & con-sensus consiliorum & voluntatum ad parandam simul ac firmandam amicitiam momenti plu-rimum afferat: sane Deo gratiores effici non possumus, quam illius ipsius imitatione. Ac quo-niam ad imitatione requiritur exemplum optimum & perfectissimum: Moses exemplum i-psum quidem primum ponit ob oculos, ac deinceps ad ipsum quo pacto comparemur docet.
units.tr: This whole thing that we are saying is accomplished by imitation. For since like delights in like, and agreement of counsels and wills carries very great weight in forming and strengthening friendship, we cannot be made more pleasing to God than by imitating him. And since imitation requires an excellent and most perfect example, Moses first sets the example itself before our eyes, and then teaches us how we may be conformed to it.

units.la: Exemplum autem idipsum proponit, secundum quod initio fueramus conditi: nempe ut ad archetypum reformaremur. Ad imaginem Dei creati sumus. Qualis igitur est Deus? Ius dicit pupillo & viduæ, & tanto peregrinos homines amore prosequitur, ut eisdem vitium[?] & amicitium large suppeditet. Quid tum postea? Sane quid mundus iis benefacit ferè à quibus remunerationem expectet, & eos suspicit, ac sequitur qui sunt gloriosi & præpotentes: contra hos negligit qui sunt obscuri atque inglorii: Deus inopes, contemptos, miseros, curat, ac iuvat maxime: Id nos consoletur inopes, exules. Etid adeò verum est ut longiore non e-geat demonstratione.
units.tr: He sets forth this example, indeed, in the same way as we were originally created, namely that we should be remade after the archetype: we were created in the image of God. What, then, is God like? "He executes justice for the fatherless and the widow, and loves the strangers so greatly that he richly supplies them with food and clothing." What follows from this? Indeed, the world does good mostly to those from whom it expects a return, and it admires and follows those who are glorious and powerful; but it neglects those who are obscure and without renown. God cares for and helps most of all the poor, the despised, and the wretched. This should console us who are poor and exiles. And this is so true that it needs no longer demonstration.

units.la: Sed in eius imitationem quomodo fit incumbenbum. 1. Ut hospites ipsi quoque diliga-mus. Iam cum veniant ad nos exules, præsertim Christiani, pii innocentes, euangelij nomine missi in exilium: caue ne eos livore, convitiis, odio, cogas abire. Ubi ubi fuerint pascet & ve-stiet eos Dominus. Si illis hic sit locus, nec illis nec tibi cōmeatus deerit. Sin abire coegeris quid fiet aliud quàm quod exeunte Noha, Lotho, Dauide, discipulis sequebantur diluvium, ignis, bellum difficile, Hierosolymarum excidium? Quin nobis gratulamur dignis visis, qui-bus hospitibus uti voluerit Dominus? Nil aliud quàm benedictionem secum afferunt, & precibus suis urbem agrumque Deo conciliant. Dicit Moses eos hoc debere facere, quia fuerint ipsi quoque hospites: dicam ego posse fieri, ut & nos mittamur in exilium. Quod caue-bitur si nostrum agrum piis fratribus asylum permittamus.
units.tr: But how are we to labour in his imitation? (1) We should also love strangers. When exiles come to us, especially Christians, pious and innocent people sent into exile for the sake of the gospel, take care not to drive them away with spite, reproaches, and hatred. Wherever they are, the Lord will feed and clothe them. If there is room for them here, neither they nor you will lack provision. But if you force them to leave, what will happen other than what followed the departure of Noah, Lot and David's companions: the flood, fire, a hard war, the destruction of Jerusalem? Why do we not rejoice that we are worthy to be seen as the guests whom the Lord has chosen to use? They bring nothing but a blessing with them, and by their prayers they win over to God the city and the countryside. Moses says they ought to do this because "you yourselves also were strangers"; I would add that it may happen that we ourselves are sent into exile. We shall guard against this if we grant a refuge to pious brothers in our land.

units.la: 2 Illum time, sequere, & dilige, & iurans testem adhibe. Iuramentum est quasi quedam vo-stræ[?] fidei confessio. Per quem enim iuramus, eum testem nobis asciscimus, quem nec li-ceat nec libeat fallere: quemque arbitremur nos periuros puniturum, vera iurantes in vita conseruaturum. Inde vetat Deus per creaturas iurari. Esa. 56. Qui vult iurare, iuret in Do-mino. Hierem.5. Filii tui deseruerunt me, iurarunt per eos qui Dii non sunt. Quid nos in or-be Christiano facimus? An non ab eo qui verus est, & vnus Deus, descivimus ac iuramus per eos qui Dii non sunt? Etenim Divi quos iurantes Deo socios asciscimus, Dii non sunt: & tamen eos quasi cordium cognitores & vindices deos iurantes adhibemus.
units.tr: (2) "Fear him, follow him, and love him, and swear by his name." An oath is, as it were, a confession of our faith. For by whomever we swear, we take him as witness, one whom it is neither permitted nor pleasing to deceive, and whom we believe will punish us if we swear falsely and preserve those who swear truly in life. Therefore God forbids swearing by creatures. Isaiah 56: "Whoever wishes to swear, let him swear in the Lord." Jeremiah 5: "Your sons have forsaken me and sworn by those who are not gods." What do we do in the Christian world? Have we not turned away from him who is true and the one God, and swear by those who are not gods? For the saints, whom we take as companions to God when we swear, are not gods; yet we call them in as gods who know and avenge the hearts, as if they were those who know and judge the heart.

units.la: Nobis Deus sufficiet, qui, ut ait Moses, est laus nostra & res magnas in repub. nostra ges-sit. Nam illud inclytum & gloriosum urbis huius nomen ex euangelij professione compara-vimus: & res præclaras Deo vires suppeditáte gessimus. Ex paucis fecit plurimos. Eiigitur[?] sit honos in secula. Amen.
units.tr: God alone is sufficient for us, who, as Moses says, is "our praise" and has done great things in our commonwealth. For we have acquired that famous and glorious name of this city through the profession of the gospel, and we have accomplished splendid things, God supplying the strength. "Out of a few he has made many." Therefore let his honour be for ever and ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT XI. SERMO XVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI. SERMON XVI.

units.la: Diligite itaq; Dominum Deum tuum & obserua custoditionem eius, ritus eius, iudicia eius, & præcepta eius, idq; cunctis diebus.
units.tr: Therefore love the Lord your God, and keep his charge, his rites, his judgments, and his precepts, all the days.

units.la: 2 Cognoscite hodie (quoniam non cum filijs vestris, qui non cognouerunt neque viderunt disciplinam Domini Dei vestri) magnalia eius, manum eius validam & brachium eius extentum.
units.tr: 2 Know this day (for not with your children, who have not known nor seen the discipline of the Lord your God) his greatness, his strong hand and his outstretched arm.

units.la: 3 Et signa eius & opera eius, quae fecit inter Aegyptios, Pharaoni regi Aegypti, & vniuersae regioni eius.
units.tr: 3 And his signs and his works, which he did among the Egyptians, to Pharaoh the king of Egypt and to all his land.

units.la: 4 Quae deniq; fecit copijs Aegypti, equis eius, atq; curribus eius, quomodo reduxerit aquas maris carestosi super eos, dum illi insectarentur vos a tergo, perdide [?] ritq; eos vsq; in praesentem diem,
units.tr: 4 And what he did to the army of Egypt, to its horses and its chariots: how he brought the waters of the Red Sea over them while they pursued you from behind, and destroyed them even to this day.

units.la: 5 Sed & quae fecit vobis in deserto, donec veneritis ad locum istum;
units.tr: 5 But also what he did for you in the desert, until you came to this place.

units.la: 6 Item quae fecit ipsi Dathan & Abiram, & filijs Eliab filij Ruben, dum terra os suum aperiret, & deuoraret eos, simulq; domus eorum, & tentoria eorum, & cunctam substantiam eorum, quam habebant in medio vniuersi Israelis.
units.tr: 6 Likewise what he did to Dathan and Abiram, the sons of Eliab, the son of Reuben, when the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them up, together with their houses, their tents, and all their substance which they had in the midst of all Israel.

units.la: 7 Etenim oculi vestri viderunt vniuersum opus Domini magnum quod fecit.
units.tr: 7 For your eyes have seen all the great work of the Lord which he did.

units.la: CUm praeceptum primum hoc potissimum vrgeat, vt genus nostrum cum Deo, ceu summo bono, coniungatur, atq; eo pacto in bonorum omnium possesionem veniat: sane ex eo cuiuis est perspicuum, in hoc ipso praecepto momenti plurimum situm esse: ac si hic quis impingat, in portu impegerit; sin quis hinc bene sit auspicatus, factum dimidij, ceu qui bene coeperit habeat. Qua de causa Moses in huius legis expositione summa fide & diligentia versatur: ac non solum quae ad eam ipsam tuendam videntur pertinere ea assert: verumetiam quae ei ipsi videbuntur obstare, in praesentia remouet. Quae expositio quatuor aut quinque capp. comprehenditur.
units.tr: Since this first precept urges above all that our race be joined to God, as to the supreme good, and that in this way we come into possession of all good things, it is plain to anyone that the greatest weight lies in this very precept: if one stumbles here, he has stumbled at the harbour itself; but if one has made a good beginning here, he has, as it were, done half the work, since he has begun well. For this reason Moses, in expounding this law, labours with great faithfulness and diligence; and he not only sets forth what seems to pertain to defending it, but also at once removes whatever seems to stand in its way. This exposition is contained in four or five chapters.

units.la: Ei vero nunc epilogum subiungit artificiose fabrefactum: in quo primum summam ac ca-put legis, tum confirmationem, deniq; conclusionem affert.
units.tr: Now he appends to it a skilfully constructed epilogue, in which he first sets out the sum and head of the law, then its confirmation, and finally its conclusion.

units.la: Summam ac caput sic proponit: Dilige itaq; Dominum Deum tuum, & observa custoditionem eius, ritus eius, &c. Quibus verbis & legis summam proponit, & eius etiam effecta ponit. Summam dicit dilectionem dicens: Dilige itaq; Dominum Deum tuum & observa custodi-tionem eius &c. Iam quod dilectionem Dei dicit huius legis summam ac scopum esse, id ipsum etiam Christo placet, qui Matth. 22. de summa legis rogatus hoc ipsum quod hic Moses dicit, respondit: diliges Dominum Deum tuum: ac deinceps qualem hanc dilectionem esse oporteat, addens quaedam ostendit. Nam perfectionem ijsdem quibus Moses supra, notis definit, corde videlicet, anima, viribus quantis possumus maximis.
units.tr: He sets out the sum and head thus: Therefore love the Lord your God, and observe his charge, his rites, etc. In these words he both states the sum of the law and sets down its effects. He names the sum as love, saying: Therefore love the Lord your God and observe his charge, etc. Now that he says the love of God is the sum and aim of this law is also pleasing to Christ, who, asked about the sum of the law in Matthew 22, answered with the very thing Moses says here: you shall love the Lord your God; and afterwards, showing what sort of love this ought to be, he adds certain particulars. For he defines its completeness by the same marks Moses used above: namely, with the heart, the soul, and the strength, as greatly as we can.

units.la: In quo morbus noster cernitur, quod videlicet Deum non diligamus: alioquin non praeciperetur. At grande nefas est authorem nostrae vitae simul & salutis, & Dominum cuius ser-ui sumus, non diligere.
units.tr: In this our disease is seen, namely that we do not love God; otherwise it would not be commanded. But it is a great wickedness not to love the author of our life and salvation at once, and the Lord whose servants we are.

units.la: At, inquis, diligo: concedo. Sed non toto corde, cum eius partem mundo, peccatis, carni-tribuas. Ideo hoc praecepto requiritur, vt Deum plane diligamus & rebus omnibus antepo-namus. Sic eum dilexit Abraham, qui ipsum relictis parentibus, amicis, patria quocunq; vo-cantem secutus est, & filium sacrificari sibi requirenti morem gerere voluerit. Sic eum dili-gunt quibus verbi diuini professio pluris est, quam patria, quam vxor, quam liberi. Sic eum diligunt qui mandata diuina malunt sequi, quam vel caducas voluptates vel quascunq; car-nis illecebras. Sed quemadmodum vxorem suam nondum rite diligit, qui scortum nondum deseruit: sic qui mundum, caducas voluptates, malam consuetudinem, turpe lucrum, aliaq; eiusdem generis non potest deserere: hic Deum nondum ita vti lege hac requiritur diligit. Audiens enim Deum haec odisse, si pluris Deum faceret, etiam ipse haec odio prosequetur.
units.tr: But, you say, I do love him. I grant it. But you give him only a part of your heart, and the other part to the world, to sins, and to the flesh. Therefore this precept requires that we love God plainly and set him before all things. Thus Abraham loved him, who, leaving his parents, friends and country, followed him calling wherever he went, and was willing to obey him when he required his son to be sacrificed. Thus they love him to whom the profession of the divine word is worth more than country, wife, or children. Thus they love him who choose to follow the divine commands rather than either fleeting pleasures or whatever allurements of the flesh. But just as a man does not yet rightly love his wife if he has not yet given up a harlot, so he who cannot yet forsake the world, fleeting pleasures, evil custom, shameful gain, and other things of this kind, does not yet love God in the way this law requires. For if he hears that God hates these things, and he holds God in higher esteem, he himself will pursue them with hatred too.

units.la: Iam quomodo hoc praeceptum seruemus secum ipse quisq; reputet. Non est quod praeceptionum diuinarum studium risum iocumq; putes, cum ne primum quidem seruaueris: Nam cum eius summa ac caput sit, Deū sic diligere, vt nihil diligas magis: tu, qui te ipse, tuas voluptates, opes, dignitates pluris facis, ab hac longe deerrasti.
units.tr: Now let each one consider for himself how we keep this precept. You should not think that the study of the divine commandments is a laughing matter, since you have not yet kept even the first. For since its sum and head is to love God so that you love nothing more, you, who value yourself, your pleasures, wealth and honours above him, have wandered far from it.

units.la: Prodest igitur summa capita nostrae fidei tenere, & animis sedulo versari, ne videlicet in portu impingens iter ad Deum parum fastum habeas. Ac certe summum dedecus est esse in orbe Christiano homines qui decalogum, precationem Dominicam, articulos fidei non teneant. Recte ergo Moses summam huius legis repetit.
units.tr: It is therefore useful to hold fast to the chief heads of our faith and to dwell on them diligently, lest, stumbling at the harbour, you have little regard for the way to God. And certainly it is the greatest disgrace to be, in the Christian world, people who do not know the Decalogue, the Lord's Prayer, and the articles of faith. Rightly, therefore, Moses repeats the sum of this law.

units.la: Iam vero ne qua falsa specie legis quasi seruatae decipiare: dilectionis huius effecta refert, d'icens, Et obserua tuftoditionem eius,ritus eius,&c. Quibus verbis quasi notis summam in hu-ius egis studio curam & diligentiam indicat, nempe ut eam ne qua parte vel tantillum negligamus. Custoditionis appellatione curam illam significat, quam rei carissimae custodiendae solemus adhibere.
units.tr: Now, lest you be deceived by a false appearance of having kept the law, he states the effects of this love, saying, And observe the keeping of it, its rites, etc. By these words, as by marks, he indicates the care and diligence that must be shown in studying this law, namely that we neglect it in no part, not even a little. By the word keeping he signifies that care which we are accustomed to apply to guarding what is most dear to us.

units.la: Dein quibus in rebus hæc cura requirat ur sigillatim docet. Primum in ritibus, hoc est, ceremoniis, sacramentis, drecibus[?], doctrina. Hæ[?] etsi salutem ipsæ minime conferant, tamen quia sunt quasi quædam diuinitus institutæ consuetudines, atque ad salutem nostram momenti multum afferunt, magno sint in precio, minimeq; negligantur necesse est. Christus ipse voluit implere omnem iustitiam, propterea baptismum & circumcisionem, quibus minimè indiguit, non dedignatus est accipere: unde & per ipsum sanctificata credimus. Idem Cornelius Centurio, Philippus, reliquiq; Apostoli & beati martyres factitarunt.
units.tr: Then he teaches in particular in what matters this care is required. First in rites, that is, ceremonies, sacraments, prayers, and doctrine. Although these do not of themselves confer salvation, yet, since they are in a way customs instituted by God, and contribute much to our salvation, they must be held in high esteem and cannot be neglected. Christ himself willed to fulfil all righteousness, and therefore he did not disdain to receive baptism and circumcision, which he did not need; whence we believe that these things were also sanctified by him. Cornelius the centurion, Philip, the rest of the apostles, and the blessed martyrs did the same.

units.la: Nos autem quia verbum, preces, sacramenta, quacunque leui de causa negligimus: parum diligentes sumus in custodiendis ritibus, quod argumento est Deum non ita uti par erat, magno apud nos esse in precio: præsertim quando conuiuia, deambulationes, aliasq; res leuissimas istis rebus anteferimus.
units.tr: But we, because we neglect the word, prayers, and sacraments for any slight reason, are not careful enough in keeping the rites; which is proof that we do not hold God in the great esteem that he deserves among us, especially when we put feasts, walks, and other most trivial things before these matters.

units.la: Post dicit iudicia, hoc est leges ciuiles, & statuta, & consuetudines, & omnino quicquid vel magistratibus vel principi placuit quod verbo Domini fit consentaneum. At eas alius odit, alius negligit: pleriq; sui iuris esse volunt, hoc est, sibi quod libet licere. Atqui Deum uere diligunt, ij pluris eius leges, quàm suos impuros motus faciunt.
units.tr: Afterwards he mentions judgments, that is, civil laws, statutes, customs, and in general whatever has pleased the magistrates or the prince, insofar as it agrees with the word of the Lord. But some hate these, others neglect them; most want to be their own masters, that is, to be allowed whatever they please. Yet those who truly love God make his laws more precious than their own impure impulses.

units.la: Postremo præcepta dicit, hoc est logos paraeneticos, seu præcepta de moribus, cuiusmodi sunt Phocilydis & Pythagoræ & aliorum, & in primis illa diuina, quæ sunt duabus illis de scripta tabulis. Illis enim summatim quid Deo, quid item hominibus debeatur, comprehenditur. At ea si commodu fit, placent: sin minus, displicet. Unde cognoscitur quo loco Deũ habeas. Quæ cum ita sint operæpreciu est haberi vitæ nostræ examina, quibus cognoscatur, quando mores nostri sacris literis, seu voluntati Domini sint consentanei: ac rursus quando ab hoc tramite deerratũ fit. Nam hæc negligentia nos à vero & bono seducit longius. Quamobrem Mosem imitati cum verbi Dei summam animis nostris comprehensam, habeamus: tum vitam ac mores nostros cum ea quàm plurimum conferamus.
units.tr: Lastly he mentions precepts, that is, exhortatory discourses [λόγοι παραινετικοί], or precepts concerning morals, such as those of Phocylides and Pythagoras and others, and above all those divine ones which are written on the two tablets. For these summarily comprise what is owed to God and likewise what is owed to men. But people approve of these if they are convenient, and if not, they dislike them. By this one may tell in what regard you hold God. Since these things are so, it is worth while to hold examinations of our life, by which it may be known when our morals agree with the Holy Scriptures or the will of the Lord, and again when we have strayed from this path. For this negligence leads us far away from the true and the good. Therefore, imitating Moses, let us keep the sum of God's word fixed in our minds, and let us compare our life and morals with it as closely as possible.

units.la: Confirmationis pars prior exempla affert, quibus docet quàm iustum atq; æquum sit huic legi stare, quantæq; ex eius obseruatione utilitates percipiantur: quippe quod eo ipso gratiam referamus Deo de nobis tam benemerito. Sunt autem exempla tria: quorum primum quæ eis in Ægypto, secundum quæ in deserto, tertium quæ in seditione diuinitus eis data sint beneficia commemorant.
units.tr: The first part of the confirmation brings forward examples, by which he teaches how just and fair it is to stand by this law, and what great benefits are gained from keeping it, since by this very thing we give thanks to God, who has deserved so well of us. There are three examples: the first recalls the benefits given to them in Egypt, the second those in the desert, the third those given by God in the sedition.

units.la: In Ægxpto[?], ut est Exod. 14. liberauit suos miris modis, hostes autem potentissimè repressit ac deleuit. Quo refer istic edita miracula. In quibus videmus summam potentiam, bonitatem, iustitiam. Quod enim oppressos suos è tyranni faucibus eripuit, est potentiæ, cuius nomine eum veneremur, & in illo omnes spes opesq; sitas esse velimus. Quod suis etiam indignis opem tulit, est misericordiæ: ad eam quis non confugeret? hic fons est gratiæ. Quod iniurias suis illatas ultus est & tyrannum oppressit, id est iustitiæ: id miseros consoletur, ac de sua causa bene sperare iubeat. Sic opem Sufannæ, Dauidi, alijsq; tulit oppressis hominibus. Sic nos omnes per Christum liberati sumus è faucibus diaboli, & mortuis vita restituta est. Idem euenit uniuersis & singulis quotidie.
units.tr: In Egypt, as in Exod. 14, he delivered his people in wonderful ways and most mightily restrained and destroyed their enemies. The miracles wrought there are to be referred to this point. In them we see supreme power, goodness and justice. That he snatched his oppressed people from the jaws of the tyrant belongs to power, in whose name we venerate him and in whom we wish all our hopes and resources to be placed. That he brought help even to his unworthy people belongs to mercy: to whom would anyone not flee for refuge? This is the fountain of grace. That he avenged the wrongs done to his people and crushed the tyrant belongs to justice: this comforts the wretched and bids them hope well for their cause. So he brought aid to Susanna, David and others oppressed. So we all have been freed through Christ from the jaws of the devil, and life has been restored to the dead. The same happens to all and to each one daily.

units.la: Atq; sic exemplum præsens docet legis primæ studium requiri iure optimo: cum Deus eum se præbeat hominibus qui desiderari possit.
units.tr: And so this example teaches that the study of the first law is rightly required, since God shows himself to men as one who can be desired.

units.la: In deserto, ut est Exod.16. populum istum tulit mirabili patientia. Siue enim peccarent ignouit: siue se sequerentur, fouit: semper passus est eos sibi reconciliari. In quo perspici potest eum nihil illorum saluti prius habuisse: nihil sua, illorum causa fecisse omnia. Quod patris est benigni & longanimis. Cur ergo non obsequeremur ei soli, qui nisi nostram salutem quærit nihil.
units.tr: In the wilderness, as in Exod. 16, he bore this people with remarkable patience. Whether they sinned, he forgave; whether they followed him, he cherished them; he always allowed them to be reconciled to him. In this it can be seen that he held nothing more important than their salvation, and did everything for their sake and nothing for his own. This is the mark of a kind and long-suffering father. Why then should we not obey him alone, who seeks nothing but our salvation?

units.la: In seditione, ut est Num.16. seditiosi puniti sic sunt ut parceretur bonis. Quod est optimi principis, qui non sic punit malos, ut inde redeat damnum ad bonos. Malos hos absterreat à malo: posse eos puniri vel saluis atq; superstitibus bonis. Multi nunc peccant quasi impunè, & alios rapturi secum in exitium, sed falli ipsos hoc exemplo discimus. Rursus bonos hoc soletur, quod ipsi vel in medio malorum conseruari possunt. Ut in diluuio Noha, in Sodomis Lothus, in Ægypto Israel, alibi alij. Quis huiusmodi Deum non diligeret? Ei sit honos in secula, Amen.
units.tr: In the rebellion, as in Num. 16, the seditious were punished in such a way that the good were spared. This is the mark of an excellent prince, who does not punish the wicked in such a way that the loss falls back on the good. It should frighten the wicked away from evil: they learn that they can be punished while the good remain safe and unharmed. Many now sin as if with impunity, intending to drag others with them into destruction, but from this example we learn that they are deceived. Again, this comforts the good, because they can be preserved even in the midst of the wicked: as Noah in the flood, Lot in Sodom, Israel in Egypt, and others elsewhere. Who would not love a God of this kind? To him be honour for ever, Amen.

units.la: SERMO XVII.
units.tr: SERMON XVII.

units.la: 8 Custodite igitur omnia præcepta, quæ ego præcipio tibi hodie, ut corroborati introeatis, & possideatis terram, ad quam vos transitis possidendam.
units.tr: 8 Keep therefore all the commandments which I command you this day, that you may be strengthened, and go in and possess the land into which you are passing to possess it.

units.la: 9 Et ut prolongetis dies super terram quam iurauit Dominus patribus ve-stris, ut daret illis atq; semini eorum terram fluentem lacte et melle.
units.tr: 9 And that you may prolong your days upon the earth which the Lord swore to your fathers, to give to them and to their seed, a land flowing with milk and honey.

units.la: 10 Quoniam terra ista ad quam tu iam proficisceris, ut occupes eam, non est si-cut terra Ægypti,de qua egressi estis, ubi seminabas semen tuum, & rigabas pedibus tuis quemadmodum hortum olerum.
units.tr: 10 For the land to which you now go, to take possession of it, is not like the land of Egypt from which you came out, where you sowed your seed and watered it with your feet, as a garden of herbs.

units.la: 11 Terra autem ista ad quam tu transis ut eam possideas,montes habet & valles,& ex aquis cœlestibus irrigatur.
units.tr: 11 But the land to which you pass over to possess it has mountains and valleys, and is watered by the waters of heaven.

units.la: 12 Hanc terram Dominus Deus tuus inuisit, suntq; oculi Domini Dei tui iugiter super eam, ab initio anni ad finem usq;.
units.tr: 12 The Lord your God visits this land, and the eyes of the Lord your God are continually upon it, from the beginning of the year to its end.

units.la: 13 Si itaq; diligenter audieritis præcepta mea, quæ ego præcipio vobis hodie, ut diligatis Dominum Deum vestrum, & seruieritis ei toto corde vestro, & toto animo vestro:
units.tr: 13 If therefore you diligently hear my commandments which I command you this day, to love the Lord your God and to serve him with your whole heart and with your whole soul:

units.la: 14 Dabo pluuiam terræ vestræ suo quoq; tempore, pluuiam tempestiuam et se-rotinam, ut colligas frumentum tuum, vinum tuum & oleum tuum.
units.tr: 14 I will give the rain of your land in its season, the early and the latter rain, that you may gather in your corn, your wine and your oil.

units.la: 15 Dabo insuper herbam in agro tuo pro iumentis tuis, ut & tu comedas & satieris.
units.tr: 15 I will moreover give grass in your field for your cattle, that you may both eat and be filled.

units.la: 16 Cauete autem ne cor vestrum seducatur, ut recedatis & seruiatis diis alie-nis, adoretisq; eos.
units.tr: 16 But take heed lest your heart be deceived, so that you turn aside and serve other gods and worship them.

units.la: 17 Et exardescat ira Domini contra vos, claudatq; cœlum ne veniat pluuia, et terra non det prouentum suum, pereatisq; cito de terra ista bona, quam Dominus dat vobis.
units.tr: 17 And the anger of the Lord be kindled against you, and he shut up heaven that there be no rain, and the earth not yield its increase, and you perish quickly from that good land which the Lord gives you.

units.la: 18 Reponite itaq; verba ista mea in cor vestrum & in animu vestru, eaq; ut si-gnum ligate ad manum vestram, ut sint veluti monimentum inter oculos vestros.
units.tr: 18 Therefore lay up these my words in your heart and in your soul, and bind them as a sign upon your hand, that they may be as a memorial between your eyes.

units.la: 19 Docete etiam ea filios vestros, ut feriò loquantur de eis, quum desides domi tuæ, & quum es in itinere, quum cubitum vadis, quum surgis.
units.tr: 19 Teach them also to your sons, that they may speak of them diligently, when you sit in your house, and when you are on the way, when you lie down and when you rise up.

units.la: 20 Scribes quoq; ea super postes domus tuæ, & in portis tuis.
units.tr: 20 You shall also write them upon the posts of your house and upon your gates.

units.la: 21 Ut prorogentur dies vestri, & dies filiorum vestrorum super terram, quam iurauit Dominus patribus vestris, ut daret eis, tantisper dum dies cœlorum sunt su-per terram.
units.tr: 21 That your days may be prolonged, and the days of your sons, upon the earth which the Lord swore to your fathers to give them, as long as the days of heaven are upon the earth.

units.la: 22 Si diligenter custodieritis omnia præcepta illa quæ ego præcipio vobis, ut faciat ea, nempe ut diligatis Dominum Deum vestrum, & ambuletis in omnibus viis eius, adhæreatisq; ei.
units.tr: 22 If you diligently keep all these commandments which I command you, to do them, namely to love the Lord your God, and to walk in all his ways, and to cleave to him,

units.la: 23 Exterminabit Dominus cunctas gentes istas à facie vestra, & vos occupa-bitis gentes magnas, & quæ robustiores sunt vobis.
units.tr: 23 then the Lord will drive out all these nations from before you, and you shall possess nations greater and stronger than yourselves.

units.la: 24 Omnis locus quoniam planta pedis vestri calcauerit, vester erit, à deserto et Libano, à fluuio inquam Euphratis usq; ad mare ultimum erunt limites vestri.
units.tr: 24 Every place on which the sole of your foot treads shall be yours: from the wilderness and Lebanon, from the river, I say, Euphrates to the western sea, shall be your borders.

units.la: 25 Nemo audebit vobis resistere, quoniam pauorem vestrum & timorem ve-strum dabit Dominus Deus vester super faciem totius terræ, quam calcaturi estis, si-cut loquutus est vobis.
units.tr: 25 No one shall dare to resist you, for the Lord your God will lay the fear and dread of you upon the face of the whole land on which you are about to tread, as he has spoken to you.

units.la: PRoxima concione diximus Mosem hoc ii.cap.explicationem primæ legis concludere, & eam conclusionem tribus partibus absoluere: quarum prima summam eius repetit, altera hanc ipsam primum exemplis tum argumentis firmat, ultima paucis quid saluti quid-ue fit exitio doceat. Igitur explicata summa ac pertractatis exemplis, nunc argumenta qua-tuor,quæ Moses verbis illis affert, exponemus. Ea sunt sumpta ab utili,à contrario,à facili,deniq; ab honesto. Vtile sic effert, Custodite igitur omnia præcepta quæ ego præcipio tibi hodie, vt corroborati introeatis &c. Quibus verbis Moses indicat possessionem eius ad quam contendebant terræ tum tum demum potituros, cum Deum amplexi sint summa pietate & diuini verbi studio. Ac quoniam illis nihil perinde esset in votis ac terra promissa potiri: dicit illis qualem eius fruitionem diuinæ legis huius studium efficiat: nempe facilem, diuturnam, diuitem.
units.tr: In the last sermon we said that Moses concludes the explanation of the first law in this second chapter, and completes that conclusion in three parts: the first repeats its summary, the second confirms this very summary first by examples and then by arguments, and the last teaches in a few words what leads to salvation and what leads to ruin. Therefore, having explained the summary and treated the examples, we will now set out the four arguments which Moses brings forward in those words. They are drawn from what is useful, from the contrary, from what is easy, and finally from what is honourable. He states the useful argument thus: Keep therefore all the commandments which I command you this day, that you may be strengthened and go in, etc. By these words Moses indicates that they will at last obtain possession of the land for which they were striving, when they embrace God with the greatest piety and devotion to his word. And since nothing was more desired by them than to possess the promised land, he tells them what kind of enjoyment of it this study of the divine law will bring about: namely, an easy, lasting and rich one.

units.la: Facilem eo ipso probat fore, quod obseruantes præcepta Dei corroboraturus sit eos Dominus ita, vt veniant, & possideant terram, quam illis daturus sit Dominus. Quod verum esse res gestæ comprobant. Nam Deum in columna nubis & ignis præeuntem secuti progressus magnos faciebant: at contra nitentes ac vel idolis, vel seditione, vel murmure, vel reditu in Ægyptum semper sese remorati sunt. Ex quo colligimus, facilia fore quæ suscipimus om-nia, si verbo Dei sint consentanea.
units.tr: He proves that it will be easy by this very thing, that by keeping the commandments of God the Lord will strengthen them so that they may come in and possess the land which the Lord is going to give them. The events themselves confirm that this is true. For when they followed God going before them in a pillar of cloud and fire, they made great progress; but on the contrary, whenever they struggled, whether through idols, or sedition, or murmuring, or the wish to return to Egypt, they always held themselves back. From this we gather that all the things we undertake will be easy, if they are in agreement with the word of God.

units.la: Diuturnam probat, Quod dies vitæ prorogaturus sit illis in terra promissa, quando præceptis ipsius steterint. Est & id probatum illorum exemplis: nam Aharon, Maria, Moses, aliquot innumeri ideo terræ promissæ coaspectu & possessione potiti non sunt, quod transgressione Deum offendissent.
units.tr: He proves that it will be lasting, because he will prolong their life in the promised land, when they have stood fast by his precepts. This too is proved by their examples: for Aaron, Miriam, Moses, and many others did not attain the sight and possession of the promised land, because they had offended God by transgression.

units.la: Diuitem pluribus verbis probat: dicit enim fluentem lacte & melle, eamq; etiam cum Æ-gypto comparat. Quæ lata ac plana est, & Nili inundatione fœcundatur: Chananæa vero valles habet & montes, & cœlestibus aquis est irrigua, & oculus Domini super eam est intentus.
units.tr: He proves that it will be rich with more words: for he says it is flowing with milk and honey, and he also compares it with Egypt. Egypt is broad and flat, and is made fertile by the flooding of the Nile; but the Canaanite land has valleys and mountains, is watered by the waters of heaven, and the eye of the Lord is fixed upon it.

units.la: Quæ docent magnos ex pietate fructus percipi. Nam cum supra summum finem nihil sit quod posset exoptari: Deus autem hunc eis promittat, siquidem ipsum ampleCtantur: sanè videmus verbi diuini studio nihil esse vtilius. Israelis labores eò tendebant omnes, vt terra promissa potirentur & fruerentur: eam Moses possessionem ex pietate promittit facilem, diuturnam, diuitem. Sic nos opes & pacatam vitam quærimus: ea bona comparantur pietate facillimè: Veni, vidi, vici. At impij multum mouendo nihil promouent: pij vigent & florent. Pij suis bonis diu fruuntur, impij surgunt & emergunt subito, caduntq; subito. Exemplo sunt Saul, Absalon, Alexander Magnus, Cæsar aliqui. Ita nostra ætate emergunt aliqui subito, malis artibus videlicet: sed subito ceu flores cadunt. Bonis quod est sufficit: impijs multum quod est non sufficit. Pietas facit, vt nihil cum sit, nihil desit tamen. Atq; his quidem promissis ad pietatem quisquis non allicitur impius sit ac maneat necesse est.
units.tr: These things teach that great fruits are gathered from piety. For since there is nothing above the highest end that could be desired, and God promises this to them, provided they cling to him, we surely see that nothing is more useful than devotion to the divine word. All the labours of Israel tended to this, that they might obtain and enjoy the promised land; Moses promises that possession, easy, lasting and rich, from piety. So we seek wealth and a peaceful life; these goods are obtained most easily by piety: I came, I saw, I conquered. But the wicked, by much stirring, accomplish nothing; the pious flourish and thrive. The pious enjoy their goods for a long time; the wicked rise and emerge suddenly, and fall suddenly. Examples are Saul, Absalom, Alexander the Great, and certain Caesars. So in our own age some emerge suddenly, by evil arts no doubt; but like flowers they fall suddenly. For the good, what they have is enough; for the wicked, much that they have is not enough. Piety makes it so that, though a man has little, he lacks nothing. And whoever is not drawn to piety by these promises must needs remain wicked.

units.la: Contrarium, Cauete (inquit) ne cor vestrum seducatur, vt seruiatis Dijs alienis, adoretisq; eos & exardeat in vos ira Domini, &c. Ostendit illis, si contra ac Deus iubeat religionem instituant, fore, vt contra ac velint, res omnes succedant. Si Dijs alienis seruiant, ardebit in illos ira Domini, claudetur cœlum ne pluat, ipsi pereant in terra, quam acceperint. Summa, Wider Gott so ist er ouch wider Sich. Saul, Achab, Pharao, Iudæi. Nostra tempora publicorum iuxta ac priuatorum exemplorum plena sunt.
units.tr: The contrary argument: Take heed (he says) lest your heart be deceived, so that you serve other gods and worship them, and the anger of the Lord be kindled against you, etc. He shows them that if they set up a religion contrary to what God commands, it will come about that all things turn out contrary to what they wish. If they serve other gods, the anger of the Lord will burn against them, heaven will be shut so that it does not rain, and they themselves will perish in the land which they have received. In short, against God, so he is also against himself. Saul, Ahab, Pharaoh, the Jews. Our own times are full of examples, public and private alike.

units.la: Facile: Reponite (inquit) verba ista mea in cor vestrum. Quibus docet nullam esse in hoc studio difficultatem: si modo res ritè & recte suscipiatur. Sed quo pacto oporteat eam suscipi iam indicat: exercitatione videlicet, quippe qua facilia fiunt etiam quæ fuerant difficilli-ma. Exercitationem igitur qualem requirat indicat.
units.tr: Easy: Lay up (he says) these my words in your heart. By which he teaches that there is no difficulty in this pursuit, provided that the matter is taken up rightly and properly. But he now indicates how it ought to be taken up: namely by practice, since by practice even the most difficult things become easy. He therefore indicates what kind of practice he requires.

units.la: 1 Recolendo ponite (inquit) verba mea in cor vestrum et in animū: hoc est facite memori mente verbum meum teneatis. Nihil scimus, nisi quod tenemus memoria. Meditatio, auditio, scriptio requiruntur. Honestum hoc est ocium: tale enim Solomon, Dauid alijq; viri principes amplexi sunt. Ac Scipio dicebat se nunquam minus ociosum esse, quam cum esset in ocio. Nihil dicam de lectionibus Alexandri Magni, Iulij Cæsaris, Ciceronis & aliorum complurium. Quid enim in re meliore nos deceat facere cum hæc illi in deteriore fecerint, nemo non perspicit. Sed deploranda in nobis, inprimisq; ijs qui versantur in repub. socordia cernitur. Aut enim lectioni vacant nunquam aut perraro: nec accedunt conciones sacras nisi raro. Mihi non fit verisimile boni in illis quicquam non plantatum excrescere. Vt fundi, sic ingenia cultura habent opus. Sed ideo difficile est eos à vitijs abstrahere, quod mox obliti cionum redeant ad ingenium.
units.tr: 1 By recollecting (he says), lay up my words in your heart and in your soul: that is, make your mind hold my word in memory. We know nothing except what we hold in memory. Meditation, hearing and writing are required. This leisure is honourable: for Solomon, David and other principal men embraced such leisure. And Scipio used to say that he was never less idle than when he was at leisure. I will say nothing about the reading of Alexander the Great, Julius Caesar, Cicero and many others. For what ought we to do in a better matter, when they did these things in a worse, no one fails to see. But the carelessness which is seen in us, and especially in those who are engaged in public affairs, is to be lamented. For they either never or very rarely devote themselves to reading, and they attend sacred sermons only rarely. It does not seem likely to me that anything good grows in them that has not been planted. As fields, so minds need cultivation. But it is therefore difficult to draw them away from vices, because, having forgotten the sermons, they soon return to their natural disposition.

units.la: Moses autem quo pacto fit succurrendum memoriæ docet: vsum monumentorum monstrans: Vt alliges (inquit) manibus, vt sint in medio oculorum, &c. In quo discimus ea habere ornamenta quæ diuinæ voluntatis admoneant nos: non item ea quæ nos faciant elatiores.
units.tr: Moses also teaches how the memory should be aided, pointing to the use of reminders: "Thou shalt bind them for a sign upon thine hand, and they shall be as frontlets between thine eyes," and so on. In this we learn that the ornaments which admonish us of the divine will are the ones to use, not those which make us more proud.

units.la: 2 Docendo liberos. Docendo namq; discimus. Vnde patriarcharum domus quasi scholæ erant. Nostræ domus sunt exempla vitierum[?] liberis ob oculos versantia.
units.tr: 2 By teaching our children. For by teaching we ourselves learn. Hence the households of the patriarchs were like schools. Our households, by contrast, set the examples of vices before the eyes of our children.

units.la: 3 Colloquiis inde petitis, nempe ut domi sedens, obambulans, dormiturus, surgens, semper exerceas te. Etenim usus quotidiani sermonis prodest plurimum. Quæ enim ita sedulò versamus ea cum addiscimus optime, tum verò subinde magis ac magis amplectimur. At nostra colloquia sunt obtrectationes, obscœni sales, aut etiam blasphemiæ. Ideo difficile est pietatis officiis assuescere, quippe à quibus hæc colloquia subinde nos retrahant.
units.tr: 3 Then by conversation, namely, that you should always exercise yourself while sitting at home, walking about, lying down to sleep, and rising up. For the daily use of speech helps greatly. Indeed, what we handle so diligently we learn best, and afterwards embrace more and more. But our conversations are backbiting, obscene jokes, or even blasphemies. Hence it is hard to become accustomed to the duties of piety, since these conversations keep drawing us back from them.

units.la: 4 Scribendo in postes, portas, &c. Hoc anxium habuit diabolum quod quocunq; iter haberet, semper ei verbum divinum esset obvium. Quare effecit pulchris, si Diis placet, prætextibus, ut deletis scripturis, gentilium hominum more ponerentur statuæ & pingerentur imagines. Sicq; effecit ut divini verbi usus omnis evanuerit, factumq; sit pietatis studium difficillimum. Nos exercitatione iam præscripta facile nobis efficiemus.
units.tr: 4 By writing on the doorposts, the gates, and so on. The devil was troubled by this, because wherever he went the Word of God was always before him. So he contrived, under the fine pretext (as God would have it!) of erasing the Scriptures, to have statues set up and images painted, in the manner of the heathen. And so he brought it about that all use of the divine Word vanished, and the study of piety became most difficult. We, by the exercise already prescribed, can easily bring it about for ourselves.

units.la: Honestum: Si diligenter custodieritis omnia præcepta quæ ego præcipio vobis, ut faciatis illa, nempe ut diligatis Dominum Deum vestrum, &c. Ostendit eos si Deum amplexi fuerint fore victores ac dominos omnium gentium & tertremendos principes. Ac ne somnium sibi fingi putent, quo pacto hoc fit futurum docet. Dominus, inquit, exterminabit gentes a facie vestra. Er wirt wyte machen. Quemcunque planta pedis vestri locum calcaverit, eum habebitis proprium. Nemo vobis audebit repugnare: quia Deus efficiet ut timendi sitis, ac videamini. Testis est historia. Rahab dicebat ipsorum corda quasi ceram diffluxisse. Testes sunt Davidis & Salomonis victoriæ. Idem accidit Helvetiis maioribus nostris: diversum nobis non ita Deum diligentibus.
units.tr: The honour of it: "If you diligently keep all these commandments which I command you, to do them, namely to love the Lord your God, and so on." He shows that if they embrace God they will be victors and lords over all nations, and most dreaded princes. And lest they think this is a dream made up for them, he teaches how it will come to pass: "The Lord, he says, will drive out the nations from before you." <bl>He will make the way wide.</bl> "Whatever place the sole of your foot shall tread upon, that shall be yours. No one will dare to resist you, because God will make you feared and held in reverence." History bears witness. Rahab said that their hearts had melted like wax. The victories of David and Solomon are witnesses. The same happened to our Swiss forebears, though it has not gone so for us, who do not love God in the same way.

units.la: Iam quoniam intelligimus ex his quàm sit utile Deum unum sequi: quàm perniciosum ab illo deficere: quàm facile eius voluntati parere: quàm honestum eum patronum habere & vindicem: quis non videt præceptum primum, uti Moses suadet, observandum esse, nempe ut in Deo maneamus, per Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum. Amen.
units.tr: Now since we understand from these things how useful it is to follow the one God, how destructive it is to fall away from him, how easy it is to obey his will, how honourable it is to have him as our patron and defender, who does not see that the first precept, as Moses urges, must be observed, namely that we abide in God, through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

units.la: SERMO XVIII.
units.tr: SERMON XVIII.

units.la: 26 En ego pono hodie in conspectu tuo benedictionem & execrationem.
units.tr: 26 Behold, I set before you this day a blessing and a curse;

units.la: 27 Benedictionem, si obtemperaveritis præceptis Domini Dei vestri, quæ ego præcipio vobis hodie:
units.tr: 27 A blessing, if ye obey the commandments of the LORD your God, which I command you this day:

units.la: 28 Execrationem verò, si non obedieritis præceptis Domini Dei vestri, & recesseritis à via quam ego præcipio vobis hodie, ut sequamini deos alios, quos non noveritis.
units.tr: 28 And a curse, if ye will not obey the commandments of the LORD your God, but turn aside out of the way which I command you this day, to go after other gods, which ye have not known.

units.la: 29 Quum itaque Dominus Deus tuus introduxerit te in terram, ad quam tu proficiseris, ut eam possideas, pones benedictionem super montem Garizim, & execrationem super montem Ebal.
units.tr: 29 And it shall be, when the LORD thy God shall have brought thee in unto the land whither thou goest to possess it, that thou shalt put the blessing upon mount Gerizim, and the curse upon mount Ebal.

units.la: 30 Qui sunt trans Iordanem post viam occasus solis in terra Chananæi, qui habitant in planitie e regione Gilgal, iuxta querceta More.
units.tr: 30 Are they not on the other side Jordan, by the way where the sun goeth down, in the land of the Canaanites, which dwell in the champaign over against Gilgal, beside the plains of Moreh?

units.la: 31 Vos transibitis Iordanem, ut introeuntes possideatis terram, quam Dominus Deus vester dat vobis, hæreditate accipietis eam, & habitabitis in ea.
units.tr: 31 For ye shall pass over Jordan to go in to possess the land which the LORD your God giveth you, and ye shall possess it, and dwell therein.

units.la: 32 Observate ergo ut faciatis omnia statuta & iudicia, quæ ego hodie vobis propono.
