units.tr: 32 And ye shall observe to do all the statutes and judgments which I set before you this day.

units.la: CUm nos ad omne genus rerum nihil perinde pertrahat atq; spes utilitatis, & ab ijsdem nihil æque facile revocet atq; metus mali: rectè sanè Moses sub finem huius expositionis bonum simul ac malum sibi ipsis opposita proponit, iuxtaq; docet, nos si legibus divinis studeamus, bona, sin ab illis deflectamus habituros mala. Atq; hoc quidem ut & intelligatur rectius & animis hæreat altius, sic persequitur, ut primum illam boni maliq; contentionem ponat ob oculos: dein ostendat quomodo eius memoria conservetur sempiterna: deniq; ipsis Israelitis quomodo accommodet.
units.tr: Since nothing draws us to every kind of action so much as the hope of advantage, and nothing turns us back from them so easily as the fear of harm, Moses rightly, near the end of this exposition, sets good and evil before them as opposites, and teaches that if we devote ourselves to the divine laws we shall have good things, but if we turn aside from them we shall have evils. He does this so that it may be understood more correctly and cling more deeply to their minds, and he pursues it in this order: first he places before their eyes the contrast between good and evil; then he shows how its memory may be preserved for ever; and finally he shows how it applies to the Israelites themselves.

units.la: Boni & mali contentionem proponit ad hunc modum: En (inquit) ego pono hodie in con-spectu tuo benedictionem & maledictionem. Benedictionem, si audieritis, &c. Quibus verbis pri-mum summum bonum simul & ultimum exitium comprehendit: tum quomodo hoc qui-dem incurras, illo vero potiare docet.
units.tr: He sets out the contest between good and evil in this way: Behold, he says, I set before you this day a blessing and a curse. A blessing, if you obey, etc. In these words he first comprehends the highest good and, at the same time, the ultimate ruin; then he teaches how one incurs the one and obtains the other.

units.la: Summum bonum & malum ultimum benedictionis & maledictionis nominibus significat. Qu[?]d igitur est benedictio? Benedictionem Graeci εὐλογίαν perinde ut Latini compo-sito nomine, Germani vero quasi κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν[?] simplici <bl>sagen</bl> appellant. Est autem benedicere bona alicui, imprecari: quod animi benevoli indicium est: quando videlicet amor animo latens verbis effertur atque exprimitur. Iam quemadmodum homo benedicendo, sic etiam Deus benedictione sua propensam suam erga nos benevolentiam patefacit.
units.tr: By the names blessing and curse he signifies the highest good and the final evil. What then is a blessing? The Greeks call a blessing eulogia [εὐλογία], as the Latins do with their compound word, and the Germans, as if by a simple word, call it sagen. To bless someone is to wish good things for them, which is a sign of a kindly mind, when, namely, love that lies hidden in the heart is expressed and brought out in words. Now just as a man blesses, so God by his blessing shows his well-disposed goodwill towards us.

units.la: Sed amplius quiddam est Dei, quàm hominis benedictio. Homo enim, quoniam & malus est & imbecillis, propterea nec vult semper, nec potest etiam si velit, quae praeca-tur bona suis amicis impertire: Deus autem, quoniam & mere bonus est & omnipotens: quae verbis effert ac promittit, ea non modo vult, sed etiam potest largiri beneficia. Veluti de con-stantia voluntatis illius erga nos bonae Christus Jesus Dominus noster testis locupletiifi-mus[?] in Evangelio disserit, & potentiam mundi creatio significat. Nam quae dixit ea voluisse eum etiam Christus docet: & quae fieri voluit eum potuisse efficere creatio rerum indicant.
units.tr: But God's blessing is something more than a man's. For man, since he is both wicked and weak, therefore neither always wills nor, even if he wills, is able to bestow the good things he wishes upon his friends. But God, since he is wholly good and almighty, not only wills but is also able to grant the benefits that he expresses and promises in words. Christ Jesus our Lord, the most reliable witness to the constancy of that good will towards us, speaks of it in the Gospel, and the creation of the world signifies his power. For Christ also teaches that he willed what he said, and the creation of things shows that he was able to bring about what he willed.

units.la: Ex quibus perspicuum est illius benedictionem non esse vanam aliquam imprecationem, sed efficacem & diuitem bonorum maximorum largitionem. Atque sic exponitur Psal. 107. Benedicit eis (inquit) & multiplicantur valde, en ut dicat benedictionem eius sequi divitias. Contra Psalm. 3. Domini est salus, & super populum tuum benedictio tua. Quo loco dicit salutem omnem penes Deum esse, & ex eo fonte benedictionem, hoc est, salutis communicationem in ecclesiam manare. Idem docet, Israelitis olim usurpatum proverbium: Benedicat tibi Dominus sicut Ephraim. At quae erat illi tribui benedictio? penes eam & locus tabernaculi fuerat, & imperium. Ex quibus potest intelligi benedictionis nomine venisse, quod eos Dominus opibus & honoribus auxisset.
units.tr: From these things it is plain that his blessing is not some empty wish but an effective and rich bestowal of the greatest goods. And so Psalm 107 is explained: He blesses them, it says, and they are multiplied greatly, so that it shows the blessing of God to be followed by riches. Against this, Psalm 3: Salvation is of the LORD, and thy blessing is upon thy people. In this place it says that all salvation is with God, and that from that fountain the blessing, that is, the communication of salvation, flows into the Church. The same thing is taught by the proverb once used among the Israelites: The LORD bless thee as Ephraim. But what blessing was given to that tribe? The place of the tabernacle belonged to it, and rule as well. From these things it can be understood that the name of blessing came to be applied because the Lord had enriched them with resources and honours.

units.la: Quae cum ita sint consequens est benedictionem esse quicquid ad bene beateque viuendum requiritur: maledictionem autem esse quidquid ad ultimam miseriam pertinet. Et hoc ipsum, si quemadmodum benedictio considerata fuit, sic ipsa quoque aestimetur maledictio, sic habere se cuiuis est perspicuum. Ac quemadmodum laeta ac fausta precari benevolentiae est indicium: sic imprecari tristia & mala animi indignantis est & maleuoli.
units.tr: Since these things are so, it follows that a blessing is whatever is required for living well and happily, and a curse is whatever pertains to utter wretchedness. And if the blessing has been considered in this way, the curse too should be judged in the same way; that this is so is plain to anyone. And just as to wish happy and prosperous things is a sign of goodwill, so to wish sad and evil things is a sign of an indignant and malevolent mind.

units.la: Caeterum ut inter hominis & Dei benedictionem, sic inter hominis & Dei maledictionē interest. Quae enim homo precatur, ea vult quidem, sed non potest dare damna, <bl>(Rätzen ge-bärt gadr nit ȝhimmel[?])</bl> quae vero Deus imprecatur, ea potest etiam immittere incommoda. Quamobrem ut benedictio sic etiam maledictio domini minime est vana minimeque contemnenda.
units.tr: Moreover, there is as much difference between the blessing of man and the blessing of God as between the curse of man and the curse of God. For what a man wishes he indeed wills, but he cannot inflict harm; what God calls down, he is also able to send as misfortunes. Therefore, just as the blessing of the Lord is by no means empty, so neither is his curse at all to be despised. (A German gloss in the margin, illegible in the scan.)

units.la: Atque haec quidem duo sic ponit Moses, ut inter ea nihil sit medium: quod etiam Christus asserit, cum duas tantum facit portas ac vias, cumque Marc. ultimo salvari & condemnari dicat: salvari credentes evangelio, condemnari incredulos. Igitur hic non licet esse neutrarum partium: alterutra secanda via est.
units.tr: Moses sets these two things before them so that there is nothing between them, as Christ also asserts when he makes only two gates and two ways, and when in Mark's last chapter he says that men are saved and condemned: those who believe the gospel are saved, and the unbelieving are condemned. Therefore here it is not permitted to be neutral; one of the two ways must be taken.

units.la: Sed cum utriusque viae finem habeamus: jam quomodo ad felicitatem perveniatur, ac rursus infelicitas caveatur cognoscendum est: et iam hoc ipsum Moses docet. Benedictionem (inquit) si audieris praecepta Domini Dei vestri, quae ego praecipio vobis hodie. Ex quo colligi potest verbi divini studio summum bonum acquiri. Atque hoc docet etiam David Psalm. 1. dicens, beatus qui meditatur in lege Domini, &c. Et Psal. 102. beatum esse, hoc est, potentem, divitem, celebrem eum, qui Deum revereatur. Et Psalm. 118.[?] toto hoc ipsum probat David.
units.tr: But since we have the end of both ways, we must now learn how one comes to happiness, and again how unhappiness is avoided; and Moses teaches this very thing. If you hear, he says, the blessing, the commandments of the LORD your God, which I command you this day. From this it can be gathered that the highest good is acquired by zeal for the Word of God. David also teaches this in Psalm 1, saying, Blessed is the man who meditates in the law of the Lord, etc. And in Psalm 102 he says that he is blessed, that is, powerful, rich and renowned, who reverences God. And in Psalm 118 David proves this very thing throughout.

units.la: Nec non Christus Mosi & Psalthi[?] servis suis assentitur: Dicente enim quadam beatu esse ven-trem, qui Dominum gestasset, & beata ubera quae Dominus suxisset, ipse ait: Quin imo beati sunt qui Dei verbum audiunt & custodiunt. Hoc scire est summa sapientia: sunt enim multi (inquit Dominus) qui cum voluissent ea videre, quae viderunt Apostoli, nec tamen potuerunt: beati, inquit, oculi qui vident quae vos videtis. Quantopere enim o bone Deus, se tor-ferunt Aristoteles & Plato, & ante hos Socrates, Pythagoras? At Moses, & prophetae, & post hos Christus & Apostoli qua via ad beatam vitam pervenires viderunt & docuerunt.
units.tr: Nor does Christ fail to agree with Moses and the Psalmist, his servants. For when a certain woman said that the womb was blessed which had carried the Lord, and the breasts blessed which the Lord had sucked, he himself said: Nay rather, blessed are they who hear the Word of God and keep it. To know this is the highest wisdom; for (says the Lord) there are many who wished to see the things that the Apostles saw, and yet could not; blessed, he says, are the eyes that see what you see. For, good God, how greatly did Aristotle and Plato torment themselves, and before them Socrates and Pythagoras? But Moses and the prophets, and after them Christ and the Apostles, saw and taught by what way one may come to a blessed life.

units.la: Sed quale sit hoc divini verbi studium jam ex ipsius verbis intelligemus. Si audieritis,in-quit. An vero satis est audisse? Minime vero, audire aliquem est eo praeceptore, consultore, magistro uti: quod est officium discipuli, qui praecepta magistri cum discit tum sequitur. Un-de & servare & custodire quandoque jubemur etiam quae audivimus. Nam audire non autem servare est, ut docet Matt. 7. Dominus, hominis desipientis & fatui. Quamobrem ut pater a filiis postulat, ut ipsum audiant, in [illegible, ~7 letters], eoque requirit obedientiā: sic Deus hoc ipso quod se vult audiri debitam obedientiam postulat.
units.tr: But what kind of zeal for the divine Word this is we shall now understand from his own words. If you hear, he says. But is it enough merely to have heard? By no means: to hear someone is to use him as adviser, counsellor and teacher, which is the duty of a disciple, who both learns and follows the teacher's precepts. Hence we are sometimes commanded to keep and preserve even what we have heard. For to hear and not to keep is the mark of a foolish and senseless man, as the Lord teaches in Matthew 7. Just as a father demands of his sons that they hear him, and requires obedience in return, so God, by the very fact that he wishes to be heard, demands the obedience that is owed.

units.la: Id nequaquam faciunt qui sua consilia, suos impuros affectus, suas illebras sequi malunt quàm verbum Domini:quibus difficile est iugum Domini.
units.tr: Those who prefer to follow their own counsels, their own impure desires and their own allurements rather than the Word of the Lord, by no means do this; for them the yoke of the Lord is hard to bear.

units.la: Sed quid,inquis,audiam? Præcepta Domini Dei tui dicit Moses,eoq; ipso traditiones hominum, quibus vti in Prophetis ab ipso dictum est Domino,frustra colitur,omnes reijcit. Quæ vero sunt illæ? Quæ ego(inquit)præcipio vobis hodie: quo scripturas canonicas ostendit verbi diuini nomine censendas esse,humana vero somnia respui debere. Nisi enim humanis somnijs hoc poneres repagulum: pro verbo Dei suas quisque fictiones venditaret. Quare verbi Dei studium quo solo via ad beatam vitam sternitur,his constat quas dixi partibus.
units.tr: But what, you may ask, am I to hear? Moses says, the commandments of the LORD your God, and by this very phrase he rejects all the traditions of men, by which, as the Lord himself says through the prophets, God is worshipped in vain. What then are those commandments? Which I command you this day, he says; by which he shows that the canonical Scriptures are to be counted as the Word of God, and that human dreams ought to be rejected. For unless you set this barrier against human dreams, each person would be peddling his own fictions in place of the Word of God. Therefore the zeal for the Word of God, the only road by which the way to a blessed life is laid, consists of the parts I have mentioned.

units.la: Sed qua via ad malum itur,vt eam caueam? Maledictionem (inquit) fi non obedieritis præceptis Domini Dei vestri, & receffueritis à via,quam ego præcipio vobis hodie,&c. En quibus ex rebus oriri calamitates soleant. His verbis limitatur,vt lure coss.more loquar, hac ætate frequenter agitata quæstio de causis & origine calamitatum. Plerique bellorum, morborum,caritatis,scelerum omnium causas imputant Euangelio:ac fi quid ingruat mali,conclamatur in verbi ministros quos odioso nomine pfaffos vocant. O scelera,ô genera sacrilega.Hoccine est officium hominis,Deum videlicet atq; eius verbum, vnde bonum omne pro manat,habere pro sentina malorum & calamitatum.
units.tr: But by what way does one go to evil, that I may guard against it? "A curse, if you will not obey the commandments of the Lord your God, and turn aside from the way which I command you today, etc." Behold the things from which calamities are wont to arise. By these words is set out, to speak in the manner of the lawyers, the question about the causes and origin of calamities, which is much debated in this age. Most people impute the causes of wars, plagues, dearth and all crimes to the Gospel, and whenever some evil threatens, they cry out against the ministers of the Word, whom they call by the hateful name of "pfaffen." O crimes, O sacrilegious kind! Is this the duty of a man, to hold God himself and his Word, from which every good flows, to be a sewer of evils and calamities?

units.la: Sed eorum causam veram Moses dicit. Primum, non audire præcepta Domini Dei nostri. Etid quidem fit hodie plerifq; in locis. Pars enim verbum Domini mandatum literis comburunt,ficq; suos verbo Dei spoliant:cur non corrigenda suis sacrificis committunt biblia,quæ à nobis conqueruntur esse depravata? Sed verbum Dei fontem rerum fecundarum atq; omnis boni suis sic auferunt:pars feruat quidem atq; audit conciones atq; libros, sed concionibus quidem quaslibet res ludicras,biblijs autem cantilenas & obscænas fabulas anteponit. Sane hæc est eorum quæ patimur malorum causa prima.
units.tr: But Moses names their true cause. First, "not to hear the commandments of the Lord your God." And this indeed happens today in many places. For some burn the books containing the Word of the Lord, and so strip themselves of the Word of God; why do they not entrust their Bibles, which we complain have been corrupted, to their sacrificers to be corrected? But others so cut off the Word of God, the source of all fruitful things and of every good, while some indeed keep and hear sermons and books, yet prefer to sermons any trifling matters, and to the Bibles songs and obscene tales. Surely this is the first cause of the evils we suffer.

units.la: Tum(inquit)à via quam ego hodie vobis tradidi recesseritis. Idipsum à nobis quoq; factum est,qui loco Mosis, Prophetarum,Apostolorum, ad papæ decreta & monachorum somnia defleximus.
units.tr: "Then (he says) you will turn aside from the way which I have handed down to you today." This too has been done by us, who, instead of the law of Moses, the Prophets and the Apostles, have turned aside to the decrees of the pope and the dreams of the monks.

units.la: Denique Deos alienos(inquit)& vobis incognitos secuti fucritis. Et nos Deos non paueiores nec minus varios quàm olim Græci & Romani coluerunt, adorauimus:quafiq; demortuo aut saltem ad res gerendas inepto facto Deo Optimo Maximo:sic orbis gubernatio nem Diuis alijs atque alijs distribuimus. Quæ cum ita sint,non est mirum nos esse miseros, & omni genere calamitatum obrui. Sed de hls[?] fatis est dictum sapientibus.
units.tr: "Finally (he says) you will have followed other gods unknown to you." And we have worshipped gods no less numerous or varied than those the Greeks and Romans once worshipped, as if God Most Good and Most Great had died or at least become unfit for governing affairs, and we have distributed the governance of the world to various other divinities. Since these things are so, it is no wonder that we are wretched and overwhelmed by every kind of calamity. But enough has been said on these matters for wise men.

units.la: Hanc antithefin Dauid etiam psalmo primo ponit, quippe quo beatos esse dicat eos, qui iugi legis[?] diuinæ meditatione sese exerceant:ac rursus infelices & perituros eos,qui curam ac studium huius abiecerint. Igitur diuinis legibus studendum erit, vt viuas ac valeas.
units.tr: David also sets out this antithesis in the first Psalm, since he says that those are blessed who exercise themselves in continual meditation on the divine law, and again that those are unhappy and will perish who have cast off care and zeal for it. Therefore one must devote oneself to the divine laws, that one may live and prosper.

units.la: Ad conferuandam huius antitheseos memoriam quid facto opus fit iam docet. Cum in terram promissam ventum erit,in duorum montium Garizimi & Hebali verticibus erigendæ e-runt columnæ,quarum altera benedictio,maledictio deferibatur altera: vt inde recitentur videli-cet. Atque hæc quidem figuræ fuerunt verbi diuini publicè prædicandi in Ecclesia. Non erigit statuas quibus quasi libris homines rudes erudiri velit, sed emisit Prophetas & Apostolos. Sic in orbem exire iussi Apostoli. Sic etiamnum sunt montes in quibus extat benedictionis simul atq; maledictionis sempiterna recordatio. Ne quis sibi viæ ducem defuisse possit conqueri.At hosce lapides demoliuntur quoad possunt Antichriftiani:quippe qui mallent habere mutas statuas,ex quibus nihil cognoscerent præterquam quod cuiq; liberet.At Deus vult verbum suum prædicari.
units.tr: He now teaches what must be done to preserve the memory of this antithesis: "When you have come into the promised land, on the summits of the two mountains, Gerizim and Ebal, columns are to be erected, one of which is to be inscribed with the blessing and the other with the curse, that from there they may be read aloud." And indeed these were figures of the divine Word being publicly proclaimed in the Church. He does not set up statues by which he wishes rude men to be taught as if from books, but he sent forth Prophets and Apostles. Thus the Apostles were ordered to go out into the whole world. Thus even now there are mountains on which stands the perpetual memorial of both blessing and curse. Let no one be able to complain that he lacked a guide on the way. But the Antichristians demolish these stones as far as they can, since they would rather have dumb statues, from which they would learn nothing except whatever each pleases.  But God wills his Word to be preached.

units.la: Ad ipsos accomodat dicens,Iam ingrederis in terram,igitur seruabis omnia verba, &c. Pe-rinde est hoc ac fi dicat,æquum esse,vt quoniam Deus benefaciat, nos ei referamus gratiam quantam possumus maximam. Sic doctrinam hanc sibi quisque accomodet. Deus talenta cuique sua distribuit, eorum omnium est cogitare quid fe deceat facere:nempe vt viam rectà,hoc est,Chri-ftum ingrediantur,per quem rectà ad patrem itur,ac æternum viuitur,Amen.
units.tr: He adapts this to them, saying, "Now you are entering the land; therefore you shall keep all the words, etc." It is just as if he said that it is fitting that, since God does good to us, we should return to him the greatest thanks we can. Let each one apply this teaching to himself. God distributes talents to each, and it is for each to consider what he ought to do: namely, that they enter the right way, that is, Christ, through whom one goes straight to the Father and lives eternally. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT XII. SERMO XIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII. SERMON XIX.

units.la: 1 Hæc sunt statuta & iudicia, quæ custodietis, vt faciatis in terra, quam Dominus patrum tuorum tibi dedit, vt illam possideas cunctis diebus quibus victurus es super terram.
units.tr: 1 These are the statutes and judgments which you shall observe, that you may do them in the land which the Lord, the God of your fathers, has given you, to possess all the days that you live upon the earth.

units.la: 2 Omnino vastabitis omnia loca in quibus coluerunt gentes, quas vos occupabitis, deos suos super montes excelsos, super colles, & sub omni arbore frondosa.
units.tr: 2 You shall utterly destroy all the places in which the nations whom you shall dispossess served their gods, upon the high mountains, upon the hills, and under every leafy tree.

units.la: 3 Diruetis aras eorum, & statuas eorum confringetis, atq; lucos eorum igne cōburetis, & sculptilia deorum quos habent concidetis, & abolebitis nomen eorum de loco illo.
units.tr: 3 You shall overthrow their altars, break their statues, burn their groves with fire, hew down the graven images of their gods, and blot out their name from that place.

units.la: QUEMADMODUM Deus in prima lege requirit fidem in se veram & pietatem, in qua cultus internus, qui verus & gratisimus est Domino, consistit potis-simum: sic in reliquis tribus tabulæ primæ legibus, quæ ad externum cultum ceu veræ pietatis exercitia pertinere videbantur, requirit atq; explicat. Ac quoniam Moses præceptū primū ijs, quæ intra ca. quintū & 12. medita sunt capitibus, expositi, eaq; ex positione & pietatem veram docuit & ab ea quicquid solet avocare vetuit: in ijs quæ sequuntur vsq; ad 17. cap. externum cultum ceu pietatis exercitia commemorat. Eius generis exercitia sunt verbi diuini studium, sacramenta atq; sacrificia, cerimoniæ, charitatis opera: quibus fides & exprimitur & exercetur & confirmatur.
units.tr: Just as in the first law God requires true faith and piety toward himself, in which above all the inward worship, which is true and most acceptable to the Lord, consists, so in the remaining laws of the first table he requires and explains those things which seemed to pertain to outward worship, as exercises of true piety. And since Moses, having expounded the first commandment in the chapters that lie between the fifth and the twelfth, taught true piety from that exposition and forbade whatever is wont to draw us away from it, in what follows, up to the seventeenth chapter, he recounts outward worship as the exercises of piety. Of this kind are the study of the divine Word, the sacraments and sacrifices, the ceremonies, and the works of charity, by which faith is expressed, exercised and confirmed.

units.la: Intelligendum est autem quod Dominus recens eductum ex Ægypto populum, & externis cultibus assuetum & ad idololatriam procliuem hac pædagogia voluit intra veræ pietatis limites continere, ne videlicet extra eas in gentiles superstitiones excurrerent: & ad Christum in quo solo Deus rite & salubriter colitur adducere. Quod ipsum Paulus hoc ipso docet, quo legem pædagogum vocat, innuens videlicet Iudæos rudes esse, & figuris istis ad Christum deduci oportere: tum etiam prophetæ magis animos quàm sacrificia requirebant, ostendentes fore vt cessent eæ cerimoniæ.
units.tr: It must be understood, however, that the Lord wished, by this pedagogy, to hold within the limits of true piety the people newly led out of Egypt, accustomed to outward rites and prone to idolatry, lest they should run out beyond those limits into heathen superstitions, and to lead them to Christ, in whom alone God is rightly and savingly worshipped. Paul teaches this very thing by the very fact that he calls the law a schoolmaster, implying that the Jews were untrained and had to be led to Christ by those figures. Likewise the prophets, too, sought hearts rather than sacrifices, showing that those ceremonies would cease.

units.la: Quæ tamen sunt multæ & variæ: & partim in personis positæ, partim in rebus. Personæ quidem erant Israelitæ, quos Deus sibi peculiariter coniunctos sui populi nomine dignatus est: tum Leuitæ & sacerdotes, quorum erat dispensatio religionis & cerimoniarum. Res erant locus, vt templū & tabernaculum: tempus, vt dies festi & solennes: res, vt sacrificia, decimæ, vestes sacræ & alia quibus eos voluit & docere quasi internarum rerum typis atq; umbris, & exercere quasi Deo debitis officijs. Atq; hæc quidem omnia non describit multis verbis, sed antea descripta libris prioribus modo repetit & commendat.
units.tr: These are, nevertheless, many and various, and some are placed in persons, others in things. The persons were the Israelites, whom God deigned to honour with the name of his people, joined to himself in a special way; then the Levites and priests, to whom the dispensing of religion and the ceremonies was committed. The things were the place, such as the temple and the tabernacle; the time, such as the feast days and solemn festivals; and the objects, such as sacrifices, tithes, sacred garments and other things by which he wished both to teach them, as it were through the types and shadows of inward realities, and to train them, as it were, in the duties owed to God. Moses does not describe all these things in many words, but merely repeats and commends what was described earlier in the preceding books.

units.la: Sed ad id priusquam veniat, idololatriam atq; omnē superstitiosum cultū secunda lege vetitū, abrogandū docet. Et rectè quidem mea sententia: quis enim tutò poneret ædificiū non remotis prius ruderibus, & benè locata basi. Igitur initio tractationis huius gentilismum omnem demoliendum docet: ac primum religionem veram commendat, tum falsam repellit.
units.tr: But before he comes to that, he teaches that idolatry and every superstitious worship, forbidden by the second law, must be abolished. And rightly so, in my judgment; for who would safely build a structure without first clearing away the rubble and laying a well-placed foundation? Therefore at the beginning of this discussion he teaches that all heathenism must be torn down; and first he commends the true religion, then repels the false.

units.la: Religionem commendat dicens, Hæc sunt statuta & iudicia quæ custodietis vt faciatis in terra, quam Dominus patrum tuorum & c. Quibus verbis ostendit religionis veræ studium multis de causis debere esse magno in precio. Ac primum ipsum commendat à definitione: dicit enim hos ritus, quos tradat, esse statuta & iudicia, hoc est, cerimonias & authoritate Dei præcipientis & illius etiam ipsius confirmatas iudicio. Nam quæ consuetudines non temerè irrepunt, sed præmeditatò seu consultò sunt inventæ & receptæ & vsu confirmatæ: eæ sunt omnium religiosissimè retinendæ quoad verbo Dei sint consentaneæ. His etiam iudiciorum nomen tribuit vt ostendat summa fide & diligentia ponderatis in vtramque partem rebus omnibus factas esse.
units.tr: He commends religion, saying: These are the statutes and judgments which you shall observe, that you may do them in the land which the Lord of your fathers has given you, etc. By these words he shows that zeal for true religion ought to be held in high esteem for many reasons. First, he commends it from its definition: he calls the rites that he delivers "statutes and judgments," that is, ceremonies both commanded by the authority of God and confirmed by his judgment. For those customs which do not creep in carelessly, but have been devised, received and confirmed by use after deliberate and considered thought, are to be retained most scrupulously of all, so far as they agree with the Word of God. He also gives them the name of judgments, to show that all these things were done with the highest faith and diligence, after weighing both sides of every matter.

units.la: Atq; sic æstimare sacrosanctum Euangelium, & ritus ei consentaneos ad pietatem veram multum momenti affert. Vt enim consultor nihil apud te proficiet sine authoritate: sic Euangelij prædicatio illis inutilis est, qui ipsum habent nullo in precio. Inde adeò accidit, vt satan euangelium, quo nos carere velit, nominibus hæreticorum hominum, alijs atque alijs modis invisum reddat: tum etiam apud eos, qui ipsum liberè doceri patiuntur, contemptum reddit, quò minus docendo, monendo, consolando proficiat. Et sacros ritus quasi deliramenta quaedam despicit. Moses autem religionis commendatione pietatem excitat. Sic Paulus Corinthiis scribit se, reliquosque Apostolos habendos esse pro divinorum mysteriorum di-spensatoribus. Sic Dei verbum auditurus, persuasum tibi fac habeas audire te non hominis, sed Dei vocem: tunc enim adduceris citius, ut imperata facias.
units.tr: And so, to esteem the most holy Gospel and the rites agreeable to it in this way contributes much to true piety. For just as a consultation with someone who lacks authority profits you nothing, so the preaching of the Gospel is useless to those who hold it in no esteem. From this it comes about that Satan, wishing us to be deprived of the Gospel, makes it hateful by calling it by the names of heretics and by one device after another; and even among those who allow it to be taught freely, he makes it contemptible, so that it accomplishes less by teaching, admonishing and consoling. He also looks down on the sacred rites as certain follies. Moses, however, by commending religion, stirs up piety. So Paul writes to the Corinthians that he and the other apostles are to be regarded as dispensers of the divine mysteries. So too, when you are about to hear the Word of God, make yourself persuaded that you are hearing not the voice of man but the voice of God; for then you will be brought more readily to do what is commanded.

units.la: Deinde commendat à fine, quæ custodietis ut faciatis, inquit. Deus ideo dedit & tulit has leges, ut eas ratas habeamus, non uti contemnamus: nec eas, ut dici solet, tulit anseribus, sed hominibus servandas. Sic verbi prædi-catio non est parietibus, & vacuis templis, sed destina-ta frequentibus concionibus. Sic sabbatha, sacramenta & quæ sunt huius generis alia data sunt nobis observanda,
units.tr: Second, he commends religion from its end: "which you shall observe, that you may do them," he says. God therefore gave and enacted these laws so that we might hold them valid, not so that we might despise them; and he did not give them, as the saying goes, to geese, but to men to be kept. So the preaching of the Word is not for walls and empty temples, but is appointed for crowded sermons. So the sabbaths, the sacraments and other things of this kind have been given to us to be observed.

units.la: Tertio commendat à facili, cum ostendit adiumenta divinitus eis ad hoc studium præ-bita, nempe terram in qua tuto possit hoc fieri. In Ægypto enim non adeo liberè licebat religionis studiis incumbere: sed terra sua potitis nemo erat impedimento futurus quo minus servarent hæc omnia. Sic nobis terra libera, pax, libertas, ubertas, sanitas, opes, quæ præclara sunt Dei munera, ad virtutem adiumenta divinitus concessa. Sed proh Deum immortalem quàm his abutimur. Multi dum valent, dum vacant à negotiis aliis, possent, sed nolunt audire euangelium: quo deinceps magno cum incommodo suo carent miseri.
units.tr: Third, he commends religion from its ease, when he shows the aids divinely provided for them for this pursuit, namely a land in which this could be done safely. For in Egypt it was not so easy to devote oneself freely to the study of religion; but once they possessed their own land, no one would be an obstacle to their keeping all these things. So for us there is a free land, peace, liberty, abundance, health and wealth, which are splendid gifts of God, divinely granted as aids to virtue. But, good God, how we abuse them! Many, while they are strong and free from other business, could hear the Gospel, but will not; and afterwards, to their great loss, the wretched men go without it.

units.la: Quarto commendat à fructu: Possideas (inquit) terram omnibus diebus vitæ tuæ. Ut supra demonstratum est felices esse, qui verbum Domini servant: ita hoc loco dicit terræ promissæ possessionem diuturnam esse sine verbi Dei studio nequaquam posse. At hodie Satan hoc in culcat potius, miseros esse eos, qui verbo Dei studeant: cur non quod est verius cogitamus ex ebrietate & scortatione & cæteris flagitiis oriri mala? Sed felix ac faustum est Euangelii studium. Atque his commendationibus ideo subinde Moses utitur, ut pietatem magis excitet.
units.tr: Fourth, he commends religion from its fruit: "you shall possess," he says, "the land all the days of your life." As has been shown above, those who keep the Word of the Lord are happy; so in this passage he says that a lasting possession of the promised land cannot be had without zeal for the Word of God. But today Satan rather inculcates that those who are zealous for the Word of God are wretched; why do we not consider the truer thing, that evils arise from drunkenness, whoring and the other vices? But happy and prosperous is zeal for the Gospel. And Moses uses these commendations again and again, so that he may stir up piety all the more.

units.la: Falsam hoc ipso repellit quod dicit, Omnino vastabitis omnia loca, &c. Hisce enim verbis ostendit loca Diis alienis sacra, itemq; aras & statuas, & solennem eorum memoriam deleri debere. Loca illa in quibus Dii isti culti sunt sive in montibus, sive in collibus destruenda &c. In quo videmus quid nostra tempestate fieri expediat, nempe ut templa & sacella diruantur. Nam si nolis ciconias, nidos tolle.
units.tr: He repels false religion by what he says: "You shall utterly destroy all the places," etc. For in these words he shows that the places consecrated to alien gods, likewise the altars and statues, and the solemn memory of them, must be wiped out. Those places in which these gods were worshipped, whether upon mountains or upon hills, are to be destroyed, etc. From this we see what it is expedient to do in our own time, namely that temples and chapels be pulled down. For, as the saying goes, if you do not want storks, remove the nests.

units.la: Dein aras (inquit) diruetis & imagines sive statuas atq; lucos. Quare & pictas & sculptas superstitioni factas imagines diruemus.
units.tr: Then (he says) you shall overthrow the altars, and the images or statues and groves. Wherefore we shall also overthrow the painted and carved images made for superstition.

units.la: Deniq; etiam nomen eorum, inquit, abolendum. Jam quoniam nomen habet notam rei, & conservat eius memoriam: quis neget dedicationes papisticas & solennes dies festos creaturis sacros abolendos esse?
units.tr: Finally, he says, their name is also to be abolished. Now since a name carries the mark of a thing and preserves its memory, who would deny that papistical dedications and solemn feast days held sacred to creatures are to be abolished?

units.la: Ex illis omnibus perspicuum est Deum velle templa creaturis sacra dirui, idola nulla poni, festos creaturis dies nullos esse: qua partium enumeratione quicquid idololatriam sapit, repellit.
units.tr: From all these things it is clear that God wills that temples consecrated to creatures be torn down, that no idols be set up, and that there be no feast days held sacred to creatures; by this enumeration of parts he rejects whatever savours of idolatry.

units.la: Sed quod Deus, qui sapientissimus est legislator, quiq; sic rerum, quàm verborum, ratio-nem habet magis, ut nihil habeat in suis præceptionibus superfluum: hoc mali genus tam sæpe & graviter vetuit: argumento est nobis hoc eius studium, quanti referat ea ab re prorsus abstinere. Et certè ex eo Domini studio perspicuum Deum jam inde ab æterno præuidisse quantopere mentes humanæ in hanc luem propendeant, utq; sit idololatria rudium hominum stipata satellitio: deniq; uti sit hæc bestia multiplex & varia. Procliues in eam esse mortales eorum dementia docet, qui nostra ætate syncerioris doctrinæ studio tantopere perpoliri nequiuere, ut idolis velint valedicere, vel pro iis ceu aris & focis pugnare desinant.
units.tr: But God, who is the wisest of lawgivers and cares more for the substance of things than for words, so that he leaves nothing superfluous in his precepts, has so often and so gravely forbidden this kind of evil. The proof for us is his zeal in this matter, and how much it matters to abstain from it altogether. Indeed, from that zeal of the Lord it is plain that God foresaw from eternity how strongly human minds incline towards this plague, and how the idolatry of untutored men is surrounded by a retinue of followers, and finally how this beast is manifold and varied. The folly of those mortals proves how prone they are to it: in our own age, though they have been so greatly refined by the study of purer doctrine, they have not been able to renounce idols, or they cease to fight for them as for their altars and hearths.

units.la: Aiunt Turcarum & Judæorum esse in statuas furere: ego vero hoc ipso meliores hosce puto quod in suis tenebris plus videant, quàm Euangelici illi in sua luce.
units.tr: They say that the Turks and the Jews rage against images; but I think these men are better for this very reason, that in their darkness they see more than those Evangelicals do in their light.

units.la: Aiunt oportere prius, imaginem Dei mente comprehendi, quàm coli queat, proptereaq; minimè male fingi: at ego statuo hoc ipsum parum theologicè dici, cum Deus non corporeus, sed immensus, æternus, omnipotens animo cogitari debeat.
units.tr: They say that the image of God must first be grasped by the mind before it can be worshipped, and that therefore it is by no means wrong to make no image; but I hold that this very statement is said with little theological precision, since God, who is not corporeal but immeasurable, eternal and almighty, ought to be conceived in the mind.

units.la: Aiunt idolum nihil esse Pauli testimonio, sed eò gravius peccant illi, qui rebus nihili divinos honores perhibent.
units.tr: They say that an idol is nothing, by the testimony of Paul; but those who ascribe divine honours to things of no account sin all the more gravely.

units.la: Aiunt idola cuiusq; animo hærere, nec eorum animos destrui: ego vero dico simulachra hæc quoq; destruenda esse: quod citra animorum incommodum accidit. Nam ut aurum & argentum, quæ in omni metallorum genere principem locum tenent in idolorum fabricam conuertenda non sunt: sic ceu Dij quærendi & feruandi non erunt: quod auari & præpar[?] solent homines. Nec pium est etiam alijs seruire turpiter ob hoc ipsum quod abundantau[?]-ro: quod genus idololatriæ per orbem vniuersum excurrit.
units.tr: They say that idols cling to the minds of each person, and that their minds are not destroyed; but I say that these images too must be destroyed, and this can happen without harm to the minds. For just as gold and silver, which hold the chief place among all kinds of metals, are not to be turned into the making of idols, so they are not to be sought and preserved as gods, as covetous men and those who are ... usually do. Nor is it pious to serve others basely for this very reason, that they abound in ... ; this kind of idolatry runs through the whole world.

units.la: Iam quoniam huic peccato patrocinantur docti & indocti, quis non videat quā de causa Deus iterum atq; iterum hoc vetuerit? Dein quia tam varium est & in omnes sese vertit formas: recte & fideliter & amanter ipsum Deus adeo multis in locis repellendum censuit: ac quemadmodum ipse quæ seriò curata velis iterum atq; iterum præcipis, sic ille quæ sanctissimè seruari voluit non vno loco mandasse contentus fuit. Præclarum videri poterat exemplum Cananæorum, qui plus minus 600. annis florentem viribus atq; opibus rempub. obti-nuerant etiam in maximo idololatriæ studio, sed id ipsum remouet iusto iudicio Dominus. Sic nos abstinebimus & à malis exemplis & à falso cultu, vt erigatur & conseruetur cultus bonus & verus in Iesu Christo Domino nostro, Amen.
units.tr: Since learned and unlearned men alike defend this sin, who does not see for what reason God has forbidden it again and again? Moreover, because it is so varied and turns itself into every form, God has judged that it must be repelled, rightly, faithfully and lovingly, in so many places; and just as you yourselves, when you wish something to be seriously attended to, command it again and again, so he was not content to have commanded what he wished to be most holily kept in only one place. The example of the Canaanites might seem a striking one: they held their commonwealth flourishing in strength and wealth for about 600 years, even in the greatest zeal for idolatry, yet the Lord removed them by his just judgment. Thus may we abstain both from evil examples and from false worship, so that good and true worship may be raised up and preserved in Jesus Christ our Lord, Amen.

units.la: SERMO XX.
units.tr: SERMON XX.

units.la: 4 Vos non sic facietis Domino Deo vestro.
units.tr: 4 You shall not do so to the Lord your God.

units.la: 5 Sed eum locum (quem elegerit Dominus Deus vester ex cunctis tribubus vestris, vt ponat nomen suum ibi, habitetq; illic) quæretis, atq; illò venietis.
units.tr: 5 But you shall seek the place which the Lord your God shall choose out of all your tribes, to put his name there, and to dwell there; and thither you shall come.

units.la: 6 Illuc adferetis holocausta vestra, victimas vestras, decimas vestras, munus liberale manus vestræ, vota vestra, voluntaria vestra munera, atque primogenita armentorum, & gregum vestrorum.
units.tr: 6 Thither you shall bring your burnt offerings, your sacrifices, your tithes, the offering of your hand, your vows, your free will offerings, and the firstborn of your herds and flocks.

units.la: IN explicatione legis secundæ, quam Moses hoc cap. exorsus est, ostendimus fidelium hominum interesse, vt à peregrinis cultibus omnibus abstineant: ne videlicet abstrahantur à Domino, ac creaturas secuti, in præsenti quidem seculo consolatione & animi tranquillitate, in altero vero illo, gaudiorum æternorum fruitione destituantur. Iam vero cultum Deo præcitum proponit, ac docet quo in loco, quid, quo pacto sit offerendum Domino. Et in præsentia locum & sacrificia ipsa commemorat.
units.tr: In explaining the second law, with which Moses began this chapter, we showed that it concerns the faithful to abstain from all foreign worship, lest they be drawn away from the Lord and, following creatures, be deprived in the present age of consolation and peace of mind, and in the age to come of the enjoyment of eternal joys. Now he sets out the worship to be offered to God, and teaches in what place, what, and in what manner it is to be offered to the Lord. For the present, he mentions the place and the sacrifices themselves.

units.la: Locum sic indicat: Vos (inquit) non sic facietis Deo vestro, sed eum locum, quem elegerit Dominus Deus vester ex cunctis tribubus vestris, vt ponat nomen suum ibi &c. Ex quo perspicuum est fideles non eodem quo gentiles more loca promiscua diuinis cultibus vsurpare debere, vt vbilibet sacrificent videlicet: sed eo quem elegerit Deus loco suas hostias offerant. Quod certè maius est multò quàm videatur, quippe quo & remoueatur superstitio, & præbeantur adiumenta religionis veræ.
units.tr: He indicates the place thus: You (he says) shall not do so to the Lord your God, but to the place which the Lord your God shall choose out of all your tribes, to put his name there, and so on. From this it is clear that the faithful ought not to use places for divine worship indiscriminately, as the Gentiles did, sacrificing wherever they please; they must offer their victims in the place God has chosen. This is certainly far more important than it seems, since by it superstition is removed and the aids of true religion are provided.

units.la: Nam hæc in religionis rebus vsurpata gentibus licentia, quantum Deorum chaos, quanta superstitionum molem, quàm tetram errorum lernam inuexerit, quis est qui nescit? Idem nostra memoria sic experti sumus, vt exemplis peregrinis opus non habeamus. Quemadmodum enim Paufanias refert varios casus quibus adducti Græci vel Bacchum, vt est apud eum in Corinthiacis, vel Æsculapium, vel alium quempiam Deorum loco habere cœperint: sic nostra tempestate quando portentum alicubi visum, aut cadauer alicuius ad præsentiam latronis sanguine fudarit, aut homo timidus spectro aliquo territus sit: ibi statim statuæ, aræ, sacella erigenda visa sunt. Omitto regulas atq; ordines, indulgentias, sanctorum nouorum canonizationes quas vocant, quæ nihil aliud erant, quàm more priscorum Romanorum aliquem in numerum Deorum referre.
units.tr: For who does not know how much chaos of gods, how great a mass of superstitions, how foul a Lernaean hydra of errors, has been introduced by the licence the Gentiles took in matters of religion? We have experienced the same in our own memory, so that we have no need of foreign examples. For just as Pausanias relates the various occasions by which the Greeks were led to regard Bacchus, as he tells it in the Corinthiaca, or Aesculapius, or some other person as a god, so in our own time, whenever some portent has been seen somewhere, or the corpse of someone has bled in the presence of a robber, or a timid man has been terrified by some spectre, statues, altars and little shrines have straightway been thought fit to be set up there. I pass over the rules and orders, the indulgences, and the so-called canonizations of new saints, which were nothing other than, in the manner of the ancient Romans, enrolling someone among the number of the gods.

units.la: Quibus rebus hominum animi perturbatæ sunt magis & perditæ, quàm seruatæ. Quod in omni vitæ parte potest perspici. Quemadmodum enim ægrotorum multorum medicorum cura perdidit, & multa variaq; co[?]silia Terentianum illū sene fecerant multò quàm effetantea[?] perplexum magis: sic indulgentiæ illæ & missæ, & vigiliæ & factæ creaturis supplicationes adeo non paucum reddunt, vt quoties afferuntur nouæ, toties ille sibi nouas quærat. Et quemadmodum Paulus sacrificia Iudaica propterea dicit esse imperfecta, quod sint in singulos annos redintegrari solita: sic illa quoq; sese ipsa docent imperfecta esse, quia semel emptis, conscientiæ tranquillitas nulla cóparata est. Cur igitur vnum Deũ non colimus? cur ad vnum non confugimus?
units.tr: By these things the minds of men have been disturbed and ruined rather than saved. This can be seen in every part of life. For just as the care of many physicians has destroyed the sick, and many and various counsels have made that Terentian old man far more perplexed than he was before, so those indulgences, masses, vigils and supplications made to creatures do not in the least give peace, but as often as new ones are brought forward, so often does the man seek new ones for himself. And just as Paul says that the Jewish sacrifices were imperfect because they had to be renewed every year, so these things too show by themselves that they are imperfect, since after they have been bought, no tranquillity of conscience is obtained. Why then do we not worship the one God? Why do we not flee to the one?

units.la: Sanè Moses hoc iam docet ostendens Deo placere vt vno aliquo loco Deus adoretur ab omni simul populo. Vnde post tabernaculum, quod fuit in Silo, mons Sion ad cultū diuinum electus est, & nomē hoc deinceps accepit ipsa quoq; ecclesia. Qua de re scriptū extat Leuit.
units.tr: Moses now teaches this clearly, showing that it pleases God that God be worshipped by the whole people together in one particular place. Hence, after the tabernacle, which was at Shiloh, Mount Zion was chosen for divine worship, and the Church herself also received this name in time. Concerning this matter it is written in Leviticus
17. Paralipomenon 6, 7, and Psalm 78.

units.la: Quod autem Deus hoc præcipit & constituit id factum est de magnis causis. Vna, vt su- us esset honos sacerdotio & salua maneret toti religioni sua authoritas, nec sibi quisq; esset sacerdos vbilibet. Nam quod cuiuis vbiuis licet, id in contemptum mox abit, veluti si Sena- tus vbique conueniret, ac non potius in Curia loco deliberationibus publicis deputato.
units.tr: The reason God commanded and established this was for great causes. One was that the priesthood might have its honour and that his authority might remain secure for the whole of religion, and that no one might be a priest wherever he liked. For what is permitted to anyone everywhere soon falls into contempt, as if the Senate were to meet everywhere, and not rather in the Curia, a place assigned for public deliberations.

units.la: Altera, vt idololatriæ & falsis cultibus omnis auferretur occasio, nec alium cultum re-ciperent ab eo, quem præscripsisset Dominus. Quod Moses docet in Leuitico ad hunc modum scribens: Sparget sacerdos sanguinem super altare Domini ante ostium tabernaculi Domini, & incendet adipem in odorem suauitatis Domino, & nequaquam vltra sacrificent dæmonibus. Quod genus dæmonia <bl>שעירים</bl> Hebræi satyros Latini nominant. Huc refer quæ supra dicta sunt de occasionibus inuentarum superstitionum.
units.tr: The other was that every occasion for idolatry and false worship might be removed, and that they might not receive any worship other than that which the Lord had prescribed. Moses teaches this in Leviticus, writing in this manner: The priest shall sprinkle the blood upon the altar of the Lord before the door of the tabernacle of the Lord, and shall burn the fat for a sweet savour to the Lord, and they shall by no means sacrifice any more to demons. The kind of demons which the Hebrews call [שעירים], the Latins call satyrs. Refer here what was said above about the occasions of the superstitions that have been invented.

units.la: Tertia, vt quemadmodum Deus vnus est, sic esset vnus populus, vna religio, vnum templum. Iam Christus nobis est sacerdos & victima. Is respiciendus fuit.
units.tr: The third reason was that, just as God is one, so there should be one people, one religion, one temple. Now Christ is our priest and victim, and it was to him that they had to look.

units.la: Atque hæc lex devno eodemque religionis loco tanti momenti fuit, vt Leuitici 17.ca- pite Dominus sacrificium oblatum alio in loco cedi comparauerit. Et Isaias dicat, Qui im- molat bouem quasi qui occidat virum. Et Israelitæ legis huius neglectæ graues pœnas sem-per dedere. Vt secundo libro Paralip. 28. capite Achaz vbiuis sacra faciens à Domino tra-ditur in manus Syriæ regis. Et capite 29. peccauerunt patres nostri, incensum non adole-uerunt & holocausta non obtulerunt in Sanctuario Deo Israel: concitatus est itaque furor Domini contra Iudam & Hierusalem tradiditque eos in commotionem, in interitum, & in Sibilum. Eadem de re quæreláe sunt Ezechielis 6. capite, Oseæ 4. capite & alibi. Sic nostra ætate propter missas priuaras, passim erectas aras atq; statuas, factaq; sacrificia, Christianus or-bis miserè discerpitur.
units.tr: And this law concerning the one and the same place of religion was of such great importance that in Leviticus chapter 17 the Lord ordained that a sacrifice offered in another place should be treated as a murder. And Isaiah says: He who slays an ox is as if he slew a man. And the Israelites who neglected this law always paid heavy penalties. Thus in the second book of Paralipomenon chapter 28, Ahaz, sacrificing everywhere, is handed over by the Lord into the hands of the king of Syria. And in chapter 29, our fathers sinned, they did not burn incense nor offer burnt offerings in the sanctuary to the God of Israel; so the wrath of the Lord was kindled against Judah and Jerusalem, and he delivered them to trouble, to destruction, and to hissing. The same complaint is made in Ezekiel chapter 6, Hosea chapter 4, and elsewhere. So in our own age, because of the private masses, the altars and statues set up everywhere, and the sacrifices made, the Christian world is miserably torn apart.

units.la: Neque vero Deus his legibus aliud quæsiuit, quàm vt cultus vnus ei, qui Deus vnus sit per vnum Christum concorditer exhibeatur ab vna Ecclesia: & vt in simplicitate fidei, do-ctrinæ Apostolicæ & propheticæ, quæ verè diuina est, manentes, à peregrinis cultibus absti-neamus. Quod Hebræis suis Paulus etiam quasi acceptum à Mose consulit Hebræ. deci-motertio cap.
units.tr: Nor indeed did God seek anything else by these laws than that one worship be offered harmoniously to him, who is one God, through the one Christ by the one Church, and that, remaining in the simplicity of faith, in the apostolic and prophetic doctrine, which is truly divine, we abstain from foreign worship. Paul also advises this to his Hebrews, as if received from Moses, Hebrews chapter 13.

units.la: Quid sacrificandum sit commemoratione omnis generis sacrificiorum indicat. Ac pri- mum ea refert quæ Hebræi <bl>עולה</bl> ab ascendendo, Græci ὁλοκαυτώματα ab eo quod tota comburantur, nos Brandopffer appellamus: quod tota in fumum abeuntia sursum lata eua-nescant. Quod genus est præcipuum, quippe quo sint vsi in maximis periculis Vt Iudic. 20. cap. Israelitæ ob acceptas à Beniamitis duas magnas clades exitium veriti Domino ho-locausta sacrificant. In primo lib. Regum 7. Israelitis Philistinorum metu deiectis Samuel hæc offert. 2. Regum 24. grassante peste Dauid his Deum placat. Et 3. Regum 3. cap. Solo-mon Deo sic illis vsus se & regnum commendat.
units.tr: As to what is to be sacrificed, he indicates by mention of every kind of sacrifice. And first he mentions those which the Hebrews call [עולה], from ascending, which the Greeks call holocausts [ὁλοκαυτώματα] from being wholly burnt, and which we call burnt offerings, because they are wholly turned into smoke, rising upward and vanishing. This is the principal kind, since they were used in the greatest dangers, as in Judges chapter 20, where the Israelites, fearing destruction after two great defeats they had received from the Benjamites, offer burnt offerings to the Lord. In the first book of Kings chapter 7, when the Israelites were cast down by fear of the Philistines, Samuel offers these. In 2 Kings 24, when the plague was raging, David appeases God with them. And in 3 Kings chapter 3, Solomon, using them thus, commends himself and his kingdom to God.

units.la: Alterum eorum est, quæ nomen suum à <bl>זבח</bl> apud Hebræos & apud Græcos θυσίαs- μάτα ταῖς θύειν, nobis vero schlachtopffer à mactando habent. Ibi enim sanguis expians peccata funditur.
units.tr: The second kind is those sacrifices which the Hebrews call [זבח], and the Greeks θυσίαι [thysiai], from θύειν [thyein] to sacrifice, and which we call slaughter-offerings, from slaying. For in these the blood that makes atonement for sins is poured out.

units.la: Tertium locum decimis tribuit: quarum ius vetustissimum est, & iam inde ab origine rerum natum. Abraham enim reuersus à cæde quatuor regum persoluit suas Melchisedecco decimas. Esauum fratrem fugiens Iacob opum suarum decimas sacris in Bethel instituendis Deo si ipsum saluum reduceret, vouit,
units.tr: He assigns the third place to tithes, whose right is most ancient and has existed from the beginning of things. For Abraham, returning from the slaughter of the four kings, paid his tithes to Melchizedek. Jacob, fleeing from his brother Esau, vowed the tithes of his possessions to God, if he should bring him back safe, for the establishing of sacred rites at Bethel.

units.la: Erant autem tria decimarum genera: vt Leuitis annuæ: sacerdotibus eæ, quas eis Leui- tæ ex suis dabant: pauperibus eæ, quas præter Leuiticas populus tertio quoque anno per-soluebat.
units.tr: There were three kinds of tithes: the annual ones, which the Levites gave from their own tithes to the priests; those which the people paid every third year, besides the Levitical ones, for the poor.

units.la: Et dignum obseruatu est, quod decimas oblationum numero comprehendit, nempe vt bona fide eas quasi Deo offerens reddas, nec Caini instar sacrifices.
units.tr: And it is worth noting that he includes tithes in the number of offerings, namely so that you may offer them as if to God, in good faith, and not sacrifice them like Cain.

units.la: Quarto refert <bl>מנחה</bl> quæ à verbo <bl>נדר</bl>, hoc est cleuando nomen habent. Larga vocant munera. Notandum est etiam quod liberalitas est vice sacrificij Domino.
units.tr: Fourthly, he mentions the offering [מנחה], which takes its name from the verb [נדר], that is, from lifting up. They call these gifts generous offerings. It should also be noted that liberality takes the place of sacrifice to the Lord.

units.la: Quinto, Vota de quibus est Leuit. 27. dicitur.
units.tr: Fifthly, vows, of which Leviticus 27 speaks.

units.la: Sexto dona dicit.
units.tr: Sixthly, he speaks of gifts.

units.la: Septimo primogenita, quæ nomen apud Græcos ex eo habent, quod augeant potius fructus, quam minuant.
units.tr: Seventhly, firstborn offerings, which among the Greeks have their name from the fact that they increase the fruits rather than diminish them.

units.la: Hæc & quæ sunt alibi scripta de omni sacrificiorum genere, quantum ad Christianos pertinet duabus generibus comprehendi possunt omnia, ita vt prius genus expiationi, po- sterius actioni gratiarum seruiat. Expiandis peccatis parata sacrificia nihil aliud significabant Iudaeis, quàm peccata, quibus requireret persoluenda satisfactio: fore ergo summum pontificem qui mediatoris inter Deum & hominem partes agat, ac suo sanguine satisfaceret diuinae iustitiae. Quod Paulus in Epistola ad Hebraeos multis verbis docet, vt & Rom. tertio, priore ad Corinthios primo, Ephes. 1. Colossen. 1. priori ad Timotheum 1. cap. Huc refer vacam rufam extra castra caesam, holocaustum, sitientem scilicet in cruce Dominum, effluentem e latere Domini sanguinem simul & aquam.
units.tr: These and the other things written elsewhere about every kind of sacrifice can, as far as Christians are concerned, all be comprehended under two kinds, so that the first kind serves for expiation and the second for thanksgiving. The sacrifices prepared for expiating sins signified to the Jews nothing other than the sins for which a satisfaction had to be paid, and that there would be a high priest who would act as mediator between God and man and satisfy divine justice with his own blood. Paul teaches this at length in the Epistle to the Hebrews, as also in Romans 3, 1 Corinthians 1, Ephesians 1, Colossians 1 and 1 Timothy 1. To this belongs the red heifer slain outside the camp, the burnt offering, namely the Lord thirsting on the cross, and the blood and water flowing together from the side of the Lord.

units.la: Iam quoniam hoc Christi sacrificium omnia consummauit ac perfecit, vt ipse in cruce dicens, Consummatum est, & velum templi scissum indicat: consequens est Christianis ad expianda peccata sacrificium aliud nullum esse necessarium: hoc autem eos non minus solari & seruare, quàm prisca illa Iudaeam gentem & conseruarunt & confirmarunt.
units.tr: Since this sacrifice of Christ has accomplished and perfected all things, as he himself indicates on the cross, saying "It is finished," and as the rending of the temple veil shows, it follows that Christians have no other sacrifice necessary for expiating sins. This comforts and preserves them no less than those ancient sacrifices both sustained and confirmed the Jewish nation.

units.la: Sed quae gratis agendis instituta sunt sacrificia, ea Christianis sunt reliqua vel Iudaeis ipsis testibus: quippe qui dicant, Messiam aduentu suo omnia sacrificia aboliturum praeter vnum laudis sacrificium, quod תודה[?] vocant. Eo gratias agimus Domino cum pro eo quod subinde nos seruat ac nutrit, tum vero de communi illa per Christum praestita liberatione. Vnde Eucharistia prisci sacrificij nomen accepit.
units.tr: But the sacrifices instituted to be offered freely remain for Christians, as the Jews themselves bear witness, for they say that the Messiah at his coming will abolish all sacrifices except one, the sacrifice of praise, which they call thodah [תודה]. By it we give thanks to the Lord both for what he continually keeps and nourishes us, and above all for that common deliverance procured through Christ. Hence the Eucharist took the name of the ancient sacrifice.

units.la: Est autem sacrificium laudis triplex. 1. Seipsum offerret homo, quemadmodum ad Romanos duodecimo capite docet Apostolus, hostiam sanctam, viuam, gratam Deo. Et vt id efficiat, sese ipsum abneget ac Christo totum mancipet. Quo pertinet, vt affectus impuros & scelera exuas atq; abijcias. Dein suas Deo preces offerat ceu fructum labiorum, vt scriptu-ra vocat. Qua de re Psalmo 50. docet. In quo videndum est vt piae, purae, constantes offerantur preces. Tertia charitas & misericordia offerantur Domino. In quo suas quisq; vires respiciet atq; opes. Sed quanto peius est nos non solum non dare, sed etiam inuidere[?] Quin fi-mus misericordes, vt etiam in nos sit misericors Dominus. Atq; hic quidem est ille cultus quem Deus requirit quasi quoddam pietatis exercitium. Nos eum illi reddamus in Iesu Christo Domino nostro, Amen.
units.tr: There are three kinds of the sacrifice of praise. (1) A person offers himself, as the Apostle teaches in Romans chapter 12, a holy and living sacrifice, acceptable to God. And to achieve this, he must deny himself and surrender himself wholly to Christ, which requires that he strip off and cast away impure affections and crimes. (2) Next, he offers his prayers to God as the fruit of the lips, as Scripture calls them; Psalm 50 teaches this. Here one must take care that prayers are offered that are pious, pure and steadfast. (3) Third, love and mercy are offered to the Lord, and in this each one should consider his own strength and resources. But how much worse it is not only not to give, but even to grudge! Rather let us be merciful, so that the Lord may also be merciful to us. And this indeed is the worship that God requires, as a kind of exercise of piety. Let us render it to him in Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

units.la: SERMO XXI.
units.tr: SERMON XXI.

units.la: 7 Ibi epulabimini coram Domino Deo vestro, & laetabimini in omnibus (ad quae admoliti estis manum vestram) vos & domus vestrae, in quibus benedixit te Dominus Deus tuus.
units.tr: 7 There you shall eat before the LORD your God, and you shall rejoice in all that you put your hand to, you and your households, in which the LORD your God has blessed you.

units.la: 8 Ne feceritis iuxta omnia quae nos hodie hic facimus, vnus quisque scilicet quod sibi rectum visum fuerit.
units.tr: 8 You shall not do after all the things that we do here today, every man doing whatever seems right in his own eyes.

units.la: 9 Nec enim adhuc venistis ad requiem, & hereditatem, quam Dominus Deus tuus daturus est tibi.
units.tr: 9 For you have not yet come to the rest and the inheritance which the LORD your God is going to give you.

units.la: 10 Quum vero transmisso Iordane in terra habitaueritis, quam Dominus Deus vester tradidit vobis possidendam (& requiem vobis dederit de cunctis hostibus vestris, qui circumquaq; sunt[?], sederitisq; securi.)
units.tr: 10 But when you have crossed the Jordan and dwell in the land which the LORD your God gives you to possess, and he gives you rest from all your enemies who are round about, and you sit down in safety.

units.la: 11 Ad locum quem elegerit Dominus Deus vester, vt in eo ponat nomen suum, adducetis omnia quae ego praecipio vobis, nempe holocausta vestra, sacrificia vestra, decimas vestras, munus liberale, manus vestrae, omnia vota vestra selecta quae voue-ritis Domino.
units.tr: 11 To the place which the LORD your God shall choose, to make his name dwell there, you shall bring all that I command you: your burnt offerings, your sacrifices, your tithes, the offering of your hand, and all your choice vows which you vow to the LORD.

units.la: 12 Et laetabimini coram Domino Deo vestro, vos & filii vestri, filiae vestrae, ser-vi vestri, & ancillae vestrae, sed & Leuita qui est intra portas vestras, quoniam nec partem nec hereditatem habet vobiscum.
units.tr: 12 And you shall rejoice before the LORD your God, you and your sons, your daughters, your menservants and your maidservants, and the Levite who is within your gates, since he has no portion or inheritance with you.

units.la: 13 Caue ne forte sacrifices holocausta tua in omni loco quem videris.
units.tr: 13 Take care lest you offer your burnt offerings in every place that you see.

units.la: 14 Sed in loco quem elegerit Dominus Deus vester in vna tribuum tuarum, ibi in-quam sacrifices holocausta tua, & illic facies quaecunq; ego praecipio tibi.
units.tr: 14 But in the place which the LORD your God shall choose in one of your tribes, there, I say, you shall offer your burnt offerings, and there you shall do all that I command you.

units.la: 15 Veruntamen pro omni animi tui desiderio mactabis & comedes carnem, iuxta benedictionem Domini Dei tui, quam dedit tibi, in omnibus portis tuis: tam im-mundus quam mundus ex ea comedent quemadmodum capream aut ceruum;
units.tr: 15 Nevertheless, according to all the desire of your soul you may slaughter and eat flesh, according to the blessing of the LORD your God which he has given you in all your gates; the unclean and the clean may eat of it, as of the roe or the hart.

units.la: 16 Modo sanguine ne edatis, sed in terram effundatis veluti aquam.
units.tr: 16 Only you shall not eat the blood; you shall pour it out on the earth like water.

units.la: 17 Non poteris comedere in portis tuis decimam frumenti tui, nec musti tui, nec olei tui, nec primogenita armentorum tuorum, & gregum tuorum, sed nec omnia vota tua quae tu voueris, nec voluntaria tua, nec munus magnificum manus tuae.
units.tr: 17 You may not eat within your gates the tithe of your grain, nor of your wine, nor of your oil, nor the firstborn of your herds and your flocks, nor any of your vows which you vow, nor your freewill offerings, nor the offering of your hand.

units.la: 18 Sed coram Domino Deo tuo comedes ea, in loco quem elegerit Dominus Deus tuus, tu & filius tuus atq; filia tua, seruus tuus & ancilla tua, atq; Leuita qui est intra portas tuas. Laetaberis coram Domino Deo tuo in cunctis ad quae admoueris manum tuam.
units.tr: 18 But you shall eat them before the LORD your God in the place which the LORD your God shall choose, you and your son and your daughter, your manservant and your maidservant, and the Levite who is within your gates; and you shall rejoice before the LORD your God in all to which you put your hand.

units.la: Postquam Moses in hac sua de cerimonijs instructione quo loco, quaeque sacrificia sint Domino verbis ijs, quae nuper expolita sunt, monstrauit, praesentibus sacrificandi modum ac rationem docet. Ac quoniam in omni rerum gerendarum ratione praecipue cogitandum est quid deceat, quidue dedeceat: eandem ipse rationem secum reputans quae cauenda, quibus rursus studendum sit rebus indicat.
units.tr: After Moses, in this his instruction on the ceremonies, has shown by the words just set out in what place and which sacrifices are to be offered to the Lord, he now teaches the manner and method of sacrificing. And since in every way of conducting affairs one must above all consider what is fitting and what is unfitting, he himself, reckoning in the same way, indicates what must be avoided and, again, what must be pursued.

units.la: Quae cauenda sint, hoc ipso monstrat quod dicit: Comedetis & laetabimini coram Deo, &c. Sed non facietis secundum quod nos hodie facimus, nec quod rectum fit in[?] placidum fit tuiq;&c. Quo docet in cerimonijs duo potissimum esse deuitanda consuetudines prauas & humana iudicia.
units.tr: That which must be avoided he shows by the very thing he says: "You shall eat and rejoice before God, etc. But you shall not do according to what we do today, nor whatever is right in one's own eyes, etc." By this he teaches that in ceremonies two things above all must be avoided: depraved customs and human judgments.

units.la: Consuetudines enim quocunq; modo introductae sint, & vsu longo confirmatae penè vim legis obtinent. Nam & antiquitatis & maiorum, à quibus ortae sunt magna apud omnes homines est authoritas atq; admiratio: & cum diu seruatae sint, sine motu ciuili mutari difficulter aut abrogari possunt, quod fit vt pars nolint pars non ausint [?] illis contradicere. Quae cum ita sint, grande est malum vitiosis ritibus assueuisse [?].
units.tr: For customs, however they have been introduced, and confirmed by long use, almost obtain the force of law. For great authority and admiration among all men attach to antiquity and to ancestors, from whom they arose; and since they have been kept for a long time, they can be changed or abrogated only with difficulty and not without civil upheaval, so that some are unwilling and others do not dare to contradict them. Since this is so, it is a great evil to have become accustomed to vicious rites.

units.la: Recte ergo Moses suos admonet, vt ne morentur eas, quibus exitinere assueuerint, cerimonias: quasi dicat, vos ex Aegypto per desertum profecti modo hoc, modo illo loco sacrificatis [?] Domino: vbi vero terra promissa potiti fueritis, Deus volet vno, eoq; abs se monstrato, & definito loco sacrificari. Quare nullum tunc erit ius vestrae consuetudinis.
units.tr: Rightly, therefore, Moses warns his people not to keep up those ceremonies to which they were accustomed on their journey, as if he were saying: you, having set out from Egypt through the desert, now sacrifice to the Lord in this place, now in that; but when you have gained possession of the promised land, God will will one place, shown and defined by himself, for sacrifice. Therefore there will then be no right of your custom.

units.la: Hoc exemplum nunquam recte perpensum est à posteris. Quoties enim populus ad gentilitatis superstitiones defecisset, ac inde eum prophetae reuocarent ad veros cultus: vetusta-tis & consuetudinis ratio semper opposita est. Sic Helias videbatur Achabo receptos ritus turbare, & Christus Iudaeis res nouas moliri, & nos papistis nouas hereses ferere. Caeterum si illi rem recte secum reputent atq; aestiment primaeuos illi ritus abiecerunt, & receperunt nouos, quos nunc falso priscos vocant. Quemadmodum igitur qui imbutus à maledocto & inepto artifice, si se tradat erudiendum bono, prius male cognita dedis-cere, & deinceps necesse habet nouis melioribus assuefacere: sic prius vetus fermentum deponemus ipsi, quam nos Christianae doctrinae tradamus. Ergo Ioannes Christo datus est, qui praecedens dehortatur homines à pristinis studijs:
units.tr: This example has never been rightly weighed by posterity. For as often as the people fell away to the superstitions of the Gentiles, and the prophets called them back from these to true worship, the plea of antiquity and custom was always set against them. Thus Elijah seemed to Ahab to disturb the received rites, and Christ seemed to the Jews to bring in new things, and the Papists charge us with bringing in new heresies. Moreover, if they would weigh and consider the matter rightly, they themselves cast off those primitive rites and received new ones, which they now falsely call ancient. Just as one who, imbued with bad and foolish teaching from an inept craftsman, if he hands himself over to be taught by a good one, must first unlearn what was badly learned and then necessarily accustom himself to new and better things, so we ourselves must first put away the old leaven before we hand ourselves over to Christian doctrine. Therefore John was given to Christ as forerunner, who, going before, turns men back from their former pursuits:

units.la: Humana iudicia ipsa quoq; reijcit, dicens, non faciendum quod cuiq; rectum videatur. Remouenda est ergo, qua nihil est ad concordiae studium nocentius ἐθελοθρησκεία. Nam cum sint quot capita tot sensus: si quid quisq; sibi finxerit, habendum sit loco: fiet vt quot sunt capita, tot sint etiam religionis genera. Vbi igitur illa quam Deus tantopere flagitat religionis consensio?
units.tr: Moses also rejects human judgments themselves, saying that one should not do whatever seems right to each. Self-chosen worship [ἐθελοθρησκεία] must therefore be removed, than which nothing is more harmful to the pursuit of concord. For since there are as many minds as there are heads, if whatever each person has devised for himself is to be held in place, it will come about that as there are heads, so there will be as many kinds of religion. Where then is that agreement in religion which God so earnestly demands?

units.la: Nos dissensionum authores videri non possumus, qui Deum vnum in vno Christo secundum vnius spiritus sancti placitum colendum & adorandum dicimus. Illi turbas mouent, qui Deum in multis & varijs mediatoribus secundum multa & varia Decreta atq; concilia colendum docent.
units.tr: We cannot be seen as the authors of dissensions, we who say that the one God is to be worshipped and adored in the one Christ, according to the pleasure of the one Holy Spirit. Those are the ones who stir up disturbances who teach that God is to be worshipped through many and various mediators, according to many and various decrees and councils.

units.la: Nec moror quod sua ieiunia, suas peregrinationes, & omnia sua deniq; opera bonae intentionis nomine excusant: Moses hic docet non faciendum, quod cuiusq; oculis placuerit. Et recte quidem. Neq; enim priuata est religionis potesio [?]: quin & Dei authoris est praece-ptio, & omnium communis hominum.
units.tr: Nor do I dwell on the fact that they excuse their own fasts, their own pilgrimages, and all their works in the name of good intention. Moses here teaches that one must not do what pleases each man's eyes, and rightly so. For the authority of religion is not private; indeed it is the command of God its author and common to all men.

units.la: Quamobrem Deus author respiciendus est, vt eius stetur iudicio. Ecclesiae res ex ipso Dei verbo omnes pendent. Non sunt religio, probitas, improbitas, gratia, maledictio, ecclesia, membra ecclesiae, nisi quae scripturae sacrae iudicio hoc nomen acceperint. Et ipsius doc-trinae iudicium penes scripturam est sacram. Quare Moses à consuetudine, ab humanis iu-dicijs, ad Dei placitum reuocat.
units.tr: Therefore God the author must be regarded, that we may stand by his judgment. All the affairs of the Church depend entirely on the Word of God itself. Religion, uprightness, wickedness, grace, curse, church, members of the church are not such unless they have received this name by the judgment of Holy Scripture. And the judgment of doctrine itself rests with holy Scripture. Therefore Moses calls us back from custom and from human judgments to the pleasure of God.

units.la: Sed causam addit, quando promissa terra nondum potiti necesse habuistis hinc inde sa-cra facere, & ex tempore & loco quoq; consilia capere: tunc Deus hoc permisit vobis: iam vero terra promissa potitis cultum certum & definitum mandat. Ad eum modum nobis per Christum requie potitis, vera adoratio quæ fit in veritate & spiritu, prodita est. Quemadmodum docent Malachias cap.1. & Christus Ioan.4. Primum igitur erit vt in religionis veræ studio, mala maiorum exempla & prauas consuetudines quas iniquum est patrocinari superstitiosis cultibus, deponamus: tum humana iudicia, quoniam iniquum est minorem maiori conditioni præscribere, missa faciamus. Quo fiet vt humanis rationibus vacui diuina capiamus atq; amplectamur.
units.tr: But he adds the reason: since you had not yet gained possession of the promised land, you had to make sacrifices here and there, and to take counsel from time and place as well; then God allowed this to you, but now that you possess the promised land, he commands a fixed and defined worship. In the same way, now that we have come to rest through Christ, true worship, which is performed in truth and in spirit, has been handed down, as Malachi chapter 1 and Christ in John 4 teach. First, therefore, in the pursuit of true religion, we must put away the evil examples of our ancestors and the depraved customs which it is wrong to defend in support of superstitious worship; then we must set aside human judgments, since it is wrong for the lesser to lay down terms for the greater. So it will come about that, free of human reasonings, we take hold of and embrace divine things.

units.la: Quibus studendum. Cum inquit, transmisso Iordane, &c. Ostendit adeo exactè cultus formam vt loci, sacrificiorum, modi rationem iam coniungat. Locum quem elegit Deus, in quo ponat nomen suum. Idem iterum repetit vt intelligamus quanti referat loco diuinitus constituto sacra fieri, propter concordiam videlicet. Vbi enim vna & simplex est religio, ibi in vnum quasi corpus omnium animi coalescunt: in dissensione & dissimilitudine religionis sub Hieroboam & Abia magni tumultus erant. Semel & vno loco passus Christus vt Paulus docet Hebr.7.9.10. & Psalm.110. Dauid, & Esa.53. Zacharias denique cap.3. Sic nostra ætate nemo discordias ferit, nisi qui passim sacrificant non contenti perenni sacrificio, quod in ara crucis pro peccatis Christus Iesus obtulit. Quod si in vno sacrificio corporis Christi spes omnibus vna esset posita, summa foret vbiq; concordia.
units.tr: What is to be pursued: "When you have crossed the Jordan, etc." He sets out the form of worship so exactly that he now joins together place, sacrifices, and manner. "The place which God has chosen, in which he will put his name." He repeats the same again so that we understand how much it matters that sacred rites be performed in a place divinely appointed, namely for the sake of concord. For where religion is one and simple, there the minds of all grow together into one body; in dissent and dissimilarity of religion there were great tumults under Jeroboam and Abijah. Christ suffered once and in one place, as Paul teaches in Hebr. 7.9.10, and Psalm 110 (David), and Isa. 53, and lastly Zechariah chap. 3. Thus in our age no one stirs up discords except those who sacrifice everywhere, not content with the perpetual sacrifice which Christ Jesus offered on the altar of the cross for sins. If in the one sacrifice of Christ's body the hope of all were placed as one, there would be the greatest concord everywhere.
