units.tr: The deed: they entice the citizens of their city, saying, Let us go and serve other gods, whom you have not known. He teaches that they draw people away from the true worship of God. And they do this with all the greater harm, the more numerous and powerful they are. Satan does this, so that what he cannot accomplish privately he may accomplish by public violence. Thus Jeroboam, Jezebel, Nebuchadnezzar, Antiochus, the Jewish high priests, the Arians, the popes, Mahomet, and the Anabaptists have defended blasphemous errors by public force. Of this kind are the conspiracies which sometimes arise even in civil affairs, with Satan as author: such as the Catilinarian conspiracy at Rome, the Peasants' War in Germany, and several tumults in Switzerland. By such instruments as these Satan seizes both bodies and souls, so that you may see that sevenfold spirit of which Christ speaks in the Gospel. These are by no means things to be despised, but things against which one must act promptly. How this is to be done has been debated by many and variously. Augustine at first denied that such men should be punished by death, but afterwards, better taught by experience, he thought otherwise. Moreover, from the word of the Lord and the example of the ancient Church, Moses teaches what must be done.

units.la: De judicij in illos exercendi forma adhunc modum disserit. Inquiras,, inquit,inuestiges, interroges diligenter etsi verum est,&c. Quibus verbis docet processum juri communi consentaneum[?]. Veluti enim in omni judicio personæ tres concurrunt,actor,reus,judex: sic ille in hoc judicio tria requiri,actionem,defensionem,judicium. Actionis onus imponit magistratui,cuius sit in hæc intentum esse: reo defensionem,nempe,ut nequis indicta causa condemnetur,sed verum ne sit an falsum inquiratur: ipsi deinceps etiam magistratui pœnam irrogandi potestatem videlicet ut cognitum peccatu digno supplicio afficiatur,cedit[?]. Hæc sigillatim Moses persequitur.
units.tr: He sets out the form of judgment to be exercised against them in this way. You shall inquire, he says, search out, examine diligently, whether it is true, etc. In these words he teaches a procedure agreeable to common law. For just as in every trial three parties meet, accuser, defendant, and judge, so in this trial he requires three things: accusation, defence, and judgment. He imposes the burden of accusation on the magistrate, whose duty it is to be intent on this; to the accused he grants defence, namely that no one be condemned without a hearing, but that it be inquired whether the matter is true or false; and to the magistrate himself he grants the power of imposing punishment, namely that, once the crime is known, it be visited with a fitting penalty. Moses pursues these points one by one.

units.la: Magistratui dicit ut inquirat ac sequatur famam:minimeq; famam negligat. Semper enim, ut præclare est apud Plautum à Palinuro seruo dictum,tu scito, flamma fumo est proxima. Sæpe quidem exhalant putidi vapores flammarum similes: qui tamen ipsi etiam animadverti debent,nempe ut obtrectationes & calumniæ coerceantur. Ac si veri sint,qui de re aliqua spargun-tur,rumores consulitur tranquillitati publicæ,si tempestive malis itum sit obviam:sin falsi sint itidem prodest sycophantas reprimi,ac sua cuiq; salva sit fama. Eiusmodi in magistratibus requiritur vigilantia. At in graves res & enormia scelera sæpe impingunt pri-us quàm animadvertant.
units.tr: He tells the magistrate to inquire, and to follow the report, and by no means to neglect the report. For, as Palinurus the slave well says in Plautus, you should know that the flame is near the smoke. Indeed foul vapours often rise that resemble flames, and these too must be noticed, namely so that detraction and calumny may be restrained. If the rumours spread about some matter are true, it serves public tranquillity to meet the evils in time; if they are false, it is likewise useful to restrain the sycophants, so that each man's reputation remains intact. Such vigilance is required of magistrates. But they often stumble upon grave matters and enormous crimes before they notice them.

units.la: Defensio vero postulat,ut ne quis temere,& indicta causa condemnetur,ac prius audiatur quam condemnetur reus. Temeritatis gravissimæ semper existunt pœnæ. Nec fama tantopere curanda est,ut ea quisquam ad irrogandam pœnam facile moveatur. Hæc enim cre-scendo[?]. Et verè dicit vulgus nostrum,<bl>wen Ver wagen fallt fo find Ver reberen vieren[?].</bl> Melius etiam est quod dici solet audiendas esse partas ambas.. Omnium optimè rem perpendit Alexander rex Macedonum, qui reo vacuam aurem unam servans actori prebuit alteram. At videmus fieri ut aures ambas prebeant actoribus aliqui,& deinceps quæ dicit reus quasi causa tota cognita: cum dimidiam tantum norit,qui partem unam audiverit: sic non audiant amplius. Id si in rebus civilibus turpe est & perniciosum,quanto peius est in religione? At semper hoc fidelibus usu venit,ut Heliæ,Christo,apostolis. Nos etiam non auditi condemnati fumus. Sed pios decet ius servare,& secundum id adversus improbos homines procedere. Quæ ratio servanda adversus Anabaptistas est.
units.tr: Defence, however, requires that no one be condemned rashly and without a hearing, and that the accused be heard before he is condemned. Punishments always follow the gravest rashness. Nor should reputation be so greatly regarded that anyone is easily moved to impose punishment on account of it. For such reports grow as they go. And our common people rightly say: "Whoever ventures, falls; whoever ventures not, wins" [in German: Wer wagen fellt, so sind wer reberen vieren]. It is also better, as is commonly said, that both parties be heard. Alexander, king of the Macedonians, judged this best of all, who kept one ear free for the accused and offered the other to the accuser. But we see that some give both ears to accusers, and afterwards believe what the accused says as if the whole cause were known, when someone who has heard only one side knows only half of it; so they no longer hear the other side at all. If this is shameful and harmful in civil affairs, how much worse is it in religion? Yet this has always happened to the faithful, as it did to Elijah, Christ, and the apostles. We too have been condemned without a hearing. But the pious ought to keep the law, and proceed against wicked men according to it. This is the rule to be kept against the Anabaptists.

units.la: Judicium autem dicit esse penes magistratum, qui si verum esse quod ferebatur explorarit, malum dignis supplicijs ulciscatur.
units.tr: He says, moreover, that judgment rests with the magistrate, who, if he has ascertained that what was reported is true, shall avenge the evil with fitting punishments.

units.la: Sed quod qualeque debeat esse supplicium, & quibus de causis par ipsum sic exerceri, jam etiam docet. 1. Omnes incolas simul cum jumentis gladio plectes. Nam hominis maledictio, quam peccando in se vocavit, etiam in pecora atque in omnes eius possessiones serpit: velu-ti initio terra Adæ peccato maledicta est. Miraris tam dirum supplicium: sed audiens causas mirari desines. Vna est, Quod etiam dirum sit peccatum,abominatio in medio tui: res Deo summe displicens, quippe à qua ceu amarore aliquo aut stercore abhorreas: pestis, morbus,&c. Jam si furem plectas,cur non eum etiam qui solicitavit ad defectionem à Deo? Et tantum abest, ut ex eo malo quicquam velit esse reliquum, ut ea quoque consumi velit quæ in usus tuos converti possent. Omnia sibi vult devoveri: minimeque ex impiorum hominum spoliis te locupletari.
units.tr: But he now also teaches what kind of punishment it ought to be, and for what reasons it is to be carried out in this way. "You shall strike all the inhabitants together with their cattle with the sword." For the curse that a man brought upon himself by sinning creeps also into his cattle and all his possessions, just as at the beginning the earth was cursed because of Adam's sin. You wonder at so dreadful a punishment, but when you hear the reasons you will cease to wonder. The first is that sin itself is dreadful, "an abomination in the midst of you," a thing highly displeasing to God, from which you would recoil as from bitterness or filth: plague, disease, and so on. Now if you punish a thief, why not also the one who has enticed others to fall away from God? And he is so far from wanting anything of that evil to remain that he wants even those things consumed which could have been turned to your use. He wills everything to be devoted to destruction, and by no means that you be enriched from the spoils of impious men.

units.la: Altera, ut iram Deus remittat suam: etenim is nisi sublato peccato non placatur.
units.tr: The second reason: "that God may turn away his anger," for he is not appeased unless the sin is removed.

units.la: Tertia, ut te diligat & augeat opibus pariter & honoribus.
units.tr: The third reason: "that he may love you and increase you with wealth and honours alike."

units.la: Atque hanc disciplinam Christus non tulit é medio, sed magistratui gladium dedit teste Rom.13.apostolo.
units.tr: And Christ did not remove this discipline from the midst, but gave the sword to the magistrate, as the apostle bears witness in Rom. 13.

units.la: Exempla sunt passim. Ut Moses in destructo vitulo & plexis idololatris. Ipse enim pri-mum audita fama facti, vidit quale esset, & Aaronem rogat qui factum sit: tum dicit, qui Dei sit sibi jungatur, incurabiles gladio domat. Exemplum in Beelphegor,itemq; Heliæ & aliorum. Ex quibus omnibus perspicuum est Dei gloriam omni studio promouendam, & huic aduersum satanam reprimendum, vti in Deo manentes æterna vita ac felicitate perfruamur per Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum. Amen.
units.tr: Examples are found everywhere: Moses, when the calf was destroyed and the idolaters were slain. For when he first heard the report of the deed, he himself saw what sort of thing it was, and asked Aaron what had happened; then, when whoever was on the Lord's side joined himself to him, he subdued the incurable with the sword. There is the example at Baal-peor, and likewise those of Elijah and of others. From all these things it is clear that the glory of God is to be promoted with every effort, and that Satan is to be checked in this matter, so that, remaining in God, we may enjoy eternal life and happiness through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT XIIII. SERMO XXVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER 14. SERMON 26.

units.la: Filij vos estis Domini Dei vestri, ne ergo laceretis vos ipsos, neq; ponetis caluitium inter oculos vestros propter mortuum.
units.tr: "You are the sons of the Lord your God; therefore you shall not cut yourselves, nor make any baldness between your eyes for the dead."

units.la: 2 Nam populus sanctus es Domino Deo tuo, & te elegit Dominus, vt sis ei populus peculiaris pra omnibus populis, qui sunt super superficiem terræ.
units.tr: "For you are a holy people to the Lord your God, and the Lord has chosen you to be his peculiar people above all the peoples that are upon the face of the earth."

units.la: QVONIAM[?] in falsa religione eò diriguntur omnia, vt splendoré sanctimoniæ magis habeant, quàm ipsam sanctimoniam: nec quicquam ex vera fide fiat: fit vt quo quisq; plus splendoris præstet, hoc illis sit ac videatur religiosior: unde & modum excedunt omnem, & suis sese cultibus atq; cerimonijs conficiunt. Atq; id fit non solum in doctrinæ splendore, in extructione templorum, in ponendis atq; exornandis statuis, in sacrificijs deniq;: verù etiam in sepeliendis & deflendis mortuis, in ieiunijs atq; in delectu ciborum, in decimis, atq; etiam in alijs pietatis officijs. Quemadmodum igitur priores illas superioribus aliquot cap.profligauit: sic illo præsenti posteriores hasce etiam repellit.
units.tr: Since in false religion all things are directed toward having the show of holiness rather than holiness itself, and nothing is done from true faith, it follows that the more splendour anyone displays, the more religious he is thought and seen to be. Hence they exceed every measure and wear themselves out with their own rites and ceremonies. This happens not only in the splendour of doctrine, in the building of temples, in the setting up and adorning of statues, and finally in sacrifices, but also in the burial and mourning of the dead, in fasts, in the selection of foods, in tithes, and in other duties of piety. Just as in the earlier chapters he overthrew the former practices, so in the present chapter he also rejects these latter ones.

units.la: Ac prima parte capitis agit de sepultura, seu de ijs quæ defunctis exhibentur officijs. Qua in re cum ferè tot abusus ac superstitiones essent, quot sunt in hoc orbe nationes: earum ipsarum genus vnum atque alterum commemorat, quippe ex quibus reliqua genera possis æstimare. Sed vt remoueat argumentis vtrinq; admotis oppugnat.
units.tr: In the first part of the chapter he deals with burial, or with the funeral rites performed for the dead. In this matter, since there were almost as many abuses and superstitions as there are nations in the world, he mentions one or another kind of them, from which the remaining kinds may be judged. But in order to remove them, he attacks them with arguments brought against them from both sides.

units.la: Abusus ipsos verbis illis reddit, Ne laceretis vos ipsos, neq; decaluetis vos inter oculos vestros propter mortuum. Quibus verbis ritus duos notat: quorum vnus est affliction seu incisio corporum: alter capillorum abrasio. De priore dicit, ne laceretis vos ipsos, hoc est, ne corpora vel cultris scindatis, vel manibus siue vnguibus lacerétis vt eliciatis sanguinem: neue conducatis alios, qui in vos seuiant. Hoc enim solebant eius generis homines facere, vt est, in 3.Reg.18.de Baalis sacrificis.
units.tr: He states the abuses themselves in these words: "Do not cut yourselves, nor make baldness between your eyes for the dead." By these words he marks two rites: one is the affliction or cutting of the body, the other the shaving of the hair. Of the first he says, "Do not cut yourselves," that is, do not gash your bodies with knives, or tear them with your hands or nails so as to draw blood, nor hire others to rage against you. For men of this kind used to do this, as is told in 3 Kings 18 concerning the sacrifices of Baal.

units.la: De posteriore dicit, ne ponatis caluitium inter oculos vestros propter mortuum. Notat autem eos qui in funeribus vel barbam, vel capita tonderent. Quod Herodotus de Ægyptijs scri-bit: à quibus id illi fortasse didicerunt. Persæ etiam Mafestium suum ab Atheniensibus cesum[?] sic luxerunt, vt & se & iumenta atq; equos tonderent. Ab his superstitionibus abstinere suos homines voluit Dominus.
units.tr: Of the second he says, "Do not make baldness between your eyes for the dead." He means those who at funerals shaved either their beards or their heads. Herodotus writes this of the Egyptians, from whom they perhaps learned it. The Persians also mourned their Masistius, slain by the Athenians, in such a way that they shaved both themselves and their beasts of burden and horses. The Lord wanted his people to abstain from these superstitions.

units.la: Ac quanquam nos legis huius iugo Dominus liberauerit hoc ipso, quod onus eius ipse sibi imposuit: ac propterea liberum fit capillos vel abradere vel nutrire: tamen eorum qui Christo nomina dederunt interest abstinere abijs moribus atque cultibus, qui sunt similes idololatrarum. Vere enim est dictum ex plumis autem agnosci: sic etiam ex superstitiosis ritibus atq; moribus ethnicum.
units.tr: Although the Lord has freed us from the yoke of this law by the very fact that he himself took its burden upon himself, so that it is now permitted to shave or to grow the hair, nevertheless it is in the interest of those who have given their names to Christ to abstain from those customs and rites which are like those of idolaters. For it is rightly said: "As the bird is known by its feathers, so is the heathen known by superstitious rites and customs."

units.la: Quos dices igitur Christianos ne, an ethnicos nostros illos rasos monachos & sacrifi-cos? quid si illa videas, quorum nomine sibi Franciscani placent, stigmata? Profecto si liceret tamen non debebat libere propter offendiculum. Quis enim ista non putet ethnica poti-us, quàm Christiana?
units.tr: Shall we then call those shaven monks and sacrificers Christians, or heathens? What if you see those stigmata in which the Franciscans take pleasure? Surely, even if it were lawful, it ought not to be done freely, because of the stumbling block. For who would not think these things to be heathen rather than Christian?

units.la: Sic quicquid Antichristum sapit, hoc debebat à nobis Christianis respui: nec minus erat nostrum abrogare festa Bachanalia, quàm ieiunia.
units.tr: Thus whatever savours of Antichrist ought to be rejected by us Christians; nor was it less our duty to abolish the feasts of Bacchus than the fasts.

units.la: In primis autem in sepeliendis & lugendis mortuis recta ratio requiritur. Et impium est, & alienum ab homine defunctos non lugere: sed modum excedere æque est alienum à spe vitæ beatæ, & omnino in vitio.
units.tr: In particular, in burying and mourning the dead right reason is required. It is both impious and foreign to a man not to mourn the dead; but to exceed the measure is equally foreign to the hope of a blessed life, and is altogether a vice.

units.la: Argumenta quibus illas superstitiones demoliatur duo affert: quorum vnum sic habet: Filij estis Domini Dei vestri. Argumentum minime malum. Nam filij ingenui referunt parentum mores: cauent ne sint parentibus dedecori: spem habent non dubiam fore se & nominis & fortunarum & omnino bonorum, quæ pater habeat, omnium hæredes & possessores. Eadem spes nobis est certissima simul ac firmissima: eædem etiam rationes.
units.tr: To overthrow those superstitions he brings forward two arguments, of which one runs thus: "You are the sons of the Lord your God." This is by no means a weak argument. For free-born sons reflect the manners of their parents; they take care not to bring dishonour on their parents; they hold the undoubted hope that they will be heirs and possessors of their name, their fortunes, and in short of all the goods their father has. We have the same hope, most certain and most firm, and the same grounds for it.

units.la: At suapte natura Deus abhorret ab omni superstitione : nec ei, quoniam zelotypus est quicquam adeo aduersum est , atq; illi quorum in honorem & gratiam superstitiones exi- stunt Dij alieni. Quocirca nos,fi ingenui fimus filij Dei, ab illis ritibus prorsus abhorrebi- bimus. Unde Matth.3.Baptista non concedebat Judaeis, quod Abrahamo patre nati essent, quando essent degeneres.Et Joa. 8. Christus dicit eos esse diaboli patris filios,quando instar satanae caedem & mendacia spirarent.Paulus autem Ephes.5.Este,aut imitatores Dei,sicut filij charissimi.
units.tr: But by its very nature God abhors every superstition, and since he is jealous, nothing is so hostile to him as the false gods in whose honour and favour superstitions exist. Therefore, if we are free-born sons of God, we shall utterly abhor those rites. Hence in Matthew 3 the Baptist did not allow the Jews to claim that they were born of Abraham as their father, when they were degenerate. And in John 8 Christ says they are the sons of their father the devil, since they breathed out murder and lies like Satan. Paul, however, says in Ephesians 5: "Be imitators of God, as dear children."

units.la: In quo speculo qui qualesq; nos simus filij contemplemur: qui nec blasphemijs nec turpi scelestaque praesentis saeculi vita, nec ulla superstitionum abominatione movemur ad vindicandam suam Deo patri gloriam. Eodem modo in funere & ubique superstitiosos ritus, quos scimus Deum odisse, cavebimus.
units.tr: Let us look into this mirror and consider what sort of sons we are, we who are moved neither by blasphemies, nor by the base and wicked life of the present age, nor by any abomination of superstitions, to vindicate the glory of God the Father. In the same way, at funerals and everywhere else, we shall beware of superstitious rites which we know God hates.

units.la: Iam filiorum est etiam ne parentibus dedecori sint cavere: nam quia ex fortibus fortes procreantur, & soboles patrem refert: certe male Deus audit, si nos peccemus: rursus bene si vitam eius verbo conformem egerimus. Unde precari nos voluit, Sanctificetur nomen tuum.
units.tr: Now it is also the duty of sons to take care not to bring dishonour on their parents. For since strong children are born of strong parents, and the offspring bears the likeness of the father, certainly God hears ill of us if we sin, and again well if we live a life conformed to his word. Hence he willed that we should pray, "Hallowed be your name."

units.la: Jam etiam Dei bonorum omnium haeredes sumus, cum eius simus filij. Quare cum hic vitam morte superata recuperarit, eius fruitio nobis indubia spe est expectanda. Sic Christus colligit Matth.22.Deum non esse eius qui sit mortuus: igitur defunctos vivere. Sic idem Joannis 13. mortem quandam ex hoc mundo ad Deum patrem transitionem. Ergo qui sumus corpus Christi, filij Dei, haeredes regni Dei: morte ceu profectione, ex hoc ipso, in quo peregrinamur mundo, ad patrem Deum commigramus. Quae cum eiusmodi sit mortuorum conditio, non est quod adeo lugeantur, quasi non sint superstites qui moriuntur in Domino. Docet hoc Apostolus 1.Thess.4.&c.
units.tr: Moreover, since we are sons of God, we are also heirs of all his goods. Therefore, since here he has recovered life by overcoming death, its enjoyment is to be awaited by us with sure hope. So Christ concludes in Matthew 22 that God is not the God of one who is dead; therefore the dead live. Likewise the same Christ in John 13 calls death a certain passing from this world to God the Father. Therefore we who are the body of Christ, sons of God, heirs of the kingdom of God, by death, as by a departure, pass over from this very world in which we are pilgrims to God the Father. Since the condition of the dead is of this kind, there is no reason to mourn them so greatly, as if those who die in the Lord were not still alive. The Apostle teaches this in 1 Thessalonians 4, etc.

units.la: Argumentum alterum sic habet: Nam populus sanctus sis Domino Deo tuo, & elegit te Dominus,&c. Argumentum ab electione ductum. Segregavit vos, inquit, Dominus à populis reliquis, igitur iniquum est cum illis iterum commisceri. Nos quoq; segregati à papistis, à mundo, &c. ne rursus misceamur. Ne ceu sues ad cœnum revertamur, inquit Apostolus. Dicit Dominus ab illo sanctificatos non debere prophanis ritibus inquinari.
units.tr: The second argument runs thus: "For you are a holy people to the Lord your God, and the Lord has chosen you," etc. It is an argument drawn from election. The Lord, he says, has separated you from the other peoples; therefore it is wrong to mix with them again. We too, separated from the Papists, from the world, etc., must not mix with them again. "Lest we return like swine to the mire," the Apostle says. The Lord says that those sanctified by him ought not to be defiled by profane rites.

units.la: Ex quibus intelligimus Deum non prohibere, quin nostrorum, quos charos habuimus, hominum mortem lugeamus: sed propter vitae aeternae, qua jam frui coeperunt, spem certam, & quia populus Deo sacer sumus, modo eã in re servari velle. Quod fiet si illi gratias habeamus, qui illorum caducam vitam cum aeterna beatâ; commutarit [?]: ac eum precemur, ut co-dem nos [?] beneficio dignetur aliquando per Jesum Christum Dominum nostrum. Amen.
units.tr: From these things we understand that God does not forbid us to mourn the death of men we have held dear; but on account of the sure hope of eternal life, which they have now begun to enjoy, and because we are a people sacred to God, he wishes us to observe this in the matter. This will be done if we give thanks to him who has exchanged their fleeting life for a blessed eternal one, and pray that he may at some time deign to grant the same benefit to us, through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

units.la: SERMO XXVII.
units.tr: SERMON XXVII.

units.la: 3 Nihil ergo quod abominandum est comedas.
units.tr: 3 Eat nothing that is abominable.

units.la: 4 Hoc est pecus quod comedetis, bovem, pecudem ovium, & pecudem caprarum.
units.tr: 4 These are the beasts you may eat: the ox, the sheep, and the goat.

units.la: 5 Ceruum, capreani, ibicem, bircoceruum, unicornem, vrum & tarandum.
units.tr: 5 The hart, the roebuck, the wild goat, the chamois, the unicorn, the wild ox, and the gazelle.

units.la: 6 Et omne animal quod separat ungulam, & findit fissuram utriusq; ungulae, ruminationem sursum revocans in pecoribus, hoc comedetis.
units.tr: 6 Any animal that parts the hoof and cleaves the cloven hoof, and that chews the cud among the cattle, you shall eat.

units.la: 7 Hoc tamen non comedetis ex his qui ruminationem sursum revocant, & ex his qui ungulam separant ac fissuram, nempe camelum, leporem, & cuniculum, quae quidem ruminationem revocant, at ungulam non separant, immunda ergo erunt vobis.
units.tr: 7 But you shall not eat of those that chew the cud or that part the hoof: the camel, the hare, and the coney. They chew the cud but do not part the hoof, so they shall be unclean to you.

units.la: 8 Et sus tametsi ungulam separat, non tamen ruminat, ideo immundus sit vobis. De carne talium non comedetis, & cadaver eorum non tangetis.
units.tr: 8 The swine, though it parts the hoof, does not chew the cud, so it is unclean to you. You shall not eat of their flesh, nor touch their carcasses.

units.la: 9 Hoc vero comedetis ex omnibus quae in aqua sunt. Quicquid pinnulas habet & squammas comedetis:
units.tr: 9 Of all that are in the water you may eat these: whatever has fins and scales, you shall eat.

units.la: 10 Quicquid vero pinnulas & squammas non habet, non comedetis, immundum sit vobis.
units.tr: 10 But whatever has no fins and scales, you shall not eat; it is unclean to you.

units.la: 11 Omnem avem mundam comedetis.
units.tr: 11 Every clean bird you may eat.

units.la: 12 Haec vero sunt de quibus non comedetis. Aquila, accipiter, aquila marina
units.tr: 12 But these are the ones you shall not eat: the eagle, the osprey, the sea eagle,

units.la: 13 Vultur, pica, & miluus iuxta speciem suam.
units.tr: 13 the vulture, the kite, and the falcon, according to their kind.

units.la: 14 Omnis quoq; coruus iuxta speciem suam.
units.tr: 14 Every raven according to its kind.

units.la: 15 Struthio, noctua, cuculus, nisus iuxta speciem suam.
units.tr: 15 The ostrich, the owl, the cuckoo, and the hawk, according to their kind.

units.la: 16 Nycticorax, bubo, Porphyrio,
units.tr: 16 The night owl, the horned owl, the swan,

units.la: 17 Ibis, Pelecanus, & mergulus.
units.tr: 17 the ibis, the pelican, and the cormorant.

units.la: 18 Ciconia, graculus iuxta speciem suam, vpupa & vespertilio.
units.tr: 18 The stork, the heron according to its kind, the hoopoe, and the bat.

units.la: 19 Quicquid ex volucribus repit, immundum sit vobis, nec comedatur.
units.tr: 19 Whatever creeps among the winged creatures is unclean to you and shall not be eaten.

units.la: 20 Omnem vero volucrem mundam edere poteritis.
units.tr: 20 But every clean winged creature you may eat.

units.la: 21 Ne edatis vllum morticinum, sed peregrino qui est intra portas tuas dabis illud, vt ipsum comedat, aut vendas ipsum alieno, quia tu populus sanctus es Domino Deo tuo. Ne coquas hædum in lacte matris suæ.
units.tr: 21 You shall not eat any carcass; you may give it to the stranger who is within your gates, that he may eat it, or sell it to a foreigner, for you are a holy people to the Lord your God. You shall not boil a kid in its mother's milk.

units.la: QVÆ[?] Moses in secunda parte præsentis capitis de delectu ciborum, id est, quæ Deus animalia suo populo comedenda concesserit, quæq; ne comederent vetuerit, iam afferr, ea ab hominibus Christianis sic percipienda atq; ponderanda sunt, vt intelligamus eorum externu vsum solis Israelitis mandatu esse, spiritualem autem illum & internum, quem Deus etiam tunc potissimum respiciebat, & illis ipsis & nobis commendari.
units.tr: When Moses, in the second part of this chapter, sets out the choice of foods, that is, which animals God allowed his people to eat and which he forbade them to eat, Christians must take and weigh these things in such a way that we understand that their outward use was commanded to the Israelites alone, while the spiritual and inward meaning, which God chiefly regarded even then, is commended both to them and to us.

units.la: Ac primum quidem est intelligendum, Deum quæ creauit spectasse & pro bonis habuisse: sed verum contracta noxa sic deprauata fuisse mortalium corpora, vt non omnia eis conuenirent in cibum animalia, atq; à quibusdam ceu immundis statim ceperint abhorrere. Enim[?] à cibis immundis horrorem Moses è patriarchis acceptum lege post expressit: vt quemadmodum alimentorum immunditie corpora viderent infici, ita peccatis etiam animas ceu veneno vitiari cogitarent.
units.tr: First of all we must understand that God looked upon the creatures he made and regarded them as good. But through the corruption that came later, the bodies of mortals were so depraved that not all animals suited them as food, and some they began at once to shrink from as unclean. For Moses later expressed in the law the horror of unclean foods that he had received from the patriarchs, so that, just as people saw their bodies infected by the impurity of food, they would also think their souls were tainted by sins, as by poison.

units.la: Illas enim de ciborum delectu leges ideo suo populo Deus tulit, vti quam de illorum salute semper habeat curam eis attestetur: atq; etiam eos his cerimonijs à cæteris gentibus seiunctos quasi quadam disciplina gubernaret atq; exerceret. Ac profecto cum alimenta salubria præbeat, noxia subtrahat ceu pater liberis: quis non videat eum, ne quo veneno conficiamur, folicite laborare? Exercet autem animos fideles altiarum rerum cogitatione, dum nostræ nos admonet miseriæ, cuius tædio moti bonis cœlestibus inhiemus: dum prudentiam sic commendat & studium in rerum æstimatione: dum monet abstinendum ab omni rapina, libidine, & scelere, quo puris sint pura quæ creata sunt omnia.
units.tr: God therefore gave those laws about the choice of foods to his people so that he might show that he always cares for their health, and also so that he might guide and train them, set apart from the other nations by these ceremonies, as by a kind of discipline. Indeed, since he provides wholesome food and withholds harmful food, as a father does for his children, who would not see that he labours anxiously lest we be poisoned by something? Moreover, he trains the faithful in thinking of higher things, while he reminds us of our misery, and, moved by weariness of it, we long for heavenly goods. He commends prudence and diligence in judging things, and he warns us to abstain from all plunder, lust, and wickedness, so that all the things created may remain pure for those who are pure.

units.la: Atq; hæc quidem pij Israelitæ & externè seruarunt, quo Dei patris voluntati, cui iure parent homines satisfacerent: & interne secum sic reputarunt, vt illis quasi typis & figuris ad Christum legis perfectionem deducerentur. Extat Gen.7. patriarcharum exemplum. Ezechiel etiam immunda placenta vesci iussus ait, ah Domine Deus anima mea non est polluta nec venit caro abominabilis in os meum. Daniel & sui leguminibus vesci maluerunt, quàm regijs epulis. Machabæorum tempestate Iudæi trucidari maluerunt, quàm cibis immundis inquinari. Præclara sunt exempla septem fratrum, & senis Eleazari, & aliorum, qui in his Dei voluntatem secuti sunt, & quod Deus purum duxit ipsi quoq; purum, quod is impurum, illi rursus impurum habuerunt. Per fidem enim cognouerunt gratissimam esse Deo obedientiam. Parui momenti res videbatur pomum edisse: verum hoc tam paruum mandatum ne transgrederetur, quod Adamum si mille mandata habuisset alia, nullum seruaturum fuisse. Quamobrem obedientia ceu nota populi fidelis Israelitæ à reliquis gentibus seligendi & secernendi fuerunt.
units.tr: These things the godly Israelites observed both outwardly, so that they might satisfy the will of God the Father, to whom people rightly owe obedience, and inwardly, reasoning with themselves in such a way that the perfection of the law was led on to Christ through these things as types and figures. There is an example of the patriarchs in Genesis 7. Ezekiel, too, when ordered to eat unclean bread, said: "Ah, Lord God, my soul has not been defiled, nor has any abominable flesh come into my mouth." Daniel and his companions preferred to eat vegetables rather than the royal feasts. In the time of the Maccabees the Jews chose to be slaughtered rather than defiled with unclean foods. There are famous examples of the seven brothers, of the old man Eleazar, and of others, who in these matters followed the will of God, and because God held as pure what was pure, they held as impure what he held as impure. For through faith they knew that obedience is most pleasing to God. Eating an apple seemed a matter of little importance, yet Adam did not keep this very small commandment; if he had had a thousand other commandments, he would not have kept any of them. Therefore, by obedience, as the mark of a faithful people, the Israelites were to be chosen and set apart from the other nations.

units.la: Iam maceria quæ erat inter ambos populos media, destructa, atq; ouibus in stabulum vnum coactis Christus veritas ipsa fugatis vmbris lucet, & docet Deum patrem in spiritu & veritate esse adorandum. Quæ cum ita sint non necesse habemus nos hunc delectum seruare: verum potius prodest, quid istis typis Deus significarit explorare.
units.tr: Now the wall that stood between the two peoples has been broken down, and with the sheep gathered into one fold, Christ, the truth itself, shines out, the shadows having fled, and teaches that God the Father is to be worshipped in spirit and in truth. Since these things are so, we do not need to keep this choice; it is rather profitable to examine what God signified by these types.

units.la: Ponit autem tria genera, à quibus sit abstinendum: vnum viuorum, mortuorum alterum, tertium eorum quæ sunt adhuc tenera.
units.tr: He sets out three kinds from which we must abstain: one of living creatures, a second of dead ones, and a third of those that are still tender.

units.la: Viuorum autem alia sunt terrestria, alia aquatilia, volatilia alia, quibus ea quæ humi repunt addit. De terrestribus hoc præcipit: Quæ simul & ruminant, & vngulam diuidunt, ea ceu pura ac sana permittit: quæ ruminant quidem, vngulam autem non diuidunt, ea ceu impura vetat: quæ deniq; vngulam quidem diuidunt, non autem ruminant, eorum ipsorum etiam ceu immundorum esu suos prohibet.
units.tr: Of the living, some are land animals, some water animals, and some winged, to which he adds the creatures that creep on the ground. Of land animals he commands this: those that both chew the cud and divide the hoof he permits as pure and wholesome; those that chew the cud but do not divide the hoof he forbids as impure; and finally those that divide the hoof but do not chew the cud he also prohibits from being eaten as unclean.

units.la: Atq; his rebus Deus altisimam philosophiam adumbrauit. Nam quod Deus illa,quæ & ruminant & vngulam diuiduntpro puris habet id eiusmodi est.Ruminare, quia idipsum est cibum sumptum remandere , significat eos qui verbum Dei suis animis acceptum subinde secum reputant & considerant,vti bene concoctum in alimentu salubre conuertatur.Quod requirit Dauid Psal.i.quo docet beatum esse eum,qui iugi meditatione legis diuinæ sit dedi- tus.Christus etiam Matth.13.docet semen verbi diuini minimè permittendum esse volucri- bus cogitationibus,verum hauriendum alta mente,vt istic in bonum fructum exuberet.Hoc est verbum Dei ruminare.
units.tr: And in these things God has shadowed forth a most lofty philosophy. For that God holds those animals that both chew the cud and divide the hoof to be pure is of this kind: to chew the cud, that is, to take food and chew it again, signifies those who, having received the word of God into their minds, keep turning it over and considering it, so that, being well digested, it is turned into wholesome nourishment. David seeks this in Psalm 1, where he teaches that he is blessed who is given over to continual meditation on the divine law. Christ also teaches in Matthew 13 that the seed of the divine word must not be allowed to be taken by fleeting thoughts like birds, but must be received into a deep mind, so that it may grow abundantly into good fruit. This is to chew the word of God.

units.la: Non ruminant verbum,qui tantum legunt ipsum & audiunt, & ore seu lingua versant, nec simul commutantur in melius,& verbum mente non retinent; Θαατμέν ἡμεῖς οὐ ἡμεῖς γ. yn ʒuum anderen vsi.
units.tr: Those who merely read and hear the word, and move it about with the mouth or tongue, do not chew the word, and they are not changed for the better at the same time, and do not hold the word in their mind. "We marvel [Θαατμέν] ... not we ... " and so on in the other way [yn ʒuum anderen vsi].

units.la: Iam vngulam diuidere,est iudicio in rebus versari,easq; inter se rite discernere, & quid inter Mosem & Christum:inter legem & euangelium : inter naturam & gratiam: inter literam & spiritum:inter vetus & nouum fœdus interfit nosse. Qui vero noua simul ac vetera confundunt,sacra miscent prophanis,humana spargunt diuinis , ij vere dicuntur vngulam non diuidere.Quamobrem hæ nobis cerimoniæ significant eos Deo placere,qui verbum eius & alta mente reponunt & in omnibus eius partibus cum iudicio versantur.
units.tr: Now to divide the hoof is to be engaged in judgement about things, and to distinguish them properly from one another, and it is necessary to know the difference between Moses and Christ, between law and gospel, between nature and grace, between letter and spirit, between the old and the new covenant. Those, however, who confuse the new with the old, mix sacred things with profane, and scatter human things among divine, are truly said not to divide the hoof. Therefore these ceremonies signify to us that they please God who take his word into a deep mind and who engage with judgement in all its parts.

units.la: At quæ ruminant quidem; vngulam autem non diuidunt animalia,ea significant hoc hominum genus,quod multum operæ in verbi diuini cogitatione ponit ; sed omni prorsus destitutum est iudicio.Vnde Paulus 1. Tim.4.cap.iubet recte secare verbum Dei.
units.tr: But the animals that chew the cud and yet do not divide the hoof signify that kind of people who spend much effort in meditating on the divine word, but who are wholly lacking in judgement. Hence Paul, in 1 Timothy 4, bids us to handle the word of God rightly.

units.la: Quæ vero diuiduntvngulam quidem non autem ruminant , eorum ipsa typum habent, qui subtiliter quidem sed leuiter tamen versantur in verbi Dei tractatione:possunt omnia se cernere,verum nihil sibi sumunt,quo fiant meliores.
units.tr: But those that divide the hoof and yet do not chew the cud bear the type of those who engage subtly, yet superficially, in the handling of God's word. They can discern all things, yet they take nothing to themselves by which they might become better.

units.la: Aquatilia ea pro mundis habet , quæ pinnas simul & squammas habent.Iam pinnis ceu alis vehuntur,squammis autem ceu plumis integuntur pisces : vnde eos referunt homines qui fide & verbi diuini studio cum supra lutum vehuntur in vitæ puritate;tum aduersus im munditiem mundanam atq; malorum omne genus probè sese confirmatos atq; communitos tenent.
units.tr: He counts as clean those aquatic creatures that have both fins and scales. Now fish are carried along by their fins as if by wings, and they are covered by their scales as if by feathers; hence they stand for those men who, by faith and devotion to the divine Word, are borne above the mire in purity of life, and who hold themselves well fortified and armed against worldly uncleanness and every kind of evil.

units.la: Volatilia vetat,& ea potissimum,quæ ex rapto viuunt, quasiq; in fui generis pernitie procreata sint sic grassantur ac sæuiunt. Ex quo perspicuum est Deum pro impuro & fœlesto habere eum,qui ex cæde & sanguine suum sibi victum quærat, & omnino omnem qui cum alterius detrimento rem suam augeat familiarem.
units.tr: He forbids birds, and especially those that live by rapine, and that rage and ravage as if they were born for the destruction of their own kind. From this it is plain that God regards as unclean and wicked the one who seeks his livelihood by slaughter and blood, and in general anyone who increases his own property to the loss of another.

units.la: Reptilium nomine eos,qui humi repunt,hoc est dediti sunt ventri,nec vnquam ex cœno mundanarum voluptatum ad cœlestia bona suis animis eriguntur. Præclarè monet hos Ouidius dicens,
units.tr: By the name of creeping things he means those who crawl upon the ground, that is, those who are given over to their belly, and who never lift their souls from the mire of worldly pleasures to heavenly goods. Ovid rightly warns against these, saying:

units.la: Os homini sublime dedit,cœlumq; videreIussit & erectos ad sydera tollere vultus.
units.tr: He gave man a face raised high, and bade him see the heavens and lift his upright gaze to the stars.

units.la: Melius Apostolus Coloss. scribens dicit, ad cœlum respiciamus, in quod Christus nos- ter ascenderit.Summa,quorum Deus venter est,eos Deus pro impuris habet.
units.tr: The Apostle writing to the Colossians says it better: let us look up to heaven, into which our Christ has ascended. In sum, those whose god is their belly, God counts as unclean.

units.la: Mortuorum genus dicit,Ne comedatis morticinum,hoc est pestæ extinctum,à feris dilania- tum.Eiusmodi sunt,qui posthabito verbi diuini cibo vitali, traditiones humanas sibi sumunt: qui relicto Christo creaturas implorant:qui relicto viuifico Dei regno præsens seculum amplectuntur:qui deniq; vera per Christum donata peccatorum expiatione spreta, ad papistica indulgentias,atq; etiam sua ipsorum merita,quibus perpurgentur confugiunt:hi impuri sint ac maneant necesse est,quandoquidem rebus quibus ablui poterant ipsis,in cœno suo sese,si Dijs placet,egregie lauant.
units.tr: He speaks of a kind of carrion, "Do not eat what is dead," that is, what has died of plague or been torn by wild beasts. Such are those who, rejecting the living food of the divine Word, take up human traditions for themselves; who, leaving Christ, call upon creatures; who, leaving the life-giving kingdom of God, embrace the present age; who, finally, having scorned the forgiveness of sins truly given through Christ, flee to papistical indulgences and even to their own merits, by which they hope to be cleansed. Such people must be and remain unclean, since, though they could be washed with the things by which they might have been cleansed, they splendidly wash themselves, if it please the gods, in their own mire.

units.la: Sugentium hæc est ratio:Ne coquas(inquit) hædum in lacte matris suæ. Vt imbecillibus parcamus,ac ne libeat ex infirmorum fratrum cæde & sanguine saginari. Qua de re Paulus & scripto & exemplo nos docuit.
units.tr: The reason for the sucklings is this: "Do not boil a kid in its mother's milk." This is so that we may spare the weak, and that we may not be tempted to fatten ourselves on the slaughter and blood of our weak brothers. On this matter Paul taught us both by writing and by example.

units.la: Sed de immundis istis citius vt dictum est iudicabimus.Quid enim aliud est edere,quàm vt Christus docet Ioannis sexto capite;credere?Ergo rebus immundis vesci, idem est quod rebus illicitis,prophanis,impijs,pernitiosis animum pascere,deditum esse,fidem habere.Vt de etiam ipsi impuri euadamus.Vertitur enim id quod alitur in alimenti naturam.
units.tr: But we shall judge these unclean things more quickly, as has been said. For what else is to eat than, as Christ teaches in the sixth chapter of John, to believe? Therefore to feed on unclean things is the same as to feed the mind on unlawful, profane, impious and pernicious things, to be given over to them, to hold them as faith. Thus we ourselves too become unclean. For what is fed upon is turned into the nature of the food.

units.la: Ex quibus omnibus est perspicuum decere & saluti nobis esse ,vt spretis atq; abiectis impuris rebus ad Christum transeamus, eoque vescentes sanctificemur, viuificemur,& in naturam cœlitum transeamus,&c.
units.tr: From all these things it is plain that it is fitting and salutary for us, having rejected and cast off unclean things, to pass over to Christ, and by feeding on him to be sanctified, quickened, and transformed into the nature of the heavenly ones, etc.

units.la: SERMO XXVIII.
units.tr: Sermon XXVIII.

units.la: 22 Exactè decimabis cunctos prouentus Jementis tuæ, quos ager singulis annis profundit.
units.tr: 22 You shall surely tithe all the increase of your seed, that the field bringeth forth year by year.

units.la: 23 Et comedes coram Domino Deo tuo (in loco quem elegerit, vt nomen suum illic ponat) decimam frumenti tui, vini tui, & olei tui, atq; primogenita armentorum tuorum, & gregum tuorum, vt discas timere Dominum Deum tuum cunctis diebus.
units.tr: 23 And you shall eat before the Lord your God, in the place which he shall choose to place his name there, the tithe of your corn, of your wine, and of your oil, and the firstlings of your herds and of your flocks, that you may learn to fear the Lord your God always.

units.la: 24 Quod si longior fuerit via, quam tu fis ferendo, quandoquidem procul est à te locus ille quem elegerit Dominus Deus tuus, vt ponat nomen suum illic, fortunaritq; te Dominus Deus tuus.
units.tr: 24 But if the way be too long for you to carry it, since the place which the Lord your God shall choose, to put his name there, is far from you, and the Lord your God shall bless you.

units.la: 25 Dabis pro pecunia, & colligata pecunia infasciculum in manum tuam, ibis ad locum quem elegerit Dominus Deus tuus.
units.tr: 25 Then you shall turn it into money, and bind up the money in your hand, and go to the place which the Lord your God shall choose.

units.la: 26 Et exponas pecuniam pro omnibus quæ desiderat animus tuus, pro bobus & pro ouibus, pro vino & sicera, pro cunctis deniq; quæ auet animus tuus, & comedes ibi coram Domino Deo tuo, & lætaberis tu atq; domus tua.
units.tr: 26 And you shall spend the money on whatever your soul desires: on oxen and on sheep, on wine and strong drink, on whatever else your soul craves. And you shall eat there before the Lord your God, and you and your household shall rejoice.

units.la: 27 Et Leuita qui est intra portas tuas ne deseras, quia nec partem, nec hæreditatem tecum habet.
units.tr: 27 And you shall not forsake the Levite who is within your gates, for he has neither portion nor inheritance with you.

units.la: 28 A fine tertij anni selige omnes decimas annonæ tuæ illius anni, & repones intra portas tuas.
units.tr: 28 At the end of every third year, you shall bring forth all the tithes of your produce of that year, and lay them up within your gates.

units.la: 29 Venietq; Leuita, qui non habet partem, & hæreditatem tecum, & peregrinus, pupillus atq; vidua, qui sunt intra portas tuas, & comedent atque saturabuntur, vt locupletet te Dominus Deus tuus in cunctis opere manus tuæ quod fecerit.
units.tr: 29 And the Levite, who has no portion or inheritance with you, shall come, and the stranger, the fatherless and the widow who are within your gates, and they shall eat and be satisfied, that the Lord your God may bless you in all the work of your hand which you do.

units.la: EXternorum seu eorum, quibus fides exercetur, operum genere & numero decimę quoque continentur, quæ sustentandis ecclesijs, ministris, pauperibus colliguntur. Parum enim fidei syncerię, in Deum amoris ij habere videntur, qui verbi ministris & egenis & omnino reipub. ex eo, quod accipiunt ipsi diuinitus, grauatè partem decimam pendunt. Sed huius rei ratione perexigua habita complures semper extitere, qui Dei non maiore amore moti, quàm vt has vel ægre, vel iniquè darent, vel omnino omnes pernegarent. Quod malum vt declinaret Deus, omnium gentium animis indidit, vt feruandæ reipub. & æquitatis gratia decimas quisq; suas in eos quos diximus vsus suppeditarent: & idipsum deinceps sua per Mosem lata lege confirmauit.
units.tr: The tithes are also included among the kinds and numbers of external works, by which faith is exercised, and which are gathered for the support of the churches, the ministers and the poor. For those who grudgingly pay the tenth part, from what they receive from God himself, to the ministers of the Word, to the needy and to the commonwealth as a whole, seem to have little sincere faith and love towards God. Yet while little regard has been paid to this matter, there have always been many who, moved by no great love of God, gave these tithes either reluctantly or unfairly, or refused them altogether. To remedy this evil, God put into the minds of all nations that each man should supply his tithes to those we have named, for the preservation of the commonwealth and for the sake of fairness. Afterwards, by the law given through Moses, he confirmed the same thing.

units.la: Nam ius decimarum non Mose primum authore, sed communi gentium omnium consensu productum est & confirmatum. Abraham reuersus à cæde quatuor regum dedit Melchisedecco sacerdoti magno spoliorum suorum decimas, Iacob fratrem iratum fugiens vouit Deo, si ipsum saluum reduxisset, decimá omnium facultatum ad constituenda in Bethel sacra. Et Herculi Romæ eodem penè quo hic scriptum est, modo persolutas decimas Plutarchus & Varro scribunt. Nec mirum est ius decimarum cosensu gentium firmatum esse, cum simul etiam religio atq; pauperum sustentatio firmata sint.
units.tr: For the right of tithes was not first brought in and confirmed by Moses as its author, but by the common consent of all nations. Abraham, returning from the slaughter of the four kings, gave to Melchizedek the priest the tenth of his spoils. Jacob, fleeing his angry brother, vowed to God that, if he brought him back safe, he would give a tenth of all his goods to establish a sanctuary at Bethel. Plutarch and Varro also write that tithes were paid to Hercules at Rome, in almost the same manner as is written here. Nor is it surprising that the right of tithes was confirmed by the consent of the nations, since at the same time religion and the support of the poor were also confirmed.

units.la: Qua tamen in re sic versatur Moses, vt 1. quę nam eæ sint. 2. quomodo cōferendę. 3. in quos vsus referendæ sint indicetur.
units.tr: Yet Moses handles this matter in such a way that it is shown: (1) what these tithes are; (2) how they are to be brought; (3) to what uses they are to be applied.

units.la: Quæ verò sint, si Leuit. vltimum, & Numerorum decimumoctauum cum præsenti loco conferuleris, intelliges esse tria potissimum decimarum genera. Vnum earum quas Leuitis Ilaelitæ singuli persoluebant annuas. Alterum earum quas de suis Leuitæ sacerdotibus dabant. Tertium earum quas tertio quoq; anno ad pauperum inopiam subleuandam populus omnis dabat. De primo genere passim scriptum extat. De secundo Num. 18. quas Aharoni ceu summo sacerdoti Leuitæ dabant. De tertio hoc ipso loco.
units.tr: As to what they are, if you compare the last chapter of Leviticus and the eighteenth chapter of Numbers with the present passage, you will understand that there are chiefly three kinds of tithes. One is the tithe which each of the Israelites paid yearly to the Levites. The second is the tithe which the Levites paid from their own tithes to their priests. The third is the tithe which all the people gave every third year to relieve the poverty of the poor. Of the first kind, much is written everywhere. Of the second, Numbers 18 speaks, where the Levites gave tithes to Aaron as high priest. Of the third, this very passage speaks.

units.la: Iam verum est nos libertate per Christum potitos esse, propterea; Mosis legibus non teneri, sed ideo iuri decimarum nihil detrahemus, si quemadmodum antea dictum est, eius originem,tam etiam vsum consideremus. Primum enim cum multò ante latam legem hoc ius introductum sit & confirmatum: ipsum profectò non minus ratum habebimus, quàm ius contractuum, quod ipsum etiam iure gentium firmatum est. Causæ deinceps eædem sunt nobis, quæ fuerunt olim Israelitis, nempe vt ministri foueantur & pauperes. Christo quidem & Apostolis nil dabatur, quia videbantur esse quasi hæretici, Ioan. 6. 16. at illis pij dabant. Luc. 8. Actor. 4. 6. & passim per Paulinas Epistolas, & 1. Tim. 5. Deinceps vbi imperio Rom. suscepta religio Constantinus, & alij fideles exemplo veteris ecclesiæ decimarum ius receperunt. Iam quoniam Christo debemus omnia, atque etiam iusti fumus bonis nostris venditis ipsum sequi, nemo est qui negare decimas audet ei, cui totum debet, vt ait Diuus Hieronymus.
units.tr: Now, it is true that we have been set free through Christ, and so we are not bound by the laws of Moses. Yet we shall not take anything away from the right of tithes, if, as was said before, we consider both its origin and its use. For since this right was introduced and confirmed long before the law was given, we shall certainly hold it to be no less binding than the right of contracts, which has also been confirmed by the law of nations. Next, the causes are the same for us as they were once for the Israelites, namely, that the ministers and the poor may be supported. Indeed, nothing was given to Christ and the Apostles, because they seemed to be almost heretics (John 6:16); but godly people gave to them (Luke 8; Acts 4 and 6), and throughout the Pauline Epistles, and in 1 Timothy 5. Afterwards, when the Roman empire had embraced the religion, Constantine and other believers, following the example of the early Church, received the right of tithes. Now, since we owe everything to Christ, and since we are indeed righteous, having sold our goods to follow him, there is no one who dares to deny tithes to him to whom he owes everything, as Saint Jerome says.

units.la: Igitur pietas iubet eos fouere, quos ad nos mittit Dominus: & chariras iubet eos alere, qui sunt vnum nobiscum in Christo corpus. Est autem summa æqualitas si ex suo quisque soluat decimas: sicut Iudæ bona fuerunt vectigalia, ruri verò sunt impositæ decimæ. Postremo nostros nos agros sic acquirimus, vti decimas persoluamus: ac qui liber est à decimis fundus, is multò maioris venit. Quo fit vt iure debeantur. Sed & si liberi simus à numero, tamen ad sustentanda reipub. necessaria munia non possumus quas debemus, siue nonas siue decimas negare: ac quemadmodum dictum est, ne decimæquidem negari possunt ab eo, qui fundum hac lege emerit, vt pendat decimas. Itaque cogitandum est Christum ministerium ecclesiæ & curam pauperum minimè sustulisse.
units.tr: Therefore godliness bids us cherish those whom the Lord sends to us, and charity bids us feed those who are one body with us in Christ. Moreover, there is the greatest fairness if each man pays tithes from what is his own, just as the goods of Judah were taxed, while tithes were imposed on the land. Finally, we acquire our fields on condition that we pay tithes, and a field that is free of tithes sells for much more. Hence they are owed by right. But even if we were free of the tithe, we could not refuse the duties necessary for supporting the commonwealth, whether we refuse tithes or tenths; and, as has been said, even the tithe cannot be refused by one who buys a field on this condition, that he pay tithes. Therefore we must consider that Christ did not in any way take away the ministry of the Church or the care of the poor.

units.la: Quomodo verò dandæ sint docet, Decimas decimabis omnium proucntuum: ac si possis, fruges ipsas afferes: sin minus, tantundem pecuniarum solues. Ex quo perspicuum est, decimas, quoniam in vsus sacros conferuntur, offerri debere Domino, quasi quædam sacrificia: Vnde constat in Deum ipsum male fidum esse quisquis eas perfidè soluerit. Etenim si quis te fallat æ gre ferres: ac malles tantum dici, quantum datur, quàm plus simulari. Hilarem datorem diligit Dominus: perfidorum sacrificia respuit. Exemplo sunt Cain, Ananias, &c. Hæc cogitanda sunt ijs qui soluùt decimas. Mentiuntur enim, inquit Petrus, spiritui sancto: quod grande scelus est. Huc impellat quod dicit dandas esse decimas, vt discas timere Dominum Deum tuum: tum vt fidem tuam exerceas.
units.tr: As to how they are to be given, he teaches: "You shall surely tithe all the increase." And if you can, bring the produce itself; if not, pay the equivalent in money. From this it is clear that tithes, since they are applied to sacred uses, ought to be offered to the Lord, as certain sacrifices. Hence it is established that whoever pays them deceitfully is false towards God himself. For if someone deceives you, you would take it badly, and would rather be told only what is given than have more pretended. The Lord loves a cheerful giver; he rejects the sacrifices of the faithless. Cain and Ananias are examples. These things ought to be considered by those who pay tithes. For, says Peter, "you have lied to the Holy Spirit", which is a great wickedness. Let this move us to what he says, that tithes are to be given, "that you may learn to fear the Lord your God", and also that you may exercise your faith.

units.la: Causæ decimarum tres potissimum hic referuntur, nempe vt ministris ecclesiæ, vt paupe ribus, vt singulis ciuibus cedant. Ministris, inquit, Et Leuitam intra portas tuas ne deseras, &c. En primam partem: Leuitis debeni, qui sunt ministri ecclesiæ.
units.tr: Three chief causes of tithes are mentioned here, namely that they go to the ministers of the Church, to the poor, and to each of the citizens. As to the ministers, he says: "And you shall not forsake the Levite within your gates," and so on. Here is the first part: the Levites, who are the ministers of the Church, are owed.

units.la: At quidam dicunt, gratis accepistis, gratis date, & negant ministris stipendia. Sed hæc illorum verba Christus dixit de miraculis, seu donis saluandi, quæ noluit esse venalia. Exemplo sunt Helizei seruus & Simon magus.
units.tr: But some say: "You have received freely, give freely," and they deny stipends to the ministers. But Christ spoke these words of miracles, or of the gifts of healing, which he would not have be for sale. Elisha's servant and Simon Magus are examples.

units.la: Sed veniamus ad causas. 1. Quia ministri sunt. De ijs Christus dicit, dignus est operarius mercede sua. Et ex, Os boui triturant non obligabis. Multa sunt. 1. Cor. 9. in hanc sententiâ. Et 2. Cor. 11. nihil Paulus accepit à Corinthijs, sed ab ijs qui veniebant è Macedonia fratribus. Alios depredatus sum, inquit, vt vobis oneri non essem. Et vt 1. Cor. 9. spiritualia dedi, recepi temporalia.
units.tr: But let us come to the causes. First, because they are ministers. Of these Christ says, "the labourer is worthy of his hire" (Luke 10:7). And, "You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out the corn" (Deut. 25:4). There are many passages to this effect in 1 Corinthians 9. And in 2 Corinthians 11, Paul received nothing from the Corinthians, but from the brethren who came from Macedonia. "I robbed other churches," he says, "so as not to be a burden to you." And, as in 1 Corinthians 9, "if we have sown to you spiritual things, is it a great thing if we reap your carnal things?"

units.la: 2. Quia Leuitæ non habent partem: nulla enim eis terræ portio fuerat assignata: Ergo vt fratribus datæ decimæ. Sic ministri verbi nunc quidem habent sacerdotia, sed cum nullas possint neque artes neque merces exercere: an non iustum est vt alicunde victum habeant, has eis dari? An enim ciues non sunt? Ex quibus perspi potest, quàm iniquum & absurdum sit hac de re vel dubitare.
units.tr: 2. Because the Levites have no portion: for no portion of the land had been assigned to them; therefore tithes were given to them as to brothers. So the ministers of the Word now indeed have their benefices, but since they can practise neither crafts nor trade, is it not just that they should have sustenance from somewhere, and that this be given to them? Are they not citizens? From which it can be seen how unjust and absurd it is even to doubt about this matter.

units.la: Pauperibus, vt peregrinis, pupillis, viduis, &c. Extant passim testimonia, quibus iubemur pauperibus benefacere, præcipuè: vt ait Apostolus, domesticis fidei. Et debet exemplum Cananæorum & Sodomitarum nos terrere, ne malimus esse inhospitalis Caucasus, quam patriarcharum similes in beneficentia.
units.tr: For the poor, as for strangers, orphans, widows, etc. There are testimonies everywhere by which we are commanded to do good to the poor, especially, as the Apostle says, to the household of faith. The example of the Canaanites and the Sodomites ought to terrify us, lest we prefer to be an inhospitable Caucasus rather than be like the patriarchs in beneficence.

units.la: Tibi ipsi, Vt locupletet te Dominus Deus tuus in omnibus, inquit, operibus manus tuæ. Præclarè dixit Paulus: Vt sementà feceris ita & metes. Matth. 25. parabola docet, quomodo redditur, quæ expendimus in pauperes. Sunt etiam egregia exempla Tobiæ, Iobis, Abrahæ, & cæterorum.
units.tr: To yourself: That the Lord your God may bless you in all the works of your hands. Paul spoke excellently: as you sow, so also shall you reap. The parable of Matthew 25 teaches how what we spend on the poor is repaid. There are also outstanding examples in Tobit, Job, Abraham, and others.

units.la: Atqui ex his quidem discimus quis sit vsus bonorum ecclesiasticorum. Gregorius I. episcopus Rom. dicit sua ætate bona ecclesiastica partibus quatuor esse distributa: quarum prima cederet episcopo & eius familiæ: secunda clero: tertia pauperibus: quarta ecclesijs reparandis. Eiusmodi reformatio nobis etiam esset necessaria. Episcoporum vicem tenent, qui præsunt Ecclesijs docendo pastores: cleri loco putes esse, qui in scholis exercent & exercentur. vt decedentibus parochis succedant: pauperum nomine censunur ægri, leprosi, debiles e-meriti, exules: item calamitates publicæ siue bello siue frugum penuria, siue peste natæ.
units.tr: Indeed, from these things we learn what the use of ecclesiastical goods is. Gregory I, bishop of Rome, says that in his age the ecclesiastical goods were divided into four parts: of which the first was to go to the bishop and his household; the second to the clergy; the third to the poor; the fourth to the repair of churches. Such a reform would also be necessary for us. They hold the place of bishops, who preside over the churches by teaching as ministers; you may consider them to hold the place of the clergy, who teach and are taught in the schools, so that they may succeed departing parish ministers. Under the name of the poor are counted the sick, lepers, the disabled, the aged and retired, exiles; likewise public calamities, whether arising from war, scarcity of crops, or plague.

units.la: Cæterum hoc sanctum opus has ærumnas & molestias mitigandi prophanat vtrinq; fa-tan. Apud papistas decimæ partim surreptæ sunt parochijs, partim misere perditæ, omnes ferè in scelestos vsus absumptæ. Apud eos qui nomine euangelij recepti sibi placent non mi-nor est eorum prophanatio. Magistratus ipsi primum illa sibi vendicarunt ceu sua, ijsq; par-tim latam sibi faciunt ditionem, partim arces atq; ædificia struunt, partim thesauros augent, neglectis interim aut perparce habitis ministris, ecclesijs, pauperibus. Dein ijs œconomos præficiunt duros simul ac rigidos, qui malint derogare quam erogare, vt gratum faciant do-minis. At vt de nobis dicam, non solum in curia nostra, verumetiam coram tribunali Christi reddenda est ratio. Iam accusabunt te animæ neglectæ & pabulo verbi diuini spoliatæ: accusa-bunt te pauperes, qui tantum non rumpuntur inedia, accusabunt ipsi etiam ciues, quibus illi mendicijunt oneri magno simul ac detrimento: surgent deniq; contra te monachi, qui tot aluerunt personas: Hæc etiam atq; etiá cogitanda sunt, vt ne hoc auro Tolosano inficiamur, ac quam augere volumus, deijciamus inclytam rempub. Quam Deus faxit sibi ornamento & saluti, conseruemus per Iesum Christum dominum nostrum. Amen.
units.tr: Otherwise, this holy work of alleviating these miseries and troubles is profaned in both ways. Among the Papists, tithes have partly been seized from the parishes and partly wretchedly squandered, almost all of them consumed in wicked uses. Among those who have been received in the name of the gospel and are pleased with themselves, their profanation is no less. The magistrates themselves first claimed these things for themselves as their own, and from them partly enlarge their domain, partly build citadels and buildings, partly increase their treasuries, while meanwhile the ministers, the churches and the poor are neglected or treated very sparingly. Then they set over these as stewards men both harsh and rigid, who would rather take away than give out, so that they may please their lords. But to speak for ourselves: an account must be rendered not only in our court but also before the judgment seat of Christ. Now the souls neglected and deprived of the food of the divine Word will accuse you; the poor, who are all but breaking down from hunger, will accuse you; the citizens themselves will accuse you, to whom those beggars are a great burden and at the same time a loss; finally the monks, who have supported so many persons, will rise up against you. These things too must be considered again and again, lest we be stained with this Toulouse gold, and by casting down what we wish to increase, overthrow the famous commonwealth. May God grant that it be preserved for its own ornament and welfare, through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT XV. SERMO XXIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XV. SERMON XXIX.

units.la: APrincipio septimi anni facias remissionem. Hæc vero sit ratio remissionis. Omnis creditor remittere debet manum suam, is scilicet qui mutuo dedit proximo suo, neq; urgeat proximum suum aut fratrem suum, nam indicta est remissio Domini.
units.tr: At the beginning of the seventh year you shall make a release. And this is the manner of the release: every creditor shall release what he has lent to his neighbour; he shall not press his neighbour or his brother, because the Lord's release has been proclaimed.

units.la: 3 Ab alieno poteris exigere: qui vero frater tuus est, hunc requiescere sinat manus tua.
units.tr: 3 Of a foreigner you may exact it; but whatever is owed by your brother, let your hand let it rest.

units.la: VM Moses præcedenti Cap. eam quæ in pensione decimarum requiritur fidem & iustitiam, quasi verae fidei quoddam exercitium suis hominibus commendarit, atq; etiam inter alias institutarum decimarum causas pauperes ipsos numerarit: opportune inde ad aliud exercitium verae fidei transit explicandum, nempe vt vbi fides in vera ac viua, ibi non possit fieri quin summa sit erga pauperes liberalitas.
units.tr: Moses, in the preceding chapter, commended to his people the faith and justice required in the payment of tithes, as a kind of exercise of true faith, and he also counted the poor among the other reasons for instituting the tithes. Here he fittingly moves on to explain another exercise of true faith, namely that where faith is true and living, generous kindness toward the poor cannot fail to be great.

units.la: Ac quanquam hæc tractatio videatur in numerum secunda tabula descriptorum præ-ceptorum referenda, qua de rebus ad proximum spectantibus agitur: tamen eam Moses, quoniam est vt diximus exercitium veræ in Deum fidei rectè ad primam tabulam refert. Quem admodum enim philosophi statuerunt naturam esse principium, ex quo honestum omne manat, atq; à quo nihil alienum vir bonus committit, propterēaq; eam qui sit vna virtute prædītus, omnes habere: sic Christiana doctrina voluntarem diuinam ceu ipsam honestarum actionum normam tradit, quam qui fide est præditus vnicè respicit, nec alienum ab ea quicquam facit; ficq; fit vt ex fide ceu fonte & principio omnes honestæ & bonæ actiones manant. Alioquin multi præclaras res gerunt, sed ducti causis aliis atq; aliis. Vt quidam miseretur inopis quodam naturæ motu: quidam egenum iuuat laudis studio: pleriq; sui commodi promouendi gratia, ac vel vt id eis Deus vel is cui benefecerit remunerent: vt videas diuersissimis exfo-tibus opus vnum & idem promanare. Sed illud verum est virtutis opus quod ex fide prosi-ciscitur. Qua de causa Moses ad externum Dei cultum seu ad exercitia fidei beneficentiam refert, atq; in primæ classis legibus numerat. Quæ eò pluribus commemorare libuit, vt confirmaret etiam Mosem ipsum plus fidei pietatiq; veræ quàm externis operibus tribuere: vt nefas sit Christianos homines, quibus velum debebat esse depositum ab oculis, ab operibus ad pietatem argumenta ducere.
units.tr: Although this subject might seem to belong to the second table of the precepts, which deals with duties toward our neighbour, Moses rightly assigns it to the first table, since, as we have said, it is an exercise of true faith in God. For just as the philosophers held that nature is the principle from which every honourable act flows, and that a good man commits nothing foreign to it, and therefore that whoever has one virtue has them all; so Christian doctrine sets forth the divine will as the very rule of honourable actions, which the man endowed with faith regards alone and does nothing contrary to. Thus it comes about that all honourable and good actions flow from faith as from a spring and principle. Otherwise, many men perform excellent deeds, but are moved by different and various causes: one pities the needy from a certain natural impulse; another helps the poor from desire for praise; many for the sake of advancing their own advantage, or so that God or the one they have benefited may reward them. So you may see one and the same work springing from very diverse sources. But that is the true work of virtue which proceeds from faith. For this reason Moses refers beneficence to the outward worship of God, or to the exercises of faith, and counts it among the laws of the first class. I have been pleased to recall these things at length so as to confirm that Moses himself ascribes more to faith and true piety than to external works; so that it is wrong for Christians, from whose eyes the veil ought to have been removed, to draw proofs of piety from works.

units.la: Beneficentiam autem sic commendat Moses vt proponat legem quandam, qua Deus inopiæ consuluerat, de anno septimo videlicet, in quo remissio quædam erat debitorū & seruitutis. Eam remissionem primum paucis proponit: tum quibus in rebus fit propositā mon-strat, nempe in remissione debitorum & seruitutis: quibus addit nonnulla de primogenitis. At hic quidem remissionem æris alieni primum docet.
units.tr: Moses commends beneficence in this way: he sets out a certain law by which God provided for the needy, namely concerning the seventh year, in which there was a certain release of debts and of bondage. First he briefly sets out this release; then he shows in what matters it is proposed, namely in the remission of debts and of bondage, to which he adds some points about firstborn animals. But here he first teaches the remission of financial debt.

units.la: A termino septimi anni facies remissionem. Hæc vero sit ratio remissionis. Omnis creditor re-mittere debet manum suam, is scilicet qui mutuo dedit proximo suo, &c. Quibus ostendit quæ qualisq; ea sit æris alieni remissio, & quos spectet potissimum. Ergo talis esto, ut ne debito-res urgeantur: sed quoniam à terra quiescente & fructus nullos proferente nihil accipiunt ipsi, ideo nihil etiam solvere teneantur.
units.tr: "At the end of the seventh year you shall make a release. And this is the manner of the release: every creditor shall release what he has lent to his neighbour," and so on. By these words he shows what kind of release of debt this is and whom it chiefly concerns. The law is thus to be observed so that debtors are not pressed; but since they receive nothing from the land, which lies fallow and yields no produce, they are therefore not bound to pay anything either.

units.la: Atque hæc lex quatenus civilis est, docet bonitatem & beneficentiam erga proximum, quæ est charitatis species, ut ne nimis rigidi simus in exigendis debitis. In quo permultum situm est, præsertim quando rigidus creditor ædibus propulsat atq; in exilium agit familias, quæ si ipse esset mitior starent. Iam Moses voluit hoc fratres dare fratribus ut alius alij parceret. Quid dices Christum, in quo restauruntur ac perficiuntur omnia, requirere? Iam si parabolas illas euangelicas non solum allegorice, verumetiá civiliter accipias, nempe ut cogitetur quantum Deo tu ipse debeas, & quam clementer ille moram sustineat: simul [?]discesquam ipse in proximum tibi minus debentem benignus esse debeas.
units.tr: And this law, insofar as it is civil, teaches goodness and beneficence toward our neighbour, which is a form of charity: that we should not be too harsh in exacting what is owed. Much depends on this, especially when a harsh creditor drives families out of their houses into exile, which they would have kept if he himself had been gentler. Now Moses wished brothers to give this to brothers, so that each should spare the other. What will you say Christ, in whom all things are restored and perfected, requires? Now if you take those gospel parables not only allegorically but also in their civil sense, namely that you should consider how much you yourself owe to God, and how patiently he bears with you, you should at the same time learn how kind you ought to be toward a neighbour who owes you less.

units.la: Sed ipsis etiam debitoribus cogitandum est, quod Paulus Rom.13. dicit omnibus sua red-denda debita. Anabaptistæ vocum naturam inverterunt, quando mutuum ceu donum acci-piunt, cum interpretantur illud dictum Domini, mutuum dantes, nihil inde sperantes. Quod si ne fortem quidem reddi volunt, dicant donum, non mutuum, ut res verbis propriis ex-primant. Summa, charitas utrique mandatur & debitori & creditori. At eam, si cum alterius detrimento rem suam familiarem augeat, debitor omnem prætorit.
units.tr: But debtors too must consider what Paul says in Rom. 13: that debts are to be paid to all. The Anabaptists have turned the nature of words upside down when they take a loan as a gift, interpreting that saying of the Lord, "lending, expecting nothing in return," in this way. But if they do not even want the principal to be repaid, let them call it a gift, not a loan, so that they express the matter in proper words. In short, charity is commanded to both debtor and creditor. But if the debtor, by enriching his own household at another's expense, neglects that charity, he commits every fault.

units.la: Sed hæc ipsa quam præscribit Moses debitorum remissio, quatenus est ex cerimoniarum genere, multa ac magna habet mysteria, quæ si considerentur multum prosunt.
units.tr: But this very remission of debts which Moses prescribes, insofar as it belongs to the kind of ceremonies, has many great mysteries, which, if considered, greatly benefit us.

units.la: 1 Discerent homines parsimoniam: ac ne sua abligurirent omnia, verum reconderent ali-qua quibus viverent anno septimo. Quod utinam hoc tam profuso seculo reputaretur: quo non vivitur, ut possimus quicquam commodare egenis, imo sic vivimus potius, ut ipsi subin de accipiamus mutuum. Quin multi mutuum accipiunt, quæ sciunt se non posse persolvere: quid hoc est aliud quàm ex alieno vivere? Dein culpam in res alias atq; alias reicimus, ut in populi multitudinem, in artes, in alia. Ergo legem hanc rectè ponderemus, ut ne sit fera in fundo parsimonia.
units.tr: 1 Men would learn thrift, and not squander everything they have, but would put something aside to live on in the seventh year. Would that this were considered in this so extravagant age, in which people live in such a way that they cannot lend anything to the needy; rather, we live in such a way that we ourselves now and then have to borrow. Indeed, many borrow what they know they cannot repay: what is this other than living on what belongs to others? Then we blame other things, such as the multitude of the people, the trades, and other things. Let us therefore weigh this law rightly, so that thrift does not become wild and reckless.

units.la: 2 Discerent homines se esse feudatarios Dei, cuius terra sit propria. Multi suis opibus quasi propriis abutuntur, cum potius earum sint quæstores. Unde eiusmodi profusos & ma-lefidos quæstores interdum officio removet Dominus. Ergo res aliter erat existimanda. Ac quemadmodum non nobis nascimur docti, prudentes, eloquentes, fortes: sic non nobis etiam nascimur divites. Ergo sua quibus nati sunt impertiant bona.
units.tr: 2 Men would learn that they are stewards of God, whose land is his own. Many misuse their wealth as if it were their own, when in fact they are rather its stewards. Therefore the Lord sometimes removes such wasteful and dishonest stewards from their office. So things ought to have been regarded differently. And just as we are not born learned, wise, eloquent, or brave, so too we are not born rich. Let them therefore share the goods with which they were born.

units.la: 3 Ut suam in Deum hoc ipso exercerent fidem: veluti cum viderent vno anno tantum fru-ctuum provenire, quod in plures sufficeret, de benedictione sic semper animis perfusu[?] ha-berent: etiamsi minus fertilis vnus annus esset, tamen Deum posse suos salvos conservare, cum vno toto anno nihil proveniat, & tamen in vita conserventur. Quod nostra ætate cogi-tatum faceret, ut animis æquioribus calamitates ferremus.
units.tr: 3 That they might exercise their faith in God in this very matter: for example, when they saw that in one year so much produce came forth that it would suffice for more people, they would always have their minds filled with the blessing; and even if one year were less fruitful, they would still believe that God could keep his people safe, since in a whole year nothing might be produced and yet they would be preserved in life. If this were considered in our own age, it would make us bear calamities with more even minds.

units.la: 4 Ut admonerentur peccati, quod sterilitatis efficiens est causa. Etenim terra licet non culta tamen vberes fructus antea proferebat quàm peccatum esset. Unde si peccata peccatis cumulemus sterilitates aliæ alias comitantur.
units.tr: 4 That they might be reminded of sin, which is the efficient cause of barrenness. For the land, though untilled, used to yield abundant fruits before sin existed. Hence, if we heap sins upon sins, one barrenness follows another.

units.la: 5 Remissionis eius quæ per Christum fidelibus obtigit admonerentur: Quod est augu-stissimum mysterium. Sed de eo aliàs. Hæc de remissione.
units.tr: 5 That they might be reminded of the remission which has come to believers through Christ. This is the most august mystery. But of that on another occasion. Let this suffice concerning the remission.

units.la: Quos vero hæc remissio respiciat, sic docet: Ab alieno poteris exigere, qui vero frater tuus est, hunc requiescere sinat manus tua. Quibus verbis docet ipsis Israelitis ac non etiam exteris hominibus hoc indultum esse. Ac quoniam civilis lex esset, iuri civili voluit esse consenta-neam.
