Etenim in rebus quæ spectant animam, nulla est personarum ratio, cum sola fides re-spiciatur. Sed in externis & civilibus rebus est ius personarum, ut inter indigenam & pe-regrinum interfit aliquid. Indigena cum sua tum maiorum causa prærogativam habet, & si vir bonus sit, est melius meritus de patria. Magistratus ergo eos ceu pater in liberos affectus esse debet. Peregrinis dein atq; exteris hominibus concedit etiam ut detur mutuum, aliàs re-mitti non vetaret.
units.tr: As to whom this remission concerns, he teaches thus: "Of a foreigner you may exact it; but whatever is owed by your brother, let your hand let it rest." By these words he teaches that this indulgence was granted to the Israelites themselves, and not to foreigners. And since it is a civil law, he wished it to agree with civil right. For in matters that concern the soul there is no distinction of persons, since faith alone is regarded. But in external and civil matters there is a right of persons, so that there is some difference between a native and a foreigner. A native has a prerogative both on his own account and on account of his ancestors, and if he is a good man he has deserved better of his country. The magistrate therefore ought to be disposed toward them as a father toward his children. Moreover, he also allows that loans be given to foreigners and strangers; otherwise he would not have forbidden their release.

units.la: In quo videmus ut sua cuique iura salva Deus esse semper voluerit.
units.tr: In this we see that God has always wanted each person's rights to remain intact.

units.la: Sed typus hic etiam considerandus est, ut videlicet Deum veris & Christo infitis Ifrae-litis debita condonare: exteris autem benefacere quidem & indulgere tempus pœnitentiæ, sed quod extra Christi septa manent, nihil remittere. Enitendum est deinceps, vt omnibus be nefaciamus, in primisq; domesticis fidei. Christo sit honos, Amen.
units.tr: But this type should also be considered, namely that God forgives debts to the true Israelites who are grafted into Christ, while to foreigners he indeed does good and grants a time of repentance, but remits nothing to those who remain outside the fold of Christ. From now on we must strive to do good to all, and especially to those of the household of faith. To Christ be honour. Amen.

units.la: SERMO XXX.
units.tr: Sermon XXX.

units.la: 4 Omnino non sit in te mendicus, quoniam vbertim locupletabit te Dominus in terra quam Dominus Deus tuus dat tibi, vt eam haereditate possideas.
units.tr: 4 There shall be no beggar among you, for the Lord will richly bless you in the land which the Lord your God gives you to possess as an inheritance.

units.la: 5 Modo diligenter audias vocem Domini Dei tui, vt custodias & facias tutum istud praeceptum, quod ego tibi hodie praecipio.
units.tr: 5 Only diligently obey the voice of the Lord your God, so that you keep and do this command which I give you today.

units.la: 6 Quandoquidem Dominus Deus tuus te locupletauit quemadmodum pollicitus est tibi: mutuo dabis multis gentibus, tu vero mutuo nihil accipies: dominaberis gentibus multis, ipsa vero tibi non dominabuntur.
units.tr: 6 For the Lord your God has blessed you as he promised you. You will lend to many nations, but you will borrow from none. You will rule over many nations, but they will not rule over you.

units.la: 7 Si fuerit in te pauper aliquis, scilicet ex fratribus tuis, intra vnam portarum tuarum, in terra tua, quam Dominus Deus tuus dabit tibi, ne obfirmes cor tuum, neq; contrahas manum tuam a fratre tuo paupere.
units.tr: 7 If there is any poor man among you, that is, one of your brothers, within any of your gates in your land which the Lord your God gives you, do not harden your heart or close your hand against your poor brother.

units.la: 8 Sed liberaliter aperies illi manum tuam, & des illi mutuum, quod satis sit penuriae eius qua laborat.
units.tr: 8 But you shall open your hand freely to him and lend him whatever is enough for the need under which he labours.

units.la: 9 Caue ne forte subeat cor tuum cogitatio impia, talis scilicet. Accelerat annus septimus, annus videlicet remissionis, & ob hoc malignus sit oculus tuus erga fratrem tuum pauperem, ita vt non des ei, & ille clamet contra te ad Dominum, fiatque tibi peccatum.
units.tr: 9 Beware lest an impious thought come into your heart, namely this: the seventh year, the year of release, is approaching, and so your eye is evil toward your poor brother, so that you do not give him anything, and he cries out against you to the Lord, and it becomes a sin for you.

units.la: 10 Omnino dabis ei, & non sit pectus tuum malignum quum tu das ei, nam huius rei gratia Dominus Deus tuus locupletabit ac fortunabit te in cunctis operibus, & in cunctis ad quae admoueris manum tuam.
units.tr: 10 You shall certainly give to him, and your heart shall not be grudging when you give to him, for on account of this thing the Lord your God will bless you and enrich you in all your works and in all that you put your hand to.

units.la: 11 Quoniam nunquam deerunt pauperes in terra, proinde praecipio tibi, dicens, Liberaliter aperi manum tuam fratri tuo, pauperi tuo atq; inopi tuo in terra tua.
units.tr: 11 For there will never be lack of poor in the land; therefore I command you, saying: Open your hand freely to your brother, to your poor and needy one in your land.

units.la: QVemadmodum Dominus apud Esaiam profitetur, se nolle sacrificijs, verum misericordia atque erga pauperes beneficentia coli: sic Moses in expositione earum, quae verum Dei cultum spectant, legum, docet, nullum cultum esse Deo gratiorem eo qui in beneficentia consistit. Ac quo sciamus quis hac in re modus requiratur, tria virtutis eius genera ponit: vnum, quando debitores non vrgemus iniquis ac nimium rigidis exactionibus: alterum, quando mutuum damus egentibus: tertium, quando in seruos propitij & clementes sumus.
units.tr: As the Lord professes through Isaiah that he does not wish to be worshipped with sacrifices, but with mercy and beneficence toward the poor, so Moses, in setting out the laws that concern the true worship of God, teaches that no worship is more pleasing to God than that which consists in beneficence. And so that we may know what measure is required in this matter, he sets out three kinds of this virtue: first, when we do not press our debtors with unjust and excessively harsh demands; second, when we lend to the needy; third, when we are gracious and merciful toward our servants.

units.la: Iam quia primum genus est expositum, dicit de secundo. In quo sic versatur, vt ostendat mutuum omnino dandum esse, sed eo ipso tamen hoc respiciendum, vt nulli sint in ciuitate pauperes, verum omnibus quod sufficiat suppeditetur. In quo primum confirmando la borat, tum autem docendo atq; exponendo.
units.tr: Now since the first kind has been set out, he speaks of the second. In this he works to show that a loan must certainly be given, yet that in giving it we must also take care that there are no poor in the city, but that everyone is supplied with what is sufficient. In this he labours first to confirm the point, and then to teach and explain it.

units.la: Vt confirmet dicit, Omnino non sit in te inops, quoniam vbertim locupletabit te Dominus, &c. Inopem eum significat Hebraea dictio, qui non sua culpa, sed aliqua mala fortuna ad inopiam redactus sit: quem vult, si ditari nequeat, tamen mendicitatis miserijs & molestijs liberari.
units.tr: To confirm it, he says: Let there be no needy one among you, since the Lord will richly bless you, and so on. The Hebrew word signifies one who has been reduced to want not through his own fault but through some misfortune; he wishes that, even if such a person cannot be made rich, he at least be freed from the miseries and troubles of begging.

units.la: Atque haec quidem lex & honesta reipub. est & vtilis. Quid enim est turpius quam homines alios opibus abundare, pauperie contra alios ringi? quid pernitiosius quam multos esse in repub. pauperes?
units.tr: Indeed this law is both honourable and useful to the commonwealth. For what is more shameful than that some men should abound in wealth while others are worn down by poverty? What is more pernicious than that there should be many poor in a commonwealth?

units.la: Sed ipse rationes affert. Vnam, quoniam vbertim locupletabit te Dominus Deus tuus. Minime mala ratio. Nam haec est illa, quam Deus in rebus humanis feruat aequalitas, vt alios vel esse diuites, pauperes alios: ac quemadmodum diuites facit propter pauperes, sic eosdem pauperes propter diuites: nempe vt hi liberalitate, illi patientia, vtrique fide exerceantur. Quamobrem si diues sis cogita, hanc ipsam ob causam opes tibi datas esse, vt pauperibus opem feras. Eadem ratio patriarchis, Abrahamo, Iobi, Tobiae, caeterisque fuit. Et natura fert, vt diues in alios redundet, pauper indigus id accipiat quo caret. Sic Israelitæ monen- tur, vt quando ipsi terram fertilem acceperint, sua in alios bona redundare patiantur.
units.tr: But he gives his reasons. The first is: since the Lord your God will richly bless you. This is by no means a poor reason. For this is that equality which God maintains in human affairs: some are rich and others poor, and just as he makes some rich for the sake of the poor, so he makes those same poor for the sake of the rich, namely so that the one may be exercised in liberality, the other in patience, and both in faith. Therefore, if you are rich, consider that riches have been given you for this very reason, that you may bring help to the poor. The same reason applied to the patriarchs: Abraham, Job, Tobit, and others. Nature also brings it about that the rich overflow toward others, and the needy poor receive what they lack. In this way the Israelites are warned that when they have received a fertile land, they should allow their good things to overflow to others.

units.la: Quanto magis hoc decebit populum Christianum, qui se ipso charitatis nexu debet con- tinere? Luc. 4. mulieres diuites dabant Christo egenti. In Act. habes: Nō erit inter eos egens. Corpus vnum fumus: igitur naturæ consentaneum est, vt alter alterius inopiæ succurrat. Est turpissimum nos opibus affluere, alijs contra malè esse propter inopiam. Est etiam per- nitiosum ecclesiæ non haberi curam pauperum, quod ab ea pauperes ad papatum secedant, & in ea sint propter inæqualitatem æmulationes.
units.tr: How much more will this befit the Christian people, who ought to be bound together by the bond of charity? In Luke 4 wealthy women gave to Christ in his need. In Acts you have: there will be no needy among them (Acts 4). We are one body; therefore it accords with nature that one should help the want of another. It is most shameful that we should abound in riches while others fare badly through poverty. It is also pernicious for the Church not to take care of the poor, since because of this the poor fall away to Papacy, and because of inequality there are rivalries within the Church.

units.la: Obijcias: At fieri potest, vt etiam ipse egeam. Respondeo: Solent hoc auari prætexere: verum præuenit eam obiectione Moses hoc ipso, quod dicit, fatis fore eis si audiát, custodiát, faciant verbū Do. En causas inopiæ, vel non audire, vel audire quidem, sed non seruate ver- bum Domini. Pijs semper est fatis: ac nihil cum sit, nihil defit tamen. Exemplo sunt Abraham, Iacob, Dauid, Solomon, Christus, Apostoli. Iam egeni fumus, quia forte nostra parum con- tenti, quia luxu perditi. Multum superesset quod pauperibus dares, si luxus esset minor. Quare fis pius & locupletabit te Dominus: & si fiat idipsum propterea factum esse memine ris, vt pauperibus subuenias.
units.tr: You may object: but it may happen that I too become needy. I answer: the covetous commonly put forward this excuse. But Moses forestalls this objection by the very thing he says, that it will be enough for them if they hear, keep, and do the word of the Lord. Here are the causes of want: either not to hear, or to hear but not keep the word of the Lord. For the godly there is always enough, and though they have nothing, yet nothing is lacking to them. Abraham, Jacob, David, Solomon, Christ, and the Apostles are examples. Now we are in need because perhaps we are little content with what we have, because we are ruined by luxury. There would be much left over to give to the poor if luxury were less. Therefore be godly, and the Lord will enrich you; and remember that this very thing has been done so that you might help the poor.

units.la: Altera, Dominaberis, &c. Beatius simul ac magnificentius est dare, quàm accipere: iam si Deus vt possis dare dedit, fac des: ne res eò redigantur tuæ, vt accipere cogare potius quàm dare, nec detur tamen.
units.tr: The second reason: you will rule, and so on. It is at once more blessed and more magnificent to give than to receive. Now if God has given you the means to give, then give; lest your affairs be brought to such a state that you are compelled to receive rather than to give, and yet even then nothing is given.

units.la: Quomodo verò efficiatur, vt rebus ad vitam necessarijs, egeat nemo, hoc ipso Moses do cet, quod mutuum introductum est. Dicit enim: Si fuerit in te pauper aliquis, des illi mutuum, &c. In quo profecto Mosem iura gentium sequuntur: nec quicquam est ad vitam humanam sustentandam magis aptum atque idoneum. Etenim si quis habeat pecuniam, re verò ca- reat, vel contra: in promptu sunt emptio & venditio: sin res alias habeat, alijs indigeat, per- mutatio: si nec pecunia, nec res suppetant, aut Dominus alienare sua nolit, accommodatio est: at vbi periculum est, ne res vsu consumantur, mutuum præsto est, in quo nullum esse potest accommodanti incommodum. Vnde mutuum ex eo nominatur quod de meo fit tuum, autho re Paulo Iureco s. l. 2. §. appellata ff. fi certum petatur.
units.tr: How it may be brought about that no one lacks the things necessary for life, Moses teaches by this very thing, that a loan has been introduced. For he says: If there is any poor man among you, give him a loan, and so on. In this the laws of the nations surely follow Moses, and nothing is more suitable and fitting for sustaining human life. For if someone has money but lacks goods, or the reverse, there are buying and selling at hand; if he has other goods but needs other things, there is exchange; if neither money nor goods are available, or the owner is unwilling to part with his own, there is lending on loan; but where there is danger that things will be consumed by use, a loan is ready to hand, in which there can be no disadvantage to the lender. Hence a loan (mutuum) is so named because what is mine becomes yours (de meo fit tuum), as the jurist Paulus says, in law 2, §. appellata, ff. si certum petatur.

units.la: Atque sic Deus humanam vitam deuinxit mutuis operis atq; auxilijs. In quo quid sit e- nitendum, quid item cauendum hoc loco docet.
units.tr: And thus God has bound human life together by mutual works and helps. Here he teaches what must be striven for, and likewise what must be avoided.

units.la: Enitendum quid sit demonstrat antithesi. Primum, ne obfirmes cor, neue contrahas manu. Cor obfirmare est durum esse in pauperes. Sic enim natura comparati sumus, vt obtutu ca- lamitatum & miseriarum moueantur, quando cor habet villos in hoc factos, vt moueatur. Sed sunt aliqui vel invidia, vel avaritia, vel alijs affectibus indurati, vti moueri nullo modo possint: veluti Pharao, Amelech, Saul, Iudæi, persequutores Euangelij, & rigidi distributores eleemosynarum. Notandum est illud de Samaritani misericordia positum in Euan- gelio Lucæ verbum, σπλαγχνίσθη: quod ei viscera commota aspectu miseri hominis docet.
units.tr: He shows what must be striven for by means of an antithesis: first, do not harden your heart or close your hand. To harden the heart is to be hard toward the poor. For we are so constituted by nature that we are moved by the sight of calamities and miseries, since the heart has been made with fibres that it may be moved. But some are hardened by envy, avarice, or other passions, so that they cannot be moved in any way: as Pharaoh, Amalek, Saul, the Jews, the persecutors of the Gospel, and the stingy distributors of alms. It must be noted that the word in the Gospel of Luke describing the mercy of the Samaritan, esplanchnisthē [σπλαγχνίσθη], shows that his bowels were moved at the sight of the wretched man.

units.la: Manum contrahere, est parcum esse erga miseros: sicuti illam aperire est esse li- beralem: quod ipse exponit dicens, vt sis liberalis, & des ei quod satis est.
units.tr: To close the hand is to be sparing toward the wretched, just as to open it is to be generous; this he himself explains, saying: that you be generous and give him what is enough.

units.la: Atque hoc enitendum esse, docent sacræ literæ: Psalmo iii. dicitur pius hoc ipso beatus esse, quod propter beneficentiam Deo sit proximus. Esaiæ quinquagesimo octauo cap. Dominus pro ieiunijs & sacrificijs vult misericordiam. Et beneficentiam Paulus λειτουργίαν appellat. Idem Coloffenf. fecundo cap. Bonum (inquit) facientes non deficiamus: tempore enim suo metemus. In priori Ioannis tertio cap. Qui habuerit substantiam mundi huius, & viderit fratrem suum egere, & clauserit viscera sua ab eo, quomodo charitas manet in eo? fi- lioli non diligamus tantum verbo neque lingua, sed opere & veritate. Ex quo perspicuum est enitendum nobis esse, vt in pauperes munifici simus.
units.tr: Holy Scripture teaches that we must strive for this. In Psalm 3 the godly man is called blessed for the very reason that, by his beneficence, he is near to God. In Isaiah 58 the Lord desires mercy rather than fasts and sacrifices. Paul calls beneficence a service [λειτουργίαν]. The same apostle, in the second chapter of Colossians, says: "Let us not be weary in well doing, for in due season we shall reap." In the first chapter of the First Epistle of John: "But whoso hath this world's good, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him? My little children, let us not love in word, neither in tongue, but in deed and in truth." From this it is plain that we must strive to be generous to the poor.

units.la: Cauendum autem est, ne prætextu propinqui anni remissionis quod posses dare neges. Et hoc quasi genere prætextus omnes tollit. Christus dicit, Mutuum dantes nihil inde spe- rantes. Charitas nescit vllos prætextus, quibus tamen abundat auaritia.
units.tr: We must take care, however, that under the pretext of the approaching year of release you do not refuse what you could give. Such a pretext, as it were, removes all giving. Christ says: "Lend, hoping for nothing again." Love knows no pretexts, yet covetousness abounds in them.

units.la: Nota Mosis phrases: Oculus malignus. In oculis apparet animus fortis & timidus: tristis & lætus: amicus & liuidus. Vnde oculus bonus pro bono animo & contra accipitur. Solo- mon in Prouerb. Oculus bonus benedicetur quia dat de cibo suo pauperi.
units.tr: Note Moses' phrase, "an evil eye." The mind shows itself in the eyes: whether it is bold or timid, sad or glad, friendly or spiteful. Hence "a good eye" is taken for a good disposition, and the reverse for the opposite. Solomon in Proverbs: "He that hath a bountiful eye shall be blessed, for he giveth of his bread to the poor."

units.la: Ne clamet contra te, quippe quasi ius naturæ violaris ceu Cain Abelum occidens. Ve- luti quidam reprehensus quod improbo dedisset munus, non homini dedi, sed humanæ forti. Et apud Plutarchum in libro de Sera vindicta Numinis scriptum extat hirundinem stridore seu clamoribus commotum latronem, vt se ipse latrocinij ante annos triginta com-misi reum fecerit. Quod indicio est peccata contra nos clamare. Iam si Dominus pauperum curam tantam habet, certum est eorum ipsum esse vindicem. Vnde Psalmus dicit, Oculi Domini pauperem respiciunt. Et Christus summam paupertatem expertus, non potest non misereri pauperum. Quicunque ergo sunt diuites, aut opum ecclesiasticarum quaestores, ij se meminerint vocibus & clamatibus pauperum apud Deum accusari, si illis non opem ferant.
units.tr: Lest he cry out against you: for you would be violating, as it were, the law of nature, like Cain slaying Abel. Like a certain man who, when rebuked for having given a gift to a wicked person, replied that he had not given it to a man but to humanity at large. And in Plutarch's book On the Delay of Divine Justice it is written that a swallow, stirred by the shrieks and cries of a robber, made him the accuser of a theft he had committed thirty years before. This is evidence that sins cry out against us. Now if the Lord has such great care for the poor, it is certain that he is their avenger. Hence the Psalm says: "The eyes of the Lord look upon the poor." And Christ, who experienced the utmost poverty, cannot but have compassion on the poor. Therefore, whoever are rich, or are collectors of church revenues, let them remember that they will be accused before God by the voices and cries of the poor if they do not bring them help.

units.la: Et fiat tibi in peccatum, hoc est, peccati poenam. Quae exprimitur Matth.25.capite, Ite in ignem, &c.
units.tr: And let it be to you a sin, that is, the punishment of sin. This is expressed in Matthew 25, "Depart into the fire," etc.

units.la: Vt benedicat. Idem dicit Solomon in Prouer. faeneratur Domino qui miseretur pauperis. Luc.6.date & dabitur vobis. 1.Tim.6. reponi in coelis thesauros dicit. Matth.25. Venite benedicti patris mei, &c. Quae cum ita sint enitendum nobis est, vt ne quem fratrum nostrorum egere patiamur, sed vt tales in eos simus, quales in nos esse Christum volumus. Id Deus faxit. Amen.
units.tr: That he may bless you. Solomon says the same in Proverbs: "He who has pity on the poor lends to the Lord." Luke 6: "Give, and it shall be given to you." 1 Timothy 6 speaks of laying up treasure in heaven. Matthew 25: "Come, ye blessed of my Father," etc. Since this is so, we must strive so that we never allow any of our brothers to be in need, but so that we are towards them such as we want Christ to be towards us. May God grant it. Amen.

units.la: SERMO XXXI.
units.tr: SERMON XXXI.

units.la: 12 Si venditus fuerit tibi frater tuus Hebraeus aut Hebraea, seruierit tibi sex annis, anno septimo manumittes eum à te.
units.tr: 12 If your brother, a Hebrew man or woman, is sold to you, he shall serve you six years; in the seventh year you shall let him go free from you.

units.la: 13 Quum eum à te manumiseris, ne amandes eum vacuum:
units.tr: 13 When you let him go free from you, you shall not send him away empty.

units.la: 14 Sed munifice eum circumcingas de gregibus tuis, de horreo tuo, atq; de torcular tuo, quibus te locupletauit Dominus Deus tuus, vt des illi.
units.tr: 14 But you shall furnish him generously from your flocks, from your threshing floor and from your winepress, with which the Lord your God has blessed you, so that you give to him.

units.la: 15 Reuoca in memoriam quod & tu seruus fuisti in terra Ægypti, & quod te liberauerit Dominus Deus tuus, ob quam causam ego tibi hoc praecipio hodie.
units.tr: 15 Remember that you too were a servant in the land of Egypt, and that the Lord your God redeemed you; for this reason I command you this today.

units.la: 16 Quod si dixerit ad te, Non egrediar à te, diligo enim te & familiam tuam, eo quod fuerit ei bene apud te.
units.tr: 16 But if he says to you, I will not go out from you, for I love you and your household, because it has gone well with him with you,

units.la: 17 Sumes subulam, & transfiges ea aurem ad ostium, seruiet tibi perpetuo, quin & famulae tuae sic facies.
units.tr: 17 you shall take an awl and pierce his ear against the door, and he shall serve you forever. And you shall do the same to your female servant.

units.la: 18 Ne graueris eum manumittere à te, quoniam duplex est merces mercenarij sex illis annis quibus tibi seruiuit, & Dominus Deus tuus dedit tibi rerum successum, & felicitatem in omnibus quae fecerit.
units.tr: 18 Do not be grieved to let him go free from you, since the wages of a hired man for the six years he served you are double; and the Lord your God has given you success and prosperity in all that you do.

units.la: Vera illa ac pia hominum erga homines charitas, quam requirit Moses, ceu quoddam fidei verae exercitium, ea non solum in mutuo & in beneficentia, verum etiam in omni genere contractuum versatur. Sunt autem eorum multa & varia genera. Saepe enim pecunia sic datur vt videatur esse vendita, ita vt eam accipiens annuo censu sibi illam redimat, ac sortem simul cum censu fundo ceu pignori imponat: saepe etiam hypotheca datur: nec raro quis se ipse pro ea vendit & obstringit.
units.tr: That true and pious love of men toward men, which Moses requires, as a kind of exercise of true faith, is practised not only in lending and in beneficence but also in every kind of contract. And there are many and various kinds of these. For often money is given in such a way that it seems to be sold: the recipient redeems it for himself by an annual rent, and places the principal together with the rent upon the estate as a pledge. Often too it is given on mortgage; and not seldom a man sells and binds himself for it.

units.la: Ac quoniam graue est debitori suo ipsius corpore cauere, de eo ipso Moses hic sermonem instituit, ac dicit: Si quis pauper Hebraeus sese tibi in seruitutem dedat, anno septimo eum manumittes & quidem auctum beneficijs: quippe quod aequum sit te meminisse tuae ipsius fortunae, illius operarum atque officiorum, itemque benedictionis diuinae. Vtilis quidem locus est, verum vt rectius intelligi posit atque ad nostra tempora accommodari, operaepretium est, vt paulo altius repetamus qualis fuerit haec prisca seruitus, quaeq; fit illa quae nostris est vsitata temporibus.
units.tr: And since it is a grave matter to stand surety for a debt with one's own body, Moses here takes up this very subject and says: If a poor Hebrew sells himself to you into servitude, in the seventh year you shall let him go free, and indeed laden with benefits. For it is fitting that you remember your own fortune, his labours and services, and likewise the divine blessing. The passage is certainly useful; but so that it may be understood more correctly and applied to our times, it is worth our while to go back a little further and consider what this ancient servitude was, and what that servitude is which is customary in our own times.

units.la: Olim erat constitutio iuris gentium, qua quis dominio alieno contra naturam subijce-retur. Et serui aut nascebantur ex ancillis nostris, vt vernae: aut fiebant vel iure gentium, vt mancipia, vel iure ciuili, vt qui ad pretium participandum sese ipsi vendidissent.
units.tr: Formerly there was a rule of the law of nations by which a man was made subject to another's dominion against nature. Slaves were either born of our female slaves, as home-born slaves; or they were made slaves either by the law of nations, as captives, or by civil law, as those who had sold themselves to share in the price.

units.la: Iam vt olim paupertas, sic eadem ipsa multos nunc seruos facit. Et sunt diuersa genera. Aut enim sunt qui seruitutem annuam seruiant, vt quos domi nostrae fouemus seruos & ancillas: aut qui in diem seruiût, vt mercenarij: aut qui pro pecunia nobis aliquid efficiunt, vt artifices.
units.tr: Just as poverty once made men slaves, so it still does today. And there are different kinds. For some serve for a year, like the male and female slaves we keep in our households; others serve by the day, like hired labourers; others do some work for us for money, like craftsmen.

units.la: Hos quicunque sint omnes piè & iuste tractandos Moses hoc loco docet. Ac primum qualis in eos vir bonus esse debeat: tum qua de causa talis in eos esse iubeatur.
units.tr: Moses teaches in this place that all of these, whoever they are, must be treated piously and justly. He first shows what sort of man a good man ought to be towards them, and then why he is commanded to be such towards them.

units.la: Qualem te eis præbeas dicit, Si venditus tibi fuerit frater Hebræus &c. Quo docet seruum bonum & manumittendum tandem & beneficijs augendum esse. Id argumento est seruis fauendum & benefaciendum esse. Agnouerunt hoc Impp. qui dominorum in seruos effrenem potestatem coercendam esse ll.arbitrati sunt. Antoninus vitæ necisque potestatem dominis in seruos abstulit, voluitque eos humanius haberi, in alijs vitæ & iuris partibus suam illis potestatem reliquit illibatam. Leo Imp. arbitratus hominem nequaquam duriore potestate premendum esse, concesit seruis vti possent & sibi acquirere & testamentum facere. Cato dixit, homines esse meminerimus. Hanc æquitatē docuit Christus per Apostolum, qui capite quarto Colossensibus scribens ait: Vos Domini æqualitatem seruis exhibete, scientes quod & vos habeatis Dominum in cœlis.
units.tr: He says what sort of person you should show yourself to them: If your Hebrew brother is sold to you, etc. By this he teaches that a good servant must in the end be let go free and enriched with benefits. This is an argument that servants are to be favoured and benefited. The emperors recognised this, who thought that the unbridled power of masters over servants must be restrained by laws. Antoninus took from masters the power of life and death over their slaves, and wished them to be treated more humanely; in other parts of life and law he left their power over them unimpaired. The Emperor Leo, thinking that a man must by no means be oppressed by a harsher power, allowed slaves to be able both to acquire property for themselves and to make a will. Cato said that we should remember that they are men. This fairness Christ taught through the Apostle, who in the fourth chapter writing to the Colossians says: Masters, give your servants what is just and equal, knowing that you too have a Master in heaven.

units.la: Iam nostrum est cogitare quantam humanitatem & beneuolentiam seruo, mercenario, opificibus nostris debeamus: non eos despiciamus, sed in idem mali genus etiam nos posse incurrere cogitemus: non eos premamus, sed quid posit natura cogitemus: non eos sua mer-cede priuemus, sed hoc aratrum eorum esse cogitemus. Nec parua causa mendicitatis est, quod pauperes debita sibi mercede fraudantur. Vnde mendicare malunt, quàm magno cum labore esurire, opprimi, despici. Sed & pietatem imbibant cogita, clementer & benignè tracta, & opera tua quantum potes subleua: nec ægros eijce domo, quocunque tandem labo-rent morbo. Memento quod Paulus dixit seruum Dei te esse, qui si inutilem te vellet eijcere, iamdudum nullus esses. Et quemadmodum Moses petentibus libertatem seruis dare iubet: sic tu seruum ancillamque non quia frugi sunt, impedi quo minus suis fortunis atque bonis perfruantur: <bl>Hinders nit an güten schicken/hilff jnen Sarzü</bl>[?]. Quanto peius est si quis filium filiamue impediat? Sanè secus te Moses hic docet.
units.tr: Now it is our task to consider how much kindness and goodwill we owe to a servant, a hired man, our workers: let us not despise them, but let us consider that we too could fall into the same kind of misfortune; let us not oppress them, but consider what nature can bear; let us not deprive them of their wages, but consider that this is their plough. Nor is it a small cause of beggary that the poor are cheated of the wages due to them. Hence they prefer to beg rather than to starve, be oppressed and be despised after great labour. But also, consider that they have imbibed piety; treat them gently and kindly, and relieve their labour as much as you can; do not cast out the sick from your house, whatever illness they may be suffering from. Remember what Paul said, that you are a servant of God, who, if he wished to cast you out as useless, would long ago have left you none. And just as Moses commands that freedom be given to servants who ask for it, so you must not, because male and female servants are thrifty, hinder them from enjoying their own fortunes and goods: [German marginal note, garbled in the scan: "Do not hinder them from good things; help them along"]. How much worse is it if someone hinders his son or daughter? Certainly Moses teaches otherwise here.

units.la: Obijciat aliquis. At si manere quàm manu mitti malit, cur eum ipse non retineam? cur alij potius eum permittam, quàm mihi seruem? Respondit imò præuenit obiectionem occupatione, atque id non solum concedit, verum etiam quo pacto fieri debeat declarat. Si (inquit) voluerit manere, quia bene ei fuerit in tua familia, subula aurem transfigas, eoq; seruo perpetuo licet vtare. Qua cerimonia seruum Domino perinde obstrictum ad obediendum notat, atque antea Dominum seruo ad beneficentiam obstrinxerat. Nam subula ferrea significat herile imperium etiam durum, acutum atque asperum: auris obedientiam domino debitam: officium introeundi & exeundi quouis officium, vt admoneatur seruus obligationis qua toti familiæ est obstrictus ad afferendum & exportandum quoduis onus. Ac quemadmodum aurem subula penetrat, sic animum herile mandatum moueat.
units.tr: Someone may object: But if he would rather remain than be set free, why should I not keep him myself? Why should I rather let another have him than keep him as my servant? He answers this objection, or rather anticipates it, and not only concedes the point but also declares how it ought to be done: If (he says) he wishes to remain, because it has gone well with him in your household, you shall pierce his ear with an awl, and you may use him forever. By this ceremony he marks the servant as bound to obedience to his master just as the master had previously been bound to kindness to the servant. For the iron awl signifies the master's authority, even harsh, sharp and rough; the ear signifies the obedience owed to the master; the office of coming in and going out signifies any task at all, so that the servant is reminded of the obligation by which he is bound to the whole household to carry and export any burden whatever. And just as the awl pierces the ear, so let the master's command pierce the mind.

units.la: In quo videmus sacras literas Iuri personarum minime repugnare, sed suum cuique tributum velle. Fuere quidem & adhuc sunt ætate nostra Catabaptistæ fanaticum hominum genus, qui prætextu libertatis euangelicæ res nouas moliti sunt, & omnes homines promiscuè debitis censibus, vectigalibus, operis, obedientia liberare voluere: similes Euno illi Syro, qui Syriæ deæ ceremonias iactitans, ad libertatem & arma seruos vocabat. At Paulus hoc ipso quod dixit inter baptizatos, hoc est, Christo initiatos neq; liberum esse neq; seruum, de spiritali seruitute verba fecit. Ac tantum abest vt vir diuinus iura ciuilia sublata voluerit, vt ea se rata habere cum doctrina tum facto commonstrarit. Nam Eph. 6. cum ex lege de honorandis parentibus colligit iustè defendi potestatem dominorum in seruos, vultq; seruos ijs syncerè & ex animo parere: quid aliud docet quàm suum cuiq; tribuere? Dum idem 1. Tim. 6. monet, coercendam esse seruorum cotumaciam, ne turbetur herilis potestas, eaq; de causa malè audiat nomen Christianum, & rebellionis nota inuratur euangelio: an non Anabaptistarum errorem tollit? Hæc est eius doctrina. Sed hoc ipso quod Onesimum Philemoni remisit, idem se reuera sentire mihi videtur, etiam facto testatus esse. Et his apostolicæ doctrinæ veltigijs insistere voluisse & solitos esse Christianos Gangrenæ Synodi decretum significat, quod sic habet: εἰ τις δοῦλον προσφάσει θεοσεβίας διδάσκει καταφρονεῖν τῶν ἰδίων δεσποτῶν, καὶ ἀναχωρεῖν τῆς ὑπηρεσίας, καὶ μὴ μετ᾽ ὀνοίας καὶ πάσης τιμῆς τῷ ἑαυτῶ δεσπότῃ ἐξυπηρετεῖσθαι, ἀνάθεμα ἔστω. In quo videmus idem patres illos egisse, quod paulò ante dictum est Apostolo curæ fuisse, nempe vt ne quis Euangelicæ libertatis prætextu suum cuiquam ius negaret, eoque facto notam iniustitiæ verbo Dei inureret. Vnde & Theodoretus in eo sermone, quo docet ὅτι τὰς [?]ἐν φεύγοντας [?]ἀλλὰ ἐν τῷ πονηρῷ [?]δικαίως [?]λυμαίνεσθαι [?], multis ratio-nibus colligit seruitutem humanæ vitæ necessariam, ipsis feruis rectè rem reputantibus mi-nimè grauem esse. Ac mihi quidem dubium non est, quin præstaret multos nostræ ætatis ho-mines seruos quàm mendicos esse, operas suas præstare ciuibus, quàm otiosè circuire & e-leemosynis victitare: artibus liberalibus vacare & iuuare ciuitates, & dominis honestè, quàm suis affectibus & libidini turpiter inseruire. Quamobrem Abrahami, Iacobi, Iosephi, Mosis & aliorum exempla seruì sibi sumant ad obediendum, vti sese excitent. Nam vt dominos vult esse humanos, sic seruos requirit obedientes.
units.tr: In this we see that the sacred letters by no means oppose the right of persons, but wish each to have his due. There were indeed, and there still are in our own age, the Anabaptists, a fanatical kind of men, who under the pretext of evangelical liberty have attempted revolutions and wished to free all men indiscriminately from fixed taxes, tributes, services and obedience: like that Syrian Eunus, who, boasting of the ceremonies of the Syrian goddess, called slaves to liberty and arms. But Paul, by the very fact that he said that among the baptised, that is, those initiated into Christ, there is neither free nor slave, was speaking of spiritual servitude. And so far is the divine man from wishing civil rights to be abolished, that he has shown by both doctrine and deed that he holds them valid. For in Ephesians 6, when from the law concerning the honouring of parents he infers that the power of masters over servants is rightly defended, and wishes servants to obey them sincerely and from the heart, what else does he teach than to give each his due? And when he advises in 1 Timothy 6 that the stubbornness of servants must be restrained, lest the master's authority be disturbed and for that reason the Christian name be ill spoken of, and the mark of rebellion be branded upon the gospel, does he not remove the error of the Anabaptists? This is his teaching. But by the very fact that he sent Onesimus back to Philemon, he seems to me to show that he really thought the same, attesting it also by deed. And that Christians wished to follow these traces of apostolic doctrine and were accustomed to do so is shown by the decree of the Synod of Gangra, which reads thus: If anyone, under the pretext of piety, teaches a slave to despise his own masters, and to withdraw from service, and not to serve his own master with goodwill and all honour, let him be anathema. [εἰ τις δοῦλον προσφάσει θεοσεβίας διδάσκει καταφρονεῖν τῶν ἰδίων δεσποτῶν, καὶ ἀναχωρεῖν τῆς ὑπηρεσίας, καὶ μὴ μετ᾽ ὀνοίας καὶ πάσης τιμῆς τῷ ἑαυτῶ δεσπότῃ ἐξυπηρετεῖσθαι, ἀνάθεμα ἔστω.] In this we see that those Fathers did the same thing that was said a little earlier to have been the Apostle's concern, namely that no one should deny to another his right under the pretext of evangelical liberty, and by that act brand the word of God with the mark of injustice. Hence also Theodoret, in that sermon in which he teaches [that the things (?) should not be fled from, but the wickedness ... rightly ...] [ὅτι τὰς ἐν φεύγοντας ἀλλὰ ἐν τῷ πονηρῷ δικαίως λυμαίνεσθαι], gathers by many arguments that servitude is necessary for human life, and that to the servants themselves, reckoning the matter rightly, it is by no means grievous. And for my part there is no doubt that many men of our age would do better to be servants than beggars: to perform their services for the citizens rather than wander about idly and live on alms; to devote themselves to the liberal arts and help the cities, and to serve their masters honourably, rather than to serve their own passions and lusts shamefully. Therefore let servants take to themselves the examples of Abraham, Jacob, Joseph, Moses and others, so as to rouse themselves to obedience. For just as he wishes masters to be humane, so he requires servants to be obedient.

units.la: Cur autem talem te seruis præbere debeas, causas tres affert. Vnam; Quod & tu seruus fuisti in Ægypto. Bona quidem hæc & ad reprimendam superbiam momenti multum afferens causa est. Nihil enim perinde surgentes spiritus reprimit, ac fortunæ prioris recordatio. Quod tibi non vis fieri alteri ne feceris. Nemo bene imperat, nisi qui paruerit imperio. At vulgus nostrum dicit rusticum hominem, si in virum principem euaserit quauis nou-cula acutiorem esse. Quamobrem paupertatis tuæ memineris, vt pauperibus tanto sis magis propitius: ignobilitatis tuæ memor esto, vt homines obscuros atque inopes minus despicias.
units.tr: Moses gives three reasons why you should treat your servants in this way. The first is: For you too were a servant in Egypt. This is a good reason and a powerful check on pride. Nothing restrains rising spirits so well as the memory of one's former fortune. Do not do to another what you would not have done to yourself. No one commands well unless he has first obeyed. Yet our common saying is that a country fellow who rises to be a great man becomes sharper than any razor. So remember your own poverty, so that you may be all the more kind to the poor, and remember your own lowly birth, so that you may look down less on obscure and needy people.

units.la: Seruitus ipsa per se est tristis & misera, si præterea grauis sis tanto magis eos premet onus. Non abs re est quod Aristophaneus ille famulus conqueritur, dicens,
units.tr: Servitude in itself is sad and wretched, and if you add a heavy master, the burden crushes them all the more. The complaint of that servant in Aristophanes is not out of place, when he says:

units.la: ὡς ἀργαλέον [?]πρᾶγμα [?]δεῖν ὦ [?]ζῶ καὶ θεοί / [?]δ' ἄλλον γενέσθαι [?]δούλου [?]ἐλευθέρου δεσπότου [?].
units.tr: How grievous a thing it is to be a slave, and to live under the gods, and to have as master one who is not a slave but free. [ὡς ἀργαλέον πρᾶγμα δοῦλον εἶναι, ὦ ζῶ καὶ θεοί, ἕτερον δὲ γενέσθαι δούλου ἐλευθέρου δεσπότου]

units.la: Quod ipsum interpres poetæ minimè malè rem reputans pulchrè exponit, dicens, χαλεπὸν ὄντ' [?]τῇ φύσει τῷ δ' ἐλευθέρῳ χαλεπώτερον γίνεται, ἐὰν καὶ ἀνοήτῳ τις δεσπότῃ ὑπηρετῇ [?].
units.tr: The translator of the poet, reckoning the matter not badly, explains it nicely, saying: It is hard in itself to be a slave, but for a free man it becomes harder still if he serves a foolish master. [χαλεπὸν ὄντ' ἐν τῇ φύσει, τῷ δ' ἐλευθέρῳ χαλεπώτερον γίνεται, ἐὰν καὶ ἀνοήτῳ τις δεσπότῃ ὑπηρετῇ]

units.la: Ergo si Deo placuit seruum aliquem iugo tuæ potestatis præter naturam premi, tu ne quid oneris vltra quod nolit Deus illi imponas, cogitans te, si eodem esses loco, id minimè posse ferre. Atque hoc illud est quod Ægyptiacæ seruitutis eum admonet.
units.tr: Therefore, if it has pleased God that a servant be burdened under the yoke of your power beyond his nature, do not lay on him any burden beyond what God wills, and consider that if you were in the same position you could not bear it at all. This is what the memory of Egyptian servitude reminds him of.

units.la: Alteram causam Moses à mercede ducit, æquum esse vt meminerit seruum ipsi duplo potiorem fuisse mercenario: ac si mercenarium nec iugo seruitutis premere, nec inaneni [?]dimittere potuisset, certè seruum hoc beneficio multò minus esse spoliandum. Quæ causa gratitudinem postulat, quam negare pugnat cum natura. Etenim terra, animalia pro sump-tibus atque operis sibi præbitis fructus quantos maximos possunt reddunt: quid tu facias ô homo, cui seruus tantum acquisiuit.
units.tr: Moses takes the second reason from wages: it is fitting that he remember a servant was worth twice as much to him as a hired man. If he could not press a hired man with the yoke of servitude, nor dismiss him empty-handed, then a servant should be far less likely to be robbed of this kindness. This reason calls for gratitude, which it is contrary to nature to deny. For the earth and the animals return the greatest harvest they can for the expenses and labour given them. What, then, will you do, O man, to whom a servant has gained so much?

units.la: Tertia causa est benedictio Domini, qua qui fidelis est omnino solet adiuuari. Eam re-bus nostris immittat Pater cœlestis per Iesum Christum, Amen.
units.tr: The third reason is the blessing of the Lord, by which whoever is faithful is usually helped in every way. May the heavenly Father bestow it upon our affairs through Jesus Christ. Amen.

units.la: SERMO XXXII.
units.tr: Sermon XXXII.

units.la: 19 Omne primogenitum quod natum fuerit in armento tuo, & in grege tuo quod masculum est, conseruabis Domino Deo tuo, nec operaberis primogenito boum tui, nec tondebis primogenitum gregis tui.
units.tr: 19 All the firstborn males that are born of your herd and your flock, you shall consecrate to the Lord your God. You shall not work with the firstborn of your ox, nor shear the firstborn of your flock.

units.la: 20 In conspectu Domini Dei tui comedes illud per singulos annos, in loco quem elegerit Dominus, tu & domus tua.
units.tr: 20 Before the Lord your God you shall eat it year by year, in the place which the Lord shall choose, you and your household.

units.la: 21 Quod si vitium aliquod fuerit in eo, nempe si fuerit claudum, vel cæcum, vel habuerit aliud malum vitium, non mastabis [?]illud Domino Deo tuo.
units.tr: 21 But if there is any blemish in it, namely if it is lame or blind, or has any other serious defect, you shall not sacrifice it to the Lord your God.

units.la: 22 Sed intra portas tuas comedes illud, tam immundus quàm mundus pariter, vt capreamp & ceruum.
units.tr: 22 Within your gates you shall eat it, the unclean and the clean alike, as the roe and the hart.

units.la: 23 Modo ne sanguinem eius edas, sed in terram eum vt aquam fundes.
units.tr: 23 Only you shall not eat its blood, but you shall pour it out on the ground like water.

units.la: CUm divinus Moses fecundi praecepti vim & sententiam hoc ipso quod requireret ex terna quaedam religionis exercitia, satis superq; explicarit, & eorum exercitiorum alia Deu, alia proximum spectarint: iā sub huius expositionis fine, eiusmodi religionis exercitiū ponit, quod & Deum respiciat & proximum. Idipsum est primogenitorum Domino oblatum sacrificium. De primogenitis autem quae dicuntur hoc loco, tum demum intelligentur rectius cum primum de eorum causis & origine, & deinceps de eorum oblatione dicemus: Ac de causis quidem & origine primogenitorum sic statuendum est. Quanquam in Ægypto multa maxima facta sint miracula, tamen ex eorum omnium numero duo potissimum sunt quae censentur maxima. Vnum est, quod Dominus Ægyptiorum primogenita vna nocte per emeritatq; Israelitis pepercerit. Alterū quod durissimus Pharao hoc facto sic emollitus est, vt populum Israeliticum adeo propere exire coegerit; vt ne fermentandis panibus ocium daret. Horum memoriam duabus cerimonijs consecratam voluit, vsu intermentatorum panum & oblatione primogenitorum, quae Deus & ex hominibus, & ex iumentis sacra sibi voluit.
units.tr: Since divine Moses, in explaining the force and meaning of the second precept, has already set out sufficiently the various outward exercises of religion that it requires, and since some of these exercises regard God and others regard our neighbour, at the close of this exposition he now lays down an exercise of religion that concerns both God and neighbour. This is the sacrifice of the firstborn offered to the Lord. Concerning the firstborn spoken of here, we shall understand them more rightly once we have first said something of their causes and origin, and then of their offering. As to the causes and origin of the firstborn, the following must be held. Although many great miracles were wrought in Egypt, two of them are chiefly reckoned as the greatest. The one is that the Lord, in a single night, destroyed the firstborn of the Egyptians while sparing the Israelites. The other is that the most hard-hearted Pharaoh was so softened by this deed that he compelled the Israelite people to depart so hastily that they had no leisure even to leaven their bread. God wished the memory of these things to be consecrated by two ceremonies: the eating of unleavened bread, and the offering of the firstborn, which God claimed as holy to himself both from men and from beasts of burden.

units.la: Ea ratio sic erat. Hominum primogenita pecunia redimi consuêuerant, ac pro redemptis Leuitæ Deo sacri deuotiq; erant: animaliū immundorum primogenita itidem pecunia redimebantur, munda vero sacerdotibus tradebantur. Quae de re Exod. 13.22. Num.3.8.18.&c. scriptum est.
units.tr: The reason was this. The firstborn of men were customarily redeemed with money, and the Levites, being given in exchange for the redeemed, were consecrated and devoted to God. The firstborn of unclean animals were likewise redeemed with money, but the firstborn of clean animals were handed over to the priests. Concerning this matter, it is written in Exodus 13, Numbers 3, Numbers 18, and so on.

units.la: Et originem huius oblationis hanc ipsam esse quam diximus ipsa scriptura testis est cum dicit: si te filius tuus rogarit dicens, quid est hoc? respondebis: Eduxit nos Dominus manu potenti de terra Ægypti de domo seruitutis. Nam cum induratus esset Pharao, & nollet nos dimittere, occidit Dominus omne primogenitum in terra Ægypti. Idcirco sacrificio Domino omne quod aperit vuluam masculini sexus. Quae verba sacrificium hoc ipsum magnis vehunt laudibus, atq; etiam innuunt alias in eo repositas nobis esse vtilitates.
units.tr: That the origin of this offering is the one we have mentioned is attested by Scripture itself, when it says: "If your son shall ask you, saying, 'What is this?' you shall answer, 'The Lord brought us out of the land of Egypt with a mighty hand, out of the house of bondage. For when Pharaoh was hardened and would not let us go, the Lord slew every firstborn in the land of Egypt. Therefore I sacrifice to the Lord every male that opens the womb.'" These words commend this sacrifice with high praise, and they also indicate that other benefits are laid up for us in it.

units.la: Primum vt sacrificium ipsum rei gestae memoriam renouans, simul etiam Deum, quis qualisq; esset ex facti qualitate demonstraret, videlicet omnipotentem suorum vindicem & vltorem iniuriarum suis illatarum: quarum rerum cogitatio fidem, spem, obedientiam in hominibus ad suam ipsorum salutem excitaret.
units.tr: First, the sacrifice, by renewing the memory of the deed, at the same time shows forth God, who and what he is, from the quality of the deed: namely, as the almighty avenger and punisher of the wrongs done to his people. The thought of these things stirs up faith, hope, and obedience in men for their own salvation.

units.la: Deinceps, vt quemadmodum in decimis agnoscimus Deum nostris opibus non egere, sed vt ne nos agnoscere quae habemus esse Dei beneficia: sic in primogenitis agnoscamus eum primitias & initia bonorum nostrorum sibi vendicare, vt intelligamus sequentia ab ipso proficisci: Velut Dominus feudi munus accipit à feudatario. Gratitudo praeclara virtus est & naturae consentanea.
units.tr: Next, just as in tithes we acknowledge that God has no need of our wealth, but so that we may recognise what we have as God's benefits, so in the firstborn we acknowledge that he claims for himself the first-fruits and beginnings of our goods, so that we may understand that what follows proceeds from him, just as a lord receives a gift from his vassal. Gratitude is an excellent virtue and agreeable to nature.

units.la: Tertio, vt suus sacerdotibus victus esset. Nam è terra nihil illis cederat, haec ergo debebantur eis, vt ἵνα [illegible, ~4 letters] ac quo quisque esset Dei pariter & religionis amantior hoc ad tam sustentandum esset alacrior. Eadem in pendendis decimis nobis debebat esse ratio. Qui hic parcus est, in ipsum Deum parcus est. Vnde & munificis ciuibus sua benedictione Deus opes augebat, & efficiebat, vt quae dedissent ad illos redirent cum fœnore.
units.tr: Third, the sacrifice was to provide sustenance for the priests. For nothing came to them from the land, so these things were owed to them, so that each man, the more he loved God and religion, the more eagerly he would support them. The same reasoning ought to apply to our payment of tithes. He who is sparing here is sparing towards God himself. Hence God also increased the wealth of generous citizens with his blessing, and made it so that what they had given returned to them with interest.

units.la: Quarto, Christum ipsum his voluit repraesentare. Is enim est primogenitus omnis creaturae, quippe per quem omnia creata sunt & gubernantur. Quod pluribus verbis docet apostolus Coloss. 1. &c. Is etiam primogenitus est multorum fratrum, hoc est electorum, qui per ipsum placati Deo, sanctificati, haeredes facti sunt. Vnde & caput est nostrum. Habes eandem de re plura Roman. 8. cap. Is ipse est primogenitus resurgentium, quippe quem spiritus Dei primum suscitarit à mortuis, vt idem Colossen. scribens docet apostolus. Quarum rerum cogitatione fides, spes, charitas mirum in modum augentur: fides, quod scimus nos per Christum patri reconciliatos esse: charitas, quod in illo fratres simus: spes, quod in illo resurrecturi simus, & aeternum victuri.
units.tr: Fourth, God wished to represent Christ himself through these offerings. For he is the firstborn of every creature, since through him all things were created and are governed. The apostle teaches this at greater length in Colossians 1 and following. He is also the firstborn of many brethren, that is, of the elect, who through him have been reconciled to God, sanctified, and made heirs; hence he is also our head. You have more on this matter in Romans 8. He is himself the firstborn of those who rise again, since the Spirit of God first raised him from the dead, as the apostle teaches in writing to the Colossians. By the thought of these things, faith, hope, and love are wonderfully increased: faith, because we know that we have been reconciled to the Father through Christ; love, because in him we are brothers; hope, because in him we shall rise and live for ever.

units.la: Caeterum de eorum oblatione pauca dicit, ac solum ostendit locum, tempus, modum. Locum hoc ipso dicit, quod ait in conspectu Domini. Id enim perinde est, ac si locum eum dicat, in quo praesentiam suam attestetur, vt primum in Silo, tum in templo. Etsi enim Deus vbique suis ads[?]it, tamen sacris coetibus in primis sese praesentem praebet: Ac par est de beneficio communiter omnibus praestito publice Deo gratias agi. Vnde nos eucharistiam, quoniam est solennis gratiarum actio de beneficio publico, non priuatim aut seorsim à reliquis fratribus, sed publice celebramus. Et Paulus 1.Cor. 11.docet coenam dominicam non esse, quae non sit publica, cum dicit, non licere ijs coenam dominicam edere, qui propriam coenam oc cupent in edendo. Et baptismum priuatum esse nolumus cum infantes debeant offerri Do-[?] mino. Et matrimonium publice debet confirmari, cum Deus & ecclesia testes eam ad rem requiruntur. Valeant igitur qui priuata conuenticula quaerunt atq; amant.
units.tr: Otherwise, he says little about their offering, and shows only the place, the time, and the manner. He indicates the place by saying "before the Lord." For this is just as if he were saying the place where he attests his presence, as first at Shiloh, then in the temple. For although God is present everywhere, yet he shows himself especially present in sacred assemblies. It is fitting too that thanks be given to God publicly for a benefit bestowed on all in common. Hence we celebrate the Eucharist, since it is a solemn thanksgiving for a public benefit, not privately or apart from the other brethren, but publicly. And Paul, in 1 Corinthians 11, teaches that the Lord's Supper is not what is not public, when he says that those who take up their own supper in eating are not permitted to eat the Lord's Supper. We also do not want baptism to be private, since infants ought to be offered to the Lord. And marriage ought to be confirmed publicly, since God and the Church are required as witnesses to it. Let those then fare well who seek and love private little conventicles.

units.la: Tempus annum docet quemq; & merito. Nam cum Deus & opibus & familia in singulos annos augeat, cur non in singulos dies gratias ageremus? Quin si cogites continuatam esse diuinarum beneficiorum largitionem, facile est colligere gratiarum actionem Deo debitam; tam oportere etiam ipsam esse assiduam.
units.tr: Time teaches that the year is the proper measure. For since God increases both our wealth and our family year by year, why should we not give thanks every day? Indeed, if you consider that the bestowal of divine benefits is continuous, it is easy to conclude that the thanksgiving due to God ought also to be constant.

units.la: Modus sic describitur, vt intelligas quid eniti, quid item cauere debeas. Enitendum hic est, vt Domino consecres primogenita mascula: contra vero caueas, ne vel vitiosa Deo offeras & ea quae tibi non sint vsui, vel quae offers in vsus tuos conferas.
units.tr: The manner is described thus, so that you may understand what you must strive for and also what you must guard against. Here you must strive to consecrate to the Lord the firstborn males. On the contrary, you must take care neither to offer to God what is blemished, nor to keep for your own use what ought to be offered.

units.la: In quo mandata sunt illa. 1. Quae praecipua sunt ex illis quae diuinitus accepimus bonis, ea deberi Domino, hoc est, in gloriam Domini & salutem proximi cedere debere. Sic enim & Deo & proximo quod suum cuiusque est tribues, si diligas alterum, alterum reuereare.
units.tr: In this are contained those commands: first, that the chief of those goods we have received from God is owed to the Lord, that is, it ought to be given to the glory of the Lord and the salvation of our neighbour. For in this way you will render to God and to your neighbour what is each one's own, if you love the one and reverence the other.

units.la: Rursum cauendum ne tibi vsurpes, neue bonorum seces Deo tribuas, optimam partem ferues tibi, nec tibi tantum seruias, vt sunt qui tantum quae sua sunt quaerunt, de quibus etiam apostolus conqueritur.
units.tr: Again, you must beware lest you claim for yourself, and lest you withhold from God any part of your goods; you keep the best part for yourself, and serve only yourself, as those do who seek only what is their own. The apostle also complains of such people.

units.la: Hic feriuntur eorum conscientiae, qui Deo claudos & mutilos filios deputant ad euangelij praedicandi studium, qui suae aetatis florem libidine consumunt ac decrepitam senectam pietati, si Dijs placet, fouent, qui decimas ex paleis, eleemosynas ex reliquijs pendunt.
units.tr: Here the consciences are struck of those who consider their lame and maimed sons fit for the zeal of preaching the gospel; who spend the flower of their age in lust, and then, if it pleases the gods, cherish a decrepit old age for piety; who pay their tithes out of chaff and their alms out of leftovers.

units.la: Atq; haec affert Moses ceu conclusionem huius explicationis, ex qua discimus proximum diligere, Deum colere. Ei sit honos in secula, Amen.
units.tr: And Moses brings forward these things as the conclusion of this exposition, from which we learn to love our neighbour and to worship God. To him be honour for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT XVI. SERMO XXXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI. SERMON XXXIII.

units.la: Observa mensem Abib, vt facias Passah Domino Deo tuo, quoniam in mense Abib Dominus Deus tuus de Ægypto nocte te eduxit.
units.tr: Observe the month Abib, and keep the Passover to the Lord your God, for in the month Abib the Lord your God brought you out of Egypt by night.

units.la: 2 Sacrificabis igitur Passah Domino Deo tuo, oues & boues in loco, quem elegerit Dominus, vt illuc nomen suum ponat.
units.tr: 2 You shall therefore sacrifice the Passover to the Lord your God, sheep and oxen, in the place which the Lord shall choose, to cause his name to dwell there.

units.la: 3 Non comedas in eo fermentatum, sed septem diebus placentas infermenta-tas comedes, panes afflictionis, eo quod festinanter egressus fis de terra Ægypti, vt recorderis diei exitus tui de terra Ægypti cunctis diebus vitae tuae.
units.tr: 3 You shall eat no leavened bread with it; seven days you shall eat unleavened bread with it, the bread of affliction, for you came out of the land of Egypt in haste, that you may remember the day you came out of the land of Egypt all the days of your life.

units.la: 4 Nec videbitur tibi fermentum in omnibus finibus tuis septem diebus, neq; pernoctet ad lucem vsq;, de carne quam mactasti in vespera prioris diei.
units.tr: 4 No leaven shall be seen with you in all your borders for seven days, and none of the flesh which you sacrificed on the evening of the first day shall remain until morning.

units.la: 5 Non poteris mactare Passah intra vnam portarum tuarum, quas Dominus Deus tuus dederit tibi.
units.tr: 5 You may not sacrifice the Passover within any of your gates which the Lord your God gives you.

units.la: 6 Duntaxat in loco, quem elegerit Dominus Deus tuus, vt collocet nomen suum illic, mactabis Passah ad vesperam, quum sol occidit, stato tempore, quo egressus es ex Ægypto.
units.tr: 6 But at the place which the Lord your God shall choose, to cause his name to dwell there, you shall sacrifice the Passover in the evening, at sunset, at the time you came out of Egypt.

units.la: 7 Coques itaq;, & comedes in loco, quem elegerit Dominus Deus tuus, manere verteris[?] & ibis ad tentoria tua.
units.tr: 7 And you shall cook it and eat it in the place which the Lord your God shall choose; and in the morning you shall turn and go to your tents.

units.la: 8 Sex diebus comedes infermentatas placentas, die vero septimo fit coetus Domino Deo tuo, nullum opus facies.
units.tr: 8 Six days you shall eat unleavened bread, and on the seventh day there shall be a solemn assembly to the Lord your God; you shall do no work.

units.la: VANQVAM Deus neq; in veteri neq; in Nouo testamento religionem externis rebus velut locis & temporibus alligarit, tamen, vt ostendit apostolus, vult omnia in ecclesia decenter & ordine fieri. Quamobrem delectum, & obseruatione dierum, atq; temporum quoad cum verbo Dei non pugnauerint, fidelis nullus improbabit, verum ceu rem externae religioni cumprimis necessariam seruabit. Externa enim religio quasi quaedam imago est internae, & propterea ei ipsi consentanea fit necesse est: ni vel in su-perstitionem vel in impietatem degenerare debeat. Iam si Deum ceu summum veneretur interna religio, atque ad eius generis obsequia externam formet, locum & tempus sibi vendicabit.
units.tr: Although God, neither in the Old nor in the New Testament, has bound religion to external things such as places and times, yet, as the apostle shows, he wills that all things in the Church be done decently and in order. Therefore no faithful person will disapprove of the choice and observance of days and times, so far as they do not conflict with the Word of God; rather he will keep them as something especially necessary to external religion. For external religion is, as it were, an image of internal religion, and so it must necessarily agree with it, unless it is to degenerate into either superstition or impiety. Now if internal religion reveres God as supreme, and shapes external observances of this kind to serve him, it will claim for itself a place and a time.

units.la: Quemadmodum igitur Deus in Sina monte leges eas primum tulit, quae cultum internum simul & externum formant, eiq; deinceps quartā lege suum tempus assignauit: sic illarum legum expositionem Moses etiam instituit, ut primum de religione, tum de tempore exercendae religioni debito differat. Ac tribus tabulae prioris legibus expositis ad quartum transfit. Quod quoniam est de sabbatho, &c, ut supra dictum est, sabbathi nomine reliquas ferias ceu suo genere continet: iam ad id ipsum illustrandum, hunc de feriis tractatum instituit. Neque vero magnum feriarum numerum instituit, sed de tribus praecipuis hic disserit, ut de pascha, pentecoste, festo tabernaculorum. Ac in praesentia paschatis tempus, ritu, locum describit.
units.tr: Therefore, just as God on Mount Sinai first gave those laws which shape both internal and external worship, and afterwards assigned his own time to worship by the fourth law, so Moses also arranges the exposition of those laws, so that he first treats of religion and then of the time due for exercising it. And having expounded the laws of the first table, he passes to the fourth. Since this law concerns the sabbath, etc., and as has been said above, the name Sabbath comprehends the other feasts under its own kind, he now sets out this treatment of feasts in order to illustrate that very point. Nor does he set out a great number of feasts, but here discourses on three principal ones: the Passover, Pentecost, and the Feast of Tabernacles. And for the present, he describes the time, rite, and place of the Passover.

units.la: De tempore quo festum hoc celebrari debeat, Moses ad hunc modum verba facit. Obserua mensem Abib, ut facias Pascha Domino Deo tuo: quoniam in mense Abib de Ægypto, &c. Quibus verbis tempus huius festi sic ostendit, ut simul etiam qua de causa, & in cuius honorem fit institutum intelligamus. Tempus est mensis Abib, sic dictus a nouis fructibus, vel ut apud Latinos Aprilis ab aperiendo, quod tunc omnia renouentur, ac reuirescant praesertim in calidis regionibus.
units.tr: Concerning the time at which this feast ought to be celebrated, Moses speaks in this manner: Observe the month Abib, to keep the Passover to the Lord your God, for in the month Abib out of Egypt, etc. By these words he shows the time of this feast in such a way that we may at the same time understand for what cause and in whose honour it was instituted. The time is the month Abib, so called from new fruits; or, as among the Latins April is named from opening (aperiendo), because then all things are renewed and revive, especially in hot regions.

units.la: Hoc tempus & veteris historiae, & rerum futurarum adumbrationem habuit, & memoriam: ut educti ex Ægypto populi Israelitici, & redempti per Christum humani generis, itemq; resurrectionis Dominicae. Quare vetus ecclesia cum veteris populi, tum Christi atq; apostolorum exemplo docta tempus hoc eruci & resurrectioni Christi sacrum esse voluit. De die quondam varie certatum est: sed etsi fideles nullis neq; locis alligati sunt, neq; temporibus, decore tamen & ordine fieri, in ecclesia Paulus omnia voluit.
units.tr: This time had the character of a figure and a memorial of ancient history and of things to come: of the people of Israel led out of Egypt, of the human race redeemed through Christ, and likewise of the Lord's resurrection. Therefore the ancient Church, taught both by the example of the ancient people and by that of Christ and the apostles, willed that this time be sacred to the cross and resurrection of Christ. Concerning the day there was once varied dispute; but although the faithful are bound neither to places nor to times, Paul nevertheless wished all things in the Church to be done decently and in order.

units.la: Est autem prophanum quiddam dies magnis Dei laudibus, beneficijs & mysterijs consecratos Bacho, Veneri, Mercurio tribuere. Intra papatum hic peccatur & extra.
units.tr: It is, however, something profane to assign days consecrated to the great praises, benefits, and mysteries of God to Bacchus, Venus, or Mercury. Within the papacy this is done, and outside it as well.

units.la: Quin Dei laudibus sacros solennesq; dies tribuimus. Unde Moses hic dicit, Domino Deo tuo, &c. Est autem hoc generale, ut omnes feriae Deo summo sacrae sint, nec quicquam est gentilismo similius, & Christianismo dissimilius, quam Diuis atq; angelis feriari, quod solent pa-stas facere, quasi ipsi sint patroni atq; vindices. Et eo res deuenit ut sacti sint pleni illis nominibus.
units.tr: Indeed we assign to the praises of God days holy and solemn. Hence Moses here says, to the Lord your God, etc. It is a general principle that all feasts be holy to God Most High, and nothing is more like paganism and more unlike Christianity than to keep holidays in honour of the saints and angels, which they are accustomed to do as though these were their patrons and avengers. And so matters have come to the point that the calendars are full of those names.

units.la: Causa vero propter quam sestum ipsum instituit Dominus est illis expressa verbis. Quoniam (inquit) hoc mense Dominus eduxit te de Ægypti. Eius igitur beneficij memoriam sic isto tempore celebrari voluit. Rem ipsam quidem literis mandauerat, sed quia sumus ob liuió[?], ideo memoria rerum praeteritarum istis caerimonijs videbatur esse refricanda. Eodem modo quas in articulis fidei pariter & in sacris libris descriptas habemus natiuitatem, resurrectionem, adsensionem, spiritus sancti missionem, tamen sestis ad id factis recolimus.
units.tr: The cause for which the Lord himself instituted this feast is stated by him in these words: For (he says) in this month the Lord brought you out of Egypt. He therefore willed that the memory of this benefit be celebrated at that time in this way. He had indeed committed the thing itself to writing, but because we are forgetful, the memory of past events seemed to need to be refreshed by these ceremonies. In the same way, although we have the nativity, resurrection, ascension, and sending of the Holy Spirit described in the articles of faith and in the sacred books, we nonetheless recall them by feasts set up for that purpose.

units.la: Ritum autem, quoniam pluribus verbis antea descripserat, nunc exponit breuius: nihil tamen omittit, quod ad rei summam pertinere videatur. 1. Iubet sacrificare pascha. At pascha significat transilire: Unde nomen rei datum Dominus ipse exponit quando dicit, se occidere velle primogenita, viso vero agni sanguine postibus aspersio transfire & parcere ei familiae velle, reliquos percussurum: quod factu etiam filijs de mysterio scisitantibus dicere parentes debeant. Mactabatur agnus masculus suus cuiq; patrifamilias de grege suarum ouium. Eius sanguis aspergebatur postibus, reliqua comedebant.
units.tr: Now, since he had earlier described the rite at greater length, he now sets it out more briefly, yet omits nothing that seems to pertain to the substance of the matter. 1. He commands the Passover to be sacrificed. But pascha signifies passing over; the Lord himself explains the name given to the thing when he says that he would slay the firstborn, but that on seeing the blood of the lamb sprinkled on the doorposts he would pass over and spare that household, and strike the rest. Parents ought to tell this to their sons who ask about the mystery. Each head of a household sacrificed his own male lamb from the flock of his sheep. Its blood was sprinkled on the doorposts, and they ate the rest.

units.la: Iam Christus agnus ille est ut Baptista Ioan. 1. & Paulus 1. Corinth. 5. docent: de grege errantium ouium sumptus non de angelis Hebr. 2. Hic ara crucis semel mactatus, eius memoria sacrificij nomen à priscis accepit, ut scribit in suis ad Hebraeos homiliis Chrysostomus. Sanguis eius conscentijs aspersus quoniā emundat nos à peccatis nostris, facit ut iudicans mundum angelus Domini nos transeat.
units.tr: Now Christ is that lamb, as John the Baptist (John 1) and Paul (1 Cor. 5) teach: taken from the flock of erring sheep, not from the angels (Heb. 2). Here, slain once on the altar of the cross, his memorial has received the name of sacrifice from the ancients, as Chrysostom writes in his homilies on Hebrews. His blood sprinkled on our consciences, since it cleanses us from our sins, causes the angel of the Lord, judging the world, to pass over us.

units.la: In eo festo comedebantur infermentati panes, qui & afflictionis dicebantur, nempe ut veteris afflictionis memoriam renouarent, & synceritatis atque veritatis admonerentur. Quod 1. Corinth. 5. docet apostolus: tum ut falsam doctrinam fugerent, quam fermentum Matth. 16. vocat Dominus. Ambo Deus expurgari vult & requirit in redemptis mores aliòs: ut Exod. duodecimo cap. accincti, calceati, tenentes baculum, propere comedentes. Eadem nobis in celebranda coena Dominica est ineunda ratio. Quam pluribus verbis in 1. Corinth. 11. docet apostolus.
units.tr: At that feast unleavened bread was eaten, which was also called the bread of affliction, namely so that they might renew the memory of their former affliction and be reminded of sincerity and truth. The apostle teaches this in 1 Cor. 5; also so that they might flee false doctrine, which the Lord calls leaven in Matt. 16. God wills both to be purged and requires in the redeemed a different manner of life: as in Exodus chapter twelve, girded, shod, holding a staff, eating in haste. The same method must be followed by us in celebrating the Lord's Supper. The apostle teaches this at greater length in 1 Cor. 11.

units.la: De loco Moses ad hunc modum dicit. Non poteris eum mactare. Studiosè Deus hoc semper cauet, ut priuati cultus in ecclesia sint nulli: sed omnium communis sit & publica religio. Tum etiam Christus tantum Hierosolymis erat immolandus.
units.tr: Moses speaks about the place in this way: You may not sacrifice it. God carefully guards this throughout, so that there be no private worship in the Church, but religion be common and public to all. Likewise Christ was to be sacrificed only at Jerusalem.

units.la: Prius exemplo est ne sint coenæ privatæ, sed quemadmodum beneficium est publicum, sic etiam publica fit gratiarum actio. Dein Christus non iterum mactetur, uno loco mactatus cum sit. Missa vergit in Christi contumeliam.
units.tr: The first thing by way of example is that there should be no private suppers; but just as the benefit is public, so also the thanksgiving is made public. Next, Christ is not to be sacrificed again, since he was sacrificed once in one place. The Mass tends to the dishonour of Christ.

units.la: Atq; sic habemus festum primum: in quo nos audiamus prædicationem beneficiorum Dei: ea suo pondere metiamur: Deo gratias agamus per Christum. Amen.
units.tr: And so we have the first feast, in which we should hear the proclamation of God's benefits, weigh them by their weight, and give thanks to God through Christ. Amen.

units.la: SERMO XXXIIII.
units.tr: SERMON XXXIV.

units.la: 9 Numerabis deinde tibi septem hebdomadas, postquam coeperis falcem (mit-tere) in segetem, incipies numerare septem hebdomades.
units.tr: 9 Then you shall number seven weeks for yourself, from the time you begin to put the sickle to the standing grain; you shall begin to count seven weeks.

units.la: 10 Faciesq; festum diem hebdomadum Domino Deo tuo: voluntarium munus dabit manus tua, quemadmodum fortunarit te Dominus Deus tuus.
units.tr: 10 And you shall keep the feast of weeks to the Lord your God: your hand shall give a freewill offering, according as the Lord your God has blessed you.

units.la: 11 Et lætaberis coram Domino Deo tuo, tu & filius tuus, filia tua, seruus tu-us, ancilla tua, atq; Leuites qui est intra portas tuas, sed & peregrinus, pupillus, & vidua qui tecum versantur, in loco quem elegerit Dominus Deus tuus, ut habitet nomen suum illic.
units.tr: 11 And you shall rejoice before the Lord your God, you and your son, your daughter, your manservant, your maidservant, and the Levite who is within your gates, and also the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow who dwell among you, in the place which the Lord your God shall choose, that he may cause his name to dwell there.

units.la: 12 Memineris quod & tu seruus fuisti in Ægypto, ideo custodi, & sacri-tus[?] illos.
units.tr: 12 Remember that you too were a servant in Egypt; therefore keep and observe these things.

units.la: QVemadmodum Deus hoc ipso, quod illa, quam in Ægypto pertulit grauissima ser-uitute populum suum leuauit, atque ex ea prorsus eripuit & in libertatem auitam asseruit contentus non fuit, verum etiam illis conseruandæ libertatis gratia bonas leges tu-lit, quarum ductu se cum erga Deum ipsum, tum etiam erga sese inuicem recte gererent: sic fidelium hominum etiam interest non modo Deo de libertate reparata, verum etiam de be-neficio datæ legis, qua libertas conseruetur gratias agere. Qua de causa Moses iussu Dei pa-scha non solum instituit, quo die libertate reparata gratias agerent Domino, verum etiam septum[?] pentecostes fecit, quo de datis ad conseruandam libertatem legibus Deo grati forent. Idipsum sic describit Moses ut 1.nomen. 2.ritum.3.causam vel visum eius describat.
units.tr: Just as God, by this very act of freeing his people from the most grievous slavery they endured in Egypt, was not content merely to relieve them and wholly snatch them from it and restore them to their ancestral liberty, but also, to preserve that liberty, gave them good laws, under whose guidance they might conduct themselves rightly both toward God himself and toward one another; so it is also in the interest of faithful people to give thanks not only to God for their restored liberty, but also for the gift of the law by which liberty is preserved. For this reason Moses, at God's command, instituted not only the Passover, on whose day they were to give thanks to the Lord for their restored liberty, but also made the feast of Pentecost, on which they were to be pleasing to God for the laws given to preserve their liberty. Moses describes this feast in such a way that he sets out (1) its name, (2) its rite, (3) its cause or purpose.

units.la: De nomine dicit, Numerabis dein tibi septem septimanas postquam falcem miseris, &c. Faciesque festum diem hebdomadarum Domino Deo tuo. Quibus ostendit interpretatio-nem nominis apud Græcos, Latinos, Germanos, Italos usitati. Hebræi vocant festum hebdomadarum, quod septem essent septimanæ ab eo die qui manipuli dicitur. Græcis autem di-citur pentecoste quod ab eo die, ut ait Philo, sepies septimus, hoc est, quinquagesimus Græcis ἡμέρᾳ πεντηκοστή[?] dicitur. Unde & Germani festum hoc Pfingsten appellant. Ut exactis ab Israelis exitu quinquaginta diebus lex data, sic quinquagesimo post dominicam resurre-ctionem die spiritus sanctus legis interpres missus est. Unde festus hic dies & Iudæis & Christianis est celebris. Numerabantur, ut supra à die manipuli qui secundus erat Azymorum, Iosepho teste.
units.tr: Concerning the name he says: "Then you shall number seven weeks for yourself, after you have put the sickle to the grain," etc., and "you shall keep the feast of weeks to the Lord your God." By these words he indicates the explanation of the name in use among the Greeks, Latins, Germans and Italians. The Hebrews call it the feast of weeks, because there are seven weeks from the day called the sheaf. The Greeks call it Pentecost, because from that day, as Philo says, which is seven times seven, that is the fiftieth day, the Greeks call it [ἡμέρᾳ πεντηκοστή]. Hence the Germans also call this feast Pfingsten. Just as the law was given after fifty days had passed from Israel's departure, so on the fiftieth day after the Lord's resurrection the Holy Spirit was sent as the interpreter of the law. Hence this festive day is celebrated by both Jews and Christians. They counted, as above, from the day of the sheaf, which was the second day of Unleavened Bread, as Josephus testifies.

units.la: Iam quoniam hoc ipso panes primitiarum offerebantur, alterum nomen festo datum est primitiarum.
units.tr: Now since on this same feast the loaves of the firstfruits were offered, a second name was given to the feast: the feast of firstfruits.
