units.la: Quod igitur idem dies & promulgandæ legi, & missioni spiritus sancti diuinitus est attributus, id non caret mysterio. Primum significat spiritum sanctum esse legis interpretem. Unde Christus cui spiritus idem est cum patre, dicit se legem non tollere, sed exponere: dicit de summa legis Matth.22. dicit cum Sadducæis disputans de eo quod dicitur, Ego sum Deus tuus: dicit de diis alienis auertens & expellens mammona: dicit de sumpto inaniter nomine Domini: dicit de sabbatho quod propter hominem factum sit: de pietate in parentes corri-piens corbonam Pharysaicam, & de magistratu iubens dare Cæsari quæ sint Cæsaris: de causis cedis ira & maledicentia: de concupiscentia, &c.
units.tr: That the same day was divinely appointed both for the promulgation of the law and for the sending of the Holy Spirit is not without mystery. First, it signifies that the Holy Spirit is the interpreter of the law. Hence Christ, whose Spirit is the same as the Father's, says that he does not abolish the law but expounds it. He says of the sum of the law in Matthew 22; he says, disputing with the Sadducees, concerning what is said, "I am your God"; he says, turning away and driving out the strange gods and mammon; he says, concerning the name of the Lord taken in vain; he says that the sabbath was made because of man; rebuking the Pharisaic corban for lack of piety toward parents; and bidding them give to Caesar what is Caesar's, concerning the magistrate; concerning the causes of murder, anger and slander; concerning lust, etc.

units.la: Sic apostoli spiritu sancto accepto Christum finem legis dixerunt, & quid sibi festa, purgationes, sacrificia, circumcisio, sacerdotium, reliquique ritus vellent explanarunt. Iam cum spiritus sanctus in Christo & apostolis legem exponat: quid opus hominum iudicio? Cur hu-ius sententiæ non statur?
units.tr: So the apostles, having received the Holy Spirit, declared Christ to be the end of the law, and explained what the feasts, purifications, sacrifices, circumcision, priesthood and the remaining rites meant. Since, then, the Holy Spirit expounds the law in Christ and the apostles, what need is there for human judgment? Why is this opinion not upheld?

units.la: Dein cum lex & euangelium eodem authore spiritu sancto, eodemq; tempore sint prodita, videmus eorum concordiam esse inter se mutuam.
units.tr: Next, since the law and the gospel were revealed by the same author, the Holy Spirit, and at the same time, we see that they agree mutually with each other.

units.la: Præterea cum legis & Euangelicæ veritatis origo partim ad Mosem, partim supra eum ipsum referatur: quis nostram dicet esse recens natam, quæ sit hausta ex fontibus antiquissimis? qui rursus eorum erit vetus religio, quæ postremis ijsdemq; putidissimis ex sententis est deducta.
units.tr: Moreover, since the origin of the law and of the evangelical truth is traced partly to Moses and partly to something above him, who will say that ours is newly born, when it has been drawn from the most ancient fountains? And who again will say that theirs is an ancient religion, when it has been derived from the latest and most rotten opinions?

units.la: Ergo tempus [?] hoc recolemus in Dei gloriam, cui Moses hic sub finem dicit esse celebrandum.
units.tr: Let us therefore call this time to mind, to the glory of God, to whom Moses here, near the end, says the feast is to be celebrated.

units.la: Ritus autem sic à Mose describitur, vt quid, atq; à quibus fieri debeat facile videamus. Et vt intelligamus quidnam fieri debeat, sacrificia festo hoc offerenda commemorat. Offerebatur igitur Gomer seu nouarum frugum manipulus. Ei sacrificio addebatur holocaustum angiculi cum minha.
units.tr: The rite is described by Moses in such a way that we may easily see what must be done and by whom. And so that we may understand what ought to be done, he recalls the sacrifices to be offered at this feast. There was offered therefore the omer, or the sheaf of new fruits. To this sacrifice was added a burnt offering of a lamb with a meal offering.

units.la: Hæc oblatio partim sacras, partim ciuiles causas habet. Primum enim voluit eos ad gratiarum actionem assuefacere veluti suos quisque liberos cum eos ante & post sumptum cibum orare facit. Dein quod inde festus ille dies, quemadmodum paulo ante ex Philone dictum est. Postremo ne agricolæ, qui sunt alias impatientes moræ, prius non meterent.
units.tr: This offering has both sacred and civil causes. For first, he willed them to be accustomed to giving thanks, just as parents make their own children pray before and after taking food. Next, because from this the feast day itself takes its name, as was said a little before from Philo. Lastly, so that the farmers, who are otherwise impatient of delay, might not reap before the time.

units.la: Iam addit à quibus hoc fieri debeat, nempe à tota ecclesia: quasi enim fit vnus quisque ...
units.tr: Now he adds by whom this ought to be done, namely by the whole congregation: as it were, each one is made ...

units.la: am sic omnes alloquitur, dicens, tu, tui liberi, &c. Obserua autem quos homines Deus in primis commendatos habeat, liberos videlicet: eos sibi Christus adduci præcipit. Quo refer catechismos, & omnem puerilem educationem.
units.tr: ...so he addresses all, saying, you, your sons, etc. Observe, however, which people God especially commends to himself, namely children: Christ also commands that they be brought to him. To this belong catechisms and all childhood education.

units.la: Serui & ancillæ etiam curæ sint Domino: Vnde de eis recte tractandis præcepta diuinitus tradita pasim extant.
units.tr: Servants and maidservants too are a concern of the Lord; hence precepts for treating them rightly are found everywhere, delivered by God.

units.la: Leuitæ, vt qui sint & ministri & legati Dei.
units.tr: The Levites, since they are both the ministers and the envoys of God.

units.la: Peregrini, pupilli & viduæ, quibus cum patroni desint Deus patronum se pollicetur ac præbet.
units.tr: Strangers, orphans and widows, for whom, since they lack patrons, God promises and provides himself as their patron.

units.la: En colleʃtam ex omni hominum genere ecclesiam. Tota concio debet coire ad cultum Dei. Sacrificia, quæ Christianos offerre deceat, Roman. 12. tum fient deuotio, & preces, elee-mosynæ, collectæ.
units.tr: Behold the church gathered from every kind of people. The whole assembly ought to come together for the worship of God. The sacrifices that Christians ought to offer are set out in Romans 12: then there will be devotion and prayers, alms, and collections.

units.la: Vsus festi sic exponitur: Meminerit quod & tu seruus fuisti in Ægypto, ideo custodi, &c. Id idem est, ac si diceret: Hoc festum ideo sancio, vt recolas præterita, è seruitute in libertatem assertus es, nec eam nisi recte constituta repub. poteris obtinere, quare legem educto dedi, eius beneficij memoriam perinde vt prioris volo esse celebrem. Quemadmodum enim opes dare magnum est & maius earum vsum tradere: sic libertatis vsus per legem præbitus est ipsa libertate maior.
units.tr: The use of the feast is set out thus: Remember that you too were a servant in Egypt; therefore keep, etc. This is the same as if he were to say: I ordain this feast so that you may recall the past: you were freed from slavery into liberty, and you cannot keep that liberty unless the commonwealth is rightly constituted; therefore I have given you the law once led out, and I want the memory of this benefit to be celebrated just as much as that of the earlier one. For just as it is a great thing to give wealth, and a greater thing to hand down its use, so the use of liberty provided through the law is greater than liberty itself.

units.la: Eodem modo festum pentecostes nobis datum spiritum sanctum docet, qui magister & dux est docens nos euangelio prius allato recte vti, secundum illud viuere, & faciens in illo perseuerare. Hic agit primum externo verbo dum per ministros prædicat, dein operatione interna dum animos intus agitat. Hic magister nisi audiatur, euangelij nullus vsus erit. Ac si velit sublatum euangelium satan, agitat homines, vt huic magistro valedicant. Dum agitur de religionis capitibus, nihil de Deo, imaginibus, iuramento, sabbatho, vult exponi: sin agitur de vita ac moribus, nihil vult de magistratus deque singulorum hominum vitijs dici: deniqué hoc agit vt tacens & mutum verbi ministerium homines velint. Quod si fiat actum est de euangelio.
units.tr: In the same way the feast of Pentecost teaches us about the Holy Spirit given to us, who is the teacher and guide, teaching us to use the gospel previously brought rightly, to live according to it, and making us persevere in it. He acts first through the external word, while through ministers he preaches, and then through inward operation, while he stirs the minds within. If this teacher is not listened to, there will be no use of the gospel. And if Satan wished the gospel abolished, he stirs men up to bid farewell to this teacher. When matters of the chief points of religion are in question, he wills that nothing be said about God, images, oath, or sabbath; but when matters of life and morals are at issue, he wills that nothing be said about the magistrate or about the faults of individual men. In short, he brings it about that men wish the ministry of the word to be silent and dumb. If this happens, it is all over with the gospel.

units.la: Atque hæc meditari, est festum pentecostes recte celebrare in Dei gloriam & salutem nostram. Amen.
units.tr: To meditate on these things is to celebrate the feast of Pentecost rightly, to the glory of God and our salvation. Amen.

units.la: SERMO XXXV.
units.tr: SERMON XXXV.

units.la: 13 Facies deinde tibi festum diem tabernaculorum septem dies, quum colligeris de area tua, atq; de torcularii tuo.
units.tr: 13 You shall then keep the feast of tabernacles for seven days, when you have gathered in from your threshing floor and from your winepress.

units.la: 14 Lætaberis in die festo tuo, tu & filius tuus, filia tua, seruus tuus, atq; ancilla tua, Leuita, peregrinus, pupillus atque vidua, qui sunt intra portas tuas.
units.tr: 14 You shall rejoice in your feast, you and your son, your daughter, your manservant and your maidservant, the Levite, the stranger, the fatherless and the widow who are within your gates.

units.la: 15 Septem diebus festum diem ages Domino Deo tuo, in loco quem elegerit Dominus, quoniam felicem rerum successum dedit tibi Dominus Deus tuus in cunctis prouentibus tuis, & in omni opere manuum tuarum, omnino igitur sis lætus.
units.tr: 15 For seven days you shall keep a feast to the Lord your God in the place which the Lord shall choose, because the Lord your God has given you a prosperous outcome in all your produce and in all the work of your hands. Therefore you shall surely be joyful.

units.la: 16 Ter in anno apparebit omnis mas tuus coram Domino Deo tuo, in loco, quem elegerit,nempe in die festo infermentatorum,in die festo hebdomadum,in die festo tabernaculorum,nec apparebit in conspectu Domini vacuus.
units.tr: 16 Three times in the year shall all your males appear before the Lord your God in the place which he shall choose, namely at the feast of unleavened bread, at the feast of weeks, and at the feast of tabernacles; and they shall not appear before the Lord empty-handed.

units.la: 17 Quisq; iuxta donum manus suæ, & iuxta benedictionem Domini Dei tui, quod dedit tibi.
units.tr: 17 Each shall give according to the gift of his hand, and according to the blessing of the Lord your God which he has given you.

units.la: CUm Dominus Deus non solum animam,ceu precipuam nostri partem,omni periculorum genere eripuerit,atque etiam etiam etiā verbi sui pabulo subinde conseruet,verum etiā corpora nostra cibo potuq; & omnis generis opibus & delicijs cum seruare tum iuuare so-leat:æquum est & iustum nos ei non tam de spiritualibus,quàm de externis bonis agere gra-tias.Atq; Deū hoc velle Moses eo ipso docet, quod paschatis & pentecostes festis solenni-bus tabernaculorum festum adiungit,nempe vt quemadmodum prioribus illis spiritualium donorū est renouata memoria,sic illo tertio bona corporalia celebremus. Nā hoc festū col-lectis omnis generis frugibus anno euolluto celebrari consueuerat:quo & veteris miseriæ re-cordatione & præsentis vbertatis consideratione debitam Deo pietatem & gratitudinem excitarent.Qua de re Moses hic agit,& primum hoc ipsum festum describit, dein illam de-festis tractationem vno epilogo omnem claudit.
units.tr: Since the Lord God not only snatches our soul, as the chief part of us, from every kind of danger, and also from time to time preserves it with the food of his word, but customarily also preserves and helps our bodies with food and drink and every kind of wealth and delight, it is right and just that we give him thanks not so much for spiritual goods as for external ones. And Moses teaches by this very thing that God wills this: in that, after the feasts of the Passover and of Pentecost, he adds the solemn feast of tabernacles. The purpose is that, just as the memory of those earlier spiritual gifts is renewed, so at that third feast we should celebrate the goods of the body. For this feast was customarily celebrated each year, once the fruits of every kind had been gathered in, so that by remembering their former misery and considering their present abundance, the people might stir up the piety and gratitude owed to God. On this account Moses here deals with the matter: first he describes this very feast, and then he closes the whole discussion of the feasts with a single epilogue.

units.la: Ac festum quidem paucis,sed accuratè tamen & adhibitis circumstantijs describit. Eæ sunt nomen,tempus,personæ,locus,causa.Nomen festo datum à tabernaculis, in quibus per eos dies populus habitabat,vt reuocaret in memoriam sortem maiorum.
units.tr: He describes the feast briefly, yet accurately and with its circumstances. These are the name, the time, the persons, the place, and the cause. The feast takes its name from the tabernacles, in which the people dwelt during those days, so that they might call to mind the lot of their forefathers.

units.la: In quo videmus vt Deus nobis consulat monumentis aliquibus. Obliuiscimur rerum, sed is ita nos earum admonet.Eius generis sunt lapides in Iordanis aquis positi, arcus fœderis,& alia. Cauendum est autem ne qua monumenta recipiamus ab illo nec probata nec po-sita,vt sunt idola passim vetita.
units.tr: Here we see how God provides for us by certain memorials. We forget things, but he thus reminds us of them. Of this kind are the stones set in the waters of the Jordan, the bow of the covenant, and others. Yet we must take care not to accept any memorials from him that are neither approved nor appointed, such as the idols that are everywhere forbidden.

units.la: Tempus dicit,Cum collegeris de ara tua atq; de torcularitu[?] o. Hoc est, cum fruges college-ritis, tempus postulat, vt quietem eam non ocio turpi, sed pia gratiarum actione con-sumatis.
units.tr: He speaks of the time: "When you have gathered in from your threshing floor and from your winepress." That is, when you have gathered in the fruits, the time requires that you spend that rest not in shameful idleness but in a pious giving of thanks.

units.la: Vide vt ocium sit sumendum partis opibus,superatis miserijs & molestijs, parta victo-ria,&c:tunc alij putant aspirandum ad altiora,alij indulgendum genio.Vt ille diues Euange-licus ampliabat horrea,& Dauid Ioabo cedens copias incidit in amore Bersabeæ.Pessimum hoc est & accidit sæpe & multum,vt ecclesia abutatur diuinitus data pace.
units.tr: Note that leisure is to be taken from the wealth you have gained, after misery and troubles have been overcome and victory won, and so on. Then some think they should aim at higher things, others that they should indulge their own inclination. Just as that rich man in the Gospel enlarged his barns, and David, when he gave way to Joab and his forces, fell into love for Bathsheba. This is the worst thing, and it happens often and widely, that the Church abuses the peace given it by God.

units.la: Personæ,liberi,serui,pupilli,vidua,Leuitæ,totam simul concionem postulat. Non autem principes tantum,sed etiam infimi quiq; veluti Luc.14.prandium non tantum diuitibus,sed pauperibus etiam parari vult. Sic Paulus 1. Corinth. 11.cœnam dominicam celebrari vult cómuniter ab omnibus. Sunt quædam personarum seu iura seu discrimina varijs ex causis orta,vt ætate,fortuna,iure:quibus non vt causis contentionũ vtamur,memores quod in regno Dei non est Græcus seruus,iuuenis,diues.Sunt quæ nobis ipsi fingimus discrimina, ve-luti cum ego mihi videor nobilior,doctior,melior quibusdam alijs:Vnde efferor eosque de-spicio.At Ecclesia Christi corpus est vnum,cuius nos sumus membra,ac si quis supra quod est efferatur,quid aliud erit quam tuber in eo corpore? Igitur ad illam celebritatem etiam infimos quosq; vocat.
units.tr: The persons: children, servants, orphans, the widow, the Levites, demand the whole assembly together. Not only the princes, but also all the lowest people, likewise, as in Luke 14, he wills that a feast be prepared not only for the rich but also for the poor. So Paul, in 1 Corinthians 11, wills that the Lord's Supper be celebrated in common by all. There are certain distinctions of persons, whether of rights or of rank, arising from various causes, such as age, fortune, or law. We should not use these as causes of contention, remembering that in the kingdom of God there is neither Greek nor slave, young nor rich. There are also distinctions that we ourselves invent, as when I seem to myself more noble, more learned, and better than certain others. From this I am puffed up and despise them. But the Church of Christ is one body, of which we are the members; and if anyone exalts himself above what he is, what else will he be than a swelling on that body? Therefore he calls even the lowliest to that gathering.

units.la: Locus,Quem elegit Dominus,in quo erat arca propitiatorij, quæ primum erat in Schilo, post Hierosolymam translata. Quò qui veniebant ij in conspectum Domini venire diceban-tur, quia Dominus supra propitiatorium dicebatur habitare. Quid illud propitiatorium? Paulus Rom.3. dicit. Christum proposuit Deus ἱλαστήριον per fidem interueniente ipsius sanguine.Et1.Ioan.4.Deus misit filium suum propitiationem pro peccatis nostris.
units.tr: The place: "which the Lord shall choose," in which was the ark of the mercy seat, which was first at Shiloh and afterwards transferred to Jerusalem. Those who came there were said to come into the presence of the Lord, because the Lord was said to dwell above the mercy seat. What is that mercy seat? Paul says in Romans 3 that God set forth Christ as a propitiation [ἱλαστήριον] through faith, by his blood intervening. And in 1 John 4, God sent his Son as a propitiation for our sins.

units.la: Præclarum profecto argumentum Christum esse eum in quo Deum inuocare simul & celebrare laudibus debeamus:ac quemadmodum Deus alibi noluit,quam in loco abs se ele-ćto festa celebrari:sic alijs in creaturis non vult preces,sed in Christo solo offerri.Matth.3.in illo placitum est patri. Quid igitur templa diuis structa? preces illis factæ? nullus hic cultus Deo gratus,nulla recta religio. Dei debent esse domus non Martini,Petri, Virginis matris, in quibus Deus adoratur.
units.tr: This is surely an excellent argument that Christ is the one in whom we ought both to invoke God and to celebrate him with praises. Just as God elsewhere would not have feasts celebrated except in a place he had chosen, so in other creatures he does not wish prayers to be offered, but in Christ alone. In Matthew 3, he is well pleased in him. What then of temples built to the saints? Prayers made to them? There is no worship here pleasing to God, no right religion. The houses of God ought to be not the houses of Martin, of Peter, or of the Virgin Mother, in which God is worshipped.

units.la: Obseruandum est autem quod Moses locum ea de causa subinde iterum atque iterum cultui debitum asignat.
units.tr: It must be observed, however, that for this reason Moses again and again assigns the place due for worship.

units.la: Causæ exprimuntur hoc ipso quod dicit, quoniam dedit tibi Dominus prouentus,&c.&c. in opere manuum tuarum, &c. Hoc est, ut eorum, quae divinitus in te collata sunt beneficiorum memoriam gratam testeris: nam Deus & successus dedit prosperos & proventus uberes. En tibi causas festi instituti, quae nos docent id ipsum instituto Christi celebrare. Dicit Leuit. 23. capite: Omnis indigena Israel habitabit his diebus in tabernaculis: quare, ut sciant posteri vestri, quod in tabernaculis habitare fecerim filios Israel cum educerem eos de terra Aegypti.
units.tr: The causes are expressed in the very words he uses: "because the Lord has given you increase," and so on, "in the work of your hands," and so on. That is, that you may bear witness to a grateful remembrance of the benefits bestowed on you by God; for God gave prosperous outcomes and abundant produce. Here you have the causes of the feast's institution, which teach us to celebrate it in accordance with the institution of Christ. Leviticus 23 says: "Every native of Israel shall dwell in these days in tabernacles, so that your descendants may know that I made the children of Israel dwell in tabernacles when I led them out of the land of Egypt."

units.la: En habes quod initio datum est: vult recordationem eius, quam tulissent miseriae, & praesentis fortunae considerationem. In deserto tabernacula, in Canaan amplissima palatia: in deserto penuriam, in Canaan magnam copiam. Sic disce meminisse malorum, ut bonis quae nactus es rectius utare. Ioan. 5. fanatum abs se hominem Christus in eandem sententiam monet dicens, Ecce sanus factus es, ne posthac pecces, ne quid deterius tibi contingat. Sic festum hoc Christiani celebrant ut Zach. 14. dicitur, Omnes qui reliqui fuerint de universis gentibus, quae venerunt contra Hierusalem ascendent ab anno in annum, ut adorent regem Dominum exercituum & celebrent festivitatem tabernaculorum. Sic Christiani celebrent festum illud. Ac nobis certe perbonum esset hoc festum recte & rite celebrari, quod fieret si vestes rusticas haberemus, quae nos admonerent aviatae frugalitatis & conditionis: at eos referimus, quos nostri maiores his finibus pepulerunt.
units.tr: Here you have what was given at the beginning: he wills a remembrance of the misery they had endured, and a consideration of their present fortune. In the wilderness, tabernacles; in Canaan, most spacious palaces. In the wilderness, want; in Canaan, great plenty. So learn to remember evils, so that you may use the goods you have obtained more rightly. In John 5, Christ warns the man he had healed in the same sense, saying: "Behold, you are made whole; sin no more, lest something worse befall you." So Christians celebrate this feast, as Zechariah 14 says: "All who remain of all the nations which came against Jerusalem shall go up year by year to worship the King, the Lord of hosts, and to celebrate the feast of tabernacles." So Christians should celebrate that feast. And it would certainly be very good for us to celebrate this feast rightly and duly; this would happen if we had rustic garments that reminded us of our former frugality and condition. But instead we bring back those whom our forefathers drove out of these borders.

units.la: Epilogus idem ille etiam Exod. 23. describitur ad hunc modum: Ter in anno celebrabitis mihi dies festos, &c. Quibus verbis ostendit praeter sabbatum alia festa, paschae videlicet & pentecostes, & tabernaculorum. Primum est azymorum nominatum ab azymis, quibus vescebantur panibus.
units.tr: The same epilogue is described also in Exodus 23, in this way: "Three times in the year you shall keep feasts to me," and so on. In these words he shows that, besides the sabbath, there are other feasts, namely the Passover, Pentecost, and tabernacles. The first is called that of unleavened bread, from the unleavened bread which they ate.

units.la: Alterum est festum pentecostes, quod Exod. 23. vocatur messis primitivorum, & hic festum hebdomadarum: erat quasi legis memoria, quae celebraretur quinquagesimo die post egressum ex Aegypto Israelem.
units.tr: The second is the feast of Pentecost, which in Exodus 23 is called the feast of the firstfruits of harvest, and here the feast of weeks. It was a kind of memorial of the law, to be celebrated on the fiftieth day after Israel's going out of Egypt.

units.la: Tertium festum tabernaculorum, quod Exod. 23. dicitur festum collectionis: erat de ea causa statutum, ut recordarentur Israelitae factorum a maioribus tabernaculorum.
units.tr: The third is the feast of tabernacles, which in Exodus 23 is called the feast of ingathering. It was appointed for this reason, that the Israelites might remember the things done by their forefathers in tabernacles.

units.la: Haec festa ut frequentarentur duabus legibus indictum fuit. 1. Ter in anno apparebit omne masculinum tuum coram Domino dominatore, & hic dicitur, tribus vicibus.
units.tr: That these feasts should be frequented was enjoined by two laws. (1) "Three times in the year shall all your males appear before the Lord, the ruler," and here it is said, "three times."

units.la: 2 Non apparebitis in conspectu meo vacui, sed offeret unusquisque, &c. ut declararet se gratos, & ut alerentur sacerdotes. Quod & Psalmus docet 125. Venientes autem veniant in exaltatione portantes manipulos suos. Quod fiet si non sine fide veniamus ad Dominum illum adorantes in Iesu Christo Domino nostro. Amen.
units.tr: (2) "You shall not appear before me empty-handed, but each shall offer," and so on, so that they would show themselves grateful, and so that the priests might be supported. The Psalm 125 also teaches this: "Those who come shall come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves." This will happen if we come to the Lord not without faith, worshipping him in Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT XVII. SERMO XXXVI.
units.tr: CAPUT XVII. SERMO XXXVI.

units.la: Iudices & apparitores constitues tibi secundum tribus tuas in omnibus civitatibus tuis, quas Dominus Deus tuus dat tibi, qui iudicent populum iusto iudicio.
units.tr: "You shall appoint judges and officers in all your towns, which the LORD your God gives you, according to your tribes, who shall judge the people with just judgment."

units.la: 2 Ne flectas iudicium, neq; agnoscas personas, neq; accipias munus, quoniam munus excaecat oculos sapientium, & peruertit causas iustas.
units.tr: 2 "You shall not pervert judgment, you shall not respect persons, nor take a bribe, for a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise and subverts righteous causes."

units.la: 3 Iustitiam iustitia persequaris, ut vivas, & possideas terram quam Dominus Deus tuus dat tibi.
units.tr: 3 "Justice, justice you shall pursue, that you may live and possess the land which the LORD your God gives you."

units.la: N ijs quae sunt a 6. vsq; ad 17. explicata, capitibus retulit Moses interpretationem quatuor praeceptorum, quae in priore tabula posita ad Deum, atq; ad eius cultum pertinent: hic vero auspicatur explicationem tabulae secundae, quae leges de proximo atq; eius dilectione comprehendit.
units.tr: In the chapters from the 6th to the 17th, Moses has explained the four commandments of the first table, which concern God and his worship. Here he begins the explanation of the second table, which contains the laws about our neighbour and our love for him.

units.la: Ac quoniam omnis de Deo deq; eius cultu cum doctrina, tum cognitio superuacua est, ni disciplina quaedam instituatur, per quam in usu atque exercitatione doctrinae sanae & ab ineunte aetate educemur & adulti retineamur: opportune & plane è re nostra factum est, ut sub finem earum quae religionem spectant legum, & in principio illarum, quae ad tuendam humanae vitae societatem referuntur, praeceptionum pulchrum illud praecepti de parentibus debita reverentia atq; obedientia ponit. Est autem idipsum eiusmodi: Honora patrem & matrem, &c. Eius explicationem Mo-ses iam auspicans, quid iis personis, quæ parentum nomine continentur, ut magistratibus & verbi Dei ministris debeamus docet.
units.tr: Since all knowledge of God and of his worship, both teaching and understanding, is useless unless some discipline is established by which we are trained from early youth in the practice and exercise of sound doctrine and kept in it when grown, it was fitting and wholly to our advantage that, at the end of the laws concerning religion and at the beginning of those that serve to protect the fellowship of human life, the fine commandment about due reverence and obedience to parents should be placed. It runs thus: "Honour your father and your mother," etc. Beginning its explanation, Moses teaches what we owe to those persons who are included under the name of parents, namely magistrates and the ministers of the Word of God.

units.la: Ac de magistratibus quidem in præsentia sic scribit, ut 1.illorum institutionem, 2.officium,3.huius ordinis utilitatem indicet.
units.tr: On magistrates, at present, he writes in such a way as to show (1) their institution, (2) their duty, and (3) the usefulness of this office.

units.la: Ac de creatione magistratuum quæ paucis affert hæc sunt: Judices & apparitores constitu-es tibi secundum tribus tuas in omnibus civitatibus tuis, quas Dominus Deus tuus dat tibi, qui iu-dicent justo judicio. Quibus verbis & ipsa functionum genera nominat, & quomodo sint creandi monstrat, & qua de causa creari illos necesse sit dicit.
units.tr: On the creation of magistrates, he briefly says this: "You shall appoint judges and officers in all your towns, which the LORD your God gives you, who shall judge the people with just judgment." In these words he names the kinds of office, shows how they are to be appointed, and states why it is necessary that they be appointed.

units.la: Munerum publicorum genera duo facit, judices & apparitores. Judices à jure dicendo nomen habent quod eius potestatem sibi commissam habeant. Est enim judex, ut à iurecons.[?] definitur, vir bonus, juris dicendi & æquitatis statuendæ peritus.
units.tr: He makes two kinds of public office, judges and officers. Judges take their name from dicere ius (declaring the law), because they hold the power of this entrusted to them. For a judge, as a jurist defines him, is a good man skilled in declaring the law and establishing equity.

units.la: Ex quo perspicuum est quos nam censeas ad id munus idoneos. Primum viros dicit, non fœminas, quibus ob judicium fragile & inconstantiam hæc officia non concedunt. In quo discimus etiam muliebribus viris ut timidis, mollibus, delicatis, inconstantibus hoc munus non esse deferendum. Multo minus iis qui sunt impuberes, & per ætatem suæ rei tuendæ pares nondum euaserunt: quomodo enim publicam rem & dignitatem tueretur, qui suam non possit? Unde & apostolus episcopum eum negat eligendum esse, qui propriæ domui præesse nequeat multoque minus ecclesiam Dei curare possit. Igitur ut adolescentibus ceu arrogantibus, temerariis, libidinosis: sic iis qui juveniles[?] animos habent hæc officia tuto commiti non possunt. <bl>Sie[?] sind allt[?] von jaaren/iung von sinnen.</bl> Quomodo enim regat qui ipse regendus est?
units.tr: From this it is clear what sort of men you would think suitable for the office. First, he says men, not women, to whom these offices are not granted on account of their frail judgment and inconstancy. Here we learn also that this office is not to be given to effeminate men, who are timid, soft, delicate and inconstant. Much less should it be given to those who are under age and have not yet grown to the maturity to look after their own affairs: for how could he protect the public good and dignity who cannot protect his own? Hence the Apostle also says that a bishop is not to be chosen who cannot rule his own household, much less be able to care for the Church of God. Therefore, just as these offices cannot safely be entrusted to young men as arrogant, rash and lustful, so they cannot be entrusted to those who have youthful minds. They are old in years, young in understanding. For how can he govern who is himself still to be governed?

units.la: Secundò vult bonum. At bonum est commune rebus honestis simul & utilibus nomen, iisque etiam qui misericordes & benefici & clementes sunt attribuitur. Est etiam in suo quodque genere bonum quicquid suum facit officium: ut bonus poeta, bonus orator, bonus operarius, bonus in suo quisque est genere, cum id egregie præstat, quod debet. Igitur bonus senator erit, qui summa fide & industria, tum etiam prudenter & dextrè quod debet facit.
units.tr: Secondly, he requires goodness. Now "good" is a name common to things both honourable and useful, and it is also applied to those who are merciful, beneficent and kind. In its own kind, too, whatever performs its proper function is good: a good poet, a good orator, a good workman, each is good in his own kind when he excellently does what he ought. Therefore a good senator will be one who does what he ought with the utmost fidelity and diligence, and also prudently and skilfully.

units.la: Tertiò requirit eum, qui sit jurisdicendi, & æquitatis statuendæ peritus.
units.tr: Thirdly, he requires one who is skilled in declaring the law and establishing equity.

units.la: Quod argumento est requiri in principe viro duo potissimum & cognitionem & interpretationem legum. Unde etiam in Officijs Cicero scribit cum multa præclara maiorum, tum quàm optimè constituti juris civilis summo semper in honore fuisse cognitionem atq; interpretationem.
units.tr: This is evidence that two things above all are required in a magistrate: knowledge and interpretation of the laws. Hence also Cicero, in his De Officiis, writes that, although many fine things were handed down by our ancestors, and the civil law was most excellently established, the knowledge and interpretation of it was always held in the highest honour.

units.la: Primum igitur opus est viro principi, ut legum cognitione sit instructus: turpe enim foret, ut ait Quintus Mutius, Patricio & nobili viro & causas oranti jus in quo versatur ignorare.
units.tr: First, then, a man who is to be a magistrate must be instructed in the knowledge of the laws; for it would be shameful, as Quintus Mutius says, for a patrician and noble man, and one who pleads causes, to be ignorant of the law in which he is engaged.

units.la: Deinceps autem opus est ut eas quas norit leges possit etiam explicare, vel ut docet Aristoteles ad rempublicam eam, in qua magistratum gerit accommodare. Sæpe enim eæ sunt factorum circumstantiæ, quæ requirunt ut rigorem legum moderemur æquitate. Nam ut Paulus Iureconsultus ait, in omnibus quidem, maximè tamen iure æquitas spe-ctanda est.
units.tr: Next, he must also be able to explain the laws he knows and to adapt them, as Aristotle teaches, to the commonwealth in which he holds office. For often there are circumstances of the facts which require that we temper the rigour of the laws with equity. For, as the jurist Paul says, equity is to be considered in all things, but most of all in law.

units.la: Hæc qui norit ac possit præstare eum judicis appellatione dignum, atq; ad id quod Moses postulat aptum arbitror.
units.tr: I judge that the man who knows these things and can perform them is worthy of the name of judge, and suited to what Moses requires.

units.la: Jam illis judicibus ministros ordinat apparitores, qui decreta exequantur, quos decet esse fidos, probos & industrios.
units.tr: Now he appoints officers as ministers to those judges, to carry out their decrees; these ought to be faithful, upright and diligent.

units.la: Eorum autem omnium electio secundum tribus, & civitates fieri solebat.
units.tr: Now the choice of all these was usually made according to tribes and cities.

units.la: En tibi quasi quandam societatem civilem, in qua ne suspicio quidem ulla sit tyranni-dis. Et profecto optima reip. forma ea est, quæ Deo probatur & placet. Et est quasi ex tribus illis monarchia, aristocratia, democratia: mixtum quoddam imperium, non absimile Venetorum reip.
units.tr: Here you have, as it were, a kind of civil fellowship in which there is not even a suspicion of tyranny. And indeed the best form of commonwealth is the one that is approved and pleasing to God. It is, as it were, a mixture of those three forms, monarchy, aristocracy and democracy: a certain mixed government, not unlike that of the Venetian commonwealth.

units.la: Hic etiam cernimus quanto in precio sit libertas: ea servari melius non potest, quam si caveantur ambitus, & inæqualitas: hinc enim differentiones & simultates civiles & tandem ruina publica. Exemplo fit Romana Respublica.
units.tr: Here too we see how highly liberty is to be valued; it cannot be better preserved than if ambition and inequality are guarded against, for from these come civil quarrels and enmities, and at last public ruin. The Roman commonwealth is an example.

units.la: Causam autem creandorum magistratuum sic exprimit, qui judicent (inquit) populum in iusto judicio, hoc est qui forenses lites & controversias discutiant, ac ne quid alteri sit iniurium caveant, suum cuique tribuant.
units.tr: He states the reason for appointing magistrates thus: "who shall judge the people," he says, "in just judgment"; that is, who shall settle the lawsuits and disputes of the courts, take care that no one suffers wrong from another, and give each his due.

units.la: In quo videmus, quod præclare est à Cicerone dictum constituendorum regum cau-sam eandem fuisse, quæ legum. Non poterant homines hominibus gubernandis præfici, vt nec oues ouibus, verum sublimius & diuinius quiddam requirebatur, vt lex, donum Deo-rum, Iurecoss. testibus. Sed vt ait Pomponius frustra ius in eiuitate fuisset, ni simul essent per quos iura redderentur. Ergo iuris decernendi causa iudices constituti sunt, vt hoc loco Moses indicat. Nam si in sua sibi quenq; causa ius dicere potuisset: quid non sibi vel opulenti in pauperes, vel astuti in simplices permisissent.
units.tr: In this we see what Cicero said well: that the cause of establishing kings was the same as that of establishing laws. Men could not be set over men to govern them, any more than sheep over sheep; something higher and more divine was required, namely law, the gift of the gods, as the jurists testify. But, as Pomponius says, the law in a state would be in vain unless at the same time there were persons through whom the laws were rendered. Therefore judges were appointed for the sake of deciding law, as Moses here indicates. For if each man could pronounce law in his own case, what would the wealthy not have allowed themselves against the poor, or the cunning against the simple?

units.la: Deinceps hoc agitur, vt sua legibus salua semper esset authoritas. Vnde etiam Cicero di-cit, vt magistratibus leges sic populo præsunt magistratus, vereq; dici potest magistratum le-gem esse loquentem, legem vero magistratum mutum.
units.tr: Next, this is done so that the authority of the magistrates is always preserved by the laws. Hence Cicero also says that as the laws are over the magistrates, so the magistrates are over the people; and it may truly be said that the magistrate is a speaking law, and the law a silent magistrate.

units.la: Postremo colligimus Deum hoc modo velle ciuium inter se coniunctionem firmare, & omnibus intestinis & externis motibus tutam atque incolumem conseruare. Quod fit recta premiorum & pœnarum distributione, cura publica, defensione. Valeant igitur, anaba ptistæ, & eorum similes qui magistratum tollunt. Secus docent Rom. 13. Paulus & 1. ep. 2. Pe-trus, qui potius sunt audiendi.
units.tr: Finally, we gather that God in this way wills to strengthen the union of citizens among themselves, and to preserve them safe and sound against all internal and external disturbances. This is done by the right distribution of rewards and punishments, by public care and by defence. Let the Anabaptists and their like, who abolish the magistracy, therefore go their way. Romans 13 by Paul and 1 Peter 2 teach otherwise, and these are rather to be heeded.

units.la: Officium magistratuum sic docet, Ne flectas iudicium, neque agnoscas personas, ne-que accipias munus, quoniam munus excæcat oculos sapientum & peruertit causas iustas. A contrario quid facto opus fit docet, quasi dicat hæc si caueas rectè munus administrati-tuum.
units.tr: He teaches the duty of magistrates thus: "You shall not pervert judgment, neither respect persons, nor take a bribe, for a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise and subverts righteous causes." By the contrary he shows what must be done, as if to say: if you avoid these things, you will administer the office rightly.

units.la: 1 Ne flectas iudicium. Iudicium autem est illa quæ super re controuersa pronuntiatur sententia. Hæc debet esse iusta secundum legem æque & bene explicatam facta, vt mediam secet viam ac recta fit: at si flectitur fit obliqua, si deerret à lege bene explicata.
units.tr: 1 "You shall not pervert judgment." Now judgment is the sentence pronounced on a disputed matter. It ought to be just, made according to the law, fairly and well explained, so that it cuts the middle way and is straight; but if it is bent, it becomes crooked, if it strays from the law well explained.

units.la: 2 Ne agnoscas personas. Heb. facies, seu vultus dicitur. Aspectus enim alius alio gratior est, & magis mouet. Sed eum consequuntur attributa quædam: Vt ciuis ne sit an peregrinus: pauper an diues: magistratus an priuatus: vir an mulier: in his spes commodi vel metus ma-li, officij vel offensæ memoria. Harum rerum ratione nulla duci, scripturæ est personam non accipere.
units.tr: 2 Do not recognise persons. In Hebrew it is called "face" or "countenance," because one look is more pleasing than another and moves us more. Certain attributes usually go with such a look: whether a man is a citizen or a foreigner, poor or rich, a magistrate or a private person, a man or a woman. Hope of advantage or fear of harm, and memory of a favour or an offence, attach to these attributes. Scripture forbids us to be swayed by any of these considerations, which is what "not accepting persons" means.

units.la: Eius rei pulchrum & perfectum exemplum Deus ipse est, qui, vt Petrus Astorum de-cimo capite dicit pios vbique terrarum, & cuiuscunque conditionis respicit ac feruat. Eo-dem modo nos in iudicijs innocentiam & iustitiam, non illa quæ diximus personarum attri-buta respiciamus.
units.tr: God himself is the fine and perfect example of this. As Peter says in the tenth chapter of Acts, he regards and cares for the godly everywhere on earth, of whatever condition they are. In the same way, in judgments we should look to innocence and justice, not to the personal attributes we have mentioned.

units.la: 3 Neque accipias munus. Corruptela munerum pernicies est reipublicæ: sed qualis sit, quid afferat, ipsius Mosis verba non obscure significant. 1. Excæcat oculos sapientum, hoc est, efficit, vt quæ videas esse iniquissima, non persequare, nec punias: interdum etiam probes tricas quæras & effugia. Id fit etiam si magistratus magna scelera malit pecunia redimi, quam puniri supplicijs.
units.tr: 3 Nor take a bribe. Corruption of gifts is the ruin of a commonwealth, and what it is and what it brings about, Moses' own words make clear. (1) It blinds the eyes of the wise, that is, it brings it about that you do not pursue or punish what you see to be most unjust, and sometimes you even approve of tricks, pretexts and evasions. This also happens when a magistrate prefers to let great crimes be bought off with money rather than punished with penalties.

units.la: 2 Peruertit causas iustas, hoc est, facit vt suum bono viro ius non reddatur, si quæ cau-dat, qui potior sit iure.
units.tr: 2 (2) It perverts just causes, that is, it means that the right is not rendered to a good man when the cause of the one who has the stronger claim in law is preferred.

units.la: Ergo præsens exitium affert rebus publicis auri sacra fames. Sparta, Roma testes sunt. Vtinam à nobis, vt cepit, auertat malum hoc Deus. Sed bene quadrat in hæc tempora quod dicit Ouidius, Aurea sunt vere nunc sæcula, Plurimus auro, sit honos. Sed hæc de officio.
units.tr: Therefore the accursed hunger for gold brings present destruction on commonwealths. Sparta and Rome are witnesses. May God turn this evil away from us, as he has begun to do. What Ovid says fits these times well: "The golden ages are truly now here; honour goes to the man with most gold." But this is enough on the duty itself.

units.la: De eius vtilitate pauca quidem, sed satis multa dicit. Iustitiam (inquit) iustitia persequa-quare, vt viuas & possideas terram quam Dominus Deus tuus dat tibi. Duo bona promittit ijs qui magistratum pium, iustum, prudentem & gnauum sibi imperantem habent. Vnum vt viuant, id est valeant: at viuimus ex verbo Dei, itemque frugibus quas terra Deo benedi-cente profert.
units.tr: Concerning its benefit, the text says only a little, but it says enough: "You shall follow justice, justice alone, that you may live and possess the land which the Lord your God gives you." It promises two blessings to those who have a godly, just, prudent and diligent magistrate ruling over them. The first is that they live, that is, they thrive; for we live by the word of God, and also by the fruits that the earth brings forth at God's blessing.

units.la: Vt possideas terram diuinitus datam alterum est. Non possumus simul habitare, non po-test inter homines retineri societas sine legibus atque iusto imperio. Prouerb. 29. Ruente magistratu ciuitatem ruere dicit Solomon. Ergo Deus o-randus est vt magistratum in officio contineat per spi-ritum suum in Iesu Christo Domino nostro. Amen.
units.tr: That you may possess the land given by God is the second. We cannot live together, and society among men cannot be maintained, without laws and just government. Solomon says in Proverbs 29 that when the magistrate falls, the city falls. Therefore God must be prayed to, so that he keeps the magistrate in his duty through his Spirit in our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

units.la: 4 Non plantabis tibi lucum ex vllis arboribus iuxta aram Domini Dei tui, quam facies ibi.
units.tr: 4 You shall not plant for yourself a grove of any trees beside the altar of the Lord your God, which you shall make there.

units.la: 5 Neq; eriges tibi statuam quam odit Dominus Deus tuus.
units.tr: 5 Nor shall you raise up for yourself a statue, which the Lord your God hates.

units.la: Hic vulgo incipit caput XVII.
units.tr: Here commonly begins chapter 17.

units.la: 6 Non sacrificabis Domino Deo tuo bouem aut pecudem, in quibus sit vitium aut vllum malum, quoniam abominatur hoc Dominus Deus tuus.
units.tr: 6 You shall not sacrifice to the Lord your God an ox or a sheep in which there is a blemish or any defect, for the Lord your God abominates this.

units.la: CVm magistratus ciuiles non solum à Deo declarati sint, vt suum illi populum in vera pietate & probitate contineant, sed etiam Deorum nomen diuinitus consecuti sint, vt intelligant in his terris Dei se ministros esse: facile est cuiuis etiam rudi atq; simplici homini cogitare, quod simul eis sit imposita religionis verae cura atque defensio. Quae tamen res dextrè & vt par est existimari simul ac tractari debet: ac non veluti nunc videmus fieri, cum alij sic eam curant, vt praestaret ab eis negligi, alij sub eius curę praetextu suam quaerunt atque augent potentiam. Sic autem est curanda, vt quae verbo Dei puro puto conueniunt ea promoueat simul ac tueatur: quae ei sint vel admixta falsa vel opposita contraria, ea profligata atq; deleta velit. Quod ipsum Deus hoc loco per Mosem docet. Nam cum in tractatione de magistratu incidisset, primum eius electionem, dein officium, postremo finem indicat. Locus pulcherrimus, cum quia breuis est, si verba numeres: tum quia prolixus est & late patens, si res consideres.
units.tr: Magistrates have been appointed by God not only to keep his people in true piety and uprightness, but they have also received the name of gods from him, so that they may understand that in this earth they are ministers of God. It is easy for anyone, even a rude and simple person, to see that the care and defence of the true religion is laid on them at the same time. Yet this matter must be understood and handled skilfully and as it ought to be. It is not handled as we now see it done: some care for it in such a way that it would be better for them to neglect it, while others, under the pretext of caring for it, seek and increase their own power. It must be cared for in this way: that magistrates promote and protect whatever agrees with the pure Word of God, and wish whatever is mixed with falsehood or opposed to it to be overthrown and destroyed. This is exactly what God teaches here through Moses. For when he had come to the discussion of the magistracy, he first states its election, then its duty, and finally its end. It is a most excellent passage, both because it is short, if you count the words, and because it is wide-ranging and broad, if you consider the matter.

units.la: Iam cum eam magistratui circa quam versatur materiam proponere velit: primo loco religionem ponit ceu summam ac caput rerum omnium.
units.tr: Now, since he wishes to set before the magistrate the subject with which he is concerned, he first places religion, as the sum and head of all things.

units.la: Ac quemadmodum antea in officij descriptione, non quae facienda, verum quae cauen-da essent indicauit: sic in rebus religionis, non quibus studendum, sed à quibus sit abstinendum dicit. Præstat enim vt ex ijs quae cauenda sunt facienda cognoscamus, quam procedatur ordine contrario: quando natura nostra ad malum adeò procliuis est, vt haud facile ex faciendis cauenda colligamus, ac nobis quae vetita non sunt permissa esse putemus.
units.tr: And just as earlier, in describing the duty, he indicated not what must be done but what must be avoided, so in matters of religion he says not what must be pursued but what must be abstained from. For it is better that we learn what we must do from what we must avoid, than to proceed in the opposite order, since our nature is so prone to evil that we hardly infer from what must be done what must be avoided, and we think that whatever is not forbidden is permitted.

units.la: Sunt autem tria quae ad cauenda & extirpanda sunt magistratui. 1. ne lucos faciant. 2. ne ponant statuas. 3. ne vitiosum quicquam sacrificent. Quae res primo obtutu parui momenti videntur esse, verum habent magna mysteria.
units.tr: There are three things the magistrate must guard against and root out: (1) that they make groves; (2) that they set up statues; (3) that they sacrifice anything defective. At first sight these matters seem of little importance, but they contain great mysteries.

units.la: Ac de primo sic dicit Moses: Non plantabis tibi lucum ex vllis arboribus iuxta aram Domini Dei tui, quam facies ibi. Deus aram iusserat, fieri in qua sacrificaretur: ara crucis mysterium habuit.
units.tr: Concerning the first, Moses speaks thus: You shall not plant for yourself a grove of any trees beside the altar of the Lord your God, which you shall make there. God had ordered an altar to be made on which sacrifice would be offered; the altar had the mystery of the cross.

units.la: Inde ea religio, ceu reliquae etiam cerimoniae sacrae ad gentes deuenere, sed per eum qui zizania seminat depravata promanauit. Ergo gentiles homines suis aris lucos consecrarunt. Tacitus author est Germanis templa nulla, ac tantum nemora dijs sacra fuisse. Idem obseruat Seruius in Virgilio dicente Nulli certa domus lucis habitamus opacis. Vnde & Israelitae ad speciosos istos ritus defleCtebant.
units.tr: From there this religion, like the other sacred ceremonies, came to the nations, but it issued forth corrupted through him who sows the tares. Therefore the Gentiles consecrated groves beside their altars. Tacitus is authority that the Germans had no temples, but only woods sacred to their gods. Servius makes the same observation on Virgil's line, "We dwell in no fixed house, in the shady groves." Hence the Israelites too were drawn aside to those splendid rites.

units.la: Sed vnde quaeso hic eis ortus est error? Ex eo videlicet quod eis prisca simplicitas ceperet dispicere, Adam, Abel, Iacob, Abraham & caeteri patriarchae aris erant contenti: illi censebant addendos lucos, quo videlicet Dei cultus esset ornatior. At Deus illos in prophetis & historiis sacris excindi iubet.
units.tr: But whence, I ask, did this error arise for them? Clearly from this: the old simplicity began to be dissatisfied. Adam, Abel, Jacob, Abraham and the other patriarchs were content with altars alone. These men thought groves should be added, so that the worship of God might be more adorned. But God commands them to be cut down, in the prophets and in the sacred histories.

units.la: Quorsum haec nobis? Vt diuni verbi simplicem & purum vsum retineamus, nec velimus ea commentis nostris exornare. Inde enim sequitur ea corruptio vt veritas amplius agnosci non queat. Sic coena dominica missae cerimonijs, baptismus exorcismis, verbum Dei glosis, additionibus, replicis sic perfusa permixtaq; sunt vt prae humanis inuentis quod diuinum est vix cerni queat.
units.tr: Why does this concern us? So that we may keep the simple and pure use of the divine Word, and not wish to decorate it with our own inventions. For from this follows such corruption that the truth can no longer be recognised. So the Lord's Supper is drenched and mixed with the ceremonies of the Mass, baptism with exorcisms, the Word of God with glosses, additions and repetitions, so that, amid human inventions, what is divine can hardly be discerned.

units.la: Pulchre quidem splendent haec omnia, sed quid tum postea? Haec magistratus inspiciat ac deleat. Quod Iosias, Constantinus & eorum similes alij strenue praestiterunt. Eorum exemplo delubra Diuorum & sacella sunt destruenda nostris temporibus.
units.tr: These things indeed shine brightly, but what then? The magistrate should look upon them and destroy them. This Josiah, Constantine and others like them did vigorously. Following their example, the shrines and chapels of the gods must be destroyed in our own times.

units.la: De statuis dicit, Neque eriges tibi statuam, quam odit Dominus Deus tuus. Idem secunda lege cauit.Idolis multum tributum,vt essent libri laicorum,qui docerent,m onerent,moue-rent: Quæ Spiritus sancti propria sunt opera. At quid illa docebant, si seor sim & secundum seipsa considerest præsefertunt quod non sunt,nec habent corporis,animi,fortunæ bona. Sin ea secundum Deum considerest,ligneum aut lapideum qui cum incorporeus tum viuus est: bicubitalem aut tricubitalem qui immensus est: hominum indigum qui illis est copiæ cornu. Vnde scriptura dixit mendacia. Quid moneat ni astet qui doceat illa hieroglyphica,nemo quid sibi velint norit. Erunt fastorum notæ rusticæ,quas antea nunquam visas, quid significent,nemo scibit. Ac quemadmodum in Arte Memoriæ loci ponuntur & imagines, & struitur tam operosa materia,vt quæ memoria tenere velis citius edidiceris , quam hoc modo possis imbibere:sic verbum Dei ipsum audire & legere præstat,quam ex istis mutis & nihil monstrantibus magistris discere.
units.tr: Concerning statues he says, Neither shall you set up for yourself a statue, which the Lord your God hates. He laid down the same thing in the second law. Much weight was given to idols, so that they might be books for the laity, which would teach, admonish and move; yet these are the proper works of the Holy Spirit. But what did they teach? If considered in themselves, they present what they are not, and they have none of the goods of body, mind or fortune. But if considered according to God, they are a thing of wood or stone, which is both incorporeal and yet living; a thing two or three cubits high, which is immense; a needy man, who is a horn of plenty to them. Whence Scripture called them lies. What would it admonish, unless someone stood by to teach those hieroglyphics? No one would know what they mean. There will be rustic marks of the calendar, which no one has ever seen before, and no one will know what they signify. And just as in the Art of Memory places and images are set down and such laborious material is built up, so that what you wish to hold in memory you learn more quickly than you could absorb it in this way, so it is better to hear and read the Word of God itself than to learn from those mute teachers who show nothing.

units.la: Alia monumenta Christus posuit: si vitem videas,aut viam,aut aquam, aut panem,aut ostium Christum idem tibi præstare cogites. Quid vero moueant si concionatur clamitans, magistratus edicens,parens admonens,repugnans conscientia non moueant ? si paupertas, exilium,vlulatus miserorum non moueant? Papam idola mouent, Christianorum homi-num miseriæ non mouent.
units.tr: Christ has set up other memorials: if you see a vine, or a road, or water, or bread, or a door, consider that Christ is offering the same thing to you. But what will move you if the preacher speaks, if the magistrate issues edicts, if a parent admonishes, if your conscience struggles against you? What will not move you: poverty, exile, the wailing of the wretched? Idols move the Papists; the miseries of Christian men do not move them.

units.la: Deus idola cum hic tum alibi vetuit. Causa,quia odit. Cur igitur in Dei domum hospi-tem odiosum introducimus? Nostrum nemo ferret istam iniuriam.
units.tr: God forbade idols both here and elsewhere. The reason is: because he hates them. Why then do we bring a hateful guest into the house of God? No one of us would endure such an injury.

units.la: De sacrificijs dicit,Non sacrificabis Domino Deo tuo, &c. Hoc Deus exigit cum propter ipsum sacrificium,tum vero propter sacrificantem.Quoad sacrificium id erit purum vt Christi typum gerat: Vitiosum enim vitia non expiaret. Igitur in rebus nihili ne queras peccatorum remissionem,vt in Missis atq; indulgentijs.
units.tr: Concerning sacrifices he says, You shall not sacrifice to the Lord your God, etc. God requires this both on account of the sacrifice itself and on account of the one who sacrifices. As regards the sacrifice, it must be pure so that it bears the type of Christ; for a defective victim would not atone for sins. Therefore do not seek forgiveness of sins in trivial things, as in the Masses and indulgences.

units.la: Quoad sacrificantem,quoniam ex fide proficisci debet opus bonum,fides non est par-ca,auara,sordida, præsertim in Deum. Bonum pecus aratro vitiosum Deo tribui prohibet. Sic quidam ætatis suæ florem mundo,senectam ceu secem Deo, mutilos & claudos liberos diuinis officijs,tempus minimum religioni,raras horas precibus, plus operæ diuitijs & honoribus quam Deo tribuunt honorando.Paulus Rom.12.hostiam viuam,sanctam, Deo gratam iubet offeramus in Christo Iesu Domino nostro.Amen.
units.tr: As regards the one who sacrifices: since a good work must proceed from faith, faith is not sparing, greedy or mean, especially towards God. It forbids giving to God a defective animal that is good enough for the plough. So some give the flower of their age to the world and old age, as the leavings, to God; they give maimed and lame children to the divine offices; the least time to religion, a few hours to prayers; and more effort to riches and honours than to God, who is to be honoured. Paul, in Rom. 12, bids us offer a living, holy sacrifice, pleasing to God, in Christ Jesus our Lord. Amen.

units.la: SERMO XXXVIII.
units.tr: SERMON XXXVIII.

units.la: 7 Quando inuentus fueritin medio tui, intra vnam portarum tuarum, quas DominusDeus tuus dat tibi,vir siue mulier,qui fecerit quod malum est in oculis Domini Dei tui,vt transgrediatur fœdus eius.
units.tr: 7 When there shall be found in the midst of thee, within one of thy gates which the Lord thy God giveth thee, a man or a woman that hath wrought that which is evil in the sight of the Lord thy God, so as to transgress his covenant,

units.la: 8 Iueritq; & coluerit deos alienos,& adorauerit eos,veluti solem aut lunam, aut quemcunq; exercitum cœlorum,de quo non præcepi.
units.tr: 8 And hath gone and served strange gods, and worshipped them, either the sun or the moon, or any of the host of heaven, which I have not commanded;

units.la: 9 Et indicatum fuerit tibi,& audieris,diligenter inquire, & en fi verum & certum est,factam esse istam abominationem in Israel.
units.tr: 9 And it be told thee, and thou hast heard of it, then shalt thou diligently inquire, and if it be true and certain that such abomination is done in Israel,

units.la: DOcet Romanis scribens apostolus magistratum nobis diuinitus institutum esse: ac quo bonum illud sciatur,id idem ipse etiam exponit 1.Tim.2.vt placidam videlicet & quietam vitam in pietate & honestate transfigamus.Ex quo perspicuum est magistratui diui-nitusid commissum esse, vt sibi creditos populos in pietate & honestate contineat, ac pa-cem & tranquillitatem publice & priuatim tueatur.At homo neque cum proximo suo,neq; secum ipse concors esse potest, si fidem in Deum rectam non habeat: quod ætate nostra hominum constantia & doctorum dissensiones docent,itemque motus populorum. Eius mandat omnis idololatriæ & superstitionis coercitio nem,atque vt in cultu vnius veri Dei suos homines retineant. Ac profecto si, quemadmodum Paulus 1.Tim.2.dicit,agnoscerem us Deum vnum esse,atque etiam vnum Dei & homi-num mediatorem,nulla poflet esse discordia.Igitur ab hac veritatis via qui seducunt, publi-cam pacem turbant propterea; iudicio Dei sunt coercendi.
units.tr: The apostle, writing to the Romans, teaches that the magistracy is instituted by God for us, and he himself also sets out the purpose of this good, namely that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in godliness and honesty (1 Tim. 2). From this it is plain that the magistrate has been entrusted by God with the task of keeping the peoples committed to him in godliness and honesty, and of defending public and private peace and tranquillity. But a man cannot be at peace with his neighbour, nor even with himself, if he does not hold a right faith in God; the constancy of men and the disagreements of teachers in our own age show this, and so do the uprisings of peoples. It is the magistrate's duty to restrain all idolatry and superstition, and to keep his people in the worship of the one true God. And indeed, if we acknowledged, as Paul says in 1 Tim. 2, that God is one, and that there is also one mediator between God and men, there could be no discord at all. Therefore those who lead men away from this path of truth disturb the public peace, and for that reason they are to be restrained by the judgment of God.

units.la: Docet id Moses hoc loco pulcherrime & ita vt habeas formam eius iudicij: primum enim omnes circumstantias notat:tum de pœnis,de testibus,de appellatione disserit. Iam de iudicio. In cuius descriptione locum, personam, factum, cognitionē, decisionem fiue latam sententiam exponit.
units.tr: Moses teaches this in this place most beautifully, and so that you may have the form of this judgment: he first notes all the circumstances, then speaks of the penalties, the witnesses and the appeal. Now concerning the judgment itself. In describing it he sets out the place, the person, the deed, the examination, and the decision or sentence pronounced.

units.la: De loco dicit, Intra vnam portarum tuarum, quas Dominus Deus tuus dat tibi. Periphrasis ciuitatis est vsitata sacris literis, vt intelligat magistratus se Dei ministrum esse, quippe qui non abs se ipso populos suos habeat, sed eos diuinitus acceperit custodiendos. Vnde eos Christus in Euangelio colonos vineæ domini vocat & Græci ποιμένες λαοῦ[?]. Si igitur tui non sunt, sed Dei, non illos tibi, sed Deo sacros esse velis: at multi suos populos à Deo reuel-lunt. Saul, Ieroboam, &c.
units.tr: Concerning the place he says, within one of thy gates which the Lord thy God giveth thee. The periphrasis for a city is customary in Holy Scripture, so that the magistrate may understand that he is God's minister, since he does not have his people from himself but has received them from God to keep. Hence Christ in the Gospel calls them the husbandmen of the Lord's vineyard, and the Greeks call them shepherds of the people [ποιμένες λαοῦ]. If therefore they are not yours but God's, you should wish them to be consecrated not to you but to God; yet many tear their peoples away from God: Saul, Jeroboam, and others.

units.la: Dein cum Dei donum sint, erunt magno in precio, pura ac sancta Dei ecclesia. Igitur donum hoc propter eum qui dedit magno in precio habeas. Deus indignissime tulit scelera, quæ in suo populo impune fiebant, vt in exercitu Iosue furem, in illa navi Ionam. Idem Hesiodus docet dicens, vnius ob noxam sæpe totam ciuitatem perire, vt Asia propter Paridem. Ergo & magistratus & suam quisque familiam Deo deuouebunt.
units.tr: Again, since they are God's gift, the pure and holy church of God will be of great value. Therefore you should hold this gift in high esteem on account of him who gave it. God took the greatest offence at the crimes that went unpunished among his people, as the thief in Joshua's army and Jonah in that ship. Hesiod teaches the same, saying that often a whole city perishes because of the guilt of one man, as Asia did because of Paris. Therefore both the magistrates and each one his own household shall be devoted to God.

units.la: De persona, sive vir inquit, sive mulier. Sexus vtriusque nomine comprehendit omne hominum genus. Cum enim omnes crearit, alat, conseruet, æquum est omnes ei seruiant. Ac præterea vult ne magistratus vel negligat, vel parcat, vel timeat quenquam, præsertim in hoc genere. Negliguntur multorum blasphemiæ propter personas alioquin infames. At i-deo impunè peccare non debet qui est infamis: nam corrumpunt bonos mores colloquia prava. Parcitur interdum propter sexum aut ætatem, delinquentibus: at omnium Deus hic est iudex & vindex. Si miser fit, cauendum est ne cumulet sibi mala: sin potens enitendum vt ne suo exemplo plures post se trahat. Quales enim in rep. principes solent esse viri, tales reliquos solere esse ciues. Vxores autem hoc ipso debent esse probiores, ne fœtus cum lacte improbitatem fugat. Bene Plutarchus de liberorum educatione scribens matres monet.
units.tr: Concerning the person: whether man or woman, he says. By the name of either sex he comprehends the whole human race. For since God created all, nourishes all and preserves all, it is right that all should serve him. Moreover, he wills that the magistrate neither neglect, nor spare, nor fear anyone, especially in this class of offence. The blasphemies of many are overlooked on account of their otherwise notorious persons. But a man of ill repute ought not to sin with impunity, for wicked conversations corrupt good morals. Sometimes offenders are spared on account of their sex or age; but God here is the judge and avenger of all. If the offender is poor, care must be taken lest he heap evils upon himself; if he is powerful, care must be taken that by his example he does not draw many after him. For as the princes in a commonwealth are usually men of a certain sort, so the rest of the citizens are usually of the same sort. Wives, moreover, ought for this very reason to be the more upright, lest the offspring drink in wickedness with the milk. Plutarch, writing well on the upbringing of children, admonishes mothers.

units.la: De facto sic disserit vt quale fit, ac Deo videatur intelligamus. Dicit malum in oculis Domini: At grauibus sceleribus hoc attribuitur.
units.tr: Concerning the deed he speaks in such a way that we may understand what it is and how it appears to God. He says evil in the sight of the Lord: and this is ascribed to grave crimes.

units.la: Dein transgressionem fœderis dicit: Fœdus enim Genesis 17. cap. Deum nobis ad omnia sufficientem pollicetur: hac illi promisione spreta creaturas, mundum, ventrem, appetitum spectant. Malè statur diuino fœderi. Baptismū respiciamus. Saul irritum Ioseph ratum habuit, exempla sunt alia.
units.tr: Then he speaks of the transgression of the covenant. For the covenant in Genesis 17 promises us God as sufficient for all things; when this promise is scorned, men look to creatures, the world, the belly and appetite. It goes badly with the divine covenant. Let us look to baptism. Saul made void what Joseph held firm; there are other examples.

units.la: At ipsum factum notat deos colere alienos, solem, lunā, astra, de quo non mandauerit. En vt abs te totos nos pendere velit. Vnde deflexio? Quia nobis per creaturas benefacit, ideo ad illas ipsas conuertimur. Titan solis frater habebatur quia nosset astra: Æsculapius, Theseus, Romulus, Hercules & alij propter beneficia suis præbita in numerum Deorum relati sunt. Vt & Petrus & Ioannes sanato claudo, itemque Paulus & Barnabas curata puella adorari cœperant.
units.tr: But the deed itself is marked as serving strange gods, the sun, the moon, the stars, which he did not command. See how he wishes us to depend wholly upon him. Whence the turning aside? Because creatures do us good, we therefore turn to those very creatures. Titan was held to be the brother of the sun because he knew the stars; Aesculapius, Theseus, Romulus, Hercules and others, on account of the benefits they conferred on their people, were numbered among the gods. So too, when Peter and John had healed the lame man, and likewise Paul and Barnabas when the girl was cured, they began to be worshipped.

units.la: Vides hic astrorum, hominum, creaturarum omnium cultum prohiberi.
units.tr: You see here that the worship of the stars, of men, and of all creatures is forbidden.

units.la: Et notandum hoc est quod dicit, de quo non præcepi: Nam frustra Deus colitur traditio-nibus hominum. Ergo magistratus hæc non feret.
units.tr: And this must be noted, what he says: which I have not commanded. For God is worshipped in vain by the traditions of men. Therefore the magistrate will not tolerate these things.

units.la: De cognitione causæ dicit, Si vel indicetur, vel audieris, vt vt cognoueris, non expectanda[?] da actio, sed ipsa fama causa impellens esto. Si verum, ne conniuens assentiri videare: sin falsum, vt ne noceat innocenti fama. Dein inquire [illegible, ~5 letters].
units.tr: Concerning the examination of the cause he says: If it is either shown or you have heard, then inquire diligently; the action is not to be awaited, but the very report of the matter ought to be what moves you. If it is true, lest by conniving you seem to assent; if false, lest the report harm the innocent. Then inquire [illegible].

units.la: De iudicio seu ferenda in reum sententia. Morte moriētur, inquit. De poenis post dicetur. Iam discimus magistratus oportere eos esse, qui suum Deo populum in pietate & hone-state retineant: quo placidam hic & quietam, istic vero beatam ac sempiternam vitam agant, in Christo Iesu Domino nostro. Amen.
units.tr: Concerning the judgment, that is, the pronouncing of sentence against the accused: he shall be put to death, he says. The penalties will be spoken of afterwards. Now we learn that the magistrates ought to be those who keep their people in godliness and honesty, so that they may lead a quiet life here and a blessed and everlasting life there, in Christ Jesus our Lord. Amen.

units.la: SERMO XXXIX.
units.tr: SERMON XXXIX.

units.la: 10 Educes virum huiusmodi, aut mulierem talem, qui perpetrauerunt rem istam malam, ad portas tuas, virum aut mulierem, & obrues eos lapidibus & mo-riantur.
units.tr: Thou shalt bring forth that man or that woman who has committed this wicked thing to thy gates, even that man or that woman, and shalt stone them with stones, and they shall die.

units.la: 11 Iuxta os duorum aut trium testium morte multetur, iuxta os vnius testis non interficiatur.
units.tr: At the mouth of two or three witnesses shall he be put to death; he shall not be put to death at the mouth of one witness.

units.la: 12 Manus testium prima erit contra eum ad interficiendum eum, deinde manus totius populi, exterminabuq[?], malum e medio tui.
units.tr: The hands of the witnesses shall be first upon him to put him to death, and afterwards the hand of all the people; so shalt thou put away the evil from among you.

units.la: 13 Si causa aliqua insolita & difficilior, quam vt te ex ea explicare possis, in iudicio orta fuerit inter sanguinem & sanguinem, inter litem & litem, & inter plagam & plagam, in actionibus iudicialibus, in portis tuis, surge & ascende ad locum, quem elegerit Dominus Deus tuus.
units.tr: If a matter arise in judgment that is too strange and too hard for thee to settle, between blood and blood, plea and plea, or stroke and stroke, being matters of contention within thy gates, then shalt thou arise and go up to the place which the LORD thy God shall choose.

units.la: 14 Veniesq; ad sacerdotes Leuitici generis, & ad iudicem qui in diebus illis fuerit, & inquire, illiq; indicabunt tibi quod aequum est & iustum.
units.tr: And thou shalt come to the priests of the Levitical race, and to the judge who shall be in those days, and enquire; and they shall declare to thee what is right and just.

units.la: 15 Tu ages iuxta praescriptum quod tibi indicarunt de loco illo, quem elegit Dominus, & observa ut facias secundum omnia, quae te docuerint.
units.tr: Thou shalt act according to the decision which they declare to thee from that place which the LORD shall choose, and take care to do according to all that they teach thee.

units.la: 16 Iuxta legem quam tibi praescribent, & iuxta sententiam quam dicent tibi, ages, nec declinabis a verbo, quod tibi annuntiant, neque ad dextram, neque ad sinistram.
units.tr: According to the law which they prescribe to thee, and the sentence which they pronounce to thee, thou shalt act; nor shalt thou turn aside from the word which they announce to thee, either to the right hand or to the left.

units.la: 17 Si quis contumaciter & superbe egerit, ita ut nolit audire sacerdotem, qui astat coram Domino Deo tuo, ut ibi ministret, aut iudicem, vir talis morietur, & ex terminabis malum ex Israele.
units.tr: If anyone acts stubbornly and proudly, so that he refuses to hear the priest who stands before the LORD thy God to minister there, or the judge, that man shall die, and thou shalt put away the evil from Israel.

units.la: 18 Idq; audiant omnes in populo, timeantq;, ne ultra contumaciter agant.
units.tr: And let all the people hear this, and fear, lest they act stubbornly any more.

units.la: CUm vera fides & religio nos & Deo & nobisipsis coiunctos teneat, eaq; de causa Deus magistratum nobis constituit, ut per eum & religio & societas humana conseruari possent: recte sane Moses suis iudicibus officij sui formam in facto fidem spectante praebet, eoque docet & in religionis & in vitae communis rebus pie prudenterq; se gerere, atque etiam Dei gloriam, aequum & bonum, suorumque hominum salutem atque incolumitatem spectare.
units.tr: Since true faith and religion bind us to God and to one another, and for this reason God has appointed the magistrate for us, so that through him both religion and human society may be preserved, Moses rightly sets before his judges the pattern of their office in a matter touching the faith, and thereby teaches them to conduct themselves piously and prudently in the affairs both of religion and of common life, and also to aim at the glory of God, at what is equitable and good, and at the salvation and safety of their people.

units.la: Estq; haec verborum eius summa, ut ubi ubi sint qui seducant a Deo plebem, eos magistratus persequatur, ac pro ut meriti fuerint plectat. Ac ne vel parcatur malis, vel iniuria fiat in-nocentibus: diligentissime de poenis, de testibus, de causarum difficiliorum relatione disserit. Poenam enim delictis parem, testimonia plena, fide digna, iure sumpta atq; dicta, relatio-nem in causis difficilibus vult ab inferiore ad superiorem magistratum fieri. Quod partim ex ijs quae nuper sunt expositi, partim etiam ex ijs quae sequuntur verbis perspicuum est.
units.tr: And the sum of his words is this: wherever there are those who lead the people astray from God, the magistrate should pursue them and punish them as they deserve. And lest the wicked be spared or the innocent be wronged, he discourses most carefully on penalties, on witnesses, and on the reference of more difficult cases. For he wishes the penalty to match the offence, the testimony to be full and trustworthy, taken and given according to law, and the reference in difficult cases to be made from the lower magistrate to the higher. This is clear partly from what has just been set out, and partly from the words that follow.

units.la: Ac primum de poenis differens, iubet capitali supplicio affici debere eos, qui vel crimen falsi in sacrosanctum Dei verbum committunt, vel statuas rudibus hominibus adorandas & colendas ponant, vel in ijs qui revera Dij non sunt, & opem quaerere, & spes suas ponere doceant.
units.tr: And first, dealing with penalties, he orders that those be punished with capital punishment who either commit the crime of falsifying the most sacred Word of God, or set up statues to be worshipped and honoured by unlearned men, or teach people to seek help and place their hopes in those who are not truly gods.

units.la: Atq; haec Dei lex omnium gentium consensu probata atq; etiam recepta est. Nam si crimen falsi in scriptis humanis commissum est capitale, quanto magis erit in verbo Dei? Si plebem a magistratu cui fit iurata, atq; etiam obligata abducere fit capitale: quanto magis a Deo cui fumus deuincti ad creaturas abduci quenquam capitale est? Sed & Luciferum, qui primus defecit ex angelo diabolu fecit, & Pharaone, & Saulem, & reliquos principes, qui populos abduxerunt ad creaturas puniuit Deus. Igitur Impp. hac sunt usi lege diuina ad coercendam eorum impietatem, qui rumores falsos & errores & impios ritus spargerent. Ut est vi-dere in C. de haeresi, & Manichaeis, quibus & priuilegia adempta & supplicia capitis irroga-ta. Vbi vero ab ea discessum est, Arius Christi diuinitatem negans Turcicae in Oriente natae sectae viam ad arma patefecit: in Occidente Rom. pontifices & ambitu suo & cultu imagi-num & ieiunijs atque coelibatu Christianos homines cum a fide catholica, tum a puritate vitae seduxerunt. Hi ambo iam in eorum posteros grassantur, quorum maiores eis contra Dei legem pepercerunt. Ex eo magistratus qui nunc sunt omnes discant coercere Anabap-tistas, blasphemos, obtrectatores ministrorum atq; legum, ne ea mala serpant magis. Caete-rum ne quis innocens opprimatur ad diligentem eam, quam requirit Dominus inquisitio-nem locus est de testibus.
units.tr: And this law of God has been approved and indeed received by the consent of all nations. For if a crime committed in human writings is capital, how much more will it be so in the Word of God? If to lead a people away from the magistrate to whom they have sworn allegiance and are also bound is a capital matter, how much more is it a capital matter to lead anyone away from God, to whom we are bound by oaths, to creatures? But God punished Lucifer, who was the first to fall and made the devil out of an angel, and Pharaoh, and Saul, and the other princes who drew peoples away to creatures.
