Therefore the emperors have used this divine law to restrain the impiety of those who spread false rumours, errors and impious rites; as may be seen in the Code, On Heresy, and in the case of the Manichaeans, from whom privileges were taken away and capital punishments imposed. But where that practice was abandoned, Arius, denying the divinity of Christ, opened the way to arms for a sect born among the Turks in the East; in the West the Roman pontiffs, by their ambition, their worship of images, their fasts and their celibacy, have led Christians astray both from the catholic faith and from purity of life. These two evils now rage against their descendants, whose ancestors spared them contrary to God's law. Hence all the magistrates who now exist should learn to restrain the Anabaptists, the blasphemers, and those who disparage the ministers and the laws, lest these evils creep on further. But so that no innocent person be oppressed, there is room, for the careful inquiry which the Lord requires, to speak of witnesses.

units.la: De testibus hoc dicit, Iuxta os duorum aut trium testium moriatur: iuxta os vnius non moriatur. Manus testium prima, &c. Quibus verbis id omne quod de testibus dici potest pe-nè comprehendit: quid in illis iudex, quid partes, quid illi ipsi qui testimonium dicunt, con-siderent.
units.tr: Concerning witnesses he says: At the mouth of two or three witnesses let him die; at the mouth of one he shall not die. The hands of the witnesses shall be first, etc. In these words he comprehends almost everything that can be said about witnesses: what the judge should consider about them, what the parties should consider, and what the witnesses themselves who give testimony should consider.

units.la: Iudici praescribit numerum. Is legitimus est, quando rei de qua cōtrouertitur fidem facit, ut est in l. iij §. eiusdē. ff. de testibus. In quibus rebus minus est periculi, in ijs pauciorum: in quibus plus momenti sit rebus, in ijs plurium vsus est testiū. Veluti in ciuitate contractus fit per literas cum imperito, & literarum ignaro homine, testes quinq; requiruntur: ad depositum datum asseuerandum tres requiruntur. Vnius testis fidem in nulla re probanda sufficere, vt emineat, dignitate populorum atq; gentium omnium consensu constat, l. iurisiurandi, C. de testibus. Et id ipsum prouerbio vulgari comprobatur, <bl>Ein man, fein[?] man/ eine mano[?] Fundtschafft kan man nit bōzen[?].</bl> Ita Moses vnum reijcit, duobus aut tribus fidem habet. Vnde regulare est duorum testimonium sufficere, nisi in iis casibus quibus lege expressum est requiri plures, vt l. vbi numerus ff. de testibus.
units.tr: He prescribes to the judge the number. That number is lawful when it makes proof of the matter in dispute, as is stated in law 3, §. eiusdem, Digest, On Witnesses. In matters where there is less danger, fewer witnesses are used; where a matter has greater weight, the use is of more witnesses. For example, in a city, when a contract is made by letter with an unskilled man who does not know letters, five witnesses are required; for a deposit given to be sworn to, three are required. That one witness is insufficient to prove anything, so that he stands out, is agreed by the dignity of peoples and the consent of all nations: law iurisiurandi, Code, On Witnesses. And this is confirmed by a common proverb: One man is no man; one witness cannot be believed. So Moses rejects one, and gives credence to two or three. Hence it is the rule that the testimony of two is sufficient, unless in those cases where the law expressly requires more: law ubi numerus, Digest, On Witnesses.

units.la: Iam cum haec de numero testium Moses tam sedulo proponat atq; inculcet, minimè dubium est eum, quoniam authoritas non solum ex numero, verum etiam ex fide & authoritate dicentium pendeat, velle vt nisi probata pietate & integritate viri testimonium non dicant. Non admittentur igitur impubes iuxta gl. l. inuiti testimonii ff. de testibus: inops mentis, quia talis persona nullo officio publico fungi potest, iij. q. vij. ca. j. & fi. mulier, l. ex eode ff. de testibus: seruus, libertus, coniunx, vasallus, & quicunq; in ea sunt conditione, vt qui producit ijs posset imperare, l. idonei ff. de testibus. infamis, quia eius generis hominibus omnes actus legitimi sunt vetiti, C. licet ex quadam. in fi. §. prin. ex. de testibus. Quicunq; praeterea suspicione metus speciue sunt grauati, ij omnes remouentur. l. iij. §. pri. ff. de testibus.
units.tr: Now since Moses sets forth and presses this matter of the number of witnesses so carefully, there is no doubt that he wishes witnesses not to give testimony unless the man's piety and integrity have first been proved; for authority depends not only on number but also on the faith and authority of those who speak. Therefore the following are not admitted, according to the gloss on law Inviti testimonii, Digest, On Witnesses: minors, because they are under age; the mentally incapable, because such a person can perform no public office, 3 q. 7 c. 1 and the end; women, law ex eodem, Digest, On Witnesses; slaves, freedmen, spouses, vassals, and whoever is in such a condition that the one who produces them could command them, law idonei, Digest, On Witnesses; the infamous, because all legal acts are forbidden to men of that sort, Code, licet ex quadam, at the end, and §. prin., ex., On Witnesses. Moreover, all who are burdened with suspicion or the appearance of fear are excluded: law 3, §. pri., Digest, On Witnesses.

units.la: Quae iudex omnia diligentissime consideret, ac ne patris personam deponat vnquam, vt permittat cuiquam suorum damnum vllum praeter meritum suum dari: quin etiam si poena fit irrogãda, hac ipsa poenitentiam quaerat ac fontem prius non condemnet, quàm patria tisceleris rite conuictum teneat. Atque haec omnino vult Moses considerari in testibus.
units.tr: The judge should consider all these matters most carefully, and never lay aside the character of a father, so as to allow any of his own people to suffer any loss beyond what they deserve. Indeed, even if a penalty is to be imposed, he should seek repentance by this very means, and not condemn the source before the guilt of the crime is duly proved. And this is what Moses wishes to be considered in regard to witnesses.

units.la: Illis autem ipsis, contra quos sistuntur testes, hoc dicit: Manus testium in reos prima, nempe pe vt rei ipsi eorumque parentes, affines, cognati, amici illos propterea neque odio neque vi vlla persequantur quod aduersum suos testimonium dixerint: verum id cogitent iure & authoritate publica fieri oportuisse: ac quemadmodum inuiti lapidibus reum petant, sic ipsum etiam inuiti suo testimonio grauent: in eo nihil se praeter aequum & bonum spectare. Vnde alicubi testium publicatio magis vsu fori, quàm vigore legum valet: alicubi mos obtinuit, vt nisi in praesentia partium audita sint testimonia, non videantur esse rite recepta. Quamobrem hoc in primis cogitandum est, testes iuris promouendi causa iussos esse dicere: ac quoniam ius & veritatem amicitijs anteponunt, indignos esse, quos odio prosequantur. Ac periculum est, ne dum nolumus alter ab altero moneri, castigari, accusari: fiat vt commune malum ingruat, quo simul omnes reformemur. Sed ipsis testibus hoc onus in reos primum iaciendi propterea est impositum, vt si inuiti id facerent, inuiti quoq; dicerent, quod ad ferendam hanc sententiam iudicem adigeret.
units.tr: Concerning those very persons against whom the witnesses are brought, he says: The hands of the witnesses shall be first upon the accused, that is, that the accused themselves, their parents, relatives, kinsmen and friends should not on that account pursue those witnesses with hatred or any violence, because they have spoken against their own people; rather let them consider that this has been done by right and by public authority: and just as the witnesses reluctantly seek the accused's life with stones, so reluctantly they should burden him with their testimony, seeing that in this they aim at nothing beyond what is equitable and good. Hence in some places the publication of witnesses holds more by the practice of the court than by the force of law; in some places the custom has prevailed that testimony is not considered duly received unless it has been heard in the presence of the parties. Wherefore this above all must be borne in mind: witnesses are ordered to speak for the sake of advancing justice, and since they put right and truth before friendships, they are not to be regarded as objects of hatred. And there is a danger that, while we are unwilling to be admonished, corrected or accused by one another, a common evil may fall upon us, by which we would all be reformed together. But this burden of first casting stones at the accused was laid upon the witnesses themselves so that, if they did this reluctantly, they would also speak reluctantly, which would compel the judge to pronounce this sentence.

units.la: Leuitas enim intollerabilis est, quod in proximi necem vergat. Vnde falsi testimonij ra-tionem in illa breuissima suae voluntatis summa, qua nisi necessaria non dixit, comprehendam censuit: innuens magno hoc scelus esse. Et certe peccatu est multum & varium. 1. Peccant in veritatem, quae sola est ea lux in qua rerum posita fit notitia, quam obscurant illi falso testimonio. 2. in eos quos testimonio suo grauant iniurij sunt: quicquid enim illis sententia iudicis adimitur, id culpa falsi testis accidit. 3. in iudices, qui secundum testium verba ceu regulam pronunciant, eoq; ipso opinionem iniquitatis acquirunt. 4. in Deum quem periurij testem habent. 5. in seipsos quibus bona adimunt omnia animi, corporis, fortunae. Quamobrem hunc locum & iudex & partes, & ipsi testes Mose monitore prudentissimè considerabunt.
units.tr: Levity is intolerable, since it tends toward the death of a neighbour. Hence he judged that the reason for false witness should be included in that very brief summary of his will, in which he said nothing that was not necessary, signalling that this is a great crime. And indeed the sin is great and manifold. (1) It sins against the truth, which is the only light in which the knowledge of things is set, and which those false witnesses obscure. (2) It does injury to those whom they burden with their testimony, for whatever is taken from them by the judge's sentence comes about through the fault of the false witness. (3) It wrongs the judges, who pronounce according to the words of the witnesses as if by a rule, and so acquire a reputation for iniquity. (4) It wrongs God, whom they have as witness of their perjury. (5) It wrongs themselves, from whom they take away all good of soul, body and fortune. Wherefore the judge, the parties and the witnesses themselves, with Moses as their adviser, will consider this point most prudently.

units.la: Caeterum si quid vel iudici vel partibus obstiterit, iam sunt eis praebita remedia: partibus duo, iudicibus vnum. Partibus quidem vel suspecti iudicis recusatio vel appellatio. Nam Alexander Seuerus ff. de appellat. referibens dicit bono principi non minori curae esse debere, vt libertas subditis sua quàm officialibus magistratibus sua fit obedientia salua atq; in-columis. Libertas autem non est obedientia, vt quod libet liceat, potare, ludere, sua prodige-re, alienis inhiare, sed aequis & bonis legibus gubernari, & suis rebus nemine prohibente vti frui posse. Quod vt obtineant subditi concessa sunt eis suspecti iudicis recusatio & ap-pellatio.
units.tr: Moreover, if anything should stand in the way of either the judge or the parties, remedies have now been provided: two for the parties and one for the judge. For the parties, there is the challenge to a suspect judge, or appeal. For Alexander Severus, writing in the Digest on appeals, says that a good prince ought to take no less care that the freedom of subjects remains safe and unharmed in their obedience to the magistrates set over them. Freedom, however, is not obedience, so that one may do whatever he pleases: drink, gamble, squander his property, covet what belongs to others. Rather, it is being governed by equitable and good laws, and being able to use and enjoy one's own goods with no one forbidding it. So that subjects may obtain this, the challenge of a suspect judge and appeal have been granted to them.

units.la: Ipsi vero iudici datum hoc est, vt de re controuersa ad principem quae sint illi difficilia referat. Qua de re dicit hoc loco Moses.
units.tr: But the referral itself has been given to the judge himself, so that he may refer to the prince those matters in the dispute which are difficult for him. Moses speaks to this point here.

units.la: De relatione, Si inciderit (inquit) causaque, &c. Quibus verbis indicat iudici concessum hoc esse, vt de rebus arduis cognitionem summo magistratui remittat. Ac dicit quid & quo remittat. Quid fit referendum primum in genere tum enumeratione partium docet. Causa quæ remota fit à iudicio tuo, seu vt minime male reddidere nostri, quæ fit insolita & difficilis. Quod indicio fuerit causas bene iudicari ab ijs,qui rerum vsu pariter,ac cognitione valeant: ac si quid vel non bene sit perceptum animo,vel antehac non auditum,vt super ea quod iustum sit pronunciari nequeat:id omne magistratibus sapientia & prudentia maiore prædi-tis esse remittendum. Vnde & relatio Iurecoss.definitur esse iudicis de iure dubitantis missa ad principem consultatio.Eius forma describitur l.j. C.de rela.&l.quæcunq;§.j.ff.de iudi.
units.tr: On referral: "If a cause arises," he says, "etc." By these words he indicates that this has been granted to the judge, namely to remit the examination of arduous matters to the supreme magistrate. And he says what he is to remit, and to whom. He first teaches in general what is to be referred, and then by enumeration of the parts. It is a cause that is remote from your judgment, or, as our people have rendered it rather poorly, one that is unusual and difficult. This would be a sign that causes are rightly judged by those who are strong both in practical experience and in knowledge of affairs. And if anything is not well grasped by the mind, or was not heard of before, so that what is just cannot be pronounced upon, all of that is to be referred to magistrates endowed with greater wisdom and prudence. Hence also the jurists define a referral as the judge's consultation of the prince, sent when he doubts about the law. Its form is described in l. 1 C. de relat. and in l. quaecunque §1 ff. de iudic.

units.la: Quæ ratio omnis documento est, Deum velle[?] vt ne quid temere, præpropere,parum prudenter statuatur.Deliberandum est diu quod statuendum semel, præsertim in rebus capitalibus.
units.tr: This reasoning is a lesson in itself, that God wills nothing to be decided rashly, hastily or imprudently. What is to be decided once must be deliberated long, especially in capital matters.

units.la: Sed exponit ipse casus,vt vocant. 1. inquit,Inter sanguinem & sanguinem:id est in causa capitali. Veluti si quis Ezechia regnante solis adorati reus fuisset,ac secundum legem,quæ pœnam capitis hoc facientibus minatur, sit condemnandus : prætendit ipse legis ignoran-tiam,ex eo,quod Hieroboami dolo detenti legem Hierosolymis discere nequiuerint,natam: ac solem à quo bona haberet maxima,sibi colendum arbitratus fit.De ea re sit relatio.
units.tr: But the case itself, as they call it, explains this. (1) He says, "between blood and blood," that is, in a capital case. For example, if someone under King Hezekiah had been accused of worshipping the sun, and was to be condemned under the law which threatens the death penalty for those doing this, he pleads ignorance of the law, arising from the fact that, detained by the guile of Jeroboam, they could not learn the law at Jerusalem. He thought the sun, from which he had his greatest goods, was to be worshipped by himself. A referral is made about this matter.

units.la: 2 Inter causam & causam,hoc est,cum agitur de corporis aut fortunæ bonis,vt cum ser-uiens opulento ciui pauperculæ vigo ab herili filio comprelsa, aut Tyrio cuidam in fœnus data sit pecunia,quam dein proselytus factus nolit reddere.
units.tr: (2) "Between cause and cause," that is, when the matter concerns goods of body or of fortune: for example, when a servant has ravished a poor citizen girl with the rich citizen's son, or when money was lent at interest to a Tyrian, which afterwards, having become a proselyte, he refuses to repay.

units.la: 3 Inter plagam & plagam,,cum lege talionis agitur aduersus eum qui læserit.
units.tr: (3) "Between stroke and stroke," when a case is brought under the law of retaliation against one who has inflicted a wound.

units.la: Atque hæc sunt illa ריבות ריב[?] id est, verborum contentiosorum seu, vt vere & proprie dicam,rerum quæ in dubium vocari & de quibus in vtramque partem quæri & disceptari potest, summa genera. De his docet nihil temere pronunciandum, verum potius ad principem referendum. Neque enim par est in aliena re quenquam ludere. Bene dixit ille,De tuo largitor puer. Ergo iudex, cuius interest suum cuique assignare:si quid cuius-que sit nesciat, causam ei remittat iudicandam, qui de ea possit iustè & sapienter pronun-ciare.
units.tr: And these are the matters of strife [ריבות ריב], that is, the highest kinds of contentious words, or, to speak truly and properly, the general classes of matters which can be called into doubt and about which one may inquire and dispute on either side. About these he teaches that nothing should be pronounced rashly, but rather referred to the prince. For it is not fitting for anyone to play with another's property. That man spoke well: "A boy is lavish with what is yours." Therefore the judge, whose concern it is to assign to each his own, if he does not know what belongs to whom, should remit the case for judgment to one who can pronounce on it justly and wisely.

units.la: Quò verò fit referendum paucis dicit,In eum quem Dominus elegit locum,in quo sacerdo-tes & princeps iudex habitant. Erat enim ponè tabernaculum chorus seu collegium sacer-dotum virorum legum diuinarum,atq; humanarum peritia summa prædito rum : erat ibi-dem summus gentis princeps. Ad eos pertinebat de rebus maioris momenti iudicare. Sic Lacedæmone,Athenis,Romæ principes & iuris peritia clari viri de iure solebant responde-re:sic Imperatores Romani suos sapientes , atque iuris interpretes , quos de rebus dubijs consulerent habuere:& ipsi suis procoss.quid esset de iure solebant rescribere. Vnde & li-bri Digestorum,Codicis, Nouellarum constitutionum, quid aliud sunt quàm Rom.Impp. rescriptæ?
units.tr: As to where the matter is to be referred, he says briefly, "to the place which the Lord has chosen, in which the priests and the chief judge dwell." For beside the tabernacle there was a chorus or college of sacred men, priests, endowed with the highest skill in divine and human laws; and there was the supreme prince of the nation. It belonged to them to judge matters of greater weight. So at Sparta, Athens and Rome, princes and men famous for their legal skill used to give responses about law. So the Roman emperors had their wise men and interpreters of law, whom they consulted on doubtful matters, and they themselves used to write back to their proconsuls what the law was. Hence, what are the books of the Digest, the Code and the Novels but rescripts of the Roman emperors?

units.la: Iam quicunque in Republica locum tenent , vt ad ipsos deferantur & appellationes & relationes de rebus magnis & difficillibus:ij cogitabunt quantum humeris suis onus susti-neant,quamque deceat eos & vsu & cognitione diuinarum pariter atq; humanarum legum exerceri:quorum autem est eos viros eligere,& toti Reipub.præficere, eorum etiam inter-est cogitare , vt eiusmodi illum in locum viros legant, qui & possint & velint secundum æ-quum & bonum iudicare.
units.tr: Now, whoever hold a place in the commonwealth, so that appeals and referrals about great and difficult matters are brought to them, let them consider how great a burden they bear upon their shoulders, and how fitting it is that they be trained, by practice and knowledge, in divine and human laws alike. And those whose task it is to choose such men and set them over the whole commonwealth should also consider that they choose for that office men who both can and will judge according to what is equitable and good.

units.la: Verum enim est quod supra diximus Deum hoc modo cum suis populis,tum etiam i-psis iudicibus seu minoribus magistratibus voluisse consulere. Sic Paulus prouocauit ad Cæsarem : Ambrosius Mediolani coram sua ecclesia contra Maxentium causam suam egit: Chrysostomus Imperatricis sibi infensæ dirum odium declinauit:nos papisticum concilium respuimus atque ad sacrosanæta Biblia prouocamus. Quod hic constitutum sit ratum habe a tur:contumaciæ quisquæ suæ pœnas luat. Oremus.
units.tr: Indeed, it is true, as we said above, that God in this way wished to provide for his peoples, and also for the judges themselves or lesser magistrates. So Paul appealed to Caesar; Ambrose at Milan pleaded his cause before his church against Maxentius; Chrysostom avoided the bitter hatred of an empress hostile to him. We reject the Papist council and appeal to the most sacred Bible. Whatever is established here, let it be held as valid, and let whoever is contumacious pay the penalty. Let us pray.

units.la: SERMO XL.
units.tr: Sermon 40.

units.la: Quum veneris in terram quam Dominus Deus tuus dat tibi, possederis eam, & in ea habitaueris,& dicturus es, Constituam super me regem,quemadmodum omnes gentes quæ circum me sunt.
units.tr: When you come into the land which the LORD your God gives you, and you possess it and dwell in it, and you say, "I will set a king over me, like all the nations that are around me,"

units.la: 20 Omnino regem super te ponės quem elegerit Dominus Deus tuus, de medio fratrum tuorum constituas super te regem: non autem præficere tibi potes hominem alienum, qui non est frater tuus.
units.tr: 20 you shall certainly set over you a king whom the LORD your God chooses; one from among your brothers you shall set over you as king. You may not set over you a foreigner who is not your brother.

units.la: 21 Modo ne sibi talis equos multos paret, neque populum in Ægyptum reducat, ut equos multiplicet, nam Dominus dixit vobis, Ne ultra redeatis per viam istam.
units.tr: 21 Only he shall not acquire many horses for himself, nor bring the people back into Egypt to multiply horses, for the LORD has said to you, "You shall never return that way again."

units.la: 22 Deinde ne sibi multas mulieres paret, ne recedat cor eius, neq; multiplicet sibi multum auri & argenti.
units.tr: 22 Nor shall he acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away; nor shall he multiply silver and gold for himself greatly.

units.la: 23 Quum sederit in solio regni sui, describet sibi exemplar huius legis in libro eorum sacerdotibus Leuitici generis:
units.tr: 23 When he sits on the throne of his kingdom, he shall write for himself a copy of this law in a book, from the one kept by the priests of the Levitical stock.

units.la: 24 Eritq; illud penes eum, ut legat in eo cunctis diebus vitæ suæ, ut discat timere Dominum Deum suum, & servare omnia verba legis huius atq; statuta ista, ut faciat ea.
units.tr: 24 It shall be with him, and he shall read in it all the days of his life, so that he may learn to fear the LORD his God, and to keep all the words of this law and these statutes, to do them.

units.la: 25 Et ne extollat cor suum super fratres suos, neq; recedat à præcepto neq; ad dextram, neq; ad sinistram, ut proroget dies in regno suo, ipse & filii eius in medio Israelis.
units.tr: 25 His heart shall not be lifted up above his brothers, and he shall not turn aside from the commandment, either to the right or to the left, so that he may prolong his days in his kingdom, he and his sons, in the midst of Israel.

units.la: IN exposita descriptione iudicij, quod pij magistratus in religionis reliquisq; rebus exercere debent, mentio facta est relationis, qua iudex causam difficilem atq; arduam superiori magistratui remittit discutiendam. Inde Moses occasionem sibi sumit de ea ipsa postrema potestate differendi: ac docet iam quidem ipsis præesse summum sacerdotem atque iudicem, fore tamen, ut instar aliarum gentium regem quoq; sint habitur[?]i. In quo res postulet, ut prouideant, quo rite creetur, & officio suo fungatur. Qua de re Moses sic disserit, ut primum de eius electione, tum de officio dicat.
units.tr: In the description just given of the judgment which godly magistrates ought to exercise in matters of religion and in other affairs, mention was made of the referral by which a judge sends a difficult and arduous case on to a higher magistrate for decision. Moses now takes occasion from this very last power, that of deferring cases, and teaches that, while the high priest and judge already presides over them, they will nevertheless have a king as other nations do. In that event, they must take care that he is duly created and performs his office. On this matter Moses argues in such a way that he speaks first of his election and then of his office.

units.la: Ac de electione quidem ad hunc modum dicit: Cum veneris in terram quam Dominus Deus tuus dat tibi, &c. Quibus verbis & electionis causam efficientem & electi regis personam monstrat.
units.tr: Concerning the election, he speaks in this manner: When you come into the land which the LORD your God gives you, and so on. In these words he shows both the efficient cause of the election and the person of the king who is chosen.

units.la: Electionis efficiens causa fuit, quod populus lautæ fortunæ suæ fruitione totus ebrius & pertesus huius status affectat alium splendidiorem.
units.tr: The efficient cause of the election was that the people, utterly drunk on the enjoyment of their comfortable fortune and weary of this condition, desired another, more splendid one.

units.la: Quod quale sit atq; acciderit 1.Reg.8. pluribus verbis descriptum extat. Populus iubet regem dare qui habeat equos &c. more aliarum gentium. Quod illis in suam ipsorum perni-ciem cessit. Saul primus rex initio quidem bonus, post vero crudelis bestia fuit. Dauid fe-cundus optimus quidem, & tamen rempub. adulterio perturbauit. Solomon tertius 3. Reg. 12. sapientia, potentia, divitijs pollens regnum quidem auxit, sed populum multis oneribus gravavit. Ab Roboamo, qui regnum scidit fuerunt reges octodecim, quorum tres boni, Iosaphat, Iosias. Ezechias, mediocres Abia & Asa, reliqui pessimi. Israelis reges totidem fuere, quorum unus tantum Iehu aliquid laude dignum fecit. Ex quo colligi potest idem illis accidisse, quod ranis regem requirentibus, videlicet ut haberent ciconiam.
units.tr: What kind of thing this was, and how it happened, is described at length in 1 Samuel 8. The people ask for a king who will have horses, and so on, after the manner of other nations. This turned out to their own ruin. Saul, the first king, was indeed good at the start, but afterwards he was a cruel beast. David, the second, was very good, yet he disturbed the commonwealth by adultery. Solomon, the third (1 Kings 12), excelled in wisdom, power and riches and indeed enlarged the kingdom, but he burdened the people with many burdens. From Rehoboam, who split the kingdom, there were eighteen kings of Judah: three were good (Jehoshaphat, Josiah, Hezekiah), two were middling (Abijah and Asa), and the rest were very wicked. The kings of Israel were just as many, and of them only Jehu did anything worthy of praise. From this it can be gathered that the same thing happened to them as to the frogs who asked for a king and were given a stork.

units.la: Quamobrem animis reputemus, quàm graue fit spreta libertate seruitutem sibi consci-scere. At id nunc in libera gente nostra proh dolor quàm fit priuatim & publicè: Rusticum hominem agricultura tædet, in urbem commigrat, ibi dilapidatis bonis seruit alienis, cui graue sibi ipsi seruire fuit. Opificem artis suæ tædet, & ad officia publica aspirat, ubi servus servorum est. Sic publice videmus fieri, ut qui divinitus erepti sumus ex miserrima seruitute, iam ad principum atq; regum aulas transeamus.
units.tr: Let us therefore consider in our minds how serious it is to reject liberty and bring slavery upon oneself. Yet, alas, this is what happens now among us, a free people, both privately and publicly. A country man is weary of farming, moves to the city, and there, with his goods squandered, serves other people's interests, when it was hard enough for him to serve himself. A craftsman is weary of his trade and aspires to public offices, where he becomes the servant of servants. Thus we see it happening in public life: we who were rescued by God from the most wretched slavery now pass over into the courts of princes and kings.

units.la: Unde hæc nausea ex nimia satietate scilicet: Wenn Dgeyß wol staat/so schartret sy. Dicit enim hic, Cum veneritis, possederitis, habitaveritis: id est, cum in illam terram ventum erit, & possessione eius iam recuperata, quietem nacti fueritis, atq; istis profectionis laboribus & molestijs defuncti estis, tum oriretur ista satietas.
units.tr: Whence this nausea, clearly from excessive satiety: When the donkey is well fed, it kicks up its heels. For here Moses says, When you have come, possessed and dwelt: that is, when you have arrived in that land, and, having recovered its possession, have found rest, and are released from the labours and troubles of the journey, then this satiety would arise.

units.la: Sed aliam etiam eius morbi causam dicit exemplum aliarum gentium. Quam suis ipso-rum verbis exprimunt veluti testis est historia. Nam reluctanti Samueli dicunt: Minime, sed regem habebimus nos, & erimus nos quoq; ut reliquæ omnes gentes, ut ius dicat nobis rex noster, & exeat ante nos & bella nostra gerat. Discimus ab his exemplis abstinere, & ut Solo-mon docuit, oculos, ne vanitatem videant, avertere. Sæpe enim illa externa rerum species fallit: nam fi hominem aulicum ex torquibus atq; annulis, ex vestibus, ex famulitio, ex his qui illi habentur honoribus, deniq; etiam ex victu velis æstimare, præ paupere & obscuro, & squalido & fabis vescente rustico beatus esse videbitur: sin illius aulici curas & molestias, animum modo spe suspensum, modo metu fractum, & durum seruitutis iugum cum securitate & tranquillitate & ea quæ est auro nobilior libertate rustici conferas, caulam quàm aulam malueris. Bene ergo dixere Maiores nostri, <bl>Es sye nit alls gold was ain settel bange</bl> [?] id est, phaleras illas quæ ex ephippio dependent non omnes totas esse aureas. Quamobrem ne quis inani specie decipiatur consultissimum est sua sorte contentum esse, & de ea gratias agere Domino potius, quàm conqueri & aliam assectare. Sed de his satis. Iam enim perspicuum est, quod ista populi vanitas atq; leuitas regis electi causa fuit.
units.tr: But Moses also gives another cause of this disease, namely the example of the other nations. History bears witness to how they expressed it in their own words: when Samuel resisted, they said, "Not so, but we will have a king, and we too will be like all the other nations: our king shall judge us and go out before us and fight our battles." From these examples we learn to refrain, and, as Solomon taught, to turn our eyes away lest they see vanity. For that outward appearance of things often deceives. If you judge a courtier by his necklaces and rings, by his clothing, his retinue, the honours paid him, and finally even by his food, he will seem happy compared with a poor, obscure, squalid country man who eats beans. But if you compare the cares and troubles of that courtier, his mind now held in suspense by hope, now broken by fear, and the harsh yoke of servitude, with the security, tranquillity and liberty of the countryman, which is more precious than gold, you will prefer the cottage to the court. Our forefathers rightly said: Not everything that hangs from a saddle is gold [?]. That is, not all those trappings that dangle from the saddle are wholly gold. Therefore, lest anyone be deceived by an empty appearance, it is most wise to be content with one's own lot, and to give thanks for it to the Lord, rather than to complain and pursue another. But enough of this. For it is now plain that this vanity and levity of the people was the cause of the choice of a king.

units.la: Cæterum si velimus omnino regem nobis esse, quoniam in eo multum situm est, deliberandum erit de eius quem eligamus persona. Ac circa personam quidem Moses indicat duo potissimum obseruanda. Vnum, vt sit electus à Deo, id est, à Deo probatus, & in cuius electione verbum Dei potius quàm affectus humani consulantur.
units.tr: Moreover, if we wish altogether to have a king over us, since much depends on him, we must deliberate about the person whom we choose. As to the person, Moses indicates two things above all to be observed. The first is that he be chosen by God, that is, approved by God, and that in his election the Word of God rather than human affections be consulted.

units.la: Quà præceptione Deus crimen ambitus damnat, ac cauet ne quis remp. emat post eam venditurus: tum indicat etiam magistratus eiusmodi esse debere, qui Deo potius quàm hominibus placeant ac grati sint.
units.tr: By this precept God condemns the crime of ambition, and guards against anyone buying the commonwealth in order to sell it afterwards. He also indicates that magistrates of this kind ought to be those who please God rather than men, and are acceptable to him.

units.la: Alterum est, vt ne sit alienigena, sed in ea natus ciuitate, in qua debeat imperare. Idque præcipitur primum ob religionem, ne cultus peregrinos introducat: dein propter eas quas rex gerit res, ne eæ propter ipsum insidiarum, odij, vllaue alia suspicione grauentur: deniq; propter ipsum regnum, quod is ceu suum natale solum & magis amabit & libentius tuebitur.
units.tr: The second is that he not be a foreigner, but born in the state in which he is to rule. This is commanded first on account of religion, lest he introduce foreign worship; then on account of the affairs the king conducts, lest these be burdened by suspicion of plots, hatred, or any other suspicion against him; and finally on account of the kingdom itself, which he, as one born on that soil, will both love more and defend more willingly.

units.la: Idem est obseruandum in omni munerum genere. Deus, qui est summa sapientia, non sine causa præuisum hoc malum notat ac monstrat. Atque hæc de rege eligendo satis.
units.tr: The same is to be observed in every kind of office. God, who is supreme wisdom, has noted and pointed out this evil in advance, and not without reason. So much for choosing a king.

units.la: Porro eius officium sic à Mose describitur, vt primum quibus rebus abstinere, deinceps in quarum studium incumbere debeat intelligamus.
units.tr: Next, his office is described by Moses in such a way that we understand first from what things he must abstain, and then to what pursuits he ought to devote himself.

units.la: Ac quatuor quidem docet regi cumprimis esse deuitanda, luxum, plebis seductionem, libidinem, auaritiam. Luxum quibus in rebus exerceant principes notum est, ideoq; eas non omnes refert, contentus vnam speciem retulisse, eam videlicet quæ in equis cernitur. At equi per se ipsi preciosi sunt & magnis vix aluntur sumptibus. Igitur si pluribus quàm opus sit vti rex velit & suis hominibus onus imponet graue, & sibi ipsi materiam superbiæ & ferociæ paratam dabit: qua fit vt Deus non respiciatur, nedum timeatur, & finitimi poquli contemnantur, & irritentur vtriq; Deus pariter & vicini.
units.tr: Moses teaches that four things above all must be avoided by a king: luxury, the seduction of the people, lust and avarice. The matters in which princes indulge in luxury are well known, and so Moses does not list them all, being content to mention one kind, namely that which is seen in horses. Horses are in themselves costly and can scarcely be maintained at great expense. Therefore, if the king wishes to use more than is needful and lays a heavy burden on his men, he will also give himself material for pride and arrogance; the result is that God is not regarded, much less feared, the neighbouring peoples are despised, and both God and the neighbours are provoked.

units.la: Eodem genere currus, equitatus, tormenta æanea, pedites, arces, continentur: in quibus si modum excedant, plus spéi ponitur, quàm in ipso Domino. Rex hosti thesauros ostentans punitur. Vbermut tbat me gut. Itaque quicquid nimium est rex vitabit.
units.tr: Under the same heading come chariots, cavalry, bronze artillery, infantry and fortresses. If a king exceeds the proper limit in these, he places more hope in them than in the Lord himself. A king who displays his treasures to an enemy is punished. Overconfidence does me good. Therefore the king will avoid whatever is excessive.

units.la: Plebis seductionem siue oppressionem hoc ipso cauendam dicit, quod vetat, ne reducat populum in Ægyptum, quippe ex qua liberati essent. Quid, inquis, est in Ægyptum ducere? quid, inquam, est in Ægypto esse? Docet equidem hoc Israelitarum in Ægypto dura conditio: seruiebant enim & premebantur duro seruitutis iugo, quo non solum corpus labore premeretur, sed animus etiam à salubri religionis vsu prohiberetur. Eò reducere populum est eum oneribus & superstitione premere. Quod nunc multi magistratus factitant, quibus pro pter suos liberos libet monasteria restituere, propter suas pensiones militiam mercenariam reducere. Hi lupi sunt, non pastores. De his Dominus Esa. 3. conqueritur, qui vt ipsi in tuto sint, Ægyptijs regibus populum obstringunt. Atq; hoc cauendum viro principi, cui salus populi sit credita.
units.tr: Moses says that the oppression or seduction of the people is to be guarded against for this very reason: he forbids leading the people back into Egypt, from which they had been freed. "What," you ask, "does it mean to lead someone into Egypt? What does it mean to be in Egypt?" The harsh condition of the Israelites in Egypt teaches us this. They were enslaved and crushed under the hard yoke of bondage, which burdened not only their bodies with labour but also kept their minds from the wholesome practice of religion. To lead the people back there is to weigh them down with burdens and superstition. Many magistrates do this now: for the sake of their own children they are pleased to restore monasteries, and for the sake of their own pensions they bring back mercenary soldiery. These are wolves, not shepherds. The Lord complains of such men in Isaiah 3, who, so that they themselves may be safe, bind the people to Egyptian kings. This is what a prince, to whom the safety of the people has been entrusted, must guard against.

units.la: Libidinem, ne multiplicet, inquit mulieres: hoc est vt sanctum custodiat ac seruet matrimonium, & ab omni libidine abstineat. Et causas addit, 1. quia auocatur animus à cura populi ad voluptates. Quid autem huiusmodi profuerit periclitanti patriæ, notum est omnibus exemplum Paridis, 2. Auocat à recto, vt Samsonem, Solomonem, alios. Ac si vna Eua seduxit Adamum, quanto facilius erit pluribus vnum seducere?
units.tr: He tells the king not to multiply wives: that is, he should keep marriage holy and preserved, and abstain from all lust. He adds two reasons: (1) because the mind is drawn away from care for the people to pleasures, and what good such things have done for a country in peril is known to all from the example of Paris; (2) because lust leads men away from what is right, as it did Samson, Solomon and others. If Eve alone seduced Adam, how much easier will it be for many women to seduce one man?

units.la: Eodem pertinet etiam vt ab otio, ab alea, à nimio venatu, reliquisq; rebus generis eiusdem abstineat. Nam cum magistratum deceat diuina quædam morum grauitas, eaq; destruatur le uitate & harum rerum studio, dabunt operam principes in rep. viri, vt istas valere iubeant: <bl>Sfinden schüch abzüchund.</bl>
units.tr: To the same purpose belongs the command that he abstain from idleness, from gambling, from excessive hunting, and from other things of that kind. For since a magistrate ought to have a certain divine seriousness of character, and this is destroyed by frivolity and devotion to such pursuits, the leading men in the commonwealth will take care to bid these things farewell: <bl>Sünden scheuchen und abziehen</bl> (shun sins and turn away from them).

units.la: Auaritiam etiam caueat, inquit, Ne sibi multiplicet aurum & argentum. Pecunia belli ner-vus est & medulla civitatis: ideo curandum ut habeatur. Sed nimium thesaurizare & auarū esse cum turpe est viris principibus, tum etiam nocens reipub. Ac praestat operam dare, ut quàm optimè gubernentur homines, quàm in hoc solū incumbere, ut crescat pecunia. Exemplo fit pater sordidus operam dans potius cumulandis opibus, quàm rectè educandis liberis: sibi sordido & auaro nutrit prodigos concoctores. Quid magistratui profuerint ingentes thesauri, cum habeat parum fidos eoq; etiam imbelles homines? Thesauri illi aliis parati sunt gentibus. Atq; haec omnia dicit Moses esse cavenda viro principi.
units.tr: He also says the king should guard against avarice: Let him not multiply to himself gold and silver. Money is the sinew and marrow of the state, so it must be looked after so that it is kept. But to hoard too much and be greedy is shameful in princes and harmful to the commonwealth. It is better to take pains that the people are governed as well as possible than to devote oneself only to making money grow. A miserly father who is more concerned with piling up wealth than with bringing up his children well, rears for himself spendthrift heirs who will squander it. What good are huge treasures to a magistrate who has few faithful men and those unwarlike? Such treasures are ready for other nations. Moses says all these things are to be guarded against by the prince.

units.la: Enitendum est autem contra, ut hoc ipsum penes se habeat sibique prorsus impresserit, quo possunt haec omnia vitia reprimi, nempe studium verbi divini. In quo Moses proponen-do atq; explicando sic versatur, ut ostendat primum quomodo legibus divinis sit studendū, tum quem nam studij illius habere debeat finem monstret.
units.tr: On the contrary, he must strive to possess the very thing by which all these vices can be restrained, and to impress it upon himself entirely: namely, zeal for the Word of God. In setting this out and explaining it, Moses shows first how one must be devoted to the divine laws, and then indicates what end such devotion ought to have.

units.la: Ac de ratione studij divini sic disserit. Cum sederit, inquit, in folio regni sui describet sibi ex-emplar huius legis in libro coram sacerdotibus Levitici generis, eritq; illud penes eum ut legat in eo cunctis diebus vitæ suæ. Quibus verbis ad studij sacri rationem duo præcepta affert: quorum altero scribendi, altero legendi usum atq; exercitium requirit.
units.tr: He speaks about the manner of studying the divine law thus: When he has sat on the throne of his kingdom, he shall write for himself a copy of this law in a book, before the priests of the Levitical tribe; and it shall be with him, that he may read in it all the days of his life. By these words he gives two precepts for the practice of sacred study: the one requires writing, the other the use and exercise of reading.

units.la: Ac scriptionem quidem hoc ipso mandat, quod vult regem ipsum sibi librum hunc de-scribere. Quod ipsum Philo in lib. de creatione principis etiam docet ad hunc modum: ἀφ᾽ ἧς(inquit) αὖ ἡμέρας παρέλθῃ τῆς ὅτι τῶν ἀρχῶν κελεύει τῶν [illegible, ~8 letters] αὐ-τοχειρίᾳ κεφαλαιώδη τύπον περιέχουσαν ἀπάντων τῶν ὁμοιωμάτων, βελτίονα ἐν κολλᾷ τῇ ψυχῇ [?] καὶ τὰ ἁγιατεταγμένα [?] γενέσθαι. τὸ μὲν δὴ ἀναγινώσκοντας ὑπὸ τὰ νοήματα τῇ φωνῇ [?] ἀφδατυσμένα. τὰ δὲ [illegible, ~8 letters] φραγίζεται, καὶ ἐνιδρύεται τῆς ὀρθῆς [?] ἐνευκαιρίας ἐκάστῳ, καὶ ἐπιρεπέστερον ἑαυτόν, καὶ μὴ μεταβάσεις ἐφ᾽ ἕτερον πεῖν ἢ πει-πράξεσθαι τὰ πρότερα βεβαίως. Ex quibus est perspicuum Mosem hic requirere scribendi studium & causam eius esse eam, ut altiore mente semen divinarum legum condatur.
units.tr: He commands writing by this very thing, that he wants the king himself to copy this book. Philo also teaches this very point in his book on the creation of the prince, in this way: "From the day on which he enters upon the office of rule, he is commanded to write out with his own hand a summary form of all the laws, a copy which will be better for his soul ..." [ἀφ᾽ ἧς ἡμέρας παρέλθῃ τῆς ... αὐτοχειρίᾳ κεφαλαιώδη τύπον]. From these words it is clear that Moses here requires the study of writing, and that its purpose is that the seed of the divine laws be planted in a higher mind.

units.la: Sed ne quis descriptum codicem nescio quo reponendum putet: docet etiam hoc requiri, ut princeps eum diu noctuq; legat. Idq; etiam eodem loco Philo ad hunc modum docet: ὅταν μὲν τοι γράφειν πεῖσαι κατ᾽ ἐκάστην ἡμέραν ἐντυγχάνειν καὶ ἀναγινώσκειν, ὑπέρτι συνεχοῦς καὶ ἀδιαστάτῳ μνήμης καλῶν καὶ συμφερόντων ἁπάντων [?] ἁγιάτων μάτων, &c. Ergo sic rex operam verbo Dei navabit, ut & legat & scribat.
units.tr: But lest anyone think the copied book is to be put away somewhere, he also teaches that the prince must read it by day and by night. Philo likewise teaches this in the same place in this way: "When he is commanded to write, he should also read and study it every day, so that the memory of all noble and useful things may be continuous and unbroken ..." [ὅταν μὲν τοι γράφειν πεῖσαι κατ᾽ ἐκάστην ἡμέραν ἐντυγχάνειν καὶ ἀναγινώσκειν]. Therefore the king will so labour at the Word of God that he both reads and writes it.

units.la: Porro finis huius est studij nosse facienda & non facienda. Facienda sunt, inquit Moses, timere Dominum Deum suum, & servare omnia verba legis huius ut faciat ea. Pietas hic com-mendatur & probitas. Non facienda sunt, inquit idem, unum, ut ne efferat sese supra fratres suos: alterum, ne recedat a divinis legibus. In quo spectatur hoc unicè, ut proroget ac firmet regnum sum. Quod etiam Philo pulcherrimè tradit & pluribus. Sed hæc de principe dicta suf-ficiant, Amen.
units.tr: The aim of this study is to know what is to be done and what is not to be done. Moses says what is to be done is to fear the Lord his God and to keep all the words of this law so as to do them. Piety and uprightness are commended here. What is not to be done, he says, is twofold: first, that he should not lift himself up above his brothers; second, that he should not turn aside from the divine laws. In this one aim is plainly seen, namely that he extend and strengthen his kingdom. Philo also teaches this most beautifully and at greater length. But let these things said about the prince be enough. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT XVIII. SERMO XLI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVIII. SERMON XLI.

units.la: SAcerdotes Leuitici generis, & tota tribus Leui nec partem nec haereditatem habebunt cum Israelitis, sed sacrificia quae igne confiunt Domino & haereditatem eius comedent.
units.tr: The priests of the Levitical race, and the whole tribe of Levi, shall have neither part nor inheritance with Israel, but shall eat the sacrifices of the LORD made by fire and his inheritance.

units.la: 2 Et ob id nullam haereditatem habebunt in medio fratrum suorum, sed Dominus est haereditas eorum, sicut pollicitus est eis.
units.tr: 2 And for this reason they shall have no inheritance among their brothers, but the LORD is their inheritance, as he promised them.

units.la: 3 Porro ius sacerdotum quod eis a populo, nempe ab his qui sacrificant sacrificia, sive bos sit, sive pecus, debetur, hoc est: Dabunt sacerdoti armum, & veram-bue maxillam atq; ventriculum.
units.tr: 3 Moreover, the priests' due from the people, namely from those who offer sacrifice, whether it be an ox or a sheep, is this: they shall give the priest the shoulder, the two cheeks and the stomach.

units.la: 4 Primitias quoq; frumenti tui, vini tui & olei tui, atq; primitias velleris o-vium tuarum dabis ei.
units.tr: 4 You shall also give him the firstfruits of your grain, your wine and your oil, and the firstfruits of the fleece of your sheep.

units.la: 5 Nam illum elegit Dominus Deus tuus ex cunctis tribubus tuis, ut stet ad ministrandum in nomine Domini,ipse & filij eius cunctis diebus.
units.tr: 5 For the LORD your God has chosen him out of all your tribes to stand to minister in the name of the LORD, he and his sons all the days.

units.la: 6 Et si venerit Levita ex una civitatum tuarum ex universo Israele, ubicunq; ipse commoretur, venerit inquam ex omni desiderio animi sui, ad locum quem elegerit Dominus.
units.tr: 6 And if a Levite comes from one of your cities out of all Israel, wherever he may be living, if he comes, I say, with all the desire of his soul, to the place which the LORD shall choose.

units.la: 7 Ministrabit in nomine Domini Dei sui, quemadmodũ omnes fratres sui Levitae, qui illic stant in conspectu Domini.
units.tr: 7 He shall minister in the name of the LORD his God, as all his fellow Levites do, who stand there before the LORD.

units.la: 8 Æquales portiones comedent, praeter venditiones suas (quas habent) à pa-tribus.
units.tr: 8 They shall eat equal portions, apart from their sales (which they have) from their fathers.

units.la: Benè profecto Deus & propter agnatam nobis imbecillitatem & malitiam salubriter instituit, ut quemadmodum adolescentes à parentibus educari, à praeceptoribus autem doceri solerent, nempe ut honori pariter atque usui suis omnibus forent: sic debeant adulti à magistratibus regi, à sacerdotibus edoceri atque instituti. Sed quon jam ambo illi, quos dici-mus, duces citra authoritatem & benevolentiam vel nihil vel perparum efficient: idem ille Deus tabulae secundae lege primaria constituit quam observantiam atque obedientiam parentibus, praeceptoribus, magistratibus, doctoribus nostris debeamus. Ac quoniam de magistratu jam proximo Capite dictum est, sequitur ut hoc ipso de sacerdotum ordine & officio dicatur.
units.tr: Certainly God has wisely instituted these things, both because of the weakness and malice we are born with, so that just as young people are usually brought up by their parents and taught by their tutors, so that they may be useful and honoured in all their affairs, so adults ought to be ruled by magistrates and instructed and trained by priests. But since those two kinds of leaders, of whom we speak, will accomplish nothing, or very little, without authority and goodwill, that same God, in the primary law of the second tablet, laid down the observance and obedience we owe to our parents, tutors, magistrates and teachers. And since the magistracy was discussed in the immediately preceding chapter, it follows that the order and office of the priests should be discussed in this one.

units.la: Quod perinde est observandum atque illud superius. Nam quemadmodum Deo resistit & publicam pacem turbat qui magistratus authoritati & potestati derogat: sic peccat in Deum qui ministris verbi suam authoritatem & potestatem lædit.
units.tr: This is to be observed in the same way as that earlier point. For just as he who detracts from the authority and power of the magistrate resists God and disturbs public peace, so he who injures the authority and power of the ministers of the Word sins against God.

units.la: Quamobrem Moses in hac tractatione versatur summa fide & diligentia: & causam eam duabus partibus absoluit. Primùm enim agit de sacerdotibus, deinceps autem de prophetia.
units.tr: Therefore Moses handles this subject with the greatest faith and diligence, and he completes the matter in two parts. First he deals with the priests, and then with prophecy.

units.la: Ac de sacerdotibus quidem sic scribit, ut primum de omni illorum genere tum de advenis differat.
units.tr: And concerning the priests he writes in such a way that he first discusses the whole class of them, and then the outsiders.

units.la: De omni genere dicit, Sacerdotes Leuitici generis, & tota tribus Levi nec partem nec hæreditatem, &c. Quibus verbis illorum personam, victum, officium dicit. Personae tribuit sacerdotes Leuitici generis & totam tribum Levi. Haec tribus sacerdotij dignitate potita est ob res praeclarè gestas: quippe quae gentem Israeliticam ex Aegypto eduxit, & idololatras affecit supplicio: velut Exodi 32. scribitur: Consecrate hodie manus vestras Domino quisque in filio suo & in fratre suo, ut detur vobis hodie benedictio. Unde eos Dominus selegit Numeri 3. Ecce ego (inquit Dominus ad Mosem dicens) selegi Levitas è medio filiorum Israel pro omni primogenito quod primum nascitur in filiis Israel & Levitae erunt mei. Quam electionem, etiam cum oppugnaretur seditione, Dominus miraculo confirmavit. Numeri decimo sexto decimoseptimo cap.
units.tr: He speaks of the whole class when he says: The priests of the Levitical race, and the whole tribe of Levi, shall have neither part nor inheritance, etc. In these words he describes their person, their sustenance and their office. To their person he assigns the priests of the Levitical race and the whole tribe of Levi. This tribe obtained the dignity of the priesthood on account of its outstanding deeds: it led the Israelite nation out of Egypt and punished the idolaters, as is written in Exodus 32: Consecrate your hands today to the LORD, each man in his son and in his brother, that a blessing may be given you today. Hence the LORD chose them, Numbers 3: Behold, I (says the LORD speaking to Moses) have chosen the Levites from among the sons of Israel in place of every firstborn that first opens the womb among the sons of Israel, and the Levites shall be mine. This choice the LORD confirmed by a miracle, even when it was attacked by rebellion: Numbers 16 and 17.

units.la: Jam quoniam Dominus & primogenita sibi delegit, & bene meritos feruentique zelo praeditos ad sacerdotij munus asciuit, eo facto nobis & Christi typum & utilia ad conservandam ecclesiam documenta praebet. Est enim hoc nobis argumento optimo quales ad ecclesiae ministerium homines sint eligendi, videlicet optimi & selectissimi: quando hoc ipsum & decet & necesse est nos facere. Decet ut floré[?] nostrum Deo dicemus, quo benedicat caeteras. Necessarium est ut pio, magno, prudenti sint animo, qui tantum munus velit sustinere: prudens qui res gerat, sapiens qui inter res discernat, magnus qui superbiam superet & despiciat minas & pericula, pius qui mundo posthabito respiciat ac sequatur Deum.
units.tr: Now since the LORD has chosen for himself the firstborn, and has taken to the priestly office those who have deserved well and are endowed with fervent zeal, by this act he presents us both with a type of Christ and with useful lessons for preserving the Church. For this gives us a very good argument as to what kind of men are to be chosen for the ministry of the Church: namely the best and most select, since this is both fitting and necessary for us to do. It is fitting that we offer God the best of our flock, so that he may bless the rest. It is necessary that the one who is to bear so great an office be of a devout, great and prudent mind: prudent to manage affairs, wise to discern among them, great to overcome pride and to despise threats and dangers, devout to put the world aside and look to and follow God.

units.la: Christum autem repraesentat, qui propter eam ipsam dignitatem primogenitus nobis praedicatur, ut unde solus sit ille summus sacerdos intelligamus. Nam quia primogenitus est omnis creaturae, ideo sacerdotij, id est docendi, benedicendi, sacrificandi, Deum pro nobis orandi munus illi soli competit & tribuitur. Jam quemadmodum olim reliqui sacerdotes summum illum respiciebant, sic nos qui teste Petro sacerdotes sumus, summum pontificem nostrum respiciemus & sequemur. Quae de re Psalmo 110. & in Pauli ad Hebraeos epistola.
units.tr: But he represents Christ, who on account of this very dignity is proclaimed to us as the firstborn, so that we may understand from this that he alone is the highest priest. For because he is the firstborn of all creation, the office of the priesthood, that is, of teaching, blessing, sacrificing and praying to God for us, belongs and is granted to him alone. Now just as the other priests of old looked to that highest priest, so we, who by the testimony of Peter are priests, shall look to and follow our high priest. On this matter see Psalm 110 and the Epistle of Paul to the Hebrews.

units.la: Sed haec de persona, jam de victu dicit: Nec partem nec hæreditatem habebunt cum filiis Israel, &c. Quibus verbis docet nullam terrae promissae portionem Levitis assignatam esse de cimasque[?] & sacrificia in victum cessisse. Causae quoad Levitas manifestae sunt, & in ipso textu quasi quodam modo exprimuntur. Sed Dominus est hereditas eorum sicut pollicitus est eis, inquit Moses. Quod argumento est voluisse Deum honoris causa possessionem & for-tem eorum esse. Quæ enim terræ portio Deo datori comparanda? Si dicat Dominus, accipite vos hanc, illam vos: ego sua Leuitis ero: quid maius? Dein sumimus eorum honor est, earum que Deo sacra sunt participem fieri. Præterea voluit Dominus illos solà religionis cu-ra atq; occupatione teneri, ceu esset hæc ipsorum propria.
units.tr: But he speaks thus of the person; now he speaks of their sustenance: They shall have neither part nor inheritance with the sons of Israel, etc. In these words he teaches that no portion of the promised land was assigned to the Levites, and that tithes and sacrifices went to their sustenance. The reasons for the Levites are plain, and they are in a certain way expressed in the text itself. But the LORD is their inheritance, as he promised them, says Moses. This is a sign that God willed their possession and lot to be the LORD himself, as a mark of honour. For what portion of land can be compared with God, the giver? If the LORD were to say, take this one and that one, and I will be the Levites' own: what could be greater? Moreover, it is an honour to become a sharer in what is sacred to God. Furthermore, the Lord willed that they be occupied and held solely by the care and business of religion, as if this were properly their own.

units.la: In quo nos etiamnum cernimus quanto sit ecclesiastæ[?] plus operæ sacris in rebus, quàm prophanis collocandum. Exemplo sunt Apostoli, qui noluerunt mensis relicto verbi mi-nisterio seruire. Sic qui nostra ætate verbo ministramus, propterea nec mercaturam nec ar-tes mœchanicas exercemus, ut liberius operam verbo demus explicando. Atque hæc est in Leuitarum persona posita causa propter quam nulla terræ portio sit eis assignata sed pro ea decimæ decretæ.
units.tr: In this we still see how much more care the minister of the Church ought to devote to sacred matters than to profane ones. The Apostles are an example, who would not leave the ministry of the Word to serve tables. So we who in our own age minister the Word therefore do not engage in trade or mechanical arts, so that we may give more freedom to the labour of explaining the Word. And this is the reason, stated in the person of the Levites, why no portion of the land was assigned to them, but tithes were ordained in its place.

units.la: Cæterum in reliquorum Israelitarum persona quædam etiam causæ exprimuntur. Decimæ enim, de quibus hic nihil dicitur, supra seorsim dictum est satis, in ipsis agris & torcu-laribus dabantur: sacrificia vero in templis offerebantur non Leuitis, sed Domino: nempe, ut Israelitæ scirent se eas Deo dare, & ijs ipsis Leuitas ideo frui quod ipsorum pars esset Dominus. Ergo Deus voluit Israelitarum pietati consulere, ne quæ Deo darent mala fide persoluerent: ut eius obliuione nulla unquam obruerentur.
units.tr: Moreover, in the person of the rest of the Israelites certain reasons are also expressed. For the tithes, of which nothing is said here, were given in the fields and winepresses themselves, as has been said sufficiently above separately. The sacrifices, however, were offered in the temples not to the Levites but to the LORD, so that the Israelites might know they were giving them to God, and that the Levites enjoyed them for this reason, that the LORD was their portion. Thus God willed to provide for the piety of the Israelites, so that they would not pay with bad faith what they gave to God, and thus never be overwhelmed by forgetfulness of him.

units.la: Paulus hunc locum in priore ad Corinthios nono capite pluribus verbis exponit. Do-minus Matthæi decimo & Ioannis undecimo cap. itidem. Et certè si ministris necesse es-set ex eo quod pro sua quisque eiuis munificentia suppeditaret viuere: sanè quæ est plero-rumq; erga illos maleuolentia, prorsus actum de eorum salute esset. Etenim quas vel aliun-de suppeditatas opes habent, eas pleriq; solent illis inuidere. Si datur illis ægre ex publico, quid speres ex priuatis?
units.tr: Paul expounds this passage at length in the ninth chapter of his first Epistle to the Corinthians. Likewise the Lord in Matthew 10 and John 11. And certainly, if the ministers had to live on whatever each one supplied out of his own generosity, then, given the ill will that most people bear toward them, their salvation would indeed be utterly undone. For most people are accustomed to begrudge them whatever wealth they have from elsewhere. If they are given grudgingly from public funds, what could you hope for from private persons?

units.la: Ergo Deus ut saluum esset officium docendi, quæ dicta sunt Leuitis assignauit. Sed hæc de victu paucis dicta sufficiant.
units.tr: Therefore God, so that the office of teaching might be safe, assigned to the Levites what has been said. But let these few remarks on their sustenance suffice.

units.la: Officium sic exponit: Nam illum(inquit) Deus tuus elegit ex cunctis tribubus tuis, ut stet ad ministrandum in nomine Domini. Eius partes sigillatim commemorat. 1 Doceant omnia statuta quæ loquutus est Dominus per Mosem Leuitici decimo, Ezechielis quadragesimo quarto, Malachiæ secundo, &c. 2 Benedicant, Numeri sexto cap. præscripta formula. 3 Sa-crificent, ut est in secundo libro Paralippomenon vicesimoquarto capite, & curent templa. Sic Apostolorum & Euangelium prædicantium est docere, benedictionem in Christo monstrare, sacramenta administrare, orare pro populo. Atque hæc de communi Leuitarum genere.
units.tr: He sets out the office thus: For he (says Moses) your God has chosen out of all your tribes, to stand to minister in the name of the LORD. He mentions its parts one by one. 1. They are to teach all the statutes which the LORD spoke through Moses: Leviticus 10, Ezekiel 44, Malachi 2, etc. 2. They are to bless, using the formula prescribed in Numbers 6. 3. They are to sacrifice, as is said in 2 Chronicles 24, and to take care of the temples. So it is the task of the Apostles and of those who preach the Gospel to teach, to show the blessing in Christ, to administer the sacraments, and to pray for the people. And these things concern the common class of Levites.

units.la: De reliquis, si qui sint pauperes, vult etiam illis victum suum esse, videlicet studio co-gnoscendæ veritatis & exercendæ fidei gratia Hierosolymam euntibus. Nam pietas & studium promoueri non impediri debent. Hæc diuinitus mandata sunt, ut saluum sit inter ho-mines verbi diuini ministerium. Id ut sit Deum oremus per Iesum Christum Dominum no-strum, Amen.
units.tr: As for the rest, if there are any poor among them, he wills that they too have their livelihood, namely for the sake of diligently learning the truth and exercising faith, for those who go up to Jerusalem. For godliness and zeal ought to be advanced, not hindered. These things have been commanded by God, so that the ministry of the divine Word may be preserved among men. That this may be so, let us pray to God through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

units.la: SERMO XLII.
units.tr: SERMON XLII.

units.la: 9 Quum tu veneris in terram, quam Dominus Deus tuus dat tibi, ne assuescas facere iuxta abominandos ritus gentium istarum.
units.tr: 9 When you have come into the land which the Lord your God gives you, you shall not learn to do after the abominable customs of those nations.

units.la: 16 Non inueniatur in te qui traducat filium suum aut filiam suam per ignem, nec diuinus qui diuinando futura prædicit, nec mathematicus, nec veneficus, nec maleficus.
units.tr: 16 Let there not be found among you anyone who makes his son or daughter pass through the fire, nor a diviner who foretells the future, nor a mathematician, nor a poisoner, nor a sorcerer.

units.la: 11 Nec incantator, nec consulens pythonē, nec magus, nec à mortuis scifcitas.
units.tr: 11 Nor an enchanter, nor one who consults a python, nor a magician, nor one who seeks the truth from the dead.

units.la: 12 Abominatur enim Dominus quicunq; ista facit, & ob istas abominationes excindit eos Dominus Deus tuus ante te.
units.tr: 12 For whoever does these things is an abomination to the Lord, and because of these abominations the Lord your God drives them out before you.

units.la: 13 Sis igitur integer cum Domino Deo tuo.
units.tr: 13 You shall therefore be whole with the Lord your God.

units.la: 14 Nam gentes istæ, quas tu iam occupabis, audiunt mathematicos et diuinos: tibi vero sic facere non permittit Dominus Deus tuus.
units.tr: 14 For those nations which you are about to dispossess listen to mathematicians and diviners; but the Lord your God does not permit you to do so.

units.la: CUm Moses hoc capite de ministris Ecclesiæ dicere cœpisset: jam inde ab eorum persona atque officio ad prophetiam, ceu eam quam illi tractant materiam, delabitur.
units.tr: When Moses had begun in this chapter to speak of the ministers of the Church, he slides from their person and office into prophecy, as if that were the subject they handle.

units.la: Est autem prophetia Hebræis quidem ab enuntiando seu reuelando, Græcis autem & Latinis à prædicendo nominata: quippe quæ res abstrusas eruat, ac priusquam eueniant prædicat. Est ergo diuinæ voluntatis reuelatio & summa sapientia, & religionis Deo placitæ & nobis salutiferæ scienti a:tum etiam rerum absconditarum cognitio. Ac quanquam hæc sacer dotibus præcipuè data esset, tamen aliis tribus non omnino suit negata: veluti Mose res gerente viri 72. prophetiæ donum acceperant: post Dauid, Solomon, Esaias & alij regia, ple-beia, alijs etiam familiaribus orti prophetia donati sunt. Est autem eius summa, vt homines di-scant Deum diligere ex toto corde, bonum à malo discernere, & quæ scire nostra refert explorare.
units.tr: Now prophecy is so named by the Hebrews from declaring or revealing, but by the Greeks and Latins from foretelling, since it brings hidden things to light and announces them before they happen. It is therefore a revelation of the divine will and supreme wisdom, and knowledge of the religion pleasing to God and saving to us; it is also knowledge of hidden things. Although this gift was given chiefly to the priests, it was not wholly denied to the other tribes. For while Moses ruled, seventy-two men received the gift of prophecy; afterwards David, Solomon, Isaiah and others, both of royal and of common birth, and some even of humble family, were endowed with prophecy. Its sum is that men should learn to love God with their whole heart, to distinguish good from evil, and to examine what it concerns us to know.

units.la: Jam satan vt avellat nos à Deo, vt malum ingerat pro bono, vt futurorum malorum metum animis eximat: prophetiam falsam introducit, cuius species multæ sunt & variæ. Jam vt & falsam cavere possumus & amplecti bonam: prius dicit de falsa, post de vera. Ac in præsentia quidem de falsa sic disserit, vt eam primùm describat, tum cavendam esse doceat.
units.tr: Now Satan, in order to tear us away from God, to thrust evil upon us in place of good, and to remove from our minds the fear of future evils, introduces false prophecy, which has many and various forms. So that we may both avoid the false and embrace the true, Moses speaks first of the false and afterwards of the true. For the present he treats of the false in such a way that he first describes it and then teaches that it must be avoided.

units.la: Ac descriptionem quidem perficit enumeratione partium dicens, Cum tu veneris in terram quam Dominus Deus tuus dat tibi, ne assuescas facere iuxta abominandos ritus gentium illa-rum. Non inveniatur, &c. Quibus primùm dicit abstinendum ab omni superstitionum genere & specie: dein eas sigillatim singulas commemorat.
units.tr: He completes the description by enumerating its parts, saying: When you have come into the land which the Lord your God gives you, you shall not learn to do after the abominable customs of those nations. Let there not be found, etc. By these words he first tells us to abstain from every kind and form of superstition, and then he recounts each of them separately.

units.la: Quod omnem superstitionum vsum vetat, id ad conservandam puritatem momenti multum affert, & propterea Deo inprimis placet. Ideo Paulus 2. Cor. 6. dicit, ne ducatis iugũ cũ incredulis. Quod enim consortium justitiæ cum injustitia? Quæ communio luci cum tenebris? Quæ concordia Christo cum Belial? aut quæ pars fideli cum infideli? aut quid convenit templo Dei cum simulachris? Apostoli noluerunt Judaismum cum Christianismo confundi, vt consilium Hierosolymitanum docet. Et Paulus dicit obnoxios esse legi qui circuncisione sibi sumunt. Vtinam Papa non gentilismum simul & Judaismum Christianismo commiscuisset. Vtinam non multi nostra ætate cum euangelio papisticas superstitiones miscerent, velut[?] qui Interim illud fabricarunt. Quæ pestis ex eo nascitur quod supra modum affectamus, terrenam illam cum mundo societatem atq; amicitiam.
units.tr: That he forbids every use of superstition contributes greatly to keeping purity, and for that reason it especially pleases God. So Paul says in 2 Cor. 6, "Do not be yoked together with unbelievers. For what fellowship has righteousness with unrighteousness? What communion has light with darkness? What concord has Christ with Belial? Or what part has the faithful with the unfaithful? Or what agreement has the temple of God with idols?" The apostles would not have Judaism confused with Christianity, as the council of Jerusalem teaches; and Paul says that those who take circumcision upon themselves are bound to the law. Would that the Pope had not mixed paganism and Judaism together with Christianity! Would that in our own age many had not mixed Papistical superstitions with the gospel, as those who in the meantime devised that. This plague arises from the fact that we desire beyond measure that earthly fellowship and friendship with the world.

units.la: At hic vetat, & per partes exponit. 1. Qui suos liberos traducunt per ignem, videlicet vel prorsus comburerent, vel ita purgarent. Ignis enim & aqua, vt quæ sua natura purgant, purgandi vim repræsentabant. Veluti canit ille in V I. Aliæ pandúntur inanes / Suspensæ ad ventos, alij sub gurgite vasto, / Infectum eluitur scelus, aut exuritur igni.
units.tr: But here he forbids and sets out the matter in parts. 1. Those who make their children pass through the fire, that is, either burn them outright or purify them thus. For fire and water, as things which purify by their nature, were signs of the power of purification. So that poet sings in book VI: "Some are stretched out, hanging to the winds; others under a vast whirlpool, till the stain is washed away, or burned out by fire."

units.la: Unde crudelis hæc & immanis superstitio magnam orbis partem peruagata est, qua liberos ignibus lustrarent.
units.tr: Hence this cruel and monstrous superstition, by which they purified their children with fires, spread far over a great part of the world.

units.la: Inde etiam crudelia sacrificia Græcis gentibus vsitata: vt quod Athenienses septem pueros & totidem puellas Minotauro mittere jussi: vt Apollonius Tyaneus senem mendicum obrui lapidibus ad expiandam pestem jussit.
units.tr: From the same source came the cruel sacrifices customary among the Greek nations: as when the Athenians were ordered to send seven boys and as many girls to the Minotaur; and as Apollonius of Tyana ordered an old beggar to be pelted with stones to expiate a plague.

units.la: Sed neq; ignibus neq; aquis abluuntur animæ labes: spiritus enim sancti propria virtus est purificare.
units.tr: But souls are not cleansed of their stains either by fires or by waters: for it is the proper power of the Holy Spirit to purify.

units.la: Ac nos discimus liberos nostros non villis monachorum ordinibus, sed soli Christo of-ferre, discimus abstinere ab aqua benedicta, atq; à reliquis papisticis purificationibus. Educa-tione, disciplina, castigatione, doctrina sana ac divina quicquid sordium hæret animis pue-rilibus abstergi potest & absumi, bene fortunante nostram operam Domino.
units.tr: We learn not to offer our children to the vile orders of monks but to Christ alone; we learn to abstain from holy water and from the other Papistical purifications. By education, discipline, correction, and sound and divine teaching, whatever filth clings to childish minds can be wiped away and removed, if the Lord prospers our labour.

units.la: 2 Divini, id est, qui quacunq; arte pollicentur rerum futurarum prædictionem: quo refer gæomantiam, chiromantiam, interpretationem somniorum, & quæ sunt huius generis alia.
units.tr: 2. Diviners, that is, those who promise the foretelling of future things by whatever art: to these belong geomancy, chiromancy, interpretation of dreams, and other things of this kind.

units.la: 3 Meonenim ab onán[?] nube dicti, vt qui in superioris mundi contemplatione versantur & judicio, qui figuram cœli & positus siderum in nativitate hominis servant, qui fata gentium ex astris conjiciunt & canunt, qui diem alium alio felicior putant. Quod genus hominum quoniam & Deo suam potestatem ademptam astris attribuunt, & incorporeum ho-minis animum rebus corporeis subjiciunt, & hominibus ipsis illudunt, in Deum quidem atque homines impij sunt, sibi vero stultitiæ notam inurunt. Qua de causa magistratuum in-terest[?] hos procul arcere suis finibus, & singulorum est eos ceu pestem publicam ca-uer[?].
units.tr: 3. The Meonim are so named from the cloud (onan [עָנָן]), as those who are occupied with the contemplation and judgment of the upper world, who observe the figure of the heavens and the positions of the stars at a man's birth, who conjecture and sing the fates of nations from the stars, and who think one day luckier than another. Since this kind of men also attribute to the stars a power taken from God, subject the incorporeal soul of man to bodily things, and mock men themselves, they are impious towards God and men, and they brand themselves with the mark of folly. For this reason it is in the interest of magistrates to keep them far away from their borders, and it is the duty of each individual to beware of them as a public plague.

units.la: 4 Menachefchim qui serpentibus quasi quodam artis organo vsi diuinant. Quo genere continentur augures & eorum similes. Veluti cum vrbs Roma conderetur visi sunt duo-decim vultures : responsum est ab auguribus vrbem duraturam annis 120. & si longius staret duraturam annis 3200. Quod vndecunque dæmon acceperit, vsu compertum est verum. Eodem pertinent quæ Rabi Dauid Kimhi dicit, eum qui conijcit ex hoc ipso quod bucella cadit ex ore, baculus è manu, filius eum reuocat, coruus occlamat, cer-uus præterit, serpentem à dextris, vulpem à sinistris habet, eius generis diuinaculum esse.
units.tr: 4. The menachefchim [מְנַחֵשׁ], who practise divination by means of serpents, as if by a kind of instrument of their art. To this kind belong augurs and those like them. For example, when the city of Rome was being founded, twelve vultures were seen; it was answered by the augurs that the city would last 120 years, and if it stood longer, that it would last 3200 years. Whatever the demon received from anywhere, its truth was proved by experience. To the same category belongs what Rabbi David Kimhi says: that one who infers from the fact that a morsel falls from the mouth, a staff from the hand, that a son calls him back, a raven cries out, a stag passes by, that he has a serpent on his right and a fox on his left, is practising a divination of this sort.

units.la: 5 Qui Mechachefchim Hebraïs dicuntur nobis malefici, vt qui vel herbis vel carminibus vel alijs id genus fictitijs vocabulis, atqz characteribus vtuntur, itemqz sagæ. Ac licet vtantur aliqui sacris vocibus, tamen adeo non possunt excusari, vt etiam blasphemi diuinorum oraculorum abusus sese faciant reos.
units.tr: 5. Those whom the Hebrews call mechachefchim [מְכַשֵּׁף], we call sorcerers, that is, those who use herbs, songs, and other such fictitious words and characters, and likewise witches. And although some use sacred words, they cannot be excused on that account, since by blasphemously abusing the divine oracles they make themselves guilty.

units.la: 6 Sunt magi rerum futurarum nuncij seu coniectores, <bl>Waarsager.</bl>
units.tr: 6. There are magi, announcers or conjecturers of future things: Waarsager [soothsayers].

units.la: 7 Qui Hebraïs dicitur fefchohel off, id est, qui malos spiritus consulit. Nam אוֹב[?] vtrem significat seu lagunculam, quod rauca atq; obscura voce quasi ex lagena quadam loqui videretur qui respondet spiritus. Consulitur autem vel cranium, vel mortuus inter fœmora Pythonis. Septuaginta interpretes ἐγγαστερίμυθος[?], Tertullianus ventriloquos vocant. Videre est in historijs, vt suis illis imposturis deceperit & perdiderit homines satan. Saul sic prostratus est. Oraculum Croeso dicit, Halim transgressum euersurum maxima regna: miser ille Croesus euertit suum. Iuliano promittunt victoriam, quam ipse persequens vincitur, Et Pœno responsum est, Aio te Æacida Romanos vincere posse.
units.tr: 7. Those whom the Hebrews call shoel ob [שֹׁאֵל אוֹב], that is, those who consult evil spirits. For ob [אוֹב] means a leather bottle or a small flask, because the spirit that answers seems to speak with a hoarse and muffled voice, as if out of some kind of jar. Consultation is made either with a skull or with a dead man between the thighs of a python. The Seventy translators render it engastrimythos [ἐγγαστρίμυθος], and Tertullian calls them ventriloquists. It is clear from histories how Satan deceived and destroyed men with those impostures of his. Saul was thus laid low. An oracle said to Croesus that if he crossed the Halys he would overthrow a great kingdom: the wretched Croesus overthrew his own. They promised victory to Julian, but while pursuing it he was himself defeated. And to the Carthaginian it was answered, "I say that you, son of Aeacus, can conquer the Romans."

units.la: 8 Veiddionei sunt incantatores.
units.tr: 8. Yidde'oni [יִדְּעֹנִי] are enchanters.

units.la: 9 Qui mortuos consulunt.
units.tr: 9. Those who consult the dead.

units.la: Ex quorum omnium catalogo perspicuum est, quod genus prophetiæ satan introduxerit, nempe quod plausibile quidem esset, sed tamen pernitiosum.
units.tr: From the catalogue of all these it is plain what kind of prophecy Satan introduced: one that was indeed plausible, yet nonetheless pernicious.

units.la: Iam docet ab his abstinendum esse, & assert causas. 1. Quia Dominus abhorret ab eis, quasi ab re quam natura oderis: cur ergo velis. Leuit.20.
units.tr: Now he teaches that these must be avoided, and gives reasons. 1. Because the Lord abhors them, as things he hates by nature; why then would you wish them? Lev. 20.
