units.la: 2 Quia propterea has gentes excindit. Pœnam hanc statuit malo, quam si velis euitare, hæc vites necesse est. Ac veluti furtum laqueo, sic excidio malum hoc mulctatur. Ergo vt la-queum effugis abstinendo à furto, sic excidium auertes cauendo ab his artibus. Tu sis inter-ger coram Domino Deo tuo.
units.tr: 2 For this reason God destroys these nations. He has appointed this punishment for the evil, and if you wish to escape it, you must avoid these vices. As theft is caught in a snare, so this evil is punished by destruction. Therefore, just as you escape the snare by abstaining from theft, so you will avert destruction by guarding yourself against these arts. Be blameless before the Lord your God.

units.la: 3 Fœdus in memoriam reuocat Genesis 17. Hoc vetat alibi consilia atq; auxilia quærere, quàm apud Dominum Deum vnum. At nullum est à Domino auxilium? Ergo inquam, quod ipse vult patienter feras: vndecunq; enim opem petas illius potentiæ non reluctaberis.
units.tr: 3 The covenant recalls the memory of Genesis 17. Elsewhere it forbids seeking counsel and help from anyone but the Lord God alone. But is there no help from the Lord? Therefore, I say, bear patiently what he himself wills, for wherever you seek aid, you will not resist his power.

units.la: 4 Gentes huius terræ Domini sic consulunt ariolos, tibi id non permittit Dominus. Quod perin-de est ac si dicat: ethnicum hoc est, & ab homine fideli prorsus alienum.
units.tr: 4 "The nations of this land consult soothsayers; the Lord does not permit you to do so." This is just as if he said: this practice is heathen and wholly foreign to a faithful man.

units.la: Eadem nobis sint rationes, vt ne tantopere allubescant hæ superstitiones. Dominus re-gnat, inquit psalthes, hunc potius consulemus. Dominus verus est, illum rogemus potius, quàm eum qui in veritate non stetit & pater est mendaciorum.
units.tr: The same reasons should hold for us, so that these superstitions do not attract us so greatly. "The Lord reigns," says the psalmist; let us rather consult him. The Lord is true; let us rather ask him than him who did not stand in the truth and is the father of lies.

units.la: Sed & iura ciuilia & sacræ literæ hæc omnia confirmant suis suffragijs. Extat Constan-tini Imp. rescriptum quo iubetur aruspex concremari, & qui illum euocauerit & bonis om-nibus exui & in infulam deportari, & eorum accusator non delatoris infami nomine, sed pre-mio dignus esse: vt est in l. nullus C. de malef. & mathem. Dein Impp. Constantinus & Iulia-nus mandant, vt sileat omnibus perpetuo diuinandi curiositas, idq; pœna capitis: l. nemo. C. eod. tit. Eodem referendæ sunt aliæ ll. eiusdem tituli. Neq; vero silentio prætereundum est illud celebre Senatusconsultum de pellendis Italia Mathematicis, cum Libo Scribonius per Firmium Catum Senatorem delatus esset, quod magos super imperio consuleret, & vmbras infernas carminibus vellet euocare. Et Imp. Leo prohibuit ne quis arte magica thesauros e-tiam in suo fundo latentes perquirat, l. j. C. de thesauris. Et in ll. xij tab. sic scribitur. Qui ma-lum carmen incantarit, frugesue excantarit coercetor. Quo referri possunt ex iure pontifi-cio, vt xxvj. q. j. ij & seq. plurima.
units.tr: Civil laws and the sacred writings alike confirm all these things with their support. There is an edict of the emperor Constantine ordering that a soothsayer be burned, and that whoever summoned him be stripped of all his goods and deported to an island, and that his accuser deserves not the infamous name of informer but a reward, as is stated in the law "nullus," C. de malef. et mathem. Then the emperors Constantine and Julian commanded that the curiosity of divining be silenced for all people forever, on pain of death (law "nemo," C. eod. tit.). Other laws of the same title are to be referred to the same point. Nor must we pass over in silence that famous senatorial decree concerning the expulsion of mathematicians from Italy, when Libo Scribonius was denounced through the senator Firmius Catus because he consulted magicians about the empire and wished to summon the shades of the underworld with incantations. And the emperor Leo forbade anyone to seek treasures, even those hidden in his own field, by magical art (law 1, C. de thesauris). And in the Twelve Tables it is written thus: "Whoever has chanted an evil charm, or charmed away the crops, shall be punished." Very many texts on this point can be cited from the papal law, as in C. 26, q. 1, cc. 2 ff.

units.la: Et memorabile est Ephef. exemplum, qui cognita per Paulum verè diuina prophetia, magicam atq; impiam illam sic detestati sunt, vt libros quibus esset ea descripta simul omnes exusserint. Qu̅ d exemplum quoniam pulchre censet & exponit Oecumenius, quae sunt eius verba placuit huc ascribi. σημειωτέον δ' ἐ(inquit) καὶ ἐν τοῖς ἐφεξῆς ὅτι καὶ πολυ- μεσ οὐσας τας χρηστικας αὐτῶν βιβλως ὡς τὴν ἐν βίῳ ἐχεσῶν τὰ κάλλιστα, οἱ εἰς χριστὸν πι- σευσαντες ἐκ πολλησας ἀλλ' ἐκαυσαν καὶ τοιγε ἐκεῖσε τοιούτων τῷ θελόντων τὰς βιβλως κτήσασθαι. πρῶτον μὲν ἵνα μήτις μεταχῇ τῆς ἀπ' αὐτῶν ψυχοφθόρου λύμης, ἔπειτα δ' ἵνα μὴ δὲ τοιαύτης αἰτίας κἀσωνταῖν. ὥσπερ γὰρ τὸ ἀπὸ πορνείας κέρδος ἀπαρέυτα [?] ἐατέιν θεοῦ οὐ τως ἀλλ' τὸ τῆς αἰτίας ταύτης ἀργύριον τεθῆναι παρὰ τὰς τῶν ἀποστόλων πό- δας δ' ἱκανὸν ἐκεῖναι ἢ ἐναπόλιχθν. [?] Ex quibus verbis est perspicuum illos noluisse eos libros etiam cum possent vendere, partim vt ne quos eorum lectione corrumperent: partim vt ne viderentur ex rebus illicitis turpe lucrum captasse.
units.tr: The example of the Ephesians is also memorable. When they had come to know, through Paul, the truly divine prophecy, they so detested magic and that impious art that they all together burned the books in which it was described. Since Oecumenius judges and explains this example well, I have thought fit to add his own words here. He says: "It should be noted, also in what follows, that those who had believed in Christ, though they had many books of their magic arts, which were the most valuable they possessed, burned them all, and so they would not allow anyone who wished to acquire such books to do so. This was done first so that no one might share in the soul-destroying corruption that comes from them, and secondly so that they might not be seen to have profited from such a cause. For just as the gain from fornication was not to be received into the treasury of God, so the money from this matter was not to be laid at the feet of the apostles." From these words it is clear that they did not wish to sell those books even though they could, partly so that they would not corrupt anyone by reading them, and partly so that they would not seem to have made a shameful profit from unlawful things. [σημειωτέον δ' ἐν τοῖς ἐφεξῆς ὅτι καὶ πολυμεσούσας τὰς χρηστικὰς αὐτῶν βίβλους ... ἐκαυσαν ... τὸ τῆς αἰτίας ταύτης ἀργύριον τεθῆναι παρὰ τοὺς τῶν ἀποστόλων πόδας]

units.la: Quamobrem hac ceu peste corporum & animarum est abstinendum atq; in studium puri puti verbi Dei incumbendum per Iesum Christum, Amen.
units.tr: Therefore we must abstain from this plague of bodies and souls, and devote ourselves to the study of the pure Word of God through Jesus Christ. Amen.

units.la: SERMO XLIII.
units.tr: SERMON XLIII.

units.la: 15 Prophetam de medio tui, ex fratribus tuis sicuti me, excitabit tibi Dominus Deus tuus, illum audietis.
units.tr: 15 The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brethren, like unto me; him shall ye hear.

units.la: 16 Iuxta omnia quae postulasti à Domino Deo tuo in Horeb in die congregationis, quando dicebas, Non vltra audiam vocem Domini Dei mei, & magnum illum ignem non videbo amplius, ne moriar.
units.tr: 16 According to all that you asked of the Lord your God in Horeb in the day of the assembly, when you said, "Let me not hear again the voice of the Lord my God, nor see this great fire any more, lest I die."

units.la: 17 Dixitq; Dominus ad me, Bene egerunt in hoc quod locuti sunt.
units.tr: 17 And the Lord said to me, "They have spoken well in what they have said."

units.la: 18 Prophetam excitabo eis de medio fratrum suorum, sicut te: ponam q; verba mea in os eius, & loquetur ad eos quaecunq; mandauero illi.
units.tr: 18 I will raise them up a prophet from among their brethren, like you; and I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I command him.

units.la: 19 Et homo qui non audierit verba mea, quae loquetur in nomine meo, in illum ego inquiram.
units.tr: 19 And whoever does not hear my words, which he shall speak in my name, I myself will call him to account.

units.la: HOc Capite Moses alterum illum seniorum ordinem, cuius dignitatem & authoritatem Dominus Deus quinta lege tuendam ratus est, describit, videlicet ministros ecclesiae. In qua descriptione primum agit de ministris ipsis, tum vero de prophetia, ceu ea circa quam versantur materia. Ac quoniam satan, vti vulgo dici solet, iuxta Dei templum sibi quoq; sacellum aliquod ponit: hoc est iuxta veram prophetiam ipse falsam spargit: Moses primum repellit falsam, & deinceps docet veram.
units.tr: In this chapter Moses describes that other order of elders, whose dignity and authority the Lord thought fit to be guarded by the fifth law; namely, the ministers of the Church. In this description he treats first of the ministers themselves, and then of prophecy, as the subject with which they are concerned. And since Satan, as is commonly said, sets up a little shrine of his own beside the temple of God, that is, alongside true prophecy he spreads false prophecy, Moses first rejects the false and then teaches the true.

units.la: Iam cum de falsa dictum sit, reliquum est vt dicatur etiam de vera. Eam hoc loco sic describit, vt primum eius originem tum autem commendet authoritatem.
units.tr: Since the false has been spoken of, what remains is that the true be spoken of as well. Here he describes it in such a way that he first sets out its origin and then commends its authority.

units.la: Ac de eius origine sic dicit: Prophetam de medio tui ex fratribus tuis sicuti me suscitabit tibi Dominus Deus tuus, illum audies, &c. Quibus verbis originem prophetiae ad Deum ipsum refert, & id probat toti populi testimonio. Ad Deū sic refert vt indicet homines à Deo ipso suscitari & praeparari ad pertractandā prophetiā. Homines quidem sunt qui nos de voluntate Dei certiores faciunt, sed tamen à Deo spiritus illos habent, propterea-que sunt audiendi. Quod ipsum si cogitarent homines, aliter ac solent de ministris iudicarent.
units.tr: As to its origin he says: "The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brethren, like unto me; him you shall hear," and so on. In these words he traces the origin of prophecy back to God himself, and proves it by the testimony of the whole people. He traces it to God in order to show that men are raised up and prepared by God himself to handle prophecy. Indeed, it is men who inform us of the will of God, but they have these gifts from God, and for that reason they are to be heard. If men considered this, they would judge about ministers otherwise than they usually do.

units.la: Sed verba singula considera. Prophetam, inquit, Nabi Hebraeis significat interpretem, oratorem, internuncium Dei, qui diuinitus acceptam veram doctrinam tradit: non vt illi quos supra dixi, coniecturas afferent & somnia. Quare par est vt multum inter verum prophetam & falsum interesse scias atq; existimes. Nostrae aetatis hominibus imposuerunt pfaffi mi ris modis: atin Deum adeo sunt ingrati, vt idem nomen etiam fidelissimis euangelistis tribuant, atq; etiam de eo reprehensi idem genus esse dicant. At Paulus voluit alio loco pios doctores haberi.
units.tr: But consider the individual words. "Prophet," he says; the Hebrews signify by nabi an interpreter, a spokesman, a messenger of God, who delivers the true doctrine received from God; not like those I mentioned above, who offer conjectures and dreams. So you should know and judge that there is a great difference between a true prophet and a false one. The priests have deceived the men of our age in many ways, and they are so ungrateful to God that they give the same name even to the most faithful evangelists, and when they are rebuked for this, they say they are of the same kind. Yet Paul wished in another place that godly teachers be held in esteem.

units.la: E medio tui, ex fratribus tuis sicut me: id est, hominem tibi cognatum. Vide quibus Deus vtatur medijs. Primum nos ipse docuit, tum angelis & hominibus vsus est internuncijs. Homines quidem sunt, sed internuncij Domini.
units.tr: From among your brethren, like me: that is, a man akin to you. See what means God uses. He first taught us himself, and then he made use of angels and men as messengers. They are men indeed, but messengers of the Lord.

units.la: Suscitabit. Quasi dicat, Homo hoc ipsum nec posset nec auderet moliri, vel facere: verum Deus illos imbuit suo spiritu, ut ad tantarum rerum cognitionem atque explicationem alacres sint & idonei. Unde in priore Petri primo cap. dicit Apostolus ille prophetas spiritu Dei instructos suum manus obiisse. Matth. 10. cap. dicitur apostolis: Vos non estis illi loquentes, sed spiritus patris vestri. Et Paulus scribit Timotheo, sacras literas institutu seu revelatione spiritus sancti proditas esse. Sic acceptae conciones efficiunt aliquid in animis nostris boni: caeterum secus, nihil.
units.tr: Will raise up. As if he said: a man could neither attempt nor dare to accomplish this by himself; but God imbues them with his Spirit, so that they are eager and fit for the knowledge and explanation of such great things. Hence in the first chapter of his first epistle that apostle says the prophets, instructed by the Spirit of God, performed their duties. In Matthew 10 it is said to the apostles: "It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father." And Paul writes to Timothy that the holy letters were set forth by the inspiration or revelation of the Holy Spirit. Thus sermons received in this way work some good in our minds; otherwise they work nothing.

units.la: Illum audies, finis hic est syncerae prophetiae, ut audiatur.
units.tr: Him you shall hear: this is the aim of genuine prophecy, that it be heard.

units.la: Iam quoniam Christus princeps prophetarum est, & eius spiritu, Petro teste, prophetae locuti sunt: recte sane colligunt hinc apostoli diuinum illud de Christo vaticinium. Ut Act. 3. Petrus ait, Moses quidem ad patres dixit, &c. Et Stephanus Actor. 7. Hic est Moses qui dixerat filijs Israel &c. Prophetam igitur & quicquid hic de eo dicitur si consideres, omnia recte de Christo dici possunt. Siue enim nabi, id est, diuinorum mysteriorum interpres, siue chofen, id est, videns dicatur, Christo recte tribuetur. Nemo enim vidit patrem nisi filius. Et filius vnigenitus, qui est in sinu patris, ipse enarrauit nobis.
units.tr: Now since Christ is the chief of the prophets, and, as Peter testifies, the prophets spoke by his Spirit, the apostles rightly infer from this the divine prophecy about Christ. As Peter says in Acts 3: "Moses indeed said to the fathers," and so on. And Stephen in Acts 7: "This is Moses who said to the sons of Israel," and so on. If you consider the prophet and whatever is said of him here, all of it can rightly be said of Christ. For whether he is called nabi, that is, an interpreter of divine mysteries, or chozeh [חוזה], that is, a seer, it is rightly attributed to Christ. For no one has seen the Father except the Son. And the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him to us.

units.la: Si fratres Iudæos consideres eius gente nobilissima familia Christus verus homo natus est: neque enim assumpsit angelum, ut scribit Hebræis suis Apostolus: sed hoc dedit Iudæis, ut ex ipsis nasci vellet.
units.tr: If you consider the brethren of the Jews: from that most noble family of that nation Christ was born a true man. For, as the Apostle writes to his Hebrews, he did not take hold of angels, but he gave this to the Jews, that he would be born from them.

units.la: Sed etsi Mose multis ijsq; immensis modis superior fit, tamen ab illo ipso multis etiam typis & figuris est adumbratus. Ac primum veluti Moses cum populo Dei maluit affligi, quàm in aula Pharaonis illustris & lautus esse:sic Christus non rapinam arbitratus est, ut ait Apostolus, serui formam assumere, omninoq; maluit diros cruciatus perpeti, quàm nobis de sertis sua gloria perfrui. Et ut Moses reiectus est à suis ipsius fratribus, sic Christus venit in sua & sui illum non receperunt. Quemadmodum Moses fideles ex Ægypto, sic Christus ex orci faucibus eripuit. Omitto multa alia inter utrumq; similia.
units.tr: But although he is superior to Moses in many and immeasurable ways, yet he was also foreshadowed by Moses in many types and figures. First, just as Moses preferred to suffer affliction with the people of God rather than to be illustrious and luxurious in the court of Pharaoh, so Christ, as the Apostle says, did not think it robbery to take the form of a servant, and chose to endure the most grievous torments rather than enjoy his glory in the company of the blessed. And as Moses was rejected by his own brethren, so Christ came to his own, and his own did not receive him. As Moses led the faithful out of Egypt, so Christ snatched them from the jaws of the grave. I pass over many other likenesses between the two.

units.la: Dein ait, Suscitabit Deus. Id asseuerat Christus dicens, ex me ipso non veni, sed se missum à patre.
units.tr: Then he says, God will raise up. Christ affirms this when he says, "I have not come of myself, but I was sent by the Father."

units.la: Post, Ipsum audias, hoc pater coelestis declamat dicens, ipsum audite, Matth. 3. &c.
units.tr: Afterwards, Him you shall hear: the heavenly Father proclaims this when he says, "Hear him," Matthew 3, and so on.

units.la: Quæ cum ita sint, videmus ut ipsis prophetis exemplum Christus proponitur: sic omni generi mortalium iniungitur, ut eandem Christi ministris præstent obedientiam.
units.tr: Since these things are so, we see that Christ is set forth as an example to the prophets themselves, and is enjoined on every kind of mortal, so that they render the same obedience to the ministers of Christ.

units.la: At originem huius muneris eorum ipsorum testimonio probat Moses, referens quod in monte Sina acciderat. Quod perinde est ac si dicat, Deus ipse vobis loqui coeperat: at eum vos audire non potuistis, & petiistis ut per prophetas suam vobis voluntatem exponeret.
units.tr: But Moses proves the origin of this office of theirs by their own testimony, recounting what happened on Mount Sinai. This is just as if he said: God himself had begun to speak to you, but you could not hear him, and you asked that he set out his will to you through prophets.

units.la: Atq; sic illud officium & præclarum hunc ordinem illorum consensu diuinitus institu-tum affirmat.
units.tr: And so he affirms that this office and this excellent order were instituted by God with the consent of them all.

units.la: En quales sint qui sibi vel spiritus, vel Deum ipsum loqui vellent, cum vocem diuinam homines nequeant sustinere. Certe & satan suis spiritibus uteretur: præstabit homines pro-phetas adhiberi: sic enim si diabolus falsos subornet, minus erit periculi, quique[?] quos suis notis facile dignoscas. Spiritus alij dogmata gentilia, alij alia protulere: sed discerni po-tuere.
units.tr: See what sort of people they are who wish to have spirits, or God himself, speaking to them, when men cannot endure the divine voice. Certainly Satan too would use his spirits; the Lord will provide that men be appointed as prophets, for in this way, if the devil suborns false ones, there will be less danger, since you can easily recognise them by their marks. Other spirits have brought forth Gentile doctrines, others other things; but they could be discerned.

units.la: Ex quibus omnibus habes prophetiam esse munus Dei immortalis, & inde omnino proficisci. Æque ac magistratus vocati sumus.
units.tr: From all these things you have that prophecy is a gift of the immortal God, and wholly proceeds from him. Just as we are called to the magistracy.

units.la: Porro de authoritate prophetiae dicit ad hunc modum: dixisse Dominum: Bene ege-runt in hoc quod loquuti sunt: Prophetam excitabo eis. Quæ sunt verba Domini istum Pro-phetarum ordinem probantia & statuentia ut iusibus eius obediatur. Quod approbat Deus populi postulata: id indicio est prophetiam & populi & Dei vnanimi consensu receptam, ac propterea retinendam esse. Ut lex & consuetudo retinentur. Nefas esto quicquam contra tentare.
units.tr: Further, concerning the authority of prophecy he speaks in this manner: the Lord said, "They have spoken well in what they have said; I will raise up a prophet for them." These are the words of the Lord, approving and establishing this order of prophets so that his commands be obeyed. That God approves the request of the people is a sign that prophecy was received by both the people and God with unanimous consent, and therefore is to be retained, just as law and custom are retained. It is wrong to attempt anything against it.

units.la: Quod pœnam statuit obedientiam detrectantibus, id authoritatem etiam muneri conciliat. Obedientia verbo Dei negata semper fuit exitio: ut Nohæ, Pharaonis, Saulis, Christi tempora, atq; etiam nostra significant. Quare nos Christo, qui patris est verbum, obediamus, ut viuamus in illo piè quidem hic: at istic bene & beatè, Amen.
units.tr: That he appoints a punishment for those who refuse obedience also lends authority to the office. Obedience refused to the word of God has always been ruinous, as the times of Noah, Pharaoh, Saul, and Christ, and our own too, show. Therefore let us obey Christ, who is the Word of the Father, that we may live in him, piously here, but there well and blessedly. Amen.

units.la: SERMO XLIIII.
units.tr: SERMON XLIV.

units.la: 20 Propheta autem qui praesumpserit loqui verbum in nomine meo, quod non praecepi ei, aut qui loquitur in nomine aliorum deorum, morietur Propheta talis.
units.tr: 20 But the prophet who presumes to speak a word in my name, which I have not commanded him, or who speaks in the name of other gods, that prophet shall die.

units.la: 21 Quod si in corde tuo dixeris: Quomodo scire poterimus verbum, quod non locutus est Dominus?
units.tr: 21 And if you say in your heart: How shall we know the word which the Lord has not spoken?

units.la: 22 Quando scilicet Propheta talis loquitur in nomine Domini, & non factum fuerit verbum, neq; euenerit: hoc verbum est quod non locutus est Dominus, sed Propheta ille temerè locutus est, ne metuas ab eo.
units.tr: 22 When such a prophet speaks in the name of the Lord, and the thing does not come to pass nor happen, that is the word which the Lord has not spoken; the prophet has spoken it presumptuously, so do not be afraid of him.

units.la: Quemadmodum Deus hoc ipso quod sacrosanctum verbum suum ceu veram ac diuinam prophetiam suam reuelat salutem nostram vnice quaerit: sic eo ipso quod erro-res atq; superstitiones ceu prophetiam falsam prodit at detegitur. Vnum hoc agit, vt auer-tat a nobis perniciem sempiternam. Inde est quod Christus & apostoli non minus, quam pro phetae quondam monuerunt, vti pseudoapostolos cauerentur. Christus ait, venient in vestiitu ouium intus lupi rapaces, Matt. 7. Et, surgent pseudochristi & pseudoprophetae, &c. Mat. 24. Petrus autem 2. ep. 2. praedicit fore falsos doctores. Et Paulus 2. Thess. 2. praedicit ipsius ecclesiam aduentum Antichristi.
units.tr: Just as God, by revealing his holy word as his true and divine prophecy, seeks our salvation alone, so by the very fact that he exposes and detects errors and superstitions as false prophecy, he does the same. He does this for one purpose only: to turn us away from eternal destruction. Hence Christ and the apostles, no less than the prophets of old, warned us to beware of false apostles. Christ says: "Inwardly they are ravening wolves, though they come to you in sheepskin" (Matt. 7). And: "False Christs and false prophets will arise," etc. (Matt. 24). Peter, in 2 Peter 2, foretells that there will be false teachers. And Paul, in 2 Thess. 2, foretells the coming of Antichrist within the Church itself.

units.la: Sic Moses hac vltima concione sua, qua summa legis exponit, ceu veram prophetiam, monet populum, vt abstineant sibi; caueant a falsis doctoribus praeuidens fore, vt aliqui praeteritentes veras prophetiae species seducerent ac proderent populum eum; qui per veram potestatem ferunt, ut hae eis non possit. Nam cum veram prophetiam descripsisset, atque etiam eius caput Christum venturum vaticinatus esset, & omnino ostendisset obediendum esse eius quis posset conqueri sibi quid inter verum & falsum interesset, non constare: veluti nunc multi solent dicere, in tanta multitudine & varietate doctrinarum sibi quid fit recipiendum minime constare: docet hic probationem prophetiarum, veluti idem D. Ioannes postea factitauit. In quo sic versatur Moses, vt primum ipsa pseudoprophetarum genera, tum notas, quibus illi probari, & a veris discerni queant, tradat.
units.tr: So Moses, in this last sermon of his, in which he sets out the sum of the law, warns the people, as a true prophet would, to hold themselves back and to beware of false teachers. He foresaw that some would come who, by imitating the true forms of prophecy, would seduce and betray that people, since they bring their message with apparent authority, so that they could not be resisted. For after describing true prophecy, and foretelling that its head would be Christ who was to come, and after showing plainly that his word must be obeyed, someone might complain that it is not clear to him what difference there is between true and false, just as many people now often say that, amid so great a multitude and variety of teachings, it is not at all clear what they should accept. Here Moses teaches the testing of prophecies, as the same St John later did. In this, Moses proceeds first to set out the kinds of false prophets themselves, and then the marks by which they can be proved and distinguished from the true.

units.la: Ac duo quidem eorum genera referit: vnum videlicet eorum, qui veniunt in nomine Domini loquentes: alterum eorum qui in nomine deorum alienorum veniunt.
units.tr: He mentions two kinds of them: one kind, namely those who come speaking in the name of the Lord; the other, those who come in the name of other gods.

units.la: Prioris generis ij sunt, qui sua fe mandata diuinitus accepisse dictitant, cum ipsi illa conf-finxerint: hoc est, qui suis erroribus praetendunt sacras literas, qui gloriantur nomine vitiorum, reuelationum, legis. Iam vt omittam prisco s haereticos: quorum suam quisq; sectam fa-crarum literarum testimonijs confirmasse videbatur: habemus iam Iudaeos qui legem, tem-plum, patriarchas, prophetas, Mosem, promissiones obtinduntur: habemus Antichristum, qui duo cornua agni, & os draconis habet, hoc est, Christum simulat & euangelium & ecclesiam iactat, quos tamen persequitur. Is dicit se venire in nomine Christi, cum veniat in nomine suo. O quam verum experimur hoc oraculum Domini: Ego veni in nomine patris mei, & non accepistis me: si venerit alius in nomine suo, illum accipietis.
units.tr: Of the first kind are those who keep insisting that they have received commands from God, when they themselves have invented them; that is, those who use the holy letters as a cover for their errors, who boast in the name of visions, revelations and the law. Now, to pass over the ancient heretics, each of whom seemed to have confirmed his own sect by the testimonies of the holy letters, we have the Jews, who lay claim to the law, the temple, the patriarchs, the prophets, Moses and the promises. We have Antichrist, who has the two horns of a lamb and the mouth of a dragon; that is, he feigns Christ, boasts of the gospel and the Church, yet persecutes those same things. He says that he comes in the name of Christ, when he comes in his own name. O how truly we experience this oracle of the Lord: "I have come in the name of my Father, and you have not received me; if another comes in his own name, you will receive him."

units.la: Igitur si illi iactent praecepta Domini, videndum an Deus praeceperit. Dicit enim quae ego non praecepi. Iam videbis illum Antichristum praecipere, quae Deus non solum non manda uerit, sed etiam vetuerit. Quid enim sanctorum inuocatio? quid peregrinationes ad statuas gentilium hominum more suscepta? Ioan. 4. veniet hora & nunc est quando neque in monte hoc, neque Herosolymis adorabitis patre. Sed venit hora & nunc est quado veri adoratores adorabunt patrem spiritu ac veritate. Nam & pater talis quaerit qui adorent ipsum. An non idola statuit contra praeceptum secundum? an non deleAum ciborum & dierum, itemque caelibatum quod genus doctrinas daemonijs tribuit apostolus? Quid verbis opus est? nihil reliquum fecit ecclesiae rerum earum, quas Deus dedit praeter verbi diuini praedicationem, eamque ipsam nec puram nec integram. Hoc genus est & pestilentissimum & periculosissimum, quippe qui praetextu veri falsum spargant, hoc quo magis seducant.
units.tr: Therefore, if they boast of the commands of the Lord, we must see whether God has commanded them. For he says: "things which I did not command." Now you will see that Antichrist commands things which God not only did not command but has even forbidden. For what of the invocation of saints? What of pilgrimages to the statues of men, undertaken after the manner of the Gentiles? John 4: "The hour comes, and now is, when you shall worship the Father neither on this mountain nor at Jerusalem. But the hour comes, and now is, when true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father seeks such people to worship him." Has he not set up images against the second commandment? Has he not set up the abolition of foods and days, and likewise celibacy, which kind of doctrine the apostle ascribes to demons? Why use many words? He has left the Church nothing of those things which God gave, apart from the preaching of the divine word, and even that neither pure nor whole. This kind is both most pestilential and most dangerous, since under the pretext of truth they spread falsehood, and so all the more easily seduce.

units.la: Alterius autem generis sunt, qui vt ait Moses, loquuntur in nomine Deorum alienorum. Hi sunt aperti & profesi hostes: ab his minus est periculi. Vt sunt Iudaei, Turcae, gentes quae Christi & ecclesiae. Christum ex professo negant & oderunt. Herodes, Caiaphas, Nero, Iulianus, Porphyrius, & similes. Eorum gregis sunt, qui nunc in dubium vocant sacras literas, resurrectionem negant, poenas & praemia tollunt, qui de religione ceu astutè excogitata plebem domandi ratione iudicant. Ab his 1. Corinth. 15. Paulus dicit cauendum & abstinendum: corrumpunt enim bonos mores colloquia praua. Atqui hi sunt illi prophetæ, qui veniunt in nomine deorum alienorum puta ventris, aut Mammonæ. Vtrumq; genus est eorum, qui vel melle venenum tegunt suum, vel aperte euomunt virus.
units.tr: Those of the other kind, as Moses says, speak in the name of other gods. These are open and avowed enemies, and they are less dangerous. Such are the Jews, the Turks, and the nations which openly deny and hate Christ and the Church. Herod, Caiaphas, Nero, Julian, Porphyry and the like. Of this flock are those who now call the holy letters into doubt, deny the resurrection, abolish punishments and rewards, and judge religion to be a crafty device invented for taming the common people. From these Paul in 1 Corinthians 15 says we must beware and abstain: "evil conversations corrupt good morals." And yet these are the prophets who come in the name of other gods, namely of the belly or of Mammon. Both kinds are those who either hide their poison under honey or openly spew forth their venom.

units.la: Iam etsi pseudoprophetas ex his quæ dicta sunt, nosse possimus: tamen vltra aliquas e-tiam notas ponit. Quod si, inquit, in corde tuo dixeris, quomodo scire poterimus verbum quod non locutus est Dominus? Quando,&c. Quæ verba videntur esse eiusmodi, vt videatur ab euentu iudicium de prophetis sumi oportere. Vnde & Ezechiæ falsus vates fuisset Esaias, & Ionas Niniuitis. At erant hypothetica vaticinia, quæ poenitentiâ respiciebant. Ergo locus hic cum superiore collatus cap. 13. erit clarior. Si quid noui Deus attulit, vt legem, vt euangelium, sit mauit ipsum miraculis. Iam ne fallant miracula, ea sunt ad doctrinam adhibenda.
units.tr: Now, although from what has been said we may know false prophets, yet Moses also sets down some further marks. "But if," he says, "you say in your heart: How shall we know the word which the Lord has not spoken? When, etc." These words seem to be of such a kind that they appear to require that judgment about prophets be drawn from the outcome. On that reading Isaiah would have been a false prophet to Hezekiah, and Jonah to the Ninevites. But those were conditional prophecies, which had regard to repentance. Therefore this passage, when compared with the earlier one in chapter 13, will be clearer. If God brings anything new, such as the law or the gospel, he confirms it with miracles. But miracles can deceive, so they must be applied to doctrine.

units.la: Ergo iudicium illud non ex docentis persona, sed ex doctrina peti debet. Etenim ha-bet dogmata, Deum esse vnum & trinum: Christum esse seruatorem: peccatum esse quod fit contra verbum Domini: sacrificia celebrata atque oblata non iustificare, sed exercere fidem, & docere Christum: illa facienda, hæc cauenda. Si quis igitur docet quod erit, id est, volunta-ti Dei, quæ diuino verbo expressa est, consentaneum: is est verus & syncerus doctor. Sin dicat quod non erit scilicet diuinæ voluntati, quæ verbo diuino expressa est, consentaneum, i-ta vt Deo consolante minetur ipse, & eodem minitante ipse consoletur: hic falsus est doctor & impostor. Summa doctrina decalogi latè patens est regula, ad quam doctrinæ proba-ri debent.
units.tr: Therefore that judgment must be sought not from the person of the teacher but from the doctrine. For the doctrine holds that God is one and three, that Christ is the Saviour, that sin is whatever is done against the word of the Lord, and that the sacrifices celebrated and offered do not justify but exercise faith and teach Christ; these things are to be done, those to be avoided. If anyone therefore teaches what is in agreement with the will of God, as expressed in the divine word, he is a true and sincere teacher. But if he says what is not in agreement with the divine will as expressed in the divine word, so that he threatens with God's comfort and comforts with God's threat, he is a false teacher and an impostor. The broad rule by which doctrines ought to be tested is the sum of the doctrine of the Decalogue.

units.la: Cogitandum est quantum nefas sit monetam vitiare: quantum item <bl>παραπροσωπείας[?]</bl> crimen sit: quantum item tabulas publicas corrumpere, &c. Sic hodieq; probandi sunt spiritus ex Deo ne sint, an ex hominibus. Notandus est etiam locus 1. Ioan. 4. Omnis, inquit, spiritus qui confitetur Iesum in carne venisse, &c.
units.tr: We should consider how great a wrong it is to debase the coinage, how great the crime of impersonation [παραπροσωπείας], and likewise how great a crime it is to corrupt public records, and so on. In the same way spirits are still to be tested, whether they are from God or from men. The passage of 1 John 4 should also be noted: "Every spirit," he says, "that confesses that Jesus has come in the flesh," etc.

units.la: Iam quorum sit probare spiritus rogas? Eorum qui sciunt vtique: neque enim sutor vl-tra crepidam. Qui igitur illi[?]qui spiritum Christi habent videlicet. Is enim ducet in omnem veritatem Ioan.16.& vnctio docebit vos omnia, dicit beatus Ioan. in ep. Nam animalis homo non percipit ea quæ sunt spiritus Dei. Ergo inquis, nullus rerum erit ordo, si quiuis iudicet? minime, apostolus ait alios Euangelistas datos, alios apostolos. Cæteri iudicent, norma erit scriptura. Is hodieq; est ordo in ecclesia. Si quis docet cum sacris literis pugnantia, aut quæ non intelligantur, cur non rogetur?
units.tr: Now you ask who should test the spirits? Those who know, certainly; for the cobbler should not go beyond his last. Therefore those who have the Spirit of Christ, namely. For "he will lead you into all truth" (John 16), and "the anointing will teach you all things," says the blessed John in his epistle. For "the natural man does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God." Therefore, you say, there will be no order of things if anyone may judge? Not at all; the apostle says that some were given as evangelists and others as apostles. The rest should judge, and the norm will be Scripture. This is the order in the Church even today. If anyone teaches things that conflict with the holy letters, or things that cannot be understood, why should he not be questioned?

units.la: Ex quibus intelligimus & pseudoprophetarum genera & eorum dignoscendorum normas[?]. Christo sit honos. Amen.
units.tr: From these things we understand both the kinds of false prophets and the norms for recognising them. To Christ be honour. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT XIX. SERMO XLV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIX. SERMON XLV.

units.la: QUm excideris Dominus Deus tuus gentes, quarum terram Dominus Deus tuus daturus est tibi, & possederis eas, habitaverisq; in ciuitatibus earum, atq; in domibus earum.
units.tr: When the LORD your God has cut off the nations whose land the LORD your God is going to give you, and you have dispossessed them and dwell in their cities and in their houses,

units.la: 2 Separabis tibi tria oppida in medio terræ tuæ, quam Dominus Deus tuus tibi possidendam dabit.
units.tr: 2 you shall set apart for yourselves three cities in the midst of your land, which the LORD your God is going to give you to possess.

units.la: 3 Muniesq; tibi viam, & in tres partes diuides limitem terræ tuæ, quam Dominus Deus tuus dat tibi in hæreditatem, vt scilicet illuc confugiat omnis homicida.
units.tr: 3 You shall prepare the way for yourselves and divide into three parts the boundary of your land, which the LORD your God gives you as an inheritance, so that every manslayer may flee there.

units.la: 4 Hac vero causa homicida illuc confugiat, vt vitam seruet, id[?] scilicet, qui percusserit proximum suum per imprudentiam, nec odio prosequutus est eum antea.
units.tr: 4 And this is the reason the manslayer shall flee there, that he may save his life: namely, whoever has struck his neighbour without intent, and had not hated him before.

units.la: 5 Vt quum quis cum proximo suo proficiscitur in syluam, vt ligna cædat, & fugiente manu eius cum securi, vt succidat arborem, elabatur ferrum è capulo, & fe-riens [?]ieni proximum eius ut moriatur, si iam confugiat ad unum ex his oppidis, ut ser-uet vitam,
units.tr: 5 Thus, when someone goes into the forest with his neighbour to cut wood, and while his hand is swinging the axe to fell a tree, the iron slips from the handle and strikes his neighbour so that he dies, he may flee to one of these cities and save his life.

units.la: 6 Ne forte vindex sanguinis insequens homicidam, quum incaluerit cor eius, eum apprehendat, & quia via longa est, vitam illius tollat, qui tamen iudicium mor-tis non commeruit, eo quod non est eum prosequutus odio antea.
units.tr: 6 Lest the avenger of blood, pursuing the manslayer while his heart is hot, overtake him and, because the way is long, take the life of one who did not deserve the sentence of death, since he had not hated him before.

units.la: 7 Proinde ego praecipio tibi, dicens, Tria oppida separabis tibi.
units.tr: 7 Therefore I command you, saying: You shall set apart three cities for yourselves.

units.la: 8 Quod si Dominus Deus limitem tuum dilataverit, quemadmodum iuravit patribus tuis, dederitq; tibi universam terrā, quam pollicitus est se daturū patribus tuis;
units.tr: 8 But if the LORD your God enlarges your border, as he swore to your fathers, and gives you the whole land which he promised to give to your fathers,

units.la: 9 Tu custodies universum praeceptum istud, ut facias ipsum quod ego tibi hodie praecipio, ut diligas Dominum Deum tuum, & ambules in viis eius cun-ctis diebus, addasq; tibi adhuc tria oppida praeter tria ista.
units.tr: 9 you shall keep this whole commandment, to do it, which I command you today: to love the LORD your God and walk in his ways always, and you shall add three more cities besides these three.

units.la: 10 Ne scilicet effundatur sanguis innoxius in medio terrae tuae, quam Dominus Deus tuus daturus est tibi in hereditatem, & ne sit super te sanguis.
units.tr: 10 So that innocent blood may not be shed in the midst of your land, which the LORD your God is going to give you as an inheritance, and so that blood-guilt may not be upon you.

units.la: Vm Diuus Moses proximis illis iam explicatis capitibus alteram tabulam decem legum ceperit explicare: ac primum eius praeceptum, quo docemur quomodo parentes pariter, atque eos qui nobis praesunt magistratus & verbi ministros habere debeamus, explicarit: auspicatur iam seq. illis Capp. 19. 20. 21. secundi praecepti expositionem, quod est non occides.
units.tr: Now that the divine Moses has finished explaining the chapters just treated, and has begun to explain the first table of the ten laws, namely its first precept, by which we are taught how we ought to honour parents alike and those who rule over us, the magistrates and ministers of the Word, he now begins, in the following chapters 19, 20 and 21, the exposition of the second precept, which is "You shall not kill."

units.la: Iam quoniam caedes seu effusio sanguinis non solum ab hominibus privatis, verum etiam à summis principibus ac potentissimis populis committitur, tunc q; belli nomen accipit: de utroque genere Moses in hac secundi praecepti interpretatione disserit, atque hoc ipso 19. Cap. de ea quam privati patrant caede. Quam rem ita persequitur ut doceat cedem aliam voluntate, aliam ab invito patrari, & per imprudentiam: quid iuris de utraque: Vnde & tractatio ipsa duabus partibus est omnis distributa: quarum priore de involuntaria, posteriore de voluntaria caede dicat.
units.tr: Since slaying, or the shedding of blood, is committed not only by private persons but also by the highest rulers and the most powerful peoples, and then takes the name of war, Moses discusses both kinds of killing in this interpretation of the second precept, and in this very nineteenth chapter he speaks of the killing that private persons commit. He pursues the matter so as to teach that one killing is done by will and another by one who is unwilling and through inadvertence, and what the law is for each. Hence the whole treatment is divided into two parts: in the first he speaks of involuntary killing, in the second of voluntary killing.

units.la: Iam de priore sic agit ut primum asyla, 2. quaedam eius genera, tertio causam huius iudicij doceat.
units.tr: Now he deals with the first part in this way: first he sets out the asylums, second certain kinds of them, and third he teaches the reason for this judgment.

units.la: De asylis ad hunc modum dicit, Cum exciderit Dominus Deus tuus gentes quarum terram Dominus Deus tuus daturus est tibi, etc. Summa, Homicidis civitates quaedam seliguntor, quae commodo, atque omnibus aequo loco, situ & aditu faciles sunto. Vt isthic in tuto sint. Ea loca Hebraei civitates refugij vocant, quod isthuc homicidae confugiant ceu in portum, in quo respirandi facultas fiat: Graeci ἄσυλα [?] vocant, ut qui sint ab omni vi tuti velut olim tri-buni plebis & pontifices. Vnde & adverbij forma ἀσυλίᾳ [?] in tuto dicunt Graeci. Germani vocant <bl>fryheiten</bl>, quod isthic quisque sit liber à vindicta. Atque hoc est illud iam inde ab origi-ne rerum usque ad nostra tempora deductum usque confirmatum ius asylorum: quod Deus hoc quidem loco diligentissime sanxit ac firmavit, deinceps autem omnium gentium animis insedit.
units.tr: Concerning asylums he speaks as follows: "When the LORD your God has cut off the nations whose land the LORD your God is going to give you," and so on. The sum is this: certain cities are chosen for manslayers, which are to be convenient, easy of access and arranged so that they are equally accessible to all, that they may be safe there. The Hebrews call these places cities of refuge, because manslayers flee there as to a harbour, where they may have room to breathe. The Greeks call them asyla, as places where people are safe from all violence, just as the tribunes of the plebs and the high priests once were. Hence the Greeks also use the adverb asylia for "in safety." The Germans call them fryheiten, because whoever is there is free from vengeance. This is that right of asylum, which has been handed down and confirmed from the beginning of things to our own times, which God in this place most carefully established and ratified, and which afterwards settled in the minds of all nations.

units.la: Atque hic quidem summam in eo ponendo adhibuit diligentiam. Primum quod viam ad ea muniri voluit: argumento potest esse, omnibus etiam sceleratissimis iustam sui defen-sionem minime esse denegandam: ne causa non audita quisquam condemnetur.
units.tr: Here indeed he showed the greatest care in appointing these places. First, he wanted the way to them to be made ready. The proof that even the most wicked should by no means be denied a just defence is this: no one is to be condemned without a hearing.

units.la: At hoc iure in sanctos Christi martyres mundus hodie nequaquam utitur: sed eos inquisitoribus monachis permittit dilaniandos.
units.tr: But today the world does not at all use this right toward the holy martyrs of Christ, but hands them over to be torn apart by monk-inquisitors.

units.la: Quod omnibus aeque commodo loco sita vult, indicio sit suum cuiq; ius oportere esse aequabile: ne ad ipsum alius alio longius iter habeat. En quam cura sit Deo ut omnibus ex-æquo & bono suo ius tribuatur. Non placent illi, qui parcūt coruis, vexant censura columbas:
units.tr: That he wants them placed at equally convenient spots shows that each man's right ought to be equal, so that one person does not have a longer journey to reach them than another. See how much God cares that every man receive his right on equal and good terms. Those who spare the ravens and harass the doves do not please him.

units.la: Quod autem omnium gentium animis hoc ius indiderit, earum ipsarum nobis probant historiae. Vt apud Aegyptios Herculis templum asylum fuit. Cadmus Thebas abs se conditas sic asyla fecit, ut inde ad supplicium trahi non possent: Servius author est, Hercule mor-tuo nepotes eius eorum, quos avus afflixisset, insidias veritos Athenis in templo Misericor-diae primum asylum sibi statuisse. Vnde nemo posset trahi: Dein & Aesculapii, Mineruae, Dianae templa asyla fuere. Romae etiam Romulus asyla posuit. Postea Rom. Impp. statuae asylorum loco fuere: fortasis ad imitationem statuae Ptolemaei regis apud Cyrenas, ad quam cum alii complures, tum vero maxime Decius Magius Campanus Carthagine ducendus, ut Livius perhibet, confugientes evasere. Et statua Imperatoria quaecunq; [illegible, ~8 letters] dici consueuit, quod qui illas laesisset teneretur iudicio maiestatis, l. non contrahit. ff. ad leg. Iul. maiest.
units.tr: The histories themselves prove to us that he implanted this right in the minds of all nations. Among the Egyptians the temple of Hercules was an asylum. Cadmus made the cities he founded at Thebes asylums, so that people could not be dragged from them to punishment. Servius reports that after Hercules died, his grandsons, fearing the plots of those whom their grandfather had afflicted, first set up for themselves an asylum in the temple of Mercy at Athens; hence no one could be dragged away. Then the temples of Aesculapius, Minerva and Diana were asylums. At Rome Romulus also established asylums. Later, the statues of the Roman emperors took the place of asylums, perhaps in imitation of the statue of King Ptolemy at Cyrene, to which many fled and escaped, and above all Decius Magius of Campania, who, as Livy reports, escaped being led to Carthage. And the statue of the emperor, whatever it is called, is customarily regarded as such: whoever injured it was liable to the charge of treason, as in the law "non contrahit," Digest, on the Julian law of treason.

units.la: Quemadmodum autem asyla quondam fuere tuendis imbecillibus posita: sic etiamnū sunt multa toto orbe Christiano. Jam quia videmus Dei legem tanto in pretio pasim fuisse, nos eam quoq; ratam habeamus æquum & bonum est.
units.tr: Just as asylums were once established to protect the weak, so there are still many of them throughout the whole Christian world. Since we see that God's law was everywhere held in such high esteem, it is right and good that we also hold it valid.

units.la: Sed ne qui scelerati priuilegiis istis ad impunitatem suorum scelerum abuterentur, jam sequitur quibus homicidis asyla sint posita.
units.tr: But lest wicked men abuse these privileges to gain impunity for their crimes, he now goes on to say to which manslayers the asylums are assigned.

units.la: Quibus asyla posita. Ait, Hac vero causa homicida isthuc fugiat, vt vitam feruet, is scilicet qui percusserit proximum suum per imprudentiam, nec eum oderat antea. Quo dicit iis asyla posita, qui imprudeter & nulla nocendi voluntate quempiam interfecerint, vt isthic ipsi in tuto sint.
units.tr: To whom the asylums are assigned. He says: "And this is the reason the manslayer shall flee there, that he may save his life: namely, whoever has struck his neighbour without intent, and had not hated him before." By this he says that asylums are appointed for those who have killed someone inadvertently and without any intention to harm, so that they themselves may be safe there.

units.la: Tum ponit exempla cædis eius: Veluti si quis in sylua ligna cædens euadente è manu sua securi proximum inuitus imprudensq; interimat. Hoc genus cædis, quoniam voluntate facientis factum non est, sed nescio quo casu, meretur veniam.
units.tr: Then he gives examples of this kind of killing: as when someone, cutting wood in the forest, unwillingly and unintentionally kills his neighbour because the axe slips from his hand. This kind of killing, since it was not done by the will of the doer but by some chance, deserves pardon.

units.la: In quo videmus iure divino facta secundum voluntatem facientis æstimari, non secun-dum se ipsa: quod multum referat quo quis animo quidq; fecerit. Et Deus hoc ipse solet.
units.tr: In this we see that by divine right deeds are judged according to the will of the doer, not according to themselves; so it matters greatly with what mind someone does anything. And God himself is accustomed to do this.

units.la: Et hoc iudicium cædis imprudenter patratæ in omnes & philosophorum & pruden-tium hominum atq; etiā gentium ex sua natura Deus deriuavit. Etenim philosophi diligenter obseruant quid inter ea quæ fiunt ἑκουσίως & inter ea quæ fiunt ἀκουσίως fit differentiæ. Qua de re pulchræ extant apud Aristotelem in moralibus ad Nicomachum disputationes. Unde Jureconsulti mitiores sunt in eos, qui casu fortuito quempiam occiderint, quàm ut imprudenter & fortuito factam cædem ex præscripto legis Aquiliæ ultore ferro persequantur. Et cum puer quidam æqualem suum temperatorio cultro ita supra pubem percussisset, ut evestigio moreretur: Alciatus de pœna percussori irroganda consultus respondit, non durio re supplicio quàm exilio coercendum. Atq; id responsum ex sententia Claudij Saturnini fe-fe dedisse dicit, qui in l. aut facta. §. finali. ff. de pœn. indicet hoc genus cædis apud Græcos olim exilio voluntario puniri solitum: quod Homerus Iliad.† tale quiddam referens innuat.
units.tr: And God has derived this judgment on accidental killing from its own nature for all philosophers, prudent men and even nations. For philosophers carefully observe the difference between things done voluntarily [ἑκουσίως] and things done involuntarily [ἀκουσίως]. Fine discussions of this matter are found in Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics. Hence the jurists are milder toward those who have killed someone by chance than to pursue with the sword of avenging, under the prescription of the Aquilian law, a killing done inadvertently and by accident. And when a boy struck his equal with a surgical knife just above the groin so that he died on the spot, Alciatus, consulted on the punishment to be inflicted on the attacker, replied that it should be restrained by exile rather than by harsher punishment. He says that this answer agreed with the opinion of Claudius Saturninus, who, in the law "aut facta," final paragraph, Digest on punishments, lays down that this kind of killing was once customarily punished among the Greeks by voluntary exile, which Homer, Iliad, hints at by recounting something of the sort.

units.la: Sed id Demosthenes ἐν τῷ κατὰ μεῖζον[?] λόγῳ hoc ipsum melius exponit, ac plenius ad hunc modum dicens, ἐπειθα οἱ φόνικοι τὰς μὲν [illegible, ~12 letters] ἀποκτιναντας [?] φυγίας [?] τῶν ὑπαρχώντων ζημιωσι[?] καὶ ἀκουσίως ἀνέσιως καὶ φιλανθρωπίας πολλῆς ἠξίωσαν. Quo in loco interpres seu scholiastes Græcus pro ἀνέσιως legit αἰδέσεως[?], & dicit idem esse quod ἀξίωσιν Græci dicunt. Ex quibus omnibus multisq; aliis, quæ possent huc afferri perspicuum est, Deum quæ Mosi dictauit etiam aliis gentibus vtcunque reuelasse.
units.tr: But Demosthenes, in his speech [ἐν τῷ κατὰ μεῖζον λόγῳ], explains this very point better and more fully in these words: "Then the lawmakers, having ordered that those who killed ... be punished with exile and the loss of their possessions, thought them worthy of unintended, gentle and great kindness [ἐπειθα οἱ φόνικοι ... ἀποκτιναντας ... φυγίας ... ζημιωσι καὶ ἀκουσίως ἀνέσιως καὶ φιλανθρωπίας πολλῆς ἠξίωσαν]." In this passage the Greek interpreter or scholiast reads [αἰδέσεως] in place of [ἀνέσιως], and says that it means the same as what the Greeks call [ἀξίωσιν]. From all these and many other examples that could be brought forward, it is plain that God revealed to other nations, in some measure, what he dictated to Moses.

units.la: Est autem hoc, quod Deus etiam nostræ negligentiæ & imprudentiæ parcit atq; consulit, magnum paternæ eius in nos voluntatis indicium.
units.tr: Moreover, the fact that God also spares and provides for our carelessness and thoughtlessness is a great sign of his fatherly will towards us.

units.la: Ac quoniam hoc genus hominibus asyla posita sunt, perspicuum est, non scelera-tis sed innocentibus & imbecillioribus esse concedenda. Alienum enim est à natura Dei ne-farios homines defendere. Nec gentiles homines aliam eorum rationem habuere. Plutar-chus enim asylum definit εἶναί ἱερόντι φύξιμον τοῖς ἀφισαμένοις οἰκέταις καὶ πᾶσι τοῖς ταπεινοτέροις καὶ δικαιοτέρους κρείττονας[?]. Qui locus indicat asyla data fuisse iis qui defensione egerent aduersus potentiores. Et Tacitus author est, sic crebrescente per Græcas vrbes licentia atque impunitate asyla statuendi, vt templa complerentur ferus fugitiuis, & obaera-tis hominibus, & reis capitalium criminum: vtque nullo imperio seditiones & flagitia coer-ceri possent, Tiberium ex sententia patrum eam libidinem coercuisse. Quò pertinet etiam quod dicit Salicetus, qui confugerunt (inquit) ad statuas principis, ab omni violentia de-bent esse tuti: si tamen sine iusta causa ad eas confugerint, veniunt puniendi. Eodem refer etiam l. unicam C. de his qui ad stat. confug. Sed his omissis ad causas asylorum transeamus.
units.tr: Since asylums were set up for this kind of men, it is plain that they ought to be granted not to the wicked but to the innocent and the weaker. For it is foreign to the nature of God to defend criminals. Nor did the Gentiles have a different view of them. Plutarch defines an asylum as "a refuge for fugitive slaves and all the lowlier people, and for those who are weaker against those who are stronger and more powerful [εἶναί ἱερόντι φύξιμον τοῖς ἀφισαμένοις οἰκέταις καὶ πᾶσι τοῖς ταπεινοτέροις καὶ δικαιοτέρους κρείττονας]." This passage shows that asylums were given to those who needed protection against the more powerful. And Tacitus is the authority that, when the licence and impunity of setting up asylums grew through the Greek cities, so that temples were crowded with runaway slaves, indebted men and men accused of capital crimes, and since riots and disgraceful acts could not be restrained by any government, Tiberius, with the approval of the senators, put a stop to that lust. To this belongs also what Salicetus says: those who have fled (he says) to the statues of the prince must be safe from all violence; yet if they have fled to them without a just cause, they are to be punished. Refer to the same point also the single law in the Code, On those who flee to statues. But, setting these aside, let us pass on to the causes of asylums.

units.la: Causas Moses duas affert unam ciuilem, sacram alteram. Ciuilis est, ne vindex iratus homicidam subito perseq-uatur, opprimat, cædem cede cumulet, ac terram innocenti sanguine polluat. Atque hæc causa priuatas personas, magistratus, universos respicit. Homines priua-tos, qui cognatione vel affinitate coniuncti forent occiso homini, ac cedem irati vellent ulcisci. Mihi, vindicta ego retribuam, inquit Dominus.
units.tr: Moses gives two causes for asylums, one civil and the other sacred. The civil cause is "lest the avenger, angry, pursue the killer suddenly, overtake him, add slaughter to slaughter, and pollute the land with innocent blood." This cause concerns private persons, the magistrates and everyone in general. As for private persons, these are the relatives or kinsmen by blood or marriage of the slain man, who would want to avenge the killing in anger. "Vengeance is mine; I will repay," says the Lord.

units.la: Magistratus, ne quis subito, affectu malo incitante, cum innocens esset, tamen opprimeretur: sed audita & cognita causa, quod iuris est fiat. In quam considerationem veniunt omnes facti [illegible, ~8 letters]. Sæpe enim idem factum ratione circumstantiarum fit diuersum. Quod magistratus norit & ponderet necesse est, nit <bl>handlen</bl> vß <bl>gunst</bl> oder <bl>vngunst</bl>. Quid enim hoc est, quod dici solet, hanc illi fuisse faustam, alii infaustam fuisse horam? Ex ipsius facti qualitate conijciendum erat de condemnatione pariter & absolutione rei.
units.tr: For the magistrates, lest anyone, incited by a bad emotion, should be oppressed suddenly, although innocent, but that, once the case has been heard and examined, what the law requires be done. Into this consideration come all the circumstances of the deed. For often the same deed becomes different by reason of its circumstances. The magistrate must know and weigh this, whether it is handled with favour or disfavour. For what is it that people commonly say, that for one man the hour was lucky and for another unlucky? From the very nature of the deed one had to conjecture whether the accused should be condemned or acquitted.

units.la: Vniuersos,ne sanguinis innocentis effusione terra pollueretur. Sanguis clamat, vt Abelis:oppressorum hominum lachrimae & suspiria ad Deum tendunt,vt Israelitarum in Ægy-pto exulum: Dauidis etiam exilium Israelitae cum rege Saule luunt, vt Ægyptus cum Pharaone, Asia cum Paride & Priamo, nautae cum Iona, Israelitae cum suo fure in exercitu Iosuae; populus Iudaeus cum suis scribis & Pharisaeis Christum crucifigentibus. Quis putas est Italici, Gallici, Picardi sanguinis effusi ad Deum clamor? Quis eius qui intra nostros fines effusus est? Quod ne pijs accidat Deus asyla ad vitandam sanguinis effusionem ponit. Quae ciuilis est asylorum causa.
units.tr: For everyone, lest the land be polluted by the shedding of innocent blood. Blood cries out, as did Abel's; the tears and sighs of oppressed people rise to God, as those of the Israelites exiled in Egypt did. The Israelites also paid for David's exile along with King Saul, as Egypt did with Pharaoh, Asia with Paris and Priam, sailors with Jonah, and the Israelites with their thief in Joshua's army; the Jewish people paid with their scribes and Pharisees who crucified Christ. Who do you think is the cry to God of the blood shed in Italy, in Gaul, in Picardy? Who is the cry of him who was shed within our borders? So that this may not befall the pious, God sets up asylums for avoiding the shedding of blood. This is the civil cause of asylums.

units.la: Sacra vero Christus est, qui nos reos mortis,ne vltore gladio percu-tiamur seruat: sed vt intra septa seu muros ecclesiae maneamus, ac ne tantillum quidem in haereticorum aut impiorum hominum deuia loca euagemur. Haec sunt alta mente repo-nenda vt diligamus Dominum Deum nostrum,(inquit Moses,qui illum nobis dedit ponti-ficem,cui sit honos in secula. Amen.
units.tr: The sacred cause, however, is Christ, who keeps us, guilty of death, from being struck down by the avenging sword, but so that we remain within the enclosure or walls of the Church, and do not wander even the least bit into the devious places of heretics or impious men. These things are to be stored deep in the mind, so that we may love the Lord our God, as Moses says, who gave us that High Priest to whom be honour for ever. Amen.

units.la: SERMO XLVI.
units.tr: SERMON XLVI.

units.la: 11 Quod si quispiam oderit proximum suum, & insidians illi, insurrexerit aduersus eum,percusseritq; animam eius vt mortuus fuerit,ac deinde confugerit ad vnum istorum oppidorum.
units.tr: 11 If anyone hates his neighbour, lies in wait for him, rises up against him, and strikes him so that he dies, and then flees to one of those cities,

units.la: 12 Mittent seniores oppidi illius,& abripiant eum illinc, tradantque eum in manum vindicis sanguinis,vt moriatur.
units.tr: 12 the elders of that city shall send and fetch him from there, and hand him over to the avenger of blood, that he may die.

units.la: 13 Ne parcat ei oculus tuus,sed excindas sanguinem innoxium ex Israele,vt bene sit tibi.
units.tr: 13 Your eye shall not spare him, but you shall purge the innocent blood from Israel, that it may go well with you.

units.la: 14 Ne transferas limitem proximi tui,quoniam limitarunt priores in haredi-tate tua,quam tu occupabis in terra quam Dominus Deus tuus dat tibi possidendā.
units.tr: 14 You shall not move your neighbour's landmark, which the men of old have set in your inheritance, which you shall possess in the land that the Lord your God gives you to possess.

units.la: 15 Ne surgat testis vnus contra aliquem in quacunq; iniquitate, in quocunque peccato,& in quacunque noxa in qua peccatum fuerit: Sed in ore duorum aut in ore trium testium astio[?] confirmabitur.
units.tr: 15 One witness shall not stand against any man for any iniquity or any sin, or for any offence in which he has sinned. Only at the mouth of two or three witnesses shall a matter be established.

units.la: 16 Si surrexerit testis iniquus contra aliquē respondendo contra illū defectionē:
units.tr: 16 If a malicious witness rises up against any man to accuse him of wrongdoing,

units.la: 17 Stabunt ambo illi homines quibus lis est,in conspectu Domini coram sacer-dotibus & iudicibus qui fuerint illis diebus.
units.tr: 17 then both the men between whom the dispute is shall stand before the Lord, before the priests and the judges who are in office in those days.

units.la: 18 Et inuestigabunt iudices diligenter,& en[?],si testis huiusmodi testis mendax fuerit,mendacium respondens contra fratrem suum:
units.tr: 18 The judges shall make careful inquiry, and if the witness is a false witness, who has testified falsely against his brother,

units.la: 19 Facietis ei quemadmodum ipse scelerate cogitauerat facere fratri suo,& e-xures malum e medio tui.
units.tr: 19 you shall do to him as he had wickedly planned to do to his brother, and you shall purge the evil from your midst.

units.la: 20 Vt reliqui id audiant & timeant,neq; audeant amplius designare rem hanc malam in te.
units.tr: 20 Then the rest shall hear and fear, and they shall no longer dare to commit such evil among you.

units.la: 21 Nec parcet oculus tuus,animam pro anima,oculum pro oculo, dentem pro dente,manum pro manu,pedem pro pede.
units.tr: 21 Your eye shall not spare: life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot.

units.la: IN expositione praecepti illius,non occides,dictum est concione proxima,eorum quae fiunt a priuatis hominibus homicidiorum esse genera duo: quorum alterum imprudenter & contra animi propositum, alterum autem dedita opera velut ab irato, odio prosequente & insidiante. Et ijs qui praeter & contra animi sui propositum aliquē imprudenter occiderint, vt ab omni sint tuti violentia,per totam terram asyla diuinitus instituta sunt.
units.tr: In explaining the precept "You shall not kill," it was said at the last sermon that there are two kinds of homicide committed by private persons: one unintentional and contrary to the purpose of the mind, the other done deliberately, as by an angry man who pursues his enemy with hatred and lies in wait for him. And so that those who have killed someone unintentionally, beside and against their purpose, may be safe from all violence, places of refuge were divinely instituted throughout the whole land.

units.la: Ceterum rei[?] ijs asyla seruiant tuendis,qui data opera caedem patrant: iam Moses docet quomodo magistratus in eos animaduertere debeat, qui vim alijs non lacesiti priores infe-rant eosq; trucident. Ac ne supplicium hoc vni tantum generi irrogetur, alijs ex legibus alia quoq; caedis genera affert, vt ex furti & falsi testimonij legibus. Quod vt intelligamus confi-derandum est simplex caedis genus:tum de non mouendis terminis:postremo de non dicen-do falso testimonio.
units.tr: But these places of refuge serve to protect only those who commit the slaying deliberately. Now Moses teaches how the magistrate ought to punish those who, without being provoked, first inflict violence on others and slay them. And so that this punishment is not imposed on only one kind of killing, he brings in other kinds of slaying from other laws, such as those on theft and false witness. To understand this, we must consider three things: first, the simple kind of killing; then, the removing of landmarks; lastly, not speaking false witness.

units.la: Ac primum de simplici cedis genere dicit ad hunc modum. Quod si quispiam oderit proximum suum,& insidians illi insurrexerit aduersus eum,percusseritq; Quibus homicidium diligentissime describit, tum etiam quomodo aduersus ipsum factum procedatur ostendit. Ipsum homicidium à causa efficiente,forma,effectis depingit.
units.tr: First, he speaks of the simple kind of killing in these words: "If anyone hates his neighbour, lies in wait for him, rises up against him, and strikes him..." In these words he describes homicide very carefully, and then shows how the case against the offender is to proceed. He depicts the homicide itself by its efficient cause, its form and its effects.

units.la: Efficiens eius causa est odium. Atque hic mitiorem & minorem eius causam affert, vt doceat quanto magis sit respiciendum ad maiorem. Odium enim,quod hic causę loco affert, ira minus nocens est,& ad inferendam iniuriam haud ita prochiue: quippe quod non tantopere ardeat,ac propterea vel metu,vel spe,vel quacunq; re alia facile cohibeatur. Et ira quidem insurgit ex ea quæ nobis iam infertur iniuria:odium autem ex quauis opinione sinistra quam de aliquo concepimus.Iratus iram suam vult sentiri minimeq; clandestinam : inimicus autem tantum abeat,vt cognosci velit,vt amici loco haberi quandoque malit. Iam si cogitemus odium ex offensa quacunque etiam leui natum instar occulti veneni malam nocendi cupiditatem alere : Moses ipsum ceu huius mali causam monstrans, ostendit eo ipso omnem ergo proximum maleuolentiam, siue ea sit præceps & ad vindictam propensa, siue lenta sit & occulta:tamen esse ceu hyius mali causam procul animis humanis arcendam.
units.tr: Its efficient cause is hatred. Here he gives a milder and lesser cause, so as to teach how much more we must attend to the greater one. For the hatred he mentions here as the cause is less harmful than anger and not so ready to inflict injury, since it does not burn so fiercely and so can easily be restrained by fear, hope, or some other thing. Anger arises from an injury already done to us; hatred arises from any ill opinion we have formed of someone. The angry man wants his anger to be felt and is least of all secret; the enemy, on the other hand, so far from wishing to be known, sometimes prefers to be thought a friend. Now if we consider that hatred, born of any offence however slight, feeds the evil desire to harm like a hidden poison, then Moses, by showing hatred itself as the cause of this evil, shows that all ill will toward a neighbour, whether it is headlong and inclined to revenge or slow and hidden, must be kept far from the human heart as the cause of this evil.

units.la: In quo videmus & Christum,& Mosem eiusmodi medicos esse,qui malorum causis primum obsistant. Vt enim hic Moses odium ceu lentam & ocultam:sic Matth.5.Christus iram vt citam cędis causam tollit.Et ex eo quidem loco discimus ab ira,odio, maledictis abstinere:quippe quæ non sint ita vt videntur leuia crimina,sed cędis initia.Hæc de causa.
units.tr: In this we see that both Christ and Moses are physicians of this kind, who first resist the causes of evils. For just as Moses here treats hatred as the slow and hidden cause, so Christ in Matthew 5 removes anger as the swift cause of murder. And from that passage we learn to abstain from anger, hatred and abusive words, since these are not slight faults as they seem, but the beginnings of murder. So much for the cause.

units.la: Iusurgere[?] vero & percutere est ipsa atrox iniuria,<bl>gwaltige hand anlegen</bl>.
units.tr: To "rise up" and "strike" is the violent injury itself, to lay violent hands on someone.

units.la: Effecta mors aut diuturnus dolor morbusue sunt.Eius authorem facti si in asylum fugerit,inde extrahendum Moses dicit,& capite plectendum.
units.tr: The effects are death, or lasting pain or sickness. If the author of such a deed flees to a place of refuge, Moses says he must be dragged out from there and put to death.

units.la: Atque hoc ipsum ceu diuinum mandatum placuit omnibus gentibus. Plinius scribit Callidromum quendam seruum fugitiuum cum ad Traiani statuam confugisset, indeabreptum esse.Sed eius generis nonnulla paulò ante diximus.
units.tr: This very thing, as though it were a divine command, has pleased all nations. Pliny writes that a certain runaway slave named Callidromus, when he had fled to the statue of Trajan, was dragged away from there. But we have mentioned some examples of this kind a little earlier.

units.la: Obseruandum est autem quod iudicem in hac re vult seuerum minimeq; lenem: & addit causam,Ne parcat oculus, vt auferas sanguinem & bene fit tibi.Quod si bene est ijs quorum terra ab innocentium hominum sanguine est pura: quanto peius habent ij qui sanguine sibi vi-ctum parant? Minimeq; laudi duci debet quod quidam magistratus pecunijs multat eos, qui capite plectendi fuerant:sic enim ditescunt quidem ipsi,terra vero sceleratis & nefarijs hominibus repletur. Quod ad eius ipsius felicitatem tantum abest vt conducat, vt eam etiam imminuat.
units.tr: It should be noted, however, that in this matter he wants the judge to be severe and not lenient at all, and he adds the reason: "Your eye shall not spare, so that you may take away the blood, and it may go well with you." If it goes well with those whose land is pure of innocent blood, how much worse will it be for those who get their living by blood? And the practice of some magistrates, who fine with money those who ought to have been put to death, deserves no praise at all. For thus they grow rich indeed, but the land is filled with wicked and criminal men. This is so far from contributing to its happiness that it even diminishes it.

units.la: Iam vero quoniam de causa cædis dixit, affert quendam ex lege furti casum, qui potest etiam cędis,& interdum magnæ stragis esse causa.Is est termini suo loco moti. Ne di-moueas terminum proximi à loco quem maiores posuere. Atque hoc est magnum nefas quippe quod inter maledictiones ponat inf.ca.27. Vult igitur terminos à maioribus positos, vt ab Eleazaro sacerdote,Iosua,principibus populi,stare.
units.tr: Now, since he has spoken of the cause of killing, he brings in a case from the law on theft, which can also be a cause of killing and sometimes of great slaughter: that is, the moving of a boundary stone. "You shall not move your neighbour's landmark, which the men of old have set." And this is a great wrong, since he places it among the curses in Deut. 27. So he wants the boundaries set by our forefathers to stand, as set by Eleazar the priest and Joshua and the leaders of the people.

units.la: Nec locus est,vt videtur papistis contra nos vtilis:qui enim illis mandauit,vt nobis terminos ponerent?Illi,quos diximus,mandatum habuerunt. |
units.tr: Nor does this passage, as the Papists seem to think, serve their cause against us. For who commanded them to set boundaries for us? Those whom we have mentioned had the commission.

units.la: Hic πλεονεξίαν prohibet,vt prouerb.22. Esa.5.Si quis velit cum alterius incommodo rem suam familiarem augere,& in fines proximi irruat,is ansam ad cędem probet. Vt Achab cupiditas vineæ ad cędem pepulit, & plus vltra progrediendi libido causam bellorum nostri temporis probet.
units.tr: Here he forbids covetousness, as in Proverbs 22 and Isaiah 5. If anyone wishes to increase his property at his neighbour's expense and encroaches on his neighbour's borders, he provides an occasion for killing. As Ahab's desire for the vineyard drove him to murder, so the lust to go further than one's due has been the cause of the wars of our own time.

units.la: Lapidem loco mouere parui momenti res est & videtur: at eum mouere qui litium fe-dandarum[?] causa positus fuerat:quoniam litibus renouandis hoc ipsum seruiat, qui non ma-lum effet? Etenim Numa Pompilius fecundus Romanorum rex agros terminis, quos sacros lapides appellauit,positis definiuit:quos si quis occuluisset aut transtulisset,eum ceu sacrilegum quiuis impune potuit occidere: idemq; ius & in priuatis & in publicis possessionibus constitutum est. Eundem Plutarchus author est,terminum velut ἐπίσκοπον[?] atq; infpectorem amicitiæ & pacis custodem ab omni cæde & sanguine purum atq; illibatū esse voluisse. Olim etiam nonnulli populi defossis carbonibus agrorum fines distinguebant, quod nihil fit carbonibus terra defossis durabilius. Memorabile est etiam quod dicit Ouidius de Ter-mino, Omne (inquit) erit finefe[?] religiosus ager. Et quia publice interest agrorum limites distinctos esse, poenæ iure ciuili sunt irrogatæ ijs, qui ipsos dimouissent. Etenim pro conditione personæ & ætatis relegabantur: qui fortuitò sustulissent verberibus cædebantur leg.ij. ff. eod. Et Paulus iureconsultus in l.ff. sin. regund. dicit actionem finium regundorum in personam esse licet sit per rei vindicationem.
units.tr: To move a stone from its place seems a small matter and of little moment. But to move one that was set to settle disputes is a serious thing, since it serves to renew quarrels. For Numa Pompilius, the second king of the Romans, divided fields by setting up boundaries, which he called sacred stones; and whoever hid or moved them could be killed by anyone with impunity as a sacrilegious person. The same law was established for private and public possessions. Plutarch also relates that the same Numa wished the boundary, as an overseer and guardian of friendship and peace, to be kept free from all slaughter and blood. In former times some peoples also marked the limits of their fields by burying charcoal, since nothing is more lasting in the ground than charcoal. Also memorable is what Ovid says of the god Terminus: "Every field will be sacred to the boundary-stone," he says. And because it is a public interest that the limits of fields be kept distinct, penalties under civil law were imposed on those who had removed them. For according to the status and age of the person they were exiled; those who had removed them by chance were beaten with rods (Dig. 47.21, law 2). And the jurist Paulus, in the law on the regulation of boundaries, says that the action for regulating boundaries is directed against the person, although it is carried out by a claim of ownership.

units.la: Quamobrem cum terminorum constitutorum recta ratio tollat occasionem ciuilium dissidiorum & iniuriarum atrocium & cædis: rectissimè scelus moti termini tam seuerè coercetur.
units.tr: Therefore, since right reason ensures that boundary stones, once set up, remove the occasion of civil quarrels, of savage injuries and of bloodshed, the crime of moving a boundary is punished with such severity.

units.la: Idem ac præsentius potius malum est, quod ex lege de falso testimonio profert: quando quis testis est mendax: eoq; facit, vt proximus afficiatur capitali supplicio.
units.tr: The same applies, and perhaps more pressingly, to the evil that the law concerning false witness addresses: when a witness is lying, and by that means his neighbour is brought to capital punishment.

units.la: Docet primum testimonium rectum recipi, & secundum id iudicari debere: est enim litis decisioni commodum.
units.tr: It teaches that the first testimony is to be received as true, and judgment is to be given according to it, for this serves to settle the dispute.

units.la: Tum autem quomodo suspecti testes per sacerdotes inquiri debeant.
units.tr: Then it teaches how witnesses who are under suspicion are to be examined by the priests.

units.la: Demum deprehenso falso poenam mortis vt talionis decernit.
units.tr: Lastly, when falsehood has been detected, it decrees death as the penalty, by way of retaliation.

units.la: Ex quo colligimus obtrectationem & mendacia quoq; cædis initia haberi: Cauenda.
units.tr: From this we gather that slander and lies are also beginnings of murder: to be guarded against.

units.la: Amen.
units.tr: Amen.

units.la: CAPUT XX. SERMO XLVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XX. SERMON XLVII.

units.la: 1 Quum egressus fueris ad bellum contra hostes tuos, & videris equos, currus, & populum te maiorem, ne metuas ab eis, Dominus Deus tuus tecum est, qui eduxit te de terra Ægypti.
units.tr: 1 When thou goest out to battle against thine enemies, and seest horses, and chariots, and a people more than thou, be not afraid of them: for the LORD thy God is with thee, which brought thee out of the land of Egypt.

units.la: 2 Quum estis in procinctu ad pugnam, accedet sacerdos & loquetur ad populū.
units.tr: 2 When ye are ready to battle, the priest shall approach and speak to the people,

units.la: 3 Et dicet ad eos, Audi Israel, vos hodie congredimini cum hostibus vestris in pugnam, ne ergo mollescat cor vestrum, neq; timeatis, ne festinetis, neq; paveatis à facie eorum.
units.tr: 3 And shall say unto them, Hear, O Israel, ye approach this day unto battle against your enemies: let not your hearts faint, fear not, nor tremble, nor be terrified at them,

units.la: 4 Quoniam Dominus Deus vester proficiscitur vobiscum, vt pugnet pro vobis contra hostes vestros, & seruet vos.
units.tr: 4 For the LORD your God is he that goeth with you, to fight for you against your enemies, to save you.

units.la: 5 Præcones quoq; loquantur ad populum, dicentes, Qui extruxerit domum nouam, nec eam initiauit, abeat, & reuertatur in domum suam, ne forte in prælio occumbat, & alius quispiam initiet eam.
