units.tr: 5 And the officers shall speak further unto the people, saying, What man is there that hath built a new house, and hath not dedicated it? let him go and return unto his house, lest he die in the battle, and another man dedicate it.

units.la: 6 Qui plantauit vineam, & nondum prophanauit eam, abeat & reuertatur in domum suam, ne forte in bello cadat, & alius quispiam prophanet eam.
units.tr: 6 And what man is there that hath planted a vineyard, and hath not yet eaten the fruit thereof? let him also go and return unto his house, lest he die in the battle, and another man eat the fruit thereof.

units.la: 7 Qui sibi vxorem desponsit, & nondum accepit eam, abeat & reuertatur in domum suam, ne forte in bello cadat, & alius quispiam accipiat eam.
units.tr: 7 And what man is there that hath betrothed a wife, and hath not taken her? let him go and return unto his house, lest he die in the battle, and another man take her.

units.la: 8 Addant præterea præcones, loquanturq; ad populum huiusmodi verba: Qui formidolosus est, & pusillanimis, abeat, & reuertatur in domum suam, ne liquefaciat cor fratrum suorum, quemadmodum est cor suum.
units.tr: 8 And the officers shall speak further unto the people, and say, What man is there that is fearful and faint-hearted? let him go and return unto his house, lest his brethren's heart faint as well as his heart.

units.la: 9 Quum præcones cessauerint loqui ad populum, constituant principes exercitus in caput populi.
units.tr: 9 And it shall be, when the officers have made an end of speaking unto the people, that they shall make captains of the armies to lead the people.

units.la: VM vera mens & sententia legis, Nō occides, in occidendi verbo fit potissimum posita, nempe, vt quid sit occidere, quodq; cædis genus Deus vetuerit intelligamus: recte Moses eius genera duo facit, quorum vnum fit hominum priuatorum, publicum alterum.
units.tr: Since the true mind and meaning of the law, "You shall not kill," lies chiefly in the word "kill", we must understand what it is to kill and what kind of slaying God has forbidden. Moses rightly makes two kinds of it, one committed by private persons, the other public.

units.la: Iam quoniam de priuato superiore capite dixit, hoc de publico quoque dicit, hoc est de bello, deq; disciplina militari. Ac primum quidem dicit quomodo sese populus ad bellum comparet, tum autem qualem eum esse in hostes velit.
units.tr: Since he has spoken of private killing in the preceding chapter, he speaks here of the public kind, that is, of war and of military discipline. First he says how the people are to prepare themselves for war, and then what kind of people he wants them to be towards their enemies.

units.la: In quo discimus quod quemadmodum Deus eam, quæ fit à priuatis odio, ira reliquisq; af-fectibus cædem vetuit: sic bellum pacis obtinendæ gratia susceptum non modo non vetitu, sed & adhibita gerendi illius rectione concessum esse. Qua de causa quicunq; bellum iuste riteq; susceptum Christianis hominibus illicitum esse contendunt, ij non modo legis huius verba, sed etiam iustam illam super his allatam Christi interpretationem minimè rectè percipiunt.
units.tr: From this we learn that, just as God forbade the slaying that arises from private hatred, anger and other passions, so war undertaken for the sake of securing peace is not only not forbidden but is permitted, provided it is properly conducted. For this reason, those who contend that a war justly and lawfully undertaken is unlawful for Christians do not rightly grasp either the words of this law or the just interpretation of Christ given concerning these matters.

units.la: Cur enim fit illicitum? An quia dixit Esaias populo Christiano pacem fore? an quia Christus dixit, omnino non occides? rectè scilicet. Christiani pacis sunt amantes, & eodem eos exhortatur Apostolus dicens, Si fieri potest, quantum in vobis est, cum omnibus hominibus in pace viuite, non vos metipsos vlciscentes. At fieri non potest interdum per alios: vt sunt aliqui instar ferarum procliues ad nocendum: quid tum fiet? non ipsi vlciscemur: igitur impune vexabimur? subdit Apostolus: magistratum non frustra gestare gladium, & esse ministrum Dei. Baptista dedit praecepta militibus, non abstinere militia iussit. Christus vectigalia tributaq; magistratibus iure belli debita reddi voluit, cum dicit, Date Cæsari quæ sunt Cæsaris. Paulus Hebr. 11. prisca bella per fidem gesta dicit esse. Quare fi magistratus est minift iusta, cum hostibus, inquit. Sunt autem hostes, qui cum oderunt, tum damnum dant quantum maximum possunt. Qui locus est ijs, qui bellum gerunt etiam atque etiam considerandus. Nam sibi ipsi causam belli iniquam esse qui putet, quomodo vim exterorum propulsabit? Exempla sunt in nostris ipsorum historijs.
units.tr: For why should it be unlawful? Is it because Isaiah said there would be peace for the Christian people? Or because Christ said, "You shall by no means kill"? Surely not! Christians are lovers of peace, and the Apostle exhorts them to the same, saying: If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men, not avenging yourselves. But it is sometimes not possible through others, since some are like wild beasts, prone to harm. What then? We shall not avenge ourselves: shall we therefore be harassed with impunity? The Apostle adds that the magistrate does not bear the sword in vain and is God's minister. John the Baptist gave precepts to soldiers; he did not order them to abstain from military service. Christ wished that taxes and tributes owed to the magistrates by right of war be paid, when he says, Render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's. Paul in Hebrews 11 says that the wars of old were waged by faith. Wherefore, if the magistrate is a minister of God, just, with enemies, he says. Now there are enemies who, when they hate, also do as much harm as they can. Those who wage war must consider this again and again. For how will one repel the violence of foreigners if he thinks his own cause of war is unjust? There are examples in our own histories.

units.la: 2. Formam belli pugnæ appellatione describit. Etenim in pugna sic res geruntur, ut neque parcatur hostibus, neq; damnum accersatur patriæ: sed vt fortiter, prouide, pro falutæ ciuium administrentur omnia.
units.tr: 2. He describes the form of war by the word "battle". For in battle things are so managed that the enemy is not spared, nor is harm brought upon the homeland, but everything is carried out bravely, wisely and for the safety of the citizens.

units.la: 3. Euentus asscribendus Deo: is pugnat pro nobis vt feruet: nec poenitentia nostra effera-mur, nec ea deficiente desperemus. Deus est victor.
units.tr: 3. The outcome is to be ascribed to God: he fighteth for us to save us. Neither are we to be puffed up by our own valour, nor to despair if it fails. God is the victor.

units.la: Hoc docebunt sacerdotes. Nec par est illos abesse à ciuibus in periculo constitutis.
units.tr: The priests will teach this. Nor is it fitting that they be absent from the citizens who are placed in danger.

units.la: Iam principibus delectum militum habendum dicit. Neque enim prodest, vti turba promiscua, in qua alij impediant alios: multò minus rem facit qui venatur inuitis canibus.
units.tr: Next he says that the leaders are to make a levy of soldiers. For it does no good to have a mixed crowd in which some hinder others; much less does he accomplish anything who hunts with unwilling dogs.

units.la: Quis igitur delectus? Qui domo, vinea, vxore, quas recens acquisiit, nondum frui cepit. Quæ remissio duabus de causis videtur concessa: quarum altera est, Cum bellorum casus in-certi sint, ne quis otiosus fruatur alienis laboribus: vt ædes extructas ab alio habitet alius: vineam ex confitis ab alio vitibus vindemiam faciat alius: vxore vix impetrata potiatur alius. Altera, ne rerum harum cura & cogitatione detenti præsentes corporibus animis autem absint: si-let enim eò mens inclinare sese, quo desiderio suo rapitur, vt esurienti parasito in patinis est animus. Quare publicæ simul & priuatæ rei consulitur hac remissione.
units.tr: Who, then, is the proper levy? He who has built a house, planted a vineyard, or taken a wife, and has not yet begun to enjoy them. This exemption seems to have been granted for two reasons. The first is that, since the outcome of wars is uncertain, no one idle should enjoy the labours of another: that another should live in houses built by someone else, that another should gather the vintage from vines planted by someone else, that another should possess a wife scarcely won by someone else. The second is that men held back by the care and thought of these things may be bodily present but absent in mind, for the mind is apt to turn wherever it is drawn by its desire, as the mind of a hungry parasite is fixed on the dishes. So by this exemption both public and private interests are served at once.

units.la: Dein singulí sunt admonendi milites, vt qui timidi sint abeant: ne videlicet liquefaciant cor fratrum suorum. Etenim timore fractus, atque infirmatus animus ipsum corpus ad res gerendas reddit inhabile. Ipsa anima corporis est magistra & gubernatrix, atque eius ipsius membris quasi quibusdam instrumentis vti consueuit. Ergo per se inepti sunt ad res gerendas qui timent, tum etiam alios inhabiles reddunt: quia vitiorum contagio reliqua turba facile inficitur: præsertim cum suum quique inprimisque timidi morbum occultant & colore virtutis illinunt: Voluntq; qui sunt ignaui sese pro cautis, timidi pro consultis haberi.
units.tr: Next the soldiers are to be warned individually that the fearful are to depart, lest they make the hearts of their brothers faint. For a spirit broken and weakened by fear renders the body itself unfit for doing its work. The soul is the teacher and governor of the body, and customarily uses the members of the body as certain instruments. Therefore those who fear are by themselves unfit for action, and they also make others unfit, because the rest of the crowd is easily infected by the contagion of vices, especially since each man, and above all the timid, hides his own sickness and paints it with the colour of virtue. And the idle want to be taken for cautious men, and the timid for prudent ones.

units.la: Quibus rebus & consilijs efficitur, vt bella iure suscipiantur, & rite gerantur, & feliciter perficiantur.
units.tr: By these means and counsels it is brought about that wars are undertaken lawfully, conducted properly, and brought to a happy end.

units.la: In milite Christiano Dominus Christus easdem virtutes requirit. Luc. 9. Qui manu admota aratro à tergo respicit, non est me dignus. Phil. 3. Paulus vult nos eorum quæ à tergo sunt obliuisci. Vxor Lothi, inuitati ad nuptias exempla sunt. Vtinam nos sub Christi signis hic geramus quo simus illi honori, regno Dei vsui, nobis saluti sempiternæ. Amen.
units.tr: Our Lord Christ requires the same virtues in the Christian soldier. Luke 9: "No man, having put his hand to the plough and looking back, is fit for me." Philippians 3: Paul wishes us to forget the things that are behind. The wife of Lot is an example for those invited to the wedding. Would that we here so fight under the banners of Christ that we may be to him for honour, to the kingdom of God for use, and to ourselves for eternal salvation. Amen.

units.la: SERMO XLVIII.
units.tr: SERMON XLVIII.

units.la: 10 Quum autem accesseris ad ciuitatem, vt illam oppugnes, offeras ei pacem.
units.tr: 10 When you draw near to a city to attack it, offer it peace.

units.la: 11 Si pacate responderit tibi, aperueritq; tibi, omnis populus qui in ea inuentus fuerit, sint tibi tributarij, seruiantq; tibi.
units.tr: 11 If it answers you peaceably and opens to you, then all the people found in it shall be tributary to you and serve you.

units.la: 12 Quod si nulla tecum fecerit pacem, sed pugnauerit contra te, oppugnabis eam:
units.tr: 12 But if it makes no peace with you, and makes war against you, you shall besiege it.

units.la: 13 Et quum Dominus Deus tuus tradiderit eam in manum tuam, feries in ea gladio omnem marem.
units.tr: 13 And when the Lord your God delivers it into your hand, you shall strike every male in it with the sword.

units.la: 14. Duntaxat mulieres, pubem, iumenta, & quicquid fuerit in ciuitate, sed & omnia spolia eius tibi diripies, & frueris spolijs hostium tuorum, quos tradidit tibi Dominus Deus tuus.
units.tr: 14 Only the women, the children, the cattle, and whatever is in the city, all its spoil, you shall plunder for yourselves, and you shall enjoy the spoils of your enemies, whom the Lord your God has given you.

units.la: 15. Sic facies omnibus ciuitatibus, quæ procul à te sunt, quæ non sunt de vrbibus istarum gentium.
units.tr: 15 So you shall do to all the cities that are far from you, which are not cities of those nations.

units.la: 16 Veruntamen de ciuitatibus istorum populorum, quos Dominus tibi dedit in hereditatem, nihil viuum permittes quod spirat.
units.tr: 16 But of the cities of those peoples, whom the Lord gives you for an inheritance, you shall let nothing that breathes remain alive.

units.la: 17 Sed omnino vastabis eos ad internecionem: vsque, nempe Hittheum, Amorræum[?], Chananæum, Pherisæum, Hiuæum & Iebusæum, quemadmodum præcepit tibi Dominus Deus tuus.
units.tr: 17 But you shall utterly destroy them to the point of extermination: namely the Hittite, the Amorite[?], the Canaanite, the Perizzite, the Hivite and the Jebusite, just as the Lord your God has commanded you.

units.la: 18 Ne scilicet doceant vos facere secundum cunctas suas abominationes, quas ipsi fecerunt diis suis, & peccetis in Dominum Deum vestrum.
units.tr: 18 So that, of course, they do not teach you to do according to all their abominations, which they have done for their gods, and so that you do not sin against the Lord your God.

units.la: 19 Quum obsederis civitatem diebus multis, & pugnaueris contra eam, vt oc-cupes eam, ne perdes arbores eius vt impellas securim in eas, sed comedas ex eis, & non succidas: num enim arbor campi homo est, vt veniat coram te in obsidionem?
units.tr: 19 When you have besieged a city for many days, and fought against it to take it, you shall not destroy its trees by lifting an axe against them, but you shall eat of them and not cut them down. For is the tree of the field a man, that it should come before you into the siege?

units.la: 20 Duntaxat illam arborem, quam nosti esse arborem quae fructum non ferat, nec esui aptam, illam inquam perdes & succides, atq; extrues propugnancula contra istam civitatem, quae contra te belligerat, donec subijcies eam.
units.tr: 20 Only the tree which you know is not a fruit tree, nor fit for food, that one you shall destroy and cut down, and build siegeworks against that city which makes war against you, until you subdue it.

units.la: IN prima parte cap.huius ostendit Moses quomodo fideles in bellis sese gerere, quamque militarem disciplinam seruare debeant in suis ipsorum copijs atque exercitibus: iam sequitur altera pars, qua docet quales in hostem esse debeant. In quo primum quid de hoste: tum quid de eorum agris sit statuendum monstrat.
units.tr: In the first part of this chapter Moses shows how the faithful should conduct themselves in wars, and what military discipline they must keep among their own troops and armies. Now follows the second part, in which he teaches how they ought to behave towards the enemy. In this he first shows what is to be decided concerning the enemy, and then what concerning their lands.

units.la: Ac primum quidem duo hostium genera facit: vnum eorum qui sunt remoti, quibus pax prius offerri, quàm bellum indici queat: alterum eorum qui sint vicini, cum quibus nulla pax vnquam coire posit sine reip. & diuinae gloriae periculo.
units.tr: And first he makes two kinds of enemies: one of those who are remote, to whom peace can be offered before war is declared; the other of those who are near, with whom no peace can ever be made without danger to the commonwealth and to the glory of God.

units.la: De priore genere sic dicit. Cum accesseris ad ciuitatem, &c. Quibus verbis ostendit bel-lum non nisi pacis recuperandæ gratia debere suscipi: pacem offerendam, ac si recipiatur concedendam etiam hostibus. Augustus Cæsar dictitabat quasi quendam aureum hamum esse: quippe quoniam instrumento precij maioris piscetur aliquis, quàm pisces capiat. Bellum enim in periculum trahit quaecunque bona dedit hominibus Dominus salutaria, vtilia, suauia: vt libertatem, religionem, probitatem, opes, honores, quietem, securitatem: pax haec affert omnia, excolit artes, auget opes. Vnde Menander, Εἰρήνη (inquit) [?] [illegible, ~40 letters]. Et Herodo.lib.1.hist ait, Οὐδεὶς γὰρ οὕτως ἀνόητος ὅστις πόλεμον πρὸ εἰρήνης αἱρέεται [?]. Magna est ergo & ardua pacis belli q; deli-beratio. Thucydides lib.1.in Concio.3.Corinth.ait, ἀλλ᾽ ἀσφαλῶς [?] [illegible, ~50 letters]. Vnde Romulus non sibi soli, licet regi, sed etiâ populo de pace belloq; deliberandi & statuendi facultate esse voluit: qua libertate post annis 700. demum in Augustû translato Imperio hoc iure spoliati sunt. Ex quibus intelligimus pacis studiû omnibus commendari: sed si nequeat hæc pia, honesta, vtilis obtineri, bellum ei præferendum. Præstat enim honestè mori, quàm turpiter viuere.
units.tr: Concerning the former kind he speaks thus: When you draw near to a city, etc. By these words he shows that war ought not to be undertaken except for the sake of recovering peace, and that peace is to be offered, and granted even to enemies if it is accepted. Augustus Caesar used to say that peace was like a golden hook: for someone fishes with an instrument of greater value than the fish he catches. For war puts in peril all the good, salutary, useful and pleasant things the Lord has given to men: liberty, religion, uprightness, wealth, honours, quiet, security. Peace brings all these, cultivates the arts, and increases wealth. Hence Menander says, "Peace..." (text illegible in the scan). And Herodotus, in book 1 of his History, says: "For no one is so foolish as to choose war rather than peace" [Οὐδεὶς γὰρ οὕτως ἀνόητος ὅστις πόλεμον πρὸ εἰρήνης αἱρέεται]. Great and difficult, therefore, is the deliberation about peace and war. Thucydides, in book 1, in the third speech of the Corinthians, says: "But safely..." [ἀλλ᾽ ἀσφαλῶς] (remainder illegible). Hence Romulus wished the power of deliberating and deciding about peace and war to belong not to himself alone, although he was king, but also to the people; and after about 700 years, when the empire was transferred to Augustus, they were at last deprived of this right. From these things we understand that the pursuit of peace is to be commended to all; but if this pious, honourable and useful peace cannot be obtained, war is to be preferred to it. For it is better to die honourably than to live shamefully.

units.la: Sed ostendit hic etiam qualis pax recipientibus sit concedenda, qualeq; bellum ijs intentari debeat, qui pacem nolunt. Pacem eiusmodi dicit quæ tributum requirat Israelitis lacessitis ad expeditionem. Idq; iusto domini iudicio. Seruiet æternû qui paruo nescient vti. In quo videmus ob peccata, vt luxum, fastum, superbiam, bella diuinitus immitti.
units.tr: But here he also shows what kind of peace is to be granted to those who accept it, and what kind of war is to be threatened against those who do not want peace. He speaks of a peace of this kind, which requires tribute from the Israelites when they have provoked him to an expedition. And this is by the just judgment of the Lord. He will serve forever who knows not how to use little. In this we see that, on account of sins such as luxury, pride, arrogance, wars are sent down from God.

units.la: Seruitute coercetur abusus libertatis, vt sunt etiam prodigi qui puniuntur inopia, & qui domestica libertate spreta in bellum ierunt, fiunt mancipia. Cham statu libertatis abu-tens factus est seruus seruorum. Dauid in Psalmo dicit auctos opibus & honoribus pios, sub iugum missos malos. Vnde & Israelitæ postea facti sunt tributarij, qui ipsi tributarios habebant. Romani libertatem omnium gentium fregerunt, tandem etiam ipsi suam amise-runt. Idem est nobis pertimescendum iudicium.
units.tr: The abuse of liberty is restrained by servitude; just as prodigals too, who are punished by poverty, and those who, having despised their domestic liberty, went to war, become slaves. Ham, abusing the state of liberty, became a servant of servants. David says in a Psalm that the pious, when increased in wealth and honours, and the wicked, are sent under the yoke. Hence also the Israelites afterwards became tributaries, though they themselves had tributaries. The Romans broke the liberty of all nations, and at last they themselves lost their own. The same judgment is to be feared by us.

units.la: Bellum vero sic erit, inquit Moses, vt occidantur gladio masculi, salui sint fœminæ, & liberi, idq; etiâ ipsum iusto Dei iudicio. Vt enim seruitus abusum libertatis coercet, sic abusum pacis bello coercet Deus. Testimonia habes Leuit.26. Deut.28. inter maledictiones refertur bellum & vastatio. Exempla sunt Iudic.2. cum Baalim Israelitæ colerent abiecto veri Dei cultu, traditi sunt vicinis gentibus, quorum deos coluere. Iudic.3. Cusam Risathaim illis dominatur annis octo, quando infidelibus vxoribus iuncti essent. Iud.4. Defuncto Ehud peccant & traduntur Iabin regi Canaan annis 20. Idem illis accidit Iudic.6.10.13.capp. Ita bello parta bello dilabuntur. Roma, Niniue, Heluetia quæ ex Germania, Italia, Gallia, Neapoli mul-tum auri contulit. Atq; sic primum genus hostium tractari debet. Alterum autem eorum est, qui iusto Dei iudicio condemnati sunt, quibus cum iusta pax esse non potest, neque etiam offerri debet. Quas gentes enumerat. Hi populi quadringen-tis ante annis condemnati propterea que delendi fuerant. Et causæ referuntur. Primo quia Deus præcepit. Vt in omnibus rebus, sic in bello, vt re maxima, verbum Dei respiciendum est. 2. Ne doceant superstitionem, neue sint exemplo malo. Malorum enim consortio tam senes quam iuuenes inficimur. Vt igitur pater liberis malas sodalitia, sic Deus suo populo ho-minum infidelium fœdera pariter & connubia vetuit : tum noluit illorum quicquam reliquum.
units.tr: But war will be of this kind, Moses says: that the males be slain with the sword, while the women and children are spared, and this too is by the just judgment of God. For as servitude restrains the abuse of liberty, so God restrains the abuse of peace by war. You have testimonies in Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28: war and devastation are reckoned among the curses. There are examples in Judges 2: when the Israelites worshipped Baalim, abandoning the true worship of God, they were handed over to the neighbouring nations whose gods they worshipped. Judges 3: Cushan-rishathaim ruled over them for eight years, when they were joined to unbelieving wives. Judges 4: after the death of Ehud they sinned and were delivered to Jabin, king of Canaan, for twenty years. The same happened to them in Judges 6, 10 and 13. Thus those things gained by war are lost by war. Rome, Nineveh, Helvetia, which brought much gold from Germany, Italy, Gaul and Naples. And so the first kind of enemy is to be treated in this way. The other kind, however, are those who have been condemned by the just judgment of God, with whom a just peace cannot exist, nor ought it even to be offered. He enumerates the nations. These peoples had been condemned four hundred years earlier, and therefore were to be destroyed, and the reasons are given. First, because God commanded it. In all things, and so in war, as in the greatest matter, the Word of God is to be regarded. Second, so that they do not teach superstition, nor be a bad example. For by the company of the wicked we are infected, old and young alike. Therefore, just as a father forbids his children bad companionships, so God forbade his people alliances and marriages with unbelieving men, and then he wished nothing of them to be left.

units.la: Hæc enim est causa belli iusta, vt eradicetur malum & suum cuique sit saluum bonum. Vt fuit bellum Abrahæ Genesis 14. Iof. 10. cum Gabaon obsidione soluitur. Iudic.19.20.cum punitur scelus Beniamitarum. Et 1.Regum 30.cum Ziclaga ab Amelechitis vastata, per Dauid recuperatur. 2.Regum 10. cum Dauid contra Ammonem Ammonitarum regem bellum gerit. Eiusdem generis sunt illa maiorum nostrorum contra Austriacos, Burgundos, Sueuos.
units.tr: For this is a just cause of war: that evil be uprooted and each one's good be kept safe. So it was Abraham's war in Genesis 14; in Joshua 10 the siege of Gibeon is loosed; in Judges 19 and 20 the crime of the Benjamites is punished; in 1 Samuel 30 Ziklag, laid waste by the Amalekites, is recovered through David; in 2 Samuel 10 David wages war against Hanun, king of the Ammonites. Of the same kind were those wars of our ancestors against the Austrians, Burgundians and Suevi.

units.la: Adest socius hæc bella gerentibus Dominus. Insignis in hanc sententiam locus est Exod. 17.quo monstratur quæ vis sit precum fidelium pro victoria.
units.tr: The Lord is present as an ally to those who wage these wars. A notable passage to this effect is Exodus 17, which shows what power the prayers of the faithful have for victory.

units.la: Malum dicit totum extirpandum. In quo plurimum situm est momenti. Ne fit illud in nos, Vincere scis Hannibal victoria vti nescis. Ne ferantur reliquiæ mali.
units.tr: He says that the evil must be utterly rooted out. In this there is much weight. Lest that happen to us, "You know how to conquer, Hannibal, but you do not know how to use victory." Lest the remnants of the evil survive.

units.la: In hostium bona, vt arbores, quæ frugiferæ sunt, eas ne corrumpant neue perdant vetat: steriles in vsus suos, vt aggeres, vtantur ijs licet. Militum petulantia coercetur. Causam addit, quia arbor non oppugnat. Bella crudelia sunt, in quibus non tam laboratur in perniciem hostium, quàm suorum etiam hominum, agros vastando & populando.
units.tr: He forbids the enemy's goods to be corrupted or destroyed, such as trees that bear fruit; but barren trees they may use for their own purposes, for siegeworks, for example. The wantonness of soldiers is restrained. He adds the reason: because the tree does not fight against you. Cruel are the wars in which effort is spent not so much on the destruction of the enemy as on that of one's own people too, by laying waste and ravaging the fields.

units.la: Discimus non ita vt solent pleriq; fruges consumere etiam in pace: vt qui plus quàm opus sit edunt & bibunt esurientibus cæteris: quíue fruges aliorum decerpunt & suffurantur. Quare abstineamus. Christo sit honos in secula. Amen.
units.tr: We learn not to consume the fruits, as most people do even in peace, eating and drinking more than is needed while others go hungry, or snatching and pilfering the fruits of others. Therefore let us abstain. To Christ be honour for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT XXI. SERMO XLIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER 21. SERMON 49.

units.la: Si in terra, quam Dominus Deus tuus dat tibi possidendam, interfectus inuentus fuerit iacens in campo, neq; scitur quis eum occiderit.
units.tr: If in the land which the Lord your God gives you to possess, a slain man is found lying in the field, and it is not known who has killed him,

units.la: 2 Egredientur seniores tui atq; iudices tui, & metientur vsq; ad ciuitates quæ sunt circum interfectum.
units.tr: then your elders and your judges shall come out and measure the distance to the cities which lie around the slain man.

units.la: 3 Ciuitas quæ propior fuerit interfecto, illius ciuitatis seniores vitulam ex armento accipiant, cum quâ adhuc nihil operis factum est, quæque iugum non traxit.
units.tr: The city nearest to the slain man: the elders of that city shall take a heifer from the herd, one on which no work has yet been done and which has never drawn the yoke.

units.la: 4 Et deducant seniores illius ciuitatis vitulam illam in vallem solidam quæ nec colitur nec feritur, & illinc incidant ei ceruicem in valle.
units.tr: And the elders of that city shall bring the heifer down to a rough valley, which is neither tilled nor sown, and there they shall break its neck in the valley.

units.la: 5 Accedentque Sacerdotes filij Leui (quos elegit Dominus Deus tuus, vt ministrent ei, & benedicant in nomine Domini, & iuxta quorum os omnis forensis actio & plaga finitur.)
units.tr: Then the priests, the sons of Levi (whom the Lord your God has chosen to minister to him and to bless in the name of the Lord, and by whose word every legal dispute and stroke is settled),

units.la: 6 Et omnes seniores ciuitatis illius, qui accesserint ad interfectum, lauabunt manus suas super vitulam, cui incisa est ceruix in valle.
units.tr: and all the elders of that city who are nearest the slain man shall wash their hands over the heifer whose neck was broken in the valley.

units.la: 7 Respondebuntq; dicentes, manus nostrae non fuderunt sanguinem istum, nec oculi nostri viderunt.
units.tr: And they shall answer and say: Our hands have not shed this blood, nor have our eyes seen it.

units.la: 8 Propitius esto populo tuo Israel, quem redemisti Domine, & ne imputes sanguinem innoxium in medio populi tui Israel, vt expientur à sanguine.
units.tr: Be merciful, O Lord, to your people Israel, whom you have redeemed, and do not impute innocent blood in the midst of your people Israel; so they shall be atoned from the blood.

units.la: 9 Et tu expurgabis sanguinem innocentem de medio tui, si volueris facere quod rectum est in oculis Domini.
units.tr: So you shall purge the innocent blood from among you, when you do what is right in the eyes of the Lord.

units.la: Nexpositione legis non occides, de privata simul ac publica caede summa fide & diligentia disservit: quemadmodum ex praeced. duob. Capp. est perspicuum. Sed quoniam eam ad rem amplius quiddam pertinet, quod partim est omnino praetermissum, partim leviter perstrictum: iam ne quid desit, ad eam suae legis huius expositionem hoc etiam caput addit, quo plenius ac melius exponat adducta, & apponat etiam praetermissa. Eius generis sunt illa. Ad privatam caedem refert: si quis occisus reperiatur, homicida vero neque comprehendi queat, neque sciri, quid facto opus esse videatur. Ad eadem publicam, si in bello, ut dictum est, formosae foeminae capiantur, quo loco sint habendae: si qui domi liberos & uxores habeant, quid tum de matrimonio deq; primogenitura sit iuris: si qui sint rebelles, quomodo in eos magistratus animadvertat.
units.tr: In expounding the law "You shall not kill," he treats with the greatest faith and diligence both private and public murder, as is clear from the two preceding chapters. But since there is still something more pertinent to this matter, some of it wholly passed over and some only lightly touched, he now adds this chapter, so that nothing is lacking, to expound his law more fully and better, and to supply what was omitted. Of this kind are the following. He refers to private murder: if a slain man is found but the killer can be neither seized nor known, what must be done seems plain. He refers to public murder: if, in war, as was said, beautiful women are taken captive, where they are to be kept; if men have children and wives at home, what right there is then concerning marriage and the firstborn; if there are rebels, how the magistrate is to punish them.

units.la: Atque haec quidem toto hoc capite, sed cognitionem caedis incerto authore patratae docet in praesentia. Si cuius hominis cadauer repertum sit & ignoretur author: ineundam rationem ditionis, in qua cedes sit patrata dicit: inde eius loci principes & sacerdotes quosdam divinitus instituto ritu profiteantur, se suosq; homines cedis huius omni culpa vacare, propterea; & Deum precari ne suam terram sanguine pollutam aestimet: & infamiae notam abstergat. Mirabilis locus est, & in recessu plus habet, quam prima fronte promittat. Quod nobis erit perspicuum si ritus illius causas omnes, ut efficientem, materiam, formam, finem aestimemus.
units.tr: And these things indeed belong to the whole chapter, but for the present it teaches the investigation of a killing committed by an unknown author. If the corpse of a man is found and its author is unknown, it says that the district in which the killing was committed must be examined; then the princes and priests of that place, by a rite divinely instituted, must profess that they and their people are free from all guilt for this killing, and pray God not to reckon their land polluted with blood, and to wipe away the stain of infamy. It is a wondrous place, and holds more in its depths than it promises at first sight. This will become clear to us if we weigh all the causes of this rite: the efficient, the material, the formal and the final.

units.la: Causa efficiens sunt, quibus ea de ritu mandatum est feruando, ut seniores & Leuitae. Id diligenter exponit. Primum quod magistratui & Leuitis mandat, ut in eadem patratam inquirant, & de populi sibi creditii innocentia sint solliciti: id est argumento velle Deum, ut verbi ministri moneant magistratus, quo exequantur quaecunque ad auertendam peccati noxam pertinent. Unde ministris nomen pastorum, vigilum, speculatorum inditum: Unde eos Christus appellat lumen ostendens maculas, vias, colores: & [?]talem quicquid est putridum mordentem. Id Esaias, Helias, Baptista, Christus, Petrus, Apostoli fecere. Qui cum malam gratiam reportarint, ne mirere si nobis idem accidat. Aegre ferunt conciones, quibus dicitur bella mercenaria vocare in nos sanguinem, quibus etiam castigantur reliqua scelera, at vides hoc opus esse consilio.
units.tr: The efficient causes are those to whom the rite was commanded to be observed, namely the elders and the Levites. He sets this out carefully. First, he commands the magistrate and the Levites to inquire diligently into the murder committed in that place, and to be anxious about the innocence of the people entrusted to them. This is proof that God wills the ministers of the Word to warn the magistrates, so that they may carry out whatever pertains to averting the harm of sin. Hence the ministers are called shepherds, watchmen and scouts; hence Christ says they are a light showing spots, paths and colours, and whatever is rotten and biting [?]. Isaiah, Elijah, the Baptist, Christ, Peter and the apostles did this. Since they gained an ill reward for it, do not be surprised if the same happens to us. Sermons are hard to bear in which it is said that mercenary wars bring blood upon us, and in which other crimes are rebuked as well; yet you see that this work requires counsel.

units.la: Magistratus autem hic discit quantopere eniti in studium innocentiae debeat: habeatq; terram a caede puram. Sed eo res redijt ut ipsi magistratus atque sacerdotes eadem & bella spirent.
units.tr: But the magistrate here learns how greatly he ought to strive for zeal for innocence, and to keep the land pure from murder. But the matter has come to this: the magistrates themselves and the priests breathe the same wars.

units.la: Post quomodo factum sit cognoscendi docet Moses. Metiantur, inquit, locum. Vide ut Deus velit distincta rerum dominia atque iura.
units.tr: Afterwards Moses teaches how the matter is to be established: "Let them measure," he says, "the place." See how God wills distinct dominions and rights over things.

units.la: Caeterum si materiam & formam consideres, vitulam quae sub iugum non venerit vult accipi, in quam manus abluant, &c. Vitula Christum, armentum gregem patriarcharum & stirpem Iessaeam significant: Christus enim iugum peccati nunquam traxit, quippe qui sit natus ex casta virgine conceptus e spiritu sancto, demissus in vallem asperá nempe hunc mundum. Is nos sua morte perpurgavit, ac nerei caedis effemus fecit: testantur hoc seniores populi, Patriarchae videlicet & Moses & Prophetae, itemq; Apostoli & Martyres. Cadauer mortuum est genus humanum occulta atque subdola satanae fraude circumuentum, atque oppressum. Quo pertinent & referri possent plurima Scripturae testimonia.
units.tr: Moreover, if you consider the matter and the form, the heifer which has not come under the yoke is to be taken, over which they wash their hands, and so on. The heifer signifies Christ, the herd the patriarchs and the stock of Jesse; for Christ never bore the yoke of sin, being born of a chaste virgin, conceived of the Holy Spirit, and sent down into the valley, that is, this rough world. He cleansed us by his death and freed us from the guilt of murder. The elders of the people bear witness to this, namely the patriarchs, Moses and the prophets, and likewise the apostles and martyrs. The corpse is the human race, dead, beset and oppressed by the hidden and subtle deceit of Satan. Very many testimonies of Scripture pertain to this and could be cited.

units.la: Ritus autem ipsius formâ si consideres, non pauca bona disces. 1. Sacerdotes benedicunt. Forma benedictionis extat Num. 6. ij non ipsi benedictionem habent, sed accepta divinitus afferunt: per eos ceu instrumenta Deus agit. Benedictio in corpus, animum, externa bona se extendit. Gene. 17. ero Deus Schaddai, dabo terram lacte melleq; manantem. Vide pro caede quaerendum.
units.tr: If you consider the form of the rite itself, you will learn not a few good things. (1) The priests bless. The form of the blessing stands in Num. 6. They do not have the blessing themselves, but bring it when received from God; God acts through them as instruments. The blessing extends to body, soul and external goods: Gen. 17, "I am God Almighty; I will give you a land flowing with milk and honey." Note that it is to be sought against bloodshed.

units.la: 2. Seniores manus abluunt: id est signum innocentiae, ut Psal. 25. Esa. 1. Matt. 27. quo testantur se nec fecisse quod quaeritur, nec eius esse conscij. Quanti [?]innocentia. Ne communices peccatis alienis. At plerique nunc multum alieni peccati suis sibi humeris imponunt.
units.tr: (2) The elders wash their hands. This is a sign of innocence, as in Ps. 25, Isa. 1 and Matt. 27, by which they testify that they neither did what is being inquired into nor are party to it. How great is innocence! Do not share in other people's sins. But most people now load much of another's sin upon their own shoulders.

units.la: 3. Ipsa professio quoque adscribitur. Quae omnia quasi quoddam speculum sunt bonae conscientiae. Enitendum est nobis ut & hic & in die iudicij possimus gloriari.
units.tr: (3) The profession itself is also added. All these things are like a mirror of a good conscience. We must strive that, both here and on the day of judgement, we may be able to glory.

units.la: Finem sic docet: Et tu expurgabis, &c. Quo horrore cedis & sanguinis incutit: est enim res naturae cumprimis contraria. Neque enim homo nascitur armatus ut reliqua animalia, sed nudus: homini sunt data principia pacis artium, in iisq;, si modo diligenter excolantur, excellit. Quare furit cum his desertis ad ferinam crudelitatem conuertitur. Pugnat cum narutà & voluntate Dei:homo ad vitam, ad imaginem Dei, ad beneficentiam conditus est, vt Deus non lupus sit homini.
units.tr: He sets out the end thus: "And you shall purge," and so on. By this he instils horror of murder and blood, for it is a thing most contrary to nature. Man is not born armed as the other animals are, but naked; the beginnings of the arts of peace are given to man, and in these, if they are diligently cultivated, he excels. Therefore, when he deserts these, he turns to savage cruelty. He fights against nature and the will of God: man was made for life, for the image of God, for beneficence, so that God may not be a wolf to man.

units.la: Sanguis clamat ad Deum, Abelis, Israelis in Ægypto, puerorum Bethelemiticorum, prophetarum, Apostolorum, martyrum. Quid nostra tempora commemorem?
units.tr: The blood cries out to God: the blood of Abel, of Israel in Egypt, of the boys of Bethlehem, of the prophets, the apostles, the martyrs. Why should I mention our own times?

units.la: 2 Vt etiam à suspicione cædis alieni simus. Nam cum Christus dira quoque imprecetur ei, qui fratrum aliquem offendérit, & Paulus dicat abstinendum etiam esse ab omni specie mali: sanè cuius est perspicuum quanti referat ex præscripto Mosis in patrata maleficia diligenter animaduertere, suam innocentiam profiteri, & suspiciones sinistras declinare.
units.tr: (2) So that we may also be free from suspicion of another's killing. For since Christ calls down dire curses on whoever offends one of the brethren, and Paul says that one must abstain from every appearance of evil, it is surely clear how much it matters to attend carefully, according to Moses' prescription, to crimes committed, to profess one's innocence and to avoid sinister suspicions.

units.la: Ex quibus omnibus intelligimus quantopere sit abstinendum à cæde & sanguine & potius enitendum, vt benedictione, quæ est in Christi sanguine, potiti, benè beateque viuamus. Amen.
units.tr: From all these things we understand how greatly we must abstain from murder and blood, and rather strive that, having obtained the blessing which is in the blood of Christ, we may live well and happily. Amen.

units.la: SERMO LI.[?]
units.tr: SERMON LI.[?]

units.la: 10 Quando egressus fueris in bellum contra hostes tuos, tradideritq; eos Dominus Deus tuus in manum tuam, vt ducas eos captiuos.
units.tr: 10 When you go out to war against your enemies, and the Lord your God delivers them into your hand, so that you lead them away captive,

units.la: 11 Viderúq; inter captiuos mulierem formâ venustam, deperisq; eam, poteris eam tibi accipere in vxorem.
units.tr: 11 and you see among the captives a woman beautiful in form, and you desire her, you may take her to yourself as a wife.

units.la: 12 Introduces ergo eam in domum tuam, illaque radet caput suum, aptabitq; vngues suos.
units.tr: 12 You shall bring her into your house, and she shall shave her head and pare her nails.

units.la: 13 Auferet quoq; vestimentum captiuitatis suæ à se, & sedebit in domo tua, deplorabit patrem suum & matrem suam integrum mensem, & tum tandem introibis ad eam, & eris maritus eius; ipsaq; erit tibi vxor.
units.tr: 13 She shall also put off the garment of her captivity, and she shall sit in your house and mourn her father and mother for a full month. And then at last you shall go in to her, and be her husband, and she shall be your wife.

units.la: 14. Sin tibi non placuerit, patiaris eam abire pro voto suo, neque tamen eam pecunia vendere, neq; ad opus vt ea poteris, eo quod oppressisti eam.
units.tr: 14 But if she does not please you, you shall let her go wherever she wishes, but you shall not sell her for money, nor treat her as a slave, since you have humbled her.

units.la: 15 Si viro alicui fuerint duæ vxores, altera dilectâ, altera odiosa, genuerintq; ei filios tam dilectâ quam odiosâ, & filius odiosæ fuerit primogenitus.
units.tr: 15 If a man has two wives, one loved and the other hated, and they bear him sons, both the loved and the hated, and the firstborn son is the son of the hated one,

units.la: 16 Aduenerit dies, quo diuisurus est filijs suis, quos habet, hereditatem suam, non poterit primogenitum facere filium dilectæ, donec superstes est primogenitus filius odiosæ.
units.tr: 16 then on the day when he divides his inheritance among his sons, he may not make the son of the loved wife the firstborn, before the firstborn son of the hated wife.

units.la: 17 Sed filium odiosæ agnoscet primogenitum, dabitq; ei portionem duplicem de omnibus quæ possidet, quandoquidem is principium est virtutis eius, & ob hoc debe-tur ei ius primogenituræ.
units.tr: 17 But he shall acknowledge the firstborn son of the hated wife, and give him a double portion of all that he possesses, since he is the beginning of his strength, and the right of the firstborn is due to him.

units.la: INilla, quam legis non occides expositioni Moses addit, appendice subinde recolendum est, tædem aliam esse priuatâ, aliam publicam. Jam quoniam ad priuatæ cædis expositionem casum nouum adduxit supra: nunc ad publicam etiam alium affert. Etenim in bello iusserat mulieribus atque liberis parcere: in quo si quis alicuius captiuæ mulieris forma captus, inq; eius amorem illectus eam ducere cupiat, quid iuris sit edocet. Ex quo deinceps alia quæstio de iure primogenitorum oritur, quam & ipsam explanat.
units.tr: In the appendix which Moses adds to the exposition of "You shall not kill," it must be recalled that there is one kind of killing that is private and another that is public. Since above he has brought in a new case to explain private killing, now he also brings another for public killing. For in war he had ordered that women and children be spared; and he teaches what the law is in the case where someone, taken by the beauty of a captive woman and enticed by love, wishes to marry her. From this another question arises concerning the right of the firstborn, which he also explains.

units.la: Quas ad res æstimandas, ne quis error ingruat, in primis pertinet, vt intelligamus leges Mosis alios esse typos siue cerimonias, alias ciuiles, rursus morales alias. Ex quibus typos Christiani, quoniam Christum habent, tantum cognoscent, non autem exercebunt. Ciuiles leges non obligant eos, quibus non late sunt & aptæ, sed tantum sunt exemplo. Morales quoniam & omnium gentium & diuino iure nituntur nos sibi deuinciunt.
units.tr: In weighing these matters, so that no error creeps in, it is above all important that we understand that the laws of Moses are of different kinds: some are types or ceremonies, others civil, and others again moral. Of these, Christians, since they have Christ, will recognise the types only and will not practise them. Civil laws do not bind those to whom they are not widely and suitably applicable, but are only an example. Moral laws, since they rest on the law of all nations and on divine law, bind us to themselves.

units.la: Illæ duæ de disciplina militari, deq; potestate patria, quicquid secundum verbum diuinum constitui posit nostris hominibus & temporibus salutare, vt id statuatur & seruetur monent. Sed & typo quodam Christianæ modestiæ nos admonent, & mores emendant præceptis disciplinæ & temperantiæ. Quod intelligemus si primum de disciplina militari, deinceps de potestate patria quid dicat videamus.
units.tr: Those two laws, on military discipline and on paternal power, advise that whatever may be established according to the divine word as salutary for our people and times should be established and kept. But they also admonish us with a certain type of Christian modesty, and correct morals by the precepts of discipline and temperance. We shall understand this if we first see what he says about military discipline, and then what he says about paternal power.

units.la: Ad disciplinam militarem pertinet quod dicit: Quando egressus fueris in bellum, &c. Quibus verbis legem militarem de mulieribus captiuis affert: quae licet ad praeceptum de adulterio pertineat: tamen quia bellicae libidini fuit opposita, recte eam Moses huic de caede commentationi miscet. Ac summa est, ne quis captiua muliere ceu scorto abutatur, sed si placeat eam uxorem ducat.
units.tr: To military discipline belongs what he says: "When you go out to war," and so on. In these words he sets out the military law concerning captive women. Although this pertains to the precept on adultery, nevertheless, since it was opposed to warlike lust, Moses rightly mingles it with this discussion of killing. The sum is that no one should abuse a captive woman as a prostitute, but if he wishes, he should take her as his wife.

units.la: In quo si singula ponderes, & causas remedia mali cernes. 1. Si in bellum egressus fueris & Deus dederit hostes tuos, &c. Ostendit victoriam divinum munus esse. Hinc efferimur quod Deus favet nostris conatibus. Accidit hoc privatim & publice: dum premimur sumus humiles & modesti: sed onere per Deum levati convertimur ad ocium. Exempla sunt & in repub. & in ecclesia eaq; & vetera & recentia.
units.tr: If you weigh the individual points in this, you will see the causes of the evil and its remedies. (1) "If you go out to war and God gives your enemies into your hand," and so on: he shows that victory is a divine gift. Hence we are elated that God favours our undertakings. This happens both privately and publicly: while we are pressed, we are humble and modest, but when God has lifted the burden, we turn to ease. There are examples both in the commonwealth and in the Church, both ancient and recent.

units.la: 2 Videris & amaveris. Ocium est materia & occasio malorum. Unde Dauid impositis Ioabo duci bellicis oneribus & molestijs ipse ocio deditus incidit in adulterium. Solomoni illius filio idem accidit ad ocium conuerso. Et Paris dicitur ociosus illuc devenisse. Et idem de Ægisto dicit Ouidius ad hunc modum:
units.tr: (2) "You see and you love." Ease is the matter and occasion of evils. Whence David, when the military burdens and troubles were laid on Joab his commander, himself given over to idleness, fell into adultery. The same happened to Solomon, his son, when he turned to ease. And Paris is said to have come there in idleness. And Ovid says the same of Aegisthus in this manner:

units.la: Quæritur Ægistus quare sit factus adulter:In promptu causa est desidiosus erat.
units.tr: "Why did Aegisthus become an adulterer? The cause is ready to hand: he was idle."

units.la: Quae cum ita sint ocium vitare multum momenti poterit eam ad rem afferre.
units.tr: Since these things are so, avoiding idleness can contribute much to this matter.

units.la: Sed affert remedia. 1. Uxorem ducces[?]. Matth. 19. Christus idem & 1. Cor. 7. Paulus remedium hoc affert.
units.tr: But he also offers remedies. (1) "Take a wife." Christ in Matthew 19 and Paul in 1 Corinthians 7 offer this same remedy.

units.la: Dein ritum quendam praescribit quo subitus aestus Veneris restingui queat. Nam ritus iubet interponi moram, unius mensis videlicet interuallum, nec statim est obediendum affectibus. Unde ille volebat iratum literarum elementa prius numerare quam tentaret quicquam.
units.tr: Then he prescribes a certain rite by which a sudden heat of desire can be quenched. For the rite orders that a delay be interposed, namely an interval of one month, and that one should not yield to the passions at once. Whence that man wished, when angry, to count over the letters of the alphabet before he attempted anything.

units.la: 2 Vetus homo deponendus est: vult enim Moses purificari illam quae fuerat ethnica. Nos illum aegerrime deponimus, quippe qui ceu papistae essemus Bacchanalia celebramus. Moderata laetitia non improbatur, sed vides ut in licentiam degeneret. Volumus esse sponsa Christi, & tamen amictum & mores sponsae gentilis non deponimus, & retinemus illas ethnicas simul ac papisticas illecebras. Si papatum superasti, depone eius illecebras.
units.tr: (2) The old man must be put off, for Moses wishes her who had been a heathen to be purified. We put him off most reluctantly, we who, as if we were Papists, celebrate Bacchanalia. Moderate joy is not disapproved, but you see how it degenerates into licence. We want to be the bride of Christ, and yet we do not put off the dress and manners of a heathen bride; we retain those heathen allurements as well as the Papistical ones. If you have overcome Popery, put off its allurements.

units.la: Sed ex tota lege perspicuum est Deo displicere militarem licentiam & libidinem. At quid his temporibus aliud cernimus quam agmina scortorum, stupra, adulteria? Helvetii maiores nostri victo ad Sempachium oppidum Leopoldo, cauerunt ne qui milites libidini in feminas captivas obsequerentur.
units.tr: But it is plain from the whole law that military licence and lust displease God. But what do we see in these times other than troops of whores, rapes, and adulteries? Our forefathers the Swiss, after defeating Leopold at the town of Sempach, took care that no soldiers should indulge their lust on female captives.

units.la: Ex his potest intelligi lautam fortunam & ocium quasi quandam occasionem huius mali solere esse: matrimonium autem & moram eius ipsius etiam esse remedia.
units.tr: From these things it can be understood that a comfortable fortune and ease are wont to be, as it were, an occasion of this evil, but marriage and the delay of lust itself are remedies.

units.la: De potestate patriae: Si vero (inquit) alicui duae fuerint uxores, &c. Summam patriae potestati terminum ponit, occasione sumpta ex eo, quem de captiuis adduxerat exemplo. Nam si quis in bello coepisset foeminam formosam & amabilem: uxorem ducat, non ea tanquam scorto abutatur. Iam sit ut habeant uxores duas. Quod si suscipiat ex utraq; liberos: quaeritur utrius liberis cedat ius primogeniturae, dicat caro, eius quae est charior: at secus placet & videtur Domino, ei videlicet qui sit primus natus, cuiuscunque sit matris, odiosae videlicet an formosae.
units.tr: On paternal power: "But if," he says, "a man has two wives," and so on. He sets a limit to paternal power, the occasion being taken from the example of captives which he had just given. For if someone in war has taken a beautiful and lovable woman, let him marry her and not abuse her as a prostitute. Now it may come about that he has two wives. If he has children by both, the question is whose children have the right of the firstborn. The flesh would say: the child of the one who is dearer. But it pleases the Lord otherwise, namely that the one who is born first, whoever his mother is, whether hated or beloved, should have it.

units.la: Erat ius primogeniturae magnum bonum: etenim qui primogenitus esset, habebat duplā portionem, primatum, sacerdotium.
units.tr: The right of the firstborn was a great good, for the firstborn had a double portion, primacy, and the priesthood.

units.la: Iam hinc non colligendum ius polygamiae: Nobis enim illuxerunt correctionis tempora, & venit Christus legem perficiens & reformans universam. Unde & matrimonium reformavit ad primā regulam, erunt duo in carne una. Gen.3[?]. Matth.19. Id firmavit Apostolus 1. Cor. 7. dicens, Habeat quisq; suam uxorem.
units.tr: From this, a right to polygamy is not to be inferred. For the times of correction have dawned upon us, and Christ has come, fulfilling and reforming the whole law. Whence he also restored marriage to its first rule: "they shall be two in one flesh" (Gen. 3[?]; Matt. 19). The Apostle confirmed this in 1 Corinthians 7, saying, "Let each man have his own wife."

units.la: Tum etiam iura emendata matrimonium in integrum restituerunt. Gell. lib. 18. cap. 5. Binas habere uxores quidam infamiae nonnulli stupri poena plecti voluere. in l. neminem. C. de incestis nuptiis, & l. eum qui duas. C. de adult. Quod & moribus receptum & principum constitutionibus firmatum. Unus Valentinianus Imp. suae libidinis tuendae gratia mutavit, ac permisit cuiq; binas.
units.tr: Also, the laws as they were amended have restored marriage to its integrity. Gellius, book 18, chapter 5: some wished that a man with two wives be punished with the penalty of infamy, others with that of stuprum. See the law "neminem" in C. "De incestis nuptiis," and the law "eum qui duas" in C. "De adulteriis." This was both received by custom and confirmed by the constitutions of the emperors. Only the emperor Valentinian changed it for the protection of his own lust, and permitted each man to have two.

units.la: Patriarcharum exemplum non iuvat, cum non habeat coniunctam legem.
units.tr: The example of the patriarchs does not help, since it has no accompanying law.

units.la: Illud autem observandum est quod Moses patriae potestati fines ponat. Videmur in liberos, uxores, in bona habere quantum libet potestatis. Facit ac suadet hoc arrogantia. Veluti[?] cum dicunt aliqui, Quid huius refert, quomodo ego tractem meam in bonis, ego meas opes quolibet legabo,& prodigam.At prophana libido haec est. Dionysius Halicarnafs. referte Romulum dedisse patribus potestatem vitae necisq; liberorum. Numam post in eum qui Juxiffet vxorem potestatem hanc non permisse. Magnum est ius patribus debitum, sed hoc est nimium. Christianis aliter est sentiendum. Vxorem & liberos esse Dei munera, perindeq; his vt Dei beneficijs rite recteq; fruendum. Et bonorum omnium nos quaefto-res non dominos esse meminerimus. Iniqui sunt dispensatores qui rapiunt haeredibus,& dant alienis. Vtraque ex lege discimus domi forisq; Deo grati, modesti, iusti esse, Amen.
units.tr: It must also be observed that Moses sets limits to paternal power. We seem to have as much power as we like over children, wives, and goods. Arrogance makes and urges this; as when some say, "What does it matter to you how I handle my property? I will bequeath my wealth to whomever I please, and squander it." But this is profane lust. Dionysius of Halicarnassus reports that Romulus gave fathers power over the life and death of their children, but that afterwards Numa did not allow this power over a man who had taken a wife. The right owed to fathers is great, but this is excessive. Christians must think otherwise: wives and children are gifts of God, and so they must be enjoyed properly and rightly as the benefits of God. Let us remember that we are stewards, not masters, of all goods. Unjust are the stewards who snatch from the heirs and give to strangers. From both laws we learn to be pleasing to God, modest and just, at home and abroad. Amen.

units.la: SERMO LI.
units.tr: SERMON LI.

units.la: 18 Si quispiam filium habuerit defectorem & rebellem, qui vocem patris fui, & vocem matris suae audire noluerit, quumq; castigauerint eum, noluerit eis obtemperare.
units.tr: 18 If anyone have a son who is defiant and rebellious, who will not hear the voice of his father or the voice of his mother, and who, though they have chastened him, will not obey them.

units.la: 19 Apprehendent eum pater eius & mater eius, educentq; eum ad seniores ciuitatis illius, & ad portam eius loci.
units.tr: 19 Then his father and his mother shall take hold of him, and bring him out to the elders of that city, and to the gate of that place.

units.la: 20 Dicentq; ad seniores ciuitatis illius, Filius hic noster defector est & rebellis, nec vult audire vocem nostram, comeftator est & potator.
units.tr: 20 And they shall say to the elders of that city, This son of ours is defiant and rebellious; he will not hear our voice; he is a glutton and a drunkard.

units.la: 21 Lapidibusq; eum obruent omnes ciues illius ciuitatis, donec moriatur, & expurgabis[?] malum de medio tui, vt omnes Israelitae audientes timeant.
units.tr: 21 And all the citizens of that city shall stone him with stones until he dies, and you shall purge the evil from among you, so that all Israel, hearing of it, may fear.

units.la: 22 Quando fuerit in aliquo peccatum morte dignum, & interfectus fuerit, age[?] eum in crucem.
units.tr: 22 When there is in someone a sin worthy of death, and he has been put to death, and you hang him on a cross.

units.la: 23 Cadauer vero eius non pernox erit in ligno, sed mox sepelies illud, illo eodem die, quoniam maledictio Dei est suspensus, & non pollues terram tuam, quam Dominus Deus tuus dat tibi in hereditatem.
units.tr: 23 But his body shall not remain upon the wood overnight; you shall bury it at once, on that same day, because whoever is hanged is cursed of God, and you shall not defile your land, which the Lord your God gives you for an inheritance.

units.la: AD vera germanamq; legis Nō occides, mente & sententia multum conducit scire magistratui publicae pacis & salutis coseruandae tuendaeq; gratia gladiu in eos, qui hanc turbant, stringendum datum esse: ea lege vt is suos aduersus omnem hominum exterorum vim & iniuriam tueretur: priuatos autem homines qui scelerati sint dignis poenis afficeret. Iniurios enim & seditiosos & nefarios homines, si quis lege non occides velit defendere, is non modo rerum omnium publicarum atq; etiam pacis euersionem, verumetiam omnium malorum atque scelerum prouentum efficeret. Quamobrem vti Moses de caede & bello deque rebus in his euenientibus disseruit, ita iam de poenis in personas priuatas decernendis dicit. In quo primum de poenis, tum de fontium cadaueribus humanis indicat.
units.tr: To grasp the true and genuine sense of the law "You shall not kill," it is very helpful to know that the sword was given to the magistrate, to be drawn against those who disturb the public peace, for the sake of preserving and protecting public peace and safety. The law was given so that the magistrate would defend his subjects against every violence and injury from outsiders, and would punish with fitting penalties private persons who are wicked. For if anyone wished to use the law "You shall not kill" to defend injurious, seditious and criminal men, he would bring about not only the overthrow of all public affairs and of peace, but also the outbreak of every kind of evil and crime. Therefore, just as Moses spoke about slaughter and war and the matters that arise from them, so now he speaks about the penalties to be decreed against private persons. In this he first indicates the penalties, and then the burial of human corpses.

units.la: Ac primum quoniam eorum quae rempub. turbant scelerum omnium catalogus afferri non potest, vnum quod reliquorum omnium quasi caput est commemorat, atq; etiam qualem fit ac fiat: qualis in ipsum actio: quod ei fit irrogandum supplicium, ordine persequitur.
units.tr: First, since a complete catalogue of the crimes that disturb the commonwealth cannot be given, he mentions one crime which is, as it were, the head of all the rest, and he goes on in order to describe what kind of crime it is, what sort of action it involves, and what punishment should be inflicted on it.

units.la: Quale fit ac fiat sic docet: Si quispiam filium habuerit defectorem & rebellem, qui vocem patris fui & vocem matris suae audire noluerit, cumq; castigauerint eum, noluerit eis obtemperare. Quibus verbis initia simul ac progressus pingit. Primum enim enim סורר[?] eum qui declinauit & alienore est factus à parentibus animo, & ab illis fidissimis atq; amantissimis parentum monitis alias ad res animum adiecit. Eius generis sunt qui sufq; deq; ferunt quaecunq; patres monent: audiunt quidem illa, & tacent, sed ijs minime permouentur. [illegible, ~8 letters] anderen wider vß gaan. Atq; hęc sunt inobedientiae principia.
units.tr: He teaches what sort of crime it is and how it comes about in these words: "If anyone have a son who is defiant and rebellious, who will not hear the voice of his father or the voice of his mother, and when they have chastened him, will not obey them." In these words he portrays both the beginnings and the progress of the evil. For first he describes the one who is סורר [sorer], that is, one who has turned aside and become estranged from his parents in mind, and who has set his mind on other things, away from the most faithful and loving admonitions of his parents. Of this kind are those who make light of whatever their fathers advise: they do hear these things and say nothing, but they are in no way moved by them. [illegible] ... they go against one another. And these are the beginnings of disobedience.

units.la: Tum מורה[?] rebellis, qui dicta parentum amare excipit, atq; in sinistram partem capit. En progressus, qui fiunt ab animis ad verba. Quo pertinēt subsannationes, oblocutiones, responsiones, quibus filij rebelles dicta parentum excipiunt.
units.tr: Then he describes the one who is מורה [morer], rebellious, who receives his parents' words with bitterness and takes them in the wrong sense. Here is the progress from attitudes of mind to words. To this belong the mockings, the back-talk and the retorts by which rebellious sons receive their parents' words.

units.la: Postremo, Qui nolit obtemperare castigantibus: in quo sceleris perfectio cernitur. Nam qui posthabitis parentum iussibus, sequitur suam libidinem, is vere est rebellis.
units.tr: Finally, "who will not obey those who chastise him," in which the completion of the crime is seen. For the one who, setting aside his parents' commands, follows his own lust, is truly rebellious.

units.la: Atq; hęc quidem non tam liberis scribuntur, quàm parentibus, nempe vt illi visis his initijs è vestigio cogitent principijs obstandum esse. Id fiet si degeneris animi signa ac verba viderint,verbis ac gestibus quàm primum obuiam eant: <bl>[illegible, ~20 letters]</bl>
units.tr: These things are written not so much for the children as for the parents, namely so that, when they see these beginnings, they may at once consider that the principles must be resisted. This will happen if, when they see the signs and words of a degenerate mind, they meet them as quickly as possible with words and gestures.

units.la: Sed est pessima nunc liberorum educatio: ad fastum vestitu, ad luxum epulis, ad proca-ciam & petulantiam irritatione & applausibus, ad omne scelerum genus indulgentia ducun-tur: ac si quis moneat vicinus offendimur. Inde sequitur, vt neq; parentibus domi, neq; ma-gistris in schola, neq; magistratibus in ciuitate pareant. Vnde & iuuenum & senum enormis est rebellio: quæ etiam fit intolerabilis.
units.tr: But the upbringing of children is now very bad: they are led on by dress to pride, by feasting to luxury, by irritation and applause to forwardness and wantonness, and by indulgence to every kind of crime; and if a neighbour advises otherwise, we take offence. From this it follows that they obey neither their parents at home, nor their teachers at school, nor the magistrates in the city. Hence the rebellion of young and old alike is monstrous, and it is becoming intolerable.

units.la: Quid tandem fiet? quod nolis quidem, sed quod oporteat tamen: Apprehendent (inquit) eum pater & mater eius educentq; eum ad seniores ciuitatis illius, & adportam eius loci dicentq; & c. Filius hic noster defector est, & c. Quibus verbis ostendit actionem in rebelles liberos patribus competere: hi,inquit,adducent: hi illos accusabunt, quasiq; eorum necis authores e-runt,prodita scilicet eorum nequitia. Graue est hoc: quis enim suo sanguine satos traderet? Cur hoc legislator iniungit hominibus? Desines mirari si quid nostris hominibus accidat recolas. Non lex est,quæ parentes cogat hoc facere,&c tamen fit vt vel parentes vel agnati ma-gistratuum opem implorent in eo genere.
units.tr: What, then, will happen? What you may not wish, but what nevertheless must be done: "His father and mother shall take hold of him" (it says) "and bring him out to the elders of that city, and to the gate of that place, and shall say, This son of ours is defiant, and so on." By these words he shows that the action against rebellious children belongs to the parents: they, he says, shall bring him; they shall accuse him; and they will be as the authors of his death, since the wickedness of their son has obviously been made known. This is a grievous thing; for who would hand over those born of his own blood? Why does the lawgiver impose this on men? Cease to wonder if something of the kind happens among our people, if you consider it. It is not the law that compels parents to do this, yet it happens that either parents or kinsmen implore the help of the magistrates in such a case.

units.la: Dirum profecto remedium est, ac veluti membro corpus ægrum mutiles: sed tamen ne necessarium[?], si mitiora non proficiant: & tamen parentibus magis incumbit, quàm ipsis qui pu-niuntur liberis. Illi enim vel desperati sunt, &negligunt vitam pariter ac famam: aut si curent maximè, tamen morte solicitudinem eam finiunt. Igitur incumbit parentibus.
units.tr: It is indeed a dreadful remedy, and like cutting off a limb to save a sick body; but it is nonetheless not to be used unless milder measures fail. And the burden falls more on the parents than on the children who are punished. For the children are either past hope and neglect both life and reputation, or, if they care most of all, they still end that anxiety by death. Therefore the burden falls on the parents.

units.la: Qui id ita? ut discant educatione tam horrendum euentum præuenire & auertere: do-ceant & corripiant. Doctrina sint pietas & religio: artes, quarum studio suos ciues volebant esse deditos, qui Massiliæ quondam rerum summa potiebantur, quasq; coluisse Bianti, Dionysio al.ijsq; profuit. Correptio sit paterna & emendationis efficiens. Præstet illos quàm te emittere lachrymas. Matri Æsopicæ quid acciderit, omnium est & notare & cauere. In idem studium incumbendum est etiam magistratui: Nam malè educatæ plebis præmia quæ qua-liaq;,sint nostra nobis exempla satis indicant.
units.tr: Why so? So that they may learn to forestall and avert so dreadful an outcome by their upbringing: let them teach and correct. Let doctrine be piety and religion; let the arts be taught, to the study of which the citizens of Massilia, who once held the chief power in public affairs, were devoted, and by which Bias, Dionysius and others profited. Let correction be paternal and effective in amendment. It is better to correct them than to shed tears over them. What befell Aesop's mother is known and noted by all, and must be guarded against. The magistrate, too, must apply himself to the same aim; for the rewards of badly brought-up common people, and what kind they are, our own examples sufficiently show.

units.la: Supplicium dicit, Lapidibus eum obruent ciues eius ciuitatis dum moriatur, & expurgabis malum de medio tui, vt omnes Israelitæ audientes timeant. Dirum dicit supplicium, sed si rectè rem reputes, dignum patrato scelere. Primum enim pugnat cum salute familiæ, quæ nequit conseruari, sed statim soluitur: estq; nostra memoria princeps paupertatis causa quod liberi non sunt assuefacti à teneris, vti parentes honorent, sese mutuum diligant: vnde existunt dissidia & diuisiones bonorum, & lites &c.
units.tr: He names the punishment: "The citizens of that city shall stone him with stones until he dies, and you shall purge the evil from among you, so that all Israel, hearing of it, may fear." He calls it a dreadful punishment, but if you weigh the matter rightly, it is fitting for the crime committed. For first, it runs against the safety of the family, which cannot be preserved but is at once dissolved; and in our own memory the chief cause of poverty has been that children were not accustomed from their tender years to honour their parents and to love one another; hence arise quarrels and divisions of goods, lawsuits, and so on.

units.la: Dein pugnat cum vtilitate publica : Nam qui puer assueuerit patris iussa ttque moni-ta contemnere, quantò magis audebit edicta magistratuum despicere? Sunt etiam hoc i-pso ciues inutiles quod nihil bonorum habent, sed egerent potius hospitali proprio suo.
units.tr: Next, it runs against the public good. For if a boy has been accustomed to despise his father's commands and admonitions, how much more will he dare to despise the edicts of magistrates? Such citizens are also useless by this very fact, that they have no goods, but would rather live at the expense of others.

units.la: Tertio, quia sunt ingrati: ac cum omnia grate reddant sibi præbita, vt agri[?] sua femina, coniæ[?] præmium educationis : hi parentibus non reddunt gratiam quam debebant ma-ximam.
units.tr: Third, because they are ungrateful; for while everything is returned gratefully to those who provide for it, as a field returns its produce, and a vine its reward for cultivation, these children do not return to their parents the greatest gratitude they owe.

units.la: Quarto cum Deo, qui id in primis mandat & neglectum punit, prorsus pugnat: veluti pa-rentum neglectorum pœnas dedere Chamus, Absolon, & alij.
units.tr: Fourth, it is altogether opposed to God, who especially commands this and punishes its neglect: thus Ham and Absalom, and others, paid the penalty for neglecting their parents.

units.la: Ex quo perspicuum est cur tam diro supplicio Deus hoc scelus vlcisci voluerit.
units.tr: From this it is clear why God wished to avenge this crime with so dreadful a punishment.

units.la: Sed & exacerbanda supplicia sunt, quoties nimium multis personis grassantibus opus est l.aut facta.§.vltimo.ff.de pœnis. Quod Senatus Tigurinus considerauit in vlcisncenda viola-tione pacis factæ inter pugnantes priuatas personas. Ita lex in homicidas lata non prohibet quo minus hos occidat magistratus.
units.tr: But punishments must also be made severer whenever there are too many persons rampaging, as the law "Facta" in the last paragraph of the Digest "De poenis" teaches. The Senate of Zurich considered this in avenging the violation of peace made between fighting private persons. Thus the law passed against homicides does not prevent the magistrate from killing them.

units.la: Iam extirpato malo & exemplo omnibus facto magistratus contentus esto. Nam cum omnis supplicij finis sit emendatio: comparata hac nihil amplius erat perquirendum. Sæui-unt quidam in viuos ita diris supplicijs, vt simul cum corporibus etiam animas videantur enecare velle: tum etiam in ipsa mortuorum cadauera, perinde ac si his gaudeant aspectibus ita suam crudelitatem exercent. Vetat hoc Moses.
units.tr: Now, once the evil has been rooted out and an example made for all, let the magistrate be content. For since the aim of all punishment is amendment, and this has been achieved, nothing more was to be sought. Some rage against the living with such dreadful punishments that they seem to wish to destroy their souls along with their bodies; and they even turn their cruelty against the corpses of the dead, as if they took pleasure in the sight. Moses forbids this.

units.la: Obseruandum est autem quod Christus pro nobis factus est maledictum, eoq; ipso vt nos benedicereimus[?] effecit. In posteriore ad Corinthios sexto, & ad Galathas tertio cap.di-cit Apostolus: Christus nos redemit ab execratione legis, dum pro nobis factus est e-xecratio. Scriptum est enim: Execrabilis omnis qui pendet in ligno, vt in gentes benedictio Abrahæ peruenirct[?] per Christum Ie-sum. Cui sit honos in secula, Amen.
units.tr: It is to be observed that Christ was made a curse for us, and by that very fact he brought it about that we might be blessed. In the later letter to the Corinthians, chapter six, and in Galatians chapter three, the Apostle says: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us. For it is written: Accursed is everyone who hangs on a tree, so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles through Jesus Christ. To whom be honour for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT XXII. SERMO LII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXII. SERMON LII.

units.la: Si videris bouem aut pecudem fratris tui fugatos; ne dissimules occultando te ab eis, sed plane reduces eos ad fratrem tuum.
units.tr: If you see your brother's ox or sheep straying, do not ignore it by hiding yourself from them, but by all means bring them back to your brother.

units.la: 2 Quod si frater tuus non est prope apud te, nec nosti eum, adsume illos in domum tuam, vt sint tecum donec quæsierit eos frater tuus, restituasq; eos illi.
units.tr: 2 But if your brother is not near you, or you do not know him, take them into your house, and they shall stay with you until your brother seeks them, and then you shall restore them to him.

units.la: 3 Sic quoq; facies asino eius, & sic ages cum vestimento eius: sic quoq; facies cum omni eo quod amisit frater tuus, quod perdidit, & tu inuenisti illud: neq; enim id dissimulare aut celare poteris.
units.tr: 3 So also shall you do with his donkey, and so shall you do with his garment; so also shall you do with everything that your brother has lost, and you have found: for you cannot overlook it or conceal it.

units.la: 4 Si videris asinum fratris tui aut bouem eius cadentes in itinere, ne dissimules abscondendo te ab eis, quin subleuando subleues eos.
units.tr: 4 If you see your brother's donkey or ox fallen on the road, do not ignore them by hiding yourself from them, but by all means help them up.

units.la: 5 Mulier ne gerat arma virilia, nec vir induatur vestimento muliebri, quoniam abominandus est Domino Deo tuo quisquis illa fecerit.
units.tr: 5 A woman shall not wear men's weapons, nor shall a man put on a woman's garment, for whoever does these things is abominable to the Lord your God.

units.la: 6 Quando occurrerit conspectui tuo in itinere nidus avium in quacunq; arbore aut in terra, in quo sunt pulli aut ova, matre incubante aut pullis ipsis, aut ouis, non tollas matrem cum pullis.
units.tr: 6 When you come upon a bird's nest on the road, in any tree or on the ground, with young birds or eggs in it, and the mother sitting on the young or the eggs, do not take the mother together with the young.

units.la: 7 Sed omnino dimittas matrem, pullos verò capies tibi, vt scilicet bene tibi sit & proroges dies.
units.tr: 7 But by all means let the mother go, and take the young for yourself, so that it may go well with you and you may prolong your days.

units.la: 8 Quum extruis domum nouam, facias loricam tecto tuo, ne ponas sanguinem in domum tuam, quum quispiam caderet ex ea.
units.tr: 8 When you build a new house, make a parapet for your roof, so that you do not bring blood upon your house if anyone should fall from it.

units.la: 9 Ne conseras vineam tuam diuersis generibus, ne forte sanctifices vniuersum semen quod conseris, atq; vinea prouentum.
units.tr: 9 Do not sow your vineyard with mixed kinds of seed, lest the whole crop you sow, and the yield of the vineyard, be made holy.

units.la: 10 Non arabis eum bouè & asino simul.
units.tr: 10 You shall not plough with an ox and an ass together.

units.la: 11 Ne induas vestem quæ ex lana & lino simul contexta est.
units.tr: 11 Do not wear a garment woven of wool and linen together.

units.la: 12 Fimbrias crassiores facito tibi in quatuor alis vestimenti tui quo te operiris.
units.tr: 12 Make thick tassels on the four corners of the garment with which you cover yourself.

units.la: C[?]UM ex decem præceptis priora sex eam impletatem atq; improbitatem tollant, quæ præcipitem hominum ruinam minitantur ac doceant, ne diuini cultus contemptu simul cum corporibus animas eamus perditum: ne rebellione & inobedie-tia salubrem hominum societatem turbemus: ne violenter fundamus sanguinem innoxium: sanè Moses ea præcepta sigillatim singula explicauit, atq; etiam omnes eò spectantes quæstio-nes euoluit: veluti iam inde à quinto capite hucusq; satis superq; est cognitum.
units.tr: Since the first six of the Ten Commandments remove that impiety and wickedness which threaten men with headlong ruin, and teach that by despising divine worship we must not destroy souls together with bodies, nor disturb the wholesome fellowship of men by rebellion and disobedience, nor shed innocent blood violently: Moses indeed explained each of those precepts separately, and unfolded all the questions bearing on them, as has been known well enough, and more than enough, from the fifth chapter up to this point.

units.la: Iam quoniam quatuor reliqua ad perfectionem ciuilis probitatis & iustitiæ, seu vt sacræ literæ dictitant, Christianæ charitatis præcipue pertinent, atq; etiam omnes cuiuscunq; ordinis & fortunæ homines docent quo pacto proximo suo non solum non obesse verumetiam prodesse debeant: rectè Moses earum expositionem in sequentibus capitibus simul omnem affert, ac summos pariter atq; imos docet, quomodo iustitiæ studeant in suo quisq; genere. Iustitia enim quæ constans est & perpetua voluntas, suum cuiq; tribuendi non modo versa-tur in commutatione & communicatione rerum, sed etiam in distributione pœnarum & præmiorum.
