Quò fit, vt ad iustam rerum communicationem seruentur matrimonia, distincta rerum dominia, iura personarum & legitimæ commutationum formæ, nec cuiquam fit liberum alterius vxoris, bonorum, seruorum vsum sibi rapere: in distributione præmiorum & pœnarum, vt ne qui indigni ciuitate & honoribus potiantur, exclusis dignioribus. De quibus suo loco dicetur pluribus. Sufficit enim argumenti vice hæc dixisse.
units.tr: Now, since the remaining four pertain chiefly to the perfection of civil uprightness and justice, or, as the Holy Scriptures call it, Christian charity, and teach men of every rank and fortune how they ought not merely to avoid harming their neighbour but actually to benefit him, Moses rightly sets out all their exposition together in the following chapters, and teaches high and low alike how each, in his own sphere, should strive for justice. For justice, which is a constant and perpetual will to give each his due, is concerned not only with the exchange and sharing of goods, but also with the distribution of punishments and rewards. Hence, for the just sharing of goods, marriages are preserved, distinct property rights are kept, the rights of persons and lawful forms of exchange are maintained, and no one is free to seize for himself the use of another's wife, goods or servants. In the distribution of rewards and punishments, no one unworthy is to hold citizenship and honours while the more worthy are excluded. These matters will be discussed at more length in their place; for it is enough to have said this much by way of introduction.

units.la: Cæterum hoc capite peculiares quasdam leges affert, quæ pertinere videntur ad qua-tuor illarum expositionem, nempe ad legem furti, concupiscentiæ, falsi testimonij, inprimis-que adulterij. Sunt autem earum nouem. De prioribus octo in præsentia:
units.tr: Moreover, in this chapter he sets out certain particular laws which seem to pertain to the exposition of those four commandments, namely the laws against theft, covetousness, false witness, and especially adultery. There are nine of them. Of the first eight, for the present:

units.la: Prima, Si bouem, &c. Quibus verbis ostendit iumenta aut quaecunq; bona, quae quidem proximus noster amiserit, nos autem reperiremus, esse restituenda. Quae lex ad legem furti pertinet explicandam, nempe ut intelligas furtum non tunc solum committi, cum quis alienam rem inuito & nesciente Domino sibi tulerit: sed etiam cum quid retines, quod scis tuum ipsius non esse.
units.tr: First, If you see an ox, etc. By these words he shows that the beasts of burden, or whatever goods our neighbour has lost and we happen to find, must be restored. This law pertains to the explanation of the law against theft, namely that you understand theft is committed not only when someone takes another's property for himself against the owner's will and without his knowledge, but also when you keep something that you know is not your own.

units.la: Ac quoniam inuentio annumeratur iis, qui rerum acquirendarum sunt jure gentium in trodu&ti[?] modis, non temere; seu cupidè retinenda sunt quae repereris. Ac pro dominio locorum, in quibus inuentae res sunt, aliud atq; aliud ius inuentori competit.
units.tr: And since finding is counted among those modes of acquiring things that are introduced by the law of nations, what you have found is not to be kept rashly or greedily. And, according to the ownership of the places where the things were found, a different right belongs to the finder.

units.la: Quid vitium bonum deceat Moses docet. Veluti si pecus alienum forte repereris, si cuius sit noris, redde: si nescias, dum cuius sit explores, retineto: non autem retineas quod scias tuum non esse. Ita lege furti non solum furto prohibemur, sed etiam sua cuiusq; reddere jubemur: ne quis aliquid inueniat prius quàm possessor amiserit.
units.tr: Moses teaches what a good man ought to do. For example, if you happen to find another's flock, and you know whose it is, return it; if you do not know, keep it while you search out whose it is; but do not keep what you know is not yours. Thus by the law against theft we are not only forbidden to steal, but are also commanded to return to each what is his, so that no one should find something before its possessor has lost it.

units.la: Secunda, Mulier ne gerat arma virilia, nec vir induatur veste muliebri. Quibus verbis prauae[?] concupiscentiae, ne damnum det, repagulum ponit. Etenim quae sunt in precio, quaeq; i-psi suspicimus, ea fere solemus impotenter appetere: jam quia nostra nobis sunt taedio, allu-bescunt aliena, accidit quod Poeta dicit,
units.tr: Second, A woman shall not wear men's weapons, nor shall a man put on a woman's garment. By these words he sets a barrier against depraved covetousness, lest it do harm. For we are usually inclined to desire immoderately the things that are prized and that we ourselves admire; and since our own things grow tedious to us, others' things tempt us, and what the poet says comes to pass:

units.la: Optat ephippia bos piger, optat arare caballus.
units.tr: The lazy ox desires the saddle, the horse desires to plough.

units.la: Cui malo sic est eundum obuiam, ut Martialis censuit dicens, Quod sis esse velis nihilq; malis. Qui diuini verbi ministrum agit, ne magistratum ambiat: qui priuatus homo est, ne se publicis ingerat negotiis: eodemq; modo in reliquis rebus omnibus. Ciuilis est harmonia, quàm turbant qui deserta statione sua in alios inuolant.
units.tr: This evil must be met as Martial advised, saying, "Be what you are, and wish for nothing else." He who serves the ministry of the divine word should not aspire to the magistracy; he who is a private man should not thrust himself into public affairs; and likewise in all other matters. Civil harmony is disturbed by those who, abandoning their own post, rush off into the posts of others.

units.la: Id Moses producto ex re familiari exemplo docet. Deus initio fecit marem & foeminam. Ac quemadmodum jure gentium sunt distincta rerum dominia: sic certa sunt & firma sexuum discrimina. De sexus utriusq; officio Solomon dicit, ac primum de mulieris officio, quaesiuit lanam, & digiti eius apprehenderunt fusum: tum viri sic describit munia: nobilis in portis eius vir quando sederit cum senatoribus terrae. Jam ne qua fiat harmoniae ciuilis perturbatio, dicit legislator, ut sua quisq; coniunx obeat officia.
units.tr: Moses teaches this by an example taken from the household. God made male and female at the beginning. And just as the ownership of things is distinct by the law of nations, so the distinctions of the sexes are certain and firm. Solomon speaks of the duty of each sex, and first describes the duty of the woman: she seeks wool, and her fingers take hold of the spindle; then he describes the duties of the man: a noble man when he sits in her gates with the senators of the land. Now, lest any disturbance of civil harmony arise, the lawgiver says that each spouse should perform their own duties.

units.la: Damnat morem Ægyptium, quo fiebat ut mulieres negotiarentur, viri familiarem rem administrarent: damnat Amazones quę spreta atq; abiecta muliebri verecundia ceu viri es-sent bella gerebant: damnat Marinam Ungariae dominam, quae posthabito reginae appellatione ne perinde ac si masculus esset regis sibi nomen usurpauit. Quo referes eas, quae in regno Neapolitano magnas res gesserunt Joannas duas: item puellam Francicam Anglos quae bello superauit, & foeminas in Bohemia rerum summa potitas, nec non Suecam quandam Heroinam.
units.tr: He condemns the Egyptian custom by which women carried on business while men managed the household property. He condemns the Amazons, who, having scorned and cast off feminine modesty, waged war as if they were men. He condemns Marina, lady of Hungary, who, disdaining the title of queen, usurped for herself the name of king, as if she were a man. To these may be added the two Joannas who accomplished great deeds in the kingdom of Naples, likewise the French maiden who defeated the English in war, the women in Bohemia who gained control of affairs of state, and also a certain Swedish heroine.

units.la: Contra damnatur in viris haec mollities, qua sibi quod natura dedit auferri[?] sinunt.
units.tr: On the other hand, this effeminacy is condemned in men, by which they allow what nature gave them to be taken away.

units.la: In utroq; sexu requirit rationem & naturae & mysterii. Homo qui naturae leges transit monstri similem sese facit, quae etiam ipsa extra naturam exorbitant.
units.tr: In each sex he requires regard both to nature and to mystery. A man who transgresses the laws of nature makes himself like a monster, which themselves also go beyond nature.

units.la: Mysterium autem grande est Christi & ecclesiae, nempe ut ne Christum submittas ecclesiae. Peccauit in utrumq; papa'ille qui peperit: peccant in sacrosanctum hoc mysterium An-tichristi illi omnes, qui constitutionibus ecclesiasticis omnia Christi dicta subiciunt.
units.tr: The mystery, however, is great, namely that of Christ and the Church, so that you do not subject Christ to the Church. That pope who gave birth sinned in both respects; and all those Antichrists sin against this sacred mystery who subject all the sayings of Christ to ecclesiastical constitutions.

units.la: Sed quid Moses? Abominabilis est apud Deum, hoc est Deus abhorret ab his monstris.
units.tr: But what does Moses say? It is abominable before God, that is, God abhors these monstrosities.

units.la: Tertia, Si ambulaueris per viam, &c. Hęc etiā cōcupiscentię coercendę causa est lata. Sę-pe enim in res aliquas nobis aliquid licet, sed nō quicquid libet, seruanda semper est moderatio. Ut si quos habeas subditos homines, seruos, amicos & alios: illorum uteris, non abuteris opera.
units.tr: Third, If you walk along the way, etc. This too is given to restrain covetousness. For often we are permitted some things, but not whatever we like; moderation must always be observed. For example, if you have subjects, servants, friends and others, you should make use of their labour, not abuse it.

units.la: Id docet exemplo brutorum eorumq; vilium animantium. Auium nidum reperiens pullos licet accipias, sed non simul etiam matrem, in qua spes est prolis alterius.
units.tr: This is taught by the example of brute beasts and of worthless animals. If you find a bird's nest, you may take the young, but not also the mother, in whom lies the hope of another brood.

units.la: Quae humanitas multò magis est exhibenda hominibus. Nam exhaustis tuorum viribus quid facies? Anus Æsopica gallina, quae ova aurea pariebat, trucidata nihil habebat rei simul ac spei reliquum: <bl>Willige rögli sol man nit üben[?] triben.</bl>
units.tr: This kindness must be shown much more to people. For when your own strength is used up, what will you do? The old woman's hen in Aesop, which laid golden eggs, was killed, and so had nothing left, neither profit nor hope: <bl>Willing hens should not be driven badly.</bl>

units.la: Quarta, Cum aedificaueris domum, &c. Et haec nostram concupiscentiam coerceat. Solemus aedificare quod nobis sit voluptati, sed quod sit interdum aliis detrimento. Id ne fiat legislator hic cauet. Habebant ut in Misnia & inferiore Germania domos magnificas, in quibus tecta essent plana, non decliuia[?], ut nostra: quod colligi potest ex Rahabae meretricis historia. In his fiebant ludi & conuiuia.
units.tr: Fourth, When you build a house, etc. This too restrains our desire. We are accustomed to build what gives us pleasure, but what may sometimes be harmful to others. The lawgiver guards against this. In Meissen and lower Germany they had fine houses whose roofs were flat, not sloping as ours are, as can be gathered from the story of Rahab the harlot. In these they held games and feasts.

units.la: Jam ne quis inde decideret muro seu lorica cingi tecta jubet: neq; enim ob prospectum quæsitum & optatum vult aliquem delabi.
units.tr: Lest anyone fall from them, he orders the roofs to be surrounded with a parapet or railing, for he does not want anyone to fall down for the sake of the view that is sought and desired.

units.la: Ergo summè est enitendum ut ne quis ædificando damnum det alteri. Unde & iura ciuilia vetant, ne cui sua vel temeritas vel auiditas lucro fit, ac ponunt regulam. Ea quæ sunt vel bona vel mala fide alieno solo affixa, cedunt solo. l. adeo. §. cum in suo. ff. de acquir. rer. dom. Eodem pertinet quod est expressum iure ciuili de speciali-bus in factum actionibus rei fami-liaris causa proditis. Et ne quis suis rebus consuleret cum detrimento alterius extant in iure ciuili multi super hac re tituli. Ut in Digestis, Si quadrupes pauperiem fecisse dicatur: De damno infecto & suggrundis vel protectionibus. Quo in titulo Paulus Iureconsultus dicit, Trebatio videri illum etiam damnum accipere, cuius ædium luminibus officiatur. Et de aqua & aquæ pluuiæ arcendæ, & alij similes tituli.
units.tr: Therefore every effort must be made that no one, in building, causes loss to another. Hence the civil laws also forbid that anyone should profit from his own rashness or greed to another's loss, and they lay down the rule: things that are attached to another's ground, whether in good or bad faith, belong to the ground. l. adeo. §. cum in suo. ff. de acquir. rer. dom. To the same point belongs what the civil law expressly provides, the special actions brought in the case of property (the actions in factum given for the protection of one's household goods). And so that no one should provide for his own affairs at another's expense, there are many titles on this matter in the civil law: in the Digest, If a four-footed animal is said to have caused harm; On damage not yet done; and On projections or overhanging eaves and penthouses. In that title Paulus the jurist says that Trebatius thought that he also suffers loss whose buildings are deprived of light. And there are other similar titles, On water and on keeping off rainwater.

units.la: Quinta, Ne feras vineam, &c. Hæc lege damnum quod dari poterat nimio suam rem familiarem augendi studio vetat. Exemplo, Ex vineto des decimam: tum feras simul femina alia de quibus non des: fit fraus Leuitis fratribus tuis. Non simul ministrum & mercatorem esse: non, &c.
units.tr: Fifth, Thou shalt not sow thy vineyard, etc. This law forbids the harm that could be done through an excessive zeal for increasing one's own property. For example: you give the tithe from the vineyard; then if you also bring in another kind of seed of which you give nothing, a fraud is made against your brothers the Levites. It is not right to be at once minister and merchant; not, etc.

units.la: Sexta, Non arabis simul cum boue & asino. Æqualitas Deo placet. Bos aratione creatus, asinus oneri ferendo, suum cuique tribuendum. Non petendum à paupere quod diues: non à rudi quod doctus ægre præstent, est proportio Geometrica.
units.tr: Sixth, Thou shalt not plough with an ox and an ass together. Equality pleases God: the ox created for ploughing, the ass for bearing burdens, each is to be given its due. What the rich man has is not to be demanded of the poor, nor what the learned can scarcely supply of the unlearned: this is geometrical proportion.

units.la: Septima, ne induas vestem, &c. Nihil est ad hominum usum ineptius homine versipelle & lubrico. Igitur candor requiritur, ut sit sermo noster est, est, non, non. Depingit hoc veste. Ea mores repræsentat. Jam ne fit mollis & dura, &c. requirit simplicem. Prudens simplicitas, pares amici, dixit bene Martialis. ἁπλούστατα.
units.tr: Seventh, Thou shalt not put on a garment, etc. Nothing is more unfit for human use than a man who is two-faced and slippery. Therefore sincerity is required, so that our speech may be yea, yea, nay, nay. The garment depicts this; it represents the character. Again, so that it should not be soft and hard, etc., it requires simplicity. Prudent simplicity, equal friends, as Martial rightly said: most simple [ἁπλούστατα].

units.la: Octaua, funiculos in fimbriis. Vestem astrictam & professione religionis insignem dicit: ne erumpas in omnem libidinem, sed recordatione legis te cohibeas. Pulcherrimæ sunt, & symbolis pythagoricis præstantiores leges, quibus adducimur ad Jesum Christum Dei filium, cui sit honos in seculá. Amen.
units.tr: Eighth, cords on the fringes. He speaks of a garment bound up and marked as a sign of the profession of religion: so that you may not break out into every lust, but restrain yourself by remembering the law. The laws are most beautiful, and better than the Pythagorean symbols, by which we are led to Jesus Christ, the Son of God, to whom be honour for ever. Amen.

units.la: SERMO LIII.
units.tr: SERMON LIII.

units.la: 13 Si quispiam uxorem duxerit, accesserit ad eam, & odisse eam cæperit:
units.tr: 13 If any man take a wife, and go in unto her, and hate her,

units.la: 14 Obtruserit ei technas verborum, divulgans de ea famam, ut si dicat, Du-xi hanc mulierem, & quum essem ad eam ingressus, nō inueni in ea signa virginitatis.
units.tr: 14 And give occasions of speech against her, and bring up an evil name upon her, and say, I took this woman, and when I came to her I found not in her the tokens of virginity:

units.la: 15 Tollent pater puellæ, & mater eius, & proferent signa virginitatis puellæ ad seniores ciuitatis, qui sunt in porta.
units.tr: 15 Then shall the father of the damsel, and her mother, take and bring forth the tokens of the damsel's virginity unto the elders of the city in the gate:

units.la: 16 Dicetq; pater puellæ ad seniores: Hanc filiam meam dederam viro uxorem, cepitq; eam odisse.
units.tr: 16 And the damsel's father shall say unto the elders, I gave my daughter unto this man to wife, and he hateth her;

units.la: 17 Et en obtrudit ei commenta verborum, & dicit: Non inueni in filia tua virginitatem: hæc vero sunt signa virginitatis filiæ meæ, & expandent vestimentum coram senioribus ciuitatis.
units.tr: 17 And, lo, he hath given occasions of speech against her, saying, I found not in thy daughter the tokens of virginity; and yet these are the tokens of my daughter's virginity. And they shall spread the cloth before the elders of the city.

units.la: 18 Tollentq; seniores ciuitatis illius virum illum, & castigabunt eum.
units.tr: 18 And the elders of that city shall take that man and chastise him;

units.la: 19 Damnabuntq; eum centum (siclis) argenti, quos dabunt patri puellæ, eò quod sparsit famam malam de virgine Israelitica, habebitq; ea in uxorem, nec poterit ea dimittere cunctis diebus suis.
units.tr: 19 And they shall amerce him in a hundred shekels of silver, and give them unto the damsel's father, because he hath brought up an evil name upon a virgin of Israel: and she shall be his wife; he may not put her away all his days.

units.la: 20 Quod si verum est verbum istud, et signa virginitatis in puella non fuerint inuenta.
units.tr: 20 But if this thing be true, and the tokens of virginity be not found in the damsel:

units.la: 21 Ducent puellam ad ostium domus patris sui, obruentq; eam cives illius ciuitatis lapidibus, ut moriatur, quia fecit nephas in Israel, scortando in domo patris sui, et exures malum è medio tui.
units.tr: 21 Then they shall bring out the damsel to the door of her father's house, and the men of her city shall stone her with stones that she die, because she hath wrought folly in Israel, to play the whore in her father's house: so shalt thou put away evil from among you.

units.la: CVm Diuus Moses hoc 22.cap.quatuor ultimarum legum expositionem occepisset, atque etiam peculiares quasdam leges adduxisset, quibus furti & concupiscentiæ præceptum explicaret, ac deinceps adulterij legem quoque posset illustrare: interponit illis explanationem falsi testimonij, qua,ne quis alteri verbis det damnum,cauet. Ac qui dixerat de concupiscentia, & post dicturus erat de adulterio: cognatum utriusque rei exemplum ad explicandum hoc praeceptum affert. Si videlicet aliquis seu tedio seu odio suæ, & desiderio mulieris alterius incitatus, ut altera liberaretur potiretur altera, crimen læsæ pudicitiæ impingeret suæ: quod quoniam graue est & offendit ciuitatem, parentum est hoc ipsum minimè ferre, sed iure cum eo experiri & de fonte fumere supplicium.
units.tr: When holy Moses had begun, in the twenty-second chapter, the exposition of the last four laws, and had also adduced certain particular laws by which he might explain the commandment against theft and covetousness, and afterwards illustrate the law against adultery as well, he inserts among them an explanation of false witness, by which he guards against anyone harming another by words. And he who had spoken of covetousness, and was afterwards to speak of adultery, brings forward an example related to both things to explain this commandment. Namely, if someone, moved by weariness or hatred of his own wife and by desire for another woman, were to bring a charge of violated chastity against his wife so that the one might be freed and the other obtained, since this is a grave offence and wounds the city, it is the business of the parents not to bear it at all, but to proceed against him by right and to take punishment from its source.

units.la: Quo discemus Deum lege falsi testimonij mendacibus, sycophantis, calumniatoribus & id genus hominibus repagulum posuisse.
units.tr: From this we learn that God, by the law of false witness, set a barrier against liars, sycophants, calumniators and men of that kind.

units.la: Quod ut sit perspicuum magis, egregio ordine persequitur. 1. Ipsum crimen calumniæ,
units.tr: That this may be more plain, he pursues it in an excellent order: 1. The very crime of calumny.

units.la: 2. Actionem aduersus calumniatorem.
units.tr: 2. The action against the calumniator.

units.la: 3. Sumendum de eo iudicium.
units.tr: 3. The judgement to be taken concerning him.

units.la: Calumniæ crimen describit à duabus causis potissimis, quibus etiam reliquas comprehendit, efficiente scilicet & forma. De efficiente dicit, Si quispiam uxorem duxerit, accesserit ad eam & odisse eam ceperit, &c. Quibus verbis odium offendit ceu mali causam efficientem, quod sit motus animi suadens teterrima quæq; scelera. Etenim quem quis odit, eum si factis nequeat, saltem verbis lædit. Atque ex eo calumnia nascitur. Eodem etiam auxilia sua confert inuidia. Qua de causa Scriptura sacra cum odium tum inuidiam tantopere detestatur. Solomon in Prouerb.cap.10. Odium (inquit) suscitat rixas. Moses Leuit.10. Non oderis fratrem tuum, &c. Christus odium homicidij causam dicit, Matth.15. Principium odii videlicet iram nominans. Diuus Ioannes 1.epist.3. Omnis, inquit, qui odit fratrem suum homicida est. Et certe videmus causam obtrectationum & calumniarum eandem etiam esse nostro tempore. Inuidia simul & odio pleni sunt plærorumq; animi: inde fit, ut obuium quemq; ledamus verbis, imprimisq; eos quibus Deus fauet & est auxilio. Crescit enim cum honoribus atque opibus inuidia, quæ parit calumnias. Igitur indicantem huius mali causas scripturam audiamus, & erit consultum, causas morbi videlicet ut tollamus. Quæ bona Deus alicui fauerit, ea tu quæso ne ei inuideas. Odio & inuidia agitatus Cain, item Saul, Josephi fratres & alii designarunt alia.
units.tr: He describes the crime of calumny from two chief causes, under which he also comprehends the rest, namely the efficient cause and the form. Concerning the efficient cause he says: "If any man take a wife, and go in unto her, and hate her," etc. By these words he sets hatred before us as the efficient cause of evil, since it is a movement of the mind that prompts the most horrible crimes. For whomever a man hates, if he cannot harm him by deeds, he harms him at least by words, and from this calumny arises. Envy also brings its aid to the same end. For this reason Holy Scripture so greatly detests both hatred and envy. Solomon in Proverbs 10: "Hatred," he says, "stirs up strife." Moses in Leviticus 19: "Thou shalt not hate thy brother," etc. Christ names hatred the cause of murder, Matthew 15, calling it by the name of the beginning of hatred, namely anger. The blessed John, 1 John 3: "Everyone," he says, "who hateth his brother is a murderer." And certainly we see that the cause of detraction and calumnies is the same in our own time too. The minds of many are full of envy and hatred at once; hence it happens that they injure with words whomever they meet, and above all those whom God favours and helps. For envy grows with honours and wealth, and it gives birth to calumnies. Therefore let us hear Scripture indicating the causes of this evil, and it will be wise to remove the causes of the disease. Whatever goods God has bestowed on anyone, I beg you, do not envy him for them. Cain, moved by hatred and envy, and likewise Saul, the brothers of Joseph and others, were driven by other motives.

units.la: De forma dicit, Obtruserit ei technas verborum, &c. Quo crimen ipsum describit: Si quis uxoris odio ductus fingat in illam crimina. Magnum flagitium est, si quis cum persona rem ipsam conferat. Uxoris fama bona ac laus pudicitiæ præcipuum in his terris bonum est, & omnibus gentibus celebre. Nam ut impudicitia matrum est ignominiosa posteris: sic illarum castitas sobolem ornat. Iam illam hac priuari sit ex malis maximis necesse est. Unde & Esa.13. uxorum pudicitiæ violationem ceu diram pœnam minitatur. Et grande nephas semper est habitum matronæ, viduæ, virginis pudicitiam ledere. Qua de causa laudatur Josephi probitas, qui beatam virginem noluit infamare, cum eam deprehendisset esse grauidam. Nec impune tulit unquam quisquis insidiatur virginis pudicitiæ. Sed tamen si personam consideres, longè maius est scelus si maritus uxorem afficiat ignominia, qui debebat eius esse tutor & patronus.
units.tr: Concerning the form he says: "And give occasions of speech against her," etc. By this he describes the crime itself: if someone, led by hatred of his wife, invents charges against her. It is a great disgrace if someone attacks the thing itself through the person. A good name for a wife and the praise of chastity are the chief good in this earthly life, and are celebrated among all nations. For just as the unchastity of mothers is shameful to their descendants, so their chastity adorns their offspring. To deprive her of this must therefore be among the greatest evils. Hence also Isaiah 13 threatens violation of wives' chastity as a dreadful punishment. And it has always been regarded as a great wickedness to injure the chastity of a matron, a widow or a virgin. For this reason the uprightness of Joseph is praised, who refused to defame the blessed Virgin when he found her to be with child. Nor has anyone who lies in wait for a virgin's chastity ever gone unpunished. But even so, if you consider the person, it is a far greater crime when a husband brings disgrace upon his wife, since he ought to be her guardian and protector.

units.la: Eodem modo calumniarum omne genus metiemur. Est præcipuum in his terris bonum fama: quippe qua semel amissa postea nullus eris. Etsi falsum sit quod sparseris, tamen grauat suspicio. At si nobis eam ledant, qui id omnium minimè debebant facere, ut episcopus episco-po, senator senatori, affinis affini, vicinus vicino, eò grauior est calumnia.
units.tr: In the same way we shall measure every kind of calumny. A good name is the chief good in this earthly life, since once it is lost you will never be restored to it. Even if what you have spread is false, the suspicion nonetheless weighs heavily. But if they wound us, those who least of all ought to do it, as a bishop a bishop, a senator a senator, a kinsman a kinsman, a neighbour a neighbour, the calumny is all the heavier.

units.la: Sed quantum sit hoc scelus ex ipso iudicio post fiet perspicuum, quàm non sit ferendum hoc semper, ex actione disci poterit. Sunt enim Christianis hominibus, quos decet patientia, quædam conuitia ferenda: sunt magistratibus quædam dissimulanda, sunt contra quǣda tan-ti momenti, ut nequaquam dissimulanda sint minimeq; toleranda.
units.tr: But how great this wickedness is will become plain afterwards from the judgement itself, and how little it is to be borne at any time can be learned from the action. For there are certain reproaches that Christian people, whom patience becomes, must bear; there are certain things that magistrates must overlook; and there are others of such weight that they must by no means be overlooked or tolerated.

units.la: Igitur actionem in sycophantam sic decernit: tollent, inquit, pater puellæ & mater eius, &c. Quibus verbis mandat & decernit actionem parentibus, nempe ut intelligamus quanti cuique esse debeat honos & existimatio, quàmque ferendum non sit quod quis famam nostram lesserit.
units.tr: Therefore he decrees the action against the sycophant thus: "Then shall the father of the damsel and her mother take," etc. By these words he commands and decrees the action to be brought by the parents, so that we may understand how great honour and esteem each person ought to have, and how little it is to be borne that someone should harm our good name.

units.la: In quo si quid alibi quoque præcipitur consideres, facile cognitu fuerit, quando calumniæ sint aut non sint dissimulandæ. In illis, esse nos superbos, ambitiosos, auaros, imprudentes, &c. itemque si quis vitia corporis exprobret, ferendum est. Et multæ causæ sunt: primum nemo dicet omni se vacare superbia: tum præditum se esse his aut illis virtutibus arrogantium est magis, quàm prudentium. Et hominibus hoc datum est, ut quæ comprehensa animis habeant, ea verbis efferre queant: alijs animantibus hoc non licet: cum illis liceat, etiam per nos liceat.
units.tr: If you consider what is taught elsewhere on this matter, it will be easy to know when calumnies are to be overlooked and when they are not. In the matter of being called proud, ambitious, avaricious, imprudent, and so on, and likewise if someone reproaches us for bodily faults, it must be borne. And there are many reasons for this: first, no one will say that he is free from all pride; then, to claim that one is endowed with this or that virtue belongs more to the arrogant than to the prudent. And it has been granted to men that they can express in words what they hold in their minds; other living creatures do not have this; since they are allowed to speak, it is allowed to us too.

units.la: Illud sibi quisque praefixum habeat, quae dicuntur aut esse vera, aut falsa: vera si sint quae de te dicuntur mala, potius emendanda, quàm de iniuria conquerare: sin mentita sint hoc ipso tibi gratulabere, quod vera ne sint ope Dei factum sit. His adde quod patientiam in no-bis Christus desideret: quodq; exprobrare calumnias plus afferat incommodi, quàm boni. Exemplo sunt Dauid Semeij contumelias aequanimiter sustinens, tum Christus & Apostoli simili praediti patientia.
units.tr: Let everyone keep this before him: whatever is said about him is either true or false. If what is said about you is true and evil, you should rather amend it than complain of the injury; but if it is false, you will rejoice on that very account, that by the help of God it is not true. Add to this that Christ requires patience in us, and that to complain of calumnies brings more harm than good. David, bearing the insults of Shimei with equanimity, is an example, and Christ and the Apostles, endowed with like patience.

units.la: In illis autem quae famam pietatis, probitatis, innocentiae lædunt, ut si blasphemum, homicidam, adulterum, furem quis te esse diceret: sanè & sua cuiusque & publicae rei interest, id ne dissimuletur, nec toleretur. Nam optimo cuique nihil esse debet antiquius laude, probitatis atque innocentiae: tum civitatis est oneratum tali infamia vel ut purgetur & exonerretur suspicione, vel ut deprehensus reus afficiatur supplicio. Itaq; criminis huius suspicionem tolli cum puellae, tum parentum, denique etiam civitatis interesse Moses docet: <bl>Vil bü-ren ceren ein statt nit</bl> [?]. Improbat igitur Dominus peruersam patientiam.
units.tr: But in those charges which wound the reputation for piety, uprightness and innocence, such as if someone were to call you a blasphemer, a murderer, an adulterer or a thief, it is certainly in the interest both of each individual and of the public that this should not be overlooked or tolerated. For nothing should be more precious to every good man than the praise of uprightness and innocence; and it is the concern of the city, when burdened with such infamy, either to be cleared and freed from suspicion, or to have the accused, if caught, punished. Therefore Moses teaches that it concerns the damsel, the parents, and finally the city as well that the suspicion of this crime be removed: <bl>Vil bü-ren ceren ein statt nit</bl> [?] (the wicked thing is not to be turned aside from the city). Therefore the Lord condemns perverse patience.

units.la: Iudicium de calumnia secundum haec Mosis verba sic habet. Primum si inquisitione facta falsum fuerit quod ille de vxore sua dixerit, puniendus est. Et quidem poena triplex decernitur, videlicet corporis, pecuniae, retinendae vxoris iugum. Ex quo perspicuum est grande nephas esse Dei iudicio calumniam. Vnde Leuit. 19. dicit: Non facies calumniam. Et in Decalogo, non dices falsum testimonium, idem indicat. Hic magistratui mandatur iudicium. Recte sanè Hippias, authore Plutarcho, iudicauit grauissimam rem esse calumniam, & debuisse non minus sycophantis quàm furibus poenam irrogatam esse, quod amicitiam quae sit ἄριστον κτῆμα [?] suffuretur. Sic contumelia famam ledit.
units.tr: The judgment on slander, according to these words of Moses, is as follows. First, if the inquiry shows that what the man said about his wife was false, he is to be punished. The penalty is threefold: of the body, of money, and the yoke of keeping his wife. From this it is plain that slander before God's judgment is a great wickedness. Hence Leviticus 19 says: You shall not make a slander. The commandment, You shall not bear false witness, in the Decalogue indicates the same thing. Here the judgment is committed to the magistrate. Hippias, as Plutarch reports, rightly judged that slander is a most serious matter, and that the penalty should have been imposed no less on sycophants than on thieves, because it steals friendship, which is the best possession [ἄριστον κτῆμα]. So insult injures reputation.

units.la: Vnde factum est vt plerique impp. vtriusque sceleris vindices extiterint. Domitianus enim dictitabat: princeps qui delatores non castigat, irritat. Et Pertinax, authore Herodiano, cum ita instituerat imperium, quo Marcum Imperatorem referret συκοφάντας vrbe exegit & vbi vbi inuenirentur puniri iussit, omninoq; cauere voluit, ne cui μεταίοις ἐγκλήμασι [?] periculum conflaretur. Iustinianus Const. 50. vult iurare actores ὡς ἂν συκοφαντοῦντες ἐπάγωσι τὰς ἐγκλήσεις [?]. Et vetus actio calumniae sycophantis adimebat decimam litis temere motae partem poenae nomine. Apud Athenienses mulctabatur deposita pecunia, quae dicebatur παρακαταβολή [?], qui temere litigasset. Romanis erat sponsio, pecunia scilicet interposita quam perderet temerarius litigator. Iurabant etiam actores se litem non mouere animo calumniandi, verum persuasos esse se habere bonam causam. Vt est l. ij. C. de iur. propter calum-dan. Quae leges omnes hinc videntur manasse quod Deus hac lege eum qui periculum vxori calumnijs conflasset ita grauiter puniri imperauit.
units.tr: Hence most emperors appeared as avengers of both crimes. Domitian used to say that a prince who does not punish informers encourages them. Pertinax, according to Herodian, when he set up his rule so as to restore the emperor Marcus, drove the sycophants [συκοφάντας] out of the city, ordered that they be punished wherever they were found, and wished altogether to guard against anyone being exposed to danger from other charges [μεταίοις ἐγκλήμασι]. Justinian (Const. 50) wants plaintiffs to swear that they bring their accusations not as sycophants [ὡς ἂν συκοφαντοῦντες ἐπάγωσι τὰς ἐγκλήσεις]. The old action for calumny took from the sycophant a tenth part of a lawsuit rashly begun, as a penalty. Among the Athenians, the money deposited by one who had litigated rashly, called the deposit [παρακαταβολή], was forfeited. The Romans had the sponsio, that is, money staked which the rash litigant would lose. Plaintiffs also swore that they did not bring suit with intent to slander, but were persuaded that they had a good cause, as in law 2 of the Code, On the law concerning calumny. All these laws seem to have sprung from the fact that God, by this law, commanded that one who had brought danger upon his wife by slanders be punished so severely.

units.la: Ac si nostra memoria magistratus omnes omniu [?] calumniarum, contumeliarum, temere motarum litium tam seueri vindices essent, multò plus pacis & tranquillitatis, minus turbarum esset ac litium.
units.tr: If, in our memory, all magistrates were such severe avengers of slanders, insults and rashly begun lawsuits, there would be much more peace and tranquillity, and fewer disturbances and lawsuits.

units.la: Sin verum sit quod maritus vxori impingit crimen, videlicet non fuisse virginem: morte (inquit) morietur. En quale Dei sit de scortatione iudicium.
units.tr: But if the charge the husband brings against his wife is true, namely that she was not a virgin, she shall surely be put to death, he says. See what kind of judgment God passes on fornication.

units.la: Ante ædes parentum vult de ea supplicium fumi [?]: nimirum vt exemplo hoc admoniti caeteri diligentiores in educandis liberis essent, si quidem vellent habere posteritatis spem meliorem.
units.tr: He wills that she be punished before her parents' house, by stoning. Doubtless the purpose is that others, warned by this example, should be more careful in bringing up their children, if they wish to have a better hope of posterity.

units.la: Atq; his quidem legem falsi testimonij, quae longè lateq; patet, exposuit, ac docuit Deo, qui ipse est veritas, gratissimum esse veritatis studium. Amen.
units.tr: With these words he has set out the law against false witness, which extends far and wide, and has taught that zeal for the truth is most pleasing to God, who is himself truth. Amen.

units.la: SERMO LIIII.
units.tr: SERMON LIV.

units.la: 22 Si deprehenditur quispiam qui dormierit cum muliere, quae habet maritum, morientur ambo illi, tam vir qui iacuit cum muliere, quam mulier ipsa, & exures malum ex Israele.
units.tr: 22 If a man is caught lying with a woman who has a husband, then both shall die, the man who lay with the woman and the woman herself. So you shall put away the evil from Israel.

units.la: 23 Si fuerit alicui desponsa puella virgo, inuenerit eam quispiam in civitate, & dormierit cum ea.
units.tr: 23 If a virgin is betrothed to a man, and another man finds her in the city and lies with her,

units.la: 24 Educetis vtrunq; ad portam ciuitatis illius, & obruetis eos lapidibus, vt moriantur: puella quidem quod non clamauit in ciuitate, vir autem quod oppresserit proximi sui, & exuresq; malum e medio tui.
units.tr: 24 then you shall bring both of them out to the gate of that city and stone them with stones until they die: the girl, because she did not cry out in the city, and the man, because he violated his neighbour's wife. So you shall put away the evil from among you.

units.la: 25 Si in agro deprehenderit vir puellam desponsam, & vim illi intulerit, dormieritq; cum ea, morietur vir qui dormierit cum ea, solus.
units.tr: 25 But if a man finds a betrothed girl in the field, and forces her and lies with her, then the man who lay with her shall die alone.

units.la: 26 Puella nihil facies, quum culpam mortis non habeat: quoniam sicut consurgit quis contra proximum suum, & interficit animam eius, sic se habet res ista.
units.tr: 26 You shall do nothing to the girl, for she has no sin deserving death. For this case is like that of a man who rises against his neighbour and kills him.

units.la: 27 Nam in agro inuenit eam, clamauit, puella desponsa, & non fuit qui eam liberaret.
units.tr: 27 For he found her in the field; the betrothed girl cried out, but there was no one to save her.

units.la: 28 Si inuenerit vir puellam virginem, quæ nondum desponsa est, apprehensaque ea dormierit cum ea, & deprehensi fuerint.
units.tr: 28 If a man finds a virgin girl who is not yet betrothed, seizes her and lies with her, and they are discovered,

units.la: 29 Dabit vir ille qui cum ea concubuit patri puellæ quinquaginta argenteos, habebitq; eam vxorem, eo quod oppresserit eam, nec poterit eam dimittere cunctis diebus suis.
units.tr: 29 then the man who lay with her shall give the girl's father fifty shekels of silver, and she shall be his wife, because he has violated her; he may never put her away all his days.

units.la: 30 Nemo ducet vxorem patris sui, neq; alam patris sui retegęt[?].
units.tr: 30 A man shall not take his father's wife, nor uncover his father's skirt.

units.la: LEgitima viri & fœminæ coniunctio non est à Mose solum, verum etiam à Deo primum instituta, & ex ipso naturæ atque omnium gentium iure deducta, & vt Paulus ait habita magno in precio. Qua de causa multis & varijs legibus tentatum est, vt virginitas ad matrimonium vsq; casta atq; illibata conseruari posset, ac deinceps in matrimonio fides atq; pietas inter coniuges mutua perduraret. Earum legum summa ac caput est quod in Decalogo dicitur: Non committes adulterium. Quam Moses hoc cap. exponit ac docet quid circa legem eam fit considerandum, quidq; ea ipsa fit vetitum. Ac quoniam adulterij lege cauere voluit Deus matrimonij, quod sacrosanctum esse debebat, prophanationem: satis perspicuum est quicquid fit, quo ipsum inquinetur, id omne esse vetitum. Quamobrem legem ipsam hoc loco latius extendit, ac dicit primum de adulterio, tum de stupro, post de incestu: quibus rebus matrimonium polluitur.
units.tr: Lawful union of man and woman was instituted first not by Moses alone but by God himself, and it is derived from the very law of nature and of all nations, and, as Paul says, it is held in great honour. For this reason many and various laws have been devised so that virginity might be kept chaste and unblemished up to marriage, and afterwards that faith and piety might endure mutually between spouses in marriage. The sum and head of these laws is what is said in the Decalogue: You shall not commit adultery. Moses in this chapter sets out and teaches what must be considered concerning that law and what exactly is forbidden by it. And since God willed by the law of adultery to guard against the profanation of marriage, which ought to be held sacred, it is quite plain that whatever defiles it is all forbidden. Therefore in this place he extends the law more widely, and speaks first of adultery, then of fornication, and afterwards of incest, by which things marriage is polluted.

units.la: Ac primum quidem adulterij genera duo refert, quorum vnum cum matrona matrefamilias, alterum cum desponsa virgine committatur.
units.tr: And first he sets out two kinds of adultery, one committed with a married matron, the other with a betrothed virgin.

units.la: De eo quod cum matrona fiat dicit ad hunc modum. Si deprehenditur quispiam qui dor-mierit cum muliere quæ maritum habeat, &c. Quo ostendit adulterium cum alicuius vxore factum capitale esse debere.
units.tr: Concerning what is done with a matron he speaks in this manner: If a man is caught lying with a woman who has a husband, etc. By this he shows that adultery committed with another's wife ought to be a capital crime.

units.la: Qua de re tametsi plura supra dixerimus, tamen pauca sunt addenda, vt intelligamus atrocitate criminis legislatorem adductum, vt ei tam duram pœnam irrogaret. Primum enim dissipatur prima ac diuinitus instituta maris & fœminæ coniunctio: de qua dictum: Mascu-lum & fœminam creauit eos: &c, relinquet homo patrem & matrem & adhærebit vxori suæ. Hanc societatem vitæ, bonorum, & omnino rerum bonarum & malarum omnium dissipat adulterium.
units.tr: Although we have said more on this matter above, still a few things must be added, so that we may understand that the lawgiver was moved by the atrocity of the crime to impose so harsh a penalty. For first, the primary union of male and female, instituted by God, is destroyed; of it was said: Male and female he created them, etc.; a man shall leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife. Adultery dissolves this fellowship of life, of goods, and in short of all good and bad things.

units.la: Dein turbatur ciuilis societas, quod quæ sunt inter ciues distincta rerum dominia, & legitimæ hęreditates, ea inter se confundantur adulterijs: fiatq; vt alter alterius & liberos & hęredes fouere necesse habeat. Vt adulterium furto deterius esse dixerit Solomon, quod & honorem & pudicitiam bona quæ restitui nunquam possint, abripiat. Qua de causa in reos adulterij dura lex est Iulia, vt etiam Romuli, Constantini, Cæsarum, Saxonum[?], aliorumq; populorum.
units.tr: Next, civil society is thrown into confusion, because the distinct ownership of property among citizens and lawful inheritances are mingled together by adulteries, so that each is obliged to support the children and heirs of the other. Solomon said that adultery is worse than theft, because it snatches away honour and chastity, goods which can never be restored. For this reason the Julian law is harsh against adulterers, as are the laws of Romulus, Constantine, the Caesars, the Saxons, and other peoples.

units.la: Postremo leditur Christiana societas, cum sacra illa Christi & ecclesiæ coniunctio hoc crimine prophanetur. Vnde Ephesijs scribens apostolus ait, Suam quisq; vxorem diligat tanquam seipsum, sicut & dominus ecclesiam, quoniam sumus membra corporis eiusdem. Et Solomon vt dirum illud flagitium caueatur amorem coniugis ceu remedium ab adulterio reuocans præbet, Prouerb.5.
units.tr: Finally, the Christian fellowship is harmed, since that holy union of Christ and the Church is profaned by this crime. Hence the apostle, writing to the Ephesians, says: Let each one of you love his wife as himself, just as the Lord loves the Church, since we are members of the same body. And Solomon, calling back the love of a spouse as a remedy against adultery, in order that this dreadful disgrace be guarded against, offers it, Prov. 5.

units.la: Iam quoniam intelligimus grande nephas esse adulterium mirum nemini videri debet quod ei tam grauis est irrogata pœna. Gen.12.in Pharaonem ob raptum Sarę, Gen.20.in Abimelechum ob raptum eiusdem, in Israelitas ob flagitium in Leuitæ concubinam commissum, in Asiam ob raptum Helenæ, in Tarquinium ob compressam Lucretiam. Et Hiero. 5. minatur Dominus exitium adulteris. Ex quibus est perspicuum nostrum illud adulterium decretum supplicium priscis illis iudicijs minimè respondere. Ambitione & auaritia quidam cohiberi poterant, verum tanto melius habet, quod pro macra aliqua propter adulterium amissa prouincia pinguior potest acquiri. Est & illud dolendum quod adeo non pudet nos eius,vt etiam iocum ludumq; putemus esse. At Deus insontem non habebit eum, qui leges ipsius transgrediatur.
units.tr: Now since we understand that adultery is a great wickedness, no one should think it strange that so grave a penalty has been imposed for it. Gen. 12, against Pharaoh for the taking of Sarah; Gen. 20, against Abimelech for the taking of the same; against the Israelites for the outrage committed upon the Levite's concubine; against Asia for the abduction of Helen; against Tarquin for the violation of Lucretia. And in Jer. 5 the Lord threatens destruction upon adulterers. From these examples it is plain that our present decreed punishment does not at all match those ancient judgments. Some men could be restrained by ambition and greed; but it is so much better that a richer province may be gained in exchange for some lean one lost on account of adultery. It is also to be lamented that we are so shameless about it that we even regard it as a joke and a game. But God will not hold guiltless him who transgresses his laws.

units.la: Alterum genus adulterij in nuptam quidem,sed nondum coniunctampuella marito com mittitur. Videlicet quando desponsa non cohabitauit. Id adulterium fit bifariam: aut enim in factum consentit,aut vi cogitur & opprimitur.
units.tr: The second kind of adultery is committed with a girl who is married indeed, but not yet joined to her husband. That is, when she is betrothed and has not yet cohabited. This adultery takes place in two ways: either she consents to the deed, or she is forced and overpowered by violence.

units.la: Consensus exprimitur vita ac moribus,vt quæ ceu Thamar in biuio consederit. Sed quo supplicio puniendum sit vtrumq; dicit etiam,nempe lapidibus obruantur: Et quæ confen-tit eodem affici supplicio iubetur.
units.tr: Consent is shown by the manner of life and conduct, as in the case of one who, like Tamar, sat at the crossroads. But he also says by what punishment each should be punished, namely that they be stoned with stones; and she who consented is ordered to suffer the same punishment.

units.la: In quo videmus quanti fidem coniugalem faciat Deus:hæc nondum venit in societatem vitæ & bonorum,sed promisit fidem,quæ tamen seruanda fuerat.
units.tr: Here we see how highly God values conjugal faith: she had not yet come into fellowship of life and goods, but had pledged faith, which nevertheless had to be kept.

units.la: Quod consensum tam diligenter notat,id est indicio quantam in vxoribus requirat pudicitiam. Vnde & Apostolus Saram hoc ipso commendat quod Abrahamum suum heri no-mine dignata fit.
units.tr: That he marks consent so carefully is an indication of how much chastity he requires in wives. Hence also the apostle commends Sarah for this very thing, that she honoured her Abraham with the name of lord.

units.la: Quæ vero violenter opprimitur, ipsa quidem rea non est, sed qui scelus patrauit capitali supplicio afficitur. Magnum etiam iure ciuili supplicium huic flagitio est irrogatum. Neque enim ferendi sunt,qui insidiantur aliorum pudicitiæ.
units.tr: But the woman who is violently overpowered is not herself guilty; the one who committed the crime is punished with capital punishment. Great punishment is also imposed by civil law for this offence. For those who lie in wait for the chastity of others must not be tolerated.

units.la: Signa seu coniecturas ex loco sumit. Multum enim docent circumstantiæ. Summa,per-spicuum quanto odio persequatur adulterium.
units.tr: He takes the signs or conjectures from the place. For the circumstances teach much. In sum, it is plain how much hatred adultery deserves.

units.la: De stupro legem alteram addit:Si inuenerit vir puellam virginem,&c. Stuprum est & ip-sum grande nephas. Vnde qui id virgini intulit, cogitur eam habere loco vxoris. Quia summum in his terris bonum est virgini laus pudicitiæ salua conseruata:quam stupro sublatam ei nisi ducat,reddere nequaquam potest. Qua de causa manet eos miseria perpetua qui stu-prum virgini intulerit:nec debent pij magistratus eis fauere.
units.tr: He adds a second law concerning fornication: If a man finds a virgin girl, etc. Fornication too is a great wickedness. Hence the man who has inflicted it on a virgin is compelled to take her in place of a wife, because the highest good on earth for a virgin is the preserved praise of chastity; and if he does not marry her, after her chastity has been taken away he can by no means restore it to her. For this reason those who have done violence to a virgin remain in perpetual misery, and righteous magistrates ought not to favour them.

units.la: Verum hæc lex non fauet cuilibet suam pudicitiam prostituenti fœminæ,sed tantum virgini. At virginitatis indices sunt pij,probi,pudici mores.
units.tr: Yet this law does not favour any woman who prostitutes her own chastity, but only a virgin. And the marks of virginity are the pious, upright, and modest manners of a girl.

units.la: Hoc operam dabunt pij magistratus,vt prorsus nulla sit scortatio. Paulus dicit, Omne peccatum quodcunq; fecerit homo extra corpus est:sed qui scortatur in proprium corpus peccat. Et an nescitis quod templum estis habitantis in vobis spiritus sancti, quem non habetis à vobis,& non estis vestri iuris. Quæ rationes si cogitentur, facile videmus cur ex-cludat regno Dei.Et inter diluvij causas hoc quoq; scelus recensetur. Notæ sunt lex Attica & lex Iulia.Haud obscurum est etiam quod in Apologetico suo Tertullianus gloriatur eam esse Christianorum suæ ætatis hominum castitatem,vt de hac lenones conqueri confueuis-sent. Ea vero nostri temporis impuritas est & libido, vt Solonem potius quàm Mosem imitari maluerimus in tolerandis alicubi lupanaribus ceu scholis libidinis. Ergo ius ciuile cum sacris literis atq; legibus hoc scelus persequitur.
units.tr: Righteous magistrates will take care that there be absolutely no fornication. Paul says: Every sin that a man commits is outside the body, but he who fornicates sins against his own body. And do you not know that your body is the temple of the Holy Spirit who dwells in you, whom you have from God, and that you are not your own? If these reasons are considered, we easily see why fornicators are shut out of the kingdom of God. Among the causes of the flood this crime too is counted. The Attic law and the Julian law are well known. It is also no secret that Tertullian in his Apology boasts that the chastity of the Christians of his age was such that pimps used to complain about it. But our own age's impurity and lust is such that we have preferred to imitate Solon rather than Moses in tolerating brothels in some places, as if they were schools of lust. Therefore civil law, together with the sacred writings and the laws, pursues this crime.

units.la: De incestu sic dicit,vt vno eius genere cætera comprehendat. Est autem locus de nefarijs & illegitimis nuptijs. Matrimonium legibus instituitur & defenditur, & omnium gentium iure probatur: sed inter eos est nefarium quibus iure coire non licet, vt qui cognatione seu affinitate coniuncti sunt. Leuit.18.
units.tr: He speaks of incest in such a way that by one kind of it he takes in the rest. Now this is a passage about wicked and unlawful marriages. Marriage is instituted and defended by laws, and is approved by the law of all nations; but it is wicked for those between whom it is not lawful to couple, such as those joined by kinship or affinity. Lev. 18.

units.la: Sed & iura Cæsarea quibusdam gradibus contrahi matrimonij prohibuerunt, vltra quos progressi pontifices lucri bonam ansam acceperunt. Omitto quas de compaternitate cogi-tarunt fabulas. Nam si id impediat,quo minus in legitimum aliâs matrimonium coeamus, quid de eo dicent,quod in Christum baptizati fratres sororesq; sumus?
units.tr: But also the Caesarean laws have forbidden marriage between certain degrees, and beyond these the popes have seized the chance of a good profit. I pass over the fables they have devised about spiritual kinship as godparents. For if that hinders us from coupling in lawful marriage, what will they say about this, that we are brothers and sisters, baptized into Christ?

units.la: Sed personas,inter quas iure diuino matrimonium fieri non licet, coire, quod scelus in-cestum vocant,etiam ethnici Paulo teste non tolerarunt.
units.tr: But that persons between whom marriage is not lawful by divine law should couple, which they call the crime of incest, even the heathen did not tolerate, as Paul bears witness.

units.la: Quin etiâ naturalis pudor hoc docuit bruta animalia,si Plinio credimus & Aristoteli bru-torum animantium exempla referentibus. In quam sententiam Iustinianus quoq; Nouell. Const.xij.scribit.Et Socrates apud Xenophontem lib. 3[?]. testatur diuinitus latam esse legem, qua nuptiæ inter parentes atq; liberos nefariæ haberentur.
units.tr: Indeed, natural shame has taught even brute animals this, if we believe Pliny and Aristotle, who relate examples of brute creatures. Justinian also writes to the same effect in Novel 12. And Socrates, in Xenophon, book 3[?], testifies that a law was given by divine inspiration by which marriages between parents and children were held to be wicked.

units.la: Vnde & Iura ciuilia eum qui sciens incestum admiserit adulterij pœna plectunt: sin absq; contumacia iuris commissus fit pœnam solent mitigare. l.si adulterium.ff.ad l.Iul.de adult. coer.& stupro.
units.tr: Hence also the civil laws punish with the penalty of adultery the one who knowingly commits incest; but if it is committed without contumacy towards the law, they are accustomed to mitigate the penalty. Law "si adulterium", Digest, on the Julian law concerning adultery, restraint and rape.

units.la: Ex quibus omnibus intelligimus lege Non mœchaberis omnem impuram vitam & libidinem coerceri,omninoq; statui sanctum vt sit inter homines matrimoniû,quale Deus inter Christum & ecclesiam esse voluit. Id Deus faxit per Jesum Christum Dominum nostrum. Amen.
units.tr: From all of these we understand that by the commandment "You shall not commit adultery" every impure life and lust is restrained, and that marriage is established among men as holy, such as God willed it to be between Christ and the Church. May God grant this through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT XXIII. SERMO LV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIII. SERMON LV.

units.la: Non intrabit qui laceratus est (testiculis) attritus, aut exectto veretro, in coetum Domini.
units.tr: He who is crushed or bruised in the testicles, or whose member is cut off, shall not enter into the assembly of the Lord.

units.la: 2 Mamser[?] non ingredietur in coetum Domini, ne decima quidem generatione introibit sibi in coetum Domini.
units.tr: A bastard shall not enter into the assembly of the Lord; even to the tenth generation he shall not enter into the assembly of the Lord.

units.la: 3 Ammonites & Moabites in congregationem Domini non introibit, ne decima quidem generatione quisquam ex ipsis ingredietur in coetum Domini, idq; perpetuo.
units.tr: An Ammonite or a Moabite shall not enter into the congregation of the Lord; even to the tenth generation none of them shall enter into the assembly of the Lord, and this for ever.

units.la: 4 Causa, quod non anteverterunt vos pane & aqua in via quum exiretis ex Ægypto, & quod conduxerit adversum te Biliam filium Beor de Pethor Aram Naharaim, ut te execraretur.
units.tr: The reason is that they did not come to meet you with bread and water on the way when you came out of Egypt, and because they hired against you Balaam son of Beor, from Pethor of Aram Naharaim, to curse you.

units.la: 5 At noluit Dominus Deus tuus audire Bileam, quin potius convertit Dominus Deus tuus execrationē tibi in benedictionem, nam diligit te Dominus Deus tuus.
units.tr: But the Lord your God would not listen to Balaam; rather, the Lord your God turned the curse into a blessance for you, for the Lord your God loves you.

units.la: 6 Ne queras quod ad eorum pacem ac salutem pertineat cunctis diebus tuis in seculum.
units.tr: You shall not seek their peace or their welfare all your days for ever.

units.la: 7 Edomæum ne abominerís, quia frater tuus est: nec abomineris Ægyptium, quandoquidem peregrinus fuisti in terra eius.
units.tr: You shall not abhor the Edomite, for he is your brother; nor shall you abhor the Egyptian, since you were a stranger in his land.

units.la: 8 Filij qui ex eis nati fuerint, tertia tandem generatione in coetum Domini venient.
units.tr: The children who are born of them shall enter into the assembly of the Lord in the third generation.

units.la: Jus & leges sunt Dei Immortalis beneficia, quibus regimur & conseruamur: sed quoniam ipsæ per se leges sunt inermes, ac nihil quicquam prosunt ni custodes gnavos atque fidos habeant: opus est illis custode, qui velit & possit eas conservare. Nam ut parum fidus tutor æquè pupilli bona perdit, ac si nullus sit qui curet ea tutor: sic legum custos nullus & malus perinde prosunt. Quæ cum ita sint, recte sapientes viri non solum de jure & justitia, quam quisq; servare erga alterum debet: sed etiam ea præcipiunt, quæ servanda si[?] in distributione præmiorum & pœnarum, ac suadent ad officia publica, qui indignus sit & ineptus, admittendum esse neminem, nempe ut legum custodes sint boni, periti, gnavi, fortes viri.
units.tr: Laws and rights are the benefits of the immortal God, by which we are governed and preserved. But since laws in themselves are unarmed and of no use at all unless they have diligent and faithful guardians, they need a guardian who both wishes and is able to keep them. For just as a poorly trustworthy guardian loses a ward's goods no less than if there were no guardian at all to look after them, so a bad or absent keeper of the laws is equally of no use. Since this is so, wise men rightly teach not only about right and justice, which each person ought to observe towards another, but also prescribe those things which must be observed in the distribution of rewards and punishments, and advise that in public offices no one who is unworthy and unfit should be admitted; namely, that the guardians of the laws should be good, skilled, diligent and brave men.

units.la: Quam rationem etiam Moses servat. Dixit de pleonexia, quæ evertit eam, quæ in rerum commutatione servanda est, justitiam. Jam dicit de distribuente justitia. Ea docet cavendā esse ἀνισότητα[?], matrem seditionum & ruinæ publicæ, quod cavetur, si indigni & inepti à reip. muniis arceantur.
units.tr: Moses also observes this principle. He spoke of greed (pleonexia), which subverts the justice that must be kept in the exchange of goods. Now he speaks of the one who distributes justice. He teaches that inequality [ἀνισότητα], the mother of sedition and public ruin, must be guarded against, and this is guarded against if the unworthy and unfit are kept away from the offices of the commonwealth.

units.la: Et in præsentia quidem tria indignorum genera commemorat, spadones, spurios, peregrinos. Id ut intelligas, primum vide unde excludat, deinde quos. Unde, Dicit, Non introibit in coetum Domini. &c. Coetum Domini dicit ipsam populi Dei rempublicam: sunt enim alias coetus etiam alij.
units.tr: For the present he names three kinds of unworthy persons: eunuchs, bastards, and foreigners. To understand this, first see from where he excludes them, and then whom. From where? He says: "shall not enter into the assembly of the Lord," etc. By the assembly of the Lord he means the commonwealth of the people of God itself; for there are other assemblies as well.

units.la: Jam venire in concionem est ad tractanda publica civitatis negocia accedere: veluti nostra lingua solemus dicere, <bl>ins Gott gon/an Gemeind gon/in rhat gon/an gericht gon/&c.</bl> Ergo vult indignos, ineptos, odio gravatos arcere procul à rep. ut salva fit εὐταξία[?].
units.tr: Now to come into the assembly is to take part in dealing with the public affairs of the state; as we in our own language are accustomed to say: <bl>ins Gott gon/an Gemeind gon/in rhat gon/an gericht gon/&c.</bl> Therefore he wills that the unworthy, the unfit and those burdened with hatred be kept far away from the commonwealth, so that good order [εὐταξία] may be preserved.

units.la: Sunt quædam officiorum rationes considerandæ propter rempublicam & propter cives. Propter rempublicam ut ea ne ruat. Sunt in populo Dei gradus officiorum: primus est explicandi & judicandi doctrinam: secundus est potestas atq; cura juris & judiciorum: tertius reddituum & ædificiorum: quarum rerum cuiq; est idoneus aliquis præficiendus.
units.tr: There are certain considerations of offices to be weighed, on account of the commonwealth and on account of the citizens. On account of the commonwealth, so that it may not fall. In the people of God there are grades of office: the first is the explaining and judging of doctrine; the second is the power and care of law and judgments; the third is of revenues and buildings. For each of these matters someone suitable must be set over it.

units.la: Doctrinæ judicium requirit virum, qui pietate & prudentia reliquis antecellat: juris administratio fortitudinem, prudentiam & justitiam postulant: bonorum publicorum cura fidem & diligentiam desiderant. Si rationem invertas, illam remp. is perditum. Moses dux eligitur, quia fortis & prudens: Aharon sacerdos declaratur, quia doctus & eloquens. In regno Dauidis Ioab dux exercituum, Abiathar sacerdos. Sic Saba regina Solomonis familiam concinnè dispositam est admirata. Marius in Cymbros mittitur Catulus reip. gubernandæ. Eadem est inter Ciceronem atque Cæsarem proportio.
units.tr: The judgment of doctrine requires a man who excels the rest in piety and prudence; the administration of law demands courage, prudence and justice; the care of public goods requires faithfulness and diligence. If you reverse this order, you ruin the commonwealth. Moses was chosen as leader because he was brave and wise; Aaron was declared priest because he was learned and eloquent. In David's kingdom Joab was commander of the armies, and Abiathar was priest. So the Queen of Sheba admired the well-ordered household of Solomon. Marius was sent against the Cimbri, Catulus to govern the commonwealth. The same proportion holds between Cicero and Caesar.

units.la: Quæ ratio nobis quoque & seruanda & retinenda. Nam quia ambimus officia publica quibus obeundis nequaquam sumus idonei sanè reip. existit inde pernicies. Quare prior est officiorum, posterior autem personarum habenda ratio.
units.tr: This principle must also be kept and retained by us. For when we seek public offices, for which we are by no means fit, this surely brings ruin upon the commonwealth. Therefore the consideration of the office must come first, and that of the person afterwards.

units.la: Sunt quædam ex quibus plus honoris quàm vtilitatis habeatur officia: ac ne stolidi ineptique homines affectarent ea, in quibus potissimum consistit salus reipublicæ, voluerunt viri sapientes, ex illis quàm minimum vtilitatis percipi. Sunt alia rursus officia ciuibus gerentibus vtilia, quæ male meritis & indignis potius cöferre quàm dignis & bene meritis, id verò maximè est indignum & iniquum, atque etiam reipublicæ perniciosum. Ibi enim boni solent esse ciues vbi bonum esse est vtile & honestum. Querebantur olim nonnulli pijs & sacrarum concionum studiosis delata publica munera: quibus autem iam deferuntur[?] Vtile sanè est, & honestum reipub. eam seruare in distribuendis muneribus æqualitatem, quàm hic videmus Mosi placuisse,
units.tr: There are some offices from which more honour than usefulness is had; and so that foolish and unfit men should not aspire to those offices in which the safety of the commonwealth chiefly consists, the wise men wished that as little usefulness as possible be gained from them. Other offices, again, are useful to citizens who hold them, and it is most unworthy and unjust, and even harmful to the commonwealth, to bestow these upon the ill-deserving and unworthy rather than upon the worthy and well-deserving. For good citizens are usually found where what is good is also useful and honourable. Once some complained that public offices were conferred on those who were devout and devoted to sacred sermons, but now they are conferred on... It is certainly useful and honourable for the commonwealth to keep equality in distributing offices, which we see here pleased Moses.

units.la: Iam vt constet quos excludet & officijs seu honoribus publicis indignos iudicet: tres eorum gradus in præsentia commemorat.
units.tr: Now, so that it is clear whom he will exclude from offices or public honours and judge unworthy, he names the three grades of them for the present.

units.la: In quo considerandum est ante omnia Deum magis animi, quàm corporis rationem habere, magisque pietatem, sapientiam, iustitiam, fortitudinem, constantiam, quàm externa aut corporis bona requirere.
units.tr: In this matter one must consider above all that God has more regard for the mind than for the body, and seeks piety, wisdom, justice, courage and steadfastness more than external or bodily goods.

units.la: Sunt tamen quædam notæ vitiorum animi in ipso corpore, velut indicia tempestatum sunt in aere. Vt medici docent corporis constitutione quasi quodam indice monstrari quàm bene vel male temperati sint animi. Vnde & Therfitis apud Homerum descriptio tam diligenter consideratur. Sunt etiam in fortunis quædam animorum notæ, veluti paupertate præsisi multo sunt seruiliore quàm diuites ingenio: eodemq; modo in reliquis.
units.tr: Nevertheless there are certain marks of the vices of the mind in the body itself, just as signs of storms are in the air. As physicians teach, the constitution of the body shows, as it were by a certain indicator, how well or badly the mind is tempered. Hence also the description of Thersites in Homer is considered so carefully. There are also in external fortunes certain marks of the mind: for example, those who are oppressed by poverty are much more servile in disposition than the rich; and so it is in other cases.

units.la: Qua de causa Moses ex his indicijs colligit qui sint vel ad reipub. curam admittendi vel ab hac arcendi. Exectis,testiculis,seu spadones. Hic enim vt ait Philo in suo [illegible, ~8 letters] libro [?]ἔτε ἄρρην ὢν, ἔτε θήλεια[?]. Habentur hi quoque iure ciuili vitiosi l.fi autem quis, ff. de ædil. edic. Igitur sunt rebus vilibus & muliebribus aptiores, quando videntur esse effœminati & rebus gerendis inepti. Effœminati enim duces si meros leones ducerent minime vincerent. Narses eius generis homo Gothos Italia profligarat: sed tamen ei vitiû hoc obiecit Sophia Imperatrix.
units.tr: For this reason Moses, from these signs, gathers who are to be admitted to the care of the commonwealth or kept from it. Cut in the testicles, or eunuchs. For here, as Philo says in his [illegible] book, "neither male nor female" [οὔτε ἄρρην ὢν, οὔτε θήλεια]. Such persons are also held to be defective by civil law. (See the law "But if anyone...", Digest, on the edict of the aediles.) Therefore they are more suited to base and feminine tasks, since they seem effeminate and unfit for carrying out affairs. For effeminate commanders, if they led lions themselves, would by no means conquer. Narses, a man of that kind, had nonetheless destroyed the Goths in Italy; yet the Empress Sophia cast this defect in his teeth.

units.la: Discimus etiam magnorum virorum esse affectibus vt imperent, eosq; reprimant.
units.tr: We also learn that the affections of great men must rule, and that they must restrain them.

units.la: II. Mamferes Spurij. Hos verisimile est ex ortu vitioso aliquid vitij contraxisse, licet interdum ex malis boni gnauiq; viri nati sunt: tum hoc fit etiam, vt ne vilescat matrimonium. Ac si natus ex serua matre seruus est, quid de eo qui natus est ex scorto matre dices? Summa Vel reip. interest nihil viro principi turpe seu probrosum obijci posse, ne videlicet hoc ipse veritus minus fortiter obeat officium. Vnde & Plutarchus de liberorum educatione scribens, parentibus egregios sibi liberos nasci cupientibus suadet ne cum obuijs quibusq; mulieribus coeant, vt scortis. (causam addens anquit) [illegible, ~45 letters] [?] [illegible, ~40 letters] καλὸς ἂν παῤῥησίας θησαυρὸς εὐγένεια.[?] Ex quo potest intelligi quas res veriti legislatores hos homines reip. cura atque administratione prohibendos exiftimarint.
units.tr: II. Bastards. It is likely that such persons, from a defective origin, have contracted some vice, although sometimes good and diligent men are born from bad parents. Moreover this is also done so that marriage may not be held cheap. And if one born of a slave mother is a slave, what will you say of one born of a harlot mother? It is of the highest concern to the commonwealth that nothing shameful or disgraceful can be thrown at a leading man, lest he, fearing this, should discharge his office less bravely. Hence Plutarch too, writing on the education of children, advises parents who wish to have outstanding children not to couple with just any women, as with harlots, adding the reason: "noble birth is a fine treasure of frankness" [καλὸς ἂν παῤῥησίας θησαυρὸς εὐγένεια]. From this it can be understood what things the lawgivers feared, and so judged that these men should be kept from the care and administration of the commonwealth.

units.la: III. Peregrini. In illis delectum habendum monet. Ammonitæ & Moabitæ nunquam admittendi, quod sint ciuitatis hostes, nec possunt vllam suæ erga rempublicam pietatis bonam spem sustinere.
units.tr: III. Foreigners. In these he advises that a selection be made. The Ammonites and Moabites are never to be admitted, because they are enemies of the state, and cannot hold out any good hope of piety towards the commonwealth.

units.la: Id exemplo potest esse omnibus, penes quos ius est eligendorum magistratuum, vt ne lupo committant ouem. Quid enim is curet aut pascat, quos oderit cane peius & angue? qui proueheret eos, quos oppressos vellet?
units.tr: This example can serve everyone who has the right to elect magistrates, that they not entrust the sheep to the wolf. For what would he care for or feed, those whom he hated worse than a dog or a snake? Who would advance those whom he wished to be crushed?

units.la: At Edomitæ & Ægyptij meliores tertia post generatione sunt admittendi.
units.tr: But the Edomites and the Egyptians are to be admitted in the third generation, as being the better.

units.la: In quo videmus, ijs qui licet oderint nos, tamè iuxta benefecerint etiam, plus apud nos prodesse oportere beneficiorum, quàm iniuriarum memoriam.
units.tr: In this we see that those who, although they hated us, nevertheless also did us good, ought to have more weight with us in the memory of their kindnesses than of their injuries.

units.la: Ex omni illa tractatione discimus sic in iustitia distribuente versari, vt & Reipublicæ consulamus, & dignis præmia non subtrahamus. Amen.
units.tr: From that whole discourse we learn to conduct ourselves in distributive justice in such a way that we both look to the welfare of the commonwealth and do not withhold rewards from the deserving. Amen.

units.la: SERMO LVI.
units.tr: SERMON LVI.

units.la: 9 Quum egressus fueris exercitu contra hostes tuos, custodies te ab omni re mala.
units.tr: 9 When you go out with the army against your enemies, you shall keep yourself from every evil thing.

units.la: 10 Si fuerit in te vir, qui non sit mundus ex eventu aliquo nocturno, is egrediatur extra castra, nec revertatur in castra.
units.tr: 10 If there is a man among you who is not clean because of some nocturnal emission, let him go out of the camp; he shall not return into the camp.

units.la: 11 Sed sub vesperam lauet se aqua, & post solis occasum ingrediatur iterum in castra.
units.tr: 11 But toward evening he shall wash himself with water, and after sunset he may come back into the camp.

units.la: 12 Locus quoq; sit tibi extra castra, ad quem foras egrediaris.
units.tr: 12 You shall also have a place outside the camp, to which you shall go out.

units.la: 13 Lignum prœacutum in baltheo, cum quo foris sedens fodias, conuerfuq; operias excrementum tuum.
units.tr: 13 You shall have a peg with your equipment, and when you sit outside, you shall dig with it and cover over your excrement.

units.la: 14 Nam Dominus Deus tuus versatur in medio castrorum tuorum, ut te eripiat, & tradat hostes tuos ante te, & ob hanc causam castra tua sancta sint, ne quam rem obscœnam videat, & se à te auertat.
units.tr: 14 For the Lord your God walks in the midst of your camps, to deliver you and to give your enemies before you. Therefore your camps must be holy, so that he may not see anything unclean among you and turn away from you.

units.la: Vemadmodum in tranquilla pacataque Republica Moses eam, quae in distribuendo versatur, iustitiam mandat, ac praecipit, vt suum cuique assignetur supplicium & praemium, quo pius & probus sit populus: qua de re dictum est in huius Capitis principio: sic docet nunc & requirit, vt belli tempore probitati pariter & temperantiae studeant.
units.tr: Just as in a peaceful and tranquil commonwealth Moses commands and prescribes the justice that consists in distribution, so that each person is assigned punishment or reward, and the people may be pious and upright, as was said at the beginning of this chapter, so now he teaches and requires that in time of war they be equally zealous for uprightness and self-restraint.

units.la: Ac quoniam in castris pleriq; sibi videntur & pietatis & iuris, atq; legum vinculis soluti liberatiq; esse: ne quis in effrenem erumpat impudicitiam atq; malitiam: duo exempla Moses affert, quae nobis rationem nostram respicientibus fortasse non ita magni precij videntur esse, nempe vt illis ipsis indicet quàm purum sanctumq; populum Deus sibi velit esse, praesertim belli tempore, ne qui velint de malis sumere supplicium, sint ijs quos punire volunt deteriores.
units.tr: And since in the camp many men think themselves free of the bonds of piety, of right, and of laws, so that they break out into unbridled immorality and wickedness, Moses brings forward two examples. To us, considering our own situation, these may perhaps seem not of great importance. Yet he shows by them how pure and holy God wishes his people to be, especially in time of war, lest those who wish to take vengeance for wrongs should be worse than those whom they wish to punish.

units.la: Quamobrem hae leges non carent rerum maiorum mysterio suntq; propterea diligentissimè ponderandae. Eam autem ad rem quasi viam author hoc ipso munit, quod primum proponit tum haec exempla explanat.
units.tr: Therefore these laws are not without the mystery of greater things, and they must for that reason be weighed most diligently. Toward this end the author, as it were, prepares the way by first setting forth these examples and then explaining them.

units.la: Proponit ad hunc modum: Cum egressus fueris exercitu contra hostes tuos, custodies te ab omni re mala. Quo docet populi Dei, quando fit cum aliquibus hostibus belligerandum, referre vt ipse quoad posit studeat omni culpa vacare. Nam cum bellum fit vindicta publica, minimè decet eos qui hanc suscipiunt esse ijs qui castigentur, indigniores: qui nec authoritatem habeant vllam tanta re dignam, nec fortunam satis amicam.
units.tr: He sets them forth in this manner: "When you go out with the army against your enemies, you shall keep yourself from every evil thing." By this he teaches that when the people of God must wage war against some enemies, it matters that each man should strive, as far as he can, to be free of every fault. For since war is public vengeance, it is very unfitting that those who undertake it should be more unworthy than those they are to punish, men who have neither the authority befitting so great a matter nor fortune sufficiently favorable.

units.la: Authoritatem autem habere non potest is, qui res gerit timidè, quod faciunt qui graua tuorum scelerum conscientia metuunt opprobria. Vt concionator auarus, ambitiosus, inuidus, ebrius qui poterit ipsum vitijs inquinatos homines castigare? quo ore eorum macu-las abstergeret suis ipse foedatus? Sanè si fecerit, tamen nil profecerit. Idem esto de magistratu, parentibus, praeceptoribus, senibus iudicium. Nec vlla alia causa est tam petulantis adolescentiae, quàm haec tam impura tamq; impudica senum vita. Quamobrem opus est vt qui ve lint alijs festucam oculis eximere, suis ipsi trabem non habeant. Alias dicetur, Medice cura teipsum.
units.tr: A man cannot have authority if he conducts affairs timidly, as those do who, conscious of their grave sins, fear reproach.
