How can a preacher who is covetous, ambitious, envious, or drunken rebuke men who are stained by vices? With what mouth would he wipe away their stains when he is himself defiled? Indeed, even if he should do so, he would accomplish nothing. The same holds for the magistrate, parents, teachers, and elders who sit in judgment. Nor is there any other cause of such wanton youth than this impure and shameless life of the old. Therefore it is necessary that those who wish to remove a speck from others' eyes should not themselves have a beam. Otherwise it will be said, "Physician, heal yourself."

units.la: Fortunam autem amicam habere non possunt, quibus ira Dei propter sua ipsorum peccata grauiter incumbit. Exemplo sunt Israelitarum cum Amalechitis pugna prior, Achan, nos ipsi. Ergo bellum prosperè non gerent aduersus malos, qui laborant pari malitia. In orbe Christiano sunt ac fiunt magna flagitia: sed qui nomen vitae melioris habent, ij sunt vitijs alijs perinde obnoxij. Illic principum exterorum stipendia atq; munera, libertatis, iuris, religionis oppressio: hic sacrilegium, peculatus, pupillorum atq; pauperum oppressio: vtrinq; ebrietas, scortatio, fœnus, blasphemiæ. Quæ cum ita sint ac negari non possint, si nos cum illis committat Deus an non malos opera malorum punit? Inde perspicuum est cur Turcæ papistis, nobis illis sint superiores. Sic in Christiana militia quisq; cogitet se cum alijs bono exemplo esse debeat, ni prorsus à malo abstineat, iusto Domini iudicio contemptum fore. Quamobrem Mosem audientes abstinebimus à malo. Exempla duo tantum commemorat, eaque rebus (vt videntur) leuibus adumbrat. 1. Si fuerit in te vir qui non fuerit mundus ex euentu noctuno aliquo, &c. Minimi momenti res vide-tur esse, quam quis somnians fecerit: sed tamen haec esse expressa legibus non caret mysterio. Primum enim somnia sunt aut rerum praeteritarum anteaue cogitatarum reliquiae, aut futu-rarum nuncia. Unde & mentis videntur esse quasi quaedam indicia.
units.tr: Those, however, cannot have favorable fortune on whom the wrath of God lies heavily on account of their own sins. Examples are the first battle of the Israelites against the Amalekites, and Achan, and ourselves. Therefore they will not wage war successfully against wicked men when they labor under the same wickedness. In the Christian world there are and occur great crimes, but those who bear the name of a better life are equally subject to other vices. There, among foreign princes, are mercenary service and bribes, oppression of liberty, of right, and of religion; here, sacrilege, embezzlement, and oppression of orphans and the poor; on both sides, drunkenness, whoredom, usury, and blasphemies. Since these things are so and cannot be denied, if God should bring us into conflict with them, does he not punish the wicked by the works of the wicked? From this it is plain why the Turks are superior to the Papists, and to us. Thus in the Christian warfare each man should consider that, since he ought to be a good example to others, unless he refrains entirely from evil, he will be despised by the just judgment of the Lord. Therefore, hearing Moses, we shall refrain from evil. He mentions only two examples, and he sketches them with things that seem trivial. (1) "If there is a man among you who is not clean because of some nocturnal emission," and so on. The matter seems of very slight importance, what someone does while dreaming. Yet these things, set down in the laws, are not without mystery. For first, dreams are either remnants of past or previously considered things, or announcements of future ones. Whence they also seem to be, as it were, certain indications of the mind.

units.la: Si igitur impura somnia vituperet, certe docet Deum velle procul a castris abesse eos, quibus salus publica, quae bello queritur aut defenditur, non magis curae sit, quam vt his occupetur somnijs. Vrias prius nec lauare nec vxori misceri voluit, quam regno pax esset recu-perata. Moses maluit angi cum populo suo, quam viuere in delicijs regijs. Idem senserunt Da-uid iuuenis, Paulus omnia factus omnibus, in primisque Christus non rapinam arbitratus ferui formam nostrae salutis recuperandae gratia assumere. Sic Epaminondas conuiuantibus ciuibus moenia circumijt. Et Regulus ad Poenos redire moriturus maluit, quam suae vitae pretio patriae graues hostes emere. Eodem refer Decios, Horatios, Ciceronem: & ex nostris Vuincelriedum, Stufsium, & alios. Sed o degeneres animos.
units.tr: If, therefore, he condemns impure dreams, he certainly teaches that God wills those to be far from the camp whose concern is not so much the public safety, which is sought or defended in war, as to be occupied with such dreams. Uriah would neither wash himself nor lie with his wife before peace had been restored to the kingdom. Moses preferred to be distressed with his people rather than to live in royal delights. David, when young, Paul, who became all things to all men, and above all Christ, who did not think it robbery to take the form of a servant in order to recover our salvation, felt the same. So Epaminondas walked around the walls while his citizens feasted. And Regulus, about to die, preferred to return to the Carthaginians rather than buy grave enemies for his country with the price of his own life. Refer to the same spirit the Decii, the Horatii, Cicero, and among our own, Winkelried, Stucius, and others. But oh, degenerate spirits!

units.la: Existimandum est etiam Deum etiam clam facta detestari, & velle nobis esse puras con-scientias. Atq; hae illarum rerum significatio nostrorum nos admonet, quae temporum, nos minime patiuntur esse libidinibus atque luxui deditos.
units.tr: We must also think that God detests even secret deeds and wishes us to have pure consciences. And the meaning of these things admonishes us, who in these times are hardly suffered to be given over to lusts and luxury.

units.la: II. Locus quoque tibi sit extra castra, &c. Iam requisita naturae vetat in castris fieri: non odio naturae quam condiderat, sed studio verecundiae, quae & viros decet & foeminas. Excrementa bifariam sunt abijcienda atque expurganda: cum quia foetore suo offendunt & suaues salubresq; odores, quo minus illis recreemur, impediut[?]: tum quia nocent bonae valetudini.
units.tr: (2) "Let there also be a place for you outside the camp," and so on. Now, the things that nature requires are forbidden in the camp, not from hatred of the nature that he had created, but from zeal for modesty, which befits both men and women. Excrement must be cast away and cleansed in two ways: partly because it offends by its stench and hinders us from being refreshed by pleasant and wholesome odors, and partly because it harms good health.

units.la: Offendere perinde est hoc loco, atque voluptatem & quietem publicam turbare: infi-cere bonam valetudinem repraesentat contagium improbae consuetudinis. Vae, inquit Do-minus, ei per quem veniunt offendicula.
units.tr: To offend here is the same as disturbing the public pleasure and quiet; to corrupt good health is represented by the contagion of an evil custom. "Woe," says the Lord, "to him through whom offenses come."

units.la: Atque eiusmodi mundiciem requirit Dominus in suorum coetu. 1. Etsi non afferat ve-ram salutem, tamen & decet hominem & conducit eius ipsius valetudini. 2. Deus habitat cum suo tabernaculo in hoc coetu, vt sanctifimus[?] quemadmodum ipse est. 3. Cum agnitio peccati fit ex lege, Spiritus sanctus harum enumeratione eius quae nobis est innata immunditiei nos admonet, eamque vult subinde perpurgari. Tito scribens ait apostolus, pol-lutis & infidelibus nihil est purum, sed polluta est illorum mens & conscientia. Illi igitur & belli & pacis tempore studebimus.
units.tr: And the Lord requires this kind of cleanliness in the assembly of his people. (1) Although it does not bring true salvation, it both becomes a man and profits his own health. (2) God dwells with his tabernacle in this assembly, so that it may be holy as he himself is holy. (3) Since the knowledge of sin comes from the law, the Holy Spirit, by enumerating these things, admonishes us of the uncleanness innate in us, and wills that it be cleansed from time to time. Writing to Titus, the apostle says: "To the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure, but both their mind and conscience are defiled." Therefore we shall be zealous for this both in time of war and in time of peace.

units.la: Causam Moses addit quod Deus ipse in nobis habitat, atque a nobis, si impuri simus auerte-retur. Quod ne fiat purae castaeque vitae studio consequemur per Iesum Christum. Amen.
units.tr: Moses adds the reason, that God himself dwells among us and would turn away from us if we were unclean. So that this may not happen, we shall attain it through Jesus Christ, by zeal for a pure and chaste life. Amen.

units.la: SERMO LVII.
units.tr: SERMON LVII.

units.la: 15 Ne includas seruum hero suo, qui ereptus ad te (venit) ab hero suo. 16 Tecum habitabit in medio tui, vbicunque elegerit locum in vna ciuitatum tua-rum, vt ipsi fuerit visum, nec inferas ei vim. 17 Ne fit scortum de filiabus Israel, neque pathicus fit de filijs Israel.
units.tr: 15 Do not hand over a slave to his master, who has fled from his master to you. 16 He shall dwell with you in the midst of you, in whatever place of your towns he chooses, where it seems good to him; do not oppress him. 17 There shall not be a harlot among the daughters of Israel, nor a male prostitute among the sons of Israel.

units.la: ET suum cuiq; reddit ac permittit, & idipsum vt vel amissum recuperet vel acquisitum obtineat omnibus opem fert iustitiae: idq; ab iis qui iusti sunt fieri consueuit priuatim & publicè. Publicè cum magistratus vim arcet ab iis qui contra ius & fas opprimuntur: pri-uatim, quando vir bonus pupillos vel quoscunque alios aduersus magnatum iniurias & li-bidinem tuetur.
units.tr: Moses gives each man his due and permits it, and he brings the aid of justice to all, so that whatever has been lost may be recovered or whatever has been acquired may be kept. This is usually done by good men, both privately and publicly. It is done publicly when the magistrate wards off violence from those who are oppressed against right and law. It is done privately when a good man defends orphans, or anyone else, against the wrongs and lust of the great.

units.la: Sunt autem omnium quae mortalibus euenient iniuriae minime leuissimae, quae vel ad oppressionem, vel ad infamiam in corpus fiunt. Illis ambabus leges duas hic opponit Moses: primum ne qui seruus fugitiui temere ab iratis heris opprimerentur, statuit ne seruus heri-lem vim atq; iram fugiens irato domino statim reddatur: tum ne quis pecunijs blanditijsue corruptus corpus suum tradat polluendum aliqua infami libidine. Quae duae res hoc prae-sertim tempore sunt etiam atque etiam considerandae.
units.tr: Of all the injuries that befall mortals, the least trivial are those done to the body, whether to oppression or to disgrace. Against these two Moses sets two laws here. First, that slaves who flee from violence and the anger of their masters should not be carelessly oppressed by angry lords: he decrees that a slave fleeing the violent anger of his master is not to be handed back at once to the angry lord. Second, that no one, corrupted by money or flattery, should hand over his body to be defiled by some shameful lust. These two matters especially deserve our careful consideration in the present time.

units.la: Prior lex sic habet: Ne tradas seruum hero suo qui ad te confugerit, &c. Summa ac caput huius legis est, vt imbecilliores ab iniurijs & violentia potentiorum vindicemus: idq; docet exemplo feruorum, qui vim & potentiam herilem veriti confugiunt ad vicinum aliquem sui defendendi gratia. Quod ex verbis legis intelligetur, quae causam propinant huius bonitatis exhibendae.
units.tr: The former law reads: You shall not deliver up to his master a slave who has fled to you, etc. The sum and chief point of this law is that we should protect the weaker from the wrongs and violence of the powerful. It teaches this by the example of slaves, who, fearing their master's power and might, flee to some neighbour for protection. This will be understood from the words of the law, which set out the reason for showing this kindness.

units.la: Serui nomine significat oppressum, imbecillem, iugo aliquo grauatum: est enim serui-tus ingens miseria & molestia praesertim si sit herus durus & stolidus. At quis dignior auxi-lijs quàm is ipse, qui his eget? non opus est diuiti vt des, firmum ac vegetum vt robores, sapi-entem vt doceas, prudentem vt consilijs instruas, victoré vt subleues: sed pauperi dandum, imbecilli robur addendum, stulto & imprudenti consulendum, victo succurrendum est.
units.tr: By the word slave is meant one who is oppressed, weak, and burdened by some yoke. For slavery is a great misery and burden, especially if the master is harsh and foolish. But who is more worthy of help than he who lacks it? You need not give to the rich, nor strengthen the strong and vigorous, nor teach the wise, nor advise the prudent with counsel, nor raise up the victor. But to the poor one must give, to the weak one must add strength, for the foolish and the imprudent one must provide counsel, and to the vanquished one must bring succour.

units.la: Heri nomine vim & potentiam significat & vim imbecillibus metuendam: quę si in per-niciem pauperum conuertatur est reprimenda.
units.tr: By the word master is meant power and might, and force to be feared by the weak. If this is turned to the destruction of the poor, it must be restrained.

units.la: Confugiendi verbo docet, eum hoc quæsisse, vt apud te quasi in tuto conquiescerit. Iam honestissimum & naturæ & officio hominis conuenientissimum est miseris succurrere, hominem homini deum esse. Sed & opresso & vindici conducit officium hoc præstitisse, quippe quod alter accipit salubre, alter serit cum multo fructu demetendum beneficium.
units.tr: By the word flee he teaches that the slave has sought refuge with you, so that he may rest with you as if in safety. Now it is most honourable, most agreeable to nature and to the duty of man, to help the wretched: man is God to man. But it also profits the one oppressed and the protector to have performed this duty, since the one receives a healthful benefit and the other sows a benefit that will be reaped with much fruit.

units.la: Exempla sunt in historijs passim obuia. Pharao rex Ægypti Iacobum patriarcham liberaliter excipiens & Israelem affecit beneficio & sibi suisq; omnibus diuinam gratiam atq; benevolentiam accersivit. Contrarium exemplum est eius posterorum. Laudantur etiam Abdias qui prophetis asylum se praebuit, & Sareptana vidua quæ prophetam excepit hospitio. Et nostri maiores Helvetij sic in fœdus coierunt & iurarunt vt oppressis hominibus opem ferrent. Unde Gradelerum baronem ex Athesina valle profugum suscep-tum à populo Tigurino omnes Helvetij defenderunt. Eadem extitit nostrorum maiorum in Schaffhusiũ, Mulhusiũ, Alsatiam beneficentia, itemq; in Lotharingiæ Principe. Sed ô degeneres animos. Quorum maiores impotentes animos tyrannorum vimque iniustam repressierunt, ij nunc à tyrannis se conduci patiuntur ad exercenda bella iniustissima. Sed & privatim pupillos negligimus, ac salui ne sint an opprimantur susque deque ferimus.
units.tr: Examples lie everywhere in the histories. Pharaoh, king of Egypt, receiving the patriarch Jacob generously, showed kindness to Israel and drew down divine grace and goodwill upon himself and all his people. The contrary example is that of his descendants. Obadiah is also praised, who gave a refuge to the prophets, and the widow of Zarephath, who received the prophet into her house. And our ancestors, the Swiss, so joined in covenant and swore that they would bring aid to oppressed men. Hence all the Swiss defended Baron Gradeler, who had fled from the Adige valley and was received by the people of Zurich. The same kindness of our ancestors was shown to Schaffhausen, Mulhausen, and Alsace, and likewise to the prince of Lorraine. But oh, degenerate spirits! Our ancestors restrained the unruly spirits of tyrants and their unjust violence, and yet we now allow ourselves to be hired by tyrants to wage most unjust wars. Moreover, we neglect orphans in private life, and we care nothing whether they are safe or oppressed.

units.la: At hæc lex mandat neque publicè neque privatim patiamur quenquam iniustè premi.
units.tr: But this law commands that we suffer no one to be unjustly oppressed, neither publicly nor privately.

units.la: Et id quidem in causa religionis præcipuè spectandum est, vt pro viribus obstemus ne piorum hominum conscientiæ grauentur.
units.tr: And this indeed must be chiefly considered in the matter of religion: that we should resist, as far as our strength allows, the burdening of the consciences of pious men.

units.la: Neque vero præcipitur hoc loco quod legi supra Cap.22. contrarium sit, ac prohibeat, quò minus suum cuíque reddatur: quod iubeat nebulones ullos defendere: sed hoc agitur vt iure potius, quàm vi res geri velimus, idque vt fiat enitamur. Neq; enim laudi fuit Ammo-nitis quod Ismaeli patrocinati sunt: neq; Ægyptijs expediebat fugitivos Iudæos excepisse.
units.tr: Nor is anything here commanded that is contrary to the law above in chapter 22, or that forbids each man to be given his due, or that orders us to defend any scoundrels. Rather, the point is that we should wish matters to be conducted by right rather than by force, and that we should strive to bring this about. For the Ammonites gained no praise for having protected Ishmael, nor was it advantageous for the Egyptians to have received fugitive Jews.

units.la: Altera lex est de tollenda scortatione. Non erit, inquit, meretrix de filiabus Israel, nec scortator de filijs Israel. Quibus verbis & scelus ipsum notat & personas, à quibus vult alienum hoc esse. Scelus est scortatio, nempe inter matrimonio solutos, de quo nostra memoria, an sit in vitio, quæritur. Et sanè erat opus interdicto scortationis, quando spurijs nulla patebat ad honores via.
units.tr: The other law is concerned with removing fornication. There shall be no harlot, it says, among the daughters of Israel, nor a whoremonger among the sons of Israel. By these words he marks both the crime itself and the persons from whom he wishes it to be kept far away. The crime is fornication, namely between those free of marriage; whether it is a vice is disputed in our own time. And indeed there was need of a prohibition on fornication, since there was no path to honours open to bastards.

units.la: Sed scortatio multos & prætextus & patronos habet, quia satan sic nouit inescare homines. Ac primum iuventam obijciunt, quæ se cœlo nequeat appendere: quis verò hoc iu-bet: ac cœlo quidem te nequaquam appendis, sed tartaro potius quisquis scortaris. Sed ad vitandam scortitionem mitrimonium Deus instituit Paulo teste, qui dicit, vt vitetur scortatio suam quisque habeat uxorem.
units.tr: But fornication has many pretexts and defenders, because Satan knows how to entice men in this way. First they object their youth, which cannot weigh itself against heaven. But who commands this? You do not weigh yourself against heaven at all; rather, whoever fornicates weighs himself toward hell. But God instituted marriage to avoid fornication, as Paul bears witness, who says: To avoid fornication, let each man have his own wife.

units.la: Deinceps aiunt non cuiuis opportuenum esse matrimonium: at si commodum non sit pietati & probitati studere, saltem ne sis improbus atque impius est enitendum. Et est fre-num optimum pietas, qua exulante mirum non est effrenem esse adolescentiam.
units.tr: Next they say that marriage is not suitable for everyone. But if it is not convenient, one must strive at least not to be wicked and impious, if one cannot devote oneself to piety and integrity. Piety is the best bridle, and it is no wonder that youth is unbridled when piety is absent.

units.la: Præterea queruntur aliqui matrimonio fieri vt multi ad mendicitatem deveniant: at ego puto plures ex scortatione morbo Gallico infectos esse: & quæro an qui spurius nascitur legitimo sit ditior? Conqueri solent etiam de morosis mulieribus: at ego illos impuros amores non credo vacare molestijs, cum ipsi quoque amantes de imperio suarum domina-rum, deque molestijs, quod verum est, fateri soleant. Sed an non scorta vexant, infamant, ex-hauriunt? Ex quibus omnibus multisque alijs generis eiusdem rationibus perspicuum est scortationem non afferre minores molestias quàm matrimonium: quinimò longè maiores, & esse tetrum flagitium.
units.tr: Besides, some complain that marriage brings many to beggary. But I think more have been infected with the French disease through fornication; and I ask whether the bastard born is richer than the legitimate child? People also tend to complain about difficult wives. But I do not believe that those impure loves are free of troubles, since lovers themselves are wont to confess, and truly so, about the rule of their mistresses and about their troubles. But do not harlots harass, disgrace, and drain men? From all these and many other reasons of the same kind it is plain that fornication brings no smaller troubles than marriage; indeed it brings far greater ones, and it is a foul crime.

units.la: Sed quibus ab hominibus potissimum requirit Dominus, vt ab illa sibi caveant? à filijs Israel, inquit: hoc est à fidelibus.
units.tr: But from which men does the Lord chiefly require that they guard themselves against this? From the sons of Israel, he says: that is, from the faithful.

units.la: Et rationes afferunt sacræ literæ non paucas, easque magnas. Ac primum scortator pec-cat in suum ipsius corpus: vt, inquit apostolus: at nostra corpora sunt membra Christi teste eodem: unde sequitur eum in ipsum Christi corpus peccare. Quare fœdū est Christo quod suum est auferre, & idipsum scorto sociare. Deinceps idem dicit nos magno precio redemptos nostriq; iuris non esse, sed Dei, vn de & necesse est nos Dei potius quàm scortorum esse oportere.
units.tr: And the sacred letters offer not a few reasons, and great ones. First, the fornicator sins against his own body, as the apostle says. But our bodies are members of Christ, as the same apostle testifies; hence it follows that he sins against the very body of Christ. Therefore it is foul to take away from Christ what is his and to join it to a harlot. Next, the same apostle says that we have been redeemed at a great price and are not our own but God's, and therefore it is necessary that we belong to God rather than to harlots.

units.la: Tertiò sumus Paulo teste templa spiritus Dei in nobis habitantis, quæ scortatione pol lui nefas esset.
units.tr: Third, by Paul's testimony we are the temples of the Spirit of God dwelling in us, which it would be wicked to pollute by fornication.

units.la: Quartò Paulus docet illud ipsum peccatum nobis cœlum claudere. In quam sententi am habemus multa Rom.1.1.Cor.5.6.Gal.5.Eph.5.1.Thess 4.Quin & Hebræis scribit Aposto lus Deum punire scortatores & adulteros. Dicit eadem de re Solomon Prou.5.
units.tr: Fourth, Paul teaches that this very sin shuts heaven against us. On this point we have many texts: Rom. 1; 1 Cor. 5, 6; Gal. 5; Eph. 5; 1 Thess. 4. Moreover, the apostle writes to the Hebrews that God punishes fornicators and adulterers. Solomon says the same on this matter in Prov. 5.

units.la: Quamobrem bene dicit Thessalonicensibus futura nuncians Apostolus diaboli inuen tum esse quod vsu matrimonij Antichristus interdicat.
units.tr: Therefore the apostle rightly says to the Thessalonians, announcing future things, that it is a device of the devil that Antichrist forbids the use of marriage.

units.la: Quæ cum ita sint, graviter peccant magistratus qui impura atque obscœna carmina, ob scœna dicteria, impudicas choreas, nedum vaga scorta aut etiam lupanaria quasi scortationi factas academias tolerant. Lactantius enim libr. 6.cap.23. lupanarium authorem facit ipsum diabolum. Vnde veteres Christiani adeo noluerunt esse lupanaria, vt Tertullianus in Apolo getico scribat lenones ethnicos de ipsorum pudicitia conqueri solitos fuisse. Et Iustinianus Nouell.Const.14.scribit, Ἐπὶ τὰ μὴ εἰ) πορνοβόσκως ἐν μηδενὶ τόπῳ τῆς τῶν Ῥωμαίων πολιτείας[?]. Igitur ij magistratus Athenienses,Corinthios,Romanos priscos magis, quàm Mosem diuinum legislatorem & veterem ecclesiam & Christianos principes imitati sunt, qui in suis ciuitatibus lupanaria fouent.
units.tr: Since these things are so, magistrates sin gravely who tolerate impure and obscene songs, lewd jokes, shameless dances, and still more wandering harlots, or even brothels, as if they were academies made for fornication. For Lactantius, book 6, chapter 23, makes the devil himself the author of brothels. Hence the ancient Christians were so unwilling to have brothels that Tertullian, in his Apologeticus, writes that pimps among the pagans used to complain about their own chastity. And Justinian, Novel 14, writes [Ἐπὶ τὰ μὴ εἶναι πορνοβόσκως ἐν μηδενὶ τόπῳ τῆς τῶν Ῥωμαίων πολιτείας] — that there should be no brothel-keeping in any place of the Roman state. Therefore those Athenian, Corinthian, and early Roman magistrates imitated the divine lawgiver Moses, the ancient Church, and Christian princes less than they did, those who keep brothels in their cities.

units.la: Quin ergo enitantur pij magistratus vt neque in vim, neque in impuram libidinem incidant suorum hominum corpora; verum vt ab omni malo præcipueq; impuritate & libidine sint immunia, ac Christo Iesu domino nostro sacra, cui sit honos in secula, Amen.
units.tr: Let the pious magistrates therefore strive that the bodies of their people fall neither into violence nor into impure lust, but rather that they be free from every evil, and above all from impurity and lust, and be consecrated to Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be honour for ever. Amen.

units.la: SERMO LVIII.
units.tr: SERMON 58.

units.la: 18 Ne inferas mercedem meretricis aut pretium canis in domum Domini Dei tui, in quocunque voto, quoniam abominatio est Domino Deo tuo utrumque.
units.tr: Thou shalt not bring the hire of a harlot, or the price of a dog, into the house of the Lord thy God for any vow: for even both these are abomination unto the Lord thy God.

units.la: 19 Ne morsum inferas fratri tuo fœnore pecuniæ, aut fœnore alicuius esculenti, imo fœnore cuiuscunque rei qua morderi possit.
units.tr: Thou shalt not lend upon usury to thy brother; usury of money, usury of victuals, usury of anything that is lent upon usury.

units.la: 20 Alienum mordebis fœnore, fratrem autem tuum non mordebis, vt felicites ac fortunet te Dominus Deus tuus in omni re ad quam extendis manum tuam, in ter ra ad quam tu proficisceris vt eam possideas.
units.tr: Unto a stranger thou mayest lend upon usury; but unto thy brother thou shalt not lend upon usury: that the Lord thy God may bless thee in all that thou settest thine hand to in the land whither thou goest to possess it.

units.la: 21 Quum votum voueris Domino Deo tuo, ne differas præstare illud, nam Dominus Deus tuus omnino requiret hoc à te, ne fiat tibi peccatum.
units.tr: When thou shalt vow a vow unto the Lord thy God, thou shalt not slack to pay it: for the Lord thy God will surely require it of thee; and it would be sin in thee.

units.la: 22 Si vero à fouendo cessas, non erit in te peccatum.
units.tr: But if thou shalt forbear to vow, it shall be no sin in thee.

units.la: 23 Si quid egressum est è labijs tuis, fac vt serues & præstes, sicut vouisti Domino Deo tuo sponte, & quem admodum locutus es ore tuo.
units.tr: That which is gone out of thy lips thou shalt keep and perform; even a freewill offering, according as thou hast vowed unto the Lord thy God, which thou hast promised with thy mouth.

units.la: 24 Quum veneris in vineam proximi tui, vuas comede pro animi tui desyderio, quantum satis est, at in vas tuum nihil reponas.
units.tr: When thou comest into thy neighbour's vineyard, then thou mayest eat grapes thy fill at thine own pleasure; but thou shalt not put any in thy vessel.

units.la: 25 Si veneris in segetem proximi tui, spicas manu tua decerpas, falcem autem segeti proximi tui ne admoveas.
units.tr: When thou comest into the standing corn of thy neighbour, then thou mayest pluck the ears with thy hand; but thou shalt not move a sickle unto thy neighbour's standing corn.

units.la: Quanquam ea ipsa, cuius nomine tantopere gloriamur, iustitia lineam rectam ducit, atque etiam ab hominibus vult teneri: tamen agitat nos habendi studium, ita vt à proximo nostro ad nos eam reflectamus. Ac si, quod solet, reclamet conscientia, nec desistat etiam post factum accusatione & querelis: videmur eam hoc ipso sopire pacareque posse, quod partem prædæ quantulamcunq; Deo offeramus. Quæ opinio nos etiam eò impietatis atque impudentiæ propellit, vt oppressionem proximi & vsuras impudenter exerceamus: ac tan dem sic in nobis crescat pleonexia, vt neq; suum rapere proximo, neq; deo factu votum habe re irritum nos pudeat.Sed & egeni laborant eodem morbo, qui locupletum hominum agros & prædia solent depopulari, inq; messes & vindemias alienas suam falcem mittunt. Quibus rebus omnibus hæc ipsa quam docet & commendat, negligitur ac violatur iustitia.
units.tr: Although that very justice, of which we boast so greatly, draws a straight line and also wishes to be kept by men, nevertheless the desire of having drives us, so that we turn it back from our neighbour to ourselves. And if conscience, as it usually does, protests, and does not cease even after the deed with accusation and complaints, we seem to be able to lull it to sleep and calm it by this very thing, that we offer some portion of the plunder, however small, to God. This opinion drives us further into impiety and shamelessness, so that we shamelessly practise oppression of our neighbour and usury; and at last covetousness grows in us to such a degree that we are not ashamed to snatch what is our neighbour's, nor to have made a vow that is void. But also the needy suffer from the same disease, who are accustomed to lay waste the fields and estates of the wealthy, and send their sickle into other men's harvests and vintages. In all these things justice, which this very law teaches and commends, is neglected and violated.

units.la: Ergo de rebus illis omnibus vt iustitiæ prophanatione Moses hoc loco disserit ac docet. 1. Deum his muneribus non ita corrumpi, vt placetur & conniueat ad malum. 2. Ab vsuris, vt iniquissima acquirendi ratione, prorsus abstinendum. 3. Vota reddenda, quæ promiseris. 4. Non diripienda bona proximi. De quibus sigillatim est dicendum.
units.tr: Therefore, concerning all these things, Moses in this place discusses and teaches the profaning of justice. (1) God is not so corrupted by these gifts that he is appeased and winks at evil. (2) Usury, as the most unjust way of acquiring, must be entirely abstained from. (3) Vows that you have promised must be paid. (4) The goods of a neighbour must not be plundered. These must be dealt with one by one.

units.la: Ac primum vetat, ne quis offerat pretium meretricis aut canis, quod hoc genus sacrificij Deus oderit. Verum mercedem meretricis vocat quæstum ex re nefaria, ut quæ suum corpus prostituat lucri gratia: pretium canis pecuniam ex re sordida atque abiecta comparatam.
units.tr: And first he forbids that anyone should offer "the price of a harlot or of a dog," because God hates this kind of sacrifice. But he calls the hire of a harlot the gain from a wicked business, since she prostitutes her body for the sake of gain; the price of a dog is money obtained from a filthy and abject thing.

units.la: Iam quoniam avaritia & vita impura Deo displicent, non potest is perinde ut homines impuris illis muneribus corrumpi, ut impune peccare quenquam sinat. Nobis in pretio sunt qui divites sunt, etsi maximè sint, ac semper fuerint infames. Verè enim dixit Ovidius, aurea nunc verè esse secula, quod plurimus auro fiat honos. At Deus homines impuros, avaros atque sordidos nihil hoc ipsum quod splendent aurum moratus, odit & punit.
units.tr: Now since covetousness and an impure life displease God, he cannot be corrupted by such impure gifts, as men are, so that he would allow anyone to sin with impunity. With us those who are rich are held in esteem, even though they are most infamous, and always have been. For Ovid truly said, "Now truly is the age of gold, since honour is paid to gold by the great majority." But God, who is not moved by the very gold that shines, hates and punishes impure, covetous and filthy men.

units.la: ...Quæ ergo malum infamia est, meretrices suam libidinem Magdalenæ vel Aphræ cultu de-[?]fendere? Moniales ubi scortatum evagantur beatæ virginis operam audere postulare? Quæ im-pudentia est papam ex meretricibus habere vectigal? Episcopos pati ut parochi usum scor-torum pecuniis sibi redimant, quando nato spurio solvunt illis nescio quam multam? Sed illis est lucri bonus odor ex re qualibet, & bene secum actum putant, si quam illius partem in usum suæ religionis vertant.
units.tr: ...What great evil is infamy, then, that harlots should defend their lust under the worship of Magdalen or Aphra? That nuns should dare to demand the service of the blessed Virgin, where they wander about in fornication? What shameless thing is it for the pope to have a tax from harlots? For bishops to suffer parish priests to redeem the use of whores with money for themselves, since they pay them some fine or other when a bastard is born? But they have a fine smell of profit from any matter whatever, and they think they have done well if they turn some part of it to the use of their religion.

units.la: ...Sic usurarij, mercenarij milites si suas iniquas ac sudore atque sanguine pauperum acqui-sitas opes plerasque sibi reponant, ac minimam earum portionem offerant Domino, bene se peccatum expiasse suum arbitrantur. Idem de illis esto iudicium, qui illo ipso quod verbum Domini bis terve in septimana audiverint, quicquid postea fecerint minus esse in vitio putant.
units.tr: ...So too, if usurers and mercenary soldiers lay up for themselves for the most part the wealth they have acquired unjustly, and by the sweat and blood of the poor, and offer the smallest portion of it to the Lord, they think they have atoned well for their sin. The same judgement is to be made of those who, because they have heard the word of the Lord twice or three times a week, think that whatever they afterwards do is less of a fault.

units.la: Bene profecto vulgo dici solet, Für fallen den schwang durch Gottes willen gen[?]. Esa. 1. Manus vestræ plenæ sanguinibus sunt, non audiam vos. Matth. 9. Misericordiam volo non sacrificium. In quo cernimus pietatem in mactandis bubus iis, quos ex furto, abnegato depositio, fraudato creditore, cæde & rapina, aliisque sceleribus acquisiveris, minimè consistere. Quod genus hominum recte compellat Philo cum in libro περὶ φυζυρίας[?] dicit, Deum hæc sacrifi-cia respuere, & Mosem ea vocare θυσίαν ἀναμιμνήσκουσαν ἁμαρτίαν[?]. Nec dubium est, quin his ceu monimentis iniquitatis Deus magis irritetur, quàm placetur. Quin ita statuendum est, Deum quoniam abhorret ab omni iniustitia, vel minimam eius portionem sibi velle conferri.
units.tr: It is indeed well said commonly among the people: "For what falls, the tail goes out for God's sake." Isa. 1. "Your hands are full of blood; I will not hear you." Matt. 9. "I desire mercy, not sacrifice." In which we see that piety does not consist at all in slaughtering those oxen which you have acquired by theft, by denying a deposit, by defrauding a creditor, by murder and robbery, and by other crimes. Philo rightly addresses this kind of men when, in his book On Exile [περὶ φυγῆς], he says that God rejects these sacrifices, and that Moses calls them "a sacrifice reminding of sin" [θυσίαν ἀναμιμνήσκουσαν ἁμαρτίαν]. And there is no doubt that God is provoked rather than appeased by these as memorials of iniquity. Indeed it must be established that God, since he abhors every injustice, does not wish even the smallest portion of it to be brought to him.

units.la: Ab usuris abstinendum sic docet, Nemorsum[?] inferas fratri tuo. Quibus verbis usuram vetat in fratres, permittit autem in exteros. Utrunq; considerandum.
units.tr: That we must abstain from usury he teaches thus: "Thou shalt not lend upon usury to thy brother." By these words he forbids usury toward brethren, but permits it toward strangers. Both points must be considered.

units.la: Deus instituit hominum inter se coniunctionem multam & variam: aut enim sunt coniugia, aut societates, aut commercia, aut civitates & amicitiæ cum privatæ tum publicæ. In his opus est æqualitate, ut ne cum alterius detrimento commodum queras tuum: animus co-ercetur lege naturæ: quod tibi non vis fieri, id alteri ne feceris. Igitur si te divitem roget egens, ut pecuniam des mutuam, iniquissimè est sic dare, ut tu fias ditior, is evadat pauperior: tunc enim pauperem non iuvas, sed mordes, oneras, præmis, is perditum. Qua de causa morsum appellat Moses. <bl>Schmirst in Nearmut/du Gyßt im Nyn/so wirt der schmerz noch größer.</bl>[?] Nos vocamus premere. <bl>Dem armen ligt Thand vndern faß/du trucfst im sy gar ab.</bl>[?]
units.tr: God has instituted among men a manifold and varied fellowship: for there are marriages, partnerships, commerce, and both private and public citizenships and friendships. In these there is need of equality, so that you do not seek your own advantage to another's loss: the mind is restrained by the law of nature: what you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another. Therefore, if a needy man asks you, being rich, to give him money as a loan, it is most unjust to give in such a way that you become richer and he becomes poorer; for then you do not help the poor man, but bite him, burden him, press him, and ruin him. For this reason Moses calls it "biting." "Schmirst in Nearmut, du Gyßt im Nyn, so wirt der Schmerz noch größer" (you smear it on in poverty, you pour on envy, so the pain grows greater). We call it pressing: "Dem armen ligt Thand vndern faß, du trucfst im sy gar ab" (you lay the poor man's hand under the cask, and press it off entirely).

units.la: Qua de causa iure divino interdictum est usuris omnibus: ut Exod. 22. Si mutuo dederis pecuniam populo meo pauperi, nempe qui tecum est, non eris ei tanquam exactor, neque incumbes ei morsu. Levit. 25. Si ad inopiam redactus fuerit frater tuus, corrobora eum, ut queat tecum vivere, ne fœnus accipias neve excessum, sed time Deum, ut tecum vivere possit frater tuus. Ezech. 22: fœnus & excessum accepisti & emolumentum tuum promovisti cum iniuria proximi tui. Et 2. Esdr. 5. Spiritus sanctus graviter in usurarios invehitur. Et Ps. 15. Ezec. 18. Bonorum atq; innocentium numero comprehenditur is qui ab usuris abstinet. Et Solomon Prov. 22. Mutuum accipiens dicitur usurario laborare.
units.tr: For this reason usury of every kind is forbidden by divine law, as in Exod. 22: "If you lend money to my people, to the poor among you, you shall not be to him as an exactor, neither shall you lay upon him usury." Lev. 25: "If thy brother be waxen poor, and fallen in decay with thee, then thou shalt relieve him, that he may live with thee: take thou no usury of him, or increase; but fear thy God, that thy brother may live with thee." Ezek. 22: "You have taken usury and increase, and you have increased your gain by the injury of your neighbour." And 2 Esdras 5: the Holy Spirit inveighs severely against usurers. And Ps. 15; Ezek. 18: among the number of good and innocent men is counted he who abstains from usury. And Solomon, Prov. 22: he who takes a loan is said to be a slave to the usurer.

units.la: Eodem pertinet quod Rom. legislatores usuris, quas videbant iniquas esse, modum posuere. Erant usuræ centesimæ, nauticæ: erant aliæ rursus hominum illustrium, aliæ plebeiorum.
units.tr: To the same purpose belongs the fact that the Roman lawgivers set a limit to usury, which they saw to be unjust. There were centesimal usuries, and maritime ones; there were again some for men of rank and others for plebeians.

units.la: Intelligendum est autem usuras esse in mutuo tantum, ac non etiam in emptione & contractibus reliquis. Quare dextrè & secundum ius & æquum est exponendum illud Christi dictum Luc. 6. Mutuum dantes nihil inde sperantes. Ibi enim Christus ex mutuo data pecunia, quæ mea esse non desiit, fructum nullum sperare me voluit: contra ex rebus locatis & venditis pretium debitum capere minimè vetuit. Ex quo potest intelligi fœnus esse in mutuo, & pugnare cum natura cumq; iure diuino. Belle etiam Ariftophani [illegible, ~4 letters] dicitur, quod fcropha fit alba fœcundius.
units.tr: It must be understood, however, that usury applies only to a loan, and not to purchase and other contracts. Therefore that saying of Christ in Luke 6, "lending, hoping for nothing again," must be expounded rightly and according to law and equity. For there Christ wished me to hope for no return from money lent, which does not cease to be mine; but he by no means forbade taking the due price from goods let out and sold. From this it can be understood that usury is in a loan, and that it is contrary to nature and to divine law. Aristophanes also is elegantly said to be "a white sow more fruitful" [illegible].

units.la: Sed in exteros permisit usuras Dominus.Nec desunt causæ. 1. Israelitæ suos alebant ipsi pauperes, ut ne cuiquá esset oneri, contra aliorum ipsi mendicis alimenta submin istrabant. Qua de causa poterant suum damnum hoc modo farcire. 2. Proselytos ut suos habebant: unde & eis Deus hoc indulsit, quasi iure ciuili consentaneum priuilegium.
units.tr: But the Lord permitted interest to be taken from foreigners, and there are reasons for this. (1) The Israelites themselves supported their own poor, so that no one would be a burden to them, whereas they provided food for the beggars of other peoples; for this reason they could make good their loss in this way. (2) They regarded proselytes as their own people, and so God granted them this as a privilege consistent with civil law.

units.la: Iam vero sublata lege destructaq; illa inter utrumque populum posita maceria per Christum omnes fratres inter se euaserunt, nec est reliquum peregrinitatis quicquam: unde sequitur rationem fratrum habendam atque omni generi hominum datum hoc esse diuinitus, ut ne quibus usuris opprimatur. Quod eo magis est enitendum, quod inimicis benefaciendum dixit Dominus, & Ioan.13. præceptum charitatis supra modum commendauit.
units.tr: Now, however, the law has been abolished and that wall of division between the two peoples has been broken down through Christ; all have become brothers to one another, and no remnant of foreignness is left. It follows that regard must be had for brothers, and that this has been given by God to every kind of man, so that no one is oppressed by any interest. This must be striven for all the more because the Lord said that we must do good to our enemies, and in John 13 he commended the command of love beyond measure.

units.la: Vota reddenda quæ promiseris. Si quid voueris. Aliquando solet usu venire, ut voueas, sed dein moram trahas, nec votum tempestiuè reddas: id facit auaritia. Votum quidem est religionis opus: sed qui Deum fefellerit, fallere quanto magis audebit homines? Ideo ceu exemplo iustitiæ Deo debitæ monstrat, quanta fide sit agendum cum proximo. Cras cras, inquit ille, sic omnis elabitur ætas. In omnibus rebus in primis; in religione malum est, quo maturè facto opus est, id subinde in posterum differre. De votis alias plura.
units.tr: "Vows must be paid which you have promised. If you have vowed anything." It sometimes happens that you make a vow, but then delay and do not pay the vow in good time; this is the work of avarice. A vow is indeed an act of religion, but whoever has deceived God, how much more will he dare to deceive men? So, as an example of the justice owed to God, he shows with what good faith we must deal with our neighbour. "Tomorrow, tomorrow," says that man, "thus all of life slips away." In all matters, and above all in religion, it is an evil to postpone from time to time what must be done as soon as possible. More on vows elsewhere.

units.la: De non diripiendis bonis proximi duæ sunt coniunctæ leges. Si quis vineam alterius ingressus uvas comedat non accusatur furti: contra si quis vase condita asportet. Si quis per fata iter faciens aristas vellicans, ut apostoli, non peccat ille quidem, nisi manipulos exportet.
units.tr: Concerning not plundering the goods of a neighbour there are two laws joined together. "If someone enters his neighbour's vineyard and eats grapes, he is not accused of theft"; but on the contrary, if someone carries off what has been preserved in a vessel. If someone, passing through a field, plucks ears of grain as the apostles did, he does not sin, provided he does not carry away sheaves.

units.la: Summa,Discimus proximi rebus utendum mediocriter, & haud secus ac illum velimus uti nostris. Peccatum est haud paruum quod ætate nostra quidam arbores, vites, & nihil non depopulari consueuere.
units.tr: In sum: we learn that our neighbour's property must be used moderately, and no differently from how we would wish our own to be used. It is no small sin, which in our age certain people are accustomed to do, to lay waste trees, vines, and everything else.

units.la: Sed ex his ll.omnibus intelligi potest charitatem utrinque feruandam esse:ac quemadmodum est diuitum pauperes iuuare, sic pauperum est diuitibus referre gratiam, nec velle esse oneri. Omnibus enim ex æquo charitatis lex posita est. Christo sit honos in secula, Amen.
units.tr: But from all these laws it can be understood that charity must be kept on both sides: just as it is the duty of the rich to help the poor, so it is the duty of the poor to return thanks to the rich and not to wish to be a burden. For the law of charity has been laid down equally for all. To Christ be honour for ever, Amen.

units.la: CAPUT XXIIII. SERMO LIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER 24. SERMON 59.

units.la: CVm quispiam ducit uxore, maritaueritq;, eam (sibi:) Euenit autem, ut hac nihil gratiæ in oculis eius impetret, ut si inueniat in ea rem aliquam fœdam, scribat ei libellum abscisionis, quem det ei in manum, & eijciat eam è domo sua.
units.tr: When a man takes a wife and marries her, and it happens that she finds no favour in his eyes, because he finds some indecent thing in her, he shall write her a bill of divorce, put it in her hand, and send her out of his house.

units.la: 2 Quæ exiens è domo eius, si abiens alij viro nupserit.
units.tr: (2) And when she has left his house and goes and becomes another man's wife,

units.la: 3 Ac is posterior maritus coeperit eam odisse, scripserit & ipse ei libellum abscisionis, tradiderit ei in manum eius, amandauerit eam de domo sua, aut si vir ille posterior, qui illam uxorem duxerat, mortuus fuerit.
units.tr: (3) and that second husband comes to hate her, and writes her a bill of divorce, puts it in her hand and sends her out of his house, or if that second husband who took her as his wife dies,

units.la: 4 Non poterit eam maritus prior, qui illam à se repudiarat, rursus ducere sibi uxorem, quandoquidem polluta est. Nam abominatio hæc est coram Domino, & ne feceris peccare terram, quam Dominus Deus tibi dat, ut hæreditate eam possideas.
units.tr: (4) her former husband, who divorced her, may not take her back as his wife, since she has been defiled. For that is an abomination before the LORD, and you shall not bring sin upon the land which the LORD your God gives you as an inheritance.

units.la: 5 Quum duxerit quispiam uxorem nouam, ne egrediatur in militiam, nec quid quam aliud ei iniungatur, sed immunis sit pro domo sua anno uno, lætetur, cum uxore sua quam duxit.
units.tr: (5) When a man has taken a new wife, he shall not go out to war, nor shall any other duty be laid upon him; he shall be free at home for one year and shall bring joy to the wife whom he has taken.

units.la: UEMADMODUM Deus & suapte natura purus & sanctus, & erga suas creaturas iustus & benignus est: sic à nobis qui cupimus illi coniungi & sociari, postulat, ut ipsi quidem puri, innocentes, sancti, in alios autem homines iusti benigniq; sumus. Quas ad res impelliunt nos etiam huius coniunctionis sacramenta baptismus & circumcisio: quibus monemur, ut impuros motus putemus, & sordes abluamus: tum ut socios fœderis propter ipsum coniunctionis huius caput amplectamur. Sed quoniam à casta sanctaque uita pruritu carnis & libidine, ab iustitia & misericordia vi pleonexias abstrahimur: libidini quidem matrimonio, auaritiæ vero legibus iustitiam & misericordiam urgentibus medicinam affert. Quibus de rebus Moses ait hoc cap. nempe de diuortio primum diffe-rens, itemq; de rebus ad matrimonium pertinentibus: tum leges de seruanda erga omnes iu-stitia & beneficentia affert.
units.tr: Just as God, who is pure and holy by his very nature, is also just and kind towards his creatures, so he requires of us, who desire to be joined and united to him, that we ourselves be pure, innocent and holy, and just and kind towards other people. The sacraments of this union, baptism and circumcision, also urge us to this: they remind us to regard impure motions as defilement and to wash away filth, and so to embrace as fellow members of the covenant those who share this very head of the union. But since we are drawn away from a chaste and holy life by the itch of the flesh and lust, and from justice and mercy by the violence of greed [πλεονεξίας], marriage offers a remedy for lust, and the laws that press justice and mercy offer one for greed. On these matters Moses speaks in this chapter: first on divorce, and likewise on things pertaining to marriage; then he sets out laws requiring justice and kindness towards all.

units.la: Jam de matrimonio sic agit, ut primum dicat de diuortio, tum de noui mariti priuilegijs.
units.tr: Now he treats of marriage in such a way that he first speaks of divorce, and then of the privileges of a new husband.

units.la: Ac primum quidem, quod ad diuortia pertinet, intelligendum est: ad puram castamq; vi-tam, qualem Deus postulat, in primis requiri matrimonium: quando iis, qui se continere non possunt, hoc remedium præbet apostolus in 1.Cor.7.& Hebræis scribens ait omnibus genti-bus sanctum habitum matrimonium.
units.tr: As to the first point, concerning divorces, it must be understood that marriage is chiefly required for a pure and chaste life such as God demands. God offers this remedy to those who cannot contain themselves, as the apostle shows in 1 Cor. 7; and writing to the Hebrews he says that marriage is an honourable state among all peoples [Heb. 13].

units.la: Sed cum in matrimonio, ut alijs rebus omnibus, accidant mala, culpa vitioq; coniugum, his ipsis est etiam consulendum. Ex quo diuortia nascuntur. Quæ non lege commendantur, sed ne eueniant deteriora, permittuntur. Veluti medicus in diætæ præscriptione aliud suadet edendum, aliud solum permittit, si se æger nequeat continere: in quo non ægri sanitatem, sed appetitum respicit medicus. Eodem modo Deus permittit diuortia, non quod hæc ei tam topere placeant, sed quod ea postulat nostra durities.
units.tr: But since, in marriage as in all other things, evils arise through the fault and vice of the spouses, provision must be made for these very evils, and from them divorces arise. These are not commended by the law, but are permitted lest worse things happen. Just as a physician, in prescribing a diet, advises one food to be eaten and only permits another if the patient cannot restrain himself, so the physician looks not to the health of the sick man but to his appetite. In the same way God permits divorces, not because they please him so much, but because our hardness of heart requires them.

units.la: Quod Dominus docet Matth.19.Mar.10.Luc.16. Eorum summa ac caput est. Diuortia Deo displicere: primum quia coniunctionem hanc maris & fœminæ primus ipse sanxerit ac propterea velit esse stabilem: tum quod uni masculo unam fœminam & uni contra fœminæ masculum unum produxerit: tertio, quod in carnem, id est & arctam & perpetuam societatem coniunctos velit: quarto, quod hanc societatem reliquis omnibus anteponendam esse duxerit, ac propterea parentes potius deserendos esse censuerit quam coniugem. Nihil igitur coniuges à coniugibus debet separare.
units.tr: The Lord teaches this in Matt. 19, Mark 10 and Luke 16, and this is the sum and head of the matter: divorce displeases God. First, because he himself first ordained this union of male and female and therefore wills it to be stable; second, because he made one man for one woman and one woman for one man; third, because he wills them to be joined into one flesh, that is, into a close and perpetual fellowship; fourth, because he judged this fellowship to be preferred above all others, and therefore thought that parents rather than a spouse should be forsaken. Therefore nothing should separate spouses from one another.

units.la: Sed tamen aliquibus de causis diuortia permittuntur, ut quod Christus aperte de diuor-tio loquitur ob stuprum concedendo. Nam & Germanis adulterium dicitur [illegible, ~5 letters] quod matrimonium eo ipso scissum sit ac violatum. Nec obstant à papistis detorti Christi atq; Pau-li loci. Dein & in impari religione quid facto opus sit docet apostolus 1.Cor.7, Præclarè enim dictum est abAmbrosio non deberi coniugij reuerentiam ei, qui coniugij authorem horreat. Accedit his etiam quod ubi liberorum procreationis & sedandæ libidinis, quarum rerum causa coniugium institutum est, spes nulla possit esse, ibi quoque moderationem illam esse adhibendam.
units.tr: Yet for some causes divorces are permitted, as when Christ clearly speaks of divorce, granting it on account of fornication. For among the Germans adultery is called [illegible] because a marriage is thereby broken and violated. Nor do the passages of Christ and Paul twisted by the Papists stand in the way. Moreover, the apostle teaches what must be done in a marriage with someone of a different religion, 1 Cor. 7; for it has been well said by Ambrose that reverence for marriage is not owed to one who abhors the author of marriage. To these is added that where there can be no hope of children's procreation and of quieting lust, for whose sake marriage was instituted, that moderation must be applied there too.

units.la: Ex quibus omnibus est perspicuum hoc Deum velle, ut firma sint coniugia, sed si graues causæ postulent diuortia postulantibus non negare.
units.tr: From all these things it is plain that God wills marriages to be firm, but if grave causes require it, divorce is not to be denied to those who ask for it.

units.la: In eam sententiam scribit etiam hoc loco Moses. 1. Si nihil gratiæ in oculis, hoc est, ubi nulla amoris synceri spes est reliqua, omniaq; tentata nil proficiunt: ad diuortium ceu ultimum & quidem acerbissimum remedium confugitur.
units.tr: Moses also writes to this effect in this passage. (1) "If she finds no favour in his eyes": that is, where no hope of sincere love remains, and all attempts have failed, recourse is had to divorce as the last and indeed most bitter remedy.

units.la: 2. Si fœdam rem aliquam inueniat, quam ערות דבר[?] vocat, eaq; cauet, neq; immerito oderit uxorem, ac tantum si dedecus sit aut adulterium.
units.tr: (2) "If he finds some indecent thing": which he calls [ערות דבר], a thing of nakedness, and which he guards against; and he may justly hate his wife only if it is a shameful matter or adultery.

units.la: 3. Scribat libellum repudij: quod fiebat publicè & æstimante causam magistratu: neque enim par est maritum ipsum esse sibi iudicem.
units.tr: (3) "He shall write a bill of divorce": which was done publicly, with the magistrate judging the cause; for it is not fitting that the husband himself should be his own judge.

units.la: 4. Non recipiat repudiatam: quo leuitatem illam prohibet, qua fit ut instar nundinationis alicuius sint & habeantur matrimonia. Quod cauere cum magistratus debent, tum etiam singuli homines.
units.tr: (4) "He shall not take her back": by which he forbids that levity by which marriages become, and are held to be, like a kind of bargaining in the market. Magistrates ought to guard against this, and so should individuals too.

units.la: De priuilegio noui mariti lex eodem ipsa quoq; pertinet, ut matrimonia sancta ac firma sint atque in amore mutuo coniugum amborum animi cum bene coalescant, tum etiam piè conquiescant. Interest enim reip,pia,casta,pacataq; esse matrimonia.
units.tr: The law also concerns the privilege of a new husband, so that marriages may be holy and firm, and that the minds of both spouses, being joined well in mutual love, may also rest devoutly. For it matters to the commonwealth that marriages be pious, chaste and peaceful.

units.la: Igitur marito noua concedit legislator annua à militia vacationem. 1. Ut animi illorum non seiungantur, sed usu vitæ continuato roboretur amor. Suspiciones enim & rumores, & obtrectationes, & alia plurima solent illum vel soluere vel saltem minuere inter absentes.
units.tr: Therefore the lawgiver grants a new husband a year's exemption from military service. (1) So that their minds are not separated, but love is strengthened by the continued practice of living together. For suspicions, rumours, detraction and many other things are wont to loosen this love, or at least to lessen it, between those who are absent.

units.la: 2. Ut ne sint in acie, quibus animus sit in cubili. Sunt enim ad tuendam patriam inepti, qui respiciunt aliud. Nostri homines defertis uxoribus atq; liberis militatum abeunt. Sed eni-tendum est omnibus cum liberorum atq; coniugum, causa tum vero patriæ conseruandæ, atque adiuuandæ gratia matrimonijs bene conseruandis studere, Amen.
units.tr: (2) So that those whose mind is in the bed are not in the battle line; for those who look to something else are unfit to defend the fatherland. Our own people go off to war leaving their wives and children behind. But everyone must strive, for the sake of children and spouses and then indeed for the preservation and support of the fatherland, to keep marriages well preserved. Amen.

units.la: SERMO LX.
units.tr: SERMON LX.

units.la: 6 Nemo pignorum loco accipiat inferiorem et superiorem molam, nam ĩ[?] vitam oppigneranit[?].
units.tr: 6 No one shall take the lower or the upper millstone in pledge, for that would be pledging his life.

units.la: 7 Si deprehensus fuerit quispiam[?], qui fuerit furatus animam ex fratribus suis de filijs Israel, & ad opus suum fuerit eo usus, aut vendiderit eum, morietur fur talis exurefq; malum è medio tui.
units.tr: 7 If anyone is caught stealing a man from among his brothers, the children of Israel, and makes use of him as a slave or sells him, that thief shall die, and you shall purge the evil from your midst.

units.la: 8 Sis cautus in macula lepræ, obseruaq; diligenter, facietisq; juxta omnia, quæ docuerint vos sacerdotes Leuitici generis: quemadmodum præscripsi eis, sic obseruabitis, & facietis.
units.tr: 8 Take heed in the case of leprosy, watch diligently, and do according to all that the Levitical priests teach you. Just as I commanded them, so you shall observe and do.

units.la: 9 Meminisse oportet quid Dominus Deus tuus fecerit Mariæ in itinere cum egrederemini ex Ægypto.
units.tr: 9 Remember what the Lord your God did to Miriam on the journey when you came out of Egypt.

units.la: 10 Quum mutuo dederis aliquid proximo tuo, ne introeas domum eius, vt pi-gnus illinc tollas.
units.tr: 10 When you lend something to your neighbour, do not go into his house to take his pledge from there.

units.la: 11 Sed sta foris, & vir ille cui tu mutuo dedisti, proferat ad te pignus foras.
units.tr: 11 Stand outside, and the man to whom you lent shall bring the pledge out to you.

units.la: 12 Quod si vir huiusmodi pauper est, non dormies in pignore eius.
units.tr: 12 But if the man is poor, you shall not sleep with his pledge.

units.la: 13 Omnino reddes ei pignus quum solo occidit, vt is dormiat in vestimento suo, beneq;[?] tibi ac fausta imprecetur: atq; id justitia tibi erit coram Domino Deo tuo.
units.tr: 13 You shall certainly return the pledge to him when the sun goes down, so that he may sleep in his garment and bless you; and this will be righteousness for you before the Lord your God.

units.la: 14 Ne neges aut ui retineas mercenario pauperi & inopi mercedem, siue fit de fratribus tuis, siue de peregrinis tuis, qui sunt in terra tua, atq; intra portas tuas.
units.tr: 14 You shall not withhold or keep by force the wages of a poor and needy hired man, whether he is one of your brothers or one of the strangers who are in your land and within your gates.

units.la: 15 Die suo dabis ei mercedem suam, neq; sol occidat super eum, quoniam pauper est, & ad eam (mercedem) attollit animum suum, ne contra te ad Dominum clamet, & cedat tibi in peccatum.
units.tr: 15 You shall give him his wages on the same day, and the sun shall not go down on it, for he is poor and sets his heart on it; otherwise he will cry out against you to the Lord, and it will be sin for you.

units.la: CUm & sacrarum literarum lectione, & jure naturæ, & ipso rerum usu cognitum habea-mus hominem homini ut consolationi sit, & saluti procreatum esse: sane lex charitatis & misericordiæ erga proximum debebat nobis inolescere, veluti cuncta animalia, quas ad res efficiendas procreata sunt, ad eas gerendas propendent mirificè.
units.tr: Since we know, both from the reading of the sacred letters, from the law of nature, and from the very use of things, that man was born to be a comfort and a help to man, the law of charity and mercy towards our neighbour ought truly to have grown in us, just as all the animals, which were created for their own tasks, are wonderfully inclined to carry them out.

units.la: Sed quoniam in nobis, ut Paulus ait, alia lex est & voluntas, quæ pugnat cum voluntate & proposito Dei, quæq; nos ipsos solum respicit, atq; in nostram ipsorum & dignitatem & u-tilitatem & voluptatem intenta est: sequitur ut ipsi à proximi studio ad nostra commoda pro movenda convertamur, nostriq; commodi gratia proximum non solum, pro eo ac par est, beneficio nullo, verum etiam contumelia atque damno afficiamus.
units.tr: But since, as Paul says, there is in us another law and will, which fights against the will and purpose of God, and which looks only to ourselves and is bent on our own dignity, advantage and pleasure, it follows that we are turned away from concern for our neighbour towards our own interests; and for the sake of our own advantage we injure our neighbour, not only by withholding the benefit he rightly deserves, but even by insult and loss.

units.la: Quibus malis atq; vitijs declinandis Deus & in novo & in veteri Testamento legem di-lectionis adhibitis alijs atq; alijs præceptiunculis explanat, eoq; ipso adulterij, furti, falsi testimonij, concupiscentiæ pestem repellit. Et earum quidem legum aliquas etiam hoc cap.com memorat, ut de duabus dictum est nuper: quinq; refert in præsentia.
units.tr: To avert these evils and vices, God, in both the New and the Old Testament, explains the law of love by means of various precepts, and by this very means he drives away the plague of adultery, theft, false witness and covetousness. Indeed, this chapter also records some of these laws, as was said recently about two of them; at present it mentions five.

units.la: Prima, Nemo vice pignoris accipiat inferiorem & superiorem molarem: nam is vitam oppignoratur. Qua lege cauit ne creditor nimio habendi studio debitorem bonis omnibus prorsus exuat, & ad mendicitatem redigat, sed eius misericordia tangatur.
units.tr: The first: No one shall take the lower or the upper millstone as a pledge, for that is pledging a life. By this law he provides that a creditor, in his eagerness to possess, does not strip a debtor of all his goods and reduce him to beggary, but is moved by pity for him.

units.la: Est autem pignus id de quo inter creditorem & debitorem convenit, ut sit pro debito obligatum, §.item Seruiana Instit.de actio.
units.tr: Now a pledge is that thing about which creditor and debtor agree, that it be bound as security for the debt; see the paragraph "item Serviana" in the Institutes, on actions.

units.la: Jam pignore sibi cavere velle jure divino minimè prohibitum est: cur enim alius fruetur, alius damnum pateretur? sed modum in pignoribus accipiendis ponit, nempe ut ne molarem, quo quis victum sibi querit, pignori capias: quare? quia victum seu vitam oppignorat, unde nec sibi suisq; sustentando, nec tibi solvendo foret.
units.tr: Indeed, to wish to secure oneself by a pledge is by no means forbidden by divine law; why should one person enjoy the benefit and another suffer the loss? But he sets a limit on the taking of pledges, namely that you may not take as a pledge the millstone by which a man seeks his food. Why? Because it pledges his food, or rather his life, and so he could neither support himself and his family nor pay you back.

units.la: In quo videmus quantam Dominus misericordiam atq; æquitatem postulet. Vult credi tori cautum, sed ita ut ne debitori sit exitio. Quid enim si molam molitor, currum atq; equos auriga, fabricam faber oppignoret, habebit reliquum? Sic si nimijs impensis, si carcere, si ana-themate, si deniq; exilio debitores opprimas, quæ hæc est immanitas?
units.tr: In this we see how much mercy and equity the Lord requires. He wills that the creditor be careful, but in such a way that it does not ruin the debtor. For what if a miller pledged his millstone, a charioteer his chariot and horses, a craftsman his workshop; would he have anything left? So if you crush debtors with excessive expenses, with prison, with excommunication, and finally with exile, what cruelty is this?

units.la: Sed quemadmodum nostrum, hoc est, singulorum interest debitoribus parcere: sic ma-gistratuum est illorum versutiam & perfidiam legibus coercere. Atq; hoc & alibi sacræ literæ præcipiunt, & jura civilia passim statuunt. Unde extant in ff.&C.multi in eam sententiam tituli.
units.tr: But just as it is in the interest of us all, that is, of each individual, to spare debtors, so it is the duty of magistrates to restrain the craftiness and treachery of such men by law. This the sacred letters also enjoin elsewhere, and the civil laws everywhere establish. Hence there are many titles in the Digest and the Code to this effect.

units.la: Secunda, Si quis deprehensus fuerit furatus animam ex, &c. Furti legem hac exponit, qua plagium quoq; prohiberi docet. Fur graviter peccat cum aurum, argentum, vestes, alia bona aufert: sed si quis filium aut filiam auferat, non dupli quadrupliuè, sed capitis pœnam subit.
units.tr: Second: If anyone is caught stealing a man, and so on. Here he explains the law against theft, by which he also teaches that kidnapping is forbidden. A thief sins gravely when he carries off gold, silver, clothing or other goods; but if someone carries off a son or a daughter, the penalty is not double or fourfold but death.

units.la: Nam eum qui liber est, seruum facere crimen est inprimis detestandum. Est enim 1. miserrima res seruitus. 2. Israelitam, Dei fœderatum cum turpe tum miserum seruũ fieri. 3. Eum qui fit ex Ægypto diuinitus redemptus in hominis seruitutem redigi. Sed ipse etiam hoc ex se potest æstimare plagiarius, qui libertate seruitutem ægre sibi comperaret. Quamobrem Jure ciuili quoq; hæc est capitalis pœna: quanquam judici concedatur, ut secundum delicti modū eam possit vel mitigare vel intendere, l. ultima. ff. ad l. sauia. de plagiar.
units.tr: For to make a free man a slave is a crime above all to be detested. For (1) slavery is a most wretched condition; (2) for an Israelite, a member of God's covenant, to become a slave is both shameful and miserable; (3) and for one who was redeemed by God out of Egypt to be reduced to the slavery of a man. The kidnapper can judge this for himself from his own case, since he would find it hard to obtain slavery for himself in exchange for freedom. For this reason the civil law also imposes capital punishment, although the judge is permitted to lessen or increase the penalty according to the measure of the offence; see the last law, in the Digest, on the Fabian law, concerning kidnapping.

units.la: Cæterum Doctores circa §. omnes autem actio. Inst. de actio. docent eodem etiam pœnæ genere plecti eos, qui corruperint alicuius liberos. Quo referes etiam ff. & C. tit. de seruo corrupto: dein & nostros plagiarios, qui in malis abducunt homines parentibus & magistratibus inuitis: qui malis moribus juuentutem inficiunt, qui Christo dicatos homines vel Mammonæ, vel idolis, vel Antichristianis ordinibus sacros faciunt.
units.tr: Moreover, the teachers, on the paragraph "omnes autem actio" in the Institutes, on actions, teach that those who corrupt the children of another are punished by the same kind of penalty. To this belongs also the Digest and Code title on the corrupted slave; then also our kidnappers, who in wickedness lead men away from their parents and magistrates against their will; who infect youth with bad morals; who make men dedicated to Christ sacred to Mammon, or to idols, or to antichristian orders.

units.la: Tertia, Sis cautus in lepræ macula, &c. Hac lege docet etiam publicè suum cuíque saluum permittere: ut si quid acciderit quo possit infici proximus, judex ne parcat uni cum periculo totius ciuitatis.
units.tr: Third: Take heed in the case of leprosy, etc. By this law he teaches also that public safety is to be preserved for each person: so that if anything happens by which a neighbour could be infected, the judge should not spare one person at the risk of the whole city.

units.la: Exempli gratia lepram ponit. Sunt Leuit. xi. 13. &c. Leges de cognoscenda judicandaque lepra quibus est standum: nempe ut quicunq; sint hac infecti excludantur, nec ulli parcatur.
units.tr: He gives leprosy as an example. See Leviticus 13 and following, the laws concerning how leprosy is to be recognised and judged, which must be observed: namely, that all who are infected with it be shut out, and no one spared.

units.la: Exemplo fit Maria soror summi ducis Mosis, cui is minimè pepercerat.
units.tr: Miriam, the sister of the great leader Moses, serves as an example, whom he did not spare at all.

units.la: Accidit lepra judicio Domini ceu quoddam infortunij, & tamen vult nemini quicquam remitti, quia plus est pluribus, quàm uni tribuendum.
units.tr: Leprosy comes by the judgement of the Lord, as if it were some misfortune, and yet he wills that nothing be remitted to anyone, because more must be given to the many than to one.

units.la: Ita in vitijs, ut scortatione, adulterijs blasphemijs nemini parcendum est, ne contagio morbi latius serpente pluribus ingruat malū. Qua de re præclarè est ad Corinthios scriptum à Paulo præcipiente ut incestum nebulonem suo cœtu eijcerent.
units.tr: So in the case of vices, such as fornication, adultery, and blasphemy, no one must be spared, lest the evil, spreading through contagion, attack many more. Concerning this, Paul wrote to the Corinthians, commanding them to cast out the incestuous wretch from their assembly.

units.la: Discimus quoq; lepram esse pœnam inobedientiæ eius, qua verbum Dei despicitur, ut in Maria & Ozia.
units.tr: We also learn that leprosy is the punishment for disobedience, by which the word of God is despised, as in the case of Miriam and Uzziah.

units.la: Sed & standum est magistratuum judicio, & secundum jus & æquum judicandum. Cæterùm bonas leges negligere & secundum malas viuere perinde est in vitio.
units.tr: But one must also abide by the judgement of the magistrates, and judge according to what is right and fair. Moreover, to neglect good laws and to live according to bad ones is equally a fault.

units.la: Quarta, Cum mutuo dederis aliquid proximo tuo, &c. Iterum hac etiam lege commendat bonitatem & misericordiam, quam diuites in primis deceat seruare. Qui mutuo dat & sibi cauet pignore, is non ingressus domum accipiat vice pignoris quod voluerit: sed & pignus ei reddat, si illo debitorem magnopere egere videat.
units.tr: Fourth: When you lend something to your neighbour, etc. Again, by this law he commends kindness and mercy, which the rich above all ought to practise. He who lends money and secures himself with a pledge should not enter the house and take as a pledge whatever he wishes; but he should return the pledge to him, if he sees that the debtor is in great need of it.

units.la: Et hæc facienti benedictionem Domini pollicetur Moses. Magnum profectò præmium & dignum quod respiciamus. Solent enim plærique pauperes, obscuros, exules, juuenes, orphanos propterea non juuare, quod ab his spem remunerationis habeant nullam: at quantam habeant, qui per fidem vident quæ beneficentiæ præmia sint in cœlis reposita, cum hic ipse tum alij complures sacræ Scripturæ loci docent. Est & nostrum prouerbium minimè falsum:
units.tr: And Moses promises the blessing of the Lord to those who do this. Surely a great reward, and one worth regarding. For most people are accustomed not to help the poor, the obscure, the exiles, the young and the orphans, for the reason that they have no hope of any return from them; but how great a reward those have who see by faith what rewards of kindness are laid up in heaven, both this passage and many other places of sacred Scripture teach. There is also a proverb of ours that is by no means false:

units.la: <bl>Der jung stier Fouffi[?]/jung lüt rousst[?]/ Dem trüyt und wachst all tag unglück</bl>. At quemadmodum iniuriarū, sic etiam officiorū sunt bene memores, & cum adoleuerint gratiam referunt. Orphani vero si nihil aliud possunt, hoc saltè dant operâ, ut te Deo precibus commendent.
units.tr: The young ox ... young folk ... misfortune grows and wakes against them every day. But just as they are mindful of injuries, so too they are mindful of kindnesses, and when they grow up they repay them. Orphans, if they can do nothing else, at least give this much: they commend you to God in their prayers.

units.la: Quinta, Ne neges aut vi retineas mercenario pauperi aut inopi, &c. Hæc lex & ipsa docet ju stitiam, nempe ut debitam mercenario mercedem soluas. In quo sic diligenter versatur, ut & cui & quomodo, qua re soluas ostendat.
units.tr: Fifth, You shall not withhold or keep by force from a hired poor man or a needy one, etc. This law also teaches justice, namely that you must pay the hired man the wage he is owed. It deals with this so carefully that it shows to whom, how and with what you should pay.

units.la: Cui, inquit, mercenario, qui suam operam locauit tibi, quiq; abs te conductus est: pauperi & inopi, qui nihil aliàs habet propterea q; est mercenarius quia pauper est & laboribus acqui rit, & cui vel hoc ipso quod æget est dandum: siue sit de fratribus, siue de peregrinis. Sæpe enim si nostras sit ægrè ferimus repeti, & putamus non debere solui: si peregrinus despicimus, & putamus eum debere hoc ipso quod illum nostris negotijs adhibuimus contentum esse. Magna vero superbia atque stoliditas.
units.tr: To the hired man, he says, who has let his labour to you and has been engaged by you; to the poor and needy, who has nothing else and is therefore a hired man because he is poor and earns by his labour, and to whom this very need makes payment due; whether he is of your brothers or of the strangers. For often, if we are asked to pay, we take it badly and think that it need not be paid; if he is a stranger, we despise him and think that, since we have employed him in our business, he ought to be content with that alone. This is great pride and stupidity.

units.la: <bl>Gibst jm den lon nit/ so machst jnn sü ein[?] fronarbeiter/ Der aber ein taglöner ist.</bl>
units.tr: If you do not give him his wage, you make him a forced labourer, though he is a day-labourer.

units.la: Quomodo, die suo dabis illi mercedem suam, neq; sol occidat super eum, &c. Quo docet mercedem & fideliter & tempestiuè reddendā esse. Sunt qui malint uniuersas simul accipere, quàm sigillatim singulas: his, si ita videatur, obsequi in vitio minimè fuerit: at differre & egentibus & requirentibus solutionem graue est. Summa, sic soluas ut is aliquem ex eo fructum sentiat ac percipiat.
units.tr: How? On the same day you shall give him his wage, nor shall the sun go down upon him, etc. By this he teaches that wages must be paid both faithfully and in good time. Some would rather receive all their wages at once than in separate instalments; to humour them in this, if it seems so, is by no means wrong. But to put off payment is serious, both for the needy and for those who ask for it. In short, pay in such a way that he feels and receives some benefit from it.

units.la: Facilè est multis instruere conuiuia, domos ædificare, vestibus luxuriari, prædia atque agros colere: interea vero carent & egent suis debitis mercatores, artifices, mercenarius. Verum hoc ipsum etiam pœna peccati illorum est, qui depravatas merces vendunt, parum fideles operas nauant.
units.tr: It is easy for many to furnish feasts, build houses, indulge in fine clothes, and cultivate estates and fields; yet meanwhile merchants, craftsmen and the hired man go without what is owed them and are in want. But this very thing is also the punishment of those who sell spoiled goods and perform their work carelessly.

units.la: Quare, Causas duplices reddit, quæ & ex mercenario & ex te nascantur. Mercenarius pauper est, ac propterea diuinitus in conspectum tuum deductus vt illum, si laborare nequeat, ad iuuares. Iam cum tam bono, probo, graui, excelsoque sit praeditus animo vt labore potius, quàm mendicando velit victum parare, quanto est dignior auxilio? quanto est dignior cui quod debes reddas?
units.tr: Wherefore, he gives a twofold cause, which arises both from the hired man and from you. The hired man is poor, and therefore has been brought before your eyes by God's providence, so that you may help him if he cannot work. Now since he is endowed with so good, upright, serious and lofty a spirit that he prefers to earn his living by labour rather than by begging, how much more worthy is he of help? How much more worthy is he to whom you should render what you owe?

units.la: Deinceps, inquit, ad mercedem attollit animam suam: hoc est, quemadmodum tu tuis ex prouentibus atq; censibus, sic ex mercede merita victum ille sibi suum habet: tibi in censibus & prouentibus annuis, illi in mercede merita spes victus sui est posita. Ac mirum est artifices quibus ingrati quidam diu debitas mercedes non soluunt posse vitam suam suorumq; fuften tare: cum in eo sit illis sui victus spes omnis, quo tam diu carent.
units.tr: Next, he says, he sets his soul upon the wage: that is, just as you have your living from your yields and revenues, so he has his living from the wage he has earned. For you have your hope of living in annual revenues and yields, and he has his hope of living placed in the wage he has earned. And it is remarkable that craftsmen, whom some ungrateful people do not pay their due wages for a long time, can sustain their own lives and those of their families, when all their hope of living lies in that which they go so long without.

units.la: Ex te verò qui debes, hoc est, quod consideres, Ne contrate ad Dominum clamet & cedat tibi in peccatum: [?]st ein schreyende sünd. Illius vxor & liberi fame cruciati lugent, & clamant ad Deum: is auditis illis indignatur & punit. Ex quibus omnibus discimus quod Paul. Ro. 13. do-cet, suum cuiq; esse reddendum, proximum diligendum. Id Deus faxit, Amen.
