units.tr: But from you, who owe it, this is what you should consider: lest he cry out to the Lord against you, and it become sin for you. It is a crying sin. His wife and children, tormented by hunger, mourn and cry out to God; when He hears them, He is indignant and punishes. From all these things we learn what Paul teaches in Rom. 13., that each is to be given what is his due, and the neighbour is to be loved. May God grant this, Amen.

units.la: SERMO LXI.
units.tr: Sermon 61.

units.la: 16 Non interficientur patres pro filijs, nec filij occidantur pro patribus, sed quis- que pro peccato suo interficiatur.
units.tr: 16 The fathers shall not be put to death for the children, nor the children put to death for the fathers; every man shall be put to death for his own sin.

units.la: 17 Ne declines iudicium peregrini & pupilli, neq; pignoris loco vestem viduae accipias.
units.tr: 17 Thou shalt not pervert the judgment of the stranger, nor of the fatherless; nor take the widow's raiment to pledge.

units.la: 18 Quin potius meminerit quod et tu seruus fuisti in Ægypto, & redemit te Dominus Deus tuus inde: idcirco praecipio tibi vt hanc rem facias.
units.tr: 18 But thou shalt remember that thou wast a bondman in Egypt, and the LORD thy God redeemed thee thence: therefore I command thee to do this thing.

units.la: 19 Quum messueris messem tuam in agro tuo, & oblitus fueris manipuli in agro, ne reuertaris vt illum tollas, sed erit peregrini, pupilli & viduae, vt felicitet & locupletet te Dominus Deus tuus in omni opere manus tuae.
units.tr: 19 When thou cuttest down thine harvest in thy field, and hast forgotten a sheaf in the field, thou shalt not go again to fetch it: it shall be for the stranger, for the fatherless, and for the widow: that the LORD thy God may bless thee in all the work of thine hands.

units.la: 20 Quum strinxeris oleam tuam, ne diligentius stringas post te: peregrini, pupilli & viduae erit.
units.tr: 20 When thou beatest thine olive tree, thou shalt not go over the boughs again: it shall be for the stranger, for the fatherless, and for the widow.

units.la: 21 Quum vindemiaueris vineam tuam, ne racemationem facias post te, erit peregrini, pupilli & viduae.
units.tr: 21 When thou gatherest the grapes of thy vineyard, thou shalt not glean it afterward: it shall be for the stranger, for the fatherless, and for the widow.

units.la: 22 Et meminerit te quoq; seruum fuisse in terra Ægypti, idcirco ego praecipio tibi, vt hanc rem facias.
units.tr: 22 And thou shalt remember that thou wast a bondman in the land of Egypt: therefore I command thee to do this thing.

units.la: CVm homines, vt nuper dictum est, sic à Deo procreati sint, vt non solum non damno, sed etiam beneficijs mutuum afficere debeant: sanè mirum non est Deum & ne iniurij in nos inuicem simus prohibere, & vt alius alium beneficijs afficiat praecipere. Ac certè laudi summæ ducitur non solum iniuria neminem afficere, verumetiam in omnes esse beneficium: vnde & iustitia cum beneficentia principem in virtutum choro locum tenent, quod hæc iniurijs ab stineat ipsa, atque etiam his prohibeat alios, illa verò non solum consilijs, verumetiam opibus iuuet. Et in harum quidem virtutum studium atq; exercitium singulì mortales in primisq; principes, diuites, præpotentes homines sibi incumbendum arbitrabuntur. Ac sin- guli quidem qui diuites fuerint pauperibus opes: prudentes imprudentibus consilia: poten- tes imbecillibus patrocinium præbeant. Iam magistratus, quæstores, ædiles, præfecti, tutores sint benefici in inferiores, cum illi vocentur [illegible, ~12 letters], & [illegible, ~12 letters]. Ergo tantum abest, vt iniurios nos esse Deus patiatur, vt etiam iubeat esse beneficos. Nec Christus contentus est hac ethnica iustitia, quæ solum in benemeritos, ac non etiam in inimicos est bœnefica. In quo officij genere nos continebunt iustitia & beneficentia.
units.tr: Since human beings, as was said recently, have been created by God in such a way that they ought to show one another not only freedom from harm but also kindness, it is surely no wonder that God forbids us to wrong one another and commands that each should benefit the other. Indeed, it is considered the highest praise not only to injure no one but also to be a benefit to all. Hence justice and beneficence hold the leading places in the company of the virtues: justice refrains from injuries itself and keeps others from them too, while beneficence helps not only with counsel but also with resources. Every mortal, and especially rulers, rich men and the powerful, will think it incumbent upon them to pursue and practise these virtues. Each of the rich should give resources to the poor, the wise should give counsel to the unwise, and the powerful should offer protection to the weak. Now magistrates, quaestors, aediles, prefects and guardians should be kind to their inferiors, since they are called [illegible]. So far is God from permitting us to be unjust that he even commands us to be beneficent. Nor is Christ satisfied with this heathen justice, which is kind only to those who deserve it and not also to enemies. In this kind of duty justice and beneficence will hold us.

units.la: Eas Moses commendat hoc loco, reuocans ab iniurijs concupiscentiam, ac primum de iustitia, tum de beneficentia disserens.
units.tr: Moses commends these virtues in this passage, calling us back from the lust for injury, and he discusses first justice and then beneficence.

units.la: Ac iustitia quidem, quoniam bipertita est, versaturq; & in commutatione rerum, & in distributione pœnarum & præmiorum, sic docet, vt inde vtraq; addiscatur.
units.tr: Justice, since it is twofold and concerns both the exchange of goods and the distribution of punishments and rewards, he teaches in such a way that both may be learned from it.

units.la: Dicit enim primum de pœnis, deinceps de patrocinio pauperum.
units.tr: For he speaks first of punishments and then of the protection of the poor.

units.la: De pœnis ad hunc modum. Non interficientur patres pro filijs, nec occidantur filij pro patri- bus, sed pro suo quisque peccato occidatur. Quibus verbis ostendit eam in pœnis seruandam esse iustitiam, ut qui peccatum commiserit luat: qui reus non sit idem etiam sit immunis à pœna,
units.tr: About punishments, in this manner: The fathers shall not be put to death for the children, nor the children put to death for the fathers; each shall be put to death for his own sin. By these words he shows that justice must be observed in punishments, so that whoever has committed a sin pays for it, and whoever is not guilty is likewise free from punishment.

units.la: Et ponit exempla arctissimę videlicet eius quæ est inter patrem & filium coniunctionis. Hic posset videri quædam consiliorum & voluntatum consensio, factiq; communicatio pro-pter arctam coniunctionem: item communis utilitatis spes propter ius successionis: denique natura duce vellet alter pro altero mortem oppetere. Sed lex neq; iudici, neq; illis permittit, ut affectibus indulgeant suis potius quàm iuri. Etenim iure puniri is debet, qui peccavit.
units.tr: He gives examples of the closest kind of union, namely that between father and son. Here one might suppose there is a certain agreement of counsels and wills and a sharing of deeds on account of the close bond, and likewise a hope of common advantage on account of the right of succession; and finally, by the guidance of nature, one might wish to die in place of the other. But the law permits neither judges nor them to indulge their feelings rather than the right. For he who has sinned ought to be punished by right.

units.la: Hanc legem Saul in Nobitis non servavit, 1.Reg.22. At servat David, 2.Reg.3. & 4. Servavit etiam Amazias patris mortem ulcisens, ubi locus hic allegatur. Obtinet hæc lex etiam Hierem.31. Unusquisq;, inquit, in iniquitate sua morietur, & quicunq; comederit uvam acerbam, illius dentes obstupescent. Ezech.18. Anima quæ peccaverit ipsa morietur, filius non portabit iniquitatem patris, neq; pater portabit iniquitatem filii, sed iustitia iusti erit super eum & impietas impii erit super eum.
units.tr: Saul did not keep this law in the case of the Nobites, 1 Kings 22. But David keeps it, 2 Kings 3 and 4. Amaziah also kept it, avenging his father's death, where this passage is cited. This law holds also in Jeremiah 31: Every one shall die for his own iniquity, and whoever eats the sour grape, his teeth shall be set on edge. Ezekiel 18: The soul that sins, it shall die; the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor the father bear the iniquity of the son; the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him.

units.la: Quo legis & ipsius etiam Dei patris exemplo pii magistratus discunt neque propter im-probitatem parentū frugi filios premere, neq; propter improbos filios parentes despicere.
units.tr: By this example of the law, and of God the Father himself, godly magistrates learn neither to oppress virtuous sons on account of the wickedness of their parents, nor to despise parents on account of wicked sons.

units.la: Deinceps singuli quoq; discent non odisse alios ob alios, quin suum cuiq; reddant.
units.tr: Next, individuals too will learn not to hate others on account of others, but rather to render to each his own.

units.la: At objicias Deum ipsum huic legi non stare, qui, ut est Exod.22. vindicat iniquitatem patrum in filios usque in tertiam & quartam generationem: qui in diluvio parentes cum liberis perdiderit, qui nulli in Sodomis neq; sexui neq; ætati pepercerit, qui gentem Amelechiti-cam funditus omnem excindi, iusserit, qui Achan cum liberis pœnas dare voluerit, qui Hiero-solymarum incolas omnes simul exciderit.
units.tr: But you may object that God himself does not stand by this law, since, as is said in Exodus 22, he visits the iniquity of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation; who destroyed parents together with their children in the flood; who spared neither sex nor age in Sodom; who commanded the whole Amalekite nation to be utterly destroyed; who wished Achan to pay the penalty together with his children; who destroyed all the inhabitants of Jerusalem at once.

units.la: In promptu ratio est. Nos quid animis intus foveant ac volvant homines ignoramus, sed reus ne an innocens sit coniecturis utcunq; assequimur. Qua de causa iubemur ab omni temeritate iudiciorum abstinere, ne quem innocentem occidamus: at Deus corda rimatur ac novit: is ubi scit hominem intus & in cute esse perditum, ibi severo iudicio procedit adver-sus progeniem viperarum, de cuius profectu nulla spes est reliqua, nec quisquam habet quod conquæratur. Sic profecto proh dolor in Helvetia nos gerimus, ut sive genus virile, sive muliebrem sexum, sive senes, sive pueros atq; iuvenes magnis malis afficiet Dominus, vel nos ipsi iudices nullius eum iniustitiæ posimus accusare. Ex viris enim alii sanguine, alii sudore pauperum victitant: ex mulieribus plærœq; luxu fastuq; sint perditæ: liberi his ipsis vitiis in primisq; impietate laborant & petulantia: passim regnat ambitio, avaritia, invidia, tuma aut superstitio aut omnis religionis ignorantia, negligentia, despectio. Quibus de causis mirum non sit calamitatum genus omne nobis advenire. Sed id eius quæ hic præcipitur iu-stitiæ studio devitatur.
units.tr: The reason is at hand. We do not know what men cherish and turn over within their minds, but we can in some measure infer whether a man is guilty or innocent. For this reason we are commanded to abstain from all rashness in judging, lest we put any innocent person to death. But God searches the hearts and knows them; when he knows that a man is lost within and to the core, then he proceeds with severe judgment against that brood of vipers, of whose progress there is no remaining hope, and no one has any ground for complaint. Alas, this is indeed how we conduct ourselves in Helvetia: whether the Lord afflicts with great evils the male sex, or the female, or the old, or boys and youths, we ourselves as judges cannot accuse him of any injustice. For some of the men live on the blood, others on the sweat of the poor; most of the women have been ruined by luxury and pride; the children labour under these same vices, and above all under impiety and wantonness; ambition, avarice, envy, arrogance, superstition or complete ignorance of religion, negligence and contempt reign everywhere. For these reasons it is no wonder that every kind of calamity comes upon us. But this is avoided by zeal for the justice commanded here.

units.la: Iam & de pauperum defensione disserit. Non peruertes, inquit, iudicium advenæ, &c. Peregrini, pupilli, viduæ, quia non possunt seipsos tueri, ideo Deus eos magistratibus ceu vicariis suis commendat. Qua de re cum & superioribus capp. dictum sit, & aliis compluribus in locis fiat mentio, non opus est hic plura disseri.
units.tr: He also discusses the defence of the poor: Thou shalt not pervert the judgment of the stranger, etc. Strangers, orphans and widows, because they cannot defend themselves, God therefore commends to the magistrates as his deputies. Since this matter has been mentioned in the preceding chapters, and is mentioned in many other places, there is no need to discuss more here.

units.la: De beneficentia tres casus, in quibus exerceatur affert: ut in messis, autumni seu vindemiæ, reliquorumq; fructuum collectione.
units.tr: As for beneficence, he brings forward three cases in which it is exercised: in the harvest, in the autumn gathering of the vintage, and in the collection of the other fruits.

units.la: Causam refert, quod etiam Deus in nos benignus sit & liberalis. Sane Christus etiam docet Deum imitari, velut apud Matthæum dicens, Estote misericordes sicut & pater vester Deus misericors est. Ita Christiani Christum imitari debent: ac quemadmodum ipse etiam in Malchum, atque in omnes inimicos suos benignus fuit, sic nos etiam inimicis benefaciamus.
units.tr: He gives the reason: that God too is kind and generous towards us. Indeed Christ also teaches us to imitate God, as in Matthew, saying: Be merciful, as your Father in heaven is merciful. So Christians ought to imitate Christ; and just as he himself was kind to Malchus and to all his enemies, so we too should do good to our enemies.

units.la: Alia causa est, quod et tu, inquit, fuisti servus, & posis etiâ è domino servus fieri. Qua vero bonitate alios in te velis uti, illa ipsa tu quoque in alios utere.
units.tr: The other reason is that you too, he says, were a servant, and you could also be made a servant by a master. In whatever kindness you wish others to use toward you, use that same kindness toward others.

units.la: Ex quibus omnibus intelligimus decere nos, ut imitati Deum & suum cuiq; tribuamus, & in omnes benefici simus. Quod Deus faxit in Iesu Christo Domino nostro. Amen.
units.tr: From all these things we understand that it becomes us, as imitators of God, to render to each his own and to be beneficent to all. May God grant this in Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT XXV. SERMO LXII.
units.tr: Chapter 25. Sermon 62.

units.la: SI fuerit oborta lis inter aliquos, venient ad iudicium, & iudicent eos, iustumq; pronuntient eum qui iustus est, impium vero condemnent.
units.tr: If a dispute arises between some people, they shall come to judgment, and the judges shall decide the case, acquitting the one who is righteous and condemning the wicked.

units.la: 2 Quod si impius cædendus est, prosternat eum index, & iubeat eum cædi in conspectu suo iuxta impietatem eius: idq; (certo) numero.
units.tr: 2 But if the wicked man deserves to be beaten, the judge shall have him lie down and be beaten in his presence, according to his wickedness, with a fixed number of blows.

units.la: 3 Quadragenis (plagis) verberet eum, nec ultra addet, ne forte si verberando plura bisce verbera addita fuerint, frater tuus vilis reddatur in oculis tuis.
units.tr: 3 He shall beat him with forty stripes and no more, lest, if more blows are added to these, your brother be made contemptible in your eyes.

units.la: 4 Ne obvincias (os) bovis in tritura tua.
units.tr: 4 You shall not muzzle the mouth of an ox while it treads out your grain.

units.la: 5 Si habitauerint unà fratres, mortuusq; fuerit alter eorum absq; filio, ne nu-bat uxor demortui alieno viro foris, sed levir eius ingrediatur ad eam, & ducat eam sibi uxorem, cognationisq; iure erga eam utatur.
units.tr: 5 If brothers have lived together and one of them dies without a son, the wife of the dead man shall not marry outside the family to a stranger, but his brother-in-law shall go in to her, take her as his wife, and perform the duty of a kinsman toward her.

units.la: 6 Et primogenitus, quoniam illa pepererit, succedat in nomen fratris sui defun-cti, ut non deleatur nomen eius ex Israele.
units.tr: 6 And the firstborn son she bears shall succeed to the name of his dead brother, so that his name is not blotted out from Israel.

units.la: 7 Quod si vir ille uxorem fratris sui ducere noluerit, ascendat fratria[?] eius ad portam, dicatq; senioribus, Levir meus recusat fratri suo suscitare semen in Israel, nec vult me iure propinquitatis ducere.
units.tr: 7 But if the man is unwilling to take his brother's wife, his sister-in-law shall go up to the gate and say to the elders: "My brother-in-law refuses to raise up a seed for his brother in Israel; he will not perform the duty of a kinsman toward me."

units.la: 8 Quem vocabunt seniores civitatis eius, & loquentur cum eo. Quod si perstat dicendo: Non placet mihi ut eam ducam.
units.tr: 8 The elders of his city shall summon him and speak with him. But if he persists and says, "I am not willing to take her,"

units.la: 9 Accedat fratria eius ad eum in conspectu seniorum, & detracto calceo leviri sui de pede eius, spuat coram eo: conceptisq; verbis dicat: Sic fiat viro qui non ædificat domum fratris sui.
units.tr: 9 then his sister-in-law shall come to him in the sight of the elders, pull his sandal from his foot, spit before him, and speak these set words: "So shall it be done to the man who does not build up his brother's house."

units.la: 10 Vocaturq;[?] nomen eius in Israele domus spoliati calceo.
units.tr: 10 And his name shall be called in Israel: "The house of the one whose sandal was pulled off."

units.la: VANQVAM Deus in altera decem legum tabula præcipuè hoc spectet, ut er-ga proximum nostrum bene affecti simus, suumq; ei cum reddamus, tum auxilio & consilio ad id obtinendum simus: dein officium iusti boniq; viri quicquid le-dit sigillatim adductis legibus vetet: tamen unam in fine legem fert prauæ con-cupiscentiæ aduersariam: quò ceu in medio potissimum ab iustitia, hoc est, ab il-la constanti perpetuaq; suum cuiq; reddendi voluntate non retrahamur. Etenim animi libi-do prauaq; nostri commodi, voluptatis, honorum cupiditas sic hominem agitat, ut si id aliun-dè nequeat obtinere, certè à cumulo proximi rapiat: ut qui de suo non habent ad aliena rapi-enda conuertuntur. Quare cum plurimum ponderis momentiq; situm in hac sit lege quæ ra-dicem transgressionis reliquarum huius tollat: sanè Moses etiam in hac ipsa pluribus verbis laborat explicanda, atq; etiam reliquas sigillatim singulas ceu exempli vice sub hanc ipsam re-fert. Quemadmodum superioribus aliquot capitibus vidimus, & sequentibus videbimus.
units.tr: Although God, in the second table of the ten laws, mainly intends this, that we be well disposed toward our neighbour and render him his due, and that we both help and advise him to attain it; and then, by taking the laws one by one, forbids whatever harms the duty of a just and good man; nevertheless, at the end he sets down one law opposed to depraved desire, so that, as if from its very centre, we may not be drawn away from justice, that is, from that constant and steady will to render each man his due. For the lust of the mind and the depraved desire for our own advantage, pleasure and honours so drive a man that, if he cannot obtain these things otherwise, he will surely snatch them from his neighbour's store; so those who have nothing of their own turn to seizing what belongs to others. Therefore, since the greatest weight and importance lies in this law, which removes the root of the transgressions of the rest, Moses indeed labours in this very law with many words to explain it, and he also refers the remaining laws individually, as it were by way of example, under this same one, as we have seen in some earlier chapters and shall see in those that follow.

units.la: Et in præsenti quidem capite leges quinq; tradit, quibus omnibus concupiscentiam pra-uam frenat, ac suum cuiq; reddi iubet.
units.tr: And in the present chapter he gives five laws, by all of which he restrains depraved desire and orders that each man be given his due.

units.la: Ac prima quidem lege, ut iustitia vigeat & suum cuiq; tribuatur, quo pacto & actori & iu-dici concupiscentia frenanda fit docet.
units.tr: And by the first law, that justice may flourish and each man receive what is his, he teaches how desire must be restrained both in the plaintiff and in the judge.

units.la: Actori libidinem in vindicta prosequenda coercet dicens, Venient, inquit, ad iudicium quibus oborta lis est aliqua de re. Quo vindictæ cupiditatem reprimit & eam animi libidinem frenat, qua nonnunquam eo propellimur, ut in nostris ipsorum causis ipsi velimus esse iudi-ces. Magistratui datus est ultor gladius, Rom.13. at Domino Deo, si magistratus negligat vin-dicta remittenda, Deut.21. Rom.12. At hæc libido sæpe vincit ut in Deum & in nos ipsos pec-cemus. Proinde venient (inquit) ad iudices. Non vetat usum fori, sed vindictæ prauam libidinem. Atq; hæc quidem actorem decent.
units.tr: To the plaintiff he restrains the desire for revenge in pursuing a case, saying: "They shall come to judgment," that is, those between whom some dispute has arisen over some matter. By this he curbs the lust for vengeance and restrains that desire of the mind by which we are sometimes driven to wish to be judges in our own causes. The sword of avenging has been given to the magistrate (Rom. 13), but vengeance belongs to the Lord God, and if the magistrate neglects to remit vengeance (Deut. 21; Rom. 12). Yet this lust often prevails so that we sin against God and against ourselves. Therefore, he says, let them come to the judges. He does not forbid the use of the courts, but the depraved lust for revenge. And this indeed befits the plaintiff.

units.la: Iudici vero hoc dicit: Iustum absoluant, iniustum condemnent, & si pœna, &c. Quibus ver-bis & in ferenda & in exequenda sententia cupiditatem frenat. In ferenda ut iustum, iustum: iniustum, iniustum pronunciet.
units.tr: But to the judge he says: "They shall acquit the righteous and condemn the wicked, and if a penalty is due, etc." By these words he restrains desire both in pronouncing and in carrying out the sentence. In pronouncing, let him declare the just man just and the unjust man unjust.

units.la: Atq; hic peccatur multum & variè. Diues est, igitur reddat, licet iure non debeat: insolens est, igitur condemnandus, ne fiat infolentior: pauper est, quid facias? &c. At Deus non vult hic nostrum iudicium respici, sed ipsam iustitiam.
units.tr: And here people sin much and in various ways. A man is rich, so let him be given his way, though by law he need not be; a man is insolent, so he must be condemned, lest he become more insolent; a man is poor, what is to be done? and so on. But God does not want our judgment to look to these things here, but to justice itself.

units.la: In exequenda, ut par sit peccato pœnæ moderatio: primum publica, ut quemadmodum malo exemplo ad iniustitiam alios traxit, sic inde exemplo pœnæ retrahat: tum moderata, se-cundum peccatum, & certo numero, & ut ne perditum eas reum.
units.tr: In carrying out the sentence, the punishment must be moderated to match the offence: first, it must be public, so that just as a bad example drew others into injustice, so the example of the punishment may call them back from it; then it must be moderate, according to the sin, and by a fixed number, and such that the guilty man is not destroyed.

units.la: Multum hic delinquitur: aut enim leues pœnæ grauibus malis, aut mediocribus sceleri-bus atroces pœnæ solent irrogari. Leuibus fit ut abeant in contemptum scelera: atrocibus, ut aut non accusentur & puniantur rei, aut in desperatione ruant. Quamobrem nihil hic agendum est duce concupiscentia. Horrenda sunt exempla tyrannorum Siciliæ, monachorum in bonos Christianos, & innocentes. At Iudæis blasphemis in orbis vindicem parcitur, itemque scortatoribus, adulteris, & id genus hominibus.
units.tr: Much error is committed here. For either light punishments are imposed for grave crimes, or savage punishments for moderate offences. From light punishments it comes about that crimes are despised; from savage ones, that either the guilty are not accused and punished, or they rush into despair. Therefore nothing is to be done here under the guidance of desire. Horrible are the examples of the tyrants of Sicily and of the monks against good and innocent Christians. Yet the blasphemous Jews are spared the avenger of the world, and likewise fornicators, adulterers, and that kind of people.

units.la: Lege secunda iustitiam eam docet, quæ suum cuiq; priuatim reddit, vt ei, qui suam nobis operam nauat, mercedem debitam persoluamus: idq; bouis aratoris exemplo repræsentat. Bouì, inquit, trituranti os non obligabis. Id eiusmodi est. Bos triturans dignus est qui vescatur aliqua frugis abs se calcatæ parte, cum labores subeat hominibus salutares: cur ergo homo tam sit ingratus qui sibi laborantem hominem pabulo prohibeat? Id quale sit quoue spectet docet apostolus, 1.Co.9.dicens: Etenim in Moysis lege scriptum est, non obligabis os bouis trituranti. Num boues curæ sunt Deo? an non hoc propter nos omnino dicit? Propter nos enim scriptum est, quod sub spe debeat is, qui arat, arare: & qui triturat sub spe sua particeps esse spei suæ.
units.tr: By the second law he teaches that justice which renders to each man privately what is his, so that we pay the due wage to one who labours for us; and he presents this by the example of the ox that ploughs. You shall not muzzle the ox while it treads, he says. The matter is of this kind: an ox that treads out the grain deserves to eat some part of the corn it trampled, since it undergoes labours that are useful to men. Why then should a man be so ungrateful as to deny food to a fellow man who labours for him? What this law looks to and what it means is taught by the apostle, who says in 1 Cor. 9: "For it is written in the law of Moses, you shall not muzzle the ox that treads out the grain. Is God concerned about oxen? Or does he not say this altogether on our account? For it was written on our account, that he who ploughs ought to plough in hope, and he who threshes, in hope to share in his hope."

units.la: Quo docet apostolus Deum perinde legibus ad bruta curanda latis hominum saluti con- fulere, vt in vsum hominum ipsa bruta procreauit, nempe vt inde ad officia atque commoda nostra argumentemur. Vt illa de asino proximi leuando: an non decet multo magis leuan- dum & reducendum hominem? Sic Paulus colligit si boui Deus alimentum non negari vo- luit, quanto minus negari debet aranti homini? Quamobrem ex fructu cultæ vitis vinitor, ex aratione arator, ex pastura pastor. Eodem ex loco Paulus colligit ministris ecclesiæ sua de beri stipendia, 1.Cor.9.1.Tim.5. Sic mercenario debitam mercedem reddi voluit, vt supra.
units.tr: By this the apostle teaches that God, by laws given concerning brute beasts, provides for the welfare of men, since he created the brutes for human use, namely so that from them we may argue to our duties and advantages. Just as in the case of the neighbour's ass, which is to be lifted up, is it not much more fitting that a man be lifted up and restored? Thus Paul reasons: if God did not will the ox to be denied its food, how much less should the labouring man be denied it? Wherefore the vinedresser shares in the fruit of the cultivated vine, the ploughman in the ploughing, the shepherd in the pasture. From this same place Paul infers that the ministers of the Church ought to receive their stipends (1 Cor. 9; 1 Tim. 5). So he wished the hireling to be given his due wage, as above.

units.la: At secus fit, ac qui laborant maximè, suorum laborum fructum minimum percipiunt. Vnde illud dici solet. Sic vos non vobis vellera fertis oues. Sed quemadmodum iniquum est quenquam gloriam alieno labore partam verbis in se transmouere: sic iniquum est etiam alios sementem facere, alios metere. Igitur hoc Deus præcipit, vt in eos qui de te bene meriti sunt sis liberalis.
units.tr: But it happens otherwise: those who labour most receive the smallest share of the fruit of their labours. Hence the saying commonly used: "So you bear fleeces, sheep, not for yourselves." But just as it is unjust for anyone to transfer to himself by words the glory won by another's labour, so it is unjust for some to sow and others to reap. Therefore God commands this: that you be generous to those who have deserved well of you.

units.la: Lege tertia docet iustitiam erga mortuos quoque seruandam esse. Ea res paulò altius est repetenda. Vxorem fratris mortui ducendam esse vt ei soboles suscitetur, nec eius nomen è populo deleatur.
units.tr: By the third law he teaches that justice must be observed even toward the dead. The matter must be taken up a little higher. The wife of a dead brother must be taken so that offspring may be raised up for him, and his name not be blotted out from the people.

units.la: Hæc lex videtur cum ea, quæ Leuit.19.de non ducenda fratria promulgata fuit, pugnare: sed tantum est prioris illius hæc exceptio, videlicet si frater sine liberis decessert: & causa, vt ne deleatur nomen eius ex Israel. Voluit enim Deus familias conseruare, ne confunderentur posessiones, & delerentur familiæ, ex quarum vna Mesias erat oriundus.
units.tr: This law seems to conflict with the one promulgated in Lev. 18 about not taking a sister-in-law; but this is only an exception to that former law, namely if a brother dies without children, and the reason is that his name may not be blotted out from Israel. For God willed to preserve families, lest the possessions be confused and the families destroyed, from one of which the Messiah was to be descended.

units.la: Iam hac non opus est amplius cum & Christus iam dudum natus, & terra cum illis pof- sessionibus vastata sit.
units.tr: Now there is no further need for this, since Christ was born long ago and the land has been laid waste with those possessions.

units.la: Verum sensus mysticus vt in alijs sic etiam in hac est optimus. 1. Christus Adamo fratri mortuo semen suscitauit. 2. Ecclesiæ ministri mortuo Christo fratres suscitabunt. 3. Magistratus orbis viduis atque liberis benefaciat: idem agnati, affines, consanguinei, vicini. Omnes enim in Christo fratres sumus, propterea que decet vt amicorum demortuorum posteritati consulamus. Iudicium & supplicium posita transgressoribus, quantum scelus iudicet Deus, id non præstare suis officium, satis magno est indicio.
units.tr: Yet the mystical sense is, as in other cases, so also in this one, most excellent. (1) Christ raised up seed for Adam, his dead brother. (2) The ministers of the Church, with Christ dead, will raise up brothers. (3) The magistrate should do good to the widows and children of the world, and likewise the agnates, kinsmen, blood relations and neighbours. For we are all brothers in Christ, and therefore it is fitting that we look after the posterity of our deceased friends. That God has set judgement and punishment against transgressors, and that such men do not perform their duty, is a sufficiently great indication of how great a crime God judges it to be.

units.la: Atq; ex his perspicuum est & publicè & priuatim studendum esse iustitiæ. Id faxit Deus per Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum, Amen.
units.tr: And from these things it is clear that both publicly and privately we ought to pursue justice. May God grant this through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

units.la: SERMO LXIII.
units.tr: SERMON LXIII.

units.la: 11 Si rixati fuerint viri inter se, alter scilicet cum altero, accesserit& alterius vxor vt eripiat maritum suum de manu percutientis eū, missaq; manu sua verenda eius apprehenderit.
units.tr: 11 If men strive together, one with another, and the wife of one come near to rescue her husband out of the hand of him that smiteth him, and put forth her hand and take him by the secrets:

units.la: 12 Abscindas manum eius, nec parcat oculus tuus.
units.tr: 12 Then thou shalt cut off her hand, and thine eye shall not spare her.

units.la: 13 Ne sint tibi in sacculo tuo diuersi lapides, magnus scilicet & parvus.
units.tr: 13 Thou shalt not have in thy bag divers weights, a great and a small.

units.la: 14 Ne sint tibi in domo tua diuersa Epha, magnum scilicet & parvum.
units.tr: 14 Thou shalt not have in thy house divers measures, a great and a small.

units.la: 15 Quin pondus æquum & iustum sit tibi, & Epha æquum & iustum sit tibi, vt prorogentur dies tui super terram, quam Dominus Deus tuus daturus est tibi.
units.tr: 15 But thou shalt have a perfect and just weight, and a perfect and just measure shalt thou have: that thy days may be lengthened in the land which the Lord thy God giveth thee.

units.la: 16 Nam abominatio Domino Deo tuo est quicunq; ista facit, & quicunq; iniquitatem perpetrat.
units.tr: 16 For all that do such things, and all that do unrighteously, are an abomination unto the Lord thy God.

units.la: 17 Meminerit quæ fecerit tibi Amalec in via cum exiret ex Ægypto.
units.tr: 17 Remember what Amalek did unto thee by the way, when ye came forth out of Egypt;

units.la: 18 Quomodo occurrerit tibi in itinere, & detruncarit in extremo agmine lassos quosq; qui erant in extrema parte exercitus tui, cum tu esses lassus & defessus, & non timuerit Deum.
units.tr: 18 How he met thee by the way, and smote the hindmost of thee, even all that were feeble behind thee, when thou wast faint and weary; and he feared not God.

units.la: 19 Cum igitur Dominus Deus tuus tibi requiem dederit de omnibus hostibus tuis qui circum te sunt, in terra quam Dominus Deus tuus dat tibi hereditatem, ut possideas eam, delebis memoriam Amalec sub cœlo, ne obliuiscaris.
units.tr: 19 Therefore it shall be, when the Lord thy God hath given thee rest from all thine enemies round about, in the land which the Lord thy God giveth thee for an inheritance to possess it, that thou shalt blot out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven; thou shalt not forget it.

units.la: Quoniam concupiscentia, ceu eorum quæ in proximum committimus peccatorum omnium radix, sic nos impedit, ut proximo nostro non solum non, uti par erat, benefaciamus: verum etiam damnum demus, propter eaque ei multis & variis legibus est eundum obuiam: aliquas Moses ad diuinæ legis illustrationem alias leges affert, quibus eam reprimat atque coerceat. Eius generis legum sex hoc ipso capite comprehendit.
units.tr: Since concupiscence, the root of all the sins we commit against our neighbour, so hinders us that we not only fail to do good to our neighbour, as we ought, but even do him harm, it must be met by many and various laws. Moses, to illustrate the divine law, adds other laws by which it may be restrained and checked. In this chapter he sets out six laws of this kind.

units.la: Vna est, ut in iudicio bonum absoluas, malum condemnes, in eoq; sic frenes animi libidinem, ut nec pœnam atrociorem de quoquam sumas, quam par sit eius flagitio: quoniam in pœnis quid eius qui castigatur restitutio, non quid animi libido suadeat, est intelligendum.
units.tr: The first is that in judgement you should acquit the good and condemn the wicked, and so curb the lust of the mind that you do not exact from anyone a punishment more severe than his offence deserves. For in punishments we must consider the restoration of the one who is punished, not what the lust of the mind suggests.

units.la: Altera, ut boui trituranti non obliges os suum: hoc est, sui quoque laboris fructum percipere ne vetes: æquum est enim labori quies & recreatio sua reddatur.
units.tr: The second is that you should not muzzle the ox as it treads out the grain: that is, you must not forbid the labourer to take the fruit of his own toil. For it is right that rest and refreshment be given to labour.

units.la: Tertia, ut fratri mortuo orbo semen suscites. Quæ lex ciuilibus de causis verè & proprie solis Iudæis seruit, nobis autem affert bona salubria q; mysteria: nempe ut famæ, bonis, liberis, corporibus mortuorum bene prospiciamus. In primis q; eorum liberos sic educemus, ut illis pariter, ac nobis honesti fiant. Quam in curam si incumbamus actum est de concupiscentia bonis fratrum mortuorum inhiante, sed de his II. supra dictum est satis.
units.tr: The third is that you should raise up seed for a brother who died childless. This law, for civil reasons, truly and properly served only the Jews; but for us it brings wholesome and saving mysteries: namely, that we should provide well for the good name, goods, children and bodies of the dead. Above all, we should bring up their children so that they become honourable to them as to us. If we apply ourselves to this care, the greed that covets the goods of dead brothers is dealt with; but concerning the second, enough has been said above.

units.la: Sequuntur iam tres aliæ, quibus etiam ipsis concupiscentia coercetur. Prima, Si rixati fuerint inter se vir & frater eius, &c. Quibus verbis ostendit etiam in priuata ea, qua quis se suosq; defendere necesse habeat, vindicta modum præteriri solere, propellente videlicet concupiscentia. Eius exemplum rei præbet. Si cuius maritus versetur in periculo, non alienum esse ab vxoris officio quæ ad tuendam mariti salutem atque incolumitatem pertinent parare & facere: sed in eo si libidini obtemperet facilè peccari potest, quando & personæ suæ decorum & vindictæ modum transeat, si viri cum marito suo pugnantis pudenda comprehendat. Sat erat propulsare iniuriam, nimium erat ea parte petere, qua cum perditum iret aduersarium, tum isthic præhenderet vbi mulieris verecundia prohiberet.
units.tr: Now follow three others, by which concupiscence itself is restrained. The first: If men strive together, a man and his brother, etc. By these words he shows that in private matters, where a man must defend himself and his own, the bounds of revenge are usually overstepped, since concupiscence drives him on. He gives an example of this. If someone's husband is in danger, it is not foreign to a wife's duty to take steps and act to preserve her husband's safety and well-being. But if she gives way to lust in this, she can easily sin, when she goes beyond both the decency of her own person and the measure of revenge by seizing the private parts of a man fighting with her husband. It was enough to repel the injury; it was too much to attack the adversary in the very part where, while he was going to his ruin, she grasped him where a woman's modesty forbids it.

units.la: In quo discunt mulieres. 1. Rationem habere sexum suum vnicè decentis verecundiæ. Summum eius est ornamentum pudicitia, qua abiecta postea nulla erit, seruat hanc in vestitu, incessu, consuetudine, colloquio.
units.tr: From this women learn: (1) to keep in view that their sex has one peculiar decency, which is modesty. Chastity is its chief ornament, and once it is cast aside nothing else remains; they keep it in their dress, their bearing, their habits and their conversation.

units.la: 2. Ne cuius famam, quā præhensa nullus fuerit, verbis lædat: ad quam rem procliue est genus mulierum.
units.tr: (2) Not to injure by their words the reputation of anyone whom they have not laid hold of; a failing to which the female sex is quite prone.

units.la: Viri discunt. 1. Suæ personæ rationem habere etiam in vindicta non illicita: ne quia læsi fiat propterea conuitia regerant: neque enim hoc decet. <bl>Bschiffest oder Grämbtest sich selb am tessy[?].</bl>
units.tr: Men learn: (1) to have regard for their own dignity even in lawful revenge, so that they do not return abuse because they have been wronged; for this is not becoming. Beschiffest oder Grämbtest sich selb am tessy[?] (You will soil or vex yourself ...).

units.la: 2. Vt modū in vindicta feruet, ac nō tam proximi necem quàm vitam suam quærat. In quo pesfimi deprehenduntur esse ij qui veneno gladios atq; tela sua inficiunt. Id si mulierē, quem admodum hic cernitur, dedecet: quanto magis virum? Animorum impotentia semper est habita in vitio. Nihil iratus agas. Literas prius numeres quàm iratus aliquid statuas. Laudatur ille philosophus qui seruum iratus verberare noluit.
units.tr: (2) To observe moderation in revenge, and to seek not so much the death of a neighbour as the preservation of their own life. Those are found to be most wicked who poison their swords and weapons. If this disgraces a woman, such as is seen here, how much more does it disgrace a man? Lack of self-control has always been counted a vice. Do nothing in anger. Count to ten before you decide anything in anger. That philosopher is praised who, when angry, refused to beat his slave.

units.la: Secunda, Ne sint tibi in faculo tuo, &c. Eam hac lege docet, quæ seruari in ponderibus & mensuris debet iustitiam. De qua alibi quoque præcipitur: vt Prouerb. 20. Diuersso pondere vti, aut diuersa mensura ambo hæc detestatur Dominus, Mich. 7. Num mundus ero cum bilance iniqua. & cum saculo in quo sunt lapides fraudulenti? Inde etiam Leuit. 19. Ezech. 45. Plurima in eandem sententiam.
units.tr: The second: Thou shalt not have in thy bag, etc. By this law he teaches the justice that ought to be observed in weights and measures. This is also commanded elsewhere: as in Prov. 20: "Divers weights and divers measures, both of them are alike abominable to the Lord"; Mic. 7: "Shall I count pure the wicked balances, and the bag of deceitful weights?" Hence also Lev. 19 and Ezek. 45, and many other passages to the same effect.

units.la: At iura & canones eum puniunt qui mensuris & ponderibus quenquam fallat, extra de empt. & vend. ca. vt mensuræ. Et Dores σαχάνλῳ[?] id trutinæ genus habebant, quo vel minutissimum ponderis genus dignosci posset. Sic Moses docet iustè contrahi debere, nec quenquam falli debere.
units.tr: But the laws and canons punish anyone who cheats another with weights and measures (Extra, de empt. et vend., c. ut mensurae). The Dorians also had a kind of balance by which even the smallest quantity of weight could be detected. So Moses teaches that contracts must be made justly, and that no one must be deceived.

units.la: Eodem pertinent qui vitiatas seu corruptas merces pro bonis vendunt: qui gravant u-suris & nimio precio: itemq; ij qui personas respiciunt, nec æqua lance pœnas & præmia, hæ-reditates, & his similia alia distribuunt: qui in religione modo minora modo maiora ponde-ra appendunt: hoc est, alijs aliter prædicant euangelium, quos apostolus cauponantes ver-bum Dei vocat. In quam sententiam etiam Diuus Hieronymus lib.13. Com.in Ezech.cap.45. legem hanc exponit. Quod quidem (inquit) non solum in commercijs & in vsu quotidianæ vitæ nobis est obseruandum, sed in omnibus custodienda iustitia: dicente Scriptura: Sermo-nibus tuis facies stateram & appendiculum (Eccles.28.) vt & in verbis & in opere & cogita-tionibus omnia ponderata & ratione faciamus. Huic Diui Hieronymi sententiæ cum Latini tum Germani suum assensum præbent. Germani enim quas res diligenter existimari volunt eas dicunt vt Latini ponderandas esse, erwägen/ermässen. Sed & Iureconsultis, qui quidem in hoc genere versantur, familiaris est locutio. Vt apud Modestinum in l.non tantum.ff.de re iudica. videre est, qui dicit: Quod & in persona mulieris æqua lance seruari æquitatis ratio suggerit. Quæ cum ita sint, & in vsu vitæ seu commercijs & in dictis atq; factis est habenda sui cuiq; decori ratio.
units.tr: To the same purpose belong those who sell spoiled or adulterated goods as good; who burden others with usury and excessive prices; likewise those who regard persons, and do not distribute punishments and rewards, inheritances and similar things, with an even balance; and those who in religion hang now lighter, now heavier weights, that is, who preach the gospel differently to different people, whom the apostle calls hucksters of the word of God. Saint Jerome also expounds this law in this sense, in book 13 of his Commentary on Ezekiel, chapter 45: "This (he says) must be observed not only in commerce and in the daily use of life, but justice must be kept in all things, since Scripture says: 'You shall make your words a balance and a weight' (Ecclus. 28), so that in words, deeds and thoughts we do everything weighed and with reason." Both Latins and Germans give their assent to this opinion of Saint Jerome. For the Germans, when they wish a matter to be carefully considered, say that it must be weighed, erwägen/ermässen, just as the Latins do. And this way of speaking is also familiar to the jurists, who are concerned with this kind of matter. As may be seen in Modestinus, in l. non tantum, ff. de re iudicata, who says: "What reason of equity suggests is also to be kept, with an even balance, in the person of a woman." Since this is so, both in the use of life and in commerce, and in words and deeds, regard must be had for each person's own decency.

units.la: Sed quantopere cauendæ sint in ponderibus[?] & mensuris fraudes tribus causis Moses docet. Vna, vt prorogentur dies tui in terra quam Dominus,&c. Hoc est, vt opibus diuturnis & fœli cibus potiare. Quid enim profuerit omnia acquirere, si cum ira Dei coniuncta sint, vt ijs per-frui nequeas? Atq; hoc ipso vetat quod in primis respicit concupiscentia: videlicet hæc illis addita cumulum fore, quo tibi bene consultum sit.
units.tr: But Moses teaches with three reasons how greatly frauds in weights and measures are to be avoided. The first: that thy days may be lengthened in the land which the Lord, etc. That is, that you may enjoy lasting wealth and prosperity. For what would it profit to acquire everything if it were joined with the wrath of God, so that you could not enjoy it? And by this he forbids what concupiscence chiefly looks to: namely, the idea that such gains would be added as a heap, by which you would be well provided for.

units.la: Altera quia abominatio est Domino, Hoc est, Deus suapte natura ab his abhorret dolis & versutijs. Ergo manendi locus est nuspiam ei, quem Deus, qui vbiq; est, horret. Quamobrem cum his fraudibus nec tibi consulas, nec possis vspiam consistere: præstat his abstinere & frenare concupiscentiam.
units.tr: Second, because it is an abomination to the Lord. That is, God by his very nature abhors these deceits and tricks. Therefore there is nowhere for one to remain whom God, who is everywhere, abhors. Wherefore, since you can neither consult your own good by these frauds nor stand firm anywhere with them, it is better to abstain from them and to restrain your desire.

units.la: Tertia lex, Meminerit, &c. In vindicta non solum peccatur si frenum remittas vltrici concupiscentiæ, verum etiam si spe boni alicuius adductus nimis remisè punias quod maiorem seueritatem postulat. Quale est in Amelechitis iudicium. Amelech nepos est Efau inter Sur & Hauila, ad Sin & mare rubrum habitans. De ijs Exod.17.1.Reg.15.
units.tr: The third law: "Remember, etc." In vengeance one sins not only if one lets go the rein to the avenging desire, but also if, led by the hope of some gain, one punishes too leniently what demands greater severity. Such is the judgment concerning the Amalekites. Amalek was a grandson of Esau, born between Shur and Havilah, dwelling toward Sin and the Red Sea. Concerning them, see Exod. 17; 1 Sam. 15.

units.la: Hæc Domini seueritas ostendit, quàm graue sit afflicto in vocatione Dei ambulanti no-uis iniurijs molestum esse. Etenim ea de causa tam graui supplicio censet afficiendos ob hoc Amelechitas, quod populum Israeliticum aliàs satis afflictum pluribus iniurijs & molestijs affligerent. Saul autem his parcens peccat grauissimè. Neque enim laudabilis est clementia, quæ parcit ijs, quos Deus vult punitos esse.
units.tr: This severity of the Lord shows how grave a thing it is to be a burden to one who is afflicted and walks in the calling of God by new injuries. For on this account he judges that the Amalekites, who otherwise oppressed the Israelite people, already sufficiently afflicted, with many injuries and troubles, must be punished with so grievous a penalty. Saul, however, sparing them, sins most gravely. For clemency is not praiseworthy when it spares those whom God wills to be punished.

units.la: Ex quibus omnibus est perspicuum quantopere requiratur concupiscentiæ nostræ mo-deratio, & vt neutram in partem hæc deflectat, inq; ea quam Dei verbum monstrat via media consistat per Iesum Christum, Amen.
units.tr: From all these things it is clear how greatly the moderation of our desire is required, and that it should not turn aside to either side, but should stand in the middle way which the word of God shows, through Jesus Christ. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT XXVI. SERMO LXIIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVI. SERMON LXIIII.

units.la: Cum ingressus fueris in terram, quam Dominus Deus tuus daturus est tibi hæreditatem, possederisq; eam, inhabitauerisq; eam.
units.tr: When you have entered the land which the Lord your God is going to give you as an inheritance, and have possessed it and dwelt in it.

units.la: 2 Tolles de primitijs cunctorum fructuum telluris, quos inuehis[?] de terra tua, quam Dominus Deus tuus dat tibi, & ponens in sporta, proficisceris ad locum quem eliget Dominus Deus tuus, vt collocet nomen suum illic.
units.tr: 2 You shall take some of the first-fruits of all the produce of the earth, which you bring in from your land that the Lord your God gives you, and putting them in a basket, you shall go to the place which the Lord your God will choose, so that he may place his name there.

units.la: 3 Veniensq; ad sacerdotem qui in diebus illis fuerit, dices ad eum: Agnosco hodie Domino Deo tuo, quod veni in terram quam Dominus patribus nostris daturum se nobis iurauit.
units.tr: 3 And you shall come to the priest who will be in those days, and say to him: I acknowledge today to the Lord your God that I have come into the land which the Lord swore to our fathers he would give us.

units.la: 4 Accipietq; sacerdos sportam de manu tua, & reponet eam coram ara Domini Dei tui.
units.tr: 4 The priest shall take the basket from your hand and set it down before the altar of the Lord your God.

units.la: 5 Et tu conceptū verbū perges dicere coram Domino Deo tuo. Syrus pater meus periturus erat, & descendit in Ægyptum, ibiq; peregrinus fuit cum valdè pau-ci hominibus: at auctus est illic in gentem amplissimam, fortem & multam.
units.tr: 5 And you shall go on, speaking the words conceived before the Lord your God: "My father Syrus was about to perish, and went down into Egypt, and lived there as a stranger with very few men; but he grew there into a great, strong and numerous nation."

units.la: 6 Afflixeruntq; nos Ægyptij, & subiugarunt nos, posuerunt q; super nos durif-simam seruitutem.
units.tr: 6 The Egyptians afflicted us, oppressed us, and laid upon us the hardest bondage.

units.la: Note: none.
units.tr: Note: none.

units.la: 7 Et cum clamassemus ad dominũ Deum patrũ nostrorũ, exaudiuit Dominus vocem nostram, viditq; afflictionẽ nostram, laborem nostrum, & oppressionẽ nostram.
units.tr: 7 And when we cried to the Lord God of our fathers, the Lord heard our voice, and saw our affliction, our labour and our oppression.

units.la: 8 Et eduxit nos Dominus de Ægypto robusta manu, extentoq; brachio, & terrore magno, signis & prodigiis.
units.tr: 8 And the Lord brought us out of Egypt with a strong hand, and with an outstretched arm, and with great terror, with signs and wonders.

units.la: 9 Et introducens nos in locum istum, dedit nobis terram hanc fluentem lacte & melle.
units.tr: 9 And leading us into this place, he gave us this land flowing with milk and honey.

units.la: 10 Nunc igitur offero primitiuas fructus terræ, quam dedisti mihi Domine. Tu verò dimisisti illã coram Domino Deo tuo, adorabis coram Domino Deo tuo.
units.tr: 10 Now therefore I offer the first-fruits of the land which you, O Lord, have given me. And you shall set it down before the Lord your God, and worship before the Lord your God.

units.la: 11 Et lætaberis in omni bono, quod dedit Dominus Deus tuus tibi, & domui tuæ, tu & Leuita atq; peregrinus, qui est in medio tui.
units.tr: 11 And you shall rejoice in all the good which the Lord your God has given you and your house, you and the Levite and the stranger who is among you.

units.la: VM[?] nuda verbi diuini cognitio ad bene beateq; viuendum minimè sufficiat, omnì noq;[?] amplius quiddã requiratur, nempe vt ad illud ipsum vitam ac mores nostros accommodemus: Moses profecto dat operam, vt diuinæ voluntatis nō modo nos certiores faciat, verum etiam vt optimis quibusq; argumentis ad perficiendā eam nos adducat. Qua de causa cum præcedentibus cap. mentem & sententiam decem legum & reliquarum etiam generis eiusdem præceptionum pluribus verbis explicasset: Iam ijs quæ- quuntur vsque ad epilogum capitibus causas mouentes seu argumenta affert, & ad diuina- rum legum studium omnis generis adiumenta præbet.
units.tr: Since the bare knowledge of the divine word is by no means sufficient for living well and blessedly, and something more is required, namely that we accommodate our life and morals to it, Moses indeed takes pains not only to make us more certain of the divine will, but also to lead us by the strongest arguments to carry it out. For this reason, after explaining at length in the preceding chapters the meaning and sense of the ten laws and of the other precepts of the same kind, he now, in the chapters that follow up to the epilogue, sets forth causes and arguments, and provides aids of every kind for the study of the divine laws.

units.la: Et hoc quidem capite vt ad præstanda Deo debita pietatis officia nos excitemur, exer-nis[?] quibusdam de quibus etiam supra dixit, officijs suscitari in animis gratam eorũ, quę Deus in nos contulit beneficiorum memoriam indicat: qua deinceps inflammata fieri non possit, quin quicquid ei scimus esse gradu, id simus animis libentissimis effecturi. Vt qui parentum amicorum, & omnium omniũ à quibus acceperit aliquid beneficij, officia recolit, is nunquam non paratus est illis vicissim gratum facere: qui nunquam beneficiorum acceptorum memi- nit, is nihil contra gratum facit. Igitur hic quid diuinitus acceperint, quid Deo vicissim debe ant iuxta ponit, vt inde virtutem, quæ est in mediocritate posita colligant.
units.tr: And in this chapter, in order that we may be roused to perform the duties of piety owed to God, he indicates that by certain outward duties, of which he also spoke above, there is aroused in our minds a grateful remembrance of the benefits God has bestowed upon us. Once this is kindled, it cannot but be that we shall gladly bring about whatever we know to be in our power in return. For one who recalls the kindnesses of parents, friends, and all from whom he has received any benefit is never unready to make them a grateful return; one who never remembers received benefits does nothing grateful in return. Therefore here he sets out what they have received from God and what they owe God in return, so that from this they may gather virtue, which lies in the mean.

units.la: Gratitudinem autem externo aliquo, vt supra dictum est, officio significandam monet. Neq; enim nudam virtutis opinionem, sed virtutem ipsam postulat, quæ in dictis atque factis cernitur. Arbor bona fructus fert bonos: Abrahæ filij quæ digna sunt patre tanto faciunt opera: fideles re ipsa præstant eius qua sunt præditi fidei indicia.
units.tr: Moreover, he bids gratitude be signified by some outward duty, as was said above. For he requires not a bare opinion of virtue, but virtue itself, which is seen in words and deeds. A good tree bears good fruit: the sons of Abraham do works worthy of so great a father; the faithful, in fact, show the marks of faith with which they are endowed.

units.la: Eorum hic operam genera duo refert, primitiarum videlicet & decimarum oblationem. Et in primitiarum oblatione sic versatur vt quando, quo loco, quomodo offeras monstret.
units.tr: Here he sets out two kinds of this work, namely the offering of first-fruits and of tithes. And in the offering of first-fruits he deals with it so as to show when, where, and how you should offer.

units.la: Quando, cum ingressus fueris in terram, quam dominus Deus tuus daturus est tibi, &c. Quibus verbis quid in lauta fortuna facto opus sit docet, nempe, quod rebus ex animi sententia affluentibus pietati cumprimis studendum sit. Videas qui in exilio, paupertate, in humili, abiecta atq; ingloria vita pietati vtcunq; studeant: at in patriam restituti, opibus & honoribus aucti mirum in modum superbiant. Vnde dicit Dominus, difficile esse diuiti intrare in regnum cœlorum: opes esse spinas: & laqueos, vt docet apostolus. Quid facias? an vt ille philosophus o- lim, eas in mare abijcias? minimè, bonum ingens sunt. Recte eas, & quomodo locus hic do- cet, considera.
units.tr: When: "when you have entered the land which the Lord your God is going to give you," etc. By these words he teaches what must be done in a prosperous fortune, namely that, when things flow in according to one's wish, one must above all devote oneself to piety. You may see people who in exile, poverty, and a lowly, abject and inglorious life somehow apply themselves to piety; but once restored to their country and increased in wealth and honours, they grow wondrously proud. Hence the Lord says it is hard for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven; riches are thorns and snares, as the apostle teaches. What are you to do? Are you, like that philosopher of old, to cast them into the sea? By no means; they are a great good. Consider them rightly, and as this place teaches.

units.la: Datas esse hæreditatem à Deo: quoad tu velis habiturus benigni patris donum: non vt vi detur manu tua partas, verum Dei beneficio concessas.
units.tr: That the inheritance is given by God: you are to have it as the gift of a kind father, for as long as you wish; not as if it were acquired by your own hand, but granted by the benefit of God.

units.la: Cum possederis & habitaueris, tunc gratus fis Domino: cum bene se res habent, tunc pieta-ti in primis stude. Diuitiæ si affluant nolite cor apponere. In cœlis, quò nulli fures penetrant, thesauros atq; cor repone. Exemplo sint Nabal, Balthassar, diues euangelicus, & alij. Recte So- lomon petijt ne nimias opes ceu irritamenta malorum acciperet. Cauendum ne fortunæ ar-ridentis blanditijs dementati nosmet ipsi eamus perditum: ac velut ab inimico blandiente ca-uemus, sic ab opibus quarum auxilio caro freta aduersus bonum Dei spiritum ferociret. Qui in altà ac præcipiti via graditur, ne labatur caueat necesse est. Saul, Dauid, Solomon, Haman, alijq; sic lapsi sunt. Sed hoc quicquid est periculi pietatis vsu atq; exercitio prouidetur. Itaq; rebus ita bene constitutis primitias hic offerendas suadet.
units.tr: "When you have possessed and dwelt in it": then you are grateful to the Lord. When things go well, above all apply yourself to piety. If riches flow in, do not set your heart upon them. Lay up treasures and your heart in heaven, where no thieves break in. Let Nabal, Belshazzar, the rich man of the Gospel, and others be examples. Solomon rightly asked not to receive excessive wealth as an incitement to evils. We must beware lest, maddened by the caresses of smiling fortune, we go to our own ruin; and as we beware of a flattering enemy, so we must beware of riches, by whose help the flesh, trusting in them, would grow fierce against the good Spirit of God. He who walks a high and precipitous road must necessarily take care lest he fall. Saul, David, Solomon, Haman and others have so fallen. But whatever danger there is, it is provided against by the practice and exercise of piety. Therefore, when things are so well arranged, he urges that first-fruits be offered here.

units.la: Quid, primitias, inquit, omnium fructuum terræ eius, quam Dominus dederit. Sunt autem cau-sæ propter quas primitias voluit offerri duæ. Vna, vt grati sint & esse discant Deo datori. Id est optimum. Ergo liberos precibus assuefacito, teq; etiam ipsum, vt vobis constet à Deo vos custodiri & pasci,
units.tr: "What, he says, the first-fruits of all the produce of that land which the Lord shall have given." There are two reasons for which he wished first-fruits to be offered. One is that they may be grateful and learn to be grateful to God the giver; that is best. Therefore accustom your children to prayer, and yourself too, so that it may be clear to you that you are kept and fed by God.

units.la: Altera,ut per oblatam particulam sanctificaretur quicquid prouentuum erat reliquum. Nam ob peccatum & terra & ex hac quicquid prouenit est obnoxium maledictioni : at per verbi diuini & pietatis vsum sanctificantur omnia.
units.tr: The other is that by the offered portion whatever remains of the produce might be sanctified. For on account of sin both the earth and whatever grows from it are liable to the curse; but through the use of the divine word and of piety all things are sanctified.

units.la: Igitur qui in bonis suis impie vitam agunt & superbiunt,ij seq; suasq; opes obnoxias ma-gis faciunt maledictioni. Exemplo sunt Saul,Nabal,alij. Quo sanctius coles Deum,hoc ille te propensius amabit:quo maiore fide primitias illi offeres,hoc sanctior & felicior erit reliqua-rum opum tuarum possessio. Sunt autem, vt docet,Philo bonorum etiam corporis atque ani-mi primitiæ Deo offerendæ.
units.tr: Therefore those who live impiously in their goods and become proud make themselves and their wealth more liable to the curse. Saul and Nabal and others are examples. The more holily you worship God, the more kindly he will love you; the more faithfully you offer him first-fruits, the holier and happier will be the possession of your remaining wealth. Moreover, as Philo teaches, the first-fruits of the goods of body and soul also are to be offered to God.

units.la: Est autem Christus in omnibus primas tenens:vt primogenitus omnis creaturæ, primi-tiæ resurgentium,&c.
units.tr: Now Christ holds the first place in all things: as firstborn of every creature, first-fruits of those who rise, etc.

units.la: Quo loco,in eo videlicet quem elegerit Dominus. Studiose præcipit,vt ne quid fiat seor-sim ab ecclesia. Est oblatio Deo debita. Simus hodieque propensi ad promouendam rem Christianam.
units.tr: In the place which, namely, "the Lord shall have chosen." He carefully commands that nothing be done apart from the Church. It is an offering owed to God. Let us also today be ready to advance the Christian cause.

units.la: Quomodo,verbis & factis : verba sunt index animi, facta sunt quasi quædam verborum probatio. Verbis profitebitur quam requirit gratitudinem.1. Agnosco. Est enim agnoscen-dum quod diuinitus accipitur beneficium : itemque gratis animis accipienda sunt quo paren-tes,agnati,tutores, magistratus dant beneficia. Nolle agnoscere & suo modo metiri benefi-cia ingratitudinis omnis causa est.
units.tr: How: by words and deeds. Words are the index of the mind, and deeds are as it were a proof of the words. By words one professes the gratitude required. 1. "I acknowledge." For the benefit received from God must be acknowledged; likewise benefits given by parents, kinsmen, guardians and magistrates are to be received with a grateful mind. Refusing to acknowledge, and measuring benefits by one's own standard, is the whole cause of ingratitude.

units.la: 2.Syrus pater,&c.Prioris fortunæ recordatio præsentem gratam facit:at rerum quam tu leris[?] aduersarum obliuisci,id vero causa est, vt præsenti minus contenti in ingratitudinis crimen incidamus.Saul,&c.Honores mutant mores,&c.
units.tr: 2. "A Syrian father, etc." Remembrance of former fortune makes the present one pleasing; but to forget the adversities you have endured is the cause that, being less content with the present, we fall into the crime of ingratitude. Saul, etc. Honours change manners, etc.

units.la: 3.Cum clamassemus,&c.Auxilij comparati forma ac ratio est Deum patrum inuocare,ab illo audiri,& eripi.Atque hæc est illa professio.
units.tr: 3. When we cried out, etc. The manner and method of obtaining help is this: to call upon the God of our fathers, to be heard by him, and to be rescued. And this is that profession.

units.la: Sed facta,tu, inquit,adorabis & vesceris cum tuis,&c. Non solus adorabis,nec solus etiam vesceris,& frueris bonis.Sed ut Deus in te liberalis est,& bonus, sic in alios ipse quoque munificus esto. Sic enim Deum imitatus beatæ vitæ possessione potiere per Iesum Christum, Amen.
units.tr: But in fact, "You shall worship and eat with your own, etc." You shall not worship alone, nor eat and enjoy the good things alone. But as God is generous and good toward you, so you too should be bountiful toward others. For by imitating God in this way you will obtain the possession of a blessed life, through Jesus Christ. Amen.

units.la: SERMO LXV.
units.tr: SERMON LXV.

units.la: 12 Cumq; compleueris dare decimas,omnes scilicet decimas prouentus tui,in anno tertio,qui est annus decimarum,dabis Leuitis,peregrinis,pupillis & viduis, vt comedant intra portas tuas,& saturentur.
units.tr: 12 When you have finished paying all the tithes of your produce, that is, all the tithes of your yield, in the third year, which is the year of tithes, you shall give them to the Levites, the strangers, the fatherless and the widows, so that they may eat within your gates and be filled.

units.la: 13 Dicesq; coram Domino Deo tuo, Sustuli Sanctum de domo,dedi ipsum Leuitis,peregrinis,pupillis & viduis,iuxta vniuersa præcepta tua quæ præcepisti mihi: non sum transgressus præcepta tua,nec obliuioni tradidi.
units.tr: 13 And you shall say before the Lord your God: I have taken the holy thing out of the house and have given it to the Levites, the strangers, the fatherless and the widows, according to all your commandments which you commanded me. I have not transgressed your commandments, nor have I forgotten them.

units.la: 14 Non comedi in dolore meo ex eo,nec sustuli quidquam ex eo in immunditia, neq; dedi ex eo quid mortuis,sed audiui vocem Domini Dei mei,& feci iuxta omnia quæ præcepisti mihi Domine.
units.tr: 14 I have not eaten of it in my sorrow, nor have I taken any of it away in uncleanness, nor have I given any of it to the dead. But I have obeyed the voice of the Lord my God, and have done according to all that you commanded me, O Lord.

units.la: 15 Aspice de habitaculo sancto tuo de cœlis,& benedic populum tuum Israel,atque terrā quam dedisti nobis,quemadmodum iurasti patribus nostris,terram lacte & melle manantem.
units.tr: 15 Look down from your holy dwelling in heaven, and bless your people Israel, and the land which you have given us, as you swore to our fathers, a land flowing with milk and honey.

units.la: 16 Hodie Dominus Deus tuus præcepit tibi,vt facias statuta ista atq; iudicia vt serues & facias ea toto corde tuo,& tota anima tua.
units.tr: 16 This day the Lord your God commands you to do these statutes and judgements; you shall keep and do them with all your heart and all your soul.

units.la: 17 Tu hodie fecisti dicere Dominum quod velit esse Deus tuus,vtq; ambules in viis eius,obserues statuta eius atq; iudicia eius,audiasq; vocem eius.
units.tr: 17 You have today caused the Lord to declare that he will be your God, and that you will walk in his ways, keep his statutes and his judgements, and hear his voice.

units.la: 18 Dominus rursum te fecit dicere hodie,vt esses ei populus peculiaris,sicut locu-tus est tibi,& custodias omnia mandata eius.
units.tr: 18 And the Lord has again caused you to declare today that you will be his peculiar people, as he has spoken to you, and that you will keep all his commandments.

units.la: 19 Et vt ponat te excelsiorem cunctis gentibus quas fecit,vt sis in laudem & celebre nomen,& in gloriam,& sis populus sanctus Domino Deo tuo,sicut loquutus est.
units.tr: 19 And that he will set you higher than all the nations which he has made, for praise, for renown and for glory, and that you will be a holy people to the Lord your God, as he has spoken.

units.la: CUm Dei beneficia agnoscere,& gratam erga tam benignum patrem animo voluntatem habere nos eo propellat, vt præceptis eius tanto magis studeamus, ac quod ipsi placeat facere, quod displiceat cauere velimus : sanè Moses nos ad diuinarum præceptionum studium propositis quibusdam gratitudinis exercitijs adiuuat atque promouet : veluti cum proponit oblationem primitiarum, quæ agnoscimus prouentus annuos esse Dei munerà, nosq; Deo datori tum demum gratos esse, quando vt ille nobis seruandis & fouendis studet sic nos illius voluntati faciendæ dediti fimus.
units.tr: Since the recognition of God's benefits and a grateful will towards so kind a Father move us to study his precepts all the more, and to wish to do what pleases him and avoid what displeases him, Moses certainly helps and advances us in the study of the divine precepts by setting before us certain exercises of gratitude. For example, when he sets forth the offering of firstfruits, we acknowledge that the yearly produce is God's gift, and that we are then pleasing to God the giver when, as he takes care to preserve and cherish us, we in turn devote ourselves to doing his will.

units.la: Iam aliud sequitur exercitium, videlicet decimarum oblatio. De quibus quoniam supra quoque dictum est, iam paucis agit, ac tantum huc respicit, vt gratitudinem erga Deum exerceamus. Dicit enim quibus, quomodo, qua de causa decimas offeramus.
units.tr: Next follows another exercise, namely the offering of tithes. Since these were also spoken of above, he now treats them briefly, and looks only to this: that we exercise gratitude towards God. For he says to whom, how and for what reason we are to offer tithes.

units.la: Ac quibus sint dandæ decimæ hoc ipso monstrat quod signillatim singulos eos refert, qui bus eas Deus vult reddi: dabis, inquit, Leuitis, peregrinis, pupillis, viduis. Atque hic catalogus ostendit quomodo grati in Deum simus, quasq; ei gratias referre deceat.
units.tr: That to whom tithes are to be given he shows by this very thing, that he names each of those to whom God wills them to be returned: you shall give them, he says, to the Levites, the strangers, the fatherless, the widows. And this list shows how we may be grateful to God, and what thanks it is fitting to render to him.

units.la: Multum hic peccatur. Dedit Deus opes, volumus largo patri gratias debitas referre: quid facimus? alius templa, alius statuas, alius vestes sacrificas, oleum, lucernas, templa, monasteria vouet & reddit: alius fruges sacrificat. At his nostris siue donis siue cultibus Deus nec opus habet vt Esaias indicat, nec afficitur, cum oderit suo verbo aduersa officia. Quare perditur quicquid in vanum absumitur.
units.tr: Much error is committed here. God has given us wealth, and we wish to repay the bountiful Father the thanks due. What do we do? One vows temples, another statues, another sacred vestments, oil, lamps, temples and monasteries; another sacrifices fruits. But God has no need of these gifts or worships of ours, as Isaiah points out, nor is he moved by them, since he hates by his word such offices as these. Therefore whatever is spent on them in vain is wasted.

units.la: Iam abstinent qui sapiunt ab hoc gratiarum genere: sed nullas afferre malum est: cui inquis referam, si Deus nec opus his habet, nec in res illas absumi velit? Moses hoc docet. Pri- mum Leuitis, ij terræ promissæ partem non habebant, & propterea iure postulabant deci-mas. Sic ministri nec mercaturæ, nec artibus sunt dediti, quibus quenquam grauent, propte- rea q; æquum est, vt quoniam publicâ rem iuuant è publicis quoq; bonis stipendia accipiant.
units.tr: Now those who are wise abstain from this kind of thanksgiving. But it is no harm to bring something: "To whom," you ask, "shall I give it, if God has no need of these things and does not wish them spent on those things?" Moses teaches this. First, to the Levites: they had no share in the promised land, and so they rightly demanded tithes. Likewise ministers are not given to trade or to crafts by which they might burden anyone; therefore it is fair that, since they serve the public good, they receive their stipends from public goods too.

units.la: Qui bona publica ministris verbi, ceu Dei nuncijs atq; interpretibus inuident sua stipen-dia, eaq; vel auferunt vel diminuunt, hi quàm ingrati in Deum sint hoc ipso produnt. Quasi vero magnum quiddam sit pro cœlestibus caduca suppeditare. Et est profecto magna nostro- rum hominum ingratitudo & inuidia, qui non tam gratis animis accipiunt euangeliū, quàm vt eius ministris quicquid habent inuideant. Quantum enim à priscorum fidelium verbi mi-nistros suis sumptibus fouentium alieni sint, hoc ipsum docet, quod non solum de suo dent illis nihil, sed etiam alienas illis opes inuideant. Onus graue sustinent, & cum hoc ipso con-temptum, odia, insidias. Quamobrem si illa spiritualia Dei munera gratis animis, vti par est, accipimus: in ministros eorum liberaliores simus necesse est.
units.tr: Those who begrudge the ministers of the Word, as messengers and interpreters of God, their stipends, and either take them away or reduce them, by this very act show how ungrateful they are towards God. As if it were a great thing to supply perishable things in return for heavenly ones! Indeed our people's ingratitude and envy is great, for they receive the gospel not so much with grateful minds as to envy its ministers whatever they have. How far they are from the ancient faithful, who supported the ministers of the Word at their own expense, this very fact shows: they not only give them nothing of their own, but even begrudge them the wealth of others. They bear a heavy burden, and with it contempt, hatred and plots. Therefore, if we receive those spiritual gifts of God with grateful minds, as is fitting, we must needs be more generous to their ministers.

units.la: 2. Peregrinis, Miserum est exulare patria solo natali dulcissimo: tum etiam multas ob res incommodum. Hæc onera leuiora fient illis, si benignè & liberaliter foueamus. Ingrati igitur in Deum sunt qui illis non modo nihil de suo largiuntur, sed etiam ipsorum ære comparatas res inuident.
units.tr: 2. To the strangers. It is a wretched thing to be exiled from one's native soil, most sweet to us, and also in many ways a hardship. These burdens will be made lighter for them if we cherish them kindly and generously. Therefore those are ungrateful to God who not only give them nothing of their own, but even begrudge them the goods they have acquired with their own money.

units.la: 3. Pupillis & viduis, quibus & detrahendum est nihil, & quod deest suppeditandum. En tibi quibus vsibus bona publica sint comparata, nempe vt egentibus succurratur. Ita fiebat vt secundum legem supra positam mendici in Israel essent nulli. Quod etiam ecclesia primitiua factitauit secundum legem charitatis. Iam rebus ad occasum vergentibus turbæ mendicorum sunt, quibus succurri posset bonis ecclesiasticis, prouentibus parochiarum, & collectis singulorum.
units.tr: 3. To the fatherless and the widows, from whom nothing is to be taken away, and to whom what they lack is to be supplied. See here the purpose for which public goods were provided: namely, that the needy might be helped. So it came about that, according to the law set down above, there were no beggars in Israel. The primitive Church also did this, according to the law of charity. But now that affairs are declining, there are crowds of beggars who might be helped from ecclesiastical goods, the revenues of parishes, and the collections of individuals.

units.la: Deus hos posuit ob oculos, vt in quibus misericordiam exerceas. Velut eum, qui in latrones incideret, Leuitæ & Samaritano curandum obiecerat. Omnes potuisset ditare, sed di-uitibus pauperes, ægrotos sanis obiecit ceu materiam, in qua virtutem exerceant suam.
units.tr: God has set these before our eyes, so that you may exercise mercy towards them. Just as he presented to the Levite and the Samaritan the man who had fallen among robbers to be cared for. He could have enriched them all, but he set the poor before the rich, and the sick before the healthy, as material on which they might exercise their virtue.

units.la: Quomodo dandæ posita confessionis forma docet. Ea refert hæc ab eo præstita, quę sua lege requirat Deus. Quod non est in eam sententiam accipiendum vt existimes spiritum sanctum docere iactantiam: qualis erat illius diuitis, qui præcepta diuina commemoranti Domino dixit, hæc omnia ab ineunte ætate abs se seruata esse: vel illius Pharisæi, quem cap.18. Lucas refert in templo suas virtutes magnificè prædicasse. Verum hæc confessio quasi quædam conscientiæ testatio est: qua profitetur & se bene sibi conscium esse bene vsurpatarum opum, & intelligere non sua factum hoc esse virtute propria, sed spiritus Dei impulsu atq; auxilio: tum sperare sese diuinam benedictionem & præmia.
units.tr: The form of confession laid down for giving shows how this is to be done. It records those things done by the one who gives, which God requires by his law. This is not to be taken in the sense that you should think the Holy Spirit teaches boastfulness, such as that of the rich man who, when the Lord recounted the divine precepts, said that he had kept all these from his youth; or that of the Pharisee whom Luke, in chapter 18, reports magnificently proclaiming his virtues in the temple. Rather, this confession is a kind of testimony of conscience, by which the giver professes that he is conscious of having used his wealth rightly, and understands that this was done not by his own strength but by the impulse and help of the Spirit of God; and then that he hopes for the divine blessing and rewards.

units.la: Opum vsus bonus & rectus in hoc consistit, vt non modo suum auferas nemini, verum etiam quod iusto titulo possides id in res malas minimè conuertas. Quare dicit in hac con-sessione ab vtroq; sese abstinuisse.
units.tr: The good and right use of wealth consists in this: not only that you take what is another's from no one, but also that you do not turn what you rightly possess to evil uses. Therefore in this confession he says that he has abstained from both.

units.la: De priore dicit: Sustuli sanctum de domo, dedi, ipsum Leuitis, peregrinis, &c. iuxta omnia praecepta, &c. En bonum ingens, si quis posit verè testari quod decimas & eleemosynas summafide præstiterit. Rationes sunt. Quia sanctum sanctuario debetur loco remunerationis Deo debitæ:ac quicquid das,id reliqua bona tua sanctificat,quicquid retines iniustè, id reliquas opes inficit quasi Tholosanum aurum. 2. Quia Deus præcepit,quod transfire vel obliuione tradere summum peccatum est.In hoc speculo contemplemur nos.
units.tr: Of the first he says: I have taken the holy thing out of the house, and have given it to the Levites, the strangers, etc., according to all the precepts, etc. Here is a great good, if anyone can truly testify that he has paid tithes and alms with the utmost fidelity. The reasons are these.
