Verum si qui sunt bonorum auidi, in ipsis fontibus ea quaerant,videlicet diuini verbi studio: rursus si qui malis declinandis studeant, ij ne latum vnguem à verbi studio discedant.Omnino paternae sunt minae quibus vt ad bonum contendamus impellit.Haec ad nos pertinere docet,1.Tim.1.Gal.5.apostolus.Igitur vt in benedictionibus primum bonorum causas, deinceps ipsa mala retulit: sic in maledictionibus primum malorum causas,tum ipsa mala refert.
units.tr: When all men are so constituted by nature that they are eager for their own honour, advantage and pleasure, and are able and willing to pursue these most readily, but are shaken by the dread of their own shame, loss and ruin, so that they can be driven to any course of action by nothing so effectively as by the promise of good and the warning of evil: God, out of his supreme and singular care for our preservation, everywhere promises good things to those who hear and follow him, and in turn threatens evil to the rebellious. For he does not promise good in order to attest to us in words the grace he already declares in deed, nor does he threaten evil in order to display his omnipotence to us; rather, he promises good to lead us to what is good, and threatens evil to turn us away from evil. This must also be considered in this 28th chapter, where blessings are assigned to the good and curses to the wicked: God does not promise good things in order to boast of his goodness and beneficence in the manner of men. For who, looking upon this world and what is in it, and recalling the immense benefits of God toward us, does not know this? Nor does he threaten evil so as to make himself terrible, and, like a proud man, strike fear into the feeble as a man of pride does. For who, weighing the sins that have been severely punished and his justice, would not perceive this? But if there are those who are eager for good things, let them seek them at their very source, namely in zealous attention to the divine Word. Again, if there are those who strive to avoid evils, let them not depart a finger's breadth from zeal for the Word. Truly, these are the threats of a father, by which he urges us to strive toward what is good. The apostle teaches that these things pertain to us (1 Tim. 1; Gal. 5). Therefore, just as in the blessings he first related the causes of good things and then the good things themselves, so in the curses he first sets out the causes of evils and then the evils themselves.

units.la: Causam sic exprimit: Si vocem Domini Dei tui non audieris; vt custodias & facias omnia mandata, &c. Quibus verbis docet omnis mali causam duabus hisce rebus oriri: nempe si non audiatur vox Domini,& si reipsa non custodiatur.
units.tr: He states the cause thus: If thou wilt not hearken to the voice of the LORD thy God, to observe all his commandments, etc. By these words he teaches that the cause of every evil arises from two things: namely, if the voice of the LORD is not heeded, and if it is not actually kept.

units.la: In quo diligenter est considerandum qui nam ij sint, qui non audiant. Sunt autem eorum qui non audiunt genera duo: quorum illi id sibi dici prorsus nolunt,hi ferunt quidem sed certa cum conditione. Qui prorsus respuunt ij vel malitia, vel ignoratione, vel zelo stulto ducuntur. Ignoratione & zelo ducti conuerti possunt, vt Paulus & Iudaei multi Actor. 4. &3. Multi item papistae: quia nihil illos quo minus assensum veritati praberent suum impedijt, quam quod opinati fuissent veritatem esse,quam profesi essent: hacq; opinione per doctrinam remota euadunt pij & boni. Qui vero malitia ducti veritatem euangelicam respuunt ac tenebras quam lucem malunt,de his spes est parua. Nam quas illi res quaerunt & amplectuntur,eas verbum Dei non solum non propinat,sed etiam aufert: vt suam clericis luxuriam,auaritiam,inertiam:vt suas Epicureis libidines, pensiones,dignitates. Exemplo sunt Pilatus,Herodes,Caiaphas,& alij qui nunc sunt hostes acerrimi.
units.tr: Here we must carefully consider who those are who do not hear. There are two kinds of those who do not hear: some utterly refuse to have it said to them at all, while others bear it, but on certain conditions. Those who utterly reject it are led either by malice, by ignorance, or by foolish zeal. Those led by ignorance and zeal can be converted, as Paul and many Jews were (Acts 4 and 3). Likewise many Papists: for what hindered them from giving assent to the truth was nothing but their opinion that the faith they professed was the truth; and when this opinion is removed through teaching, they become godly and good. But those who, led by malice, reject the evangelical truth and prefer darkness to light, for them there is little hope. For the Word of God not only does not offer them the things they seek and embrace, but even takes them away: such as the clergy's luxury, avarice and idleness; such as the Epicureans' lusts, pensions and dignities. Examples are Pilate, Herod, Caiaphas, and others who are now the bitterest enemies.

units.la: Alterum autem genus ferret quidem verbum sed quàm leuissimè praedicatum & ita vt affectus ne tangerentur asperius. Vt in religione,qui intrant alia quàm per Christum via, ne fures appellentur: nèue missas in contumeliam atque ignominiam Christi celebrari quisquam dictitet: in vita ac moribus ne Solomonis illud de adulterio & furto iuditium promatur:ne Iudae marsupium quod multi nunc euangelij,si dijs placet,assertores ipso Christo charius habent,publice dicatur.
units.tr: The other kind would indeed bear the Word, but only when it is preached very mildly, and in such a way that their feelings are not touched too harshly. In religion, for instance, they would have it that those who enter by a way other than through Christ are not called thieves; nor does anyone insist that the Masses are celebrated to the contumely and shame of Christ; in life and morals, they would not have the judgement of Solomon on adultery and theft put forward, nor have it publicly said that Judas's money-bag, which many now, God help them, hold as the champions of the gospel, is dearer to them than Christ himself.

units.la: At hic docet omnis mali causam ex eo proficisci, quod vel totum verbum vel aliquam eius partem respuamus.Idem ca.30.Efaias dicit.Populus iste contumax est,inquit, filij men daces,qui nolunt audire legem Domini. Qui dicunt videntibus ne videatis,loquamini nobis blanda.Sed quis finis? Vt murus,inquit,& ruent vas figuli.Hiere. 9.dicit ab eo tempore quo sint ex Ægypto liberati semper clamasse Dominum & iussisse: audite vocem meam, sed non audierunt, nec inclinarunt aurem suam qui magis inceferunt in praua cordis sui libidine mali.Sed finis quis? sequitur.Iccirco dicit Dominus. Ecce ego adduco super eos malum de quo eluctari non poterunt,clamabunt q; ad me & non exaudiam eos.
units.tr: But here he teaches that every evil arises from this: that we reject either the whole Word or some part of it. Isaiah says the same in chapter 30: "This people is rebellious," he says, "lying sons who refuse to hear the law of the Lord; who say to the seers, 'Do not see,' and to the prophets, 'Speak to us smooth things.'" But what is the end of it? "Like a wall," he says, "and like a potter's vessel that is broken." Jeremiah 9 says that from the time they were freed from Egypt the Lord always cried out and commanded, "Hear my voice"; but they did not hear, nor did they incline their ear, but walked the more in the wickedness of their own hard hearts. But what is the end? It follows: "Therefore the Lord says, 'Behold, I will bring upon them an evil from which they will not be able to escape; they will cry out to me, and I will not hear them.'"

units.la: Quare bene suadent Esa.51. Sectatoribus iustitiae,vt audiant legem Domini, & qui eam cognorunt gaudium fore, Matthaei 17. ipsum audite. Matth.7. Vir sapiens audit & custodit verbum Domini. Addit enim & hic idipsum dicens, vt custodiant & faciant. Rectè ergo Ro. 9.Non auditores sed factores legis iustificantur.Sic nos habuisse non autem obseruasse euangelium nihil adiuuerit.At cum nec audire pars velit, nec seruare omnes soleamus, non mirum est tam miseram esse Germaniam,quippe in qua pars respuit pars non praestet euangelium.Id si caueas,maledictiones caues.
units.tr: Therefore he rightly urges, in Isaiah 51, that those who pursue righteousness should hear the law of the Lord, and that those who know it will have joy. In Matthew 17: "Hear him." Matthew 7: "The wise man hears and keeps the word of the Lord." He adds here the same thing, saying that they may keep and do it. Rightly, then, in Romans 9, "It is not the hearers but the doers of the law who are justified." So to have had the gospel, but not to have observed it, will profit nothing. But since we are accustomed neither to want to hear nor to keep it, all of us, it is no wonder that Germany is in such a wretched state, since in it one part rejects the gospel and the other does not live up to it. If you take care of this, you will avoid the curses.

units.la: Mala vero,quae ex hoc diuini verbi contemptu proueniunt; primum bonis ex eius studio proudentibus opposita,dein tribus potisimum capitibus comprehensa refert.
units.tr: He then sets out the evils that come from this contempt of the divine Word: first, those opposed to the blessings that come from zealous attention to it; and then he describes them, comprehended under three main heads.

units.la: Bonis opposita,Execratus,inquit,in vrbe & agro:sporta & reliquijs:fructu ventris, telluris, pecoris:in introitu & exitu. Quibus in rebus ante benedictum dixerat eum, qui verbum diuinum sequeretur,& ad illud ipsum vitam accommodaret suam, in ijs iam infelicem atque miserum eum pronunciat qui Dei verbum vel odit vel negligit.
units.tr: Opposed to the blessings: Cursed shall you be, he says, in the city and in the field; your basket and your store; the fruit of your womb, of your land, and of your cattle; in your coming in and your going out. In these same things, before, he had said that the one who followed the divine Word and fitted his life to it would be blessed; now he pronounces unhappy and wretched in these same things the one who either hates or neglects the Word of God.

units.la: Tribus generibus comprehensa,vt egestate,peste, bello refert.Egestate, Mittet te Dominus in,&c. Quibus tria mala coniungit: Primùm, vt egeas rebus ad vitam tuendam necessarijs:dein vt perturbato,incerto, perplexo fis animo, omninoque rationem & consilium illas parandi nescias omnes: tertiò, vt te ipse increpes, impatiens tui ipsius fias, omnem egestatis culpam ac caufaminte [?] ref eras, teq; propterea ipse oderis. His addit pestiferas pluuias, rubigi-nem, & alia: post etiam amentiam, tacitatem, cor pauidum, mala maxima.
units.tr: He comprehends them under three kinds: want, pestilence, and war. For want: The Lord will send upon you, etc. In these he joins three evils. First, that you lack the things necessary for sustaining life; next, that you become troubled, uncertain, and perplexed in mind, and altogether do not know how to get those things or what plan to make for them; third, that you rebuke yourself, become impatient with yourself, and lay all the blame and cause of the want upon yourself, and so hate yourself. To these he adds pestilential rains, rust, and other things; then also madness, blindness, and a fearful heart, the greatest evils.

units.la: Peste comprehendit hæc : Adhærere faciet tibi Dominus pestem donec consumat te. Addit morbos, tumores, ardores, &c. vt sunt nunc plurimi.
units.tr: He includes these under pestilence: The Lord will make the pestilence cling to you until it consumes you. He adds diseases, swellings, burnings, etc., such as there are now in great number.

units.la: Bello comprehendit, Dabit prostratum ante hostes, contra ac supra dixit. Iniuriam patieris, nec eripieris. Quod quale sit facile exemplo nostro cognoscimus. Uxore, domo, vinea iumento, pecore, potietur alius. Diligens est ruentis reip. descriptio.
units.tr: Under war he includes: He will give you up, struck down before your enemies, contrary to what he said above; you will suffer wrong and will not be rescued. How true this is we easily know from our own experience. Another will possess your wife, your house, your vineyard, your ox, your flock. It is a careful description of a commonwealth going to ruin.

units.la: Hæc si quis horret, vt sunt horrenda, verbi Dei negligentiam prius horreat & declinabit per Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum, Amen.
units.tr: If anyone shudders at these things, as they are dreadful, let him first shudder at neglect of the Word of God, and he will turn aside from it through Jesus Christ our Lord, Amen.

units.la: SERMO LXX.
units.tr: Sermon 70.

units.la: 45 Venient deniq; in te omnes execrationes istæ, quæ & insequentur te, & apprehendent te, donec consumaris, eo quod non audiuisti vocem Domini Dei tui, vt custodires præcepta eius atq; statuta eius, quæ præcepit tibi.
units.tr: 45 And all these curses shall come upon thee, and shall pursue thee, and overtake thee, till thou be destroyed; because thou hearkenedst not unto the voice of the LORD thy God, to keep his commandments and his statutes which he commanded thee.

units.la: 46 Erunt in signum & in portentum in te, & in semine tuo perpetuò.
units.tr: 46 And they shall be upon thee for a sign and a wonder, and upon thy seed for ever.

units.la: 47 Eo quod non seruieris Domino Deo tuo in lætitia & bonitate cordis tui, quum tamen tibi omnia affluerent.
units.tr: 47 Because thou servedst not the LORD thy God with joyfulness, and with gladness of heart, for the abundance of all things.

units.la: 48 Seruies igitur hosti tuo, quem immittet Dominus tibi, in fame, siti, nuditate & omni rerum penuria. Et ponet iugum ferreum super collum tuum, donec ipse te deleat.
units.tr: 48 Therefore shalt thou serve thine enemy which the LORD shall send against thee, in hunger, and in thirst, and in nakedness, and in want of all things: and he shall put a yoke of iron upon thy neck, until he have destroyed thee.

units.la: 49 Excitabit contra te Dominus gentē è longinquo ab extremitate terræ, quæ involabit vt aquila, gentem cuius linguam tu non capies.
units.tr: 49 The LORD shall bring a nation against thee from far, from the end of the earth, as swift as the eagle flieth; a nation whose tongue thou shalt not understand.

units.la: 50 Gentem impudentem facie, quæ faciem senis non reuerebitur, nec miserebitur adolescentis.
units.tr: 50 A nation of fierce countenance, which shall not regard the person of the old, nor shew favour to the young.

units.la: 51 Hæc comedet fœtum iumentorum tuorum, & fructum telluris tuæ, donec te deleat vt nihil reliquum faciat tibi, neq; frumenti, neq; vini, neq; olei, neq; fœtus boum tuorum, neq; gregis ouium tuarum, donec te perdat.
units.tr: 51 And he shall eat the fruit of thy cattle, and the fruit of thy land, until thou be destroyed: which also shall not leave thee either corn, wine, or oil, or the increase of thy kine, or flocks of thy sheep, until he have caused thee to perish.

units.la: 52 Et premet te in omnibus portis tuis, donec deiecerit muros tuos sublimes, & munitiones in quas tu per totam terram tuam fiduciam collocas, & premet te in omnibus vrbibus tuis per vniuersam terram tuam, quam dedit tibi Dominus Deus tuus.
units.tr: 52 And he shall besiege thee in all thy gates, until thy high and fenced walls come down, wherein thou trustedst, throughout all thy land: and he shall besiege thee in all thy gates throughout all thy land, which the LORD thy God hath given thee.

units.la: 53 Et in hac obsidione & afflictione, quibus te affliget hostis tuus in cunctis vrbibus tuis, comedes fructum ventris tui, carnem filiorum tuorum & filiarum tuarum, quas dedit tibi Dominus Deus.
units.tr: 53 And thou shalt eat the fruit of thine own body, the flesh of thy sons and of thy daughters, whom the LORD thy God hath given thee, in the siege and in the straitness wherewith thine enemies shall distress thee.

units.la: 54 Oculus viri teneri & valde delicatuli qui in te est, inuidebit fratri suo, atq; uxori gremij sui, & his qui ex filijs eius reliqui sunt.
units.tr: 54 The man that is tender among you, and very delicate, his eye shall be evil toward his brother, and toward the wife of his bosom, and toward the remnant of his children which he shall leave.

units.la: 55 Ne scilicet det alicui eorum de carnibus filiorum suorum quos comedet, quia doquidem ex omnibus nihil aliud illi reliquum est in obsidione & afflictione, quibus te affliget hostis tuus in cunctis vrbibus tuis.
units.tr: 55 So that he will not give to any of them of the flesh of his children whom he shall eat, because he hath nothing left him in the siege and in the straitness wherewith thine enemies shall distress thee in all thy gates.

units.la: 56 (Mulier) quoq; tenera & delicatula, quæ in te est, quæ præ delicijs & teneritudine nunquam tentauit planta pedis sui super terram collocare, inuidebit oculo suo viro gremij sui, filio suo & filiæ suæ.
units.tr: 56 The tender and delicate woman among you, which would not adventure to set the sole of her foot upon the ground for delicateness and tenderness, her eye shall be evil toward the husband of her bosom, and toward her son, and toward her daughter.

units.la: 57 Felicitati quoq; sua recens à se edita, & filijs suis quos gignet, quoniam comedet eos in secreto, cum iam omnia desunt, in obsidione & afflictione, quibus te affliget hostis tuus in portis tuis.
units.tr: 57 And toward her young one that cometh out from between her feet, and toward her children which she shall bear: for she shall eat them for want of all things secretly in the siege and straitness wherewith thine enemy shall distress thee in thy gates.

units.la: 58 Si non seruaueris vt facias omnia verba legis huius, quæ scripta sunt in libro isto, & non timueris nomen hoc gloriosum et tremendum Dominum Deum tuum.
units.tr: 58 If thou wilt not observe to do all the words of this law that are written in this book, that thou mayest fear this glorious and fearful name, THE LORD THY GOD.

units.la: 59 Noua quædam, rara & magna atq; durabilia verbera, tum etiam infirmitates malas & durabiles infliget Dominus tibi & semini tuo.
units.tr: 59 Then the LORD will make thy plagues wonderful, and the plagues of thy seed, even great plagues, and of long continuance, and sore sicknesses, and of long continuance.

units.la: 60 Reducet, in te omnem morbum Ægypti, à quibus tu metuisti, & adhære-scent tibi.
units.tr: 60 Moreover he will bring upon thee all the diseases of Egypt, which thou wast afraid of; and they shall cleave unto thee.

units.la: 61 Omnem quoq; languorem, & omnes afflictiones, quae non sunt scriptae in libro legis huius, adducet Dominus super te, donec te deleat.
units.tr: 61 Also every sickness, and every plague, which is not written in the book of this law, them will the LORD bring upon thee, until thou be destroyed.

units.la: 62 Et pauci numero (ex vobis) reliqui erunt, cum essetis ante multi ut stellae cæ-li, quod non audiuisti vocem Domini Dei tui.
units.tr: 62 And ye shall be left few in number, whereas ye were as the stars of heaven for multitude; because thou wouldest not obey the voice of the LORD thy God.

units.la: 63 Fiet, ut sicut Dominus lætatus est de vobis, ut vobis benefaceret, et vos multiplicaret, sic lætabitur Dominus de vobis, ut perdat vos, & ut deleat vos, atque euellemini à superficie terræ in quam tu venis ut eam possideas.
units.tr: 63 And it shall come to pass, that as the LORD rejoiced over you to do you good, and to multiply you; so the LORD will rejoice over you to destroy you, and to bring you to nought; and ye shall be plucked from off the land whither thou goest to possess it.

units.la: 64 Disjiciet quoq; te Dominus in omnes populos, à fine terræ vsq; ad finem ter-ræ: ibi seruies diis aliis, quos neq; tu neq; patres tui noverunt: ligno nempe & lapidi.
units.tr: 64 And the LORD shall scatter thee among all people, from the one end of the earth even unto the other; and there thou shalt serve other gods, which neither thou nor thy fathers have known, even wood and stone.

units.la: 65 Et apud gentes huiusmodi requiem non invenies, neq; erit quo plantam pe-dis tui colloces, & dabit tibi Dominus cor palpitans, consumptionem oculorum, et mæ-rorem animi.
units.tr: 65 And among these nations shalt thou find no ease, neither shall the sole of thy foot have rest: but the LORD shall give thee there a trembling heart, and failing of eyes, and sorrow of mind.

units.la: 66 Et pendebit vita tua ante te, pauebis nocte et interdiu, nec fidere poteris vi-ta tuæ.
units.tr: 66 And thy life shall hang in doubt before thee; and thou shalt fear day and night, and shalt have none assurance of thy life.

units.la: 67 Mane dices, quis dabit vesperum? propter pauorem cordis tui, quo pauebis, & propter visum oculorum quod videbis.
units.tr: 67 In the morning thou shalt say, Would God it were even! and at even thou shalt say, Would God it were morning! for the fear of thine heart wherewith thou shalt fear, and for the sight of thine eyes which thou shalt see.

units.la: 68 Et reducet te Dominus in Ægyptum navibus, per viam quam dixi tibi: Non videbis eam amplius, & venum exponerus ibidem hostibus tuis in servos & ancillas, & non erit qui emat.
units.tr: 68 And the LORD shall bring thee into Egypt again with ships, by the way whereof I spake unto thee, Thou shalt see it no more again: and there ye shall be sold unto your enemies for bondmen and bondwomen, and no man shall buy you.

units.la: Quemadmodum Deus nobis, ut ad bonum nos propellat, multa magnaque bona polliceatur, ac rursus, ut abstrahat à malo, gravissima quaeq; mala comminatur: sic satan, qui semper ei reluctatur, minis à bono, ac rursus falsa specie bonorum ad mala trahit. Videmus e-nim quae minitetur studiosis evangelii, pietatis, sobrietatis, justitiae: ut rursus bona promittat improbis atq; impiis. Sed hoc non solum agit, verum etiam in confutationem verbi divini, sive bona sive mala promittentis incumbit: ac si bella, annonae caritatem, pestem minitatur, nihil ait esse nisi pfafforum terrores quibus fortunam dulcem nobis amaram reddant: negat-que etiam daemones & tartara: sed semper fuisse bella, non posse fieri quin ingruat aliquando rerum aliqua penuria, mirum non esse nec alienum à natura vel morte vel morbis obrui: à primo sic cepisse & ad ultimum usq; duraturam hanc rerum vicissitudinem: multum etiam uti sese quisque gerat, seq; praesentibus rebus & temporibus accommodet, referre: velle multos esse miseros, & suae sibi vel necis, vel fugae, vel penuriae causas ipsos esse: deniq; etiam ipsa sic elevat atque extenuat vitia, ut ne videantur esse in vitio.
units.tr: As God, to drive us towards what is good, promises many great blessings, and again, to draw us away from evil, threatens the gravest evils, so Satan, who always struggles against him, draws men from good by threats and again to evil by a false show of good. For we see what he threatens to the students of the gospel, of piety, of sobriety, of justice; and again what good things he promises to the wicked and the impious. But he does not only do this; he also sets himself against the divine word, whether it promises good or evil, in order to refute it. If he threatens wars, dearth of provisions, or plague, he says these are nothing but the terrors of priests, by which they make our fortune, which is sweet, seem bitter to us. He denies demons and hell too, and says that there have always been wars, that it cannot but be that some scarcity of goods comes at some time, that it is no wonder and not contrary to nature to be overwhelmed by death or disease; that this change of circumstances has begun from the first and will last to the very end; that it matters much how each man conducts himself and adapts himself to present things and times; that many wish to be wretched, and that they themselves are the causes of their own death, flight or want. Finally, he so raises up and belittles vices that they do not even seem to be vices at all.

units.la: Quaecum ita sint ac multum etiam moveant homines: sanè Moses omnia mala verbi divini contemptoribus divinitus irrogata commemorat, eaq; deinceps sic exaggerat ut pro le-vibus terriculamentis haberi non queant. Atque hoc quidem loco, ut quanti velitisthæc[?] fie-ri intelligas, malorum jam antea commemoratorum catalogum claudit repetita propositione & summa rei, tum etiam ἀξίωσις[?] qua permoveat.
units.tr: Although these things are so, and move men greatly, Moses certainly recalls all the evils divinely inflicted on the despisers of the divine word, and afterwards so magnifies them that they cannot be regarded as light scares. And indeed in this place, so that you may understand how much these things are to be valued, he closes the catalogue of evils already mentioned with a repeated statement and summary of the matter, and then with an appeal [ἀξίωσις] by which he may move us.

units.la: Ac summam quidem sic proponit, ut & illa mala certò adventare, & causam eorum effi-cientem iterum monstret. Etenim ea certò ventura quasi quadam hypotyposi probat. 1. Ve-nient in te, suo videlicet motu quodam. Nam quod veniendi vim & propensionem habet, de eo quin veniat non est dubitandum.
units.tr: He sets out the summary in such a way that he both shows that those evils are certainly coming and again points out their efficient cause. For he proves by a kind of outline that they will certainly come. 1. They shall come upon you, that is, by some motion of their own. For what has the power and tendency to come, there is no doubt that it will come.

units.la: 2. Insequentur te, videlicet evitare & astu nescio quo conantem & cupientem declinare. Quod argumento est mala divinitus decreta nullo consilio, nullo astu posse declinari: & ad-versus hæc nisi pœnitentiam non esse ullum remedium. Exemplo sunt Saul, Jonas, Judæi, alii.
units.tr: 2. They shall pursue you, that is, they cannot be avoided by one trying and desiring to evade them by some cunning device. This is an argument that evils decreed by God cannot be turned aside by any counsel or any cunning, and that against them there is no remedy except repentance. Examples are Saul, Jonah, the Jews, and others.

units.la: 3. Apprehendent: vim evadendi præripient omnem. Ut enim peccatis sic illorum pœnis homines irretiri solent, nempe ut quemadmodum peccandi finem nullum facis & in aliud la-beris ex alio, sic calamitatum finis nullus est & alia aliam consequitur.
units.tr: 3. They shall overtake you: they will snatch away every power of escape. For men are usually entangled in their punishments just as in their sins: just as there is no end to sinning, and one slides from one sin into another, so there is no end of calamities, and one follows another.

units.la: Omnium ultimus finis est, ut consumarit, inquit. Exemplo sunt & homines innumeri & complures cum imperiis civitates.
units.tr: The last end is that he consume you, he says. Examples are countless men and many cities together with their empires.

units.la: Causa est, quod non audieris. Una malorum omnium causa est Dei verbum audire nolle. Vide ergo quanto mundum fallat ac seducat satan. Malorum omnium causam atq; culpam imputat verbi Dei doctrinae & studio. Veluti Saul Dauidi, Heliae Isabella, Iudaeis Antiochus, Christo & Apostolis Iudaei. Venient Romani & tollent gentem & locum hunc. Eadem ex-probratio priscis Christianis & Augustino & Arnobio fuit refutanda. Nec nostris ipsorum e-xemplis destituimur. Nam & nobis aerumnas & miserias objiciunt adversarij, quasi illae ex E-uangelio obortae sint: cum aliis inobedientiae poenas bella, caritatem annonae, pestem minite-mur, ipsi quasi mala minime rara saepe q; euenire solita despiciunt. At hic inobedientiam mali causam & fontem dicit: Deum quia non obsequamur ei sic nos punire solere.
units.tr: It is because you did not listen. The one cause of all evils is refusing to hear the word of God. See, then, how far Satan deceives and seduces the world. He lays the cause and blame for all evils on the teaching and practice of God's word, just as Saul blamed David, Ahab blamed Elijah, the Jews blamed Antiochus, and the Jews blamed Christ and the apostles. "The Romans will come and take away our nation and this place." The same reproach had to be answered for the early Christians, and by Augustine and Arnobius. Nor are we left without examples from our own time. Our opponents also throw our miseries and troubles in our faces, as if they had arisen from the Gospel. Yet they threaten others with wars, dearth of food and plague as punishments for disobedience, and themselves overlook the fact that such evils are not rare and often happen as a matter of course. But here Moses names disobedience as the cause and source of evil: this is how God is accustomed to punish us, because we do not obey him.

units.la: Sed objiciat aliquis: An vero Deus ita suo honori ceu tyrannus consulit: si illius dicta nō audias ille quasi vindicans iniuriam, sic te statim eat perditum? Minime vero, Deus bonus est, & nostra causa vult nos verbis eius obsequentes esse. Et quàm aequum sit hoc eius iudici-um dicit. Erit in signum, &c. Id est, cum Deo danti bona animi, corporis, externa maxima ac plurima non obsecutus sis: merito & iure eius quem is immittet hostis iugum tete[?] ferre. Æ-quum est enim omnium gentium consensu puniri ingratitudinem & servire qui sunt abusi libertate, pauperes esse qui divitias turpiter abligurierunt, parere tyrannis qui noluere pijs magistratibus obtemperare, perire cum scorto qui cum proba matrona pie viuere noluerit, ex-bauriri indulgentijs & papisticis exactionibus illos qui repudiarunt euangelium. Hoc enim etiam leges monent ut ingratus libertus in servitutem retrahatur. Igitur verbi Dei negligen-tia atque contemptio malorum omnium fons sunt.
units.tr: But someone may object: does God, like a tyrant, look so jealously to his own honour that, if you do not heed his words, he immediately destroys you, as though avenging an injury? By no means. God is good, and he wills that we obey his words for our own sake. And see how just this judgment of his is. He says: It shall be for a sign, etc. That is, when you have not obeyed God, who gave you the greatest and most numerous good things of soul, body and outward life, it is rightly and justly done that you should bear the yoke of an enemy whom he sends against you. For it is fair, by the agreement of all nations, that those who abuse liberty should be punished by slavery for their ingratitude; that those who shamefully squander their riches should become poor; that those who refuse to obey godly magistrates should obey tyrants; that those who will not live chastely with a respectable matron should perish with a harlot; and that those who have rejected the Gospel should be drained by papal indulgences and exactions. For the laws too direct that an ungrateful freedman be returned to servitude. Therefore neglect and contempt of God's word are the source of all evils.

units.la: Ipsa vero mala praecipueq; bellum ceu malorum omnium fontem refert egregiè, & per hypotyposim sic describit ut ipsam calamitatem quasi coram atq; ob oculos versantem videa-ris spectare. Nam personam, facta, eventum pingit & proponit. Personam, excitabit, inquit, contra te Dominus gentem e longinquo ab extremitate terra quae involabit ut aquila, gentem cuius linguam tu non capies, gentem impudentem facie. Quę singula vim habent suam & personam ter tremendam notant.
units.tr: Moses also describes the evils themselves, and above all war, as the fountain of all evils, and he does so admirably, through a vivid portrayal, so that you seem to see the calamity as if it were before your eyes. For he paints and sets forth the enemy, the deeds and the outcome. The enemy: The Lord will raise up against you a nation from afar, from the end of the earth, which will swoop down like an eagle, a nation whose language you will not understand, a nation shameless of face. Each of these words has its own force and marks the enemy as truly dreadful.

units.la: 1. Venturum hostem mandato Dei, providentia Dei, iusto iudicio Dei: Dicit enim, Do-minus excitabit contra te. Habes authorem bellorum alium quàm qui videtur prophanis gentibus. Nihil enim erat quod duo Martis templa haberent Romani: unum intra urbem Quirini ad conservandam in tranquillo rempublicam: alterum extra urbem Gradiui ad ar-cendos & profligandos hostes. Eodem loco putabis esse sive Bellonam sive Duellonam foro rem & uxorem Martis, quae ei in bella eunti currus & equos parare dicebatur. Moses contra Deum authorem dicit bellorum, qui illa sceleratis immittit iusto iudicio proptereaque dici-minus exercituum. Et Esaias dicit Dominum Ægyptijs & Assyrijs sibilaturum ut veniant ul-tum contemptum verbi Domini.
units.tr: 1. The enemy comes by God's command, God's providence and God's just judgment. For he says: the Lord will raise up against you. You have as the author of wars someone other than the one the profane nations imagine. The Romans had two temples of Mars, for no other reason than that one within the city, of Quirinus, was to keep the commonwealth in peace, and the other outside the city, of Gradivus, was to ward off and crush enemies. You would think that in the same place there were Bellona or Duellona, the wife of Mars, who was said to prepare chariots and horses for him when he went to war. Moses, against this, names God as the author of wars, who by just judgment sends them upon the wicked; for this reason he is called Lord of hosts. Isaiah also says that the Lord will whistle for the Egyptians and Assyrians to come and avenge the contempt of the Lord's word.

units.la: Nos abundantia ac tedio pacis bellum, in bello quancunq; pacem affectamus: at id omne est positum in manu Domini. Sæpe ut adversus hostiles incursiones tuti simus & muniti in fœdera venimus: sæpe malum quiddam committimus, & Deum negamus pacis obtinendæ studio: sed Deus iratus alias[?]. Exemplo sunt vel Iudæi Romanos hoc ipso offendentes quo sibi studebant conciliare. Rectè ergo dicit Moses Deum excitare & movere in rebelles hostem.
units.tr: We, in our abundance and weariness of peace, desire war; and in war we seek peace in every way. But all this lies in the hand of the Lord. Often, to be safe and protected against hostile raids, we enter into covenants; often we commit some wrong and deny God in our eagerness to obtain peace; but God is angry in other ways. The Jews are an example, who offended the Romans by the very means by which they strove to win their favour. Rightly, then, Moses says that God raises up and stirs up an enemy against rebels.

units.la: 2. Gens remota, non coniuncta fœdere, cuius conditionibus impedita damnum dare non posit. Verum remota à vicinia.
units.tr: 2. A remote nation, not joined by covenant, whose conditions could not hinder it from doing harm. That is, remote from the neighbourhood.

units.la: 3. Velox instar aquilae. Altissimus & pernicissimus est volatus aquilae. Quo ducem fortunatum ac fœlicem vocat. Optimum enim est & maximum boni ducis in velocitate positum præsidium. Præstat enim prævenire, quàm præveniri, inquit ille. Et ut Sallustianus ille dux praeclarè statuit, deliberandum est diu quod statuendum semel: at ubi deliberaveris maturè facto opus est.
units.tr: 3. Swift as an eagle. The flight of the eagle is the highest and swiftest. By this he calls the leader fortunate and happy. For the best and greatest defence of a good leader lies in speed. As that man said, it is better to forestall than to be forestalled. And, as that Sallustian general wisely laid down: one should deliberate long over what must be decided once; but when you have deliberated, action must be taken promptly.

units.la: 4. Cuius tu linguam non intelligas: nempe ut nec deprecari culpam, nec pacisci vitam, nec supplex quicquam postulare queas, ac diversum quiddam ab eo quod sentias dicas. Veluti in bello, quod Helvetij maiores nostri contra Maximilianum Romanorum regem gesserunt, quidam in fuga viuum se conservari postulans insequentem Helvetium alloquebatur, mein sü[?] maul laß mich läben, existimans hoc proprium esse gentis nomen, quod vicini ignominiae causa indiderant, atque ipse in sua procul hinc remota terra solum audiuerat. Magni igitur in mali sit loco nescire gentis eius linguam, à qua superaris, quippe cum qua nulla possit inter-eedere[?] familiaritas.
units.tr: 4. Whose language you do not understand: namely, so that you cannot plead for mercy, bargain for your life, or humbly ask for anything, and so that you say something other than what you actually feel. For example, in the war which our Swiss forebears waged against Maximilian, king of the Romans, a certain man, fleeing and begging to be spared alive, called out to a pursuing Swiss, "Mein süess maul, lass mich läben" ("my sweet mouth, let me live"), supposing this to be the proper name of the people, which their neighbours had given them as a term of abuse and which he himself had heard only in his own distant land. It is therefore a great evil to be ignorant of the language of the people by whom you are overcome, since no familiarity can exist with them.

units.la: 5. Facie impudente. Nec sexus nec ætatis rationem habeat, sed immisericorditer in omne
units.tr: 5. Of a shameless face. It shows no regard for sex or age, but rages without mercy against every kind of person.

units.la: { } Gloss text not legible as separate note on this page. genus hominum grassetur. Vnde prophetæ minantur prægnantes dissecatum, & inde pueros ex vteris extractum iri. Ac quoniam in vultu notæ sunt animi siue boni siue trucis & maligni, dicit impudentę vultum gentis illius esse, velut ille apud Homerum aduersarium suum κλωσπῶπις appellat. At eum quis non metuat quem nullius neq; maleficij, neque iniuriæ pudeat? Ex quibus omnibus intelligimus hostem, si personam eius consideres, fatis grauem & durum immissum iri.
units.tr: [Gloss text not legible as a separate note on this page.] It will rage against the human race. Hence the prophets threaten that pregnant women will be ripped open and children torn from their wombs. And since the marks of the mind, whether good or fierce and malicious, are written in the face, he says that the face of that nation is shameless, as the adversary in Homer is called brazen-faced [κλωσπῶπις]. But who would not fear a man whom no crime or wrong makes ashamed? From all these things we understand that, if you consider the character of the enemy, a very grave and harsh one will be sent against you.

units.la: Facta etiam ipsa commemorat. Hæc, inquit, comedet fœtum iumentorum tuorum, &c. Quo ostendit, 1. Absumpturum fruges, pecoris quicquid est, & alimentorum quo viuit homo. Hinc rerum omnium penuria: ac fit vt quemadmodum antea tuo, sic iam alieno luxu tuæ facultates concoquantur.
units.tr: He also recalls the deeds themselves: This nation will eat the offspring of your cattle, etc. By this he shows: 1. that it will consume the crops, whatever livestock there is, and all the food by which man lives. Hence comes a shortage of everything; and as before your wealth was consumed by your own extravagance, so now it is consumed by the extravagance of others.

units.la: 2. Oppida atq; arces in quibus spei plurimum effet diruent. Illi enim relicto domino sidebant muris, & inde facti securi quicquid diceretur de diuino iudicio vel ridebant vel negligebant: nec cogitabant homines frustra vigilare non custodiente Deo. Quare brachium hoc carnis Deus aufert, & suis eos destituit præsidijs.
units.tr: 2. They will destroy the towns and strongholds in which you placed most of your hope. For they, having left their Lord, trusted in their walls, and, made secure by this, either laughed at or neglected whatever was said about divine judgment; nor did they consider that men keep watch in vain when God does not guard the city. Therefore God takes away this arm of flesh and abandons them to their own defences.

units.la: 3. Premente te paßim, vt supra, iugo ferreo. Nullus erit locus quietis, sic lege talionis vlciscitur Deus scelera.
units.tr: 3. When he presses you everywhere, as above, with an iron yoke. There will be no place of rest. So God avenges crimes by the law of retaliation.

units.la: Euentus, Et in hac, inquit, obsidione, &c. Docet 1. Tantam fore inediam vt devoraturi sint suos ipsorum liberos. 2. Grauissimis etiam morbis affligantur, nempe ex intemperato victu & mala vitæ ratione contractis. 3. Deus quasi lætabundus pugnabit. 4. Disiiciet, Videlicet ceu quisquilias. 5. Cor pauidum. Exempla harum calamitatum sunt & in sacris & in prophanis in primisque huius gentis historijs. Vt 4. Reg. 16. obsessa Samaria: vt quod Hieremias in Threnis factum dicit: quod Hierosolymis in obsidione vltima factum Egesippus refert. Vbi Titus dicebat, quod hic Moses comminetur, Deum cum illis pugnare.
units.tr: The outcome: And in this siege, etc. He teaches: (1) that there will be such want of food that they will devour their own children; (2) that they will be afflicted with the gravest diseases, namely those contracted from intemperate diet and a bad manner of life; (3) that God will fight as if rejoicing; (4) He will scatter, that is, as though they were rubbish; (5) a fearful heart. Examples of these calamities are found both in sacred and in profane writers, and especially in the histories of this nation: as in 4 Kings 16, when Samaria was besieged; as Jeremiah in the Lamentations says was done; and as Hegesippus reports was done at Jerusalem in the final siege, where Titus used to say that this is what Moses threatens, that God fights against them.

units.la: Ex quibus est colligendum, quod Christus vineæ plantatæ & colonis alijs elocatæ parabola significat, Matth. 21. Quare qui sibi confultum volunt ij legi diuinæ studendum existimabunt, fèque hoc ipso beabunt, per Christum Dominum nostrum, Amen.
units.tr: From these things it is to be gathered that Christ signifies, in the parable of the vineyard planted and let out to other husbandmen, Matt. 21. Therefore those who wish to look to their own good will think they must study the divine law, and will thereby make themselves blessed, through Christ our Lord. Amen.

units.la: IOANNIS VVOLPHII TIGVRINI IN DEVTERONOMIVM SERMONVM LIBER QVARTVS. CAPUT XXIX. SERMO I.
units.tr: JOHANN WOLF OF ZURICH, FOURTH BOOK OF SERMONS ON DEUTERONOMY. CHAPTER 29. SERMON 1.

units.la: HÆc sunt verba fœderis, quod præcepit Dominus Mosi, vt feriret cum filijs Israel in terra Moab, præter fœdus illud quod ferijt cum eis in Horeb.
units.tr: These are the words of the covenant which the Lord commanded Moses to make with the children of Israel in the land of Moab, besides the covenant which he made with them in Horeb.

units.la: 2 Vocato autem omni Israele Moses, dixit ad eos: Vos vidistis omnia quæ fecit Dominus vobis spectantibus in terra Ægypti, Pharaoni & omnibus seruis eius, atq; vniuersæ terræ eius.
units.tr: And Moses called all Israel and said to them: You have seen all that the Lord did before your eyes in the land of Egypt, to Pharaoh and all his servants and all his land.

units.la: 3 Tentationes magnas, quas viderunt oculi tui, signaq; illa magna atque portenta.
units.tr: The great trials which your eyes have seen, those great signs and wonders.

units.la: 4 Nec dedit vobis Dominus cor ad intelligendum, & oculos ad videndum, atque aures ad audiendum vsq; in præsentem diem.
units.tr: Yet the Lord has not given you a heart to understand, or eyes to see, or ears to hear, to this present day.

units.la: 5 Ego quidem duxi vos quadraginta annis per desertum, nec sunt vetustate attrita vestimenta vestra super vos, nec calceamentum tuum vetustate consumptū est in pede tuo.
units.tr: I have led you forty years through the wilderness. Your clothes have not worn out upon you, nor has your sandal worn out upon your foot.

units.la: 6 Panem non edistis, nec vinum aut siceram bibistis, vt sciretis quod ego sum Dominus Deus vester.
units.tr: You have not eaten bread, nor drunk wine or strong drink, so that you might know that I am the Lord your God.

units.la: 7 Et venistis ad locum, egressusq; obuiam vobis Sihon rex Hesbon, & Og rex Basan congressus est (nobiscum) quos percussimus.
units.tr: When you came to this place, Sihon king of Heshbon and Og king of Bashan came out against us, and we defeated them.

units.la: 8 Accipientes autem terram eorum, dedimus eam in hæreditatem Rubenitis et Gaditis, & dimidiæ tribui Manasse.
units.tr: We took their land and gave it as an inheritance to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh.

units.la: 9 Custodietis itaq; verba fœderis huius, vt faciatis ea, vt prudenter agatis omnia quæ facturi estis.
units.tr: Keep, therefore, the words of this covenant and do them, so that you may act wisely in everything you are about to do.

units.la: 10 Vos omnes hodie statis coram Domino Deo vestro, capita vestra, tribus vestras, seniores vestri, & præcones vestri atq; omnes viri Israelitæ.
units.tr: You all stand today before the Lord your God: your heads, your tribes, your elders, your officers, and all the men of Israel.

units.la: 11 Pubes vestra, vxores vestræ, & peregrinus tuus qui est in castris tuis, à lignatore tuo vsq; ad aquatores tuos.
units.tr: Your little ones, your wives, and the stranger who is in your camp, from the one who hews your wood to the one who draws your water.

units.la: 12 Vt transeat in fœdus Domini Dei tui, & in iuramentum eius, quod Dominus Deus tuus hodie ferit tecum.
units.tr: That you may enter into the covenant of the Lord your God and into his oath, which the Lord your God makes with you today.

units.la: 13 Vt erigat te hodie sibi in populum, & ipse sit tibi Deus quemadmodum pollicitus est tibi, et quemadmodū iurauit patribus tuis, Abrahamo scilicet, Isaac et Iacob.
units.tr: That he may today establish you as his people, and that he may be your God, just as he promised you and swore to your fathers, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

units.la: 14 Non autem vobiscum duntaxat ego ferio pactum istud, et iuramentū illud.
units.tr: I do not make this covenant and this oath with you alone.

units.la: 15 Sed & cum omni eo qui hodie apud nos hic stat coram Domino Deo nostro, & cum eo qui hodie non est hic nobiscum.
units.tr: But I make it with whoever stands here with us today before the Lord our God, and with whoever is not here with us today.

units.la: 16 Vos enim scitis qualiter habitauerimus in terra Ægypti, & quomodo transierimus per medias gentes, per quas transistis.
units.tr: For you know how we dwelt in the land of Egypt, and how we passed through the nations through which you went.

units.la: 17 Vidistis quoq; abominationes eorum, & idola eorum, lignum & lapidem, argentum & aurum, quæ apud illos erant.
units.tr: You have seen their abominations and their idols, wood and stone, silver and gold, which were among them.

units.la: CVM doctrina de voluntate Dei & salute mortalium Thora Hebręis appelletur, id est, recta via dirigendi ratio siue regula: tum eius interpres omnis sit quasi qui dam Moreh, id est director, gubernator, magister: sane quando homines sese dirigi non patiantur, nisi eas ad res, quas sibi saluti fore norint: oportet bonum interpretem & docere & mouere: id est, non modo verbis rem efferre, verum etiam ad eius studium incitare. Docere enim ad intellectum & memoriam, mouere vero ad voluntatem pertinet:vtrunq; efficitur expositione,exemplis, sententijs, amplificatione, & alijs generis eiusdem rebus.
units.tr: Since the doctrine of God's will and the salvation of mortals is called Torah by the Hebrews, that is, a rule or method for guiding one straight, its interpreter must be a kind of Moreh, that is, a director, guide and teacher. Indeed, when men will not allow themselves to be directed except towards those things they know to be good for their salvation, a good interpreter must both teach and move. That is, he must not only set the matter forth in words, but also stir people to take it up eagerly. For teaching concerns the understanding and memory, while moving concerns the will. Both are achieved by exposition, examples, maxims, amplification, and other things of this kind.

units.la: Quamobrem cum Moses ceu Dei Opt.Max. interpres hoc libro summam ac caput coe-lestis doctrinae cum exponat tum commendet suis hominibus: primum animos ad eam acci-piendam accommodat:dein eius summam quandam ponit ob oculos: postremo eam expo-nit atque omnis generis argumentis & exemplis munit. Quas partes superioribus libris ut-cunq; explanatas puto.
units.tr: Therefore, since Moses, as interpreter of God the Best and Greatest, sets out and recommends to his people in this book the sum and chief point of heavenly doctrine, he first prepares their minds to receive it, then places before their eyes a certain summary of it, and finally sets it out and fortifies it with arguments and examples of every kind. I think I have explained these parts, in some measure, in the earlier books.

units.la: Iam quoniam conclusiones ex initiorum natura fluunt,funtq; totius orationis quasi qui-dam portus: Moses etiam hanc suam de doctrina coelesti sane quam fabrefactam orationem eiusmodi peroratione claudit, quae praecipuis eius partibus respondeat, & ab illo docendi mouendiq; proposito no modo non aberret, sed idipsum cumulatissime praestet. Nam cum omnis recta conclusio duabus constet partibus, enumeratione & motu, ealq; etiam ipsas hoc habeat: enumeratio quidem principio huiusce concionis, motus autem expositioni seu confirmationi videntur respondere. Ac quemadmodum exordio progymnasmata quaedam proposuit, quibus ad doctrinam ipsam animos hominum quasi quodammodo praepararet atque accommodaret: sic illa priore conclusionis parte quaecunq; videntur ab eius studio retrahere, ea omnia hic repellit, rursus vt expositione seu confirmatione doctrinae exempla sententias, leges, argumenta, cerimonias, promissiones affert atque minas ei videlicet stabiliendae: sic parte conclusionis posteriore suum discessum, carmen & benedictiones commouendis hominum animis adducit.
units.tr: Now, since conclusions flow from the nature of the beginnings, and are like a harbour for the whole discourse, Moses also closes this carefully wrought discourse on heavenly doctrine with a peroration that corresponds to its principal parts, and that not only does not stray from his purpose of teaching and moving, but fulfils it most fully. For every proper conclusion consists of two parts, recapitulation and appeal, and these have their own parts. Recapitulation seems to correspond to the beginning of this sermon, and appeal to the exposition or confirmation. Just as in the exordium he set forth certain preliminary exercises by which he might, as it were, prepare and dispose the minds of men towards the doctrine itself, so in the first part of the conclusion he rejects everything that seems to draw them away from its pursuit. Again, in the exposition or confirmation of the doctrine, he brings forward examples, maxims, laws, arguments, ceremonies, promises, and threats, to establish it. So in the latter part of the conclusion he brings forward his departure, his song and his blessings, to stir the hearts of men.

units.la: Sed impedimenta primum duobus his 29.&30. cap.repellit.Eorum primum est peruersa personarum ratio. De qua sic disserit hoc loco, vt primum proponat: tum commemoratio-ne singularum partium repellat: postremo omnes ordines appellans ad propositum suum omnia accommodet.
units.tr: But he first removes the obstacles, in these two chapters, 29 and 30. The first of these is a perverse view of persons. He discusses this in the following way: first he sets it out; then, by recalling the individual parts, he refutes it; finally, by addressing all the orders, he adapts everything to his purpose.

units.la: Vt proponat impedimentum hoc considerandum : Haec sunt, inquit, verba foederis quod praecepit Dominus Mosi vt feriret cum filijs Israel in terra Moab, praeter foedus illud quod fecerat cum illis in Horeb. Id est, Ne qui in Horeb vel Sina propositam doctrinam ipsi non acceperunt, multoq; post alio loco sunt nati, putent eam ad se minime pertinere: Moses iussus est eam posteris in terra Moab repetere, & ostendere tam illis quam maioribus: tam in Chananaea terra quam in deserto: tam secundis his quam illis tristibus rebus & temporibus seruandam esse.
units.tr: That he may set out this obstacle for consideration: These are the words of the covenant which the Lord commanded Moses to make with the children of Israel in the land of Moab, besides the covenant which he made with them in Horeb, he says. That is, lest those who did not receive the proposed doctrine in Horeb or Sinai, and were born long afterwards in another place, should think it has nothing to do with them, Moses was commanded to repeat it to the descendants in the land of Moab, and to show it to them as well as to their fathers; it is to be kept both in the land of Canaan and in the wilderness, in prosperity as well as in those sad times and circumstances.

units.la: Quae res etiam nostris hominibus est obseruanda, quando nobis res gestas patrum atq; Christi, temq;[?] leges, prophetas, euangelistas, apostolos enarrantibus atq; ad haec nostra tempora accomodantibus obijcitur: haec olim patriarchis, Israelitis, Iudaeis, alijs prisci populis proposita atque mandata nihil ad nos pertinere. At quemadmodum per Mosem olim sic per Christum deinceps renouatum est foedus, & diruta maceria, factumq; ouile vnum.
units.tr: This point must also be observed by our people, when they are told the deeds of the fathers and of Christ, and when the laws, prophets, evangelists and apostles are related and applied to our own times. It is objected that the precepts and commands once given to the patriarchs, Israelites, Jews and other ancient peoples have nothing to do with us. But just as the covenant was once renewed through Moses, so it was afterwards renewed through Christ, the wall was broken down, and there was made one fold.

units.la: Quod quoniam Moses ipse docet, eius verbis insistemus. Ac quoniam de personis agitur[?], vt ne quod dubium vlli relinquatur, personas omnes ponderat: vt Dei, vt ipsorum, vt incolarum seu aduenarum cum illis habitantium, vt earum quas imitabantur gentium.
units.tr: Since Moses himself teaches this, we shall follow his words. And since the matter concerns persons, so that no doubt may remain for anyone, he weighs all the persons: those of God, those of the people themselves, those of the sojourners or strangers who lived among them, and those of the nations they imitated.

units.la: De Dei persona dicit ad hunc modum : Vos vidistis omnia quae fecit Deus vobis spectantibus in terra Aegypti, &c. Quibus verbis quid Deus fecerit ordine commemorat: vt quid in Aegypto, quid in deserto, quid in Moab. In Aegypto primum Pharaonem regni caput, malo-rum authorem ipsum petijt: tum seruos ei in re tam scelesta cum applaudentes, tum opem ferentes, vltus est dignis suppliciis: deniq; terram ipsam his sceleribus contaminatam quasiq; veneno aliquo infectam diris plagis afflixit.
units.tr: He speaks of God's person in this way: You have seen all that God did before your eyes in the land of Egypt, etc. In these words he recalls in order what God did: first in Egypt, then in the wilderness, then in Moab. In Egypt, he first attacked Pharaoh, the head of the kingdom and the author of the evils himself. Then he punished with fitting penalties the servants who applauded and lent aid to him in so wicked a matter. Finally he afflicted the land itself, contaminated by these crimes and as if infected with some poison, with dreadful plagues.

units.la: At neque signis neque plagis vllis emolliri gens indurata potuit. Vnde haec eis & caecitas & duricies? Dicit Moses. Nec dedit Dominus cor ad intelligendum, nec aures ad audiendum, nec oculos ad videndum. Inerat illis ἀναισθησία quaedam, qua fiebat vti nullis obiectis eorum sen-sus permoueri possent: ac veluti somno altissimo presi, nec voce nec pulsu, nec vllo modo se se patiuntur excitari: sic illi in veternum peccati sui demersi nihil eorum quae Deus emollien-dis adhibebat, sentiebant. Sin Deus hoc det vt sentiamus, tunc potest fieri vt excitemur. Huic, inquit Moses, Deus non dedit cor vt intelligeret: id est, Deus non illuminauit, non mouit, non aperuit.
units.tr: But a people hardened could not be softened by any signs or plagues. Whence this blindness and hardness? Moses says: Nor has the Lord given a heart to understand, nor ears to hear, nor eyes to see. There was in them a certain insensibility [ἀναισθησία], by which their senses could not be moved by any objects; and as if held by the deepest sleep, they allowed themselves to be roused by neither voice nor touch nor any means at all. So they, sunk in the lethargy of their sin, perceived nothing of those things by which God applied means to soften them. But if God gives us to perceive, then it can happen that we are roused. To this people, says Moses, God did not give a heart to understand: that is, God did not enlighten, did not move, did not open.

units.la: En Deum authorem beatis sapientiae. Psal.39. quoniam apud te est fons vitae & in lumi-ne tuo videbimus lumen. Et 1. Cor.12. dicit apostolus neminem posse dicere Dominum Iesum nisi in spiritu sancto. Ioh.3. Baptista videns stuporem discipulorum exclamat: neminem posse quicquam accipere, nisi datum fuerit illi desuper. Ioh. 6. Christus ait neminem ad se venire posse, nisi cui id sit datum à patre. Sic Moses populo suam obliuionem exprobrans docet in operibus Dei nos non sapere, nisi Dei dono atque beneficio: quo suscitaret in illorum animis pietatem & preces, quibus peterent sibi cor, aures, oculos diuinitus dari. Velut Hierem.24. promisit illis cor ut ipsum cognoscant. Eodem modo nostrum est potius à Deo petere cor, aures, oculos quibus illum plene cognoscamus, audiamus, videamus quàm illius verba atq; opera dicamus nihil ad nos pertinere.
units.tr: Behold God as the author of blessed wisdom: "For with thee is the fountain of life; and in thy light shall we see light" (Psal. 39). And the apostle says in 1 Cor. 12 that no one can say "Jesus is Lord" except in the Holy Spirit. John the Baptist, seeing the amazement of the disciples, cries out (John 3) that no one can receive anything unless it has been given to him from above. Christ says (John 6) that no one can come to him unless it is given to him by the Father. So Moses, rebuking the people for their forgetfulness, teaches that we do not understand the works of God except by God's gift and blessing. His aim was to stir up in their minds piety and prayers, by which they might ask that heart, ears and eyes be given them from God. Thus in Jer. 24 God promised them a heart to know him. In the same way, it is our duty to ask God for a heart, ears and eyes, so that we may fully know, hear and see him, rather than to say that his words and works are no concern of ours.

units.la: Nam hæc in conspectu nostro non sine causa fecit: sed hoc egit, ut alieno exemplo nos ad emendationem propelleret. Ac veluti magistratus fures & latrones publicè plectit, ut exemplo sint toti populo: sic Deus etiam ipse exempla facit. Quod igitur in Ægypto Pharaonem atque eius homines omnes primum quidem afflixit, deinceps autem funditus sustulit, idque publicè[?] & in conspectu totius populi sic[?] id tantum abest nihil ut ad posteros pertineat, uti Deus hoc exemplo voluerit omnem posteritatem quantum sit nefas impietas, edocere.
units.tr: He did these things before our eyes not without reason, but to drive us to amendment by another's example. Just as the magistrate punishes thieves and robbers publicly so that they may be examples to the whole people, so God too makes examples. Therefore, what he did in Egypt, first afflicting Pharaoh and all his people, and afterwards utterly destroying them, and doing so publicly and in the sight of the whole people, is by no means of no concern to later generations. God willed to teach all posterity by this example how great a wickedness impiety is.

units.la: Iam in deserto quod neq; vestimenta atq; calceamenta attrita sunt, neq; eis cibus potuis-que defuere: id non tam eorum qui tunc beneficijs illis fruebantur est factum causa, verum omnibus hominibus documento potest esse, quàm non difficile sit Deo vel in desertis atq; in cultis locis ecclesiam suam sustentare. Sic vnius Sareptanæ viduæ & vnius Nahaamani Syri exemplis quid de Dei potentia sit statuendum Christus ipse docet Luc.4. Quamobrem quæ in deserto maiores experti sunt eorum omnibus prodest cognitio.
units.tr: Again, in the desert, the clothes and shoes were not worn out, and they lacked neither food nor drink. This was done not so much for the sake of those who then enjoyed those benefits, but it can serve as a lesson to all men of how not difficult it is for God to sustain his church even in deserts and in uninhabited places. Christ himself teaches in Luke 4 what is to be concluded about God's power from the examples of the one widow of Sarepta and the one Syrian Naaman. Therefore, the knowledge of what our forefathers experienced in the desert profits all of them.

units.la: Iam in terra Moab reges deuicti, & eorum bonis ipsi ditati sunt, easq; terras acceperant ac possederant ex parte, quarum occupandarum gratia maiores Ægypto erepti, per illa aspera desertaq; loca traducti fuerant, cum istis gentibus grauia bella gesserant. Iam si leges maioribus latas ceu nihil ad ipsos pertinerent respuebant: cur terris & à Deo promissis & maiorum sanguine partis fruebantur? Hoc nimirum agebant ut bonis fruerentur, oneraque leges detestarent. At diuersum etiam ipsa suadet ratio. Si velint esse Dei peculium, Dei socij, amici, populus, cum occupanda est terra: sint etiam cum standum est pactis atq; fœderi.
units.tr: Again, in the land of Moab the kings were conquered and their goods made the Israelites rich. They had received and possessed in part those lands, for the sake of occupying which their forefathers had been led out of Egypt and through those harsh and desert places, and had waged grievous wars with those peoples. Now, if they rejected the laws given to their forefathers as though they did not concern them, why did they enjoy the lands promised by God and won with their forefathers' blood? Clearly they did this in order to enjoy the goods while detesting the burdens of the laws. Yet reason itself suggests the opposite. If they wished to be God's peculiar people, God's associates, friends and people, then, just as they had to seize the land, so too they must abide by the pacts and covenant.

units.la: Eadem nobis est ineunda ratio. Si maiorum bonæ leges & consuetudines, probitas, pietas nihil ad nos pertinent, quid illorum nomine gloriamur? cur illorum fruimur libertate & priuilegijs? cur illorum res gestas legimus & canimus? si quæ fiunt ab alijs gentibus atque populis nihil ad nos attinent, cur earum visendaram gratia peregre proficiscimur? Cur seniibus[?] vsu rerum prudentiam consecutis tantum tribuimus si res olim gestas nihil ad nos pertinere ducimus? Sed cum aliena exempla docent, tū in doctrinā nostram omnia mandata sunt literis, ut inquit apostolus. Qui igitur Deus non tantum nostris maioribus verumetiam nobis ipsis perinde vult à nobis coli atq; voluit olim ab illis adorari.
units.tr: The same reasoning must be applied to us. If the good laws and customs of our forefathers, their uprightness and piety, are no concern of ours, why do we glory in their name? Why do we enjoy the liberty and privileges they won? Why do we read and sing of their deeds? If what is done by other nations and peoples is no concern of ours, why do we set out abroad for the sake of seeing them? Why do we give so much honour to the old, who have gained wisdom through experience of affairs, if we consider the deeds of past times to be no concern of ours? But as the examples of others teach us, so all things have been committed to writing for our instruction, as the apostle says. Therefore, God wills to be worshipped by us, and not only by our forefathers but by ourselves, just as he once willed to be adored by them.

units.la: Quamobrem hoc addit Moses dicens: Custodietis itaq; verba fœderis huius, ut faciatis ea, ut prudenter agatis omnia quæ facturi estis. Id est, Quamobrem cum hæc Deus publicè, & non minus in vestram, quàm maiorum vestrorum salutem atq; utilitatem fecerit: vestra profecto, si quidem sapere velitis & vestræ incolumitati studere, non minus refert quàm patrum vestrorum hæc præcepta seruare.
units.tr: Therefore Moses adds this, saying: Therefore you shall keep the words of this covenant, that you may do them, and act wisely in all that you are about to do. That is: since God has done these things publicly, and for your salvation and welfare no less than that of your forefathers, it is certainly of no less importance to you, if indeed you wish to be wise and to care for your own safety, to keep these precepts than it was for your fathers.

units.la: Iam de ipsorum persona ad hunc modum dicit: Vos omnes hodie statis coram Domino Deo vestro, capita vestra, tribus vestri, seniores vestri, &c. Sigillatim singulos ab imo ad summum appellat: tum addit, Ut transeas in foedus Domini Dei tui, in iuramentum eius, quod hodie facit tecum. Ut erigat te in populum & ipse sit Deus, ut promisit patribus. En præceptum magistratibus, plebeijs, senibus, iuuenibus, masculis fœminis, feruis, liberis, indigenis exteris effugium, & omnes & singulos appellat: tum addit vinculum, fœdus Domini, iuramentum Domini, populi Dei dignitatem. Ex quo colligitur eum qui velit hac societate comprehendi, promissis patrum gaudere, bonis optatis aliquando potiri, eum leges fœderis etiam seruare oportere.
units.tr: Further, concerning their persons he speaks in this way: You all stand today before the Lord your God, your heads, your tribes, your elders, etc. He addresses each individual, from the lowest to the highest. Then he adds: That you may enter into the covenant of the Lord your God, and into his oath, which he makes with you today; that he may establish you as a people, and that he himself may be your God, as he promised your fathers. Behold, he addresses and includes all and each: magistrates, commoners, elders, young men, men and women, servants, free men, natives and foreigners. He adds the bond, the covenant of the Lord, the oath of the Lord, the dignity of the people of God. From this it is gathered that whoever wishes to be bound by this fellowship, rejoices in the promises made to the fathers, and will one day obtain the desired goods, ought also to keep the laws of the covenant.

units.la: In quo videmus quàm calua sit nostrorum hominum excusatio, qui vel Iudaeis latas leges de moribus tanquam abs sua forte remotas auersantur: vel diuini verbi studium atq; professionem, quasi rem ministris solis competentem respuunt, cum tamen promisso Messia, & omnibus in illo expectatis bonis frui velint. Roganti de Deo, de bonis moribus, de legibus, de religione, non sum inquiunt, Pfaffus[?], non habeo vllum ex quo victitem[?] sacerdotium: curâ hanc Pfaffis[?] remitto. Sed o bone vir, an non habes etiam Deum, an non ab illo vitam, alium pro sacerdotio victum accepisti? annon illius beneficio liberatus es? non per multa pericula vectus? An verò Christianus non es? Sanè si Christianus velis esse, & à Christo olim agnosci atq; recipi, illum hic colas, obserues, sequaris, confitearis necesse est. Ut fruitione gaudiorum. cœlestium excludi nemo volet,sic imitatione & profesione Christi nemo se exemptum ar-bitrator.
units.tr: In this we see how feeble is the excuse of our own people, who both reject the laws concerning morals given to the Jews, as if they were far removed from their own affairs, and despise the study and profession of the divine word, as if it were a matter belonging to ministers alone, though they wish to enjoy the promised Messiah and all the goods expected in him. When asked about God, about good morals, about laws, about religion, they say: "I am no priest, I have no means of living from the priesthood; I leave this care to the priests." But, good sir, do you not also have God? Have you not received your life from him, and your livelihood, which replaces the priesthood? Have you not been freed by his benefit? Have you not been carried through many dangers? Or are you not then a Christian? Certainly, if you wish to be a Christian, and to be acknowledged and received by Christ, you must honour, observe, follow and confess him here. As no one will wish to be shut out from the enjoyment of heavenly joys, so no one should think himself exempt from imitating and professing Christ.

units.la: De aJuenárum[?] persona dicit,Non autem vobiscum duntaxat ego ferio pallum[?] illud & iura mentum illud,sed & cum omni eo qui,&c. Quo docet homines exteros,qui solent ad populum Dei commugrare[?],quoniam beneficiis divinis etiam ipsi fruantur, debere divinis quoq; legi-bus stare. Nihil enim est quod debeat vel impietati vel improbitati patrocinari. Nam si lice-ret exteris leges divinas impunè violare,certè vel eorum exemplo solo cùm leges in conte-ptum abirent,tum exemplo eorum malo civitatem infici necesse esset.
units.tr: Concerning the strangers he says: Not with you only do I make this covenant and this oath, but with all those who are here, etc. By this he teaches that foreigners, who are accustomed to migrate to the people of God, since they too enjoy the divine benefits, ought also to abide by the divine laws. For there is nothing that should defend impiety or wickedness. For if it were permitted to foreigners to violate the divine laws with impunity, then, when the laws fell into contempt through their example alone, the state would necessarily be infected by their bad example.

units.la: Quod nobis est documento,ut quibus legibus peregrinos obligari quondam placuit,iis nihildum detractum patiamur. Etenim si nostra libertate & pace,& reliquis Dei beneficiis frui datur illis,cur non starent his etiam legibus atq; cultibus,quibus observatis nobis certò constat Deo nos gratissimum facere?
units.tr: This is a lesson for us, that we should not allow anything to be taken away from the laws by which it once pleased that strangers should be bound. For if they are granted to enjoy our liberty, our peace and the other benefits of God, why should they not also abide by these laws and worships, by keeping which we are certain that we make ourselves most pleasing to God?

units.la: De gentium vicinarum persona dicit:Vidistis quoq; abominationes earum, & idola earum,&c. Quasi dicat,Si voluissem illis vos esse similes,minimè vos ab eorum commixtione segregassem: si illorum superstitiosos ritusatque cultus approbassem,non dixissem eos esse,à quibus abhorrerem. Summa,idololatria,quia fœtet coram Domino,est omnis euertenda.
units.tr: Concerning the neighbouring nations he says: You have also seen their abominations and their idols, etc. It is as if he said: If I had wished you to be like them, I would not have separated you from their intermingling at all; if I had approved their superstitious rites and worships, I would not have called them those from whom I abhor. In sum, all idolatry, because it stinks before the Lord, is to be utterly overthrown.

units.la: Atque his quidem omnibus docet omnino divinis legibus standum esse omnibus omnium ordinum hominibus,cum Deus omnium sit hominum salus & gaudium. Ei sit honos in fœcula,Amen.
units.tr: By all these things he teaches, indeed, that the divine laws must be abided by entirely, by men of all orders, since God is the salvation and joy of all men. To him be honour for ever and ever. Amen.

units.la: SERMO II.
units.tr: SERMON II.

units.la: 18 Ne forte fit in vobis vir aut mulier,familia aut tribus aliqua,cuius cor se auertat hodie à Domino Deo nostro,ut abeat,& seruiat diis gentium istarum,& ne forte sit in vobis radix germinans fel & absynthium.
units.tr: 18 Lest perhaps there be among you a man or woman, a family or a tribe, whose heart turns away today from the Lord our God, to go and serve the gods of those nations, and lest perhaps there be among you a root bearing gall and wormwood.

units.la: 19 Sed & cum audierit verba execrationis huius,felicitatem sibi promittat in corde suo,dicens: Pax erit mihi,etiamsi incessero iuxta libidinem cordis mei, ut finiatur ebria cum sitiente.
units.tr: 19 And when he hears the words of this curse, let him promise himself happiness in his heart, saying: I shall have peace, even though I walk according to the lust of my heart, so that the drunkard may be swept away with the thirsty.

units.la: 20 Non vult Dominus huic propitius esse,sed tum fumabit furor Domini, & indignatio eius adversum virum talem , & cubabit super eum omnis execratio,quæ scripta est in hoc libro,delebitq; Dominus nomen eius sub cœlo.
units.tr: 20 The Lord will not be gracious to him, but then the fury of the Lord and his indignation will smoke against such a man, and every curse that is written in this book will lie upon him, and the Lord will blot out his name from under heaven.

units.la: 21 Separabitq; Dominus eum ad malum ex omnibus tribubus Israel, iuxta omnes execrationes fœderis,quod scriptum est in libro huius legis.
units.tr: 21 And the Lord will separate him for evil from all the tribes of Israel, according to all the curses of the covenant that is written in the book of this law.

units.la: 22 Et dicet generatio posterior,scilicet filii vestri,qui post vos exorientur,& alienum qui veniet de terra remota,quum visuri sunt verbera huius terræ,& languores,quibus Dominus illam languere facit.
units.tr: 22 And the later generation, namely your sons who will rise up after you, and the foreigner who comes from a distant land, will say, when they see the plagues of this land and the sicknesses with which the Lord has made it sick.

units.la: 23 Sulphure & sale exurentibus universam terram eius,ut seminari non possit,non germinante,neq; exoriente in ea ulla herba,sicut in loco subversionis Sodomæ & Admorae,Admæ,& Zeboim,quas subvertit Dominus in ira sua atq; in furore suo.
units.tr: 23 Its whole land burning with sulphur and salt, so that it cannot be sown, nothing sprouting and no herb coming up in it, like the overthrow of Sodom and Admah, and Zeboiim, which the Lord overthrew in his anger and in his fury.

units.la: 24 Dicent inquam omnes gentes: Cur Dominus huic terræ sic fecit? Quæ est ira furoris tam immensi?
units.tr: 24 All the nations will say, I say: Why has the Lord done this to this land? What is the meaning of such great fury of wrath?

units.la: 25 Et respondebunt: Quod fœdus Domini Dei patrum suorum deseruerint,quod pepigit cum eis cum educeret eos de terra Ægypti.
units.tr: 25 And they will answer: Because they forsook the covenant of the Lord, the God of their fathers, which he made with them when he brought them out of the land of Egypt.

units.la: 26 Nam abierunt,& servierunt diis aliis,adoraverunt q; eos,deos quos non cognoverunt,& quos non divisit eis.
units.tr: 26 For they went and served other gods, and worshipped them, gods whom they did not know, and whom he had not allotted to them.

units.la: 27 Et exarsit furor Domini contra terram illam,ut induceret super eam omnem execrationem,quæ scripta est in libro isto.
units.tr: 27 And the fury of the Lord burned against that land, to bring upon it every curse that is written in this book.

units.la: 28 Et evulsit eos Dominus de terra eorum in ira,furore & indignatione magna,ut testatur hæc dies.
units.tr: 28 And the Lord uprooted them from their land in anger, fury and great indignation, as this day bears witness.

units.la: 29 Abscondita Domino Deo nostro, revelata vero ad nos & ad filios nostros
units.tr: 29 The hidden things belong to the Lord our God, but the things revealed belong to us and to our sons

units.la: (attinens )dum durat seculum, ut faciamus omnia verba legis huius.
units.tr: (pertaining to) for as long as the age endures, that we may do all the words of this law.

units.la: **IN** prima parte praesentis capitis commemorat & exponit Moses impedimentum quoddam, quod nobis obstat quo minus Dei legibus qua par est, quaque expedit fide & dili-gentia nos exerceamus: videlicet peruersum discrimen personarum, quo persuasi putamus nihil nostra referre quae Deus olim praeceperit. Ea res ne nos ab omni pietate & religione reuocaret, per omnes personarum rationes est deducta atque ponderata. Deus in Ægypto Pharao-nem, eius seruos atque ipsam etiam terram populis aliis exemplum fecit: in deserto sic Israelitarum corpora, vestimenta, bona omnia conseruauit, ut quantum in illius prouidentia ac potentia spei sit omnibus hominibus testatum voluerit: in terra Moab reges vicit, eorumque terras atque opes in longam possessionem posteris quoque largitus est. Ergo Dei persona recte considerata significat ad omnes quae dicit ac facit Deus omnia pertinere, suo quoque modo. Populus Israel vocatum in foedus & receptum est: igitur eius foederis legibus etiam continetur vniuersus. Aduenae, quoniā easdem habitant sedes, quas beneficus Deus donauit, harum legum vinculis exempti esse non possunt. Gentes suo exemplo non retinent in idololatria quenquam, sed ab ea reuocant & abster-rent omnes. Quae cum ita sint ab hoc excusationum genere discimus nos etiam nobis abstinendum esse.
units.tr: In the first part of the present chapter Moses recalls and sets out a certain hindrance that stands in our way, so that we do not exercise ourselves in God's laws as we ought, nor with the faith and diligence that they require: namely, the perverse distinction of persons, by which, persuaded, we think that what God commanded long ago does not concern us. So that this matter might not call us back from all piety and religion, it is traced and weighed through every class of persons. In Egypt God made Pharaoh, his servants, and the land itself an example to other peoples; in the desert he so preserved the bodies, clothing and all the goods of the Israelites that he wished it to be witnessed to all men how great is his providence and power; in the land of Moab he conquered kings and gave their lands and wealth in long possession to their posterity also. Therefore God, rightly considered in his person, signifies that all that God says and does pertains to everyone, in its own way. The people of Israel was called into covenant and received; therefore all men are included under the laws of that covenant. Strangers, since they dwell in the same seats which the bounteous God has given, cannot be exempt from the bonds of these laws. The nations, by their example, do not keep anyone in idolatry, but call back and deter all from it. Since these things are so, we learn from this kind of excuse that we too must abstain from it.

units.la: Sed restat aliud malum securitas, quae & ipsa multum nocet. Quemadmodum enim quae inuiti facimus ea nostra ut faciamus non interesse praetendimus: sic quae fieri nolumus ea, ut-ut praeuidentur futura, tamen ut credamus euentura, aut ne eueniant declinemus, non possumus adduci. Igitur & hanc ipsam remoram Moses tollit, ac docet quae Deus vel promittit bona, vel minatur mala, ea minimè negligenda, verum pro certissimis habenda. Est autem securitas omnium penè malorum maximum, & excidij certissimum nuncium. Qua de causa Moses ipsum tractat eo diligentius. 1. Depingit quasi in tabula. 2. Docet eius finem. 3. Remouet oppositum ei malum curiositatem.
units.tr: But another evil remains, security, which also does great harm in itself. For just as we pretend that it makes no difference to us what we do unwillingly, so we cannot be brought to believe that things we are unwilling to do will come to pass, or to avoid them so that they do not happen, even when they are foreseen as future.
