Therefore Moses also removes this very delay, and teaches that the good things God promises or the evils he threatens are by no means to be neglected, but held as most certain. Now security is almost the greatest of all evils and the most certain announcement of ruin. For this reason Moses treats it more carefully. 1. He portrays it as if on a tablet. 2. He teaches its end. 3. He removes the evil opposed to it, curiosity.

units.la: Securitatem depingit ad hunc modum: Ne forte sit in vobis vir aut mulier, familia aut tri-bus aliqua cuius cor se auertat hodie à Domino, &c. Quibus verbis & personas & mores atq; fa-cta securorum hominum refert. Ac primum quia virum, mulierem, familiam, tribum refert, eo ipso offendit in omne genus hominum hoc vitium cadere. Vir quoniam à virtute, ἀνδρὸς πρὸς τῆς ἀνδρείας[?], mann von mannheit[?] dici solent, alienum à sexu suo, à natura sua, à forte sua ducunt vllius mali metu teneri: sibi conuenire potius vt sint intrepidi, vt malorum eis ne in mentem veniat quidem. At arrepta hac scala latan[?] prudentiam, quae & ipsa viri virtus est propria, atque in omnia bona malaq; oculata, caecitate ferit, impedit, ac ne mala quae vel in propinquo sunt animaduertat facit.
units.tr: He portrays security in this way: Lest perhaps there be among you a man or woman, a family or a tribe, whose heart turns away today from the Lord, etc. In these words he sets forth both the persons and the morals and deeds of secure men. And first, because he names a man, a woman, a family, a tribe, he shows by this very fact that this vice falls upon every kind of person. Vir (man), since men are usually called after virtue, ἀνδρὸς πρὸς τῆς ἀνδρείας [man from manliness], think it foreign to their sex, their nature and their strength to be held by any fear of evil; it is fitting for them rather to be fearless, so that evil does not even enter their minds. But once this ladder is seized, it strikes blindness upon prudence, which is itself the proper virtue of a man and is watchful over all good and evil things, and it hinders it, and makes it not notice the evils that are even near at hand.

units.la: At mulier, quia videt & metum esse in vitio, & eum ipsum admissum delicijs atq; illecebris suis obstare: partim dissimulat, partim voluptate quantum potest sopit. Quod vt securi-tatem efficiat satan, & illecebrarum studium suggerit & voluptates ipsas quantas potest maximas praebet. Unde existit in foeminis plerunq; maior quàm in viris securitas.
units.tr: But mulier (woman), because she sees that fear stands in the way of vice, and that the very indulgence of it is opposed to her delights and allurements, partly dissembles and partly lulls fear with pleasure as far as she can. Satan, to make her secure, suggests a zeal for allurements and offers the greatest pleasures he can. Hence security is commonly greater in women than in men.

units.la: Jam familiae & tribus, & ciuitates quoniam bona habent quibus & afficiuntur suauiter, & ita nituntur vt in illis sibi aduersus omnia mala atque pericula praesidij satis esse putent: cum facilius securae fiunt, tum in illa quoque securitate pertinacius perseuerant.
units.tr: Now families and tribes, and cities, since they have goods by which they are pleasantly affected, and so strive that they think there is enough protection for themselves in these against all evils and dangers, when they become more easily secure, then also persevere more stubbornly in that same security.

units.la: Atque hæc propterea sunt paulò altius repetenda, vt quibus in naturis atque locis radi-ces agat hoc vitium intelligas.
units.tr: And these things must be taken up a little more deeply, so that you may understand in what natures and places this vice takes root.

units.la: Progressus autem & incrementa sic docet. 1. Auertit cor à Domino, inquit. Cor aliqua ab re seuocare & auertere est eam ipsam negligere & floccifacere: nam quae magnificamus quaeque chara habemus, ad ea animum aduertimus: velut Christus dicit, vbi thesaurus vester ibi cor vestrum. Atque inde est quod cum Dominus paruo est[?] apud nos in precio, cor ab eo dicitur aduersum esse & alienum. Et dicit Dominus de Judaeis apud prophetam, cor eorum procul à se abesse.
units.tr: He teaches the progress and increase of it thus. 1. He turns the heart away from the Lord, he says. To withdraw and turn the heart away from something is to neglect it and hold it cheap; for we give our attention to what we magnify and hold dear. So Christ says: where your treasure is, there is your heart. And hence it is that when the Lord is of little account among us, the heart is said to be against him and alien to him. And the Lord says of the Jews through the prophet that their heart is far from him.

units.la: Jam si reputes animo quantum scelus sit magistratum, parentes, paedagogum, seniores despicere: certè cognitu facile est multo maius scelus esse Deum, qui his omnibus est maior & superior despicere. Is enim non modo non vult despici verum etiam toto corde amari, & quemadmodum est in vniuerso mundo sic etiam in animis nostris omnium supremus esse. Matth.22.teste Domino. At qui securi sunt, quoniam sunt humanis rebus & illecebris dediti, eaque curant quae corporis sunt, Deum sanè prorsus negligunt. Exemplo sunt Nephilim, Sodomitae, Saul, Israel, Judaei, nostra secula. Atque haec sunt mali illius initia. Seruit Diis gentium. Idololatria scelus est maximum. Suorum enim deorum ope fre-ti Deum securè negligunt: ut Cananæi, Samaritani, & papistæ. Quacunque enim iniuria Dei verbum atque eius asseclas[?] afficiant, semper idolorum suorum auxilio id impunè se auferre putant.
units.tr: Now if you consider in your mind how great a crime it is to despise magistrates, parents, teachers, elders, it is certainly easy to recognise that it is a much greater crime to despise God, who is greater and higher than all of these. For he not only does not wish to be despised, but to be loved with the whole heart, and, as he is supreme in the whole world, so he is also supreme over our minds: Matt. 22, the Lord bearing witness. But those who are secure, since they are given over to human things and allurements, and care for what belongs to the body, certainly altogether neglect God. Examples are the Nephilim, the Sodomites, Saul, Israel, the Jews, our own age. And these are the beginnings of that evil. Serving the gods of the nations. Idolatry is the greatest crime. For trusting in the help of their own gods, they carelessly neglect God, as the Canaanites, the Samaritans and the Papists do. For whatever injury they inflict on the word of God and its adherents, they always think they can carry it off with impunity by the aid of their idols.

units.la: Sit radix germinans fel & absynthium. Hoc est, intus & in cute amari toti. Nam ab amarore eos notat.
units.tr: Let there be a root that bears gall and wormwood. That is, bitterness throughout, inwardly and on the surface. For Moses marks them by their bitterness.

units.la: Cum execrationes audiat, promittat sibi felicitatem & pacem. Minatur Deus idolatris diras poenas: at illi sibi felicitatem atque pacem pollicentur. Idem de adulteris, scorta-toribus, usurarijs, alijsq; esto iudicium. Omnes historiæ docent eos qui sibi persuasum habuere nullum esse, quo possent obrui malum, in maxima improuisa incidisse. Veluti subitum erat diluuium, subitum Sodomæ incendium, improuisum Troiæ excidium, & Baltazaris, & Nabalis, & Iudæorum.
units.tr: When he hears the curses, let him promise himself happiness and peace. God threatens idolaters with dreadful punishments, yet they promise themselves happiness and peace. The same judgment applies to adulterers, fornicators, usurers and others. All histories teach that those who have persuaded themselves that there is no way by which evil could be overwhelmed have fallen into the greatest disasters they did not foresee. Thus the flood came suddenly, the burning of Sodom came suddenly, and the fall of Troy, of Belshazzar, of Nabal and of the Jews came unforeseen.

units.la: Ebrius & sitiens iungantur. Indulgeant genio, somno vinoq; sepulti pereant cum sobrijs ebrij.
units.tr: Let the drunkard and the thirsty be joined together. Let them indulge their appetites; buried in sleep and wine, the drunkards perish along with the sober.

units.la: Sed quoniam hic locus varie exponitur ab Hebraeis, vt est apud Pagninum in Dict. [illegible, ~3 letters], & apud Paul. Fagium in suis ad Deutero. locum illum Annotationibus: tum etiam à Græcis puta LXX. interpret. & Procopio: nihil hic eadem de re dicetur amplius, cum & Steuchus & Munsterus hoc exponant. Mihi quidem Pauli Fagij sententia, quoniam auctoritate LXX. interpretum & Procopij nititur, minimè displicet.
units.tr: But since this passage is explained in various ways by the Hebrews, as in Pagninus's Dictionary [illegible], and by Paulus Fagius in his notes on this place of Deuteronomy; and also by the Greeks, namely the Septuagint translators and Procopius, nothing more will be said here on this matter, since both Steuchus and Munster also expound it in this way. For my part, Paulus Fagius's opinion, since it rests on the authority of the Septuagint translators and of Procopius, does not displease me at all.

units.la: Extremum hoc est, ut ne Mammona aut ventrem Deorum loco habeamus, atque accensi libidine & habendi cupiditate insatiabili ebrij sobrij pereamus.
units.tr: This is the final point: that we should not regard Mammon or the belly as our gods, and that, inflamed by lust and by an insatiable desire to possess, we should not perish drunk while others perish sober.

units.la: Sed Dei de securitate iudicium etiam hic describit Moses. 1. Non vult Dominus huic prò pitius esse. Id est, Etsi Deus pro sua summa erga genus nostrum beneuolentia non vult mortem peccatoris, sed vt viuat: tamen superbis, insolentibus, prefractis istis & oblatæ gratiæ contemptoribus non vult peccatum condonare. Ergo hoc est peccatum in spiritum quod non remittitur. Etenim est una ad salutem via, quam Spiritus sanctus partim in mentibus hominum, partim in scripturis ostendit: hanc viam ingredi est obedientia fidei, illam malitiosè repellere est inobedientia & incredulitas: de qua Christus dicit, qui non credit est condemnatus. Atq; sic æstimat Dominus peccatum, in quo sibi increduli placent tantopere.
units.tr: But Moses also describes here God's judgment on those who are secure. First: "The Lord will not be willing to forgive him." That is, although God, in his great goodwill toward our race, does not desire the death of the sinner but that he should live, yet he is unwilling to pardon sin for the proud, the insolent, the stubborn and the despisers of the grace offered. Therefore this is the sin against the Spirit that is not forgiven. For there is one way to salvation, which the Holy Spirit shows partly in the minds of men and partly in the Scriptures. To walk in this way is the obedience of faith; to reject it wickedly is disobedience and unbelief, of which Christ says: "he who does not believe is condemned." In this way the Lord judges the sin in which unbelievers take such great pleasure in themselves.

units.la: 2. Fumabit furor Domini & indignatio. Iræ Dei effecta narrat. Et, cubabit super eum omnis execratio scripta. Dein auget hoc primum admiratione, quà ducentur posteri: deinceps & exemplo Sodomæ quasi firmat. His addit huiusce iræ causam efficientem neglectum ab his fedus Dei. Ut omnium patrem, patronum, socium, sic Deum etiam male habet perdi sua beneficia.
units.tr: Second: "The wrath and jealousy of the Lord will smoke." He describes the effects of God's anger. And: "every curse written in this book will lie upon him." Then he increases this first by the wonder with which posterity will be led, and afterwards seems to confirm it by the example of Sodom. To these he adds the efficient cause of this anger: the neglect of God's covenant by these people. Just as a father, patron and partner is wounded, so God too is grieved when his benefits are lost.

units.la: Iam obijcias, Quis reuelauit tibi ista Dei iudicia? nugaris: quis tibi dixisset? Respondeo. Sunt omnium quæ extant rerum aliæ Deo soli cognitæ, & ab hominum cognitione remotæ prorsus atq; reconditæ: sunt aliæ rursus verbo eius expressæ & hominibus propositæ atq; explicatæ. Iam nemo sibi vendicat altiorem quam quæ Dei verbo sit expressa sapientiam: atq; hic quidem ea tantum quæ sunt sacris literis reuelata nunciamus. Hę execrationes & benedictiones sunt hoc ipso libro atq; etiam alibi reuelatæ. Qua de causa non est de his quæ dicta sunt dubitandum. Ergo verbum Domini reuerenter, & remota secura eius contemptione est retipiendum[?]. Quò fiet, vt in illo cum bene, tum beatæ viuamus, Amen.
units.tr: Now you may object: "Who revealed these judgments of God to you? You are talking nonsense; who could have told you?" I answer: of all the things that exist, some are known to God alone, remote from human knowledge and wholly hidden; others, again, are expressed in his Word and set forth and explained to men. Now no one claims a wisdom higher than what is expressed in God's Word, and here we announce only those things that have been revealed in the sacred letters. These curses and blessings are revealed in this very book and also elsewhere. For this reason there is no need to doubt what has been said. Therefore the Word of the Lord must be received reverently, and its careless contempt set aside. In this way we shall live well and blessedly in him, Amen.

units.la: CAPUT XXX. SERMO III.
units.tr: Chapter 30. Sermon III.

units.la: Quum itaq; venerint super te omnia ista: nempe benedictio & execratio, quæ e-go posui ante faciem tuam, & reuocabis ad cor tuum, apud cunctas gentes, ad quas te propulerit Dominus Deus tuus.
units.tr: When all these things have come upon you, namely the blessing and the curse which I have set before your face, and you call them to mind among all the nations to which the Lord your God has driven you,

units.la: 2 Conuersusq; fueris ad Dominum Deum tuum, vocique eius obedieris iuxta omnia quæ ego præcipio tibi hodie, tu & filij tui, toto corde tuo atq; tota anima tua.
units.tr: and you turn back to the Lord your God and obey his voice according to all that I command you this day, you and your sons, with all your heart and all your soul,

units.la: 3 Conuertet quoq; Dominus Deus tuus captiuitatem tuam, & intimis visceribus miserationis afficietur erga te, & conuersus colliget te de cunctis populis, in quos te dispersit Dominus Deus tuus.
units.tr: then the Lord your God will restore your captivity, and will have compassion on you, and will turn and gather you from all the peoples among whom the Lord your God has scattered you.

units.la: 4 Etiamsi fueris eiectus tu usque ad fines cælorum, illinc te colliget Dominus Deus tuus, atq; inde te tollet.
units.tr: Even if you have been driven out to the uttermost parts of heaven, from there the Lord your God will gather you, and from there he will fetch you.

units.la: 5 Et introducet te Dominus Deus tuus in terram quam possederunt patres tui, & possidebis eam, benefacietq; tibi, & multiplicabit te magis quàm patres tuos.
units.tr: And the Lord your God will bring you into the land which your fathers possessed, and you shall possess it; he will do you good and multiply you more than your fathers.

units.la: 6 Et circumcidet Dominus Deus tuus cor tuum, & cor seminis tui, ut diligas Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde & ex tota anima tua, ut vivas.
units.tr: And the Lord your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your seed, so that you may love the Lord your God with all your heart and all your soul, that you may live.

units.la: 7 Ponet quoq; Dominus Deus tuus omnes execrationes istas super hostes tuos, & super eos qui te oderunt, & qui te persequuntur.
units.tr: The Lord your God will also lay all these curses upon your enemies and upon those who hate you and persecute you.

units.la: 8 Siquidem tu reversus audieris vocem Domini, atque feceris omnia præcepta eius, quæ ego mando tibi hodie.
units.tr: And you shall return and hear the voice of the Lord, and do all his commandments which I command you this day.

units.la: 9 Et eximium te faciet Dominus Deus tuus in omni opere manus tuæ, in fru-ctu ventris tui, & in fœtu iumentorum tuorum, & in fructu terræ tuæ ad bonum, quoniam revertetur Dominus, ut lætetur super te bono (tuo) sicut lætatus est super patres tuos.
units.tr: And the Lord your God will make you abundant in every work of your hand, in the fruit of your womb, in the young of your cattle, and in the fruit of your land, for good; for the Lord will return to rejoice over you for good, as he rejoiced over your fathers,

units.la: 10 Si modo audieris vocem Domini Dei tui, ut custodias præcepta eius & statuta eius, quæ scripta sunt in libro legis huius, & si conversus fueris ad Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo, & ex tota anima tua.
units.tr: if only you hear the voice of the Lord your God, to keep his precepts and statutes which are written in the book of this law, and if you turn to the Lord your God with all your heart and all your soul.

units.la: VEMADMODVM civilibus in rebus & quod nimium est, & quod non satis est, ambo sunt in vitio: veluti nostro prouerbio dicitur, [illegible, ~6 letters] vnd [illegible, ~11 letters] alle spil: sic usu comperimus in rebus pietatis atque fidei nobis euenire solere. Sive enim securus fis, ac neque Deum neque homines cures, omninoque tibi tutus ab omni genere calamitatum esse videare: sive despondeas animum omninoque te seclusum ab omni bonorum possessione esse putes: versaris in magno periculo, teque is perditum.
units.tr: As in civil affairs both too much and too little are faults, as our proverb says, "... und ... alle Spiel", so we find by experience that it commonly happens in matters of piety and faith. For if you become careless, caring neither for God nor for men, and seem altogether safe from every kind of calamity, or if you lose heart and think yourself utterly cut off from all possession of good things, you are in great danger, and you are ruined by either.

units.la: Securitas habet spem & fiduciam non euenturi mali, sed idipsum in peccatis maximis: quo detrahitur divinæ iustitiæ: quasi enim Deus non videat, non velit, non possit ulcisci ma-la, sic peccatur impudenter.
units.tr: Carelessness holds out the hope and confidence that no evil will come, and that precisely in the greatest sins; by this, the justice of God is diminished. For as if God did not see, did not will, or could not punish evils, so men sin shamelessly.

units.la: Partem in contrariam deflectit desperatio, quæ spem deponit omnem: & in mœrore at-que in metu pœnæ tota iacet, nec potest credere eam averti posse: quo divinæ bonitati & cle-mentiæ detrahitur: quasi enim immitis quidam atq; inexorabilis tyrannus esset, qui benignif-simus est & optimus pater, Deus, sic metuitur.
units.tr: Despair turns to the opposite side, abandoning all hope; it lies wholly in grief and in fear of punishment, and cannot believe that it can be turned aside; by this the goodness and mercy of God are diminished. For God, who is most kind and the best of fathers, is feared as if he were some harsh and inexorable tyrant.

units.la: Fouetur autem hoc genus cogitationibus desperatio. 1. Deus est suapte natura iustus, zelotes, severus peccatorum vltor: itemq; durum & difficilem & inexorabilem mens despe-rabunda sibi fingit. 2. Minas intentatas & peccatis decretis ob oculos ponit. 3. Opera divina atque iræ divinæ exempla in Pharaone, Saule, Iuda, alijsq; edita considerat. 4. Expendit vi-res adeo arduis rebus impares perficiendis. 5. Concludit,se, cum præcepta nequeat seruare maledictum esse, Deum quæ non seminauerit velle metere: veluti qui talentum vnum acce-perat dictitauit.
units.tr: Despair nourishes this kind of thought. (1) God is by his nature just, zealous, a severe avenger of sins; and the despairing mind imagines him to be hard, difficult and inexorable. (2) It sets before its eyes the threats uttered and the sins decreed. (3) It considers the works of God and the examples of divine wrath shown in Pharaoh, Saul, Judas and others. (4) It weighs its own strength, too unequal to accomplish such arduous things. (5) It concludes that, since it cannot keep the precepts, it is accursed, and that God wishes to reap where he has not sown, as the man who had received one talent used to complain.

units.la: Quamobrem ut securitatem antea remouit: sic desperationem iam oppugnat Moses: ac docet quomodo cum divina iustitia comparari debeat Dei clementia, quoque modo sit de causis immissarum calamitatum iudicandum. In malis cogitandum est, hæc propter peccata accidisse: remotis igitur peccatis ceu malorum causis ipsa quoque mala sublatum iri. Igitur pœnitentiam requiri: ac quemadmodum peccatis in mala detrudimur: sic una pœnitentia nos è malis eripi atque conservari. Est autem summa. Affligeris multis malis & molestiis: quid facies? noli desperare: si tu mutes animum, vitam, mores: Deus mutabit fortunam tuam: si fias ipse melior, fortuna quoque tua futura est melior. Iam in verbis eius ostendetur quomodo nos converti, quomodo rursus fortunam converti necesse fit.
units.tr: Therefore, as Moses earlier removed carelessness, so now he attacks despair, and teaches how the mercy of God must be reconciled with his justice, and how the causes of the calamities sent are to be judged. In evils we must think that these have happened on account of sins; therefore, with sins removed as the causes of evils, the evils themselves will also be taken away. Thus repentance is required; and just as we are thrust into evils by sins, so by repentance alone we are rescued from evils and preserved. The sum is this: you are afflicted with many evils and troubles; what will you do? Do not despair; if you change your mind, your life and your manners, God will change your fortune; if you become better yourself, your fortune too will be better. Now in his words it will be shown how we must be converted, and how it is necessary that our fortune be turned again.

units.la: Ac de nostra quidem in melius conversione Moses ad hunc modum dicit: Cum itaque venerint super te benedictio & execratio, &c. Quibus verbis ad conversionem veram sive pœni-tentiam tria requirit potissimum: ut in cor nostrum descendamus, ut ad Dominum con-vertamur, ut verbo divino obsequamur. Quæ res pœnitentiam agenti sunt considerandæ.
units.tr: Moses speaks thus of our conversion to the better: "When therefore the blessing and the curse have come upon you," etc. In these words he chiefly requires three things for true conversion, or repentance: that we descend into our heart, that we turn to the Lord, and that we obey the divine word. These things are to be considered by one who is repenting.

units.la: 1. Revocabis ad cor tuum apud cunctas gentes, ad quas te propulerit Dominus Deus tuus. Id est in te descendes, & quid feceris, quem irritaveris atque offenderis, altius animo repetendum est.Hoc primum est pœnitentis officium,in se descendere,peccatum suum agnoscere, detec-stari,odisse, idque factum dolere. Inde enim existunt illæ sanctorum hominum lachrymæ, quas dum agunt pœnitentiam solent effundere. Vt Dauid de suis sæpe & multum per Psal-mos dicit: vt Luc.7. Mulier peccatrix Domini pedes lauat:vt publicanus orans pectus tun-dens:vt Petrus flens amare:vt Niniuitæ in saeco & cinere pœnitentes. Hinc etiam ieiunia & castigatio corporum,& pœnitentia publica.
units.tr: (1) "You shall call them to your heart among all the nations to which the Lord your God has driven you." That is, you must descend into yourself, and what you have done, whom you have provoked and offended, must be traced back more deeply in the mind. This is the first duty of the penitent: to descend into himself, to acknowledge his sin, to detest it, to hate it, and to grieve for what he has done. From this arise those tears of holy men which they are accustomed to pour out while they do penance; as David often says of his own in the Psalms; as the sinful woman washes the feet of the Lord (Luc. 7.); as the publican, beating his breast while praying; as Peter weeping bitterly; as the Ninevites repenting in sackcloth and ashes. Hence also come fasting and the mortification of the body, and public penance.

units.la: Ex quo colligi potest eos peccatū suum non sentire,nec quantū sit agnoscere,qui nihilo minus indulgent genio:veluti Noħæ ætatis homines,& Sodomitæ,& vltimi seculi mortales.
units.tr: From this it can be gathered that those who indulge their own nature all the more do not feel their sin, nor recognise how great it is; such were the men of Noah's time, the Sodomites, and mortals of the last age.

units.la: Atq; hic est primus gradus pœnitentiæ videlicet in se descendere & peccatum suum agnoscere. Sed prohdolor quàm verum est quod poeta prophanus dicit;
units.tr: And this is the first step of repentance, namely to descend into oneself and acknowledge one's sin. But alas, how true is what the heathen poet says:

units.la: Vt nemo in[?] se se tentat descendere nemo, Sed præcedenti speƈtatur mantica tergo.
units.tr: "No one tries to descend into himself; no one... but the wallet is seen hanging on the back of the one who goes before."

units.la: Omnes certè sumus ad censuram aliorum proniores, quàm ad nostram ipsorum emendationem. Quod cum ita fit, ad nostri inquisitionem ătq; ăgnitionem, rem videlicet nostrae saluti necessariam, alijs atq; alijs malis nos propellit Deus. Atq; hoc ipsum est quod dicit Dominus per Mosem: Israelitas, quocunq; terrarum actì fuerint cogitare debere: quod domi in libertate, in rerum copia, in pace & odio, vbi commodissimè potuissent, se inspicere & castigare noluerint: iam in seruitute, in summa rerū penuria, atq; in perturbatione, cum fit incommodissimum, opportunum esse. O miseros Phryges qui nisi plagis emendari non possunt. Sed si secus fieri vt emendemur non potest, est aliquid eo vsq; prodire. Primus enim ad conuersionem hic est gradus.
units.tr: Certainly we are all more ready to judge others than to correct ourselves. Since this is so, God drives us by one evil after another to search and recognise ourselves, a thing necessary for our salvation. And this is what the Lord says through Moses: that the Israelites, wherever they were taken in the lands, ought to think that at home, in freedom, in abundance of goods, in peace and at ease, where they could most conveniently have examined and corrected themselves, they were unwilling to do so; now in servitude, in the greatest want of goods and in disturbance, when it is most inconvenient, it is the right time. O wretched Phrygians, who cannot be amended except by blows! But if it cannot be otherwise that we are amended, it is something to come forth to that point. For this is the first step to conversion.

units.la: Secundus est,vt conuertamur ad Dominum: dicit enim, Conuersus ad Dominum Deum tuum. Auertitur à Deo qui illo neglecto res prophanas atq; malas animo cogitat. Nam homi-nis & Dei coniunctio peccatis rumpitur. Igitur ab illis ad Deum conuertamur necesse est. Quod fecerunt Acolastus, Matthæus, Zachæus, & quotquot à peccatis suis ad Dominum sonuersi sunt.
units.tr: The second is that we turn to the Lord; for he says, "Turn back to the Lord your God." He who neglects God and thinks in his mind of profane and wicked things is turned away from God. For the union of man and God is broken by sins. Therefore we must necessarily turn from them to God. This is what Acolastus, Matthew, Zacchaeus, and all who turned from their sins to the Lord did.

units.la: Tertius ad pœnitentiam gradus est obsequi verbo Domini: dicit enim, Vocí, eius obedieris. Non hæreas in peccatorum illecebris: sed illis repudiatis Deo te seruum dedas. Quod qui fieri debeat monstrat. 1. Voci eius: hoc est, verbo per ministros prædicato. 2. Iuxta omnia, quæ ego tibi præcipio: id est, non tuis affectibus accommodato, per te mitigato: sed ad meam voluntatem exposito. 3. Tu & filij tui. Familiam omnem intelligit. 4. Toto corde & anima. Relinquas omne prorsus malum, & sequare bonum. Vt Petrus aula relicta secutus est ecclesiam. Atq; sic quidè conuertamur necesse est, modo velimus & propositû suum mutet Deus. Quod eum Moses iam dicit fratre.
units.tr: The third step to repentance is to obey the word of the Lord; for he says, "You shall obey his voice." Do not cling to the allurements of sins; but, having rejected them, give yourself as a servant to God. He shows how this must be done: (1) "to his voice," that is, to the word preached by the ministers; (2) "according to all that I command you," that is, not adapted to your own affections, not softened by you, but set forth according to my will; (3) "you and your sons": he means the whole household; (4) "with all heart and soul": you must leave behind all evil altogether, and follow good, as Peter, leaving the court, followed the Church. And so we must indeed be converted, provided we are willing, and God changes his purpose, which Moses, as already said, shows in the brother.

units.la: Quomodo vero fortunam asperâ conuertat Deus in meliorem sic docet. Conuertet quoq; Dominus Deus tuus captiuitatem tuam, &c. Quibus verbis non solum docet quomodo Deus nos agentes pœnitentiam recipiat in gratiam: verum etiam rationes affert, quibus ob patratum scelus mœrenti spem gratiæ faciat.
units.tr: Now how God turns a harsh lot into a better one, he teaches thus: "The LORD your God will also turn your captivity, etc." In these words he not only teaches how God receives into favour those who repent, but also gives reasons by which he offers hope of grace to one grieving over a crime committed.

units.la: 1. Intimis visceribus miserationis afficietur erga te. Lucas dicit, ἐσπλαγχνίσθη[?]. At misericor-dia gratiæ causa efficiens est. Vnde Dei misericordia passim prædicatur in Abrahamo, Iofepho,Ifr.&c.
units.tr: 1. "He will be moved with inward compassion toward you." Luke says, "he was moved with compassion" [ἐσπλαγχνίσθη]. Now mercy is the efficient cause of grace. Hence God's mercy is proclaimed everywhere, in Abraham, Joseph, Israel, etc.

units.la: 2. De gentibus omnibus colliget te etiam vltimis, &c. Potentiam Dei dicit ad auxilium sufficere. Vt enim potuit dispergere, sic poterit sparsa colligere. Et hæc quidem Dei potentia passim prædicatur partim vt terrori fit impijs: partim vt consolationi fit pijs.
units.tr: 2. "He will gather you from all the nations, even from the farthest." He speaks of God's power being sufficient for help. For as he was able to scatter, so he will be able to gather what has been scattered. This power of God is proclaimed everywhere, partly so that it may be a terror to the wicked, partly so that it may be a comfort to the godly.

units.la: 3. Reducet te in terram, & fœcundabit supra quàm patres. Beneficentia & liberalitas in dan do,quæ Deo passim tribuitur. Opum acquirendarum causa non est quod eum deferas: habet is vnde faciat te locupletiorem: nec deest voluntas etiam.
units.tr: 3. "He will bring you back into the land and make you more fruitful than your fathers." This is the kindness and generosity in giving that is ascribed to God everywhere. The reason you should not fear to forsake him for the sake of acquiring wealth is that he has the means to make you richer, and he lacks no will to do so.

units.la: 4. Circumcidet cor tuū, &c. Causa finalis immissarum calamitatum vt corda circumcidat. [illegible, ~35 letters] Circumcisio cordis potissimum requiritur. Qua de re Iustinus philosophus & martyr in eo quod cum Tryphone Iudæo habuit colloquio multa præclarè scripsit.
units.tr: 4. "He will circumcise your heart, etc." The final cause of the calamities sent is that he may circumcise your hearts. [illegible, about 35 letters] Circumcision of the heart is chiefly required. On this matter Justin, philosopher and martyr, wrote many excellent things in his dialogue with the Jew Trypho.

units.la: 5. Mala imponet hostibus qui sua felicitate elati spreuerunt te. Iustitiam Dei prædicat: qua fit,vt par pari referatur hostibus.
units.tr: 5. "He will lay these curses on your enemies, who, lifted up by their prosperity, have despised you." He proclaims the justice of God, by which it comes about that like is repaid with like upon your enemies.

units.la: 6. Eximium te faciet, &c. Magnitudo & celebritas nominis Dei sunt munera.
units.tr: 6. "He will make you outstanding, etc." The greatness and renown of God's name are gifts.

units.la: 7. Letabitur super te bono. Erit illi voluptas in te augendo & ornando summa. Quamobrē ad deū conuertamur, vt nos in integrū restituat ac beet per Christū dominum nostrum. Amen.
units.tr: 7. "He will rejoice over you for good." He will take the greatest delight in increasing and adorning you. Wherefore let us turn to God, that he may restore us wholly and bless us through Christ our Lord. Amen.

units.la: 11 Etenim præceptum istud quod ego tibi præcipio hodie, non est absconditum à te, nec tam remotum.
units.tr: 11 For this commandment which I command you today is not hidden from you, nor is it too far away.

units.la: 12 Non est in cælis, ut dicas: Quis ascendet nobis in cælos, ut ipsum nobis afferat, annuntietque nobis illud ut faciamus ipsum?
units.tr: 12 It is not in heaven, that you should say, "Who will go up to heaven for us, and bring it down to us, and proclaim it to us, that we may do it?"

units.la: 13 Nec est ultra mare, ut dicas: Quis traijciat nobis mare, & afferet nobis, et annuntiet nobis, ut ipsum faciamus?
units.tr: 13 Nor is it beyond the sea, that you should say, "Who will cross the sea for us, and bring it to us, and proclaim it to us, that we may do it?"

units.la: 14 Sed valdè propinquum est tibi verbum in ore tuo & in corde tuo, ut facias illud.
units.tr: 14 But the word is very near to you, in your mouth and in your heart, that you may do it.

units.la: 15 Ecce posui hodie ante te vitam atq; bonum, mortem deniq; & malum.
units.tr: 15 See, I have set before you today life and good, death and evil.

units.la: 16 Nam ego præcipio tibi, ut diligas Dominum Deū tuum, ut incedas in vijs eius, atq; custodias præcepta eius, statuta eius atq; iudicia eius, ut viuas & multiplicēris, fortunetq; te Dominus Deus tuus in terra ad quam tu iam venis ut tè[?] possideas.
units.tr: 16 For I command you to love the LORD your God, to walk in his ways, and to keep his commandments, his statutes and his judgments, that you may live and be multiplied, and that the LORD your God may bless you in the land into which you are now going to possess it.

units.la: 17 Sin retrospexerit cor tuum, et non obedieris, sed impulsus adoraueris deos alienos, seruieris{ eu.[?]
units.tr: 17 But if your heart turns away, and you do not obey, but are led astray and worship other gods and serve them,

units.la: 18 Denuncio vobis hodie quod certissimè peribitis, nec prorogabitis dies super terram, ad quam tu transmisso Iordanē iam venies ut eam possideas.
units.tr: 18 I declare to you today that you will surely perish, and you will not prolong your days upon the land to which you are crossing the Jordan now to go in and possess it.

units.la: 19 Obtestor hodie adversum vos cælum & terram, vitam & mortem proposui vobis, benedictionem & execrationem: elige igitur vitam, ut viuas tu & semen tuū.
units.tr: 19 I call heaven and earth to witness against you today: I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse. Choose therefore life, that you and your seed may live.

units.la: 20 Ut scilicet diligas Dominum Deum tuum, & obedias voci eius, adhæreasque ei: quoniam ipse est vita tua, & longitudo dierum tuorum, ut habites super terrā quam iurauit Dominus patribus tuis, Abrahamo, Isaac & Iacobo, ut ipsis (eam) daret.
units.tr: 20 That is, that you may love the LORD your God, obey his voice, and cleave to him; for he is your life and the length of your days, that you may dwell in the land which the LORD swore to your fathers, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, to give them.

units.la: Earum quæ mortales à verbi diuini studio seuocant atq; impediunt rerum, hæc etiam est vna, quæ prætenditur diuinæ voluntatis ignorantia: cum dicunt scelerati se melius nihil compertum habuisse, id ipsum aliquoquin fuisse facturos. Qua quidem de re dici multa possent, an verè hoc prætextu semper excusentur: sed non necesse est ex iure ciuili multa huc afferri: ac sufficit hoc scire quod quemadmodum iudicem dedecet iuris eius, quod sequi in iudicio debet ignorantem esse: sic hominem Christianum eius, quam profitetur atque sequi tur, religionis ignorantem esse cum turpe est, tum verè maximè perniciosum. Quare & si præ texatur illud, Nescui, simplicitati studui, pauca scire volui, quò de paucis esset reddenda ratio: tamen nihil efficietur hac excusatione, cum ignorationis causæ iustæ non sint vllæ.
units.tr: Among the hindrances that call mortals away from the study of the divine word, this is also one that is pretended: the ignorance of the divine will. Wicked men say that they have learned nothing better, and that they would in any case have done the same thing. Much could be said on this matter, whether they are truly excused by this pretext; but it is not necessary to bring many things here from civil law. It is enough to know this: just as it disgraces a judge to be ignorant of the law he ought to follow in judgment, so it is both shameful and truly most harmful for a Christian to be ignorant of the religion he professes and follows. Therefore, even if the plea is put forward, "I did not know; I cultivated simplicity; I wished to know little, so that I would have to give account for little," nothing will be gained by this excuse, since there are no just causes of ignorance.

units.la: Sed cum hic prætextus ignorantiæ plausibilis sit hominibus, ac propterea multi soleant & à lectione & ab auscultatione verbi Dei abstinere, Moses hoc impedimentum perinde ac priora repellit. Ac primum huius prætextus partes singulas sigillatim refellit & inficiatur: deinceps ostendit data potius ad diuini verbi studium auxilia. De quibus sigillatim.
units.tr: But since this pretext of ignorance is plausible to men, and for that reason many are accustomed to abstain both from reading and from hearing the word of God, Moses repels this hindrance just as he did the earlier ones. First he refutes and denies the parts of this pretext one by one, and then he shows the aids given instead for the study of the divine word. Of these, one by one.

units.la: Negat ad hunc modum: Etenim præceptum istud, quod ego tibi præcipio hodie, non est absconditum &c. Quibus verbis, ut dictum est, prætextus huius genera sigillatim enumerat & inficiatione simplici tollit, minimeq; hæc eò commemorat, ut quemadmodum Pelagiani & papistæ statuunt, vana suæ libertatis, atque virium confidentia populum accendat. Neque enim sequitur ideo positam esse in nobis salutis rationem, quia Moses doceat esse certam & apertam: unde enim est quod certa sit & expedita? Certè à Deo non à nobis, à natura simplicis & apertæ veritatis, non à nostri ingenij natura ac conditione.
units.tr: He denies it in this way: For this commandment which I command you today is not hidden, etc. By these words, as has been said, he enumerates the kinds of this pretext one by one and removes them by a simple denial, and he does not mention these things so that, as the Pelagians and Papists maintain, he may inflame the people with a vain confidence in their own freedom and powers. For it does not follow that the way of salvation is placed in us because Moses teaches that it is certain and plain. For whence is it that it is certain and easy? Surely it is from God, not from us: from the nature of simple and open truth, not from the nature and condition of our own mind.

units.la: Quin si nostram naturam, atque etiam vires nostras sat dignis modis metiamur: videbimus omnia esse quæ cogitamus & facimus in vitio. 1. Si diuinas res nostropte ingenio non assequimur: qui factis eas exprimemus? 2. Tantum defertur vbique gratiæ Christi, ut sine ea nihil sit nostrum, seu velle seu facere. 3. Hoc experimur in omni deliberatione, quod bifariam ratio nostra fallitur: primum cum rei, de qua deliberatur, natura non bene cognita falsò concludimus: tum licet probè ratiocinemur quid ex iustitia sit agendum, tamen pondere cupiditatum retrahimur & impedimur ab intelligentia simul & actione.
units.tr: Indeed, if we measure our nature, and also our powers, in sufficiently worthy ways, we shall see that everything we think and do is tainted with fault. 1. If we do not grasp divine things by our own wit, how shall we express them by our deeds? 2. Everywhere so much is ascribed to the grace of Christ that without it nothing is ours, whether to will or to do. 3. We experience this in every deliberation: our reason is deceived in two ways. First, when we conclude falsely about the nature of the matter under deliberation, not having understood it well; then, although we reason rightly about what justice requires us to do, we are nevertheless drawn back and hindered by the weight of our desires, both in understanding and in action.

units.la: Hanc nostram cæcitatem, infirmitatem, vitiositatem tantum abest ut nescieruit Moses, vt etiam Ethnici illum non ignorarint. Dicit enim Medea, video meliora proboq; , deteriora sequor. Et Laius ille in tragoedia de imbecillitate ea conqueritur, dicens:
units.tr: So far is this our blindness, weakness and wickedness from being unknown to Moses that even the heathen did not overlook it. For Medea says, "I see the better and approve it, but I follow the worse." And that Laius in the tragedy complains of this same weakness, saying:

units.la: Λέλησθε δ' ἐμ' ἀθὲν τῶν ... σὺ ν ... [illegible, ~12 letters]
units.tr: Λέλησθε δ' ἐμ' ἀθὲν τῶν ... σὺ ν ... [illegible, about 12 letters]

units.la: Γνωμήν δ' ἔχοντά' ἡ φύσις βίον ζητεῖ. [?]
units.tr: Γνωμήν δ' ἔχοντά' ἡ φύσις βίον ζητεῖ. [Gnōmēn d' echonta' hē physis bion zētei]

units.la: Et Ariftoteles fœlicitatem, id est vt ipse exponit, virtutis actionem Dei munus esse contendit. Plato quoq; virtutes non abfq; instinctu diuino afflari dixit.
units.tr: And Aristotle contends that happiness, that is, as he himself explains it, the action of virtue, is a gift of God. Plato also said that the virtues are inspired by no other source than a divine impulse.

units.la: Quamobrem fatendum est hominem imparem esse feruandae legi, proptereaq; Christo eguisse. Rom. 8. Caeterum lege nos admoneri, vt ad Deum confugiamus, atq; ab eo ad facultatem honestarum actionum opem petamus. Quod Hierem. cap. 31. docet. Conuerte me, inquiens, & conuertar: tu enim es Dominus Deus meus. Thren. 5. Conuerte nos Domine & conuertemur. Hieronymus in 31. cap. Hierem. Ergo idipsum, inquit, quod agimus poenitentiam, nisi Dei nitamur auxilio, implere non possumus. Et quod Christus dixit, apud homines non potest fieri, vt saluus quisquam fiat, apud Deum omnia possunt fieri. Exponit idem contra Pelagianos. Mandata naturae quidem impossibilia, gratiae tamen possibilia.
units.tr: Wherefore it must be confessed that man is unable to keep the law, and for that reason has needed Christ (Rom. 8). Moreover, the law admonishes us to flee to God and to seek from him help toward the ability to perform honourable actions. This Jeremiah teaches in chapter 31: "Turn me," he says, "and I shall be turned, for you are the LORD my God." Lamentations 5: "Turn us, O LORD, and we shall be turned." Jerome, on chapter 31 of Jeremiah: "Therefore," he says, "we cannot fulfil that very thing we do in repenting, unless we lean on the help of God." And what Christ said, that with men it is impossible for anyone to be saved, but with God all things are possible, he explains likewise against the Pelagians: the commandments of nature are indeed impossible, but those of grace are possible.

units.la: Quae cum ita sint, facile est colligere, non ex natura nostra hanc diuini verbi facilitatem & claritatem, sed ex ipsius veritatis, quae breuis & simplex est & propterea perspicua, natura, tum etiam ex illa fideli patris coelestis communicatione nasci.
units.tr: Since this is so, it is easy to gather that the ease and clarity of the divine word arise not from our nature but from the nature of the truth itself, which is brief and simple and therefore plain, and also from the faithful communication of the heavenly Father.

units.la: Quod igitur Moses dicit, Verbum Dei facile & perspicuum esse, eo ipso naturam nostram quae & caeca est & infirma, & perplexa, non extollit: sed bonitatem, fidem & diligentiam Dei laudat, qui illud ipsum nobis erudiendis tam benigne accommodat, quiq; in hoc ipsum sic in cumbar totus, vt quid facto opus sit nos edoceat.
units.tr: When Moses says that the word of God is easy and plain, he does not thereby exalt our nature, which is blind, weak and confused. He praises the goodness, faithfulness and diligence of God, who so kindly adapts that very word to our instruction, and who is so wholly devoted to this end that he teaches us what needs to be done.

units.la: Ac ne quis obscurum sibi fuisse quid Deus vellet, posset obijcere: iam inficiatur singula praetextus huius generis. 1. Non est insolens sive rarum, &c. quod ceu monstrum aut ostentum mirari quam cognoscere facilius existimes. Veluti cometas attoniti suspicimus, nec quid significent scimus. Eiusmodi verbum Dei non est, cum quae necessaria scitu sint doceat: argumentum tot sunt typi, sententiae, &c.
units.tr: Lest anyone object that what God wished was obscure to him, I refute each pretext of this kind. 1. It is not unusual or rare, etc. so that you would think it a monster or portent to be wondered at rather than something easily known. We look up in astonishment at comets and do not know what they signify. The word of God is not of this kind, since it teaches what is necessary to know. Its subject matter consists of so many types, sayings, etc.

units.la: 2 Non remotum: vt vel secreto dicatur aliquibus solum, aut per inuolucra proponatur: sed publice praedicatur, & ad captum atq; ingenium singulorum accommodatur: testes sunt libri, historiae, prophetae, Psalmi: testantur hoc ipsum parabolae & similitudines obscuris rebus explicandis adhibitae: probant idem ipsum exempla, res quasi in tabula depingentia: habent ipsum in vsu philosophus, rusticus, politicus, omninoq;, omnes.
units.tr: 2. It is not remote, so that it is spoken secretly to a few alone, or put forward in veils. It is preached publicly and adapted to the capacity and talent of each person. Books, histories, prophets and Psalms bear witness to this. Parables and similitudes used to explain obscure matters bear witness to it too. Examples which paint the matter as on a tablet prove the same thing. Philosopher, peasant, statesman, indeed everyone and all, have it in use.

units.la: 3. Non est in coelis, vt inde sit expetendum, vnde vix afferri possit. Deus ipse coelitus hunc thesaurum nobis attulit atque aperuit: suo spiritu patriarchas, prophetas, apostolos afflauit: quin ipsum etiam, ne quid deesset filium nobis misit.
units.tr: 3. It is not in heaven, so that it must be sought from there, whence it could hardly be brought. God himself brought and opened this treasure to us from heaven. He breathed by his Spirit upon the patriarchs, prophets and apostles. Indeed, lest anything be lacking, he sent us his Son himself.

units.la: 4. Non est trans mare. Non opus peregrinationibus Pythagorae, Platonis, Apollonij Thyanaei: nec opus est vt cum Regina Sabae longo difficilique itinere ad Solomonem contendamus: hic enim est plusquam Solomon, inquit Dominus.
units.tr: 4. It is not beyond the sea. There is no need for the journeys of Pythagoras, Plato or Apollonius of Tyana. Nor is there need for us to make a long and difficult journey, as the Queen of Sheba did, to Solomon. For, as the Lord says, "One greater than Solomon is here."

units.la: Quae cum ita sint consequens est excusationem ignorantiae nullam nobis esse reliquam: sed Deum pro sua erga genus nostrum propensa voluntate verbum suum dedisse, quod sua pte natura sit certum & expeditum. Sic Rom. 10. Paulus docet certam & bene explicatam esse fidei iustitiam.
units.tr: Since this is so, it follows that no excuse of ignorance remains for us. God, out of his favourable will towards our race, has given his word, which by its own nature is certain and clear. Thus Paul teaches in Romans 10 that the righteousness of faith is certain and well explained.

units.la: His iam addit adiuuantia verbi diuini studium auxilia, dicens: Prope te est, in ore tuo, & in corde tuo, vt facias, &c. quasi dicat. Agnoscis, & verbis effers, modo factis praestes. Deus sic reuelat, vt primum in ore sit omni populo: omnes enim possunt suis id verbis efferre. Videmus enim si sit de peccato alicuius differendum, quam graues & acuti censores simus: vt Romanis scribes haud immerito dicat apostolus: Quocirca inexcusabilis es, o homo, omnis qui iudicas: eadem enim facis quae iudicas. Et, Existimas cum iudices, &c. Quamobrem quod de reformatione, de poenitentia, de religione, & probitate tam subtiliter disputamus: idipsum te stabitur nos inexcusabiles esse.
units.tr: To the word of God he now adds helps that accompany study of it, saying: The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart, that you may do it, etc. As if he said: you acknowledge it and express it in words; only show it in deeds. God so reveals that it is first in the mouth of every people, for all can express it in their own words. For we see how sharp and severe critics we are when the sin of someone else is to be discussed. Thus the apostle rightly says to the Romans: "Therefore you are inexcusable, O man, whoever you are who judge, for you do the same things that you judge. And do you think, when you judge, etc.?" Therefore, whatever we dispute so subtly about reformation, repentance, religion and uprightness, you will be found to be inexcusable in that very matter.

units.la: Deinceps in corde est, inquit. Inscripsit in cor hominis, vt docet apostolus Rom. 1. de lege naturae. Primum enim homo habet mentem: & ea cum aliunde oriatur, nec à bruta natura possit oriri, certè aeterna mente proficisci necesse est. Vt in Pf. Dauid ait: qui fecit oculos non videret? Deinceps hoc docet inditum nobis honestorum & turpium discrimen, quod ab illa mente nascatur oportet. Docent idem tota rerum natura, leges coelestium motuum fixae, similium ex similibus ortus, & singulorum peculiaris vsus. His adde legum, reip. pastorum, præmiorum & pœnarum inuentio, distributio, cognitio. Omitto motus in humanis animis plane diuinos & complura alia: quibus euincitur mentibus humanis inscriptum atq; impressum esse verbum Domini.
units.tr: Next he says, it is in the heart. He has written it in the heart of man, as the apostle teaches in Romans 1 concerning the law of nature. For man first has a mind, and since this comes from elsewhere and cannot arise from brute nature, it must certainly proceed from an eternal mind. As David says in the Psalm: "He who made the eye, shall he not see?" Next, this teaches that the distinction between honourable and base, which is implanted in us, must arise from that mind. The whole nature of things teaches the same: the fixed laws of the heavenly motions, the birth of like from like, and the particular use of each thing. To these add the invention, distribution and knowledge of laws, of commonwealths, ministers, rewards and punishments. I pass over the movements in human souls that are plainly divine, and many other things, by which it is proved that the word of the Lord is inscribed and impressed upon human minds.

units.la: Tertiò, Ecce propono, inquit, bonum & malum, vitam & mortem. Quibus verbis eos quasi impellit, & ad recipiendum atq; retinendum verbum suum cogit. Veluti rex aliquis obsidio ne cingens vrbem nunciat obsessis rosam aut gladium proponi, vtrum accipiant optionem dari: si conditiones oblatas accipiant, ciuitatem obsidione solutum iri, pacemq; fore: sin eadem recusent atq; respuant, hostem ad expugnationem atq; delectionem vrbis omnia comparaturum. Et se deinceps exponit ipse seruantibus bona commemorans, negligentibus mala minitans.
units.tr: Thirdly, behold, he says, I set before you good and evil, life and death. By these words he as it were urges them and compels them to receive and keep his word. As some king, besieging a city, announces to the besieged that a rose or a sword is put before them, to choose which they will accept: if they accept the offered terms, the city will be released from siege and there will be peace; but if they refuse and reject them, he will make every preparation for the enemy to storm and destroy the city. And afterwards he explains himself, mentioning good things to those who keep the word and threatening evils to the negligent.

units.la: Est autem hoc ipsum, quod Deus nos quasi vi trahit, & in regnum suum cogit extrinsecus & intrinsecus instrumentis adhibitis, magni illius in nos amoris indicium: tum etiam argumento certissimo, nos si respuamus occasionem oblatam inexcusabiles fore.
units.tr: Moreover, this very fact, that God draws us as though by force and compels us into his kingdom, both outwardly and inwardly, by means of the instruments he employs, is a token of that great love of his towards us. It is also a most certain argument that if we reject the opportunity offered, we shall be inexcusable.

units.la: Verum ex his omnibus colligimus verbum diuinum nobis clare & aperte reuelari, minime esse obscurum: tum id nobis in os, in cor ingeri: denique etiam nos impelli ad ipsum accipiendum promissis pariter ac minis.
units.tr: But from all these things we gather that the divine word is clearly and openly revealed to us, is by no means obscure, and that it is thrust into our mouth and heart; and finally that we are moved to receive it, by promises as well as by threats.

units.la: Quæ cum magna sint ad beatam vitam comparandam auxilia: nobis est enitendum, vt illa ipsa gratis animis amplectamur: ac patrem Domini nostri Iesu Christi precemur, quo suo spiritu datam antea gratiam augeat ac roboret, donec nos ex his terris ad cœlitum consortium deducat, per Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum, Amen.
units.tr: Since these are great helps for gaining a blessed life, we must strive to embrace them with willing minds, and pray to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ that he may increase and strengthen by his Spirit the grace previously given, until he leads us out of these earthly places into the fellowship of the heavenly ones, through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT XXXI. SERMO V.
units.tr: Chapter 31. Sermon 5.

units.la: Abiens itaq; Moses, loquutus est verba ista ad omnem Israelem:
units.tr: And so Moses, going away, spoke these words to all Israel:

units.la: 2 Et dixit ad eos: Ego hodie sum natus centum & viginti annos, nec possum vltra egredi & ingredi, & dixit Dominus ad me: Tu non transibis Iordanem istum.
units.tr: 2 And he said to them: I am today a hundred and twenty years old, and I can no longer go out and come in. And the Lord said to me: You shall not cross this Jordan.

units.la: 3 Dominus Deus tuus ipse transibit ante te, & delebit gentes istas ante te: tu vero possidebis eas. Iehofua quoq; ille præcedet te, quemadmodum loquutus est Dominus.
units.tr: 3 The Lord your God himself will pass over before you, and will destroy these nations before you, and you shall possess them. Joshua too will go before you, as the Lord has spoken.

units.la: 4 Et faciet Dominus eis quemadmodum fecit Sihon & Og regibus Amorræorum, atq; terræ eorum quos ipse exterminauit.
units.tr: 4 And the Lord will do to them as he did to Sihon and Og, kings of the Amorites, and to their land, whom he destroyed.

units.la: 5 Tradetq; eos Dominus ante faciem vestram, vt faciatis eis iuxta totum hoc præceptum, quod mandaui vobis.
units.tr: 5 And the Lord will deliver them up before your face, so that you may do to them according to this whole commandment which I have given you.

units.la: 6 Fortes igitur estote & agite gnauiter, ne timeatis, neque terreamini ab ipsis, quia Dominus Deus tuus ipse comitatur te, non faciet te remissum neq; deseret te.
units.tr: 6 Be strong therefore and act manfully; do not fear, nor be terrified by them, for the Lord your God himself accompanies you; he will not let you go nor forsake you.

units.la: QVEMADMODVM[?] Dominus noster Iesus Christus & iturus ad supplicium mortis & in cœlum hinc ascensurus suos discipulos, ne vel offensi cruce eius desperarent, vel illo corporaliter digresso diuinam quoque eius gratiam abesse putarent, consolatur, vt Ioh.15.16. & seq.cap. sic Moses eius typus & propheta similis præuidens atq; sentiens sibi hinc emigrandum esse, populum suum consolatur, quasiq; testamentum faciens ad diuinæ legis studium impellit. Ac veluti Christus de paracleto suo loco eis affuturo, sic ille de Iosua successore: vt Christus de doctrinæ summa, veritate, vtilitate: sic ille de legis vsu, custodia, annua repetitione: vt Christus vltimo præclaras ad patrem preces fudit, sic ille carmen egregium canit cum populo in Dei laudem & gloriam. Atq; his quidem populi partim ne eius discessu tristiores essent: partim ne rebus ex animi sententia fluentibus superbiant, quasi repagulo posito cauet.
units.tr: Just as our Lord Jesus Christ, about to go to the death of the cross and to ascend into heaven from here, comforts his disciples, lest they despair when offended by his cross, or think that his divine grace is gone when he has departed bodily, so Moses, his type and a like prophet, foreseeing and sensing that he must depart from here, comforts his people and, as if making a testament, urges them to the study of the divine law. As Christ spoke of his Paraclete who would be present to them in his place, so Moses spoke of Joshua his successor; as Christ spoke of the sum, truth and usefulness of doctrine, so Moses spoke of the use, the keeping and the yearly repetition of the law; as Christ at the end poured out splendid prayers to the Father, so Moses sings a remarkable song with the people in praise and glory of God. And he does these things partly so that the people would not be made sadder by his departure, and partly so that they would not grow proud when affairs flow according to their wishes; he guards against this, as if setting a bar in place.

units.la: Continet autem hoc caput primum periocham insequentis narrationis: tum institutionem ducis seu magistratus & Leuitarum: deniq; ordinis vtriusq; confirmationem.
units.tr: This chapter contains, first, the summary of the narrative that follows; then the appointment of the leader or magistrate and of the Levites; and finally the confirmation of both offices.

units.la: Periocham verbis supra positis quasi quadam præfatione comprehendit: ita vt primum quid fecerit, dein quid dixerit Moses ostendat.
units.tr: He comprises the summary in the words set above, as a kind of preface, so that he shows first what Moses did and then what he said.

units.la: Quid fecerit hoc ipso docet quod dicit eum abiisse & omnia verba ista ad omnem Israelem dixisse dixisse. Quod perinde est ac si diceretur: Cum ætate iam ingrauescente Moses sentiret sibi iam iam moriendum esse, ne populus eius morte non prouisa consternatus animum desponderet, secundumque actum esse putaret, vel deinceps rectore & doctore destitutus terra promissa, qua neq; potiri vellet & auderet, neq; ea comparata atq; acquisita recte vteretur: vult eos consolari & de rerum suarum statu admonere.
units.tr: That he did this he shows by the very fact that he says Moses went away and spoke all these words to all Israel. This is just as if it were said: When Moses, his age now advancing, perceived that he must soon die, he wished to comfort the people and to admonish them about the state of their affairs, lest the people, dismayed by his death which they had not foreseen, should lose heart and think that they were now left in a bad state; or lest, deprived henceforth of a ruler and teacher, they should not wish or dare to take possession of the promised land, or, having obtained and acquired it, should not use it rightly.

units.la: Ac verbo eundi videtur significari ipsum Mosem per castra vniuersa circumiuisse, & ex omni populo singulos sigillatim appellasse.
units.tr: By the word going it seems to be signified that Moses himself went round the whole camp and addressed each person individually from the whole people.

units.la: Atq; hoc Mosis factum omnibus & magistratibus & priuatis hominibus est exemplo o-ptimo, quod videlicet Moses nec iniuriarum, quas multas ac magnas acceperat, meminit, aut quod illis ad peccatum impulsus obijcit: neq; curam ciuitatis eius à qua discedit iam iam moriturus deponit: sed & cum bona gratia vult discedere, & posteris suis perinde, atq; sibi, ipsis consulere. Magnus profectò & insigni pietate præditus animus, quique & magistratu fungentem & priuatum hominem deceat.
units.tr: And this action of Moses is a most excellent example for magistrates and private persons alike: namely, that Moses neither recalls the many great injuries he had received, nor throws in their faces the sins to which they were driven; nor does he lay down the care of the city from which he is departing, about to die, but he wishes to depart with good grace, and to provide for his descendants just as for himself. Truly a great spirit, endowed with remarkable piety, one that befits both a magistrate and a private man.

units.la: Magistratus interest non suorum modo temporum, sed etiam posterorum quieti, tranquillitati, fœlicitati studere. Inuenias qui putent res bene esse curatas si sibi suis tempori-bus consultum sit: at Moses etiam posteris prospicit. Ianus bifrons rex Italiæ præsentia futuraq;, pariter spectabat. Patriarchæ posterorum rationem habuere in educatione puerorum, in parandis bonis, in conciliandis amicitijs: vt Dauid, Solomon, Iosias, &c. Sic omnes magistratus in gratiam posteritatis scholas, leges, annonam, fœdera conseruabunt.
units.tr: It is the duty of a magistrate to strive for the quiet, tranquillity and happiness not only of his own times but also of posterity. You will find people who think affairs are well managed if provision is made for their own times; but Moses looks also to posterity. Janus, the two-faced king of Italy, looked equally at the present and the future. The patriarchs took account of posterity in the education of children, in acquiring goods, and in forming friendships; so did David, Solomon, Josiah and others. So all magistrates, for the sake of posterity, will preserve schools, laws, the grain supply and covenants.

units.la: Deinceps iniurias neq; priuatas neq; publicas impotenter velint vlcisci.
units.tr: Furthermore, they should not wish to avenge injuries, whether private or public, in an unrestrained way.

units.la: Sed homines priuati in educatione liberorum, in rei familiaris cura, in amicitijs, in iuris obseruantia liberos respiciant. Paulus fidelem negat esse eum, qui id non faciat. Tum moritu-ri, bona gratia discedamus potius quàm mala: remittamus vt remittatur nobis. Sic mortui sunt accersitis ad se suis Iacob, Tobias, Christus commendans alterum alteri, præmonens, consolans: sic Moses hoc loco: Paulus scribens & instituens suos ex vinculis, Iohannes acceptam diuinitus reuelationem proferens. Mali igitur sunt & inhumani, qui morituri discordiæ semina post se relinquunt: quod comes Toggeburgius olim fecit.
units.tr: But private persons, in the education of their children, in the care of household property, in friendships and in the observance of the law, should look to their children. Paul says that he is not faithful who does not do this. Then, when we are about to die, let us depart with good grace rather than bad: let us forgive, so that we may be forgiven. Thus Jacob and Tobias died, having summoned their own to them; Christ too commended one to another, giving warnings and comfort; so Moses in this place. Paul, writing and instructing his people from his chains, and John, publishing the revelation received from God, did likewise. Therefore those are wicked and inhuman who, about to die, leave seeds of discord behind them, as Count Toggenburg once did.

units.la: Quid dixerit, Ego hodie sum natus centum viginti, &c. Id est, Ego morior quidem, vosque porro nec docere potero, nec regere: Sed animos propterea non desponde-bitis: nam & ea sum ætate, vt ne multum vobis amplius prodesse possim, & Deus vester dux erit quæq; promisit dabit omnia: tum neq; duce carebitis homine videlicet Iosua, neq; diuino patrocinio. Quo docet illos morte eius nequaquam terreri debere: esse quibus eius incommodū resarciatur. Consolatur eos hoc modo & rationes eam ad rem affert.
units.tr: What he said: "I am today a hundred and twenty years old," etc. That is: I am indeed dying, and I shall no longer be able to teach or to rule you; but you should not for that reason lose heart. For I am of such an age that I can no longer be of much further use to you, but your God will be your leader and will give everything he has promised; then you will lack neither a leader in the person of Joshua, nor divine protection. By this he teaches them that they ought not to be terrified at all by his death: there are others by whom its loss will be made good. He comforts them in this way and brings reasons for it.

units.la: 1. Ab ætate: Ego hodie natus sum annos centum viginti, nec possum egredi & ingredi, & dixit Dominus ad me, tu non transibis Iordanem istum. Hoc est, mors mea duabus de causis ferenda est æquis animis. Vna, quod senex sum & functus officio. Altera, quod diuina prouidentia ac voluntate fit, vt mori nunc extra hanc terram necesse sit.
units.tr: 1. From age: I am today a hundred and twenty years old; I cannot go out and come in, and the Lord has said to me, You shall not cross this Jordan. That is: my death is to be borne with calm mind for two reasons. One, that I am old and have discharged my office. The other, that it comes about by divine providence and will, so that it is necessary for me to die now outside this land.

units.la: Senectus non potest longum vitæ cursum polliceri, quando senes quicquid temporis vi-uunt in lucro habeant. Deinde meretur hæc eadem vacationem à muneribus publicis & la-boribus, nec inuidendum est ei, qui in stadio cucurrerit, si quiescat. Sic si grandæuos diuque exercitatos antistites, magistratus, parentes amittimus, nos consolemur, quod & senibus imminebat mors, & longo labore confectis quies erat concedenda. His accedit voluntas Dei.
units.tr: Old age cannot promise a long course of life, since the aged count whatever time they still live as gain. Further, this same age deserves exemption from public duties and labours, and one who has run in the race should not be begrudged rest if he rests. So if we lose aged ministers, magistrates and parents, long practised in their work, let us console ourselves: death was hanging over the old too, and rest was to be granted to those worn out by long labour. To this is added the will of God.

units.la: 2. A promissis diuinis. Dominus Deus tuus transibit ante te &c. Allegat Dei promissa quæ non possunt non afferre consolationem. Vt in lapsu suo promissione feminis benedicti, in di-luvio [?] Nohæ, in exilio suo Abraham, Israel in Ægypto, alij in alijs molestijs & miserijs, in morbis, &c. Quæ fiducia si nutet exemplis atq; signis est confirmanda. Vnde illæ Dei voces, Ego sum Deus Abraham, &c. patrum tuorum, &c.
units.tr: 2. From God's promises: The Lord your God will pass over before you, etc. He cites God's promises, which cannot fail to bring consolation. So in the fall, with the promise made to the seed of the blessed woman; in the flood, to Noah; in his exile, to Abraham; to Israel in Egypt; and to others in other troubles and miseries, in diseases, etc. If this confidence wavers, it must be confirmed by examples and signs. Hence those voices of God: I am the God of Abraham, etc., of your fathers, etc.

units.la: Moses hic Seonis & Ogis regum deuictorum exemplis Dei promissiones firmat. Sic in morbo, habes exempla mulieris laborantis sanguinis profluuio, cœci nati, claudi ad piscinam iacentis, Lazari in sepulchro iacentis, & aliorum: in pauperie solabuntur vidua Sareptana, Lazarus receptus in sinum Abrahæ, &c. in difficili bello, Bethulia, Samaria, Hierusalem, nostra Heluetia. Sic Moses solatur exemplo suo & Iosuæ, &c.
units.tr: Here Moses confirms God's promises by the examples of the kings Sihon and Og, who were defeated. Thus in sickness you have the examples of the woman suffering from a flow of blood, of the man born blind, of the lame man lying by the pool, of Lazarus lying in the tomb, and of others. In poverty the widow of Zarephath and Lazarus, received into Abraham's bosom, will comfort you, and so on. In a hard war, Bethulia, Samaria, Jerusalem, and our own Helvetia. So Moses comforts by his own example and Joshua's, and so on.

units.la: 3. A persona successoris. Iosua, inquit, præcedet te. Ille fungetur officio ducis. Semper aliquis à Deo suscitatur qui populum regat ac gubernet: velut etiam mulieres aliquando fertur ad tuendam publicam rem suscitasse, vt Deboram, Iuditham, aliquando pueros vt Dauidem, antea Samuelem, Danielem, & alios. Et nostris temporibus non defuerunt heroes, &c.
units.tr: 3. From the person of the successor: Joshua, he says, will go before you. He will perform the office of leader. Always someone is raised up by God to rule and govern the people. Women too are said at times to have been raised up to defend the public cause, such as Deborah and Judith; at times boys, such as David, and earlier Samuel, Daniel and others. And in our own times heroes have not been lacking, and so on.

units.la: 4. Ab auxilio & patrocinio Dei. Non faciet te remissum. Non deseret te. Affuit Deus Ia-cobo, Iosepho, Helizeo, Tobiae, Hierosolymis obsessis, pueris Danielis, & angelis mandatum est de nobis, Psal. 90.
units.tr: 4. From the help and protection of God. He will not fail you. That is, he will not forsake you. God was present with Jacob, with Joseph, with Elisha, with Tobias, with Jerusalem when it was besieged, with the boys of Daniel; and the angels have been commanded concerning us, Ps. 90.

units.la: Ex quibus discimus, nos, cum simili in loco res sint nostrae, similibus ipsi nos argumen-tis consolemur, per Iesum Christum, Amen.
units.tr: From these examples we learn that, since our circumstances are like those in the same situations, we ourselves should console ourselves with similar arguments, through Jesus Christ. Amen.

units.la: SERMO VI.
units.tr: SERMO VI.

units.la: 7 Vocauit autem Moses Josuam, & dixit ad eum in oculis totius Israel: Fortis esto & gnauiter age, quoniam tu ingredieris cum populo isto in terram, quam jurauit Dominus patribus eorum, ut daret eis: & tu divides eam in hereditatem.
units.tr: 7 And Moses called Joshua, and said to him in the sight of all Israel: Be strong and act courageously, for you shall go with this people into the land which the Lord swore to their fathers to give them, and you shall divide it for an inheritance.

units.la: 8 Sed & Dominus ipse praecedet te, & ipse aderit tibi, nec remissum te faciet, nec te deseret: ne ergo timeas: ne animo frangaris.
units.tr: 8 And the Lord himself shall go before you, and he shall be with you; he will neither fail you nor forsake you. Therefore do not fear, nor be discouraged.

units.la: 9 Et scripsit Moses legem istam, & tradidit eam sacerdotibus filijs Leui, qui portabant arcam foederis Domini, atq; cunctis senioribus Israel.
units.tr: 9 And Moses wrote this law and delivered it to the priests, the sons of Levi, who carried the ark of the covenant of the Lord, and to all the elders of Israel.

units.la: 10 Praecepitq; Moses eis hisce verbis: A fine septem annorum in statuto[?] festo anni remissionis in solennitate tabernaculorum.
units.tr: 10 And Moses commanded them with these words: At the end of seven years, at the appointed feast of the year of release, at the solemnity of tabernacles,

units.la: 11 Quando convenerit cunctus Israel, ut appareat in conspectu Domini Dei tui, in loco quem sibi elegerit, leges hanc legem coram universo Israele ipsis audientibus.
units.tr: 11 When all Israel comes to appear before the Lord your God in the place which he shall choose, you shall read this law before all Israel, in their hearing.

units.la: 12 Congregabis autem populum, viros, mulieres & pubem, sed & peregrinum tuum, qui est intra portas tuas, ut audiant & ut discant, timeantq; Dominum Deum vestrum, custodiantq; & observent omnia verba legis huius.
units.tr: 12 Gather the people, men, women and children, and also your stranger who is within your gates, that they may hear and learn, and fear the Lord your God, and keep and observe all the words of this law.

units.la: 13 Filij quoq; eorum qui nihil noverunt audiant & discant, ut timeant Domi-num Deum vestrum cunctis diebus quibus vivetis super terram, in quam vos transietis Iordane introitis, ut eam possideatis.
units.tr: 13 And let their children, who have known nothing, hear and learn to fear the Lord your God all the days that you live upon the earth, into which you pass over the Jordan to possess it.

units.la: CVm Moses populum Israel velit consolari, ne dolorem ex eius morte nimis magnum caperent: & tamen ipsi duabus de causis illa dolere possent: una, quod duce: altera, quod doctore se destitui crederent: docet Moses neutra parte damnum oriri, ac Josuam ipsius loco gubernatore, Levitas autem legis doctores fore. In quo ceu speculo cernimus populi cuiusq; salutem atq; incolumitatem in hoc potissimum consistere, ut & magistratus habeant & doctores bonos.
units.tr: Since Moses wishes to console the people, so that they should not grieve too greatly over his death, they could grieve for two reasons: one, that they were deprived of a leader; the other, that they were deprived of a teacher. Moses shows that neither loss arises, and that Joshua will be their governor in his place, and the Levites will be the teachers of the law. In this, as in a mirror, we see that the safety and welfare of any people consist chiefly in this: that they have both good magistrates and good teachers.

units.la: Atq; hoc ipsum ut crederent, primum Josuam ducem sibi successurum accersit, populo sistit, eligit, instruit, confirmat, tum legem abs se mandatam literis profert, eamq; Levitis tan-quam custodibus atq; interpretibus tradit. Quae cum nobis ad imitationem sint proposita, videamus eo quo proponuntur ordine. Primo, ducem, dein Levitas. Etsi enim primum in civitate locum teneat religio, tamen ut eam à ministris traditam magistratus publica potestate tueatur necesse est: Unde & potestatem publicam ceu illius tutorem primum omnium infor-mat hoc loco.
units.tr: And so that they might believe this very thing, Moses first summons Joshua to succeed him as leader, presents him to the people, chooses him, instructs him and confirms him; then he sets forth in writing the law entrusted by him and hands it over to the Levites, as its guardians and interpreters. Since these things are set before us for imitation, let us consider them in the order in which they are set out: first the leader, then the Levites. For although religion holds the first place in the commonwealth, nevertheless, for it to be protected by public authority, once it has been handed over by the ministers, is necessary. Hence Moses, as the guardian of religion, first of all instructs us here about public authority.

units.la: De magistratu dicit: Vocauit autem Moses Josuam, &c. Quibus verbis electionem, officium, auxilium seu praesidium magistratus docet. Electionem eo ipso quod Josuam vocat, populo sistit, inq; eius omnis conspectu sui illam admonet & officij & praesidij.
units.tr: Concerning the magistrate he says: "And Moses summoned Joshua," etc. By these words he teaches the election, the office, and the help or protection of the magistrate. He teaches the election by the very fact that he summons Joshua, presents him to the people, and in the sight of all admonishes them of his office and of the protection due to him.

units.la: Id est documento magistratus electionem propterea debere esse solennem atque publi-cam, ut quid altera pars alteri debeat nemini sit incognitum. Nam oblivio officij malorum fere causa est. Ac quemadmodum pater oblitus se esse patrem cum filijs ludit seq; contemptu & filios deteriores facit: sic magistratus oblitus se ducem & rectorem esse cum subditis sibi civibus ebrietati, aliisq; vitijs inquinatur: suae existimationi & subditorum probitati damnum dat maximum. Igitur officij sui illos coram plebe Moses exemplo suo docet admonendos, ut huius solennis electionis memoria recenti in animis conservata ab officio nunquâ discedant, seq; à contemptu tueantur. Contra plebs quem videt sibi praepositum, revereatur, amet, se-quatur: ac ducis, patris, regis habeat loco. Quis enim est qui non amet ac colat eum quem sibi praefectum videt?
units.tr: This is a lesson that the election of a magistrate ought therefore to be solemn and public, so that it may be known to no one what each party owes to the other. For forgetfulness of duty is nearly always the cause of evils. And just as a father who forgets that he is a father plays with his children, and by his contempt makes them worse, so a magistrate who forgets that he is leader and ruler of the citizens committed to him is defiled by drunkenness and other vices, and does the greatest harm both to his own reputation and to the integrity of his subjects. Therefore Moses, by his example, teaches that the magistrates are to be admonished of their duty before the people, so that, with the memory of this solemn election fresh in their minds, they never depart from their duty and guard themselves against contempt. On the other side, the people should revere, love and follow whomever they see set over them, and should hold him in the place of a leader, a father, a king. For who is there who does not love and honour the one whom he sees set over him?

units.la: Ambitum autem hoc ritu praecipuè repellit, atq; expectanda cuiq; liberam vocationem suadet: tunc enim & qui praeest erit liberior, & qui paret obedientior. Nam quae vi parta sunt, & malis artibus nunquam fuere diuturna imperia.
units.tr: Moreover, by this rite he especially repels ambition, and urges that each person should await a free calling; for then the one who rules will be the freer, and the one who obeys the more willing. For empires gained by force and by wicked arts have never been lasting.

units.la: Officium autem magistratus eo ipso docet, quod ad Iosuam dicit: Fortis esto & gnauiter agito, quoniam tu ingredieris, &c. Quo dicto primum eius animum, dein facta format. Animum requirit fortem: oportet enim infracto atq; impigro sit animo quisquam non facile ijs qui fusci-tantur a tergo tumultibus terreatur. Et vere dici vulgo nostro solet leonem ceruorum agmi-ne potius vincere, quam ceruus dux leonum copijs. Vnde magnanimi illi heroes, Dauid, Iohanathas, Iudas Machabaeus, Marius, Alexander Magnus, alijq; multi paruis copijs foelicissime pugnarunt. Et in regis exemplum omnium oculi conuertuntur.
units.tr: He teaches the office of the magistrate by what he says to Joshua: Be strong and act courageously, for you shall go, etc. By this word he forms first his spirit, then his deeds. He requires a brave spirit: for a man of a broken and sluggish spirit is not easily terrified by tumults that are stirred up at his back. And indeed it is commonly said among us that a lion will rather conquer a herd of stags than a stag, as leader, the forces of lions. Hence those high-minded heroes, David, Jonathan, Judas Maccabeus, Marius, Alexander the Great, and many others, with small forces fought most successfully. And the eyes of all are turned to the example of the king.
