units.la: Facta autem requirit ea, quae gnaui induftrijq; sint animi indicia. Oportet enim virum principem esse laboriosum, vigilantem, impigrum. Οὐχ ἡ πάννυχον ἐῦδ' ἐυλπόεσσν ἀἴδρα [?] Epaminondas epulantibus suis Thebanis circuibat ac vigilabat ne quid mali paterentur ciues. Scipio sic castra sua gubernabat, vt deprehensos atque adductos ad se exploratores Hannibalis ipse per omnia castra circumduceret, & iussos quae vidissent nunciare duci suo, remitteret. Absit a principe, segnicies, somnus, crapula. Atque hoc est quod dicit Moses gnauiter agendum esse.
units.tr: He requires, moreover, deeds which are signs of a diligent and active spirit. For a prince ought to be hardworking, watchful, and vigorous. "Not the one who sleeps all night, the man of good counsel" [Οὐχ ἡ πάννυχον ἐῦδ' ἐυλπόεσσν ἀἴδρα]. Epaminondas, while his Theban men feasted, went round and kept watch so that the citizens should suffer no harm. Scipio so governed his camp that he himself led the spies of Hannibal, when they had been caught and brought before him, through all the camp, and then sent them back, ordered to report to their commander what they had seen. Let idleness, sleep and gluttony be far from a prince. And this is what Moses means when he says that one must act courageously.

units.la: Sed quid agat? Introibis, inquit, cum populo & diuides eis terram: hoc est, dabis operam vt ditescant, proficiant, augeantur opibus & honoribus: tum vt quas adepti sunt opes recte inter se riteq; distribuant. Duae enim ad salutem publicam res requiruntur: vna vt acquirat, altera vt acquisitis rebus & vtatur & fruatur iuste, pacate, liberè.
units.tr: But what is he to do? You shall go in, he says, with the people and divide the land for them: that is, you shall take care that they grow rich, prosper and are increased in wealth and honours; then that they distribute among themselves, rightly and justly, the wealth they have acquired. For two things are required for the public welfare: one, that they acquire; the other, that they use and enjoy what has been acquired justly, peacefully and freely.

units.la: Est autem magistratus & publicae vniuersorum & singulorum quoq; ciuium vtilitati studere, cum promouendae tum etiam tuendae. Vt patriae suus sit honos, suae diuitiae, sua commoda: velut annona, pax, leges. Dein vt ciues non ad egestatem aut infamiam adigantur. [illegible, ~20 letters] Ovium cura penes pastorem esto.
units.tr: It is the duty of the magistrate to care for the public advantage of all, and also for the advantage of each single citizen, both to promote it and to protect it: that his country may have its honour, its riches, its advantages, such as the food supply, peace and laws. Then that the citizens are not driven into destitution or disgrace. [illegible, about 20 letters] The care of the sheep rests with the shepherd.

units.la: Praesidium autem & auxilium vnde habeat iam dicit: Dominus ipse praecedet te, ipse aderit tibi, nec remissum te faciet, nec te deseret. Ne ergo timeas, ne animo frangaris. Quo docet magistratibus, si pij sint in Deo praesidij satis & auxilij positum esse.
units.tr: He now states whence the magistrate has his protection and help: The Lord himself shall go before you, he shall be with you; he will neither fail you nor forsake you. Therefore do not fear, nor be discouraged. By this he teaches magistrates that, if they are godly, there is enough protection and help placed in God.

units.la: Dicit enim primum, Praecedet te. Quo docet haud difficile esse quod mandet modo praeeuntem sequatur Deum. Quid enim est facilius, quàm praeeuntem qui secet glaciem & viam aperiat sequi? Illud praeire Dei lucis appellatione sacrae literae quoq; significant.
units.tr: For he says first, He shall go before you. By this he teaches that it is not difficult to do what he commands, if one follows God going before. For what is easier than to follow one who goes before, cutting through the ice and opening up the way? Holy Scripture also signifies this going before of God by the name of light.

units.la: 2. Aderit, videlicet vt socius. Affuit antea Mosi cum in illum Core, Datan, & Abiram ir-ruerent: tum dicit Iosuae Dominus, quemadmodum fui cum Mose sic ero tecum. Et certè seditiosos omnes puniuit. Nam qui magistratui resistit Deo bellum indicit.
units.tr: 2. He shall be with you, namely as a companion. He had been with Moses before, when Korah, Dathan and Abiram attacked him; then the Lord says to Joshua that, just as he was with Moses, so he will be with him. And certainly he punished all the seditious. For whoever resists the magistrate declares war on God.

units.la: 3. Non remissum te faciet, non te deseret. Omnis fortitudinis basis in Domino. Tyranni sunt meticulosi, quia cum homines tum Deum hostes habent: pij verò homines sunt animosi, quia in Deo quasi in asylo tutissimo conquiescunt, & Deus pijs magistratibus authoritatem conciliat vt Iosepho, Dauidi, Danieli: interdum etiam mulieribus vt Iudithae, Deborae, & alijs.
units.tr: 3. He will neither fail you nor forsake you. The foundation of all courage is in the Lord. Tyrants are fearful, because they have men and God as enemies; but godly men are bold, because they rest in God as in the safest refuge, and God gives authority to godly magistrates, as to Joseph, David and Daniel, and at times even to women, as to Judith, Deborah and others.

units.la: Atq; haec de magistratu Moses affert, quò videant Deum nequaquam velle populum su-su-um ducibus destitui.
units.tr: And these are the things Moses brings forward concerning the magistrate, so that they may see that God by no means wishes his people to be deprived of leaders.

units.la: Videmus quàm non possimus carere hoc ordine: quis enim praeiret? quis litigantes dirimeret? quis in moerore & luctu iacentes recrearet? Multae sunt ergo & variae causae quibus efficitur vt ne magistratu carere possimus. Sed quoniam sacerdotes, quod magistratus secundum verbum Dei mandat, ipsi docent ac suadent: ac propterea ciuitas ijs perinde opus habet, ac ducibus: iam de ijs ipsis quoq; dicit. Et scripsit, inquit, Moses legem istam, &c. Quo docet etiam altera gubernationis parte prospectum illis esse: quando legem absque mandatam lite-ris vnà cum magistratu Leuitae feruent, statoq; tempore omni populo praedicent. In quo ne qua fraus fiat, diligenter ostendit: quid, qui, quando, quibus praedicare debeant.
units.tr: We see how we cannot do without this order: for who would go before? who would settle disputes between litigants? who would revive those lying in grief and mourning? There are therefore many and various causes by which it comes about that we cannot do without the magistrate. But since the priests, whom the magistrate according to the word of God commands, themselves teach and persuade, and therefore the state needs them just as it needs leaders, he now speaks also about them. And Moses, he says, wrote this law, etc. By this he teaches that provision has been made for them in the other part of government as well: since the Levites keep the law, written down and entrusted together with the magistrate, and proclaim it to the people at the appointed time. And so that no fraud may occur in this, he shows carefully what they must proclaim, by whom, when, and to whom.

units.la: Quid, Et scripsit Moses legem istam: Hoc est, noluit viua voce tradere, ne vitiaretur: sed vt integra, pura, sancta ad posteros demitteretur, ipse descriptam eis reliquit. Et vt traditiones humanas respuat, atque verbum suum neque auctum neque diminutum velit Deus.
units.tr: "What is: And Moses wrote this law." That is, he was unwilling to hand it down by living voice, lest it be corrupted. Instead he left it to them in writing, so that it might pass to posterity whole, pure and holy. He also did this to reject human traditions, and because God wills that his word be neither added to nor diminished.

units.la: Qui, Leuitae, sacerdotes, qui fuerant ei rei deputati: & dotati decimis. Ergo sint, quorum sit in ecclesia verba ad plebem facere: nec id munus sibi quisquam arroget. Cauenda est enim cuique ciuitati [illegible, ~6 letters]. Sed his adduntur seniores: nisi enim illi quod docent Leuitae, legibus im-parent & obtineant, nihil agitur: estq; permultum in hoc situm vt ordines hi duo remp. ad-ministrent concorditer.
units.tr: "Who: the Levites," that is, the priests who had been appointed to this business and endowed with tithes. So these are the ones whose task in the church is to address the people; let no one arrogate this office to himself. For each city must be guarded [illegible]. But elders are added to these. Unless the people obey and uphold the laws that the Levites teach, nothing is accomplished, and it matters greatly that these two orders administer the commonwealth in harmony.

units.la: Ergo religionis cura magistratus sese minimè abdicabit. Nam supra 13. magistratui com-mittitur examen prophetiarum. Et supra 17. eidem mandatur ne statuas erigi, neue lucos plan-tari patiatur. Et Iosue extruxit aram in Hebal, Dauid arcam deduxit, Solomon templum extruxit:tum Abia,Iofaphat,Ezechias,Iofias religionem collapsam restaurarant. Alios,q̃ re-ligionem contempsissent, dignis supplicijs affecisse inuenias. Nabuchodonozor blasphe-mum in partes scindi,& illius domum latrinam fieri voluit.Dan. 3. Quod genus homines fi-de & spiritu Christi prædití fuisse dicuntur apostolis. Religionem quoq; restaurarunt & de-fenderunt Constantinus,Gratianus,Valentinianus,Theodosius. Quorum exempla pij ma-gistratus imitabuntur. Quando,septimo quoq; anno.Stata rebus sacris atque publicis pera-gendis tempora seruanda discimus,vt sabbata,&c.
units.tr: Therefore the magistrate will by no means abdicate the care of religion. For above, at 13, the examination of prophecies is committed to the magistrate, and above, at 17, the same magistrate is commanded not to allow statues to be erected or groves planted. Joshua built an altar on Ebal, David brought up the ark, Solomon built the temple, and then Abijah, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah and Josiah restored a religion that had fallen into ruin. You will find that they punished with fitting penalties those who had despised religion. Nebuchadnezzar wanted the blasphemer cut into pieces and his house made a latrine (Dan. 3). Men of this kind are said to have been endowed with faith and the Spirit of Christ, as the apostles were. Constantine, Gratian, Valentinian and Theodosius also restored and defended religion. Pious magistrates will imitate their examples. "When: every seventh year." We learn that fixed times must be observed for carrying out sacred and public business, such as the sabbaths, and so on.

units.la: Quibus,omnibus simul & singulis.Valeant qui sacrorum librorum vsu laicis interdicunt: cum Deus hos omnibus ceu bonum publicum impertiat. Cumq; is qui pariter omnibus sa-lutem pollicetur pariter adorandum se proponat.
units.tr: "To whom: to all together and to each one singly." Good riddance to those who forbid laymen the use of the sacred books, since God bestows them on all as a common good, and since he who promises salvation equally to all also sets himself before all as equally to be worshipped.

units.la: Quem in finem. Vt timeant Dominum. In quo verbi diuini vis cernitur. Sapientiam im-peritis suppeditat Ps.19.Cibus est Deut.8.Mat.4.Docet & solatur Ro.15. Regenerat 1. Pet.1. Tum lux,ignis,gladius,scutum est.
units.tr: "To what end? That they may fear the Lord." In this the power of the divine word is seen. It supplies wisdom to the unlearned (Ps. 19). It is food (Deut. 8; Matt. 4). It teaches and comforts (Rom. 15). It regenerates (1 Pet. 1). It is light, fire, sword and shield.

units.la: Ex quibus omnibus intelligimus tunc demum nobis bene prospectum esse,cum & magistratum habemus pium,prudentem,fortem,industriũ:& doctores verbi Dei peritos:quorum opera cum doceamur tum deducamur ad Deum, per Iesum Christum D.N.Amen.
units.tr: From all these things we understand that we are then well provided for when we have a pious, prudent, brave and diligent magistrate, and teachers of God's word who are skilled in it. Through their work we are both taught and led to God, through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

units.la: SERMO VII.
units.tr: Sermon VII.

units.la: 14 Et dixit Dominus ad Mosem: Ecce appropinquarunt dies tui vt moria-ris.Voca igitur Josuam,& collocate vos in tentorium constitutionis,vt dem ei man-data.Abijt ergo Moses & Josua,& statuerunt se in tentorium constitutionis.
units.tr: 14 And the Lord said to Moses: Behold, your days draw near that you must die. Call Joshua, therefore, and present yourselves in the tent of meeting, that I may give him his charge. So Moses and Joshua went and presented themselves in the tent of meeting.

units.la: 15 Et apparuit Dominus in tentorio in columna nubis,stetitq; columna nubis super ostio tentorij.
units.tr: 15 And the Lord appeared in the tabernacle, in a pillar of cloud, and the pillar of cloud stood over the door of the tabernacle.

units.la: 16 Et dixit Dominus ad Mosem: Ecce tu dormies cum patribus tuis,& surget populus,& scortabitur ( sequendo )deos alienos,huius terrae scilicet in quam veniet, deseret me,& irritum faciet fœdus meum quod pepigi cum eo.
units.tr: 16 And the Lord said to Moses: Behold, thou shalt sleep with thy fathers; and this people will rise up and go a-whoring after (following) the strange gods of the land into which they will come. They will forsake me and break my covenant which I made with them.

units.la: 17 Et irascetur furor meus in eum in die illo,deseramq; eos,& abscondam faciem meam ab eis,eritq; in deuorationem[?],& apprehendent eum multa mala & afflictiones[?], vt dicturus sit illo die: Annon me ideo ista mala apprehendunt, quod Deus non est in medio mei?
units.tr: 17 Then my anger will be kindled against them in that day, and I will forsake them and hide my face from them, and they shall be for devouring[?], and many evils and afflictions[?] will seize them; so that they will say in that day: Do not these evils seize us because God is not in the midst of us?

units.la: 18 Eodem die ego omnino abscondam faciem meam propter vniuersum malum quod facit,nempe quod se converterit ad deos alios.
units.tr: 18 On that day I will surely hide my face on account of all the evil that they do, namely that they have turned to other gods.

units.la: 19 Nunc igitur scribite vobis canticum istud,& doce ipsum filios Israel,& insere hoc ori ipsorum,vt sit mihi canticum istud in testem contra filios Israel.
units.tr: 19 Now therefore write for yourselves this song, and teach it to the children of Israel, and put it in their mouths, so that this song may be a witness for me against the children of Israel.

units.la: 20 Nam introducam eum in terram ,quam iuraui patribus eius,fluentem lac-te & melle, & comedens satiabitur, & pinguescet,conuertesque se ad deos alios, & seruient eis,& irritabunt me,& irritum facient fœdus meum.
units.tr: 20 For I will bring them into the land which I swore to their fathers, flowing with milk and honey; and they shall eat and be satisfied, and grow fat, and turn to other gods and serve them, and provoke me, and break my covenant.

units.la: 21 Quumq; acciderint ei multa mala atq; afflictiones, respondebit ei canticum istud coram eo tanquam testis,quoniam nunquam excidet semini eius ex ore. Nam co gnoui figmentum cordis eius,quod ipse hodie facit,antequam introducam eum in ter-ram,quam iurauì.
units.tr: 21 And when many evils and afflictions come upon them, this song will answer them face to face as a witness, for it shall not be forgotten from the mouth of their seed. For I know the imagination of their heart, which they are already forming today, before I bring them into the land which I swore.

units.la: QVanquam exemplum populi Israelitici satis ostendat, ad incolumitatem cuiusq; re-gni siue ciuitatis pertinere & omnino requiri, vt illi duo ordines,magistratus & diui-ni verbi administri summa fide & diligentia constituantur: tamen vt ne qua pateat malignis effugium:iam sequitur quo pacto Deus illos ambos confirmarit:quò fit in his atq; in præce-dentibus vt bifariam probetur citra duos hosce remp. constare nequaquam posse : partim quia populus ipse confirmandus fuit aliorum promissione,post Mosem,doctorum & ducũ: in quorum penuria nisi malum suum præuidissent,tantũ animo dolorem nequaquá accepis-sent: partim quia Deus Mosis hac de re verba atq; placita suffragio suo rata habet ac probat.
units.tr: Although the example of the Israelite people sufficiently shows that the safety of every kingdom or city depends on, and altogether requires, that those two orders, the magistracy and the ministers of the divine Word, be established with the utmost faith and diligence, nevertheless, lest the malicious have any loophole of escape, it now follows how God confirmed both of them. Hence it is proved in two ways, both here and in what precedes, that the commonwealth cannot possibly stand without these two: partly because the people itself was to be confirmed by the promise of others, after Moses, of teachers and leaders, and without foreseeing their own evil they would by no means have received such great grief in their minds; partly because God holds and approves by his own assent the words and decisions of Moses on this matter.

units.la: Quod quoniam ad existimationem horum ordinum pertinet,atq; etiam ad salutem pu-blicam:paulò altius est repetendum:ac videndum,quod dicitur Deus illis primù apparuisse, deinceps suo suffragio Mosis institutum probasse.
units.tr: Since this pertains to the esteem of these orders, and also to the public welfare, it must be taken up somewhat more deeply, and we must see what is meant when it is said that God first appeared to them and afterwards by his own assent approved the institution of Moses.

units.la: Ac quomodo Dominus apparuerit sic docet: Et ait dominus ad Mosen, Ecce appropinquant dies tui, &c. Quo ostendit primum Moses de sua morte verba diuinitus quoq; rata habet, nec de ea quicquam celatum Mosem, sed sine vlla circuitione dictum esse, appropinquarunt dies tui morieris: tum ab ipso quoq; Domino tam Mosem vt electorem, quàm Iosuam vt electum ad tabernaculum, in quo Leuitarum statio cultusq; omnis erat, conuocatos: & dato praesentiae Domini visibili indicio quid facto opus sit edoctos esse.
units.tr: And how the Lord appeared, he teaches thus: And the Lord said to Moses, Behold, thy days draw near, etc. By this he shows, first, that Moses also holds the words spoken about his death as ratified by God, and that nothing about it was hidden from Moses, but was said plainly and without circumlocution: thy days draw near, thou shalt die. Then, that both Moses, as the one choosing, and Joshua, as the one chosen, were summoned by the Lord himself to the tabernacle, where the station of the Levites and all worship was; and that, by the giving of a visible sign of the Lord's presence, they were taught what needed to be done.

units.la: Ac quod ad prius illud attinet, Mosi tam aperte dictum de morte: videmus vt scriptura nihil earum, quas nos scire nostra multum interest, rerum nos celet. Et quid est aliud quod nos scire, tenere memoria, perpetuo cogitare magis expediat, quàm quod sumus morituri? Haec cogitatio reprimet amorem huius seculi, superbiam, auaritiam, omnes effrenes atq; impuros motus: docet eum missum facere, imò potius diligere, à quibus iam iam fumus digressuri: eum contra venerari ad quem tendimus. Vnde sacrae literae nostram hanc mundanā vitam fumo, vapori, gramini, floribus similem esse ferunt. Nec cuicquam mors parcit, vtut alto fatus sit sanguine. Bene enim poeta Lyricus: Pallida mors æquo pulsat pede pauperum tabernas, regumq; turres ò Beate Sefti. Sed in illa conuocatione locum, in quo hoc fit? personae quibus cum agitur: modus quo Dominus apparuit consideremus.
units.tr: As for the first point, that Moses was so plainly told of his death: we see that Scripture conceals from us none of those things which it greatly concerns us to know. And what is more useful for us to know, to keep in memory, and to think on continually, than that we are going to die? This thought restrains the love of this world, pride, greed, and all unbridled and impure impulses; it teaches us to set aside, or rather to love less, the things from which we are soon to depart, and to revere Him toward whom we are tending. Hence the sacred letters say that this worldly life of ours is like smoke, vapour, grass, or flowers. Nor does death spare anyone, however high he may be born in blood. For the lyric poet rightly says: "Pale death with equal foot knocks at the huts of the poor and the towers of kings, O blessed Sestius." But let us consider in that summons the place where it happens, the persons with whom it is dealt, and the manner in which the Lord appeared.

units.la: Locus est tabernaculum sacrum Deo, destinatum summo pontifici: tum arae & arca, in qua tabulae: quae omnia typum coeli rerumq; coelestium habuere.
units.tr: The place is the tabernacle, sacred to God, set apart for the high priest; then the altar and the ark, in which were the tables; all of which bore the character of a type of heaven and of heavenly things.

units.la: Iam si materiam, formam, vsum tabernaculi inspicias, omniaq; augusta atq; diuina videas: arbitraberis quod res est, hos ordines magno in precio habendos esse: eorumq; contemptum ac violationem in Dei ipsius ignominiam vergere. Psalmo 81[?]. Dij vocantur. Rom. 13. Deo dicitur resistere qui resistit magistratui. Dauid noluit tangere vnctum Domini. Iam de prophetis, Leuitis, apostolis, euangelistis, episcopis cum exempla tum praecepta extant: vt Helizei violatio: vt quod Christus dicit: Qui vos contemnit me contemnit, qui me contemnit eum contemnit qui me misit. Paulus, Sic nos æstimet homo, vt dispensatores mysteriorum Dei. Haec ex loco, qui cum nobis etiā sit sacer pietatis magistratui ministrisq; debitae nos admonet.
units.tr: Now if you examine the matter, form and use of the tabernacle, and see that all things are majestic and divine, you will judge, as is the truth, that these orders are to be held in great esteem, and that their contempt and violation tends to the dishonour of God himself. Psalm 81: I have said, You are gods. Rom. 13: He who resists the magistrate resists God. David would not touch the anointed of the Lord. Moreover, concerning prophets, Levites, apostles, evangelists and bishops, both examples and precepts exist: such as the violation of Elisha; or what Christ says: He who despises you despises me, and he who despises me despises him who sent me. Paul: Let a man so regard us, as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. From this place, which is also sacred to us, we are reminded of the due reverence owed to the magistracy and its ministers.

units.la: Personae, Elector Moses, vt loci religione ductus in electione versetur religiose. Ne personas, vtilitatem priuatam respiciamus: haec enim res est, 1. Diuina, à qua falsum abesse debet: 2. Publica, in qua nulla priuati commodi sit habenda ratio: 3. Conscientiae quasi incumbens onus, quippe quae si discedamus à recto violati iuris diuini simul, atq; humani subinde reos agat: sitq; plumbo grauior iniquitatis in re tanta adhibitae funesta ac tristis recordatio.
units.tr: As for the persons: Moses, the one choosing, being moved by the sanctity of the place, is to make his choice religiously. We must not look to persons or to private advantage. For this matter is (1) divine, from which falsehood must be far removed; (2) public, in which no account of private gain is to be taken; (3) a burden lying upon the conscience, which, if we depart from what is right, at once makes us guilty of violating both divine and human law; and the grievous and sorrowful memory of iniquity committed in so great a matter is heavier than lead.

units.la: Electus autem Iosua cogitet quantam ad rem vocetur: quantopere peccet si sua sibi culpa vel contemptum vel oppressionem accersat: nam id tanto maius scelus est quanto causam effecta superant.
units.tr: But the chosen Joshua should consider to how great a matter he is called, and how greatly he sins if by his own fault he brings upon himself either contempt or oppression; for this is so much the greater a crime, the more the consequences outweigh the cause.

units.la: Iam ipsa apparitio Domini mirabilis est: apparet enim intabernaculo; vt intelligas Deum, & si passim existat, omniaq; expleat: ibi tamen potissimum praesentem esse velle, vbi doctri-na, preces, sacramenta, eleemosyna solent exerceri. Quod & Christus docet, dicens, vbi duo tresue erunt in nomine meo, ibi illis adero medius.
units.tr: The very appearance of the Lord is remarkable: for he appears in the tabernacle, so that you understand that God, although he exists everywhere and fills all things, yet wishes to be present especially there where teaching, prayers, sacraments and almsgiving are usually exercised. Christ also teaches this, saying: where two or three are gathered in my name, there I will be in the midst of them.

units.la: In columna nubis. Est autem nubes commodum diuinæ præsentiæ testimonium: quippe aqua cum sit ac promittat pluuiâ: qua vel irrigetur & fœcundetur terra, vel etiam sceleribus inquinata puniatur: nota est & gratiæ Dei & iræ. Dominus ergo potest adesse vt eripiat, iuuet, conseruet: tum etiam vt puniat. Mosi conseruando, Coræ puniendo Deus affuit: eodem-que modo in Ægypto & alibi. Est autem nubes densa caligo: non enim vult Dominus nobis in his corporibus compagibus plane videri. Nec vllam visibilem sui formam præbet, ne quam hominibus ad idololatriam alioquin pronis præbeat occasionem.
units.tr: In the pillar of cloud. A cloud is a fitting testimony of the divine presence: since water, which is condensed and promises rain, by which the earth is either watered and made fruitful or, polluted by wickedness, is punished, is a sign both of God's grace and of his wrath. The Lord therefore can be present to rescue, to help, to preserve, and also to punish. God was present to preserve Moses and to punish Korah, and in the same way in Egypt and elsewhere. A cloud is, moreover, a thick darkness: for the Lord does not wish to be plainly seen by us in these bodies and frames. Nor does he offer any visible form of himself, lest he give men, who are otherwise prone to idolatry, an occasion for it.

units.la: At Mosis institutū quomodo probet Deus vt cognoscamus, sic erit exiftimandū. 1. Quae Moses ad populum de morte sua dixerat, ea Dominus hic affirmat esse vera: sed sic, vt consolationem & salutis spem iuxta ponat. Nam qui prius dixit, morieris: idem nunc dicit dormies. Ergo mors est somnus è quo expergiscimur. Et quidem dormies cum patribus Abraham, Isaac, Iacob: quorum antea se Deum esse dixerat, vt viuentium: cum ijs igitur dormies quibus Deus est salus ac vita. Sic Iob, Scio Deum meum viuere: sic Christus de Lazari somno dixit apostolis: sic Paulus omnium resurrectionem probat 1. Theff. 4. & 1. Cor. 15. Eodem modo Mosem Deus monet primum: sed deinceps eundem hoc ipso rursus consolatur, quod mortem somnum appellat: innueas[?] vt è somno euigilamus, sic resurgamus à morte.
units.tr: But how God confirms the institution of Moses, so that we may know it, is to be considered thus. (1) What Moses had said to the people about his death, the Lord here affirms to be true; but he sets consolation and the hope of salvation alongside it. For he who first said you will die now says you will sleep. Death, therefore, is a sleep from which we awake. And indeed, you will sleep with the fathers, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, of whom he had earlier said that he was God, as of the living: so you will sleep with those for whom God is salvation and life. So Job: I know that my Redeemer lives; so Christ spoke to the apostles of Lazarus' sleep; so Paul proves the resurrection of all, 1 Thess. 4 and 1 Cor. 15. In the same way God first warns Moses, but afterwards comforts him again in this very thing, by calling death a sleep, signifying that as we awake from sleep, so we rise from death.

units.la: 2. Quae Moses de Iosua atq; Leuitis dixerat, vt approbet Dominus, fata populi illius ca-nit, eoq; docet nimirum illis opus esse duobus his ordinibus: quando saturati bonis sunt su-turi petulantes, defer-turi[?] Deum, deos alienos secuturi. Vnde malorum omne genus: ab scondet Deus faciem ab eis suam, perdet, &c. In quo duæ sunt causæ requirentes hos ordines. Vnà, petulantia: quæ & doctrina, & legibus, & supplicijs est coercenda. Altera, afflictio, in qua non modo consolatione, sed etiam consilijs & defensione est opus ciuitati. Igitur canticum ceu re medium præbet.
units.tr: 2. What Moses had said about Joshua and the Levites, so that the Lord may confirm it, he sings of the fates of that people; and he teaches, of course, that there is need of these two orders: when they are satisfied with good things they will grow wanton, they will forsake God and follow strange gods. Hence every kind of evil: God will hide his face from them, will destroy them, etc. In this there are two causes that call for these orders. One is wantonness, which must be restrained by doctrine, by laws and by punishments. The other is affliction, in which the commonwealth needs not only consolation but also counsel and defence. Therefore the song provides a remedy for both.

units.la: In quo videmus: 1. Malis desperationem & exitium potius ex saturitate, quàm penuria prouenire: & familiare esse, vt domus Domini maximis abutantur. Honos, opes, forma, robur, & his similia bona sunt egregia: sed proh Deum quam his abutimur? Ergo his carere non quantum putas malum.
units.tr: In this we see: first, that despair and ruin come to the wicked from abundance rather than from want, and that it is commonplace for men to abuse the gifts of the Lord's house in the greatest measure. Honour, riches, beauty, strength and similar goods are excellent; but, good God, how we abuse them! So to lack these is not as great an evil as you think.

units.la: Dein, omnium pessimum est Deum deserere: veluti fit simpliciter, sequendo alios, illegitimo cultu. Summa opus est vt nostra petulantia cum verbo coerceatur, tum legibus: cumque Deus det vtrumque, illis obsequamur. Amen.
units.tr: Next, the worst of all things is to desert God, as happens plainly when men follow others in illegitimate worship. There is great need, then, that our wantonness be restrained both by the word and by the laws; and since God gives both, let us obey them. Amen.

units.la: SERMO VIII.
units.tr: SERMON VIII.

units.la: 22 Scripsit igitur Moses canticum istud eadem die, & docuit ipsum filios Israel.
units.tr: 22 Moses therefore wrote this song the same day, and taught it to the children of Israel.

units.la: 23 Præcepit q; Iosuæ filio Nun dicens: Corroborare, & esto robustus, quoniam tu introduces filios Israel in terram, quam iuraui eis, & ego ero tecum.
units.tr: 23 He also charged Joshua the son of Nun, saying: Be strong, and of good courage, for thou shalt bring the children of Israel into the land which I sware unto them, and I will be with thee.

units.la: 24 Factumq; est vt cessasset Moses scribere verba legis huius in libro, & consummasset ea.
units.tr: 24 And it came to pass, when Moses had made an end of writing the words of this law in a book, until they were finished,

units.la: 25 Præcepit Moses Leuitis portantibus arcam fœderis Domini, dicens:
units.tr: 25 that Moses commanded the Levites who bare the ark of the covenant of the LORD, saying:

units.la: 26 Accipite librum legis huius, & reponite eum in latere arcæ fœderis Domini Dei vestri, vt sit tibi contra te in testimonium.
units.tr: 26 Take this book of the law, and put it in the side of the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God, that it may be there for a witness against thee.

units.la: 27 Ego enim noui rebellionem tuam, & ceruicem tuam præfractam: etenim etiam num hodie cum adhuc sum vobiscum viuens, estis rebelles Domino, quanto ergo magis post mortem meam?
units.tr: 27 For I know thy rebellion, and thy stiff neck: behold, while I am yet alive with you this day, ye have been rebellious against the LORD; and how much more after my death?

units.la: 28 Congregate ad me omnes seniores tribuum vestrarum, & præfectos vestros, vt loquar in auribus eorum verba ista, & obtestler aduersum eos cœlum & terram.
units.tr: 28 Gather unto me all the elders of your tribes, and your officers, that I may speak these words in their ears, and call heaven and earth to record against them.

units.la: 29 Noui enim quod post mortem meam certissimè perperam agetis, & deficietis de via, quam præcepi vobis, occurretq; vobis tandem malum, quoniam perperam agetis in oculis Domini, vt prouocetis eum per opus manus vestræ.
units.tr: 29 For I know that after my death ye will utterly corrupt yourselves, and turn aside from the way which I have commanded you; and evil will befall you in the latter days, because ye will do evil in the sight of the LORD, to provoke him to anger through the work of your hands.

units.la: 30 Loquutusq; est Moses in auribus totius cœtus Israelitici verba cantici huius, donec complesset ea.
units.tr: 30 And Moses spake in the ears of all the congregation of Israel the words of this song, until they were ended.

units.la: EX ijs, quæ sunt ad huius cap. expositionem hactenus allata, facilè perspici potuit, ad cuiusq; ciuitatis salutem atq; incolumitatem conseruandam præcipuè requiri, vt in ea sint qui populum quid facto opus sit admoneant, quiq; illi quid quenque deceat exponant: tum qui sui officij bene admonitos in eo quod cuiusq; est proprium officio contineant. Iam quoniam homines suapte sic sunt omnes comparati natura, imperare vt malint, quàm parere imperio: minimeq; velint ijs parere, quibus aut se pares esse existimant, aut certè etiam superiores: vnde & difficillima quædam res existit imperare: sanè qui vel doctrina vel imperio præesse debent, ij diuinum quiddam penes se habeant necesse est: cuius ipsi ductu gerant omnia, cuiusq; reuerentia populus adductus eis obediat. Quemadmodum enim nec ipsis populi ducibus sine præscripta, quam sequantur, regula tanta potestas tutò credi potest: sic nec illis populus separatim atq; extra hanc aliquid præcipientibus obsequetur.
units.tr: From what has been brought forward so far in the exposition of this chapter, it can easily be seen that for the safety and preservation of every commonwealth it is chiefly required that there be in it those who admonish the people as to what needs to be done and who set out for each person what befits him, and then those who keep those well admonished to the duty that belongs to each one's office. Now since all men are by nature so constituted that they prefer to command rather than to obey, and least of all wish to obey those whom they think to be either their equals or indeed their superiors, hence even commanding is a very difficult matter. Certainly those who ought to preside over teaching or command must necessarily have something divine in them, by whose guidance they conduct everything, and through reverence for which the people, drawn along, obey them. For just as not even the leaders of the people can safely be entrusted with such power without a prescribed rule which they follow, so the people will not obey them if they give orders apart from and outside this rule.

units.la: Qua de causa Moses Dei mandato Iosuam & Leuitas verbo Dei instruit: qua armati ipsi dextrè fungantur officijs, populus autem ceu præsenti motus numine libentius obediat.
units.tr: For this reason Moses, by God's command, instructs Joshua and the Levites in the word of God, so that, armed with it, they may discharge their offices rightly, while the people, as if moved by a present divinity, may obey more willingly.

units.la: Quod quidem ita fit, vt 1. Moses scribat & doceat canticum: 2. Iosuæ demandet imperium: 3. Leuitis committat legem.
units.tr: This is done so that: (1) Moses writes and teaches the song; (2) he commits the command to Joshua; (3) he entrusts the law to the Levites.

units.la: Canticum Moses ad hunc modum dicitur & scripsisse & docuisse. Scripsit itaq; Moses canticum eadem die, & docuit ipsum populum. In quo res & persona considerari possunt. Res quæ scribitur est verbum Domini, forma cantici descriptum atque propositum: persona scribens ac docens Moses est. Iam quod verbum Domini ceu remedium rebellioni & ingratitudini præbitum voluit scripto comprehendi: id indicio est Deum nos religionis, probitatis, officij non nostro, sed suo ipsius modo admoneri velle: quo ipso traditiones & opiniones hominum repellit & impatientes disciplinæ reprehendit. Verbum Domini plenum & perfectum est, pro pterea; nihil ei debet addi, nihil ite detrahi. Mat.15.Esa.29.supra12. Multo minus torquendum est atq; accommodandum nostris affectibus: vt suam auarus eo ipso tueri velit auaritiam, suam prodigus luxuriam, alius alia vitia. Igitur vt prudens princeps quàm minimum arbitrio iudicis permittit : verum eos vult expresso verbo stare, & secundum ius scriptum iudicare : sic Deus res religionis suo verbo mauult, quàm humana opinione censeri.
units.tr: The song is said to have been both written and taught by Moses in this way. Moses therefore wrote the song the same day and taught it to the people. In this, the matter and the person may be considered. The matter that is written is the word of the Lord, set down and presented in the form of a song; the person writing and teaching is Moses. Now, that he wished the word of the Lord, offered as a remedy for rebellion and ingratitude, to be committed to writing is a sign that God wishes to admonish us about religion, uprightness and duty not in our own way but in his own; by this very fact he rejects the traditions and opinions of men and rebukes those impatient of discipline. The word of the Lord is full and perfect; therefore nothing ought to be added to it, nothing taken away. Matt. 15. Isa. 29. Above 12. Much less is it to be twisted and adapted to our desires, so that the greedy man wishes by that very means to defend his greed, the prodigal his luxury, another his other vices. Therefore, just as a prudent prince leaves as little as possible to the judge's discretion, but wants them to abide by the express word and to judge according to the written law, so God prefers that matters of religion be judged by his word rather than by human opinion.

units.la: Persona autem Moses est, qui in tam proue&a ætate, vt ix o. annorum adeò laboriosus est, vt scribendo se & docendo exerceat. Quod est exemplum industriæ quæ laudabilis est in omnibus quidem hominibus in primisq; viris principibus. Industriæ & vigilantiæ exempla habemus Dauidem qui vacans à negotijs publicis Psalmos meditabatur: Salomonem, qui belli gerando, ædificando, ius dicendo, philosophando & commentando operam dabat: quorum tamen singulorum studium singulis satis graue existit. Et Ionathas ille 1. Machab. 12. suis hominibus vigilias & vt essent mane comparati ad prelium mandauit. Christus Matth. 26. suis dicit: Vigilate & orate. Sifara dormiens opprimitur. Iud. 5. Holophernes somno vinoq; sepultus obtruncatur, Iudith. 13.
units.tr: Moses, moreover, is the person who, at such an advanced age (a hundred and twenty years), was so hardworking that he kept himself busy with writing and teaching. This is an example of diligence, which is praiseworthy in all men, and especially in men who are princes. We have examples of diligence and vigilance in David, who, free from public business, meditated on the Psalms; and in Solomon, who devoted himself to waging war, building, dispensing justice, philosophising and commenting; yet the zeal of each of these would be enough for any one man. And Jonathan, in 1 Maccabees 12, commanded his men to keep watch and to be ready for battle in the morning. Christ says to his disciples in Matt. 26: Watch and pray. Sisera is overcome while sleeping (Judg. 5). Holofernes, buried in sleep and wine, is beheaded (Judith 13).

units.la: Sunt vtriusq; rei in gentibus exempla plurima: vt Catonis qui 86. ætatis annum agens firmus vt esset adhuc effecit labore & industria: tum penè senex Latinas, iam senex Græcas li teras & ius ciuile didicit. Liuius Drufus & senex & cæcus ius ciuile populo explanauit. Sunt exempla Pythagoræ, Chrysippi, Cleanthis, Demosthenis, Isocratis, Sophoclis, Simonidis.
units.tr: There are very many examples of both things among the nations: Cato, who at the age of eighty-six, by labour and diligence, kept himself still strong; and who, nearly an old man, learned Latin literature, and, already old, Greek literature and civil law. Livius Drusus, both old and blind, explained civil law to the people. There are examples in Pythagoras, Chrysippus, Cleanthes, Demosthenes, Isocrates, Sophocles and Simonides.

units.la: Exhortantur nos ad laborem ipsæ etiam sacræ literæ. Propter frigus piger arare noluit, mendicabit igitur æstate & non dabitur ei. Exemplo sunt locusta & formica. Iuueni laboran-dum est senex vt habeat, aut si minus habeat laboribus saltem assueuerit. Sed in religionis & Dei negocio cumprimis est adhibenda fides & diligentia. Vt Hier. 28. Maledi&us qui opus Dei facit negligenter. Contra laudem feret & præmiū quisquis fuerit impiger & industrius.
units.tr: The Holy Scriptures themselves also exhort us to labour. "The sluggard will not plough by reason of the cold; therefore shall he beg in harvest, and have nothing" (Prov. 20). The locust and the ant are examples. A young man must labour so that he may have something when he is old, or at least, if he does not have it, he will have become accustomed to labour. But in the business of religion and of God above all, faith and diligence must be applied. Hier. 28: Cursed is he that doeth the work of the LORD negligently. On the contrary, whoever is diligent and industrious will receive praise and reward.

units.la: Iosuæ mandatur imperium: Præcepitq;, inquit, Iehosua filio Nun dicens corroborare, &c. Quibus verbis sic illi committit imperium, vt & qualem velit esse magistratum, & qua ratione talis efficiatur monstret. Vult esse fortem: quid enim princeps ignauus & stolidus efficiat? Exemplo sunt Achab, qui imperij habenas permittebat mulieri: itè Balthassar ebrius & Paris adulter. Fortibus, prouidis, impigris principibus auctà sunt Lacedæmonum, Macedonum, Romanorum, Heluetiorum aliaq; imperia: at ignauia, ambitione, auaritia cum hæc ipsa, tum alia pereunt. Igitur magistratus pij, gnaui, prouidi sunto.
units.tr: The command to Joshua is given: He charged him, he says, Joshua the son of Nun, saying, Be strong, etc. By these words he commits the command to him in such a way that he both shows what kind of magistrate he wishes him to be and by what means such a one is made. He wishes him to be strong; for what would an idle and foolish prince accomplish? Examples are Ahab, who handed the reins of power to a woman; likewise Belshazzar, drunk, and Paris, an adulterer. By strong, prudent and diligent princes the empires of the Lacedaemonians, the Macedonians, the Romans, the Swiss and others were increased; but through idleness, ambition and avarice, these and other empires perish. Therefore let magistrates be pious, watchful and prudent.

units.la: Necessarium hoc est: sed quibus rationibus efficitur? Neq; enim cuiuis contingit adire Corinthum. Rationes affert. 1. Officij conscientia: vt scias, cogites, memineris te mandatum deducendi populum habere. Tu, inquit, introduces in terram. Et id addit animum. Veluti si in vinea sui domini laboret seruus non est quod quicquam metuat: sin ea neglecta genio indul-ferit, sibi timeat necesse est. In dicenda sententia, si ius respicias timebis neminem: & si enim re oderit aliquis, non id audebit profiteri nisi illum non pudeat ipsum etiam ius odisse. Sic si religionem, bonas leges, ius, innocentiä, bona pupillorum atq; pauperum tueare: neminé me-tuis: sin à religione, legibus, iure declines: pauperû bona tibi rapias, tunc time: & si enim homines parcant tamé id deus nö patietur impune te auferre. Is enim pijs fauet, impios psequitur.
units.tr: This is necessary; but by what reasons is it brought about? For it is not granted to everyone to go to Corinth. He gives reasons. (1) The consciousness of office: that you know, think about and remember that you have the commission of leading the people. "Thou shalt bring them," he says, "into the land." And he adds courage. If a servant labours in his master's vineyard, he has nothing to fear; but if he neglects it and gives himself over to pleasure, he must fear for himself. In giving your opinion, if you have regard to justice, you will fear no one; for even if someone hates it, he will not dare to profess this unless he is not ashamed to hate justice itself too. So if you protect religion, good laws, justice, innocence, and the goods of orphans and the poor, you need fear no one; but if you turn aside from religion, laws and justice, and seize the goods of the poor for yourself, then be afraid; for even if men spare you, God will not allow you to take them away with impunity. For he favours the godly and pursues the impious.

units.la: 2. Ego ero tecum. Auxilio Domini quod ille suis ministris semper præbuit, efficitur, vt magistratus fit fortis & prouidus. Adest enim res suas gerentibus tanquam socius, vt Iacobo in Mesopotamia, Josepho in Ægypto, Dauidi in exilio, Danielis socijs, apostolis, nobis. Vnde & Christus apostolos hoc ipso consolatur quod se dicit eis affore vsq; ad sine mundi, quodq; dicit non ipsos oratores, sed spiritum sanctum eius, quam sint acturi, causæ patronum fore. Ab homine quidem hæc præstari non possunt, ope Dei promoueantur necesse est.
units.tr: 2. "I will be with thee." By the help of the Lord, which he has always given to his ministers, it comes about that the magistrate becomes strong and prudent. For he is present with those who carry out their affairs, as a companion: as to Jacob in Mesopotamia, to Joseph in Egypt, to David in exile, to Daniel's companions, to the apostles, and to us. Hence Christ also consoles the apostles with this very thing, that he says he will be with them until the end of the world; and he says that it will not be they themselves who speak, but his Holy Spirit who will be the advocate of the cause they are about to plead. These things cannot be performed by man; they must be advanced by the help of God.

units.la: Leuitis datur lex asseruanda, ac ne sua nihil referre populus existimet, etiam is ipse eam ad rem aduocatur. Leuitis præcipitur vt acceptam arca fœderis, qua decem legum tabulæ & virga Aaronis & Manna conseruabantur, conderent.
units.tr: The Levites are given the law to keep, and so that the people may not think it has nothing to do with them, the people too is called in to witness this very matter. The Levites are commanded to take the book of the covenant and place it beside the ark, where the two tablets of the ten laws, the rod of Aaron and the manna were kept.

units.la: In quo videmus Dominum voluisse: 1. Leuitis sacrosanctum esse & augustum verbum Domini, <bl>heiligthumb.</bl> Quod non ceu prophanum quiddam esset sic habere tur: Quid enim de ea reliquum vulgus sentiat si custodes ipsius eam negligant?
units.tr: In this we see that the Lord wished the following: (1) that the holy and august word of the Lord should be sacred to the Levites. It was not to be handled as though it were some common thing. For what would the ordinary people think of it if its own guardians neglected it?

units.la: 2. Coniunctà esse cum lege eius explicationem. Hic enim liber erat legis explicatio: decalogus ipsa lex: ambo vult in arca reponi, decalogum videlicet vt legem, & Deuteronomiû, vt eius interpretationé. Errant igitur qui relicto textu glossas, ac rursus qui interpretatione pia posthabita legem nudam suis scilicet ipsorum affectibus permissam volunt. Et legi vult Dominus, & accommodari personis, locis, temporibus. Exemplo sunt Esdras, Christus, apostoli.
units.tr: (2) That an explanation should be joined to his law. For this book was an explanation of the law: the Decalogue was the law itself. He wanted both placed in the ark, namely the Decalogue as the law and Deuteronomy as its interpretation. Those therefore err who, abandoning the text, follow glosses, and likewise those who, setting aside pious interpretation, want the bare law left to their own inclinations. The Lord wants the law both to be read and to be adapted to persons, places and times. Ezra, Christ and the apostles are examples of this.

units.la: 3. Ipsius legis custodes esse Leuitas: ne discedant ab ea, nec cui prophanandam permit-tant eam, Neq; enim par est, vt quod suum non est mundo permittant. Ciuilibus in rebus li-cet, in diuinis minimè. Sed & populus, vt dictum est, aduocatur, admonetur rebellionis futurę. Quod indicio est quomodo verbo Dei castigandi simus. Qua disciplina semper aliqui meliores aut nitio- res fiunt. At non omnes? quid tum? illis in testimonium dicitur Matth. 10. & Act. 19.
units.tr: (3) That the Levites are the guardians of the law itself, so that they do not depart from it, nor allow it to be profaned by anyone; for it is not fitting that they should hand over to the world what is not their own. In civil matters this is allowed, but in divine matters not at all. But the people too, as has been said, is called in and warned of the rebellion to come. This is evidence of how we ought to be chastised by the word of God. By this discipline some are always made better or more attentive. But not all? What of it? Matthew 10 and Acts 19 are cited as witness to this.

units.la: Ex quibus quoniam intelligimus nostra referre, vt habeamus hos ordines, & eos quidem instructos lege Domini: legem quidem ipsam fide vera amplectamur: ipsos autem ea, quam lex præscripserit, via ducentes sequamur, nempe vt ad Deum peruenianus [?], per Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum. Amen.
units.tr: Since from these things we understand that it matters to us that we have these orders, and indeed instructed by the law of the Lord, let us embrace the law itself with true faith, and let us follow those who lead by the way which the law prescribes, so that we may come to God through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT XXXII. SERMO IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER 32. SERMON 9.

units.la: Audite cœli, nam loquar, audiatq; terra verba oris mei.
units.tr: Hear, O heavens, and I will speak; and let the earth hear the words of my mouth.

units.la: 2 Stillabit veluti pluvia doctrina mea, fluet vt ros eloquium meum, sicut im-ber pluvius super herbam, & sicut stillæ super plantulas.
units.tr: My doctrine shall drop as the rain, my speech shall distil as the dew, as the small rain upon the tender herb, and as the showers upon the grass.

units.la: 3 Quoniam invocabo nomen Domini, tribuite magnificentiam Deo nostro.
units.tr: Because I will publish the name of the LORD: ascribe ye greatness unto our God.

units.la: N principio conclusionis huius libri demonstratum est Mosem non solù quæcun- que ad legis explicationem attulerat repetere, sed & populum ad eius studium atque vsum incitare velle: qua de causa agere testamenti modo omnia: nepe, vt quem admodum testamenti institutio & vltimæ voluntatis expositio admonitione mor tis, & quod parentum atq; amicorum consuetudine sentiscimus nos priuatum iri, lugubris est & hominis animum multum mouet: sic populus Israel commemoratione voluntatis vlti- mæ & rerum omnium ordinatione per Mosem facta moueri potuit, vt omnis doctrinæ Mo- saicæ tanto magis memor esset & studiosior. Ac quanquam hæc omnia ijs quidem qui tunc vi-vebant sufficerent, nec pluribus verbis opus esset: tamen vt & eius temporis hominibus plus satis, & posteris satis ad salutem auxilij præberetur: hoc capite etiam carmen eandem ad rem faciens mandato Dei præscribitur & prælegitur, nempe vt eo ipso cum præsentium tum posterorum omnium animi permouerentur.
units.tr: At the beginning of the conclusion of this book it was shown that Moses wished not only to repeat whatever he had brought forward to explain the law, but also to stir the people to its study and use. For this reason he does all things in the manner of a testament. Just as the making of a will and the explanation of a person's last wishes, which remind us of death and of the loss of parents and friends that we feel, are sad and greatly move a man's mind, so the people of Israel could be moved by the recollection of Moses' last will and by the orderly arrangement of all things, so that they would be all the more mindful and eager for the whole Mosaic doctrine. And although all these things would have been enough for those who then lived, and no more words were needed, yet, so that help for salvation would be given both to the people of that time, more than enough, and to posterity, sufficiently, a song serving the same purpose is prescribed and read aloud in this chapter by God's command, so that by this very means the minds of both those present and all those to come might be moved.

units.la: Carmina enim, quoniam & accurata vocum atq; syllabarum collocatione & numeris:tum figuris atq; similibus, ipsa deniq; res proponendi & pertractandi ratione rara, augusta peneq; diuina maiestatis nescio quid habent, animos hominum in primis percellunt: eoq; si vox ipsa modo leuata, modo depressa, modo ad luctum, modo ad lætitiam facta permultum momenti potest afferre. Vnde & in rerum ciuilium vsu, ad imitationem virtutis auitæ posteri carminibus, vt olim in Græcia, nunc in his terris excitari consueuere: & in religione Psalmis atque Hymnis mentes permotæ sunt.
units.tr: For songs, since both their carefully arranged words and syllables and their rhythms, and also their figures and similar devices, and finally their unusual method of setting forth and treating the subject, have something of the august and almost divine majesty, strike the minds of men above all. And if the voice itself is raised at one moment, lowered at another, and made to express grief or joy, it can have very great effect. Hence also in the practice of civil affairs, posterity has been wont to be stirred by songs to imitate ancestral virtue, as formerly in Greece and now in these lands; and in religion minds have been moved by Psalms and Hymns.

units.la: Ea ipsa ratione Moses, vt populum permoueret, carmen scribit, & recitat: in quo & au-thor & argumentum, & dispositio considerari debent. Author est & impulsor qui supra præ-ceed. cap. monstratur Deus: is prævidens populi illius inconstantiam, quodq; abs atq; ab hac disciplina tota defecturus esset, eoq; sese iturus perditum: tanti mali avertendi studio carme hoc componi iussit, eoq; voluit illos in officio retinere? Ex quo perspicimus etiam finem, salutem humani generis videlicet. O bonum patrem, qui illam quoquomodo potest curat: lege naturæ, verbo, typis, sacramentis, artibus aliis atq; aliis.
units.tr: For this very reason Moses writes and recites a song to move the people, and in it both the author, the subject and the arrangement must be considered. The author and mover is God, who is shown above in the preceding chapter: foreseeing the inconstancy of that people, and that they would fall away from this whole discipline and go to their ruin, he ordered this song to be composed with the aim of averting so great an evil, and so wished to keep them in their duty. From this we also perceive the end, namely the salvation of the human race. O good Father, who cares for it in whatever way he can: by the law of nature, by the Word, by types, by sacraments, by other and other arts.

units.la: Iam vt de carminis argumento dicatur: exponitur natura Dei, cumq; ea populi illius in-genium comparatur: tum Dei in illam gentè beneficia recensentur. Ac deinceps cum ijs populi peccata conferuntur. Deniq; Domini de ea re profertur atq; exponitur iudicium.
units.tr: Now, to say something of the subject of the song: the nature of God is set forth, and the character of that people is compared with it; then the benefits of God toward that nation are recounted. And next the sins of the people are set alongside these. Finally the judgment of the Lord on this matter is brought forward and explained.

units.la: Unde colligi potest quanta sit huius carminis utilitas. Naturarum diuinæ & humanæ notitia est utilissima: & est summa sapientia se, ipsum simul ac Deum nosse. Huc omnis philosophia, huc lex & prophetæ, huc ipsum etiam tendit euangelium: te esse caducum, impurum, mise-rum: Deum æternum, sanctum, beatum: per solum Christum ad ipsum Deum iter esse. Dei beneficiorum & nostrorum in illorum peccatorum comparatio est utilis: sic enim agnoscitur peccati magnitudo, nempe quod sit ingratitudo. Iudicium Domini utile est scire, ut terreat malos, soleturbonos [?]. Ergo omnes populi carmen hoc sciant operæprecium est.
units.tr: From this it can be gathered how great the usefulness of this song is. The knowledge of the divine and human natures is most useful, and it is the highest wisdom to know oneself together with God. To this all philosophy tends, to this the law and the prophets, to this the gospel itself also tends: that you are frail, impure, wretched; that God is eternal, holy, blessed; and that the way to God himself is through Christ alone. A comparison of God's benefits with our sins is useful, for thus the greatness of sin is recognised, namely that it is ingratitude. It is useful to know the judgment of the Lord, so that it terrifies the wicked and comforts the good. Therefore it is worth the effort for all peoples to know this song.

units.la: Sed ad eius cognitionem vt nos Moses promoueat, bona ac facili methodo progreditur. Habet exordium, propositionem, expositionem, conclusionem. Exordium ducit ab attentio-ne & beneuolentia, quando inuocans elementa mouet & attentos facit: tum vtilitatem carminis explanat. Propositione summam comprehendit inuocandum & honorandum Dominum. Expositio habet comparationem quam diximus nostrarum, itemq; beneficiorum: deniq; & iudicij. Conclusio ad principium redit.
units.tr: But so that Moses may lead us to its knowledge, he proceeds by a good and easy method. He has an exordium, a proposition, an exposition and a conclusion. The exordium begins from attention and goodwill, when, by calling upon heaven and earth, he moves his hearers and makes them attentive; then he explains the usefulness of the song. In the proposition he comprehends the sum: that the Lord is to be invoked and honoured. The exposition contains the comparison, which we mentioned, of our own conduct and of the benefits, and finally of the judgment. The conclusion returns to the beginning.

units.la: Exordium sic habet: Audite cœli nam loquar, &c. Quibus verbis illos & attentos & benevolos sibi facit. Attentos hoc ipso, quòd cœlum ac terram quasi testes suis verbis accersit, ac dicit: Audite cœli nam loquar, etc. Ac cœli terræq; nomine comprehendit & vniuersum orbem, & quæ in eo sunt omnia. Terra enim punctum est orbis medium, quam habitant animalia rationæ prædita pariter & destituta: qua proueniunt bona malaq; hominibus. Cœlum autem & superior est mundus, in quo sunt astra & reliqua corpora cœlestia.
units.tr: The exordium runs thus: Hear, O heavens, for I will speak, etc. By these words he makes them both attentive and well-disposed to himself. He makes them attentive by this very fact, that he summons heaven and earth as witnesses to his words, saying: Hear, O heavens, for I will speak, etc. And by the name of heaven and earth he comprehends both the whole world and all that is in it. For the earth is the central point of the world, which is inhabited by animals endowed with reason and also by those without it, and which brings forth good and evil things for men. But heaven is the higher world, in which are the stars and the other heavenly bodies.

units.la: Hæc omnia ad dicendum testimonium citat. Vult audiri ab his illa verba & iudicia: quòd modò audient? an habeant aures? quomodò dicent? an habent os & linguam? [?] hæc dicuntur omnia. Actūrus aliquid de quo constet postea: testes qui videant audiantq; hæc adhibes: illos vt memineris obtestaris: eos cum vsus est, vt dicant titas. Sic Deus aperte, publicè, quasiq; in aprico nobiscum, vt negare non possis agit.
units.tr: He cites all these to bear witness to what he is going to say. He wants these words and judgments to be heard by them. What will they hear? Have they ears? How will they speak? Do they have a mouth and a tongue? [Such questions] are all said. When he is about to say something that will be established afterwards, he calls in witnesses who see and hear these things, and he solemnly charges them to remember, and when it is needed, to speak out. So God acts openly, publicly, and as if in the open air with us, so that you cannot deny it.

units.la: Atq; hæc externis sensibus expositæ mundi corpora siue quid secundum naturam pariant, si quid accidat eis præter naturam, docent tamen & solantur & minantur: vt annuæ vicissitudines, & grandines & pruinæ, & cometæ, &c.
units.tr: Moreover, the bodies of the world, set out to our outward senses, whether they produce something according to nature or whether something happens to them beyond nature, nevertheless teach, comfort and threaten: such as the yearly changes of the seasons, hailstorms and frosts, comets, and so on.

units.la: Quomodo testantur? cum iræ & vindictæ Dei sunt instrumenta pariter & præsagia. Vt diluuium, cœlum ferreum Heliæ tempore, frigora, terræmotus. Miracula circa mortem Christi facta: fulmen episcopum calcante segetes vicíscens. Quando enim quæ profuerant antea post nocent pluuiæ: sanè sunt accusatrices ingratitudinis humanæ. Vnde & Esa. 1. Hierem. 6: vocantur in testimonium. Hoc facit attentos: magnum enim quiddam videtur dicturus esse qui tam graviter obtestatur. Vt Iob de resurrectione dissertur us petens tabula quæ diceret describi verba. Et Christus maius quiddam dicturus clamat: qui habet aures ad audiendum audiat. Quod si tanta gravitate proponitur: quanto audietur maiore verbum Domini? Exempla sunt diligentium auditorum regina Saba, turbæ Christum sequentes, &c.
units.tr: How do they bear witness? When they are at once instruments and omens of God's wrath and vengeance: as the flood; the iron heaven in the time of Elijah; frosts; earthquakes; the miracles done at the death of Christ; lightning striking a bishop who trampled the crops. For when rains which before had been of benefit afterwards do harm, they are surely accusers of human ingratitude. Hence they are also called as witnesses in Isa. 1 and Jer. 6. This makes the hearers attentive: for he who solemnly calls witnesses seems about to say something great. So Job, speaking of the resurrection, asked for a tablet on which the words might be written. And Christ, about to say something greater, cries out: he who has ears to hear, let him hear. But if it is proposed with such gravity, with how much greater attention will the word of the Lord be heard? Examples of diligent hearers are the queen of Sheba, the crowds following Christ, and so on.

units.la: Iam verò beneuolum facit dicens: Stillabit veluti pluuia doctrina mea, fluet vt ros eloquium meum: sicut imber pluuius super herbas & sicut stillæ super plantulas. Quo docet ipsius doctrinâ, siquidem accipiatur vtilissimam pariter ac salubèrrimam fore. Idq; exponit rebus externis, pluuia scilicet & rore. Rigant, humectant ac quasi vegetantè vim creatis rebus subministrant: sic verbum diuinum mentes serpentis venenati morsu æstuantes refrigerat, rigat, ijsq; vt crescant omni in opere bono vim vegetantem subministrat. Vt Psa. 1. Arbor ad flumen plantata. 1. Cor. 3. Ego plantaui, Apollo rigauit. Et Christus verbi ministerium cum agricultura comparat: vt Matth. 13. Semente, zizania, Ioh. 6. Messe. Ioh. 15. Vite. Iam & doctrina comparatur nubi: Nubes est inanis & non statim defluit & obscurat lumen solis, seu nos eius aspectu priuat. Sic nubes inanis est humana philosophia: grauida vero diuina. Fructus diuinæ est fruges producere: lapides ex ea nihil habent nisi quod excauentur potius: vt sunt lapides gentes. At arbor bona, terra bona, herbæ crescunt ex hac pluuia. Sic est vtile verbum Domini si non cadat in silices aut pumices. Exempla habemus domestica. Satis hoc docet quid de eo sit statuendum.
units.tr: Now indeed he makes them well-disposed by saying: My doctrine shall drop as the rain, my speech shall distil as the dew: as the small rain upon the herbs, and as the showers upon the tender plants. By this he teaches that his doctrine, if it is received, will be most useful and most healthful. And he explains this by outward things, namely rain and dew. They water, moisten and, as it were, impart life-giving power to created things; so the divine word cools the minds burning with the bite of the venomous serpent, waters them, and supplies them with a growing power so that they may increase in every good work. Compare Ps. 1: a tree planted by the river; 1 Cor. 3: I planted, Apollos watered. And Christ compares the ministry of the Word with agriculture: Matt. 13, the seed and the tares; John 6, the harvest; John 15, the vine. Doctrine is also compared to a cloud: a cloud is empty and does not at once pour down, and it darkens the light of the sun, or deprives us of its sight. So human philosophy is an empty cloud, but the divine is heavy with rain. It is the nature of divine doctrine to produce fruits; stones from it have nothing but to be hollowed out, as the Gentiles are stones. But a good tree, good earth, and grass grow from this rain. So the word of the Lord is useful, provided it does not fall on flint or pumice. We have examples close to home. This sufficiently teaches what is to be concluded about it.

units.la: Propositio sic habet. Quoniam invocabo nomen Domini: tribuite magnificentiam Deo nostro. Id est, canam de colendo & adorando Deo Opt. Max. ac docebo illum vnum summum in animis nostris locum obtinere oportere.
units.tr: The proposition runs thus: "Since I will call upon the name of the LORD, ascribe greatness to our God." That is, I will sing of worshipping and adoring God, the best and greatest, and I will teach that he alone ought to hold the highest place in our minds.

units.la: Nomen Dei, id est, quod de eo solet ac potest dici: vt misericordia, sapientia, iustitia, veritas, potentia, &c.
units.tr: The name of God means what can and is usually said of him: for example, mercy, wisdom, justice, truth, power, and so on.

units.la: Invocare eum est omnem illi honorem deferre, ab eo quicquid velis petere, ab illo solo pendere illum vnum reuereri. Ergo si quid petas ab illo roges: si peccatum allubescat, illum reuererc: si tibi nimiū placeas, illius in conspectu pudeat te faxis. Magnificentiam ei tribues, si nemini plus tribues, quàm illi. Atq; in his quicquid ad verbi diuini studium pertinet, attentionem, benevolentiam, orationem habemus. Id omne est patri Deo offerendum, per Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum, Amen.
units.tr: To call upon him is to render him all honour, to seek from him whatever you wish, and to revere him alone as the one on whom everything depends. Therefore, if you seek anything, ask it of him; if sin tempts you, reverence him; if you are too pleased with yourself, be ashamed in his sight. You ascribe greatness to him if you ascribe more to no one than to him. And in these matters we have whatever pertains to the study of the divine Word: attention, goodwill, and prayer. All of this is to be offered to God the Father, through Jesus Christ our Lord, Amen.

units.la: SERMO X.
units.tr: SERMON X.

units.la: 4 Opus petræ illius solidum est, quoniam omnes viæ eius sunt iudicium, Deus verax, absq; vanitate, iustus & rectus est.
units.tr: 4 The work of that Rock is perfect, for all his ways are judgment: a God of truth without iniquity, just and right is he.

units.la: 5 Peruersa hæc & detorta generatio corrupit sibi, non filij eius in maculis suis.
units.tr: 5 They have corrupted themselves; their spot is not the spot of his children: they are a perverse and crooked generation.

units.la: 6 Hoccine rependitis Domino? stulte populè & non sapiens: annon ipse est pater tuus qui te comparauit? qui te fecit? quiq; te firmauit?
units.tr: 6 Do you thus requite the LORD, O foolish people and unwise? Is not he your father that hath bought you? hath he not made you, and established you?

units.la: EXpositis iam huius cantici duabus partibus, quibus & in eam ipsam, quam agit causam Moses, introducit, & ipsius rei summam ac caput ponit: reliquum est, vt ad tertiam ve-niamus: qua veluti nuper dictum est, tria potissimum agit. Primum Dei naturam atq; mores cum ingenio nostro confert: dein Dei in populum suum benefactum cum ipsius populi scele-ratis rebus gestis comparat: postremò Dei de nostra natura atque moribus iudicium tradit. Quæ res & utiles sunt consideratu & cognitu necessariæ, vti suo loco dicetur.
units.tr: Having now set out the two parts of this song, by which Moses leads us into the very cause he is pleading and sets forth the sum and heart of the matter, what remains is to come to the third part. As was said just now, it chiefly does three things. First, it compares the nature and character of God with our own disposition. Second, it sets God's benefits to his people against the wicked deeds of the same people. Last, it delivers God's judgment on our nature and character. These matters are both useful to consider and necessary to know, as will be shown in its place.

units.la: Iam vero hæc naturæ diuinæ & humani ingenij comparatio, quoniam & in homine atq; Dei cognitionem introducit, & quales simus qualesq; nos esse deceat atque oporteat often-dit: primum quidem animis hominum solidam sapientiâ, deinceps autem homini ipsi veram corporis atque animi incolumitatem affert. Quare eam qui velit & sapere & bene beateq; vi-uere, primum studiose cognoscere, deinceps autem altissima mente reponere atque voluere debuerit. Quam ad rem nos Moses iuuat expositione methodica: primum ponens ob ocu-los ipsam nostrarum inter se factam comparationem, dein adhibens etiam eius usum.
units.tr: Now this comparison between the divine nature and the human disposition, since it brings us to the knowledge of both man and God, and shows what and how we are, and how we ought to be, first brings to people's minds a solid wisdom, and then brings to man himself a true soundness of body and soul. Therefore whoever wishes both to be wise and to live well and happily ought first to learn this diligently and then to lay it up and turn it over in the highest regard of mind. To this end Moses helps us with a methodical exposition, first setting before our eyes the very comparison between our natures, and then also applying its use.

units.la: Ac comparatione quidem hoc agit ut priore loco Dei naturam atque mores paucis de-pingat, deinde vero hominis etiam describat ingenium. De Deo dicit: Petræ perfecta sunt ope-ra, quia omnes viæ eius iudicium: Deus veritas est nec fraus aut iniquitas: iustus & rectus ipse est. Quibus verbis Deum nominat, eius opera definit, naturam describit.
units.tr: In this comparison, Moses' aim is first to portray in a few words the nature and character of God, and then also to describe the disposition of man. Of God he says: The works of the Rock are perfect, because all his ways are judgment; God is truth, there is no deceit or iniquity; he is just and right. In these words he names God, defines his works, and describes his nature.

units.la: Dei nomen haud vulgare seu consuetum, sed augustum & quasi αἰνιγματωδῶς[?] quod-dam affert petra nominans, nimirum, ut re externa atq; omnibus cognita natura diuina adum-braret. Igitur vt est petra excelsa, inaccessa, solida, tutum omnibus, qui in eam confugiunt, præ-fidium: quippe quo nec miles ascendere nec tormenta bellica trahi possunt: ac quæ non arte & industria & viribus hominum, sed suapte natura constitit: sic Deus est excelsus, inaccessus, solidus, tutum omnibus in ipso positis præsidium: quippe quem nec hominum astutia supe-rare possit, nec eorundem frangere potentia: estque hoc ipsum quod est non vllius alterius rei, sed suo ipsius beneficio. Atque hoc ipsum spiritus sanctus adeo multis in locis docet, vt dies vnus iis haud sufficiat commemorandis.
units.tr: The name he uses for God is not common or ordinary but august, and he brings in something like a riddle [αἰνιγματωδῶς] by calling him a Rock, clearly so that the divine nature might be shadowed forth by an external thing known to all. Thus a rock is high, inaccessible, solid, a safe refuge for all who flee to it; no soldier can climb it, nor can siege engines be dragged up it; and it stands not by the skill, industry, or strength of men but by its own nature. So God is high, inaccessible, solid, and a safe refuge for all who are placed in him. No human cunning can overcome him, nor can any human power break him. And this is what he is, not by any other thing's benefit but by his own. The Holy Spirit teaches this so often in many places that a single day would not be enough to recount them.

units.la: Iam hoc nomen Christo datum est, in quo Deus nos vult saluos facere. Ex quo perspi-cuum est, in quo omnium tutissimè conquiescas, nempe in Deo per Christum. Unde & Mat. 7. qui id facit viro sapienti comparatur. Paulus, si Deus pro nobis quis contra nos? Psalm. nō timebo quia Dominus mecum est. Quæ si cogitaremus, minus in hominibus rebusque humanis spei poneremus.
units.tr: Now this name has been given to Christ, in whom God wills to make us safe. From this it is plain in whom you may rest most securely, namely in God through Christ. Hence also Matthew 7: he who does this is compared to a wise man. Paul: "If God is for us, who can be against us?" Psalm: "I will not fear, for the Lord is with me." If we considered these things, we would place less hope in men and in human affairs.

units.la: Opera Dei, inquit, sunt perfecta, quia omnes viæ eius iudicium. Obseruandum quod opera Dei dicit perfecta, immaculata, incorrupta. Verbum Hebræum tribuitur sacrificiis, vt ovi-bus, in quibus nec morbus nec macula. Sunt enim, vt in vestibus & corporibus hominum, sic etiam in dictis & factis maculæ. Velut eleemosyna solet amarulentia, ambitione, aliàve re ceu macula aspergi. At opera Dei sunt perfecta, ἀμέμπτα, quæ non possunt fieri meliora. Vide enim vt & crearit & gubernet & conseruet omnia: vt vicissitudo rerum atque tempo-rum nobis ipsis sit grata: vtut enim dura sit hyems tamen eius quies agricolis est grata: vtut quiete gaudeant tamen exoptant æstatem.
units.tr: "The works of God," he says, "are perfect, because all his ways are judgment." It is to be noted that he calls the works of God perfect, unblemished, incorrupt. The Hebrew word is applied to sacrifices, such as sheep in which there is neither disease nor spot. For as there are spots in the clothes and bodies of men, so there are spots in their words and deeds. Thus alms are commonly stained, as it were with a spot, by bitterness, ambition, or some other thing. But the works of God are perfect, ἀμέμπτα [faultless], such that they cannot be made better. For see how he both creates, governs, and preserves all things, so that the alternation of things and seasons is pleasing to us. Though winter is harsh, its rest is welcome to farmers; and though they rejoice in rest, they still long for summer.

units.la: His ortum & occasum regnorum adde, & iudicia Dei. Nohæ seculum & Lothi, & Ægyptus, & Roma, & alij nemini indignè puniti esse videntur. Sic qui Germaniæ mores intuea-tur, vt in vestitu, victu, crapula, reliquisque vitiis haud mirum ei videtur, quod Deus illis immisit Hispanos, Hussaros, Turcas. Quid de Heluetia nostra dicas? pars persequitur pars ne-gligit ac despicit euangelium: plæriq; vitam ab eo prorsus alienam agunt. Quæ mala si Deus etiam grauissimis suppliciis ulciscatur quid mirum? Ac quoniam uxores, fœminæ liberi sunt ipsis viris atque adolescentibus deteriores, quis illis dicat fieri iniuriam? Perfecta sunt, ergo nec reprehendi possunt opera Domini.
units.tr: Add to these the rise and fall of kingdoms, and the judgments of God. The age of Noah, of Lot, Egypt, Rome, and others seem to have been punished justly, and no one can say otherwise. So, if one looks at the manners of Germany, in clothing, food, drunkenness, and the other vices, it seems no wonder to him that God has sent upon them the Spaniards, the Hussars, and the Turks. What can one say of our Helvetia? Part persecutes the gospel, part neglects and despises it, and most live a life utterly alien to it. If God punishes such evils even with the most severe torments, what is surprising? And since wives and women and children are worse than the husbands and young men themselves, who could say that an injustice is done to them? The works of the Lord are perfect; therefore they cannot be blamed.

units.la: Atque in huius imitationem etiam nobis est incumbendum: nempe, vt ne quis de nobis iure possit conqueri. Nemo potest omnibus placere, sed precipuis placere nō vltima laus est.
units.tr: And in imitation of this we too must strive, so that no one may rightly complain of us. No one can please everyone, but to please the best people is no small praise.

units.la: Sed quomodo hoc ipsum consequemur? Si iis vtamur artibus quibus Deus: quæ vero sunt illæ? Dicit: quia omnes viæ eius sunt iudicium: hoc est eius dicta & facta sunt ceu prudenter & iustè lata sententia: nihil temere; prudenter facit omnia. Ac quemadmodum iustus & prudens iudex omnia in vtramque partem dicta, ante & post acta, testes ponderat, cumq; le-gibus atque moribus comparat: tum nec personarum, nec opinionum vulgarium, nec asse-ctuum habita ratione fert sententiam: sic Deus omnia prouidentissimè peragit. Unde eius dicta & facta iudicia appellantur.
units.tr: But how shall we attain this very thing? If we use the same arts as God. What are those arts? He says: "because all his ways are judgment." That is, his words and deeds are like a sentence pronounced prudently and justly. Nothing is done rashly; he does all things with prudence. And just as a just and prudent judge weighs all the things said on either side, the acts before and after, the witnesses, and compares them with laws and customs, and then gives his sentence without regard to persons, popular opinions, or partialities, so God carries out all things most providently. Hence his words and deeds are called judgments.

units.la: Ex quo colligimus tunc demum nos facturos quæ reprehendi nequeant, quando nihil temerè, inconsultò, iniustè, petulanter, ambitiosè, auarè, odiosè feceris. Nos assentus consuli- mus, opinionibus ducimur, inde fit vt peccemus. Igitur imitemur Deum: iudicium sequi- tur & perfecta sunt eius opera.
units.tr: From this we conclude that we shall then at last do what cannot be blamed, when you have done nothing rashly, thoughtlessly, unjustly, wantonly, ambitiously, greedily, or spitefully. We consult flattery, we are led by opinions, and so it comes about that we sin. Therefore let us imitate God: judgment follows, and his works are perfect.

units.la: Porrò Dei natura fert, inquit, vt sit veritas sine fraude: vt iustus & rectus. Quorum alte- rum nos consolatur alterum docet. Consolatur quod veritas sit. Nam cum vanis homini- bus tutò fides haberi nequeat, huic tutò credes qui ipsissima est veritas: cum labaris in commer- cijs quæ sunt fraudi, hic stabis, vbi fraus est nulla. Id vt teneas repete promissa diuina: quippe ex quibus præstitis Dei veritas colligitur.
units.tr: Furthermore, he says, the nature of God bears that there be truth without deceit, that he be just and right. The one of these comforts us, the other teaches us. It comforts us that there is truth. For since one cannot safely trust vain men, you may safely trust him who is truth itself. When you stumble in dealings where there is fraud, you will stand firm here, where there is no fraud.
