To hold to this, recall the divine promises, for from those that have been fulfilled the truth of God is inferred.

units.la: Docet autem nos iustitiæ studere, quod Deus ipse & iustus est & rectus: neq; enim cum illo potest esse societas ijs qui sunt eius dissimiles.
units.tr: He teaches us, moreover, to pursue justice, because God himself is both just and right; for there can be no fellowship with him for those who are unlike him.

units.la: Verum vt quales simus noris iam hominum naturam pingit. Corrupit, inquit, non filij eius, macula ipsorum, generatio praua & peruersa. Id est, praua hæc & peruersa progenies, quæ nomine Dei filiorum indigna est, in suam ipsorum contumeliam atq; ignominiam sese corrumpit. En quicquid dici potest de homine. Homo præclarum illud opus Domini, partim ad Dei gloriam, partim in suum ipsius bonum procreatum, homo, filius Dei adoptatus sese ipse init perditum: fecit vt ne fit quod esse per Christum poterat, quod ipsi probro est. Israelitæ popu li Dei nomine seipsi dedignati sunt.
units.tr: Now, that you may know what we are, he portrays the nature of man. They have corrupted, he says, not his children, their spot; a crooked and perverse generation. That is, this crooked and perverse offspring, unworthy of the name of God's children, has corrupted itself to its own dishonour and shame. Behold whatever can be said of man. Man, that noble work of the Lord, created partly for the glory of God and partly for his own good, man, adopted as a son of God, has himself rushed into ruin. He has made it so that what could have been made through Christ is not, and this is his own disgrace. The Israelites, in the name of the people of God, disdained themselves.

units.la: Sic hodieq; peccatis omnia corrumpimus quæ in nostram ipsorum salutem ac suam ipsius gloriam Deus parat.
units.tr: So today too we corrupt by our sins all the things God prepares for our own salvation and for his own glory.

units.la: Quam nostram ingratitudinè ex vtriusq; partis natura colligimus rite comparata. Ergò Deum intueamur, hominè consideremus: vt Deum adoremus, homini nõ nimiú tribuamus.
units.tr: We gather this our ingratitude from the nature of each party, when the two are rightly compared. Let us therefore look upon God and consider man, so that we may adore God and not attribute too much to man.

units.la: In vlum nostrum quomodo fit hæc comparatio conuertenda, ad hunc modum docet. Num Domino reddis hoc, populeste stulte & insipiens? an non ipse est pater tuus qui posside te, fecit te, parauit te. Quo ostendit ex illa Dei noftraq; ipsorum comparatione colligendum nos non solum miseros esse: qui cum Deus sit verax, nos fraudulenti: Deus iustus, nos iniusti sumus: verum etiam quod cum ille velit nos sui similes, id nos oblatum respuamus bonum. Sumus degeneres: malam Deo gratiam referimus. Vide quæ superfit homini gloriatio. Dicit Esa.1. Dominus: filios enutriui & euexi, & quæ sunt reliqua. Dicit Mat.3. Baptista, Iudæos non esse filios Abrahæ. Dicit Ioh.8. Christus, eos non Deo, sed diabolo patre natos.
units.tr: How this comparison is to be turned to our own use, he teaches in this way: "Do you repay the LORD thus, you foolish and senseless people? Is he not your father, who has possessed you, made you, and established you?" By this he shows that from the comparison between God and ourselves we are to conclude not only that we are wretched, since God is true and we are deceitful, God is just and we are unjust, but also that, although he wishes us to be like himself, we reject the good that is offered to us. We are degenerate and return an evil grace to God. See what room for boasting is left to man. Isaiah 1, the Lord says: "I have nourished and brought up children," and so on. Matthew 3, the Baptist says that the Jews are not sons of Abraham. John 8, Christ says that they were born not of God but of the devil as their father.

units.la: Quamobrem est enitendum, vt deposita nostra natura in bonam Dei naturam atque vitam transeamus. Quod fiet per Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum, Amen.
units.tr: Therefore we must strive to put off our nature and pass over into the good nature and life of God. This will be done through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

units.la: SERMO XI.
units.tr: SERMON XI.

units.la: 7 Memineris dierum priscorum, expendite animo annos priorum seculorum: interroga patrem tuum, & annuntiabit tibi: senes tuos, & dicent tibi.
units.tr: 7 Remember the days of old, consider the years of many generations: ask thy father, and he will shew thee; thine elders, and they will tell thee.

units.la: 8 Cum altissimus possessiones distribueret gentibus, quum dispergeret filios hominum, constituit limites populorum pro numero filiorum Israel.
units.tr: 8 When the Most High divided to the nations their inheritance, when he separated the sons of Adam, he set the bounds of the peoples according to the number of the children of Israel.

units.la: 9 Quoniam pars Domini populus eius, & Iacob funiculus hereditatis eius.
units.tr: 9 For the LORD's portion is his people; Jacob is the lot of his inheritance.

units.la: 10 Invenit eum in terra solitudinis, in vasto (loco) vlulatus & deserto. Circum duxit eum, & erudivit eum, custodiuit eum perinde ac pupillam oculi sui.
units.tr: 10 He found him in a desert land, and in the waste howling wilderness; he led him about, he instructed him, he kept him as the apple of his eye.

units.la: 11 Quemadmodum aquila excitans nidum suum, & super pullos suos volitans, expandensq; alas suas tollit illum, & portat eum super alas suas.
units.tr: 11 As an eagle stirreth up her nest, fluttereth over her young, spreadeth abroad her wings, taketh them, beareth them on her wings.

units.la: 12 Solus Dominus duxit eum, & non fuit cum eo Deus alienus.
units.tr: 12 So the LORD alone did lead him, and there was no strange god with him.

units.la: 13 Inuexit eum in sublimitatibus terræ, vt comederet prouentus agrorum, deditq; ei vt surgeret mel de petra, oleumq; è durissimo saxo.
units.tr: 13 He made him ride on the high places of the earth, that he might eat the increase of the fields; and he made him to suck honey out of the rock, and oil out of the flinty rock.

units.la: 14 Butyrum boum, & lac ouium, cum adipe arietum pinguium, & hircorum, cum adipe delicatissimi tritici, & sanguinem vuæ biberet meracum.
units.tr: 14 Butter of kine, and milk of sheep, with fat of lambs, and rams of the breed of Bashan, and goats, with the fat of kidneys of wheat; and thou didst drink the pure blood of the grape.

units.la: 15 Et pinguis factus rectus calcitrauit: crassus factus es & adipe obduétus. Dereliquit Deum factorem suum, & ingratus fuit petræ salutis suæ.
units.tr: 15 But Jeshurun waxed fat, and kicked: thou art waxen fat, thou art grown thick, thou art covered with fatness; then he forsook God which made him, and lightly esteemed the Rock of his salvation.

units.la: 16 Ad indignationem eum alienu (dijs) provocauerunt, abominationibus eum ad iracundiam concitarunt.
units.tr: 16 They provoked him to jealousy with strange gods, with abominations provoked they him to anger.

units.la: 17 Sacrificarunt cacodæmonibus, non Deo, dijs quos non nouerunt, nouis qui super exorti sunt, quos patres vestri nihil reueriti sunt.
units.tr: 17 They sacrificed unto devils, not to God; to gods whom they knew not, to new gods that came newly up, whom your fathers feared not.

units.la: Petra quæ te genuit oblitus es, excidit tibi Deus, qui te parturijt.
units.tr: Of the Rock that begat thee thou art unmindful, and hast forgotten God that formed thee.

units.la: CUm Divus Moses ijs, quæ nuper explicata sunt, verbis Dei naturam descripsset[?], cum-que ea naturam atq; ingenium hominum comparasset: eorum jam quæ Deus in homi-nes contulit beneficiorum, & multorum ab hominibus contra Deum patratorum scelerum comparationem affert. Unde facile cognosci potest peccatum, propterea quidem peccatum esse, quod cum bona recta; Dei natura pugnet atq; voluntate: sed multo maius hac de causa scelus esse, quòd facta eorum cum Dei beneficijs comparatione sit ac videatur ingratitudo. Jam si ingratitudo hominis in hominem tetrum est, & videtur vitium: quanto maius est flagi-tium in Deum peccare, qui immensa in nos confert beneficia. Sed nemo hoc agnoscit melius quàm qui Dei beneficia cum omnibus nostris dictis atq; factis contulerit, quasiq; rationem cum Deo iniens sic ultrò citròq; facta bona atq; mala contulerit atq; æstimauerit.
units.tr: When Moses, in the words just explained, had described the nature of God, and had compared with it the nature and disposition of men, he now sets out a comparison between the benefits God has conferred on men and the many wicked deeds men have committed against God. From this it can easily be seen why sin is sin: it is because it clashes with the good and right nature and will of God; but it is a far greater crime for this reason, that men's deeds, when set beside God's benefits, appear as ingratitude. Now if a man's ingratitude toward another man is foul and seen as a vice, how much greater is the wickedness of sinning against God, who bestows immense benefits upon us? But no one recognises this better than one who has set God's benefits side by side with all his own words and deeds, and, as if reckoning with God, has weighed and assessed the good and evil deeds passed back and forth between them.

units.la: Quam ad rem non parum momenti præsens hæc Dei beneficiorum & nostrarum actio-num comparatio attulerit. Eam Moses diligentissimè persequitur: primum enim Dei benefi-cia, deinceps populi facta commemorat.
units.tr: This present comparison of God's benefits with our actions has contributed no small weight to this matter. Moses pursues it most diligently: he first recounts God's benefits, and then the deeds of the people.

units.la: De Dei beneficijs ad hunc modum disserit: Memineris dierum priscorum, &c. Quibus verbis & beneficia Dei refert, & quomodo ea sint existimanda docet. Primum enim iubet ea cum ex antiquitatis memoria tum ex senibus repetere & cognoscere, cum dicit: Memineris priscorum dierum, & priora secula considera. Quod documento est nostra referre, ut annales & maiorum res gestas lustremus. Et bene Cicero, historia, inquit, est testis temporum, lux veritatis, vita memoriae, magistra vitae, nuncia vetustatis.
units.tr: He discusses God's benefits in this way: Remember the days of old, etc. In these words he both recalls God's benefits and teaches how they ought to be regarded. For first he bids us recover and learn them from the memory of antiquity and from the elders, when he says: Remember the days of old, and consider the former generations. This is a lesson for us to bring forward our records, that we may review the annals and the deeds of our ancestors. And Cicero rightly says: history is the witness of the times, the light of truth, the life of memory, the teacher of life, the messenger of antiquity.

units.la: Socordis est & ignavi prorsus hominis res civitatis suæ gestas negligere, ne dum quæ fi-unt quotidie nō observare. Exemplis indicatur id neglectum obfuisse, observatum multum conduxisse. Obfuit Pharaoni Ægyptio quod Josephum eiusque familiam ignoraret, ideoque affligeret: alioquin haud dubie futurus gratior. Assuero profuit Mardochei beneficium annotasse & relegisse postea, sic enim in illum gratus fuit & sibi suisque cauit. Sic prodest meminisse annalium, & ex ijs discere in quos gratus esse & beneficus: à quibus rursus abstinere debeas.
units.tr: It is the mark of a careless and utterly idle man to neglect the deeds of his own commonwealth, let alone not to observe what happens every day. Examples show that neglect has done harm, and observance has greatly helped. It harmed Pharaoh of Egypt that he did not know Joseph and his family, and therefore oppressed them; otherwise he would undoubtedly have been more grateful. It profited Ahasuerus that he had noted Mordecai's service and afterwards read it again; so he was grateful to him and took care for himself and his own. So it is useful to remember the annals and to learn from them whom you ought to be grateful to and generous toward, and, on the other hand, whom you ought to avoid.

units.la: Deinceps autem senes audiendos dicit, ut qui illa possint narrare Deut. 6. & alibi illis hoc beneficium narrandi imponitur. Est id documento juvenibus ut studeant senum commercijs ac colloquijs. Ex illis audies bona eum deferbuerit malitia: audies sapientiam cum usu vitæ multum didicerint. Exemplum pueritiæ Christus præstulit qui duodecennis puer in medio doctorum inventus est.
units.tr: Next he says that the elders are to be listened to, since they are able to relate these things (Deut. 6.), and elsewhere this duty of recounting such benefits is laid upon them. This is a lesson for the young to be eager for the company and conversation of their elders. From them you will hear how wickedness has lost its strength; you will hear what wisdom they have learned along with experience of life. Christ set an example for boyhood, who at twelve years old was found in the midst of the teachers.

units.la: Sed omnes discimus ab initio vitæ usque ad præsentem ætatem supputare, & quid diui-nitus acceperimus discere. Ut Dauid in Psal. dicit usu vitæ longo se didicisse eorum qui pij sunt perire neminem. Sic quid tibi, quid alijs usuenerit considerato.
units.tr: But we all learn to reckon from the beginning of life up to the present age, and to learn what we have received from God. As David says in the Psalm that, from long experience of life, he has learned that none of those who are godly perish. So consider what has happened to you and to others.

units.la: Sed enumerat.1. Quum altissimus possessiones distribuerit, &c. Dicit Deum Israelitis perinde ac suis hæredibus distribuisse terram. In quo cum modum consideremus tum causam.
units.tr: But he enumerates. 1. When the Most High divided the inheritances, etc. He says that God divided the land to the Israelites just as to his own heirs. In this we should consider both the manner and the cause.

units.la: In modo enim, quod Deus omnibus populis suas terras dederit, itemque suas Israelitis: cernimus verum esse quod Psal.104.105.106. Dauid canit: regna terrarum à Deo distribui & ab eo pendere omnia. Igitur qui velint acquirere illum honorent: qui velint parta conservare eum ipsum socium habeant necesse est. Abrahæ promittitur: Ego ero tecum. Erat cum, Mose, Dauide, Daniele, Hestere & reliquis: quo fiebat, ut invitis omnibus inimicis eveberentur. Contra Pharao, Cananæi, Saul, Philistini, Roboam, Alexandri Macedonis regnum, Babylon, Roma, quoniam hos Deus excisos voluit stare non potuere.
units.tr: As to the manner: that God gave their lands to all peoples, and likewise gave his own to the Israelites, we see that what David sings in Psalms 104, 105, 106 is true: that the kingdoms of the earth are distributed by God, and that all things depend on him. Therefore those who wish to acquire anything must honour him; those who wish to keep what they have must necessarily have him as their partner. To Abraham it was promised: I will be with thee. He was with Moses, David, Daniel, Esther and the rest; and so it came about that they were carried on although all their enemies were against them. On the other hand Pharaoh, the Canaanites, Saul, the Philistines, Rehoboam, the kingdom of Alexander of Macedon, Babylon, and Rome could not stand, because God willed them to be overthrown.

units.la: In causa vero, quod dicit: Quoniam pars Domini populus eius, & Jacob funiculus hæreditatis eius. Hoc est, quoniam populum Israel elegit sibi in peculium, ut eos loco filiorum habe-ret: hac duētus ratione Deus non potuit eos in illa distributione terrarum negligere.
units.tr: As to the cause, which he states: For the LORD's portion is his people, and Jacob the lot of his inheritance. That is: because he chose the people of Israel for himself as his special possession, so that he might have them in place of sons, led by this reasoning God could not overlook them in that division of lands.

units.la: Ex quo perspicuum est, quanti sit esse in numero amicorum Dei, hæredes & filios Dei. Curam habet omnium in primis suorum. Jam qui spiritum Christi habent, Christo insiti[?] sunt, & filij Dei. Quod si filij certè & hæredes. At hæredibus si mundana det nulla, pro ijs est haud dubiè daturus cœlestia. Hæc fides, Job, Abrahæ, Mosis, Dauidis, Apostolorum qui reli-ctis rebus omnibus Christum secuti sunt arbitrati sese eò potitos non esse ditiores.
units.tr: From this it is plain how great a thing it is to be among the friends of God, his heirs and sons. He has especially care of all his own. Now those who have the Spirit of Christ are grafted into Christ and are sons of God. If sons, then certainly heirs. And if he gives no worldly goods to his heirs, he will undoubtedly give heavenly ones in their place. This was the faith of Job, Abraham, Moses, David, and the Apostles, who, leaving all things, followed Christ, and did not consider themselves any richer for having obtained him.

units.la: 2. Inuenit eum in deserto, &c. In pauperie, mœrore & luctu jacentem quasi è mendicitate suscepit. Hoc non exprobrandi sed admonendi causa docet: plurimum enim refert qui fueris antea quique nunc fis[?] scire: ne videlicet ferocias, neve quenquam despicias, aut tibi quasi Deo tam bene meritus sis plus satis tribuas. Sic Dauidi, Sauli, alijs fortunā priore Deus obiecit. Quo in loco res nostrae sint ac fuerint antea cogitare cum priuatim tum publice nostra interesset. Obliti enim paupertatis pristinae in bonis, quae nunc habemus, superbimus.
units.tr: 2. He found him in the desert, etc. Lying in poverty, sorrow and grief, he took him up as if from beggary. He teaches this not for the sake of reproach but of admonition: for it matters greatly to know who you were before and who you now are; so that, clearly, you do not grow proud, nor despise anyone, nor credit yourself more than enough, as if you had deserved so well of God. So God threw the former fortune of David and Saul in their faces. In this place it was in our interest to think over both privately and publicly what our circumstances are and what they were before. For forgetting our former poverty, we grow proud of the goods we now have.

units.la: 3. Circumduxit,&c. Eruditus,custodiuit,&c. Officium educationis omnibus suis numeris absolutum depingit. Promouit à loco in locum, vt progrederentur: si quo loco minus bene haberent in aliū duxit: veluti parui atq; aegri infantes matrum vlnis gestantur. Eruditiuit omnibus in rebus scitu necessarijs: custodiuit à malis omnibus: muniuit legibus, magistratibus, disciplina militari simul ac ciuili.
units.tr: 3. He led him about, etc. He instructed him, kept him, etc. He portrays the office of rearing completed in all its parts. He moved him from place to place so that they might advance; if he was less well off in one place, he led him to another, just as little and sick infants are carried in their mothers' arms. He instructed him in all things needful to know; he kept him from all evils; he fortified him with laws, magistrates, and military as well as civil discipline.

units.la: Sed id ipse perpulchris perq; aptis similitudinibus exponit. Vt pupillum oculi. Nihil charius oculis: vnde nihil est cui perinde parcimus ac prospicimus: tā Deus de illis solicitus fuit. Tū vt aquila pullos suos alit, volare docet, solaribꝰ [?] radijs assuefacit, tenerrime diligit: sic deus hunc populū amat & amplectitur: testis est historia. Idē de nobis, deq; omnibus dici potest.
units.tr: But he himself sets this out with very beautiful and apt comparisons. As the apple of the eye. Nothing is dearer to the eyes; hence nothing is guarded and watched over with such care; so God was anxious for them. Then, as the eagle feeds her chicks, teaches them to fly, accustoms them to the rays of the sun, loves them most tenderly, so God loves and embraces this people; history is the witness. The same can be said of us, and of all.

units.la: 4. Solus Dominus duxit eum,& non fuit cum eo Deus alius. Solus ille seruauit, ergo solus ille colendus fuerat. Vt ergo Deus vnus creauit, alit, seruat: sic vnus est adorandus sine dijs socijs, quemadmodum sine dijs socijs nos adiuuit.
units.tr: 4. The Lord alone led him, and there was no strange god with him. He alone preserved him; therefore he alone ought to be worshipped. Just as the one God created, feeds and preserves, so he alone is to be adored, without other gods as partners, just as he alone helped us without gods as partners.

units.la: Hoc argumento Paulus docet Corinthios vnius Christi nomine gloriari, quòd nec Paulus nec Petrus, nec quisquā alius praeter solum Christum pro nobis fit crucifixus. Et certē non Iudas qui prodidit, non apostoli qui fugerunt, non Petrus qui negauit, non Simon Cyrenensis qui portauit crucem, sed qui illi solus est affixus Dominus noster Iesus Christus. Sin aliū pro nobis passum probes cedo. Sin minus ego libertus Christi illum ipsum, qui me seruitutis iugo liberauit sui sanguinis precio patroni loco solum retinebo.
units.tr: By this argument Paul teaches the Corinthians to glory in the name of Christ alone, because neither Paul nor Peter, nor anyone else except Christ alone, was crucified for us. Certainly not Judas who betrayed, not the apostles who fled, not Peter who denied, not Simon of Cyrene who carried the cross, but our Lord Jesus Christ alone was fastened to it. But if you can prove that anyone else suffered for us, then produce him. If not, I, a freedman of Christ, shall keep that very One, who freed me from the yoke of slavery by the price of his blood, as my sole patron.

units.la: 5. Inuexit eum in sublimitatibus terrae,&c. Refert magna cum paruis Dei munera: nempe vt intelligas tam minima, quàm maxima haberi à Domino, proq; omnibus illi deberi gratias. Atq; hæc docet nos Deo gratos esse.
units.tr: 5. He made him ride on the high places of the earth, etc. He sets forth God's great gifts alongside small ones, namely so that you may understand that the smallest things as well as the greatest are had from the Lord, and that thanks are owed to him for all. And this teaches us to be pleasing to God.

units.la: De populo,pinguis,&c. Quo docet quae populus contra fecerit: & initium à causa facit. Pinguis factus & obesus: lauta fortuna causa est petulantiae. Opes, honores, pax, deliciae sunt Dei munera: sed malis irritamenta malorum. Igitur si illa non habeas, ne tantopere doleas: ca res irritamento malorum: sin habeas memineris cauendum. Saul quanto peior in regno? Dauid in pace? Abfalon in forma corporis? Solomon in diuitijs?
units.tr: Concerning the people, fat, etc. By this he teaches what the people did against him, and he begins from the cause. He grew fat and gross: a lavish fortune is the cause of wantonness. Wealth, honours, peace and delights are God's gifts, but for the wicked they are incitements to evil. Therefore if you do not have these things, do not grieve too much: that condition is an incitement to evil; but if you have them, remember to be on your guard. How much worse was Saul in his kingdom? David in peace? Absalom in the beauty of his body? Solomon in his riches?

units.la: Quid fecerit sigillatim refert. Dereliquit Deum factorem suum: irritauit cultu Deorum alienorum [?] zelotem Deum: sacrificauit daemonibus: Dei qui genuit oblitus est. Summa ingratitudo il-lius, qui te genuerit: malum ouum, progenies viperarum.
units.tr: He recounts what they did, one by one. They forsook God their maker; they provoked him to jealousy with strange gods; they sacrificed to demons; they forgot God who begot them. Supreme ingratitude of that man who begot you: an evil egg, a brood of vipers.

units.la: Atq; sic si priuatim iuxta ac publice rationem iniremus: non superessent vlla nobis quae supererogationis opera vocantur: sed nos infinitis modis Deo debitores esse coftaret. Quod cum ita sit relictis his praesidijs omnibus ad Christum Dominum nostrum confugiamus, Amen.
units.tr: And so, if we went through the reckoning in private just as much as in public, no works would remain for us that are called works of supererogation; rather, it would be clear that we are debtors to God in infinite ways. Since this is so, let us, with all these supports set aside, flee for refuge to Christ our Lord. Amen.

units.la: SERMO XII.
units.tr: Sermon XII.

units.la: 19 Et vidit Dominus & irritatus est propter prouocationem filiorum suorum, & filiarum suarum.
units.tr: 19 And the Lord saw it, and was provoked to anger because of the provoking of his sons and of his daughters.

units.la: 20 Et dixit abscondam faciem meam ab eis, spectabo quid tandem (facturi) sint illi: quoniam generatio est peruersa, filij in quibus nulla est fides.
units.tr: 20 And he said: I will hide my face from them; I will see what they will at last do, for they are a perverse generation, children in whom there is no faith.

units.la: 21 Ipsi prouocauerunt me ad indignationem in eo qui non est Deus, ad iracundiam me concitarunt vanitatibus suis, & ego quoq; prouocabo eos in eo qui non est populus, in gente stulta irritabo eos.
units.tr: 21 They have provoked me to jealousy with that which is not God; they have moved me to anger with their vanities. And I also will provoke them to jealousy with that which is not a people; I will anger them with a foolish nation.

units.la: 22 Quoniam ignis succensus est in furore meo, & exardescet ad infimos inferos, vsq; deuorabit terram cum fructu eius, & inflammabit fundamenta montium.
units.tr: 22 For a fire is kindled in my wrath, and shall burn to the lowest hell, and shall devour the earth with its increase, and shall set on fire the foundations of the mountains.

units.la: 23 Congregabo super eos mala, sagittas meas euacuabo in eos.
units.tr: 23 I will heap evils upon them; I will spend my arrows upon them.

units.la: 24 Adusti fame, consumpti ardenti lue & amara agritudine, quin & dentes bestiarum immittam in eos, cum furore serpentium in pulucre.
units.tr: 24 They shall be consumed with hunger, and devoured by burning plague and bitter destruction. I will also send the teeth of beasts upon them, with the fury of serpents in the dust.

units.la: 25 Foris orbabit gladius, in penetralibus terror, tam iuuenem quàm virginem, lactentem cum viro cano.
units.tr: 25 Abroad the sword shall bereave, and at home terror, for young man and virgin alike, the suckling with the grey-haired man.

units.la: 26 Statueram quidem quod disijcere vellem eos per angulos (terra) collereque memoriam eorum è mortalibus.
units.tr: 26 I had indeed determined to scatter them into corners and to make their memory cease from among men.

units.la: 27 Nisi ferociam hostium veritus essem, ne forte hostes eorum sibi id arroga[?] rent, ne forte dicerent: Manus nostra excelsa, & non Dominus operatus est univer-sum hoc.
units.tr: 27 Had I not feared the fierceness of the enemy, lest their adversaries should claim it for themselves, lest they should say: Our hand is high, and the Lord has not wrought all this.

units.la: 28 Quoniam gens est qua perdit consilia, neq; est eis intelligentia aliqua.
units.tr: 28 For they are a nation that loses counsel, and there is no understanding in them.

units.la: 29 O si saperent intelligerentq, hoc, expenderentq, quid tandem futurum sit ipsis.
units.tr: 29 O that they were wise, and understood this, and considered what will at last become of them!

units.la: 30 Quomodo persequeretur unus mille, & duo fugarent decem millia, nisi petra eorum vendidisset eos, & Dominus conclusisset eos?
units.tr: 30 How could one chase a thousand, and two put ten thousand to flight, unless their rock had sold them, and the Lord had shut them up?

units.la: 31 Nam petra eorum non est ut petra nostra (huiusq; rei), & hostes nostri iudi-ces sunt.
units.tr: 31 For their rock is not as our Rock (even in this matter), and our enemies are judges.

units.la: 32 Quoniam de vite Sedomorum vitis eorum, atq; de arvis Amorrhæ. Uva eo-rum uva fellis, botrus amarissimus eis.
units.tr: 32 For their vine is of the vine of Sodom, and of the fields of Amorrha. Their grapes are grapes of gall; their clusters are most bitter.

units.la: 33 Virus draconum vinum eorum, & fel aspidum sævum.
units.tr: 33 Their wine is the venom of dragons, and the cruel gall of asps.

units.la: 34 An non hoc repositum est apud me, & obsignatum in thesauris meis?
units.tr: 34 Is not this laid up in store with me, and sealed among my treasures?

units.la: 35 Ultio mihi est & repensio ad tempus, labetur pes eorum, appropinquat dies quo perdantur ipsi, & festinant quæ imminent eis.
units.tr: 35 Vengeance is mine, and recompense, in due time. Their foot shall slip; the day of their destruction is near, and the things that are coming upon them hasten.

units.la: 36 Quoniam iudicabit Dominus populum suum, & in servis suis se solabitur, nam videbit vires eorum abiisse, & in nihilum abiisse conclusum & derelictum.
units.tr: 36 For the Lord shall judge his people, and relent toward his servants; for he shall see that their strength has gone, and that none is shut up or left.

units.la: 37 Et dicet: Ubi sunt dii eorum, petra, in quem speraverunt?
units.tr: 37 And he shall say: Where are their gods, the rock in which they trusted?

units.la: 38 Quorum adipem ex sacrificiis comederunt, & quorum vinum in libaminibus biberunt. Surgant & opituleniur[?] nobis, sint nobis in latibulum.
units.tr: 38 Who ate the fat of their sacrifices, and drank the wine of their drink offerings? Let them rise up and help you; let them be a covering over you.

units.la: Quemadmodum in iudiciis hominum atq; in foro civili fieri solet, ut auditis actoris atque rei partibus feratur iusta atque æqua sententia: sic in sua hac admonitione Moses primum Dei beneficia iuxtaq; mortalium scelera ponit quasi defensionem cum accusatione conferens: deinceps autem sententiam atque iudicium Domini introducit.
units.tr: As is usually done in human courts and in the civil forum, where, after the parts of plaintiff and defendant have been heard, a just and fair sentence is pronounced, so in this admonition Moses first sets God's benefits alongside the wickedness of mortals, weighing the defence against the accusation, and afterwards introduces the sentence and judgement of the Lord.

units.la: Atq; hic quidem describitur divinum de hac mortalium ingratitudine iudicium. Qua in descriptione primum minas hinc promanantium incommodorum refert: tum causas monstrat quibus adductus Deus non repente puniat, sed tarde peccata hominum ulciscatur. Postremo quomodo puniat.
units.tr: Here is described the divine judgement on this human ingratitude. In the description he first recounts the threats of the calamities that flow from it; then he shows the causes which move God not to punish at once but to be slow to avenge men's sins; and lastly, how he punishes.

units.la: Minas ad hunc modum refert: Et vidit Dominus & iratus est propter provocationem filiorum suorum. Quibus verbis tria malorum genera comminatur: sed antea quo pacto ad causas cognitionem procedat monstrat.
units.tr: He recounts the threats in this way: "And the Lord saw, and was angry because of the provoking of his sons." In these words he threatens three kinds of evil; but first he shows how he comes to know the causes.

units.la: Ait eum vidisse & iratum esse hæc à suis ipsius fieri liberis. Operæprecium est hæc scire: Deum audire & videre quæ geruntur in terris omnia. Ut Abelis sanguinem clamantem audi-vit: Israelis item in Ægypto gemitus: Rahelis lachrymas, & Paulus illū dicitur petiisse cum discipulos qui in Damasco erant petiisset. Atq; hæc cogitatio malos quidem coercet, bonos autem consolatur.
units.tr: He says that he saw and was angered at these things done by his own sons. It is worth knowing this: that God hears and sees all that is done on earth. Thus he heard the blood of Abel crying out, likewise the groaning of Israel in Egypt, and the tears of Rachel; and Saul is said to have sought the disciples who were in Damascus, and God sought him. This thought restrains the wicked and consoles the good.

units.la: Filios dein appellat suos, ut apud Esaiam, & alibi.
units.tr: Then he calls them "his sons," as in Isaiah and elsewhere.

units.la: Observandum est etiam quod dicit nostris peccatis Deum irritari: quasi quæ fiunt in illius molestiam, [illegible, ~12 letters]. Quo certè vix quicquā est peius. Eum enim irritare, qui crea-rit ac fouerit est inauditæ malitiæ. Sed proh Deum atq; homines, quàm frequens hoc est: Sci-mus Deum nolle nos alibi, quàm in ipso solo sperare & quærere auxilia: at nos ad diuos, ad ho-mines in his terris degentes confugimus: odit idola, at plena sunt horum templa Christiana: odit blasphemias, at pueris nedum senibus hoc est familiare: eodemq; modo in rebus reliquis.
units.tr: It is also to be observed that he says our sins provoke God, as if what is done is to his annoyance [illegible, ~12 letters]. Certainly there is scarcely anything worse than this. For to provoke him who created and cherished us is a malice unheard of. But, good God and men, how frequent this is! We know that God wills us to seek and look for help in him alone and nowhere else; yet we flee to the saints, to men living on this earth. He hates idols, yet Christian temples are full of them. He hates blasphemies, yet these are familiar not only to boys but to old men. And so it is in the rest as well.

units.la: Sed quid inde bonorum reportatur? Hoc ipsum Moses refert.1. Subtrahit sua Deus illis hominibus auxilia. Dicit enim, abscondam faciem meam ab eis, spectabo quid tandem facturi sint illi. Abscondere faciem Deus, cum nos non respicit, sed auersatur, & vult punire, dicitur. Est id frequens in sacris literis: ut à Cain, ab Iuda, à Saule faciem abscondit. Petrum autem respe-xit, & Elizabetham & alios. Videbit quid faciamus: hoc est, quo pacto simus res nostras admini-stratauri. Deum, sine quo nullus es, deserere quantę quæso impudentiæ?
units.tr: But what good comes from this? Moses himself reports it. First, God withdraws his help from such men. For he says: "I will hide my face from them; I will see what they will at last do." It is said that God hides his face when he does not regard us but turns away and wishes to punish. This is frequent in the sacred letters: he hid his face from Cain, from Judah, from Saul. But he looked upon Peter, and Elizabeth, and others. "He will see what we do": that is, how we will manage our affairs. To desert God, without whom you are nothing, what, I ask, is the height of impudence!

units.la: Cur autem deserit Dominus, & abscondit faciem? Caussas duas affert: unam, quòd sit perversa generatio: hoc est, intus & in cute mali. Altera, quia filii in quibus nulla sit fides, quiq; quod sua interest non faciunt. En quibus rebus remoueatur ab homine Dei gratia. Si totus caro fit, ac tantummodo malum spiret: ut idololatriam, cedem, rapinam, adulteria, scortationem: tum si filii Dei esse glorientur & toti sint degeneres, ut de Iudæis Matth.3.Ioh.8. Habes unum malum & eius causas.
units.tr: Why, however, does the Lord desert us and hide his face? He gives two causes. One is that it is a perverse generation: that is, evil within and to the skin. The other is that they are children in whom there is no faith, who do not do what is for their own good. Behold the things by which grace is removed from a man of God: if he becomes wholly flesh and breathes only evil, such as idolatry, murder, robbery, adultery, fornication; and then if men boast of being sons of God while being wholly degenerate, as the Jews were (Matt. 3; John 8). You have one evil and its causes.

units.la: 2. Subiecturus vili populo. Ipsi me provocarunt in eo qui non est Deus, inquit: ego eos sub iugum eorum, quos pro populo vix ipsi habent, mittam. En poenam talionis. Deum falsum pro vero coluerunt, eoq; dedecore maximo summum illum, verumq; Deum affecerunt: ergo par pari refert Deus bona praebens non illis, sed aliis populis, qui illis minime videbantur digni tantis bonis esse & gloria. Et certe bona Iudaeis diuinitus promissa, ut latum imperium, ingentes opes, magnam gloriam sapientiae, prudentiae, fortitudinis, iustitiae, Graeci & Romani magis habuere excellentia: contra Iudaei ab his ipsis alienissimi fuere, & adhuc sunt. Sic omnino ut bus seculis fideles his bonis propter ingratitudinem caruerunt, atque prophanis gentibus data viderunt quae Deus illis & promiserat, & si frugi fuissent dediisset. Ac multis papistas bonis abundare cernimus quae nobis, si grati essemus, Deus daret. Vtitur hoc loco Paulus Rom. 11. vide quid sit Deum prouocare.
units.tr: 2. He is about to subject them to a base people. "They provoked me with that which is not God," he says; "I will send them under the yoke of those whom they themselves scarcely count as a people." Behold the punishment of retaliation. They worshipped a false God in place of the true, and with the greatest dishonour they affronted that supreme and true God. So God, returning like for like, bestows good things not on them but on other peoples, who seemed to them least worthy of such goods and glory. And indeed the goods divinely promised to the Jews, such as wide empire, great riches, and the great glory of wisdom, prudence, fortitude and justice, the Greeks and Romans rather possessed in excellence; on the contrary the Jews were most alien to these very things, and still are. So in every age faithful people have, on account of ingratitude, lacked these goods, and have seen them given to profane nations, which God had both promised to them and would have given had they been fruitful. And we see the Papists abounding in goods which God would give us if we were thankful. Paul uses this passage in Romans 11; see what it is to provoke God.

units.la: 3. Mala minitatur: poenam, ab animatis & inanimatis rebus exitium: vt penuriam, pestem, bellum, pesima quaeq;. Exemplo sunt secula Noha, Lothi, Achab, Israel, Iuda, Germania nostra. Subtraxit auxilium, sumus praui, infideles. Subiecit ijs populis, quos ipsi semper contem pmus. Sentimus Dei vindictam, est in magna annonae copia fames & annonae caritas: morbi sunt multi & varij: ferae sunt ipsi nunc homines, prae quibus haud tuta sunt itinera: bella sunt toto orbe. Quarum rerum atque aerumnarum cogitatione si qua tangeremur: non possumus fieri quin ad dominum Deum conuerteremur.
units.tr: 3. He threatens evils: punishment, and destruction from animate and inanimate things, such as scarcity, pestilence, war, and all the worst things. Examples are the ages of Noah, Lot, Ahab, Israel, Judah, and our Germany. He withdrew his help; we are wicked and faithless. He subjected them to peoples whom they had always despised. We feel God's vengeance: amid great abundance of grain there is famine and dearth; there are many and various diseases; men themselves have now become wild beasts, before whom the roads are not safe; wars rage across the whole world. If we were moved by the thought of these things and miseries, we could not fail to turn to the Lord God.

units.la: Cur autem poenam differat, ac peccatores non statim puniat hoc ipso docet, quod dicit: Statueram quidem quod dissicere vellem, &c. Et eorum memoriam e medio tollere. Prima ac praecipua diuinae in poenis morae causa est Dei longanimitas, quae poenitentiam & conuersionem peccatoris expectat: sed aliud etiam in hoc Deus respicit, nempe sui nominis gloriam. Etenim si Dominus impiorum opera ad coercendum populum suum vtatur, illi victores triumphant, sibique tribuunt omnia: vt Pharao, Cananaei, Philistini, Senacherib, Antiochus, nostri temporis persecutores. Vnde sancti Dei serui idipsum in suis ad Deum precibus praetendere confuerunt. Veluti Moses, Samuel, Daniel, & alij. Sic Deus videns adhuc nos non resipiscere, punire quidem impoenitentes decernit, sed existimationem sui verbi respiciens moram trahit. Nec dubium est quin dudum vltus esset nostram, qua verbum eius nunc excipimus, ingratitudinem, nisi illa causa obstitisset. Eodemq; modo priuatim atque publice fera vindicta numinis est existimanda.
units.tr: Why he defers punishment and does not strike sinners at once, he shows by this very word, where he says: "I had indeed resolved that I would scatter them, &c.," and would blot out their memory from among men. The first and chief cause of God's delay in punishing is his long-suffering, which waits for the repentance and conversion of the sinner. But God has regard to something else in this as well, namely the glory of his own name. For if the Lord uses the wicked to restrain his people, the victors triumph and attribute everything to themselves, as Pharaoh, the Canaanites, the Philistines, Sennacherib, Antiochus and the persecutors of our own time did. Hence the holy servants of God have been accustomed to put this forward in their prayers to God, as Moses, Samuel, Daniel and others did. So God, seeing that we still do not repent, decrees indeed to punish the unrepentant, but out of regard for the reputation of his word he delays. Nor is there any doubt that he would long since have avenged our ingratitude, in which we now receive his word, had that consideration not stood in the way. In the same way, a fierce vengeance of the divine power is to be expected both in private and in public.

units.la: Iam eorum miseriam pluribus verbis describit, dicens, Quoniam gens est quae perdit consilia, &c. Docet illos, t. esse perplexos, stupidos, stolidos: qui non respiciant finem, fugam, vindictam Dei, quam conclusionem vocat: tum Sodomae exemplis illustrat. Sed de his satis.
units.tr: Now he describes their misery at greater length, saying: "For they are a nation that has lost its counsel, &c." He teaches that they are perplexed, dazed and foolish, who do not look to the end, the flight and the vengeance of God, which he calls the conclusion. Then he illustrates this with the example of Sodom. But enough on these points.

units.la: Poenae modum hoc ipso monstrat quod dicit: An non hoc repositum est apud me, &c. Often dicit suae prouidentiae thesauris contineri quae dicat: quos Deus cum visum fuerit aperiensefundat ita vt homines & intelligant se suaq; omnia vana esse, & sentiant Deum verum esse Deum, cuius vnius sit vltio.
units.tr: He shows the measure of the punishment by this very thing that he says: "Is not this laid up in store with me, &c.?" He often says that the things he speaks of are kept in the treasuries of his providence, which God, when it seems good to him, opens and pours out, so that men both understand that they and all their possessions are vain, and perceive that God is the true God, whose alone is vengeance.

units.la: Ex quibus omnibus perspicuum est quale sit domini de nostra vitiosa natura, deq; tetra erga illum ingratitudine iudicium: enitendum nobis esse vt nostra poenitentia mala tanta tamq; gratia praeueniamus: alieno periculo cauti in tempore ad Deum conuertamur, obnixe precati vt nos seruet in Christo Iesu Domino nostro, Amen.
units.tr: From all these things it is plain what the Lord's judgment is of our sinful nature, and of our foul ingratitude towards him. We must strive so to anticipate our own evil with repentance, that, warned by another's danger, we may turn to God in time, earnestly praying that he would keep us in Christ Jesus our Lord, Amen.

units.la: SERMO XIII.
units.tr: SERMON XIII.

units.la: 39 Videte igitur quod ego, ego inquam ipse (sum Dominus), & non est Deus praeter me: ego occido, & rursus viuificio: ego vulnus infligo, & ego medebor, nec est qui e manibus meis eripere possit.
units.tr: 39 See now that I, even I, am he, and there is no god with me: I kill, and I make alive; I wound, and I heal: neither is there any that can deliver out of my hand.

units.la: 40 Quoniam sublata manu mea in caelum, dicam: Viuo ego in aeternum.
units.tr: 40 For I lift up my hand to heaven and say, I live for ever.

units.la: 41 Quum exacuero fulgorem gladij mei, tum manus mea apprehendet iudicium, reddam & vltionem hostibus meis, simulq; odientibus me reddam.
units.tr: 41 If I whet the glittering of my sword, and my hand take hold on judgment, I will render vengeance to my enemies, and will reward those who hate me.

units.la: 42 Imbuam sagittas meas sanguine, et gladius meus devorabit carnes, propter sanguinem occisorum, propterq; captiuos, vt hosti summatim vltiones (reddam.)
units.tr: 42 I will make my arrows drunk with blood, and my sword shall devour flesh, with the blood of the slain and of the captives, from the beginning of the revenges upon the enemy.

units.la: 43 Excitate ò gentes ad iubilum populum eius, quoniam sanguinem seruorum suorum vlciscetur, & vindictam rependet hostibus suis, & propitius erit terræ suæ & populo suo.
units.tr: 43 Rejoice, O ye nations, with his people: for he will avenge the blood of his servants, and will render vengeance to his adversaries, and will be merciful unto his land, and to his people.

units.la: Benè profecto & si illius fidissimis atq; amantissimis monitis obtemperetur, sane quàm utiliter consuluit Solomon dicens: Initium sapientiæ timor Domini: quemadmodum enim equus etiam ferocissimus retineri in officio & gubernari potest: sic qui religione & reverentia numinis aliqua ducitur, quo minus mala cogitet, dicat, faciat, facile prohiberi potest: rursus ut equus freno solutus aut nunquam, aut ægrè retinetur, sic qui nullo Dei timo-re percellitur in omne scelerum genus vi cupiditatum rapiatur necesse est. Qua de causa Moses & toto hoc libro, & in primis in hoc Cantico, quò timorem numinis incutiat, omnia Dei præcepta magnis, augustis, prægnantibus rationibus firmat atque exaggerat. Ac positis actione & defensione quasi forensibus, nostra scelera, quoniam defendi non possunt, ostendit iusto Dei iudicio condemnari. Quis hoc non moueatur? præsertim si, quod facit Moses, etiam pœnarum genera depingantur.
units.tr: Truly, it is well and wisely advised by Solomon, if we obey his most faithful and loving admonitions, when he says: "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom." For just as even the most fierce horse can be held in check and steered, so one who is led by some reverence and respect for the divine power can easily be kept from thinking, saying or doing evil. Conversely, as a horse with its bridle loosed can scarcely or never be restrained, so one whom no fear of God strikes must inevitably be swept by the force of his desires into every kind of wickedness. For this reason Moses, throughout this whole book and especially in this Song, in order to strike fear of the divine power into us, supports and heightens all God's precepts with great, weighty and powerful reasons. And, setting out the case and its defence as if in a court of law, he shows that our crimes, since they cannot be defended, are condemned by the just judgment of God. Who would not be moved by this? Especially if, as Moses also does, the kinds of punishment are portrayed.

units.la: Sed ut terrent ac reuocant hæc à malo: sic ad Deum reuocant atq; inuitant, quæ in epi-logo huius cantici commonstrantur, Dei clementia & iustitia. Clementiæ est iusto iudicio percussos, si resipiscant, sanare: iustitiæ verò pœna talionis ulcisci iniurias suis illatas. Quod ut plenius intelligatur Moses canticum hoc primum enumeratione, deinceps consolatione claudit.
units.tr: But just as these things terrify us and call us back from evil, so the mercy and justice of God, which are shown in the epilogue of this Song, call us back to God and invite us. It belongs to mercy to heal those struck by a just judgment, if they repent; it belongs to justice to avenge the wrongs done to him by the punishment of retaliation. So that this may be understood more fully, Moses closes this Song first with an enumeration and then with consolation.

units.la: Ac primum antedicta sic repetit & enumerat: Videte igitur quod ego, ego inquam ipse, & non est Deus præter me, &c. Quod perinde est ac si dicat: ex eo quod ex Ægypto vos eduxi, in deserto conseruaui, tum multis & varijs bonis auxi: ac rursus huius fortunæ splendore & lautitijs elatos, ad idola gentium conuersos, mihi rebelles factos sub iugum iterum misi, bonis omnibus exui, commeritis pœnis castigaui: certè facilè fuit vobis colligere, eum me Deum esse, qui possit unus & vita donare & vita indignos in mortem præcipitare, eadem vul-nera cum instigere, tum sanare: nec esse adeò sapientem & potentem qui me possit à proposito suscepto& hoc consilio vel retrahere vel impedire, quenquam. Magnum quiddam, hoc est, atque id quidem si timorem Dei nullum incutiat, nihil est aliud quo permoueare.
units.tr: And first he repeats and enumerates what has been said: See now that I, even I, am he, and there is no god beside me, etc. This is just as if he were saying: "Because I led you out of Egypt, preserved you in the desert, and then increased you with many and various goods; and because, when you were lifted up by the splendour and luxury of this prosperity, you turned to the idols of the nations and became rebellious against me, I sent you again under the yoke, stripped you of all your goods, and chastised you with the punishments you deserved. Surely it was easy for you to gather that I am the God who alone can both give life and cast into death those unworthy of life, who can both inflict the same wounds and heal them; and that there is no one so wise or powerful who can call me back or hinder me from the purpose and plan I have undertaken." This is a great matter, and if it does not strike fear of God, nothing else can move us.

units.la: Igitur singula consideres. 1. Videte igitur. Id est, quæ cum ita facta sint & demonstrata, vos animis vestris inite rationem: & quid ex Dei natura atque factis, quid item ex natura atque factis vestris, quid denique ex cognito atque explorato vobis Dei iudicio disci queat, dispicite. En præceptorem fidelem Moses, qui nos eius discipulos officij nostri diligenter admoneat. Velut enim industrii discipuli est quid quoque die fecerit, didicerit, profecerit, quomodo diem triuerit sese examinare, ut errores diei prioris emendet insequentis diligentia: sic hominis in schola Christi intrantis erit quomodo quoque die sese gesserit, peccati quid commiserit, recti quid fecerit abs se requirere & rationem vitæ poscere. Videbit inde qualem Deum senserit, Dei beneficiis quomodo ipse responderit: quid laude quid vituperio dignum fecerit. Sanè si fierent & priuatim & publicè eiusmodi examina, videret quisq; quos fructus luxuriæ quos contra parsimoniæ: quos pietatis, quos rursus impietatis haberet: tum etiam quid se deceret intelligeret.
units.tr: Consider then each point separately. (1.) "See now." That is: since these things have been done and shown in this way, bring your minds to bear on them, and examine what can be learned from the nature and deeds of God, what likewise from your own nature and deeds, and finally from the judgment of God known and tested by you. Here is Moses as a faithful teacher, who carefully reminds us of our duty as his disciples. For just as it belongs to a diligent pupil to examine himself each day as to what he has learned, what progress he has made, and how he has spent the day, so that by careful attention he may correct the errors of the previous day in the one that follows, so it belongs to a man entering the school of Christ to ask of himself each day how he has conducted himself, what sin he has committed, what good he has done, and to demand an account of his life. From this he will see what kind of God he has perceived, how he himself has responded to God's benefits, and what he has done that is worthy of praise or blame. Indeed, if such examinations were made both privately and publicly, each person would see what fruits of luxury he had and, on the other hand, of thrift; what fruits of piety and again of impiety; and then he would also understand what befits him.

units.la: 2. Quod ego, videlicet Deus Israel. Qui dicitur alibi, ut Exod.3.5.7. Deus Hebræorum: alibi, ut apparens Mosi, Deus Abraham, Isaac, Iacob: alibi, ut in Decalogo, qui te eduxi de terra Ægypti: alibi, ut Dan.6. Deus Danielis: alibi, ut Actor.4. Deus patrum nostrorum. Ex quo po-test intelligi quem Dei loco habere debeamus: qui videlicet suam in nobis procreandis conseruandisque potentiam & bonitatem testatus est.
units.tr: (2.) "That I, namely the God of Israel." He is called in other places the God of the Hebrews (Exod. 3.5.7); elsewhere, appearing to Moses, the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; elsewhere, in the Decalogue, "who brought you out of the land of Egypt"; elsewhere, the God of Daniel (Dan. 6); elsewhere, the God of our fathers (Acts 4). From this it can be understood whom we ought to hold in the place of God: namely, him who has borne witness to his power and goodness in creating and preserving us.

units.la: 3. Ego inquam[?], & non est alius præter me, &c. Videlicet, vita, salus, patrocinium. En ut salus velit adorari, inuocari, coli: ut fit zelotes & auersetur idola, deos alienos, humanorum auxiliorum fiduciam, itemque in opibus & viribus & consilijs nostris quam ponimus spem: sed omnem in se conuersam velit hominis mentem & fiduciam. Quod cum omnes eius mini-stri ipseque etiam vnigenitus filius cognitum habuerint: nos ad ipsum inuitarunt.
units.tr: (3.) I, I say, and there is no other beside me, etc. That is: life, salvation, protection. Behold how he wishes to be worshipped, invoked and honoured as the Saviour; how he is jealous and turns away from idols, strange gods, and the trust in human help, and likewise the hope we place in our riches, strength and counsels; but he wishes the whole mind and trust of man to be turned toward himself. Since all his ministers, and his only-begotten Son himself, have known this, they have invited us to him.

units.la: At inquit Antichristus, homini peccatori non patet aditus ad Deum: & opus est aliquo internuncio. En tibi inquam Christum aduocatum, Deut.18. Esa.53. Rom.8.1. Tim.2.1. Ioh.2. Qui Deus est & homo, is ad se vocat omnes Matthæi 11. Tum ad eum pater etiam nos re-mittit. mittit Matthæi 3.17. Cur igitur vel Israelitæ, vel gentiles, vel papistæ Diuos & Diuorum si-mulachra, Deos aut Deorum imagines coluere: cum ad vnum Deum per Christum con-tendendum esset? Atque hæc non in Diuorum contumeliam dicimus: sed volumus vt suus Christo honos sit saluus.
units.tr: But Antichrist says that there is no open access for a sinful man to God, and that some intermediary is needed. Behold, I tell you, Christ as advocate (Deut. 18; Isa. 53; Rom. 8.1; 1 Tim. 2.1; John 2). He who is God and man calls all to himself (Matt. 11). Then the Father also sends us back to him (Matt. 3.17). Why then did the Israelites, or the Gentiles, or the Papists worship the saints and the images of the saints, gods or images of gods, when they ought to have strained toward the one God through Christ? And we do not say this to insult the saints; rather we wish that Christ's honour remain whole.

units.la: Simulachra Paulus dicit esse nulla: & id bene & verè exponit Alexandrinus ille Clemens docens, nec Deum qui sit incorporea substantia: nec animam, quæ & ipsa non sit obiecta sensibus illis externis: nec organa siue membra corporum, quę vitalem in se vim habent effingi posse: vnde vanum esse quicquid eiusmodi rerum simulatur.
units.tr: Paul says that images are nothing, and that Clement of Alexandria rightly and truly explains this, teaching that God is not a corporeal substance, nor is the soul, which is itself not an object of those external senses, nor can the organs or members of bodies, which have a vital force in themselves, be fashioned; hence whatever is simulated of such things is vain.

units.la: Iam in suis ipsius vel suorum opibus aut potentia spem ponere, & idipsum est à Deo ad seipsum deficere: ac quia charitas simul & in Deum pietas hac extingui solent, est idololatriæ pessimum genus. Existimant enim illi se vicinum habere in marsupio: & quem negli-gunt proxima panegyri rustica rursus reperturos. Quid hoc aliud est, quàm se Deum facere nullius indigum, sui indigos omnes homines? Idem esto de reliquis rebus iudicium, in quibus maior est quàm in Deo spes collocata.
units.tr: Now to place hope in one's own riches or power, or in those of one's friends, is also to fall away from God to oneself; and since charity and piety toward God are commonly extinguished by this, it is the worst kind of idolatry. For such men think they have a neighbour in their purse, and that they will find again the one they neglect at the nearest rural fair. What is this other than to make oneself a God who needs nothing, and to make all other men needy? Let the judgment be the same concerning the other things in which hope is placed more than in God.

units.la: 4. Occido & viuifico. Quæ sunt indicia diuinæ potentiæ. Homo enim occidit quidem sed in vitam non restituit: spoliat non autem ditat. At Deus vtrunque potest, quod in aerum nis & miserijs in primis est obseruandum. Versaris in summa paupertate: id accidisse diuini-tus arbitrator: ad illum conuertere: is te, si volet, ditare potest: vt Abrahamum abductum à suis inter exteros auxit opibus, Iobem bonis & amicis expoliatum vtrisque iterum donauit, Dauidem in exilium actum & reduxit & ad regnum euexit, Solomonem & quam optabat sapientia, & quas non expetebat opibus donauit.
units.tr: 4. I kill and I make alive. These are signs of divine power. For man indeed kills, but does not restore to life; he strips, but does not enrich. But God can do both, which is especially to be observed in troubles and miseries. If you are in the deepest poverty, consider that this has happened by divine appointment, and turn to him; he, if he will, can enrich you, as he increased Abraham, led away from his own people among strangers, with wealth; as he gave back to Job, stripped of his goods and friends, both again; as he brought back David, driven into exile, and raised him to the kingdom; and as he gave Solomon both the wisdom he desired and the riches he did not seek.

units.la: Versaris in periculo, id euenisse non sine Dei prouidentia scito: is te eruet ad se conuersum velut Iacobum ab Esauo: Dauidem ab leone, vrso, Goliatho, Saule, Philistæis, Absolone.
units.tr: You are in danger? Know that this has not happened without the providence of God. He will rescue you, if you turn to him, as he rescued Jacob from Esau, David from the lion, the bear, Goliath, Saul, the Philistines and Absalom.

units.la: Laboras morbo: recordare Deum esse eum qui te percusserit & sanare possit, vt Iobem, Mariam Mosis sororem, Ezechiam, Nahamanum Syrum, & alios. Est mors præ-foribus: recordare Deum esse & mortis & vitæ dominum, qui tibi quam misit auferre mortem potest. Exempla sunt & argumenta quibus spem robores[?] in Iobe, in Ezechiele, in euangelio, in Paulo, denique in veritate Christianæ fidei.
units.tr: You are suffering from sickness? Remember that God is the one who struck you and is able to heal you, as he did Job, Miriam the sister of Moses, Hezekiah, Naaman the Syrian, and others. Death is at the door? Remember that God is the Lord of both death and life, and that he can take away the death he has sent you. There are examples and arguments by which you may strengthen your hope: in Job, in Ezekiel, in the Gospel, in Paul, and finally in the truth of the Christian faith.

units.la: Contra si bonis abundes, ne efferare: ne si stes postea cadas. Deus est qui vulnerat, nec est qui possit eripere. Non illius manus effugerunt Sodomitæ, Cananæi, Philistæi, Iudæi, Romani. Non suum Samsoni robur, sua Solomoni sapientia, sua Nabuchodonozori potentia, sua Absoloni forma, suæ Croeso diuitiæ profuere contra Deum: hæc omnia cesserunt illi po-tentissimo.
units.tr: On the other hand, if you abound in goods, do not become proud, lest, if you stand now, you fall afterwards. It is God who wounds, and there is none who can rescue. The Sodomites, the Canaanites, the Philistines, the Jews and the Romans did not escape his hand. Samson's strength, Solomon's wisdom, Nebuchadnezzar's power, Absalom's beauty and Croesus's riches did not avail against God: all these yielded to that most powerful one.

units.la: Consolatur autem ad hunc modum. Quoniam sublata manu mea in cælum, &c. Quibus verbis consolationem sic instituit suam, vt & ad faciendam fidem argumenta solida afferat: & opem se laturum reuera monstret. Vt fidem faciat iuramento se obstringit. Quod enim manus in cælum leuat id iurantis est. Iam vero licet omnes Dei promissiones tanti apud nos ponderis esse debeant, vt de illis dubitare nefas sit: tamen vt ne quid desit earum, quæ ad faciendam fidem pertinent, rerum: iuramento, qui[?] ipsa fides est & veritas Deus nobis cauet. Et iurat per seipsum Hebr. 6. Psal. 109. Iurat enim vnigenitus eius filius magna bona pollicens in euangelio. Quare si iuranti homini creditur quanto magis est iuranti Deo credendum?
units.tr: He consoles us in this way: Since I have lifted my hand to heaven, &c. In these words he so arranges his consolation that he both brings forward solid arguments to make us believe and shows that he will truly bring help. To make his word believed, he binds himself by an oath. For lifting the hand to heaven belongs to one who swears. Now, although all God's promises ought to carry such weight with us that it is wrong to doubt them, yet, so that nothing is lacking of those things which pertain to producing faith, God guards us with an oath, he who is faith itself and truth. And he swears by himself (Heb. 6; Ps. 109). For his only-begotten Son also swears, promising great goods in the Gospel. Therefore, if a man is believed when he swears, how much more must God be believed when he swears?

units.la: Et Deus per semetipsum iurans exemplo est per quem sit iurandum, per vnum ipsum videlicet.
units.tr: And God, swearing by himself, is the example by which one ought to swear, namely by the one himself.

units.la: Iam vt ostendat se reuera iuuare velle dicit: 1. Cum exacuero fulgorem gladij mei, &c. Le-ge talionis acturum se cum hostibus sui populi minatur. Vt Ægyptios in ijs ipsis aquis suffocauit in quas Hebrei infantes erant expositi. Saulem Deus satanæ consilijs permisit cui maluerat aures antea quam Samueli præbere. Hamanum eo patibulo suspendi fecit quod Iudeis ipse pararat, vt lentis ignibus & cruciatibus fideles afficiebat Antiochus: sic lentis ipse vermium morsibus putrescens atq; fœtens confectus est. Sic qui veritatis euangelici infamiæ maculis aspergunt ijs ipsis illi verè notantur.
units.tr: Now, to show that he really wishes to help, he says: 1. When I sharpen the lightning of my sword, &c. He threatens that he will deal with the enemies of his people by the law of retaliation. Thus he drowned the Egyptians in the very waters in which the Hebrew infants had been exposed. God permitted Saul to the counsels of Satan, to whom he had previously preferred to give his ear rather than to Samuel. He caused Haman to be hanged on the gibbet which he himself had prepared for the Jews; as Antiochus afflicted the faithful with slow fires and torments, so he himself, rotting and stinking from the slow bites of worms, was worn away. So too those who besmirch the gospel of truth with the stains of infamy are truly marked by these very things.

units.la: 2. Imbuam sagittas sanguine: hoc est, ceu sanguisugas bestiolas hostili sanguine tela mea re-plebo, vt ebria decidant.
units.tr: 2. I will make my arrows drunk with blood: that is, as bloodsucking little beasts, I will fill my weapons with hostile blood, so that they fall down drunk.

units.la: 3. Propter sanguinem occisorum: En sanguinis martyrū ad Deum clamores. Abel, Naboth, Rahel, Stephanus, alij, deniq; sanguis omnium prophetarum.
units.tr: 3. Because of the blood of the slain: Behold the cries of the blood of the martyrs to God: Abel, Naboth, Rachel, Stephen and others, and finally the blood of all the prophets.

units.la: Hoc ipso tandem claudit, quod ostendit sic eum vlcisci suos, vt illis ipsis sit propitius. Id faxit in Christo, Amen.
units.tr: He closes with this, which shows that he thus avenges his people in such a way that he is propitious to those very same people. May he grant this in Christ, Amen.

units.la: SERMO XIIII.
units.tr: SERMON XIV.

units.la: 44 Veniens itaq; Moses, loquutus est omnia verbo cantici huius in auribus populi, ipse & Iofua filius Nun.
units.tr: 44 So Moses came and spoke all the words of this song in the ears of the people, he and Joshua the son of Nun.

units.la: 45 Et quum finem fecisset Moses, quumq; locutus esset omnia verba hæc ad v-niuersum populum Israel:
units.tr: When Moses had made an end of speaking, and had spoken all these words to all Israel,

units.la: 46 Dixit ad eos: Ponite cor vestrum ad omnia verba, quæ ego testificor vobis hodie, præcipietisq; ea filijs vestris, vt custodiant & faciant omnia verba legis huius.
units.tr: he said to them: Set your hearts upon all the words which I testify to you this day, and charge your children to observe and do all the words of this law.

units.la: 47 Nec sit vobis hic sermo vanus, quoniam est vita vestra, & in hoc verbo prolongabitis dies super terram, ad quam vos transmisso Iordane proficiscimini, vt possideatis eam.
units.tr: For it is no vain thing for you; it is your life, and through this word you shall prolong your days upon the land to which you go over the Jordan to possess it.

units.la: 48 Et loquutus est Dominus ad Mosem eodem die in hac verba.
units.tr: And the Lord spoke to Moses the same day, saying:

units.la: 49 Ascende montem istum Abarim, montem Nebo, qui est in terra Moab, è regione Iericho, & contemplare terram Chanaan, quam do filijs Israel possiden-dam.
units.tr: Go up this mountain, Abarim, Mount Nebo, which is in the land of Moab, over against Jericho, and behold the land of Canaan, which I give to the children of Israel for a possession.

units.la: 50 Et morere in monte quem tu ascendis, colligerisq; ad populos tuos, quemad-modum mortuus est Aharon frater tuus in monte Hor, & colleƈtus est ad populos suos.
units.tr: And die in the mountain which you ascend, and be gathered to your people, as Aaron your brother died in Mount Hor and was gathered to his people.

units.la: 51 Eò quod præuaricati estis contra me in medio filiorū Israel iuxta aquas Me-ruba in Kades deserti Zin, quod me non sanctificastis in medio filiorum Israel.
units.tr: Because you trespassed against me among the children of Israel at the waters of Meribah in Kadesh, in the wilderness of Zin, because you did not sanctify me among the children of Israel.

units.la: 52 E regione spectabis terram hanc, illuc autem non venies, ad terram inquam quam ego do filijs Israel.
units.tr: You shall see the land before you, but you shall not go there, into the land which I give to the children of Israel.

units.la: CVm omnis fidelis & syncera admonitio in finem eum fiat, vt qui monetur se moueri, & à damno impendente custodiri patiatur: sanè vt admonitio multum vi ium[?] atq; authoritatis habeat necesse est: nempe, vt in optimam partem accipiatur, & ad repellenda quæ time-bantur mala conuertatur.
units.tr: Since every faithful and sincere admonition is made with a view to its end, so that the one who is warned is moved and allows himself to be guarded from impending harm, an admonition must necessarily have much force and authority: namely, that it be taken in good part and turned to the repelling of the evils that were feared.

units.la: Qua de causa Moses hanc suam instar cantici factam admonitionem, & rationibus alijs commendat, & mortis suæ prædictione efficacem facit.
units.tr: For this reason Moses commends this admonition of his, made in the manner of a song, both by other considerations, and makes it effective by the prediction of his death.

units.la: Ex quo nobis indicari potest, de verbo Dei, quod nostri nos subinde admonet idè prorsus esse statuendum. Et certè facilè est videre, quibus rebus sua verbo Dei concilietur autho-ritas & efficacia, si in his Mosis verbis primum cantici huius commendationem, ac deinceps mortis Mosis prædictionem æstimemus.
units.tr: From this it can be shown concerning the Word of God, which our ministers admonish us from time to time, that it must be judged in exactly this way. And indeed it is easy to see by what means the authority and efficacy of God's Word are secured, if in these words of Moses we consider first the commendation of this song, and then the prediction of Moses' death.

units.la: Canticum autem hoc ipso commendat, quod adhibito Iofua successore quasi legem pro-mulgat, ac docet alta mente reponendum, liberis atq; posteris omnibus inculcandum, mini-meq; contemnendum: sed vt saluberrimum Dei immortalis munus accipiendum. Est enim reuera donū Dei, quod mala repellit, ac feruat. Vnde & Martianus Iurecos. in l.ij.ff.de ll. defi-nit legem esse donum Deorum, quod prohibeat homines malis.
units.tr: The song itself commends itself by this: that with Joshua as successor it promulgates, as it were, a law, and teaches that it is to be laid up deep in the mind, impressed upon children and all posterity, and not to be despised in any way, but received as the most wholesome gift of the immortal God. For it is truly a gift of God, which wards off evils and preserves us from them. Whence also the jurist Martianus, in l. 2 ff. de legibus, defines law as a gift of the gods, which keeps men from evils.

units.la: Ex quo nobis etiam est perspicuum quo loco verbum Domini, quod nos assiduis moni-tionibus, fidis & prudentibus consilijs, paternis & amantibus castigationibus à malis retra-hit, habeamus: ac rursus quibus rebus atq; artibus ei sua concilietur ac retineatur autho-ritas. Nam quod Moses venisse in concionem, & adhibito Iofua verba cantici huius in auribus po-puli protulisse dicitur: id, quoniam solennem, grauem, cum authoritate coniunctam ceu le-gis magnæ promulgationem refert, argumento est ad stabiliendam diuini verbi autho-ritatem pertinere, vt & eius administri in illo cognoscendo pariter atque proponendo quanta possunt maxima fide & diligentia & constantia laborent: tum vt eam ad rem pij magistratus auxilia sua ferant.
units.tr: From this we also have it clear what place we should give to the Word of the Lord, which by constant admonitions, faithful and prudent counsels, and fatherly and loving corrections draws us back from evils; and again, by what means and arts its authority is secured and maintained. For the fact that Moses is said to have come into the assembly and, with Joshua present, to have delivered the words of this song in the ears of the people, since it reports a solemn and weighty promulgation, joined with authority as of a great law, is an argument that it pertains to establishing the authority of the divine Word that its ministers labour, with all the greatest faithfulness, diligence and constancy they can, both in knowing it and in setting it forth; and then that godly magistrates bring their aid to this end.

units.la: Siue enim administri quod profiteri docereq; & propagare debent, ipsi negligant & osci tanter praedicent euangelium: siue magistratus quam promouere & tueri debent ipsi cón- temptui habeant; proculcent, & fastidiant religionem & pietatem: certe plebs quae princi- pum exempla susp icit ac sequitur, aut nihili faciet aut etiam e medio sublatam volet. Quo fit vt etiam docendo parum proficiatur: idq; testes sunt historiae. Cum penes Helium sacerdo- tem summa sacerdotij pariter & reipublicae potestas effet: atque ipse quidem remissus filij ve- ro petulantes & in plebem iniurij, tum etiam religionis contemptores: ea pestis in plebem omnis serpebat. Samuel postea strenuè quidem munus obibat suum, hocq; ipso tantum hoc efficiebat vt non deesset quibus Saulis tyrannis displiceret: sed quia Saul illius monita re- spuebat, plaerique regis exemplum imitati sic euadebant mali; vt eos Philistinorum incursio- nibus vlciscereatur Dominus. Dauide religionem tuente & habente qui illam praedicarent mystis atque vatibus florebat regnum Israel: at Achabo & Isabella reluctantibus & Baal ado- rantibus, vtut fortes Helias & Abdias essent, tamen perparum efficiebatur: quanquam & sui diuino verbo fructus essent, 7000. hominum qui nullum honorem Baali habuissent. Vbi Io- sias, Ezechias, alij; pij reges prophetas adiuuarunt, tunc bene cesit praedicatio. Christus do- cebat magna vi & gravitate, & vt Matthaeus ait, cap. 7. ὡς ἐξεσίαν ἔχων, eoq; effecit multum: sed plus effectum esset, si magistratus non tanto pere repugnassent. A postoli magna atq; etiam admirabili parrhisia docebant, eoq; multum efficiebant: sed longe plus effecissent non impe- dito per magistratus cursu euangelij. At vbi Constantinus Magnus se coniunxit episcopis iam Christiana ecclesia florere coepit & crescere. Ac nostra memoria cum ministri seduli, gra- ues, constantes essent in docendo: magistratus prouidi, acres, fortes in tuendo & promouen- do euangelio: sane magnos in abroganda superstitione, domanda libidine progressus vidi- mus; iam cum vtriq; sunt remissiores videmus, vt in Aegyptum & respiciamus & redeamus. Quamobrem est enitendum vt in suum hi incumbant officium, ac coniunctis copijs popu- lum admoneant quanta possunt gravitate & constantia.
units.tr: For if the ministers themselves neglect what they ought to profess, teach and spread, and preach the gospel coldly and carelessly; or if the magistrates hold in contempt what they ought to advance and protect, and trample upon and despise religion and piety, then surely the common people, who take up and follow the examples of their rulers, will either make nothing of it or even want it removed from the midst. Hence it comes about that little is gained even by teaching, and histories bear witness to this. When under the priest Eli the highest priestly and civil power lay together, he himself was lax, his sons were wanton and wronged the people, and moreover were despisers of religion, and that plague crept over the whole people. Afterwards Samuel discharged his office vigorously, but by this alone effected only this, that there were not lacking those who disliked Saul's tyranny; yet because Saul rejected his admonitions, many, imitating the king's example, became so wicked that the Lord avenged them by the incursions of the Philistines. While David protected religion and had those who preached it, the kingdom of Israel flourished with seers and prophets; but with Ahab and Jezebel resisting and adoring Baal, however brave Elijah and Obadiah were, very little was accomplished, although even so there were fruits of the divine Word: seven thousand men who had paid no honour to Baal. Where Josiah, Hezekiah and other godly kings aided the prophets, then preaching prospered. Christ taught with great power and gravity, and as Matthew says in ch. 7, [ὡς ἐξουσίαν ἔχων] as one having authority, and so effected much; but more would have been effected if the magistrates had not so strongly resisted. The apostles taught with great and even admirable boldness of speech, and so effected much; but far more would they have effected had the course of the gospel not been impeded by the magistrates. But when Constantine the Great joined himself to the bishops, the Christian Church began to flourish and grow. And in our own memory, while the ministers were diligent, grave and constant in teaching, and the magistrates provident, keen and brave in protecting and advancing the gospel, we saw indeed great progress in abolishing superstition and taming lust; now that both have become more remiss, we see that we look back and return to Egypt. Wherefore it must be striven for that these men apply themselves to their own duty, and, with their forces joined, admonish the people with all the gravity and constancy they can muster.

units.la: 2. Quod ait, Reponite in cor vestrum omnia verba, quae ego testificor hodie: eo ipso docet ver- bum Domini tum demum audiri magno cum fructu, quando homines ad eius studium ani- mos aduertunt. Quemadmodum enim in omni artium genere nihil proficimus animo in eam non conuerso: ita verbum Domini parum momenti vel ad instruendum vel ad emen- dandum nos afferre potest, si id animis audiamus parum attentis. Docet hoc Matth. 13. Domi- nus in seminantis parabola: cum dicit aues devorare femen, quod in viam cecidit. Solet enim fieri, vt animus rerfertus alienis à religione curis ac cogitationibus, & aegrè femen illud ad- mittat & admissum nequeat retinere. Quamobrem ponenda sunt ob oculos exempla fideli- um. Maria conseruabat omnia in corde suo de Christo dicta & facta miracula, Luc. 2. Et Matt. 9. Turbae viso circa paralyticum miraculo sunt Iesum admiratae & animo contemplatae. In quo nostri seculi negligentia supina cernitur, quando gaudio, moerore, metu, ira, spe moue- mur: at diuinis admonitionibus non item. Etiam audientes non audimus, inde nobis accidit, vt multum praedicando nihil proficiatur.
units.tr: 2. When he says, Set in your heart all the words which I testify to you today, he thereby teaches that the Word of the Lord is then heard with great fruit when men turn their minds to its study. For just as in every kind of art we make no progress unless the mind is turned to it, so the Word of the Lord can bring little weight either to instruct or to amend us if we hear it with minds that are little attentive. The Lord teaches this in the parable of the sower, Matt. 13, when he says that the birds devour the seed which fell by the way. For it often happens that a mind crowded with cares and thoughts alien to religion scarcely admits that seed, and, once admitted, cannot retain it. Therefore examples of the faithful must be set before our eyes. Mary kept all the things said about Christ and the miracles done by him in her heart, Luke 2. And in Matt. 9, the crowds, seeing the miracle around the paralytic, marvelled at Jesus and contemplated it in their minds. In this the supine negligence of our age is seen: we are moved by joy, sorrow, fear, anger and hope, but not so by divine admonitions. Even when we hear, we do not listen; hence it happens to us that by preaching much, little is gained.

units.la: 3. Praecipietis filijs vestris, vt custodiant, & faciant omnia verba legis huius. Ex quo disci- mus curam educationis puerilis nobis imponi, videlicet vt liberos adducamus Domino. In liberis spes est posteritatis: quam si velis habere bonam oportet nec sumptibus parcas, nec laboribus. Nam quo semel est imbuta recens seruabit odorem testa diu. Quamobrem stultè suis prospiciunt liberis, qui diuitijs cumulandis magis incumbunt, quàm illis pie & liberali- ter instituendis. Ac qui magistratus necessarijs ad scholas parcunt sumptibus, ij suspicionem de se praebent eos esse animis ad turpe lucrum, quàm ad pietatem & probitatem propensio- ribus. Quare vt spes possit esse retinenda veritatis euangelicae; quae nunc est iuuentus rectè educetur necesse est.
units.tr: 3. You shall charge your children to observe and do all the words of this law. From this we learn that the care of children's education is laid upon us, namely that we bring our children up to the Lord. In children lies the hope of posterity; if you wish to have it good, you must spare neither expense nor labour. For a jar, once newly imbued, will keep its odour a long time. Therefore they foolishly provide for their children who devote themselves rather to piling up riches than to bringing them up piously and generously. And those magistrates who grudge the necessary expense for schools give cause to suspect that they are more inclined in mind to base gain than to piety and uprightness. Therefore, if the hope of retaining evangelical truth is to remain, the youth who are now growing up must be rightly educated.

units.la: 4. Nec sit vobis sermo vanus. Quo contemptum repellit: hic enim est perniciosissimus.
