Vnde satan despectis nominibus pfafforum, haereticorum, impostorum verbum in contem- ptum vocat, vt eo nos gladio spoliet, quo solo possemus ipsum expugnare. Qua enim alia re icortatio, adulterium, vsurae, aliaq; scelera coercentur? at illa vt conseruet, haec patrantibus persuadet esse Luteranas, haereticas, pfafforum nenias & anilia terriculamenta, satan. Ex quo pestilens illa subsecuta est pertinacia, qua Pharao, Saul, Iudaei, impij omnes perierę.
units.tr: 4. Nor let my words be idle. Scorn would drive out the word, and that is the most destructive thing of all. For this reason Satan, by holding up to contempt the names of priests, heretics and impostors, calls the Word itself into contempt, so that he may strip us of the one sword with which alone we could overcome him. For by what other means are fornication, adultery, usury and other crimes restrained? Yet Satan persuades those who commit them to keep those things, and to call the Word Lutheran, heretical, priestly trifles and old wives' bugbears. From this came that deadly obstinacy in which Pharaoh, Saul, the Jews and all the wicked perished.

units.la: 5.Vt agnoscamus ingenteis,quas ex his percipimus vtilitates.Vita,inquit,est vestra,et hoc studio vitam longaevam atq; faustam consequemini. Vitæ cibum esse verbum Domini supra cap. 8.Matth.4.Joh.5.discimus.Fœlix eius esse, & faustum studium cum Judæorum tum vero nostra ipsorum fortuna docet.Ut enim Israelitas olim sic nos hæc studia ditarunt.Quamobrem nihil est neq; honestius neq; utilius,quàm eniti,ut verbum Dei ritè prædicetur:diligenter audiatur & teneatur:posteris inculcetur:summo sit in honore & precio pro ipsa habeatur fœlicitate & vita.
units.tr: 5. That we may recognise the great benefits we receive from these things: "It is your life," he says, "and by this diligence you will attain a long and prosperous life." We learn from chapter 8 of this book, and from Matthew 4 and John 5, that the word of the Lord is our food of life. The fortune of the Jews and our own fortune alike teach how happy and prosperous this diligence is. For these pursuits enriched the Israelites of old, and they enrich us in the same way. Therefore nothing is more honourable or more useful than to strive that the word of God be rightly preached, diligently heard and held fast, passed on to posterity, held in the highest honour and value, and regarded as the very source of our happiness and life.

units.la: Atq; his quidem argumentis & si satis sit hæc admonitio commendata,ac dictum sapien-ti sat fit:tamen ut magis animi nostri moveantur hic est adiecta mortis eius prædictio. Quæ & ipsa adhibitis omnibus circumstantijs: ut tempore, ut loco, ut re, ut causa pulchrè explicatur.
units.tr: Although this admonition has been commended to us by these arguments, and although it is enough, and a word to the wise is sufficient, nevertheless, so that our minds may be moved more, the prediction of his death is added here. This too is set out well, with all its circumstances: the time, the place, the matter and the cause.

units.la: Tempus est dies is quo hoc quicquid fuit agebatur:quod est indicio Mosem usque ad ultimum vitæ diem in vinea Domini laborasse. Unde & exemplum est omnibus,ut ne cito defi-ciant in opere Domini:sed quoad hac vita frui datur, tantisper etiam opera sui frui patiantur ecclesiam.
units.tr: The time is the day on which all this was being done. That Moses laboured in the vineyard of the Lord until the last day of his life is evidence of this. Hence he is also an example to all, that they should not quickly grow weary in the work of the Lord, but, for as long as life is granted them, should let the Church enjoy the labour of their work as well.

units.la: Locus est è regione Hierichuntis,quasi pro foribus terræ promissæ:Unde eam ipsam vi-dere detur,non autem intrare. Typus legis est,qua ducimur ad limina terræ beatæ:sed Chri-stus,quem Josua repræsentat,in ipsam terram,hoc est,cœleste regnum introducit.
units.tr: The place lies opposite Jericho, as it were at the doors of the promised land, so that he seems to see that land but not to enter it. The law is a type by which we are led to the threshold of the blessed land; but Christ, whom Joshua represents, brings us into the land itself, that is, into the heavenly kingdom.

units.la: Mors ipsa sic prædicitur, ut & Mose & nobis omnibus hæc eius prædictio consolationi possit esse.Nam primum dicitur ei moriendum esse.Quod omnibus est de se statuendum:hic enim finis omnes quanticunq; simus manet.Adamo dictum hoc est, & omnes usu cognoverunt homines.Bene enim Horatius:Pallida mors æquo pulsat pede pauperum tabernas:regumq; turres,ô beatè Sesti.
units.tr: Death itself is foretold in such a way that this prediction of it may be a comfort both to Moses and to all of us. For first he is told that he must die. Every one of us must reckon with this for himself, for this end awaits us all, however great we are. This was said to Adam, and all men have learned it by experience. For Horace says well: "Pale death knocks with impartial foot at the huts of the poor and the towers of kings, O fortunate Sestius."

units.la: Quod si memoria teneamus , & metu nos magno & cupidine prava nos levabimus. Τὸ δὲ φοβεῖσθαι τὸν θάνατον. Ἀλλ᾽ ὁ πολὺς[?] πᾶσιν δὲ ἡμῖν τὰ τ᾽ ὀφείλεται παθεῖν, inquit Aristophanes.Et certè stultum est id timere,quod est ferendum,nec potest evitari. Cupidi-tas autem,quæ est aliàs insatiabilis,nisi mortis,quæ bonis omnibus hominem exuit,memo-ria domatur,vix reprimi posse credendum est. Nec dubium est quin si illum vitæ finem animis comprehensum teneremus:multo minus esset ambitionis,auaritiæ,libidinis.
units.tr: If we keep this in memory, we shall relieve ourselves of great fear and of wicked desire. "To fear death" [Τὸ δὲ φοβεῖσθαι τὸν θάνατον]. "But it is owed by all of us to suffer" [Ἀλλ᾽ ὁ πολὺς ... τὰ τ᾽ ὀφείλεται παθεῖν], says Aristophanes. And certainly it is foolish to fear what must be endured and cannot be avoided. Desire, which is otherwise insatiable, can hardly be believed to be restrained unless by the memory of death, which strips every man of all his goods. And there is no doubt that if we kept that end of life fixed in our minds, there would be much less ambition, avarice and lust.

units.la: Deinceps dicit,Colligeris ad patres tuos,siue populus tuus:hoc est,mortuus non peribis, ve-rum in illorum qui mundo periisse videbantur consortium assumere. Est ergo mors aliud nihil nisi quædam transmigratio,eorum videlicet,qui hinc ad superos ascendunt. Agnoverunt hoc etiam prisci Græci & Romani, unde & eorum qui mortui fuerant maiorum consortium expetebant:ac si quidem licuisset id optare, noluissent repuerascere. Quanto magis hac spe Christiani sese recreabunt ut meliore & certiore?
units.tr: Next he says, "You shall be gathered to your fathers, or to your people." That is, you will not perish when dead, but will be taken into the fellowship of those who seemed to have perished from the world. Death, then, is nothing other than a kind of migration of those who depart hence to the heavenly ones. The ancient Greeks and Romans also recognised this, and so they sought the fellowship of their dead forebears; and indeed, had it been permitted to wish it, they would not have wished to become young again. How much more, then, will Christians be refreshed by this hope, as by a better and surer one?

units.la: Posthæc addit exemplum fratris:quemadmodum Aharon frater tuus,inquit.Id documen-to est Enochi, Heliæ, sanctorum omnium in primisq; Christi Domini exempla nobis esse ad consolationem proposita.Ut enim illi mortui cum Deo omnibusq; cœlitibus vivunt,& æter-nam & beatam vitam:sic nos ad illos olim transferemur.
units.tr: After this he adds the example of a brother: "as Aaron your brother," he says. This is evidence that the examples of Enoch, Elijah and all the saints, and above all of Christ the Lord, are set before us for our consolation. For just as those who have died live with God and all the inhabitants of heaven, in eternal and blessed life, so we too shall one day be transferred to them.

units.la: Causa mortis peccatum demonstratur:quia, inquit, non sanctificastis me coram hominibus Israel.Id peccatum extat Exod.20.Nu.20. Quod autem hoc ipsum ei refricatur id argumen-to est referre nostra quandoq; & in malis ac miseriis in primis, ut peccata perpetrata recola-mus.Primum enim agnoscens in malo se versari,quod sua sibi culpa accersiuit:non potest id impatienter ferre,cum quem accuset præter se solum habeat neminem.Ut qui luxu,crapula, negligentia pauperiem sibi accersiuerint: qui intemperata victus ratione & crapula quotidia-na morbum: qui turpis lucri causa libertatem cum seruitute commutarint : quem præter se solos accusabunt? Sed & hac ipsa de causa prodest peccatorum suorum meminisse, ut iuxta meminerimus quantopere divina gratia egeamus.
units.tr: The cause of death is shown to be sin: "because," he says, "you did not sanctify me before the people of Israel." This sin is recorded in Exodus 20 and Numbers 20. That this same sin is brought back to him is an argument that we too should sometimes call our sins to mind, especially in our evils and miseries. For when a man first recognises that he is in evil, which he has brought upon himself by his own fault, he cannot bear it patiently, since he has no one to accuse but himself. Those who have brought poverty upon themselves through luxury, drunkenness and negligence, who have brought disease upon themselves by intemperate diet and gluttony, who have exchanged their liberty for slavery for the sake of base gain: whom will they accuse but themselves? But remembering one's sins is useful also for this reason, that we may remember how greatly we need the grace of God.

units.la: Sed in exemplo Mosis intelligimus,quàm graue sit peccare principes in civitate viros.Illorum enim exempla multos offendunt,& post se trahunt. Igitur admonitiones divinas gratis animis amplectamur, teneamus,servemus,ut ab his malis custoditi conservemur,per Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum, Amen.
units.tr: But in the example of Moses we understand how grave a thing it is for the leading men of a state to sin. For their examples offend many and draw them after them. Let us therefore embrace the divine admonitions gladly, hold them fast and keep them, so that, guarded from these evils, we may be preserved, through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT XXXIII. SERMO XV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXIII. SERMON XV.

units.la: Hæc est benedictio, qua benedixit vir Dei filios Israel ante mortem suam.
units.tr: This is the blessing with which the man of God blessed the children of Israel before his death.

units.la: 2 Dixitq; Dominus de Sina venit, & ortus est eis ex Seir, illuxit de mõte Pharan, & venit cum decem millibus sanctorum, à dextris ignea lex adeos.
units.tr: 2 And he said: The Lord came from Sinai, and rose up for them from Seir; he shone forth from Mount Paran, and came with ten thousands of saints; from his right hand a fiery law for them.

units.la: 3 Et vehementer diligit populos, omnes sancti eius sunt in manibus tuis. Et ipsi inserti intra pedes tuos, accipient ex verbis tuis.
units.tr: 3 Indeed he loves the peoples; all his saints are in your hands. And they, placed at your feet, shall receive of your words.

units.la: 4 Legem præcepit nobis Moses hæreditariam cœtui Iacob.
units.tr: 4 Moses commanded us a law, an inheritance for the assembly of Jacob.

units.la: 5 Et fuit æquabilis rex, quum se congregarent capita populi simulque tribus Israel.
units.tr: 5 And he was a righteous king, when the heads of the people gathered together, and the tribes of Israel at once.

units.la: HOC agit Diuus Moses, ut hanc suam ad Israelitas ultimam concionem populo vehementer etiam atq; etiam probet, eumq; ad divinę legis studium permoveat: quâ de causa fit in conclusione subinde vehementior, seq; ipsum subinde magis ac magis superat. Nec dubium est quin omnium animos perculerit, quod suam eis mortem prædixit: alios in suum perinde ac iam mortuus esset locum substituit, & in publicum produxit: tum quasi, quod factum nondum fuerat, legem oblitos & transgressos, atq; ob hoc ipsum malis maximis immersos verbis castigat & in viam reducit.
units.tr: Moses here has a clear aim: he wants to commend this last address of his to the Israelites most earnestly, and to stir them up to the study of the divine law. For this reason the conclusion grows ever more vehement, and he rises above himself more and more. There is no doubt that it struck everyone when he foretold his own death. He set others in his place, as though he were already dead, and presented them in public. Then, as if the people had already forgotten the law and transgressed it, and had therefore been plunged into the greatest evils, he rebukes them with words and brings them back to the right way.

units.la: Sed omnium maximum est, quod quasi discedens illis valedicit, faustaq; omnia precatur. Quod hoc cap. describitur. Ac primum eorum quæ precatur bonorum fontem Deum monstrat: tum bona ipsa singillatim singula commemorat: deniq; eorum etiam usum atq; fructum laudibus vehit.
units.tr: Yet the greatest thing is that, as if taking leave of them on his departure, he prays for every blessing for them. This is what the chapter describes. First he shows God to be the fountain of the good things he prays for; then he recounts the blessings themselves one by one; and finally he praises their use and fruit.

units.la: Sed de eorum patre seu origine, seu fonte dicit in præsentia. Ac quoniam Deus ; qui bo-norum omnium princeps causa atque unicus fons est; hæc ipsa per secundas causas sive re-bus apta atque idonea media mortalibus impertire solet : hic de benedictionis administro prius dicit, deinceps de eius authore Deo.
units.tr: But he speaks here of their Father, or origin, or fountain. Since God, who is the prince and sole cause of all good things, is accustomed to bestow these very things on mortals through secondary causes, or through means suited and fitted to the things themselves, Moses speaks first of the minister of the blessing and afterwards of its author, God.

units.la: Ac de eius administro sic dicit: Hæc est benedictio, qua benedixit Moses vir Dei filios Israel ante mortem suam. Expende quas adhibet circumstantias. Res ipsa est benedicere: ea actio bi-sariam est consideranda, videlicet quoad ministrum sive hominem, tum quoad Deum. Quam enim & verbis imprecatur & optat minister, eam Deus revera confert pacem, salutem, fœ-licitatem.
units.tr: About its minister he speaks thus: This is the blessing with which Moses, the man of God, blessed the children of Israel before his death. Weigh the circumstances he includes. The thing itself is to bless. This action must be considered in two ways: with regard to the minister or man, and with regard to God. For what the minister invokes and wishes in words, God in truth bestows: peace, salvation, happiness.

units.la: Externæ eius, quæ fieri per ministrum solet, Num.6. extat forma. Leuit.6. usus. Ea Chri-sti simulachrum seu typus omnis fuit. Ut enim sacrificia atque adeò sacerdotium Aharonis, sic illius etiam benedictio Christi sacrificium atq; benedictionem repræsentarunt. Ac quem-admodum Aharonici illius sacerdotij papistis usitata imitatio vana est, sic benedictio illorum est inutilis & vana.
units.tr: The external form of this, which is usually performed by a minister, is found in Num. 6, and its use in Lev. 6. This was a likeness or type of Christ in every way. For just as the sacrifices and indeed the priesthood of Aaron, so also his blessing represented the sacrifice and blessing of Christ. And just as the imitation of that Aaronic priesthood practised by the Papists is vain, so their blessing is useless and vain.

units.la: Sed sunt præterea benedictionum aliæ priscis usitatæ formæ. Primum enim decedentes suis quàm optimè consulebant, ac de rebus necessarijs prospiciebant, ut Isaac, Iacob, Noe, &c. Dein prædicabant suis bona ac mala quæ prouidebant euentura: quasiq; cometæ & signa & prodigia sic illi suos terrebant & monebant. Postremo, ut precentur faulta[?] quæq; hominibus divinitus obtingere: quo propensum in suos animum testabantur. Eius generis etiam hæc ipsa Mosis est benedictio.
units.tr: There are also other forms of blessing customary among the ancients. First, those who were departing took the best care of their own, and provided for necessary matters, as Isaac, Jacob, Noah, and others did. Next, they foretold to their people the good and evil things they foresaw would happen, and so, like comets, signs, and portents, they frightened and warned them. Lastly, they prayed that all good things might fall to men from God, thereby showing their favourable disposition towards their own. Moses' blessing here is also of this kind.

units.la: Iam si personas consideres, qui benedicit est Moses vir Dei: bonum & laudabile epithe-ton. Ut enim vir Belial hominem effrenem, & vir sanguinum virum cruentum, truculentum, sanguine humano madentem significat: sic vir Dei virum divinum, spiritu Dei gubernari so-litum refert.
units.tr: Now if you consider the persons, the one who blesses is Moses, the man of God: a good and praiseworthy epithet. For just as "a man of Belial" signifies an unbridled man, and "a man of blood" a bloody, savage man steeped in human blood, so "a man of God" refers to a divine man, one accustomed to be governed by the Spirit of God.

units.la: Israelitæ vero sunt ij, quibus benedicitur.
units.tr: Those who are blessed are the Israelites.

units.la: Tempus est ut Hebræus habet, ante faciem mortis: quasi in conspectu mortis, iam iam moriturus.
units.tr: The time is, as the Hebrew has it, "before the face of death": as if in the sight of death, about to die at any moment.

units.la: Ex quibus circumstantijs, si illæ singillatim singulæ ponderentur, utilissima documenta peti possunt. In re enim ipsa cernimus omnes bonorum thesauros penes Deum esse reposi-tos: nec aliunde peti debere, nec alibi inveniri: ac stultissimos esse qui illa alibi quærunt.
units.tr: If these circumstances are weighed one by one, very useful lessons can be drawn from them. For in the matter itself we see that all the treasures of good things are laid up with God, that they must not be sought elsewhere nor found elsewhere, and that those who seek them elsewhere are most foolish.

units.la: In personis autē obseruabimus. 1. Nunquam deesse Deo ministros p e r quos benefaciat ac quandoq; mulieres rebus maximis adhiberi.
units.tr: In the persons we shall observe the following. 1. God never lacks ministers through whom he does good, and sometimes women are employed in the greatest matters.

units.la: 2. Etsi per homines aliasq; creaturas beneficia conferat in nos: tamen ideo non ab illo ad has esse deficiendum. Quis enim Mosem ideo adoraret, quod minister benedictionis fuit[?] Ex eo certè nata est omnis idololatria gentilium atq; etiam nostra. Quemadmodū enim sol quia terram calore suo fœcundat est adoratus: sic apostoli, quia per eos multa magnaq; in nos beneficia Deus contulit, adorati sunt.
units.tr: 2. Although God bestows benefits on us through men and other creatures, we must not on that account turn from him to them. For who would worship Moses merely because he was the minister of the blessing? Certainly all the idolatry of the Gentiles, and indeed of our own people, has arisen from exactly this. For just as the sun was worshipped because it makes the earth fruitful with its heat, so the apostles were worshipped because God bestowed many great benefits on us through them.

units.la: 3. Quod utile fit habere in populo multos Dei viros, hoc est pios homines, per quos to-ti populo fausta omnia accedant: contra multitudine impunitorum nebulonum maledictio populis accersitur.
units.tr: 3. It is useful to have in the people many men of God, that is, godly men, through whom every good thing comes to the whole people. On the other hand, a curse is brought upon peoples by a multitude of unpunished scoundrels.

units.la: 4. Bonorum virorum est non inuidere, male precari, malefacere: sed fauere, benedicere, benefacere. Satan maledicit non spiritus Dei. Ipsi vero Israelitæ quoniam benedictionem admittunt, exemplo sunt ut ne sana ac nobis salutaria consilia respuamus, siquidem velimus benedictionem accipere. Multi sunt pauperes quia frugalitatem suadentibus non obtemperant: eodemq; modo in cæteris.
units.tr: 4. It is the mark of good men not to envy, not to curse, not to do evil, but to favour, to bless, and to do good. Satan curses; the Spirit of God does not. But the Israelites themselves, since they accept the blessing, are an example to us that, if we want to receive a blessing, we must not reject sound counsels that are salutary for us. Many are poor because they do not obey those who urge thrift; and the same holds in other matters.

units.la: At tempus ipsum ostendit Mosem ita fauisse saluti publicæ, ut cum eam beneficijs amplius juvare non posset, benedictione tamen promoueret.
units.tr: Yet the time itself shows that Moses so served the public welfare that, since he could no longer help it by benefits, he nevertheless promoted it by blessing.

units.la: Quod optimatibus omnibus exemplo est, ut quoquo possint modo remp. semper juvent.
units.tr: This is an example for all the nobles, that they should always, in whatever way they can, help the commonwealth.

units.la: Sed & typus in hoc est aliquis. Ut enim mortuo Mose benedictio accepta est: sic abroga-ta lege Christus benedicens missus est: tum quemadmodum Moses jamjam à suis abiturus benedicit eis sic Christus ascensurus ad cœlos suis quoq; benedicit.
units.tr: There is also some type in this. For just as the blessing was received after Moses' death, so after the law was abrogated Christ was sent as the one who blesses. Then, just as Moses, about to leave his people, blesses them, so Christ, about to ascend to heaven, also blesses his own.

units.la: Sed quoniam dubium non est, quin bonis abundet Deus, & habeat penes se quicquid bonorum est uspiam: de eo vero controuersum fuerit, an vero nobis hæc etiam velit impertire: quo de multi dubitarunt quibus videlicet illius non satis est explorata bonitas & gratia. Jam quoniam ea bonorum in nos ex Deo profluentium causa est: Moses eam suis Israelitis probat, idq; ex anteactis. Ac primum tres vicinos montes appellat: Sina, Seir, Pharan: quorum nomina res isthic gestas in memoriam renouent, eoq; doceant propensam esse planeq; paternam Dei in suos voluntatem. In Sina legem dedit Dominus: in Seir remedium contra venenatos serpentes, itemq; insignem de Oge & Seone regibus victoriam: in Pharan coturnicibus pauit.
units.tr: But since there is no doubt that God abounds in good things, and holds within himself whatever good exists anywhere, the question is whether he also wills to bestow these things upon us. On this point many have doubted, namely those who have not sufficiently explored his goodness and grace. Now since this is the cause of the good things flowing to us from God, Moses proves it to his Israelites, and he does so from past events. First he names three neighbouring mountains: Sinai, Seir, and Paran. Their names are meant to recall to memory the events that took place there, and so to teach that God's will towards his people is favourable and truly fatherly. On Sinai the Lord gave the law; at Seir came the remedy against the poisonous serpents, and also the notable victory over the kings Og and Sihon; at Paran he fed them with quails.

units.la: Sed verba, quibus hoc proponit paulo altius sunt consideranda. Dominus, inquit, de Sina venit. En legem siue verbum suum afferens venire dicitur, quasiq; suos invisere. Legem enim promulgabat in Sina Dominus: id hic veniendi verbo exponit Moses: ostendens claram verbi divini prædicationem aliud nihil esse, quàm Dei ad nos descensum atque adventum. Ergo Deum adventantem respuunt, qui illius verbum fastidiunt: illum contra digne excipiunt qui magno verbum eius habent in precio. Et dicit Dominus se verbum suum exercentibus ipsum interesse, ut Matth.18. Ubi sunt duo vel tres congregati in nomine meo, ibi sum in medio eorum. Omnium autem clarissimè dicit hoc Dominus Johan.14. Si quis diliget me sermonem meum servabit, & pater meus diliget eum, & ad eum veniemus & mansionem apud eum faciemus. Ex quibus intelligitur verbi divini prædicationem apertam, synceram, iustam certissimum esse Domini ad nos adventus indicium. Rectè ergo Moses promulgatæ legis admonituros suos dicit Dominum de Sina venisse.
units.tr: But the words by which he sets this forth must be considered a little more deeply. The Lord, he says, came from Sinai. Behold, he is said to come, bringing his law or word, as if to visit his people. For the Lord proclaimed the law on Sinai; Moses here explains this by the word "came," showing that the clear preaching of the divine word is nothing other than God's descent and coming to us. Therefore they reject God when he comes who despise his word, while they receive him worthily who hold his word in high esteem. And the Lord says that he himself is present to those who exercise his word, as in Matt. 18: "Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them." Most clearly of all the Lord says this in John 14: "If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him." From these passages it is understood that the open, pure, and just preaching of the divine word is the most certain sign of the Lord's coming to us. Rightly, then, Moses says that the Lord came from Sinai to his people, to admonish them concerning the law that had been promulgated.

units.la: Sed addit: Et ortus est eis ex Seir: illuxit de monte Pharan. Verbum Hebræum [illegible, ~4 letters] de sole primum, tum de quouis lumine dicitur: sed verè proprieq; de sole dici solet: at verbum [illegible, ~4 letters] splenduit & in Hiphil, ut hic, & Psalm. 50. Deus [illegible, ~5 letters] splenduit, seu ut exponit Rabi Dauid Kimhi, manifestauit se in splendore suo & gloria.
units.tr: But he adds: And there arose for them from Seir; he shone forth from Mount Paran. The Hebrew verb is used first of the sun and then of any light, though it is said most properly and characteristically of the sun. The same verb is also used in the Hiphil form, as here, and in Psalm 50, where God shone forth. Rabbi David Kimhi explains it as God making himself manifest in his splendour and glory.

units.la: Atque his quidem verbis Moses usus est, ut mysteria sublimia quoquo modo notaret. Nam & oriri Christum huius mundi lucem, & illucescere Dei verbum, quo pelluntur tenebræ, Scripturæ passim docent. Nam quia secus verbi divini viam merè sunt tenebræ, sanè lumen oriri dicitur ijs, qui tenebris his exempti veritatis cognitione sunt assecuti. Unde & ministri verbi lumina appellantur. Ortus autem sol est Israelitis tunc aliquo modo, quando serpens æneus palo suspensus Christum mundi solem figurauit. Unde & Paulus Tito scribens, cap.2. dicit: Illuxit enim gratia Dei salutifera omnibus hominibus, erudiens nos, ut abnega-ta, &c. Ut & Matth.4. Esaiæ de lucis huius ortu testimonium adducitur ex 9. cap. Populus, inquit, qui sedebat in tenebris & umbra mortis, vidit lucem magnam: & qui sedebant in regione & umbra mortis lux orta est eis.
units.tr: Moses used these words to indicate, in some way, sublime mysteries. For the Scriptures everywhere teach that Christ arises as the light of this world and that the Word of God dawns, by which darkness is dispelled. Apart from the way of the divine Word there is only darkness, so light is said to rise for those who, freed from that darkness, have attained knowledge of the truth. Hence the ministers of the Word are also called lights. Moreover, the sun rose for the Israelites in some sense when the bronze serpent, hung on a pole, prefigured Christ, the sun of the world. Hence Paul, writing to Titus in chapter 2, says: "For the saving grace of God has appeared to all men, teaching us, that denying..." and so on. Likewise in Matthew 4 a testimony about the rising of this light is cited from Isaiah, chapter 9: "The people who sat in darkness and in the shadow of death have seen a great light; and for those who sat in the region and shadow of death, a light has risen."

units.la: Obseruandum est etiam quòd dicit: Cum decem millibus sanctorum.Id enim & Stephanus Actor.7. exponit, dicens Iudæos accepisse legem per dispositionem angelorum: & Paul.Gal. 3.dicens,Legem ordinatam per angelos,per manus intercessoris. In quo duo possunt notari. Vnum,quod in comparatione ministrorum veteris testamenti videmus quanto præstantius lege fit euangelium.Mose enim & angelis vsus legem: Christo vero vnigenito & angelis & apostolis adhibitis euangelium attulit. QuodHebræis scribens apostolus hoc ipso docet quod dicit: Deus olim multifariam,&c.
units.tr: It should also be observed that he says: with ten thousands of saints. Stephen in Acts 7 explains this, saying that the Jews received the law by the disposition of angels; and Paul in Galatians 3 says that the law was ordained by angels, through the hand of a mediator. Two things may be noted here. First, comparing the ministers of the Old Testament, we see how much more excellent the gospel is than the law: Moses used angels in giving the law, but Christ, the only-begotten, brought the gospel with angels and apostles in attendance. The apostle, writing to the Hebrews, teaches this by what he says: "God, who spoke in many portions and in many ways at various times..." Second, the one who once was mediator, who showed the distinction between us and God and brought the law, is now Christ the mediator, who removes that distinction and, by satisfying for us, takes away the law's demands.

units.la: Alterum quod olim mediator erat,qui quod inter nos & Deum est discrimen monstrans legem attulit: iam Christus mediator est, qui discrimen illud aufert legi latæ pro nobis satisfaciens.
units.tr: The other point is this: the one who was once mediator, who brought the law and showed the separation between us and God, is now Christ the mediator, who removes that separation by satisfying for us the law that was given.

units.la: Porro ignis natura quæ diuinæ legis vis sit ostendit,quod instar ignis illustret, accendat, consumat omnia:quæ etiam eius vtilitas,nempe vt ad omnem vsum vitæ conducat. Vnde & Spiritus sanctus,Actor.2.igneis linguis adumbratur.
units.tr: Moreover, the nature of fire shows what the force of the divine law is: as fire lights up, kindles and consumes everything, so the law does the same. Its usefulness is also of this kind, namely that it serves every use of life. Hence the Holy Spirit is also foreshadowed by tongues of fire (Acts 2).

units.la: His Moses illud addit:Vehementer diligit populos: omnes sancti eius sunt in manibus tuis.Quæ Chaldæus sic profert:Etiam diligit tribus,omnes sanctos suos de domo Israel.Procopius dicit omnes sanctos patri Deo ceu ministros à dextris astare. Alijs videtur Christum hic conuersus alloqui tanquam mediatorem & sanctorum patronum:ad cuius pedes sedeant angeli,discipuli,verbi ministri vt discant ab eo. Quo videtur etiam Diuus Augustinus in lib.de eff. diui.respicere.Sed & Christus profitetur in Euangelio sibi creditos esse suos,seq; dare operam vt ne quos perdat.Videntur enallagæ personarum hic esse. Sed suum illum amorem eo ipso declarauit quod & legem & gubernatorem quasi regem dedit.
units.tr: Moses adds this: Yes, he loves the peoples; all his holy ones are in your hands. The Chaldee paraphrast renders it thus: "Yes, he loves the tribes; all his holy ones of the house of Israel." Procopius says that all the saints stand at the right hand of God the Father as his ministers. To others it seems that Christ, to whom the speech is turned here, is addressed as mediator and patron of the saints, at whose feet the angels, the disciples and the ministers of the Word sit, that they may learn from him. Saint Augustine also seems to look to this in his book on the effects of the divine. But Christ too declares in the Gospel that his own have been entrusted to him, and that he takes care that he lose none of them. There seem to be shifts of persons here. Yet he has declared that love precisely by giving both the law and a governor, as it were a king.

units.la: Ex quibus omnibus intelligimus à Deo per manum Christi mediatoris benedictionem expectandam esse; Amen.
units.tr: From all these things we understand that a blessing is to be looked for from God through the hand of Christ the mediator. Amen.

units.la: SERMO XVI.
units.tr: Sermon XVI.

units.la: 6 Viuat Ruben, & non moriatur, sintq; homines illius pauci numero.
units.tr: 6 Let Reuben live, and not die, and let his men be few in number.

units.la: 7 Et hæc est (benedictio) Iudæ: & dixit: Audi Domine vocem Iudæ, & ad populum suum duc eum: manus eius multæ erunt ei, tu opem ei feres contra hostes suos.
units.tr: 7 And this is the blessing of Judah. He said: Hear, Lord, the voice of Judah, and bring him to his people. His hands shall be many for him; you will bring him help against his enemies.

units.la: 8 Et ad Leui sic dixit: Thummim[?] sunt tui, tui sunt Urim, viroque qui in te pius fuerit, quem tentasti in Massa, & quem ad contentionem provocasti ad aquas Meriba.
units.tr: 8 And to Levi he said: Your Thummim and your Urim belong to your godly man, whom you tested at Massah and with whom you contended at the waters of Meribah.

units.la: 9 Qui dicit patri suo & matri suæ: Non vidi eum, & fratres suos non cognouit, neq; filios suos agnoscit: quoniam custodierunt eloquia tua, & fœdus tuum tenaciter seruabunt.
units.tr: 9 He who says to his father and his mother, "I have not seen him," and does not acknowledge his brothers or know his own sons, because they have kept your words and will firmly observe your covenant.

units.la: 10 Docebunt ipsum Iacob iudicia tua, & Israelem legem tuam. Incensum ponent coram naribus tuis, & holocaustum in aram tuam.
units.tr: 10 They shall teach Jacob your judgments and Israel your law. They shall put incense before your nostrils and whole burnt offerings on your altar.

units.la: 11 Benedic Domine opibus eius, & opus manuum eius tibi probetur. Contunde lumbos eorum qui insurgunt aduersus eum, & eorum qui odio eum habent ne insurgant.
units.tr: 11 Lord, bless his substance, and accept the work of his hands. Break the loins of those who rise up against him and of those who hate him, that they may not rise again.

units.la: 12 Ad Beniamin dixit: Dilectus Domini securus habitabit, iuxta eum inumbrabit super eum tota die, & inter humeros eius habitabit.
units.tr: 12 To Benjamin he said: The beloved of the Lord shall dwell in safety; he shall cover him all day long, and he shall dwell between his shoulders.

units.la: Postquam Diuus Moses ijs, quæ nuper explicata sunt, verbis indicauit, unde & per quæ media bonorum omne genus Israelitis fit expectandum: iam sigillatim singulis sua pecuniaria bona commemorat. In quo non minus atque in toto hoc Mosis officio,totaq; eius rep. Christi typus insignis est. Vt enim hic per Mosem ceu mediatorem,sic per Christum passim fidelibus mediatorem vnicum à patre cœlesti omnia bona conferuntur: vtq; singulorum cuiuram Moses habet,sic in ecclesia nemo tam abiectus est, qui non sit in manu curaq; Iesu Christi. Iam vero sua singulis beneficia commemorat.
units.tr: After Moses, the divine, had shown in the words just explained whence and by what means the Israelites are to expect every kind of good, he now recounts to each tribe in turn its own temporal blessings. In this, no less than in the whole of this office of Moses, his entire government is a notable type of Christ. For just as here blessings come through Moses as mediator, so through Christ, the one mediator, all good things are conferred on the faithful by the heavenly Father; and just as Moses has the care of each individual, so in the Church no one is so lowly as not to be in the hand and care of Jesus Christ. Now he recounts the particular benefits of each.

units.la: Ac quanquam Simeonem in his silentio prætereat, quem eis benedicens Iacob Leuitis annumerauit:tamen vniuersorum communi benedictione, quam & in principio & in fine ponit, satis superq; docet eodem numero ipsum quoq; comprehendi minimeq; excludendum.
units.tr: And although he passes over Simeon in silence, whom Jacob numbered among the Levites when he blessed them, yet by the common blessing of all, which he places both at the beginning and at the end, he teaches abundantly enough that Simeon too is included in that number and by no means excluded.

units.la: Quæ cum sic se habeant sitq; Simeon neq; hic recensitus,neq; hinc exclusus:eorum sane typus videtur esse,qui cum sint ignobiles,tamen ideo nō sunt prorsus miseri,verum aliquem in ecclesia locū habent. Eius igitur exemplo discimus de mundana hac gloria non magnopere laborare, verum ante omnia,quod Christus consulit regnum Dei quærere,ea spe freti non defutura cætera. Communi salute potiri sufficiat.
units.tr: Since these things stand thus, and Simeon is neither listed here nor excluded from here, he seems to be a type of those who, though of humble status, are nevertheless not utterly wretched, but have a place in the Church. From his example we learn not to labour greatly over this worldly glory, but above all, since Christ bids us seek the kingdom of God, to be confident that the rest will not be lacking. It is enough to share in the common salvation.

units.la: Ruben viuat, & non moriatur, sintq; homines eius numero pauci. Quibus verbis hic Iacobi patriarchae de eadem tribu iam olim dicta verba adseuerat. Erat autem Ruben primogenitus Israelis filiorum, eaq; dignitate propter inceftu pollutum patris thorum exciderat. Gene.35. res gesta, at peccati poena Gen.49. recitatur. Dicit enim Iacob, Ruben primogenitus meus es tu: robur quidem meum: at principium doloris mei. Tunc Iacobus primogenitura ad Ephraim & Manasse filios Iosephi transfert, regnum ad Iuda, sacerdotium & primogenita ad Leui, vt est i. Para.5.
units.tr: "Let Reuben live, and not die, and let his men be few in number." In these words Jacob the patriarch confirms what he had already said long before about the same tribe. Reuben was the firstborn of Israel's sons, but because of his incest, which defiled his father's bed, he had lost that dignity. The deed is recounted at Gen. 35, and the punishment for his sin at Gen. 49. For Jacob says: "Reuben, you are my firstborn, my might, and the beginning of my sorrow." Then Jacob transferred the birthright to Ephraim and Manasseh, the sons of Joseph, the kingdom to Judah, and the priesthood and the firstborn rights to Levi, as is recorded at 1 Chron. 5.

units.la: Caeterum quod hic dicit eius homines fore numero paucos: quae poena peccati est: ab Iacobo dicitur: ne excellas caeteros. Sed consolatur eum Moses dicens, viuat & non moriatur.
units.tr: But that he says here that his men will be few in number, which is the punishment for sin, Jacob says so that he should not surpass the others. Moses, however, consoles him, saying: "Let him live and not die."

units.la: In quo videmus vt fit natura mortalium misera: qui non possunt ijs quae habent bonis vti, quin illis ipsis excidant. Vt enim ille peccato tetraq; libidine sua se dignitate & felicitate exuit, sic etiamnum videmus honoribus, opibus, amicis sua se culpa multos priuare.
units.tr: In this we see how wretched the condition of mortals is: they cannot enjoy the goods they have without losing them. For just as he, by his sin and foul lust, stripped himself of dignity and happiness, so even now we see many people deprived of honours, wealth and friends through their own fault.

units.la: Quod autem eorum peccatum sic punitur vt non omnis extirpetur familia: bonitatis diuinae est indicium clarissimum: quippe qui non perdit sed coercet & humiliat vt adducat ad poenitentiam ac conseruet. Exemplis abundant sacrae literae. Sed & praeclarus in Ruben typus est Iudeorum: quorum & si plerique sint reprobi, multi tamen in Christo sunt electi & coseruantur.
units.tr: That his sin is punished in such a way that his whole family is not rooted out is a most clear sign of divine goodness, since God destroys not but restrains and humbles in order to lead to repentance and preserve. Holy Scripture abounds in examples. But Reuben is also a notable type of the Jews: although most of them are reprobate, many are nonetheless elect in Christ and preserved.

units.la: Iuda. Et hoc est, inquit, benedictio Iudae: audi Domine vocem Iudae, &c. Quibus conuersus ad Deum precatur ei tribui laudem & dignitatem, qua reliquis post praeluxit. Ac quae Gen. 49. pluribus verbis Iacob narrat, ea paucis hic exponit. Et certe strenua & in acie prima semper fuit: secundus gentis Israelis rex Dauid ea natus fuit, potentissimus, & pietate clarus & armis: itidem Solomon cum opibus tum sapientia toti terrarum orbi suspiciendus.
units.tr: "Judah." "And this," he says, "is the blessing of Judah: Hear, Lord, the voice of Judah," and so on. Turning to God, Moses prays that the praise and dignity which that tribe has shone with above the rest be granted to it. And what Jacob narrates in more words at Gen. 49, he sets out here in few. Indeed, Judah was always vigorous and in the front line. The second king of the Israelite nation, David, was born of it, most powerful, renowned for piety and arms; likewise Solomon, to be admired by the whole world both for his wealth and for his wisdom.

units.la: Vaticinatur autem hoc loco eos orraturos vt ab hostibus suis incolumes redirent. Quod Dauid saepissime, Iosaphat cum Ammonitis bellum gerens, Ezechias obsessus ab Assyrijs.
units.tr: Moreover, in this place he prophesies that they will fight so that they return unharmed from their enemies. This David did very often; Jehoshaphat did so when waging war with the Ammonites, and Hezekiah when besieged by the Assyrians.

units.la: Obseruandum est autem quod Iudaeis ceu beneficium promittitur fore, vt laboribus & molestijs exerceantur. Quippe quo euchantur ad gloriam.
units.tr: It must be noted, however, that it is promised to the Jews as a benefit that they will be exercised by labours and troubles. For by these they are trained for glory.

units.la: In quo disce primum, fortitudinem & laudem virtutis bellicae Dei donum esse: quam qui suis tribuunt viribus repugnantur. Dein victoriam in pietate & precibus potissimum esse post, sitam: vt in pugna cum Amalek, in Samariae, Bethuliae, Hierusalem obsidionibus. Postremo laboribus & molestijs exerceri mundo quidem malum, at Deo bonum videri. Veluti Cato nolebat dirutam Carthaginem ceu cotem virtutis Romanae. Sane & Heluetiae nostrae res ocio deteriores factae sunt.
units.tr: In this, learn first that courage and the praise of military virtue are a gift of God, and that those who ascribe them to their own strength are refuted. Next, that victory depends above all on piety and prayers, as in the battle with Amalek and in the sieges of Samaria, Bethulia and Jerusalem. Lastly, that to be exercised by labours and troubles seems an evil to the world, but a good to God. Thus Cato did not wish Carthage destroyed, regarding it as the whetstone of Roman virtue. Indeed, our own Helvetia has been made worse off by idleness.

units.la: Leui dicit vtcunq; multa, sed quae sacerdotij munus illi impositum pene spectent omnia. 1. Thumim et Vrim tui sunt. Quid ij sint, de eo sunt interpretes multae & variae sententiae: paucis sic habeto. Exod.28. Hosehen sacerdotis habuit Vrim & Thumim. Vrim sunt ignes: Thumim integri, perfecti, impolluti Hebraea lingua. Graeci reddiderunt Δήλωσιν καὶ ἀλήθειαν. Quo significabatur doctrinam claram & synceram penes sacerdotem oportere esse depositam.
units.tr: He says many things to Levi, however they may be arranged, but nearly all of them concern the office of the priesthood entrusted to him. (1) "Your Thummim and your Urim." What these are, interpreters hold many and various opinions; briefly, take it thus. The high priest Aaron's breastplate had the Urim and the Thummim (Exod. 28). The Urim are lights; the Thummim are whole, perfect, unblemished, in the Hebrew tongue. The Greeks rendered them as "declaration and truth" [δήλωσιν καὶ ἀλήθειαν]. By this was signified that clear and sincere teaching ought to be kept with the priest.

units.la: Sint illi custodes legis diuinae. Atq; huius quidem rei eo ipso admonebantur, quod ad pectus penderent splendentes gemmae & integrae.
units.tr: Let them be the guardians of the divine law. And they were reminded of this very thing by the fact that bright and flawless gems hung upon the breast.

units.la: 2. Viro qui in te pius, &c. Leui tentatus in Massa, murmurante populo praeclarum sese praestitit: in Cades rursus tentati ceciderunt: adeo nihil est integrum in humano ingenio. Et obseruandum est non tam virtutes quam vitia a spiritu sancto notari: nempe, vt ne nimium nobis ipsi tribuentes in peccata grauiora illabamur.
units.tr: (2) "To the man who is godly towards you," and so on. Levi, when tested at Massah, showed himself admirable while the people murmured; but at Kadesh those who were tested again fell. So nothing in the human mind is whole. And it must be noted that the Holy Spirit marks not so much virtues as vices, namely so that we, attributing too much to ourselves, may not slip into graver sins.

units.la: 3. Qui patri, &c. Commendatur in tribu Leui syncerum & incorruptum iudicium, quam do Mosi contra idololatras opem tulerunt nulla habita personarum ratione, seq; potius imperio diuino, quam suis affectibus accomodarunt. Sic Phinees Nu.25. zelo diuino ductus est.
units.tr: (3) "Who said to his father," and so on. The sincere and incorruptible judgment of the tribe of Levi is commended, which brought help to Moses against the idolaters, paying no regard to persons, and adapted themselves to the divine command rather than to their own feelings. So Phinehas was led by divine zeal (Num. 25).

units.la: 4. Docebunt iudicia & legem: quod est eorum officium potissimum.
units.tr: (4) "They shall teach judgments and law," which is above all their duty.

units.la: 5. Incensum ponent coram naribus tuis & holocaustum in aram tuam. Psal. Dirigatur oratio mea sicut incensum in conspectu tuo. Apoc. Et ascendit fumus incensorum de precibus sanctorum e manu angeli. Significat ascendens τὸ κυρὸν quod natura sit precum ad coelestem partem penetrare & ascendere: significat etiam odor suauis gratus naribus quam gratae sint Deo preces nostrae.
units.tr: (5) "They shall put incense before your nostrils and a whole burnt offering on your altar." Psalm: "Let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight." Revelation: "And the smoke of the incense rose from the prayers of the saints from the hand of the angel." The rising smoke signifies [τὸ κυρὸν] that the nature of prayers is to penetrate and ascend to the heavenly region; it also signifies, by its sweet odour, how pleasing our prayers are to God.

units.la: 6. Benedic Domine, &c. Orat vt ad conseruandum sacerdotium Leuitis opes & authoritatem concedat: quae res ad id in primis requiruntur officium. Propter multos, eosq; vehementes aduersarios.
units.tr: (6) "Bless, Lord," and so on. He prays that God grant the Levites wealth and authority for the preservation of the priesthood, which above all is required for that office, because of the many and fierce adversaries.

units.la: Beniamin dicit: Dilectus Domini, &c. Quibus illi pauca quidem, sed tria maxima bona precatur. Vnum, diuinam gratiam: vocat enim dilectum Domini: quod est non tam magnum quam quàm necessarium. Alterum, fortitudinem, qua aliquando sunt abusi Beniamitae. Tertium, templum scilicet Hierusalem: locum religioni destinatum.
units.tr: Benjamin says: "The beloved of the LORD, &c." With these words he prays for a few things, but for three very great blessings: first, the grace of God (for he calls him the beloved of the LORD, which is not so much great as it is necessary); second, strength, with which the Benjamites at times abused themselves; third, namely the temple at Jerusalem, the place set apart for religion.

units.la: Ex quibus discimus quae potissimum bona sint diuinitus expetenda. In Simeon vt pri-ma cura sit beatorum numero non excludi: in Ruben, vt poenas peccatorum patienter fera-mus, gauisi quod non pro eo ac fueramus meriti funditus extirpemus: in Iuda laudem virtu-tis bellicae Dei donum esse, victoriam pijs precibus diuinitus impetrari, sub cruce exerceri in bonis, non malis esse: in Leui doctrinam, pietatem, authoritatem, victum verbi diuini mini-stris esse necessaria: in Beniamin, diuinam gratiam, fortitudinem, religionem esse praecipua Dei beneficia. Oremus.
units.tr: From these things we learn which blessings above all are to be sought from God. In Simeon, that our first care should be not to be excluded from the number of the blessed; in Reuben, that we should patiently bear the punishments of sins, rejoicing that we have not been utterly uprooted as we deserved; in Judah, that praise for martial valour is a gift of God, that victory is obtained from God by pious prayers, and that to be exercised under the cross is a good thing and not an evil; in Levi, that teaching, piety, authority and sustenance from the divine Word are necessary for the ministers; in Benjamin, that the grace of God, strength and religion are the chief benefits of God. Let us pray.

units.la: SERMO XVII.
units.tr: SERMON XVII.

units.la: 13 Ad Iosephi[?] dixit, Benedicta est[?] à Domino terra eius à delicatissimis & dulcissimis fructibus cœli, à rore & ab abysso inferne cubante.
units.tr: 13 And of Joseph he said: Blessed of the LORD be his land, with the most precious fruits of heaven, with the dew, and with the deep that lies beneath.

units.la: 14 A delicatissimis & dulcissimis fructibus solis, & à delicatissimis & dulissimis fructibus mensium.
units.tr: 14 With the most precious fruits of the sun, and with the most precious and sweet fruits of the months.

units.la: 15 Et à capitibus montium orientalium, & à delicatissimis fructibus collium, qui iam olim fuerunt, à fructu delicatissimo terrae, & à copia eius.
units.tr: 15 And with the tops of the eastern mountains, and with the most precious fruits of the hills that have stood from of old, with the most precious fruit of the earth and its abundance.

units.la: 16 Et fauor habitantis in rubo, veniat in caput Ioseph, & in verticem Naza-rei inter fratres suos.
units.tr: 16 And let the favour of him who dwelt in the bush come upon the head of Joseph, and upon the crown of the Nazarite among his brothers.

units.la: 17 Decor eius vt primogeniti bouis illius, & cornua illius vt cornua vnicor-nis, quibus populos deturbabit pariter vsq; ad fines terrae: atq; haec sunt decem millia Ephraim, & ista millia Manasse.
units.tr: 17 His glory is like the firstborn of his bullock, and his horns are like the horns of a unicorn, with which he shall push the peoples together to the ends of the earth; and these are the ten thousands of Ephraim, and these are the thousands of Manasseh.

units.la: 18 Ad Zebulon ait: Latare Zebulon in exitu tuo, & Isachar in tabernaculis tuis.
units.tr: 18 Of Zebulun he said: Rejoice, Zebulun, in your going out, and Issachar in your tents.

units.la: 19 Populos ad montem vocabunt, vbi sacrificabunt sacrificia iustitiae, quoniam inundationem marium sugent[?], & reconditos thesauros arenae.
units.tr: 19 They shall call the peoples to the mountain, where they shall offer the sacrifices of righteousness; for they shall suck the abundance of the seas and the hidden treasures of the sand.

units.la: 20 Et ad Gad dixit: Benedictus qui dilatat Gad, vt leo moratur, qui lacerat brachium cum vertice.
units.tr: 20 And of Gad he said: Blessed is he who enlarges Gad; he dwells like a lion, and tears the arm together with the crown of the head.

units.la: 21 Primum sibi prospexit, quod illic essET portio legislatoris laqueati, & veniet cum principibus populi, & faciet iustitiam Domini, atq; iudicia eius cum Israele.
units.tr: 21 He provided the first part for himself, because there was the portion of the lawgiver, who was laid up; and he shall come with the leaders of the people, and he shall execute the justice of the LORD and his judgments with Israel.

units.la: 22 Ad Dan ait, Dan catulus leonis, desilit à Basan.
units.tr: 22 Of Dan he said: Dan is a lion's whelp, leaping forth from Bashan.

units.la: 23 Et ad Naphtali dixit: Naphtali satur est (diuino) beneplacito, atq; plenus benedictione Domini: occidentem & meridiem occupabit.
units.tr: 23 And of Naphtali he said: Naphtali is satisfied with the favour (of God), and full of the blessing of the LORD; he shall possess the west and the south.

units.la: 24 Ad Aser quoq; ait: Aser benedictus ob filios, gratus fratribus suis, in oleo tinget pedem suum. Ferrum & aes sub calceamentis tuis, & longaeuus eris in senectute tua.
units.tr: 24 Of Asher also he said: Asher is blessed above his sons, acceptable to his brothers, and he shall dip his foot in oil. Iron and brass shall be under your shoes, and you shall be long-lived in your old age.

units.la: COmmemorata quatuor tribuum benedictione Moses reliquis sua quoque fata refert. In quo speculo videmus quae quantaq; Dei sint in genus nostrum beneficia, quæq; ei de his debeantur gratiæ. Sed ad propositum.
units.tr: When Moses had recalled the blessing of the four tribes, he also relates his own fate to the rest. In this mirror we see what great benefits of God toward our race there are, and what thanks are owed to him for them. But back to our purpose.

units.la: Ephraim & Manasse Iosephi nomine coniunguntur: atq; his assignat tria bonorum genera: annonae copiam, diuinam gratiam, magnam vim ciuium atque incolarum. Annonae copiam ex soli fertilitate, aeris bona temperie, faustŏq; rerum omnium prouentu: quae sunt causae mediae. Dicit enim fructus de cœlo, rore; abysso: tum & sole & luna: dem collibus & vallibus.
units.tr: Ephraim and Manasseh are joined under the name of Joseph, and to them he assigns three kinds of good things: abundance of produce, divine grace, and a great strength of citizens and residents. The abundance of produce comes from the fertility of the soil, the good temperature of the air, and the prosperous yield of all things; these are the intermediate causes. For he speaks of fruits from heaven, dew, the deep, then also of the sun and moon, and of the hills and valleys.

units.la: Videmus igitur Deum & aeris & astrorum gubernatore esse, eaq; pro eo ac vult modo in vtilitatem, modo in salutem nostram conuertere. Iratus enim cœlum æneum, ferreum, durum præbet, vt Heliæ tempore, pro leni fuauiq; aura & pluuia: pruinam demittit pro rore: magnas siccitates quasique Phaetonteum incendium pro pluuia, placatus autem sole calido fœcundat interdiu, eademq; noctu lunæ frigidis humoribus humectat ac refrigerat.
units.tr: We see, therefore, that God is the governor both of the air and of the stars, and turns them to our benefit or our salvation, as he wills. For when angry, he makes the sky brass and iron, hard, as in the time of Elijah, instead of gentle and pleasant breezes and rain; he sends down hoarfrost instead of dew; he sends great droughts, almost a Phaethon-like fire, instead of rain; but when appeased, he warms the day with the hot sun, and at night he moistens and cools the earth with the cold moisture of the moon.

units.la: Hic existunt iræ pariter & beneuolentiæ Domini indicia. Si tempestates sint solito aspe-riores vulgus existimat id inde euenire, quod forsan aliquis mortem sibi consciuerit: quin cōgites hoc illius mali causam esse quod turpiter, impudenter, obstinatè peccando multi sese eunt perditum. Diuinam gratiam hoc ipso promittit quod dicit: Fauor habitantis in rubo venit in vertice? Quæ verba sunt altissima mente reponenda. Nam quod Deum quasi quadam visus periphrasi in rubo habitantem vocat, id argumento est Dei afflictis & miseris potissimum accurrere solere: quando rebus Israeliticis in Ægypto desperatis, & Mosi quasi inde exulanti Deus in rubo apparet. Qua de re est Exod. 3. Ibi in rubo visus Mosi Deus opem promittit, & officium educendi populum imponit. Itaque cum videamus Deum [illegible, ~8 letters] apparere solere miseris:nos afflicti bene de eo speremus, quod sit finem tragœdijs nostris impositurus.
units.tr: Here are the signs of the anger and the goodwill of the Lord alike. If the storms are harsher than usual, the common people suppose this happens because perhaps someone has committed suicide; rather, consider that the cause of this evil is that many have ruined themselves by sinning shamefully, shamelessly and stubbornly. He promises divine grace by this very thing when he says: The favour of him who dwelt in the bush comes upon the head? These words are to be laid up with the highest mind. For that he calls God, as it were by a certain periphrasis, the one who dwells in the bush, is a proof that God is accustomed especially to run to the afflicted and wretched, when the affairs of Israel in Egypt were despaired of, and God appeared in the bush to Moses, who was as it were an exile from there. On this matter there is Exodus 3. There God, seen in the bush by Moses, promises help and imposes on him the duty of leading the people out. Therefore, since we see that God is accustomed to appear to the wretched, let us afflicted hope well of him, that he will put an end to our tragedies. [illegible]

units.la: Quod autem Iosephum, cui bona hæc precatur & pollicetur, Nazaræum vocat: hoc est, peculiaribus donis excellentem & singulari quadam pietate Deo seruientem: id est documento, tunc nobis hæc Dei beneficia potissimum esse expectanda cum Iosephum imitati fratres nostros reliquos Christianos pietate & probitate anteire studuerimus. Et certè Samuel,Dauid,Daniel,& ante hos Iosephi,Samson alijque ab ineunte ætate diuinis studijs dediti hoc ipsum sunt diuinitus consecuti: vt quemadmodum pietate & vitæ innocentia reliquos antecelluerunt, sic ijsdem etiam virtutum splendore superiores essent. Quod ipsum est etiam atque etiam cogitandum iamq; inde ab ineunte ætate conseruandum memoria.
units.tr: Moreover, that he calls Joseph, to whom he prays for and promises these good things, a Nazarite, that is, one excelling in singular gifts and serving God with a certain singular piety: this is a lesson that these benefits of God are then especially to be expected by us, when we, imitating Joseph, strive to surpass our other Christian brothers in piety and uprightness. And indeed Samuel, David, Daniel, and before them Joseph and Samson, and others devoted to divine studies from their early age, obtained this very thing from God: that just as they excelled the rest in piety and innocence of life, so they were also superior in the splendour of virtues. This too is to be thought over again and again, and from early age kept in memory.

units.la: Magnam vim hominum & robustos ciues pollicetur: quos tauro primogenito & vnicorni comparat animantibus & robustis & suaptæ naturæ ad tuendum se munitis. Quo pollicetur eos ciues qui possint humi sternere irruentes hostes. Atq; hæc bona quoniam diuinitus accipimus, Deo largitori grati vt simus est enitendum.
units.tr: He promises a great number of men and robust citizens, whom he compares to the firstborn bull and the unicorn, animals both strong and by their own nature equipped to defend themselves. By this he promises citizens who can throw down invading enemies to the ground. And since we receive these goods from God, we must strive to be grateful to God the giver.

units.la: Zabulon & Ifachar etiam ipsæ ambæ tribus coniunguntur: de quarum situ, studijs, successu verba facit. Situs erat inter mare mediterraneum & lacum Tiberiadis. Vnde & dicuntur opes maris fugere.
units.tr: Zebulun and Issachar, both tribes, are also joined together, and he speaks of their situation, their pursuits and their success. Their situation was between the Mediterranean Sea and the Lake of Tiberias. Hence they are said to suck the riches of the sea.

units.la: Studia diuersa dicit: Zabulon in exitu, id est, peregrinationibus: Ifachar in tentoriis, id est, re pecuaria benedicit. Vehebat Zabulon merces: domi in amœnis pascuis Ifachar quiescebat. Vtrinq; multum augebantur opibus.
units.tr: He names different pursuits: Zebulun in his going out, that is, in journeys; Issachar in the tents, that is, he blesses them in herding flocks. Zebulun carried merchandise; at home Issachar rested in pleasant pastures. Both were greatly increased in wealth.

units.la: Sed in quos vsus hæc bona conferebant? dicit, in victimas, &c.
units.tr: But to what uses did these goods contribute? He says, for sacrifices, etc.

units.la: In quo obseruandum est: quemquæ gens suæ regionis habeat situm, vt quas aptas ei viderit artes, eas studiosè diligenterq; exerceat: tum enitendum vt operæ & artes vigeant, procul absit ocium: quod & Massilienses factitarunt. Nobis & nocet & turpe est ocium.
units.tr: In this it is to be observed: whatever people has a situation suited to its region, it should diligently and eagerly practise those arts which it sees to be fitting for it; then it must strive that its works and arts flourish, and that idleness be kept far away, as the Massilians also did. Idleness both harms us and is shameful.

units.la: Dein vt opes in regni Dei promotionem conferamus. Vnde & successus lætisperari possunt.
units.tr: Next, that we should contribute our wealth to the advancement of the kingdom of God. From this, too, joyful success may be hoped for.

units.la: Gad tribui hæc bona promittit & precatur: 1. Quod læta sit eius futura portio: videlicet pulsis Oge & Seone regibus: quorum illi terra atq; opibus sint fruituri. Sic Carolus Burgundionum dux Heluetios maiores nostros, quos medicos appellauit suis opibus locupletauit.
units.tr: He promises and prays that these good things belong to the tribe of Gad: (1) that his portion will be happy in the future, namely, once the kings Og and Sihon have been driven out, and the one will enjoy their land and wealth. So Charles, duke of the Burgundians, enriched with his wealth the Helvetians, our ancestors, whom he called doctors.

units.la: 2. Magnanimitatem, quam leoni comparat.
units.tr: (2) Greatness of spirit, which he compares to a lion.

units.la: 3. Sed 3. Philautiæ quoq; suæ eam tribum commonefacit: verum adhibita quoq; laude iustitiæ. Vt enim auaritiæ speciem referat quod omnium primi sibi terræ portionem vendicabant: sic iustitiæ quoq; magnum exemplum erat nullum sibi quietis locum dare prius, quàm reliquæ etiam tribus in suas possessiones missæ essent.
units.tr: (3) But he also reminds that tribe of its own self-love; yet praise of justice is added too. For, though it resembles avarice that they first of all claimed for themselves a portion of the land, so too it was a great example of justice that they gave themselves no place of rest until the other tribes also had been sent into their own possessions.

units.la: Quorum altero discimus auaritiam ne ceu hydrops crescat verbo diuino coercere: semper est enim radix omnium malorum auaritia: altero, vt non tam nostri quàm nostrorum cura tangamur: vtq; fidem datam seruemus.
units.tr: From the one we learn that we must restrain avarice with the word of God, lest it grow like dropsy; for avarice is always the root of all evils. From the other, that we be moved not so much by care for our own affairs as for those of our people, and that we keep the faith given.

units.la: Dan, inquit, catulus leonis desilit à Bafan. In hoc fortitudinem laudat eius & virtutem bellicam, similitudinem sumit à leonis catulo desiliente ex Bafan opimis pascuis celebri monte. Quo docet fore vt isti bene curata, vegeta, robusta corpora sint habituri, vnde etiam animus suus adsit vigor. Vit [illegible, ~16 letters] haben. Iam quicquid ocij ad corpus siue recreandum siue confirmandum datur: id nostræ ætatis homines, hoc ipso quod sese Baccho & Venere eneruant, in suam ipsorum pernitiem conuertunt, nulla coluntur prisca exercitia.
units.tr: Of Dan he says: Dan is a lion's whelp, leaping forth from Bashan. In this he praises his strength and warlike virtue, taking the likeness from a lion's whelp leaping forth from Bashan, a mountain famous for rich pastures. By this he teaches that those men are to have well-kept, vigorous, robust bodies, from which their spirit also has its vigour. [illegible passage] Now whatever leisure is given to refresh or strengthen the body, men of our age turn it to their own destruction, by weakening themselves with Bacchus and Venus, and the ancient exercises are neglected by all.

units.la: Naphtali tribuitur quod plenus fauore Domini sit habitaturus ad occidentem. Iacobus patriarcha hanc gratiam exponit & docet esse doctrinam & eloquentiam. Exemplum in Barac duce & Debora prophetissa Iud. cap. 4. & 5. Est autem Spiritus sancti munus eximium eloquentia. Sed mundus ingratus est, vt testantur historiæ.
units.tr: Naphtali is said to be going to dwell in the west full of the favour of the Lord. The patriarch Jacob explains this grace and teaches that it is learning and eloquence. The example is Barak the leader and Deborah the prophetess, Judges 4 and 5. Moreover, eloquence is a distinguished gift of the Holy Spirit. But the world is ungrateful, as histories bear witness.

units.la: Afer hoc ipso beatus futurus esse prædicatur, quod sit abundaturus sobole: gratia apud suos & benevolentia: opibus subterraneis, vt ferri, æris, chalybis, & omnis generis metallorum. Vnde & Iacobus ait panem eius pinguem fore. Atque ex his omnibus colligendum est, nos decere, ut siue bonorum illorum aliqua, siue ea omnia habeamus, Deo gratos esse. Quod fiet si Christum in quo dat hæc omnia quanta possumus maxima fide constantia amplectimur. Ei sit honos in sæcula; Amen.
units.tr: Asher is also declared to be blessed in this very respect: that he will abound in offspring, in favour and goodwill among his own people, and in riches from beneath the earth, such as iron, bronze, steel, and every kind of metal. Hence Jacob also says that his bread will be rich. From all these things we must conclude that it becomes us, whether we have some of those goods or all of them, to be pleasing to God. This will happen if we embrace Christ, in whom he gives all these things, with the greatest faith and constancy we can. To him be honour for ever and ever; Amen.

units.la: SERMO XVIII.
units.tr: SERMON XVIII.

units.la: 26 Non est Deus ut (Deus) Israelis, qui cœlos inæquitat, auxiliator tuus, & magnificentia eius æther est.
units.tr: There is none like God, O Israel, who rides the heavens to be your helper, and whose majesty is the sky.

units.la: 27 Qui iam olim habitatio Dei est, & inferne brachia in mundo (extendit) Et expellet ante faciem tuam hostem, & dicit: Vastato.
units.tr: He who from of old is the dwelling of God, and beneath are the everlasting arms; he shall drive out the enemy from before you, and say, Destroy.

units.la: 28 Habitabit itaq; solus Israel securus, & oculus Iacob ad terram frumenti et uini, quin & cœli eius stillabunt rorem.
units.tr: So Israel shall dwell alone in safety, and the eye of Jacob shall be upon a land of grain and wine; yea, his heavens shall drop down dew.

units.la: 29 Beatus es tu o Israel, quis tui similis o populé? salvus in Domino, qui est clypeus auxilij tui, & gladius gloriationis tuæ. Et mentientur tibi inimici tui, & tu calcabis in excelsis eorum.
units.tr: Happy are you, O Israel; who is like you, O people? Saved in the Lord, who is the shield of your help and the sword of your glory. Your enemies shall lie to you, and you shall tread upon their high places.

units.la: CVm diuinus Moses hoc Cap. benedictionem suo populo commemorarit, suaq; fata sic exposuerit, uti quæ bona, à quo, quibusq; hominibus expectanda sint intelligi posset: eam narrationem nunc concludit ad hunc modum, ut earum simul omnium rerum suos admoneat. Igitur Deum datorem, primo: bona, quæ dantur, secundo: populum, cui datur, tertio loco laudibus vehit.
units.tr: Since divine Moses, in this chapter, has recounted the blessing to his people and set out their future in such a way that it might be understood what good things are to be expected, from whom, and for what kind of people, he now concludes that account in this manner, so as to remind them of all these things at once. He therefore extols, first, God the giver; second, the good things that are given; and third, the people to whom they are given.

units.la: Ac Deum datorem sic commendat: Nemo est, inquit, ut Deus Israel, &c. Quibus verbis Dei maiestatem, bonitatem, prouidentiam extollit. Maiestatis enim est & gloriæ quod dicit, Nemo est ut Deus rectorum, qui cœlos inæquitat. Multi sunt qui vocantur, reuera autem non sunt dij: ut Iupiter, Apollo, &c. At huic Deo non est quisquam conferendus. Atque hoc suum excellere Deus ipse docet eo ipso, quod nullum sibi nomen proprium sumit: sed alibi dicitur Iehoua, alibi Schaddai, alibi omnipotens, misericors: videlicet quod cum omnium summus sit, non habeat opus quo seiungatur ab aliis nomine.
units.tr: He commends God the giver thus: There is no one, he says, like the God of Israel, etc. By these words he extols God's majesty, goodness and providence. It belongs to majesty and glory that he says, There is none like the God of the upright, who rides the heavens. There are many who are called gods, yet in truth are not gods, such as Jupiter, Apollo, and so on. But there is no one who may be compared with this God. That God himself teaches his own excellence by the very fact that he takes no proper name for himself; rather he is called Jehovah in one place, Shaddai in another, Almighty and Merciful elsewhere. Clearly, since he is the highest of all, he has no need of a name to distinguish him from others.

units.la: Obseruandum est autem quod dicitur Deus rectorum: hoc est, eorum qui se thora seu normæ & rectæ regulæ solent accommodare, & ut omnia dicta ac facta sint recta studere.
units.tr: It must be observed that it says God of the upright: that is, of those who are accustomed to conform themselves to the law, or norm, and right rule, and who strive that all their words and deeds be upright.

units.la: Quod & pijs & impijs vitæ doctrinæq; documenta præbet. Pijs quidem ut sciant se Deum habere patronum quoad recti fuerint: ut Iosephi, Dauid, &c. Impijs ut ne efferantur animis si Deus cedat illis victoriam in suos à via recta exorbitantes: est enim rectorum non obliquorum Deus, bonorum non malorum patronus: nec tuetur malas causas.
units.tr: This also offers instruction in life and doctrine both to the godly and to the ungodly. To the godly, so that they may know that they have God as their patron, as long as they are upright, as with Joseph, David, and others. To the ungodly, so that they may not be puffed up in mind if God grants victory to their own people when they stray from the straight path. For he is the God of the upright, not of the crooked; the patron of the good, not of the wicked; nor does he defend bad causes.

units.la: Addit etiam ad Dei celsitudinem: qui cœlos inæquitat: qui magnus sit & excelsus Dominus. Alibi thronus hic equus Dei dicitur cœlum. Vtrumq; est maiestatis & gloriæ. Quare si quæ magna atque excelsa sunt magnificamus: certè Deum, qui maximus est, faciemus maximi.
units.tr: He adds, to the loftiness of God, who rides the heavens: that is, the Lord who is great and high. Elsewhere this heaven is called the footstool of God's throne. Both belong to majesty and glory. Therefore, if we magnify whatever is great and lofty, we will surely hold God, who is greatest, in the highest esteem.

units.la: Bonitatis vero est quod dicitur auxiliator tuus. Oportet enim natura bonum esse qui tam ta cum sit maiestate & gloria præstans & homini misero opem ferat. Neque enim promittit solum, ut consoletur: verum etiam opem fert ut iuvet. Dixit, in die tribulationis inuoca me & eruam te. Venite qui estis onerati. Affuit periclitantibus Mosi, Iosuæ, Dauidi, Ezechiæ, &c. Estq; eius quasi proprium afflictis accurrere.
units.tr: It belongs to goodness that he is called your helper. For he who is so excellent in majesty and glory, and yet brings aid to wretched man, must be good by nature. For he does not merely promise to console; he also brings help to assist. He said, Call upon me in the day of trouble, and I will deliver you. Come to me, all you who are burdened. He stood by those in peril: Moses, Joshua, David, Hezekiah, and others. It is, as it were, his proper task to run to the afflicted.

units.la: Prouidentiæ deniq; est quod magnificentia eius æther est, & inferne brachia in mundo: hoc est, ut Psalm.113. dicitur, qui tam excelsam domum habitat, & nihilominus res humanas respicit & gubernat. Exempla habes in sacris literis & multa & pulchra. Exod.3. & Psalm.105. Columna nubis & ignis ducens populum. Expandit nubem ad tegendum, inquit. Vt duxit & defendit Christum puerum? ut ecclesiam Hierosolymis Pellam vocauit priusquam vrbs excinderetur? Habet Deus sua pijs liberandis decreta tempora, ut ostendit Act.7. Stephanus. Vt euehit pauperes? ut deijcit principes? Agnoruntque hanc eius prouidentiam, & ea notitia sese consolati sunt in maximis miserijs & molestijs boni: ut Iosephi dicens, Vos non, sed Deus præmisit me ante vos in Ægyptum: Iob, Dominus dedit, Dominus abstulit: Dauid, Dominus iussit, ut mihi malediceret. Quid verbis opus est? nihil illius mentem latet: nihil est quod eius manus effugiat: unde ut regum sic illius manus longè esse dici possunt. Rectè Basilius: Οὐδ' ἀπεγνωσμένου[?] ἡμελημένον[?] ὁ Θεὸς πάντα σκοπεύει[?] ὁ ἀκοίμητος ὀφθαλμὸς πᾶσι παρ[?] ῥέσι,σκοπτίζων ἑκάσῳ τῶν σωτηρίαν[?]. Atque hæc consideratio non solùm nos ad cultū nu-minis accendit, verumetiam in omnibus nostris rebus & dirigit & consolatur.
units.tr: Finally, it belongs to providence that his majesty is the sky, and beneath are the everlasting arms: that is, as Psalm 113 says, he who dwells in so lofty a house nevertheless looks upon and governs human affairs. You have many fine examples in Holy Writ: Exodus 3 and Psalm 105, the pillar of cloud and fire leading the people. He spread out a cloud for a covering, it says. How did he lead and defend the boy Christ? How did he call the Church out of Jerusalem to Pella before the city was overthrown? God has appointed times for the deliverance of his people, as Stephen shows in Acts 7. How does he raise up the poor? How does he cast down princes? The good have acknowledged this providence, and by that knowledge they have consoled themselves in the greatest miseries and troubles: as Joseph said, It was not you, but God sent me before you into Egypt; Job, The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; David, The Lord has bidden him curse me. What need is there of words? Nothing is hidden from his mind; nothing escapes his hand. Hence, while the hands of kings can be said to be far off, his cannot. Basil rightly says: [Οὐδὲν ἀπεγνωσμένον ἠμελημένον· ὁ Θεὸς πάντα σκοπεῖ· ὁ ἀκοίμητος ὀφθαλμὸς πᾶσι παρῇ, σκοπῶν ἑκάστῳ τὴν σωτηρίαν.] Nothing is neglected or forsaken; God looks upon all things; his unsleeping eye is present to all, watching over the salvation of each. And this consideration not only kindles us to the worship of the divine power, but also directs and comforts us in all our affairs.

units.la: Bona diuinitus expectanda sic refert: Expelle ante faciem tuam hostem, & dicet vastato. Habitabit itaq; solus Israel securus, &c. Quibus verbis ea refert quæ ad tuendam dignitatem, tranquillitatem, facietatem, sanitatem ciuium reiq; publicæ pertinent.
units.tr: He sets forth the good things to be expected from God in this way: He shall drive out the enemy from before you, and say, Destroy. So Israel shall dwell alone in safety, etc. By these words he sets forth those things which pertain to protecting the dignity, tranquillity, fertility and health of the citizens and of the commonwealth.

units.la: Ad dignitatem confert, vt hostes & quicunq; vim faciunt repelli possint. Vnde enim maior est populo vel gloria, quàm si vincat: vel ignominia quàm si sub iugum mittatur? Exemplo sunt Græci, Romani, Heluetij nostri, & hi ipsi Israelitæ, qui rebus præclarè gestis nomen & authoritatem sibi compararunt.
units.tr: He confers dignity, so that enemies and all who use violence may be repelled. For what greater thing can befall a people, either in glory, if it conquers, or in disgrace, if it is sent under the yoke? Examples are the Greeks, the Romans, our own Swiss, and these very Israelites, who by their famous deeds won for themselves name and authority.

units.la: Ad tranquillitatem pertinet vt securè & citrà metum insidiarum horroremque rumorū bellicorum viuat ac valeat. Contrà malè habet quæ continuis motibus affligitur.
units.tr: Tranquillity pertains to living and thriving securely, without fear of ambushes and the dread of rumours of war. On the contrary, a land that is racked by constant upheaval fares badly.

units.la: Satietati feruit magna annonæ copia. Sanitatem iuuat bona cœli temperies: vnde & fru-gibus & corporibus salubre fit alimentum.
units.tr: Plenty comes from a great abundance of grain. The good temperature of the sky promotes health, and so the fruits of the earth and the bodies of men become wholesome food.

units.la: Hæc omnia diuina bona agnoscamus, vt ei qui largitur ea grati simus.
units.tr: Let us acknowledge all these divine goods, so that we may be thankful to the one who bestows them.

units.la: Populum autem cui hæc promittit iam ipsum quoque suis laudibus vehit, vt quis quan-tusq; fit Dei beneficio intelligat. Beatus es, inquit, tu o Israel, quis tui similis? Vt Deum excellen-tem dixit, sic etiam ei ipsi coniunctum populum. Et certè vt dij fictitij nullius sunt precij, sic illis qui seruiunt etiam abiecti sunt stultique homines. Rursus vt Deus est beatus, excellens, magnus: sic qui illi fide vera coniungitur homo.
units.tr: He also extols the people to whom he promises these things, so that one may understand how great and of what kind a people becomes by God's benefit. Happy are you, he says, O Israel; who is like you? As he declared God to be excellent, so he also declares the people joined to him. And indeed, as false gods are worth nothing, so those who serve them are abject and foolish men. Conversely, as God is blessed, excellent and great, so is the man who is joined to him by true faith.

units.la: Sed in quo nobis hæc bona sint reposita scire multum refert. Dicit igitur nos saluos esse in Domino, qui sit clypeus auxilij, gladius gloriationis. Huius generis extant permulta præsertim in Psalmis testimonia.
units.tr: But it matters greatly to know in whom these goods are laid up for us. He says, therefore, that we are saved in the Lord, who is the shield of help and the sword of glorying. Very many testimonies of this kind exist, especially in the Psalms.

units.la: Deinde dicit, Gentes mentiuntur: hoc est, simulabunt, quam coacti seruant, amicitiam. Vt, &c.
units.tr: Then he says, the nations lie: that is, they will pretend a friendship which they keep only under compulsion. As, etc.

units.la: Atque hæc sunt etiam referenda ad ecclesiam. Eius benedictionis minister est Christus, Marci vltimo, benedicens nobis in cœlù ascensurus. Pater cœlestis bonus & prouidus hunc dedit rectis, hoc est, credentibus. Bona quæ habemus in eo, sunt: victoria contra sathanam, conscientiæ tranquillitas, satietas cibi corporibus atque animabus idonei, salubres etiam animas. Sumus autem ipsi magnus in Christo populus & vt ait Petrus, regale sacerdotium. Christo sit honos in secula, Amen.
units.tr: These things are also to be applied to the Church. Christ is the minister of this blessing, as the last chapter of Mark shows, where he blesses us as he is about to ascend into heaven.
